title: RingBFT: Resilient Consensus over Sharded Ring Topology
text: The recent surge in federated data management applications has brought forth concerns about the security of underlying data and the consistency of replicas in the presence of malicious attacks. A prominent solution in this direction is to employ a permissioned blockchain framework that is modeled around traditional Byzantine Fault-Tolerant (BFT) consensus protocols. Any federated application expects its data to be globally scattered to achieve faster access. But, prior works have shown that traditional BFT protocols are slow. This has led to the rise of sharded-replicated blockchains. Existing BFT protocols for these sharded blockchains are efficient if client transactions require access to a single-shard, but face performance degradation if there is a cross-shard transaction that requires access to multiple shards. As cross-shard transactions are common, to resolve this dilemma, we present RingBFT, a novel meta-BFT protocol for sharded blockchains. RingBFT requires shards to adhere to the ring order, and follow the principle of process, forward, and re-transmit while ensuring the communication between shards is linear. Our evaluation of RingBFT against state-of-the-art sharding BFT protocols illustrates that RingBFT achieves up to 18x higher throughput, gracefully scales to nearly 500 globally distributed nodes, and achieves a peak throughput of 1.2 million transactions per second.

title: RingBFT: Resilient Consensus over Sharded Ring Topology
text: The proliferation of federated data management applications has heightened concerns about data security and replica consistency in the face of malicious attacks. To address these concerns, permissioned blockchain frameworks modeled around traditional Byzantine Fault-Tolerant (BFT) consensus protocols have emerged as a promising solution. In federated applications, data is typically dispersed globally to facilitate rapid access. However, traditional BFT protocols have been shown to be slow, leading to the development of sharded-replicated blockchains. While existing BFT protocols for sharded blockchains are efficient for single-shard transactions, they experience performance degradation when handling cross-shard transactions that require access to multiple shards. Given the prevalence of cross-shard transactions, we propose RingBFT, a novel meta-BFT protocol designed for sharded blockchains. By enforcing a ring order among shards and adhering to a process-forward-retransmit principle, RingBFT ensures linear communication between shards. Our evaluation demonstrates that RingBFT outperforms state-of-the-art sharding BFT protocols, achieving up to 18x higher throughput, scaling to nearly 500 globally distributed nodes, and reaching a peak throughput of 1.2 million transactions per second.

title: Removing Operational Friction Using Process Mining: Challenges Provided by the Internet of Production (IoP)
text: Operational processes in production, logistics, material handling, maintenance, etc., are supported by cyber-physical systems combining hardware and software components. As a result, the digital and the physical world are closely aligned, and it is possible to track operational processes in detail (e.g., using sensors). The abundance of event data generated by today's operational processes provides opportunities and challenges for process mining techniques supporting process discovery, performance analysis, and conformance checking. Using existing process mining tools, it is already possible to automatically discover process models and uncover performance and compliance problems. In the DFG-funded Cluster of Excellence "Internet of Production" (IoP), process mining is used to create "digital shadows" to improve a wide variety of operational processes. However, operational processes are dynamic, distributed, and complex. Driven by the challenges identified in the IoP cluster, we work on novel techniques for comparative process mining (comparing process variants for different products at different locations at different times), object-centric process mining (to handle processes involving different types of objects that interact), and forward-looking process mining (to explore "What if?" questions). By addressing these challenges, we aim to develop valuable "digital shadows" that can be used to remove operational friction.

title: Removing Operational Friction Using Process Mining: Challenges Provided by the Internet of Production (IoP)
text: The increasing adoption of the Internet of Production (IoP) has led to a surge in the generation of industrial process data, offering unprecedented opportunities for process optimization. However, the sheer volume and complexity of this data also introduce significant operational friction, hindering the realization of IoP's full potential. Process mining, a technique that extracts knowledge from event data, has emerged as a promising approach to address this challenge. In this context, we investigate the challenges and opportunities of applying process mining to remove operational friction in IoP environments. We propose a novel framework that integrates process mining with IoP-specific data sources, such as machine sensors and product lifecycle management systems. Our approach is evaluated on a real-world dataset from a leading manufacturing company, comprising over 10 million events from 500 machines. The results show that our framework can identify and eliminate up to 37% of unnecessary process steps, leading to significant reductions in production time and cost. Our findings highlight the importance of considering IoP-specific challenges, such as data quality issues and equipment heterogeneity, when applying process mining in industrial settings.

title: HTF: Homogeneous Tree Framework for Differentially-Private Release of Location Data
text: Mobile apps that use location data are pervasive, spanning domains such as transportation, urban planning and healthcare. Important use cases for location data rely on statistical queries, e.g., identifying hotspots where users work and travel. Such queries can be answered efficiently by building histograms. However, precise histograms can expose sensitive details about individual users. Differential privacy (DP) is a mature and widely-adopted protection model, but most approaches for DP-compliant histograms work in a data-independent fashion, leading to poor accuracy. The few proposed data-dependent techniques attempt to adjust histogram partitions based on dataset characteristics, but they do not perform well due to the addition of noise required to achieve DP. We identify density homogeneity as a main factor driving the accuracy of DP-compliant histograms, and we build a data structure that splits the space such that data density is homogeneous within each resulting partition. We show through extensive experiments on large-scale real-world data that the proposed approach achieves superior accuracy compared to existing approaches.

title: HTF: Homogeneous Tree Framework for Differentially-Private Release of Location Data
text: Location-based mobile applications are ubiquitous, encompassing diverse domains including transportation, urban planning, and healthcare. A plethora of critical use cases rely on statistical queries, such as identifying areas of high user activity, which can be efficiently addressed through histogram construction. However, precise histograms can compromise individual user privacy by revealing sensitive information. To mitigate this, differential privacy (DP) has emerged as a widely adopted protection model. Nevertheless, existing DP-compliant histogram approaches often sacrifice accuracy for privacy, particularly when employing data-independent methods. A few data-dependent techniques attempt to adapt histogram partitions to dataset characteristics, but are hindered by the necessary addition of noise to achieve DP. We uncover density homogeneity as a key determinant of DP-compliant histogram accuracy and propose a novel data structure that partitions the space to ensure homogeneous data density within each partition. Through comprehensive experimentation on large-scale real-world datasets, our approach demonstrates superior accuracy compared to existing methods.

title: Machine Learning over Static and Dynamic Relational Data
text: This tutorial overviews principles behind recent works on training and maintaining machine learning models over relational data, with an emphasis on the exploitation of the relational data structure to improve the runtime performance of the learning task. The tutorial has the following parts: 1) Database research for data science 2) Three main ideas to achieve performance improvements 2.1) Turn the ML problem into a DB problem 2.2) Exploit structure of the data and problem 2.3) Exploit engineering tools of a DB researcher 3) Avenues for future research

title: Machine Learning over Static and Dynamic Relational Data
text: This tutorial synthesizes the fundamental principles underlying recent advances in training and maintaining machine learning models over relational data, highlighting the strategic leveraging of relational data structures to enhance runtime performance. The tutorial is organized around three primary themes: the intersection of database research and data science, three key strategies for achieving performance gains, and future research directions, including the reformulation of machine learning problems as database queries, exploiting data and problem structure, and harnessing database engineering expertise.

title: Towards Semantic Interoperability in Historical Research: Documenting Research Data and Knowledge with Synthesis
text: A vast area of research in historical science concerns the documentation and study of artefacts and related evidence. Current practice mostly uses spreadsheets or simple relational databases to organise the information as rows with multiple columns of related attributes. This form offers itself for data analysis and scholarly interpretation, however it also poses problems including i) the difficulty for collaborative but controlled documentation by a large number of users, ii) the lack of representation of the details from which the documented relations are inferred, iii) the difficulty to extend the underlying data structures as well as to combine and integrate data from multiple and diverse information sources, and iv) the limitation to reuse the data beyond the context of a particular research activity. To support historians to cope with these problems, in this paper we describe the Synthesis documentation system and its use by a large number of historians in the context of an ongoing research project in the field of History of Art. The system is Web-based and collaborative, and makes use of existing standards for information documentation and publication (CIDOC-CRM, RDF), focusing on semantic interoperability and the production of data of high value and long-term validity.

title: Towards Semantic Interoperability in Historical Research: Documenting Research Data and Knowledge with Synthesis
text: Historical research is a data-intensive discipline, yet the heterogeneity of data sources, formats, and knowledge representations hinders the integration and reuse of research findings. The advent of digital humanities has exacerbated this issue, as the volume and variety of digital data have increased exponentially. To address this challenge, we present Synthesis, a novel framework for documenting research data and knowledge in historical research. Synthesis leverages semantic web technologies and cognitive architectures to establish a common understanding of historical concepts, entities, and relationships. Our approach is grounded in a rigorous methodology, involving the development of a domain-specific ontology, the design of a knowledge graph data model, and the implementation of a web-based annotation platform. We evaluate Synthesis through a case study on the French Revolution, demonstrating its ability to integrate disparate data sources, facilitate knowledge discovery, and enable semantic queries. The results show a significant improvement in data interoperability, with an average increase of 35% in data reuse and a 25% reduction in data integration time. Our findings have important implications for the development of digital infrastructures in historical research, highlighting the potential of semantic interoperability to transform the way researchers collaborate, share, and build upon each other's work.

title: Safest Nearby Neighbor Queries in Road Networks (Full Version)
text: Traditional route planning and k nearest neighbors queries only consider distance or travel time and ignore road safety altogether. However, many travellers prefer to avoid risky or unpleasant road conditions such as roads with high crime rates (e.g., robberies, kidnapping, riots etc.) and bumpy roads. To facilitate safe travel, we introduce a novel query for road networks called the k safest nearby neighbors (kSNN) query. Given a query location $v_l$, a distance constraint $d_c$ and a point of interest $p_i$, we define the safest path from $v_l$ to $p_i$ as the path with the highest path safety score among all the paths from $v_l$ to $p_i$ with length less than $d_c$. The path safety score is computed considering the road safety of each road segment on the path. Given a query location $v_l$, a distance constraint $d_c$ and a set of POIs P, a kSNN query returns k POIs with the k highest path safety scores in P along with their respective safest paths from the query location. We develop two novel indexing structures called Ct-tree and a safety score based Voronoi diagram (SNVD). We propose two efficient query processing algorithms each exploiting one of the proposed indexes to effectively refine the search space using the properties of the index. Our extensive experimental study on real datasets demonstrates that our solution is on average an order of magnitude faster than the baselines.

title: Safest Nearby Neighbor Queries in Road Networks (Full Version)
text: The proliferation of location-based services has spawned a surge of interest in spatial queries, particularly nearest neighbor (NN) searches, which are crucial in various applications such as route planning, traffic management, and emergency response systems. However, the traditional NN query paradigm, which focuses on finding the closest point of interest, often neglects the inherent risks associated with the recommended routes, such as accidents, traffic congestion, and road closures. To address this limitation, we propose a novel concept, Safest Nearby Neighbor (SNN) queries, which aim to identify the nearest neighbors while minimizing the risk of traversing the corresponding routes. We formalize the SNN problem in the context of road networks and develop an efficient algorithm, dubbed SafeRoute, to solve it. SafeRoute leverages a combination of graph-based techniques and risk assessment models to identify the safest routes to nearby neighbors. Our approach is designed to accommodate various risk factors, including accident history, traffic patterns, and road conditions. Experimental evaluations on real-world road networks demonstrate that SafeRoute outperforms traditional NN query algorithms in terms of safety, while incurring only moderate overhead in terms of query response time. The results of our study show that SNN queries can significantly reduce the risk of accidents and traffic congestion in various scenarios, including emergency response, ride-hailing, and logistics services. Furthermore, we demonstrate the scalability and flexibility of our approach by integrating it with existing spatial databases and query processing systems. The proposed SNN framework has far-reaching implications for the development of safer and more efficient location-based services.

title: Interactive Region-of-Interest Discovery using Exploratory Feedback
text: In this paper, we propose a geospatial data management framework called IRIDEF which captures and analyzes user's exploratory feedback for an enriched guidance mechanism in the context of interactive analysis. We discuss that exploratory feedback can be a proxy for decision-making feedback when the latter is scarce or unavailable. IRIDEF identifies regions of interest (ROIs) via exploratory feedback and highlights a few interesting and out-of-sight POIs in each ROI. These highlights enable the user to shape up his/her future interactions with the system. We detail the components of our proposed framework in the form of a data analysis pipeline and present the aspects of efficiency and effectiveness for each component. We also discuss evaluation plans and future directions for IRIDEF.

title: Interactive Region-of-Interest Discovery using Exploratory Feedback
text: The proliferation of large-scale datasets has necessitated the development of efficient methods for identifying regions of interest (ROIs), a crucial step in various data analysis pipelines. Existing ROI discovery approaches often rely on manual annotation or batch processing, which can be time-consuming and ineffective. We propose an interactive ROI discovery framework that leverages exploratory feedback to guide the discovery process. Our approach utilizes a novel combination of density-based clustering and active learning, allowing users to provide corrective feedback on the fly. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art batch processing techniques, achieving a 3.5x reduction in labeling effort while maintaining a high degree of accuracy. Furthermore, user studies reveal significant improvements in user satisfaction and ROI discovery efficiency.

title: Freezing Sub-Models During Incremental Process Discovery: Extended Version
text: Process discovery aims to learn a process model from observed process behavior. From a user's perspective, most discovery algorithms work like a black box. Besides parameter tuning, there is no interaction between the user and the algorithm. Interactive process discovery allows the user to exploit domain knowledge and to guide the discovery process. Previously, an incremental discovery approach has been introduced where a model, considered to be under construction, gets incrementally extended by user-selected process behavior. This paper introduces a novel approach that additionally allows the user to freeze model parts within the model under construction. Frozen sub-models are not altered by the incremental approach when new behavior is added to the model. The user can thus steer the discovery algorithm. Our experiments show that freezing sub-models can lead to higher quality models.

title: Freezing Sub-Models During Incremental Process Discovery: Extended Version
text: Process discovery typically involves learning a process model from observed behavioral data, with existing algorithms often functioning as opaque black boxes that permit limited user interaction beyond parameter tuning. In contrast, interactive process discovery enables users to leverage their domain expertise and guide the discovery process. Building upon an incremental discovery approach, where a model under construction is iteratively extended by user-selected behavior, this paper presents a novel method that allows users to freeze specific model components, thereby preserving their integrity as new behavior is incorporated. This feature enables users to steer the discovery algorithm and, as our experiments demonstrate, can result in the generation of higher-quality process models.

title: Skeena: Efficient and Consistent Cross-Engine Transactions
text: Database systems are becoming increasingly multi-engine. In particular, a main-memory database engine may coexist with a traditional storage-centric engine in a system to support various applications. It is desirable to allow applications to access data in both engines using cross-engine transactions. But existing systems are either only designed for single-engine accesses, or impose many restrictions by limiting cross-engine transactions to certain isolation levels and table operations. The result is inadequate cross-engine support in terms of correctness, performance and programmability. This paper describes Skeena, a holistic approach to cross-engine transactions. We propose a lightweight snapshot tracking structure and an atomic commit protocol to efficiently ensure correctness and support various isolation levels. Evaluation results show that Skeena maintains high performance for single-engine transactions and enables cross-engine transactions which can improve throughput by up to 30x by judiciously placing tables in different engines.

title: Skeena: Efficient and Consistent Cross-Engine Transactions
text: Distributed databases often employ multiple engines to boost performance and cater to diverse workloads, but ensuring consistency across these engines is a long-standing challenge. Existing solutions either compromise on consistency, sacrifice performance, or introduce significant engineering complexity. We present Skeena, a novel system that enables efficient and consistent cross-engine transactions. Skeena leverages a modular architecture, combining a lightweight transaction manager with engine-specific adapters to orchestrate transactions across disparate engines. Our evaluation, conducted on a heterogeneous cluster comprising PostgreSQL, Cassandra, and MongoDB, demonstrates that Skeena achieves 2-5x higher throughput and 30-50% lower latency compared to state-of-the-art solutions, while maintaining strong consistency guarantees. We also develop a formal proof of Skeena's correctness, establishing its reliability in the face of concurrent updates and engine failures. Skeena's efficiency, consistency, and flexibility make it an attractive solution for modern distributed databases.

title: Extending Sticky-Datalog+/- via Finite-Position Selection Functions: Tractability, Algorithms, and Optimization
text: Weakly-Sticky(WS) Datalog+/- is an expressive member of the family of Datalog+/- program classes that is defined on the basis of the conditions of stickiness and weak-acyclicity. Conjunctive query answering (QA) over the WS programs has been investigated, and its tractability in data complexity has been established. However, the design and implementation of practical QA algorithms and their optimizations have been open. In order to fill this gap, we first study Sticky and WS programs from the point of view of the behavior of the chase procedure. We extend the stickiness property of the chase to that of generalized stickiness of the chase (GSCh) modulo an oracle that selects (and provides) the predicate positions where finitely values appear during the chase. Stickiness modulo a selection function S that provides only a subset of those positions defines sch(S), a semantic subclass of GSCh. Program classes with selection functions include Sticky and WS, and another syntactic class that we introduce and characterize, namely JWS, of jointly-weakly-sticky programs, which contains WS. The selection functions for these last three classes are computable, and no external, possibly non-computable oracle is needed. We propose a bottom-up QA algorithm for programs in the class sch(S), for a general selection function S. As a particular case, we obtain a polynomial-time QA algorithm for JWS and weakly-sticky programs. Unlike WS, JWS turns out to be closed under magic-sets query optimization. As a consequence, both the generic polynomial-time QA algorithm and its magic-set optimization can be particularized and applied to WS.

title: Extending Sticky-Datalog+/- via Finite-Position Selection Functions: Tractability, Algorithms, and Optimization
text: The Sticky-Datalog+/- framework has emerged as a powerful tool for querying and reasoning over large-scale data repositories, leveraging the principles of stickiness and predicate invention to facilitate efficient and scalable query evaluation. However, its applicability is limited by the restrictive nature of the underlying selection functions, which preclude the incorporation of more expressive and nuanced querying capabilities. To address this limitation, we introduce finite-position selection functions, a novel extension to the Sticky-Datalog+/- framework that enables the formulation of more sophisticated and context-dependent queries. We establish the tractability of the extended framework by developing a novel algorithm for query evaluation, which leverages the properties of finite-position selection functions to reduce the complexity of query processing. Through a comprehensive analysis, we demonstrate that our algorithm exhibits polynomial time complexity, thereby ensuring the scalability and efficiency of the extended framework. Furthermore, we investigate the optimization of query evaluation in the presence of finite-position selection functions, and develop a suite of optimization techniques that exploit the structural properties of the selection functions to minimize computational overhead. Our experimental evaluation, conducted on a range of benchmarks, demonstrates the efficacy of our approach, yielding significant performance improvements over existing Sticky-Datalog+/- implementations. The contributions of this work have far-reaching implications for the development of scalable and expressive query languages, and pave the way for the integration of Sticky-Datalog+/- with other declarative programming paradigms. By extending the capabilities of Sticky-Datalog+/- via finite-position selection functions, we provide a powerful tool for querying and reasoning over complex data repositories, with applications in data integration, knowledge graph querying, and beyond.

title: A Neural Database for Differentially Private Spatial Range Queries
text: Mobile apps and location-based services generate large amounts of location data that can benefit research on traffic optimization, context-aware notifications and public health (e.g., spread of contagious diseases). To preserve individual privacy, one must first sanitize location data, which is commonly done using the powerful differential privacy (DP) concept. However, existing solutions fall short of properly capturing density patterns and correlations that are intrinsic to spatial data, and as a result yield poor accuracy. We propose a machine-learning based approach for answering statistical queries on location data with DP guarantees. We focus on countering the main source of error that plagues existing approaches (namely, uniformity error), and we design a neural database system that models spatial datasets such that important density and correlation features present in the data are preserved, even when DP-compliant noise is added. We employ a set of neural networks that learn from diverse regions of the dataset and at varying granularities, leading to superior accuracy. We also devise a framework for effective system parameter tuning on top of public data, which helps practitioners set important system parameters without having to expend scarce privacy budget. Extensive experimental results on real datasets with heterogeneous characteristics show that our proposed approach significantly outperforms the state of the art.

title: A Neural Database for Differentially Private Spatial Range Queries
text: The proliferation of location-based services has generated massive amounts of spatial data, which poses significant privacy risks when shared with untrusted parties. Differential privacy offers a robust framework for quantifying and mitigating these risks, but existing solutions for differentially private spatial range queries suffer from high computational overhead or degraded accuracy. This paper proposes a novel neural database architecture that integrates differential privacy into the query processing pipeline, enabling efficient and accurate spatial range queries while protecting user location data. Our approach leverages a neural network-based spatial index that learns to approximate the optimal private query response, eliminating the need for computationally expensive perturbation mechanisms. We develop a customized training procedure that incorporates the differential privacy constraint, ensuring that the neural index satisfies a desired level of privacy. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that our neural database outperforms state-of-the-art differentially private spatial query methods by up to 3 orders of magnitude in terms of query latency, while achieving comparable or better accuracy. Furthermore, we theoretically analyze the privacy guarantees of our approach, establishing a novel upper bound on the privacy loss. Our results pave the way for scalable and accurate spatial data analytics under differential privacy, with significant implications for location-based services and urban informatics applications.

title: Ontology Modeling for Decentralized Household Energy Systems
text: In a decentralized household energy system consisting of various devices such as washing machines, heat pumps, and solar panels, understanding the electric energy consumption and production data at the granularity of the device helps end-users be closer to the system and further achieve the sustainability of energy use. However, many datasets in this area are isolated from other domains with records of only energy-related data. This may raise a loss of information (e.g. weather) that is relevant to the energy use of each device. A noticeable disadvantage is that many of those datasets have to be used in computational modeling approaches such as machine learning models, which are vulnerable to the data feed, to advance the understanding of energy consumption and production. Although such computational methods have achieved a high benchmark merely through a local view of datasets, the reusability cannot be firmly guaranteed when the information omission is taken into account. This paper addresses the data isolation problem in the smart energy systems area by exploring Semantic Web techniques on top of a household energy system. We propose an ontology modeling solution for the management of decentralized data at the resolution of a device in the system. As a result, the scope of the data concerning each device can be easily extended to be wider across the web and more information that may be of interest such as weather can be retrieved from the Web if the data are structured by the ontology.

title: Ontology Modeling for Decentralized Household Energy Systems
text: Decentralized household energy systems comprising diverse devices, such as washing machines and solar panels, necessitate granular understanding of electric energy consumption and production data at the device level to promote end-user engagement and sustainable energy practices. However, existing datasets in this domain often suffer from isolation, capturing only energy-related data and omitting relevant contextual information like weather patterns. This limitation hinders the applicability of computational modeling approaches, including machine learning algorithms, which are susceptible to data quality issues. Although these methods have achieved notable benchmarks within local dataset contexts, their reusability is compromised by the omission of relevant information. This study tackles the data isolation problem in smart energy systems by leveraging Semantic Web techniques in a household energy system. We develop an ontology-based modeling solution for managing decentralized data at the device resolution, enabling the seamless extension of device-related data scope across the web. This structured approach facilitates the retrieval of additional relevant information, such as weather data, from the web, thereby enhancing the comprehension of energy consumption and production patterns.

title: Real-World Trajectory Sharing with Local Differential Privacy
text: Sharing trajectories is beneficial for many real-world applications, such as managing disease spread through contact tracing and tailoring public services to a population's travel patterns. However, public concern over privacy and data protection has limited the extent to which this data is shared. Local differential privacy enables data sharing in which users share a perturbed version of their data, but existing mechanisms fail to incorporate user-independent public knowledge (e.g., business locations and opening times, public transport schedules, geo-located tweets). This limitation makes mechanisms too restrictive, gives unrealistic outputs, and ultimately leads to low practical utility. To address these concerns, we propose a local differentially private mechanism that is based on perturbing hierarchically-structured, overlapping $n$-grams (i.e., contiguous subsequences of length $n$) of trajectory data. Our mechanism uses a multi-dimensional hierarchy over publicly available external knowledge of real-world places of interest to improve the realism and utility of the perturbed, shared trajectories. Importantly, including real-world public data does not negatively affect privacy or efficiency. Our experiments, using real-world data and a range of queries, each with real-world application analogues, demonstrate the superiority of our approach over a range of alternative methods.

title: Real-World Trajectory Sharing with Local Differential Privacy
text: The proliferation of location-based services has led to an unprecedented collection of trajectory data, which can be valuable for urban planning, traffic management, and personalized services. However, sharing such data poses significant privacy risks, as it can reveal sensitive information about individuals. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework for real-world trajectory sharing with local differential privacy (LDP). Our approach leverages a combination of spatial and temporal analyses to identify the most informative segments of trajectories, which are then perturbed using a customized LDP mechanism. We evaluate our framework on two large-scale datasets of human mobility, comprising over 10 million GPS samples. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves a better tradeoff between privacy and utility compared to existing LDP-based approaches, with a mean relative error of 15.3% in estimating popular routes. Furthermore, we show that our framework can be integrated with existing data sharing platforms, enabling secure and privacy-preserving trajectory sharing for a wide range of applications. Our work has important implications for the development of privacy-aware location-based services, and can facilitate the creation of more accurate and sustainable urban planning models.

title: Privacy-Preserving Synthetic Location Data in the Real World
text: Sharing sensitive data is vital in enabling many modern data analysis and machine learning tasks. However, current methods for data release are insufficiently accurate or granular to provide meaningful utility, and they carry a high risk of deanonymization or membership inference attacks. In this paper, we propose a differentially private synthetic data generation solution with a focus on the compelling domain of location data. We present two methods with high practical utility for generating synthetic location data from real locations, both of which protect the existence and true location of each individual in the original dataset. Our first, partitioning-based approach introduces a novel method for privately generating point data using kernel density estimation, in addition to employing private adaptations of classic statistical techniques, such as clustering, for private partitioning. Our second, network-based approach incorporates public geographic information, such as the road network of a city, to constrain the bounds of synthetic data points and hence improve the accuracy of the synthetic data. Both methods satisfy the requirements of differential privacy, while also enabling accurate generation of synthetic data that aims to preserve the distribution of the real locations. We conduct experiments using three large-scale location datasets to show that the proposed solutions generate synthetic location data with high utility and strong similarity to the real datasets. We highlight some practical applications for our work by applying our synthetic data to a range of location analytics queries, and we demonstrate that our synthetic data produces near-identical answers to the same queries compared to when real data is used. Our results show that the proposed approaches are practical solutions for sharing and analyzing sensitive location data privately.

title: Privacy-Preserving Synthetic Location Data in the Real World
text: The proliferation of location-based services has led to an unprecedented collection of sensitive user location data, posing significant privacy risks. Synthetic location data has emerged as a promising solution, enabling data utility while protecting user privacy. However, existing approaches are often limited to theoretical frameworks or simulations, neglecting the complexities of real-world data. This work presents the first comprehensive study on privacy-preserving synthetic location data in real-world settings. We focus on the popular Gowalla and Foursquare datasets, comprising over 10 million check-ins from 100,000 users. Our approach leverages a novel combination of differential privacy and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to generate synthetic location data that preserves individual privacy while maintaining data utility. We develop a custom GAN architecture, incorporating a privacy loss function that enforces (ε, δ)-differential privacy guarantees. Our methodology involves a rigorous evaluation framework, assessing both privacy and utility metrics. Specifically, we measure privacy using the proposed privacy loss function, while utility is evaluated through a range of tasks, including location prediction, clustering, and recommendation systems. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in privacy preservation, outperforming existing methods by up to 30%. Moreover, our synthetic data exhibits superior utility, with a maximum drop of 15% in location prediction accuracy compared to the original data. We further conduct a user study, revealing that 85% of participants are unable to distinguish between real and synthetic data. Our work provides a practical solution for privacy-preserving synthetic location data, paving the way for widespread adoption in real-world applications.

title: A FAIR and AI-ready Higgs boson decay dataset
text: To enable the reusability of massive scientific datasets by humans and machines, researchers aim to adhere to the principles of findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability (FAIR) for data and artificial intelligence (AI) models. This article provides a domain-agnostic, step-by-step assessment guide to evaluate whether or not a given dataset meets these principles. We demonstrate how to use this guide to evaluate the FAIRness of an open simulated dataset produced by the CMS Collaboration at the CERN Large Hadron Collider. This dataset consists of Higgs boson decays and quark and gluon background, and is available through the CERN Open Data Portal. We use additional available tools to assess the FAIRness of this dataset, and incorporate feedback from members of the FAIR community to validate our results. This article is accompanied by a Jupyter notebook to visualize and explore this dataset. This study marks the first in a planned series of articles that will guide scientists in the creation of FAIR AI models and datasets in high energy particle physics.

title: A FAIR and AI-ready Higgs boson decay dataset
text: Efforts to ensure the reusability of large scientific datasets by both humans and machines rely on adherence to the findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability (FAIR) principles for data and artificial intelligence (AI) models. This article presents a domain-agnostic, step-by-step evaluation framework to assess a dataset's compliance with these principles. We apply this framework to evaluate the FAIRness of an open simulated dataset from the CMS Collaboration at the CERN Large Hadron Collider, comprising Higgs boson decays and quark and gluon background, and accessible through the CERN Open Data Portal. By leveraging additional tools and incorporating feedback from the FAIR community, we validate our results. An accompanying Jupyter notebook facilitates visualization and exploration of this dataset. This study constitutes the first in a series of planned articles aimed at guiding scientists in the development of FAIR AI models and datasets in high-energy particle physics, ultimately promoting dataset reusability and collaboration.

title: Relational E-Matching
text: We present a new approach to e-matching based on relational join; in particular, we apply recent database query execution techniques to guarantee worst-case optimal run time. Compared to the conventional backtracking approach that always searches the e-graph "top down", our new relational e-matching approach can better exploit pattern structure by searching the e-graph according to an optimized query plan. We also establish the first data complexity result for e-matching, bounding run time as a function of the e-graph size and output size. We prototyped and evaluated our technique in the state-of-the-art egg e-graph framework. Compared to a conventional baseline, relational e-matching is simpler to implement and orders of magnitude faster in practice.

title: Relational E-Matching
text: By leveraging relational join techniques from database query execution, we develop a novel e-matching approach that ensures worst-case optimal runtime. Departing from traditional backtracking methods, which traverse the e-graph in a top-down manner, our relational approach capitalizes on pattern structure by executing an optimized query plan. We further establish the first data complexity result for e-matching, bounding runtime in terms of e-graph size and output size. In the egg e-graph framework, our prototyped technique exhibits marked improvements, boasting both simplicity of implementation and significant speedup – orders of magnitude faster than conventional baselines in practice.

title: IoT Notary: Attestable Sensor Data Capture in IoT Environments
text: Contemporary IoT environments, such as smart buildings, require end-users to trust data-capturing rules published by the systems. There are several reasons why such a trust is misplaced -- IoT systems may violate the rules deliberately or IoT devices may transfer user data to a malicious third-party due to cyberattacks, leading to the loss of individuals' privacy or service integrity. To address such concerns, we propose IoT Notary, a framework to ensure trust in IoT systems and applications. IoT Notary provides secure log sealing on live sensor data to produce a verifiable `proof-of-integrity,' based on which a verifier can attest that captured sensor data adheres to the published data-capturing rules. IoT Notary is an integral part of TIPPERS, a smart space system that has been deployed at the University of California Irvine to provide various real-time location-based services on the campus. We present extensive experiments over realtime WiFi connectivity data to evaluate IoT Notary, and the results show that IoT Notary imposes nominal overheads. The secure logs only take 21% more storage, while users can verify their one day's data in less than two seconds even using a resource-limited device.

title: IoT Notary: Attestable Sensor Data Capture in IoT Environments
text: The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has led to an explosion of sensor data, which is increasingly relied upon for critical decision-making. However, the integrity and trustworthiness of this data are often suspect, as IoT devices are vulnerable to tampering, manipulation, and data breaches. To address this challenge, we propose IoT Notary, a novel system for attesting sensor data capture in IoT environments. IoT Notary leverages a combination of secure boot mechanisms, trusted execution environments, and blockchain-based data provenance to ensure the integrity and authenticity of sensor data. Our approach involves instrumenting IoT devices with a lightweight, tamper-evident logging mechanism that records sensor readings and associated metadata. These logs are then anchored to a blockchain, enabling verifiable and tamper-proof data provenance. We evaluate IoT Notary using a large-scale IoT testbed, comprising 100+ devices, and demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting data manipulation attacks and ensuring data integrity. Our results show that IoT Notary achieves high accuracy in validating sensor data, with a median detection rate of 97.5% for data tampering attacks. We believe IoT Notary has significant implications for IoT applications requiring high-integrity sensor data, such as industrial automation, smart cities, and healthcare.

title: SLoClas: A Database for Joint Sound Localization and Classification
text: In this work, we present the development of a new database, namely Sound Localization and Classification (SLoClas) corpus, for studying and analyzing sound localization and classification. The corpus contains a total of 23.27 hours of data recorded using a 4-channel microphone array. 10 classes of sounds are played over a loudspeaker at 1.5 meters distance from the array by varying the Direction-of-Arrival (DoA) from 1 degree to 360 degree at an interval of 5 degree. To facilitate the study of noise robustness, 6 types of outdoor noise are recorded at 4 DoAs, using the same devices. Moreover, we propose a baseline method, namely Sound Localization and Classification Network (SLCnet) and present the experimental results and analysis conducted on the collected SLoClas database. We achieve the accuracy of 95.21% and 80.01% for sound localization and classification, respectively. We publicly release this database and the source code for research purpose.

title: SLoClas: A Database for Joint Sound Localization and Classification
text: We introduce the Sound Localization and Classification (SLoClas) corpus, a comprehensive database designed to facilitate the study and analysis of sound localization and classification. This corpus comprises 23.27 hours of recordings captured using a 4-channel microphone array, featuring 10 classes of sounds played from a loudspeaker at 1.5 meters distance, with varying Direction-of-Arrival (DoA) from 1 to 360 degrees at 5-degree intervals. To assess noise robustness, six types of outdoor noise are recorded at four DoAs using the same setup. We also propose a baseline approach, the Sound Localization and Classification Network (SLCnet), and present experimental results and analysis on the SLoClas database, achieving 95.21% accuracy for sound localization and 80.01% for classification. The SLoClas database and SLCnet source code are publicly available to support further research in this domain.

title: Handling Inconsistencies in Tables with Nulls and Functional Dependencies
text: In this paper we address the problem of handling inconsistencies in tables with missing values (also called nulls) and functional dependencies. Although the traditional view is that table instances must respect all functional dependencies imposed on them, it is nevertheless relevant to develop theories about how to handle instances that violate some dependencies. Regarding missing values, we make no assumptions on their existence: a missing value exists only if it is inferred from the functional dependencies of the table. We propose a formal framework in which each tuple of a table is associated with a truth value among the following: true, false, inconsistent or unknown; and we show that our framework can be used to study important problems such as consistent query answering, table merging, and data quality measures - to mention just a few. In this paper, however, we focus mainly on consistent query answering, a problem that has received considerable attention during the last decades. The main contributions of the paper are the following: (a) we introduce a new approach to handle inconsistencies in a table with nulls and functional dependencies, (b) we give algorithms for computing all true, inconsistent and false tuples, (c) we investigate the relationship between our approach and Four-valued logic in the context of data merging, and (d) we give a novel solution to the consistent query answering problem and compare our solution to that of table repairs.

title: Handling Inconsistencies in Tables with Nulls and Functional Dependencies
text: The presence of null values and functional dependencies in tables poses significant challenges to data consistency and quality. Inconsistencies can lead to incorrect query results, inaccurate data analysis, and poor decision-making. Existing approaches to handling inconsistencies often focus on either null values or functional dependencies separately, neglecting their interplay. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for detecting and resolving inconsistencies in tables with nulls and functional dependencies. Our approach leverages a novel combination of data profiling and constraint-based reasoning. We first employ data profiling techniques to identify potential inconsistencies and functional dependencies in the data. Then, we utilize constraint-based reasoning to detect and resolve inconsistencies, taking into account the interplay between null values and functional dependencies. Our framework is capable of handling both tuple-level and attribute-level inconsistencies, and can be applied to various types of functional dependencies, including unary and binary dependencies. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in detecting and resolving inconsistencies. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our framework achieves significant improvements in inconsistency detection accuracy and resolution efficiency. Furthermore, our approach is scalable and can handle large datasets with millions of tuples. The results of this research have important implications for data quality, data integration, and data analytics, and can be applied in various domains, including finance, healthcare, and e-commerce.

title: Four-Valued Semantics for Deductive Databases
text: In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to deductive databases meant to take into account the needs of current applications in the area of data integration. To this end, we extend the formalism of standard deductive databases to the context of Four-valued logic so as to account for unknown, inconsistent, true or false information under the open world assumption. In our approach, a database is a pair (E,R) where E is the extension and R the set of rules. The extension is a set of pairs of the form (f, v) where f is a fact and v is a value that can be true, inconsistent or false - but not unknown (that is, unknown facts are not stored in the database). The rules follow the form of standard Datalog{neg} rules but, contrary to standard rules, their head may be a negative atom. Our main contributions are as follows: (i) we give an expression of first-degree entailment in terms of other connectors and exhibit a functionally complete set of basic connectors not involving first-degree entailment, (ii) we define a new operator for handling our new type of rules and show that this operator is monotonic and continuous, thus providing an effective way for defining and computing database semantics, and (iii) we argue that our framework allows for the definition of a new type of updates that can be used in most standard data integration applications.

title: Four-Valued Semantics for Deductive Databases
text: The rising complexity of modern data management applications has led to a growing interest in deductive databases, which integrate logic programming and relational databases to enable declarative querying and reasoning. However, traditional deductive databases are limited by their reliance on two-valued semantics, which cannot effectively handle incomplete or inconsistent data. To address this limitation, we propose a novel four-valued semantics for deductive databases, which allows for the explicit representation of uncertainty and inconsistency. Our approach is based on the notion of bilattices, which provide a mathematical framework for combining multiple truth values. We define a four-valued semantics for deductive databases, where each fact or rule is assigned one of four truth values: true, false, unknown, or inconsistent. We then develop a sound and complete reasoning algorithm for this semantics, which is capable of handling complex queries and rules. Experimental evaluation on a range of benchmarks demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach, which outperforms traditional two-valued semantics in terms of both query accuracy and execution time. We also demonstrate the applicability of our approach in a case study on data integration, where it enables the effective handling of inconsistent data from multiple sources. Our results have significant implications for the development of robust and scalable deductive databases, and highlight the potential of four-valued semantics for tackling the challenges of modern data management.

title: Proof-of-Reputation: An Alternative Consensus Mechanism for Blockchain Systems
text: Blockchains combine other technologies, such as cryptography, networking, and incentive mechanisms, to enable the creation, validation, and recording of transactions between participating nodes. A consensus algorithm is used in a blockchain system to determine the shared state among distributed nodes. An important component underlying any blockchain-based system is its consensus mechanism, which principally determines the performance and security of the overall system. As the nature of peer-to- peer(P2P) networks is open and dynamic, the security risk within that environment is greatly increased mostly because nodes can join and leave the network at will. Thus, it is important to have a system that can check against malicious behaviour. In this work, we propose a reputation-based consensus mechanism for blockchain-based systems, Proof-of-Reputation(PoR) where the nodes with the highest reputation values eventually become part of a consensus group that determines the state of the blockchain.

title: Proof-of-Reputation: An Alternative Consensus Mechanism for Blockchain Systems
text: The increasing popularity of blockchain systems has led to a surge in energy consumption and scalability issues, largely attributed to traditional proof-of-work (PoW) consensus mechanisms. In response, we propose Proof-of-Reputation (PoR), a novel consensus algorithm that leverages a node's reputation, earned through consistent contributions to the network, to determine its eligibility to validate transactions. Our approach integrates a reputation system, built upon a decentralized trust graph, with a variant of the Byzantine Fault Tolerance algorithm. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that PoR achieves a 3.5x increase in transaction throughput and a 40% reduction in energy consumption compared to PoW, while maintaining a high level of security and decentralization. Furthermore, our results show that PoR incentivizes honest behavior, as nodes with higher reputations have a higher likelihood of being selected to create new blocks. This work has significant implications for the development of sustainable and scalable blockchain systems.

title: Master Graduation Thesis: A Lightweight and Distributed Container-based Framework
text: Edge/Fog computing is a novel computing paradigm that provides resource-limited Internet of Things (IoT) devices with scalable computing and storage resources. Compared to cloud computing, edge/fog servers have fewer resources, but they can be accessed with higher bandwidth and less communication latency. Thus, integrating edge/fog and cloud infrastructures can support the execution of diverse latency-sensitive and computation-intensive IoT applications. Although some frameworks attempt to provide such integration, there are still several challenges to be addressed, such as dynamic scheduling of different IoT applications, scalability mechanisms, multi-platform support, and supporting different interaction models. To overcome these challenges, we propose a lightweight and distributed container-based framework, called FogBus2. It provides a mechanism for scheduling heterogeneous IoT applications and implements several scheduling policies. Also, it proposes an optimized genetic algorithm to obtain fast convergence to well-suited solutions. Besides, it offers a scalability mechanism to ensure efficient responsiveness when either the number of IoT devices increases or the resources become overburdened. Also, the dynamic resource discovery mechanism of FogBus2 assists new entities to quickly join the system. We have also developed two IoT applications, called Conway's Game of Life and Video Optical Character Recognition to demonstrate the effectiveness of FogBus2 for handling real-time and non-real-time IoT applications. Experimental results show FogBus2's scheduling policy improves the response time of IoT applications by 53\% compared to other policies. Also, the scalability mechanism can reduce up to 48\% of the queuing waiting time compared to frameworks that do not support scalability.

title: Master Graduation Thesis: A Lightweight and Distributed Container-based Framework
text: Containerization has revolutionized the way distributed systems are designed and deployed, offering improved resource utilization, scalability, and isolation. However, existing container-based frameworks often incur significant overhead in terms of resource consumption, complexity, and single-point-of-failure risks. To address these limitations, we present a novel, lightweight, and distributed container-based framework, specifically tailored for large-scale data processing and analytics workloads. Our framework, dubbed "Master Graduation Thesis," leverages a micro-kernel architecture, where a minimal, fault-tolerant core orchestrates a fleet of autonomous, stateless container managers. This design enables efficient resource allocation, reduced latency, and improved fault resilience. We employ a hierarchical, distributed scheduling strategy, which optimizes container placement, reduces network overhead, and ensures workload balancing across the cluster. Through a comprehensive evaluation using realistic workloads and benchmarks, we demonstrate that our framework achieves significant performance gains, reducing container startup times by up to 75%, and improving overall system throughput by up to 40%, compared to state-of-the-art container orchestration systems. Furthermore, our framework exhibits improved scalability, supporting up to 50% more concurrent containers, while maintaining a 30% reduction in overall system resource utilization. Our findings have significant implications for the design and deployment of large-scale distributed systems, enabling more efficient, scalable, and resilient data processing and analytics pipelines. The "Master Graduation Thesis" framework is open-sourced, and we envision its widespread adoption in various domains, including scientific computing, IoT, and cloud-native applications.

title: Organization and Understanding of a Tactile Information Dataset TacAct During Physical Human-Robot Interactions
text: Advanced service robots require superior tactile intelligence to guarantee human-contact safety and to provide essential supplements to visual and auditory information for human-robot interaction, especially when a robot is in physical contact with a human. Tactile intelligence is an essential capability of perception and recognition from tactile information, based on the learning from a large amount of tactile data and the understanding of the physical meaning behind the data. This report introduces a recently collected and organized dataset "TacAct" that encloses real-time pressure distribution when a human subject touches the arms of a nursing-care robot. The dataset consists of information from 50 subjects who performed a total of 24,000 touch actions. Furthermore, the details of the dataset are described, the data are preliminarily analyzed, and the validity of the collected information is tested through a convolutional neural network LeNet-5 classifying different types of touch actions. We believe that the TacAct dataset would be more than beneficial for the community of human interactive robots to understand the tactile profile under various circumstances.

title: Organization and Understanding of a Tactile Information Dataset TacAct During Physical Human-Robot Interactions
text: The lack of standardization in tactile information datasets hinders the development of effective human-robot interaction systems. To address this, we introduce TacAct, a novel dataset designed to capture the complexity of physical human-robot interactions. TacAct comprises 360,000 tactile samples collected from 30 participants interacting with a robotic arm in 12 distinct scenarios, yielding a diverse range of tactile patterns and pressure distributions. Each sample is annotated with corresponding action labels, allowing for the exploration of tactile-action correlations. We employ a hybrid data collection approach, combining high-fidelity tactile sensors with computer vision and motion capture systems to provide a comprehensive understanding of the interaction dynamics. Our analysis reveals that TacAct exhibits a long-tail distribution of tactile patterns, with a small set of frequent patterns accounting for a significant portion of the interactions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TacAct by training a deep neural network to recognize actions from tactile inputs, achieving an accuracy of 85.2%. The release of TacAct is expected to facilitate the development of more sophisticated human-robot interaction systems that can effectively interpret and respond to tactile cues.

title: "What makes my queries slow?": Subgroup Discovery for SQL Workload Analysis
text: Among daily tasks of database administrators (DBAs), the analysis of query workloads to identify schema issues and improving performances is crucial. Although DBAs can easily pinpoint queries repeatedly causing performance issues, it remains challenging to automatically identify subsets of queries that share some properties only (a pattern) and simultaneously foster some target measures, such as execution time. Patterns are defined on combinations of query clauses, environment variables, database alerts and metrics and help answer questions like what makes SQL queries slow? What makes I/O communications high? Automatically discovering these patterns in a huge search space and providing them as hypotheses for helping to localize issues and root-causes is important in the context of explainable AI. To tackle it, we introduce an original approach rooted on Subgroup Discovery. We show how to instantiate and develop this generic data-mining framework to identify potential causes of SQL workloads issues. We believe that such data-mining technique is not trivial to apply for DBAs. As such, we also provide a visualization tool for interactive knowledge discovery. We analyse a one week workload from hundreds of databases from our company, make both the dataset and source code available, and experimentally show that insightful hypotheses can be discovered.

title: "What makes my queries slow?": Subgroup Discovery for SQL Workload Analysis
text: Database administrators (DBAs) face the critical task of analyzing query workloads to diagnose schema issues and optimize performance. While repetitive performance bottlenecks can be readily identified, automatically discovering subsets of queries that share specific patterns and correlate with target metrics, such as execution time, remains a significant challenge. These patterns, defined by combinations of query clauses, environment variables, database alerts, and metrics, provide valuable insights into questions like what causes SQL queries to slow down and what drives high I/O communications. In the context of explainable AI, automatically uncovering these patterns in a vast search space and presenting them as hypotheses for issue localization and root-cause analysis is crucial. We propose a novel approach based on Subgroup Discovery, adapting this generic data-mining framework to identify potential causes of SQL workload issues. To facilitate interactive knowledge discovery, we also provide a visualization tool. Experimental results on a one-week workload from hundreds of databases demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, and we make the dataset and source code publicly available.

title: A Survey on Deep Reinforcement Learning for Data Processing and Analytics
text: Data processing and analytics are fundamental and pervasive. Algorithms play a vital role in data processing and analytics where many algorithm designs have incorporated heuristics and general rules from human knowledge and experience to improve their effectiveness. Recently, reinforcement learning, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) in particular, is increasingly explored and exploited in many areas because it can learn better strategies in complicated environments it is interacting with than statically designed algorithms. Motivated by this trend, we provide a comprehensive review of recent works focusing on utilizing DRL to improve data processing and analytics. First, we present an introduction to key concepts, theories, and methods in DRL. Next, we discuss DRL deployment on database systems, facilitating data processing and analytics in various aspects, including data organization, scheduling, tuning, and indexing. Then, we survey the application of DRL in data processing and analytics, ranging from data preparation, natural language processing to healthcare, fintech, etc. Finally, we discuss important open challenges and future research directions of using DRL in data processing and analytics.

title: A Survey on Deep Reinforcement Learning for Data Processing and Analytics
text: The proliferation of big data has necessitated the development of efficient data processing and analytics techniques to unlock valuable insights. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm in this context, leveraging the strengths of both deep learning and reinforcement learning to optimize complex data processing pipelines. This survey provides a comprehensive review of the current state-of-the-art in DRL for data processing and analytics, encompassing 75 research articles published in top-tier conferences and journals between 2015 and 2022. We systematically categorize existing DRL approaches based on their application domains, including data preprocessing, data warehousing, and data mining, and analyze their performance on benchmark datasets. Our analysis reveals that DRL-based methods outperform traditional techniques in terms of processing efficiency and accuracy, particularly in scenarios involving large-scale, heterogeneous, and dynamic data. However, we also identify key challenges and open research directions, including the need for more robust evaluation methodologies and the integration of DRL with domain-specific knowledge. This survey aims to provide a roadmap for researchers and practitioners seeking to harness the potential of DRL in data processing and analytics.

title: Contrained Generalization For Data Anonymization - A Systematic Search Based Approach
text: Data generalization is a powerful technique for sanitizing multi-attribute data for publication. In a multidimensional model, a subset of attributes called the quasi-identifiers (QI) are used to define the space and a generalization scheme corresponds to a partitioning of the data space. The process of sanitization can be modeled as a constrained optimization problem where the information loss metric is to be minimized while ensuring that the privacy criteria are enforced. The privacy requirements translate into constraints on the partitions (bins), like minimum occupancy constraints for k-anonymity, value diversity constraint for l-diversity etc. Most algorithms proposed till date use some greedy search heuristic to search for a locally optimal generalization scheme. The performance of such algorithms degrade rapidly as the constraints are made more complex and numerous. To address this issue, in this paper we develop a complete enumeration based systematic search framework that searches for the globally optimal generalization scheme amongst all feasible candidates. We employ a novel enumeration technique that eliminates duplicates and develop effective pruning heuristics that cut down the solution space in order to make the search tractable. Our scheme is versatile enough to accommodate multiple constraints and information loss functions satisfying a set of generic properties (that are usually satisfied by most metrics proposed in literature). Additionally, our approach allows the user to specify various stopping criteria and can give a bound on the approximation factor achieved by any candidate solution. Finally, we carry out extensive experimentation whose results illustrate the power of our algorithm and its advantage over other competing approaches.

title: Contrained Generalization For Data Anonymization - A Systematic Search Based Approach
text: Data anonymization has become a crucial step in publishing sensitive data, as it enables the sharing of valuable information while protecting individual privacy. However, existing anonymization techniques often struggle to balance data utility and privacy, leading to either over-suppression of sensitive information or insufficient protection. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach to data anonymization, Constrained Generalization (CG), which leverages systematic search to identify optimal anonymization strategies. Our CG approach formulates anonymization as a constraint optimization problem, where the goal is to maximize data utility while satisfying privacy constraints. We employ a systematic search algorithm to explore the vast space of possible anonymization strategies, navigating the trade-off between data utility and privacy. The search process is guided by a set of constraints, including k-anonymity, l-diversity, and t-closeness, which ensure that the anonymized data meets rigorous privacy standards. We evaluate the efficacy of CG using a comprehensive experimental framework, comprising real-world datasets and a range of anonymization scenarios. Our results demonstrate that CG significantly outperforms state-of-the-art anonymization techniques, achieving better data utility while maintaining robust privacy guarantees. Specifically, CG achieves an average improvement of 23.4% in data utility compared to existing approaches, while ensuring k-anonymity, l-diversity, and t-closeness constraints are met. Furthermore, our approach is shown to be scalable, with anonymization times comparable to existing techniques. The CG approach offers a promising solution for data anonymization, enabling the sharing of sensitive data while protecting individual privacy.

title: Parallel algorithms for mining of frequent itemsets
text: In the recent decade companies started collecting of large amount of data. Without a proper analyse, the data are usually useless. The field of analysing the data is called data mining. Unfortunately, the amount of data is quite large: the data do not fit into main memory and the processing time can become quite huge. Therefore, we need parallel data mining algorithms. One of the popular and important data mining algorithm is the algorithm for generation of so called frequent itemsets. The problem of mining of frequent itemsets can be explained on the following example: customers goes in a store put into theirs baskets some goods; the owner of the store collects the baskets and wants to know the set of goods that are bought together in at least p% of the baskets. Currently, the sequential algorithms for mining of frequent itemsets are quite good in the means of performance. However, the parallel algorithms for mining of frequent itemsets still do not achieve good speedup. In this thesis, we develop a parallel method for mining of frequent itemsets that can be used for an arbitrary depth first search sequential algorithms on a distributed memory parallel computer. Our method achieves speedup of ~ 6 on 10 processors. The method is based on an approximate estimation of processor load from a database sample - however it always computes the set of frequent itemsets from the whole database. In this thesis, we show a theory underlying our method and show the performance of the estimation process.

title: Parallel algorithms for mining of frequent itemsets
text: The proliferation of data collection in recent years has created an urgent need for efficient data analysis techniques. Data mining, a field dedicated to extracting valuable insights from large datasets, is severely hindered by the sheer volume of data, which often exceeds main memory capacity and leads to prohibitively long processing times. This has necessitated the development of parallel data mining algorithms. One crucial algorithm in this context is the generation of frequent itemsets, which involves identifying sets of items that co-occur in a minimum percentage of transactions. A paradigmatic example is a store owner seeking to determine the goods frequently purchased together by customers. While sequential algorithms for frequent itemset mining have demonstrated satisfactory performance, parallel algorithms have yet to achieve significant speedup. This thesis presents a novel parallel method for mining frequent itemsets, designed to be compatible with arbitrary depth-first search sequential algorithms on distributed memory parallel computers. Our approach, which leverages approximate processor load estimation from a database sample, yields a speedup of approximately 6 on 10 processors while ensuring the computation of complete frequent itemsets from the entire database. This work provides a theoretical foundation for our method and evaluates the performance of the estimation process.

title: Managing ML Pipelines: Feature Stores and the Coming Wave of Embedding Ecosystems
text: The industrial machine learning pipeline requires iterating on model features, training and deploying models, and monitoring deployed models at scale. Feature stores were developed to manage and standardize the engineer's workflow in this end-to-end pipeline, focusing on traditional tabular feature data. In recent years, however, model development has shifted towards using self-supervised pretrained embeddings as model features. Managing these embeddings and the downstream systems that use them introduces new challenges with respect to managing embedding training data, measuring embedding quality, and monitoring downstream models that use embeddings. These challenges are largely unaddressed in standard feature stores. Our goal in this tutorial is to introduce the feature store system and discuss the challenges and current solutions to managing these new embedding-centric pipelines.

title: Managing ML Pipelines: Feature Stores and the Coming Wave of Embedding Ecosystems
text: The end-to-end machine learning pipeline in industrial settings hinges on iterative refinement of model features, training, deployment, and large-scale monitoring. Feature stores have emerged as a solution to standardize and streamline this process, primarily catering to traditional tabular feature data. However, the recent paradigm shift towards leveraging self-supervised pretrained embeddings as model features has introduced novel complexities. Specifically, managing embedding training data, evaluating embedding quality, and monitoring downstream models that utilize embeddings pose significant challenges. Current feature stores are ill-equipped to address these issues, which have thus far received inadequate attention. This tutorial aims to elucidate the feature store system and explore the challenges and existing solutions for managing embedding-centric pipelines.

title: Towards Practical Learned Indexing
text: Latest research proposes to replace existing index structures with learned models. However, current learned indexes tend to have many hyperparameters, often do not provide any error guarantees, and are expensive to build. We introduce Practical Learned Index (PLEX). PLEX only has a single hyperparameter $ε$ (maximum prediction error) and offers a better trade-off between build and lookup time than state-of-the-art approaches. Similar to RadixSpline, PLEX consists of a spline and a (multi-level) radix layer. It first builds a spline satisfying the given $ε$ and then performs an ad-hoc analysis of the distribution of spline points to quickly tune the radix layer.

title: Towards Practical Learned Indexing
text: The advent of learned indexing has sparked significant interest in leveraging machine learning to optimize database indexing. However, existing approaches suffer from limitations, including high training overhead, inadequate adaptability to diverse data distributions, and inefficient index maintenance. This work presents a practical learned indexing framework that addresses these shortcomings. We propose a novel, data-driven approach to index construction, leveraging a hierarchical neural network to learn a compact, adaptive representation of the data distribution. Our experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate significant improvements in query performance and index maintenance efficiency, outperforming state-of-the-art learned indexing methods by up to 3.2x.

title: LargeEA: Aligning Entities for Large-scale Knowledge Graphs
text: Entity alignment (EA) aims to find equivalent entities in different knowledge graphs (KGs). Current EA approaches suffer from scalability issues, limiting their usage in real-world EA scenarios. To tackle this challenge, we propose LargeEA to align entities between large-scale KGs. LargeEA consists of two channels, i.e., structure channel and name channel. For the structure channel, we present METIS-CPS, a memory-saving mini-batch generation strategy, to partition large KGs into smaller mini-batches. LargeEA, designed as a general tool, can adopt any existing EA approach to learn entities' structural features within each mini-batch independently. For the name channel, we first introduce NFF, a name feature fusion method, to capture rich name features of entities without involving any complex training process. Then, we exploit a name-based data augmentation to generate seed alignment without any human intervention. Such design fits common real-world scenarios much better, as seed alignment is not always available. Finally, LargeEA derives the EA results by fusing the structural features and name features of entities. Since no widely-acknowledged benchmark is available for large-scale EA evaluation, we also develop a large-scale EA benchmark called DBP1M extracted from real-world KGs.
