Extensive experiments confirm the superiority of LargeEA against state-of-the-art competitors.

title: LargeEA: Aligning Entities for Large-scale Knowledge Graphs
text: Scalability limitations have hindered the adoption of entity alignment (EA) methods in real-world knowledge graph (KG) integration scenarios. To overcome this challenge, we introduce LargeEA, a novel framework designed to align entities across large-scale KGs. LargeEA comprises two complementary channels: a structure channel, which leverages METIS-CPS, a memory-efficient mini-batch generation strategy, to partition large KGs into smaller batches, enabling the adoption of existing EA approaches to learn structural features independently within each batch; and a name channel, which employs NFF, a name feature fusion method, to capture rich name features without complex training. We further propose a name-based data augmentation technique to generate seed alignment sans human intervention, a common constraint in real-world scenarios. The final EA results are derived by fusing the structural and name features of entities. To facilitate large-scale EA evaluation, we develop DBP1M, a benchmark extracted from real-world KGs. Our extensive experiments demonstrate LargeEA's superiority over state-of-the-art competitors, showcasing its potential for real-world KG integration applications.

title: Finite Automata Intersection Non-Emptiness: Parameterized Complexity Revisited
text: The problem DFA-Intersection-Nonemptiness asks if a given number of deterministic automata accept a common word. In general, this problem is PSPACE-complete. Here, we investigate this problem for the subclasses of commutative automata and automata recognizing sparse languages. We show that in both cases DFA-Intersection-Nonemptiness is complete for NP and for the parameterized class $W[1]$, where the number of input automata is the parameter, when the alphabet is fixed. Additionally, we establish the same result for Tables Non-Empty Join, a problem that asks if the join of several tables (possibly containing null values) in a database is non-empty. Lastly, we show that Bounded NFA-Intersection-Nonemptiness, parameterized by the length bound, is $\mbox{co-}W[2]$-hard with a variable input alphabet and for nondeterministic automata recognizing finite strictly bounded languages, yielding a variant leaving the realm of $W[1]$.

title: Finite Automata Intersection Non-Emptiness: Parameterized Complexity Revisited
text: The intersection non-emptiness problem for finite automata is a fundamental question in automata theory with numerous applications in formal verification, database theory, and programming languages. Despite its importance, the parameterized complexity of this problem remains poorly understood. In this context, we revisit the parameterized complexity of finite automata intersection non-emptiness, focusing on the number of automata and the size of the alphabet as parameters. We present a novel framework that leverages algebraic techniques and combinatorial insights to derive improved upper bounds on the complexity of this problem. Our main result establishes that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the size of the alphabet, significantly improving upon the previous best known bound. We also provide a tight lower bound, demonstrating that our algorithm is optimal under reasonable assumptions. These findings have significant implications for the design of more efficient algorithms in various areas of computer science.

title: A General Cardinality Estimation Framework for Subgraph Matching in Property Graphs
text: Many techniques have been developed for the cardinality estimation problem in data management systems. In this document, we introduce a framework for cardinality estimation of query patterns over property graph databases, which makes it possible to analyze, compare and combine different cardinality estimation approaches. This framework consists of three phases: obtaining a set of estimates for some subqueries, extending this set and finally combining the set into a single cardinality estimate for the query. We show that (parts of) many of the existing cardinality estimation approaches can be used as techniques in one of the phases from our framework. The three phases are loosely coupled, this makes it possible to combine (parts of) current cardinality estimation approaches. We create a graph version of the Join Order Benchmark to perform experiments with different combinations of techniques. The results show that query patterns without property constraints can be accurately estimated using synopses for small patterns. Accurate estimation of query patterns with property constraints require new estimation techniques to be developed that capture correlations between the property constraints and the topology in graph databases.

title: A General Cardinality Estimation Framework for Subgraph Matching in Property Graphs
text: Subgraph matching, a fundamental operation in graph databases, is crucial for various applications, including social network analysis, recommendation systems, and knowledge graph querying. However, its computational complexity renders it impractical for large-scale property graphs. A key bottleneck lies in estimating the cardinality of subgraph matches, which is essential for optimizing query plans and resource allocation. Existing approaches are either limited to simple graph structures or rely on domain-specific heuristics, lacking a general and principled solution. We propose a novel framework for cardinality estimation in subgraph matching, tailored to property graphs. Our approach leverages a probabilistic model that captures the distribution of subgraph patterns and their frequencies. By exploiting graph summarization techniques and a hierarchical decomposition of the subgraph pattern, we develop an efficient estimation algorithm with provable guarantees. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the accuracy and scalability of our framework, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by up to 3 orders of magnitude. Our work has significant implications for query optimization and performance in graph databases, enabling faster and more efficient subgraph matching for complex queries.

title: TextBenDS: a generic Textual data Benchmark for Distributed Systems
text: Extracting top-k keywords and documents using weighting schemes are popular techniques employed in text mining and machine learning for different analysis and retrieval tasks. The weights are usually computed in the data preprocessing step, as they are costly to update and keep track of all the modifications performed on the dataset. Furthermore, computation errors are introduced when analyzing only subsets of the dataset. Therefore, in a Big Data context, it is crucial to lower the runtime of computing weighting schemes, without hindering the analysis process and the accuracy of the machine learning algorithms. To address this requirement for the task of top-k keywords and documents, it is customary to design benchmarks that compare weighting schemes within various configurations of distributed frameworks and database management systems. Thus, we propose a generic document-oriented benchmark for storing textual data and constructing weighting schemes (TextBenDS). Our benchmark offers a generic data model designed with a multidimensional approach for storing text documents. We also propose using aggregation queries with various complexities and selectivities for constructing term weighting schemes, that are utilized in extracting top-k keywords and documents. We evaluate the computing performance of the queries on several distributed environments set within the Apache Hadoop ecosystem. Our experimental results provide interesting insights. As an example, MongoDB proves to have the best overall performance, while Spark's execution time remains almost the same, regardless of the weighting schemes.

title: TextBenDS: a generic Textual data Benchmark for Distributed Systems
text: The proliferation of distributed systems has been instrumental in scaling modern text-centric applications, yet the lack of a standardized benchmark for textual data hinders the evaluation and comparison of these systems. Existing benchmarks focus on specific domains or datasets, limiting their applicability and generalizability. To bridge this gap, we introduce TextBenDS, a generic textual data benchmark for distributed systems. TextBenDS is designed to provide a comprehensive evaluation framework for distributed systems processing textual data, encompassing diverse characteristics, such as data size, schema complexity, and query patterns. Our benchmark consists of five datasets, each representing a unique textual data distribution, and a suite of 15 queries that exercise various aspects of distributed system performance, including data ingestion, storage, and querying. We evaluate the performance of three prominent distributed systems, Apache Cassandra, Apache HBase, and Google's Bigtable, using TextBenDS and demonstrate its effectiveness in revealing system-specific strengths and weaknesses. Our results show that TextBenDS is able to uncover significant performance differences between the evaluated systems, highlighting the importance of a standardized benchmark for textual data in distributed systems. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis of the results, identifying key factors that influence system performance and offering insights for system designers and practitioners. TextBenDS is publicly available, facilitating its adoption and fostering further research in the development of optimized distributed systems for textual data processing.

title: Accelerating Approximate Aggregation Queries with Expensive Predicates
text: Researchers and industry analysts are increasingly interested in computing aggregation queries over large, unstructured datasets with selective predicates that are computed using expensive deep neural networks (DNNs). As these DNNs are expensive and because many applications can tolerate approximate answers, analysts are interested in accelerating these queries via approximations. Unfortunately, standard approximate query processing techniques to accelerate such queries are not applicable because they assume the result of the predicates are available ahead of time. Furthermore, recent work using cheap approximations (i.e., proxies) do not support aggregation queries with predicates. To accelerate aggregation queries with expensive predicates, we develop and analyze a query processing algorithm that leverages proxies (ABae). ABae must account for the key challenge that it may sample records that do not satisfy the predicate. To address this challenge, we first use the proxy to group records into strata so that records satisfying the predicate are ideally grouped into few strata. Given these strata, ABae uses pilot sampling and plugin estimates to sample according to the optimal allocation. We show that ABae converges at an optimal rate in a novel analysis of stratified sampling with draws that may not satisfy the predicate. We further show that ABae outperforms on baselines on six real-world datasets, reducing labeling costs by up to 2.3x.

title: Accelerating Approximate Aggregation Queries with Expensive Predicates
text: Approximate aggregation queries have become a crucial component in various data analytics and machine learning applications, enabling fast and efficient processing of large datasets. However, the presence of expensive predicates in these queries can significantly degrade their performance, leading to increased latency and reduced throughput. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework that accelerates approximate aggregation queries with expensive predicates. Our approach leverages a combination of data summarization techniques and probabilistic query optimization methods to reduce the number of predicate evaluations required during query processing. We develop a cost-model-based optimization algorithm that dynamically selects the most effective summarization strategy and predicate evaluation order based on the query workload and underlying data distribution. The proposed framework is implemented on top of a state-of-the-art approximate query processing engine and evaluated using a diverse set of real-world datasets and query workloads. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves significant performance gains, with an average speedup of 3.5x compared to the baseline approach, while maintaining a high degree of accuracy in the query results. Furthermore, our framework is shown to be robust to varying predicate selectivities and data distributions, making it a viable solution for a wide range of applications. Overall, this work contributes to the development of efficient and scalable approximate query processing techniques, enabling faster and more accurate insights from large datasets.

title: Reusable Templates and Guides For Documenting Datasets and Models for Natural Language Processing and Generation: A Case Study of the HuggingFace and GEM Data and Model Cards
text: Developing documentation guidelines and easy-to-use templates for datasets and models is a challenging task, especially given the variety of backgrounds, skills, and incentives of the people involved in the building of natural language processing (NLP) tools. Nevertheless, the adoption of standard documentation practices across the field of NLP promotes more accessible and detailed descriptions of NLP datasets and models, while supporting researchers and developers in reflecting on their work. To help with the standardization of documentation, we present two case studies of efforts that aim to develop reusable documentation templates -- the HuggingFace data card, a general purpose card for datasets in NLP, and the GEM benchmark data and model cards with a focus on natural language generation. We describe our process for developing these templates, including the identification of relevant stakeholder groups, the definition of a set of guiding principles, the use of existing templates as our foundation, and iterative revisions based on feedback.

title: Reusable Templates and Guides For Documenting Datasets and Models for Natural Language Processing and Generation: A Case Study of the HuggingFace and GEM Data and Model Cards
text: Standardizing documentation practices across natural language processing (NLP) is crucial for fostering transparency, accessibility, and reproducibility in dataset and model development. The diverse backgrounds, skills, and motivations of NLP practitioners, however, present significant hurdles to achieving this goal. To address this challenge, we present two case studies that demonstrate our efforts to develop reusable documentation templates for NLP datasets and models. Specifically, we introduce the HuggingFace data card, a general-purpose template for NLP datasets, and the GEM benchmark data and model cards, which focus on natural language generation. Our template development process involved identifying key stakeholder groups, establishing guiding principles, building upon existing templates, and refining our designs through iterative feedback incorporation. By sharing our experiences and insights, we aim to promote widespread adoption of standardized documentation practices in NLP, ultimately supporting more effective collaboration and knowledge sharing among researchers and developers.

title: Computing and Maintaining Provenance of Query Result Probabilities in Uncertain Knowledge Graphs
text: Knowledge graphs (KG) that model the relationships between entities as labeled edges (or facts) in a graph are mostly constructed using a suite of automated extractors, thereby inherently leading to uncertainty in the extracted facts. Modeling the uncertainty as probabilistic confidence scores results in a probabilistic knowledge graph. Graph queries over such probabilistic KGs require answer computation along with the computation of those result probabilities, aka, probabilistic inference. We propose a system, HAPPI (How Provenance of Probabilistic Inference), to handle such query processing. Complying with the standard provenance semiring model, we propose a novel commutative semiring to symbolically compute the probability of the result of a query. These provenance-polynomiallike symbolic expressions encode fine-grained information about the probability computation process. We leverage this encoding to efficiently compute as well as maintain the probability of results as the underlying KG changes. Focusing on a popular class of conjunctive basic graph pattern queries on the KG, we compare the performance of HAPPI against a possible-world model of computation and a knowledge compilation tool over two large datasets. We also propose an adaptive system that leverages the strengths of both HAPPI and compilation based techniques. Since existing systems for probabilistic databases mostly focus on query computation, they default to re-computation when facts in the KG are updated. HAPPI, on the other hand, does not just perform probabilistic inference and maintain their provenance, but also provides a mechanism to incrementally maintain them as the KG changes. We extend this maintainability as part of our proposed adaptive system.

title: Computing and Maintaining Provenance of Query Result Probabilities in Uncertain Knowledge Graphs
text: Probabilistic knowledge graphs (KGs) inherently harbor uncertainty in their extracted facts, which are typically modeled as probabilistic confidence scores. Querying these KGs necessitates not only answer computation but also probabilistic inference to determine result probabilities. To address this challenge, we introduce HAPPI, a system designed to process queries over probabilistic KGs. By adhering to the standard provenance semiring model, we propose a novel commutative semiring that symbolically computes query result probabilities. The resulting provenance-polynomial-like expressions encode fine-grained information about the probability computation process, enabling efficient probability computation and maintenance as the underlying KG evolves. We evaluate HAPPI's performance on a popular class of conjunctive basic graph pattern queries over two large datasets, comparing it to a possible-world model of computation and a knowledge compilation tool. Furthermore, we propose an adaptive system that leverages the strengths of both HAPPI and compilation-based techniques. Notably, HAPPI's incremental maintainability feature, which is also integrated into the adaptive system, sets it apart from existing probabilistic database systems that re-compute results upon KG updates. By providing a mechanism for incremental maintenance, HAPPI efficiently accommodates KG changes, ensuring up-to-date query results and probabilities.

title: VerSaChI: Finding Statistically Significant Subgraph Matches using Chebyshev's Inequality
text: Approximate subgraph matching, which is an important primitive for many applications like question answering, community detection, and motif discovery, often involves large labeled graphs such as knowledge graphs, social networks, and protein sequences. Effective methods for extracting matching subgraphs, in terms of label and structural similarities to a query, should depict accuracy, computational efficiency, and robustness to noise. In this paper, we propose VerSaChI for finding the top-k most similar subgraphs based on 2-hop label and structural overlap similarity with the query. The similarity is characterized using Chebyshev's inequality to compute the chi-square statistical significance for measuring the degree of matching of the subgraphs. Experiments on real-life graph datasets showcase significant improvements in terms of accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods, as well as robustness to noise.

title: VerSaChI: Finding Statistically Significant Subgraph Matches using Chebyshev's Inequality
text: The proliferation of large-scale graph-structured data has necessitated the development of efficient subgraph matching algorithms. Despite advances in this area, existing approaches often neglect the statistical significance of identified subgraphs, leading to an abundance of false positives. We propose VerSaChI, a novel framework that leverages Chebyshev's inequality to identify statistically significant subgraph matches in large graphs. By formulating the subgraph matching problem as a probabilistic inference task, VerSaChI efficiently computes the probability of observing a subgraph match by chance, thereby enabling the detection of significant patterns. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that VerSaChI outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of precision and recall, while reducing the number of false positives by up to 75%.

title: CollaborER: A Self-supervised Entity Resolution Framework Using Multi-features Collaboration
text: Entity Resolution (ER) aims to identify whether two tuples refer to the same real-world entity and is well-known to be labor-intensive. It is a prerequisite to anomaly detection, as comparing the attribute values of two matched tuples from two different datasets provides one effective way to detect anomalies. Existing ER approaches, due to insufficient feature discovery or error-prone inherent characteristics, are not able to achieve stable performance. In this paper, we present CollaborER, a self-supervised entity resolution framework via multi-features collaboration. It is capable of (i) obtaining reliable ER results with zero human annotations and (ii) discovering adequate tuples' features in a fault-tolerant manner. CollaborER consists of two phases, i.e., automatic label generation (ALG) and collaborative ER training (CERT). In the first phase, ALG is proposed to generate a set of positive tuple pairs and a set of negative tuple pairs. ALG guarantees the high quality of the generated tuples and hence ensures the training quality of the subsequent CERT. In the second phase, CERT is introduced to learn the matching signals by discovering graph features and sentence features of tuples collaboratively. Extensive experimental results over eight real-world ER benchmarks show that CollaborER outperforms all the existing unsupervised ER approaches and is comparable or even superior to the state-of-the-art supervised ER methods.

title: CollaborER: A Self-supervised Entity Resolution Framework Using Multi-features Collaboration
text: Entity resolution, a critical step in anomaly detection, seeks to determine whether two tuples represent the same real-world entity. However, existing approaches often struggle with unstable performance due to inadequate feature discovery or inherent errors. To address this, we propose CollaborER, a self-supervised entity resolution framework that leverages multi-feature collaboration to achieve reliable results without human annotations. CollaborER consists of two phases: automatic label generation (ALG) and collaborative ER training (CERT). ALG generates high-quality positive and negative tuple pairs, ensuring the accuracy of subsequent training. CERT then learns matching signals by collaboratively discovering graph and sentence features of tuples. Our comprehensive evaluation on eight real-world ER benchmarks demonstrates that CollaborER surpasses all existing unsupervised ER approaches and is comparable to or even outperforms state-of-the-art supervised methods, showcasing its effectiveness in entity resolution. By overcoming the limitations of current ER methods, CollaborER has significant implications for anomaly detection and data integration tasks.

title: Second-Order Specifications and Quantifier Elimination for Consistent Query Answering in Databases
text: Consistent answers to a query from a possibly inconsistent database are answers that are simultaneously retrieved from every possible repair of the database. Repairs are consistent instances that minimally differ from the original inconsistent instance. It has been shown before that database repairs can be specified as the stable models of a disjunctive logic program. In this paper we show how to use the repair programs to transform the problem of consistent query answering into a problem of reasoning w.r.t. a theory written in second-order predicate logic. It also investigated how a first-order theory can be obtained instead by applying second-order quantifier elimination techniques.

title: Second-Order Specifications and Quantifier Elimination for Consistent Query Answering in Databases
text: Query answers deemed consistent across a potentially inconsistent database are those derived from every possible repair, where repairs represent consistent instances minimally divergent from the original inconsistent instance. Prior research has established that database repairs can be formally characterized as the stable models of a disjunctive logic program. This study demonstrates a novel approach, leveraging repair programs to recast the problem of consistent query answering as a reasoning task concerning a second-order predicate logic theory. Furthermore, we explore the application of second-order quantifier elimination techniques to derive a first-order theory, thereby facilitating more efficient reasoning processes.

title: Byzantine Cluster-Sending in Expected Constant Communication
text: Traditional resilient systems operate on fully-replicated fault-tolerant clusters, which limits their scalability and performance. One way to make the step towards resilient high-performance systems that can deal with huge workloads, is by enabling independent fault-tolerant clusters to efficiently communicate and cooperate with each other, as this also enables the usage of high-performance techniques such as sharding and parallel processing. Recently, such inter-cluster communication was formalized as the Byzantine cluster-sending problem, and worst-case optimal protocols have been proposed that solve this problem. Unfortunately, these protocols have an all-case linear complexity in the size of the clusters involved. In this paper, we propose probabilistic cluster-sending techniques that can reliably send messages from one Byzantine fault-tolerant cluster to another with only an expected constant message complexity, this independent of the size of the clusters involved. Depending on the robustness of the clusters involved, our techniques require only two-to-four message round-trips. Furthermore, our protocols can support worst-case linear communication between clusters, which is optimal, and deal with asynchronous and unreliable communication. As such, our work provides a strong foundation for the further development of resilient high-performance systems.

title: Byzantine Cluster-Sending in Expected Constant Communication
text: Scalability and performance limitations in traditional resilient systems stem from their reliance on fully-replicated fault-tolerant clusters. To overcome these limitations and build high-performance systems capable of handling massive workloads, it is essential to enable efficient communication and cooperation between independent fault-tolerant clusters, thereby facilitating the use of high-performance techniques like sharding and parallel processing. The Byzantine cluster-sending problem, recently formalized to capture inter-cluster communication, has been addressed through worst-case optimal protocols. However, these protocols exhibit an all-case linear complexity in cluster size, which can be prohibitive. This paper presents probabilistic cluster-sending techniques that achieve reliable message transmission between Byzantine fault-tolerant clusters with an expected constant message complexity, independent of cluster size. Our protocols require only two-to-four message round-trips, depending on cluster robustness, and support optimal worst-case linear communication between clusters while tolerating asynchronous and unreliable communication. This work lays a solid foundation for the development of resilient high-performance systems.

title: Temporal Graph Functional Dependencies [Extended Version]
text: Data dependencies have been extended to graphs to characterize topological and value constraints. Existing data dependencies are defined to capture inconsistencies in static graphs. Nevertheless, inconsistencies may occur over evolving graphs and only for certain time periods. The need for capturing such inconsistencies in temporal graphs is evident in anomaly detection and predictive dynamic network analysis. This paper introduces a class of data dependencies called Temporal Graph Functional Dependencies (TGFDs). TGFDs generalize functional dependencies to temporal graphs as a sequence of graph snapshots that are induced by time intervals, and enforce both topological constraints and attribute value dependencies that must be satisfied by these snapshots. (1) We establish the complexity results for the satisfiability and implication problems of TGFDs. (2) We propose a sound and complete axiomatization system for TGFDs. (3) We also present efficient parallel algorithms to detect inconsistencies in temporal graphs as violations of TGFDs. The algorithm exploits data and temporal locality induced by time intervals, and uses incremental pattern matching and load balancing strategies to enable feasible error detection in large temporal graphs. Using real datasets, we experimentally verify that our algorithms achieve lower runtimes compared to existing baselines, while improving the accuracy over error detection using existing graph data constraints, e.g., GFDs and GTARs with 55% and 74% gain in F1-score, respectively.

title: Temporal Graph Functional Dependencies [Extended Version]
text: Temporal graphs, which capture dynamic relationships between entities, often exhibit inconsistencies that arise from evolving topological structures and attribute values over time. Existing data dependencies, designed for static graphs, fall short in characterizing these inconsistencies, which are crucial in anomaly detection and predictive dynamic network analysis. This paper introduces Temporal Graph Functional Dependencies (TGFDs), a novel class of data dependencies that generalize functional dependencies to temporal graphs. TGFDs enforce both topological constraints and attribute value dependencies across a sequence of graph snapshots induced by time intervals. We investigate the theoretical foundations of TGFDs, establishing complexity results for the satisfiability and implication problems. Furthermore, we propose a sound and complete axiomatization system for TGFDs. To facilitate efficient inconsistency detection, we develop parallel algorithms that leverage data and temporal locality, incremental pattern matching, and load balancing strategies. Experimental evaluations on real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding lower runtimes and improved accuracy compared to existing baselines, with significant gains in F1-score (55% over GFDs and 74% over GTARs).

title: Privacy-Preserving Batch-based Task Assignment in Spatial Crowdsourcing with Untrusted Server
text: In this paper, we study the privacy-preserving task assignment in spatial crowdsourcing, where the locations of both workers and tasks, prior to their release to the server, are perturbed with Geo-Indistinguishability (a differential privacy notion for location-based systems). Different from the previously studied online setting, where each task is assigned immediately upon arrival, we target the batch-based setting, where the server maximizes the number of successfully assigned tasks after a batch of tasks arrive. To achieve this goal, we propose the k-Switch solution, which first divides the workers into small groups based on the perturbed distance between workers/tasks, and then utilizes Homomorphic Encryption (HE) based secure computation to enhance the task assignment. Furthermore, we expedite HE-based computation by limiting the size of the small groups under k. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, in terms of the number of successfully assigned tasks, the k-Switch solution improves batch-based baselines by 5.9X and the existing online solution by 1.74X, with no privacy leak.

title: Privacy-Preserving Batch-based Task Assignment in Spatial Crowdsourcing with Untrusted Server
text: We investigate the privacy-preserving task assignment problem in spatial crowdsourcing, where worker and task locations are perturbed using Geo-Indistinguishability, a differential privacy notion for location-based systems, prior to their release to the server. In contrast to online settings, where tasks are assigned immediately upon arrival, we focus on the batch-based setting, where the server aims to maximize the number of successfully assigned tasks after a batch of tasks arrives. To achieve this, we propose the k-Switch solution, which partitions workers into small groups based on perturbed distances and leverages Homomorphic Encryption (HE) for secure computation to enhance task assignment. By limiting group sizes to k, we accelerate HE-based computation. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that the k-Switch solution significantly outperforms batch-based baselines by a factor of 5.9 and the existing online solution by 1.74, while maintaining privacy guarantees.

title: A computational study on imputation methods for missing environmental data
text: Data acquisition and recording in the form of databases are routine operations. The process of collecting data, however, may experience irregularities, resulting in databases with missing data. Missing entries might alter analysis efficiency and, consequently, the associated decision-making process. This paper focuses on databases collecting information related to the natural environment. Given the broad spectrum of recorded activities, these databases typically are of mixed nature. It is therefore relevant to evaluate the performance of missing data processing methods considering this characteristic. In this paper we investigate the performances of several missing data imputation methods and their application to the problem of missing data in environment. A computational study was performed to compare the method missForest (MF) with two other imputation methods, namely Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN). Tests were made on 10 pretreated datasets of various types. Results revealed that MF generally outperformed MICE and KNN in terms of imputation errors, with a more pronounced performance gap for mixed typed databases where MF reduced the imputation error up to 150%, when compared to the other methods. KNN was usually the fastest method. MF was then successfully applied to a case study on Quebec wastewater treatment plants performance monitoring. We believe that the present study demonstrates the pertinence of using MF as imputation method when dealing with missing environmental data.

title: A computational study on imputation methods for missing environmental data
text: The increasing availability of environmental data has enabled researchers to study complex ecological systems, but missing values in these datasets remain a pervasive problem, hindering the accuracy of downstream analyses. Imputation methods, which fill in missing values using statistical models, have been proposed as a solution, but their performance has not been systematically evaluated in environmental data. This study conducts a comprehensive investigation of eight popular imputation methods, including mean imputation, regression imputation, and machine learning-based approaches, on a diverse set of environmental datasets. We consider datasets from various sources, including air quality monitoring networks, water quality sensors, and climate models, encompassing different data types, spatial resolutions, and missingness patterns. Our experiments reveal that no single imputation method consistently outperforms others across all datasets, highlighting the importance of dataset-specific tuning. However, we identify a subset of methods, including random forest-based imputation and matrix factorization, which exhibit robust performance across a majority of datasets. Notably, these methods improve upon traditional mean imputation by up to 30% in terms of root mean squared error. Our findings provide valuable insights for environmental researchers and policymakers, informing the selection of imputation methods for data analysis and decision-making.

title: On Quantifying Literals in Boolean Logic and Its Applications to Explainable AI
text: Quantified Boolean logic results from adding operators to Boolean logic for existentially and universally quantifying variables. This extends the reach of Boolean logic by enabling a variety of applications that have been explored over the decades. The existential quantification of literals (variable states) and its applications have also been studied in the literature. In this paper, we complement this by studying universal literal quantification and its applications, particularly to explainable AI. We also provide a novel semantics for quantification, discuss the interplay between variable/literal and existential/universal quantification. We further identify some classes of Boolean formulas and circuits on which quantification can be done efficiently. Literal quantification is more fine-grained than variable quantification as the latter can be defined in terms of the former. This leads to a refinement of quantified Boolean logic with literal quantification as its primitive.

title: On Quantifying Literals in Boolean Logic and Its Applications to Explainable AI
text: By augmenting Boolean logic with existential and universal quantification operators, Quantified Boolean Logic (QBL) expands the scope of Boolean logic, facilitating diverse applications that have been explored extensively over the years. While the existential quantification of literals has garnered significant attention, the universal quantification of literals and its implications, particularly in the realm of explainable AI, remain understudied. This paper addresses this gap by investigating universal literal quantification and its applications, introducing a novel semantics for quantification, and examining the intricate relationships between variable/literal and existential/universal quantification. Furthermore, we identify specific classes of Boolean formulas and circuits that enable efficient quantification. Our findings demonstrate that literal quantification offers a more nuanced approach than variable quantification, which can be defined in terms of the former, thereby yielding a refined QBL framework with literal quantification as its foundation.

title: No DBA? No regret! Multi-armed bandits for index tuning of analytical and HTAP workloads with provable guarantees
text: Automating physical database design has remained a long-term interest in database research due to substantial performance gains afforded by optimised structures. Despite significant progress, a majority of today's commercial solutions are highly manual, requiring offline invocation by database administrators (DBAs) who are expected to identify and supply representative training workloads. Even the latest advancements like query stores provide only limited support for dynamic environments. This status quo is untenable: identifying representative static workloads is no longer realistic; and physical design tools remain susceptible to the query optimiser's cost misestimates. Furthermore, modern application environments such as hybrid transactional and analytical processing (HTAP) systems render analytical modelling next to impossible. We propose a self-driving approach to online index selection that eschews the DBA and query optimiser, and instead learns the benefits of viable structures through strategic exploration and direct performance observation. We view the problem as one of sequential decision making under uncertainty, specifically within the bandit learning setting. Multi-armed bandits balance exploration and exploitation to provably guarantee average performance that converges to policies that are optimal with perfect hindsight. Our comprehensive empirical evaluation against a state-of-the-art commercial tuning tool demonstrates up to 75% speed-up on shifting and ad-hoc workloads and up to 28% speed-up on static workloads in analytical processing environments. In HTAP environments, our solution provides up to 59% speed-up on shifting and 51% speed-up on static workloads. Furthermore, our bandit framework outperforms deep reinforcement learning (RL) in terms of convergence speed and performance volatility (providing up to 58% speed-up).

title: No DBA? No regret! Multi-armed bandits for index tuning of analytical and HTAP workloads with provable guarantees
text: The quest for automated physical database design has long been a crucial pursuit in database research, driven by the significant performance enhancements achievable through optimized structures. However, current commercial solutions largely rely on manual intervention, where database administrators (DBAs) are required to identify and provide representative training workloads offline. Even recent advancements, such as query stores, offer limited support for dynamic environments. This paradigm is unsustainable, as identifying representative static workloads is no longer feasible, and physical design tools remain vulnerable to cost misestimates by the query optimizer. Moreover, modern application environments, such as hybrid transactional and analytical processing (HTAP) systems, render analytical modeling impractical. To address these challenges, we propose a self-driving approach to online index selection, which eliminates the need for DBA and query optimizer intervention, instead learning the benefits of viable structures through strategic exploration and direct performance observation. By framing the problem as one of sequential decision making under uncertainty within the bandit learning setting, we can balance exploration and exploitation to guarantee average performance that converges to optimal policies. Our comprehensive empirical evaluation against a state-of-the-art commercial tuning tool demonstrates significant speed-ups of up to 75% on shifting and ad-hoc workloads, and up to 28% on static workloads in analytical processing environments. In HTAP environments, our solution achieves speed-ups of up to 59% on shifting and 51% on static workloads, outperforming deep reinforcement learning in terms of convergence speed and performance volatility, with speed-ups of up to 58%.

title: Making RDBMSs Efficient on Graph Workloads Through Predefined Joins
text: Joins in native graph database management systems (GDBMSs) are predefined to the system as edges, which are indexed in adjacency list indices and serve as pointers. This contrasts with and can be more performant than value-based joins in RDBMSs and has lead researchers to investigate ways to integrate predefined joins directly into RDBMSs. Existing approaches adopt a strict separation of graph and relational data and processors, where a graph-specific processor uses left-deep and index nested loop joins for a subset of joins. This may be suboptimal, and may lead to non-sequential scans of data in some queries. We propose a purely relational approach to integrate predefined joins in columnar RDBMSs that uses row IDs (RIDs) of tuples as pointers. Users can predefine equality joins between any two tables, which leads to materializing RIDs in extended tables and optionally in RID indices. Instead of using the RID index to perform the join directly, we use it primarily in hash joins to generate semi-join filters that can be passed to scans using sideways information passing, ensuring sequential scans. In some settings, we also use RID indices to reduce the number of joins in query plans. Our approach does not introduce any graph-specific system components, can execute predefined joins on any join plan, and can improve performance on any workload that contains equality joins that can be predefined. We integrated our approach to DuckDB and call the resulting system {\em GRainDB}. We demonstrate that GRainDB far improves the performance of DuckDB on relational and graph workloads with large many-to-many joins, making it competitive with a state-of-the-art GDBMS, and incurs no major overheads otherwise.

title: Making RDBMSs Efficient on Graph Workloads Through Predefined Joins
text: The increasing prevalence of graph-structured data has exposed the inefficiencies of traditional Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMSs) in handling graph workloads. The root cause lies in the excessive number of joins required to traverse the graph, leading to poor performance and scalability. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that leverages predefined joins to optimize RDBMSs for graph workloads. Our methodology involves a thorough analysis of graph query patterns to identify frequently occurring subgraphs and join sequences. We then develop a set of predefined joins that can be materialized and stored in the database, reducing the overhead of runtime join computation. To ensure the effectiveness of our approach, we implement a join selection algorithm that dynamically chooses the optimal predefined join based on the query workload and available system resources. Experimental evaluation on a range of graph datasets and query workloads demonstrates significant performance improvements, with an average speedup of 3.5x over traditional RDBMSs. Moreover, our approach achieves better scalability, with a reduction of 40% in memory usage and 25% in disk I/O. We also observe that the benefits of predefined joins are more pronounced for larger graphs and more complex query patterns. Our results have important implications for the efficient processing of graph data in RDBMSs, enabling a wider range of applications to leverage the benefits of relational databases. Furthermore, our approach can be extended to other data models, such as document-oriented and time-series databases, where graph-like structures are increasingly prevalent. Overall, our work contributes to the development of more efficient and scalable database systems for graph-structured data.

title: Learning GraphQL Query Costs (Extended Version)
text: GraphQL is a query language for APIs and a runtime for executing those queries, fetching the requested data from existing microservices, REST APIs, databases, or other sources. Its expressiveness and its flexibility have made it an attractive candidate for API providers in many industries, especially through the web. A major drawback to blindly servicing a client's query in GraphQL is that the cost of a query can be unexpectedly large, creating computation and resource overload for the provider, and API rate-limit overages and infrastructure overload for the client. To mitigate these drawbacks, it is necessary to efficiently estimate the cost of a query before executing it. Estimating query cost is challenging, because GraphQL queries have a nested structure, GraphQL APIs follow different design conventions, and the underlying data sources are hidden. Estimates based on worst-case static query analysis have had limited success because they tend to grossly overestimate cost. We propose a machine-learning approach to efficiently and accurately estimate the query cost. We also demonstrate the power of this approach by testing it on query-response data from publicly available commercial APIs. Our framework is efficient and predicts query costs with high accuracy, consistently outperforming the static analysis by a large margin.

title: Learning GraphQL Query Costs (Extended Version)
text: The GraphQL query language has revolutionized API interactions by providing a flexible and efficient way to fetch data from diverse sources. However, the complexity of GraphQL queries can lead to performance bottlenecks, making it crucial to estimate query costs accurately. Existing approaches rely on static analysis, which falls short in capturing the dynamic nature of GraphQL queries. To address this limitation, we propose a machine learning-based approach to learn GraphQL query costs. Our method leverages a comprehensive dataset of query executions and their corresponding costs, collected from a large-scale GraphQL deployment. We employ a combination of graph neural networks and gradient boosting to learn a cost model that accurately predicts the execution time of arbitrary GraphQL queries. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to 3.5x in terms of mean absolute error. Furthermore, we show that our learned cost model can be effectively utilized for query optimization, resulting in a significant reduction of up to 40% in query execution time. Our approach has significant implications for GraphQL-based systems, enabling developers to optimize their queries proactively and improving the overall performance of their applications. We release our dataset and implementation as open-source, facilitating further research in this area.

title: Supercomputing Enabled Deployable Analytics for Disaster Response
text: First responders and other forward deployed essential workers can benefit from advanced analytics. Limited network access and software security requirements prevent the usage of standard cloud based microservice analytic platforms that are typically used in industry. One solution is to precompute a wide range of analytics as files that can be used with standard preinstalled software that does not require network access or additional software and can run on a wide range of legacy hardware. In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, this approach was tested for providing geo-spatial census data to allow quick analysis of demographic data for better responding to emergencies. These data were processed using the MIT SuperCloud to create several thousand Google Earth and Microsoft Excel files representative of many advanced analytics. The fast mapping of census data using Google Earth and Microsoft Excel has the potential to give emergency responders a powerful tool to improve emergency preparedness. Our approach displays relevant census data (total population, population under 15, population over 65, median age) per census block, sorted by county, through a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet (xlsx file) and Google Earth map (kml file). The spreadsheet interface includes features that allow users to convert between different longitude and latitude coordinate units. For the Google Earth files, a variety of absolute and relative colors maps of population density have been explored to provide an intuitive and meaningful interface. Using several hundred cores on the MIT SuperCloud, new analytics can be generated in a few minutes.

title: Supercomputing Enabled Deployable Analytics for Disaster Response
text: Disaster response efforts rely heavily on timely and accurate situational awareness, which is often hindered by the sheer volume and velocity of relevant data. The increasing availability of IoT sensors, drones, and social media platforms exacerbates this challenge, necessitating novel analytics approaches that can handle massive datasets in real-time. This research presents a deployable analytics framework, dubbed "RAPID," which leverages supercomputing resources to facilitate swift and informed decision-making in disaster response scenarios. RAPID's architecture is centered around an in-memory data grid, which enables low-latency data ingestion and querying. We employ a distributed, GPU-accelerated machine learning pipeline to process streaming data from various sources, including satellite imagery, sensor feeds, and social media APIs. This pipeline is powered by a custom-developed, performance-optimized implementation of the Random Forest algorithm, which achieves a 5x speedup over existing GPU-based implementations. We evaluate RAPID's efficacy using a comprehensive disaster response dataset, comprising over 10 million records gathered from recent hurricane and wildfire events. Our experiments demonstrate that RAPID can process this dataset in under 10 minutes, yielding actionable insights on damage assessment, resource allocation, and evacuation routing. Notably, RAPID achieves a 92% accuracy rate in predicting disaster-affected areas, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches by 15%. We envision RAPID being deployed in the field, providing critical support to emergency responders and mitigating the devastating impacts of disasters.

title: Local Exceptionality Detection in Time Series Using Subgroup Discovery
text: In this paper, we present a novel approach for local exceptionality detection on time series data. This method provides the ability to discover interpretable patterns in the data, which can be used to understand and predict the progression of a time series. This being an exploratory approach, the results can be used to generate hypotheses about the relationships between the variables describing a specific process and its dynamics. We detail our approach in a concrete instantiation and exemplary implementation, specifically in the field of teamwork research. Using a real-world dataset of team interactions we include results from an example data analytics application of our proposed approach, showcase novel analysis options, and discuss possible implications of the results from the perspective of teamwork research.

title: Local Exceptionality Detection in Time Series Using Subgroup Discovery
text: Anomalies in time series data can significantly impact decision-making in various domains, from finance to healthcare. Local exceptions, in particular, are challenging to detect due to their subtle nature and rarity. Existing methods often rely on density-based or statistical approaches, which may overlook subtle patterns and correlations. This paper proposes a novel framework for local exceptionality detection using subgroup discovery, a technique commonly employed in data mining. Our approach leverages the ability of subgroup discovery to identify complex patterns and relationships in data. We introduce a tailored quality measure to guide the search for exceptional subgroups and demonstrate its effectiveness on real-world datasets from finance and energy consumption. Experimental results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in detecting local exceptions, achieving a 25% increase in F1-score and 30% reduction in false positives.

title: Enabling SQL-based Training Data Debugging for Federated Learning
text: How can we debug a logistical regression model in a federated learning setting when seeing the model behave unexpectedly (e.g., the model rejects all high-income customers' loan applications)? The SQL-based training data debugging framework has proved effective to fix this kind of issue in a non-federated learning setting. Given an unexpected query result over model predictions, this framework automatically removes the label errors from training data such that the unexpected behavior disappears in the retrained model. In this paper, we enable this powerful framework for federated learning. The key challenge is how to develop a security protocol for federated debugging which is proved to be secure, efficient, and accurate. Achieving this goal requires us to investigate how to seamlessly integrate the techniques from multiple fields (Databases, Machine Learning, and Cybersecurity). We first propose FedRain, which extends Rain, the state-of-the-art SQL-based training data debugging framework, to our federated learning setting. We address several technical challenges to make FedRain work and analyze its security guarantee and time complexity. The analysis results show that FedRain falls short in terms of both efficiency and security. To overcome these limitations, we redesign our security protocol and propose Frog, a novel SQL-based training data debugging framework tailored for federated learning. Our theoretical analysis shows that Frog is more secure, more accurate, and more efficient than FedRain. We conduct extensive experiments using several real-world datasets and a case study. The experimental results are consistent with our theoretical analysis and validate the effectiveness of Frog in practice.

title: Enabling SQL-based Training Data Debugging for Federated Learning
text: Debugging logistical regression models in federated learning settings poses a significant challenge, particularly when models exhibit unexpected behavior, such as rejecting loan applications from high-income customers. The SQL-based training data debugging framework has demonstrated efficacy in non-federated settings, automatically identifying and removing label errors from training data to rectify anomalous model behavior. This paper adapts this framework for federated learning, necessitating the development of a secure, efficient, and accurate security protocol. Integrating techniques from databases, machine learning, and cybersecurity, we propose FedRain, an extension of the state-of-the-art Rain framework, tailored for federated learning. However, our analysis reveals that FedRain falls short in terms of efficiency and security. To overcome these limitations, we redesign our security protocol and introduce Frog, a novel SQL-based training data debugging framework optimized for federated learning. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that Frog surpasses FedRain in security, accuracy, and efficiency. We validate Frog's effectiveness through extensive experiments on real-world datasets and a case study, with results consistent with our theoretical analysis. Our work enables the reliable debugging of logistical regression models in federated learning settings, ensuring fair and accurate decision-making processes.

title: Towards Observability for Production Machine Learning Pipelines
text: Software organizations are increasingly incorporating machine learning (ML) into their product offerings, driving a need for new data management tools. Many of these tools facilitate the initial development of ML applications, but sustaining these applications post-deployment is difficult due to lack of real-time feedback (i.e., labels) for predictions and silent failures that could occur at any component of the ML pipeline (e.g., data distribution shift or anomalous features). We propose a new type of data management system that offers end-to-end observability, or visibility into complex system behavior, for deployed ML pipelines through assisted (1) detection, (2) diagnosis, and (3) reaction to ML-related bugs. We describe new research challenges and suggest preliminary solution ideas in all three aspects. Finally, we introduce an example architecture for a "bolt-on" ML observability system, or one that wraps around existing tools in the stack.

title: Towards Observability for Production Machine Learning Pipelines
text: Machine learning (ML) pipelines have become a crucial component of modern data-driven systems, but their complexity and opaqueness hinder effective monitoring and debugging. In production environments, ML pipelines involve intricate data flows, distributed computing, and numerous dependencies, making it challenging to diagnose issues, identify performance bottlenecks, and ensure model reliability. To address these challenges, we propose a novel observability framework for production ML pipelines. Our approach combines data provenance tracking, model introspection, and real-time metrics collection to provide a unified view of pipeline behavior. We implement our framework using a combination of open-source tools, including Apache Beam, TensorFlow, and Prometheus. Experimental evaluation on real-world pipelines demonstrates that our framework reduces mean time to detect (MTTD) issues by 3.5x and mean time to resolve (MTTR) by 2.2x, compared to existing ad-hoc monitoring approaches. Our work enables data scientists and engineers to develop more reliable, efficient, and explainable ML pipelines.

title: Hierarchical Bitmap Indexing for Range and Membership Queries on Multidimensional Arrays
text: Traditional indexing techniques commonly employed in da\-ta\-ba\-se systems perform poorly on multidimensional array scientific data. Bitmap indices are widely used in commercial databases for processing complex queries, due to their effective use of bit-wise operations and space-efficiency. However, bitmap indices apply natively to relational or linearized datasets, which is especially notable in binned or compressed indices. We propose a new method for multidimensional array indexing that overcomes the dimensionality-induced inefficiencies. The hierarchical indexing method is based on $n$-di\-men\-sional sparse trees for dimension partitioning, with bound number of individual, adaptively binned indices for attribute partitioning. This indexing performs well on range involving both dimensions and attributes, as it prunes the search space early, avoids reading entire index data, and does at most a single index traversal. Moreover, the indexing is easily extensible to membership queries. The indexing method was implemented on top of a state of the art bitmap indexing library Fastbit. We show that the hierarchical bitmap index outperforms conventional bitmap indexing built on auxiliary attribute for each dimension. Furthermore, the adaptive binning significantly reduces the amount of bins and therefore memory requirements.

title: Hierarchical Bitmap Indexing for Range and Membership Queries on Multidimensional Arrays
text: The proliferation of multidimensional arrays in various domains, including scientific simulations, data analytics, and machine learning, has created a pressing need for efficient indexing techniques that support range and membership queries. Existing indexing methods, such as k-d trees and ball trees, exhibit poor performance and limited scalability when confronted with high-dimensional data. To address this challenge, we propose a novel hierarchical bitmap indexing approach that leverages the inherent sparsity of multidimensional arrays. Our method represents each array dimension as a hierarchical bitmap, enabling fast range and membership query processing through bitwise operations. We develop a rigorous cost model to guide the construction of the hierarchical index, minimizing the number of bitmap lookups and reducing storage overhead. Experimental evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art indexing techniques by up to 5x in terms of query response time, while incurring a modest storage overhead of 10-20%. We also provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis, establishing the optimality of our indexing scheme under certain assumptions. Our results have significant implications for accelerating data-intensive applications, particularly those involving complex queries on high-dimensional arrays.

title: Latency-Redundancy Tradeoff in Distributed Read-Write Systems
text: Data is replicated and stored redundantly over multiple servers for availability in distributed databases. We focus on databases with frequent reads and writes, where both read and write latencies are important. This is in contrast to databases designed primarily for either read or write applications. Redundancy has contrasting effects on read and write latency. Read latency can be reduced by potential parallel access from multiple servers, whereas write latency increases as a larger number of replicas have to be updated. We quantify this tradeoff between read and write latency as a function of redundancy, and provide a closed-form approximation when the request arrival is Poisson and the service is memoryless. We empirically show that this approximation is tight across all ranges of system parameters. Thus, we provide guidelines for redundancy selection in distributed databases.

title: Latency-Redundancy Tradeoff in Distributed Read-Write Systems
text: Distributed read-write systems are crucial for modern data-intensive applications, yet they often struggle to balance latency and redundancy. While redundancy is essential for fault-tolerance and data durability, it can significantly increase latency due to the overhead of replication and consistency protocols. This paper investigates the latency-redundancy tradeoff in distributed read-write systems, focusing on the interplay between replica placement, consistency models, and concurrency control. We develop a novel analytical framework that captures the intricate relationships between these factors and their impact on system performance. Through a comprehensive evaluation using a combination of simulations and experiments on a real-world distributed database, we demonstrate that our framework can predict optimal tradeoff points with high accuracy. Our results show that, depending on the workload and system configuration, a 30-50% reduction in latency can be achieved by judiciously adjusting redundancy levels, without compromising data durability or consistency.

title: Quantum-Inspired Keyword Search on Multi-Model Databases
text: With the rising applications implemented in different domains, it is inevitable to require databases to adopt corresponding appropriate data models to store and exchange data derived from various sources. To handle these data models in a single platform, the community of databases introduces a multi-model database. And many vendors are improving their products from supporting a single data model to being multi-model databases. Although this brings benefits, spending lots of enthusiasm to master one of the multi-model query languages for exploring a database is unfriendly to most users. Therefore, we study using keyword searches as an alternative way to explore and query multi-model databases. In this paper, we attempt to utilize quantum physics's probabilistic formalism to bring the problem into vector spaces and represent events (e.g., words) as subspaces. Then we employ a density matrix to encapsulate all the information over these subspaces and use density matrices to measure the divergence between query and candidate answers for finding top-\textit{k} the most relevant results. In this process, we propose using pattern mining to identify compounds for improving accuracy and using dimensionality reduction for reducing complexity. Finally, empirical experiments demonstrate the performance superiority of our approaches over the state-of-the-art approaches.

title: Quantum-Inspired Keyword Search on Multi-Model Databases
text: The proliferation of domain-specific applications necessitates the development of databases capable of accommodating diverse data models, thereby prompting the emergence of multi-model databases. As vendors increasingly transition their products to support multiple data models, a crucial challenge arises: the complexity of mastering multi-model query languages, which can be daunting for most users. To address this issue, we explore the feasibility of keyword searches as a more user-friendly alternative for querying multi-model databases. By leveraging the probabilistic formalism of quantum physics, we represent events as subspaces within vector spaces and encapsulate information across these subspaces using density matrices. This approach enables the measurement of divergence between queries and candidate answers, facilitating the retrieval of top-k relevant results. Furthermore, we propose the integration of pattern mining to identify compounds and dimensionality reduction to mitigate complexity. Our empirical experiments demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing state-of-the-art methods.

title: MORTAL: A Tool of Automatically Designing Relational Storage Schemas for Multi-model Data through Reinforcement Learning
text: Considering relational databases having powerful capabilities in handling security, user authentication, query optimization, etc., several commercial and academic frameworks reuse relational databases to store and query semi-structured data (e.g., XML, JSON) or graph data (e.g., RDF, property graph). However, these works concentrate on managing one of the above data models with RDBMSs. That is, it does not exploit the underlying tools to automatically generate the relational schema for storing multi-model data. In this demonstration, we present a novel reinforcement learning-based tool called MORTAL. Specifically, given multi-model data containing different data models and a set of queries, it could automatically design a relational schema to store these data while having a great query performance. To demonstrate it clearly, we are centered around the following modules: generating initial state based on loaded multi-model data, influencing learning process by setting parameters, controlling generated relational schema through providing semantic constraints, improving the query performance of relational schema by specifying queries, and a highly interactive interface for showing query performance and storage consumption when users adjust the generated relational schema.

title: MORTAL: A Tool of Automatically Designing Relational Storage Schemas for Multi-model Data through Reinforcement Learning
text: The proliferation of multi-model data, encompassing diverse data formats and structures, has created a pressing need for efficient relational storage schema design. Existing approaches rely on manual schema design, which is time-consuming, error-prone, and often suboptimal. To address this challenge, we present MORTAL, a novel tool that leverages reinforcement learning to automatically design relational storage schemas for multi-model data. MORTAL's core component is a deep Q-network that learns to navigate the vast space of possible schema designs, guided by a reward function that balances query performance, data consistency, and storage efficiency. Through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, we demonstrate that MORTAL outperforms state-of-the-art schema design techniques, achieving an average improvement of 23% in query execution time and 17% in storage compression. Furthermore, MORTAL's learned schema designs exhibit improved data integrity and consistency, reducing data anomalies by 35%. Our results underscore the potential of reinforcement learning in automating complex database design tasks, paving the way for more efficient and adaptive data management systems.

title: Storing Multi-model Data in RDBMSs based on Reinforcement Learning
text: How to manage various data in a unified way is a significant research topic in the field of databases. To address this problem, researchers have proposed multi-model databases to support multiple data models in a uniform platform with a single unified query language. However, since relational databases are predominant in the current market, it is expensive to replace them with others. Besides, due to the theories and technologies of RDBMSs having been enhanced over decades, it is hard to use few years to develop a multi-model database that can be compared with existing RDBMSs in handling security, query optimization, transaction management, etc. In this paper, we reconsider employing relational databases to store and query multi-model data. Unfortunately, the mismatch between the complexity of multi-model data structure and the simplicity of flat relational tables makes this difficult. Against this challenge, we utilize the reinforcement learning (RL) method to learn a relational schema by interacting with an RDBMS. Instead of using the classic Q-learning algorithm, we propose a variant Q-learning algorithm, called \textit{Double Q-tables}, to reduce the dimension of the original Q-table and improve learning efficiency. Experimental results show that our approach could learn a relational schema outperforming the existing multi-model storage schema in terms of query time and space consumption.

title: Storing Multi-model Data in RDBMSs based on Reinforcement Learning
text: The integration of diverse data sources into a unified framework remains a pressing concern in database research. One proposed solution is the multi-model database, which supports multiple data models via a single, unified query language. However, the widespread adoption of relational databases and the decades-long refinement of relational database management systems (RDBMSs) render it infeasible to develop a comparable multi-model database within a few years. In light of this, we revisit the possibility of leveraging relational databases for storing and querying multi-model data. Nevertheless, the mismatch between the complexity of multi-model data structures and the simplicity of flat relational tables poses a significant challenge. To overcome this, we employ reinforcement learning (RL) to learn a relational schema through interactions with an RDBMS. We introduce a variant of the Q-learning algorithm, termed Double Q-tables, which reduces the dimensionality of the original Q-table and enhances learning efficiency. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach can learn a relational schema that outperforms existing multi-model storage schemas in terms of query time and space consumption.

title: Complex Event Forecasting with Prediction Suffix Trees: Extended Technical Report
text: Complex Event Recognition (CER) systems have become popular in the past two decades due to their ability to "instantly" detect patterns on real-time streams of events. However, there is a lack of methods for forecasting when a pattern might occur before such an occurrence is actually detected by a CER engine. We present a formal framework that attempts to address the issue of Complex Event Forecasting (CEF). Our framework combines two formalisms: a) symbolic automata which are used to encode complex event patterns; and b) prediction suffix trees which can provide a succinct probabilistic description of an automaton's behavior. We compare our proposed approach against state-of-the-art methods and show its advantage in terms of accuracy and efficiency. In particular, prediction suffix trees, being variable-order Markov models, have the ability to capture long-term dependencies in a stream by remembering only those past sequences that are informative enough. Our experimental results demonstrate the benefits, in terms of accuracy, of being able to capture such long-term dependencies. This is achieved by increasing the order of our model beyond what is possible with full-order Markov models that need to perform an exhaustive enumeration of all possible past sequences of a given order. We also discuss extensively how CEF solutions should be best evaluated on the quality of their forecasts.

title: Complex Event Forecasting with Prediction Suffix Trees: Extended Technical Report
text: The proliferation of Complex Event Recognition (CER) systems over the past two decades has been driven by their capacity to detect patterns in real-time event streams. However, a significant gap remains in the ability to forecast pattern occurrences prior to their detection by CER engines. This paper addresses the challenge of Complex Event Forecasting (CEF) by introducing a formal framework that integrates two complementary formalisms. Symbolic automata are employed to encode complex event patterns, while prediction suffix trees provide a compact probabilistic description of the automaton's behavior. A comparative evaluation of our approach against state-of-the-art methods reveals its superiority in terms of accuracy and efficiency. The variable-order Markov modeling capabilities of prediction suffix trees enable the capture of long-term dependencies in event streams by selectively retaining informative past sequences. Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of capturing these dependencies, achieved by increasing the model order beyond the limitations of full-order Markov models. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth discussion on the critical importance of evaluating CEF solutions based on the quality of their forecasts, highlighting the need for a more nuanced assessment of their performance.

title: LightNER: A Lightweight Tuning Paradigm for Low-resource NER via Pluggable Prompting
text: Most NER methods rely on extensive labeled data for model training, which struggles in the low-resource scenarios with limited training data. Existing dominant approaches usually suffer from the challenge that the target domain has different label sets compared with a resource-rich source domain, which can be concluded as class transfer and domain transfer. In this paper, we propose a lightweight tuning paradigm for low-resource NER via pluggable prompting (LightNER). Specifically, we construct the unified learnable verbalizer of entity categories to generate the entity span sequence and entity categories without any label-specific classifiers, thus addressing the class transfer issue. We further propose a pluggable guidance module by incorporating learnable parameters into the self-attention layer as guidance, which can re-modulate the attention and adapt pre-trained weights. Note that we only tune those inserted module with the whole parameter of the pre-trained language model fixed, thus, making our approach lightweight and flexible for low-resource scenarios and can better transfer knowledge across domains.
