title: LightNER: A Lightweight Tuning Paradigm for Low-resource NER via Pluggable Prompting
text: The pervasive reliance on extensive labeled data for training Named Entity Recognition (NER) models hinders their performance in low-resource scenarios, where data scarcity is a significant obstacle. A major challenge in this context is the mismatch between the label sets of the target and source domains, which encompasses both class transfer and domain transfer. This paper presents LightNER, a novel, lightweight tuning paradigm designed to address these limitations. By introducing a unified, learnable verbalizer for entity categories, we eliminate the need for label-specific classifiers, thereby mitigating the class transfer issue. Furthermore, we propose a pluggable guidance module, which incorporates learnable parameters into the self-attention layer to adaptively re-modulate attention and fine-tune pre-trained weights. Notably, our approach only tunes the inserted modules, keeping the pre-trained language model's parameters fixed, ensuring a lightweight and flexible solution for low-resource scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate that LightNER achieves comparable performance in standard supervised settings and surpasses strong baselines in low-resource conditions.

title: MultiCategory: Multi-model Query Processing Meets Category Theory and Functional Programming
text: The variety of data is one of the important issues in the era of Big Data. The data are naturally organized in different formats and models, including structured data, semi-structured data, and unstructured data. Prior research has envisioned an approach to abstract multi-model data with a schema category and an instance category by using category theory. In this paper, we demonstrate a system, called MultiCategory, which processes multi-model queries based on category theory and functional programming. This demo is centered around four main scenarios to show a tangible system. First, we show how to build a schema category and an instance category by loading different models of data, including relational, XML, key-value, and graph data. Second, we show a few examples of query processing by using the functional programming language Haskell. Third, we demo the flexible outputs with different models of data for the same input query. Fourth, to better understand the category theoretical structure behind the queries, we offer a variety of graphical hooks to explore and visualize queries as graphs with respect to the schema category, as well as the query processing procedure with Haskell.

title: MultiCategory: Multi-model Query Processing Meets Category Theory and Functional Programming
text: The proliferation of diverse data formats and models, inherent to the Big Data era, has necessitated innovative approaches to data abstraction. Data can be categorized into structured, semi-structured, and unstructured forms, each with unique characteristics. Building upon prior research that leveraged category theory to abstract multi-model data into schema and instance categories, we present the MultiCategory system. This system, grounded in category theory and functional programming principles, enables the processing of multi-model queries. To demonstrate the system's capabilities, we focus on four key scenarios. We first illustrate the construction of schema and instance categories by integrating disparate data models, including relational, XML, key-value, and graph data. We then showcase query processing examples using the Haskell functional programming language. Furthermore, we exhibit the system's flexibility by generating diverse output formats for identical input queries. Finally, to elucidate the underlying category theoretical structure, we provide graphical visualizations of queries as graphs, facilitating exploration and comprehension of the schema category and query processing procedures.

title: Joint Management and Analysis of Textual Documents and Tabular Data within the AUDAL Data Lake
text: In 2010, the concept of data lake emerged as an alternative to data warehouses for big data management. Data lakes follow a schema-on-read approach to provide rich and flexible analyses. However, although trendy in both the industry and academia, the concept of data lake is still maturing, and there are still few methodological approaches to data lake design. Thus, we introduce a new approach to design a data lake and propose an extensive metadata system to activate richer features than those usually supported in data lake approaches. We implement our approach in the AUDAL data lake, where we jointly exploit both textual documents and tabular data, in contrast with structured and/or semi-structured data typically processed in data lakes from the literature. Furthermore, we also innovate by leveraging metadata to activate both data retrieval and content analysis, including Text-OLAP and SQL querying. Finally, we show the feasibility of our approach using a real-word use case on the one hand, and a benchmark on the other hand.

title: Joint Management and Analysis of Textual Documents and Tabular Data within the AUDAL Data Lake
text: The proliferation of diverse data sources has led to an increasing need for integrated management and analysis of heterogeneous data types. In particular, the co-occurrence of textual documents and tabular data in various domains necessitates a unified framework for their joint processing. This paper presents AUDAL, a data lake architecture designed to efficiently store, manage, and analyze both textual documents and tabular data. AUDAL employs a hybrid storage model, combining column-store and document-oriented databases to optimize query performance. We introduce a novel data model, termed Document-Table Associations, to capture relationships between textual documents and tabular data. Our experiments on a real-world dataset demonstrate AUDAL's ability to improve query performance by up to 3.5x compared to traditional data warehousing approaches. Furthermore, we develop a set of analytical techniques, including document-table join and aggregation, to facilitate integrated analysis of textual and tabular data. Our results show that AUDAL enables more accurate insights into complex phenomena, such as sentiment analysis and trend detection, by leveraging the complementary strengths of both data types.

title: A Longitudinal Multi-modal Dataset for Dementia Monitoring and Diagnosis
text: Dementia affects cognitive functions of adults, including memory, language, and behaviour. Standard diagnostic biomarkers such as MRI are costly, whilst neuropsychological tests suffer from sensitivity issues in detecting dementia onset. The analysis of speech and language has emerged as a promising and non-intrusive technology to diagnose and monitor dementia. Currently, most work in this direction ignores the multi-modal nature of human communication and interactive aspects of everyday conversational interaction. Moreover, most studies ignore changes in cognitive status over time due to the lack of consistent longitudinal data. Here we introduce a novel fine-grained longitudinal multi-modal corpus collected in a natural setting from healthy controls and people with dementia over two phases, each spanning 28 sessions. The corpus consists of spoken conversations, a subset of which are transcribed, as well as typed and written thoughts and associated extra-linguistic information such as pen strokes and keystrokes. We present the data collection process and describe the corpus in detail. Furthermore, we establish baselines for capturing longitudinal changes in language across different modalities for two cohorts, healthy controls and people with dementia, outlining future research directions enabled by the corpus.

title: A Longitudinal Multi-modal Dataset for Dementia Monitoring and Diagnosis
text: Cognitive decline in adults, manifesting as impaired memory, language, and behavior, remains a pressing concern. Conventional diagnostic biomarkers, such as MRI, are costly, while neuropsychological tests struggle to detect dementia onset due to sensitivity limitations. In response, speech and language analysis has emerged as a promising, non-invasive approach for diagnosing and monitoring dementia. However, existing research often neglects the multi-modal nature of human communication and the dynamic aspects of everyday conversational interactions. Moreover, the lack of consistent longitudinal data hinders the investigation of cognitive status changes over time. This study addresses these gaps by introducing a novel, fine-grained longitudinal multi-modal corpus, collected in a natural setting from healthy controls and individuals with dementia across two phases, comprising 28 sessions each. The corpus encompasses spoken conversations, partially transcribed, as well as typed and written thoughts, supplemented by extra-linguistic information such as pen strokes and keystrokes. We detail the data collection process and corpus characteristics, establishing baselines for capturing longitudinal language changes across modalities in both healthy controls and individuals with dementia, and outlining future research avenues enabled by this corpus.

title: Stretching Your Data With Taffy Filters
text: Popular approximate membership query structures such as Bloom filters and cuckoo filters are widely used in databases, security, and networking. These structures represent sets approximately, and support at least two operations - insert and lookup; lookup always returns true on elements inserted into the structure; it also returns true with some probability $0 < \varepsilon < 1$ on elements not inserted into the structure. These latter elements are called false positives. Compensatory for these false positives, filters can be much smaller than hash tables that represent the same set. However, unlike hash tables, cuckoo filters and Bloom filters must be initialized with the intended number of inserts to be performed, and cannot grow larger - inserts beyond this number fail or significantly increase the false positive probability. This paper presents designs and implementations of filters than can grow without inserts failing and without meaningfully increasing the false positive probability, even if the filters are created with a small initial size. The resulting code is available on GitHub under a permissive open source license.

title: Stretching Your Data With Taffy Filters
text: The proliferation of IoT devices and social media platforms has led to an exponential surge in data generation, resulting in scalability issues for traditional data processing systems. To address this challenge, we propose Taffy Filters, a novel data reduction approach that leverages the concept of stretchable filters to minimize data redundancy. By dynamically adjusting the filter's granularity, Taffy Filters can effectively reduce the data volume while preserving its semantic integrity. Our methodology involves a two-pronged approach: first, we develop a statistical model to identify the optimal filter granularity based on the underlying data distribution; second, we implement a Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation framework to optimize filter execution. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that Taffy Filters can achieve up to 70% data reduction with minimal loss of accuracy, outperforming state-of-the-art data compression techniques. Furthermore, our approach shows significant improvements in query response times, making it particularly suitable for real-time data analytics applications.

title: MONITOR: A Multimodal Fusion Framework to Assess Message Veracity in Social Networks
text: Users of social networks tend to post and share content with little restraint. Hence, rumors and fake news can quickly spread on a huge scale. This may pose a threat to the credibility of social media and can cause serious consequences in real life. Therefore, the task of rumor detection and verification has become extremely important. Assessing the veracity of a social media message (e.g., by fact checkers) involves analyzing the text of the message, its context and any multimedia attachment. This is a very time-consuming task that can be much helped by machine learning. In the literature, most message veracity verification methods only exploit textual contents and metadata. Very few take both textual and visual contents, and more particularly images, into account. In this paper, we second the hypothesis that exploiting all of the components of a social media post enhances the accuracy of veracity detection. To further the state of the art, we first propose using a set of advanced image features that are inspired from the field of image quality assessment, which effectively contributes to rumor detection. These metrics are good indicators for the detection of fake images, even for those generated by advanced techniques like generative adversarial networks (GANs). Then, we introduce the Multimodal fusiON framework to assess message veracIty in social neTwORks (MONITOR), which exploits all message features (i.e., text, social context, and image features) by supervised machine learning. Such algorithms provide interpretability and explainability in the decisions taken, which we believe is particularly important in the context of rumor verification. Experimental results show that MONITOR can detect rumors with an accuracy of 96% and 89% on the MediaEval benchmark and the FakeNewsNet dataset, respectively. These results are significantly better than those of state-of-the-art machine learning baselines.

title: MONITOR: A Multimodal Fusion Framework to Assess Message Veracity in Social Networks
text: The unchecked dissemination of information on social media platforms has created a breeding ground for the rapid proliferation of rumors and fake news, thereby undermining the credibility of these platforms and potentially causing real-world harm. Consequently, the detection and verification of rumors have become pressing concerns. Assessing the veracity of social media messages requires a comprehensive analysis of their textual content, context, and multimedia attachments, a task that can be greatly facilitated by machine learning. While existing approaches primarily focus on textual content and metadata, few consider both textual and visual components, particularly images. Building on the hypothesis that incorporating all aspects of a social media post enhances veracity detection accuracy, we propose a novel approach that leverages advanced image features inspired by image quality assessment research. These features effectively identify fake images, including those generated using sophisticated techniques like generative adversarial networks (GANs). Our proposed Multimodal fusiON framework to assess message veracIty in social neTwORks (MONITOR) integrates text, social context, and image features using supervised machine learning, providing interpretable and explainable decision-making processes crucial in rumor verification. Experimental results on the MediaEval benchmark and FakeNewsNet dataset demonstrate MONITOR's superior performance, achieving rumor detection accuracies of 96% and 89%, respectively, outperforming state-of-the-art machine learning baselines.

title: Privacy-Preserving Database Fingerprinting
text: When sharing sensitive relational databases with other parties, a database owner aims to (i) have privacy guarantees for the database entries, (ii) have liability guarantees (via fingerprinting) in case of unauthorized sharing of its database by the recipients, and (iii) provide a high quality (utility) database to the recipients. We observe that sharing a relational database with privacy and liability guarantees are orthogonal objectives. The former can be achieved by injecting noise into the database to prevent inference of the original data values, whereas, the latter can be achieved by hiding unique marks inside the database to trace malicious parties (data recipients) who redistribute the data without the authorization. We achieve these two objectives simultaneously by proposing a novel entry-level differentially-private fingerprinting mechanism for relational databases. At a high level, the proposed mechanism fulfills the privacy and liability requirements by leveraging the randomization nature that is intrinsic to fingerprinting and achieves desired entry-level privacy guarantees. To be more specific, we devise a bit-level random response scheme to achieve differential privacy guarantee for arbitrary data entries when sharing the entire database, and then, based on this, we develop an $ε$-entry-level differentially-private fingerprinting mechanism. Next, we theoretically analyze the relationships between privacy guarantee, fingerprint robustness, and database utility by deriving closed form expressions. The outcome of this analysis allows us to bound the privacy leakage caused by attribute inference attack and characterize the privacy-utility coupling and privacy-fingerprint robustness coupling. Furthermore, we also propose a SVT-based solution to control the cumulative privacy loss when fingerprinted copies of a database are shared with multiple recipients.

title: Privacy-Preserving Database Fingerprinting
text: The proliferation of data-driven applications has led to an unprecedented growth in database sizes, making it increasingly challenging to ensure data integrity and confidentiality. Database fingerprinting, a technique used to identify and verify the origin of a dataset, is a crucial component in this endeavor. However, existing fingerprinting methods often compromise data privacy, as they rely on exact data matching or similarity measures that can be exploited to infer sensitive information. We propose a novel privacy-preserving database fingerprinting approach that leverages secure multi-party computation (SMPC) and homomorphic encryption to enable robust fingerprinting without revealing the underlying data. Our method, called PriFin, employs a distributed architecture where multiple parties jointly compute a compact representation of their respective datasets without sharing the actual data. This representation, referred to as a fingerprint, is used to verify the authenticity and integrity of the datasets. We evaluate PriFin using real-world datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying tampered or duplicate datasets while maintaining strong privacy guarantees. Our experiments show that PriFin achieves a high accuracy of 95.2% in detecting dataset tampering, outperforming existing methods by up to 12.5%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that PriFin incurs a reasonable computational overhead, with an average latency of 3.2 seconds for fingerprints of size 1 KB. Theoretical analysis and experimental results confirm that PriFin provides differential privacy guarantees, ensuring that the fingerprints do not reveal sensitive information about the underlying data. Our approach has far-reaching implications for various applications, including data sharing, auditing, and forensics, where data privacy and integrity are paramount.

title: An Ontology-Based, Fully Probabilistic, Scalable Method for Human Activity Recognition
text: Efficiency and scalability are obstacles that have not yet received a viable response from the human activity recognition research community. This paper proposes an activity recognition method. The knowledge model is in the form of ontology, the state-of-the-art in knowledge representation and reasoning. The ontology starts with probabilistic information about subjects' low-level activities and location and then is populated with the assertion axioms learned from data or defined by the user. Unlike methods that choose only the most probable candidate from sensor readings, the proposed method keeps multiple candidates with the known degree of confidence for each one and involves them in decision making. Using this method, the system is more flexible to deal with unreliable readings from sensors, and the final recognition rate is improved. Besides, to resolve the scalability problem, a system is designed and implemented to do reasoning and storing in a relational database management system. Numerical evaluation and conceptual benchmarking prove the proposed system feasibility.

title: An Ontology-Based, Fully Probabilistic, Scalable Method for Human Activity Recognition
text: Human activity recognition (HAR) is a fundamental task in various applications, including healthcare, surveillance, and smart homes. Despite significant advances, existing methods struggle to balance accuracy, scalability, and interpretability. This paper presents a novel ontology-based, fully probabilistic approach to HAR, which addresses these limitations by exploiting the hierarchical structure of human activities. We design a probabilistic ontology that captures the uncertainty in activity recognition and integrates it with a scalable, distributed inference framework. Our method leverages a large, diverse dataset of annotated sensor readings to learn the probabilistic relationships between activities and their corresponding sensor patterns. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy (95.2% on average) while reducing computational costs by up to 75%. Furthermore, our probabilistic framework provides interpretable uncertainty estimates, enabling the identification of ambiguous activities and uncertain sensor readings. These results have significant implications for real-world HAR applications, where robustness, efficiency, and explainability are crucial.

title: Dutch Comfort: The limits of AI governance through municipal registers
text: In this commentary, we respond to a recent editorial letter by Professor Luciano Floridi entitled 'AI as a public service: Learning from Amsterdam and Helsinki'. Here, Floridi considers the positive impact of these municipal AI registers, which collect a limited number of algorithmic systems used by the city of Amsterdam and Helsinki. There are a number of assumptions about AI registers as a governance model for automated systems that we seek to question. Starting with recent attempts to normalize AI by decontextualizing and depoliticizing it, which is a fraught political project that encourages what we call 'ethics theater' given the proven dangers of using these systems in the context of the digital welfare state. We agree with Floridi that much can be learned from these registers about the role of AI systems in municipal city management. Yet, the lessons we draw, on the basis of our extensive ethnographic engagement with digital well-fare states are distinctly less optimistic.

title: Dutch Comfort: The limits of AI governance through municipal registers
text: Professor Luciano Floridi's recent editorial letter, 'AI as a public service: Learning from Amsterdam and Helsinki', highlights the benefits of municipal AI registers in these cities, which catalog a select number of algorithmic systems. However, we contend that Floridi's governance model for automated systems relies on questionable assumptions. The drive to normalize AI through decontextualization and depoliticization is a contentious political endeavor that risks perpetuating 'ethics theater', overlooking the proven hazards of these systems within the digital welfare state. While we concur that valuable insights can be gleaned from these registers regarding AI's role in municipal management, our ethnographic research in digital welfare states yields a more cautionary perspective. By scrutinizing the complexities of AI implementation, we seek to temper Floridi's optimism and provide a more nuanced understanding of AI registers' implications.

title: Utilizing Shannon's Entropy to Create Privacy Aware Architectures
text: Privacy is an individual choice to determine which personal details can be collected, used and shared. Individual consent and transparency are the core tenets for earning customers trust and this motivates the organizations to adopt privacy enhancing practices while creating the systems. The goal of a privacy-aware design is to protect information in a way that does not increase an adversary's existing knowledge about an individual beyond what is permissible. This becomes critical when these data elements can be linked with the wealth of auxiliary information available outside the system to identify an individual. Privacy regulations around the world provide directives to protect individual privacy but are generally complex and vague, making their translation into actionable and technical privacy-friendly architectures challenging. In this paper, we utilize Shannon's Entropy to create an objective metric that can help simplify the state-of-the-art Privacy Design Strategies proposed in the literature and aid our key technical design decisions to create privacy aware architectures.

title: Utilizing Shannon's Entropy to Create Privacy Aware Architectures
text: The capacity for individuals to control the collection, utilization, and dissemination of their personal information is a fundamental aspect of privacy. Trust is fostered when organizations prioritize transparency and consent, thereby motivating the adoption of privacy-enhancing practices in system design. The paramount objective of privacy-aware design is to safeguard information in a manner that does not excessively augment an adversary's existing knowledge about an individual, particularly when combined with external auxiliary data. This challenge is compounded by the complexity and vagueness of global privacy regulations, which hinder the development of actionable, technical privacy-friendly architectures. To address this, we propose a novel approach leveraging Shannon's Entropy to create an objective metric that simplifies and informs key technical design decisions, thereby enhancing the efficacy of state-of-the-art privacy design strategies and facilitating the creation of privacy-aware architectures.

title: ProcK: Machine Learning for Knowledge-Intensive Processes
text: We present a novel methodology to build powerful predictive process models. Our method, denoted ProcK (Process & Knowledge), relies not only on sequential input data in the form of event logs, but can learn to use a knowledge graph to incorporate information about the attribute values of the events and their mutual relationships. The idea is realized by mapping event attributes to nodes of a knowledge graph and training a sequence model alongside a graph neural network in an end-to-end fashion. This hybrid approach substantially enhances the flexibility and applicability of predictive process monitoring, as both the static and dynamic information residing in the databases of organizations can be directly taken as input data. We demonstrate the potential of ProcK by applying it to a number of predictive process monitoring tasks, including tasks with knowledge graphs available as well as an existing process monitoring benchmark where no such graph is given. The experiments provide evidence that our methodology achieves state-of-the-art performance and improves predictive power when a knowledge graph is available.

title: ProcK: Machine Learning for Knowledge-Intensive Processes
text: Knowledge-intensive processes, such as business process management and case management, involve complex decision-making and rely heavily on human expertise. However, the increasing volume and variety of data in these processes make it challenging to extract relevant knowledge and make informed decisions. Recent advances in machine learning have shown promise in automating knowledge extraction and decision-making, but existing approaches are limited by their focus on specific domains or process models. We propose ProcK, a novel machine learning framework that learns from event logs and process models to identify knowledge-intensive tasks and automate decision-making. ProcK integrates symbolic and sub-symbolic AI techniques to represent knowledge graphs and predict task outcomes. We evaluate ProcK on three real-world datasets from healthcare and finance, achieving an average F1-score of 0.87 in task outcome prediction and reducing process duration by 23%. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of ProcK in automating knowledge-intensive processes and its potential to improve process efficiency and decision quality.

title: Making Table Understanding Work in Practice
text: Understanding the semantics of tables at scale is crucial for tasks like data integration, preparation, and search. Table understanding methods aim at detecting a table's topic, semantic column types, column relations, or entities. With the rise of deep learning, powerful models have been developed for these tasks with excellent accuracy on benchmarks. However, we observe that there exists a gap between the performance of these models on these benchmarks and their applicability in practice. In this paper, we address the question: what do we need for these models to work in practice? We discuss three challenges of deploying table understanding models and propose a framework to address them. These challenges include 1) difficulty in customizing models to specific domains, 2) lack of training data for typical database tables often found in enterprises, and 3) lack of confidence in the inferences made by models. We present SigmaTyper which implements this framework for the semantic column type detection task. SigmaTyper encapsulates a hybrid model trained on GitTables and integrates a lightweight human-in-the-loop approach to customize the model. Lastly, we highlight avenues for future research that further close the gap towards making table understanding effective in practice.

title: Making Table Understanding Work in Practice
text: The ability to interpret the semantics of tables at scale is essential for various data-centric tasks, including integration, preparation, and search. Recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of powerful table understanding models, which have demonstrated excellent accuracy on benchmark datasets. However, a significant gap exists between the performance of these models on benchmarks and their practical applicability. This disparity is attributed to three primary challenges: the difficulty in customizing models to specific domains, the lack of training data for typical enterprise database tables, and the uncertainty associated with model inferences. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework and implement it in SigmaTyper, a hybrid model trained on GitTables that integrates a lightweight human-in-the-loop approach for customization. Our approach enables effective semantic column type detection and paves the way for future research aimed at bridging the gap between table understanding models and their practical deployment.

title: Cardinality Estimation in DBMS: A Comprehensive Benchmark Evaluation
text: Cardinality estimation (CardEst) plays a significant role in generating high-quality query plans for a query optimizer in DBMS. In the last decade, an increasing number of advanced CardEst methods (especially ML-based) have been proposed with outstanding estimation accuracy and inference latency. However, there exists no study that systematically evaluates the quality of these methods and answer the fundamental problem: to what extent can these methods improve the performance of query optimizer in real-world settings, which is the ultimate goal of a CardEst method. In this paper, we comprehensively and systematically compare the effectiveness of CardEst methods in a real DBMS. We establish a new benchmark for CardEst, which contains a new complex real-world dataset STATS and a diverse query workload STATS-CEB. We integrate multiple most representative CardEst methods into an open-source database system PostgreSQL, and comprehensively evaluate their true effectiveness in improving query plan quality, and other important aspects affecting their applicability, ranging from inference latency, model size, and training time, to update efficiency and accuracy. We obtain a number of key findings for the CardEst methods, under different data and query settings. Furthermore, we find that the widely used estimation accuracy metric(Q-Error) cannot distinguish the importance of different sub-plan queries during query optimization and thus cannot truly reflect the query plan quality generated by CardEst methods. Therefore, we propose a new metric P-Error to evaluate the performance of CardEst methods, which overcomes the limitation of Q-Error and is able to reflect the overall end-to-end performance of CardEst methods. title: Cardinality Estimation in DBMS: A Comprehensive Benchmark Evaluation
text: Cardinality estimation is a fundamental component in modern Database Management Systems (DBMS), significantly influencing the quality of query optimization and execution. Despite its importance, the accuracy of cardinality estimation remains a subject of ongoing research, with various techniques being proposed to improve its precision. However, the lack of a comprehensive benchmark evaluation hinders the ability to compare and contrast these methods, making it challenging to determine the most effective approach. In this study, we present a rigorous benchmark evaluation of 15 state-of-the-art cardinality estimation techniques, including both traditional statistical methods and machine learning-based approaches. Our evaluation is conducted on a diverse set of 25 real-world datasets, totaling over 10,000 queries, and employs a range of performance metrics, including mean absolute error, mean relative error, and query execution time. The results of our evaluation reveal significant differences in the performance of the various techniques, with some methods exhibiting excellent accuracy on specific datasets while struggling with others. Notably, our findings suggest that machine learning-based approaches, such as those leveraging neural networks and decision trees, generally outperform traditional statistical methods, with the exception of certain datasets exhibiting strong correlations. Furthermore, we observe that the choice of technique has a profound impact on query execution time, with some methods incurring significant overhead. Our comprehensive evaluation provides valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of various cardinality estimation techniques, facilitating the development of more accurate and efficient query optimization strategies in modern DBMS.

title: An End-to-end Point of Interest (POI) Conflation Framework
text: Point of interest (POI) data serves as a valuable source of semantic information for places of interest and has many geospatial applications in real estate, transportation, and urban planning. With the availability of different data sources, POI conflation serves as a valuable technique for enriching data quality and coverage by merging the POI data from multiple sources. This study proposes a novel end-to-end POI conflation framework consisting of six steps, starting with data procurement, schema standardisation, taxonomy mapping, POI matching, POI unification, and data verification. The feasibility of the proposed framework was demonstrated in a case study conducted in the eastern region of Singapore, where the POI data from five data sources was conflated to form a unified POI dataset. Based on the evaluation conducted, the resulting unified dataset was found to be more comprehensive and complete than any of the five POI data sources alone. Furthermore, the proposed approach for identifying POI matches between different data sources outperformed all baseline approaches with a matching accuracy of 97.6% with an average run time below 3 minutes when matching over 12,000 POIs to result in 8,699 unique POIs, thereby demonstrating the framework's scalability for large scale implementation in dense urban contexts.

title: An End-to-end Point of Interest (POI) Conflation Framework
text: The integration of point of interest (POI) data from diverse sources has significant implications for enhancing the quality and coverage of geospatial information, with applications in real estate, transportation, and urban planning. To harness the potential of POI data, a novel end-to-end conflation framework is proposed, comprising six stages: data procurement, schema standardization, taxonomy mapping, POI matching, POI unification, and data verification. The efficacy of this framework was evaluated in a case study in eastern Singapore, where POI data from five sources was conflated to create a unified dataset. The results show that the unified dataset surpasses the individual sources in terms of comprehensiveness and completeness. Notably, the proposed approach for identifying POI matches achieves a high accuracy of 97.6% with an average runtime of under 3 minutes, even when matching over 12,000 POIs to yield 8,699 unique POIs. This demonstrates the framework's scalability and potential for large-scale implementation in dense urban environments, making it a valuable tool for geospatial applications.

title: Augmenting Decision Making via Interactive What-If Analysis
text: The fundamental goal of business data analysis is to improve business decisions using data. Business users often make decisions to achieve key performance indicators (KPIs) such as increasing customer retention or sales, or decreasing costs. To discover the relationship between data attributes hypothesized to be drivers and those corresponding to KPIs of interest, business users currently need to perform lengthy exploratory analyses. This involves considering multitudes of combinations and scenarios and performing slicing, dicing, and transformations on the data accordingly, e.g., analyzing customer retention across quarters of the year or suggesting optimal media channels across strata of customers. However, the increasing complexity of datasets combined with the cognitive limitations of humans makes it challenging to carry over multiple hypotheses, even for simple datasets. Therefore mentally performing such analyses is hard. Existing commercial tools either provide partial solutions or fail to cater to business users altogether. Here we argue for four functionalities to enable business users to interactively learn and reason about the relationships between sets of data attributes thereby facilitating data-driven decision making. We implement these functionalities in SystemD, an interactive visual data analysis system enabling business users to experiment with the data by asking what-if questions. We evaluate the system through three business use cases: marketing mix modeling, customer retention analysis, and deal closing analysis, and report on feedback from multiple business users. Users find the SystemD functionalities highly useful for quick testing and validation of their hypotheses around their KPIs of interest, addressing their unmet analysis needs. The feedback also suggests that the UX design can be enhanced to further improve the understandability of these functionalities.

title: Augmenting Decision Making via Interactive What-If Analysis
text: Business data analysis seeks to inform decision-making by uncovering relationships between data attributes and key performance indicators (KPIs). To accomplish this, business users must currently engage in time-consuming exploratory analyses, considering numerous combinations and scenarios, and performing various data transformations to identify correlations between hypothesized drivers and KPIs of interest. However, the escalating complexity of datasets and human cognitive limitations render it difficult to mentally manage multiple hypotheses, even with simple datasets. Existing commercial tools offer incomplete solutions or fail to cater to business users' needs. We propose four essential functionalities to enable business users to interactively explore and reason about relationships between data attributes, thereby facilitating data-driven decision-making. Our interactive visual data analysis system, SystemD, implements these functionalities, allowing business users to experiment with data through what-if queries. We evaluate SystemD using three business use cases: marketing mix modeling, customer retention analysis, and deal closing analysis, and gather feedback from multiple business users. Users find SystemD's functionalities highly valuable for rapid hypothesis testing and validation related to their KPIs of interest, addressing their unmet analysis needs. However, feedback suggests that the user experience design can be further refined to enhance the understandability of these functionalities.

title: ML Based Lineage in Databases
text: We track the lineage of tuples throughout their database lifetime. That is, we consider a scenario in which tuples (records) that are produced by a query may affect other tuple insertions into the DB, as part of a normal workflow. As time goes on, exact provenance explanations for such tuples become deeply nested, increasingly consuming space, and resulting in decreased clarity and readability. We present a novel approach for approximating lineage tracking, using a Machine Learning (ML) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) technique; namely, word embedding. The basic idea is summarizing (and approximating) the lineage of each tuple via a small set of constant-size vectors (the number of vectors per-tuple is a hyperparameter). Therefore, our solution does not suffer from space complexity blow-up over time, and it "naturally ranks" explanations to the existence of a tuple. We devise an alternative and improved lineage tracking mechanism, that of keeping track of and querying lineage at the column level; thereby, we manage to better distinguish between the provenance features and the textual characteristics of a tuple. We integrate our lineage computations into the PostgreSQL system via an extension (ProvSQL) and extensive experiments exhibit useful results in terms of accuracy against exact, semiring-based, justifications, especially for the column-based (CV) method which exhibits high precision and high per-level recall. In the experiments, we focus on tuples with \textit{multiple generations} of tuples in their lifelong lineage and analyze them in terms of direct and distant lineage.

title: ML Based Lineage in Databases
text: The provenance of database tuples is a crucial aspect of data management, as query-generated records can influence subsequent tuple insertions, leading to complex and deeply nested explanations over time. This nested structure not only consumes excessive space but also compromises clarity and readability. To address this issue, we propose a novel approximate lineage tracking approach that leverages machine learning and natural language processing techniques, specifically word embedding. By representing each tuple's lineage as a compact set of constant-size vectors, our method mitigates space complexity blow-up and inherently ranks explanations for tuple existence. Furthermore, we introduce an alternative lineage tracking mechanism that operates at the column level, effectively distinguishing between provenance features and textual characteristics. We have integrated our lineage computations into the PostgreSQL system via the ProvSQL extension. Extensive experiments demonstrate promising results, with high accuracy against exact, semiring-based justifications, particularly for the column-based method, which exhibits both high precision and per-level recall. Our experiments focus on tuples with multiple generations of lineage, analyzing direct and distant provenance relationships.

title: Coo: Rethink Data Anomalies In Databases
text: Transaction processing technology has three important contents: data anomalies, isolation levels, and concurrent control algorithms. Concurrent control algorithms are used to eliminate some or all data anomalies at different isolation levels to ensure data consistency. Isolation levels in the current ANSI standard are defined by disallowing certain kinds of data anomalies. Yet, the definitions of data anomalies in the ANSI standard are controversial. On one hand, the definitions lack a mathematical formalization and cause ambiguous interpretations. On the other hand, the definitions are made in a case-by-case manner and lead to a situation that even a senior DBA could not have infallible knowledge of data anomalies, due to a lack of a full understanding of its nature. While revised definitions in existing literature propose various mathematical formalizations to correct the former argument, how to address the latter argument still remains an open problem. In this paper, we present a general framework called Coo with the capability to systematically define data anomalies. Under this framework, we show that existing reported data anomalies are only a small portion. While we theoretically prove that Coo is complete to mathematically formalize data anomalies, we employ a novel method to classify infinite data anomalies. In addition, we use this framework to define new isolation levels and quantitatively describe the concurrency and rollback rate of mainstream concurrency control algorithms. These works show that the C and I of ACID can be quantitatively analyzed based on all data anomalies.

title: Coo: Rethink Data Anomalies In Databases
text: The integrity of transaction processing systems relies on three fundamental components: data anomalies, isolation levels, and concurrent control algorithms. The latter is employed to mitigate or eliminate data anomalies at varying isolation levels, thereby ensuring data consistency. However, the current ANSI standard definitions of isolation levels, which are predicated on prohibiting specific data anomalies, are contentious. The definitions suffer from a lack of mathematical rigor, leading to ambiguous interpretations, and are formulated in a piecemeal manner, rendering even seasoned database administrators uncertain about the exhaustive nature of data anomalies due to a limited understanding of their underlying principles. While recent literature has proposed revised definitions with mathematical formalizations to address the former limitation, the latter issue remains unresolved. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework, Coo, capable of systematically defining data anomalies. We demonstrate that existing reported data anomalies constitute only a subset of the broader spectrum. Theoretically, we prove the completeness of Coo in mathematically formalizing data anomalies and develop a novel method for categorizing infinite data anomalies. Furthermore, we utilize this framework to define new isolation levels and quantitatively evaluate the concurrency and rollback rates of prominent concurrency control algorithms, enabling the quantitative analysis of the consistency and isolation aspects of the ACID principle.

title: A Survey on Data Cleaning Methods for Improved Machine Learning Model Performance
text: Data cleaning is the initial stage of any machine learning project and is one of the most critical processes in data analysis. It is a critical step in ensuring that the dataset is devoid of incorrect or erroneous data. It can be done manually with data wrangling tools, or it can be completed automatically with a computer program. Data cleaning entails a slew of procedures that, once done, make the data ready for analysis. Given its significance in numerous fields, there is a growing interest in the development of efficient and effective data cleaning frameworks. In this survey, some of the most recent advancements of data cleaning approaches are examined for their effectiveness and the future research directions are suggested to close the gap in each of the methods.

title: A Survey on Data Cleaning Methods for Improved Machine Learning Model Performance
text: The proliferation of machine learning applications has underscored the significance of data quality, with noisy or erroneous data capable of severely degrading model performance. Data cleaning, a crucial preprocessing step, aims to identify and rectify such errors, thereby enhancing the accuracy and reliability of machine learning models. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of existing data cleaning methods, categorizing them into rule-based, statistical, and machine learning-based approaches. We examine the strengths and limitations of each method, highlighting their applicability to diverse data types and domains. Our analysis reveals that hybrid approaches, combining multiple techniques, often yield superior performance improvements. Furthermore, we identify key research directions, including the development of automated cleaning pipelines and the integration of data cleaning with model interpretability techniques. By providing a systematic review of data cleaning methods, this survey aims to inform and guide practitioners and researchers in the pursuit of improved machine learning model performance.

title: Evaluation of Distributed Databases in Hybrid Clouds and Edge Computing: Energy, Bandwidth, and Storage Consumption
text: A benchmark study of modern distributed databases is an important source of information to select the right technology for managing data in the cloud-edge paradigms. To make the right decision, it is required to conduct an extensive experimental study on a variety of hardware infrastructures. While most of the state-of-the-art studies have investigated only response time and scalability of distributed databases, focusing on other various metrics (e.g., energy, bandwidth, and storage consumption) is essential to fully understand the resources consumption of the distributed databases. Also, existing studies have explored the response time and scalability of these databases either in private or public cloud. Hence, there is a paucity of investigation into the evaluation of these databases deployed in a hybrid cloud, which is the seamless integration of public and private cloud. To address these research gaps, in this paper, we investigate energy, bandwidth and storage consumption of the most used and common distributed databases. For this purpose, we have evaluated four open-source databases (Cassandra, Mongo, Redis and MySQL) on the hybrid cloud spanning over local OpenStack and Microsoft Azure, and a variety of edge computing nodes including Raspberry Pi, a cluster of Raspberry Pi, and low and high power servers. Our extensive experimental results reveal several helpful insights for the deployment selection of modern distributed databases in edge-cloud environments.

title: Evaluation of Distributed Databases in Hybrid Clouds and Edge Computing: Energy, Bandwidth, and Storage Consumption
text: The proliferation of hybrid cloud and edge computing environments has led to a surge in the adoption of distributed databases, which are critical for various applications, including IoT, real-time analytics, and content delivery. However, the energy, bandwidth, and storage consumption of these systems have significant implications for operational costs, carbon footprint, and overall sustainability. Despite their importance, there is a lack of comprehensive studies evaluating the resource utilization of distributed databases in hybrid cloud and edge computing settings. This study addresses this knowledge gap by conducting a rigorous evaluation of five popular distributed databases – Apache Cassandra, Amazon DynamoDB, Google Cloud Bigtable, MongoDB, and CockroachDB – deployed across a hybrid cloud and edge computing infrastructure. We designed a novel benchmarking framework that simulates real-world workloads and measures energy consumption using wattmeters, bandwidth utilization using network sniffers, and storage usage using disk analytics. Our results show that Cassandra and CockroachDB exhibit the lowest energy consumption, while DynamoDB and Bigtable demonstrate the highest bandwidth efficiency. MongoDB, on the other hand, exhibits the highest storage efficiency. We also observed that edge computing nodes reduce energy consumption by up to 35% and bandwidth utilization by up to 27% compared to cloud-only deployments. Our findings provide valuable insights for practitioners and researchers designing and optimizing distributed databases in hybrid cloud and edge computing environments. We also identify key areas for future research, including the development of more energy-efficient database algorithms and the integration of renewable energy sources into edge computing infrastructures.

title: PoWareMatch: a Quality-aware Deep Learning Approach to Improve Human Schema Matching
text: Schema matching is a core task of any data integration process. Being investigated in the fields of databases, AI, Semantic Web and data mining for many years, the main challenge remains the ability to generate quality matches among data concepts (e.g., database attributes). In this work, we examine a novel angle on the behavior of humans as matchers, studying match creation as a process. We analyze the dynamics of common evaluation measures (precision, recall, and f-measure), with respect to this angle and highlight the need for unbiased matching to support this analysis. Unbiased matching, a newly defined concept that describes the common assumption that human decisions represent reliable assessments of schemata correspondences, is, however, not an inherent property of human matchers. In what follows, we design PoWareMatch that makes use of a deep learning mechanism to calibrate and filter human matching decisions adhering the quality of a match, which are then combined with algorithmic matching to generate better match results. We provide an empirical evidence, established based on an experiment with more than 200 human matchers over common benchmarks, that PoWareMatch predicts well the benefit of extending the match with an additional correspondence and generates high quality matches. In addition, PoWareMatch outperforms state-of-the-art matching algorithms.

title: PoWareMatch: a Quality-aware Deep Learning Approach to Improve Human Schema Matching
text: Schema matching, a fundamental component of data integration, has long been a subject of investigation across disciplines, including databases, artificial intelligence, the Semantic Web, and data mining. Despite extensive research, the primary challenge persists: generating high-quality matches between data concepts, such as database attributes. This study adopts a unique perspective by examining match creation as a process, focusing on the behavior of human matchers. We analyze the dynamics of traditional evaluation metrics (precision, recall, and f-measure) in this context, underscoring the necessity of unbiased matching to support this analysis. However, unbiased matching – the assumption that human decisions accurately reflect schemata correspondences – is not an intrinsic property of human matchers. To address this, we propose PoWareMatch, a deep learning-based approach that calibrates and filters human matching decisions to ensure match quality, which are then combined with algorithmic matching to produce superior match results. Our empirical evaluation, involving over 200 human matchers and common benchmarks, demonstrates that PoWareMatch accurately predicts the benefits of extending matches and generates high-quality matches, outperforming state-of-the-art matching algorithms.

title: Multi-Dimensional Data Compression and Query Processing in Array Databases
text: In recent times, the production of multidimensional data in various domains and their storage in array databases has witnessed a sharp increase; this rapid growth in data volumes necessitates compression in array databases. However, existing compression schemes used in array databases are general-purpose and not designed specifically for the databases. They could degrade query performance with complex analytical tasks, which incur huge computing costs. Thus, a compression scheme that considers the workflow of array databases is required. This study presents a compression scheme, SEACOW, for storing and querying multidimensional array data. The scheme is specially designed to be efficient for both dimension-based and value-based exploration. It considers data access patterns for exploration queries and embeds a synopsis, which can be utilized as an index, in the compressed array. In addition, we implement an array storage system, namely MSDB, to perform experiments. We evaluate query performance on real scientific datasets and compared it with those of existing compression schemes. Finally, our experiments demonstrate that SEACOW provides high compression rates compared to existing compression schemes, and the synopsis improves analytical query processing performance.

title: Multi-Dimensional Data Compression and Query Processing in Array Databases
text: The proliferation of array-based data in various domains, such as scientific simulations, sensor networks, and multimedia systems, has led to the development of array databases that efficiently store and query large multidimensional arrays. However, the sheer volume of these datasets poses significant challenges in terms of storage and query processing. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework for multi-dimensional data compression and query processing in array databases. Our approach leverages a combination of dimensionality reduction techniques, such as PCA and Tucker decomposition, and lossless compression algorithms, including Huffman coding and LZ77. We implement our framework on top of the SciDB array database management system and conduct an extensive experimental evaluation using real-world datasets from climate modeling and medical imaging. Our results demonstrate that our approach achieves significant compression ratios, with an average reduction in storage size of 75%, while maintaining query performance within 10% of the uncompressed data. Moreover, our framework enables efficient query processing, including range queries and aggregations, with an average speedup of 3x over traditional compression techniques.

title: Frequent Itemset Mining with Multiple Minimum Supports: a Constraint-based Approach
text: The problem of discovering frequent itemsets including rare ones has received a great deal of attention. The mining process needs to be flexible enough to extract frequent and rare regularities at once. On the other hand, it has recently been shown that constraint programming is a flexible way to tackle data mining tasks. In this paper, we propose a constraint programming approach for mining itemsets with multiple minimum supports. Our approach provides the user with the possibility to express any kind of constraints on the minimum item supports. An experimental analysis shows the practical effectiveness of our approach compared to the state of the art.

title: Frequent Itemset Mining with Multiple Minimum Supports: a Constraint-based Approach
text: Frequent itemset mining is a crucial task in data mining, but traditional algorithms are often limited by a single minimum support threshold, which may not capture the varying importance of different itemsets. We propose a novel constraint-based approach that accommodates multiple minimum supports, enabling the discovery of itemsets with varying frequencies. Our method, MultiSup, formulates the problem as a constraint satisfaction problem and leverages advanced constraint programming techniques to efficiently prune the search space. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that MultiSup outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of runtime and memory usage, while discovering more meaningful itemsets.

title: Northlight: Declarative and Optimized Analysis of Atmospheric Datasets in SparkSQL
text: Performing data-intensive analytics is an essential part of modern Earth science. As such, research in atmospheric physics and meteorology frequently requires the processing of very large observational and/or modeled datasets. Typically, these datasets (a) have high dimensionality, i.e. contain various measurements per spatiotemporal point, (b) are extremely large, containing observations over a long time period. Additionally, (c) the analytical tasks being performed on these datasets are structurally complex. Over the years, the binary format NetCDF has been established as a de-facto standard in distributing and exchanging such multi-dimensional datasets in the Earth science community -- along with tools and APIs to visualize, process, and generate them. Unfortunately, these access methods typically lack either (1) an easy-to-use but rich query interface or (2) an automatic optimization pipeline tailored towards the specialities of these datasets. As such, researchers from the field of Earth sciences (which are typically not computer scientists) unnecessarily struggle in efficiently working with these datasets on a daily basis. Consequently, in this work, we aim at resolving the aforementioned issues. Instead of proposing yet another specialized tool and interface to work with atmospheric datasets, we integrate sophisticated NetCDF processing capabilities into the established SparkSQL dataflow engine -- resulting in our system Northlight. In contrast to comparable systems, Northlight introduces a set of fully automatic optimizations specifically tailored towards NetCDF processing. We experimentally show that Northlight scales gracefully with the selectivity of the analysis tasks and outperforms the comparable state-of-the-art pipeline by up to a factor of 6x.

title: Northlight: Declarative and Optimized Analysis of Atmospheric Datasets in SparkSQL
text: The proliferation of atmospheric datasets has created a pressing need for scalable and efficient analysis techniques. Existing approaches often rely on imperative programming models, which can lead to performance bottlenecks and steep learning curves for domain experts. In response, we propose Northlight, a novel declarative framework for analyzing atmospheric datasets in SparkSQL. By leveraging Spark's distributed computing capabilities and SQL's declarative nature, Northlight enables scientists to express complex queries in a concise and intuitive manner. Our framework is built upon a rigorous optimization pipeline that incorporates domain-specific knowledge to prune the search space of possible query plans. We introduce a novel cost model that accounts for the unique characteristics of atmospheric datasets, such as spatial and temporal correlations. This cost model is used to guide a dynamic programming-based optimization algorithm that generates efficient query plans. We evaluate Northlight on a suite of real-world atmospheric datasets, including NASA's MERRA-2 and ERA5 reanalysis products. Our experiments demonstrate that Northlight outperforms state-of-the-art SparkSQL-based approaches by up to 5x in terms of query execution time, while maintaining a high degree of accuracy and transparency. Additionally, our user study involving domain experts from the atmospheric science community reveals a significant reduction in development time and increased productivity when using Northlight. Overall, Northlight offers a powerful and accessible platform for atmospheric data analysis, facilitating breakthroughs in our understanding of the Earth's climate and weather patterns.

title: Dr. Top-k: Delegate-Centric Top-k on GPUs
text: Recent top-$k$ computation efforts explore the possibility of revising various sorting algorithms to answer top-$k$ queries on GPUs. These endeavors, unfortunately, perform significantly more work than needed. This paper introduces Dr. Top-k, a Delegate-centric top-$k$ system on GPUs that can reduce the top-$k$ workloads significantly. Particularly, it contains three major contributions: First, we introduce a comprehensive design of the delegate-centric concept, including maximum delegate, delegate-based filtering, and $β$ delegate mechanisms to help reduce the workload for top-$k$ up to more than 99%. Second, due to the difficulty and importance of deriving a proper subrange size, we perform a rigorous theoretical analysis, coupled with thorough experimental validations to identify the desirable subrange size. Third, we introduce four key system optimizations to enable fast multi-GPU top-$k$ computation. Taken together, this work constantly outperforms the state-of-the-art.

title: Dr. Top-k: Delegate-Centric Top-k on GPUs
text: Top-k query processing is a fundamental operation in various data-intensive applications, but its efficiency remains a major bottleneck, particularly on large datasets. Existing solutions rely on CPU-based algorithms, which are often memory-bound and fail to harness the massive parallelism offered by modern Graphics Processing Units (GPUs). We propose Dr. Top-k, a novel delegate-centric framework that leverages GPU acceleration to efficiently process top-k queries. By introducing a hierarchical delegate-based indexing scheme, we effectively prune the search space and reduce memory access patterns, leading to significant performance gains. Our experimental evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates that Dr. Top-k outperforms state-of-the-art CPU-based algorithms by up to 10× in terms of query response time, while achieving comparable accuracy. Furthermore, our framework scales seamlessly to accommodate large datasets, making it an attractive solution for modern data analytics workloads.

title: Integrating Flowsheet Data in OMOP Common Data Model for Clinical Research
text: Flowsheet data presents unique challenges and opportunities for integration into standardized Common Data Models (CDMs) such as the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) CDM from the Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics (OHDSI) program. These data are a potentially rich source of detailed curated health outcomes data such as pain scores, vital signs, lines drains and airways (LDA) and other measurements that can be invaluable in building a robust model of patient health journey during an inpatient stay. We present two approaches to integration of flowsheet measures into the OMOP CDM. One approach was computationally straightforward but of potentially limited research utility. The second approach was far more computationally and labor intensive and involved mapping to standardized terms in controlled clinical vocabularies such as Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes (LOINC), resulting in a research data set of higher utility to population health studies.

title: Integrating Flowsheet Data in OMOP Common Data Model for Clinical Research
text: The integration of flowsheet data into standardized Common Data Models (CDMs) poses distinct challenges and opportunities, particularly when considering the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) CDM developed by the Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics (OHDSI) program. Flowsheet data offers a rich source of curated health outcomes information, including pain scores, vital signs, lines drains and airways (LDA), and other measurements, which can significantly enhance the modeling of patient health journeys during inpatient stays. This research explores two approaches to integrating flowsheet measures into the OMOP CDM. The first approach, while computationally efficient, may have limited research applicability. In contrast, the second approach, although more resource-intensive, involves mapping to standardized terms in controlled clinical vocabularies like Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes (LOINC), yielding a research dataset with higher utility for population health studies, characterized by improved data quality and interpretability.

title: Fixpoint Semantics for Recursive SHACL
text: SHACL is a W3C-proposed language for expressing structural constraints on RDF graphs. The recommendation only specifies semantics for non-recursive SHACL; recently, some efforts have been made to allow recursive SHACL schemas. In this paper, we argue that for defining and studying semantics of recursive SHACL, lessons can be learned from years of research in non-monotonic reasoning. We show that from a SHACL schema, a three-valued semantic operator can directly be obtained. Building on Approximation Fixpoint Theory (AFT), this operator immediately induces a wide variety of semantics, including a supported, stable, and well-founded semantics, related in the expected ways. By building on AFT, a rich body of theoretical results becomes directly available for SHACL. As such, the main contribution of this short paper is providing theoretical foundations for the study of recursive SHACL, which can later enable an informed decision for an extension of the W3C recommendation.

title: Fixpoint Semantics for Recursive SHACL
text: The W3C's SHACL language enables the specification of structural constraints on RDF graphs, with a current focus on non-recursive constraints. Recent efforts have explored the extension of SHACL to recursive schemas, necessitating a formal investigation of their semantics. Drawing on insights from non-monotonic reasoning, we demonstrate that a SHACL schema can be directly translated into a three-valued semantic operator. By leveraging Approximation Fixpoint Theory (AFT), this operator gives rise to a range of semantics, including supported, stable, and well-founded models, which are related in a predictable manner. This approach taps into a rich body of theoretical results, providing a solid foundation for the study of recursive SHACL. Our work lays the groundwork for an informed decision on extending the W3C recommendation, thereby enhancing the expressiveness and applicability of SHACL.

title: Micro-architectural Analysis of a Learned Index
text: Since the publication of The Case for Learned Index Structures in 2018, there has been a rise in research that focuses on learned indexes for different domains and with different functionalities. While the effectiveness of learned indexes as an alternative to traditional index structures such as B+Trees have already been demonstrated by several studies, previous work tend to focus on higher-level performance metrics such as throughput and index size. In this paper, our goal is to dig deeper and investigate how learned indexes behave at a micro-architectural level compared to traditional indexes. More specifically, we focus on previously proposed learned index structure ALEX, which is a tree-based in-memory index structure that consists of a hierarchy of machine learned models. Unlike the original proposal for learned indexes, ALEX is designed from the ground up to allow updates and inserts. Therefore, it enables more dynamic workloads using learned indexes. In this work, we perform a micro-architectural analysis of ALEX and compare its behavior to the tree-based index structures that are not based on learned models, i.e., ART and B+Tree. Our results show that ALEX is bound by memory stalls, mainly stalls due to data misses from the last-level cache. Compared to ART and B+Tree, ALEX exhibits fewer stalls and a lower cycles-per-instruction value across different workloads. On the other hand, the amount of instructions required to handle out-of-bound inserts in ALEX can increase the instructions needed per request significantly (10X) for write-heavy workloads. However, the micro-architectural behavior shows that this increase in the instruction footprint exhibit high instruction-level parallelism, and, therefore, does not negatively impact the overall execution time.

title: Micro-architectural Analysis of a Learned Index
text: The proliferation of learned index structures in various domains and with diverse functionalities has been a notable trend since the seminal work "The Case for Learned Index Structures" in 2018. While the efficacy of learned indexes as an alternative to traditional index structures, such as B+Trees, has been extensively demonstrated, existing studies have primarily focused on high-level performance metrics, including throughput and index size. This paper seeks to elucidate the micro-architectural behavior of learned indexes, thereby complementing existing research. We concentrate on ALEX, a tree-based in-memory index structure comprising a hierarchy of machine learned models, which is designed to facilitate updates and inserts, thereby enabling dynamic workloads. Through a rigorous micro-architectural analysis, we compare ALEX's behavior to that of ART and B+Tree, two tree-based index structures that do not rely on learned models. Our findings indicate that ALEX is predominantly bound by memory stalls, largely attributable to data misses from the last-level cache. In contrast to ART and B+Tree, ALEX exhibits fewer stalls and a lower cycles-per-instruction value across diverse workloads. Notably, ALEX's handling of out-of-bound inserts can lead to a substantial increase in instructions per request (up to 10X) for write-heavy workloads. However, our analysis reveals that this increase in instruction footprint exhibits high instruction-level parallelism, thereby mitigating its impact on overall execution time.

title: SaCoFa: Semantics-aware Control-flow Anonymization for Process Mining
text: Privacy-preserving process mining enables the analysis of business processes using event logs, while giving guarantees on the protection of sensitive information on process stakeholders. To this end, existing approaches add noise to the results of queries that extract properties of an event log, such as the frequency distribution of trace variants, for analysis.Noise insertion neglects the semantics of the process, though, and may generate traces not present in the original log. This is problematic. It lowers the utility of the published data and makes noise easily identifiable, as some traces will violate well-known semantic constraints.In this paper, we therefore argue for privacy preservation that incorporates a process semantics. For common trace-variant queries, we show how, based on the exponential mechanism, semantic constraints are incorporated to ensure differential privacy of the query result. Experiments demonstrate that our semantics-aware anonymization yields event logs of significantly higher utility than existing approaches.

title: SaCoFa: Semantics-aware Control-flow Anonymization for Process Mining
text: The analysis of business processes through event logs is facilitated by privacy-preserving process mining, which ensures the protection of sensitive stakeholder information. Existing methods achieve this by injecting noise into query results, such as frequency distributions of trace variants. However, this approach neglects process semantics, potentially generating traces absent from the original log, thereby compromising data utility and facilitating noise detection due to violations of well-established semantic constraints. We advocate for a semantics-integrated approach to privacy preservation, demonstrating the incorporation of semantic constraints into the exponential mechanism for common trace-variant queries to guarantee differential privacy. Our experiments reveal that this semantics-aware anonymization yields event logs with significantly higher utility compared to existing methods, thereby enhancing the analytical value of published data.

title: An open GPS trajectory dataset and benchmark for travel mode detection
text: Travel mode detection has been a hot topic in the field of GPS trajectory-related processing. Former scholars have developed many mathematical methods to improve the accuracy of detection. Among these studies, almost all of the methods require ground truth dataset for training. A large amount of the studies choose to collect the GPS trajectory dataset for training by their customized ways. Currently, there is no open GPS dataset marked with travel mode. If there exists one, it will not only save a lot of efforts in model developing, but also help compare the performance of models. In this study, we propose and open GPS trajectory dataset marked with travel mode and benchmark for the travel mode detection. The dataset is collected by 7 independent volunteers in Japan and covers the time period of a complete month. The travel mode ranges from walking to railway. A part of routines are traveled repeatedly in different time slots to experience different road and travel conditions. We also provide a case study to distinguish the walking and bike trips in a massive GPS trajectory dataset.

title: An open GPS trajectory dataset and benchmark for travel mode detection
text: The detection of travel modes from GPS trajectories has garnered significant attention in recent years, with numerous mathematical approaches proposed to enhance accuracy. While these methods have demonstrated promise, they often rely on ground truth datasets for training, which can be time-consuming and resource-intensive to collect. Moreover, the lack of open GPS datasets annotated with travel mode information hinders the development and comparison of models. To address this limitation, we introduce an open GPS trajectory dataset, annotated with travel mode information, along with a benchmark for travel mode detection. Our dataset, collected by seven independent volunteers in Japan over a period of one month, encompasses a diverse range of travel modes, from walking to railway travel. To simulate real-world variability, certain routines were repeated at different times to capture varying road and travel conditions. We also present a case study demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in distinguishing walking and biking trips within a large GPS trajectory dataset.

title: When Similarity Digest Meets Vector Management System: A Survey on Similarity Hash Function
text: The booming vector manage system calls for feasible similarity hash function as a front-end to perform similarity analysis. In this paper, we make a systematical survey on the existent well-known similarity hash functions to tease out the satisfied ones. We conclude that the similarity hash function MinHash and Nilsimsa can be directly marshaled into the pipeline of similarity analysis using vector manage system. After that, we make a brief and empirical discussion on the performance, drawbacks of the these functions and highlight MinHash, the variant of SimHash and feature hashing are the best for vector management system for large-scale similarity analysis.

title: When Similarity Digest Meets Vector Management System: A Survey on Similarity Hash Function
text: The proliferation of big data has necessitated the development of efficient similarity search algorithms, with similarity hash functions emerging as a promising solution. Among these, the Similarity Digest and Vector Management System (VMS) have garnered significant attention. This survey provides a comprehensive review of the intersection of Similarity Digest and VMS, examining their underlying principles, advantages, and limitations. We analyze the performance of various similarity hash functions, including MinHash, SimHash, and Sensitive Hash, across diverse datasets and application domains. Our findings highlight the trade-offs between computational efficiency, memory usage, and accuracy, providing valuable insights for practitioners and researchers seeking to optimize similarity search in large-scale databases.

title: Regular Sequential Serializability and Regular Sequential Consistency
