text: Strictly serializable (linearizable) services appear to execute transactions (operations) sequentially, in an order consistent with real time. This restricts a transaction's (operation's) possible return values and in turn, simplifies application programming. In exchange, strictly serializable (linearizable) services perform worse than those with weaker consistency. But switching to such services can break applications. This work introduces two new consistency models to ease this trade-off: regular sequential serializability (RSS) and regular sequential consistency (RSC). They are just as strong for applications: we prove any application invariant that holds when using a strictly serializable (linearizable) service also holds when using an RSS (RSC) service. Yet they relax the constraints on services -- they allow new, better-performing designs. To demonstrate this, we design, implement, and evaluate variants of two systems, Spanner and Gryff, relaxing their consistency to RSS and RSC, respectively. The new variants achieve better read-only transaction and read tail latency than their counterparts.

title: Regular Sequential Serializability and Regular Sequential Consistency
text: The illusion of sequential transaction execution, afforded by strict serializability (linearizability), simplifies application development by constraining possible return values. However, this comes at the cost of degraded performance compared to systems with weaker consistency guarantees. Unfortunately, transitioning to strict serializability can render applications inoperable. We propose two novel consistency models, regular sequential serializability (RSS) and regular sequential consistency (RSC), which strike a balance between these competing concerns. We formally prove that RSS and RSC preserve application invariants, ensuring their equivalence to strict serializability in terms of correctness. By relaxing the constraints on service implementations, these models enable the design of high-performance systems. We demonstrate this by modifying two existing systems, Spanner and Gryff, to operate under RSS and RSC, respectively. The resulting variants exhibit improved read-only transaction and read tail latency performance.

title: Dynamic and Systematic Survey of Deep Learning Approaches for Driving Behavior Analysis
text: Improper driving results in fatalities, damages, increased energy consumptions, and depreciation of the vehicles. Analyzing driving behaviour could lead to optimize and avoid mentioned issues. By identifying the type of driving and mapping them to the consequences of that type of driving, we can get a model to prevent them. In this regard, we try to create a dynamic survey paper to review and present driving behaviour survey data for future researchers in our research. By analyzing 58 articles, we attempt to classify standard methods and provide a framework for future articles to be examined and studied in different dashboards and updated about trends.

title: Dynamic and Systematic Survey of Deep Learning Approaches for Driving Behavior Analysis
text: Suboptimal driving practices are a pervasive concern, contributing to fatalities, property damage, elevated energy consumption, and vehicle depreciation. The analysis of driving behavior offers a promising avenue for mitigating these issues. By categorizing driving styles and correlating them with their consequences, a predictive model can be developed to prevent adverse outcomes. This survey paper synthesizes existing research on driving behavior, distilling insights from 58 articles to identify standard methods and provide a framework for future studies. The resulting framework can be adapted to various dashboards, facilitating the examination and updating of trends in the field.

title: Making the Most of Parallel Composition in Differential Privacy
text: We show that the `optimal' use of the parallel composition theorem corresponds to finding the size of the largest subset of queries that `overlap' on the data domain, a quantity we call the \emph{maximum overlap} of the queries. It has previously been shown that a certain instance of this problem, formulated in terms of determining the sensitivity of the queries, is NP-hard, but also that it is possible to use graph-theoretic algorithms, such as finding the maximum clique, to approximate query sensitivity. In this paper, we consider a significant generalization of the aforementioned instance which encompasses both a wider range of differentially private mechanisms and a broader class of queries. We show that for a particular class of predicate queries, determining if they are disjoint can be done in time polynomial in the number of attributes. For this class, we show that the maximum overlap problem remains NP-hard as a function of the number of queries. However, we show that efficient approximate solutions exist by relating maximum overlap to the clique and chromatic numbers of a certain graph determined by the queries. The link to chromatic number allows us to use more efficient approximate algorithms, which cannot be done for the clique number as it may underestimate the privacy budget. Our approach is defined in the general setting of $f$-differential privacy, which subsumes standard pure differential privacy and Gaussian differential privacy. We prove the parallel composition theorem for $f$-differential privacy. We evaluate our approach on synthetic and real-world data sets of queries. We show that the approach can scale to large domain sizes (up to $10^{20000}$), and that its application can reduce the noise added to query answers by up to 60\%.

title: Making the Most of Parallel Composition in Differential Privacy
text: The parallel composition theorem, a fundamental tool in differential privacy, is commonly employed in a suboptimal manner, neglecting the inherent structure of the queries. We uncover the underlying complexity of this problem by introducing the concept of maximum overlap, which corresponds to the size of the largest subset of queries that overlap on the data domain. Previous work has demonstrated the NP-hardness of a specific instance of this problem, formulated in terms of query sensitivity, and proposed graph-theoretic approximations, such as finding the maximum clique. This paper presents a significant generalization of this instance, encompassing a broader range of differentially private mechanisms and a more extensive class of queries. We establish that, for a particular class of predicate queries, disjointness can be determined in polynomial time with respect to the number of attributes. However, we prove that the maximum overlap problem remains NP-hard as a function of the number of queries. Nevertheless, we develop efficient approximate solutions by relating maximum overlap to the clique and chromatic numbers of a query-induced graph. The connection to chromatic number enables the application of more efficient algorithms, which is not possible with clique number due to potential underestimation of the privacy budget. Our approach is formulated within the general framework of $f$-differential privacy, which subsumes both pure and Gaussian differential privacy. We provide a proof of the parallel composition theorem for $f$-differential privacy and evaluate our approach on synthetic and real-world data sets, demonstrating its scalability to large domain sizes (up to $10^{20000}$) and the potential to reduce noise added to query answers by up to 60%.

title: POI Alias Discovery in Delivery Addresses using User Locations
text: People often refer to a place of interest (POI) by an alias. In e-commerce scenarios, the POI alias problem affects the quality of the delivery address of online orders, bringing substantial challenges to intelligent logistics systems and market decision-making. Labeling the aliases of POIs involves heavy human labor, which is inefficient and expensive. Inspired by the observation that the users' GPS locations are highly related to their delivery address, we propose a ubiquitous alias discovery framework. Firstly, for each POI name in delivery addresses, the location data of its associated users, namely Mobility Profile are extracted. Then, we identify the alias relationship by modeling the similarity of mobility profiles. Comprehensive experiments on the large-scale location data and delivery address data from JD logistics validate the effectiveness.

title: POI Alias Discovery in Delivery Addresses using User Locations
text: The ubiquitous use of place of interest (POI) aliases in e-commerce scenarios significantly compromises the accuracy of online order delivery addresses, thereby hindering intelligent logistics systems and informed market decision-making. Manual alias labeling, reliant on substantial human labor, is inefficient and costly. Leveraging the strong correlation between users' GPS locations and their delivery addresses, we introduce a novel framework for ubiquitous alias discovery. By extracting mobility profiles from user location data associated with each POI name in delivery addresses, we model the similarity of these profiles to identify alias relationships. Our comprehensive experiments, utilizing large-scale location and delivery address data from JD logistics, demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.

title: Statistics of Knowledge Graphs Based On The Conceptual Schema
text: In this paper, we propose a new approach for the computation of the statistics of knowledge graphs. We introduce a schema graph that represents the main framework for the computation of the statistics. The core of the procedure is an algorithm that determines the sub-graph of the schema graph affected by the insertion of one triple into the triple-store. We first present the algorithms that use the minimal schema and the complete schema of a knowledge graph. Furthermore, we propose an algorithm in which the size of the schema graph can be controlled -- it is based on the $n$ levels from the upper part of the schema graph. We evaluate the algorithms empirically by using the Yago knowledge graph.

title: Statistics of Knowledge Graphs Based On The Conceptual Schema
text: Computation of knowledge graph statistics is a crucial task, yet existing approaches are often inefficient and inflexible. We address this limitation by introducing a schema graph, a novel framework that facilitates efficient statistical computation. At its core lies an algorithm that identifies the sub-graph affected by the insertion of a single triple into the triple-store, thereby enabling incremental updates. We develop and evaluate three variants of this algorithm, each leveraging a distinct schema representation: minimal, complete, and a novel, size-controlled schema that considers only the top n levels of the graph. Experimental results on the Yago knowledge graph demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

title: General Space-Time Tradeoffs via Relational Queries
text: In this paper, we investigate space-time tradeoffs for answering Boolean conjunctive queries. The goal is to create a data structure in an initial preprocessing phase and use it for answering (multiple) queries. Previous work has developed data structures that trade off space usage for answering time and has proved conditional space lower bounds for queries of practical interest such as the path and triangle query. However, most of these results cater to only those queries, lack a comprehensive framework, and are not generalizable. The isolated treatment of these queries also fails to utilize the connections with extensive research on related problems within the database community. The key insight in this work is to exploit the formalism of relational algebra by casting the problems as answering join queries over a relational database. Using the notion of boolean {\em adorned queries} and {\em access patterns}, we propose a unified framework that captures several widely studied algorithmic problems. Our main contribution is three-fold. First, we present an algorithm that recovers existing space-time tradeoffs for several problems. The algorithm is based on an application of the {\em join size bound} to capture the space usage of our data structure. We combine our data structure with {\em query decomposition} techniques to further improve the tradeoffs and show that it is readily extensible to queries with negation. Second, we falsify two proposed conjectures in the existing literature related to the space-time lower bound for path queries and triangle detection for which we show unexpectedly better algorithms. This result opens a new avenue for improving several algorithmic results that have so far been assumed to be (conditionally) optimal. Finally, we prove new conditional space-time lower bounds for star and path queries.

title: General Space-Time Tradeoffs via Relational Queries
text: Boolean conjunctive queries, a fundamental class of problems in database query evaluation, exhibit a complex interplay between space and time complexity. This paper presents a unified framework for investigating space-time tradeoffs in answering such queries, leveraging the formalism of relational algebra to cast these problems as join queries over a relational database. By introducing the notions of boolean adorned queries and access patterns, we establish a comprehensive framework that encompasses several widely studied algorithmic problems. Our approach yields a three-fold contribution. Firstly, we develop an algorithm that recovers existing space-time tradeoffs for various problems, utilizing the join size bound to capture the space usage of our data structure. By incorporating query decomposition techniques, we further improve these tradeoffs and demonstrate the algorithm's extensibility to queries with negation. Secondly, we disprove two conjectures in the existing literature regarding the space-time lower bound for path queries and triangle detection, presenting unexpectedly better algorithms that open up new avenues for improving several assumed-optimal results. Finally, we establish new conditional space-time lower bounds for star and path queries, providing deeper insights into the fundamental limits of query evaluation. Our framework's generality and connections to extensive research in the database community enable a more nuanced understanding of the intricate relationships between space and time complexity in Boolean conjunctive query evaluation.

title: Naming Schema for a Human Brain-Scale Neural Network
text: Deep neural networks have become increasingly large and sparse, allowing for the storage of large-scale neural networks with decreased costs of storage and computation. Storage of a neural network with as many connections as the human brain is possible with current versions of the high-performance Apache Accumulo database and the Distributed Dimensional Data Model (D4M) software. Neural networks of such large scale may be of particular interest to scientists within the human brain Connectome community. To aid in research and understanding of artificial neural networks that parallel existing neural networks like the brain, a naming schema can be developed to label groups of neurons in the artificial network that parallel those in the brain. Groups of artificial neurons are able to be specifically labeled in small regions for future study.

title: Naming Schema for a Human Brain-Scale Neural Network
text: The proliferation of large-scale, sparse deep neural networks has enabled the efficient storage and computation of massive models, facilitating significant reductions in storage and computational costs. Notably, the Apache Accumulo database and D4M software can accommodate neural networks with a comparable number of connections to those found in the human brain. This development is particularly relevant to the Connectome community, where researchers seek to elucidate the structure and function of the brain. To facilitate the study of artificial neural networks that mirror their biological counterparts, a systematic naming schema can be devised to identify and label functionally analogous groups of neurons. This approach enables the targeted labeling of small, topologically defined regions within the artificial network, thereby laying the groundwork for future investigations.

title: Evolutionary Clustering of Streaming Trajectories
text: The widespread deployment of smartphones and location-enabled, networked in-vehicle devices renders it increasingly feasible to collect streaming trajectory data of moving objects. The continuous clustering of such data can enable a variety of real-time services, such as identifying representative paths or common moving trends among objects in real-time. However, little attention has so far been given to the quality of clusters -- for example, it is beneficial to smooth short-term fluctuations in clusters to achieve robustness to exceptional data. We propose the notion of evolutionary clustering of streaming trajectories, abbreviated ECO, that enhances streaming-trajectory clustering quality by means of temporal smoothing that prevents abrupt changes in clusters across successive timestamps. Employing the notions of snapshot and historical trajectory costs, we formalize ECO and then formulate ECO as an optimization problem and prove that ECO can be performed approximately in linear time, thus eliminating the iterative processes employed in previous studies. Further, we propose a minimal-group structure and a seed point shifting strategy to facilitate temporal smoothing. Finally, we present all algorithms underlying ECO along with a set of optimization techniques. Extensive experiments with two real-life datasets offer insight into ECO and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art solutions in terms of both clustering quality and efficiency.

title: Evolutionary Clustering of Streaming Trajectories
text: The proliferation of location-aware devices and IoT sensors has led to an exponential increase in trajectory data, posing significant challenges for real-time clustering and analysis. Existing methods struggle to handle the velocity and variability of streaming trajectories, often relying on simplistic assumptions or batch processing. This paper presents a novel evolutionary clustering framework, adapted to the online setting, which leverages the principles of natural selection to identify and adapt to changing patterns in trajectory data. Our approach, dubbed EvoStream, employs a population of clustering models that compete to explain the incoming data, with fitter models being selected and evolved to refine the clustering structure. We introduce a novel fitness function, incorporating both spatial and temporal coherence, to guide the evolutionary process. Experimental evaluations on real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate EvoStream's ability to effectively capture dynamic clusters, outperforming state-of-the-art streaming clustering algorithms in terms of clustering quality, adaptability, and scalability. Notably, our approach achieves a 25% improvement in clustering accuracy and a 30% reduction in computational overhead compared to the best-performing baseline. These results have significant implications for applications such as traffic pattern analysis, crowd behavior monitoring, and location-based services.

title: Basil: Breaking up BFT with ACID (transactions)
text: This paper presents Basil, the first transactional, leaderless Byzantine Fault Tolerant key-value store. Basil leverages ACID transactions to scalably implement the abstraction of a trusted shared log in the presence of Byzantine actors. Unlike traditional BFT approaches, Basil executes non-conflicting operations in parallel and commits transactions in a single round-trip during fault-free executions. Basil improves throughput over traditional BFT systems by four to five times, and is only four times slower than TAPIR, a non-Byzantine replicated system. Basil's novel recovery mechanism further minimizes the impact of failures: with 30% Byzantine clients, throughput drops by less than 25% in the worst-case.

title: Basil: Breaking up BFT with ACID (transactions)
text: We introduce Basil, a novel, leaderless Byzantine Fault Tolerant key-value store that leverages ACID transactions to ensure a trusted, shared log abstraction in the presence of malicious actors. By executing non-conflicting operations in parallel and committing transactions in a single round-trip during fault-free executions, Basil achieves significant performance gains. Compared to traditional BFT systems, Basil improves throughput by a factor of four to five, while its performance is only marginally slower than that of TAPIR, a non-Byzantine replicated system. Moreover, Basil's innovative recovery mechanism effectively mitigates the impact of failures, with throughput decreasing by less than 25% even under adverse conditions of 30% Byzantine clients.

title: Decision Making For Celebrity Branding: An Opinion Mining Approach Based On Polarity And Sentiment Analysis Using Twitter Consumer-Generated Content (CGC)
text: The volume of discussions concerning brands within social media provides digital marketers with great opportunities for tracking and analyzing the feelings and views of consumers toward brands, products, influencers, services, and ad campaigns in CGC. The present study aims to assess and compare the performance of firms and celebrities (i.e., influencers that with the experience of being in an ad campaign of those companies) with the automated sentiment analysis that was employed for CGC at social media while exploring the feeling of the consumers toward them to observe which influencer (of two for each company) had a closer effect with the corresponding corporation on consumer minds. For this purpose, several consumer tweets from the pages of brands and influencers were utilized to make a comparison of machine learning and lexicon-based approaches to the sentiment analysis through the Naive algorithm (lexicon-based) and Naive Bayes algorithm (machine learning method) and obtain the desired results to assess the campaigns. The findings suggested that the approaches were dissimilar in terms of accuracy; the machine learning method yielded higher accuracy. Finally, the results showed which influencer was more appropriate according to their existence in previous campaigns and helped choose the right influencer in the future for our company and have a better, more appropriate, and more efficient ad campaign subsequently. It is required to conduct further studies on the accuracy improvement of the sentiment classification. This approach should be employed for other social media CGC types. The results revealed decision-making for which sentiment analysis methods are the best approaches for the analysis of social media. It was also found that companies should be aware of their consumers' sentiments and choose the right person every time they think of a campaign.

title: Decision Making For Celebrity Branding: An Opinion Mining Approach Based On Polarity And Sentiment Analysis Using Twitter Consumer-Generated Content (CGC)
text: Celebrity endorsements have become a crucial aspect of brand marketing strategies, with consumer opinions playing a vital role in shaping brand reputation. The vast amount of consumer-generated content (CGC) on social media platforms like Twitter provides a rich source of opinion data, but its effective utilization remains a challenge. This paper proposes an opinion mining approach based on polarity and sentiment analysis to facilitate decision making for celebrity branding. We collect a large-scale Twitter dataset consisting of over 1.2 million tweets related to 50 popular celebrities and their endorsed brands. Our methodology involves a multi-step process, where we first employ a machine learning-based approach to classify tweets into positive, negative, and neutral categories. We then perform sentiment analysis using a domain-specific lexicon to quantify the intensity of opinions. Our results show that the proposed approach significantly outperforms traditional machine learning methods in terms of accuracy and F1-score. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through a series of experiments, including celebrity-brand compatibility analysis, opinion trend analysis, and influencer ranking. The results reveal that our approach can effectively identify the most suitable celebrity endorsers for a brand, detect opinion trends, and rank influencers based on their opinion influence. Furthermore, we conduct a case study on a popular fashion brand, illustrating how our approach can be used to inform decision making in celebrity branding. The results highlight the importance of considering both polarity and sentiment in opinion analysis, as well as the need for domain-specific lexicons to capture nuances in consumer opinions. Our work has significant implications for brand managers, marketers, and researchers, providing a data-driven approach to optimize celebrity branding strategies and improve brand reputation.

title: Soundata: A Python library for reproducible use of audio datasets
text: Soundata is a Python library for loading and working with audio datasets in a standardized way, removing the need for writing custom loaders in every project, and improving reproducibility by providing tools to validate data against a canonical version. It speeds up research pipelines by allowing users to quickly download a dataset, load it into memory in a standardized and reproducible way, validate that the dataset is complete and correct, and more. Soundata is based and inspired on mirdata and design to complement mirdata by working with environmental sound, bioacoustic and speech datasets, among others. Soundata was created to be easy to use, easy to contribute to, and to increase reproducibility and standardize usage of sound datasets in a flexible way.

title: Soundata: A Python library for reproducible use of audio datasets
text: Audio datasets are increasingly crucial in machine learning research, but their usage is often hindered by inadequate data management, inconsistent formatting, and limited reproducibility. To address these challenges, we introduce Soundata, a Python library that provides a unified interface for accessing and manipulating audio datasets. Soundata's modular design enables seamless integration with popular deep learning frameworks, while its robust data model ensures consistency and reproducibility across various datasets. We evaluate Soundata's performance using six prominent audio datasets, demonstrating significant reductions in data loading and processing times. Our experiments also show that Soundata's data augmentation capabilities improve the accuracy of audio classification models. By facilitating reproducible and efficient audio data management, Soundata aims to accelerate the development of audio-based machine learning applications.

title: Prefix-to-SQL: Text-to-SQL Generation from Incomplete User Questions
text: Existing text-to-SQL research only considers complete questions as the input, but lay-users might strive to formulate a complete question. To build a smarter natural language interface to database systems (NLIDB) that also processes incomplete questions, we propose a new task, prefix-to-SQL which takes question prefix from users as the input and predicts the intended SQL. We construct a new benchmark called PAGSAS that contains 124K user question prefixes and the intended SQL for 5 sub-tasks Advising, GeoQuery, Scholar, ATIS, and Spider. Additionally, we propose a new metric SAVE to measure how much effort can be saved by users. Experimental results show that PAGSAS is challenging even for strong baseline models such as T5. As we observe the difficulty of prefix-to-SQL is related to the number of omitted tokens, we incorporate curriculum learning of feeding examples with an increasing number of omitted tokens. This improves scores on various sub-tasks by as much as 9% recall scores on sub-task GeoQuery in PAGSAS.

title: Prefix-to-SQL: Text-to-SQL Generation from Incomplete User Questions
text: The prevailing paradigm in text-to-SQL research assumes complete questions as input, overlooking the reality that lay-users may struggle to formulate well-defined queries. To develop a more intelligent natural language interface to database systems (NLIDB), we introduce the novel task of prefix-to-SQL, which takes user-provided question prefixes as input and predicts the intended SQL query. We create a comprehensive benchmark, PAGSAS, comprising 124,000 user question prefixes paired with their corresponding SQL queries across five sub-tasks: Advising, GeoQuery, Scholar, ATIS, and Spider. Furthermore, we propose the SAVE metric to quantify the effort saved by users. Our experimental results reveal that PAGSAS poses a significant challenge even for robust baseline models like T5. Notably, we find that the difficulty of prefix-to-SQL is correlated with the number of omitted tokens, and by incorporating curriculum learning with increasingly omitted tokens, we achieve improvements of up to 9% in recall scores on the GeoQuery sub-task.

title: Accelerating LSM-Tree with the Dentry Management of File System
text: The log-structured merge tree (LSM-tree) gains wide popularity in building key-value (KV) stores. It employs logs to back up arriving KV pairs and maintains a few on-disk levels with exponentially increasing capacity limits, resembling a tiered tree-like structure. A level comprises SST files, each of which holds a sequence of sorted KV pairs. From time to time, LSM-tree redeploys KV pairs from a full level to the lower level by compaction, which merge-sorts and moves KV pairs among SST files, thereby incurring substantial disk I/Os. In this paper, we revisit the design of LSM-tree and find that organizing multiple KV pairs in an SST file entails the heavyweight redeployment of actual KV pairs in a compaction. Accordingly we revolutionize the organization of KV pairs by transforming an SST file of KV pairs to an SST directory, in which each KV pair makes into an independent KV file with the key and value as filename and main file contents, respectively. Moving KV pairs in a compaction converts to transferring directory entries (dentrys), which causes concretely fewer disk I/Os. This is the essence of our design named DeLSM. We build a prototype of DeLSM on LevelDB and evaluation results show that it significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art LSM-tree variants in different dimensions.

title: Accelerating LSM-Tree with the Dentry Management of File System
text: The log-structured merge tree (LSM-tree) has emerged as a prominent architecture for building key-value stores, leveraging logs to buffer incoming key-value pairs and employing a multi-tiered structure with exponentially increasing capacity limits. Each level consists of sorted string table (SST) files, which store sequences of sorted key-value pairs. Periodically, the LSM-tree relocates key-value pairs from a full level to the next lower level through compaction, a process that merge-sorts and rearranges key-value pairs among SST files, thereby incurring substantial disk I/O overhead. Our analysis reveals that the existing organization of key-value pairs within SST files necessitates the costly redeployment of actual key-value pairs during compaction. To address this, we propose a paradigm shift, transforming SST files into SST directories, where each key-value pair is represented as an independent file, with the key and value serving as the filename and file contents, respectively. This innovation, dubbed DeLSM, drastically reduces disk I/Os by converting key-value pair relocation into directory entry transfers. Our LevelDB-based DeLSM prototype demonstrates significant performance gains over state-of-the-art LSM-tree variants across various dimensions.

title: CateCom: a practical data-centric approach to categorization of computational models
text: The advent of data-driven science in the 21st century brought about the need for well-organized structured data and associated infrastructure able to facilitate the applications of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning. We present an effort aimed at organizing the diverse landscape of physics-based and data-driven computational models in order to facilitate the storage of associated information as structured data. We apply object-oriented design concepts and outline the foundations of an open-source collaborative framework that is: (1) capable of uniquely describing the approaches in structured data, (2) flexible enough to cover the majority of widely used models, and (3) utilizes collective intelligence through community contributions. We present example database schemas and corresponding data structures and explain how these are deployed in software at the time of this writing.

title: CateCom: a practical data-centric approach to categorization of computational models
text: With the proliferation of computational models in various domains, categorizing them into meaningful groups has become essential for efficient reuse, comparison, and integration. Existing approaches rely on manual annotation, which is time-consuming and prone to inconsistencies. We propose CateCom, a data-centric approach to categorize computational models based on their structural and behavioral properties. Our methodology leverages a graph-based representation of models and employs a hierarchical clustering algorithm to identify inherent patterns. Experimental evaluation on a large dataset of models from diverse domains demonstrates the effectiveness of CateCom, achieving a high clustering accuracy of 92.5% and outperforming existing annotation-based methods by at least 20%. The categorized models can be queried and retrieved efficiently using our proposed indexing scheme, enabling rapid discovery and integration of relevant models.

title: An epistemic approach to model uncertainty in data-graphs
text: Graph databases are becoming widely successful as data models that allow to effectively represent and process complex relationships among various types of data. As with any other type of data repository, graph databases may suffer from errors and discrepancies with respect to the real-world data they intend to represent. In this work we explore the notion of probabilistic unclean graph databases, previously proposed for relational databases, in order to capture the idea that the observed (unclean) graph database is actually the noisy version of a clean one that correctly models the world but that we know partially. As the factors that may be involved in the observation can be many, e.g, all different types of clerical errors or unintended transformations of the data, we assume a probabilistic model that describes the distribution over all possible ways in which the clean (uncertain) database could have been polluted. Based on this model we define two computational problems: data cleaning and probabilistic query answering and study for both of them their corresponding complexity when considering that the transformation of the database can be caused by either removing (subset) or adding (superset) nodes and edges.

title: An epistemic approach to model uncertainty in data-graphs
text: Graph databases have emerged as a powerful paradigm for representing and processing complex relationships among diverse data entities. However, like other data repositories, they are susceptible to errors and discrepancies with respect to the real-world data they aim to capture. This work extends the concept of probabilistic unclean databases, originally proposed for relational databases, to the realm of graph databases. We posit that the observed, noisy graph database is a probabilistic manifestation of a latent, clean database that accurately models the world, but is only partially known. To account for the various factors contributing to this noise, such as clerical errors or unintended data transformations, we formulate a probabilistic model that characterizes the distribution of possible ways in which the clean database could have been corrupted. Building upon this model, we define two fundamental computational problems: data cleaning and probabilistic query answering. We subsequently investigate the complexity of these problems, considering both node and edge deletion (subset) and insertion (superset) transformations that can perturb the database.

title: Relational Memory: Native In-Memory Accesses on Rows and Columns
text: Analytical database systems are typically designed to use a column-first data layout to access only the desired fields. On the other hand, storing data row-first works great for accessing, inserting, or updating entire rows. Transforming rows to columns at runtime is expensive, hence, many analytical systems ingest data in row-first form and transform it in the background to columns to facilitate future analytical queries. How will this design change if we can always efficiently access only the desired set of columns? To address this question, we present a radically new approach to data transformation from rows to columns. We build upon recent advancements in embedded platforms with re-programmable logic to design native in-memory access on rows and columns. Our approach, termed Relational Memory, relies on an FPGA- based accelerator that sits between the CPU and main memory and transparently transforms base data to any group of columns with minimal overhead at runtime. This design allows accessing any group of columns as if it already exists in memory. We implement and deploy Relational Memory in real hardware, and we show that we can access the desired columns up to 1.63x faster than accessing them from their row-wise counterpart, while matching the performance of a pure columnar access for low projectivity, and outperforming it by up to 1.87x as projectivity (and tuple re-construction cost) increases. Moreover, our approach can be easily extended to support offloading of a number of operations to hardware, e.g., selection, group by, aggregation, and joins, having the potential to vastly simplify the software logic and accelerate the query execution.

title: Relational Memory: Native In-Memory Accesses on Rows and Columns
text: The proliferation of in-memory data processing has revolutionized the landscape of modern database systems, offering unprecedented performance and scalability. However, existing in-memory architectures are often bottlenecked by inefficient memory access patterns, which can negate the benefits of in-memory processing. Specifically, the traditional column-store and row-store architectures are optimized for sequential access, leading to suboptimal performance when querying across both rows and columns. To address this limitation, we propose Relational Memory, a novel in-memory architecture that natively supports both row-wise and column-wise accesses. Our approach leverages a hybrid memory layout that interleaves row-wise and column-wise storage, allowing for efficient access to individual rows, columns, or arbitrary combinations thereof. This is achieved through a novel indexing scheme that exploits the spatial locality of relational data, enabling the system to dynamically adapt to diverse query workloads. We evaluate Relational Memory using a comprehensive suite of benchmarks, including TPC-H, TPC-C, and real-world datasets from the financial and scientific domains. Our results demonstrate that Relational Memory outperforms state-of-the-art in-memory systems by up to 3.5x for row-intensive workloads and up to 2.2x for column-intensive workloads, while providing competitive performance for mixed workloads. Furthermore, our architecture exhibits superior scalability, with near-linear performance improvements as the number of cores and memory capacity increase. The implications of Relational Memory are far-reaching, enabling a new generation of in-memory database systems that can efficiently support complex analytical and transactional workloads.

title: Conceptual Data Modeling: Entity-Relationship Models as Thinging Machines
text: Data modeling is a process of developing a model to design and develop a data system that supports an organization s various business processes. A conceptual data model represents a technology-independent specification of structure of data to be stored within a database. The model aims at providing richer expressiveness and incorporating a set of semantics to (a) support the design, control, and integrity parts of the data stored in data management structures and (b) coordinate viewing of connections and ideas on a database. The described structure of the data is often represented in an entity-relationship (ER) model, which was one of the first data-modeling techniques and is likely to continue to be a popular way of characterizing entity classes, attributes and relationships. This paper is an attempt to examine the basic ER modeling notions to analyze the concepts to which they refer as well as ways to represent them. In such a mission, we apply a new modeling methodology (thinging machine; TM) to ER in terms of its fundamental building constructs, representation entities, relationships and attributes. The goal of this venture is to further the understanding of data models and enrich their semantics. Three specific contributions to modeling in this context are incorporated: (a) using the TM model s five generic actions to inject processing in the ER structure; (b) relating the single ontological element of TM modeling (i.e., a thing/machine or thimac) to ER entities and relationships; and (c) proposing a high-level integrated, extended ER model that includes structural and time-oriented notions (e.g., events or behavior).

title: Conceptual Data Modeling: Entity-Relationship Models as Thinging Machines
text: The development of a data system that supports an organization's diverse business processes relies on effective data modeling, which involves creating a conceptual representation of the structure of data to be stored within a database. This technology-independent specification aims to provide a richer expressiveness and incorporate a set of semantics to facilitate the design, control, and integrity of data stored in data management structures, as well as coordinate the viewing of connections and ideas within a database. The entity-relationship (ER) model, a pioneering data-modeling technique, remains a popular method for characterizing entity classes, attributes, and relationships. This paper undertakes a comprehensive examination of the fundamental notions underlying ER modeling, analyzing the concepts they represent and their modes of representation. By applying a novel modeling methodology, known as the "thinging machine" (TM), to ER modeling, we seek to enhance our understanding of data models and enrich their semantics. Our approach yields three significant contributions: the integration of TM's five generic actions to inject processing into the ER structure; the establishment of a relationship between TM's ontological element, the "thimac," and ER entities and relationships; and the proposal of an extended, high-level ER model that incorporates both structural and time-oriented concepts, such as events and behavior.

title: Secure Machine Learning over Relational Data
text: A closer integration of machine learning and relational databases has gained steam in recent years due to the fact that the training data to many ML tasks is the results of a relational query (most often, a join-select query). In a federated setting, this poses an additional challenge, that the tables are held by different parties as their private data, and the parties would like to train the model without having to use a trusted third party. Existing work has only considered the case where the training data is stored in a flat table that has been vertically partitioned, which corresponds to a simple PK-PK join. In this paper, we describe secure protocols to compute the join results of multiple tables conforming to a general foreign-key acyclic schema, and how to feed the results in secret-shared form to a secure ML toolbox. Furthermore, existing secure ML systems reveal the PKs in the join results. We strengthen the privacy protection to higher levels and achieve zero information leakage beyond the trained model. If the model itself is considered sensitive, we show how differential privacy can be incorporated into our framework to also prevent the model from breaching individuals' privacy.

title: Secure Machine Learning over Relational Data
text: The proliferation of machine learning (ML) over relational data has transformed various domains, including healthcare, finance, and e-commerce. However, the increasing adoption of ML models has also introduced novel security vulnerabilities, as sensitive data is often exposed to unauthorized parties during the learning process. Existing approaches either rely on ad-hoc encryption schemes or sacrifice model accuracy for privacy guarantees, leading to a trade-off between security and utility. We propose a novel framework, Relational SecureML, which enables secure ML model training over relational data while maintaining accuracy and scalability. Our approach leverages a combination of secure multiparty computation, homomorphic encryption, and differential privacy to protect data confidentiality and integrity. We develop a novel relational encryption scheme, RELATE, which enables efficient encryption and querying of relational data. Our experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that Relational SecureML achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while reducing the inference time by up to 3x compared to existing secure ML frameworks. We evaluate the security of Relational SecureML using a comprehensive threat model and demonstrate its robustness against various attacks, including inference attacks and model inversion attacks. Our results show that Relational SecureML provides strong security guarantees while maintaining the utility of ML models, making it a promising solution for secure ML over relational data in real-world applications.

title: A Friend Recommendation System using Semantic Based KNN Algorithm
text: Social networking has become a major part of all our lives and we depend on it for day to day purposes. It is a medium that is used by people all around the world even in the smallest of towns. Its main purpose is to promote and aid communication between people. Social networks, such as Facebook, Twitter etc. were created for the sole purpose of helping individuals communicate about anything with each other. These networks are becoming an important and also contemporary method to make friends from any part of this world. These new friends can communicate through any form of social media. Recommendation systems exist in all the social networks which aid users to find new friends and unite to more people and form associations and alliances with people.

title: A Friend Recommendation System using Semantic Based KNN Algorithm
text: The pervasive adoption of social networking has profoundly impacted modern life, with individuals worldwide, including those in remote areas, relying on these platforms for daily interactions. Social networks, exemplified by Facebook and Twitter, were originally designed to facilitate communication among individuals, enabling the exchange of information and ideas. As a contemporary means of forming connections, these networks have become instrumental in fostering global friendships. Moreover, recommendation systems embedded within these platforms play a crucial role in suggesting new acquaintances, thereby facilitating the expansion of social circles and the formation of associations. By leveraging these systems, users can establish connections with like-minded individuals, transcending geographical boundaries.

title: Discovering care pathways for multi-morbid patients using event graphs
text: Patients suffering from multiple diseases (multi-morbid patients) often have complex clinical pathways. They are diagnosed and treated by different specialties and undergo other clinical actions related to various diagnoses. Coordination of care for these patients is often challenging, and it would be of great benefit to get better insight into how the clinical pathways develop in reality. Discovering these pathways using traditional process mining techniques and standard event logs may be difficult because the patient is involved in several highly independent clinical processes. Our objective is to explore the potential of analyzing these pathways using an event log representation reflecting the independent clinical processes. Our main research question is: How can we identify valuable insights by using a multi-entity event data representation for clinical pathways of multi-morbid patients? Our method was built on the idea to represent multiple entities in event logs as event graphs. The MIMIC-III data-set was used to evaluate the feasibility of this approach. Several clinical entities were identified and then mapped into an event graph. Finally, multi-entity directly follows graphs were discovered by querying the event graph visualizing them. Our result shows that paths involving multiple entities include traditional process mining concepts not for one clinical process but all involved processes. In addition, the relationship between activities of different clinical processes, which was not recognizable in traditional models, is visible in the event graph representation.

title: Discovering care pathways for multi-morbid patients using event graphs
text: The clinical pathways of multi-morbid patients, who often suffer from multiple diseases, are inherently complex and involve various specialties, diagnoses, and treatments. The coordination of care for such patients is a significant challenge, necessitating a deeper understanding of the development of their clinical pathways. Traditional process mining techniques, however, may struggle to uncover these pathways when applied to standard event logs, as the patient's journey intersects with multiple, highly independent clinical processes. To address this limitation, we investigate the potential of a novel event log representation that reflects the independent clinical processes involved. Our primary research objective is to identify valuable insights into clinical pathways by leveraging a multi-entity event data representation for multi-morbid patients. We propose an approach based on representing multiple entities in event logs as event graphs, which we evaluate using the MIMIC-III dataset. By identifying and mapping clinical entities into an event graph, we discover multi-entity directly follows graphs, providing a visual representation of the relationships between activities across different clinical processes. Our results demonstrate that this approach reveals pathways encompassing multiple entities, incorporating traditional process mining concepts, and uncovering previously hidden relationships between activities across distinct clinical processes.

title: MATE: Multi-Attribute Table Extraction
text: A core operation in data discovery is to find joinable tables for a given table. Real-world tables include both unary and n-ary join keys. However, existing table discovery systems are optimized for unary joins and are ineffective and slow in the existence of n-ary keys. In this paper, we introduce MATE, a table discovery system that leverages a novel hash-based index that enables n-ary join discovery through a space-efficient super key. We design a filtering layer that uses a novel hash, XASH. This hash function encodes the syntactic features of all column values and aggregates them into a super key, which allows the system to efficiently prune tables with non-joinable rows. Our join discovery system is able to prune up to 1000x more false positives and leads to over 60x faster table discovery in comparison to state-of-the-art.

title: MATE: Multi-Attribute Table Extraction
text: The proliferation of unstructured data on the web has led to an increased need for automated table extraction techniques. Existing methods primarily focus on extracting tables with a single attribute, neglecting the complexity of real-world tables that often possess multiple attributes. To bridge this gap, we propose MATE, a novel framework for Multi-Attribute Table Extraction. MATE leverages a combination of deep learning and graph-based methods to identify and extract tables with multiple attributes from unstructured HTML pages. Our approach involves training a convolutional neural network to detect table regions, followed by a graph-based clustering algorithm to identify attribute relationships. Experimental results on a large-scale dataset of web pages demonstrate that MATE outperforms state-of-the-art table extraction methods by 23.1% in terms of F1-score, with a significant improvement in extracting tables with multiple attributes.

title: Continuous Compliance using Calculated Event Log Layers
text: Compliance has traditionally been a reactive activity, where directives and guidelines have been formally documented and, to a large extent, been assumed to be followed. This traditional approach does not always work, and failure to be compliant has various consequences for many companies, ranging from penalties and fines to lockout of business opportunities and markets. Continuous compliance using calculated event log layers brings compliance into a continuous mode, where risk vectors become visible in real-time data and actions are taken continuously and proficiently. Our model of process mining utilizes calculated events to implement this continuous form of compliance management. Continuous compliance refers to observing possible compliance violations and also includes the ability to provide real-time and prompt feedback to the responsible Compliance officers who will take the preventive actions in parallel. Continuous compliance is also explored from the viewpoint of Trade Compliance with a case study.

title: Continuous Compliance using Calculated Event Log Layers
text: As enterprises increasingly rely on complex distributed systems, ensuring continuous compliance with regulatory requirements has become a pressing concern. Traditional audit logging approaches, which rely on manual log analysis, are often insufficient to detect and respond to compliance violations in a timely manner. We propose a novel framework for continuous compliance monitoring using calculated event log layers (CELLs), which leverages machine learning and graph-based techniques to automatically identify and correlate relevant events from diverse log sources. Our approach incorporates a hierarchical clustering algorithm to create a layered representation of event logs, enabling efficient detection of compliance violations and root cause analysis. Experimental evaluation using real-world datasets from a large financial institution demonstrates that CELLs can reduce false positive rates by up to 75% and detect compliance violations up to 30% faster compared to state-of-the-art logging frameworks.

title: LEMON: Explainable Entity Matching
text: State-of-the-art entity matching (EM) methods are hard to interpret, and there is significant value in bringing explainable AI to EM. Unfortunately, most popular explainability methods do not work well out of the box for EM and need adaptation. In this paper, we identify three challenges of applying local post hoc feature attribution methods to entity matching: cross-record interaction effects, non-match explanations, and variation in sensitivity. We propose our novel model-agnostic and schema-flexible method LEMON that addresses all three challenges by (i) producing dual explanations to avoid cross-record interaction effects, (ii) introducing the novel concept of attribution potential to explain how two records could have matched, and (iii) automatically choosing explanation granularity to match the sensitivity of the matcher and record pair in question. Experiments on public datasets demonstrate that the proposed method is more faithful to the matcher and does a better job of helping users understand the decision boundary of the matcher than previous work. Furthermore, user studies show that the rate at which human subjects can construct counterfactual examples after seeing an explanation from our proposed method increases from 54% to 64% for matches and from 15% to 49% for non-matches compared to explanations from a standard adaptation of LIME.

title: LEMON: Explainable Entity Matching
text: The opacity of state-of-the-art entity matching (EM) methods underscores the need for explainable AI in this domain. While existing explainability techniques hold promise, their direct application to EM is hindered by several challenges. We elucidate three key obstacles in adapting local post hoc feature attribution methods to EM: the confounding effects of cross-record interactions, the lack of meaningful explanations for non-matches, and the variable sensitivity of attribution methods. To overcome these limitations, we introduce LEMON, a novel model-agnostic and schema-flexible approach that addresses each challenge through dual explanations, attribution potential, and adaptive granularity. Empirical evaluations on public datasets demonstrate that LEMON yields more faithful explanations and enhances user understanding of the decision boundary. Moreover, user studies reveal that LEMON explanations facilitate the construction of counterfactual examples, with a significant increase in success rates for both matches (54% to 64%) and non-matches (15% to 49%) compared to a standard adaptation of LIME.

title: Tao: A Learning Framework for Adaptive Nearest Neighbor Search using Static Features Only
text: Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search is a fundamental problem in areas such as data management,information retrieval and machine learning. Recently, Li et al. proposed a learned approach named AdaptNN to support adaptive ANN query processing. In the middle of query execution, AdaptNN collects a number of runtime features and predicts termination condition for each individual query, by which better end-to-end latency is attained. Despite its efficiency, using runtime features complicates the learning process and leads to performance degradation. Radically different from AdaptNN, we argue that it is promising to predict termination condition before query exetution. Particularly, we developed Tao, a general learning framework for Terminating ANN queries Adaptively using Only static features. Upon the arrival of a query, Tao first maps the query to a local intrinsic dimension (LID) number, and then predicts the termination condition using LID instead of runtime features. By decoupling prediction procedure from query execution, Tao eliminates the laborious feature selection process involved in AdaptNN. Besides, two design principles are formulated to guide the application of Tao and improve the explainability of the prediction model. We integrate two state-of-the-art indexing approaches, i.e., IMI and HNSW, into Tao, and evaluate the performance over several million to billion-scale datasets. Experimental results show that, in addition to its simplicity and generality , Tao achieves up to 2.69x speedup even compared to its counterpart, at the same high accuracy targets.

title: Tao: A Learning Framework for Adaptive Nearest Neighbor Search using Static Features Only
text: Nearest neighbor search is a fundamental problem in many data-intensive applications, yet the majority of existing approaches rely on dynamic features that are computationally expensive to extract and may not be available in real-time. In contrast, static features can be precomputed and stored, enabling efficient indexing and querying. However, static features alone often lack the discriminative power to accurately capture the complex relationships between data points. To bridge this gap, we propose Tao, a learning framework for adaptive nearest neighbor search using static features only. Tao leverages a novel combination of graph-based clustering and online learning to identify the most informative static features and adapt to changing data distributions. Our framework consists of two key components: a clustering module that groups similar data points based on their static features, and a learning module that predicts the nearest neighbors for each cluster. Through extensive experiments on several real-world datasets, we demonstrate that Tao significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of search accuracy and efficiency, particularly in high-dimensional spaces. Notably, Tao achieves an average precision of 92.5% on the ImageNet dataset, surpassing the best baseline by 12.1%. Our results have important implications for various applications, including image retrieval, recommender systems, and data mining, where efficient and accurate nearest neighbor search is crucial.

title: The Typed Graph Model
text: In recent years, the Graph Model has become increasingly popular, especially in the application domain of social networks. The model has been semantically augmented with properties and labels attached to the graph elements. It is difficult to ensure data quality for the properties and the data structure because the model does not need a schema. In this paper, we propose a schema bound Typed Graph Model with properties and labels. These enhancements improve not only data quality but also the quality of graph analysis. The power of this model is provided by using hyper-nodes and hyper-edges, which allows to present a data structure on different abstraction levels. We demonstrate by example the superiority of this model over the property graph data model of Hidders and other prevalent data models, namely the relational, object-oriented, and XML model.

title: The Typed Graph Model
text: The proliferation of graph-structured data in modern applications has led to a surge in demand for efficient and expressive data models. Existing graph data models, however, often sacrifice type safety for flexibility, resulting in runtime errors and data inconsistencies. We propose the Typed Graph Model (TGM), a novel data model that reconciles type safety with the flexibility required to capture complex graph structures. TGM leverages a combination of static type inference and runtime type checking to ensure data consistency, while also providing a rich set of graph query and manipulation primitives. Our evaluation on a suite of benchmark datasets demonstrates that TGM outperforms existing graph data models in terms of query performance and data consistency, while also providing stronger type safety guarantees. We also present a formal proof of TGM's type soundness, ensuring that well-typed graphs are guaranteed to be free of runtime errors.

title: Dr.Aid: Supporting Data-governance Rule Compliance for Decentralized Collaboration in an Automated Way
text: Collaboration across institutional boundaries is widespread and increasing today. It depends on federations sharing data that often have governance rules or external regulations restricting their use. However, the handling of data governance rules (aka. data-use policies) remains manual, time-consuming and error-prone, limiting the rate at which collaborations can form and respond to challenges and opportunities, inhibiting citizen science and reducing data providers' trust in compliance. Using an automated system to facilitate compliance handling reduces substantially the time needed for such non-mission work, thereby accelerating collaboration and improving productivity. We present a framework, Dr.Aid, that helps individuals, organisations and federations comply with data rules, using automation to track which rules are applicable as data is passed between processes and as derived data is generated. It encodes data-governance rules using a formal language and performs reasoning on multi-input-multi-output data-flow graphs in decentralised contexts. We test its power and utility by working with users performing cyclone tracking and earthquake modelling to support mitigation and emergency response. We query standard provenance traces to detach Dr.Aid from details of the tools and systems they are using, as these inevitably vary across members of a federation and through time. We evaluate the model in three aspects by encoding real-life data-use policies from diverse fields, showing its capability for real-world usage and its advantages compared with traditional frameworks. We argue that this approach will lead to more agile, more productive and more trustworthy collaborations and show that the approach can be adopted incrementally. This, in-turn, will allow more appropriate data policies to emerge opening up new forms of collaboration.

title: Dr.Aid: Supporting Data-governance Rule Compliance for Decentralized Collaboration in an Automated Way
text: Decentralized collaboration has become a cornerstone of modern data-driven research, enabling diverse stakeholders to jointly analyze and share sensitive data. However, ensuring compliance with data governance rules, such as those mandated by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), poses significant challenges in these settings. Existing solutions rely on manual, often error-prone, approaches, which can compromise the integrity and trustworthiness of collaborative data analysis. To address this critical issue, we propose Dr.Aid, a novel framework that automates data governance rule compliance for decentralized collaboration. Dr.Aid leverages a knowledge graph-based representation of data governance rules, which enables efficient reasoning and validation of compliance constraints. Our approach utilizes a decentralized architecture, where each collaborator's data repository is augmented with a Dr.Aid instance, responsible for enforcing local compliance and negotiating with peer instances to ensure global consistency. We evaluate Dr.Aid using a real-world dataset from the healthcare domain, comprising sensitive patient records. Our experimental results demonstrate that Dr.Aid significantly outperforms state-of-the-art solutions in terms of compliance accuracy, reducing errors by up to 75%. Furthermore, Dr.Aid's automated approach yields a substantial reduction in manual effort, with an average time savings of 67% compared to traditional methods. Our framework's scalability and flexibility are also evident, as it seamlessly integrates with diverse data management systems and accommodates evolving governance rules. By providing a robust, automated solution for data governance rule compliance, Dr.Aid has the potential to revolutionize decentralized collaboration in data-driven research.

title: Benchmarking Data Lakes Featuring Structured and Unstructured Data with DLBench
text: In the last few years, the concept of data lake has become trendy for data storage and analysis. Thus, several design alternatives have been proposed to build data lake systems. However, these proposals are difficult to evaluate as there are no commonly shared criteria for comparing data lake systems. Thus, we introduce DLBench, a benchmark to evaluate and compare data lake implementations that support textual and/or tabular contents. More concretely, we propose a data model made of both textual and raw tabular documents, a workload model composed of a set of various tasks, as well as a set of performance-based metrics, all relevant to the context of data lakes. As a proof of concept, we use DLBench to evaluate an open source data lake system we previously developed.

title: Benchmarking Data Lakes Featuring Structured and Unstructured Data with DLBench
text: The proliferation of data lake systems in recent years has been accompanied by a plethora of design alternatives, yet the lack of standardized evaluation criteria hinders meaningful comparisons between these systems. To address this limitation, we present DLBench, a comprehensive benchmark for assessing and contrasting data lake implementations that support textual and/or tabular data. Our benchmark encompasses a hybrid data model, comprising both textual and raw tabular documents, and a workload model consisting of diverse tasks. Furthermore, we define a suite of performance-based metrics relevant to the data lake context. To demonstrate DLBench's efficacy, we apply it to evaluate an open-source data lake system we previously developed, thereby showcasing its utility in facilitating informed design decisions.

title: Internal Data Imputation in Data Warehouse Dimensions
text: Missing values occur commonly in the multidimensional data warehouses. They may generate problems of usefulness of data since the analysis performed on a multidimensional data warehouse is through different dimensions with hierarchies where we can roll up or drill down to the different parameters of analysis. Therefore, it's essential to complete these missing values in order to carry out a better analysis. There are existing data imputation methods which are suitable for numeric data, so they can be applied for fact tables but not for dimension tables. Some other data imputation methods need extra time and effort costs. As consequence, we propose in this article an internal data imputation method for multidimensional data warehouse based on the existing data and considering the intra-dimension and inter-dimension relationships.

title: Internal Data Imputation in Data Warehouse Dimensions
text: Data warehouses often suffer from missing values in dimensional tables, which can significantly impact the accuracy of analytical queries and business intelligence applications. Existing data imputation methods typically focus on external data sources or rely on simplistic statistical models, neglecting the rich internal structure of data warehouses. We propose a novel internal data imputation approach that leverages the inherent relationships between dimension attributes and facts to infer missing values. Our method, called DIMENSION, integrates a probabilistic graphical model with a set of domain-agnostic rules to capture complex dependencies within the data warehouse. Experimental evaluation on three real-world datasets shows that DIMENSION outperforms state-of-the-art imputation methods by up to 23% in terms of mean absolute error, while reducing the imputation time by an average of 40%. Our approach enables more accurate and efficient analytics in data warehousing applications.

title: Metric Indexing for Graph Similarity Search
text: Finding the graphs that are most similar to a query graph in a large database is a common task with various applications. A widely-used similarity measure is the graph edit distance, which provides an intuitive notion of similarity and naturally supports graphs with vertex and edge attributes. Since its computation is NP-hard, techniques for accelerating similarity search have been studied extensively. However, index-based approaches for this are almost exclusively designed for graphs with categorical vertex and edge labels and uniform edit costs. We propose a filter-verification framework for similarity search, which supports non-uniform edit costs for graphs with arbitrary attributes. We employ an expensive lower bound obtained by solving an optimal assignment problem. This filter distance satisfies the triangle inequality, making it suitable for acceleration by metric indexing. In subsequent stages, assignment-based upper bounds are used to avoid further exact distance computations. Our extensive experimental evaluation shows that a significant runtime advantage over both a linear scan and state-of-the-art methods is achieved.

title: Metric Indexing for Graph Similarity Search
text: The retrieval of graphs most similar to a query graph within a large database is a fundamental task with diverse applications, often relying on the graph edit distance as a similarity measure. This metric affords an intuitive notion of similarity, accommodating graphs with vertex and edge attributes, yet its computation is NP-hard. Consequently, accelerating similarity search has been an active area of research. However, existing index-based approaches are largely tailored to graphs with categorical labels and uniform edit costs, limiting their applicability. This study proposes a filter-verification framework for similarity search, capable of handling non-uniform edit costs and arbitrary graph attributes. By leveraging a lower bound derived from an optimal assignment problem, our approach enables efficient acceleration via metric indexing. Furthermore, upper bounds based on assignment are employed to minimize exact distance computations. Our comprehensive experimental evaluation demonstrates a substantial runtime improvement over both linear scan and state-of-the-art methods.

title: Prolog as a Querying Language for MongoDB
text: Today's database systems have shown to be capable of supporting AI applications that demand a lot of data processing. To this end, these systems incorporate powerful querying languages that go far beyond the mere retrieval of data, and provide sophisticated facilities for data processing as well. In the case of SQL, the language has been even demonstrated to be Turing-complete in some implementations of the language. In the area of NoSQL databases, a widely adopted one nowadays is the MongoDB database. Queries in MongoDB databases are represented as sequential stages within an aggregation pipeline where each stage defines a transformation of the input data, and passes the transformed data to the next stage. But aggregation queries tend to become rather large for more complex computational problems, lack organization into re-usable pieces, and are thus hard to debug and maintain. We propose a new database querying language called Mongolog which is syntactically a subset of the Prolog language, and we define its operational semantics through translations into aggregation pipelines. To this end, we make use of and extend the formal framework of the MQuery language which characterizes the aggregation framework set-theoretically.

title: Prolog as a Querying Language for MongoDB
text: The increasing demand for data-intensive AI applications has driven the development of sophisticated querying languages in modern database systems, enabling them to support complex data processing tasks. Notably, certain SQL implementations have been shown to be Turing-complete, demonstrating the language's expressive power. In the realm of NoSQL databases, MongoDB has emerged as a widely adopted solution. Its query model relies on aggregation pipelines, where sequential stages perform data transformations, passing the output to subsequent stages. However, as computational problems escalate in complexity, aggregation queries tend to become unwieldy, lacking modularity and reusability, which hinders debugging and maintenance. To address this limitation, we introduce Mongolog, a novel querying language that leverages the expressive power of Prolog, while ensuring seamless integration with MongoDB through a formal framework that translates Mongolog queries into aggregation pipelines. Building upon the set-theoretic characterization of the MQuery language, we extend its formalism to define the operational semantics of Mongolog, thereby providing a robust and maintainable querying solution for complex data processing tasks.

title: Weakly Durable High-Performance Transactions
text: Existing disk-based database systems largely fall into two categories -- they either provide very high performance but few guarantees, or expose the transaction abstraction satisfying the full ACID guarantees at the cost of lower performance. In this paper, we present an alternative that achieves the best of both worlds, namely good performance and transactional properties. Our key observation is that, because of the frequent use of synchronization primitives, systems with strong durability can hardly utilize the extremely high parallelism granted by modern storage devices. Thus, we explore the notion of weakly durable transactions, and discuss how to safely relax durability without compromising other transactional properties. We present AciKV, a transactional system whose design is centered around weak durability. AciKV exposes to users the normal transactional interface, but what sets it apart from others is a new "persist" primitive that decouples durability from commit. AciKV is a middle ground between systems that perform fast atomic operations, and ones that support transactions; this middle ground is useful as it provides similar performance to the former, while prevents isolation and consistency anomalies like the latter. Our evaluation using the YCSB benchmark shows that AciKV, under workloads that involve write requests, exhibits more than two orders of magnitude higher throughput than existing strongly durable systems.

title: Weakly Durable High-Performance Transactions
text: The rise of distributed databases and cloud-based applications has led to a growing need for high-performance transactional systems that can efficiently process large volumes of concurrent requests. However, ensuring strong durability guarantees in these systems can come at the cost of reduced performance and availability. Weak durability, which relaxes the traditional notion of durability by allowing for a bounded number of writes to be lost in the event of a failure, has emerged as a promising approach to mitigate this tradeoff. In this context, we present a novel transactional protocol, dubbed WDTP, that leverages weak durability to achieve high performance while maintaining strong consistency guarantees. WDTP employs a hierarchical architecture, wherein a primary node executes transactions and maintains a durable log, while a set of secondary nodes replicate the log and execute read-only transactions. We introduce a novel write-back cache mechanism that enables the primary node to buffer writes and asynchronously replicate them to secondary nodes, thereby reducing the latency and overhead of durability enforcement. Our experimental evaluation, conducted on a 15-node cluster using the TPC-C benchmark, demonstrates that WDTP outperforms state-of-the-art transactional protocols, including Calvin and FaRM, by up to 2.5x in terms of throughput, while incurring a bounded loss of at most 5 writes in the event of a failure. We also conduct a thorough analytical modeling of WDTP, which reveals that our protocol achieves optimal throughput and latency under various system loads and failure scenarios.

title: Scalable Relational Query Processing on Big Matrix Data
text: The use of large-scale machine learning methods is becoming ubiquitous in many applications ranging from business intelligence to self-driving cars. These methods require a complex computation pipeline consisting of various types of operations, e.g., relational operations for pre-processing or post-processing the dataset, and matrix operations for core model computations. Many existing systems focus on efficiently processing matrix-only operations, and assume that the inputs to the relational operators are already pre-computed and are materialized as intermediate matrices. However, the input to a relational operator may be complex in machine learning pipelines, and may involve various combinations of matrix operators.
