Hence, it is critical to realize scalable and efficient relational query processors that directly operate on big matrix data. This paper presents new efficient and scalable relational query processing techniques on big matrix data for in-memory distributed clusters. The proposed techniques leverage algebraic transformation rules to rewrite query execution plans into ones with lower computation costs. A distributed query plan optimizer exploits the sparsity-inducing property of merge functions as well as Bloom join strategies for efficiently evaluating various flavors of the join operation. Furthermore, optimized partitioning schemes for the input matrices are developed to facilitate the performance of join operations based on a cost model that minimizes the communication overhead.The proposed relational query processing techniques are prototyped in Apache Spark. Experiments on both real and synthetic data demonstrate that the proposed techniques achieve up to two orders of magnitude performance improvement over state-of-the-art systems on a wide range of applications.

title: Scalable Relational Query Processing on Big Matrix Data
text: The proliferation of machine learning applications in diverse domains, from business intelligence to autonomous vehicles, relies heavily on complex computation pipelines that integrate various operations. These pipelines typically involve relational operations for data pre-processing and post-processing, as well as matrix operations for core model computations. While existing systems primarily focus on optimizing matrix-only operations, they often assume that inputs to relational operators are pre-computed and materialized as intermediate matrices. However, in machine learning pipelines, inputs to relational operators can be intricate, involving combinations of matrix operators. Therefore, it is essential to develop efficient and scalable relational query processors that can directly operate on large matrix data. This paper proposes novel relational query processing techniques for in-memory distributed clusters, which leverage algebraic transformation rules to rewrite query execution plans and minimize computation costs. A distributed query plan optimizer is designed to exploit the sparsity-inducing property of merge functions and Bloom join strategies, enabling efficient evaluation of various join operations. Additionally, optimized partitioning schemes for input matrices are developed to reduce communication overhead, based on a cost model that minimizes this overhead. The proposed techniques are implemented in Apache Spark, and experiments on real and synthetic data demonstrate performance improvements of up to two orders of magnitude over state-of-the-art systems across a wide range of applications.

title: Version Reconciliation for Collaborative Databases
text: We propose MindPalace, a prototype of a versioned database for efficient collaborative data management. MindPalace supports offline collaboration, where users work independently without real-time correspondence. The core of MindPalace is a critical step of offline collaboration: reconciling divergent branches made by simultaneous data manipulation. We formalize the concept of auto-mergeability, a condition under which branches may be reconciled without human intervention, and propose an efficient framework for determining whether two branches are auto-mergeable and identifying particular records for manual reconciliation.

title: Version Reconciliation for Collaborative Databases
text: Collaborative databases enable multiple users to concurrently modify shared data, but reconciling conflicting updates remains a challenging problem. We propose a novel version reconciliation framework that leverages a combination of operational transformation and conflict-free replicated data types. Our approach ensures consistency and convergence in the presence of network partitions and concurrent updates. Experimental evaluation on a real-world dataset demonstrates a significant reduction in reconciliation latency and improved data freshness compared to existing solutions.

title: Mobile authentication of copy detection patterns: how critical is to know fakes?
text: Protection of physical objects against counterfeiting is an important task for the modern economies. In recent years, the high-quality counterfeits appear to be closer to originals thanks to the rapid advancement of digital technologies. To combat these counterfeits, an anti-counterfeiting technology based on hand-crafted randomness implemented in a form of copy detection patterns (CDP) is proposed enabling a link between the physical and digital worlds and being used in various brand protection applications. The modern mobile phone technologies make the verification process of CDP easier and available to the end customers. Besides a big interest and attractiveness, the CDP authentication based on the mobile phone imaging remains insufficiently studied. In this respect, in this paper we aim at investigating the CDP authentication under the real-life conditions with the codes printed on an industrial printer and enrolled via a modern mobile phone under the regular light conditions. The authentication aspects of the obtained CDP are investigated with respect to the four types of copy fakes. The impact of fakes' type used for training of authentication classifier is studied in two scenarios: (i) supervised binary classification under various assumptions about the fakes and (ii) one-class classification under unknown fakes. The obtained results show that the modern machine-learning approaches and the technical capacity of modern mobile phones allow to make the CDP authentication under unknown fakes feasible with respect to the considered types of fakes and code design.

title: Mobile authentication of copy detection patterns: how critical is to know fakes?
text: The proliferation of mobile devices has led to an unprecedented rise in digital content creation and dissemination, rendering copy detection a crucial task to combat misinformation. Copy detection patterns, in particular, have emerged as a promising approach to identify duplicates in multimedia data. However, the authenticity of these patterns in mobile authentication scenarios remains a pressing concern. The ability to distinguish between genuine and fake patterns is critical, as fake patterns can be intentionally crafted to evade detection or inject malicious content. This study investigates the criticality of knowing fake copy detection patterns in mobile authentication. We propose a novel framework, MobileAuth, which integrates a pattern recognition module with a fake pattern detection mechanism. Our approach leverages a comprehensive dataset of 10,000 images, comprising 5,000 authentic and 5,000 fake patterns, to train a deep neural network-based classifier. The classifier achieves an accuracy of 96.5% in distinguishing between genuine and fake patterns. Experimental results on three popular mobile devices demonstrate that MobileAuth incurs an average latency of 0.35 seconds and energy overhead of 12.7% while maintaining a detection accuracy of 94.2%. We also conduct a user study involving 100 participants, which reveals that users can be deceived by fake patterns with a probability of 0.42, highlighting the importance of fake pattern detection in mobile authentication. Our findings have significant implications for the design of secure and efficient copy detection systems in mobile devices, emphasizing the need to prioritize fake pattern detection to prevent potential security breaches.

title: The Typed Graph Model -- a Supermodel for Model Management and Data Integration
text: In recent years, the Graph Model has become increasingly popular, especially in the application domain of social networks. The model has been semantically augmented with properties and labels attached to the graph elements. It is difficult to ensure data quality for the properties and the data structure because the model does not need a schema. In this paper, we propose a schema bound Typed Graph Model with properties and labels. These enhancements improve not only data quality but also the quality of graph analysis. The power of this model is provided by using hyper-nodes and hyper-edges, which allows to present data structures on different abstraction levels. We prove that the model is at least equivalent in expressive power to most popular data models. Therefore, it can be used as a supermodel for model management and data integration. We illustrate by example the superiority of this model over the property graph data model of Hidders and other prevalent data models, namely the relational, object-oriented, XML model, and RDF Schema.

title: The Typed Graph Model -- a Supermodel for Model Management and Data Integration
text: The prevalence of graph models in social network applications has led to the augmentation of graph elements with properties and labels, thereby introducing semantic richness. However, the schema-less nature of these models compromises data quality and structural integrity. To address this limitation, we introduce the Typed Graph Model, a schema-bound paradigm that incorporates properties and labels, thereby enhancing data quality and facilitating robust graph analysis. The model's expressiveness is attributed to the use of hyper-nodes and hyper-edges, which enable the representation of data structures across multiple abstraction levels. We formally demonstrate the model's equivalence in expressive power to prominent data models, including relational, object-oriented, XML, and RDF Schema models, as well as the property graph data model proposed by Hidders. The Typed Graph Model's versatility renders it an ideal candidate for model management and data integration, as exemplified by its superiority over existing models in a range of applications.

title: Data Validation for Big Live Data
text: Data Integration of heterogeneous data sources relies either on periodically transferring large amounts of data to a physical Data Warehouse or retrieving data from the sources on request only. The latter results in the creation of what is referred to as a virtual Data Warehouse, which is preferable when the use of the latest data is paramount. However, the downside is that it adds network traffic and suffers from performance degradation when the amount of data is high. In this paper, we propose the use of a readCheck validator to ensure the timeliness of the queried data and reduced data traffic. It is further shown that the readCheck allows transactions to update data in the data sources obeying full Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability (ACID) properties.

title: Data Validation for Big Live Data
text: Heterogeneous data integration typically employs one of two approaches: periodic bulk data transfer to a physical data warehouse or on-demand retrieval from sources, yielding a virtual data warehouse. The latter is preferred when up-to-date data is crucial, but it incurs increased network traffic and performance degradation with large datasets. We propose a readCheck validator to ensure timely data querying and reduce traffic. Notably, our approach enables transactions to update data sources while maintaining full adherence to Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability (ACID) properties, thereby guaranteeing reliable data integration. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our method in mitigating performance degradation and ensuring data freshness in virtual data warehouses.

title: Visualizing Trace Variants From Partially Ordered Event Data
text: Executing operational processes generates event data, which contain information on the executed process activities. Process mining techniques allow to systematically analyze event data to gain insights that are then used to optimize processes. Visual analytics for event data are essential for the application of process mining. Visualizing unique process executions -- also called trace variants, i.e., unique sequences of executed process activities -- is a common technique implemented in many scientific and industrial process mining applications. Most existing visualizations assume a total order on the executed process activities, i.e., these techniques assume that process activities are atomic and were executed at a specific point in time. In reality, however, the executions of activities are not atomic. Multiple timestamps are recorded for an executed process activity, e.g., a start-timestamp and a complete-timestamp. Therefore, the execution of process activities may overlap and, thus, cannot be represented as a total order if more than one timestamp is to be considered. In this paper, we present a visualization approach for trace variants that incorporates start- and complete-timestamps of activities.

title: Visualizing Trace Variants From Partially Ordered Event Data
text: The execution of operational processes yields event data, which inherently contains information about the process activities that have been performed. Process mining techniques enable the systematic analysis of such event data to gain valuable insights, ultimately informing process optimization strategies. Visual analytics play a crucial role in process mining, with the visualization of unique process executions, known as trace variants, being a prevalent approach in both academic and industrial settings. However, most existing visualization methods assume a total ordering of process activities, implying atomicity and instantaneous execution. In reality, process activities are non-atomic, with multiple timestamps, such as start and complete timestamps, often recorded for a single activity. This allows for the possibility of overlapping activity executions, rendering total ordering inadequate when multiple timestamps are considered. Our proposed visualization approach addresses this limitation by incorporating both start and complete timestamps, providing a more accurate representation of trace variants.

title: Phoebe: A Learning-based Checkpoint Optimizer
text: Easy-to-use programming interfaces paired with cloud-scale processing engines have enabled big data system users to author arbitrarily complex analytical jobs over massive volumes of data. However, as the complexity and scale of analytical jobs increase, they encounter a number of unforeseen problems, hotspots with large intermediate data on temporary storage, longer job recovery time after failures, and worse query optimizer estimates being examples of issues that we are facing at Microsoft. To address these issues, we propose Phoebe, an efficient learning-based checkpoint optimizer. Given a set of constraints and an objective function at compile-time, Phoebe is able to determine the decomposition of job plans, and the optimal set of checkpoints to preserve their outputs to durable global storage. Phoebe consists of three machine learning predictors and one optimization module. For each stage of a job, Phoebe makes accurate predictions for: (1) the execution time, (2) the output size, and (3) the start/end time taking into account the inter-stage dependencies. Using these predictions, we formulate checkpoint optimization as an integer programming problem and propose a scalable heuristic algorithm that meets the latency requirement of the production environment. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Phoebe in production workloads, and show that we can free the temporary storage on hotspots by more than 70% and restart failed jobs 68% faster on average with minimum performance impact. Phoebe also illustrates that adding multiple sets of checkpoints is not cost-efficient, which dramatically reduces the complexity of the optimization.

title: Phoebe: A Learning-based Checkpoint Optimizer
text: Checkpointing is a ubiquitous technique in database systems and scientific simulations to ensure fault tolerance and reduce the overhead of failures. However, the frequency and placement of checkpoints significantly impact the performance and resource utilization of these systems. Existing checkpoint optimizers rely on heuristics, static analysis, or manual tuning, which often lead to suboptimal performance. We propose Phoebe, a learning-based checkpoint optimizer that leverages machine learning to adaptively determine the optimal checkpointing strategy for a given workload. Phoebe uses a novel combination of online learning and offline training to minimize the overhead of checkpointing while meeting the desired recovery time objectives. Our approach involves training a deep neural network to predict the optimal checkpoint interval based on workload characteristics, system resources, and failure patterns. We evaluate Phoebe using a diverse set of benchmarks, including TPC-C, TPC-H, and scientific simulations, on a distributed database system. Our results show that Phoebe outperforms state-of-the-art checkpoint optimizers by up to 35% in terms of throughput and reduces the recovery time by up to 50%. We also demonstrate the robustness of Phoebe under varying workload and failure patterns. Our analysis reveals that Phoebe's adaptive checkpointing strategy can effectively balance the trade-off between performance and reliability. The key contributions of this work include the design and implementation of Phoebe, a novel learning-based checkpoint optimizer, and a thorough evaluation of its effectiveness in real-world scenarios. Our approach has implications for a wide range of applications, from high-performance computing to cloud-based database systems, where fault tolerance and performance are critical.

title: How to Query An Oracle? Efficient Strategies to Label Data
text: We consider the basic problem of querying an expert oracle for labeling a dataset in machine learning. This is typically an expensive and time consuming process and therefore, we seek ways to do so efficiently. The conventional approach involves comparing each sample with (the representative of) each class to find a match. In a setting with $N$ equally likely classes, this involves $N/2$ pairwise comparisons (queries per sample) on average. We consider a $k$-ary query scheme with $k\ge 2$ samples in a query that identifies (dis)similar items in the set while effectively exploiting the associated transitive relations. We present a randomized batch algorithm that operates on a round-by-round basis to label the samples and achieves a query rate of $O(\frac{N}{k^2})$. In addition, we present an adaptive greedy query scheme, which achieves an average rate of $\approx 0.2N$ queries per sample with triplet queries. For the proposed algorithms, we investigate the query rate performance analytically and with simulations. Empirical studies suggest that each triplet query takes an expert at most 50\% more time compared with a pairwise query, indicating the effectiveness of the proposed $k$-ary query schemes. We generalize the analyses to nonuniform class distributions when possible.

title: How to Query An Oracle? Efficient Strategies to Label Data
text: The problem of querying an expert oracle for dataset labeling in machine learning is inherently costly and time-consuming, necessitating efficient solutions. Conventional approaches rely on pairwise comparisons between each sample and class representatives, resulting in an average of N/2 queries per sample for N equally likely classes. We propose a novel k-ary query scheme, where k ≥ 2 samples are batched in a single query, effectively leveraging transitive relations to identify (dis)similar items. Our randomized batch algorithm operates in a round-by-round manner, achieving a query rate of O(N/k^2). Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive greedy query scheme, which attains an average rate of approximately 0.2N queries per sample using triplet queries. We provide analytical and simulated evaluations of the query rate performance for both algorithms. Empirical studies reveal that triplet queries require at most 50% more time from experts compared to pairwise queries, demonstrating the efficacy of our k-ary query schemes. We also extend our analyses to accommodate nonuniform class distributions whenever possible.

title: Simulation of Derivatives Post-Trade Services using an Authoritative Data Store and the ISDA Common Domain Model
text: In this paper, we present a summary of the design and implementation of a simulation of post-trade services for interest rate swaps, from execution to maturity. We use an authoritative data store (ADS) and the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA) Common Domain Model (CDM) to simulate a potential future architecture. We start by providing a brief overview of the CDM and the lifecycle of an interest rate swap. We then compare our simulated future state architecture with a typical current state architecture. Next, we present the key requirements of the simulated system, several suitable design patterns, and a summary of the implementation. The simulation uses the CDM to address the industry problems of inconsistent processes and inconsistent data, and an authoritative data store to address the industry problem of duplicated data.

title: Simulation of Derivatives Post-Trade Services using an Authoritative Data Store and the ISDA Common Domain Model
text: This study outlines the design and implementation of a post-trade services simulation for interest rate swaps, encompassing the entire lifecycle from execution to maturity. Leveraging the International Swaps and Derivatives Association's (ISDA) Common Domain Model (CDM) and an authoritative data store (ADS), we propose a future architecture for mitigating industry-wide challenges. The CDM, which standardizes the swap lifecycle, is introduced, followed by a comparative analysis of our simulated future state architecture with its current state counterpart. The system's key requirements, applicable design patterns, and implementation summary are subsequently presented. By harnessing the CDM and ADS, our simulation tackles the pervasive issues of inconsistent processes, data, and duplication, offering a promising solution for the industry.

title: Reconsidering Optimistic Algorithms for Relational DBMS
text: At DBKDA 2019, we demonstrated that StrongDBMS with simple but rigorous optimistic algorithms, provides better performance in situations of high concurrency than major commercial database management systems (DBMS). The demonstration was convincing but the reasons for its success were not fully analysed. There is a brief account of the results below. In this short contribution, we wish to discuss the reasons for the results. The analysis leads to a strong criticism of all DBMS algorithms based on locking, and based on these results, it is not fanciful to suggest that it is time to re-engineer existing DBMS.

title: Reconsidering Optimistic Algorithms for Relational DBMS
text: High-concurrency performance of StrongDBMS, a system employing optimistic algorithms, surpassed that of prominent commercial database management systems (DBMS) at DBKDA 2019. Although the demonstration was compelling, the underlying factors contributing to its success remained largely unexplored. This study delves into the analysis of these results, revealing inherent limitations of locking-based DBMS algorithms. Our findings warrant a critical reevaluation of existing DBMS designs, suggesting a pressing need for re-engineering to improve concurrency performance in modern database systems.

title: An Event Data Extraction Approach from SAP ERP for Process Mining
text: The extraction, transformation, and loading of event logs from information systems is the first and the most expensive step in process mining. In particular, extracting event logs from popular ERP systems such as SAP poses major challenges, given the size and the structure of the data. Open-source support for ETL is scarce, while commercial process mining vendors maintain connectors to ERP systems supporting ETL of a limited number of business processes in an ad-hoc manner. In this paper, we propose an approach to facilitate event data extraction from SAP ERP systems. In the proposed approach, we store event data in the format of object-centric event logs that efficiently describe executions of business processes supported by ERP systems. To evaluate the feasibility of the proposed approach, we have developed a tool implementing it and conducted case studies with a real-life SAP ERP system.

title: An Event Data Extraction Approach from SAP ERP for Process Mining
text: Event log extraction, transformation, and loading (ETL) from information systems is a crucial yet resource-intensive precursor to process mining, with significant hurdles posed by popular enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems like SAP due to their vast and complex data structures. The scarcity of open-source ETL support and commercial vendors' limited, ad-hoc connectors for ERP systems underscore the need for a more comprehensive solution. This paper presents a novel approach to facilitate event data extraction from SAP ERP systems, leveraging object-centric event logs that efficiently capture business process executions. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach through a proof-of-concept tool and case studies conducted on a real-life SAP ERP system, showcasing its potential to streamline ETL for process mining applications.

title: Workload-Aware Materialization of Junction Trees
text: Bayesian networks are popular probabilistic models that capture the conditional dependencies among a set of variables. Inference in Bayesian networks is a fundamental task for answering probabilistic queries over a subset of variables in the data. However, exact inference in Bayesian networks is \NP-hard, which has prompted the development of many practical inference methods. In this paper, we focus on improving the performance of the junction-tree algorithm, a well-known method for exact inference in Bayesian networks. In particular, we seek to leverage information in the workload of probabilistic queries to obtain an optimal workload-aware materialization of junction trees, with the aim to accelerate the processing of inference queries. We devise an optimal pseudo-polynomial algorithm to tackle this problem and discuss approximation schemes. Compared to state-of-the-art approaches for efficient processing of inference queries via junction trees, our methods are the first to exploit the information provided in query workloads. Our experimentation on several real-world Bayesian networks confirms the effectiveness of our techniques in speeding-up query processing.

title: Workload-Aware Materialization of Junction Trees
text: Optimizing query performance is crucial in large-scale data analytics, where complex queries are executed over massive datasets. Junction trees, a key data structure in probabilistic graphical models, play a vital role in inference and learning tasks. However, materializing junction trees can be computationally expensive, especially when dealing with large models and datasets. In this context, we propose a workload-aware materialization approach that considers the query workload and available computational resources to optimize junction tree materialization. Our approach leverages a cost model that estimates the materialization cost of each junction tree and a query-aware optimization framework that selects the most beneficial trees to materialize. We evaluate our approach on real-world datasets using various query workloads and demonstrate significant performance improvements compared to existing methods. Our results show that our approach achieves up to 3.5x speedup in query execution time and reduces memory usage by up to 40% while maintaining accuracy. The proposed approach can be applied to various applications, including probabilistic inference, machine learning, and data analytics.

title: Symbolic Register Automata for Complex Event Recognition and Forecasting
text: We propose an automaton model which is a combination of symbolic and register automata, i.e., we enrich symbolic automata with memory. We call such automata Symbolic Register Automata (SRA). SRA extend the expressive power of symbolic automata, by allowing Boolean formulas to be applied not only to the last element read from the input string, but to multiple elements, stored in their registers. SRA also extend register automata, by allowing arbitrary Boolean formulas, besides equality predicates. We study the closure properties of SRA under union, intersection, concatenation, Kleene closure, complement and determinization and show that SRA, contrary to symbolic automata, are not in general closed under complement and they are not determinizable. However, they are closed under these operations when a window operator, quintessential in Complex Event Recognition, is used. We show how SRA can be used in Complex Event Recognition in order to detect patterns upon streams of events, using our framework that provides declarative and compositional semantics, and that allows for a systematic treatment of such automata. We also show how the behavior of SRA, as they consume streams of events, can be given a probabilistic description with the help of prediction suffix trees. This allows us to go one step beyond Complex Event Recognition to Complex Event Forecasting, where, besides detecting complex patterns, we can also efficiently forecast their occurrence.

title: Symbolic Register Automata for Complex Event Recognition and Forecasting
text: We introduce Symbolic Register Automata (SRA), a novel automaton model that integrates the expressiveness of symbolic automata with the memory capabilities of register automata. By augmenting symbolic automata with registers, SRA enable the application of Boolean formulas to multiple input elements, thereby expanding their expressive power. In contrast to register automata, SRA support arbitrary Boolean formulas, beyond mere equality predicates. Our investigation reveals that SRA exhibit distinct closure properties under various operations, including union, intersection, concatenation, Kleene closure, and determinization. Notably, SRA are not closed under complementation and determinization in general, but these limitations can be overcome by incorporating a window operator, a crucial component in Complex Event Recognition. We demonstrate the efficacy of SRA in Complex Event Recognition, leveraging their declarative and compositional semantics to detect patterns in event streams. Furthermore, we show that the behavior of SRA can be probabilistically characterized using prediction suffix trees, enabling the transition from Complex Event Recognition to Complex Event Forecasting, where complex patterns can be both detected and efficiently predicted.

title: Graph Neural Networks in Real-Time Fraud Detection with Lambda Architecture
text: Transaction checkout fraud detection is an essential risk control components for E-commerce marketplaces. In order to leverage graph networks to decrease fraud rate efficiently and guarantee the information flow passed through neighbors only from the past of the checkouts, we first present a novel Directed Dynamic Snapshot (DDS) linkage design for graph construction and a Lambda Neural Networks (LNN) architecture for effective inference with Graph Neural Networks embeddings. Experiments show that our LNN on DDS graph, outperforms baseline models significantly and is computational efficient for real-time fraud detection.

title: Graph Neural Networks in Real-Time Fraud Detection with Lambda Architecture
text: The proliferation of online transactions has necessitated the development of efficient fraud detection systems. We propose a novel approach leveraging graph neural networks (GNNs) within a Lambda architecture to facilitate real-time fraud detection. Our system exploits the graph structure of transactional data to learn intricate patterns, enabling accurate anomaly detection. Experimental results on a large-scale dataset demonstrate a 32% reduction in false positives and a 25% increase in fraud detection rate compared to traditional machine learning approaches, while maintaining a latency of under 10ms per transaction.

title: Provenance in Temporal Interaction Networks
text: In temporal interaction networks, vertices correspond to entities, which exchange data quantities (e.g., money, bytes, messages) over time. Tracking the origin of data that have reached a given vertex at any time can help data analysts to understand the reasons behind the accumulated quantity at the vertex or behind the interactions between entities. In this paper, we study data provenance in a temporal interaction network. We investigate alternative propagation models that may apply to different application scenarios. For each such model, we propose annotation mechanisms that track the origin of propagated data in the network and the routes of data quantities. Besides analyzing the space and time complexity of these mechanisms, we propose techniques that reduce their cost in practice, by either (i) limiting provenance tracking to a subset of vertices or groups of vertices, or (ii) tracking provenance only for quantities that were generated in the near past or limiting the provenance data in each vertex by a budget constraint. Our experimental evaluation on five real datasets shows that quantity propagation models based on generation time or receipt order scale well on large graphs; on the other hand, a model that propagates quantities proportionally has high space and time requirements and can benefit from the aforementioned cost reduction techniques.

title: Provenance in Temporal Interaction Networks
text: Temporal interaction networks, which model complex relationships between entities over time, have become ubiquitous in various domains, including social media, recommender systems, and epidemiology. However, the lack of provenance information in these networks hinders our ability to understand the origins and evolution of interactions, making it challenging to identify biases, ensure accountability, and maintain transparency. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach to provenance in temporal interaction networks, focusing on the capture, representation, and querying of provenance information. Our methodology leverages a combination of graph-based data models and temporal databases to efficiently store and process provenance metadata. We introduce a set of provenance-aware query operators that enable the retrieval of interaction sequences, influence paths, and temporal dependencies. Our experimental evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach, achieving a significant reduction in query latency and an increase in data freshness compared to existing solutions. Furthermore, we apply our provenance framework to a case study on misinformation diffusion, illustrating its potential to uncover hidden relationships and identify key actors in the propagation of false information. Our work contributes to the development of transparent and trustworthy temporal interaction networks, with implications for a broad range of applications, from social network analysis to digital forensics.

title: Precision and Fitness in Object-Centric Process Mining
text: Traditional process mining considers only one single case notion and discovers and analyzes models based on this. However, a single case notion is often not a realistic assumption in practice. Multiple case notions might interact and influence each other in a process. Object-centric process mining introduces the techniques and concepts to handle multiple case notions. So far, such event logs have been standardized and novel process model discovery techniques were proposed. However, notions for evaluating the quality of a model are missing. These are necessary to enable future research on improving object-centric discovery and providing an objective evaluation of model quality. In this paper, we introduce a notion for the precision and fitness of an object-centric Petri net with respect to an object-centric event log. We give a formal definition and accompany this with an example. Furthermore, we provide an algorithm to calculate these quality measures. We discuss our precision and fitness notion based on an event log with different models. Our precision and fitness notions are an appropriate way to generalize quality measures to the object-centric setting since we are able to consider multiple case notions, their dependencies and their interactions.

title: Precision and Fitness in Object-Centric Process Mining
text: Process mining has emerged as a crucial technique for analyzing and improving business processes, but traditional approaches often struggle to accurately capture the complexities of real-world systems. Object-centric process mining, which focuses on the interactions between objects and activities, offers a promising solution. However, existing methods in this domain typically sacrifice precision for fitness, or vice versa, leading to incomplete or inaccurate process models. This paper proposes a novel approach that simultaneously optimizes precision and fitness in object-centric process mining. We develop a probabilistic framework that leverages Bayesian networks to model the relationships between objects, activities, and events. Our approach is evaluated on a comprehensive dataset of 15 real-world processes, demonstrating significant improvements in both precision (up to 23%) and fitness (up to 35%) compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we conduct a thorough sensitivity analysis to investigate the robustness of our approach under varying noise levels and data quality. The results suggest that our method is resilient to noisy data and can effectively handle missing or incomplete information. Overall, our work contributes to the development of more accurate and reliable process models, enabling organizations to make informed decisions and drive business improvement.

title: Fallout: Distributed Systems Testing as a Service
text: All modern distributed systems list performance and scalability as their core strengths. Given that optimal performance requires carefully selecting configuration options, and typical cluster sizes can range anywhere from 2 to 300 nodes, it is rare for any two clusters to be exactly the same. Validating the behavior and performance of distributed systems in this large configuration space is challenging without automation that stretches across the software stack. In this paper we present Fallout, an open-source distributed systems testing service that automatically provisions and configures distributed systems and clients, supports running a variety of workloads and benchmarks, and generates performance reports based on collected metrics for visual analysis. We have been running the Fallout service internally at DataStax for over 5 years and have recently open sourced it to support our work with Apache Cassandra, Pulsar, and other open source projects. We describe the architecture of Fallout along with the evolution of its design and the lessons we learned operating this service in a dynamic environment where teams work on different products and favor different benchmarking tools.

title: Fallout: Distributed Systems Testing as a Service
text: The efficacy of modern distributed systems hinges on their ability to balance performance and scalability. However, the vast configuration space arising from varying cluster sizes (2-300 nodes) and diverse performance optimization strategies renders manual validation of system behavior and performance impractical. Automated testing that spans the entire software stack is essential to address this challenge. We introduce Fallout, an open-source distributed systems testing service that automates provisioning, configuration, and benchmarking of distributed systems and clients. Fallout supports a range of workloads and benchmarks, generating comprehensive performance reports with visual analytics. Following five years of internal deployment at DataStax, we have open-sourced Fallout to facilitate collaboration with Apache Cassandra, Pulsar, and other open-source projects. This paper presents the Fallout architecture, its design evolution, and the insights gleaned from operating this service in a dynamic, multi-product environment with diverse benchmarking preferences.

title: Communication-Efficient Triangle Counting under Local Differential Privacy
text: Triangle counting in networks under LDP (Local Differential Privacy) is a fundamental task for analyzing connection patterns or calculating a clustering coefficient while strongly protecting sensitive friendships from a central server. In particular, a recent study proposes an algorithm for this task that uses two rounds of interaction between users and the server to significantly reduce estimation error. However, this algorithm suffers from a prohibitively high communication cost due to a large noisy graph each user needs to download. In this work, we propose triangle counting algorithms under LDP with a small estimation error and communication cost. We first propose two-rounds algorithms consisting of edge sampling and carefully selecting edges each user downloads so that the estimation error is small. Then we propose a double clipping technique, which clips the number of edges and then the number of noisy triangles, to significantly reduce the sensitivity of each user's query. Through comprehensive evaluation, we show that our algorithms dramatically reduce the communication cost of the existing algorithm, e.g., from 6 hours to 8 seconds or less at a 20 Mbps download rate, while keeping a small estimation error.

title: Communication-Efficient Triangle Counting under Local Differential Privacy
text: The problem of triangle counting in networks under Local Differential Privacy (LDP) is crucial for analyzing connection patterns and calculating clustering coefficients while safeguarding sensitive relationships from a central server. Recently, a two-round interactive algorithm has been proposed to achieve this task with reduced estimation error. However, this approach incurs a prohibitively high communication overhead due to the large noisy graphs that users must download. To address this limitation, we present novel triangle counting algorithms under LDP that strike a balance between estimation accuracy and communication efficiency. Our approach involves edge sampling and strategic edge selection to minimize the number of edges downloaded by each user, thereby reducing estimation error. Additionally, we introduce a double clipping technique that restricts the number of edges and noisy triangles, significantly diminishing the sensitivity of user queries. Through rigorous evaluation, we demonstrate that our algorithms drastically reduce the communication cost of existing methods, achieving speedups of up to three orders of magnitude (e.g., from 6 hours to 8 seconds or less at 20 Mbps) while maintaining a small estimation error.

title: Recommending POIs for Tourists by User Behavior Modeling and Pseudo-Rating
text: POI recommendation is a key task in tourism information systems. However, in contrast to conventional point of interest (POI) recommender systems, the available data is extremely sparse; most tourist visit a few sightseeing spots once and most of these spots have no check-in data from new tourists. Most conventional systems rank sightseeing spots based on their popularity, reputations, and category-based similarities with users' preferences. They do not clarify what users can experience in these spots, which makes it difficult to meet diverse tourism needs. To this end, in this work, we propose a mechanism to recommend POIs to tourists. Our mechanism include two components: one is a probabilistic model that reveals the user behaviors in tourism; the other is a pseudo rating mechanism to handle the cold-start issue in POIs recommendations. We carried out extensive experiments with two datasets collected from Flickr. The experimental results demonstrate that our methods are superior to the state-of-the-art methods in both the recommendation performances (precision, recall and F-measure) and fairness. The experimental results also validate the robustness of the proposed methods, i.e., our methods can handle well the issue of data sparsity.

title: Recommending POIs for Tourists by User Behavior Modeling and Pseudo-Rating
text: The proliferation of location-based services has generated an unprecedented amount of user-generated data, providing valuable insights into tourist behavior. However, existing point of interest (POI) recommendation systems largely rely on explicit ratings, which are often scarce and unreliable. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that leverages user behavior modeling and pseudo-ratings to recommend POIs for tourists. Our method integrates a probabilistic matrix factorization framework with a Markov chain model to capture the sequential dependencies in user behavior, thereby generating high-quality pseudo-ratings. We evaluate our approach on a large-scale dataset of tourist trajectories, comprising over 10,000 users and 5,000 POIs. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 21.4% improvement in precision and a 17.9% improvement in recall. Furthermore, we observe that our approach is particularly effective for cold-start users and POIs, where explicit ratings are scarce. Our findings have significant implications for the development of personalized tourism services, enabling tourists to discover hidden gems and experience authentic local culture.

title: Finding Materialized Models for Model Reuse
text: Materialized model query aims to find the most appropriate materialized model as the initial model for model reuse. It is the precondition of model reuse, and has recently attracted much attention. {Nonetheless, the existing methods suffer from the need to provide source data, limited range of applications, and inefficiency since they do not construct a suitable metric to measure the target-related knowledge of materialized models. To address this, we present \textsf{MMQ}, a source-data free, general, efficient, and effective materialized model query framework.} It uses a Gaussian mixture-based metric called separation degree to rank materialized models. For each materialized model, \textsf{MMQ} first vectorizes the samples in the target dataset into probability vectors by directly applying this model, then utilizes Gaussian distribution to fit for each class of probability vectors, and finally uses separation degree on the Gaussian distributions to measure the target-related knowledge of the materialized model. Moreover, we propose an improved \textsf{MMQ} (\textsf{I-MMQ}), which significantly reduces the query time while retaining the query performance of \textsf{MMQ}. Extensive experiments on a range of practical model reuse workloads demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of \textsf{MMQ}.

title: Finding Materialized Models for Model Reuse
text: The quest for the optimal materialized model to initiate model reuse hinges on the efficacy of materialized model query, a crucial precursor that has garnered significant attention of late. However, existing methods are beset by limitations, including the requirement for source data, restricted applicability, and inefficiency stemming from the lack of a suitable metric to quantify the target-related knowledge embodied in materialized models. To overcome these hurdles, we introduce MMQ, a novel framework that enables source-data-free, general, efficient, and effective materialized model querying. By leveraging a Gaussian mixture-based separation degree metric, MMQ ranks materialized models according to their target-related knowledge. Specifically, MMQ vectorizes target dataset samples into probability vectors using each materialized model, fits Gaussian distributions to these vectors, and calculates the separation degree to quantify target-related knowledge. We further propose I-MMQ, an optimized variant that significantly reduces query time while preserving MMQ's performance. Comprehensive experiments on diverse model reuse workloads empirically validate the efficacy and efficiency of MMQ.

title: Reverse Maximum Inner Product Search: How to efficiently find users who would like to buy my item?
text: The MIPS (maximum inner product search), which finds the item with the highest inner product with a given query user, is an essential problem in the recommendation field. It is usual that e-commerce companies face situations where they want to promote and sell new or discounted items. In these situations, we have to consider a question: who are interested in the items and how to find them? This paper answers this question by addressing a new problem called reverse maximum inner product search (reverse MIPS). Given a query vector and two sets of vectors (user vectors and item vectors), the problem of reverse MIPS finds a set of user vectors whose inner product with the query vector is the maximum among the query and item vectors. Although the importance of this problem is clear, its straightforward implementation incurs a computationally expensive cost. We therefore propose Simpfer, a simple, fast, and exact algorithm for reverse MIPS. In an offline phase, Simpfer builds a simple index that maintains a lower-bound of the maximum inner product. By exploiting this index, Simpfer judges whether the query vector can have the maximum inner product or not, for a given user vector, in a constant time. Besides, our index enables filtering user vectors, which cannot have the maximum inner product with the query vector, in a batch. We theoretically demonstrate that Simpfer outperforms baselines employing state-of-the-art MIPS techniques. Furthermore, our extensive experiments on real datasets show that Simpfer is at least two orders magnitude faster than the baselines.

title: Reverse Maximum Inner Product Search: How to efficiently find users who would like to buy my item?
text: The maximum inner product search (MIPS) is a fundamental problem in recommendation systems, where the goal is to identify the item with the highest inner product with a given query user. In e-commerce applications, promoting new or discounted items necessitates identifying interested users, giving rise to the reverse maximum inner product search (reverse MIPS) problem. This problem involves finding a set of user vectors whose inner product with a query vector is maximum among both user and item vectors. Despite its importance, a naive implementation of reverse MIPS is computationally prohibitive. To address this, we propose Simpfer, a fast, exact, and simple algorithm for reverse MIPS. Simpfer builds a lower-bound index in an offline phase, enabling it to determine in constant time whether a user vector can achieve the maximum inner product with a query vector. This index also facilitates batch filtering of user vectors that cannot attain the maximum inner product. We provide theoretical guarantees of Simpfer's superiority over baselines employing state-of-the-art MIPS techniques. Moreover, our comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that Simpfer outperforms baselines by at least two orders of magnitude in terms of speed.

title: Fast Data Series Indexing for In-Memory Data
text: Data series similarity search is a core operation for several data series analysis applications across many different domains. However, the state-of-the-art techniques fail to deliver the time performance required for interactive exploration, or analysis of large data series collections. In this work, we propose MESSI, the first data series index designed for in-memory operation on modern hardware. Our index takes advantage of the modern hardware parallelization opportunities (i.e., SIMD instructions, multi-socket and multi-core architectures), in order to accelerate both index construction and similarity search processing times. Moreover, it benefits from a careful design in the setup and coordination of the parallel workers and data structures, so that it maximizes its performance for in-memory operations. MESSI supports similarity search using both the Euclidean and Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) distances. Our experiments with synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that overall MESSI is up to 4x faster at index construction, and up to 11x faster at query answering than the state-of-the-art parallel approach. MESSI is the first to answer exact similarity search queries on 100GB datasets in ~50msec (30-75msec across diverse datasets), which enables real-time, interactive data exploration on very large data series collections.

title: Fast Data Series Indexing for In-Memory Data
text: The quest for efficient data series similarity search has become a pressing concern across various domains, as existing techniques struggle to provide the necessary time performance for interactive exploration and large-scale data analysis. To bridge this gap, we introduce MESSI, a novel data series index optimized for in-memory operation on modern hardware. By leveraging parallelization opportunities afforded by modern hardware, including SIMD instructions, multi-socket, and multi-core architectures, MESSI achieves significant acceleration in both index construction and similarity search processing times. A carefully designed setup and coordination of parallel workers and data structures enable MESSI to maximize its performance for in-memory operations. Supporting similarity search using both Euclidean and Dynamic Time Warping distances, our index demonstrates remarkable speedups in experiments with synthetic and real datasets. Notably, MESSI outperforms the state-of-the-art parallel approach by up to 4x in index construction and 11x in query answering, and enables real-time, interactive data exploration on large datasets by answering exact similarity search queries on 100GB datasets in approximately 50msec (30-75msec across diverse datasets).

title: Improving overlay maps of science: combining overview and detail
text: Overlay maps of science are global base maps over which subsets of publications can be projected. Such maps can be used to monitor, explore, and study research through its publication output. Most maps of science, including overlay maps, are flat in the sense that they visualize research fields at one single level. Such maps generally fail to provide both overview and detail about the research being analyzed. The aim of this study is to improve overlay maps of science to provide both features in a single visualization. I created a map based on a hierarchical classification of publications, including broad disciplines for overview and more granular levels to incorporate detailed information. The classification was obtained by clustering articles in a citation network of about 17 million publication records in PubMed from 1995 onwards. The map emphasizes the hierarchical structure of the classification by visualizing both disciplines and the underlying specialties. To show how the visualization methodology can help getting both overview of research and detailed information about its topical structure, I projected two overlay maps onto the base map: (1) open access publishing and (2) coronavirus/Covid-19 research.

title: Improving overlay maps of science: combining overview and detail
text: The proliferation of scientific literature has led to an explosion of data, rendering traditional methods of knowledge discovery and visualization inadequate. Overlay maps of science, which integrate multiple datasets to provide a comprehensive understanding of the scientific landscape, have emerged as a promising solution. However, existing approaches often sacrifice either overview or detail, limiting their utility. We propose a novel methodology that combines the strengths of both, yielding a more informative and scalable overlay map. Our approach leverages a hybrid clustering algorithm that incorporates both hierarchical and density-based techniques to identify meaningful patterns at multiple resolutions. We then employ a graph-based visualization framework that adaptively adjusts the level of detail in response to user interactions. Evaluations on a large-scale dataset of scientific publications demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both clustering quality and visualization effectiveness. Specifically, our method achieves a 25% improvement in clustering purity and a 30% reduction in visual clutter compared to existing techniques. The resulting overlay map provides a more nuanced understanding of the complex relationships between scientific domains, facilitating more effective knowledge discovery and exploration.

title: A Survey on State-of-the-art Techniques for Knowledge Graphs Construction and Challenges ahead
text: Global datasphere is increasing fast, and it is expected to reach 175 Zettabytes by 20251 . However, most of the content is unstructured and is not understandable by machines. Structuring this data into a knowledge graph enables multitudes of intelligent applications such as deep question answering, recommendation systems, semantic search, etc. The knowledge graph is an emerging technology that allows logical reasoning and uncovers new insights using content along with the context. Thereby, it provides necessary syntax and reasoning semantics that enable machines to solve complex healthcare, security, financial institutions, economics, and business problems. As an outcome, enterprises are putting their effort into constructing and maintaining knowledge graphs to support various downstream applications. Manual approaches are too expensive. Automated schemes can reduce the cost of building knowledge graphs up to 15-250 times. This paper critiques state-of-the-art automated techniques to produce knowledge graphs of near-human quality autonomously. Additionally, it highlights different research issues that need to be addressed to deliver high-quality knowledge graphs

title: A Survey on State-of-the-art Techniques for Knowledge Graphs Construction and Challenges ahead
text: The proliferation of large-scale knowledge graphs has fueled numerous applications in artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and data mining. However, the construction of these graphs poses significant challenges, including data heterogeneity, entity disambiguation, and scalability. This survey provides a comprehensive review of state-of-the-art techniques for knowledge graph construction, categorizing them into three primary approaches: entity-centric, relation-centric, and hybrid methods. We analyze the strengths and limitations of each approach, highlighting their applicability to diverse domains and data sources. Our methodology involves a systematic review of 120 research articles published in top-tier conferences and journals between 2015 and 2022, identifying key trends, and knowledge gaps. The survey reveals that while significant progress has been made in addressing the challenges of knowledge graph construction, several open issues remain, including the lack of standardized evaluation metrics, limited scalability, and inadequate handling of dynamic data. We conclude by outlining future research directions, emphasizing the need for interdisciplinary approaches to overcome the challenges ahead in knowledge graph construction.

title: A Static Analysis Framework for Data Science Notebooks
text: Notebooks provide an interactive environment for programmers to develop code, analyse data and inject interleaved visualizations in a single environment. Despite their flexibility, a major pitfall that data scientists encounter is unexpected behaviour caused by the unique out-of-order execution model of notebooks. As a result, data scientists face various challenges ranging from notebook correctness, reproducibility and cleaning. In this paper, we propose a framework that performs static analysis on notebooks, incorporating their unique execution semantics. Our framework is general in the sense that it accommodate for a wide range of analyses, useful for various notebook use cases. We have instantiated our framework on a diverse set of analyses and have evaluated them on 2211 real world notebooks. Our evaluation demonstrates that the vast majority (98.7%) of notebooks can be analysed in less than a second, well within the time frame required by interactive notebook clients

title: A Static Analysis Framework for Data Science Notebooks
text: The flexibility of notebooks, which integrate code development, data analysis, and visualization, is tempered by the challenges posed by their out-of-order execution model. This paradigm can lead to unexpected behavior, compromising notebook correctness, reproducibility, and cleanliness. To address these issues, we present a static analysis framework that accommodates the unique execution semantics of notebooks, enabling a broad range of analyses tailored to diverse use cases. We instantiated our framework across multiple analyses and evaluated its performance on a corpus of 2211 real-world notebooks. The results demonstrate that our approach can efficiently analyze the vast majority (98.7%) of notebooks, with processing times under one second, well within the requirements of interactive notebook clients.

title: Hydra: A System for Large Multi-Model Deep Learning
text: Scaling up model depth and size is now a common approach to raise accuracy in many deep learning (DL) applications, as evidenced by the widespread success of multi-billion or even trillion parameter models in natural language processing (NLP) research. Despite success in DL research and at major technology companies, broader practical adoption of such large models among domain scientists and businesses is still bottlenecked by GPU memory limits, high training costs, and low GPU availability, even on public clouds. Model selection needs further compound these resource challenges: users often need to compare dozens of models with different hyper-parameters or neural architectures to suit their specific task and dataset. In this paper, we present Hydra, a system designed to tackle such challenges by enabling out-of-the-box scaling for multi-large-model DL workloads on even commodity GPUs in a resource-efficient manner. Hydra is the first approach to holistically optimize the execution of multi-model workloads for large DL models. We do this by adapting prior "model-parallel" execution schemes to work with scalable parameter offloading across the memory hierarchy and further hybridizing this approach with task-parallel job scheduling techniques. Hydra decouples scalability of model parameters from parallelism of execution, thus enabling DL users to train even a 6-billion parameter model on a single commodity GPU. It also fully exploits the speedup potential of task parallelism in multi-GPU setups, yielding near-linear strong scaling and making rigorous model selection perhaps more practical for such models. We evaluate end-to-end performance by fine-tuning GPT-2 for language modeling. We find that Hydra offers between 50% and 100% higher training throughput than even the best settings of state-of-the-art industrial frameworks such as DeepSpeed and GPipe for multi-large-model training.

title: Hydra: A System for Large Multi-Model Deep Learning
text: Deep learning has revolutionized numerous domains, but its adoption in large-scale settings is hindered by the limitations of existing training and deployment systems. These systems struggle to accommodate the complexity and diversity of modern deep learning models, leading to inefficient resource utilization, prolonged training times, and suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we present Hydra, a system designed to support large multi-model deep learning. Hydra's core innovation lies in its novel hierarchical architecture, which enables the seamless integration of multiple models, each with its own unique characteristics, into a unified framework. This allows Hydra to dynamically allocate resources, optimize data processing, and facilitate knowledge sharing across models. We propose a suite of algorithms that leverage Hydra's architecture to improve training efficiency, including a novel model-parallelism strategy and a data-aware scheduling mechanism. Our evaluation on a diverse set of deep learning workloads demonstrates Hydra's efficacy, achieving speedups of up to 5.2x compared to state-of-the-art systems. Furthermore, Hydra's ability to accommodate heterogeneous models enables the exploration of novel ensemble methods, resulting in significant accuracy improvements of up to 3.5% on several benchmark datasets. We also demonstrate Hydra's scalability by training a large-scale multi-model ensemble comprising 15 distinct models, showcasing its potential to support complex AI applications. By providing a flexible, efficient, and scalable platform for large multi-model deep learning, Hydra has the potential to transform the landscape of AI research and deployment.

title: Visualization of Real-time Displacement Time History superimposed with Dynamic Experiments using Wireless Smart Sensors (WSS) and Augmented Reality (AR)
text: Wireless Smart Sensors (WSS) process field data and inform structural engineers and owners about the infrastructure health and safety. In bridge engineering, inspectors make decisions using objective data from each bridge. They decide about repairs and replacements and prioritize the maintenance of certain structure elements on the basis of changes in displacements under loads. However, access to displacement information in the field and in real-time remains a challenge. Displacement data provided by WSS in the field undergoes additional processing and is seen at a different location by an inspector and a sensor specialist. When the data is shared and streamed to the field inspector, there is a inter-dependence between inspectors, sensor specialists, and infrastructure owners, which limits the actionability of the data related to the bridge condition. If inspectors were able to see structural displacements in real-time at the locations of interest, they could conduct additional observations, which would create a new, information-based, decision-making reality in the field. This paper develops a new, human-centered interface that provides inspectors with real-time access to actionable structural data (real-time displacements under loads) during inspection and monitoring enhanced by Augmented Reality (AR). It summarizes the development and validation of the new human-infrastructure interface and evaluates its efficiency through laboratory experiments. The experiments demonstrate that the interface accurately estimates dynamic displacements in comparison with the laser. Using this new AR interface tool, inspectors can observe and compare displacement data, share it across space and time, and visualize displacements in time history.

title: Visualization of Real-time Displacement Time History superimposed with Dynamic Experiments using Wireless Smart Sensors (WSS) and Augmented Reality (AR)
text: Real-time monitoring of structural displacements under load is crucial for informed decision-making in bridge engineering, yet accessing this data in the field remains a significant challenge. Currently, Wireless Smart Sensors (WSS) provide displacement data that undergoes additional processing before being viewed by inspectors and sensor specialists at a separate location, leading to interdependence among stakeholders and limiting the actionability of the data. This paper presents a novel, human-centered interface that empowers inspectors with real-time access to actionable structural data, including displacements under load, during inspection and monitoring, augmented by Augmented Reality (AR) technology. This innovative interface enables inspectors to conduct additional observations, fostering a data-driven decision-making paradigm in the field. We describe the development and validation of this human-infrastructure interface and evaluate its efficacy through laboratory experiments. Our results demonstrate that the interface accurately estimates dynamic displacements, comparable to laser measurements. By leveraging this AR interface tool, inspectors can observe, compare, and share displacement data across space and time, visualizing time histories of displacements, thereby revolutionizing the bridge inspection process.

title: Low-Precision Quantization for Efficient Nearest Neighbor Search
text: Fast k-Nearest Neighbor search over real-valued vector spaces (KNN) is an important algorithmic task for information retrieval and recommendation systems. We present a method for using reduced precision to represent vectors through quantized integer values, enabling both a reduction in the memory overhead of indexing these vectors and faster distance computations at query time. While most traditional quantization techniques focus on minimizing the reconstruction error between a point and its uncompressed counterpart, we focus instead on preserving the behavior of the underlying distance metric. Furthermore, our quantization approach is applied at the implementation level and can be combined with existing KNN algorithms. Our experiments on both open source and proprietary datasets across multiple popular KNN frameworks validate that quantized distance metrics can reduce memory by 60% and improve query throughput by 30%, while incurring only a 2% reduction in recall.

title: Low-Precision Quantization for Efficient Nearest Neighbor Search
text: An efficient k-Nearest Neighbor search in real-valued vector spaces is crucial for information retrieval and recommendation systems. We propose a novel approach that leverages reduced precision representations of vectors through quantized integer values, thereby reducing memory overhead and accelerating distance computations at query time. Unlike traditional quantization methods that prioritize reconstruction error minimization, our methodology focuses on preserving the intrinsic properties of the underlying distance metric. This implementation-level quantization strategy is compatible with existing KNN algorithms, enabling seamless integration. Experimental results on diverse datasets across popular KNN frameworks demonstrate that our quantized distance metrics achieve a 60% memory reduction and 30% query throughput improvement, while incurring a mere 2% recall degradation.

title: Fast and Exact Outlier Detection in Metric Spaces: A Proximity Graph-based Approach
text: Distance-based outlier detection is widely adopted in many fields, e.g., data mining and machine learning, because it is unsupervised, can be employed in a generic metric space, and does not have any assumptions of data distributions. Data mining and machine learning applications face a challenge of dealing with large datasets, which requires efficient distance-based outlier detection algorithms. Due to the popularization of computational environments with large memory, it is possible to build a main-memory index and detect outliers based on it, which is a promising solution for fast distance-based outlier detection. Motivated by this observation, we propose a novel approach that exploits a proximity graph. Our approach can employ an arbitrary proximity graph and obtains a significant speed-up against state-of-the-art. However, designing an effective proximity graph raises a challenge, because existing proximity graphs do not consider efficient traversal for distance-based outlier detection. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel proximity graph, MRPG. Our empirical study using real datasets demonstrates that MRPG detects outliers significantly faster than the state-of-the-art algorithms.

title: Fast and Exact Outlier Detection in Metric Spaces: A Proximity Graph-based Approach
text: The versatility of distance-based outlier detection has led to its widespread adoption in data mining and machine learning, owing to its unsupervised nature, applicability in generic metric spaces, and absence of assumptions regarding data distributions. However, the scalability of these algorithms becomes a critical issue when dealing with large datasets, a common challenge in data mining and machine learning applications. The increasing availability of computational environments with large memory capacities presents an opportunity to develop efficient distance-based outlier detection methods leveraging main-memory indexing. In this context, we propose a novel approach that utilizes a proximity graph to accelerate outlier detection. Our method is designed to accommodate arbitrary proximity graphs and demonstrates significant performance gains over state-of-the-art algorithms. We also introduce a novel proximity graph, MRPG, optimized for efficient traversal in distance-based outlier detection. Experimental evaluations on real datasets confirm that MRPG achieves substantial speedups in outlier detection compared to existing algorithms.

title: MetricHaven -- More Than 23,000 Metrics for Measuring Quality Attributes of Software Product Lines
text: Variability-aware metrics are designed to measure qualitative aspects of software product lines. As we identified in a prior SLR , there exist already many metrics that address code or variability separately, while the combination of both has been less researched. MetricHaven fills this gap, as it extensively supports combining information from code files and variability models. Further, we also enable the combination of well established single system metrics with novel variability-aware metrics, going beyond existing variability-aware metrics. Our tool supports most prominent single system and variability-aware code metrics. We provide configuration support for already implemented metrics, resulting in 23,342 metric variations. Further, we present an abstract syntax tree developed for MetricHaven, that allows the realization of additional code metrics. Tool: Video:

title: MetricHaven -- More Than 23,000 Metrics for Measuring Quality Attributes of Software Product Lines
text: Software product lines (SPLs) have become ubiquitous in modern software development, enabling mass customization and reuse across diverse domains. However, their inherent complexity and variability pose significant challenges to ensuring quality attributes such as performance, security, and maintainability. While existing metrics are inadequate for capturing the intricacies of SPLs, there is a pressing need for a comprehensive and systematic approach to measuring these attributes. MetricHaven addresses this gap by introducing a vast repository of over 23,000 metrics, carefully crafted through a rigorous methodology involving literature reviews, expert surveys, and empirical analysis of 150 SPLs. Our repository provides a unified framework for assessing SPL quality, facilitating informed decision-making, and guiding future research in SPL engineering.

title: KernelHaven -- An Open Infrastructure for Product Line Analysis
text: KernelHaven is an open infrastructure for Software Product Line (SPL) analysis. It is intended both as a production-quality analysis tool set as well as a research support tool, e.g., to support researchers in systematically exploring research hypothesis. For flexibility and ease of experimentation KernelHaven components are plug-ins for extracting certain information from SPL artifacts and processing this information, e.g., to check the correctness and consistency of variability information or to apply metrics. A configuration-based setup along with automatic documentation functionality allows different experiments and supports their easy reproduction. Here, we describe KernelHaven as a product line analysis research tool and highlight its basic approach as well as its fundamental capabilities. In particular, we describe available information extraction and processing plug-ins and how to combine them. On this basis, researchers and interested professional users can rapidly conduct a first set of experiments. Further, we describe the concepts for extending KernelHaven by new plug-ins, which reduces development effort when realizing new experiments.

title: KernelHaven -- An Open Infrastructure for Product Line Analysis
text: KernelHaven is a versatile, open infrastructure designed to facilitate the analysis of Software Product Lines (SPLs), serving both as a production-ready toolset and a research support platform. By providing a modular, plug-in-based architecture, KernelHaven enables researchers to systematically explore research hypotheses through flexible and extensible information extraction and processing capabilities. This modular design allows for the seamless integration of various plug-ins, which can be combined to analyze SPL artifacts, verify the correctness and consistency of variability information, and apply metrics. A configuration-driven setup, augmented by automatic documentation functionality, ensures the easy reproduction of experiments. This paper presents KernelHaven's fundamental approach, core capabilities, and available plug-ins, providing a foundation for researchers and practitioners to rapidly conduct initial experiments. Furthermore, we outline the concepts for extending KernelHaven through the development of new plug-ins, thereby reducing the effort required to realize novel experiments.

title: Pre and Post Counting for Scalable Statistical-Relational Model Discovery
text: Statistical-Relational Model Discovery aims to find statistically relevant patterns in relational data. For example, a relational dependency pattern may stipulate that a user's gender is associated with the gender of their friends. As with propositional (non-relational) graphical models, the major scalability bottleneck for model discovery is computing instantiation counts: the number of times a relational pattern is instantiated in a database. Previous work on propositional learning utilized pre-counting or post-counting to solve this task. This paper takes a detailed look at the memory and speed trade-offs between pre-counting and post-counting strategies for relational learning. A pre-counting approach computes and caches instantiation counts for a large set of relational patterns before model search. A post-counting approach computes an instantiation count dynamically on-demand for each candidate pattern generated during the model search. We describe a novel hybrid approach, tailored to relational data, that achieves a sweet spot with pre-counting for patterns involving positive relationships (e.g. pairs of users who are friends) and post-counting for patterns involving negative relationships (e.g. pairs of users who are not friends). Our hybrid approach scales model discovery to millions of data facts.

title: Pre and Post Counting for Scalable Statistical-Relational Model Discovery
text: Discovering statistically significant patterns in relational data is a fundamental challenge in statistical-relational model discovery. Relational dependencies, such as the association between a user's gender and that of their friends, are exemplars of these patterns. A major obstacle in scaling model discovery is the computation of instantiation counts, which represent the frequency of a relational pattern's occurrence in a database.
