This problem is reminiscent of propositional graphical models, where pre-counting and post-counting strategies have been employed to mitigate the computational burden. This study provides a comprehensive examination of the memory and speed trade-offs between these two approaches in the context of relational learning. We propose a novel hybrid method that leverages the strengths of both strategies, applying pre-counting to patterns involving positive relationships and post-counting to those involving negative relationships. This tailored approach enables model discovery to scale to datasets comprising millions of facts, thereby significantly advancing the state-of-the-art in statistical-relational model discovery.

title: An Interoperable Open Data Portal for Climate Analysis
text: This work proposes an open interoperable data portal that offers access to a Web-wide climate domain knowledge graph created for Ireland and England's NOAA climate daily data. There are three main components contributing to this data portal: the first is the upper layer schema of the knowledge graph -- the climate analysis (CA) ontology -- the second is an ad hoc SPARQL server by which to store the graph data and provide public Web access, the last is a dereferencing engine deployed to resolve URIs for entity information. Our knowledge graph form of NOAA climate data facilitates the supply of semantic climate information to researchers and offers a variety of semantic applications that can be built on top of it.

title: An Interoperable Open Data Portal for Climate Analysis
text: Climate change mitigation and adaptation efforts rely heavily on the availability of high-quality, interoperable climate data from diverse sources. Existing data portals often lack standardization, hindering data integration and analysis. To address this, we designed and implemented an interoperable open data portal for climate analysis, leveraging semantic web technologies and standardized metadata vocabularies. Our portal, ClimateHub, integrates datasets from multiple providers, including NASA, NOAA, and the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, and provides a unified query interface for spatiotemporal data retrieval. Experimental results demonstrate improved data discovery and integration capabilities, with an average query response time of 3.2 seconds for complex queries. ClimateHub has been successfully applied in several use cases, including climate model evaluation and urban planning, and is poised to support a wide range of climate-related research applications.

title: Using RDMA for Efficient Index Replication in LSM Key-Value Stores
text: Log-Structured Merge tree (LSM tree) Key-Value (KV) stores have become a foundational layer in the storage stacks of datacenter and cloud services. Current approaches for achieving reliability and availability avoid replication at the KV store level and instead perform these operations at higher layers, e.g., the DB layer that runs on top of the KV store. The main reason is that past designs for replicated KV stores favor reducing network traffic and increasing I/O size. Therefore, they perform costly compactions to reorganize data in both the primary and backup nodes, which hurts overall system performance. In this paper, we design and implement Talos, an efficient rack-scale LSM-based KV store that aims to significantly reduce the I/O amplification and CPU overhead in backup nodes and make replication in the KV store practical. We rely on two observations: (a) the increased use of RDMA in the datacenter, which reduces CPU overhead for communication, and (b) the use of KV separation that is becoming prevalent in modern KV stores. We use a primary-backup replication scheme that performs compactions only on the primary nodes and sends the pre-built index to the backup nodes of the region, avoiding all compactions in backups. Our approach includes an efficient mechanism to deal with pointer translation across nodes in the region index. Our results show that Talos reduces in the backup nodes, I/O amplification by up to $3\times$, CPU overhead by up to $1.6\times$, and memory size needed for the write path by up to $2\times$, without increasing network bandwidth excessively, and by up to $1.3\times$. Overall, we show that our approach has benefits even when small KV pairs dominate in a workload (80%-90%). Finally, it enables KV stores to operate with larger growth factors (from 10 to 16) to reduce space amplification without sacrificing precious CPU cycles.

title: Using RDMA for Efficient Index Replication in LSM Key-Value Stores
text: The rise of big data and cloud computing has led to an increasing demand for efficient and scalable key-value stores. Log-Structured Merge (LSM) trees have emerged as a popular indexing strategy in modern key-value stores due to their high write throughput and efficient storage utilization. However, LSM trees rely on index replication to ensure data durability and availability, which can introduce significant overhead in terms of network bandwidth and CPU utilization. To address this challenge, we explore the potential of Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) in optimizing index replication in LSM key-value stores. RDMA enables direct access to remote memory, eliminating the need for CPU involvement in data transfer and reducing latency. We design and implement a novel RDMA-based index replication mechanism, called RIR, which leverages RDMA's zero-copy data transfer and asynchronous communication capabilities to minimize the overhead of index replication. Our evaluation, conducted on a 10-node cluster using the YCSB benchmark, demonstrates that RIR can achieve up to 2.5x higher replication throughput and 40% lower latency compared to traditional TCP-based replication mechanisms. Moreover, RIR reduces the CPU utilization of the replica nodes by up to 60%, allowing them to handle a higher volume of client requests. We also investigate the impact of RDMA on the overall system performance, including the effects of network congestion and node failures. Our results show that RIR can improve the overall throughput of the key-value store by up to 15% and reduce the average latency by up to 25%. We conclude that RDMA-based index replication is a promising approach for optimizing the performance and scalability of LSM key-value stores, and our proposed RIR mechanism provides a practical solution for achieving efficient and reliable index replication in these systems.

title: Collective Shortest Paths for Minimizing Congestion on Temporal Load-Aware Road Networks
text: Shortest path queries over graphs are usually considered as isolated tasks, where the goal is to return the shortest path for each individual query. In practice, however, such queries are typically part of a system (e.g., a road network) and their execution dynamically affects other queries and network parameters, such as the loads on edges, which in turn affects the shortest paths. We study the problem of collectively processing shortest path queries, where the objective is to optimize a collective objective, such as minimizing the overall cost. We define a temporal load-aware network that dynamically tracks expected loads while satisfying the desirable `first in, first out' property. We develop temporal load-aware extensions of widely used shortest path algorithms, and a scalable collective routing solution that seeks to reduce system-wide congestion through dynamic path reassignment. Experiments illustrate that our collective approach to this NP-hard problem achieves improvements in a variety of performance measures, such as, i) reducing average travel times by up to 63%, ii) producing fairer suggestions across queries, and iii) distributing load across up to 97% of a city's road network capacity. The proposed approach is generalizable, which allows it to be adapted for other concurrent query processing tasks over networks.

title: Collective Shortest Paths for Minimizing Congestion on Temporal Load-Aware Road Networks
text: Road networks are increasingly overwhelmed by growing traffic demands, resulting in congestion, pollution, and decreased quality of life. Existing routing strategies focus on individual shortest paths, neglecting the collective impact on network congestion. We propose a novel approach, Collective Shortest Paths (CSP), that optimizes route assignments to minimize congestion on temporal load-aware road networks. Our method leverages real-time traffic data and incorporates time-dependent traffic patterns to compute CSPs. We formulate the problem as a mixed-integer linear program, solving it using a customized column generation approach. Experimental evaluations on a large-scale road network demonstrate that CSP reduces congestion by up to 23% compared to traditional shortest path algorithms. Moreover, CSP achieves a 17% reduction in travel time and a 12% decrease in fuel consumption. We also show that CSP is robust to varying traffic conditions and network sizes. Our results have significant implications for intelligent transportation systems, highlighting the potential for CSP to mitigate urban traffic congestion and improve overall network efficiency. By addressing the intricate relationships between traffic flow, road capacity, and time-dependent demand, our approach paves the way for more sustainable and efficient urban mobility.

title: Collaboration Challenges in Building ML-Enabled Systems: Communication, Documentation, Engineering, and Process
text: The introduction of machine learning (ML) components in software projects has created the need for software engineers to collaborate with data scientists and other specialists. While collaboration can always be challenging, ML introduces additional challenges with its exploratory model development process, additional skills and knowledge needed, difficulties testing ML systems, need for continuous evolution and monitoring, and non-traditional quality requirements such as fairness and explainability. Through interviews with 45 practitioners from 28 organizations, we identified key collaboration challenges that teams face when building and deploying ML systems into production. We report on common collaboration points in the development of production ML systems for requirements, data, and integration, as well as corresponding team patterns and challenges. We find that most of these challenges center around communication, documentation, engineering, and process and collect recommendations to address these challenges.

title: Collaboration Challenges in Building ML-Enabled Systems: Communication, Documentation, Engineering, and Process
text: The integration of machine learning (ML) components into software projects necessitates interdisciplinary collaboration between software engineers, data scientists, and other specialists. This collaboration is fraught with unique challenges stemming from ML's distinct characteristics, including its exploratory development process, requisite specialized skills, difficulties in testing, and need for continuous monitoring and evolution. Furthermore, ML systems introduce non-traditional quality attributes such as fairness and explainability. Our study, based on 45 in-depth interviews with practitioners from 28 organizations, reveals key challenges that teams encounter when developing and deploying ML systems in production environments. We identify common collaboration points and corresponding team patterns and challenges in requirements, data, and integration, highlighting communication, documentation, engineering, and process as primary areas of concern. Our findings provide recommendations for addressing these challenges.

title: 2020 State of the Octoverse: Securing the World's Software
text: Open source is the connective tissue for much of the information economy. You would be hard-pressed to find a scenario where your data does not pass through at least one open source component. Many of the services and technology we all rely on, from banking to healthcare, also rely on open source software. The artifacts of open source code serve as critical i infrastructure for much of the global economy, making the security of open source software mission-critical to the world.

title: 2020 State of the Octoverse: Securing the World's Software
text: The pervasive adoption of open source software has rendered it a linchpin of the modern information economy, with virtually all data traversing at least one open source component. The provision of essential services, encompassing banking and healthcare, is heavily reliant on open source technologies. Consequently, the integrity of open source codebases assumes paramount importance, as they constitute critical infrastructure underpinning the global economy, rendering their security a mission-critical imperative.

title: JavaBERT: Training a transformer-based model for the Java programming language
text: Code quality is and will be a crucial factor while developing new software code, requiring appropriate tools to ensure functional and reliable code. Machine learning techniques are still rarely used for software engineering tools, missing out the potential benefits of its application. Natural language processing has shown the potential to process text data regarding a variety of tasks. We argue, that such models can also show similar benefits for software code processing. In this paper, we investigate how models used for natural language processing can be trained upon software code. We introduce a data retrieval pipeline for software code and train a model upon Java software code. The resulting model, JavaBERT, shows a high accuracy on the masked language modeling task showing its potential for software engineering tools.

title: JavaBERT: Training a transformer-based model for the Java programming language
text: The development of high-quality software code necessitates the employment of effective tools to guarantee functionality and reliability. Despite the potential benefits, machine learning techniques remain underutilized in software engineering tools. Natural language processing has demonstrated its capacity to handle various tasks involving text data, suggesting that similar models could be leveraged for software code processing. This paper explores the application of natural language processing models to software code analysis. We design a data retrieval pipeline for software code and train a model on Java code, resulting in JavaBERT. Our evaluation reveals that JavaBERT achieves a high accuracy on the masked language modeling task, underscoring its potential as a valuable asset for software engineering tools.

title: KabOOM: Unsupervised Crash Categorization through Timeseries Fingerprinting
text: Modern mobile applications include instrumentation that sample internal application metrics at regular intervals. Following a crash, sample metrics are collected and can potentially be valuable for root-causing difficult to diagnose crashes. However, the fine-grained nature and overwhelming wealth of available application metrics, coupled with frequent application updates, renders their use for root-causing crashes extremely difficult. We propose KabOOM, a method to automatically cluster telemetry reports in intuitive, distinct crash categories. Uniquely, KabOOM relies on multivariate timeseries fingerprinting; an auto-encoder coupled with a cluster centroid optimization technique learns embeddings of each crash report, which are then used to cluster metric timeseries based crash reports. We demonstrate the effectiveness of KabOOM on both reducing the dimensionality of the incoming crash reports and producing crash categories that are intuitive to developers.

title: KabOOM: Unsupervised Crash Categorization through Timeseries Fingerprinting
text: The proliferation of instrumentation in modern mobile applications enables the collection of internal metrics at regular intervals, providing a valuable opportunity for root-causing crashes. However, the sheer volume and fine-grained nature of these metrics, compounded by frequent application updates, render their analysis extremely challenging. To address this, we introduce KabOOM, a novel method for automatically clustering telemetry reports into distinct, intuitive crash categories. By leveraging multivariate timeseries fingerprinting, KabOOM employs an auto-encoder coupled with cluster centroid optimization to learn embeddings of each crash report, facilitating the clustering of metric timeseries-based crash reports. Our approach is shown to effectively reduce dimensionality and produce crash categories that are readily interpretable by developers.

title: On the Effectiveness of Clone Detection for Detecting IoT-related Vulnerable Clones
text: Since IoT systems provide services over the Internet, they must continue to operate safely even if malicious users attack them. Since the computational resources of edge devices connected to the IoT are limited, lightweight platforms and network protocols are often used. Lightweight platforms and network protocols are less resistant to attacks, increasing the risk that developers will embed vulnerabilities. The code clone research community has been developing approaches to fix buggy (e.g., vulnerable) clones simultaneously. However, there has been little research on IoT-related vulnerable clones. It is unclear whether existing code clone detection techniques can perform simultaneous fixes of the vulnerable clones. In this study, we first created two datasets of IoT-related vulnerable code. We then conducted a preliminary investigation to show whether existing code clone detection tools (e.g., NiCaD, CCFinderSW) are capable of detecting IoT-related vulnerable clones by applying them to the created datasets. The preliminary result shows that the existing tools can detect them partially.

title: On the Effectiveness of Clone Detection for Detecting IoT-related Vulnerable Clones
text: The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has introduced a plethora of vulnerabilities, many of which stem from cloned code. Clone detection, a technique originally designed for identifying duplicate code in software systems, has been touted as a potential solution for detecting vulnerable clones in IoT firmware. However, the effectiveness of clone detection in this context remains largely unexplored. This study investigates the efficacy of clone detection in identifying IoT-related vulnerable clones. We propose a novel approach that combines clone detection with vulnerability analysis, leveraging a dataset of 1500 IoT firmware images. Our results show that clone detection can identify up to 75% of vulnerable clones, with a precision of 85%. Notably, we find that the most effective clone detection techniques are those that incorporate semantic analysis, such as graph-based and token-based methods. These findings have significant implications for the development of automated tools for securing IoT devices.

title: Investigating Reversibility of Steps in Petri Nets
text: In reversible computations one is interested in the development of mechanisms allowing to undo the effects of executed actions. The past research has been concerned mainly with reversing single actions. In this paper, we consider the problem of reversing the effect of the execution of groups of actions (steps). Using Petri nets as a system model, we introduce concepts related to this new scenario, generalising notions used in the single action case. We then present properties arising when reverse actions are allowed in place/transition nets (pt-nets). We obtain both positive and negative results, showing that allowing steps makes reversibility more problematic than in the interleaving/sequential case. In particular, we demonstrate that there is a crucial difference between reversing steps which are sets and those which are true multisets. Moreover, in contrast to sequential semantics, splitting reverses does not lead to a general method for reversing bounded pt-nets. We then show that a suitable solution can be obtained by combining split reverses with weighted read arcs.

title: Investigating Reversibility of Steps in Petri Nets
text: Reversibility, a fundamental concept in concurrency theory, enables the design of fault-tolerant and flexible systems. Petri nets, a widely-used formalism for modeling concurrent systems, lack a comprehensive understanding of reversibility, particularly with respect to the reversibility of individual steps. This knowledge gap hinders the development of reversible Petri net-based systems, which could significantly benefit from the ability to undo erroneous or unwanted actions. To address this limitation, we present a systematic investigation into the reversibility of steps in Petri nets. Our approach involves developing a novel notion of step reversibility, which we formalize using a set of necessary and sufficient conditions. We then propose an algorithm to determine the reversibility of a given step in a Petri net, with a proof of its correctness and an analysis of its computational complexity. Experimental evaluations on a large benchmark of Petri nets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, revealing that a significant proportion of steps in real-world models are reversible. Our findings have important implications for the design and implementation of reversible Petri net-based systems, enabling the creation of more robust and dependable concurrent systems.

title: Color Teams for Machine Learning Development
text: Machine learning and software development share processes and methodologies for reliably delivering products to customers. This work proposes the use of a new teaming construct for forming machine learning teams for better combatting adversarial attackers. In cybersecurity, infrastructure uses these teams to protect their systems by using system builders and programmers to also offer more robustness to their platforms. Color teams provide clear responsibility to the individuals on each team for which part of the baseline (Yellow), attack (Red), and defense (Blue) breakout of the pipeline. Combining colors leads to additional knowledge shared across the team and more robust models built during development. The responsibilities of the new teams Orange, Green, and Purple will be outlined during this paper along with an overview of the necessary resources for these teams to be successful.

title: Color Teams for Machine Learning Development
text: The convergence of machine learning and software development has led to the adoption of similar processes and methodologies for delivering reliable products to customers. This paper introduces a novel teaming construct for machine learning teams, specifically designed to counter adversarial attacks in cybersecurity. By integrating system builders and programmers, these teams can enhance the robustness of infrastructure platforms. The color team construct assigns distinct responsibilities to team members, encompassing the baseline (Yellow), attack (Red), and defense (Blue) phases of the pipeline. The intersection of these colors fosters knowledge sharing and yields more resilient models during development. This paper elaborates on the roles of Orange, Green, and Purple teams, and outlines the necessary resources for their success.

title: Bootstrapping confidence in future safety based on past safe operation
text: With autonomous vehicles (AVs), a major concern is the inability to give meaningful quantitative assurance of safety, to the extent required by society - e.g. that an AV must be at least as safe as a good human driver - before that AV is in extensive use. We demonstrate an approach to achieving more moderate, but useful, confidence, e.g., confidence of low enough probability of causing accidents in the early phases of operation. This formalises mathematically the common approach of operating a system on a limited basis in the hope that mishap-free operation will confirm one's confidence in its safety and allow progressively more extensive operation: a process of "bootstrapping" of confidence. Translating that intuitive approach into theorems shows: (1) that it is substantially sound in the right circumstances, and could be a good method for deciding about the early deployment phase for an AV; (2) how much confidence can be rightly derived from such a "cautious deployment" approach, so that we can avoid over-optimism; (3) under which conditions our sound formulas for future confidence are applicable; (4) thus, which analyses of the concrete situations, and/or constraints on practice, are needed in order to enjoy the advantages of provably correct confidence in adequate future safety.

title: Bootstrapping confidence in future safety based on past safe operation
text: The inability to provide quantitative safety assurances for autonomous vehicles (AVs) that meet societal expectations, such as parity with a proficient human driver, poses a significant concern prior to their widespread adoption. We propose an approach to establish moderate yet meaningful confidence in AV safety, particularly during the early operational phases, by quantifying the probability of accident occurrence. This method formalizes the common practice of deploying systems in a limited capacity, with the expectation that incident-free operation will incrementally build confidence in their safety, thereby enabling more extensive use – a process we term "confidence bootstrapping." By translating this intuitive approach into mathematical theorems, we demonstrate that it is substantially sound under specific circumstances, providing a viable framework for deciding on early AV deployment. Our results also provide a nuanced understanding of the confidence that can be derived from cautious deployment, avoiding over-optimism, and outline the conditions under which our formulas for future confidence are applicable, thereby informing the analyses and practical constraints necessary to ensure provably correct confidence in adequate future safety.

title: Scheduling of Graph Queries: Controlling Intra- and Inter-query Parallelism for a High System Throughput
text: The vast amounts of data used in social, business or traffic networks, biology and other natural sciences are often managed in graph-based data sets, consisting of a few thousand up to billions and trillions of vertices and edges, respectively. Typical applications utilizing such data either execute one or a few complex queries or many small queries at the same time interactively or as batch jobs. Furthermore, graph processing is inherently complex, as data sets can substantially differ (scale free vs. constant degree), and algorithms exhibit diverse behavior (computational intensity, local or global, push- or pull-based). This work is concerned with multi-query execution by automatically controlling the degree of parallelization, with overall objectives including high system utilization, low synchronization cost, and highly efficient concurrent execution. The underlying concept is three-fold: (1) sampling is used to determine graph statistics, (2) parallelization constraints are derived from algorithm and system properties, and (3) suitable work packages are generated based on the previous two aspects. We evaluate the proposed concept using different algorithms on synthetic and real world data sets, with up to 16 concurrent sessions (queries). The results demonstrate a robust performance in spite of these various configurations, and in particular that the performance is always close to or even slightly ahead of the performance of manually optimized implementations. Furthermore, the similar performance to manually optimized implementations under extreme configurations, which require either a full parallelization (few large queries) or complete sequential execution (many small queries), shows that the proposed concept exhibits a particularly low overhead.

title: Scheduling of Graph Queries: Controlling Intra- and Inter-query Parallelism for a High System Throughput
text: The proliferation of graph-structured data has led to a surge in graph query workloads, which often exhibit complex dependencies and varying computational intensities. Efficient scheduling of these queries is crucial to achieve high system throughput, particularly in modern distributed graph processing systems. Existing scheduling strategies, however, focus primarily on intra-query parallelism, neglecting the significant opportunities for inter-query parallelism. In this context, we propose a novel scheduling framework that holistically controls both intra- and inter-query parallelism to maximize system throughput. Our approach leverages a combination of query graph analysis, workload characterization, and dynamic scheduling to optimize the allocation of computational resources. We devise a query graph decomposition technique to identify opportunities for inter-query parallelism and develop a novel cost model to estimate the execution time of each query fragment. Our scheduling framework is designed to adapt to changing workload conditions and query characteristics, ensuring high system utilization and responsiveness. We evaluate our approach using a diverse set of graph query workloads on a distributed graph processing system. Experimental results demonstrate that our scheduling framework achieves an average system throughput improvement of 2.5x compared to state-of-the-art scheduling strategies, while reducing query latency by up to 40%. Furthermore, our framework exhibits robustness to varying workload conditions and query characteristics, making it a promising solution for large-scale graph query processing systems.

title: Ethics-Based Auditing of Automated Decision-Making Systems: Nature, Scope, and Limitations
text: Important decisions that impact human lives, livelihoods, and the natural environment are increasingly being automated. Delegating tasks to so-called automated decision-making systems (ADMS) can improve efficiency and enable new solutions. However, these benefits are coupled with ethical challenges. For example, ADMS may produce discriminatory outcomes, violate individual privacy, and undermine human self-determination. New governance mechanisms are thus needed that help organisations design and deploy ADMS in ways that are ethical, while enabling society to reap the full economic and social benefits of automation. In this article, we consider the feasibility and efficacy of ethics-based auditing (EBA) as a governance mechanism that allows organisations to validate claims made about their ADMS. Building on previous work, we define EBA as a structured process whereby an entity's present or past behaviour is assessed for consistency with relevant principles or norms. We then offer three contributions to the existing literature. First, we provide a theoretical explanation of how EBA can contribute to good governance by promoting procedural regularity and transparency. Second, we propose seven criteria for how to design and implement EBA procedures successfully. Third, we identify and discuss the conceptual, technical, social, economic, organisational, and institutional constraints associated with EBA. We conclude that EBA should be considered an integral component of multifaced approaches to managing the ethical risks posed by ADMS.

title: Ethics-Based Auditing of Automated Decision-Making Systems: Nature, Scope, and Limitations
text: The increasing ubiquity of automated decision-making systems (ADMS) in high-stakes domains has sparked concerns about their potential to perpetuate biases, discriminate against vulnerable populations, and erode trust in institutions. As a response, ethics-based auditing has emerged as a crucial mechanism to ensure ADMS align with societal values and norms. Despite its importance, the nature, scope, and limitations of ethics-based auditing remain poorly understood. This study aims to address this knowledge gap by providing a comprehensive framework for ethics-based auditing of ADMS. We conducted a systematic review of 135 papers from top-tier computer science and ethics journals, which revealed a lack of standardized auditing methodologies and inconsistent reporting of auditing outcomes. To address these limitations, we developed a novel auditing framework that integrates value alignment, transparency, and accountability principles. We applied this framework to three real-world ADMS case studies, including a criminal risk assessment tool, a loan approval system, and a personalized healthcare platform. Our findings indicate that ethics-based auditing can identify subtle biases and discriminatory patterns, but its effectiveness is hindered by the complexity of ADMS, the lack of domain-specific expertise, and the conflicting priorities of stakeholders. This study contributes to the development of a rigorous and systematic approach to ethics-based auditing, highlighting the need for continued research into the challenges and limitations of auditing ADMS.

title: Automated Climate Analyses Using Knowledge Graph
text: The FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles are fundamental for climate researchers and all stakeholders in the current digital ecosystem. In this paper, we demonstrate how relational climate data can be "FAIR" and modeled using RDF, in line with Semantic Web technologies and our Climate Analysis ontology. Thus, heterogeneous climate data can be stored in graph databases and offered as Linked Data on the Web. As a result, climate researchers will be able to use the standard SPARQL query language to query these sources directly on the Web. In this paper, we demonstrate the usefulness of our SPARQL endpoint for automated climate analytics. We illustrate two sample use cases that establish the advantage of representing climate data as knowledge graphs.

title: Automated Climate Analyses Using Knowledge Graph
text: Climate research relies heavily on the FAIR data principles, which ensure that data are findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. We propose a methodology for modeling relational climate data according to these principles, leveraging RDF and Semantic Web technologies in conjunction with our Climate Analysis ontology. This approach enables the storage of heterogeneous climate data in graph databases, making them available as Linked Data on the Web. Consequently, researchers can utilize the standardized SPARQL query language to directly query these sources online. We demonstrate the efficacy of our SPARQL endpoint in facilitating automated climate analytics, illustrating its benefits through two exemplary use cases that showcase the advantages of representing climate data as knowledge graphs, thereby enhancing data discoverability and reuse.

title: DeLag: Using Multi-Objective Optimization to Enhance the Detection of Latency Degradation Patterns in Service-based Systems
text: Performance debugging in production is a fundamental activity in modern service-based systems. The diagnosis of performance issues is often time-consuming, since it requires thorough inspection of large volumes of traces and performance indices. In this paper we present DeLag, a novel automated search-based approach for diagnosing performance issues in service-based systems. DeLag identifies subsets of requests that show, in the combination of their Remote Procedure Call execution times, symptoms of potentially relevant performance issues. We call such symptoms Latency Degradation Patterns. DeLag simultaneously searches for multiple latency degradation patterns while optimizing precision, recall and latency dissimilarity. Experimentation on 700 datasets of requests generated from two microservice-based systems shows that our approach provides better and more stable effectiveness than three state-of-the-art approaches and general purpose machine learning clustering algorithms. DeLag is more effective than all baseline techniques in at least one case study (with p $\leq$ 0.05 and non-negligible effect size). Moreover, DeLag outperforms in terms of efficiency the second and the third most effective baseline techniques on the largest datasets used in our evaluation (up to 22%).

title: DeLag: Using Multi-Objective Optimization to Enhance the Detection of Latency Degradation Patterns in Service-based Systems
text: Latency degradation patterns in service-based systems can have profound implications on system performance, reliability, and user experience. Despite their significance, detecting these patterns remains a challenging task due to the inherent complexity of modern software systems. Existing approaches often rely on simplified models, neglecting the multifaceted nature of latency degradation. To address this limitation, we propose DeLag, a novel multi-objective optimization-based approach for detecting latency degradation patterns in service-based systems. DeLag formulates the detection problem as a Pareto optimization problem, simultaneously minimizing false positives, false negatives, and detection latency. We evaluated DeLag on a real-world dataset from a large-scale e-commerce platform, comprising over 10,000 service interactions. Our results show that DeLag outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, achieving an average F1-score of 0.93, a 15% improvement over the best-performing baseline. Furthermore, DeLag identifies novel patterns that were previously undetected, including a 30% increase in latency degradation instances attributed to third-party service dependencies. Our findings have significant implications for the design and operation of service-based systems, highlighting the potential of multi-objective optimization in enhancing latency degradation pattern detection.

title: Viash: from scripts to pipelines
text: Most bioinformatics pipelines consist of software components that are tightly coupled to the logic of the pipeline itself. This limits reusability of the individual components in the pipeline or introduces maintenance overhead when they need to be reimplemented in multiple pipelines. We introduce Viash, a tool for speeding up development of robust pipelines through "code-first" prototyping, separation of concerns and code generation of modular pipeline components. By decoupling the component functionality from the pipeline logic, component functionality becomes fully pipeline-agnostic, and conversely the resulting pipelines are agnostic towards specific component requirements. This separation of concerns improves reusability of components and facilitates multidisciplinar and pan-organisational collaborations. It has been applied in a variety of projects, from proof-of-concept pipelines to supporting an international data science competition. Viash is available as an open-source project at and documentation is available at

title: Viash: from scripts to pipelines
text: The proliferation of scripting languages in data science has led to an abundance of bespoke scripts, hindering reproducibility and scalability. To address this, we present Viash, a novel framework for transforming scripts into reusable, modular pipelines. By abstracting away implementation details, Viash enables users to define high-level data flows, which are then optimized and executed on various platforms. Our approach leverages a domain-specific language (DSL) for pipeline specification, allowing users to focus on the logic of their workflows. We evaluate Viash using a suite of real-world bioinformatics pipelines, demonstrating significant improvements in execution time and developer productivity. Notably, our results show that Viash pipelines achieve an average speedup of 3.2x compared to their script-based counterparts, while reducing development time by 45%. These findings underscore the potential of Viash to streamline data science workflows and improve collaboration across domains.

title: Methodology for Assessing the State of the Practice for Domain X
text: To improve software development methods and tools for research software, we first need to understand the current state of the practice. Therefore, we have developed a methodology for assessing the state of the software development practices for a given research software domain. For each domain we wish to answer questions such as: i) What artifacts (documents, code, test cases, etc.) are present? ii) What tools are used? iii) What principles, process and methodologies are used? iv) What are the pain points for developers? v) What actions are used to improve qualities like maintainability and reproducibility? To answer these questions, our methodology prescribes the following steps: i) Identify the domain; ii) Identify a list of candidate software packages; iii) Filter the list to a length of about 30 packages; iv) Gather source code and documentation for each package; v) Collect repository related data on each software package, like number of stars, number of open issues, number of lines of code; vi) Fill in the measurement template (the template consists of 108 questions to assess 9 qualities (including the qualities of installability, usability and visibility)); vii) Interview developers (the interview consists of 20 questions and takes about an hour); viii) Rank the software using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP); and, ix) Analyze the data to answer the questions posed above. A domain expert should be engaged throughout the process, to ensure that implicit information about the domain is properly represented and to assist with conducting an analysis of the commonalities and variabilities between the 30 selected packages. Using our methodology, spreadsheet templates and AHP tool, we estimate (based on our experience with using the process) the time to complete an assessment for a given domain at 173 person hours.

title: Methodology for Assessing the State of the Practice for Domain X
text: Understanding the current state of software development practices is crucial for improving methods and tools in research software. To this end, we have devised a comprehensive methodology for assessing the software development practices prevalent in a given research software domain. Our approach seeks to elucidate key aspects, including the presence and characteristics of various artifacts, toolchains employed, and principles, processes, and methodologies adopted. Additionally, we aim to identify pain points faced by developers and strategies employed to enhance qualities such as maintainability and reproducibility. The methodology comprises nine steps: domain identification, candidate software package selection, filtering, data collection (including source code, documentation, and repository metrics), completion of a 108-question measurement template assessing nine software qualities (installability, usability, visibility, and others), hour-long developer interviews, ranking via the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), and data analysis. A domain expert's involvement is essential throughout the process to ensure implicit domain knowledge is adequately captured and to facilitate analysis of commonalities and variabilities across the selected packages. Based on our experience, we estimate that completing an assessment for a given domain using our methodology, spreadsheet templates, and AHP tool requires approximately 173 person hours.

title: Creating Knowledge Graphs Subsets using Shape Expressions
text: The initial adoption of knowledge graphs by Google and later by big companies has increased their adoption and popularity. In this paper we present a formal model for three different types of knowledge graphs which we call RDF-based graphs, property graphs and wikibase graphs. In order to increase the quality of Knowledge Graphs, several approaches have appeared to describe and validate their contents. Shape Expressions (ShEx) has been proposed as concise language for RDF validation. We give a brief introduction to ShEx and present two extensions that can also be used to describe and validate property graphs (PShEx) and wikibase graphs (WShEx). One problem of knowledge graphs is the large amount of data they contain, which jeopardizes their practical application. In order to palliate this problem, one approach is to create subsets of those knowledge graphs for some domains. We propose the following approaches to generate those subsets: Entity-matching, simple matching, ShEx matching, ShEx plus Slurp and ShEx plus Pregel which are based on declaratively defining the subsets by either matching some content or by Shape Expressions. The last approach is based on a novel validation algorithm for ShEx based on the Pregel algorithm that can handle big data graphs and has been implemented on Apache Spark GraphX.

title: Creating Knowledge Graphs Subsets using Shape Expressions
text: The widespread adoption of knowledge graphs, pioneered by Google and subsequently adopted by major companies, has led to a surge in their popularity. This paper introduces a formal framework for three distinct knowledge graph paradigms: RDF-based graphs, property graphs, and Wikibase graphs. To ensure the quality and validity of knowledge graphs, various approaches have emerged, including Shape Expressions (ShEx), a concise language for RDF validation. We provide an overview of ShEx and propose two extensions, PShEx and WShEx, which can be applied to property graphs and Wikibase graphs, respectively. A significant challenge in knowledge graph adoption is the enormous volume of data they contain, hindering practical application. To mitigate this issue, we propose generating subsets of knowledge graphs tailored to specific domains. Five approaches are presented: entity-matching, simple matching, ShEx matching, ShEx plus Slurp, and ShEx plus Pregel, which enable declarative definition of subsets based on content matching or Shape Expressions. Notably, the latter approach leverages a novel ShEx validation algorithm, built upon the Pregel algorithm, capable of handling large-scale data graphs and implemented on Apache Spark GraphX.

title: cleanTS: Automated (AutoML) Tool to Clean Univariate Time Series at Microscales
text: Data cleaning is one of the most important tasks in data analysis processes. One of the perennial challenges in data analytics is the detection and handling of non-valid data. Failing to do so can result in inaccurate analytics and unreliable decisions. The process of properly cleaning such data takes much time. Errors are prevalent in time series data. It is usually found that real world data is unclean and requires some pre-processing. The analysis of large amounts of data is difficult. This paper is intended to provide an easy to use and reliable system which automates the cleaning process of univariate time series data. Automating the process greatly reduces the time required. Visualizing a large amount of data at once is not very effective. To tackle this issue, an R package cleanTS is proposed. The proposed system provides a way to analyze data on different scales and resolutions. Also, it provides users with tools and a benchmark system for comparing various techniques used in data cleaning.

title: cleanTS: Automated (AutoML) Tool to Clean Univariate Time Series at Microscales
text: Microscale univariate time series data, commonly encountered in IoT, financial, and sensor applications, are prone to errors, outliers, and missing values, which can significantly impact the accuracy of machine learning models and downstream analytics. Existing cleaning methods often rely on manual inspection, heuristics, or simplistic statistical techniques, leading to suboptimal results. We propose cleanTS, an automated tool that leverages AutoML principles to clean microscale univariate time series data. cleanTS combines a novel, density-based anomaly detector with a robust, regression-based imputation method, and a sophisticated, reinforcement learning-driven data repair strategy. Evaluation on a diverse set of real-world datasets demonstrates that cleanTS outperforms state-of-the-art cleaning techniques, achieving a mean absolute error reduction of 34.7% and a precision improvement of 21.3%. Furthermore, cleanTS exhibits robustness to varying levels of noise, outliers, and missingness, making it a reliable solution for real-world time series data cleaning tasks. The cleanTS tool is available as an open-source Python package, facilitating widespread adoption in the data science community.

title: REACH: Refining Alloy Scenarios by Scope
text: Writing declarative models has numerous benefits, ranging from automated reasoning and correction of design-level properties be-fore systems are built, to automated testing and debugging of their implementations after they are built. Alloy is a declarative modeling language that is well suited for verifying system designs. A key strength of Alloy is its scenario-finding toolset, the Analyzer, which allows users to explore all valid scenarios that adhere to the model's constraints up to a user-provided scope. In Alloy, it is common for users to desire to first validate smaller scenarios, then once confident, move onto validating larger scenarios. However, the Analyzer only presents scenarios in the order they are discovered by the SAT solver. This paper presents Reach, an extension to the Analyzer which allows users to explore scenarios by size. Experimental results reveal Reach's enumeration improves performance while having the added benefit of maintaining a semi-sorted ordering of scenarios for the user. Moreover, we highlight Reach's ability to improve the performance of Alloy's analysis when the user makes incremental changes to the scope of the enumeration.

title: REACH: Refining Alloy Scenarios by Scope
text: The Alloy specification language has emerged as a prominent tool for modeling and analyzing complex systems, relying on scenario-based reasoning to validate system properties. However, the inherent ambiguity of natural language scenarios can lead to inconsistencies and inaccuracies, hindering the effectiveness of Alloy's analysis. To address this limitation, we propose REACH, a novel approach for refining Alloy scenarios by scope. REACH leverages a combination of natural language processing and machine learning techniques to identify and disambiguate ambiguous scenario phrases, subsequently generating a refined set of scenarios that capture the intended system behavior. Our evaluation on a benchmark of 150 Alloy models demonstrates that REACH reduces the number of spurious counterexamples by an average of 37%, while increasing the accuracy of property validation by 24%. Furthermore, our approach is shown to be robust against variations in scenario phrasing and syntax, making it a valuable addition to the Alloy ecosystem. By refining Alloy scenarios, REACH enables more precise and efficient system analysis, ultimately contributing to the development of more reliable and trustworthy software systems.

title: RDD-Eclat: Approaches to Parallelize Eclat Algorithm on Spark RDD Framework (Extended Version)
text: Frequent itemset mining (FIM) is a highly computational and data intensive algorithm. Therefore, parallel and distributed FIM algorithms have been designed to process large volume of data in a reduced time. Recently, a number of FIM algorithms have been designed on Hadoop MapReduce, a distributed big data processing framework. But, due to heavy disk I/O, MapReduce is found to be inefficient for the highly iterative FIM algorithms. Therefore, Spark, a more efficient distributed data processing framework, has been developed with in-memory computation and resilient distributed dataset (RDD) features to support the iterative algorithms. On this framework, Apriori and FP-Growth based FIM algorithms have been designed on the Spark RDD framework, but Eclat-based algorithm has not been explored yet. In this paper, RDD-Eclat, a parallel Eclat algorithm on the Spark RDD framework is proposed with its five variants. The proposed algorithms are evaluated on the various benchmark datasets, and the experimental results show that RDD-Eclat outperforms the Spark-based Apriori by many times. Also, the experimental results show the scalability of the proposed algorithms on increasing the number of cores and size of the dataset.

title: RDD-Eclat: Approaches to Parallelize Eclat Algorithm on Spark RDD Framework (Extended Version)
text: The Eclat algorithm is a popular method for mining frequent itemsets in transactional databases, but its sequential nature hinders its scalability for large datasets. To address this limitation, we explore approaches to parallelize the Eclat algorithm on the Spark Resilient Distributed Dataset (RDD) framework. Our proposed RDD-Eclat method leverages Spark's in-memory computing and distributed processing capabilities to significantly accelerate the itemset mining process. We present two novel strategies for parallelizing Eclat on RDDs: (1) a horizontal partitioning approach, which distributes the transactional database across multiple nodes, and (2) a vertical partitioning approach, which splits the itemset lattice into smaller sub-lattices. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that RDD-Eclat achieves significant speedups over the sequential Eclat implementation, with up to 15x performance improvement on a 16-node Spark cluster. Furthermore, our approach exhibits strong scalability, with near-linear speedup as the number of nodes increases. Our findings have important implications for large-scale data mining applications, enabling the efficient discovery of frequent itemsets in massive datasets.

title: Development of Semantic Web-based Imaging Database for Biological Morphome
text: We introduce the RIKEN Microstructural Imaging Metadatabase, a semantic web-based imaging database in which image metadata are described using the Resource Description Framework (RDF) and detailed biological properties observed in the images can be represented as Linked Open Data. The metadata are used to develop a large-scale imaging viewer that provides a straightforward graphical user interface to visualise a large microstructural tiling image at the gigabyte level. We applied the database to accumulate comprehensive microstructural imaging data produced by automated scanning electron microscopy. As a result, we have successfully managed vast numbers of images and their metadata, including the interpretation of morphological phenotypes occurring in sub-cellular components and biosamples captured in the images. We also discuss advanced utilisation of morphological imaging data that can be promoted by this database.

title: Development of Semantic Web-based Imaging Database for Biological Morphome
text: The exponential growth of biological imaging data necessitates the development of sophisticated databases to facilitate knowledge discovery and integration. Current imaging repositories lack semantic annotation, hindering the identification of complex patterns and relationships between morphological features and biological processes. We present a novel Semantic Web-based imaging database, BioMorphoDB, designed to address these limitations. Our approach leverages ontology-based modeling, integrating domain-specific knowledge from the Open Biological and Biomedical Ontology (OBO) Foundry. A semantic data model is constructed using Resource Description Framework (RDF) and Web Ontology Language (OWL), enabling inference-based querying and reasoning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of BioMorphoDB through a use case involving the analysis of morphological patterns in zebrafish embryogenesis, illustrating improved data integration and discovery capabilities. Our framework provides a foundation for the development of advanced imaging informatics systems, facilitating insights into the complex relationships between biological morphology and function.

title: An Empirical Study of Blockchain System Vulnerabilities: Modules, Types, and Patterns
text: Blockchain, as a distributed ledger technology, becomes increasingly popular, especially for enabling valuable cryptocurrencies and smart contracts. However, the blockchain software systems inevitably have many bugs. Although bugs in smart contracts have been extensively investigated, security bugs of the underlying blockchain systems are much less explored. In this paper, we conduct an empirical study on blockchain's system vulnerabilities from four representative blockchains, Bitcoin, Ethereum, Monero, and Stellar. Specifically, we first design a systematic filtering process to effectively identify 1,037 vulnerabilities and their 2,317 patches from 34,245 issues/PRs (pull requests) and 85,164 commits on GitHub. We thus build the first blockchain vulnerability dataset. We then perform unique analyses of this dataset at three levels, including (i) file-level vulnerable module categorization by identifying and correlating module paths across projects, (ii) text-level vulnerability type clustering by natural language processing and similarity-based sentence clustering, and (iii) code-level vulnerability pattern analysis by generating and clustering code change signatures that capture both syntactic and semantic information of patch code fragments. Our analyses reveal three key findings: (i) some blockchain modules are more susceptible than the others; notably, each of the modules related to consensus, wallet, and networking has over 200 issues; (ii) about 70% of blockchain vulnerabilities are of traditional types, but we also identify four new types specific to blockchains; and (iii) we obtain 21 blockchain-specific vulnerability patterns that capture unique blockchain attributes and statuses, and demonstrate that they can be used to detect similar vulnerabilities in other popular blockchains, such as Dogecoin, Bitcoin SV, and Zcash.

title: An Empirical Study of Blockchain System Vulnerabilities: Modules, Types, and Patterns
text: The burgeoning adoption of blockchain technology has precipitated a surge in the development of cryptocurrencies and smart contracts. However, the underlying blockchain software systems are not immune to errors, with a substantial number of bugs and vulnerabilities lurking beneath the surface. While the security of smart contracts has garnered significant attention, the vulnerabilities inherent to blockchain systems themselves remain understudied. This paper presents a comprehensive empirical examination of system vulnerabilities in four prominent blockchain platforms: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Monero, and Stellar. From a corpus of 34,245 issues/PRs and 85,164 commits on GitHub, we devise a systematic filtering process that yields 1,037 vulnerabilities and their corresponding 2,317 patches, thereby creating the first comprehensive blockchain vulnerability dataset. We subject this dataset to a multifaceted analysis, encompassing file-level categorization of vulnerable modules, text-level clustering of vulnerability types via natural language processing, and code-level analysis of vulnerability patterns via the generation and clustering of code change signatures. Our findings reveal that certain blockchain modules are disproportionately prone to errors, with consensus, wallet, and networking modules exhibiting over 200 issues each. Furthermore, we identify four novel vulnerability types specific to blockchain systems, in addition to 21 blockchain-specific patterns that can be leveraged to detect similar vulnerabilities in other popular blockchains, such as Dogecoin, Bitcoin SV, and Zcash.

title: Towards User Engagement Dynamics in Social Networks
text: The engagement of each user in a social network is an essential indicator for maintaining a sustainable service. Existing studies use the $coreness$ of a user to well estimate its static engagement in a network. However, when the engagement of a user is weakened or strengthened, the influence on other users' engagement is unclear. Besides, the dynamic of user engagement has not been well captured for evolving social networks. In this paper, we systematically study the network dynamic against the engagement change of each user for the first time. The influence of a user is monitored via two novel concepts: the $collapsed~power$ to measure the effect of user weakening, and the $anchored~power$ to measure the effect of user strengthening. We show that the two concepts can be naturally integrated such that a unified offline algorithm is proposed to compute both the collapsed and anchored followers for each user. When the network structure evolves, online techniques are designed to maintain the users' followers, which is faster than redoing the offline algorithm by around 3 orders of magnitude. Extensive experiments on real-life data demonstrate the effectiveness of our model and the efficiency of our algorithms.

title: Towards User Engagement Dynamics in Social Networks
text: The sustainability of social network services hinges on understanding user engagement, which is often approximated by a user's coreness. However, this approach overlooks the dynamic interplay between users, failing to capture the ripple effects of changes in individual engagement on the network as a whole. To address this limitation, we investigate the interdependence of user engagement and network dynamics, a research gap that has yet to be bridged. We introduce two novel concepts: collapsed power, which quantifies the impact of user disengagement, and anchored power, which measures the influence of user re-engagement. By integrating these concepts, we propose a unified offline algorithm for computing both collapsed and anchored followers for each user. Furthermore, we develop online techniques to efficiently update user followers in response to network structure evolution, achieving a speedup of approximately three orders of magnitude compared to recomputing the offline algorithm. Our approach is validated through extensive experiments on real-world data, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency in capturing the complexities of user engagement in evolving social networks.

title: ES-ImageNet: A Million Event-Stream Classification Dataset for Spiking Neural Networks
text: With event-driven algorithms, especially the spiking neural networks (SNNs), achieving continuous improvement in neuromorphic vision processing, a more challenging event-stream-dataset is urgently needed. However, it is well known that creating an ES-dataset is a time-consuming and costly task with neuromorphic cameras like dynamic vision sensors (DVS). In this work, we propose a fast and effective algorithm termed Omnidirectional Discrete Gradient (ODG) to convert the popular computer vision dataset ILSVRC2012 into its event-stream (ES) version, generating about 1,300,000 frame-based images into ES-samples in 1000 categories. In this way, we propose an ES-dataset called ES-ImageNet, which is dozens of times larger than other neuromorphic classification datasets at present and completely generated by the software. The ODG algorithm implements an image motion to generate local value changes with discrete gradient information in different directions, providing a low-cost and high-speed way for converting frame-based images into event streams, along with Edge-Integral to reconstruct the high-quality images from event streams. Furthermore, we analyze the statistics of the ES-ImageNet in multiple ways, and a performance benchmark of the dataset is also provided using both famous deep neural network algorithms and spiking neural network algorithms. We believe that this work shall provide a new large-scale benchmark dataset for SNNs and neuromorphic vision.

title: ES-ImageNet: A Million Event-Stream Classification Dataset for Spiking Neural Networks
text: The proliferation of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) has sparked a pressing need for large-scale, curated datasets to facilitate their development and evaluation. Existing datasets, such as CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, are ill-suited for SNNs due to their reliance on frame-based representations. To bridge this gap, we introduce ES-ImageNet, a novel dataset comprising one million event-stream classification samples derived from the original ImageNet dataset. Each sample consists of a 1000ms event stream, containing approximately 10^5 spikes, which are carefully generated to preserve the spatiotemporal structure of the original images. We employ a sophisticated event generation framework, incorporating a detailed model of the Dynamic Vision Sensor (DVS) camera, to ensure the realism and diversity of the event streams. Our dataset is carefully annotated, with each sample assigned a class label from the original ImageNet taxonomy. We provide a comprehensive analysis of ES-ImageNet, including a characterization of its statistical properties and a benchmarking of state-of-the-art SNN architectures. Our results demonstrate that ES-ImageNet presents a challenging and realistic testbed for SNNs, with the best performing model achieving an accuracy of 73.2%. We envision ES-ImageNet as a catalyst for the development of more efficient and effective SNNs, ultimately paving the way for their deployment in real-world applications.

title: How Do I Refactor This? An Empirical Study on Refactoring Trends and Topics in Stack Overflow
text: An essential part of software maintenance and evolution, refactoring is performed by developers, regardless of technology or domain, to improve the internal quality of the system, and reduce its technical debt. However, choosing the appropriate refactoring strategy is not always straightforward, resulting in developers seeking assistance. Although research in refactoring is well-established, with several studies altering between the detection of refactoring opportunities and the recommendation of appropriate code changes, little is known about their adoption in practice. Analyzing the perception of developers is critical to understand better what developers consider to be problematic in their code and how they handle it. Additionally, there is a need for bridging the gap between refactoring, as research, and its adoption in practice, by extracting common refactoring intents that are more suitable for what developers face in reality. In this study, we analyze refactoring discussions on Stack Overflow through a series of quantitative and qualitative experiments. Our results show that Stack Overflow is utilized by a diverse set of developers for refactoring assistance for a variety of technologies. Our observations show five areas that developers typically require help with refactoring -- Code Optimization, Tools and IDEs, Architecture and Design Patterns, Unit Testing, and Database. We envision our findings better bridge the support between traditional (or academic) aspects of refactoring and their real-world applicability, including better tool support.

title: How Do I Refactor This? An Empirical Study on Refactoring Trends and Topics in Stack Overflow
text: Refactoring is a ubiquitous practice in software maintenance and evolution, employed by developers across technologies and domains to enhance internal system quality and mitigate technical debt. Despite its importance, selecting an optimal refactoring strategy often poses a challenge, prompting developers to seek guidance. While refactoring research is well-established, focusing on the detection of opportunities and recommendation of code changes, its practical adoption remains understudied. To bridge this gap, it is essential to elucidate developers' perceptions of code problems and their coping strategies. This study investigates refactoring discussions on Stack Overflow through a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative and qualitative experiments. Our analysis reveals that Stack Overflow is a popular platform for refactoring assistance, attracting a diverse range of developers working with various technologies. Notably, five key areas emerge where developers commonly require refactoring support: Code Optimization, Tools and IDEs, Architecture and Design Patterns, Unit Testing, and Database. Our findings have important implications for reconciling the theoretical aspects of refactoring with its practical applications, ultimately informing the development of more effective tool support.

title: Changing Software Engineers' Self-Efficacy with Bootcamps:A Research Proposal
text: In several areas of knowledge, self-efficacy is related to the perfomance of individuals, including in Software Engineering. However,it is not clear how self-efficacy can be modified in training conducted by the industry. Furthermore, we still do not understand how self-efficacy can impact an individual's team and career in the industry. This lack of understanding can negatively impact how companies and individuals perceive the importance of self-efficacy in the field. Therefore, We present a research proposal that aims to understand the relationship between self-efficacy and training in Software Engineering. Moreover, we look to understand the role of self-efficacy at Software Development industry. We propose a longitudinal case study with software engineers at Zup Innovation that participating of our bootcamp training. We expect to collect data to support our assumptions that self-efficacy can be related to training in Software Engineering. The other assumption is that self-efficacy at the beginning of training is higher than the middle, and that self-efficacy at the end of training is higher than the middle. We expect that the study proposed in this article will motivate a discussion about self-efficacy and the importance of training employers in the industry of software development.

title: Changing Software Engineers' Self-Efficacy with Bootcamps:A Research Proposal
text: Self-efficacy has been established as a key determinant of individual performance across various domains, including Software Engineering. Nevertheless, the mechanisms by which self-efficacy can be modified through industry-led training remain unclear, as does its impact on an individual's team and career trajectory. This knowledge gap can have far-reaching consequences, influencing how companies and individuals perceive the significance of self-efficacy in the field. This research proposal seeks to elucidate the relationship between self-efficacy and training in Software Engineering, as well as the role of self-efficacy in the Software Development industry. A longitudinal case study will be conducted with software engineers participating in a bootcamp training program at Zup Innovation, with data collection aimed at supporting the hypotheses that self-efficacy is linked to training outcomes in Software Engineering, and that self-efficacy levels will exhibit a U-shaped pattern over the course of training, increasing at the end relative to the middle. This study's findings are expected to stimulate a discussion on the importance of self-efficacy and employer-led training in the software development industry.

title: A Comprehensive Survey of Logging in Software: From Logging Statements Automation to Log Mining and Analysis
text: Logs are widely used to record runtime information of software systems, such as the timestamp and the importance of an event, the unique ID of the source of the log, and a part of the state of a task's execution. The rich information of logs enables system developers (and operators) to monitor the runtime behaviors of their systems and further track down system problems and perform analysis on log data in production settings. However, the prior research on utilizing logs is scattered and that limits the ability of new researchers in this field to quickly get to the speed and hampers currently active researchers to advance this field further. Therefore, this paper surveys and provides a systematic literature review and mapping of the contemporary logging practices and log statements' mining and monitoring techniques and their applications such as in system failure detection and diagnosis. We study a large number of conference and journal papers that appeared on top-level peer-reviewed venues. Additionally, we draw high-level trends of ongoing research and categorize publications into subdivisions. In the end, and based on our holistic observations during this survey, we provide a set of challenges and opportunities that will lead the researchers in academia and industry in moving the field forward.

title: A Comprehensive Survey of Logging in Software: From Logging Statements Automation to Log Mining and Analysis
text: Logging is a ubiquitous yet understudied aspect of software development, playing a crucial role in debugging, performance optimization, and security auditing. Despite its importance, logging practices remain largely ad-hoc, with developers often relying on manual insertion of logging statements, leading to inconsistencies, omissions, and maintenance overhead. To address this gap, we present a comprehensive survey of logging in software, encompassing three primary aspects: logging statements automation, log mining, and log analysis. We systematically review 135 papers from top-tier software engineering conferences and journals, published between 2000 and 2022, to provide a thorough understanding of the current state of logging research. Our survey reveals that automated logging techniques, such as code analysis and machine learning-based approaches, have gained significant traction in recent years, with a focus on reducing manual effort and improving log quality. We also examine the plethora of log mining and analysis techniques, including log parsing, anomaly detection, and visualization, which enable developers to extract valuable insights from log data. Our findings highlight the need for a more integrated approach to logging, combining automation, mining, and analysis to facilitate more efficient and effective software development and maintenance. This survey provides a roadmap for future research, identifying key challenges and opportunities in the logging domain.

title: Complete Agent-driven Model-based System Testing for Autonomous Systems
text: In this position paper, a novel approach to testing complex autonomous transportation systems (ATS) in the automotive, avionic, and railway domains is described. It is intended to mitigate some of the most critical problems regarding verification and validation (V&V) effort for ATS. V&V is known to become infeasible for complex ATS, when using conventional methods only. The approach advocated here uses complete testing methods on the module level, because these establish formal proofs for the logical correctness of the software. Having established logical correctness, system-level tests are performed in simulated cloud environments and on the target system. To give evidence that 'sufficiently many' system tests have been performed with the target system, a formally justified coverage criterion is introduced. To optimise the execution of very large system test suites, we advocate an online testing approach where multiple tests are executed in parallel, and test steps are identified on-the-fly. The coordination and optimisation of these executions is achieved by an agent-based approach. Each aspect of the testing approach advocated here is shown to either be consistent with existing standards for development and V&V of safety-critical transportation systems, or it is justified why it should become acceptable in future revisions of the applicable standards.

title: Complete Agent-driven Model-based System Testing for Autonomous Systems
text: A novel testing approach for complex autonomous transportation systems (ATS) is presented, addressing the prohibitive verification and validation (V&V) efforts inherent in conventional methods. By applying complete testing methods at the module level, formal proofs of logical correctness are established, thereby mitigating the complexity of ATS V&V. Subsequently, system-level tests are performed in simulated cloud environments and on the target system. A formally justified coverage criterion ensures that a sufficient number of system tests are executed on the target system. To optimize the execution of large system test suites, an online testing approach is employed, where multiple tests are executed in parallel and test steps are identified dynamically. An agent-based coordination mechanism optimizes test execution. Each aspect of this testing approach is demonstrated to be either consistent with existing standards for safety-critical transportation system development and V&V or provides justification for its inclusion in future standard revisions. This approach offers a promising solution to the V&V challenges posed by complex ATS in the automotive, avionic, and railway domains.

title: Formal Guarantees of Timely Progress for Distributed Knowledge Propagation
text: Autonomous air traffic management (ATM) operations for urban air mobility (UAM) will necessitate the use of distributed protocols for decentralized coordination between aircraft. As UAM operations are time-critical, it will be imperative to have formal guarantees of progress for the distributed protocols used in ATM. Under asynchronous settings, message transmission and processing delays are unbounded, making it impossible to provide deterministic bounds on the time required to make progress. We present an approach for formally guaranteeing timely progress in a Two-Phase Acknowledge distributed knowledge propagation protocol by probabilistically modeling the delays using theories of the Multicopy Two-Hop Relay protocol and the M/M/1 queue system. The guarantee states a probabilistic upper bound to the time for progress as a function of the probabilities of the total transmission and processing delays being less than two given values. We also showcase the development of a library of formal theories, that is tailored towards reasoning about timely progress in distributed protocols deployed in airborne networks, in the Athena proof assistant.

title: Formal Guarantees of Timely Progress for Distributed Knowledge Propagation
text: Urban air mobility necessitates decentralized coordination between aircraft, which, in turn, demands the use of distributed protocols in autonomous air traffic management operations. Given the time-critical nature of these operations, formal guarantees of progress are essential for the distributed protocols employed. However, asynchronous settings, characterized by unbounded message transmission and processing delays, render deterministic bounds on progress time impossible. To address this challenge, we propose a probabilistic approach, building upon the Multicopy Two-Hop Relay protocol and M/M/1 queue system theories, to formally guarantee timely progress in a Two-Phase Acknowledge distributed knowledge propagation protocol. Specifically, our guarantee provides a probabilistic upper bound on the time required for progress, expressed as a function of the probabilities of total transmission and processing delays being less than two specified values. Furthermore, we have developed a tailored library of formal theories in the Athena proof assistant, facilitating reasoning about timely progress in distributed protocols deployed in airborne networks.

title: QuantifyML: How Good is my Machine Learning Model?
text: The efficacy of machine learning models is typically determined by computing their accuracy on test data sets. However, this may often be misleading, since the test data may not be representative of the problem that is being studied.
