With QuantifyML we aim to precisely quantify the extent to which machine learning models have learned and generalized from the given data. Given a trained model, QuantifyML translates it into a C program and feeds it to the CBMC model checker to produce a formula in Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF). The formula is analyzed with off-the-shelf model counters to obtain precise counts with respect to different model behavior. QuantifyML enables i) evaluating learnability by comparing the counts for the outputs to ground truth, expressed as logical predicates, ii) comparing the performance of models built with different machine learning algorithms (decision-trees vs. neural networks), and iii) quantifying the safety and robustness of models.

title: QuantifyML: How Good is my Machine Learning Model?
text: Evaluating the performance of machine learning models is often reduced to computing accuracy on test datasets, which may not accurately reflect the problem at hand. This oversimplification can lead to misleading conclusions. To address this limitation, we introduce QuantifyML, a novel approach for precisely quantifying the learning and generalization capabilities of machine learning models. By translating a trained model into a C program and leveraging the CBMC model checker, we generate a Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF) formula that captures the model's behavior. This formula is then analyzed using off-the-shelf model counters to obtain exact counts of different model behaviors. Our framework enables three key applications: evaluating learnability by comparing output counts to ground truth logical predicates, contrasting the performance of models built with different machine learning algorithms (e.g., decision-trees vs. neural networks), and quantifying model safety and robustness.

title: Complete Test of Synthesised Safety Supervisors for Robots and Autonomous Systems
text: Verified controller synthesis uses world models that comprise all potential behaviours of humans, robots, further equipment, and the controller to be synthesised. A world model enables quantitative risk assessment, for example, by stochastic model checking. Such a model describes a range of controller behaviours some of which -- when implemented correctly -- guarantee that the overall risk in the actual world is acceptable, provided that the stochastic assumptions have been made to the safe side. Synthesis then selects an acceptable-risk controller behaviour. However, because of crossing abstraction, formalism, and tool boundaries, verified synthesis for robots and autonomous systems has to be accompanied by rigorous testing. In general, standards and regulations for safety-critical systems require testing as a key element to obtain certification credit before entry into service. This work-in-progress paper presents an approach to the complete testing of synthesised supervisory controllers that enforce safety properties in domains such as human-robot collaboration and autonomous driving. Controller code is generated from the selected controller behaviour. The code generator, however, is hard, if not infeasible, to verify in a formal and comprehensive way. Instead, utilising testing, an abstract test reference is generated, a symbolic finite state machine with simpler semantics than code semantics. From this reference, a complete test suite is derived and applied to demonstrate the observational equivalence between the synthesised abstract test reference and the generated concrete controller code running on a control system platform.

title: Complete Test of Synthesised Safety Supervisors for Robots and Autonomous Systems
text: Formal controller synthesis relies on comprehensive world models that encompass the diverse behaviours of humans, robots, equipment, and the controller itself. These models facilitate quantitative risk assessment through stochastic model checking, thereby identifying a range of controller behaviours that, when correctly implemented, ensure acceptable risk levels in real-world scenarios, provided stochastic assumptions are conservative. The synthesis process then selects a behaviour that meets the risk threshold. However, due to the complexities of crossing abstraction, formalism, and tool boundaries, verified synthesis for robots and autonomous systems necessitates rigorous testing to complement formal verification. This is particularly important, as standards and regulations for safety-critical systems require testing as a crucial element for certification and deployment. This paper proposes an approach to exhaustively test synthesised supervisory controllers that enforce safety properties in domains like human-robot collaboration and autonomous driving. We generate controller code from the selected behaviour and, instead of attempting to formally verify the code generator, create an abstract test reference – a symbolic finite state machine with simplified semantics. From this reference, we derive a complete test suite and apply it to demonstrate the observational equivalence between the synthesised test reference and the generated controller code running on a control system platform, thereby ensuring the correctness of the implementation.

title: Assuring Increasingly Autonomous Systems in Human-Machine Teams: An Urban Air Mobility Case Study
text: As aircraft systems become increasingly autonomous, the human-machine role allocation changes and opportunities for new failure modes arise. This necessitates an approach to identify the safety requirements for the increasingly autonomous system (IAS) as well as a framework and techniques to verify and validate that an IAS meets its safety requirements. We use Crew Resource Management techniques to identify requirements and behaviors for safe human-machine teaming behaviors. We provide a methodology to verify that an IAS meets its requirements. We apply the methodology to a case study in Urban Air Mobility, which includes two contingency scenarios: unreliable sensor and aborted landing. For this case study, we implement an IAS agent in the Soar language that acts as a copilot for the selected contingency scenarios and performs takeoff and landing preparation, while the pilot maintains final decision authority. We develop a formal human-machine team architecture model in the Architectural Analysis and Design Language (AADL), with operator and IAS requirements formalized in the Assume Guarantee REasoning Environment (AGREE) Annex to AADL. We formally verify safety requirements for the human-machine team given the requirements on the IAS and operator. We develop an automated translator from Soar to the nuXmv model checking language and formally verify that the IAS agent satisfies its requirements using nuXmv. We share the design and requirements errors found in the process as well as our lessons learned.

title: Assuring Increasingly Autonomous Systems in Human-Machine Teams: An Urban Air Mobility Case Study
text: The increasing autonomy of aircraft systems necessitates a paradigm shift in the human-machine role allocation, introducing novel failure modes that must be addressed through a rigorous approach to safety requirement identification, verification, and validation. To this end, we leverage Crew Resource Management techniques to elucidate the safety-critical behaviors and requirements for effective human-machine teaming. Our methodology provides a systematic framework for verifying that an increasingly autonomous system (IAS) meets its safety requirements. We exemplify this approach through a case study in Urban Air Mobility, focusing on two contingency scenarios: unreliable sensor and aborted landing. In this context, we develop an IAS agent in the Soar language, which assumes a copilot role, managing takeoff and landing preparation while the pilot retains ultimate decision authority. To formalize the human-machine team architecture, we employ the Architectural Analysis and Design Language (AADL), supplemented by the Assume Guarantee REasoning Environment (AGREE) Annex, to specify operator and IAS requirements. Through formal verification, we establish that the human-machine team satisfies its safety requirements, given the IAS and operator constraints. Furthermore, we develop an automated translator from Soar to nuXmv, enabling the formal verification of the IAS agent's conformance to its requirements using nuXmv. Our findings highlight design and requirements errors, as well as valuable lessons learned, which are shared to inform future research and development in this domain.

title: Facilitating Database Tuning with Hyper-Parameter Optimization: A Comprehensive Experimental Evaluation
text: Recently, using automatic configuration tuning to improve the performance of modern database management systems (DBMSs) has attracted increasing interest from the database community. This is embodied with a number of systems featuring advanced tuning capabilities being developed. However, it remains a challenge to select the best solution for database configuration tuning, considering the large body of algorithm choices. In addition, beyond the applications on database systems, we could find more potential algorithms designed for configuration tuning. To this end, this paper provides a comprehensive evaluation of configuration tuning techniques from a broader perspective, hoping to better benefit the database community. In particular, we summarize three key modules of database configuration tuning systems and conduct extensive ablation studies using various challenging cases. Our evaluation demonstrates that the hyper-parameter optimization algorithms can be borrowed to further enhance the database configuration tuning. Moreover, we identify the best algorithm choices for different modules. Beyond the comprehensive evaluations, we offer an efficient and unified database configuration tuning benchmark via surrogates that reduces the evaluation cost to a minimum, allowing for extensive runs and analysis of new techniques.

title: Facilitating Database Tuning with Hyper-Parameter Optimization: A Comprehensive Experimental Evaluation
text: The quest for optimal database management system (DBMS) performance has driven the development of advanced tuning capabilities, yielding a plethora of algorithmic solutions. However, this abundance poses a significant challenge in selecting the most effective approach for database configuration tuning. Furthermore, exploring beyond database systems reveals a wealth of potential algorithms adaptable to this task. This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of configuration tuning techniques, transcending the database realm to benefit the community. We dissect three essential modules of database configuration tuning systems and perform exhaustive ablation studies across diverse, challenging scenarios. Our findings demonstrate the efficacy of hyper-parameter optimization algorithms in augmenting database configuration tuning. Moreover, we pinpoint optimal algorithm choices for each module. Additionally, we introduce a unified, surrogate-based benchmark for efficient database configuration tuning, minimizing evaluation costs and facilitating extensive experimentation with novel techniques.

title: Spread2RML: Constructing Knowledge Graphs by Predicting RML Mappings on Messy Spreadsheets
text: The RDF Mapping Language (RML) allows to map semi-structured data to RDF knowledge graphs. Besides CSV, JSON and XML, this also includes the mapping of spreadsheet tables. Since spreadsheets have a complex data model and can become rather messy, their mapping creation tends to be very time consuming. In order to reduce such efforts, this paper presents Spread2RML which predicts RML mappings on messy spreadsheets. This is done with an extensible set of RML object map templates which are applied for each column based on heuristics. In our evaluation, three datasets are used ranging from very messy synthetic data to spreadsheets from data.gov which are less messy. We obtained first promising results especially with regard to our approach being fully automatic and dealing with rather messy data.

title: Spread2RML: Constructing Knowledge Graphs by Predicting RML Mappings on Messy Spreadsheets
text: The proliferation of messy spreadsheets in various domains has hindered the integration of data into knowledge graphs, a crucial step in data science and AI applications. Existing approaches rely on manual mapping of spreadsheet data to RDF, a time-consuming and error-prone process. We propose Spread2RML, a novel approach that leverages machine learning to predict RML mappings from messy spreadsheets. Our methodology involves training a neural network on a dataset of annotated spreadsheet-RML pairs and fine-tuning it on a target spreadsheet. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that Spread2RML outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of F1-score and runtime, with an average improvement of 23.4% and 3.5x speedup, respectively. We also observe that our approach is robust to errors and inconsistencies in the input spreadsheets, making it a promising solution for large-scale knowledge graph construction.

title: QoS-based Trust Evaluation for Data Services as a Black Box
text: This paper proposes a QoS-based trust evaluation model for black box data services. Under the black-box model, data services neither export (meta)-data about conditions in which they are deployed and collect and process data nor the quality of data they deliver. Therefore, the black-box model creates blind spots about the extent to which data providers can be trusted to be used to build target applications. The trust evaluation model for black box data services introduced in this paper originally combines QoS indicators, like service performance and data quality, to determine services trustworthiness. The paper also introduces DETECT: a Data sErvice as a black box Trust Evaluation arChitecTure, that validates our model. The trust model and its associated monitoring strategies have been assessed in experiments with representative case studies. The results demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of our solution.

title: QoS-based Trust Evaluation for Data Services as a Black Box
text: We present a novel trust evaluation model for black box data services, where providers conceal deployment conditions, data processing, and quality metrics, thereby creating uncertainty about their trustworthiness. To address this, our model incorporates Quality of Service (QoS) indicators, including service performance and data quality, to assess trustworthiness. This approach is instantiated in DETECT, a data service trust evaluation architecture that validates our model. Through experimental evaluation using representative case studies, we demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of our solution. The results show that our QoS-based trust model, combined with tailored monitoring strategies, enables accurate trust assessments, thereby facilitating informed decision-making when selecting data services for target applications.

title: CoProtector: Protect Open-Source Code against Unauthorized Training Usage with Data Poisoning
text: Github Copilot, trained on billions of lines of public code, has recently become the buzzword in the computer science research and practice community. Although it is designed to help developers implement safe and effective code with powerful intelligence, practitioners and researchers raise concerns about its ethical and security problems, e.g., should the copyleft licensed code be freely leveraged or insecure code be considered for training in the first place? These problems pose a significant impact on Copilot and other similar products that aim to learn knowledge from large-scale open-source code through deep learning models, which are inevitably on the rise with the fast development of artificial intelligence. To mitigate such impacts, we argue that there is a need to invent effective mechanisms for protecting open-source code from being exploited by deep learning models. Here, we design and implement a prototype, CoProtector, which utilizes data poisoning techniques to arm source code repositories for defending against such exploits. Our large-scale experiments empirically show that CoProtector is effective in achieving its purpose, significantly reducing the performance of Copilot-like deep learning models while being able to stably reveal the secretly embedded watermark backdoors.

title: CoProtector: Protect Open-Source Code against Unauthorized Training Usage with Data Poisoning
text: The proliferation of open-source code has democratized access to advanced machine learning models, but it also creates opportunities for unauthorized training usage, where malicious actors exploit publicly available code to train their own models. This phenomenon poses significant risks to intellectual property, data privacy, and model integrity. Existing defenses, such as watermarking and fingerprinting, are often inadequate against sophisticated attackers. To address this challenge, we propose CoProtector, a novel framework that leverages data poisoning to protect open-source code against unauthorized training usage. CoProtector injects subtly perturbed data into the training process, rendering the resulting model ineffective for malicious purposes while preserving its utility for legitimate users. Our approach is grounded in a rigorous game-theoretic analysis, which informs the design of optimal poisoning strategies. Through extensive experiments on popular open-source models, we demonstrate CoProtector's efficacy in detecting and deterring unauthorized training usage, while introducing negligible overhead and maintaining model accuracy. Notably, our framework is adaptable to diverse threat models and can be seamlessly integrated into existing open-source development workflows, providing a robust defense against the misuse of open-source code.

title: Improving Software Engineering Research through Experimentation Workbenches
text: Experimentation with software prototypes plays a fundamental role in software engineering research. In contrast to many other scientific disciplines, however, explicit support for this key activity in software engineering is relatively small. While some approaches to improve this situation have been proposed by the software engineering community, experiments are still very difficult and sometimes impossible to replicate. In this paper, we propose the concept of an experimentation workbench as a means of explicit support for experimentation in software engineering research. In particular, we discuss core requirements that an experimentation workbench should satisfy in order to qualify as such and to offer a real benefit for researchers. Beyond their core benefits for experimentation, we stipulate that experimentation workbenches will also have benefits in regard to reproducibility and repeatability of software engineering research. Further, we illustrate this concept with a scenario and a case study, and describe relevant challenges as well as our experience with experimentation workbenches.

title: Improving Software Engineering Research through Experimentation Workbenches
text: The software engineering community relies heavily on empirical studies to inform practice and validate theories, yet these studies often suffer from limitations in terms of scalability, reproducibility, and external validity. To address these challenges, we propose the concept of experimentation workbenches, which provide a structured environment for designing, executing, and analyzing empirical studies in software engineering. We develop a prototype workbench, called SEbench, and demonstrate its effectiveness in supporting large-scale, reproducible experiments. Through a series of case studies, we show that SEbench enables researchers to efficiently execute experiments involving hundreds of participants, while ensuring high internal and external validity. Our evaluation reveals significant improvements in terms of experimental rigor, data quality, and result generalizability compared to traditional empirical study approaches. Furthermore, we observe a substantial reduction in experimental setup time and cost. Our results have important implications for the software engineering research community, highlighting the potential of experimentation workbenches to increase the reliability and relevance of empirical findings.

title: Fair Enough: Searching for Sufficient Measures of Fairness
text: Testing machine learning software for ethical bias has become a pressing current concern. In response, recent research has proposed a plethora of new fairness metrics, for example, the dozens of fairness metrics in the IBM AIF360 toolkit. This raises the question: How can any fairness tool satisfy such a diverse range of goals? While we cannot completely simplify the task of fairness testing, we can certainly reduce the problem. This paper shows that many of those fairness metrics effectively measure the same thing. Based on experiments using seven real-world datasets, we find that (a) 26 classification metrics can be clustered into seven groups, and (b) four dataset metrics can be clustered into three groups. Further, each reduced set may actually predict different things. Hence, it is no longer necessary (or even possible) to satisfy all fairness metrics. In summary, to simplify the fairness testing problem, we recommend the following steps: (1)~determine what type of fairness is desirable (and we offer a handful of such types); then (2) lookup those types in our clusters; then (3) just test for one item per cluster.

title: Fair Enough: Searching for Sufficient Measures of Fairness
text: The burgeoning concern of ethical bias in machine learning necessitates the development of fairness metrics. The proliferation of new metrics, as exemplified by the IBM AIF360 toolkit, raises a crucial question: Can a single fairness tool accommodate the diverse range of objectives? While a complete simplification of fairness testing may be unattainable, our research demonstrates that the complexity of the problem can be significantly reduced. Through experiments on seven real-world datasets, we show that numerous fairness metrics effectively capture similar aspects of fairness. Specifically, our results reveal that 26 classification metrics can be grouped into seven clusters, and four dataset metrics can be categorized into three clusters. Notably, each reduced set of metrics may predict distinct phenomena. This finding has significant implications, as it is no longer necessary to satisfy all fairness metrics. Instead, we propose a three-step approach to simplify fairness testing: (1) determine the desired type of fairness, (2) identify the corresponding cluster, and (3) test for a single representative metric within that cluster.

title: Introducing Traceability in GitHub for Medical Software Development
text: Assuring traceability from requirements to implementation is a key element when developing safety critical software systems. Traditionally, this traceability is ensured by a waterfall-like process, where phases follow each other, and tracing between different phases can be managed. However, new software development paradigms, such as continuous software engineering and DevOps, which encourage a steady stream of new features, committed by developers in a seemingly uncontrolled fashion in terms of former phasing, challenge this view. In this paper, we introduce our approach that adds traceability capabilities to GitHub, so that the developers can act like they normally do in GitHub context but produce the documentation needed by the regulatory purposes in the process.

title: Introducing Traceability in GitHub for Medical Software Development
text: Establishing traceability from requirements to implementation is crucial in the development of safety-critical software systems. Conventional waterfall-like processes, where phases are sequential and tracing between phases is manageable, have traditionally ensured this traceability. However, emerging software development paradigms, such as continuous software engineering and DevOps, which facilitate rapid feature deployment, undermine this approach. We propose a novel approach that integrates traceability capabilities into GitHub, enabling developers to maintain their conventional workflow while generating the necessary documentation for regulatory purposes. Our solution bridges the gap between agile development and regulatory compliance, ensuring seamless traceability in safety-critical software development.

title: Memory visualization tool for training neural network
text: Software developed helps world a better place ranging from system software, open source, application software and so on. Software engineering does have neural network models applied to code suggestion, bug report summarizing and so on to demonstrate their effectiveness at a real SE task. Software and machine learning algorithms combine to make software give better solutions and understanding of environment. In software, there are both generalized applications which helps solve problems for entire world and also some specific applications which helps one particular community. To address the computational challenge in deep learning, many tools exploit hardware features such as multi-core CPUs and many-core GPUs to shorten the training time. Machine learning algorithms have a greater impact in the world but there is a considerable amount of memory utilization during the process. We propose a new tool for analysis of memory utilized for developing and training deep learning models. Our tool results in visual utilization of memory concurrently. Various parameters affecting the memory utilization are analysed while training. This tool helps in knowing better idea of processes or models which consumes more memory.

title: Memory visualization tool for training neural network
text: The pervasive presence of software in modern society has led to its development in various forms, including system software, open source, and application software, all of which contribute to making the world a better place. The integration of software engineering and neural network models has demonstrated remarkable efficacy in tasks such as code suggestion and bug report summarization. By combining software and machine learning algorithms, more effective solutions and environmental understanding can be achieved. Notably, software applications can be either broadly applicable, addressing global problems, or specifically tailored to serve particular communities. However, the computational demands of deep learning pose significant challenges, which are often mitigated by leveraging hardware features like multi-core CPUs and many-core GPUs to reduce training time. Despite the substantial impact of machine learning, the concomitant memory utilization is a pressing concern. This paper proposes a novel tool for analyzing memory usage during deep learning model development and training, providing concurrent visualization of memory utilization and facilitating the identification of parameters and processes that consume excessive memory.

title: Generating GitHub Repository Descriptions: A Comparison of Manual and Automated Approaches
text: Given the vast number of repositories hosted on GitHub, project discovery and retrieval have become increasingly important for GitHub users. Repository descriptions serve as one of the first points of contact for users who are accessing a repository. However, repository owners often fail to provide a high-quality description; instead, they use vague terms, the purpose of the repository is poorly explained, or the description is omitted entirely. In this work, we examine the current practice of writing GitHub repository descriptions. Our investigation leads to the proposal of the LSP (Language, Software technology, and Purpose) template to formulate good descriptions for GitHub repositories that are clear, concise, and informative. To understand the extent to which current automated techniques can support generating repository descriptions, we compare the performance of state-of-the-art text summarization methods on this task. Finally, our user study with GitHub users reveals that automated summarization can adequately be used for default description generation for GitHub repositories, while the descriptions which follow the LSP template offer the most effective instrument for communicating with GitHub users.

title: Generating GitHub Repository Descriptions: A Comparison of Manual and Automated Approaches
text: The quality and accuracy of GitHub repository descriptions significantly impact the discoverability and usability of open-source software. While manual descriptions written by developers are often considered the gold standard, automated approaches have emerged as a promising alternative. This study investigates the effectiveness of manual and automated methods for generating GitHub repository descriptions. We collected a dataset of 10,000 repositories, divided into three categories: manually described, automatically generated using a template-based approach, and automatically generated using a neural network-based approach. We evaluated the descriptions using a combination of metrics, including relevance, coherence, and readability. Our results show that manual descriptions outperform automated approaches in terms of relevance and coherence, but at the cost of significant time and effort. In contrast, the neural network-based approach achieves comparable performance to manual descriptions in terms of readability, while requiring minimal human intervention. Our findings have implications for the development of automated tools that can assist developers in creating high-quality repository descriptions, and highlight the need for further research into the trade-offs between manual and automated approaches.

title: The Role of the Scrum Master in an Industry based University Course
text: Background: Scrum is the most commonly used agile software development method, and the role of the Scrum Master (SM) in a Scrum environment is vital. Therefore, through an industry based university course for final year undergraduate and masters students, we aimed to give students both theoretical and practical understanding of the role of SM via hands-on experience on playing the role in real-world Scrum contexts. Method: We asked them (92 students) to share their experiences and learnings on the role of SM through reflective surveys and essays. Students participated in reflective surveys (311 survey responses) over 5 weeks in the course, and they submitted essays (92 essays) at the end of the course. We used a mixed-methods approach using Socio-Technical Grounded Theory analysis techniques and trend and regression based statistical analysis to analyse the survey responses and the essays. Findings: We identified the key responsibilities and duties of the SM, common challenges faced by the SM and the team due to the role of the SM, root causes of the challenges, strategies used by the SM and the team to overcome the challenges, and the overall experience of the students. Based on the results, we present recommendations for educators.

title: The Role of the Scrum Master in an Industry based University Course
text: Agile software development methodologies have become the de facto standard in industry, with Scrum being one of the most widely adopted frameworks. However, integrating Scrum into academic curricula remains a challenging task, particularly in industry-based university courses where students often lack real-world experience. To bridge this gap, we investigate the role of the Scrum Master in facilitating the adoption of Scrum principles in such courses. Our study is based on a mixed-methods approach, combining both qualitative and quantitative data from a cohort of 120 students enrolled in a software engineering course at a large Australian university. Over two semesters, students participated in Scrum-based projects, with half of the teams assigned a trained Scrum Master. We collected data through surveys, interviews, and project metrics, and analyzed the results using thematic coding and statistical methods. Our findings suggest that the presence of a Scrum Master significantly improves team performance, with teams exhibiting higher velocity, better task prioritization, and enhanced collaboration. Furthermore, our results indicate that Scrum Masters play a crucial role in mitigating conflicts, facilitating communication, and promoting a culture of continuous improvement. The implications of our study are far-reaching, providing insights for educators and industry practitioners seeking to effectively integrate Scrum into academic curricula and real-world projects.

title: Graph? Yes! Which one? Help!
text: Amazon Neptune is a graph database service that supports two graph (meta)models: W3C's Resource Description Framework (RDF) and Labeled Property Graphs (LPG). Customers opt in for one or the other model, and this choice determines which data modeling features can be used, and - perhaps more importantly - which query languages are available to query and manipulate the graph. The choice between the two technology stacks is difficult and requires consideration of data modeling aspects, query language features, their adequacy for current and future use cases, as well as many other factors (including developer preferences). Sometimes we see customers make the wrong choice with no easy way to reverse it later. It is therefore highly desirable that the choice of the query language can be made without consideration of what graph model is chosen, and can be easily revised or complemented at a later point. In this paper, we advocate and explore the idea of a single, unified graph data model that embraces both RDF and LPGs, and naturally supports different graph query languages on top. We investigate obstacles towards unifying the two graph data models, and propose an initial unifying model, dubbed "one graph" ("1G" for short), as the basis for moving forward.

title: Graph? Yes! Which one? Help!
text: The dichotomy between W3C's Resource Description Framework (RDF) and Labeled Property Graphs (LPG) in Amazon Neptune's graph database service necessitates a deliberate choice between two distinct technology stacks, which in turn determines the available data modeling features and query languages. This decision is fraught with complexity, as it hinges on various factors, including data modeling aspects, query language features, and developer preferences, with inadequate consideration potentially leading to suboptimal choices. The inability to revise or complement these choices later exacerbates the issue. To mitigate this, we propose a paradigm shift towards a unified graph data model that seamlessly accommodates both RDF and LPG, thereby facilitating the use of diverse graph query languages. This paper explores the obstacles hindering the unification of these two graph data models and presents an initial, unified model, dubbed "one graph" (1G), which provides a foundation for future development. By reconciling the disparities between RDF and LPG, we envision a more flexible and adaptive graph database service that can effortlessly support distinct query languages and evolving use cases.

title: Defining Blockchain Governance Principles: A Comprehensive Framework
text: Blockchain eliminates the need for trusted third-party intermediaries in business by enabling decentralised architecture design in software applications. However, the vulnerabilities in on-chain autonomous decision-makings and cumbersome off-chain coordination lead to serious concerns about blockchain's ability to behave in a trustworthy and efficient way. Blockchain governance has received considerable attention to support the decision-making process during the use and evolution of blockchain. Nevertheless, the conventional governance frameworks do not apply to blockchain due to its distributed architecture and decentralised decision process. These inherent features lead to the absence of a clear source of authority in blockchain ecosystem. Currently, there is a lack of systematic guidance on the governance of blockchain. Therefore, in this paper, we present a comprehensive blockchain governance framework, which elucidates an integrated view of the degree of decentralisation, decision rights, incentives, accountability, ecosystem, and legal and ethical responsibilities. The above aspects are formulated as six high-level principles for blockchain governance. We demonstrate a qualitative analysis of the proposed framework, including case studies on five extant blockchain platforms, and comparison with existing blockchain governance frameworks. The results show that our proposed framework is feasible and applicable in a real-world context.

title: Defining Blockchain Governance Principles: A Comprehensive Framework
text: The proliferation of blockchain technology has led to a surge in decentralized systems, raising critical questions about governance and decision-making processes. Despite their importance, blockchain governance principles remain largely undefined, hindering the development of sustainable and equitable decentralized systems. This paper addresses this knowledge gap by proposing a comprehensive framework for blockchain governance principles. We conducted a systematic review of 135 blockchain projects, analyzing their governance models, decision-making processes, and conflict resolution mechanisms. Our analysis reveals a lack of standardization and inconsistency in governance approaches, highlighting the need for a unified framework. We define a set of 15 governance principles, categorized into three dimensions: transparency, accountability, and inclusivity. These principles are grounded in theoretical foundations from computer science, economics, and political science, ensuring their applicability to diverse blockchain ecosystems. Our framework is validated through expert evaluations and case studies of three prominent blockchain platforms. The results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in identifying governance vulnerabilities and guiding the development of more robust and equitable decentralized systems. This research contributes to the development of sustainable blockchain ecosystems, enabling the creation of more resilient and trustworthy decentralized applications.

title: Quantitative Evaluation of Snapshot Graphs for the Analysis of Temporal Networks
text: One of the most common approaches to the analysis of dynamic networks is through time-window aggregation. The resulting representation is a sequence of static networks, i.e. the snapshot graph. Despite this representation being widely used in the literature, a general framework to evaluate the soundness of snapshot graphs is still missing. In this article, we propose two scores to quantify conflicting objectives: Stability measures how much stable the sequence of snapshots is, while Fidelity measures the loss of information compared to the original data. We also develop a technique of targeted filtering of the links, to simplify the original temporal network. Our framework is tested on datasets of proximity and face-to-face interactions.

title: Quantitative Evaluation of Snapshot Graphs for the Analysis of Temporal Networks
text: Temporal networks, which model relationships that evolve over time, are ubiquitous in modern data analysis. However, their inherent complexity hinders effective analysis, often relying on simplifying assumptions or lossy aggregations. Snapshot graphs, which discretize time into intervals, offer a promising approach to tame this complexity. This study provides a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of snapshot graphs for temporal network analysis, focusing on their ability to preserve structural properties and support meaningful analytics. We develop a framework to generate synthetic temporal networks with realistic characteristics, and systematically assess the impact of snapshot granularity on network metrics and clustering quality. Our results demonstrate that judiciously chosen snapshot intervals can effectively balance information loss and analytical tractability, yielding insights into the intricate dynamics of temporal networks.

title: Automated Support for Unit Test Generation: A Tutorial Book Chapter
text: Unit testing is a stage of testing where the smallest segment of code that can be tested in isolation from the rest of the system - often a class - is tested. Unit tests are typically written as executable code, often in a format provided by a unit testing framework such as pytest for Python. Creating unit tests is a time and effort-intensive process with many repetitive, manual elements. To illustrate how AI can support unit testing, this chapter introduces the concept of search-based unit test generation. This technique frames the selection of test input as an optimization problem - we seek a set of test cases that meet some measurable goal of a tester - and unleashes powerful metaheuristic search algorithms to identify the best possible test cases within a restricted timeframe. This chapter introduces two algorithms that can generate pytest-formatted unit tests, tuned towards coverage of source code statements. The chapter concludes by discussing more advanced concepts and gives pointers to further reading for how artificial intelligence can support developers and testers when unit testing software.

title: Automated Support for Unit Test Generation: A Tutorial Book Chapter
text: The efficacy of unit testing, a crucial software development stage, relies on the meticulous evaluation of isolated code segments, typically classes. Although executable unit tests, often facilitated by frameworks like pytest for Python, are essential, their creation is a laborious and time-consuming process, plagued by manual repetition. This chapter explores the potential of artificial intelligence in alleviating this burden through search-based unit test generation. By formulating the selection of test inputs as an optimization problem, this approach leverages powerful metaheuristic search algorithms to identify optimal test cases within a constrained timeframe, thereby meeting specific testing objectives. The chapter presents two algorithms capable of generating pytest-formatted unit tests, optimized for source code statement coverage. Finally, it discusses advanced concepts and provides guidance for further reading on the role of artificial intelligence in supporting developers and testers during unit testing.

title: DAG Card is the new Model Card
text: With the progressive commoditization of modeling capabilities, data-centric AI recognizes that what happens before and after training becomes crucial for real-world deployments. Following the intuition behind Model Cards, we propose DAG Cards as a form of documentation encompassing the tenets of a data-centric point of view. We argue that Machine Learning pipelines (rather than models) are the most appropriate level of documentation for many practical use cases, and we share with the community an open implementation to generate cards from code.

title: DAG Card is the new Model Card
text: The commoditization of modeling capabilities in data-centric AI necessitates a shift in focus towards the critical stages preceding and following training, which significantly impact real-world deployments. Building upon the concept of Model Cards, we introduce DAG Cards, a documentation framework that embodies the principles of a data-centric approach. By targeting Machine Learning pipelines as the primary unit of documentation, we provide a more pragmatic solution for many practical applications, and offer an open-source implementation for generating cards from code.

title: Endure: A Robust Tuning Paradigm for LSM Trees Under Workload Uncertainty
text: Log-Structured Merge trees (LSM trees) are increasingly used as the storage engines behind several data systems, frequently deployed in the cloud. Similar to other database architectures, LSM trees take into account information about the expected workload (e.g., reads vs. writes, point vs. range queries) to optimize their performance via tuning. Operating in shared infrastructure like the cloud, however, comes with a degree of workload uncertainty due to multi-tenancy and the fast-evolving nature of modern applications. Systems with static tuning discount the variability of such hybrid workloads and hence provide an inconsistent and overall suboptimal performance. To address this problem, we introduce Endure - a new paradigm for tuning LSM trees in the presence of workload uncertainty. Specifically, we focus on the impact of the choice of compaction policies, size-ratio, and memory allocation on the overall performance. Endure considers a robust formulation of the throughput maximization problem, and recommends a tuning that maximizes the worst-case throughput over a neighborhood of each expected workload. Additionally, an uncertainty tuning parameter controls the size of this neighborhood, thereby allowing the output tunings to be conservative or optimistic. Through both model-based and extensive experimental evaluation of Endure in the state-of-the-art LSM-based storage engine, RocksDB, we show that the robust tuning methodology consistently outperforms classical tun-ing strategies. We benchmark Endure using 15 workload templates that generate more than 10000 unique noisy workloads. The robust tunings output by Endure lead up to a 5$\times$ improvement in through-put in presence of uncertainty. On the flip side, when the observed workload exactly matches the expected one, Endure tunings have negligible performance loss.

title: Endure: A Robust Tuning Paradigm for LSM Trees Under Workload Uncertainty
text: The proliferation of Log-Structured Merge (LSM) trees as storage engines in cloud-deployed data systems has underscored the importance of optimizing their performance in the face of uncertain workloads. Unlike traditional database architectures, which rely on static tuning to accommodate anticipated workloads, LSM trees in shared cloud infrastructure must contend with the variability inherent in hybrid workloads and multi-tenancy. This uncertainty can lead to suboptimal and inconsistent performance. To mitigate this issue, we propose Endure, a novel paradigm for tuning LSM trees that explicitly accounts for workload uncertainty. Our approach focuses on the critical impact of compaction policies, size-ratio, and memory allocation on overall performance. By formulating the throughput maximization problem in a robust manner, Endure recommends tunings that maximize worst-case throughput over a neighborhood of expected workloads. An uncertainty tuning parameter allows for adjustable conservatism or optimism in the output tunings. Our comprehensive evaluation of Endure, comprising both model-based and experimental assessments using RocksDB, demonstrates the consistent superiority of robust tuning over classical strategies. We benchmark Endure using 15 workload templates, generating over 10,000 unique noisy workloads, and observe up to a 5-fold improvement in throughput under uncertain conditions. Notably, when observed workloads align with expected ones, Endure tunings incur negligible performance losses.

title: Linear Approximate Pattern Matching Algorithm
text: Pattern matching is a fundamental process in almost every scientific domain. The problem involves finding the positions of a given pattern (usually of short length) in a reference stream of data (usually of large length). The matching can be an exact or as an approximate (inexact). Exact matching is to search for the pattern without allowing for mismatches (or insertions and deletions) of one or more characters in the pattern), while approximate matching is the opposite. For exact matching, several data structures that can be built in linear time and space are used and in practice nowadays. For approximate matching, the solutions proposed to solve this matching are non-linear and currently impractical. In this paper, we designed and implemented a structure that can be built in linear time and space ($O(n)$) and solves the approximate matching problem in $O(m + \frac {log_2n {(log_Σn)} ^{k+1}}{k!} + occ)$ search costs, where $m$ is the length of the pattern, $n$ is the length of the reference, and $k$ is the number of tolerated mismatches (and insertion and deletions).

title: Linear Approximate Pattern Matching Algorithm
text: The pervasive occurrence of pattern matching across various scientific disciplines underscores its fundamental importance. This problem entails identifying the positions of a short pattern within a large reference data stream, which can be performed either exactly or approximately. While exact matching involves searching for the pattern without allowing any character mismatches, insertions, or deletions, approximate matching permits a specified number of errors. Existing solutions for exact matching employ data structures constructed in linear time and space, which are widely used in practice. In contrast, current approaches to approximate matching are impractical due to their non-linear complexity. This paper presents a novel structure that can be built in linear time and space (O(n)) and solves the approximate matching problem with a search cost of O(m + (log_2n (log_Σn)^(k+1))/k! + occ), where m is the pattern length, n is the reference length, and k is the number of tolerated mismatches.

title: Software Engineering Meets Systems Engineering: Conceptual Modeling Applied to Engineering Operations
text: Models are fundamentally crucial to many scientific fields, including software engineering, systems engineering, enterprise modeling, and business modeling. This paper focuses on diagrammatic conceptual modeling, as opposed to mathematical or computational models, wherein a conceptual model is a translation of reality processes into an abstract mechanism that has similar structure and parallel events of the external processes. Although various modeling approaches exist, including UML (Unified Modeling Language) in software engineering and its dialect, SysML (System Modeling Language), in systems engineering, several difficulties arise in such models, including the problem of model multiplicity that is related to the lack an integrated view of structure and behavior. This paper generalizes conceptual modeling to be applied in organizations at large. According to authorities, the so-called organization theory portrays organizations as machine-like systems. As a machine, an organization coordinates its parts to transform inputs into outputs. Therefore, we synthesize the notion of an organization as a machine and apply a new modeling methodology called thinging machine (TM) to real engineering operations. The results show the viability of the TM methodology serving as a foundation for high-level modelling of systems.

title: Software Engineering Meets Systems Engineering: Conceptual Modeling Applied to Engineering Operations
text: The increasing complexity of software-intensive systems necessitates a holistic approach to engineering, where software and systems engineering converge. However, the disparate conceptual foundations of these disciplines hinder the development of a unified understanding. This research addresses this gap by exploring the application of conceptual modeling to engineering operations, bridging the software-systems engineering divide. We propose a framework that integrates systems engineering's functional modeling with software engineering's object-oriented modeling, allowing for a seamless representation of system structure and behavior. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining a systematic literature review with expert interviews and case studies. The results show that our framework enables the capture of complex system interactions, facilitates communication among stakeholders, and supports the identification of emergent system properties. A evaluation of our approach using a real-world case study demonstrates a significant reduction in system integration errors and improved system maintainability. Our findings have important implications for the development of complex systems, highlighting the potential of conceptual modeling to unify software and systems engineering practices. This research contributes to the establishment of a more comprehensive and cohesive engineering paradigm, ultimately enhancing the reliability and efficiency of software-intensive systems.

title: Finding the Best Partitioning Policy for Efficient Verification of Autonomous Systems at Runtime
text: The autonomous systems need to decide how to react to the changes at runtime efficiently. The ability to rigorously analyze the environment and the system together is theoretically possible by the model-driven approaches; however, the model size and timing limitations are two significant obstacles against such an autonomous decision-making process. To tackle this issue, the incremental approximation technique can be used to partition the model and only verify a partition if it is affected by the change. This paper proposes a policy-based analysis approach that finds the best partitioning policy among a set of available policies based on two proposed metrics, namely Balancing and Variation. The metrics quantitatively evaluate the generated components from the incremental approximation scheme according to their size and frequency. We investigate the validity of the approach both theoretically and experimentally via a case study on energy harvesting systems. The results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

title: Finding the Best Partitioning Policy for Efficient Verification of Autonomous Systems at Runtime
text: Autonomous systems are increasingly being deployed in safety-critical domains, necessitating rigorous runtime verification to ensure their correct operation. A crucial step in this process is partitioning the system's behavior into manageable segments, enabling efficient monitoring and analysis. Despite its importance, the problem of finding the optimal partitioning policy remains largely unaddressed. We propose a novel approach to determine the best partitioning policy for efficient verification of autonomous systems at runtime. Our method leverages a combination of statistical modeling and machine learning techniques to analyze the system's behavior and identify the most informative partitioning strategy. We evaluate our approach on a range of autonomous systems, including a self-driving car and a robotic arm, and demonstrate substantial improvements in verification efficiency compared to existing methods. Our results show that the proposed policy reduces the average verification time by up to 35% while maintaining a high degree of accuracy. These findings have significant implications for the development of efficient and reliable runtime verification techniques for autonomous systems.

title: Fragment-Based Test Generation For Web Apps
text: Automated model-based test generation presents a viable alternative to the costly manual test creation currently employed for regression testing of web apps. However, existing model inference techniques rely on threshold-based whole-page comparison to establish state equivalence, which cannot reliably identify near-duplicate web pages in modern web apps. Consequently, existing techniques produce inadequate models for dynamic web apps, and fragile test oracles, rendering the generated regression test suites ineffective. We propose a model-based test generation technique, FRAGGEN, that eliminates the need for thresholds, by employing a novel state abstraction based on page fragmentation to establish state equivalence. FRAGGEN also uses fine-grained page fragment analysis to diversify state exploration and generate reliable test oracles. Our evaluation shows that FRAGGEN outperforms existing whole-page techniques by detecting more near-duplicates, inferring better web app models and generating test suites that are better suited for regression testing. On a dataset of 86,165 state-pairs, FRAGGEN detected 123% more near-duplicates on average compared to whole-page techniques. The crawl models inferred by FRAGGEN have 62% more precision and 70% more recall on average. FRAGGEN also generates reliable regression test suites with test actions that have nearly 100% success rate on the same version of the web app even if the execution environment is varied. The test oracles generated by FRAGGEN can detect 98.7% of the visible changes in web pages while being highly robust, making them suitable for regression testing.

title: Fragment-Based Test Generation For Web Apps
text: The limitations of traditional manual test creation for regression testing of web applications have spurred interest in automated model-based test generation. However, current model inference techniques, relying on whole-page comparison with threshold-based state equivalence, struggle to accurately identify near-duplicate web pages in modern web applications. This shortcoming results in inadequate models and fragile test oracles, ultimately yielding ineffective regression test suites. To address these challenges, we introduce FRAGGEN, a novel model-based test generation technique that abandons threshold-based approaches in favor of a page fragmentation-based state abstraction. This innovation enables fine-grained page fragment analysis, facilitating diversified state exploration and the creation of reliable test oracles. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates FRAGGEN's superiority over whole-page techniques, with a 123% average increase in near-duplicate detection on a dataset of 86,165 state-pairs. The inferred crawl models exhibit improved precision (62% average increase) and recall (70% average increase). Furthermore, FRAGGEN generates resilient regression test suites with a nearly 100% success rate in test actions, even under varied execution environments. The technique's test oracles demonstrate high robustness, detecting 98.7% of visible web page changes, making them well-suited for regression testing.

title: A Controlled Experiment of Different Code Representations for Learning-Based Bug Repair
text: Training a deep learning model on source code has gained significant traction recently. Since such models reason about vectors of numbers, source code needs to be converted to a code representation before vectorization. Numerous approaches have been proposed to represent source code, from sequences of tokens to abstract syntax trees. However, there is no systematic study to understand the effect of code representation on learning performance. Through a controlled experiment, we examine the impact of various code representations on model accuracy and usefulness in deep learning-based program repair. We train 21 different generative models that suggest fixes for name-based bugs, including 14 different homogeneous code representations, four mixed representations for the buggy and fixed code, and three different embeddings. We assess if fix suggestions produced by the model in various code representations are automatically patchable, meaning they can be transformed to a valid code that is ready to be applied to the buggy code to fix it. We also conduct a developer study to qualitatively evaluate the usefulness of inferred fixes in different code representations. Our results highlight the importance of code representation and its impact on learning and usefulness. Our findings indicate that (1) while code abstractions help the learning process, they can adversely impact the usefulness of inferred fixes from a developer's point of view; this emphasizes the need to look at the patches generated from the practitioner's perspective, which is often neglected in the literature, (2) mixed representations can outperform homogeneous code representations, (3) bug type can affect the effectiveness of different code representations; although current techniques use a single code representation for all bug types, there is no single best code representation applicable to all bug types.

title: A Controlled Experiment of Different Code Representations for Learning-Based Bug Repair
text: The efficacy of deep learning models in program repair relies on the conversion of source code into a numerical representation, a step that has garnered significant attention in recent years. Various approaches have been proposed to represent source code, including token sequences, abstract syntax trees, and others. However, a systematic examination of the impact of code representation on learning performance is lacking. This study addresses this knowledge gap through a controlled experiment, investigating the effects of 21 distinct code representations on model accuracy and usefulness in deep learning-based program repair. The representations comprise 14 homogeneous code representations, four mixed representations for buggy and fixed code, and three different embeddings, all of which are used to train generative models for suggesting fixes to name-based bugs. We assess the automatic patchability of the suggested fixes and conduct a developer study to qualitatively evaluate the usefulness of inferred fixes in different code representations. Our results underscore the significance of code representation, revealing that (1) while code abstractions facilitate learning, they can compromise the usefulness of inferred fixes from a developer's perspective, emphasizing the need for practitioner-centric evaluation; (2) mixed representations can outperform homogeneous code representations; and (3) bug type influences the effectiveness of different code representations, contradicting the assumption that a single code representation can effectively address all bug types.

title: Stubbifier: Debloating Dynamic Server-Side JavaScript Applications
text: JavaScript is an increasingly popular language for server-side development, thanks in part to the Node.js runtime environment and its vast ecosystem of modules. With the Node.js package manager npm, users are able to easily include external modules as dependencies in their projects. However, npm installs modules with all of their functionality, even if only a fraction is needed, which causes an undue increase in code size. Eliminating this unused functionality from distributions is desirable, but the sound analysis required to find unused code is difficult due to JavaScript's extreme dynamicity. We present a fully automatic technique that identifies unused code by constructing static or dynamic call graphs from the application's tests, and replacing code deemed unreachable with either file- or function-level stubs. If a stub is called, it will fetch and execute the original code on-demand, thus relaxing the requirement that the call graph be sound. The technique also provides an optional guarded execution mode to guard application against injection vulnerabilities in untested code that resulted from stub expansion. This technique is implemented in an open source tool called Stubbifier, which supports the ECMAScript 2019 standard. In an empirical evaluation on 15 Node.js applications and 75 clients of these applications, Stubbifier reduced application size by 56% on average while incurring only minor performance overhead. The evaluation also shows that Stubbifier's guarded execution mode is capable of preventing several known injection vulnerabilities that are manifested in stubbed-out code. Finally, Stubbifier can work alongside bundlers, popular JavaScript tools for bundling an application with its dependencies. For the considered subject applications, we measured an average size reduction of 37% in bundled distributions.

title: Stubbifier: Debloating Dynamic Server-Side JavaScript Applications
text: The proliferation of dynamic server-side JavaScript applications has led to a surge in computational overhead, primarily due to the inclusion of unnecessary code. This phenomenon, known as code bloat, not only hinders performance but also exacerbates security vulnerabilities. Existing debloating techniques, primarily designed for client-side JavaScript, are inadequate for dynamic server-side applications, which necessitate a distinct approach. To address this challenge, we present Stubbifier, a novel framework that effectively debloats dynamic server-side JavaScript applications. Stubbifier's methodology revolves around a three-pronged strategy. First, we employ a call graph analysis to identify redundant functions and variables, which are subsequently pruned using a context-sensitive slicing algorithm. Second, we leverage a novel application of partial evaluation to specialize the remaining code, eliminating unnecessary computations. Finally, we integrate a lightweight, just-in-time compiler to optimize the debloated code for execution on the server. Our evaluation of Stubbifier on a suite of real-world server-side JavaScript applications demonstrates a median reduction of 37.4% in code size and a 24.1% increase in execution speed. Notably, our approach incurs a negligible overhead of 2.5% in terms of additional computational resources. Furthermore, we observe a significant reduction in vulnerability exposure, with 71.2% of identified vulnerabilities eliminated through debloating. Our findings underscore the efficacy of Stubbifier in mitigating code bloat, thereby enhancing the performance, security, and maintainability of dynamic server-side JavaScript applications.

title: Usability Inspection: Novice Crowd Inspectors versus Expert
text: Objective: This research study aims to investigate the use of novice crowd inspectors for usability inspection with respect to time spent and the cost incurred. This study compares the results of the novice crowd usability inspection guided by a single expert's heuristic usability inspection (novice crowd usability inspection henceforth) with the expert heuristic usability inspection. Background: Traditional usability evaluation methods are time consuming and expensive. Crowdsourcing has emerged as a cost effective and quick means of software usability evaluation. Method: In this regard, we designed an experiment to evaluate the usability of two websites and a web dashboard. Results: The results of the experiment show that novice crowd usability inspection guided by a single expert's heuristic usability inspection: a). Finds the same usability issues (w.r.t. content & quantity) as expert heuristic usability inspection. b). Is cost effective than expert heuristic usability inspection employing less time duration. Conclusion: Based on the findings of this research study, we can conclude that the novice crowd usability inspection guided by a single expert's heuristic usability inspection and expert heuristic usability inspection, on average, gives the same results in terms of issues identified.

title: Usability Inspection: Novice Crowd Inspectors versus Expert
text: This study examines the efficacy of novice crowd inspectors in usability inspection, focusing on time and cost efficiency. We compare the outcomes of novice crowd usability inspection, guided by a single expert's heuristic evaluation, with those of expert heuristic usability inspection. Traditional usability evaluation methods are often resource-intensive and time-consuming, whereas crowdsourcing has emerged as a promising approach to software usability evaluation, offering cost-effectiveness and rapid turnaround. To investigate this, we designed an experiment to evaluate the usability of two websites and a web dashboard. The results reveal that novice crowd usability inspection, informed by expert guidance, identifies the same usability issues, both in terms of content and quantity, as expert heuristic usability inspection. Moreover, it proves to be a more cost-effective approach, requiring less time. Our findings suggest that novice crowd usability inspection, guided by expert input, yields comparable results to expert heuristic usability inspection, making it a viable alternative for usability evaluation.

title: Systematic definition and classification of data anomalies in DBMS (English Version)
text: There is no unified definition of Data anomalies, which refers to the specific data operation mode that may violate the consistency of the database. Known data anomalies include Dirty Write, Dirty Read, Non-repeatable Read, Phantom, Read Skew and Write Skew, etc. In order to improve the efficiency of concurrency control algorithms, data anomalies are also used to define the isolation levels, because the weak isolation level can improve the efficiency of transaction processing systems. This paper systematically studies the data anomalies and the corresponding isolation levels. We report twenty-two new data anomalies that other papers have not reported, and all data anomalies are classified miraculously. Based on the classification of data anomalies, two new isolation levels systems with different granularity are proposed, which reveals the rule of defining isolation levels based on data anomalies and makes the cognition of data anomalies and isolation levels more concise.

title: Systematic definition and classification of data anomalies in DBMS (English Version)
text: The concept of data anomalies, referring to specific data operation modes that potentially compromise database consistency, lacks a unified definition. Well-documented anomalies include Dirty Write, Dirty Read, Non-repeatable Read, Phantom, Read Skew, and Write Skew. The characterization of data anomalies is crucial for defining isolation levels, as weaker isolation can enhance the efficiency of transaction processing systems. This study provides a systematic examination of data anomalies and their corresponding isolation levels. We identify 22 previously unreported data anomalies and develop a comprehensive classification framework. Building upon this framework, we propose two novel isolation level systems with varying granularity, elucidating the principle of defining isolation levels based on data anomalies and providing a more concise understanding of their interrelationship.

title: CG2A: Conceptual Graphs Generation Algorithm
text: Conceptual Graphs (CGs) are a formalism to represent knowledge. However producing a CG database is complex. To the best of our knowledge, existing methods do not fully use the expressivity of CGs. It is particularly troublesome as it is necessary to have CG databases to test and validate algorithms running on CGs. This paper proposes CG2A, an algorithm to build synthetic CGs exploiting most of their expressivity. CG2A takes as input constraints that constitute ontological knowledge including a vocabulary and a set of CGs with some label variables, called $γ$-CGs, as components of the generated CGs. Extensions also enable the automatic generation of the set of $γ$-CGs and vocabulary to ease the database generation and increase variability.

title: CG2A: Conceptual Graphs Generation Algorithm
text: Representing knowledge through Conceptual Graphs (CGs) necessitates a comprehensive database, yet existing methodologies fail to fully leverage their expressivity, hindering the testing and validation of CG-based algorithms. This limitation is addressed by CG2A, a novel algorithm designed to generate synthetic CGs that capitalize on their expressive capabilities. By incorporating constraints grounded in ontological knowledge, including a vocabulary and γ-CGs with label variables, CG2A produces diverse CG databases. Furthermore, extensions to this algorithm enable the automatic generation of γ-CGs and vocabulary, thereby streamlining database creation and enhancing variability.

title: From Complexity Measurement to Holistic Quality Evaluation for Automotive Software Development
text: In recent years, the role and the importance of software in the automotive domain have changed dramatically. Being able to systematically evaluate and manage software quality is becoming even more crucial. In practice, however, we still find a largely static approach for measuring software quality based on a predefined list of complexity metrics with static thresholds to fulfill. We propose using a more flexible framework instead, which systematically derives measures and evaluation rules based on the goals and context of a development project.

title: From Complexity Measurement to Holistic Quality Evaluation for Automotive Software Development
text: The growing complexity of automotive software poses significant challenges to ensuring reliability, safety, and performance. Existing quality evaluation approaches focus on isolated metrics, neglecting the intricate interdependencies between components. We bridge this gap by proposing a holistic quality evaluation framework that integrates complexity measurement, architectural analysis, and empirical validation. Our approach is grounded in a comprehensive study of 15 industrial automotive projects, involving 2.5 million lines of code. Results show that our framework effectively identifies quality flaws, improves defect prediction, and enhances maintainability, thereby supporting informed decision-making in automotive software development.

title: Deep Transfer Learning for Multi-source Entity Linkage via Domain Adaptation
text: Multi-source entity linkage focuses on integrating knowledge from multiple sources by linking the records that represent the same real world entity. This is critical in high-impact applications such as data cleaning and user stitching. The state-of-the-art entity linkage pipelines mainly depend on supervised learning that requires abundant amounts of training data. However, collecting well-labeled training data becomes expensive when the data from many sources arrives incrementally over time. Moreover, the trained models can easily overfit to specific data sources, and thus fail to generalize to new sources due to significant differences in data and label distributions. To address these challenges, we present AdaMEL, a deep transfer learning framework that learns generic high-level knowledge to perform multi-source entity linkage. AdaMEL models the attribute importance that is used to match entities through an attribute-level self-attention mechanism, and leverages the massive unlabeled data from new data sources through domain adaptation to make it generic and data-source agnostic. In addition, AdaMEL is capable of incorporating an additional set of labeled data to more accurately integrate data sources with different attribute importance. Extensive experiments show that our framework achieves state-of-the-art results with 8.21% improvement on average over methods based on supervised learning. Besides, it is more stable in handling different sets of data sources in less runtime.

title: Deep Transfer Learning for Multi-source Entity Linkage via Domain Adaptation
text: Entity linkage, a fundamental task in data integration, aims to identify and merge duplicate entity references across multiple sources. The increasing availability of large-scale datasets has led to a pressing need for scalable and accurate entity linkage methods. However, traditional approaches often rely on handcrafted features, domain-specific knowledge, and extensive manual annotation, limiting their applicability to diverse domains. This paper presents a novel deep transfer learning framework for multi-source entity linkage via domain adaptation. Our approach leverages the power of pre-trained language models and adaptively fine-tunes them on target domains to learn domain-invariant entity representations. We introduce a novel multi-source attention mechanism that selectively weighs the importance of each source during the adaptation process. Experimental results on three real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance with an average improvement of 11.4% in F1-score compared to existing methods. Notably, our framework exhibits robustness to domain shift, achieving a 21.1% relative improvement in F1-score on unseen domains. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the learned domain-invariant representations can be successfully transferred to new domains with minimal additional training data, highlighting the potential for large-scale entity linkage applications.

title: An exploratory study on the effects of event-driven architecture on software modularity
text: Event-driven architecture has been widely adopted in the software industry, emerging as an alternative to the development of enterprise applications based on the REST architectural style. However, little is known about the effects of event-driven architecture on modularity while enterprise applications evolve. Consequently, practitioners end up adopting it without any empirical evidence about its impacts on essential indicators, including separation of concerns, coupling, cohesion, complexity and size. This article, therefore, reports an exploratory study comparing event-driven architecture and REST style in terms of modularity. A real-world application was developed using an event-driven architecture and REST through five evolution scenarios. In each scenario, a feature was added. The generated versions were compared using ten metrics. The initial results suggest that the event-driven architecture improved the separation of concerns, but was outperformed considering the metrics of coupling, cohesion, complexity and size. The findings are encouraging and can be seen as a first step in a more ambitious agenda to empirically evaluate the benefits of event-driven architecture against the REST style.

title: An exploratory study on the effects of event-driven architecture on software modularity
text: The proliferation of distributed systems and microservices has led to a resurgence of interest in event-driven architecture (EDA) as a means of facilitating communication and scalability. Despite its popularity, the impact of EDA on software modularity remains poorly understood. This study seeks to contribute to the ongoing discussion by conducting an exploratory analysis of the relationship between EDA and modularity in software systems. We employed a mixed-methods approach, combining a systematic literature review with a case study of three industrial-scale systems that have adopted EDA. Our results suggest that EDA can have a positive impact on modularity, particularly in terms of reducing coupling and increasing cohesion. However, our findings also indicate that the effectiveness of EDA in promoting modularity is highly dependent on the presence of certain architectural and organizational factors, such as well-defined event schemas and a culture of event-driven design. These insights have important implications for software engineers and architects seeking to leverage EDA to improve the modularity and maintainability of their systems.

title: Finding a Concise, Precise, and Exhaustive Set of Near Bi-Cliques in Dynamic Graphs
text: A variety of tasks on dynamic graphs, including anomaly detection, community detection, compression, and graph understanding, have been formulated as problems of identifying constituent (near) bi-cliques (i.e., complete bipartite graphs). Even when we restrict our attention to maximal ones, there can be exponentially many near bi-cliques, and thus finding all of them is practically impossible for large graphs.
