Then, two questions naturally arise: (Q1) What is a "good" set of near bi-cliques? That is, given a set of near bi-cliques in the input dynamic graph, how should we evaluate its quality? (Q2) Given a large dynamic graph, how can we rapidly identify a high-quality set of near bi-cliques in it? Regarding Q1, we measure how concisely, precisely, and exhaustively a given set of near bi-cliques describes the input dynamic graph. We combine these three perspectives systematically on the Minimum Description Length principle. Regarding Q2, we propose CutNPeel, a fast search algorithm for a high-quality set of near bi-cliques. By adaptively re-partitioning the input graph, CutNPeel reduces the search space and at the same time improves the search quality. Our experiments using six real-world dynamic graphs demonstrate that CutNPeel is (a) High-quality: providing near bi-cliques of up to 51.2% better quality than its state-of-the-art competitors, (b) Fast: up to 68.8x faster than the next-best competitor, and (c) Scalable: scaling to graphs with 134 million edges. We also show successful applications of CutNPeel to graph compression and pattern discovery.

title: Finding a Concise, Precise, and Exhaustive Set of Near Bi-Cliques in Dynamic Graphs
text: The identification of constituent near bi-cliques, or complete bipartite graphs, is a fundamental problem in dynamic graph analysis, with applications in anomaly detection, community detection, compression, and graph understanding. However, the number of maximal near bi-cliques can grow exponentially with graph size, rendering exhaustive enumeration infeasible for large graphs. This raises two critical questions: what constitutes a "good" set of near bi-cliques, and how can we efficiently identify such a set in a large dynamic graph? To address the first question, we develop a systematic evaluation framework based on the Minimum Description Length principle, which assesses the quality of a near bi-clique set in terms of its conciseness, precision, and exhaustiveness in describing the input graph. To tackle the second question, we propose CutNPeel, a fast search algorithm that adaptively re-partitions the input graph to reduce the search space while improving search quality. Experimental results on six real-world dynamic graphs demonstrate that CutNPeel outperforms state-of-the-art competitors, yielding near bi-cliques with up to 51.2% better quality, while achieving speedups of up to 68.8x and scalability to graphs with 134 million edges. Furthermore, we illustrate the effectiveness of CutNPeel in graph compression and pattern discovery applications.

title: SMORE: Knowledge Graph Completion and Multi-hop Reasoning in Massive Knowledge Graphs
text: Knowledge graphs (KGs) capture knowledge in the form of head--relation--tail triples and are a crucial component in many AI systems. There are two important reasoning tasks on KGs: (1) single-hop knowledge graph completion, which involves predicting individual links in the KG; and (2), multi-hop reasoning, where the goal is to predict which KG entities satisfy a given logical query. Embedding-based methods solve both tasks by first computing an embedding for each entity and relation, then using them to form predictions. However, existing scalable KG embedding frameworks only support single-hop knowledge graph completion and cannot be applied to the more challenging multi-hop reasoning task. Here we present Scalable Multi-hOp REasoning (SMORE), the first general framework for both single-hop and multi-hop reasoning in KGs. Using a single machine SMORE can perform multi-hop reasoning in Freebase KG (86M entities, 338M edges), which is 1,500x larger than previously considered KGs. The key to SMORE's runtime performance is a novel bidirectional rejection sampling that achieves a square root reduction of the complexity of online training data generation. Furthermore, SMORE exploits asynchronous scheduling, overlapping CPU-based data sampling, GPU-based embedding computation, and frequent CPU--GPU IO. SMORE increases throughput (i.e., training speed) over prior multi-hop KG frameworks by 2.2x with minimal GPU memory requirements (2GB for training 400-dim embeddings on 86M-node Freebase) and achieves near linear speed-up with the number of GPUs. Moreover, on the simpler single-hop knowledge graph completion task SMORE achieves comparable or even better runtime performance to state-of-the-art frameworks on both single GPU and multi-GPU settings.

title: SMORE: Knowledge Graph Completion and Multi-hop Reasoning in Massive Knowledge Graphs
text: Knowledge graphs (KGs) have emerged as a crucial component in various AI systems, capturing knowledge in the form of head-relation-tail triples. Two fundamental reasoning tasks on KGs are single-hop knowledge graph completion, which involves predicting individual links, and multi-hop reasoning, where the goal is to identify entities satisfying a given logical query. Embedding-based methods, which compute entity and relation embeddings to form predictions, have been widely employed to address these tasks. However, existing scalable KG embedding frameworks are limited to single-hop knowledge graph completion and are incapable of handling the more challenging multi-hop reasoning task. We introduce Scalable Multi-hOp REasoning (SMORE), a novel framework that efficiently supports both single-hop and multi-hop reasoning on KGs. Notably, SMORE can perform multi-hop reasoning on the large-scale Freebase KG (86M entities, 338M edges) using a single machine, surpassing the size of previously considered KGs by a factor of 1,500. The key to SMORE's exceptional runtime performance lies in its innovative bidirectional rejection sampling, which achieves a square root reduction in the complexity of online training data generation. Additionally, SMORE leverages asynchronous scheduling, overlapping CPU-based data sampling, GPU-based embedding computation, and frequent CPU-GPU IO to optimize performance. Our experimental results demonstrate a 2.2-fold increase in throughput over prior multi-hop KG frameworks, while requiring minimal GPU memory (2GB for training 400-dim embeddings on 86M-node Freebase) and achieving near-linear speedup with the number of GPUs. Furthermore, SMORE exhibits comparable or superior runtime performance to state-of-the-art frameworks on both single GPU and multi-GPU settings for single-hop knowledge graph completion.

title: Be Lean -- How to Fit a Model-Based System Architecture Development Process Based on ARP4754 Into an Agile Environment
text: An emerging service is moving the known aviation sector in terms of technology, paradigms, and key players - the Urban Air Mobility. The reason: new developments in non-aviation industries are driving technological progress in aviation. For instance electrical motors, modern sensor technologies and better energy storage expand the possibilities and enable novel vehicle concepts which require also novel system architectures for flight control systems. Their development is governed by aviation authority and industry recognized standards, guidelines and recommended practices. Comprehensive methods for Model-Based Systems Engineering exist which address these guidance materials but their setup and their application can be quite resource-demanding. Especially the new and rather small key players - start-ups and development teams in an educational environment - can be overwhelmed to setup such development processes. For these clients, the authors propose a custom workflow for the development of system architectures. It shall ensure development rigor, quality and consistency. The authors show how the custom workflow has been established based on the ARP4754A and its level of compliance to the standard's process objectives. Based on automation of life cycle activities, manual effort can be reduced to allow the application even in small teams. The custom workflow's activities are explained and demonstrated within a case study of an Experimental Autopilot system architecture.

title: Be Lean -- How to Fit a Model-Based System Architecture Development Process Based on ARP4754 Into an Agile Environment
text: The Urban Air Mobility sector is undergoing a transformative shift, driven by technological advancements originating from non-aviation industries. Breakthroughs in electric motors, sensor technologies, and energy storage have opened up new possibilities for novel vehicle concepts, necessitating innovative system architectures for flight control systems. The development of these architectures is governed by stringent standards, guidelines, and recommended practices set forth by aviation authorities and industry stakeholders. While comprehensive Model-Based Systems Engineering methods exist to address these guidance materials, their implementation can be resource-intensive, posing a significant challenge for small key players, including start-ups and educational development teams. To address this, we propose a customized workflow for system architecture development, ensuring rigor, quality, and consistency. Our approach leverages automation of life cycle activities to reduce manual effort, rendering it feasible for small teams to apply. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our custom workflow, established in accordance with ARP4754A, through a case study of an Experimental Autopilot system architecture, showcasing its compliance with the standard's process objectives.

title: On the Importance and Shortcomings of Code Readability Metrics: A Case Study on Reactive Programming
text: Well structured and readable source code is a pre-requisite for maintainable software and successful collaboration among developers. Static analysis enables the automated extraction of code complexity and readability metrics which can be leveraged to highlight potential improvements in code to both attain software of high quality and reinforce good practices for developers as an educational tool. This assumes reliable readability metrics which are not trivial to obtain since code readability is somewhat subjective. Recent research has resulted in increasingly sophisticated models for predicting readability as perceived by humans primarily with a procedural and object oriented focus, while functional and declarative languages and language extensions advance as they often are said to lead to more concise and readable code. In this paper, we investigate whether the existing complexity and readability metrics reflect that wisdom or whether the notion of readability and its constituents requires overhaul in the light of programming language changes. We therefore compare traditional object oriented and reactive programming in terms of code complexity and readability in a case study. Reactive programming is claimed to increase code quality but few studies have substantiated these claims empirically. We refactored an object oriented open source project into a reactive candidate and compare readability with the original using cyclomatic complexity and two state-of-the-art readability metrics. More elaborate investigations are required, but our findings suggest that both cyclomatic complexity and readability decrease significantly at the same time in the reactive candidate, which seems counter-intuitive. We exemplify and substantiate why readability metrics may require adjustment to better suit popular programming styles other than imperative and object-oriented to better match human expectations.

title: On the Importance and Shortcomings of Code Readability Metrics: A Case Study on Reactive Programming
text: The maintainability of software and the success of collaborative development efforts hinge on the quality of source code, which is characterized by its structure and readability. Automated static analysis can extract metrics that quantify code complexity and readability, providing valuable insights for improvement and serving as an educational tool to promote best practices among developers. However, the accuracy of readability metrics is a subject of ongoing debate, as code readability is inherently subjective. Recent advances in readability modeling have primarily focused on procedural and object-oriented languages, while functional and declarative languages, as well as language extensions, have gained popularity for their potential to produce more concise and readable code. This paper examines whether existing complexity and readability metrics adequately capture the nuances of emerging programming paradigms. We present a case study comparing traditional object-oriented and reactive programming approaches in terms of code complexity and readability. By refactorizing an open-source project from an object-oriented to a reactive implementation, we observe a significant decrease in both cyclomatic complexity and readability metrics, contrary to expectations. Our findings suggest that existing readability metrics may need to be reevaluated to better accommodate modern programming styles, moving beyond imperative and object-oriented paradigms to align with human perceptions of code quality.

title: Fuzzm: Finding Memory Bugs through Binary-Only Instrumentation and Fuzzing of WebAssembly
text: WebAssembly binaries are often compiled from memory-unsafe languages, such as C and C++. Because of WebAssembly's linear memory and missing protection features, e.g., stack canaries, source-level memory vulnerabilities are exploitable in compiled WebAssembly binaries, sometimes even more easily than in native code. This paper addresses the problem of detecting such vulnerabilities through the first binary-only fuzzer for WebAssembly. Our approach, called Fuzzm, combines canary instrumentation to detect overflows and underflows on the stack and the heap, an efficient coverage instrumentation, a WebAssembly VM, and the input generation algorithm of the popular AFL fuzzer. Besides as an oracle for fuzzing, our canaries also serve as a stand-alone binary hardening technique to prevent the exploitation of vulnerable binaries in production. We evaluate Fuzzm with 28 real-world WebAssembly binaries, some compiled from source and some found in the wild without source code. The fuzzer explores thousands of execution paths, triggers dozens of crashes, and performs hundreds of program executions per second. When used for binary hardening, the approach prevents previously published exploits against vulnerable WebAssembly binaries while imposing low runtime overhead.

title: Fuzzm: Finding Memory Bugs through Binary-Only Instrumentation and Fuzzing of WebAssembly
text: The prevalence of memory bugs in WebAssembly (WASM) code poses a significant threat to the security and reliability of web applications. Despite recent advancements in static analysis and fuzz testing, detecting memory bugs in WASM remains a challenging task due to the lack of source code and complexity of the compilation process. To address this issue, we present Fuzzm, a novel approach that combines binary-only instrumentation and fuzzing to identify memory bugs in WASM modules. Fuzzm leverages a custom instrumentation framework to inject fault detection mechanisms into the WASM binary, enabling the identification of memory corruption errors at runtime. Our fuzzing engine then generates a vast range of input stimuli to exercise the instrumented binary, increasing the likelihood of triggering memory bugs. We evaluate Fuzzm on a diverse set of real-world WASM applications and compare its performance with existing state-of-the-art tools. Our results show that Fuzzm can detect a significant number of previously unknown memory bugs, including use-after-free, buffer overflows, and data races, with a low false positive rate. Furthermore, Fuzzm's binary-only approach makes it applicable to a wide range of WASM deployments, providing a crucial step towards securing the web ecosystem.

title: On Wasted Contributions: Understanding the Dynamics of Contributor-Abandoned Pull Requests
text: Pull-based development has enabled numerous volunteers to contribute to open-source projects with fewer barriers. Nevertheless, a considerable amount of pull requests (PRs) with valid contributions are abandoned by their contributors, wasting the effort and time put in by both the contributors and maintainers. To better understand the underlying dynamics of contributor-abandoned PRs, we conduct a mixed-methods study using both quantitative and qualitative methods. We curate a dataset consisting of 265,325 PRs including 4,450 abandoned ones from ten popular and mature GitHub projects and measure 16 features characterizing PRs, contributors, review processes, and projects. Using statistical and machine learning techniques, we find that complex PRs, novice contributors, and lengthy reviews have a higher probability of abandonment and the rate of PR abandonment fluctuates alongside the projects' maturity or workload. To identify why contributors abandon their PRs, we also manually examine a random sample of 354 abandoned PRs. We observe that the most frequent abandonment reasons are related to the obstacles faced by contributors, followed by the hurdles imposed by maintainers during the review process. Finally, we survey the top core maintainers of the studied projects to understand their perspectives on dealing with PR abandonment and on our findings.

title: On Wasted Contributions: Understanding the Dynamics of Contributor-Abandoned Pull Requests
text: The adoption of pull-based development in open-source projects has lowered barriers to entry for volunteer contributors, yet a substantial proportion of pull requests (PRs) with valid contributions are ultimately abandoned by their authors. This phenomenon entails significant waste of effort and time for both contributors and maintainers. To elucidate the underlying mechanisms driving contributor-abandoned PRs, we employ a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative and qualitative analyses. Our dataset comprises 265,325 PRs, including 4,450 abandoned instances, from ten prominent and mature GitHub projects, which we characterize using 16 features spanning PR attributes, contributor profiles, review processes, and project properties. Statistical and machine learning techniques reveal that complex PRs, novice contributors, and protracted reviews are associated with a higher likelihood of abandonment, with the abandonment rate varying in tandem with project maturity and workload. A manual examination of 354 randomly sampled abandoned PRs uncovers that contributor-faced obstacles and maintainer-imposed hurdles during reviews are the primary reasons for abandonment. Furthermore, we survey top core maintainers to gather their insights on PR abandonment and our findings, providing a comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon.

title: AWSOM-LP: An Effective Log Parsing Technique Using Pattern Recognition and Frequency Analysis
text: Logs provide users with useful insights to help with a variety of development and operations tasks. The problem is that logs are often unstructured, making their analysis a complex task. This is mainly due to the lack of guidelines and best practices for logging, combined with a large number of logging libraries at the disposal of software developers. There exist studies that aim to parse automatically large logs. The main objective is to extract templates from samples of log data that are used to recognize future logs. In this paper, we propose AWSOM-LP, a powerful log parsing and abstraction tool, which is highly accurate, stable, and efficient. AWSOM-LP is built on the idea of applying pattern recognition and frequency analysis. First, log events are organized into patterns using a simple text processing method. Frequency analysis is then applied locally to instances of the same group to identify static and dynamic content of log events. When applied to 16 log datasets of the the LogPai project, AWSOM-LP achieves an average grouping accuracy of 93.5%, which outperforms the accuracy of five leading log parsing tools namely, Logram, Lenma, Drain, IPLoM and AEL. Additionally, AWSOM-LP can generate more than 80% of the final log templates from 10% to 50% of the entire log dataset and can parse up to a million log events in an average time of 5 minutes. AWSOM-LP is available online as an open source. It can be used by practitioners and researchers to parse effectively and efficiently large log files so as to support log analysis tasks.

title: AWSOM-LP: An Effective Log Parsing Technique Using Pattern Recognition and Frequency Analysis
text: The analysis of log data is a crucial aspect of software development and operations, as it provides valuable insights into system behavior and performance. However, the lack of standardized logging practices and the proliferation of diverse logging libraries often result in unstructured log data, rendering analysis a complex and daunting task. Existing studies have sought to develop automated log parsing techniques, with the primary goal of extracting templates from log samples to facilitate the recognition of future log events. This paper presents AWSOM-LP, a novel log parsing and abstraction tool that leverages pattern recognition and frequency analysis to achieve high accuracy, stability, and efficiency. By organizing log events into patterns using a simple text processing method and applying frequency analysis to identify static and dynamic content, AWSOM-LP outperforms five state-of-the-art log parsing tools, achieving an average grouping accuracy of 93.5% on 16 log datasets from the LogPai project. Furthermore, AWSOM-LP can generate over 80% of final log templates from a small fraction of the entire log dataset (10%-50%) and parse up to one million log events in an average time of 5 minutes. As an open-source tool, AWSOM-LP is readily available for practitioners and researchers to efficiently and effectively parse large log files, thereby supporting a wide range of log analysis tasks.

title: The Structure-Behavior Coalescence Method --Toward a Unified View of the Software System in Model-Driven Engineering
text: In Model-Driven Engineering (MDE), the Unified Modeling Language (UML) 2.0 specification includes a metamodel that defines the language concepts and a user model that defines how the language concepts are represented. In UML 2.0, an important use of metamodel is to provide an integrated semantic framework that every diagram in the user model can be projected as a view of the metamodel. However, most existing UML 2.0 metamodels lack the ability to serve as the basis for unifying different views of a software system. To overcome the shortcomings of the current UML 2.0 metamodel approaches, we developed Operation-Based Multi-Queue Structure-Behavior Coalescence Process Algebra (O-M-SBC-PA), which provides an integrated semantic framework that is able to integrate structural and behavioral constructs. Using O-M-SBC-PA as the metamodel of UML 2.0, each diagram in the user model can be projected as a view of the MDE metamodel.

title: The Structure-Behavior Coalescence Method --Toward a Unified View of the Software System in Model-Driven Engineering
text: Model-driven engineering (MDE) has revolutionized the software development landscape by emphasizing the role of models as primary artifacts. However, the traditional separation between structural and behavioral aspects of software systems in MDE frameworks hinders a comprehensive understanding of the system's overall behavior. To address this limitation, we introduce the Structure-Behavior Coalescence Method (SBCM), a novel approach that reconciles the structural and behavioral views of a software system. By leveraging a rigorous ontological analysis and a set of well-defined transformation rules, SBCM integrates the system's static structure and dynamic behavior into a unified model. Our evaluation, conducted on a corpus of 20 industrial-scale case studies, demonstrates that SBCM enables the discovery of emergent behavior and facilitates the identification of structural flaws that would remain hidden in traditional MDE approaches. The results pave the way for a more holistic understanding of software systems, ultimately leading to improved system design, development, and maintenance.

title: A Comprehensive Study on Learning-Based PE Malware Family Classification Methods
text: Driven by the high profit, Portable Executable (PE) malware has been consistently evolving in terms of both volume and sophistication. PE malware family classification has gained great attention and a large number of approaches have been proposed. With the rapid development of machine learning techniques and the exciting results they achieved on various tasks, machine learning algorithms have also gained popularity in the PE malware family classification task. Three mainstream approaches that use learning based algorithms, as categorized by the input format the methods take, are image-based, binary-based and disassembly-based approaches. Although a large number of approaches are published, there is no consistent comparisons on those approaches, especially from the practical industry adoption perspective. Moreover, there is no comparison in the scenario of concept drift, which is a fact for the malware classification task due to the fast evolving nature of malware. In this work, we conduct a thorough empirical study on learning-based PE malware classification approaches on 4 different datasets and consistent experiment settings. Based on the experiment results and an interview with our industry partners, we find that (1) there is no individual class of methods that significantly outperforms the others; (2) All classes of methods show performance degradation on concept drift (by an average F1-score of 32.23%); and (3) the prediction time and high memory consumption hinder existing approaches from being adopted for industry usage.

title: A Comprehensive Study on Learning-Based PE Malware Family Classification Methods
text: The proliferation of Portable Executable (PE) malware has spawned a surge in research focused on family classification, driven by the lucrative nature of this threat. Machine learning algorithms have emerged as a prominent approach in this domain, with three primary categories of methods distinguished by their input formats: image-based, binary-based, and disassembly-based techniques. Despite the abundance of published studies, a systematic comparison of these approaches is lacking, particularly from the perspective of practical industry adoption. Furthermore, the impact of concept drift, an inherent challenge in malware classification due to the rapidly evolving nature of malware, remains unexplored. This study presents a comprehensive empirical evaluation of learning-based PE malware classification approaches on four diverse datasets, employing consistent experimental settings. Our findings indicate that no single class of methods exhibits superior performance, and all approaches suffer from significant performance degradation (averaging 32.23% F1-score decline) when confronted with concept drift. Additionally, our results, corroborated by industry partner feedback, highlight the limitations of existing methods, including prolonged prediction times and excessive memory consumption, which hinder their adoption in real-world industrial settings.

title: Crowd-sensing Enhanced Parking Patrol using Trajectories of Sharing Bikes
text: Illegal vehicle parking is a common urban problem faced by major cities in the world, as it incurs traffic jams, which lead to air pollution and traffic accidents. The government highly relies on active human efforts to detect illegal parking events. However, such an approach is extremely ineffective to cover a large city since the police have to patrol over the entire city roads. The massive and high-quality sharing bike trajectories from Mobike offer us a unique opportunity to design a ubiquitous illegal parking detection approach, as most of the illegal parking events happen at curbsides and have significant impact on the bike users. The detection result can guide the patrol schedule, i.e. send the patrol policemen to the region with higher illegal parking risks, and further improve the patrol efficiency. Inspired by this idea, three main components are employed in the proposed framework: 1)~{\em trajectory pre-processing}, which filters outlier GPS points, performs map-matching, and builds trajectory indexes; 2)~{\em illegal parking detection}, which models the normal trajectories, extracts features from the evaluation trajectories, and utilizes a distribution test-based method to discover the illegal parking events; and 3)~{\em patrol scheduling}, which leverages the detection result as reference context, and models the scheduling task as a multi-agent reinforcement learning problem to guide the patrol police. Finally, extensive experiments are presented to validate the effectiveness of illegal parking detection, as well as the improvement of patrol efficiency.

title: Crowd-sensing Enhanced Parking Patrol using Trajectories of Sharing Bikes
text: Urban parking management faces significant challenges due to the increasing number of vehicles and limited parking infrastructure. Traditional parking patrol methods relying on fixed sensors or patrol cars are often ineffective and resource-intensive. Meanwhile, the proliferation of bike-sharing systems offers an underutilized opportunity to leverage the trajectories of these bikes as a crowd-sensing approach to enhance parking patrol. This paper presents a novel framework that integrates bike trajectory data with machine learning and spatial analysis to detect parking violations and optimize patrol routes. Our approach exploits the inherent mobility patterns of bike-sharing users to identify high-probability parking violation areas, which are then fed into a graph-based optimization model to generate efficient patrol routes. We evaluate our framework using a large-scale bike trajectory dataset from a major city, comprising over 1 million trips and 10,000 parking events. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach can detect parking violations with an accuracy of 85.2% and reduce patrol route lengths by 23.4% compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, we show that our framework can adapt to varying bike usage patterns and parking demand, making it a robust solution for real-world parking management. Our work has significant implications for smart city initiatives, highlighting the potential of crowd-sensing and mobility data to enhance urban transportation management.

title: A Demonstration of Benchmarking Time Series Management Systems in the Cloud
text: Time Series Management Systems (TSMS) are Database Management Systems that have been configured with the primary objective of processing and storing time series data. With the IoT expanding at exponential rates and there becoming increasingly more time series data to process and analyze, several TSMS have been proposed and are used in practice. Each system has its own architecture and storage mechanisms and factors such as the dimensionality of the dataset or the nature of the operators a user wishes to execute can cause differences in system performance. This makes it highly challenging for practitioners to determine the most optimal TSMS for their use case. To remedy this several TSMS benchmarks have been proposed, yet these benchmarks focus primary on simple and supported operators, largely disregarding the advanced analytical operators (ie. Normalization, Clustering, etc) that constitute a large part of the use cases in practice. In this demo, we introduce a new benchmark that enables users to evaluate the performance of four prominent TSMS (TimescaleDB, MonetDB, ExtremeDB, Kairos-H2) in their handling of over 13 advanced analytical operators. In a simple and interactive manner, users can specify the TSMS(s) to compare, the advanced analytical operator(s) to execute, and the dataset(s) to utilize for the comparison. Users can choose from over eight real-world datasets with varying dimensions or upload their own dataset. The tool then provides a report and recommendation of the most optimal TSMS for the parameters chosen.

title: A Demonstration of Benchmarking Time Series Management Systems in the Cloud
text: The proliferation of IoT devices and ubiquitous sensing has led to an exponential growth in time series data, prompting the development of dedicated Time Series Management Systems (TSMS). Cloud-based TSMS, in particular, have emerged as a promising solution to tackle the scalability and performance challenges associated with massive time series data. However, the lack of standardized benchmarking frameworks hinders the comparison and evaluation of these systems, making it difficult for practitioners to choose the most suitable TSMS for their specific use case. To address this gap, we design and implement a comprehensive benchmarking framework for cloud-based TSMS, encompassing a diverse set of workloads and performance metrics. Our framework encompasses three primary components: a data generator capable of producing realistic time series datasets, a workload simulator mimicking real-world query patterns, and a performance monitoring module tracking system-level metrics such as latency, throughput, and resource utilization. We apply our benchmarking framework to four popular cloud-based TSMS: TimescaleDB, InfluxDB, OpenTSDB, and Amazon Timestream. Our results reveal significant performance differences across the systems, with TimescaleDB exhibiting the highest ingestion throughput (350,000 points per second) and InfluxDB demonstrating the lowest latency (15ms) for aggregation queries. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the critical role of data compression and storage layouts in determining TSMS performance. Our benchmarking framework and findings provide valuable insights for practitioners, researchers, and TSMS developers, ultimately contributing to the maturation of the TSMS ecosystem.

title: Simpli-Squared: A Very Simple Yet Unexpectedly Powerful Join Ordering Algorithm Without Cardinality Estimates
text: The Join Order Benchmark (JOB) has become the de facto standard to assess the performance of relational database query optimizers due to its complexity and completeness. In order to compute the optimal execution plan -- join order -- existing solutions employ extensive data synopses and correlations -- functional dependencies -- between table attributes. These structures incur significant overhead to design, build, and maintain. In this paper, we present \textit{Simpli}city \textit{Simpli}fied (\textit{Simpli-Squared}), a very simple join ordering algorithm that achieves unexpectedly good results. Simpli-Squared computes the join order without using any statistics or cardinality estimates. It takes as input only the referential integrity constraints declared at schema definition and the number of tuples (size) in the base tables. The join order of a given query is computed by splitting the join graph along the many-to-many joins and sorting the tables based on their size. The tables involved in one-to-many joins are greedily included based on size and the query join graph. The resulting plan can be efficiently generated by a lightweight query rewriting procedure. Experiments on the JOB benchmark in PostgreSQL show that Simpli-Squared achieves runtimes having an increase of only up to 16\% -- and sometimes even a reduction -- compared to four state-of-the-art solutions that are considerably more intricate. Based on these results, we question whether JOB adequately tests query optimizers or if accurate cardinality estimation is such a fundamental requirement for performing well on the JOB benchmark.

title: Simpli-Squared: A Very Simple Yet Unexpectedly Powerful Join Ordering Algorithm Without Cardinality Estimates
text: Optimizing join ordering is a crucial step in query optimization, yet existing algorithms rely heavily on accurate cardinality estimates, which are often unavailable or unreliable in practice. Moreover, the search space for optimal join orders is exponentially large, making exhaustive search impractical even for moderate-sized queries. Recently, there has been a growing interest in cardinality-estimate-free join ordering algorithms, but these methods typically sacrifice optimality for simplicity. We present Simpli-Squared, a novel join ordering algorithm that eschews cardinality estimates altogether, instead relying on a simple, yet powerful, heuristic-based approach. Our algorithm iteratively applies a set of carefully crafted rules to prune the search space, effectively reducing the problem to a series of tractable sub-problems. This allows Simpli-Squared to efficiently explore the vast space of possible join orders, often discovering near-optimal solutions. Our comprehensive evaluation on a range of real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrates that Simpli-Squared consistently outperforms state-of-the-art cardinality-estimate-free algorithms, while often rivaling the performance of more complex, estimate-based methods. Notably, Simpli-Squared exhibits exceptional robustness in the face of uncertain or missing statistics, making it an attractive choice for real-world query optimization. We further analyze the theoretical properties of Simpli-Squared, providing insights into its convergence behavior and optimality guarantees. Overall, our results firmly establish Simpli-Squared as a competitive and practical solution for join ordering in modern database systems.

title: A Non-Deterministic Multiset Query Language
text: We develop a multiset query and update language executable in a term rewriting system. Its most remarkable feature, besides non-standard approach to quantification and introduction of fresh values, is non-determinism - a query result is not uniquely determined by the database. We argue that this feature is very useful, e.g., in modelling user choices during simulation or reachability analysis of a data-centric business process - the intended application of our work. Query evaluation is implemented by converting the query into a terminating term rewriting system and normalizing the initial term which encapsulates the current database. A normal form encapsulates a query result. We prove that our language can express any relational algebra query. Finally, we present a simple business process specification framework (and an example specification). Both syntax and semantics of our query language is implemented in Maude.

title: A Non-Deterministic Multiset Query Language
text: The proliferation of multisets in modern data analysis has led to a pressing need for expressive and efficient query languages. Despite advances in set-based querying, existing languages often fail to capture the inherent non-determinism of multisets, relying on ad-hoc workarounds or probabilistic approximations. We introduce NDML, a novel non-deterministic multiset query language that leverages the mathematical foundations of multisets to provide a rigorous framework for querying and manipulating uncertain data. NDML's syntax is designed to accommodate the inherent ambiguity of multisets, featuring probabilistic selection, aggregation, and grouping operators. We formalize the language's semantics using a probabilistic relational algebra, ensuring soundness and completeness. Experimental evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates NDML's ability to efficiently process complex queries, outperforming existing approaches by up to 3x. Our results have significant implications for data integration, data mining, and machine learning applications involving uncertain data.

title: Chaos Engineering of Ethereum Blockchain Clients
text: In this paper, we present ChaosETH, a chaos engineering approach for resilience assessment of Ethereum blockchain clients. ChaosETH operates in the following manner: First, it monitors Ethereum clients to determine their normal behavior. Then, it injects system call invocation errors into one single Ethereum client at a time, and observes the behavior resulting from perturbation. Finally, ChaosETH compares the behavior recorded before, during, and after perturbation to assess the impact of the injected system call invocation errors. The experiments are performed on the two most popular Ethereum client implementations: GoEthereum and Nethermind. We assess the impact of 22 different system call errors on those Ethereum clients with respect to 15 application-level metrics. Our results reveal a broad spectrum of resilience characteristics of Ethereum clients w.r.t. system call invocation errors, ranging from direct crashes to full resilience. The experiments clearly demonstrate the feasibility of applying chaos engineering principles to blockchain systems.

title: Chaos Engineering of Ethereum Blockchain Clients
text: We propose ChaosETH, a novel chaos engineering methodology for evaluating the resilience of Ethereum blockchain clients against system call invocation errors. This approach involves three primary stages: initially, ChaosETH profiles the normal behavior of Ethereum clients through monitoring; subsequently, it introduces system call invocation errors into individual clients, observing the resultant behavioral perturbations; and finally, it compares pre-, during-, and post-perturbation behavior to quantify the impact of the injected errors. Experiments were conducted on the two predominant Ethereum client implementations, GoEthereum and Nethermind, examining the effects of 22 distinct system call errors on 15 application-level metrics. Our findings reveal a diverse range of resilience characteristics in Ethereum clients, spanning from immediate crashes to complete fault tolerance. These results underscore the viability of applying chaos engineering principles to blockchain systems, providing valuable insights into their robustness and fault resilience.

title: A Hybrid Software Test Automation for Educational Portals
text: Educational portal (EP) is a multi-function website that allows access to activities such as public and private sections, data retrieval and submission, personalized content and so on for the educational system. This study investigated the specific requirement for the enhancement of quality and behavior of EP with regards to time and cost using Obafemi Awolowo University (OAU), Ile-Ife, Nigeria as a case study. A test automation framework was designed using unified modelling language and implemented in Java programming language. MySQL and Excel database were used to store test data. The framework developed was evaluated using Test Time Performance (TTP), Performance Test Efficiency (PTE) and Automation Scripting Productivity (ASP) metrics. The results from the evaluation of the sample data provided showed that ASP produced a tested outcome of 360 operations per hour, PTE yielded 80% and TTP was just 4%. Based on the recorded performance, it is evident that the research can provide quick and firsthand information to quality assurance analyst and software testers, thereby reducing maintenance cost during software development.

title: A Hybrid Software Test Automation for Educational Portals
text: This study examines the quality and behavioral enhancements of an educational portal (EP), a multifaceted website facilitating various activities within the educational system, with a focus on time and cost efficiency. Obafemi Awolowo University (OAU), Ile-Ife, Nigeria, serves as the case study. A test automation framework was designed using the unified modelling language and implemented in Java, utilizing MySQL and Excel databases for storing test data. The framework's effectiveness was assessed through three key metrics: Test Time Performance (TTP), Performance Test Efficiency (PTE), and Automation Scripting Productivity (ASP). The evaluation results reveal that ASP enables 360 operations per hour, PTE achieves 80% efficiency, and TTP registers a mere 4% overhead. These findings demonstrate the framework's potential to provide rapid and direct insights for quality assurance analysts and software testers, ultimately reducing maintenance costs during software development.

title: Utility-driven Mining of Contiguous Sequences
text: Recently, contiguous sequential pattern mining (CSPM) gained interest as a research topic, due to its varied potential real-world applications, such as web log and biological sequence analysis. To date, studies on the CSPM problem remain in preliminary stages. Existing CSPM algorithms lack the efficiency to satisfy users' needs and can still be improved in terms of runtime and memory consumption. In addition, existing algorithms were developed to deal with simple sequence data, working with only one event at a time. Complex sequence data, which represent multiple events occurring simultaneously, are also commonly observed in real life. In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm, fast utility-driven contiguous sequential pattern mining (FUCPM), to address the CSPM problem. FUCPM adopts a compact sequence information list and instance chain structures to store the necessary information of the database and candidate patterns. For further efficiency, we develop the global unpromising items pruning and local unpromising items pruning strategies, based on sequence-weighted utilization and item-extension utilization, to reduce the search space. Extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that FUCPM outperforms the state-of-the-art algorithms and is scalable enough to handle complex sequence data.

title: Utility-driven Mining of Contiguous Sequences
text: The proliferation of sequence data in various domains has spawned a growing interest in discovering contiguous sequences, a crucial task in data mining and knowledge discovery. Existing approaches, however, often overlook the inherent utility of these sequences, leading to the extraction of patterns that may not be meaningful or actionable. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework for utility-driven mining of contiguous sequences. Our approach leverages a probabilistic model to quantify the utility of each sequence, incorporating domain-specific knowledge and user preferences. We develop an efficient algorithm, termed UCMine, which integrates a dynamic programming strategy with a greedy optimization technique to identify high-utility contiguous sequences. Experimental evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates the efficacy of UCMine, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of precision, recall, and F1-score. Furthermore, our approach is shown to be robust to varying utility functions and sequence lengths. The results of this study have significant implications for applications such as recommender systems, bioinformatics, and text analysis, where the extraction of meaningful contiguous sequences can inform critical decision-making processes.

title: FUIM: Fuzzy Utility Itemset Mining
text: Because of usefulness and comprehensibility, fuzzy data mining has been extensively studied and is an emerging topic in recent years. Compared with utility-driven itemset mining technologies, fuzzy utility mining not only takes utilities (e.g., profits) into account, but also considers quantities of items in each transaction for discovering high fuzzy utility itemsets (HFUIs). Thus, fuzziness can be regard as a key criterion to select high-utility itemsets, while the exiting algorithms are not efficient enough. In this paper, an efficient one-phase algorithm named Fuzzy-driven Utility Itemset Miner (FUIM) is proposed to find out a complete set of HFUIs effectively. In addition, a novel compact data structure named fuzzy-list keeps the key information from quantitative transaction databases. Using fuzzy-list, FUIM can discover HFUIs from transaction databases efficiently and effectively. Both completeness and correctness of the FUIM algorithm are proved by five theorems. At last, substantial experiments test three terms (runtime cost, memory consumption, and scalability) to confirm that FUIM considerably outperforms the state-of-the-art algorithms.

title: FUIM: Fuzzy Utility Itemset Mining
text: Fuzzy data mining has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its ability to provide comprehensive and interpretable insights. In contrast to traditional utility-driven itemset mining approaches, fuzzy utility mining integrates both utility and quantity considerations to uncover high fuzzy utility itemsets (HFUIs). The fuzziness criterion plays a pivotal role in selecting high-utility itemsets, yet existing algorithms fall short in terms of efficiency. This paper presents Fuzzy-driven Utility Itemset Miner (FUIM), a novel one-phase algorithm designed to efficiently extract a complete set of HFUIs. A compact data structure, termed fuzzy-list, is introduced to store essential information from quantitative transaction databases, enabling FUIM to perform efficient HFUI discovery. The correctness and completeness of FUIM are rigorously proven through five theorems. Experimental evaluations, encompassing runtime cost, memory consumption, and scalability, demonstrate that FUIM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms.

title: TargetUM: Targeted High-Utility Itemset Querying
text: Traditional high-utility itemset mining (HUIM) aims to determine all high-utility itemsets (HUIs) that satisfy the minimum utility threshold (\textit{minUtil}) in transaction databases. However, in most applications, not all HUIs are interesting because only specific parts are required. Thus, targeted mining based on user preferences is more important than traditional mining tasks. This paper is the first to propose a target-based HUIM problem and to provide a clear formulation of the targeted utility mining task in a quantitative transaction database. A tree-based algorithm known as Target-based high-Utility iteMset querying using (TargetUM) is proposed. The algorithm uses a lexicographic querying tree and three effective pruning strategies to improve the mining efficiency. We implemented experimental validation on several real and synthetic databases, and the results demonstrate that the performance of \textbf{TargetUM} is satisfactory, complete, and correct. Finally, owing to the lexicographic querying tree, the database no longer needs to be scanned repeatedly for multiple queries.

title: TargetUM: Targeted High-Utility Itemset Querying
text: In transaction databases, traditional high-utility itemset mining (HUIM) endeavors to uncover all itemsets exceeding a minimum utility threshold, denoted as minUtil. However, in practice, not all high-utility itemsets (HUIs) are pertinent, as only specific subsets are typically required. Consequently, targeted mining that incorporates user preferences is increasingly vital. This paper pioneers the formulation of a target-based HUIM problem, formally defining the task of targeted utility mining in quantitative transaction databases. We propose TargetUM, a tree-based algorithm that leverages a lexicographic querying tree and three pruning strategies to enhance mining efficiency. Experimental validation on real and synthetic databases demonstrates the satisfactory, complete, and correct performance of TargetUM. Notably, the lexicographic querying tree eliminates the need for repetitive database scans, thereby streamlining query processing for multiple queries.

title: Text Classification for Task-based Source Code Related Questions
text: There is a key demand to automatically generate code for small tasks for developers. Websites such as StackOverflow provide a simplistic way by offering solutions in small snippets which provide a complete answer to whatever task question the developer wants to code. Natural Language Processing and particularly Question-Answering Systems are very helpful in resolving and working on these tasks. In this paper, we develop a two-fold deep learning model: Seq2Seq and a binary classifier that takes in the intent (which is in natural language) and code snippets in Python. We train both the intent and the code utterances in the Seq2Seq model, where we decided to compare the effect of the hidden layer embedding from the encoder for representing the intent and similarly, using the decoder's hidden layer embeddings for the code sequence. Then we combine both these embeddings and then train a simple binary neural network classifier model for predicting if the intent is correctly answered by the predicted code sequence from the seq2seq model. We find that the hidden state layer's embeddings perform slightly better than regular standard embeddings from a constructed vocabulary. We experimented with our tests on the CoNaLa dataset in addition to the StaQC database consisting of simple task-code snippet-based pairs. We empirically establish that using additional pre-trained embeddings for code snippets in Python is less context-based in comparison to using hidden state context vectors from seq2seq models.

title: Text Classification for Task-based Source Code Related Questions
text: The proliferation of online platforms for asking and answering programming-related questions has led to an explosion of source code-centric queries, posing significant challenges for automated question classification. In particular, task-based source code related questions (TBSCQs) – which involve resolving specific programming tasks through code snippets – require nuanced understanding of both programming concepts and natural language semantics. Existing approaches to text classification, however, often fall short in capturing the intricate relationships between code and text in TBSCQs. To address this gap, we propose a novel text classification framework tailored to TBSCQs. Our approach leverages a hybrid representation combining both code- and text-based features, extracted using a combination of syntax-aware code embeddings and contextualized language models. We evaluate our framework on a large-scale dataset of TBSCQs, annotated with fine-grained task categories, and demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art text classification models. Our experiments reveal that the incorporation of code-based features yields a 15.2% increase in macro-F1 score compared to text-only models, while our hybrid representation achieves a 21.5% improvement over code-only models. Furthermore, we observe that the effectiveness of our approach is robust across different programming languages and task categories. Our findings have important implications for the development of more accurate and efficient question classification systems, ultimately enhancing the user experience in online programming communities.

title: Challenging but Full of Opportunities: Teachers' Perspectives on Programming in Primary Schools
text: The widespread establishment of computational thinking in school curricula requires teachers to introduce children to programming already at primary school level. As this is a recent development, primary school teachers may neither be adequately prepared for how to best teach programming, nor may they be fully aware why they have to do so. In order to gain a better understanding of these questions, we contrast insights taken from practical experiences with the anticipations of teachers in training. By surveying 200 teachers who have taught programming at primary schools and 97 teachers in training, we identify relevant challenges when teaching programming, opportunities that arise when children learn programming, and strategies how to address both of these in practice. While many challenges and opportunities are correctly anticipated, we find several disagreements that can inform revisions of the curricula in teaching studies to better prepare primary school teachers for teaching programming at primary schools.

title: Challenging but Full of Opportunities: Teachers' Perspectives on Programming in Primary Schools
text: With the increasing emphasis on introducing programming concepts early in the curriculum, primary school teachers are now expected to teach programming despite often lacking formal training in the subject. This study explores the challenges and opportunities that primary school teachers face when teaching programming, shedding light on their perspectives and experiences. We conducted in-depth interviews with 25 primary school teachers from 15 schools in the UK, who had received training and support to integrate programming into their teaching practices. Thematic analysis revealed that while teachers acknowledged the importance of programming, they struggled with the abstract nature of programming concepts, limited resources, and the need to adapt their pedagogical approaches. Notably, teachers also highlighted the opportunities that programming presented, including improved problem-solving skills, enhanced digital literacy, and increased pupil engagement. Our findings provide valuable insights for policymakers, educators, and researchers, informing the development of effective strategies to support primary school teachers in teaching programming and promoting computational thinking.

title: Application-Platform Co-Design for Serverless Data Processing
text: Application-platform co-design" refers to the phenomenon of new platforms being created in response to changing application needs, followed by application design and development changing due to the emergence (and the specifics, limitations) of the new platforms, therefore creating, again, new application and platform requirements. This continuous process of application and platform (re-)design describes an engineering and management responsibility to constantly evaluate any given platform for application fit and platform-specific application design, and to consider a new or evolutionary platform development project due to evolving and changing application needs. In this paper, we study this phenomenon in the context of serverless computing and (big) data processing needs, and thus, for application-platform co-design for serverless data processing (SDP). We present an analysis of the state-of-the-art of function-as-a-service (FaaS) platforms, which reveals several configuration, deployment, execution, and measurement differences between popular platforms happening at-speed. These differences indicate already ongoing platform (re-)design processes resulting in more specialized serverless platforms and new, platform-specific challenges for application design. We discuss data processing needs of applications using the serverless model and present common initial (and undesirable) workaround solutions on the application level, giving additional argument to the creation of new SDP platforms. We present critical SDP requirements and possible new platform augmentations, but identify the need for engineering methods and tooling to better guide application-platform co-design. We argue to pay appropriate attention to the phenomenon of continuous application-platform co-design to better anticipate and to control future platform and application developments.

title: Application-Platform Co-Design for Serverless Data Processing
text: The interplay between application requirements and platform development gives rise to a dynamic co-design process, where emerging platforms influence application design, and, in turn, novel application needs drive platform evolution. This reciprocal process underscores the importance of continually assessing platform fitness for applications and considering platform-driven design adaptations or new platform developments in response to shifting application demands. We investigate this phenomenon in the context of serverless computing and big data processing, specifically focusing on application-platform co-design for serverless data processing (SDP). Our examination of the current state of function-as-a-service (FaaS) platforms reveals significant variations in configuration, deployment, execution, and measurement across popular platforms, which are already triggering platform redesign and specialization. These differences, in turn, introduce new challenges for application design. We analyze the data processing needs of serverless applications and highlight common, yet undesirable, workarounds employed at the application level, further underscoring the need for novel SDP platforms. We identify critical SDP requirements and potential platform augmentations, but emphasize the necessity for engineering methodologies and tooling to guide application-platform co-design. By acknowledging the continuous interplay between applications and platforms, we can better anticipate and direct future developments in both domains.

title: AutoShard -- Declaratively Managing Hot Spot Data Objects in NoSQL Document Stores
text: NoSQL document stores are becoming increasingly popular as backends in web development. Not only do they scale out to large volumes of data, many systems are even custom-tailored for this domain: NoSQL document stores like Google Cloud Datastore have been designed to support massively parallel reads, and even guarantee strong consistency in updating single data objects. However, strongly consistent updates cannot be implemented arbitrarily fast in large-scale distributed systems. Consequently, data objects that experience high-frequent writes can turn into severe performance bottlenecks. In this paper, we present AutoShard, a ready-to-use object mapper for Java applications running against NoSQL document stores. AutoShard's unique feature is its capability to gracefully shard hot spot data objects to avoid write contention. Using AutoShard, developers can easily handle hot spot data objects by adding minimally intrusive annotations to their application code. Our experiments show the significant impact of sharding on both the write throughput and the execution time.

title: AutoShard -- Declaratively Managing Hot Spot Data Objects in NoSQL Document Stores
text: Distributed NoSQL document stores have become a cornerstone of modern data management, offering high scalability and flexible schema designs. However, they often struggle with hot spot data objects, which can lead to performance bottlenecks and uneven resource utilization. Existing approaches to mitigating hot spots rely on manual sharding, which can be error-prone, tedious, and may not adapt well to changing workloads. This paper presents AutoShard, a novel declarative framework for managing hot spot data objects in NoSQL document stores. AutoShard allows developers to specify high-level policies for data distribution and replication, which are then automatically translated into optimal sharding strategies. Our approach leverages a cost-based optimization model that considers factors such as data access patterns, node capacities, and network topology. Experimental results on a real-world dataset demonstrate that AutoShard reduces hot spot contention by up to 75% and improves overall system throughput by up to 30%, while minimizing administrative overhead.

title: Code2Snapshot: Using Code Snapshots for Learning Representations of Source Code
text: There are several approaches for encoding source code in the input vectors of neural models. These approaches attempt to include various syntactic and semantic features of input programs in their encoding. In this paper, we investigate Code2Snapshot, a novel representation of the source code that is based on the snapshots of input programs. We evaluate several variations of this representation and compare its performance with state-of-the-art representations that utilize the rich syntactic and semantic features of input programs. Our preliminary study on the utility of Code2Snapshot in the code summarization and code classification tasks suggests that simple snapshots of input programs have comparable performance to state-of-the-art representations. Interestingly, obscuring input programs have insignificant impacts on the Code2Snapshot performance, suggesting that, for some tasks, neural models may provide high performance by relying merely on the structure of input programs.

title: Code2Snapshot: Using Code Snapshots for Learning Representations of Source Code
text: Source code analysis is a fundamental task in software engineering, relying on effective representations of code. Recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of neural models that learn from source code, but these models often struggle to capture the complexity and diversity of real-world codebases. We propose Code2Snapshot, a novel approach that leverages code snapshots, i.e., compact, abstract representations of code, to learn robust and informative representations of source code. Our method involves generating a large dataset of code snapshots from open-source projects and training a neural network to predict the snapshot from the corresponding code snippet. Experiments on a range of downstream tasks, including code classification, clone detection, and code search, demonstrate that Code2Snapshot outperforms state-of-the-art models, achieving a 15% improvement in accuracy on average. Our results suggest that code snapshots are a valuable intermediate representation for learning effective code representations.

title: Dazed and Confused: What's Wrong with Crypto Libraries?
text: Recent studies have shown that developers have difficulties in using cryptographic APIs, which often led to security flaws. We are interested to tackle this matter by looking into what types of problems exist in various crypto libraries. We manually studied 500 posts on Stack Overflow associated with 20 popular crypto libraries. We realized there are 10 themes in the discussions. Interestingly, there were only two questions related to attacks against cryptography. There were 63 discussions in which developers had interoperability issues when working with more than a crypto library. The majority of posts (i.e. 112) were about encryption/decryption problems and 111 were about installation/compilation issues of crypto libraries. Overall, we realize that the crypto libraries are frequently involved in more than five themes of discussions. We believe the current initial findings can help team leaders and experienced developers to correctly guide the team members in the domain of cryptography. Moreover, future research should investigate the similarity of problems at the API level among popular crypto libraries.

title: Dazed and Confused: What's Wrong with Crypto Libraries?
text: The widespread adoption of cryptographic primitives in modern software systems has led to a proliferation of cryptographic libraries, which, in theory, provide a secure and convenient way to integrate encryption into applications. However, our empirical analysis of 15 popular open-source cryptographic libraries reveals a concerning lack of rigor in their design and implementation. We systematically evaluated each library's API, documentation, and test suite, and found that 12 libraries exhibit at least one of the following issues: incomplete or inconsistent API documentation, inadequate test coverage, or ambiguous error handling. Furthermore, we identified 23 instances of cryptographic misuse, including the use of broken primitives, insecure key management, and incorrect protocol implementations. Our results suggest that the current state of cryptographic libraries is precarious, and that the lack of formal verification and rigorous testing is a major contributing factor. We propose a set of guidelines and tools to help library developers and users ensure the correct and secure use of cryptographic primitives, and advocate for a more principled approach to cryptographic library design and implementation.

title: Callee: Recovering Call Graphs for Binaries with Transfer and Contrastive Learning
text: Recovering binary programs' call graphs is crucial for inter-procedural analysis tasks and applications based on them.transfer One of the core challenges is recognizing targets of indirect calls (i.e., indirect callees). Existing solutions all have high false positives and negatives, making call graphs inaccurate. In this paper, we propose a new solution Callee combining transfer learning and contrastive learning. The key insight is that, deep neural networks (DNNs) can automatically identify patterns concerning indirect calls, which can be more efficient than designing approximation algorithms or heuristic rules to handle various cases. Inspired by the advances in question-answering applications, we utilize contrastive learning to answer the callsite-callee question. However, one of the toughest challenges is that DNNs need large datasets to achieve high performance, while collecting large-scale indirect-call ground-truths can be computational-expensive. Since direct calls and indirect calls share similar calling conventions, it is possible to transfer knowledge learned from direct calls to indirect ones. Therefore, we leverage transfer learning to pre-train DNNs with easy-to-collect direct calls and further fine-tune the indirect-call DNNs. We evaluate Callee on several groups of targets, and results show that our solution could match callsites to callees with an F1-Measure of 94.6%, much better than state-of-the-art solutions. Further, we apply Callee to binary code similarity detection and hybrid fuzzing, and found it could greatly improve their performance.

title: Callee: Recovering Call Graphs for Binaries with Transfer and Contrastive Learning
text: The recovery of accurate call graphs from binary programs is a fundamental prerequisite for various inter-procedural analysis tasks and applications. A crucial aspect of this problem is the identification of indirect callees, which remains a significant challenge. Existing approaches suffer from high rates of false positives and negatives, leading to inaccurate call graphs. This paper presents Callee, a novel solution that leverages the strengths of transfer learning and contrastive learning to address this challenge. By recognizing that deep neural networks can automatically identify patterns related to indirect calls, we employ contrastive learning to formulate the callsite-callee relationship as a question-answering problem. A key obstacle in this approach is the requirement for large datasets to achieve high performance, which can be computationally expensive for indirect calls. To overcome this, we exploit the similarity in calling conventions between direct and indirect calls, using transfer learning to pre-train neural networks on easily collectible direct calls and fine-tune them for indirect calls. Our evaluation demonstrates that Callee achieves an F1-Measure of 94.6% in matching callsites to callees, outperforming state-of-the-art solutions. Moreover, we show that Callee significantly improves the performance of binary code similarity detection and hybrid fuzzing when integrated into these applications.

title: Constructing a software requirements specification and design for electronic IT news magazine system
text: Requirements engineering process intends to obtain software services and constraints. This process is essential to meet the customer's needs and expectations. This process includes three main activities in general. These are detecting requirements by interacting with software stakeholders, transferring these requirements into a standard document, and examining that the requirements really define the software that the client needs. Functional requirements are services that the software should deliver to the end-user. In addition, functional requirements describe how the software should respond to specific inputs, and how the software should behave in certain circumstances. This paper aims to develop a software requirements specification document of the electronic IT news magazine system. The electronic magazine provides users to post and view up-to-date IT news. Still, there is a lack in the literature of comprehensive studies about the construction of the electronic magazine software specification and design in conformance with the contemporary software development processes. Moreover, there is a need for a suitable research framework to support the requirements engineering process. The novelty of this paper is the construction of software specification and design of the electronic magazine by following the Al-Msie'deen research framework. All the documents of software requirements specification and design have been constructed to conform to the agile usage-centered design technique and the proposed research framework. A requirements specification and design are suggested and followed for the construction of the electronic magazine software. This study proved that involving users extensively in the process of software requirements specification and design will lead to the creation of dependable and acceptable software systems.

title: Constructing a software requirements specification and design for electronic IT news magazine system
text: The proliferation of digital media has led to a surge in the popularity of electronic IT news magazines, necessitating the development of sophisticated systems to support their publication and dissemination. Despite their growing importance, existing systems often suffer from inadequate software requirements specifications and design, resulting in inefficient content management, poor user experience, and limited scalability. To address these limitations, we present a systematic approach to constructing a software requirements specification and design for an electronic IT news magazine system. Our methodology involves a comprehensive review of existing literature and industry practices, followed by a thorough analysis of stakeholder requirements using goal-oriented modeling and scenario-based design techniques. We then utilize object-oriented analysis and design principles to develop a detailed software architecture, comprising modular components for content creation, publishing, and subscription management. Our design emphasizes flexibility, scalability, and maintainability, while ensuring seamless user interaction and efficient content delivery. The resulting system supports diverse content formats, personalized user profiles, and real-time updates, thereby enhancing the overall user experience. We evaluate our approach through a case study, where we apply our methodology to develop a functional electronic IT news magazine system. The results demonstrate significant improvements in system performance, user satisfaction, and content quality, highlighting the effectiveness of our approach in constructing a software requirements specification and design for electronic IT news magazine systems.

title: MillenniumDB: A Persistent, Open-Source, Graph Database
text: In this systems paper, we present MillenniumDB: a novel graph database engine that is modular, persistent, and open source. MillenniumDB is based on a graph data model, which we call domain graphs, that provides a simple abstraction upon which a variety of popular graph models can be supported. The engine itself is founded on a combination of tried and tested techniques from relational data management, state-of-the-art algorithms for worst-case-optimal joins, as well as graph-specific algorithms for evaluating path queries. In this paper, we present the main design principles underlying MillenniumDB, describing the abstract graph model and query semantics supported, the concrete data model and query syntax implemented, as well as the storage, indexing, query planning and query evaluation techniques used. We evaluate MillenniumDB over real-world data and queries from the Wikidata knowledge graph, where we find that it outperforms other popular persistent graph database engines (including both enterprise and open source alternatives) that support similar query features.

title: MillenniumDB: A Persistent, Open-Source, Graph Database
text: Modern graph databases often sacrifice performance, scalability, or persistence to achieve high query throughput, compromising their ability to efficiently manage large-scale graph datasets. To address these limitations, we present MillenniumDB, a novel, open-source graph database that leverages a combination of advanced indexing techniques, parallel query execution, and a novel, log-structured merge-tree (LSM-tree) storage engine to achieve high performance, scalability, and persistence. Our approach exploits the inherent graph structure to enable efficient query optimization, while our LSM-tree design ensures high write throughput and efficient garbage collection. Experimental evaluation using the LDBC Social Network Benchmark and the Graph500 benchmark suite demonstrates that MillenniumDB outperforms state-of-the-art graph databases, including Neo4j and Amazon Neptune, by up to 5x in query performance and 3x in data ingestion rates, while providing strong consistency and durability guarantees. Our results have significant implications for large-scale graph data management in various domains, including social networks, recommender systems, and knowledge graphs.

title: Do Names Echo Semantics? A Large-Scale Study of Identifiers Used in C++'s Named Casts
text: Developers relax restrictions on a type to reuse methods with other types. While type casts are prevalent, in weakly typed languages such as C++, they are also extremely permissive. Assignments where a source expression is cast into a new type and assigned to a target variable of the new type, can lead to software bugs if performed without care. In this paper, we propose an information-theoretic approach to identify poor implementations of explicit cast operations. Our approach measures accord between the source expression and the target variable using conditional entropy. We collect casts from 34 components of the Chromium project, which collectively account for 27MLOC and random-uniformly sample this dataset to create a manually labelled dataset of 271 casts. Information-theoretic vetting of these 271 casts achieves a peak precision of 81% and a recall of 90%. We additionally present the findings of an in-depth investigation of notable explicit casts, two of which were fixed in recent releases of the Chromium project.

title: Do Names Echo Semantics? A Large-Scale Study of Identifiers Used in C++'s Named Casts
text: The relaxation of type restrictions to facilitate method reuse across different types is a common practice among developers, particularly in weakly typed languages like C++. However, this permissiveness can lead to software bugs when type casts are performed without careful consideration. A specific scenario prone to errors involves assigning a source expression to a target variable of a different type, which can result in type mismatches. This paper presents an information-theoretic approach to detect poor implementations of explicit cast operations by quantifying the accord between source expressions and target variables using conditional entropy. We evaluate our approach on a dataset of 271 manually labeled casts, randomly sampled from 34 components of the Chromium project totaling 27 million lines of code. Our methodology achieves a peak precision of 81% and a recall of 90%. Furthermore, we provide insights from an in-depth analysis of notable explicit casts, including two instances that were addressed in recent Chromium releases.

title: SO{U}RCERER: Developer-Driven Security Testing Framework for Android Apps
text: Frequently advised secure development recommendations often fall short in practice for app developers.
