Tool-driven (e.g., using static analysis tools) approaches lack context and domain-specific requirements of an app being tested. App developers struggle to find an actionable and prioritized list of vulnerabilities from a laundry list of security warnings reported by static analysis tools. Process-driven (e.g., applying threat modeling methods) approaches require substantial resources (e.g., security testing team, budget) and security expertise, which small to medium-scale app dev teams could barely afford. To help app developers securing their apps, we propose SO{U}RCERER, a guiding framework for Android app developers for security testing. SO{U}RCERER guides developers to identify domain-specific assets of an app, detect and prioritize vulnerabilities, and mitigate those vulnerabilities based on secure development guidelines. We evaluated SO{U}RCERER with a case study on analyzing and testing 36 Android mobile money apps. We found that by following activities guided by SO{U}RCERER, an app developer could get a concise and actionable list of vulnerabilities (24-61% fewer security warnings produced by SO{U}RCERER than a standalone static analyzer), directly affecting a mobile money app's critical assets, and devise a mitigation plan. Our findings from this preliminary study indicate a viable approach to Android app security testing without being overwhelmingly complex for app developers.

title: SO{U}RCERER: Developer-Driven Security Testing Framework for Android Apps
text: The adoption of secure development practices by app developers is often hindered by the limitations of existing approaches. Tool-driven methods, which rely on static analysis tools, fail to account for the specific context and requirements of the app being tested, resulting in an overwhelming number of security warnings. Meanwhile, process-driven approaches, such as threat modeling, demand significant resources and security expertise, making them inaccessible to small to medium-scale development teams. To address this gap, we introduce SO{U}RCERER, a guiding framework designed to facilitate security testing for Android app developers. This framework enables developers to identify domain-specific assets, detect and prioritize vulnerabilities, and develop mitigation strategies aligned with secure development guidelines. In a case study involving 36 Android mobile money apps, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SO{U}RCERER in producing a concise and actionable list of vulnerabilities, with a 24-61% reduction in security warnings compared to a standalone static analyzer. Our preliminary findings suggest that SO{U}RCERER offers a viable and accessible approach to Android app security testing, empowering developers to secure their apps without being overwhelmed by complexity.

title: International Comparative Studies on the Software Testing Profession
text: This work attempts to fill a gap by exploring the human dimension in particular, by trying to understand the motivation of software professionals for taking up and sustaining their careers as software testers. Towards that goal, four surveys were conducted in four countries - India, Canada, Cuba, and China - to try to understand how professional software engineers perceive and value work-related factors that could influence their motivation to start or move into software testing careers. From our sample of 220 software professionals, we observed that very few were keen to take up testing careers. Some aspects of software testing, such as the potential for learning opportunities and the importance of the job, appear to be common motivators across the four countries, whereas the treatment of testers as second-class citizens and the complexity of the job appeared to be the most prominent de-motivators.

title: International Comparative Studies on the Software Testing Profession
text: The software testing profession plays a vital role in ensuring the quality of software systems, yet its characteristics and dynamics remain understudied. This paper presents a large-scale international comparative study of the software testing profession, examining the demographics, skills, and practices of testers across 17 countries. We conducted a mixed-methods study, combining surveys of 2,345 professional testers with in-depth interviews of 35 testing team leaders. Our analysis reveals significant variations in testers' educational backgrounds, with a strong emphasis on computer science degrees in Europe and a more diverse range of degrees in Asia. We also found that testers in North America prioritize automation skills, while those in South America focus on manual testing. Furthermore, our results show that testing teams in developed economies tend to adopt more agile methodologies, whereas those in developing economies rely more on traditional waterfall approaches. These findings have important implications for software testing education, training, and practice.

title: An Evaluation of WebAssembly and eBPF as Offloading Mechanisms in the Context of Computational Storage
text: As the volume of data that needs to be processed continues to increase, we also see renewed interests in near-data processing in the form of computational storage, with eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) being proposed as a vehicle for computation offloading. However, discussions in this regard have so far ignored viable alternatives, and no convincing analysis has been provided. As such, we qualitatively and quantitatively evaluated eBPF against WebAssembly, a seemingly similar technology, in the context of computation offloading. This report presents our findings.

title: An Evaluation of WebAssembly and eBPF as Offloading Mechanisms in the Context of Computational Storage
text: The escalating demands of data processing have sparked a resurgence of interest in near-data processing, specifically computational storage, with eBPF emerging as a promising solution for offloading computation. Notwithstanding, existing discussions have overlooked alternative approaches, lacking a rigorous comparative analysis. This study bridges this gap by presenting a comprehensive evaluation of eBPF and WebAssembly, a comparable technology, in the context of computation offloading, providing both qualitative and quantitative insights.

title: Fair-SSL: Building fair ML Software with less data
text: Ethical bias in machine learning models has become a matter of concern in the software engineering community. Most of the prior software engineering works concentrated on finding ethical bias in models rather than fixing it. After finding bias, the next step is mitigation. Prior researchers mainly tried to use supervised approaches to achieve fairness. However, in the real world, getting data with trustworthy ground truth is challenging and also ground truth can contain human bias. Semi-supervised learning is a machine learning technique where, incrementally, labeled data is used to generate pseudo-labels for the rest of the data (and then all that data is used for model training). In this work, we apply four popular semi-supervised techniques as pseudo-labelers to create fair classification models. Our framework, Fair-SSL, takes a very small amount (10%) of labeled data as input and generates pseudo-labels for the unlabeled data. We then synthetically generate new data points to balance the training data based on class and protected attribute as proposed by Chakraborty et al. in FSE 2021. Finally, the classification model is trained on the balanced pseudo-labeled data and validated on test data. After experimenting on ten datasets and three learners, we find that Fair-SSL achieves similar performance as three state-of-the-art bias mitigation algorithms. That said, the clear advantage of Fair-SSL is that it requires only 10% of the labeled training data. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first SE work where semi-supervised techniques are used to fight against ethical bias in SE ML models.

title: Fair-SSL: Building fair ML Software with less data
text: The prevalence of ethical bias in machine learning models has sparked significant concern within the software engineering community, prompting a shift in focus from detection to mitigation strategies. While prior research has primarily relied on supervised approaches to achieve fairness, the limitations of obtaining trustworthy ground truth data and the potential for human bias in annotations hinder their effectiveness. Semi-supervised learning offers a promising alternative, where incrementally labeled data is leveraged to generate pseudo-labels for unlabeled data, facilitating model training. This study explores the application of four popular semi-supervised techniques as pseudo-labelers to develop fair classification models. Our proposed framework, Fair-SSL, requires only a minimal amount (10%) of labeled data as input, which is then used to generate pseudo-labels for the remaining data. The training data is subsequently balanced based on class and protected attribute, following the approach outlined by Chakraborty et al. (FSE 2021). Experimental results on ten datasets and three learners demonstrate that Fair-SSL achieves comparable performance to three state-of-the-art bias mitigation algorithms, while requiring significantly less labeled training data. To our knowledge, this is the first software engineering study to harness semi-supervised techniques in combating ethical bias in machine learning models.

title: Smells in System User Interactive Tests
text: Test smells are known as bad development practices that reflect poor design and implementation choices in software tests. Over the last decade, test smells were heavily studied to measure their prevalence and impacts on test maintainability. However, these studies focused mainly on the unit level and to this day, the work on system tests that interact with the System Under Test through a Graphical User Interface remains limited. To fill the gap, we conduct an exploratory analysis of test smells occurring in System User Interactive Tests (SUIT). First, based on a multi-vocal literature review, we propose a catalog of 35 SUIT-specific smells. Then, we conduct an empirical analysis to assess the prevalence and refactoring of these smells in 48 industrial test suites and 12 open-source projects. We show that the same type of smells tends to appear in industrial and open-source projects, but the symptoms are not addressed in the same way. Smells such as Obscure Test, Sneaky Checking, and Over Checking show symptoms in more than 70% of the tests. Yet refactoring actions are much less frequent with less than 50% of the affected tests ever undergoing refactoring. Interestingly, while refactoring actions are rare, some smells, such as Narcissistic, disappear through the removal of old symptomatic tests and the introduction of new tests not presenting such symptoms.

title: Smells in System User Interactive Tests
text: User interactive tests, which involve human evaluators assessing the usability and effectiveness of software systems, are essential for ensuring high-quality user experiences. However, these tests are often plagued by "smells"—subtle, pervasive, and context-dependent issues that can significantly impact test validity and reliability. Despite their importance, smells in user interactive tests have received scant attention in the software engineering community. This study aims to bridge this gap by systematically investigating smells in system user interactive tests. We conducted a mixed-methods study, combining a comprehensive literature review, a survey of 35 experienced testers, and an in-depth analysis of 150 user interactive test cases from five open-source software projects. Our results reveal 13 distinct smell types, including ambiguous task descriptions, inadequate evaluator training, and inconsistent test environment configurations. We also identify key factors contributing to smell presence, such as time pressure, limited resources, and inadequate test design. Furthermore, we develop a taxonomy of smells, which provides a framework for understanding, detecting, and mitigating these issues. Our findings have important implications for software engineering practitioners and researchers, highlighting the need for more rigorous and systematic approaches to user interactive test design and execution.

title: Can I use this publicly available dataset to build commercial AI software? -- A Case Study on Publicly Available Image Datasets
text: Publicly available datasets are one of the key drivers for commercial AI software. The use of publicly available datasets is governed by dataset licenses. These dataset licenses outline the rights one is entitled to on a given dataset and the obligations that one must fulfil to enjoy such rights without any license compliance violations. Unlike standardized Open Source Software (OSS) licenses, existing dataset licenses are defined in an ad-hoc manner and do not clearly outline the rights and obligations associated with their usage. Further, a public dataset may be hosted in multiple locations and created from multiple data sources each of which may have different licenses. Hence, existing approaches on checking OSS license compliance cannot be used. In this paper, we propose a new approach to assessing the potential license compliance violations if a given publicly available dataset were to be used for building commercial AI software. We conduct a case study with our approach on 6 commonly used publicly available image datasets. Our results show that there exists potential risks of license violations associated with all of the studied datasets if they were used for commercial purposes.

title: Can I use this publicly available dataset to build commercial AI software? -- A Case Study on Publicly Available Image Datasets
text: The proliferation of commercial AI software is largely driven by the availability of public datasets, whose usage is governed by dataset licenses that outline entitlements and obligations. Unlike standardized Open Source Software licenses, dataset licenses are often defined in an ad-hoc manner, leading to ambiguity regarding rights and obligations associated with their use. Furthermore, public datasets may be hosted across multiple locations and sourced from diverse data providers, each with distinct licenses, rendering existing OSS license compliance approaches inapplicable. This paper proposes a novel approach for assessing potential license compliance violations when utilizing publicly available datasets for commercial AI software development. A case study applying this approach to six commonly used public image datasets reveals that all datasets examined pose risks of license violations if employed for commercial purposes. These findings underscore the imperative for a systematic and standardized framework for dataset licensing to mitigate the risks of non-compliance.

title: TOSCAdata: Modelling data pipeline applications in TOSCA
text: The serverless platform allows a customer to effectively use cloud resources and pay for the exact amount of used resources. A number of dedicated open source and commercial cloud data management tools are available to handle the massive amount of data. Such modern cloud data management tools are not enough matured to integrate the generic cloud application with the serverless platform due to the lack of mature and stable standards. One of the most popular and mature standards, TOSCA (Topology and Orchestration Specification for Cloud Applications), mainly focuses on application and service portability and automated management of the generic cloud application components. This paper proposes the extension of the TOSCA standard, TOSCAdata, that focuses on the modeling of data pipeline-based cloud applications. Keeping the requirements of modern data pipeline cloud applications, TOSCAdata provides a number of TOSCA models that are independently deployable, schedulable, scalable, and re-usable, while effectively handling the flow and transformation of data in a pipeline manner. We also demonstrate the applicability of proposed TOSCAdata models by taking a web-based cloud application in the context of tourism promotion as a use case scenario.

title: TOSCAdata: Modelling data pipeline applications in TOSCA
text: The serverless computing paradigm enables customers to efficiently utilize cloud resources, with costs incurred only for the resources consumed. However, the proliferation of cloud data management tools, both open-source and commercial, has not yet yielded a mature standard for integrating generic cloud applications with serverless platforms. The Topology and Orchestration Specification for Cloud Applications (TOSCA), a prominent standard, primarily addresses application and service portability, as well as automated management of cloud application components. This paper proposes an extension to TOSCA, dubbed TOSCAdata, which specifically targets the modeling of data pipeline-centric cloud applications. By catering to the requirements of modern data pipeline cloud applications, TOSCAdata provides a suite of independently deployable, schedulable, scalable, and reusable models that effectively manage data flow and transformation in a pipeline architecture. The applicability of the proposed TOSCAdata models is demonstrated through a web-based cloud application use case scenario in the context of tourism promotion.

title: Recommendations to clarify NASA open source requirements
text: The software community has specific definitions for terms such as "open source software," "free software," and "permissive license," but scientists proposing software development efforts to NASA are not always knowledgeable about these definitions. Misunderstandings about the meaning of these terms can result in problems of fairness with solicitations, because scientists who interpret the terms differently than NASA intends may either needlessly limit the scope of their proposed work, or unwittingly propose work that does not comply with software licensing requirements. It is therefore recommended that NASA adopt definitions of the above terms that are in line with software community usage, that these definitions be communicated as part of solicitations to ensure a common understanding, and that proposals be required to identify what software licenses the proposers expect to use.

title: Recommendations to clarify NASA open source requirements
text: A lack of clarity surrounding terms like "open source software," "free software," and "permissive license" can lead to misconceptions among scientists submitting software development proposals to NASA, resulting in unfair solicitations. Divergent interpretations of these terms can cause proposers to unnecessarily restrict their project scope or unintentionally violate software licensing requirements. To mitigate these issues, we advocate for NASA to adopt definitions aligned with those established by the software community. Furthermore, these definitions should be explicitly communicated within solicitations to ensure a shared understanding among proposers. Additionally, proposals should be required to specify the software licenses expected to be used, promoting transparency and compliance with licensing requirements.

title: GraphSearchNet: Enhancing GNNs via Capturing Global Dependencies for Semantic Code Search
text: Code search aims to retrieve accurate code snippets based on a natural language query to improve software productivity and quality. With the massive amount of available programs such as (on GitHub or Stack Overflow), identifying and localizing the precise code is critical for the software developers. In addition, Deep learning has recently been widely applied to different code-related scenarios, e.g., vulnerability detection, source code summarization. However, automated deep code search is still challenging since it requires a high-level semantic mapping between code and natural language queries. Most existing deep learning-based approaches for code search rely on the sequential text i.e., feeding the program and the query as a flat sequence of tokens to learn the program semantics while the structural information is not fully considered. Furthermore, the widely adopted Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proved their effectiveness in learning program semantics, however, they also suffer the problem of capturing the global dependencies in the constructed graph, which limits the model learning capacity. To address these challenges, in this paper, we design a novel neural network framework, named GraphSearchNet, to enable an effective and accurate source code search by jointly learning the rich semantics of both source code and natural language queries. Specifically, we propose to construct graphs for the source code and queries with bidirectional GGNN (BiGGNN) to capture the local structural information of the source code and queries. Furthermore, we enhance BiGGNN by utilizing the multi-head attention module to supplement the global dependencies that BiGGNN missed to improve the model learning capacity. The extensive experiments on Java and Python programming language from the public benchmark CodeSearchNet confirm that GraphSearchNet outperforms current state-of-the-art works.

title: GraphSearchNet: Enhancing GNNs via Capturing Global Dependencies for Semantic Code Search
text: Code search, a technique aimed at retrieving relevant code snippets from natural language queries, is crucial for enhancing software productivity and quality. The vast amount of available programs on platforms like GitHub and Stack Overflow necessitates the development of accurate code localization methods. Recent advances in deep learning have been successfully applied to various code-related tasks, including vulnerability detection and source code summarization. However, automated deep code search remains a challenging problem due to the requirement of establishing a high-level semantic correspondence between code and natural language queries. Existing deep learning-based approaches to code search often rely on sequential text representations, neglecting the structural information inherent in programs. While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated effectiveness in learning program semantics, they struggle to capture global dependencies in the constructed graph, limiting their learning capacity. This paper presents GraphSearchNet, a novel neural network framework designed to facilitate accurate source code search by jointly learning the rich semantics of source code and natural language queries. We propose constructing graphs for source code and queries using bidirectional GGNN (BiGGNN) to capture local structural information. Furthermore, we enhance BiGGNN with a multi-head attention module to supplement global dependencies, thereby improving model learning capacity. Experimental results on Java and Python programming languages from the public benchmark CodeSearchNet demonstrate that GraphSearchNet outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

title: Big Data Testing Techniques: Taxonomy, Challenges and Future Trends
text: Big Data is reforming many industrial domains by providing decision support through analyzing large data volumes. Big Data testing aims to ensure that Big Data systems run smoothly and error-free while maintaining the performance and quality of data. However, because of the diversity and complexity of data, testing Big Data is challenging. Though numerous research efforts deal with Big Data testing, a comprehensive review to address testing techniques and challenges of Big Data is not available as yet. Therefore, we have systematically reviewed the Big Data testing techniques evidence occurring in the period 2010-2021. This paper discusses testing data processing by highlighting the techniques used in every processing phase. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and future directions. Our findings show that diverse functional, non-functional and combined (functional and non-functional) testing techniques have been used to solve specific problems related to Big Data. At the same time, most of the testing challenges have been faced during the MapReduce validation phase. In addition, the combinatorial testing technique is one of the most applied techniques in combination with other techniques (i.e., random testing, mutation testing, input space partitioning and equivalence testing) to find various functional faults through Big Data testing.

title: Big Data Testing Techniques: Taxonomy, Challenges and Future Trends
text: The proliferation of Big Data has significantly impacted various industrial sectors, enabling data-driven decision-making through the analysis of vast data volumes. Consequently, ensuring the reliability, performance, and quality of Big Data systems has become paramount, necessitating rigorous testing methodologies. However, the inherent complexity and diversity of Big Data pose significant challenges to testing, despite numerous research endeavors in this area. A comprehensive review of Big Data testing techniques and challenges has been lacking, prompting this systematic review of evidence from 2010 to 2021. This paper provides a detailed examination of data processing testing, highlighting the techniques employed in each processing phase. The findings reveal that a range of functional, non-functional, and combined testing approaches have been applied to address specific Big Data-related problems. Notably, the MapReduce validation phase has been identified as a critical bottleneck, with combinatorial testing emerging as a prominent technique, often used in conjunction with other methods, such as random testing and mutation testing, to detect various functional faults. This review also identifies future research directions and challenges in Big Data testing.

title: Automatic Diversity in the Software Supply Chain
text: Despite its obvious benefits, the increased adoption of package managers to automate the reuse of libraries has opened the door to a new class of hazards: supply chain attacks. By injecting malicious code in one library, an attacker may compromise all instances of all applications that depend on the library. To mitigate the impact of supply chain attacks, we propose the concept of Library Substitution Framework. This novel concept leverages one key observation: when an application depends on a library, it is very likely that there exists other libraries that provide similar features. The key objective of Library Substitution Framework is to enable the developers of an application to harness this diversity of libraries in their supply chain. The framework lets them generate a population of application variants, each depending on a different alternative library that provides similar functionalities. To investigate the relevance of this concept, we develop ARGO, a proof-of-concept implementation of this framework that harnesses the diversity of JSON suppliers. We study the feasibility of library substitution and its impact on a set of 368 clients. Our empirical results show that for 195 of the 368 java applications tested, we can substitute the original JSON library used by the client by at least 15 other JSON libraries without modifying the client's code. These results show the capacity of a Library Substitution Framework to diversify the supply chain of the client applications of the libraries it targets.

title: Automatic Diversity in the Software Supply Chain
text: The increasing reliance on open-source software (OSS) components in modern software systems has introduced a critical vulnerability: the potential for malicious or compromised libraries to spread widely and unnoticed. While various approaches have been proposed to address this issue, they often focus on detecting known vulnerabilities or enforcing strict security policies, neglecting the inherent lack of diversity in the software supply chain. This homogeneity enables a single vulnerability to have a disproportionate impact, as evidenced by recent high-profile incidents. To mitigate this risk, we propose a novel approach to automatically introduce diversity into the software supply chain, leveraging advances in program synthesis and genetic improvement. Our methodology, dubbed "DiversiChain," combines static analysis, constraint solving, and evolutionary computation to generate functionally equivalent, yet syntactically diverse, variants of OSS components. We evaluate DiversiChain on a corpus of popular OSS libraries, demonstrating its ability to produce diverse variants with minimal impact on performance and functionality. Our results show that DiversiChain can reduce the attack surface by up to 75% against certain classes of attacks, while also improving the overall resilience of the software supply chain. Furthermore, we explore the implications of our approach on the broader software ecosystem, including the potential for adaptive attackers and the need for continuous diversity injection. Our work lays the foundation for a more robust and diverse software supply chain, better equipped to withstand emerging threats.

title: An Empirical Study of the Effectiveness of an Ensemble of Stand-alone Sentiment Detection Tools for Software Engineering Datasets
text: Sentiment analysis in software engineering (SE) has shown promise to analyze and support diverse development activities. We report the results of an empirical study that we conducted to determine the feasibility of developing an ensemble engine by combining the polarity labels of stand-alone SE-specific sentiment detectors. Our study has two phases. In the first phase, we pick five SE-specific sentiment detection tools from two recently published papers by Lin et al. [31, 32], who first reported negative results with standalone sentiment detectors and then proposed an improved SE-specific sentiment detector, POME [31]. We report the study results on 17,581 units (sentences/documents) coming from six currently available sentiment benchmarks for SE. We find that the existing tools can be complementary to each other in 85-95% of the cases, i.e., one is wrong, but another is right. However, a majority voting-based ensemble of those tools fails to improve the accuracy of sentiment detection. We develop Sentisead, a supervised tool by combining the polarity labels and bag of words as features. Sentisead improves the performance (F1-score) of the individual tools by 4% (over Senti4SD [5]) - 100% (over POME [31]). In a second phase, we compare and improve Sentisead infrastructure using Pre-trained Transformer Models (PTMs). We find that a Sentisead infrastructure with RoBERTa as the ensemble of the five stand-alone rule-based and shallow learning SE-specific tools from Lin et al. [31, 32] offers the best F1-score of 0.805 across the six datasets, while a stand-alone RoBERTa shows an F1-score of 0.801.

title: An Empirical Study of the Effectiveness of an Ensemble of Stand-alone Sentiment Detection Tools for Software Engineering Datasets
text: The efficacy of sentiment analysis in software engineering has been well-documented, with applications in various development activities. This study explores the viability of creating an ensemble engine by aggregating the polarity labels of standalone sentiment detectors tailored to software engineering. Our two-phase empirical study begins with the selection of five software engineering-specific sentiment detection tools, as identified in recent publications by Lin et al. [31, 32]. These tools are evaluated using six publicly available sentiment benchmarks for software engineering, comprising 17,581 units. Our findings indicate that while the existing tools exhibit complementarity in 85-95% of cases, a majority voting-based ensemble approach fails to improve sentiment detection accuracy. We subsequently develop Sentisead, a supervised tool that combines polarity labels and bag-of-words features, achieving an F1-score improvement of 4-100% over individual tools. In the second phase, we enhance Sentisead's infrastructure by integrating Pre-trained Transformer Models (PTMs). Notably, the Sentisead ensemble, incorporating RoBERTa and the five standalone rule-based and shallow learning tools, yields an optimal F1-score of 0.805 across the six datasets, outperforming a standalone RoBERTa model with an F1-score of 0.801.

title: Discerning Legitimate Failures From False Alerts: A Study of Chromium's Continuous Integration
text: Flakiness is a major concern in Software testing. Flaky tests pass and fail for the same version of a program and mislead developers who spend time and resources investigating test failures only to discover that they are false alerts. In practice, the defacto approach to address this concern is to rerun failing tests hoping that they would pass and manifest as false alerts. Nonetheless, completely filtering out false alerts may require a disproportionate number of reruns, and thus incurs important costs both computation and time-wise. As an alternative to reruns, we propose Fair, a novel, lightweight approach that classifies test failures into false alerts and legitimate failures. Fair relies on a classifier and a set of features from the failures and test artefacts. To build and evaluate our machine learning classifier, we use the continuous integration of the Chromium project. In particular, we collect the properties and artefacts of more than 1 million test failures from 2,000 builds. Our results show that Fair can accurately distinguish legitimate failures from false alerts, with an MCC up to 95%. Moreover, by studying different test categories: GUI, integration and unit tests, we show that Fair classifies failures accurately even when the number of failures is limited. Finally, we compare the costs of our approach to reruns and show that Fair could save up to 20 minutes of computation time per build.

title: Discerning Legitimate Failures From False Alerts: A Study of Chromium's Continuous Integration
text: The reliability of software testing is compromised by flaky tests, which exhibit inconsistent pass and fail outcomes for identical program versions, thereby wasting developers' time and resources on investigating false alerts. The prevailing approach to mitigate this issue involves repeated re-execution of failed tests, hoping to identify false positives. However, this method can be computationally expensive and time-consuming, often necessitating an impractically large number of reruns. As a more efficient alternative, we introduce Fair, a lightweight framework that leverages machine learning to categorize test failures into genuine errors and false alerts. By analyzing a comprehensive set of features extracted from failure instances and test artifacts, our classifier achieves high accuracy in distinguishing between legitimate failures and false positives, with a Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) of up to 95%. We validate Fair's effectiveness using a large-scale dataset of over 1 million test failures from 2,000 builds of the Chromium project, including diverse test categories such as GUI, integration, and unit tests. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that Fair can conserve significant computational resources, saving up to 20 minutes of processing time per build compared to rerun-based approaches.

title: Numerisation D'un Siecle de Paysage Ferroviaire Français : recul du rail, conséquences territoriales et coût environnemental
text: The reconstruction of geographical data over a century, allows to figuring out the evolution of the French railway landscape, and how it has been impacted by major events (eg.: WWII), or longer time span processes : industry outsourcing, metropolization, public transport policies or absence of them. This work is resulting from the fusion of several public geographical data (SNCF, IGN), enriched with the computer-assisted addition of multiple data gathered on the Internet (Wikipedia, volunteer geographic information). The dataset compounds almost every rail stations (even simple stops) and railway branch nodes, whose link to their respective rail lines allows to build the underlying consistent graph of the network. Every rail line has a "valid to" date (or approx) so that time evolution can be displayed. The present progress of that reconstruction sums up to roughly 90% of what is expected (exact total unknown). This allows to consider temporal demographic analysis (how many cities and towns served by the railway since 1925 up on today), and environmental simulations as well (CO2 cost by given destination ).

title: Numerisation D'un Siecle de Paysage Ferroviaire Français : recul du rail, conséquences territoriales et coût environnemental
text: The French railway network has undergone significant transformations over the past century, with a notable decline in rail infrastructure and services. This phenomenon, known as "rail recession," has far-reaching territorial and environmental consequences. To quantify and analyze these impacts, we developed a novel geo-spatial database, "RailFérro," integrating historical railway maps, land use data, and environmental indicators. Our methodology employs a multi-scale approach, combining spatial autocorrelation analysis and machine learning algorithms to identify patterns of rail infrastructure decline and its relationships with land use changes, population dynamics, and environmental degradation. Our results show a significant correlation between rail recession and urban sprawl, as well as increased fragmentation of natural habitats. Furthermore, we estimate that the environmental costs of rail recession in France amount to approximately €1.3 billion annually, primarily due to increased greenhouse gas emissions and habitat destruction. The RailFérro database and our findings provide valuable insights for policymakers and stakeholders, highlighting the need for sustainable transportation infrastructure planning and environmental mitigation strategies.

title: Security Header Fields in HTTP Clients
text: HTTP headers are commonly used to establish web communications, and some of them are relevant for security. However, we have only little information about the usage and support of security-relevant headers in mobile applications. We explored the adoption of such headers in mobile app communication by querying 9,714 distinct URLs that were used in 3,376 apps and collected each server's response information. We discovered that support for secure HTTP header fields is absent in all major HTTP clients, and it is barely provided with any server response. Based on these results, we discuss opportunities for improvement particularly to reduce the likelihood of data leaks and arbitrary code execution. We advocate more comprehensive use of existing HTTP headers and timely development of relevant web browser security features in HTTP client libraries.

title: Security Header Fields in HTTP Clients
text: The prevalence and significance of security-centric HTTP headers in mobile applications remain understudied, despite their crucial role in web communication security. To bridge this knowledge gap, we conducted a large-scale analysis of 9,714 URLs spanning 3,376 mobile apps, examining the responses from each server. Our findings reveal a pervasive lack of support for secure HTTP header fields across all major HTTP clients, with servers rarely providing these critical headers in their responses. This alarming dearth of security features increases the risk of data breaches and arbitrary code execution. We propose that a more comprehensive adoption of existing HTTP headers, coupled with the timely development of pertinent security features in HTTP client libraries, is essential to mitigate these vulnerabilities and enhance web communication security.

title: CloudRCA: A Root Cause Analysis Framework for Cloud Computing Platforms
text: As business of Alibaba expands across the world among various industries, higher standards are imposed on the service quality and reliability of big data cloud computing platforms which constitute the infrastructure of Alibaba Cloud. However, root cause analysis in these platforms is non-trivial due to the complicated system architecture. In this paper, we propose a root cause analysis framework called CloudRCA which makes use of heterogeneous multi-source data including Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), logs, as well as topology, and extracts important features via state-of-the-art anomaly detection and log analysis techniques. The engineered features are then utilized in a Knowledge-informed Hierarchical Bayesian Network (KHBN) model to infer root causes with high accuracy and efficiency. Ablation study and comprehensive experimental comparisons demonstrate that, compared to existing frameworks, CloudRCA 1) consistently outperforms existing approaches in f1-score across different cloud systems; 2) can handle novel types of root causes thanks to the hierarchical structure of KHBN; 3) performs more robustly with respect to algorithmic configurations; and 4) scales more favorably in the data and feature sizes. Experiments also show that a cross-platform transfer learning mechanism can be adopted to further improve the accuracy by more than 10\%. CloudRCA has been integrated into the diagnosis system of Alibaba Cloud and employed in three typical cloud computing platforms including MaxCompute, Realtime Compute and Hologres. It saves Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) more than $20\%$ in the time spent on resolving failures in the past twelve months and improves service reliability significantly.

title: CloudRCA: A Root Cause Analysis Framework for Cloud Computing Platforms
text: The expanding global presence of Alibaba's business across diverse industries has precipitated stringent demands on the service quality and reliability of its big data cloud computing platforms, which form the backbone of Alibaba Cloud. The complexity of these platforms' system architecture, however, renders root cause analysis a formidable challenge. This paper proposes CloudRCA, a novel root cause analysis framework that leverages heterogeneous multi-source data encompassing Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), logs, and topology. By harnessing state-of-the-art anomaly detection and log analysis techniques, CloudRCA extracts salient features that are subsequently utilized in a Knowledge-informed Hierarchical Bayesian Network (KHBN) model to infer root causes with high accuracy and efficiency. Extensive experimental evaluations, including ablation studies, demonstrate that CloudRCA consistently outperforms existing frameworks in f1-score across different cloud systems, exhibits robustness to algorithmic configurations, and scales favorably with increasing data and feature sizes. Notably, the framework's hierarchical structure facilitates the handling of novel root cause types, while a cross-platform transfer learning mechanism can be employed to further enhance accuracy by over 10%. CloudRCA has been successfully integrated into Alibaba Cloud's diagnosis system, yielding significant service reliability improvements and a 20% reduction in time spent resolving failures by Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) over the past year.

title: Confidence Composition for Monitors of Verification Assumptions
text: Closed-loop verification of cyber-physical systems with neural network controllers offers strong safety guarantees under certain assumptions. It is, however, difficult to determine whether these guarantees apply at run time because verification assumptions may be violated. To predict safety violations in a verified system, we propose a three-step confidence composition (CoCo) framework for monitoring verification assumptions. First, we represent the sufficient condition for verified safety with a propositional logical formula over assumptions. Second, we build calibrated confidence monitors that evaluate the probability that each assumption holds. Third, we obtain the confidence in the verification guarantees by composing the assumption monitors using a composition function suitable for the logical formula. Our CoCo framework provides theoretical bounds on the calibration and conservatism of compositional monitors. Two case studies show that compositional monitors are calibrated better than their constituents and successfully predict safety violations.

title: Confidence Composition for Monitors of Verification Assumptions
text: Cyber-physical systems governed by neural network controllers can be endowed with robust safety assurances, contingent upon specific assumptions. Nevertheless, ascertaining the validity of these assumptions at runtime poses a significant challenge. To anticipate potential safety breaches in verified systems, we introduce a novel three-step Confidence Composition (CoCo) framework for monitoring verification assumptions. By encoding the sufficient condition for verified safety as a propositional logical formula over assumptions, we establish a rigorous foundation for our approach. Subsequently, we develop calibrated confidence monitors that estimate the probability of each assumption holding true. Finally, we derive the overall confidence in verification guarantees by composing assumption monitors via a function tailored to the logical formula. The CoCo framework provides theoretical guarantees on monitor calibration and conservatism, as demonstrated by two case studies, which showcase the superiority of compositional monitors in predicting safety violations.

title: Sunspot: A Decentralized Framework Enabling Privacy for Authorizable Data Sharing on Transparent Public Blockchains
text: Blockchain technologies have been boosting the development of data-driven decentralized services in a wide range of fields. However, with the spirit of full transparency, many public blockchains expose all types of data to the public such as Ethereum. Besides, the on-chain persistence of large data is significantly expensive technically and economically. These issues lead to the difficulty of sharing fairly large private data while preserving attractive properties of public blockchains. Although direct encryption for on-chain data persistence can introduce confidentiality, new challenges such as key sharing, access control, and legal rights proving are still open. Meanwhile, cross-chain collaboration still requires secure and effective protocols, though decentralized storage systems such as IPFS bring the possibility for fairly large data persistence. In this paper, we propose Sunspot, a decentralized framework for privacy-preserving data sharing with access control on transparent public blockchains, to solve these issues. We also show the practicality and applicability of Sunspot by MyPub, a decentralized privacy-preserving publishing platform based on Sunspot. Furthermore, we evaluate the security, privacy, and performance of Sunspot through theoretical analysis and experiments.

title: Sunspot: A Decentralized Framework Enabling Privacy for Authorizable Data Sharing on Transparent Public Blockchains
text: Decentralized services, fueled by blockchain technologies, have expanded across various domains. Nevertheless, the inherent transparency of public blockchains, exemplified by Ethereum, raises concerns about data privacy. The on-chain storage of large datasets is not only technically but also economically prohibitive, hindering the fair sharing of sensitive information while maintaining the benefits of public blockchains. Encrypting on-chain data can ensure confidentiality, but introduces additional challenges related to key management, access control, and legal rights verification. Furthermore, secure cross-chain collaboration protocols are still lacking, despite the potential of decentralized storage systems like IPFS for large data persistence. This paper presents Sunspot, a decentralized framework designed to enable privacy-preserving data sharing with access control on transparent public blockchains, addressing these challenges. We demonstrate Sunspot's practicality through MyPub, a decentralized publishing platform, and evaluate its security, privacy, and performance through theoretical analysis and experimental validation.

title: Automatic Program Repair with OpenAI's Codex: Evaluating QuixBugs
text: OpenAI's Codex, a GPT-3 like model trained on a large code corpus, has made headlines in and outside of academia. Given a short user-provided description, it is capable of synthesizing code snippets that are syntactically and semantically valid in most cases. In this work, we want to investigate whether Codex is able to localize and fix bugs, a task of central interest in the field of automated program repair. Our initial evaluation uses the multi-language QuixBugs benchmark (40 bugs in both Python and Java). We find that, despite not being trained for APR, Codex is surprisingly effective, and competitive with recent state of the art techniques. Our results also show that Codex is slightly more successful at repairing Python than Java.

title: Automatic Program Repair with OpenAI's Codex: Evaluating QuixBugs
text: We examine the capabilities of OpenAI's Codex, a large language model trained on a vast codebase, in the context of automated program repair (APR). Despite being primarily designed for code synthesis, Codex demonstrates an unexpected aptitude for localizing and fixing bugs when provided with brief user descriptions. To assess its APR capabilities, we evaluate Codex on the multi-language QuixBugs benchmark, comprising 40 bugs in both Python and Java. Our results reveal that, without explicit training for APR, Codex achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art techniques, exhibiting a slight preference for repairing Python bugs over Java ones.

title: High Performance Out-of-sample Embedding Techniques for Multidimensional Scaling
text: The recent rapid growth of the dimension of many datasets means that many approaches to dimension reduction (DR) have gained significant attention. High-performance DR algorithms are required to make data analysis feasible for big and fast data sets. However, many traditional DR techniques are challenged by truly large data sets. In particular multidimensional scaling (MDS) does not scale well. MDS is a popular group of DR techniques because it can perform DR on data where the only input is a dissimilarity function. However, common approaches are at least quadratic in memory and computation and, hence, prohibitive for large-scale data. We propose an out-of-sample embedding (OSE) solution to extend the MDS algorithm for large-scale data utilising the embedding of only a subset of the given data. We present two OSE techniques: the first based on an optimisation approach and the second based on a neural network model. With a minor trade-off in the approximation, the out-of-sample techniques can process large-scale data with reasonable computation and memory requirements. While both methods perform well, the neural network model outperforms the optimisation approach of the OSE solution in terms of efficiency. OSE has the dual benefit that it allows fast DR on streaming datasets as well as static databases.

title: High Performance Out-of-sample Embedding Techniques for Multidimensional Scaling
text: The proliferation of high-dimensional datasets has spurred significant interest in dimension reduction (DR) techniques. To accommodate the scale and velocity of modern data, high-performance DR algorithms are essential. However, traditional DR methods, including multidimensional scaling (MDS), struggle to cope with massive datasets. MDS, a popular DR approach that operates solely on dissimilarity functions, is particularly limited by its quadratic computational and memory complexity. To overcome this limitation, we propose an out-of-sample embedding (OSE) solution that extends MDS to large-scale data by leveraging the embedding of a subset of the data. Our OSE framework encompasses two techniques: an optimization-based approach and a neural network model. By accepting a minor trade-off in approximation accuracy, our OSE methods enable efficient processing of large-scale data with reasonable computational and memory requirements. A comparative evaluation reveals that the neural network model outperforms the optimization approach in terms of efficiency. Furthermore, OSE confers a dual advantage, facilitating fast DR on both streaming datasets and static databases.

title: Em-K Indexing for Approximate Query Matching in Large-scale ER
text: Accurate and efficient entity resolution (ER) is a significant challenge in many data mining and analysis projects requiring integrating and processing massive data collections. It is becoming increasingly important in real-world applications to develop ER solutions that produce prompt responses for entity queries on large-scale databases. Some of these applications demand entity query matching against large-scale reference databases within a short time. We define this as the query matching problem in ER in this work. Indexing or blocking techniques reduce the search space and execution time in the ER process. However, approximate indexing techniques that scale to very large-scale datasets remain open to research. In this paper, we investigate the query matching problem in ER to propose an indexing method suitable for approximate and efficient query matching. We first use spatial mappings to embed records in a multidimensional Euclidean space that preserves the domain-specific similarity. Among the various mapping techniques, we choose multidimensional scaling. Then using a Kd-tree and the nearest neighbour search, the method returns a block of records that includes potential matches for a query. Our method can process queries against a large-scale dataset using only a fraction of the data $L$ (given the dataset size is $N$), with a $O(L^2)$ complexity where $L \ll N$. The experiments conducted on several datasets showed the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Em-K Indexing for Approximate Query Matching in Large-scale ER
text: Entity resolution (ER) is a crucial step in various data mining and analysis projects, requiring the integration and processing of massive datasets. The development of ER solutions that facilitate rapid query responses on large-scale databases is becoming increasingly vital in real-world applications. Specifically, certain applications necessitate the expedient matching of entity queries against large-scale reference databases. This paper addresses the query matching problem in ER, wherein efficient and approximate indexing techniques are essential to reduce the search space and execution time. Although indexing and blocking techniques have been explored, scalable approximate indexing methods for very large datasets remain an open research challenge. To tackle this problem, we propose an indexing approach that leverages spatial mappings to embed records in a multidimensional Euclidean space, preserving domain-specific similarity. Utilizing multidimensional scaling and a Kd-tree with nearest neighbor search, our method returns a block of records containing potential matches for a query. With a complexity of O(L^2), where L is a fraction of the dataset size N (L ≪ N), our approach enables efficient query processing against large-scale datasets. Experimental results on multiple datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Meta Cross-Modal Hashing on Long-Tailed Data
text: Due to the advantage of reducing storage while speeding up query time on big heterogeneous data, cross-modal hashing has been extensively studied for approximate nearest neighbor search of multi-modal data. Most hashing methods assume that training data is class-balanced.However, in practice, real world data often have a long-tailed distribution. In this paper, we introduce a meta-learning based cross-modal hashing method (MetaCMH) to handle long-tailed data. Due to the lack of training samples in the tail classes, MetaCMH first learns direct features from data in different modalities, and then introduces an associative memory module to learn the memory features of samples of the tail classes. It then combines the direct and memory features to obtain meta features for each sample. For samples of the head classes of the long tail distribution, the weight of the direct features is larger, because there are enough training data to learn them well; while for rare classes, the weight of the memory features is larger. Finally, MetaCMH uses a likelihood loss function to preserve the similarity in different modalities and learns hash functions in an end-to-end fashion. Experiments on long-tailed datasets show that MetaCMH performs significantly better than state-of-the-art methods, especially on the tail classes.

title: Meta Cross-Modal Hashing on Long-Tailed Data
text: The burgeoning field of cross-modal hashing has been propelled by its dual benefits of reduced storage and accelerated query times for large-scale heterogeneous data. However, a prevailing assumption in existing hashing methods is that the training data is class-balanced, which diverges from the typical real-world scenario where data often exhibit a long-tailed distribution. To address this disparity, we propose MetaCMH, a novel meta-learning-based cross-modal hashing approach tailored to tackle long-tailed data. By acknowledging the scarcity of training samples in tail classes, MetaCMH initially extracts direct features from multi-modal data and subsequently incorporates an associative memory module to capture the memory features of tail class samples. The fusion of direct and memory features yields meta features, where the weight of direct features dominates for head classes with sufficient training data, while memory features take precedence for rare classes. Through an end-to-end likelihood loss function, MetaCMH preserves cross-modal similarity and learns hash functions. Empirical evaluations on long-tailed datasets demonstrate the superiority of MetaCMH over state-of-the-art methods, particularly in terms of its enhanced performance on tail classes.

title: OpenMP aware MHP Analysis for Improved Static Data-Race Detection
text: Data races, a major source of bugs in concurrent programs, can result in loss of manpower and time as well as data loss due to system failures. OpenMP, the de facto shared memory parallelism framework used in the HPC community, also suffers from data races. To detect race conditions in OpenMP programs and improve turnaround time and/or developer productivity, we present a data flow analysis based, fast, static data race checker in the LLVM compiler framework. Our tool can detect races in the presence or absence of explicit barriers, with implicit or explicit synchronization. In addition, our tool effectively works for the OpenMP target offloading constructs and also supports the frequently used OpenMP constructs. We formalize and provide a data flow analysis framework to perform Phase Interval Analysis (PIA) of OpenMP programs. Phase intervals are then used to compute the MHP (and its complement NHP) sets for the programs, which, in turn, are used to detect data races statically. We evaluate our work using multiple OpenMP race detection benchmarks and real world applications. Our experiments show that the checker is comparable to the state-of-the-art in various performance metrics with around 90% accuracy, almost perfect recall, and significantly lower runtime and memory footprint.

title: OpenMP aware MHP Analysis for Improved Static Data-Race Detection
text: The proliferation of multi-core processors has led to a surge in the adoption of parallel programming models, with OpenMP being a popular choice for shared-memory architectures. However, the increased concurrency introduced by parallelism also exacerbates the data-race problem, making it a significant bottleneck in the development of correct and efficient parallel software. Static data-race detection techniques, while effective in identifying races at compile-time, often suffer from high false positive rates and limited scalability. To address these limitations, we present an OpenMP-aware Multi-Hierarchical Phenomena (MHP) analysis for improved static data-race detection. Our approach leverages the structured parallelism of OpenMP to guide the MHP analysis, reducing the search space and improving the accuracy of race detection. We formally define the OpenMP-aware MHP analysis and develop a static analysis tool, OMP-MHP, to implement this approach. Experimental results on a suite of OpenMP benchmarks demonstrate that OMP-MHP achieves a significant reduction in false positives (up to 75%) and improves the detection of data-races (up to 30%) compared to existing state-of-the-art static analysis tools. Our approach has important implications for the development of more efficient and reliable parallel software, enabling developers to write correct and scalable parallel code with increased confidence.

title: How Developers and Managers Define and Trade Productivity for Quality
text: In this paper, we present the findings from a survey study to investigate how developers and managers define and trade-off developer productivity and software quality (two related lenses into software development). We found that developers and managers, as cohorts, are not well aligned in their views of what it means to be productive (developers think of productivity in terms of activity, while more managers think of productivity in terms of performance). We also found that developers are not accurate at predicting their managers' views of productivity. In terms of quality, we found that individual developers and managers have quite varied views of what quality means to them, but as cohorts they are closely aligned in their different views, with the majority in both groups defining quality in terms of robustness. Over half of the developers and managers reported that quality can be traded for higher productivity and why this trade-off can be justified, while one third consider quality as a necessary part of productivity that cannot be traded. We also present a new descriptive framework for quality, TRUCE, that we synthesize from the survey responses. We call for more discussion between developers and managers about what they each consider as important software quality attributes, and to have open debate about how software quality relates to developer productivity and what trade-offs should or should not be made.

title: How Developers and Managers Define and Trade Productivity for Quality
text: Software development organizations constantly face the challenge of balancing productivity and quality, as these two goals are often perceived to be in tension. Despite their importance, there is a lack of understanding of how developers and managers define and trade productivity for quality in real-world settings. This study aims to bridge this gap by investigating the perceptions and practices of software professionals in making productivity-quality tradeoffs. We conducted a mixed-methods study, combining a survey of 152 software developers and managers with 22 in-depth interviews. Our results show that developers and managers define productivity and quality in diverse and often conflicting ways, with developers emphasizing individual performance and managers focusing on project-level efficiency. We identified three primary strategies used to trade productivity for quality: prioritizing tasks, adjusting development processes, and allocating resources. Our analysis reveals that these strategies are influenced by factors such as project deadlines, team experience, and organizational culture. We found that developers tend to favor short-term productivity gains, while managers prioritize long-term quality benefits. Our study contributes to the understanding of the complex interplay between productivity and quality in software development, providing insights for practitioners and researchers to better navigate these tradeoffs.

title: Development of a Meta-language and its Qualifiable Implementation for the Use in Safety-critical Software
text: The use of domain-specific modeling for development of complex (cyber-physical) systems is gaining increasing acceptance in the industrial environment. Domain-specific modeling allows complex systems and data to be abstracted for a more efficient system design, development, validation, and configuration. However, no existing (meta-)modeling framework can be used with reasonable effort in certified software so far, neither for the development of systems nor for the execution of system functions. For the use of (development) artifacts from domain-specific modeling in safety-critical processes or systems it is required to ensure their correctness by either subsequent (manual) verification or the usage of (pre-)qualified software. Existing meta-languages often contain modeling elements that are difficult or impossible to implement in a qualifiable manner leading to a high manual, subsequent certification effort. Therefore, the aim is to develop a (meta-)modeling framework, that can be used in certified software. This can significantly reduce the development effort for safety-critical systems and enables the full advantages of domain-specific modeling. The framework components considered in this PhD-Thesis include: (1) an essential meta-language, (2) a qualifiable runtime environment, and (3) a suitable persistence. The essential \mbox{(meta-)}modeling language is mainly based on the UML standard, but is enhanced with multi-level modeling concepts such as deep instantiation. Supporting a possible qualification, the meta-language is implemented using the highly restrictive, but formally provable programming language Ada SPARK.

title: Development of a Meta-language and its Qualifiable Implementation for the Use in Safety-critical Software
text: The development of safety-critical software necessitates rigorous methodologies to ensure the correctness and reliability of the system. Formal methods have been increasingly adopted to address this concern, but their integration into mainstream software development remains a significant challenge. To bridge this gap, we propose a meta-language, dubbed SafeSpec, designed to facilitate the specification and verification of safety-critical systems. SafeSpec provides a formal framework for expressing safety properties, enabling the creation of qualifiable implementations that can be seamlessly integrated into existing software development workflows. We present a syntax-directed approach to the implementation of SafeSpec, which leverages a combination of model checking and proof-carrying code techniques to ensure the correctness of the generated code. Our methodology involves a two-stage process, where the SafeSpec specification is first translated into an intermediate representation, which is then compiled into executable code. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through a case study involving the development of a safety-critical automotive system, where SafeSpec is used to specify and verify the correctness of a fault-tolerant brake controller. Our evaluation shows that SafeSpec-based implementations can achieve significant reductions in verification time and effort, while maintaining the required level of safety assurance. Furthermore, we demonstrate the flexibility of our approach by integrating SafeSpec with existing software development tools, enabling a seamless transition to formal methods-based development. The proposed meta-language and its implementation provide a promising solution for the development of safety-critical software, offering a balance between formal rigor and practical applicability.

title: When Cyber-Physical Systems Meet AI: A Benchmark, an Evaluation, and a Way Forward
text: Cyber-physical systems (CPS) have been broadly deployed in safety-critical domains, such as automotive systems, avionics, medical devices, etc. In recent years, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been increasingly adopted to control CPS. Despite the popularity of AI-enabled CPS, few benchmarks are publicly available. There is also a lack of deep understanding on the performance and reliability of AI-enabled CPS across different industrial domains. To bridge this gap, we initiate to create a public benchmark of industry-level CPS in seven domains and build AI controllers for them via state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods. Based on that, we further perform a systematic evaluation of these AI-enabled systems with their traditional counterparts to identify the current challenges and explore future opportunities. Our key findings include (1) AI controllers do not always outperform traditional controllers, (2) existing CPS testing techniques (falsification, specifically) fall short of analyzing AI-enabled CPS, and (3) building a hybrid system that strategically combines and switches between AI controllers and traditional controllers can achieve better performance across different domains. Our results highlight the need for new testing techniques for AI-enabled CPS and the need for more investigations into hybrid CPS systems to achieve optimal performance and reliability.

title: When Cyber-Physical Systems Meet AI: A Benchmark, an Evaluation, and a Way Forward
text: The increasing ubiquity of artificial intelligence (AI) in cyber-physical systems (CPS) has created a pressing need to evaluate the efficacy of AI-driven decision-making in safety-critical domains. Despite the growing body of research, a comprehensive benchmark for assessing AI-infused CPS remains elusive. This paper addresses this knowledge gap by introducing CPS-AI-Bench, a novel evaluation framework that integrates realistic CPS scenarios with diverse AI algorithms. Our benchmark comprises three CPS domains (autonomous vehicles, smart grid, and industrial control systems) and six AI paradigms (deep reinforcement learning, transfer learning, etc.). We conduct a rigorous evaluation of 18 AI-CPS combinations, examining their performance under varying uncertainty, noise, and fault conditions. Our results reveal significant disparities in AI performance across domains, with deep reinforcement learning exhibiting highest variability in autonomous vehicles, but lowest in smart grid. Furthermore, we identify critical factors influencing AI-CPS interactions, including data quality, model interpretability, and human-in-the-loop feedback. Based on our findings, we propose a roadmap for future research, emphasizing the need for domain-specific AI design, robustness testing, and human-AI collaboration in CPS.

title: Is knowledge the key? An experiment on debiasing architectural decision-making -- a pilot study
text: The impact of cognitive biases on architectural decision-making has been proven by previous research. In this work, we endeavour to create a debiasing treatment that would minimise the impact of cognitive biases on architectural decision-making. We conducted a pilot study on two groups of students, to investigate whether a simple debiasing presentation reporting on the influences of cognitive biases, can provide a debiasing effect. The preliminary results show that this kind of treatment is ineffective. Through analysing our results, we propose a set of modifications that could result in a better effect.

title: Is knowledge the key? An experiment on debiasing architectural decision-making -- a pilot study
text: Architectural decision-making is a complex, high-stakes process prone to cognitive biases. While knowledge is often assumed to mitigate these biases, its impact remains unexplored. This pilot study investigates the effect of knowledge on debiasing architectural decision-making. We recruited 32 software architects and randomly assigned them to either a knowledge-enhanced or control group. Participants then made decisions on a series of architectural scenarios. Results show that the knowledge-enhanced group demonstrated a significant reduction in biases, particularly confirmation bias and availability heuristic. Our findings suggest that knowledge can play a crucial role in debiasing architectural decision-making, with implications for software development practices.

title: Senatus -- A Fast and Accurate Code-to-Code Recommendation Engine
text: Machine learning on source code (MLOnCode) is a popular research field that has been driven by the availability of large-scale code repositories and the development of powerful probabilistic and deep learning models for mining source code. Code-to-code recommendation is a task in MLOnCode that aims to recommend relevant, diverse and concise code snippets that usefully extend the code currently being written by a developer in their development environment (IDE). Code-to-code recommendation engines hold the promise of increasing developer productivity by reducing context switching from the IDE and increasing code-reuse. Existing code-to-code recommendation engines do not scale gracefully to large codebases, exhibiting a linear growth in query time as the code repository increases in size. In addition, existing code-to-code recommendation engines fail to account for the global statistics of code repositories in the ranking function, such as the distribution of code snippet lengths, leading to sub-optimal retrieval results. We address both of these weaknesses with \emph{Senatus}, a new code-to-code recommendation engine. At the core of Senatus is \emph{De-Skew} LSH a new locality sensitive hashing (LSH) algorithm that indexes the data for fast (sub-linear time) retrieval while also counteracting the skewness in the snippet length distribution using novel abstract syntax tree-based feature scoring and selection algorithms. We evaluate Senatus and find the recommendations to be of higher quality than competing baselines, while achieving faster search. For example on the CodeSearchNet dataset Senatus improves performance by 31.21\% F1 and 147.9\emph{x} faster query time compared to Facebook Aroma. Senatus also outperforms standard MinHash LSH by 29.2\% F1 and 51.02\emph{x} faster query time.

title: Senatus -- A Fast and Accurate Code-to-Code Recommendation Engine
text: Code-to-code recommendation systems have emerged as a promising approach to alleviate the burden of manual code search and discovery, particularly in large-scale software development. Despite their potential, existing solutions suffer from either high computational complexity or limited recommendation accuracy, thereby hindering their adoption in real-world development settings. To bridge this gap, we introduce Senatus, a novel code-to-code recommendation engine that leverages a synergy of natural language processing, graph-based analysis, and deep learning techniques to provide fast and accurate recommendations. Senatus's core innovation lies in its ability to learn a joint representation of code snippets and their corresponding natural language descriptions, which enables effective matching between the two modalities. We employ a graph attention network to model the intricate relationships between code entities, and a hybrid ranking mechanism that incorporates both semantic and structural features to generate a relevance score for each recommendation. Extensive experiments on a large-scale dataset of open-source projects demonstrate the superiority of Senatus over state-of-the-art baselines, with an average improvement of 21.4% in terms of recall and 18.7% in terms of mean average precision. Moreover, Senatus achieves a significant reduction in inference latency, with an average response time of 230 milliseconds, making it amenable to real-time integration into integrated development environments. Our findings suggest that Senatus has the potential to transform the code discovery process, enabling developers to quickly identify relevant code snippets and improve their overall productivity.

title: Ontology-based question answering over corporate structured data
text: Ontology-based approach to the Natural Language Understanding (NLU) processing allows to improve questions answering quality in dialogue systems. We describe our NLU engine architecture and evaluate its implementation. The engine transforms user input into the SPARQL SELECT, ASK or INSERT query to the knowledge graph provided by the ontology-based data virtualization platform. The transformation is based on the lexical level of the knowledge graph built according to the Ontolex ontology. The described approach can be applied for graph data population tasks and to the question answering systems implementation, including chat bots. We describe the dialogue engine for a chat bot which can keep the conversation context and ask clarifying questions, simulating some aspects of the human logical thinking. Our approach uses graph-based algorithms to avoid gathering datasets, required in the neural nets-based approaches, and provide better explainability of our models. Using question answering engine in conjunction with data virtualization layer over the corporate data sources allows extracting facts from the structured data to be used in conversation.

title: Ontology-based question answering over corporate structured data
text: A knowledge graph-driven approach to Natural Language Understanding (NLU) enhances the accuracy of question answering in dialogue systems. We present a novel NLU engine architecture, which translates user input into SPARQL queries executable on an ontology-based data virtualization platform. This transformation leverages the lexical level of the knowledge graph, constructed in accordance with the Ontolex ontology. Our approach has broader implications for graph data population tasks and question answering systems, including chatbots. We also describe a dialogue engine capable of maintaining conversation context and posing clarifying questions, thereby simulating aspects of human logical reasoning. By employing graph-based algorithms, our method obviates the need for dataset gathering, inherent in neural network-based approaches, and provides greater model explainability. Furthermore, integrating the question answering engine with a data virtualization layer over corporate data sources enables the extraction of facts from structured data for use in conversation.

title: Time- and Space-Efficient Regular Path Queries on Graphs
text: We introduce a time- and space-efficient technique to solve regularpath queries over labeled graphs. We combine a bit-parallel simula-tion of the Glushkov automaton of the regular expression with thering index introduced by Arroyuelo et al., exploiting its wavelettree representation of the triples in order to efficiently reach thestates of the product graph that are relevant for the query. Ourquery algorithm is able to simultaneously process several automa-ton states, as well as several graph nodes/labels. Our experimentalresults show that our representation uses 3-5 times less space thanthe alternatives in the literature, while generally outperformingthem in query times (1.67 times faster than the next best).

title: Time- and Space-Efficient Regular Path Queries on Graphs
text: Regular path queries (RPQs) are essential in graph-based data management, but their evaluation can be computationally expensive. Existing solutions often sacrifice either time or space efficiency, hindering their applicability in real-world scenarios. We propose a novel approach that achieves a balance between both efficiency metrics.
