Our method leverages a compact graph encoding and a carefully designed query rewriting strategy to reduce the search space. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, yielding up to 3.5x speedup and 5x reduction in memory consumption. Our results have significant implications for scalable graph query processing in various domains, including social networks and knowledge graphs.

title: Safety Validation of Autonomous Vehicles using Assertion Checking
text: Safety and mission performance validation of autonomous vehicles (AVs) is a major challenge. In this paper we describe a methodology for constructing and applying assertion checks to validate the behaviour of an AV operating either in simulation or in the real world. We have identified a taxonomy of assertion types and the general format of their specification, and we have developed procedures for translating driving codes of practice to yield formal logical expressions that can be monitored automatically by computer, either by direct translation or by physical modelling. We have developed examples of assertions derived from the UK Highway Code (UKHC), as an example of a code of practice. We illustrate the approach with an example of assertion checking for vehicle overtaking, using a geospatial information system in an SQL database for validation and performance assessment. We present initial simulation and runtime monitoring experiments that apply assertions relevant in this overtaking scenario together with an analysis of the safety and mission performance characteristics measured.

title: Safety Validation of Autonomous Vehicles using Assertion Checking
text: The widespread adoption of autonomous vehicles (AVs) hinges on the assurance of their safety, which is compromised by the complexity of their software systems. Traditional testing methods are insufficient to exhaustively validate the safety of AVs, necessitating the development of formal verification techniques. This paper presents a novel approach to safety validation of AVs using assertion checking, a lightweight formal method. We define a set of safety assertions based on industry-recognized standards and regulations, and integrate them into the software development process of an AV system. We then employ a satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solver to automatically check these assertions against the system's behavior, modeled using a combination of finite state machines and linear temporal logic. Our experimental evaluation on a suite of benchmarks demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach in detecting safety violations, with an average reduction of 37% in false positives compared to traditional testing methods. Our results pave the way for the integration of formal methods into the development lifecycle of AVs, enhancing their safety and reliability.

title: CORE: a Complex Event Recognition Engine
text: Complex Event Recognition (CER) systems are a prominent technology for finding user-defined query patterns over large data streams in real time. CER query evaluation is known to be computationally challenging, since it requires maintaining a set of partial matches, and this set quickly grows super-linearly in the number of processed events. We present CORE, a novel COmplex event Recognition Engine that focuses on the efficient evaluation of a large class of complex event queries, including time windows as well as the partition-by event correlation operator. This engine uses a novel automaton-based evaluation algorithm that circumvents the super-linear partial match problem: under data complexity, it takes constant time per input event to maintain a data structure that compactly represents the set of partial matches and, once a match is found, the query results may be enumerated from the data structure with output-linear delay. We experimentally compare CORE against state-of-the-art CER systems on real-world data. We show that (1) CORE's performance is stable with respect to both query and time window size, and (2) CORE outperforms the other systems by up to five orders of magnitude on different workloads.

title: CORE: a Complex Event Recognition Engine
text: Real-time complex event recognition over large data streams is a challenging task, particularly when evaluating user-defined query patterns. The primary hurdle lies in maintaining a set of partial matches, which can grow super-linearly with the number of processed events, leading to computationally prohibitive query evaluation. To address this issue, we introduce CORE, a novel Complex Event Recognition Engine designed to efficiently evaluate a broad range of complex event queries, including those featuring time windows and the partition-by event correlation operator. Our engine employs an innovative automaton-based algorithm that overcomes the super-linear partial match problem by maintaining a compact data structure in constant time per input event, allowing for output-linear delay enumeration of query results upon match detection. Experimental comparisons with state-of-the-art CER systems using real-world data reveal that CORE exhibits stable performance with respect to query and time window size, outperforming existing systems by up to five orders of magnitude across diverse workloads.

title: Machine Learning-based Test Selection for Simulation-based Testing of Self-driving Cars Software
text: Abstract Simulation platforms facilitate the development of emerging cyber-physical systems (CPS) like self-driving cars (SDC) because they are more efficient and less dangerous than field operational tests. Despite this, thoroughly testing SDCs in simulated environments remains challenging because SDCs must be tested in a sheer amount of long-running test scenarios. Past results on software testing optimization have shown that not all the tests contribute equally to establishing confidence in test subjects' quality and reliability, with some \uninformative" tests that can be skipped (or removed) to reduce testing effort. However, this problem was partially addressed in the context of SDC simulation platforms. In this paper, we investigate test selection strategies to increase the cost-effectiveness of simulation-based testing in the context of SDCs. We propose an approach called SDC-Scissor (SDC coSt-effeCtIve teSt SelectOR), which leverages machine learning (ML) strategies to identify and skip tests that are unlikely to detect faults in SDCs before executing them. Specifically, SDC-Scissor extract features concerning the characteristics of the test scenarios being executed in the simulation environment and via ML strategies predict tests that lead to faults before executing them. Our evaluation shows that SDC-Scissor achieved high classification accuracy (up to 93.4%) in classifying tests leading to a fault which allows improving testing cost-effectiveness: SDC-Scissor was able to reduce (ca. 170%) the time spent in running irrelevant tests as well as identified 33% more failure triggering tests compared to a randomized baseline. Interestingly, SDC-Scissor does not introduce significant computational overhead in the SDCs testing process, which is critical to SDC development in industrial settings.

title: Machine Learning-based Test Selection for Simulation-based Testing of Self-driving Cars Software
text: Cyber-physical systems, such as self-driving cars, rely on simulation platforms for efficient and safe development. However, exhaustive testing in simulated environments remains a significant challenge due to the vast number of long-running test scenarios required. Prior research in software testing optimization has demonstrated that not all tests contribute equally to establishing confidence in the quality and reliability of test subjects, with some tests being "uninformative" and eligible for removal to reduce testing effort. While this issue has been partially addressed in the context of simulation platforms, test selection strategies for simulation-based testing in self-driving cars remain underexplored. This paper addresses this knowledge gap by proposing SDC-Scissor, an approach that leverages machine learning strategies to identify and skip tests unlikely to detect faults in self-driving cars before execution. By extracting features related to test scenario characteristics and predicting fault-inducing tests using machine learning, SDC-Scissor achieves high classification accuracy (up to 93.4%) and improves testing cost-effectiveness. Our evaluation shows that SDC-Scissor reduces the time spent on irrelevant tests by approximately 170% and identifies 33% more failure-triggering tests compared to a randomized baseline, without introducing significant computational overhead. This approach has critical implications for the development of self-driving cars in industrial settings, where testing efficiency and effectiveness are paramount.

title: D$^2$ABS: A Framework for Dynamic Dependence Abstraction of Distributed Programs
text: As modern software systems are increasingly developed for running in distributed environments, it is crucial to provide fundamental techniques such as dependence analysis for checking, diagnosing, and evolving those systems. However, traditional dependence analysis is either inapplicable or of very limited utility for distributed programs due to the decoupled components of these programs that run in concurrent processes at physically separated machines. Motivated by the need for dependence analysis of distributed software and the diverse cost-effectiveness needs of dependence-based applications, this paper presents D$^2$ABS, a framework of dynamic dependence abstraction for distributed programs. By partial-ordering distributed method-execution events and inferring causality from the ordered events, D$^2$ABS abstracts method-level dependencies both within and across process boundaries. Further, by exploiting message-passing semantics across processes, and incorporating static dependencies and statement coverage within individual components, we present three additional instantiations of D$^2$ABS that trade efficiency for better precision. We present the design of the D$^2$ABS framework and evaluate the four instantiations of D$^2$ABS on distributed systems of various architectures and scales using our implementation for Java. Our empirical results show that D$^2$ABS is significantly more effective than existing options while offering varied levels of cost-effectiveness tradeoffs. As our framework essentially computes whole-system run-time dependencies, it naturally empowers a range of other dependence-based applications.

title: D$^2$ABS: A Framework for Dynamic Dependence Abstraction of Distributed Programs
text: The complexity of distributed systems stems from intricate dependencies among components, making it challenging to reason about their behavior. Existing approaches to dependence analysis, although effective for sequential programs, fall short in capturing the dynamics of distributed systems, where dependencies are subject to frequent changes. To bridge this gap, we propose D$^2$ABS, a novel framework for dynamic dependence abstraction of distributed programs. Our approach leverages a combination of static analysis, runtime monitoring, and machine learning to construct a dependence graph that evolves with the system's execution. We formulate the dependence abstraction problem as a graph optimization task, where the goal is to minimize the graph's size while preserving the essential dependence relationships. Our evaluation on a suite of distributed benchmarks demonstrates that D$^2$ABS can effectively capture dynamic dependencies, achieving an average precision of 93.5% and recall of 91.2%. We further show that our framework can significantly improve the performance of distributed debugging tools, reducing the average debugging time by 35.7%. The D$^2$ABS framework has far-reaching implications for the development of more efficient and reliable distributed systems, enabling practitioners to better understand and optimize the complex interactions within these systems.

title: Structure-Behavior Coalescence Process Algebra -- Toward a Unified View of the System in Model-Based Systems Engineering
text: In Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE), the Systems Modeling Language (SysML) specification includes a metamodel that defines the language concepts and a user model that defines how the language concepts are represented. In SysML, an important use of metamodel is to provide an integrated semantic framework that every diagram in the user model can be projected as a view of the metamodel. However, most existing SysML metamodels lack such capability of being a basis for unification of different views of a system. To overcome the shortcomings of the current SysML metamodel approaches, we developed Channel-Based Multi-Queue Structure-Behavior Coalescence Process Algebra (C-M-SBC-PA), which provides an integrated semantic framework that is able to integrate structural constructs with behavioral constructs. Using C-M-SBC-PA as the metamodel of SysML, each diagram in the user model can be projected as a view of the C-M-SBC-PA metamodel.

title: Structure-Behavior Coalescence Process Algebra -- Toward a Unified View of the System in Model-Based Systems Engineering
text: Model-based systems engineering (MBSE) has become a cornerstone of modern systems design, relying on the explicit representation of system structure and behavior. However, existing approaches often treat these aspects separately, leading to inconsistencies and fragmentation. This paper proposes a novel process algebra, Structure-Behavior Coalescence (SBC), which integrates the structural and behavioral facets of systems into a unified framework. SBC combines the strengths of algebraic process calculi and graph theory to provide a rigorous, compositional formalism for modeling and analyzing complex systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SBC through a series of case studies, showcasing its ability to capture subtle interactions and emergent behavior in diverse domains, including autonomous vehicles and smart grids. Our results indicate that SBC can significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of MBSE, facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of system dynamics and behavior.

title: Building an AI-ready RSE Workforce
text: Artificial Intelligence has been transforming industries and academic research across the globe, and research software development is no exception. Machine learning and deep learning are being applied in every aspect of the research software development lifecycles, from new algorithm design paradigms to software development processes. In this paper, we discuss our views on today's challenges and opportunities that AI has presented on research software development and engineers, and the approaches we, at the University of Florida, are taking to prepare our workforce for the new era of AI.

title: Building an AI-ready RSE Workforce
text: The increasing adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) in software development necessitates a workforce with interdisciplinary skills. Research Software Engineers (RSEs) play a crucial role in this landscape, but their AI-readiness remains a concern. This study investigates the development of an AI-ready RSE workforce through a mixed-methods approach, combining surveys, interviews, and skill assessments. Our results show that RSEs require targeted training in AI/ML fundamentals, data science, and collaboration tools, with a significant emphasis on domain-specific knowledge and continuous professional development.

title: An Empirical Study of Automated Unit Test Generation for Python
text: Various mature automated test generation tools exist for statically typed programming languages such as Java. Automatically generating unit tests for dynamically typed programming languages such as Python, however, is substantially more difficult due to the dynamic nature of these languages as well as the lack of type information. Our Pynguin framework provides automated unit test generation for Python. In this paper, we extend our previous work on Pynguin to support more aspects of the Python language, and by studying a larger variety of well-established state of the art test-generation algorithms, namely DynaMOSA, MIO, and MOSA. Furthermore, we improved our Pynguin tool to generate regression assertions, whose quality we also evaluate. Our experiments confirm that evolutionary algorithms can outperform random test generation also in the context of Python, and similar to the Java world, DynaMOSA yields the highest coverage results. However, our results also demonstrate that there are still fundamental remaining issues, such as inferring type information for code without this information, currently limiting the effectiveness of test generation for Python.

title: An Empirical Study of Automated Unit Test Generation for Python
text: Automated unit test generation has garnered significant attention in recent years as a means to alleviate the burden of manual testing and improve software quality. Despite the abundance of existing approaches, the effectiveness of these techniques in real-world settings remains largely unexplored. This study empirically investigates the efficacy of automated unit test generation for Python, a popular programming language with a large and active developer community. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of three state-of-the-art tools – Pynguin, Randoop, and EvoSuite – on a curated dataset of 150 open-source Python projects. Our analysis reveals that while these tools can generate tests with high code coverage, they often struggle to produce meaningful assertions, resulting in tests with limited fault-detection capabilities. Moreover, we find that the quality of generated tests varies significantly across projects, with factors such as code complexity and project size influencing tool performance. Our findings have important implications for the development of more effective automated testing strategies and highlight the need for further research into the challenges and opportunities of applying these techniques in real-world software development.

title: BreakBot: Analyzing the Impact of Breaking Changes to Assist Library Evolution
text: If we make this change to our code, how will it impact our clients?" It is difficult for library maintainers to answer this simple-yet essential!-question when evolving their libraries. Library maintainers are constantly balancing between two opposing positions: make changes at the risk of breaking some of their clients, or avoid changes and maintain compatibility at the cost of immobility and growing technical debt. We argue that the lack of objective usage data and tool support leaves maintainers with their own subjective perception of their community to make these decisions. We introduce BreakBot, a bot that analyses the pull requests of Java libraries on GitHub to identify the breaking changes they introduce and their impact on client projects. Through static analysis of libraries and clients, it extracts and summarizes objective data that enrich the code review process by providing maintainers with the appropriate information to decide whether-and how-changes should be accepted, directly in the pull requests.

title: BreakBot: Analyzing the Impact of Breaking Changes to Assist Library Evolution
text: Software libraries are essential components of modern software systems, but their evolution is often hindered by breaking changes that affect dependent projects. To mitigate this issue, library maintainers need to carefully consider the impact of such changes, which is a time-consuming and error-prone task. This paper presents BreakBot, a novel approach to analyzing the impact of breaking changes on dependent projects. BreakBot combines static analysis, repository mining, and machine learning techniques to identify, quantify, and prioritize breaking changes. We evaluate BreakBot on a dataset of 150 popular Java libraries and 10,000 dependent projects, demonstrating its ability to accurately predict the likelihood and severity of breaking changes. Our results show that BreakBot can reduce the time spent on breaking change analysis by 75% while maintaining a high accuracy of 92%. Furthermore, we observe that the majority of breaking changes (80%) affect only a small subset of dependent projects, suggesting that targeted communication and testing strategies can be employed to minimize the disruption caused by library evolution.

title: Test cases as a measurement instrument in experimentation
text: Background: Test suites are frequently used to quantify relevant software attributes, such as quality or productivity. Problem: We have detected that the same response variable, measured using different test suites, yields different experiment results. Aims: Assess to which extent differences in test case construction influence measurement accuracy and experimental outcomes. Method: Two industry experiments have been measured using two different test suites, one generated using an ad-hoc method and another using equivalence partitioning. The accuracy of the measures has been studied using standard procedures, such as ISO 5725, Bland-Altman and Interclass Correlation Coefficients. Results: There are differences in the values of the response variables up to +-60%, depending on the test suite (ad-hoc vs. equivalence partitioning) used. Conclusions: The disclosure of datasets and analysis code is insufficient to ensure the reproducibility of SE experiments. Experimenters should disclose all experimental materials needed to perform independent measurement and re-analysis.

title: Test cases as a measurement instrument in experimentation
text: The development of software systems relies heavily on experimentation, yet the measurement instruments used in these experiments are often overlooked. Test cases, a crucial component of software testing, have the potential to serve as a measurement instrument, but their validity and reliability in this context are unknown. This study investigates the use of test cases as a measurement instrument in experimentation, focusing on their ability to capture the effectiveness of software engineering techniques. We conducted a series of controlled experiments, involving 240 participants, to assess the validity and reliability of test cases in measuring the performance of three distinct software development methods. Our results show that test cases can be a reliable measurement instrument, with a high degree of correlation between test case outcomes and expert evaluations. However, our findings also highlight the importance of considering the characteristics of the test cases, such as their complexity and coverage, to ensure their validity.

title: Stateful Dynamic Partial Order Reduction for Model Checking Event-Driven Applications that Do Not Terminate
text: Event-driven architectures are broadly used for systems that must respond to events in the real world. Event-driven applications are prone to concurrency bugs that involve subtle errors in reasoning about the ordering of events. Unfortunately, there are several challenges in using existing model-checking techniques on these systems. Event-driven applications often loop indefinitely and thus pose a challenge for stateless model checking techniques. On the other hand, deploying purely stateful model checking can explore large sets of equivalent executions. In this work, we explore a new technique that combines dynamic partial order reduction with stateful model checking to support non-terminating applications. Our work is (1) the first dynamic partial order reduction algorithm for stateful model checking that is sound for non-terminating applications and (2) the first dynamic partial reduction algorithm for stateful model checking of event-driven applications. We experimented with the IoTCheck dataset: a study of interactions in smart home app pairs. This dataset consists of app pairs originated from 198 real-world smart home apps. Overall, our DPOR algorithm successfully reduced the search space for the app pairs, enabling 69 pairs of apps that did not finish without DPOR to finish and providing a 7X average speedup.

title: Stateful Dynamic Partial Order Reduction for Model Checking Event-Driven Applications that Do Not Terminate
text: Model checking event-driven applications is a crucial task, especially when dealing with non-terminating systems. However, the state explosion problem inherent to model checking hinders its applicability to real-world systems. Partial order reduction (POR) is a well-established technique to mitigate this issue by exploiting the independence of concurrent transitions. Nevertheless, existing POR methods are limited to terminating systems or require additional annotations, which can be cumbersome to provide. This work presents a novel stateful dynamic POR approach tailored to model checking non-terminating event-driven applications. Our method leverages the dynamic nature of event-driven systems to construct a partial order on the fly, eliminating the need for manual annotations. We formulate the POR problem as a constraint satisfaction problem and employ a SMT solver to efficiently compute the partial order. Experimental results on a range of benchmarks demonstrate a significant reduction in the number of explored states, with an average reduction of 75%, compared to traditional model checking. Furthermore, our approach is able to verify the correctness of non-terminating systems, which is beyond the capabilities of existing POR methods. This work paves the way for the model checking of complex, real-world event-driven systems that do not terminate.

title: An adaptive 3D virtual learning environment for training software developers in scrum
text: Scrum is one of the most used frameworks for agile software development because of its potential improvements in productivity, quality, and client satisfaction. Academia has also focussed on teaching Scrum practices to prepare students to face common software engineering challenges and facilitate their insertion in professional contexts. Furthermore, advances in learning technologies currently offer many virtual learning environments to enhance learning in many ways. Their capability to consider the individual learner preferences has led a shift to more personalised training approaches, requiring that the environments adapt themselves to the learner. We propose an adaptive approach for training developers in Scrum, including an adaptive virtual learning environment based on Felder's learning style theory. Although still preliminary, our findings show that students who used the environment and received instruction matching their preferences obtained sightly higher learning gains than students who received a different instruction than the one they preferred. We also noticed less variability in the learning gains of students who received instruction matching their preferences. The relevance of this work goes beyond the impact on learning gains since it describes how adaptive virtual learning environments can be used in the domain of Software Engineering.

title: An adaptive 3D virtual learning environment for training software developers in scrum
text: Scrum, a widely adopted agile framework, requires software developers to possess specific skills and competencies to collaborate effectively. Despite its popularity, traditional instructor-led training methods often struggle to provide immersive and interactive experiences, leading to inadequate preparedness in real-world scenarios. To address this gap, we designed and developed an adaptive 3D virtual learning environment (VLE) that simulates real-world Scrum projects, allowing developers to practice and refine their skills in a controlled setting. Our VLE leverages cognitive architectures to model individual learners' knowledge, skills, and attitudes, and adapts the learning experience accordingly. We conducted a controlled experiment with 120 software developers, randomly assigned to either the adaptive VLE or a traditional instructional method. Results show that participants in the adaptive VLE group demonstrated significant improvements in Scrum-specific knowledge (p < 0.01) and collaboration skills (p < 0.05) compared to the control group. Furthermore, the adaptive VLE group reported higher levels of engagement and satisfaction (p < 0.001). Our findings suggest that adaptive 3D virtual learning environments can be an effective tool for training software developers in Scrum, and have implications for the design of future training programs in software engineering education.

title: Statistical Perspectives on Reliability of Artificial Intelligence Systems
text: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems have become increasingly popular in many areas. Nevertheless, AI technologies are still in their developing stages, and many issues need to be addressed. Among those, the reliability of AI systems needs to be demonstrated so that the AI systems can be used with confidence by the general public. In this paper, we provide statistical perspectives on the reliability of AI systems. Different from other considerations, the reliability of AI systems focuses on the time dimension. That is, the system can perform its designed functionality for the intended period. We introduce a so-called SMART statistical framework for AI reliability research, which includes five components: Structure of the system, Metrics of reliability, Analysis of failure causes, Reliability assessment, and Test planning. We review traditional methods in reliability data analysis and software reliability, and discuss how those existing methods can be transformed for reliability modeling and assessment of AI systems. We also describe recent developments in modeling and analysis of AI reliability and outline statistical research challenges in this area, including out-of-distribution detection, the effect of the training set, adversarial attacks, model accuracy, and uncertainty quantification, and discuss how those topics can be related to AI reliability, with illustrative examples. Finally, we discuss data collection and test planning for AI reliability assessment and how to improve system designs for higher AI reliability. The paper closes with some concluding remarks.

title: Statistical Perspectives on Reliability of Artificial Intelligence Systems
text: The pervasive adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) systems across various domains has been accompanied by growing concerns regarding their reliability. As AI technologies continue to evolve, it is essential to establish their dependability to foster public trust and confidence. This paper presents a statistical perspective on AI reliability, emphasizing the temporal dimension, wherein a system's performance is evaluated over its intended operational period. We propose the SMART framework, a structured approach comprising five interconnected components: system structure, reliability metrics, failure cause analysis, reliability assessment, and test planning. A comprehensive review of traditional reliability data analysis and software reliability methods is undertaken, highlighting their applicability to AI reliability modeling and assessment. Recent advances in AI reliability modeling and analysis are discussed, alongside the identification of key statistical research challenges, including out-of-distribution detection, training set effects, adversarial attacks, model accuracy, and uncertainty quantification. The interplay between these topics and AI reliability is elucidated through illustrative examples. Furthermore, we explore data collection strategies and test planning for AI reliability evaluation, as well as design optimization techniques to enhance AI system reliability. The paper concludes with a summary of its key findings and implications.

title: Verifying Controllers with Convolutional Neural Network-based Perception: A Case for Intelligible, Safe, and Precise Abstractions
text: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) for object detection, lane detection, and segmentation now sit at the head of most autonomy pipelines, and yet, their safety analysis remains an important challenge. Formal analysis of perception models is fundamentally difficult because their correctness is hard if not impossible to specify. We present a technique for inferring intelligible and safe abstractions for perception models from system-level safety requirements, data, and program analysis of the modules that are downstream from perception. The technique can help tradeoff safety, size, and precision, in creating abstractions and the subsequent verification. We apply the method to two significant case studies based on high-fidelity simulations (a) a vision-based lane keeping controller for an autonomous vehicle and (b) a controller for an agricultural robot. We show how the generated abstractions can be composed with the downstream modules and then the resulting abstract system can be verified using program analysis tools like CBMC. Detailed evaluations of the impacts of size, safety requirements, and the environmental parameters (e.g., lighting, road surface, plant type) on the precision of the generated abstractions suggest that the approach can help guide the search for corner cases and safe operating envelops.

title: Verifying Controllers with Convolutional Neural Network-based Perception: A Case for Intelligible, Safe, and Precise Abstractions
text: The pervasive adoption of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in autonomy pipelines for object detection, lane detection, and segmentation has underscored the imperative of ensuring their safety. However, the formal analysis of these perception models poses significant challenges, primarily due to the difficulty in specifying their correctness. This paper presents a novel approach to derive intelligible and safe abstractions for perception models by integrating system-level safety requirements, data, and program analysis of downstream modules. This technique facilitates the tradeoff between safety, size, and precision in abstraction creation and subsequent verification. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through two comprehensive case studies, involving high-fidelity simulations of a vision-based lane keeping controller for an autonomous vehicle and a controller for an agricultural robot. Our results show that the generated abstractions can be seamlessly composed with downstream modules, enabling the verification of the abstract system using tools like CBMC. Furthermore, our evaluations reveal the impact of size, safety requirements, and environmental parameters (such as lighting, road surface, and plant type) on abstraction precision, thereby informing the search for corner cases and safe operating envelopes.

title: A Comprehensive Evaluation of Android ICC Resolution Techniques
text: Inter-component communication (ICC) is a widely used mechanism in mobile apps, which enables message-based control flow transferring and data passing between Android components. Effective ICC resolution requires precisely identifying entry points, analyzing data values of ICC fields, modeling related framework APIs, etc. Due to various control-flow- and data-flow-related characteristics involved and the lack of oracles for real-world apps, the comprehensive evaluation of ICC resolution techniques is challenging. To fill this gap, we collect multiple-type benchmark suites with 4,104 apps, covering hand-made apps, open-source, and commercial ones. Considering their differences, various evaluation metrics, e.g., number count, graph structure, and reliable oracle based metrics, are adopted on-demand. As the oracle for real-world apps is unavailable, we design a dynamic analysis approach to extract the real ICC links triggered during GUI exploration. By auditing the code implementations, we carefully check the extracted ICCs and confirm 1,680 ones to form a reliable oracle set, in which each ICC is labeled with 25 code characteristic tags. The evaluation performed on six state-of-the-art ICC resolution tools shows that 1) the completeness of static ICC resolution results on real-world apps is not satisfactory, as up to 38%-85% ICCs are missed by tools; 2) many wrongly reported ICCs are sent from or received by only a few components and the graph structure information can help the identification; 3) the efficiency of fundamental tools, like ICC resolution ones, should be optimized in both engineering and research aspects. By investigating both the missed and wrongly reported ICCs, we discuss the strengths of different tools for users and summarize eight common FN/FP patterns in ICC resolution for tool developers.

title: A Comprehensive Evaluation of Android ICC Resolution Techniques
text: Android's Inter-Component Communication (ICC) mechanism enables interaction between applications, but its complexity often leads to security vulnerabilities and performance issues. Resolving ICC calls is crucial for effective Android app analysis, but existing techniques exhibit limitations in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and scalability. To address these challenges, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art ICC resolution techniques, encompassing both static and dynamic analysis approaches. Our assessment framework, ICC-Evaluator, incorporates a dataset of 10,000 ICC calls extracted from 500 popular Android apps, covering diverse categories and API levels. We evaluate nine prominent ICC resolution techniques, including FlowDroid, IccTA, and Amandroid, using a combination of quantitative and qualitative metrics. Our results reveal that no single technique consistently outperforms others across all evaluation criteria. While static analysis techniques like IccTA excel in terms of efficiency, they often suffer from low accuracy due to inadequate handling of complex ICC scenarios. In contrast, dynamic analysis approaches like FlowDroid provide higher accuracy but incur significant performance overhead. We identify several key factors influencing ICC resolution effectiveness, including ICC call complexity, API level, and app category. Our findings have important implications for Android app analysis, highlighting the need for hybrid approaches that balance accuracy, efficiency, and scalability. We make our ICC-Evaluator framework and dataset publicly available to facilitate future research in this area.

title: Counterfactual Explanations for Models of Code
text: Machine learning (ML) models play an increasingly prevalent role in many software engineering tasks. However, because most models are now powered by opaque deep neural networks, it can be difficult for developers to understand why the model came to a certain conclusion and how to act upon the model's prediction. Motivated by this problem, this paper explores counterfactual explanations for models of source code. Such counterfactual explanations constitute minimal changes to the source code under which the model "changes its mind". We integrate counterfactual explanation generation to models of source code in a real-world setting. We describe considerations that impact both the ability to find realistic and plausible counterfactual explanations, as well as the usefulness of such explanation to the user of the model. In a series of experiments we investigate the efficacy of our approach on three different models, each based on a BERT-like architecture operating over source code.

title: Counterfactual Explanations for Models of Code
text: The pervasive adoption of machine learning (ML) models in software engineering tasks has introduced a pressing need for transparency in model decision-making. As deep neural networks underlie most models, understanding the rationale behind their predictions and informing subsequent actions remain significant challenges. This paper addresses this issue by exploring counterfactual explanations for source code models, which involve identifying minimal code modifications that alter the model's output. We incorporate counterfactual explanation generation into real-world source code models, highlighting key considerations that influence the discovery of realistic and plausible explanations, as well as their utility for model users. Through a series of experiments, we evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on three BERT-like models operating on source code, providing insights into the potential of counterfactual explanations to facilitate more informed model-driven decision-making.

title: Towards More Reliable Automated Program Repair by Integrating Static Analysis Techniques
text: A long-standing open challenge for automated program repair is the overfitting problem, which is caused by having insufficient or incomplete specifications to validate whether a generated patch is correct or not. Most available repair systems rely on weak specifications (i.e., specifications that are synthesized from test cases) which limits the quality of generated repairs. To strengthen specifications and improve the quality of repairs, we propose to closer integrate static bug detection techniques with automated program repair. The integration combines automated program repair with static analysis techniques in such a way that bug detection patterns can be synthesized into specifications that the repair system can use. We explore the feasibility of such integration using two types of bugs: arithmetic bugs, such as integer overflow, and logical bugs, such as termination bugs. As part of our analysis, we make several observations that help to improve patch generation for these classes of bugs. Moreover, these observations assist with narrowing down the candidate patch search space, and inferring an effective search order.

title: Towards More Reliable Automated Program Repair by Integrating Static Analysis Techniques
text: The automated program repair community has long grappled with the overfitting problem, which arises from the scarcity of comprehensive specifications to validate the correctness of generated patches. The prevalent reliance on weak specifications, typically synthesized from test cases, compromises the quality of repairs. To address this limitation, we propose a novel integration of static bug detection techniques with automated program repair. By combining these approaches, we can synthesize bug detection patterns into specifications that inform the repair process. We investigate the efficacy of this integration in the context of two bug categories: arithmetic bugs, including integer overflow, and logical bugs, such as termination bugs. Our analysis yields several key insights that enhance patch generation for these bug classes, while also facilitating the pruning of the candidate patch search space and the inference of an effective search order.

title: Symbolic Security Predicates: Hunt Program Weaknesses
text: Dynamic symbolic execution (DSE) is a powerful method for path exploration during hybrid fuzzing and automatic bug detection. We propose security predicates to effectively detect undefined behavior and memory access violation errors. Initially, we symbolically execute program on paths that don't trigger any errors (hybrid fuzzing may explore these paths). Then we construct a symbolic security predicate to verify some error condition. Thus, we may change the program data flow to entail null pointer dereference, division by zero, out-of-bounds access, or integer overflow weaknesses. Unlike static analysis, dynamic symbolic execution does not only report errors but also generates new input data to reproduce them. Furthermore, we introduce function semantics modeling for common C/C++ standard library functions. We aim to model the control flow inside a function with a single symbolic formula. This assists bug detection, speeds up path exploration, and overcomes overconstraints in path predicate. We implement the proposed techniques in our dynamic symbolic execution tool Sydr. Thus, we utilize powerful methods from Sydr such as path predicate slicing that eliminates irrelevant constraints. We present Juliet Dynamic to measure dynamic bug detection tools accuracy. The testing system also verifies that generated inputs trigger sanitizers. We evaluate Sydr accuracy for 11 CWEs from Juliet test suite. Sydr shows 95.59% overall accuracy. We make Sydr evaluation artifacts publicly available to facilitate results reproducibility.

title: Symbolic Security Predicates: Hunt Program Weaknesses
text: The discovery of security vulnerabilities in software programs remains a pressing concern, as exploits can have devastating consequences. While recent advances in symbolic execution have improved the efficiency of vulnerability detection, existing approaches often rely on simplistic error detection mechanisms, neglecting the rich semantic information present in program code. This oversight leads to a high rate of false positives and negatives, hampering the effectiveness of security auditing tools. To address this limitation, we introduce Symbolic Security Predicates (SSPs), a novel framework that integrates symbolic execution with precise, logic-based security specifications. SSPs enable the formulation of expressive security properties, capturing subtle program behaviors and data dependencies that are crucial for identifying vulnerabilities. Our approach leverages a combination of abstract interpretation, model checking, and SMT solving to systematically explore the program's symbolic state space and validate SSPs. We evaluate our framework on a suite of real-world programs, demonstrating its ability to detect previously unknown vulnerabilities and significantly reduce the number of false alarms. Notably, SSPs uncover novel attack vectors in the OpenSSL library, highlighting the importance of integrating semantic security specifications into vulnerability detection tools. Our work paves the way for the development of more accurate and efficient security auditing frameworks, ultimately enhancing the resilience of software systems.

title: MAJORCA: Multi-Architecture JOP and ROP Chain Assembler
text: Nowadays, exploits often rely on a code-reuse approach. Short pieces of code called gadgets are chained together to execute some payload. Code-reuse attacks can exploit vulnerabilities in the presence of operating system protection that prohibits data memory execution. The ROP chain construction task is the code generation for the virtual machine defined by an exploited executable. It is crucial to understand how powerful ROP attacks can be. Such knowledge can be used to improve software security. We implement MAJORCA that generates ROP and JOP payloads in an architecture agnostic manner and thoroughly consider restricted symbols such as null bytes that terminate data copying via strcpy. The paper covers the whole code-reuse payloads construction pipeline: cataloging gadgets, chaining them in DAG, scheduling, linearizing to the ready-to-run payload. MAJORCA automatically generates both ROP and JOP payloads for x86 and MIPS. MAJORCA constructs payloads respecting restricted symbols both in gadget addresses and data. We evaluate MAJORCA performance and accuracy with rop-benchmark and compare it with open-source compilers. We show that MAJORCA outperforms open-source tools. We propose a ROP chaining metric and use it to estimate the probabilities of successful ROP chaining for different operating systems with MAJORCA as well as other ROP compilers to show that ROP chaining is still feasible. This metric can estimate the efficiency of OS defences.

title: MAJORCA: Multi-Architecture JOP and ROP Chain Assembler
text: The growing complexity of modern software and the increasing sophistication of attackers have made it challenging to develop effective defenses against code reuse attacks, which exploit vulnerabilities in software by chaining together short snippets of code, known as gadgets. While several defenses have been proposed to mitigate these attacks, they often rely on assumptions about the underlying architecture or are limited to specific types of gadgets. To address these limitations, we present MAJORCA, a novel framework for assembling multi-architecture JOP (Jump-Oriented Programming) and ROP (Return-Oriented Programming) chains. MAJORCA uses a combination of static analysis, symbolic execution, and constraint solving to identify and compose gadgets across multiple architectures, including x86, ARM, and MIPS. Our evaluation shows that MAJORCA can successfully assemble JOP and ROP chains for a range of real-world exploits, including those that target multiple architectures. Furthermore, we demonstrate that MAJORCA can be used to improve the effectiveness of existing defenses, such as address space layout randomization (ASLR), by identifying and mitigating potential gadget chains. Overall, MAJORCA provides a powerful tool for understanding and defending against code reuse attacks, and has important implications for the development of more secure software systems.

title: Data-Driven AI Model Signal-Awareness Enhancement and Introspection
text: AI modeling for source code understanding tasks has been making significant progress, and is being adopted in production development pipelines. However, reliability concerns, especially whether the models are actually learning task-related aspects of source code, are being raised. While recent model-probing approaches have observed a lack of signal awareness in many AI-for-code models, i.e. models not capturing task-relevant signals, they do not offer solutions to rectify this problem. In this paper, we explore data-driven approaches to enhance models' signal-awareness: 1) we combine the SE concept of code complexity with the AI technique of curriculum learning; 2) we incorporate SE assistance into AI models by customizing Delta Debugging to generate simplified signal-preserving programs, augmenting them to the training dataset. With our techniques, we achieve up to 4.8x improvement in model signal awareness. Using the notion of code complexity, we further present a novel model learning introspection approach from the perspective of the dataset.

title: Data-Driven AI Model Signal-Awareness Enhancement and Introspection
text: The advent of AI modeling in source code understanding has sparked significant interest, with its integration into production development pipelines. Nevertheless, concerns regarding the reliability of these models persist, particularly with respect to their ability to capture task-relevant aspects of source code. Recent probing approaches have revealed a lack of signal awareness in many AI-for-code models, but fallen short of providing remedies to address this limitation. This paper presents a data-driven framework to enhance signal awareness in AI models, combining software engineering (SE) concepts with AI techniques. Specifically, we leverage code complexity and curriculum learning to improve model performance, and incorporate SE assistance through customized Delta Debugging to generate simplified signal-preserving programs, augmenting the training dataset. Our approach yields up to 4.8x improvement in model signal awareness, and facilitates a novel introspection approach to model learning from a dataset perspective, informed by code complexity metrics.

title: What Does the Post-Moore Era Mean for Research Software Engineering?
text: We are entering the post-Moore era where we no longer enjoy the free ride of the performance growth from simply shrinking the transistor features. However, this does not necessarily mean that we are entering a dark era of computing. On the contrary, sustaining the performance growth of computing in the post-Moore era itself is cutting-edge research. Concretely, heterogeneity and hardware specialization are becoming promising approaches in hardware designs. However, these are paradigm shifts in computer architecture. So what does the post-Moore era mean for research software engineering? This position paper addresses such a question by summarizing possible challenges and opportunities for research software engineering in the post-Moore era. We then briefly discuss what is missing and how we prepare to tackle such challenges and exploit opportunities for the future of computing.

title: What Does the Post-Moore Era Mean for Research Software Engineering?
text: As the semiconductor industry transitions into the post-Moore era, characterized by diminishing returns on transistor density and increasing heterogeneity in computing architectures, research software engineering (RSE) faces unprecedented challenges. To understand the implications of this paradigm shift, we conducted a mixed-methods study combining surveys, interviews, and case studies of 15 RSE teams from top-tier institutions. Our results show that the post-Moore era exacerbates existing RSE pain points, such as performance optimization, portability, and maintainability, while introducing new concerns related to hardware-aware software design and resource allocation. We identify a pressing need for novel software engineering methodologies, tools, and expertise to effectively harness emerging heterogeneous architectures. Our findings inform a research agenda for RSE in the post-Moore era, highlighting the importance of co-design, domain-specific languages, and community-driven infrastructure development.

title: SyzScope: Revealing High-Risk Security Impacts of Fuzzer-Exposed Bugs in Linux kernel
text: Fuzzing has become one of the most effective bug finding approach for software. In recent years, 24*7 continuous fuzzing platforms have emerged to test critical pieces of software, e.g., Linux kernel. Though capable of discovering many bugs and providing reproducers (e.g., proof-of-concepts), a major problem is that they neglect a critical function that should have been built-in, i.e., evaluation of a bug's security impact. It is well-known that the lack of understanding of security impact can lead to delayed bug fixes as well as patch propagation. In this paper, we develop SyzScope, a system that can automatically uncover new "high-risk" impacts given a bug with seemingly "low-risk" impacts. From analyzing over a thousand low-risk bugs on syzbot, SyzScope successfully determined that 183 low-risk bugs (more than 15%) in fact contain high-risk impacts, e.g., control flow hijack and arbitrary memory write, some of which still do not have patches available yet.

title: SyzScope: Revealing High-Risk Security Impacts of Fuzzer-Exposed Bugs in Linux kernel
text: The widespread adoption of fuzzing as a bug detection approach has led to the development of continuous fuzzing platforms, which have proven instrumental in testing critical software components, such as the Linux kernel. While these platforms have successfully identified numerous bugs and provided reproducible proof-of-concepts, a significant limitation is their failure to incorporate a crucial functionality: assessing the security implications of discovered bugs. This oversight can result in delayed bug fixes and patch propagation, as the lack of understanding of security impact can hinder remediation efforts. To address this shortcoming, we present SyzScope, a system capable of automatically uncovering high-risk security implications from seemingly low-risk bugs. Our analysis of over a thousand low-risk bugs on syzbot reveals that 183 (more than 15%) actually possess high-risk impacts, including control flow hijacking and arbitrary memory writes, with some remaining unpatched to date.

title: A Chinese Multi-type Complex Questions Answering Dataset over Wikidata
text: Complex Knowledge Base Question Answering is a popular area of research in the past decade. Recent public datasets have led to encouraging results in this field, but are mostly limited to English and only involve a small number of question types and relations, hindering research in more realistic settings and in languages other than English. In addition, few state-of-the-art KBQA models are trained on Wikidata, one of the most popular real-world knowledge bases. We propose CLC-QuAD, the first large scale complex Chinese semantic parsing dataset over Wikidata to address these challenges. Together with the dataset, we present a text-to-SPARQL baseline model, which can effectively answer multi-type complex questions, such as factual questions, dual intent questions, boolean questions, and counting questions, with Wikidata as the background knowledge. We finally analyze the performance of SOTA KBQA models on this dataset and identify the challenges facing Chinese KBQA.

title: A Chinese Multi-type Complex Questions Answering Dataset over Wikidata
text: The proliferation of knowledge base question answering (KBQA) research in recent years has been hindered by the limitations of publicly available datasets, which are predominantly English-centric and restricted to a narrow range of question types and relations. This constraint impedes the exploration of more realistic scenarios and multilingual KBQA. Furthermore, the majority of state-of-the-art KBQA models have not been trained on Wikidata, a prominent real-world knowledge base. To address these gaps, we introduce CLC-QuAD, a large-scale complex Chinese semantic parsing dataset built upon Wikidata. Accompanying the dataset is a text-to-SPARQL baseline model, capable of handling diverse complex question types, including factual, dual intent, boolean, and counting questions. Our empirical analysis of state-of-the-art KBQA models on CLC-QuAD reveals the challenges inherent to Chinese KBQA, providing valuable insights for future research.

title: Agile Information System Development Organizations Transforming to Large-Scale Collaboration
text: We report findings from a case study of a large agile information systems development (ISD) organization`s sudden transformation to distributed, digital work in the context of the Covid-19 pandemic. It seeks to understand how knowledge creation and sharing changes. The findings show various forms of distance being introduced, digital tool usage, increased task orientation, and variations across teams. To analyze the findings, we use the concepts of large-scale collaborations and sociability. Large-scale collaboration offers a socio-technical perspective on tackling distributed knowledge sharing and creation in the presence of multiple, loosely coupled partners using digital tools for collaboration. We show what the digital tools afford using the concept of sociability. We discuss how distributed digital practices make teams more task-oriented and that creating and maintaining sociability, a key issue for knowledge sharing in agile ISD organizations, require relation oriented communication during practical problem solving using digital tools.

title: Agile Information System Development Organizations Transforming to Large-Scale Collaboration
text: This case study examines the abrupt transition to distributed, digital work in a large agile information systems development organization amidst the Covid-19 pandemic, focusing on the ensuing changes in knowledge creation and sharing. The findings reveal the emergence of various forms of distance, increased reliance on digital tools, and a heightened task orientation, with notable variations across teams. Through the lens of large-scale collaborations and sociability, we analyze these findings, highlighting the socio-technical challenges of distributed knowledge sharing and creation in multi-partner settings. Our results illustrate how digital tools afford new opportunities for collaboration, yet simultaneously underscore the importance of relation-oriented communication in fostering sociability, a crucial factor in facilitating knowledge sharing within agile ISD organizations.

title: Developing and Publishing Code for Trusted Research Environments: Best Practices and Ways of Working
text: This report discusses 3 distinct, but overlapping topics. Firstly, it recommends the tools and best practices for research software engineering and data science that are most relevant to the researchers working on the Wales Multimorbidity Machine Learning (WMML) project. Secondly, it expands upon these recommendations for the specific use case of Trusted Research Environments (TREs), with development workflows for computational research in TREs offered that respect and complement existing best practices. Finally, it discusses the considerations around publishing research code that is developed to run within a TRE on sensitive data, offering practical advice that researchers using TREs can follow.

title: Developing and Publishing Code for Trusted Research Environments: Best Practices and Ways of Working
text: This study converges on three interconnected themes pertinent to the Wales Multimorbidity Machine Learning project. We distill the most relevant tools and best practices for research software engineering and data science, providing actionable guidance for WMML researchers. Furthermore, we adapt these recommendations to accommodate the unique requirements of Trusted Research Environments, outlining development workflows that harmonize with existing best practices. Lastly, we delve into the nuances of publishing research code developed for sensitive data within TREs, offering pragmatic advice to facilitate responsible knowledge sharing among TRE-based researchers.

title: Open Data Fabric: A Decentralized Data Exchange and Transformation Protocol With Complete Reproducibility and Provenance
text: Data is the most powerful decision-making tool at our disposal. However, despite the exponentially growing volumes of data generated in the world, putting it to effective use still presents many challenges. Relevant data seems to be never there when it is needed - it remains siloed, hard to find, hard to access, outdated, and of bad quality. As a result, governments, institutions, and businesses remain largely impaired in their ability to make data-driven decisions. At the same time, data science is undergoing a reproducibility crisis. The results of the vast majority of studies cannot be replicated by other researchers, and provenance often cannot be established, even for data used in medical studies that affect lives of millions. We are losing our ability to collaborate at a time when significant improvements to data are badly needed. We believe that the fundamental reason lies in the modern data management processes being entirely at odds with the basic principles of collaboration and trust. Our field needs a fundamental shift of approach in how data is viewed, how it is shared and transformed. We must transition away from treating data as static, from exchanging it as anemic binary blobs, and instead focus on making multi-party data management more sustainable: such as reproducibility, verifiability, provenance, autonomy, and low latency. In this paper, we present the Open Data Fabric, a new decentralized data exchange and transformation protocol designed from the ground up to simplify data management and enable collaboration around data on a similar scale as currently seen in open-source software.

title: Open Data Fabric: A Decentralized Data Exchange and Transformation Protocol With Complete Reproducibility and Provenance
text: The proliferation of data-driven applications has led to an explosion of data silos, hindering seamless data exchange and collaboration across organizational boundaries. Existing data integration approaches rely on centralized authorities, compromising data sovereignty and provenance. To address these limitations, we propose the Open Data Fabric (ODF), a decentralized data exchange and transformation protocol that ensures complete reproducibility and provenance. ODF is built upon a distributed ledger technology, leveraging a novel consensus mechanism that enables efficient and scalable data transactions. Our protocol features a modular architecture, comprising data providers, data transformers, and data consumers, which interact through a standardized interface. This design enables seamless data exchange, transformation, and integration, while ensuring data ownership and sovereignty. We evaluate ODF using a comprehensive experimental framework, comprising real-world datasets and diverse data transformation scenarios. Our results demonstrate that ODF achieves significant performance improvements, with an average reduction of 35% in data transaction latency and 40% in data transformation overhead, compared to existing centralized approaches. Moreover, ODF ensures complete reproducibility, with a provenance graph that captures the entire data lineage, enabling transparent and trustworthy data exchange. We further demonstrate the applicability of ODF in various domains, including healthcare, finance, and climate science, showcasing its potential to facilitate collaboration, accelerate innovation, and foster data-driven decision-making. By providing a decentralized, reproducible, and transparent data exchange and transformation protocol, ODF has the potential to revolutionize the way data is shared, transformed, and utilized, ultimately leading to more accurate, reliable, and impactful insights.

title: Detecting Quality Problems in Data Models by Clustering Heterogeneous Data Values
text: Data is of high quality if it is fit for its intended use. The quality of data is influenced by the underlying data model and its quality. One major quality problem is the heterogeneity of data as quality aspects such as understandability and interoperability are impaired. This heterogeneity may be caused by quality problems in the data model. Data heterogeneity can occur in particular when the information given is not structured enough and just captured in data values, often due to missing or non-suitable structure in the underlying data model. We propose a bottom-up approach to detecting quality problems in data models that manifest in heterogeneous data values. It supports an explorative analysis of the existing data and can be configured by domain experts according to their domain knowledge. All values of a selected data field are clustered by syntactic similarity. Thereby an overview of the data values' diversity in syntax is provided. It shall help domain experts to understand how the data model is used in practice and to derive potential quality problems of the data model. We outline a proof-of-concept implementation and evaluate our approach using cultural heritage data.

title: Detecting Quality Problems in Data Models by Clustering Heterogeneous Data Values
text: The fitness of data for its intended purpose is contingent upon its quality, which in turn is influenced by the underlying data model and its inherent quality. A significant impediment to data quality is heterogeneity, which compromises aspects such as understandability and interoperability. This issue can be attributed to flaws in the data model, leading to unstructured information and poorly captured data values. When data values lack a suitable structure, heterogeneity ensues, highlighting the need for a systematic approach to detecting quality problems in data models. We present a bottom-up method for identifying data model quality issues that manifest as heterogeneous data values. This approach facilitates exploratory analysis of existing data and can be customized by domain experts based on their expertise. By clustering data field values according to syntactic similarity, our method provides a comprehensive overview of data value diversity, enabling domain experts to discern how the data model is utilized in practice and infer potential quality problems. We describe a proof-of-concept implementation and evaluate our approach using cultural heritage data, demonstrating its efficacy in detecting data model quality issues.

title: First-Order Rewritability and Complexity of Two-Dimensional Temporal Ontology-Mediated Queries
text: Aiming at ontology-based data access to temporal data, we design two-dimensional temporal ontology and query languages by combining logics from the (extended) DL-Lite family with linear temporal logic LTL over discrete time (Z,<). Our main concern is first-order rewritability of ontology-mediated queries (OMQs) that consist of a 2D ontology and a positive temporal instance query. Our target languages for FO-rewritings are two-sorted FO(<) - first-order logic with sorts for time instants ordered by the built-in precedence relation < and for the domain of individuals - its extension FOE with the standard congruence predicates t \equiv 0 mod n, for any fixed n > 1, and FO(RPR) that admits relational primitive recursion. In terms of circuit complexity, FOE- and FO(RPR)-rewritability guarantee answering OMQs in uniform AC0 and NC1, respectively. We proceed in three steps. First, we define a hierarchy of 2D DL-Lite/LTL ontology languages and investigate the FO-rewritability of OMQs with atomic queries by constructing projections onto 1D LTL OMQs and employing recent results on the FO-rewritability of propositional LTL OMQs. As the projections involve deciding consistency of ontologies and data, we also consider the consistency problem for our languages. While the undecidability of consistency for 2D ontology languages with expressive Boolean role inclusions might be expected, we also show that, rather surprisingly, the restriction to Krom and Horn role inclusions leads to decidability (and ExpSpace-completeness), even if one admits full Booleans on concepts. As a final step, we lift some of the rewritability results for atomic OMQs to OMQs with expressive positive temporal instance queries. The lifting results are based on an in-depth study of the canonical models and only concern Horn ontologies.

title: First-Order Rewritability and Complexity of Two-Dimensional Temporal Ontology-Mediated Queries
text: Two-dimensional temporal (2DT) ontology-mediated queries (OMQs) have emerged as a crucial paradigm for querying temporal data streams in various domains, including finance, healthcare, and IoT. A fundamental problem in this context is to determine the complexity of evaluating 2DT OMQs and whether they can be rewritten into a more tractable form. In this context, first-order rewritability (FOR) has been identified as a key property, as it enables the use of standard relational database management systems to evaluate OMQs. Previous studies have investigated the complexity of evaluating OMQs in the context of one-dimensional temporal data, but the 2DT case remains largely unexplored. This paper fills this gap by providing a comprehensive analysis of the complexity of 2DT OMQs and their first-order rewritability. Our methodology involves a rigorous study of the expressive power of 2DT OMQs, leveraging techniques from finite model theory and descriptive complexity. We establish a tight connection between the complexity of evaluating 2DT OMQs and their FOR, and demonstrate that 2DT OMQs can be rewritten into first-order logic if and only if they can be evaluated in polynomial time. Our main findings are twofold. Firstly, we show that 2DT OMQs can be evaluated in polynomial time if the underlying ontology is formulated in a guarded fragment of the Description Logic (DL) ALCQIO, a popular DL used in various applications. Secondly, we provide a precise characterization of the complexity of evaluating 2DT OMQs, demonstrating that they can be evaluated in NPTime if the ontology is formulated in ALCQIO, and in PSpace otherwise. These results have significant implications for the design of efficient query evaluation algorithms and the development of scalable systems for querying temporal data streams.

title: Reliability Models for Smartphone Applications
text: Smartphones have become the most used electronic devices. They carry out most of the functionalities of desktops, offering various useful applications that suit the users needs. Therefore, instead of the operator, the user has been the main controller of the device and its applications, therefore its reliability has become an emergent requirement. As a first step, based on collected smartphone applications failure data, we investigated and evaluated the efficacy of Software Reliability Growth Models (SRGMs) when applied to these smartphone data in order to check whether they achieve the same accuracy as in the desktop/laptop area. None of the selected models were able to account for the smartphone data satisfactorily. Their failure is traced back to: (i) the hardware and software differences between desktops and smartphones, (ii) the specific features of mobile applications compared to desktop applications, and (iii) the different operational conditions and usage profiles. Thus, a reliability model suited to smartphone applications is still needed. In the second step, we applied the Weibull and Gamma distributions, and their two particular cases, Rayleigh and S-Shaped, to model the smartphone failure data sorted by application version number and grouped into different time periods. An estimation of the expected number of defects in each application version was obtained. The performances of the distributions were then compared amongst each other. We found that both Weibull and Gamma distributions can fit the failure data of mobile applications, although the Gamma distribution is frequently more suited.

title: Reliability Models for Smartphone Applications
text: The widespread adoption of smartphones has led to a surge in the development of mobile applications, which are increasingly critical to daily life, commerce, and communication. Despite their importance, smartphone applications are prone to failures, crashes, and inconsistencies, compromising user experience and trust. Reliability modeling is essential to assess and improve the dependability of these systems. Existing reliability models, however, are largely tailored to traditional desktop and server-based systems, neglecting the unique characteristics of mobile devices and applications. This study proposes a novel reliability modeling framework specifically designed for smartphone applications. We develop a hierarchical model that captures the complex interactions between the application, operating system, and hardware components. Our approach integrates Bayesian networks, fault trees, and Markov models to represent the various failure modes and error propagation mechanisms. We validate our framework using a comprehensive dataset of 150 popular Android applications, comprising over 10,000 execution traces and 500 distinct failure scenarios. Our results show that the proposed model outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and precision, with a mean absolute error of 12.4% in estimating application reliability. We identify key factors contributing to reliability, including memory leaks, network connectivity issues, and sensor malfunctions. Furthermore, our model enables the identification of critical components and failure paths, facilitating targeted optimization and debugging efforts. The findings of this study have significant implications for the development of reliable and efficient smartphone applications, ultimately enhancing user satisfaction and loyalty.

title: Revisiting Active Object Stores: Bringing Data Locality to the Limit With NVM
text: Object stores are widely used software stacks that achieve excellent scale-out with a well-defined interface and robust performance. However, their traditional get/put interface is unable to exploit data locality at its fullest, and limits reaching its peak performance. In particular, there is one way to improve data locality that has not yet achieved mainstream adoption: the active object store. Although there are some projects that have implemented the main idea of the active object store such as Swift's Storlets or Ceph Object Classes, the scope of these implementations is limited. We believe that there is a huge potential for active object stores in the current status quo. Hyper-converged nodes are bringing more computing capabilities to storage nodes --and viceversa. The proliferation of non-volatile memory (NVM) technology is blurring the line between system memory (fast and scarce) and block devices (slow and abundant). More and more applications need to manage a sheer amount of data (data analytics, Big Data, Machine Learning & AI, etc.), demanding bigger clusters and more complex computations. All these elements are potential game changers that need to be evaluated in the scope of active object stores. In this article we propose an active object store software stack and evaluate it on an NVM-populated node. We will show how this setup is able to reduce execution times from 10% up to more than 90% in a variety of representative application scenarios. Our discussion will focus on the active aspect of the system as well as on the implications of the memory configuration.

title: Revisiting Active Object Stores: Bringing Data Locality to the Limit With NVM
text: The scalability and performance of object stores, a widely employed software stack, are hindered by their traditional get/put interface, which fails to fully leverage data locality. This limitation can be addressed by the active object store paradigm, which, despite being explored in projects like Swift's Storlets and Ceph Object Classes, has yet to gain widespread adoption. The current landscape, however, presents a unique opportunity for active object stores to thrive. The increasing convergence of compute and storage capabilities in hyper-converged nodes, combined with the emergence of non-volatile memory (NVM) technology, is blurring the distinction between system memory and block devices. Moreover, the growing demand for data-intensive applications, such as data analytics, Big Data, and Machine Learning & AI, necessitates larger clusters and more complex computations. In this context, we propose an active object store software stack and evaluate its performance on an NVM-equipped node. Our results show significant reductions in execution times, ranging from 10% to over 90%, across a variety of representative application scenarios. This paper provides an in-depth examination of the active aspect of the system, as well as the implications of memory configuration, highlighting the potential of active object stores to revolutionize data storage and processing.

title: Regular Path Query Evaluation Sharing a Reduced Transitive Closure Based on Graph Reduction
text: Regular path queries (RPQs) find pairs of vertices of paths satisfying given regular expressions on an edge-labeled, directed multigraph. When evaluating an RPQ, the evaluation of a Kleene closure (i.e., Kleene plus or Kleene star) is very expensive. Furthermore, when multiple RPQs include a Kleene closure as a common sub-query, repeated evaluations of the common sub-query cause serious performance degradation. In this paper, we present a novel concept of RPQ-based graph reduction, which significantly simplifies the original graph through edge-level and vertex-level reductions. Interestingly, RPQ-based graph reduction can replace the evaluation of the Kleene closure on the large original graph to that of the transitive closure to the small reduced graph. We then propose a reduced transitive closure (RTC) as a lightweight structure for efficiently sharing the result of a Kleene closure.
