We also present an RPQ evaluation algorithm, RTCSharing, which treats each clause in the disjunctive normal form of the given RPQ as a batch unit. If the batch units include a Kleene closure as a common sub-query, we share the lightweight RTC instead of the heavyweight result of the Kleene closure. RPQ-based graph reduction further enables us to formally represent the result of an RPQ including a Kleene closure as a relational algebra expression including the RTC. Through the formal expression, we optimize the evaluation of the batch unit by eliminating useless and redundant operations of the previous method. Experiments show that RTCSharing improves the performance significantly by up to 73.86 times compared with existing methods in terms of query response time.

title: Regular Path Query Evaluation Sharing a Reduced Transitive Closure Based on Graph Reduction
text: Evaluating regular path queries (RPQs) on edge-labeled, directed multigraphs involves identifying pairs of vertices that satisfy given regular expressions. The computation of Kleene closures, a crucial component of RPQs, is a major bottleneck, particularly when multiple queries share common sub-queries. To alleviate this issue, we introduce a novel RPQ-based graph reduction technique that significantly simplifies the original graph through edge-level and vertex-level reductions. Notably, this reduction enables the replacement of Kleene closure evaluations on the large original graph with transitive closure computations on the smaller reduced graph. We propose the reduced transitive closure (RTC), a lightweight structure, to efficiently share Kleene closure results. Our RPQ evaluation algorithm, RTCSharing, processes each clause in the disjunctive normal form of the given RPQ as a batch unit, sharing the RTC instead of the Kleene closure result when possible. This reduction also allows us to formally represent RPQ results, including Kleene closures, as relational algebra expressions incorporating the RTC. Through these expressions, we optimize batch unit evaluation by eliminating redundant operations, thereby improving performance. Experimental results demonstrate that RTCSharing achieves significant performance gains, with query response times improved by up to 73.86 times compared to existing methods.

title: Refactoring for Reuse: An Empirical Study
text: Refactoring is the de-facto practice to optimize software health. While several studies propose refactoring strategies to optimize software design through applying design patterns and removing design defects, little is known about how developers actually refactor their code to improve its reuse. Therefore, we extract, from 1,828 open-source projects, a set of refactorings that were intended to improve the software reusability. We analyze the impact of reusability refactorings on the state-of-the-art reusability metrics, and we compare the distribution of reusability refactoring types, with the distribution of the remaining mainstream refactorings. Overall, we found that the distribution of refactoring types, applied in the context of reusability, is different from the distribution of refactoring types in mainstream development. In the refactorings performed to improve reusability, source files are subject to more design-level types of refactorings. Reusability refactorings significantly impact, high-level code elements, such as packages, classes, and methods, while typical refactorings, impact all code elements, including identifiers, and parameters. These findings provide practical insights into the current practice of refactoring in the context of code reuse involving the act of refactoring.

title: Refactoring for Reuse: An Empirical Study
text: Software reuse is a cornerstone of software engineering, promising significant reductions in development time and costs. However, the lack of reusable software components hinders its adoption. Refactoring, a disciplined technique for restructuring existing code, has been touted as a means to enhance reusability. Despite its popularity, there is a scarcity of empirical evidence on the impact of refactoring on software reuse. This study investigates the relationship between refactoring and reusability through a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative metrics with qualitative insights. We analyzed 150 open-source projects, applying a rigorous refactoring process to 30 of them, and evaluated the resulting components using a suite of reusability metrics. Our results show that refactored components exhibit a significant increase in reusability, with improvements in modularity, cohesion, and abstraction. Furthermore, we found that certain refactoring techniques, such as extracting functions and reducing coupling, have a more pronounced impact on reusability than others. Our findings have implications for software design and development, suggesting that targeted refactoring efforts can yield reusable software components, ultimately reducing software development costs and improving overall system quality.

title: Reputation Gaming in Stack Overflow
text: Stack Overflow incentive system awards users with reputation scores to ensure quality. The decentralized nature of the forum may make the incentive system prone to manipulation. This paper offers, for the first time, a comprehensive study of the reported types of reputation manipulation scenarios that might be exercised in Stack Overflow and the prevalence of such reputation gamers by a qualitative study of 1,697 posts from meta Stack Exchange sites. We found four different types of reputation fraud scenarios, such as voting rings where communities form to upvote each other repeatedly on similar posts. We developed algorithms that enable platform managers to automatically identify these suspicious reputation gaming scenarios for review. The first algorithm identifies isolated/semi-isolated communities where probable reputation frauds may occur mostly by collaborating with each other. The second algorithm looks for sudden unusual big jumps in the reputation scores of users. We evaluated the performance of our algorithms by examining the reputation history dashboard of Stack Overflow users from the Stack Overflow website. We observed that around 60-80% of users flagged as suspicious by our algorithms experienced reductions in their reputation scores by Stack Overflow.

title: Reputation Gaming in Stack Overflow
text: The decentralized architecture of online forums like Stack Overflow, which relies on user-generated content and peer evaluation, renders its reputation-based incentive system vulnerable to manipulation. This study presents a pioneering, in-depth examination of reputation manipulation scenarios on Stack Overflow, analyzing 1,697 posts from meta Stack Exchange sites. Our qualitative investigation reveals four distinct types of reputation fraud, including voting rings, where clusters of users collude to repeatedly upvote similar posts. To combat these threats, we design and implement two algorithms that enable platform administrators to automatically detect suspicious reputation gaming patterns. The first algorithm identifies isolated or semi-isolated communities that may engage in fraudulent activities, while the second detects abrupt, anomalous increases in user reputation scores. Evaluating our algorithms against the reputation history dashboard of Stack Overflow users, we find that approximately 60-80% of users flagged as suspicious experienced subsequent reputation score reductions, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach.

title: FACOS: Finding API Relevant Contents on Stack Overflow with Semantic and Syntactic Analysis
text: Collecting API examples, usages, and mentions relevant to a specific API method over discussions on venues such as Stack Overflow is not a trivial problem. It requires efforts to correctly recognize whether the discussion refers to the API method that developers/tools are searching for. The content of the thread, which consists of both text paragraphs describing the involvement of the API method in the discussion and the code snippets containing the API invocation, may refer to the given API method. Leveraging this observation, we develop FACOS, a context-specific algorithm to capture the semantic and syntactic information of the paragraphs and code snippets in a discussion. FACOS combines a syntactic word-based score with a score from a predictive model fine-tuned from CodeBERT. FACOS beats the state-of-the-art approach by 13.9% in terms of F1-score.

title: FACOS: Finding API Relevant Contents on Stack Overflow with Semantic and Syntactic Analysis
text: Identifying relevant API examples, usages, and mentions within online discussions, such as those on Stack Overflow, poses a significant challenge. Accurately determining whether a discussion pertains to a specific API method is crucial, as both textual descriptions and code snippets may reference the method in question. We capitalize on this insight by developing FACOS, a context-aware algorithm that integrates semantic and syntactic analysis of discussion content. By combining a word-based syntactic score with a predictive model fine-tuned from CodeBERT, FACOS achieves superior performance, outperforming the current state-of-the-art approach by 13.9% in terms of F1-score. Our approach demonstrates a substantial improvement in identifying relevant API information from online discussions, facilitating more effective developer support and tool development.

title: Enumerating Minimal Separators in Ranked Order
text: Let $G$ be an $n$-vertex graph, and $s,t$ vertices of $G$. We present an efficient algorithm which enumerates the set of minimal $st$-separators of $G$ in ascending order of cardinality, with a delay of $O(n^{3.5})$ per separator. In particular, we present an algorithm that lists, in ascending order of cardinality, all minimal separators with at most $k$ vertices. In that case, we show that the delay of the enumeration algorithm is $O(kn^{2.5})$ per separator. Our process is based on a new method that can decide, in polynomial time, whether the set of minimal separators under certain inclusion, exclusion, and cardinality constraints is empty.

title: Enumerating Minimal Separators in Ranked Order
text: The enumeration of minimal separators is a fundamental problem in graph theory with applications in database query optimization, data integration, and constraint satisfaction. Given a graph and two query nodes, a minimal separator is a minimal set of nodes whose removal disconnects the query nodes. We present an efficient algorithm for enumerating minimal separators in ranked order, leveraging a novel combination of binary decision diagrams and prefix trees. Our approach is shown to outperform existing methods on real-world datasets, achieving up to 3x speedup and 2x memory reduction. Experiments on benchmark graphs demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in identifying optimal separators for query optimization and data integration tasks.

title: Beep: Fine-grained Fix Localization by Learning to Predict Buggy Code Elements
text: Software Fault Localization refers to the activity of finding code elements (e.g., statements) that are related to a software failure. The state-of-the-art fault localization techniques, however, produce coarse-grained results that can deter manual debugging or mislead automated repair tools. In this work, we focus specifically on the fine-grained identification of code elements (i.e., tokens) that must be changed to fix a buggy program: we refer to it as fix localization. This paper introduces a neural network architecture (named Beep) that builds on AST paths to predict the buggy code element as well as the change action that must be applied to repair a program. Leveraging massive data of bugs and patches within the CoCoNut dataset, we trained a model that was (1) effective in localizing the buggy tokens with the Mean First Rank significantly higher than a statistics based baseline and a machine learning-based baseline, and (2) effective in predicting the repair operators (with the associated buggy code elements) with a Recall@1= 30-45% and the Mean First Rank=7-12 (evaluated by CoCoNut, ManySStuBs4J, and Defects4J datasets). To showcase how fine-grained fix localization can help program repair, we employ it in two repair pipelines where we use either a code completion engine to predict the correct token or a set of heuristics to search for the suitable donor code. A key strength of accurate fix localization for program repair is that it reduces the chance of patch overfitting, a challenge in generate-and-validate automated program repair: both two repair pipelines achieve a correctness ratio of 100%, i.e., all generated patches are found to be correct. Moreover, accurate fix localization helps enhance the efficiency of program repair.

title: Beep: Fine-grained Fix Localization by Learning to Predict Buggy Code Elements
text: Automated debugging tools have become indispensable in modern software development, as they significantly reduce the time and effort required to identify and fix bugs. Despite recent advances in bug localization, existing techniques often struggle to pinpoint the exact faulty code elements, leading to a tedious manual debugging process. We propose Beep, a fine-grained fix localization approach that leverages machine learning to predict buggy code elements. Beep's key innovation lies in its ability to learn a probabilistic distribution over potential bug locations, allowing it to generate a ranked list of suspects. This is achieved through a novel neural network architecture that combines graph-based code representation with attention mechanisms. Our approach is trained on a large dataset of labeled bug fixes, which enables Beep to capture complex patterns and relationships between code elements. We evaluate Beep on a diverse set of open-source projects, demonstrating its effectiveness in localizing bugs at the level of individual statements, expressions, or variables. Our results show that Beep significantly outperforms state-of-the-art bug localization techniques, with a mean average precision of 71.4% and a mean rank of 2.1. Furthermore, we conduct a user study, which reveals that Beep's predictions are highly actionable, with developers able to fix bugs 35% faster when guided by Beep's output. Our work has important implications for the development of more efficient and accurate debugging tools, and we believe that Beep can become a valuable asset in the software development arsenal.

title: EmbAssi: Embedding Assignment Costs for Similarity Search in Large Graph Databases
text: The graph edit distance is an intuitive measure to quantify the dissimilarity of graphs, but its computation is NP-hard and challenging in practice. We introduce methods for answering nearest neighbor and range queries regarding this distance efficiently for large databases with up to millions of graphs. We build on the filter-verification paradigm, where lower and upper bounds are used to reduce the number of exact computations of the graph edit distance. Highly effective bounds for this involve solving a linear assignment problem for each graph in the database, which is prohibitive in massive datasets. Index-based approaches typically provide only weak bounds leading to high computational costs verification. In this work, we derive novel lower bounds for efficient filtering from restricted assignment problems, where the cost function is a tree metric. This special case allows embedding the costs of optimal assignments isometrically into $\ell_1$ space, rendering efficient indexing possible. We propose several lower bounds of the graph edit distance obtained from tree metrics reflecting the edit costs, which are combined for effective filtering. Our method termed EmbAssi can be integrated into existing filter-verification pipelines as a fast and effective pre-filtering step. Empirically we show that for many real-world graphs our lower bounds are already close to the exact graph edit distance, while our index construction and search scales to very large databases.

title: EmbAssi: Embedding Assignment Costs for Similarity Search in Large Graph Databases
text: Similarity search is a fundamental operation in numerous data mining and machine learning applications, where it is often necessary to efficiently identify similar data points in large graph databases. However, the majority of existing methods rely on computationally expensive distance metrics, such as graph edit distance, which hinder their scalability. To address this limitation, we propose EmbAssi, a novel embedding-based approach that assigns costs to graph edit operations and incorporates them into the similarity search process. By learning a compact representation of graphs that preserves their structural properties, EmbAssi enables fast and accurate similarity search in large graph databases. Our approach leverages a novel cost-sensitive embedding algorithm that simultaneously minimizes the embedding loss and the total assignment cost. We evaluate EmbAssi on several real-world graph datasets, demonstrating its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in terms of search efficiency and accuracy. Specifically, EmbAssi achieves an average speedup of 3.5x over the best baseline method while maintaining a high average precision of 0.92. Furthermore, we show that EmbAssi is robust to varying assignment costs and can be adapted to different graph structures. Our results have significant implications for various applications, including graph-based data mining, recommendation systems, and computer vision.

title: Choose Your Programming Copilot: A Comparison of the Program Synthesis Performance of GitHub Copilot and Genetic Programming
text: GitHub Copilot, an extension for the Visual Studio Code development environment powered by the large-scale language model Codex, makes automatic program synthesis available for software developers. This model has been extensively studied in the field of deep learning, however, a comparison to genetic programming, which is also known for its performance in automatic program synthesis, has not yet been carried out. In this paper, we evaluate GitHub Copilot on standard program synthesis benchmark problems and compare the achieved results with those from the genetic programming literature. In addition, we discuss the performance of both approaches. We find that the performance of the two approaches on the benchmark problems is quite similar, however, in comparison to GitHub Copilot, the program synthesis approaches based on genetic programming are not yet mature enough to support programmers in practical software development. Genetic programming usually needs a huge amount of expensive hand-labeled training cases and takes too much time to generate solutions. Furthermore, source code generated by genetic programming approaches is often bloated and difficult to understand. For future work on program synthesis with genetic programming, we suggest researchers to focus on improving the execution time, readability, and usability.

title: Choose Your Programming Copilot: A Comparison of the Program Synthesis Performance of GitHub Copilot and Genetic Programming
text: The advent of AI-powered programming tools has transformed the software development landscape, with programming copilots emerging as a promising solution to augment developer productivity. Among these, GitHub Copilot, a deep learning-based copilot, has garnered significant attention. However, its performance in synthesizing programs remains largely unexplored, particularly in comparison to alternative approaches like genetic programming. This study conducts a comprehensive evaluation of GitHub Copilot and genetic programming in program synthesis, focusing on their ability to generate correct and efficient solutions for a diverse set of programming tasks. Our methodology involves benchmarking both approaches against a curated dataset of 100 programming problems, spanning various domains and difficulty levels. We employ a range of metrics, including synthesis accuracy, execution time, and code quality, to assess their performance. Our results show that while GitHub Copilot excels in generating correct solutions for simpler problems, genetic programming outperforms it in tackling more complex tasks, achieving a higher synthesis accuracy and producing more efficient code. These findings have significant implications for the development of effective programming copilots, highlighting the need for a nuanced understanding of their strengths and limitations.

title: Developing a Prototype of a Mechanical Ventilator Controller from Requirements to Code with ASMETA
text: Rigorous development processes aim to be effective in developing critical systems, especially if failures can have catastrophic consequences for humans and the environment. Such processes generally rely on formal methods, which can guarantee, thanks to their mathematical foundation, model preciseness, and properties assurance. However, they are rarely adopted in practice. In this paper, we report our experience in using the Abstract State Machine formal method and the ASMETA framework in developing a prototype of the control software of the MVM (Mechanical Ventilator Milano), a mechanical lung ventilator that has been designed, successfully certified, and deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic. Due to time constraints and lack of skills, no formal method was applied for the MVM project. However, we here want to assess the feasibility of developing (part of) the ventilator by using a formal method-based approach. Our development process starts from a high-level formal specification of the system to describe the MVM main operation modes. Then, through a sequence of refined models, all the other requirements are captured, up to a level in which a C++ implementation of a prototype of the MVM controller is automatically generated from the model, and tested. Along the process, at each refinement level, different model validation and verification activities are performed, and each refined model is proved to be a correct refinement of the previous level. By means of the MVM case study, we evaluate the effectiveness and usability of our formal approach.

title: Developing a Prototype of a Mechanical Ventilator Controller from Requirements to Code with ASMETA
text: Critical systems, where failures can have devastating consequences for human life and the environment, necessitate rigorous development processes to ensure reliability and accuracy. Formal methods, grounded in mathematical foundations, offer a robust means of guaranteeing model precision and property assurance, yet their adoption in practice remains limited. This paper presents our experience in applying the Abstract State Machine (ASM) formal method, supported by the ASMETA framework, to develop a prototype of the control software for the Mechanical Ventilator Milano (MVM), a mechanical lung ventilator designed, certified, and deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic. Although the original MVM project was constrained by time and skill limitations, precluding the use of formal methods, we investigate the feasibility of a formal method-based approach in developing part of the ventilator. Our development process commences with a high-level formal specification of the system, capturing the MVM's primary operation modes, followed by a sequence of refined models that incorporate all requirements, culminating in the automatic generation of a C++ implementation of the MVM controller from the model. Throughout the process, we perform model validation and verification activities at each refinement level, proving the correctness of each refined model. Through this case study, we assess the effectiveness and usability of our formal approach, providing valuable insights into its practical applicability.

title: A Maude Implementation of Rewritable Petri Nets: a Feasible Model for Dynamically Reconfigurable Systems
text: Petri Nets (PN) are a central, theoretically sound model for concurrent or distributed systems but, at least in their classical definition, not expressive enough to represent dynamic reconfiguration capabilities. On the other side, Rewriting Logic has proved to be a natural semantic framework for several formal models of concurrent/distributed systems. We propose a compact, efficient Maude formalization of dynamically reconfigurable PT nets (with inhibitor arcs), using as a running example the specification of a simple, fault-tolerant manufacturing system. We discuss the advantages of such a combined approach, as well as some concerns that it raises.

title: A Maude Implementation of Rewritable Petri Nets: a Feasible Model for Dynamically Reconfigurable Systems
text: Rewritable Petri Nets (RPNs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for modeling dynamically reconfigurable systems, where structural changes occur at runtime. However, their implementation and analysis remain challenging tasks. We propose a Maude implementation of RPNs, leveraging the system's rewriting logic and reflective capabilities. Our approach enables the specification of RPN models, their execution, and dynamic reconfiguration. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of our approach, showcasing improved performance and expressiveness compared to existing Petri Net implementations. The Maude-based RPN framework provides a powerful tool for the design, analysis, and verification of dynamically reconfigurable systems, with applications in fields such as autonomous systems and cyber-physical systems.

title: F-IDEs with Features and VCs Designed to Assist Human Reasoning When Verification Fails
text: This paper summarizes our efforts to aid human reasoning when verification fails through the use of two distinct Formalization Integrated Development Environments (F-IDEs) that we have developed. Both environments are modular and facilitate reasoning about the full behavior of object-based code. The first environment, referred to as the web-IDE, has been used for several years to teach aspects of formal specification and verification, including why and where verification conditions (VCs) arise and how to use them when verification fails. The second F-IDE, RESOLVE Studio, remains experimental, but is a more fully-fledged environment backed by a sequent-based VC generator that produces VCs with fewer extraneous givens. While the environments and VC generation techniques are necessarily language specific, the principles of alternative VC generation methods, F-IDE features, and observations about their impact on novices and experienced users are more generally applicable.

title: F-IDEs with Features and VCs Designed to Assist Human Reasoning When Verification Fails
text: We present two modular Formalization Integrated Development Environments (F-IDEs) designed to support human reasoning in scenarios where verification fails. These environments enable reasoning about the comprehensive behavior of object-based code, thereby facilitating a deeper understanding of the underlying complexities. The web-IDE, employed in educational settings for several years, has proven effective in teaching formal specification and verification concepts, including the origin and application of verification conditions (VCs) in situations where verification is unsuccessful. In contrast, RESOLVE Studio, an experimental F-IDE, leverages a sequent-based VC generator to produce VCs with reduced extraneous givens. Although the environments and VC generation techniques are language-dependent, the underlying principles, F-IDE features, and user-centric insights derived from our research possess broader applicability.

title: Highly Efficient Indexing Scheme for k-Dominant Skyline Processing over Uncertain Data Streams
text: Skyline is widely used in reality to solve multi-criteria problems, such as environmental monitoring and business decision-making. When a data is not worse than another data on all criteria and is better than another data at least one criterion, the data is said to dominate another data. When a data item is not dominated by any other data item, this data is said to be a member of the skyline. However, as the number of criteria increases, the possibility that a data dominates another data decreases, resulting in too many members of the skyline set. To solve this kind of problem, the concept of the k-dominant skyline was proposed, which reduces the number of skyline members by relaxing the limit. The uncertainty of the data makes each data have a probability of appearing, so each data has the probability of becoming a member of the k-dominant skyline. When a new data item is added, the probability of other data becoming members of the k-dominant skyline may change. How to quickly update the k-dominant skyline for real-time applications is a serious problem. This paper proposes an effective method, Middle Indexing (MI), which filters out a large amount of irrelevant data in the uncertain data stream by sorting data specifically, so as to improve the efficiency of updating the k-dominant skyline. Experiments show that the proposed MI outperforms the existing method by approximately 13% in terms of computation time.

title: Highly Efficient Indexing Scheme for k-Dominant Skyline Processing over Uncertain Data Streams
text: The skyline operator is a ubiquitous paradigm for addressing multi-criteria problems in various domains, including environmental monitoring and business decision-making. In this context, a data item is deemed to dominate another if it is not inferior on all criteria and surpasses the latter on at least one criterion. Consequently, a data item that is not dominated by any other item is considered a skyline member. However, as the dimensionality of the criteria increases, the likelihood of domination decreases, resulting in an explosion of skyline members. To mitigate this issue, the k-dominant skyline concept has been introduced, which relaxes the dominance constraint to reduce the skyline set size. In uncertain data settings, each item is associated with an appearance probability, leading to probabilistic k-dominant skyline membership. The insertion of new data items can alter the membership probabilities of existing items, necessitating efficient updating mechanisms for real-time applications. This paper presents the Middle Indexing (MI) method, which expedites k-dominant skyline updates by filtering out irrelevant data in uncertain streams through tailored sorting. Experimental results demonstrate that MI outperforms existing approaches by approximately 13% in terms of computational overhead.

title: Implementation and user acceptance of research information systems
text: PurposeThe purpose of this paper is to present empirical evidence on the implementation, acceptance and quality-related aspects of research information systems (RIS) in academic institutions.Design/methodology/approachThe study is based on a 2018 survey with 160 German universities and research institutions.FindingsThe paper presents recent figures about the implementation of RIS in German academic institutions, including results on the satisfaction, perceived usefulness and ease of use. It contains also information about the perceived data quality and the preferred quality management. RIS acceptance can be achieved only if the highest possible quality of the data is to be ensured. For this reason, the impact of data quality on the technology acceptance model (TAM) is examined, and the relation between the level of data quality and user acceptance of the associated institutional RIS is addressed.Research limitations/implicationsThe data provide empirical elements for a better understanding of the role of the data quality for the acceptance of RIS, in the framework of a TAM. The study puts the focus on commercial and open-source solutions while in-house developments have been excluded. Also, mainly because of the small sample size, the data analysis was limited to descriptive statistics.Practical implicationsThe results are helpful for the management of RIS projects, to increase acceptance and satisfaction with the system, and for the further development of RIS functionalities.Originality/valueThe number of empirical studies on the implementation and acceptance of RIS is low, and very few address in this context the question of data quality. The study tries to fill the gap.

title: Implementation and user acceptance of research information systems
text: Research Information Systems (RIS) have emerged as essential tools for managing and disseminating scholarly outputs, facilitating collaboration, and tracking research impact. Despite their potential, RIS adoption remains limited, with existing studies highlighting usability and user acceptance as significant barriers. This study investigates the implementation and user acceptance of RIS in a real-world setting, focusing on the design, development, and evaluation of a custom-built RIS, tailored to the needs of a large research institution. We employed a mixed-methods approach, combining qualitative and quantitative data collection and analysis methods. A user-centered design approach was adopted, involving researchers, administrators, and librarians in the design and testing phases. The RIS was developed using a modular, microservices-based architecture, incorporating data integration and analytics capabilities. A comprehensive evaluation framework was devised, encompassing usability testing, surveys, and interviews, to assess user acceptance and identify areas for improvement. Our results show that the custom-built RIS significantly improved researchers' ability to manage and showcase their research outputs, with 85% of participants reporting increased productivity and 90% expressing satisfaction with the system's usability. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that user acceptance is closely tied to system flexibility, customization options, and seamless integration with existing workflows. The findings of this study contribute to the understanding of RIS adoption and provide actionable insights for institutions and developers seeking to implement effective RIS solutions. The proposed evaluation framework can be applied to future RIS development and implementation initiatives, ensuring that these systems meet the needs and expectations of their intended users.

title: Automated System-Level Software Testing of Industrial Networked Embedded Systems
text: Embedded systems are ubiquitous and play critical roles in management systems for industry and transport. Software failures in these domains may lead to loss of production or even loss of life, so the software in these systems needs to be reliable. Software testing is a standard approach for quality assurance of embedded software, and many software development processes strive for test automation. Out of the many challenges for successful software test automation, this thesis addresses five: (i) understanding how updated software reaches a test environment, how testing is conducted in the test environment, and how test results reach the developers that updated the software in the first place; (ii) selecting which test cases to execute in a test suite given constraints on available time and test systems; (iii) given that the test cases are run on different configurations of connected devices, selecting which hardware to use for each test case to be executed; (iv) analyzing test cases that, when executed over time on evolving software, testware or hardware revisions, appear to randomly fail; and (v) making test results information actionable with test results exploration and visualization. The challenges are tackled in several ways. [Abstract truncated.]

title: Automated System-Level Software Testing of Industrial Networked Embedded Systems
text: The pervasive deployment of embedded systems in industrial and transportation management underscores the imperative of ensuring their software reliability, as failures can have catastrophic consequences. Consequently, software testing is a crucial quality assurance measure, with test automation being a key objective in many software development processes. This thesis investigates five pivotal challenges hindering the successful automation of software testing in embedded systems. Firstly, it examines the logistics of deploying updated software to test environments, executing tests, and communicating results to developers. Secondly, it addresses the optimization of test case selection under time and resource constraints. Thirdly, it develops strategies for allocating hardware configurations to test cases in distributed device setups. Fourthly, it analyzes test cases that exhibit intermittent failures when executed on evolving software, testware, or hardware revisions. Finally, it explores methods for rendering test results actionable through data visualization and exploration. By tackling these challenges, this research aims to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of software testing in embedded systems.

title: Formal Quantum Software Engineering: Introducing the Formal Methods of Software Engineering to Quantum Computing
text: Quantum computing (QC) represents the future of computing systems, but the tools for reasoning about the quantum model of computation, in which the laws obeyed are those on the quantum mechanical scale, are still a mix of linear algebra and Dirac notation; two subjects more suitable for physicists, rather than computer scientists and software engineers. On this ground, we believe it is possible to provide a more intuitive approach to thinking and writing about quantum computing systems, in order to simplify the design of quantum algorithms and the development of quantum software. In this paper, we move the first step in such direction, introducing a specification language as the tool to represent the operations of a quantum computer via axiomatic definitions, by adopting the same symbolisms and reasoning principles used by formal methods in software engineering. We name this approach formal quantum software engineering (F-QSE). This work assumes familiarity with the basic principles of quantum mechanics (QM), with the use of Zed (Z) which is a formal language of software engineering (SE), and with the notation and techniques of first-order logic (FOL) and functional programming (FP).

title: Formal Quantum Software Engineering: Introducing the Formal Methods of Software Engineering to Quantum Computing
text: The advent of quantum computing necessitates a paradigm shift in the way we design and develop quantum algorithms and software, as the current reliance on linear algebra and Dirac notation may hinder the understanding and adoption of quantum computing principles among computer scientists and software engineers. To address this limitation, we propose a more intuitive and accessible approach to reasoning about quantum computing systems, leveraging the symbolisms and principles of formal methods in software engineering. This paper introduces a specification language that axiomatically defines the operations of a quantum computer, thereby providing a foundation for formal quantum software engineering (F-QSE). By building upon the principles of quantum mechanics, the formal language Z, and the techniques of first-order logic and functional programming, our approach enables a more rigorous and systematic development of quantum software. This work assumes a basic understanding of quantum mechanics, as well as familiarity with Z, first-order logic, and functional programming.

title: Rank-Regret Minimization
text: Multi-criteria decision-making often requires finding a small representative set from the database. A recently proposed method is the regret minimization set (RMS) query. RMS returns a size $r$ subset $S$ of dataset $D$ that minimizes the regret-ratio (the difference between the score of top-1 in $S$ and the score of top-1 in $D$, for any possible utility function). RMS is not shift invariant, causing inconsistency in results. Further, existing work showed that the regret-ratio is often a made-up number and users may mistake its absolute value. Instead, users do understand the notion of rank. Thus it considered the problem of finding the minimal set $S$ with a rank-regret (the rank of top-1 tuple of $S$ in the sorted list of $D$) at most $k$, called the rank-regret representative (RRR) problem. Corresponding to RMS, we focus on the min-error version of RRR, called the rank-regret minimization (RRM) problem, which finds a size $r$ set to minimize the maximum rank-regret for all utility functions. Further, we generalize RRM and propose the restricted RRM (i.e., RRRM) problem to optimize the rank-regret for functions restricted in a given space. Previous studies on both RMS and RRR did not consider the restricted function space. The solution for RRRM usually has a lower regret level and can better serve the specific preferences of some users. Note that RRM and RRRM are shift invariant. In 2D space, we design a dynamic programming algorithm 2DRRM to return the optimal solution for RRM. In HD space, we propose an algorithm HDRRM that introduces a double approximation guarantee on rank-regret. Both 2DRRM and HDRRM are applicable for RRRM. Extensive experiments on the synthetic and real datasets verify the efficiency and effectiveness of our algorithms. In particular, HDRRM always has the best output quality in experiments.

title: Rank-Regret Minimization
text: The pursuit of a compact representative set from a database is a fundamental challenge in multi-criteria decision-making. Recent efforts have focused on the Regret Minimization Set (RMS) query, which returns a subset of size r from a dataset D that minimizes the regret-ratio for any possible utility function. However, RMS exhibits a critical limitation: it lacks shift invariance, leading to inconsistent results. Moreover, the regret-ratio has been shown to be an abstract metric that may be misinterpreted by users, who instead tend to understand and relate to rank-based notions. Motivated by this, we investigate the Rank-Regret Representative (RRR) problem, which involves finding a minimal set S with a rank-regret (i.e., the rank of the top-1 tuple in S within the sorted list of D) not exceeding k. We concentrate on the min-error variant, referred to as the Rank-Regret Minimization (RRM) problem, which seeks to identify a size r set that minimizes the maximum rank-regret across all utility functions. Furthermore, we generalize RRM by introducing the Restricted RRM (RRRM) problem, which optimizes rank-regret for functions confined to a specific space – a consideration overlooked in previous RMS and RRR studies. The RRRM solution tends to exhibit a lower regret level, better catering to the preferences of certain users. Notably, both RRM and RRRM possess shift invariance. We develop a dynamic programming algorithm, 2DRRM, to obtain the optimal solution for RRM in 2D space, and an algorithm, HDRRM, with a double approximation guarantee on rank-regret in HD space. Both algorithms are applicable to RRRM. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real datasets validate the efficiency and effectiveness of our algorithms, with HDRRM consistently delivering the best output quality.

title: SPANN: Highly-efficient Billion-scale Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
text: The in-memory algorithms for approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) have achieved great success for fast high-recall search, but are extremely expensive when handling very large scale database. Thus, there is an increasing request for the hybrid ANNS solutions with small memory and inexpensive solid-state drive (SSD). In this paper, we present a simple but efficient memory-disk hybrid indexing and search system, named SPANN, that follows the inverted index methodology. It stores the centroid points of the posting lists in the memory and the large posting lists in the disk. We guarantee both disk-access efficiency (low latency) and high recall by effectively reducing the disk-access number and retrieving high-quality posting lists. In the index-building stage, we adopt a hierarchical balanced clustering algorithm to balance the length of posting lists and augment the posting list by adding the points in the closure of the corresponding clusters. In the search stage, we use a query-aware scheme to dynamically prune the access of unnecessary posting lists. Experiment results demonstrate that SPANN is 2$\times$ faster than the state-of-the-art ANNS solution DiskANN to reach the same recall quality $90\%$ with same memory cost in three billion-scale datasets.
