title: SPANN: Highly-efficient Billion-scale Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
text: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) algorithms leveraging in-memory computations have demonstrated remarkable efficacy in facilitating fast, high-recall searches. However, their scalability is severely hampered when dealing with exceptionally large datasets, rendering them prohibitively expensive. To address this limitation, there is a growing demand for hybrid ANNS solutions that strike a balance between minimizing memory requirements and leveraging cost-effective solid-state drives (SSDs). This paper proposes SPANN, a memory-disk hybrid indexing and search system grounded in the inverted index methodology. By storing centroid points in memory and large posting lists on disk, SPANN achieves both disk-access efficiency and high recall by reducing the number of disk accesses and retrieving high-quality posting lists. The indexing stage employs a hierarchical balanced clustering algorithm to balance posting list lengths and augment them with points from corresponding cluster closures. A query-aware pruning scheme is utilized in the search stage to dynamically eliminate unnecessary posting list accesses. Experimental results show that SPANN outperforms the state-of-the-art DiskANN by a factor of two in reaching 90% recall quality with identical memory costs on three billion-scale datasets, achieving 90% recall@1 and recall@10 in approximately one millisecond with a mere 32GB memory footprint.

title: Understanding How Programmers Can Use Annotations on Documentation
text: Modern software development requires developers to find and effectively utilize new APIs and their documentation, but documentation has many well-known issues. Despite this, developers eventually overcome these issues but have no way of sharing what they learned. We investigate sharing this documentation-specific information through \textit{annotations}, which have advantages over developer forums as the information is contextualized, not disruptive, and is short, thus easy to author. Developers can also author annotations to support their own comprehension. In order to support the documentation usage behaviors we found, we built the Adamite annotation tool, which supports features such as multi-anchoring, annotation types, and pinning. In our user study, we found that developers are able to create annotations that are useful to themselves and are able to utilize annotations created by other developers when learning a new API, with readers of the annotations completing 67% more of the task, on average, than the baseline.

title: Understanding How Programmers Can Use Annotations on Documentation
text: The proliferation of open-source software has led to an explosion in the volume and complexity of documentation, making it challenging for developers to efficiently locate and comprehend relevant information. Annotations on documentation, such as comments and tags, have been touted as a potential solution to this problem. However, there is a lack of systematic understanding of how programmers utilize these annotations in practice. This study investigates the role of annotations in facilitating software development through a mixed-methods approach, combining a survey of 150 professional developers with a controlled laboratory experiment involving 30 participants. Our results show that annotations significantly improve documentation comprehension and reduce search time, with developers relying heavily on annotations to identify key functionality and troubleshoot issues. Furthermore, we identify specific annotation types, such as code snippets and usage examples, that are particularly effective in supporting programmer understanding. These findings have implications for the design of documentation tools and the development of more effective annotation strategies.

title: GAP Enhancing Semantic Interoperability of Genomic Datasets and Provenance Through Nanopublications
text: While the publication of datasets in scientific repositories has become broadly recognised, the repositories tend to have increasing semantic-related problems. For instance, they present various data reuse obstacles for machine-actionable processes, especially in biological repositories, hampering the reproducibility of scientific experiments. An example of these shortcomings is the GenBank database. We propose GAP, an innovative data model to enhance the semantic data meaning to address these issues. The model focuses on converging related approaches like data provenance, semantic interoperability, FAIR principles, and nanopublications. Our experiments include a prototype to scrape genomic data and trace them to nanopublications as a proof of concept. For this, (meta)data are stored in a three-level nanopub data model. The first level is related to a target organism, specifying data in terms of biological taxonomy. The second level focuses on the biological strains of the target, the central part of our contribution. The strains express information related to deciphered (meta)data of the genetic variations of the genomic material. The third level stores related scientific papers (meta)data. We expect it will offer higher data storage flexibility and more extensive interoperability with other data sources by incorporating and adopting associated approaches to store genomic data in the proposed model.

title: GAP Enhancing Semantic Interoperability of Genomic Datasets and Provenance Through Nanopublications
text: The increasing volume and diversity of genomic datasets have created a pressing need for effective semantic interoperability solutions, enabling seamless integration and meaningful analysis of data from disparate sources. Moreover, the provenance of genomic data, including its origin, processing history, and quality, is crucial for reproducibility and trustworthiness. To address these challenges, we present GAP (Genomic Annotation Platform), a novel framework designed to enhance semantic interoperability and provenance management of genomic datasets through nanopublications. GAP leverages a hybrid approach, combining semantic web technologies with a graph-based data model, to represent genomic data and its provenance as a network of interconnected nanopublications. We evaluated GAP using a corpus of 10,000 genomic datasets from diverse sources, demonstrating significant improvements in semantic interoperability, with an average increase of 37% in query recall and 25% in query precision compared to existing solutions. Furthermore, GAP's provenance tracking capabilities enabled the identification of data quality issues and inconsistencies, leading to a 30% reduction in data errors and discrepancies. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of GAP in facilitating large-scale integrative analysis of genomic data, while ensuring transparency and reproducibility.

title: Improved Pan-Private Stream Density Estimation
text: Differential privacy is a rigorous definition for privacy that guarantees that any analysis performed on a sensitive dataset leaks no information about the individuals whose data are contained therein. In this work, we develop new differentially private algorithms to analyze streaming data. Specifically, we consider the problem of estimating the density of a stream of users (or, more generally, elements), which expresses the fraction of all users that actually appear in the stream. We focus on one of the strongest privacy guarantees for the streaming model, namely user-level pan-privacy, which ensures that the privacy of any user is protected, even against an adversary that observes, on rare occasions, the internal state of the algorithm. Our proposed algorithms employ optimally all the allocated privacy budget, are specially tailored for the streaming model, and, hence, outperform both theoretically and experimentally the conventional sampling-based approach.

title: Improved Pan-Private Stream Density Estimation
text: Differential privacy provides a robust safeguard against information leakage in sensitive datasets, ensuring that analyses reveal no individual-specific details. This study presents novel differentially private algorithms for analyzing streaming data, focusing on the estimation of user density, which represents the proportion of users present in the stream. We concentrate on user-level pan-privacy, a stringent guarantee that protects individual privacy even against adversaries with occasional access to the algorithm's internal state. By optimally utilizing the allocated privacy budget, our algorithms are carefully crafted for the streaming model, thereby theoretically and empirically surpassing conventional sampling-based approaches. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our methods, which offer a significant improvement in privacy-preserving data analysis for streaming applications.

title: The Case for Learned In-Memory Joins
text: In-memory join is an essential operator in any database engine. It has been extensively investigated in the database literature. In this paper, we study whether exploiting the CDF-based learned models to boost the join performance is practical or not. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to fill this gap. We investigate the usage of CDF-based partitioning and learned indexes (e.g., Recursive Model Indexes (RMI) and RadixSpline) in the three join categories; indexed nested loop join (INLJ), sort-based joins (SJ) and hash-based joins (HJ). Our study shows that there is a room to improve the performance of INLJ and SJ categories through our proposed optimized learned variants. Our experimental analysis showed that these proposed learned variants of INLJ and SJ consistently outperform the state-of-the-art techniques.

title: The Case for Learned In-Memory Joins
text: Relational databases rely heavily on efficient join processing, yet traditional join algorithms are often bottlenecked by memory access patterns and cache locality. Recent advances in machine learning and in-memory computing have sparked interest in learned indexing and data structures. We explore the application of learned models to in-memory join processing, proposing a novel framework for Learned In-Memory Joins (LIMJ). Our approach leverages neural networks to predict join results, reducing the number of memory accesses and improving cache locality. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that LIMJ outperforms state-of-the-art join algorithms by up to 3.5x in terms of execution time, while maintaining high accuracy. We also show that LIMJ adapts well to varying data distributions and join types, making it a promising direction for future database systems research.

title: How a 4-day Work Week affects Agile Software Development Teams
text: Context: Agile software development (ASD) sets social aspects like communication and collaboration in focus. Thus, one may assume that the specific work organization of companies impacts the work of ASD teams. A major change in work organization is the switch to a 4-day work week, which some companies investigated in experiments. Also, recent studies show that ASD teams are affected by the switch to remote work since the Covid 19 pandemic outbreak in 2020. Objective: Our study presents empirical findings on the effects on ASD teams operating remote in a 4-day work week organization. Method: We performed a qualitative single case study and conducted seven semi-structured interviews, observed 14 agile practices and screened eight project documents and protocols of agile practices. Results: We found, that the teams adapted the agile method in use due to the change to a 4-day work week environment and the switch to remote work. The productivity of the two ASD teams did not decrease. Although the stress level of the ASD team member increased due to the 4-day work week, we found that the job satisfaction of the individual ASD team members is affected positively. Finally, we point to affects on social facets of the ASD teams. Conclusions: The research community benefits from our results as the current state of research dealing with the effects of a 4-day work week on ASD teams is limited. Also, our findings provide several practical implications for ASD teams working remote in a 4-day work week.

title: How a 4-day Work Week affects Agile Software Development Teams
text: The adoption of a 4-day work week has gained popularity in recent years, with proponents arguing that it can lead to increased productivity, improved work-life balance, and reduced environmental impact. However, the effects of this schedule on agile software development teams, which rely heavily on collaboration and rapid iteration, remain poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a mixed-methods study involving 12 agile teams from 6 organizations that transitioned to a 4-day work week for a period of 6 months. We collected quantitative data on team velocity, lead time, and defect density, as well as qualitative data through surveys, interviews, and focus groups. Our results show that, on average, teams experienced a 12% increase in velocity and a 9% reduction in lead time, while defect density remained largely unchanged. However, we also observed significant variation in team performance, with some teams experiencing declines in productivity. Our qualitative analysis revealed that the success of the 4-day work week was highly dependent on factors such as team composition, communication strategies, and management support. Specifically, teams with more experienced members, those that leveraged asynchronous communication tools, and those with managers who actively encouraged work-life balance were more likely to thrive in the 4-day work week environment. Our findings have important implications for software development organizations considering adopting a 4-day work week, highlighting the need for careful planning, effective communication, and tailored support to ensure success.

title: Cross-platform graphics subsystem for an ARINC 653-compatible real-time operating system
text: In the development of modern cockpits, there is a trend towards the use of large displays that combine information about air navigation and the status of aircraft equipment. Flight and equipment performance information generated by multiple flight control systems should be graphically displayed in an easy-to-read form on widescreen multifunction displays. It is usually generated by independent systems whose output must not interfere with each other in accordance with the requirements of the ARINC 653 standard. This paper presents a solution to the problem of displaying ARINC 653 applications, which further improves security and portability, when running multiple applications on a single screen of one physical device.

title: Cross-platform graphics subsystem for an ARINC 653-compatible real-time operating system
text: The proliferation of safety-critical real-time systems in avionics and automotive domains necessitates the development of reliable and efficient graphics subsystems. This paper presents a novel cross-platform graphics subsystem designed for an ARINC 653-compatible real-time operating system. Our approach leverages a microkernel-based architecture, decoupling the graphics rendering pipeline from the underlying operating system. We employ a modular design, utilizing OpenGL ES 3.0 and EGL 1.5 APIs to ensure platform independence. Experimental results on x86, ARM, and PowerPC architectures demonstrate a 30% reduction in graphics processing latency and a 25% increase in system responsiveness, while maintaining conformance to ARINC 653 and DO-178C safety standards.

title: Are automated static analysis tools worth it? An investigation into relative warning density and external software quality
text: Automated Static Analysis Tools (ASATs) are part of software development best practices. ASATs are able to warn developers about potential problems in the code. On the one hand, ASATs are based on best practices so there should be a noticeable effect on software quality. On the other hand, ASATs suffer from false positive warnings, which developers have to inspect and then ignore or mark as invalid. In this article, we ask the question if ASATs have a measurable impact on external software quality, using the example of PMD for Java. We investigate the relationship between ASAT warnings emitted by PMD on defects per change and per file. Our case study includes data for the history of each file as well as the differences between changed files and the project in which they are contained. We investigate whether files that induce a defect have more static analysis warnings than the rest of the project. Moreover, we investigate the impact of two different sets of ASAT rules. We find that, bug inducing files contain less static analysis warnings than other files of the project at that point in time. However, this can be explained by the overall decreasing warning density. When compared with all other changes, we find a statistically significant difference in one metric for all rules and two metrics for a subset of rules. However, the effect size is negligible in all cases, showing that the actual difference in warning density between bug inducing changes and other changes is small at best.

title: Are automated static analysis tools worth it? An investigation into relative warning density and external software quality
text: The efficacy of Automated Static Analysis Tools (ASATs) in enhancing software quality remains a topic of interest in software development practices. While ASATs are grounded in best practices, their impact on software quality is often mitigated by the prevalence of false positive warnings, which can lead to wasted developer resources. This study investigates the relationship between ASAT warnings and defect rates, using PMD for Java as a case study. We examine the correlation between PMD-emitted warnings and defects per change and per file, leveraging a comprehensive dataset that encompasses the version history of each file and the differences between modified files and their containing projects. Our analysis reveals that files inducing defects actually exhibit fewer static analysis warnings than other project files at a given point in time, a phenomenon attributable to the overall decline in warning density. Notwithstanding, we detect statistically significant differences in warning density between defect-inducing changes and other changes for select metrics, albeit with negligible effect sizes. These findings suggest that the disparity in warning density between defect-inducing changes and other changes is, at best, minimal.

title: The Integrated List of Agile Practices -- A Tertiary Study
text: Context: Companies adapt agile methods, practices or artifacts for their use in practice since more than two decades. This adaptions result in a wide variety of described agile practices. For instance, the Agile Alliance lists 75 different practices in its Agile Glossary. This situation may lead to misunderstandings, as agile practices with similar names can be interpreted and used differently. Objective: This paper synthesize an integrated list of agile practices, both from primary and secondary sources. Method: We performed a tertiary study to identify existing overviews and lists of agile practices in the literature. We identified 876 studies, of which 37 were included. Results: The results of our paper show that certain agile practices are listed and used more often in existing studies. Our integrated list of agile practices comprises 38 entries structured in five categories. Contribution: The high number of agile practices and thus, the wide variety increased steadily over the past decades due to the adaption of agile methods. Based on our findings, we present a comprehensive overview of agile practices. The research community benefits from our integrated list of agile practices as a potential basis for future research. Also, practitioners benefit from our findings, as the structured overview of agile practices provides the opportunity to select or adapt practices for their specific needs.

title: The Integrated List of Agile Practices -- A Tertiary Study
text: The widespread adoption of agile methods has led to a proliferation of adapted practices, resulting in a diverse landscape of agile approaches. The Agile Alliance's Agile Glossary, for instance, catalogs 75 distinct practices, which can lead to confusion due to similarities in naming and interpretation. To address this issue, our study aimed to consolidate a comprehensive list of agile practices from both primary and secondary sources. Through a tertiary study, we identified 876 relevant studies, ultimately including 37 in our analysis. Our results reveal that certain agile practices are more frequently cited and employed in existing research. We present a structured list of 38 agile practices, categorized into five groups, which provides a nuanced understanding of the agile practice landscape. The steady increase in agile practices over the past two decades underscores the need for a unified framework. Our integrated list offers a valuable resource for the research community, serving as a foundation for future investigations, and provides practitioners with a structured overview to inform their selection and adaptation of agile practices tailored to their specific needs.

title: Semantic Foundations of Seraph Continuous Graph Query Language
text: The scientific community has been studying graph data models for decades. Their high expressiveness and elasticity led the scientific community to design a variety of graph data models and graph query languages, and the practitioners to use them to model real-world cases and extract useful information. Recently, property graphs and, in particular, Cypher 9 (the first open version of the well-known Neo4j Inc.'s language) are gaining popularity. Practitioners find Cypher useful and applicable in many scenarios. However, we are living in a streaming world where data continuously flows. A growing number of Cypher's users show interest in continuously querying graph data to act in a timely fashion. Indeed, Cypher lacks the features for dealing with streams of (graph) data and continuous query evaluation. In this work, we propose Seraph, an extension of Cypher, as a first attempt to introduce streaming features in the context of property graph query languages. Specifically, we define Seraph semantics, we propose a first version of Seraph syntax, and we discuss the potential impacts from a user perspective.

title: Semantic Foundations of Seraph Continuous Graph Query Language
text: Decades of research have led to the development of various graph data models and query languages, leveraging their expressiveness and elasticity to model real-world cases and extract valuable insights. The recent popularity of property graphs, particularly Cypher 9, has further accelerated their adoption. While Cypher has proven useful in numerous scenarios, its limitations in handling streaming data and continuous query evaluation have become increasingly apparent. As data continuously flows, there is a growing need for timely decision-making, prompting Cypher users to seek continuous querying capabilities. To address this gap, we introduce Seraph, an extension of Cypher that incorporates streaming features into property graph query languages. We define the semantics of Seraph, propose an initial syntax, and explore the potential implications for users. By integrating streaming capabilities, Seraph enables real-time graph data processing, unlocking new opportunities for timely and informed decision-making.

title: Software Engineering for Responsible AI: An Empirical Study and Operationalised Patterns
text: Although artificial intelligence (AI) is solving real-world challenges and transforming industries, there are serious concerns about its ability to behave and make decisions in a responsible way. Many AI ethics principles and guidelines for responsible AI have been recently issued by governments, organisations, and enterprises. However, these AI ethics principles and guidelines are typically high-level and do not provide concrete guidance on how to design and develop responsible AI systems. To address this shortcoming, we first present an empirical study where we interviewed 21 scientists and engineers to understand the practitioners' perceptions on AI ethics principles and their implementation. We then propose a template that enables AI ethics principles to be operationalised in the form of concrete patterns and suggest a list of patterns using the newly created template. These patterns provide concrete, operationalised guidance that facilitate the development of responsible AI systems.

title: Software Engineering for Responsible AI: An Empirical Study and Operationalised Patterns
text: The increasing adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) in software systems has raised concerns about their potential impact on individuals and society. As AI systems become more pervasive, it is essential to ensure their development follows responsible practices that mitigate potential harm. This paper presents an empirical study investigating the current state of responsible AI practices in software engineering. We conducted a mixed-methods study, combining a survey of 150 software practitioners with 20 in-depth interviews and a case study of three organizations developing AI systems. Our results show that while practitioners acknowledge the importance of responsible AI, they often lack clear guidelines and operationalised practices to achieve it. We identified 15 operationalised patterns for responsible AI development, including transparent decision-making, human oversight, and value alignment. These patterns are grounded in our empirical findings and can be integrated into existing software engineering methodologies to promote responsible AI development practices.

title: InspectJS: Leveraging Code Similarity and User-Feedback for Effective Taint Specification Inference for JavaScript
text: Static analysis has established itself as a weapon of choice for detecting security vulnerabilities. Taint analysis in particular is a very general and powerful technique, where security policies are expressed in terms of forbidden flows, either from untrusted input sources to sensitive sinks (in integrity policies) or from sensitive sources to untrusted sinks (in confidentiality policies). The appeal of this approach is that the taint-tracking mechanism has to be implemented only once, and can then be parameterized with different taint specifications (that is, sets of sources and sinks, as well as any sanitizers that render otherwise problematic flows innocuous) to detect many different kinds of vulnerabilities. But while techniques for implementing scalable inter-procedural static taint tracking are fairly well established, crafting taint specifications is still more of an art than a science, and in practice tends to involve a lot of manual effort. Past work has focussed on automated techniques for inferring taint specifications for libraries either from their implementation or from the way they tend to be used in client code. Among the latter, machine learning-based approaches have shown great promise. In this work we present our experience combining an existing machine-learning approach to mining sink specifications for JavaScript libraries with manual taint modelling in the context of GitHub's CodeQL analysis framework. We show that the machine-learning component can successfully infer many new taint sinks that either are not part of the manual modelling or are not detected due to analysis incompleteness. Moreover, we present techniques for organizing sink predictions using automated ranking and code-similarity metrics that allow an analysis engineer to efficiently sift through large numbers of predictions to identify true positives.

title: InspectJS: Leveraging Code Similarity and User-Feedback for Effective Taint Specification Inference for JavaScript
text: The efficacy of static analysis in detecting security vulnerabilities has been well-documented, with taint analysis emerging as a versatile and powerful technique. This approach involves expressing security policies in terms of prohibited information flows, either from untrusted sources to sensitive sinks (integrity policies) or from sensitive sources to untrusted sinks (confidentiality policies). A key advantage of taint analysis lies in its flexibility, as a single taint-tracking mechanism can be parameterized with diverse taint specifications to identify various types of vulnerabilities. While scalable inter-procedural static taint tracking has become increasingly well-established, crafting effective taint specifications remains a labor-intensive task that relies heavily on manual effort. Recent research has focused on automating the inference of taint specifications for libraries, leveraging either implementation details or usage patterns in client code. Machine learning-based approaches have shown particular promise in this regard. This study combines an existing machine learning-based approach for mining sink specifications in JavaScript libraries with manual taint modeling within GitHub's CodeQL analysis framework. Our results demonstrate that the machine learning component can successfully identify numerous novel taint sinks not captured by manual modeling or obscured by analysis limitations. Furthermore, we present novel techniques for ranking and filtering sink predictions using code similarity metrics, enabling analysis engineers to efficiently identify true positives from large sets of predictions.

title: A Case Study on Optimization of Platooning Coordination
text: In today's world, circumstances, processes, and requirements for software systems are becoming increasingly complex. In order to operate properly in such dynamic environments, software systems must adapt to these changes, which has led to the research area of Self-Adaptive Systems (SAS). Platooning is one example of adaptive systems in Intelligent Transportation Systems, which is the ability of vehicles to travel with close inter-vehicle distances. This technology leads to an increase in road throughput and safety, which directly addresses the increased infrastructure needs due to increased traffic on the roads. However, the No-Free-Lunch theorem states that the performance of one platooning coordination strategy is not necessarily transferable to other problems. Moreover, especially in the field of SAS, the selection of the most appropriate strategy depends on the current situation of the system. In this paper, we address the problem of self-aware optimization of adaptation planning strategies by designing a framework that includes situation detection, strategy selection, and parameter optimization of the selected strategies. We apply our approach on the case study platooning coordination and evaluate the performance of the proposed framework.

title: A Case Study on Optimization of Platooning Coordination
text: The escalating complexity of software systems necessitates adaptability to dynamic environments, giving rise to the research area of Self-Adaptive Systems (SAS). One exemplar of adaptive systems in Intelligent Transportation Systems is platooning, which enables vehicles to travel in close proximity, thereby increasing road throughput and safety. This technology addresses the pressing issue of infrastructure needs exacerbated by growing traffic volumes. However, the No-Free-Lunch theorem underscores the limitations of platooning coordination strategies, emphasizing that performance is not universally transferable across problems. Furthermore, in the context of SAS, the optimal strategy selection depends on the system's current state. This paper presents a framework for self-aware optimization of adaptation planning strategies, encompassing situation detection, strategy selection, and parameter optimization. We validate our approach through a case study on platooning coordination, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework in dynamically adapting to changing system conditions.

title: Measuring source code conciseness across programming languages using compression
text: It is well-known, and often a topic of heated debates, that programs in some programming languages are more concise than in others. This is a relevant factor when comparing or aggregating volume-impacted metrics on source code written in a combination of programming languages. In this paper, we present a model for measuring the conciseness of programming languages in a consistent, objective and evidence-based way. We present the approach, explain how it is founded on information theoretical principles, present detailed analysis steps and show the quantitative results of applying this model to a large benchmark of diverse commercial software applications. We demonstrate that our metric for language conciseness is strongly correlated with both an alternative analytical approach, and with a large scale developer survey, and show how its results can be applied to improve software metrics for multi-language applications.

title: Measuring source code conciseness across programming languages using compression
text: The conciseness of source code has long been recognized as a key factor in software maintainability, readability, and overall quality. However, measuring conciseness objectively across different programming languages remains an open challenge. In this study, we propose a novel approach to quantifying source code conciseness using lossless compression algorithms. We collect a large-scale dataset of open-source projects across eight popular programming languages and apply standard compression techniques to measure the compressibility of each codebase. Our results show that, despite differences in syntax and paradigm, programming languages exhibit distinct conciseness profiles, with functional languages (Haskell, Scala) generally outperforming imperative languages (C, Java). Furthermore, we find that conciseness is strongly correlated with established software quality metrics, such as cyclomatic complexity and Halstead's effort. Our findings have implications for language design, code quality assessment, and software development best practices.

title: Improving Prediction-Based Lossy Compression Dramatically via Ratio-Quality Modeling
text: Error-bounded lossy compression is one of the most effective techniques for scientific data reduction. However, the traditional trial-and-error approach used to configure lossy compressors for finding the optimal trade-off between reconstructed data quality and compression ratio is prohibitively expensive. To resolve this issue, we develop a general-purpose analytical ratio-quality model based on the prediction-based lossy compression framework, which can effectively foresee the reduced data quality and compression ratio, as well as the impact of the lossy compressed data on post-hoc analysis quality. Our analytical model significantly improves the prediction-based lossy compression in three use-cases: (1) optimization of predictor by selecting the best-fit predictor; (2) memory compression with a target ratio; and (3) in-situ compression optimization by fine-grained error-bound tuning of various data partitions. We evaluate our analytical model on 10 scientific datasets, demonstrating its high accuracy (93.47% accuracy on average) and low computational cost (up to 18.7X lower than the trial-and-error approach) for estimating the compression ratio and the impact of lossy compression on post-hoc analysis quality. We also verified the high efficiency of our ratio-quality model using different applications across the three use-cases. In addition, the experiment demonstrates that our modeling based approach reduces the time to store the 3D Reverse Time Migration data by up to 3.4X over the traditional solution using 128 CPU cores from 8 compute nodes.

title: Improving Prediction-Based Lossy Compression Dramatically via Ratio-Quality Modeling
text: The proliferation of IoT devices and edge computing has led to an explosion in the volume of sensory data, necessitating efficient compression techniques to mitigate storage and transmission costs. Prediction-based lossy compression (PLC) has emerged as a promising approach, leveraging the inherent correlations in time-series data to achieve high compression ratios. However, existing PLC methods often rely on simplistic quality metrics, such as mean squared error or peak signal-to-noise ratio, which fail to capture the nuanced relationships between compression ratio and data quality. This paper proposes a novel ratio-quality modeling framework that fundamentally reshapes the PLC paradigm. By explicitly modeling the intricate tradeoffs between compression ratio and data quality, our approach enables the derivation of optimal compression strategies that dramatically outperform state-of-the-art PLC techniques. Our method is rooted in a probabilistic framework, wherein we jointly model the compression ratio and data quality as a bivariate distribution, allowing for the computation of conditional probabilities that inform compression decisions. Experimental evaluations on a diverse range of datasets, including climate, traffic, and financial time series, demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, yielding average compression ratio improvements of 35% and quality enhancements of 25% compared to existing PLC methods. Furthermore, our ratio-quality models exhibit superior robustness to varying data characteristics and compression settings, underscoring the versatility of our framework in real-world compression applications.

title: Method for representing an exponent in a fifth-dimensional hypercomplex number systems using a hypercomplex computing software
text: The structure of method for constructing a representation of an exponential function in hypercomplex number systems(HNS) by the method of solving an associated system of linear differential equations is considered. Brief information about the hypercomplex computing software (HCS) is given. With the use of HCS, the necessary cumbersome operations on symbolic expressions were performed when constructing the representation of the exponent in the fifth-dimensional HNS. title: Method for representing an exponent in a fifth-dimensional hypercomplex number systems using a hypercomplex computing software
text: This study explores a novel methodology for constructing exponential function representations within hypercomplex number systems (HNS) by leveraging the solution of associated systems of linear differential equations. The hypercomplex computing software (HCS) is utilized to facilitate cumbersome symbolic expression operations, enabling the successful construction of an exponential representation in a fifth-dimensional HNS. The paper presents HCS programming fragments and resultant symbolic calculation outcomes, demonstrating the efficacy of this approach.

title: Efficiently Transforming Tables for Joinability
text: Data from different sources rarely conform to a single formatting even if they describe the same set of entities, and this raises concerns when data from multiple sources must be joined or cross-referenced. Such a formatting mismatch is unavoidable when data is gathered from various public and third-party sources. Commercial database systems are not able to perform the join when there exist differences in data representation or formatting, and manual reformatting is both time consuming and error-prone. We study the problem of efficiently joining textual data under the condition that the join columns are not formatted the same and cannot be equi-joined, but they become joinable under some transformations. The problem is challenging simply because the number of possible transformations explodes with both the length of the input and the number of rows, even if each transformation is formed using very few basic units. We show that an efficient algorithm can be developed based on the common characteristics of the joined columns, and develop one such algorithm over a rich set of basic operations that can be composed to form transformations. We compare both the coverage and the running time of our algorithm to a state-of-the-art approach, and show that our algorithm covers every transformation that is covered in the state-of-the-art approach but is a few orders of magnitude faster, as evaluated on various real and synthetic data.

title: Efficiently Transforming Tables for Joinability
text: Discrepancies in data formatting are ubiquitous when integrating data from diverse sources, hindering the join and cross-referencing of entities. This mismatch is inherent when aggregating data from public and third-party sources, as commercial database systems are incapable of performing joins in the presence of representation or formatting differences. Manual reformatting is a time-consuming and error-prone solution, necessitating an efficient algorithmic approach. We investigate the problem of joining textual data with non-uniformly formatted join columns, which can be rendered joinable through suitable transformations. The complexity of this problem arises from the exponential growth of possible transformations with increasing input length and row count, despite the use of basic units. By exploiting the common characteristics of joined columns, we develop an efficient algorithm that leverages a rich set of compositional basic operations to form transformations. Our algorithm is shown to surpass a state-of-the-art approach in both coverage and running time, with evaluations on real and synthetic data demonstrating orders-of-magnitude improvements.

title: Interactive Set Discovery
text: We study the problem of set discovery where given a few example tuples of a desired set, we want to find the set in a collection of sets. A challenge is that the example tuples may not uniquely identify a set, and a large number of candidate sets may be returned. Our focus is on interactive exploration to set discovery where additional example tuples from the candidate sets are shown and the user either accepts or rejects them as members of the target set. The goal is to find the target set with the least number of user interactions. The problem can be cast as an optimization problem where we want to find a decision tree that can guide the search to the target set with the least number of questions to be answered by the user. We propose a general algorithm that is capable of reaching an optimal solution and two variations of it that strike a balance between the quality of a solution and the running time. We also propose a novel pruning strategy that safely reduces the search space without introducing false negatives. We evaluate the efficiency and the effectiveness of our algorithms through an extensive experimental study using both real and synthetic datasets and comparing them to previous approaches in the literature. We show that our pruning strategy reduces the running time of the search algorithms by 2-5 orders of magnitude.

title: Interactive Set Discovery
text: The proliferation of large-scale datasets in various domains has led to an increased interest in set discovery, a problem that involves identifying meaningful subsets within a dataset. While existing approaches have primarily focused on automated set discovery, they often fail to incorporate human intuition and domain expertise, leading to suboptimal results. Interactive set discovery, which involves soliciting user feedback to guide the discovery process, has the potential to significantly improve the quality and relevance of discovered sets. In this work, we propose an interactive set discovery framework that leverages active learning and visualization techniques to involve users in the discovery process. Our framework utilizes a novel sampling strategy that balances exploration and exploitation, allowing users to provide feedback on the most informative sets. We also develop an efficient indexing scheme to facilitate real-time visualization and exploration of the dataset. We evaluate our framework on several real-world datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in discovering meaningful sets that align with user expectations. Our results show that interactive set discovery can lead to a significant improvement in set quality and user satisfaction, compared to automated approaches. Furthermore, we observe that user feedback can be effectively incorporated into the discovery process with minimal additional overhead. Our work has important implications for various applications, including data exploration, pattern discovery, and decision-making.

title: An Index for Single Source All Destinations Distance Queries in Temporal Graphs
text: Temporal closeness is a generalization of the classical closeness centrality measure for analyzing evolving networks. The temporal closeness of a vertex $v$ is defined as the sum of the reciprocals of the temporal distances to the other vertices. Ranking all vertices of a network according to the temporal closeness is computationally expensive as it leads to a single-source-all-destination (SSAD) temporal distance query starting from each vertex of the graph. To reduce the running time of temporal closeness computations, we introduce an index to speed up SSAD temporal distance queries called Substream index. We show that deciding if a Substream index of a given size exists is NP-complete and provide an efficient greedy approximation. Moreover, we improve the running time of the approximation using min-hashing and parallelization. Our evaluation with real-world temporal networks shows a running time improvement of up to one order of magnitude compared to the state-of-the-art temporal closeness ranking algorithms.

title: An Index for Single Source All Destinations Distance Queries in Temporal Graphs
text: Temporal graphs, which model relationships between entities that evolve over time, have become increasingly important in various applications, including social network analysis and traffic pattern mining. One fundamental problem in temporal graph analysis is the single source all destinations (SSAD) distance query, which seeks to find the shortest temporal distance from a source node to all other nodes in the graph. Existing solutions for this problem have high computational costs, making them inefficient for large-scale datasets. We propose a novel index-based approach to accelerate SSAD distance queries in temporal graphs. Our method, called TempoIndex, leverages a combination of graph decomposition and interval indexing to efficiently store and query temporal shortest paths. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that TempoIndex outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to two orders of magnitude in terms of query response time, while requiring only moderate additional storage overhead. Our approach enables fast and scalable analysis of temporal graph datasets, facilitating insights into complex dynamic systems.

title: Formal verification of space systems designed with TASTE
text: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) is a development approach aiming to build correct-by-construction systems, provided the use of clear, unambiguous and complete models to describe them along the design process. The approach is supported by several engineering tools that automate the development steps, for example the production of code, documentation, test cases and more. TASTE [1] is pragmatic MBSE toolset supported by ESA that encapsulates several technologies to design a system (data modelling, architecture modelling, behaviour modelling/implementation), to automatically generate the binary application(s), and to validate it. One topic left open in TASTE is the formal verification of a system design with respect to specified properties. In this paper we describe our approach based on the IF model-checker [4] to enable the formal verification of properties on TASTE designs. The approach is currently under development in the ESA MoC4Space project.

title: Formal verification of space systems designed with TASTE
text: The development of space systems poses unique challenges, particularly in ensuring the reliability and correctness of onboard software. The TASTE (The Autonomous Spacecraft Terminal Environment) framework has gained popularity in this domain due to its model-driven engineering approach and automated code generation capabilities. However, the lack of formal verification techniques hinders the adoption of TASTE in safety-critical space applications. This paper presents a formal verification framework for TASTE-designed space systems, leveraging the expressive power of higher-order logic. We encode TASTE's AADL (Architecture Analysis and Design Language) models in the HOL4 theorem prover and develop a set of formal verification procedures to establish the correctness of system architectures and component interactions. Our evaluation on a set of case studies demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach in detecting subtle design flaws and ensuring compliance with safety standards, thereby increasing the confidence in TASTE-based space systems.

title: UEFI virtual machine firmware hardening through snapshots and attack surface reduction
text: The Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) is a standardised interface between the firmware and the operating system used in all x86-based platforms over the past ten years. A side effect of the transition from conventional BIOS implementations to more complex and flexible implementations based on the UEFI was that it became easier for the malware to target BIOS in a widespread fashion, as these BIOS implementations are based on a common specification. This paper introduces Amaranth project - a solution to some of the contemporary security issues related to UEFI firmware. In this work we focused our attention on virtual machines as it allowed us to simplify the development of secure UEFI firmware. Security hardening of our firmware is achieved through several techniques, the most important of which are an operating system integrity checking mechanism (through snapshots) and overall firmware size reduction.

title: UEFI virtual machine firmware hardening through snapshots and attack surface reduction
text: The widespread adoption of Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) as a standardized interface between firmware and operating systems in x86-based platforms over the past decade has inadvertently created a homogeneous attack surface, facilitating malware targeting of BIOS implementations. This vulnerability stems from the shift from conventional BIOS to more complex and flexible UEFI-based implementations, which are built upon a common specification. The Amaranth project addresses these contemporary UEFI firmware security concerns by leveraging virtual machines to simplify secure firmware development. Our approach employs multiple security hardening techniques, including an operating system integrity checking mechanism via snapshots and a significant reduction in firmware size. These innovations collectively enhance the security posture of UEFI firmware, mitigating the risk of widespread attacks.

title: Datasets for Online Controlled Experiments
text: Online Controlled Experiments (OCE) are the gold standard to measure impact and guide decisions for digital products and services. Despite many methodological advances in this area, the scarcity of public datasets and the lack of a systematic review and categorization hinder its development. We present the first survey and taxonomy for OCE datasets, which highlight the lack of a public dataset to support the design and running of experiments with adaptive stopping, an increasingly popular approach to enable quickly deploying improvements or rolling back degrading changes. We release the first such dataset, containing daily checkpoints of decision metrics from multiple, real experiments run on a global e-commerce platform. The dataset design is guided by a broader discussion on data requirements for common statistical tests used in digital experimentation. We demonstrate how to use the dataset in the adaptive stopping scenario using sequential and Bayesian hypothesis tests and learn the relevant parameters for each approach.

title: Datasets for Online Controlled Experiments
text: The widespread adoption of online controlled experiments (OCEs) in digital product development has underscored the need for systematic evaluation and categorization of OCE datasets. Despite notable methodological advances, the scarcity of publicly available datasets hinders further progress in this field. This study addresses this gap by presenting the first comprehensive survey and taxonomy of OCE datasets, revealing a significant lack of datasets supporting adaptive stopping, a increasingly popular approach for rapid deployment and rollback of changes. To fill this void, we introduce a novel dataset comprising daily checkpoints of decision metrics from multiple real-world experiments conducted on a global e-commerce platform. Our dataset design is informed by a thorough examination of data requirements for common statistical tests in digital experimentation. We demonstrate the dataset's utility in adaptive stopping scenarios using sequential and Bayesian hypothesis tests, and provide insights into parameter estimation for each approach.

title: A privacy-aware zero interaction smart mobility system
text: Smart cities often rely on technological innovation to improve citizens' safety and quality of life. This paper presents a novel smart mobility system that aims to facilitate people accessing public mobility while preserving their privacy. The system is based on a zero interaction approach whereby a person can use public transport services without any need to perform explicit actions. Operations related to ticket purchase and validation have been fully automated. The system is also designed with the privacy-by-design paradigm in mind, to preserve user privacy as much as possible. Throughout the paper several technical details are discussed as well to describe a prototype version of the system that was implemented. The prototype has been successfully tested in the city of Imola (Emilia Romagna, Italy) in order to prove the system validity on the field.

title: A privacy-aware zero interaction smart mobility system
text: Citizens' safety and quality of life in urban environments are increasingly dependent on technological advancements. This research proposes a novel smart mobility system that seamlessly integrates public transportation access with stringent privacy preservation. By adopting a zero-interaction approach, users can utilize public transport services without explicit actions, as ticket purchasing and validation operations are fully automated. The system's architecture is grounded in the privacy-by-design principle, ensuring optimal user privacy protection. We delve into the technical underpinnings of the system, detailing a prototype implementation that was successfully tested in Imola, Italy, thereby validating its real-world efficacy. The results of this field trial underscore the system's potential to transform urban mobility while safeguarding citizen privacy.

title: Understanding Developers Well-Being and Productivity: a 2-year Longitudinal Analysis during the COVID-19 Pandemic
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has brought significant and enduring shifts in various aspects of life, including increased flexibility in work arrangements. In a longitudinal study, spanning 24 months with six measurement points from April 2020 to April 2022, we explore changes in well-being, productivity, social contacts, and needs of software engineers during this time. Our findings indicate systematic changes in various variables. For example, well-being and quality of social contacts increased while emotional loneliness decreased as lockdown measures were relaxed. Conversely, people's boredom and productivity, remained stable. Furthermore, a preliminary investigation into the future of work at the end of the pandemic revealed a consensus among developers for a preference of hybrid work arrangements. We also discovered that prior job changes and low job satisfaction were consistently linked to intentions to change jobs if current work conditions do not meet developers' needs. This highlights the need for software organizations to adapt to various work arrangements to remain competitive employers. Building upon our findings and the existing literature, we introduce the Integrated Job Demands-Resources and Self-Determination (IJARS) Model as a comprehensive framework to explain the well-being and productivity of software engineers during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Understanding Developers Well-Being and Productivity: a 2-year Longitudinal Analysis during the COVID-19 Pandemic
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has precipitated profound and lasting transformations in various aspects of life, including the widespread adoption of flexible work arrangements. A 24-month longitudinal study, comprising six measurement points from April 2020 to April 2022, investigates the dynamics of well-being, productivity, social contacts, and needs among software engineers during this period. The results reveal systematic shifts in these variables, including increments in well-being and quality of social contacts, accompanied by decreases in emotional loneliness, as lockdown restrictions were gradually lifted. In contrast, boredom and productivity remained relatively stable. Notably, a preliminary exploration of post-pandemic work arrangements reveals a prevailing preference among developers for hybrid work models. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the significance of prior job changes and low job satisfaction as predictors of intentions to change jobs if current work conditions fail to meet developers' needs. This underscores the imperative for software organizations to accommodate diverse work arrangements to maintain their competitiveness as employers. Our findings inform the development of the Integrated Job Demands-Resources and Self-Determination (IJARS) Model, a comprehensive framework explaining the well-being and productivity of software engineers during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Fast Discovery of Nested Dependencies on JSON Data
text: Functional and inclusion dependencies are the most widely used classes of data dependencies in data profiling due to their ability to identify relationships in data such as primary and foreign keys. These relationships are equally important when dealing with nested data formats such as JSON. However, the definition of functional and inclusion dependencies makes use of a flat, unnested relational model which misses many useful types of dependencies on data which involve nested data models. In this work, we identify types of dependencies which are not captured by traditional functional and inclusion dependencies but which nevertheless capture meaningful relationships among nested data. We also demonstrate how algorithms for mining these traditional dependencies can be adapted to also mine nested dependencies. The first strategy simply flattens the input data and feeds into unmodified existing algorithms. We present a second strategy which instead adapts the algorithm to efficiently process JSON data as input which in some cases leads to a reduction in runtime by multiple orders of magnitude on real-world datasets. We further show how these algorithms can be adapted to produce useful results in the presence of a percentage of incomplete or invalid data.

title: Fast Discovery of Nested Dependencies on JSON Data
text: The discovery of relationships within data, such as primary and foreign keys, is facilitated by functional and inclusion dependencies, which are extensively employed in data profiling. Although these dependencies are equally crucial when handling nested data formats like JSON, their traditional definitions rely on a flat, relational model that overlooks numerous valuable dependencies inherent to nested data structures. This research identifies novel types of dependencies that, while not captured by conventional functional and inclusion dependencies, reveal meaningful relationships within nested data. Furthermore, we demonstrate the adaptability of existing algorithms for mining traditional dependencies to accommodate nested dependencies. Two strategies are presented: a straightforward approach involving data flattening, and a more nuanced method that efficiently processes JSON data, yielding runtime reductions of multiple orders of magnitude on real-world datasets. Additionally, we illustrate the algorithms' ability to produce useful results in the presence of incomplete or invalid data, ensuring robustness in real-world applications.

title: Modeling and Analysis of the Landing Gear System with the Generalized Contracts
text: Nowadays, there are several complex systems in different sectors such as aviation, air traffic control ...etc. These systems do not have a precise perimeter, they are open and made of various specific components built with different languages and environments. The modeling, assembly and analysis of such open and complex heterogeneous systems are challenges in software engineering. This paper describes how the Minarets method decreases the difficulty of modeling, composition and analysis of the well known case study of the landing gear system. The method consists in: equipping individual components with generalized contracts that integrate various facets related to different concerns, composing these components according to their facets and verifying the resulting system with respect to the involved facets as well. The proposed method may be used or extended to cover more facets, and by strengthening assistance tool through proactive aspects in modeling, composing multi-facets contracts and finally the verification of the heterogeneous systems.

title: Modeling and Analysis of the Landing Gear System with the Generalized Contracts
text: Complex systems, prevalent in domains such as aviation and air traffic control, often lack well-defined perimeters and comprise diverse components developed in disparate languages and environments. The modeling, assembly, and analysis of these open and heterogeneous systems pose significant software engineering challenges. This paper presents the Minarets method, which alleviates these challenges in the context of the well-known landing gear system case study. The method involves equipping individual components with generalized contracts that integrate multiple facets related to various concerns, followed by component composition based on these facets and verification of the resulting system with respect to the involved facets. The proposed approach can be extended to accommodate additional facets and reinforced through tool support, enabling proactive modeling, multi-facet contract composition, and heterogeneous system verification.

title: INCHE: High-Performance Encoding for Relational Databases through Incrementally Homomorphic Encryption
text: Homomorphic encryption (HE) offers data confidentiality by executing queries directly on encrypted fields in the database-as-a-service (DaaS) paradigm. While fully HE exhibits great expressiveness but prohibitive performance overhead, a better balance between flexibility and efficiency can be achieved by partially HE schemes. Performance-wise, however, the encryption rate of state-of-the-art HE schemes is still orders of magnitude lower than the I/O throughput, rendering the HE scheme the performance bottleneck. This paper proposes INCHE, an incrementally homomorphic encryption scheme, which aims to boost the performance of HE schemes by incrementally encrypting fields in relational databases. The key idea of INCHE is to explore the intrinsic correlation between plaintexts and cache them for future reuse such that expensive HE primitives from plaintexts to ciphertexts are avoided. We prove the semantic security of INCHE under the chosen-plaintext attack (CPA) model and show that its time complexity is linear in the plaintext length. We implement an INCHE prototype by extending the Symmetria cryptosystem and verify its effectiveness on both randomly-generated data and the TPC-H benchmark.

title: INCHE: High-Performance Encoding for Relational Databases through Incrementally Homomorphic Encryption
text: The widespread adoption of cloud-based relational databases has heightened concerns about data confidentiality, driving the need for efficient encryption techniques that preserve query functionality. Homomorphic encryption (HE) has emerged as a promising solution, enabling computations on encrypted data without decryption. However, existing HE schemes suffer from high computational overhead, rendering them impractical for large-scale relational databases. To address this limitation, we propose INCHE, a novel incrementally homomorphic encryption scheme tailored for relational databases. INCHE leverages the inherent structure of relational data to incrementally update encrypted representations, significantly reducing computational costs. Our approach exploits the monotonicity of aggregation functions, allowing for efficient evaluation of range queries and aggregations on encrypted data. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that INCHE outperforms state-of-the-art HE schemes by up to 3 orders of magnitude in terms of encryption and query processing times, while maintaining a high level of security. INCHE's performance gains make it a viable solution for encrypting large-scale relational databases, enabling secure querying and analysis of sensitive data in cloud-based environments.

title: Challenging Machine Learning-based Clone Detectors via Semantic-preserving Code Transformations
text: Software clone detection identifies similar code snippets. It has been an active research topic that attracts extensive attention over the last two decades. In recent years, machine learning (ML) based detectors, especially deep learning-based ones, have demonstrated impressive capability on clone detection. It seems that this longstanding problem has already been tamed owing to the advances in ML techniques. In this work, we would like to challenge the robustness of the recent ML-based clone detectors through code semantic-preserving transformations. We first utilize fifteen simple code transformation operators combined with commonly-used heuristics (i.e., Random Search, Genetic Algorithm, and Markov Chain Monte Carlo) to perform equivalent program transformation. Furthermore, we propose a deep reinforcement learning-based sequence generation (DRLSG) strategy to effectively guide the search process of generating clones that could escape from the detection. We then evaluate the ML-based detectors with the pairs of original and generated clones. We realize our method in a framework named CloneGen. CloneGen In evaluation, we challenge the two state-of-the-art ML-based detectors and four traditional detectors with the code clones after semantic-preserving transformations via the aid of CloneGen. Surprisingly, our experiments show that, despite the notable successes achieved by existing clone detectors, the ML models inside these detectors still cannot distinguish numerous clones produced by the code transformations in CloneGen. In addition, adversarial training of ML-based clone detectors using clones generated by CloneGen can improve their robustness and accuracy. CloneGen Meanwhile, compared with the commonly-used heuristics, the DRLSG strategy has shown the best effectiveness in generating code clones to decrease the detection accuracy of the ML-based detectors.

title: Challenging Machine Learning-based Clone Detectors via Semantic-preserving Code Transformations
text: Code clone detection, a fundamental task in software engineering, has witnessed significant advancements with the advent of machine learning-based approaches. These techniques leverage patterns learned from large codebases to identify duplicated code segments, facilitating code reuse, plagiarism detection, and software maintenance. However, the robustness of these detectors against adversarial code transformations remains unexplored. In this context, we investigate the vulnerability of state-of-the-art machine learning-based clone detectors to semantic-preserving code transformations. We propose a systematic framework to generate transformed code variants that preserve the original code's semantics but alter its syntactic structure. Our framework combines program analysis, code refactoring, and machine learning-driven perturbations to create a diverse set of challenging code samples. We evaluate the resilience of six prominent machine learning-based clone detectors against our generated code transformations. The experimental results reveal that these detectors are susceptible to significant performance degradation, with accuracy drops ranging from 15% to 43%, when confronted with transformed code. Notably, we observe that detectors relying on syntactic features are more vulnerable to our transformations than those incorporating semantic features. Our findings have important implications for the development of robust code clone detection systems, highlighting the need for detectors that can effectively generalize across diverse code representations. Furthermore, our framework provides a valuable tool for benchmarking the robustness of clone detectors and guiding the design of more resilient approaches.

title: Experience-Enhanced Learning: One Size Still does not Fit All in Automatic Database
text: Recent years, the database committee has attempted to develop automatic database management systems. Although some researches show that the applying AI to data management is a significant and promising direction, there still exists many problems in implementing these techniques to real applications (long training time, various environments and unstable performance). In this paper, we discover that traditional rule based methods have the potential to solve the above problems. We propose three methodologies for improving learned methods, i.e. label collection for efficiently pre-training, knowledge base for model transfer and theoretical guarantee for stable performance. We implement our methodologies on two widely used learning approaches, deep learning and reinforcement learning. Firstly, the novel experience enhanced deep learning (EEDL) could achieve efficient training and stable performance. We evaluate EEDL with cardinality estimation, an essential database management. The experimental results on four real dataset [1] show that our EEDL could outperforms the general DL model [2]. Secondly, we design a novel experience-enhanced reinforcement learning (EERL), which could efficiently converge and has better performance than general RL models [3]. We test EERL with online index tuning task. The experiments on TPC-H shows that EERL could accelerate the convergence of agent and generate better solution that generalizes the reinforcement learning.

title: Experience-Enhanced Learning: One Size Still does not Fit All in Automatic Database
text: The quest for a one-size-fits-all approach to automatic database tuning has been a longstanding challenge in the database community. Despite significant advances in machine learning-based tuning, existing solutions often neglect the crucial role of experience in informing the optimization process. We argue that incorporating experience-driven insights can significantly enhance the effectiveness of automatic database tuning. To this end, we propose Experience-Enhanced Learning (EEL), a novel framework that integrates human expertise with machine learning-based optimization. EEL leverages a multi-modal knowledge graph that captures both database-specific knowledge and expert feedback, which is then used to guide the search for optimal configurations. Our experimental evaluation on a diverse set of real-world databases reveals that EEL outperforms state-of-the-art automatic tuning approaches by up to 35% in terms of query performance and 25% in terms of resource utilization. Furthermore, we observe that EEL's performance gains are most pronounced in scenarios characterized by high variability in workload patterns and database schema complexity. Our findings suggest that experience-enhanced learning can be a game-changer in automatic database tuning, and we envision EEL as a key enabler of more efficient, adaptable, and human-centered database systems.

title: A Software Tool for Evaluating Unmanned Autonomous Systems
text: The North Carolina Agriculture and Technical State University (NC A&T) in collaboration with Georgia Tech Research Institute (GTRI) has developed methodologies for creating simulation-based technology tools that are capable of inferring the perceptions and behavioral states of autonomous systems. These methodologies have the potential to provide the Test and Evaluation (T&E) community at the Department of Defense (DoD) with a greater insight into the internal processes of these systems. The methodologies use only external observations and do not require complete knowledge of the internal processing of and/or any modifications to the system under test. This paper presents an example of one such simulation-based technology tool, named as the Data-Driven Intelligent Prediction Tool (DIPT). DIPT was developed for testing a multi-platform Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) system capable of conducting collaborative search missions. DIPT's Graphical User Interface (GUI) enables the testers to view the aircraft's current operating state, predicts its current target-detection status, and provides reasoning for exhibiting a particular behavior along with an explanation of assigning a particular task to it.

title: A Software Tool for Evaluating Unmanned Autonomous Systems
text: The development of Unmanned Autonomous Systems (UAS) has seen significant growth in recent years, with applications in various domains such as surveillance, search and rescue, and environmental monitoring. However, evaluating the performance of UAS in complex scenarios remains a challenging task. Existing evaluation methods rely on manual observation, simulation, or ad-hoc testing, which are time-consuming, prone to human error, and lack standardization. To address these limitations, we propose a software tool for evaluating UAS performance in a systematic and reproducible manner. Our tool, called UAS-Evaluator, provides a comprehensive framework for designing and executing experiments, collecting and processing data, and analyzing performance metrics. We implemented UAS-Evaluator using a modular architecture, allowing for easy integration with various UAS platforms and sensors. Experimental results using a quadcopter platform demonstrate the effectiveness of UAS-Evaluator in evaluating navigation, control, and sensing performance in real-world scenarios. Our tool reduces evaluation time by 60% and improves accuracy by 25% compared to traditional methods, enabling faster and more reliable development of UAS applications.

title: Explainable Software Defect Prediction: Are We There Yet?
text: Explaining the prediction results of software defect prediction models is a challenging while practical task, which can provide useful information for developers to understand and fix the predicted bugs. To address this issue, recently, Jiarpakdee et al. proposed to use {two state-of-the-art} model-agnostic techniques (i.e., LIME and BreakDown) to explain the prediction results of bug prediction models. Their experiments show these tools can generate promising results and the generated explanations can assist developers understand the prediction results. However, the fact that LIME and BreakDown were only examined on a single software defect prediction model setting calls into question about their consistency and reliability across software defect prediction models with various settings. In this paper, we set out to investigate the consistency and reliability of model-agnostic technique based explanation generation approaches (i.e., LIME and BreakDown) on software defect prediction models with different settings , e.g., different data sampling techniques, different machine learning classifiers, and different prediction scenarios. Specifically, we use both LIME and BreakDown to generate explanations for the same instance under software defect prediction models with different settings and then check the consistency of the generated explanations for the instance. We reused the same defect data from Jiarpakdee et al. in our experiments. The results show that both LIME and BreakDown generate inconsistent explanations under different software defect prediction settings for the same test instances, which makes them unreliable for explanation generation. Overall, with this study, we call for more research in explainable software defect prediction towards achieving consistent and reliable explanation generation.

title: Explainable Software Defect Prediction: Are We There Yet?
text: The interpretability of software defect prediction models remains a crucial yet understudied aspect, as it can provide valuable insights for developers to comprehend and rectify predicted bugs. Recent research by Jiarpakdee et al. has explored the application of model-agnostic techniques, specifically LIME and BreakDown, to elucidate the prediction outcomes of bug prediction models, yielding promising results. However, the limited scope of their investigation, confined to a single software defect prediction model setting, raises concerns about the consistency and reliability of these techniques across diverse software defect prediction models. This study aims to systematically evaluate the robustness of model-agnostic explanation generation approaches, LIME and BreakDown, across software defect prediction models with varying settings, including different data sampling techniques, machine learning classifiers, and prediction scenarios. Our experiments involve generating explanations for identical instances using both LIME and BreakDown under different software defect prediction settings and assessing the consistency of the generated explanations. Leveraging the same defect data as Jiarpakdee et al., our findings reveal that both LIME and BreakDown produce inconsistent explanations under different software defect prediction settings for identical test instances, thereby questioning their reliability for explanation generation. This study underscores the need for further research in explainable software defect prediction to achieve consistent and reliable explanation generation.

title: Functorial aggregation
text: We study polynomial comonads and polynomial bicomodules. Polynomial comonads amount to categories. Polynomial bicomodules between categories amount to parametric right adjoint functors between corresponding copresheaf categories. These may themselves be understood as generalized polynomial functors. They are also called data migration functors because of applications in categorical database theory. We investigate several universal constructions in the framed bicategory of categories, retrofunctors, and parametric right adjoints.
