We then use the theory we develop to model database aggregation alongside querying, all within this rich ecosystem.

title: Functorial aggregation
text: This work explores the realm of polynomial comonads and bicomodules, which can be viewed as categorical structures. Specifically, polynomial bicomodules between categories correspond to parametric right adjoint functors between their associated copresheaf categories, thereby generalizing polynomial functors. Referred to as data migration functors, these constructions have significant implications for categorical database theory. We establish various universal constructions within the framed bicategory of categories, retrofunctors, and parametric right adjoints, and demonstrate their applicability in modeling database aggregation and querying.

title: Precise Learning of Source Code Contextual Semantics via Hierarchical Dependence Structure and Graph Attention Networks
text: Deep learning is being used extensively in a variety of software engineering tasks, e.g., program classification and defect prediction. Although the technique eliminates the required process of feature engineering, the construction of source code model significantly affects the performance on those tasks. Most recent works was mainly focused on complementing AST-based source code models by introducing contextual dependencies extracted from CFG. However, all of them pay little attention to the representation of basic blocks, which are the basis of contextual dependencies. In this paper, we integrated AST and CFG and proposed a novel source code model embedded with hierarchical dependencies. Based on that, we also designed a neural network that depends on the graph attention mechanism.Specifically, we introduced the syntactic structural of the basic block, i.e., its corresponding AST, in source code model to provide sufficient information and fill the gap. We have evaluated this model on three practical software engineering tasks and compared it with other state-of-the-art methods. The results show that our model can significantly improve the performance. For example, compared to the best performing baseline, our model reduces the scale of parameters by 50\% and achieves 4\% improvement on accuracy on program classification task.

title: Precise Learning of Source Code Contextual Semantics via Hierarchical Dependence Structure and Graph Attention Networks
text: The ability to accurately capture source code contextual semantics is crucial for a wide range of software engineering tasks, including code comprehension, bug detection, and program repair. Despite significant advances in deep learning-based approaches, existing methods often struggle to effectively model the complex, hierarchical relationships inherent in source code. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework that leverages hierarchical dependence structures and graph attention networks to learn precise contextual semantics from source code. Our approach first constructs a hierarchical dependence graph from the abstract syntax tree of the input code, which captures both local and global dependencies between program elements. We then employ a graph attention network to learn a contextualized representation of each node in the graph, incorporating both syntactic and semantic information. Experimental results on a range of programming languages demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in source code modeling tasks, including code summarization, method name prediction, and bug detection. Furthermore, we show that our learned representations can be effectively fine-tuned for downstream software engineering tasks, achieving competitive performance with task-specific models.

title: Columnar Formats for Schemaless LSM-based Document Stores
text: In the last decade, document store database systems have gained more traction for storing and querying large volumes of semi-structured data. However, the flexibility of the document stores' data models has limited their ability to store data in a columnar-major layout - making them less performant for analytical workloads than column store relational databases. In this paper, we propose several techniques based on piggy-backing on Log-Structured Merge (LSM) tree events and tailored to document stores to store document data in a columnar layout. We first extend the Dremel format, a popular on-disk columnar format for semi-structured data, to comply with document stores' flexible data model. We then introduce two columnar layouts for organizing and storing data in LSM-based storage. We also highlight the potential of using query compilation techniques for document stores, where values' types are known only at runtime. We have implemented and evaluated our techniques to measure their impact on storage, data ingestion, and query performance in Apache AsterixDB. Our experiments show significant performance gains, improving the query execution time by orders of magnitude while minimally impacting ingestion performance.

title: Columnar Formats for Schemaless LSM-based Document Stores
text: Schemaless log-structured merge (LSM) tree-based document stores have gained popularity due to their ability to efficiently handle high ingestion rates and scalable query performance. However, their row-oriented storage layout can lead to poor storage efficiency and slow query execution for certain workloads. To address these limitations, we investigate the application of columnar formats to schemaless LSM-based document stores. We propose a novel storage architecture that integrates a columnar format with the LSM tree, enabling efficient storage and query processing of documents. Our approach, called ColumnLSM, uses a hybrid storage layout that combines row-oriented and column-oriented storage to leverage the strengths of both formats. We evaluate ColumnLSM using a variety of real-world workloads and demonstrate significant improvements in storage efficiency and query performance compared to traditional row-oriented LSM tree-based document stores. Specifically, our experiments show that ColumnLSM achieves up to 3.7x better storage efficiency and up to 2.5x faster query execution times while maintaining similar write performance. Our results suggest that columnar formats can be effectively applied to schemaless LSM-based document stores, enabling more efficient and scalable data management.

title: The Complexity of Conjunctive Queries with Degree 2
text: We study the tractability of conjunctive query answering for queries with unbounded arity. It is well known that tractability of the problem can be characterised in terms of the queries treewidth under the assumption of bounded arity. We extend this result to cases with unbounded arity but degree 2. To do so, we introduce hypergraph dilutions as an alternative method to primal graph minors for studying substructures of hypergraphs. Using dilutions we observe an analogue to the Excluded Grid Theorem for degree 2 hypergraphs. In consequence, we show that that the tractability of conjunctive query answering can be characterised in terms of generalised hypertree width. A similar characterisation is also shown for the corresponding counting problem. We also generalise our main structural result to arbitrary bounded degree and discuss possible paths towards a characterisation of the bounded degree case.

title: The Complexity of Conjunctive Queries with Degree 2
text: The evaluation of conjunctive queries is a fundamental problem in database theory, with significant implications for query optimization and parallelization. While the complexity of conjunctive queries with arbitrary degree has been extensively studied, the special case of degree 2 queries has received relatively little attention. In this setting, we investigate the complexity of evaluating conjunctive queries with degree 2, where each variable appears in at most two atoms. We employ a combination of graph-theoretic and algebraic techniques to establish a dichotomy theorem, classifying queries into either PTIME or NP-complete according to the structure of their query graphs. Our main result shows that the evaluation problem for degree 2 conjunctive queries is inherently linked to the complexity of graph homomorphism, yielding a rich landscape of tractable and intractable cases. We also provide a comprehensive characterization of the tractable queries, leading to improved optimization strategies for practical query evaluation.

title: Developments in Connected Vehicles and the Requirement for Increased Cybersecurity
text: The increase in popularity of connected features in intelligent transportation systems, has led to a greater risk of cyber-attacks and subsequently, requires a more robust validation of cybersecurity in vehicle design. This article explores three such cyber-attacks and the weaknesses in the connected networks. A review is carried out on current vulnerabilities and key considerations for future vehicle design and validation are highlighted. This article addresses the vehicle manufactures desire to add unnecessary remote connections without appropriate security analysis and assessment of the risks involved. The modern vehicle is All Connected and only as strong as its weakest link.

title: Developments in Connected Vehicles and the Requirement for Increased Cybersecurity
text: The proliferation of connected vehicles has introduced a multitude of benefits, including enhanced safety and improved traffic flow. However, this increased reliance on networked systems has also created a vast attack surface, rendering vehicles vulnerable to cyber threats. This study investigates the cybersecurity implications of connected vehicles and proposes a novel, multi-layered defense framework. Through a combination of static analysis, penetration testing, and simulation-based evaluation, we identify key vulnerabilities in existing systems and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in mitigating attacks. Our findings underscore the urgent need for increased cybersecurity measures in the development of connected vehicles.

title: RepoMiner: a Language-agnostic Python Framework to Mine Software Repositories for Defect Prediction
text: Data originating from open-source software projects provide valuable information to enhance software quality. In the scope of Software Defect Prediction, one of the most challenging parts is extracting valid data about failure-prone software components from these repositories, which can help develop more robust software. In particular, collecting data, calculating metrics, and synthesizing results from these repositories is a tedious and error-prone task, which often requires understanding the programming languages involved in the mined repositories, eventually leading to a proliferation of language-specific data-mining software. This paper presents RepoMiner, a language-agnostic tool developed to support software engineering researchers in creating datasets to support any study on defect prediction. RepoMiner automatically collects failure data from software components, labels them as failure-prone or neutral, and calculates metrics to be used as ground truth for defect prediction models. We present its implementation and provide examples of its application.

title: RepoMiner: a Language-agnostic Python Framework to Mine Software Repositories for Defect Prediction
text: Software quality enhancement can be facilitated by leveraging data from open-source software projects, particularly in the realm of software defect prediction. However, the extraction of valid data about failure-prone software components from these repositories poses significant challenges. The process of collecting data, calculating metrics, and synthesizing results from these repositories is notoriously time-consuming and error-prone, often necessitating proficiency in the programming languages utilized in the mined repositories. This has led to the proliferation of language-specific data-mining software, hindering research efforts. To address this limitation, we introduce RepoMiner, a language-agnostic tool designed to support software engineering researchers in creating datasets for defect prediction studies. By automatically collecting failure data, labeling components as failure-prone or neutral, and calculating relevant metrics, RepoMiner provides a robust foundation for defect prediction models. This paper details the implementation and application of RepoMiner, demonstrating its potential to streamline software defect prediction research.

title: Can Pre-trained Language Models be Used to Resolve Textual and Semantic Merge Conflicts?
text: Program merging is standard practice when developers integrate their individual changes to a common code base. When the merge algorithm fails, this is called a merge conflict. The conflict either manifests in textual merge conflicts where the merge fails to produce code, or semantic merge conflicts where the merged code results in compiler or test breaks. Resolving these conflicts for large code projects is expensive because it requires developers to manually identify the sources of conflict and correct them. In this paper, we explore the feasibility of automatically repairing merge conflicts (both textual and semantic) using k-shot learning with large neural language models (LM) such as GPT-3. One of the challenges in leveraging such language models is to fit the examples and the queries within a small prompt (2048 tokens). We evaluate LMs and k-shot learning for two broad applications: (a) textual and semantic merge conflicts for a divergent fork Microsoft Edge, and (b) textual merge conflicts for a large number of JavaScript projects in GitHub. Our results are mixed: one one-hand, LMs provide the state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on semantic merge conflict resolution for Edge compared to earlier symbolic approaches; on the other hand, LMs do not yet obviate the benefits of fine-tuning neural models (when sufficient data is available) or the design of special purpose domain-specific languages (DSL) for restricted patterns for program synthesis.

title: Can Pre-trained Language Models be Used to Resolve Textual and Semantic Merge Conflicts?
text: The integration of individual code changes into a common code base, a ubiquitous practice in software development, is often hindered by merge conflicts. These conflicts arise when the merge algorithm fails, resulting in either textual inconsistencies or semantic errors that manifest as compiler or test failures. The manual resolution of such conflicts in large-scale projects is a costly and time-consuming endeavor, as it requires developers to painstakingly identify and correct the sources of conflict. This paper investigates the viability of automating merge conflict resolution (both textual and semantic) using k-shot learning with large neural language models, such as GPT-3. A significant challenge in harnessing these models lies in accommodating the examples and queries within a constrained prompt size of 2048 tokens. We assess the efficacy of language models and k-shot learning across two application domains: (1) resolving textual and semantic merge conflicts in a divergent fork of Microsoft Edge, and (2) addressing textual merge conflicts in a large corpus of JavaScript projects on GitHub. Our findings are nuanced, revealing that language models achieve state-of-the-art performance in semantic merge conflict resolution for Edge, surpassing earlier symbolic approaches, yet they do not supplant the benefits of fine-tuning neural models or designing domain-specific languages for restricted patterns in program synthesis when sufficient data is available.

title: ptype-cat: Inferring the Type and Values of Categorical Variables
text: Type inference is the task of identifying the type of values in a data column and has been studied extensively in the literature. Most existing type inference methods support data types such as Boolean, date, float, integer and string. However, these methods do not consider non-Boolean categorical variables, where there are more than two possible values encoded by integers or strings. Therefore, such columns are annotated either as integer or string rather than categorical, and need to be transformed into categorical manually by the user. In this paper, we propose a probabilistic type inference method that can identify the general categorical data type (including non-Boolean variables). Additionally, we identify the possible values of each categorical variable by adapting the existing type inference method ptype. Combining these methods, we present ptype-cat which achieves better results than existing applicable solutions.

title: ptype-cat: Inferring the Type and Values of Categorical Variables
text: The accurate identification of data types in columns is a fundamental task in data preprocessing, known as type inference. While existing methods can recognize common data types such as Boolean, date, float, integer, and string, they often fail to distinguish non-Boolean categorical variables, which are instead annotated as integer or string types. This limitation necessitates manual transformation by the user. To address this shortcoming, we develop a probabilistic type inference approach that can identify general categorical data types, including non-Boolean variables. By integrating our method with the existing ptype algorithm, which detects possible values for categorical variables, we introduce ptype-cat. Experimental results demonstrate that ptype-cat outperforms existing applicable solutions in type inference accuracy.

title: Identifying the Units of Measurement in Tabular Data
text: We consider the problem of identifying the units of measurement in a data column that contains both numeric values and unit symbols in each row, e.g., "5.2 l", "7 pints". In this case we seek to identify the dimension of the column (e.g. volume) and relate the unit symbols to valid units (e.g. litre, pint) obtained from a knowledge graph. Below we present PUC, a Probabilistic Unit Canonicalizer that can accurately identify the units of measurement, extract semantic descriptions of quantitative data columns and canonicalize their entries. We present the first messy real-world tabular datasets annotated for units of measurement, which can enable and accelerate the research in this area. Our experiments on these datasets show that PUC achieves better results than existing solutions.

title: Identifying the Units of Measurement in Tabular Data
text: The proliferation of datasets in various domains has led to an increased need for automated data analysis and understanding. A crucial step in this process is identifying the units of measurement associated with each column in tabular data, as it enables meaningful interpretation and further processing of the data. Existing approaches rely on manual annotation or simple heuristics, which are often incomplete or inaccurate. We propose a novel, machine learning-based approach that leverages linguistic and statistical features to identify units of measurement in tabular data. Our method achieves an F1-score of 0.92 on a benchmark dataset, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches by 15%. We also demonstrate the applicability of our approach on real-world datasets from diverse domains, showcasing its potential in facilitating more accurate and efficient data analysis.

title: Context-based navigation for ground mobile robot in a semi-structured indoor environment
text: There is a growing demand for mobile robots to operate in more variable environments, where guaranteeing safe robot navigation is a priority, in addition to time performance. To achieve this, current solutions for local planning use a specific configuration tuned to the characteristics of the application environment. In this paper, we present an approach for developing quality models that can be used by a self-adaptation framework to adapt the local planner configuration at run-time based on the perceived environment. We contribute a definition of a safety model that predicts the safety of a navigation configuration given the perceived environment. Experiments have been performed in a realistic navigation scenario for a retail application to validate the obtained models and demonstrate their integration in a self-adaptation framework.

title: Context-based navigation for ground mobile robot in a semi-structured indoor environment
text: Navigation in semi-structured indoor environments remains a significant challenge for ground mobile robots, owing to the lack of a priori maps and the presence of dynamic obstacles. This paper presents a context-based navigation approach that leverages semantic information about the environment to guide the robot's motion. Our method integrates a convolutional neural network (CNN) for scene understanding with a probabilistic graph-based planning framework. The CNN extracts contextual features from visual and lidar data, which are then used to infer the robot's position and orientation within the environment. Experimental results in a realistic office setting demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional SLAM-based methods in terms of navigation accuracy and robustness, with a 25% reduction in navigation errors. Furthermore, our method enables the robot to adapt to changes in the environment, such as relocated furniture, and to navigate through unfamiliar areas.

title: Bounding Box-Free Instance Segmentation Using Semi-Supervised Learning for Generating a City-Scale Vehicle Dataset
text: Vehicle classification is a hot computer vision topic, with studies ranging from ground-view up to top-view imagery. In remote sensing, the usage of top-view images allows for understanding city patterns, vehicle concentration, traffic management, and others. However, there are some difficulties when aiming for pixel-wise classification: (a) most vehicle classification studies use object detection methods, and most publicly available datasets are designed for this task, (b) creating instance segmentation datasets is laborious, and (c) traditional instance segmentation methods underperform on this task since the objects are small. Thus, the present research objectives are: (1) propose a novel semi-supervised iterative learning approach using GIS software, (2) propose a box-free instance segmentation approach, and (3) provide a city-scale vehicle dataset. The iterative learning procedure considered: (1) label a small number of vehicles, (2) train on those samples, (3) use the model to classify the entire image, (4) convert the image prediction into a polygon shapefile, (5) correct some areas with errors and include them in the training data, and (6) repeat until results are satisfactory. To separate instances, we considered vehicle interior and vehicle borders, and the DL model was the U-net with the Efficient-net-B7 backbone. When removing the borders, the vehicle interior becomes isolated, allowing for unique object identification. To recover the deleted 1-pixel borders, we proposed a simple method to expand each prediction. The results show better pixel-wise metrics when compared to the Mask-RCNN (82% against 67% in IoU). On per-object analysis, the overall accuracy, precision, and recall were greater than 90%. This pipeline applies to any remote sensing target, being very efficient for segmentation and generating datasets.

title: Bounding Box-Free Instance Segmentation Using Semi-Supervised Learning for Generating a City-Scale Vehicle Dataset
text: The task of vehicle classification in computer vision has garnered significant attention, with applications in remote sensing extending from understanding urban patterns to traffic management. However, pixel-wise classification in top-view imagery poses unique challenges, including the dominance of object detection methods in existing studies and the labor-intensive creation of instance segmentation datasets. Furthermore, traditional instance segmentation approaches often underperform when dealing with small objects. This research addresses these limitations by proposing a novel semi-supervised iterative learning framework, leveraging Geographic Information System (GIS) software, and introducing a box-free instance segmentation approach. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive city-scale vehicle dataset. Our iterative learning procedure involves initial labeling of a small vehicle subset, followed by model training, image classification, and polygon shapefile conversion. Error-prone areas are corrected and incorporated into the training data, with this process repeated until satisfactory results are achieved. To isolate individual instances, we exploit vehicle interior and border features, utilizing a U-net architecture with an Efficient-net-B7 backbone. By removing borders, vehicle interiors become distinct, enabling unique object identification. A simple border recovery method is also proposed to expand predictions. Our approach yields superior pixel-wise metrics, achieving an IoU of 82% compared to Mask-RCNN's 67%. Per-object analysis reveals overall accuracy, precision, and recall exceeding 90%. This efficient pipeline is adaptable to various remote sensing targets, offering a valuable tool for segmentation and dataset generation.

title: Panoptic Segmentation Meets Remote Sensing
text: Panoptic segmentation combines instance and semantic predictions, allowing the detection of "things" and "stuff" simultaneously. Effectively approaching panoptic segmentation in remotely sensed data can be auspicious in many challenging problems since it allows continuous mapping and specific target counting. Several difficulties have prevented the growth of this task in remote sensing: (a) most algorithms are designed for traditional images, (b) image labelling must encompass "things" and "stuff" classes, and (c) the annotation format is complex. Thus, aiming to solve and increase the operability of panoptic segmentation in remote sensing, this study has five objectives: (1) create a novel data preparation pipeline for panoptic segmentation, (2) propose an annotation conversion software to generate panoptic annotations; (3) propose a novel dataset on urban areas, (4) modify the Detectron2 for the task, and (5) evaluate difficulties of this task in the urban setting. We used an aerial image with a 0,24-meter spatial resolution considering 14 classes. Our pipeline considers three image inputs, and the proposed software uses point shapefiles for creating samples in the COCO format. Our study generated 3,400 samples with 512x512 pixel dimensions. We used the Panoptic-FPN with two backbones (ResNet-50 and ResNet-101), and the model evaluation considered semantic instance and panoptic metrics. We obtained 93.9, 47.7, and 64.9 for the mean IoU, box AP, and PQ. Our study presents the first effective pipeline for panoptic segmentation and an extensive database for other researchers to use and deal with other data or related problems requiring a thorough scene understanding.

title: Panoptic Segmentation Meets Remote Sensing
text: Panoptic segmentation, which integrates instance and semantic predictions, offers a unified framework for detecting "things" and "stuff" in remotely sensed data. The ability to accurately perform panoptic segmentation in this domain has significant implications for various challenging problems, including continuous mapping and object counting. However, the development of this task in remote sensing has been hindered by several challenges, including the limitations of traditional image-based algorithms, the complexity of annotating both "things" and "stuff" classes, and the need for a standardized annotation format. To address these challenges, this study pursues five primary objectives: (1) developing a novel data preparation pipeline for panoptic segmentation, (2) creating an annotation conversion software to generate panoptic annotations, (3) constructing a novel urban area dataset, (4) adapting the Detectron2 framework for this task, and (5) evaluating the difficulties of panoptic segmentation in urban environments. Our approach utilizes aerial images with a 0.24-meter spatial resolution, encompassing 14 classes, and involves a three-input pipeline with point shapefiles converted to COCO format. The resulting dataset comprises 3,400 samples with 512x512 pixel dimensions. We evaluate the performance of Panoptic-FPN with ResNet-50 and ResNet-101 backbones using semantic instance and panoptic metrics, achieving mean IoU, box AP, and PQ scores of 93.9, 47.7, and 64.9, respectively. This study presents a pioneering pipeline for panoptic segmentation in remote sensing and a comprehensive database for future research, enabling thorough scene understanding and addressing a range of related problems.

title: Filter Methods for Feature Selection in Supervised Machine Learning Applications -- Review and Benchmark
text: The amount of data for machine learning (ML) applications is constantly growing. Not only the number of observations, especially the number of measured variables (features) increases with ongoing digitization. Selecting the most appropriate features for predictive modeling is an important lever for the success of ML applications in business and research. Feature selection methods (FSM) that are independent of a certain ML algorithm - so-called filter methods - have been numerously suggested, but little guidance for researchers and quantitative modelers exists to choose appropriate approaches for typical ML problems. This review synthesizes the substantial literature on feature selection benchmarking and evaluates the performance of 58 methods in the widely used R environment. For concrete guidance, we consider four typical dataset scenarios that are challenging for ML models (noisy, redundant, imbalanced data and cases with more features than observations). Drawing on the experience of earlier benchmarks, which have considered much fewer FSMs, we compare the performance of the methods according to four criteria (predictive performance, number of relevant features selected, stability of the feature sets and runtime). We found methods relying on the random forest approach, the double input symmetrical relevance filter (DISR) and the joint impurity filter (JIM) were well-performing candidate methods for the given dataset scenarios.

title: Filter Methods for Feature Selection in Supervised Machine Learning Applications -- Review and Benchmark
text: The proliferation of data in machine learning (ML) applications has led to an exponential increase in both the number of observations and measured variables, rendering feature selection a crucial determinant of ML success in business and research. The abundance of filter-based feature selection methods (FSMs), which operate independently of ML algorithms, has created a daunting task for researchers and quantitative modelers in selecting the most suitable approaches for typical ML problems. To address this challenge, this review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the literature on feature selection benchmarking and evaluates the performance of 58 methods within the R environment. Focusing on four prototypical dataset scenarios that pose significant challenges for ML models - noisy, redundant, imbalanced data, and cases with more features than observations - we assess the performance of these methods according to four key criteria: predictive performance, feature selection efficacy, stability, and runtime. Our results indicate that methods leveraging the random forest approach, double input symmetrical relevance filter (DISR), and joint impurity filter (JIM) emerge as top-performing candidates for these dataset scenarios, providing concrete guidance for researchers and practitioners.

title: Style-Guided Web Application Exploration
text: A wide range of analysis and testing techniques targeting modern web apps rely on the automated exploration of their state space by firing events that mimic user interactions. However, finding out which elements are actionable in web apps is not a trivial task. To improve the efficacy of exploring the event space of web apps, we propose a browser-independent, instrumentation-free approach based on structural and visual stylistic cues. Our approach, implemented in a tool called StyleX, employs machine learning models, trained on 700,000 web elements from 1,000 real-world websites, to predict actionable elements on a webpage a priori. In addition, our approach uses stylistic cues for ranking these actionable elements while exploring the app. Our actionable predictor models achieve 90.14\% precision and 87.76\% recall when considering the click event listener, and on average, 75.42\% precision and 77.76\% recall when considering the five most-frequent event types. Our evaluations show that StyleX can improve the JavaScript code coverage achieved by a general-purpose crawler by up to 23\%.

title: Style-Guided Web Application Exploration
text: The automation of web application exploration via event firing relies on identifying actionable elements, a task that poses significant challenges. To enhance the efficacy of event space exploration, we introduce a novel, browser-independent, and instrumentation-free approach that leverages structural and visual stylistic cues. Our methodology, embodied in the StyleX tool, utilizes machine learning models trained on a large dataset of 700,000 web elements from 1,000 real-world websites to predict actionable elements on a webpage a priori. The approach further incorporates stylistic cues to rank actionable elements during exploration. Our actionable predictor models exhibit high accuracy, achieving 90.14% precision and 87.76% recall for the click event listener, and average precision and recall of 75.42% and 77.76%, respectively, for the top five event types. Evaluations demonstrate that StyleX can significantly improve JavaScript code coverage, outperforming a general-purpose crawler by up to 23%.

title: The Reproducibility of Programming-Related Issues in Stack Overflow Questions
text: Software developers often look for solutions to their code-level problems using the Stack Overflow Q&A website. To receive help, developers frequently submit questions containing sample code segments and the description of the programming issue. Unfortunately, it is not always possible to reproduce the issues from the code segments that may impede questions from receiving prompt and appropriate solutions. We conducted an exploratory study on the reproducibility of issues discussed in 400 Java and 400 Python questions. We parsed, compiled, executed, and carefully examined the code segments from these questions to reproduce the reported programming issues. The outcomes of our study are three-fold. First, we found that we can reproduce approximately 68% of Java and 71% of Python issues, whereas we were unable to reproduce approximately 22% of Java and 19% of Python issues using the code segments. Of the issues that were reproducible, approximately 67% of the Java code segments and 20% of the Python code segments required minor or major modifications to reproduce the issues. Second, we carefully investigated why programming issues could not be reproduced and provided evidence-based guidelines for writing effective code examples for Stack Overflow questions. Third, we investigated the correlation between the issue reproducibility status of questions and the corresponding answer meta-data, such as the presence of an accepted answer. According to our analysis, a reproducible question has at least two times higher chance of receiving an accepted answer than an irreproducible question. Besides, the median time delay in receiving accepted answers is double if the issues reported in questions could not be reproduced. We also investigate the confounding factors (e.g., reputation) and find that confounding factors do not hurt the correlation between reproducibility status and answer meta-data.

title: The Reproducibility of Programming-Related Issues in Stack Overflow Questions
text: The proliferation of online platforms for crowdsourced knowledge sharing has revolutionized the way programmers seek and provide assistance for programming-related issues. Stack Overflow, a prominent question-and-answer website, has become a go-to resource for millions of developers worldwide. However, the reliability of the solutions and the reproducibility of the issues reported on the platform remain understudied. We investigate the reproducibility of programming-related issues in Stack Overflow questions, focusing on the Java and Python programming languages. Our methodology involves a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative analysis of a large dataset of Stack Overflow questions with qualitative coding of a subset of questions. We collect a dataset of 10,000 questions from each language, annotated with metadata such as question tags, votes, and answer counts. We then develop a reproducibility framework, consisting of a set of criteria to assess the reproducibility of an issue, including the presence of a minimal, complete, and verifiable example, as well as the availability of relevant system and library information. Our quantitative analysis reveals that only 23.4% of Java questions and 17.9% of Python questions meet our reproducibility criteria, indicating a significant reproducibility gap. Furthermore, our qualitative coding of 200 questions from each language identifies several factors contributing to this gap, including incomplete or inaccurate problem descriptions, inadequate code snippets, and insufficient system information. We also find that questions with higher vote counts and more answers are more likely to be reproducible, suggesting a relationship between community engagement and issue reproducibility. Our findings have implications for the design of online platforms for collaborative problem-solving, highlighting the need for features that promote reproducibility and facilitate more effective knowledge sharing among programmers. By shedding light on the reproducibility of programming-related issues on Stack Overflow, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of the complexities of crowdsourced knowledge sharing in the context of software development.

title: Scale-Invariant Strength Assortativity of Streaming Butterflies
text: Bipartite graphs are rich data structures with prevalent applications and identifier structural features. However, less is known about their growth patterns, particularly in streaming settings. Current works study the patterns of static or aggregated temporal graphs optimized for certain down-stream analytics or ignoring multipartite/non-stationary data distributions, emergence patterns of subgraphs, and streaming paradigms. To address these, we perform statistical network analysis over web log streams and identify the governing patterns underlying the bursty emergence of mesoscopic building blocks, 2,2-bicliques known as butterflies, leading to a phenomenon that we call "scale-invariant strength assortativity of streaming butterflies". We provide the graph-theoretic explanation of this phenomenon. We further introduce a set of micro-mechanics in the body of a streaming growth algorithm, sGrow, to pinpoint the generative origins. sGrow supports streaming paradigms, emergence of 4-vertex graphlets, and provides user-specified configurations for the scale, burstiness, level of strength assortativity, probability of out-of-order records, generation time, and time-sensitive connections. Comprehensive Evaluations on pattern reproducing and stress testing validate the effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness of sGrow in realization of the observed patterns independent of initial conditions, scale, temporal characteristics, and model configurations. Theoretical and experimental analysis verify the robust ability of sGrow in generating streaming graphs based on user-specified configurations that affect the scale and burstiness of the stream, level of strength assortativity, probability of-of-order streaming records, generation time, and time-sensitive connections.

title: Scale-Invariant Strength Assortativity of Streaming Butterflies
text: The widespread adoption of distributed stream processing systems has necessitated the development of novel, scalable graph processing algorithms capable of handling massive, dynamic datasets. Among the most fundamental graph primitives is the butterfly, a motif crucial in modeling various real-world phenomena. Despite their importance, the strength assortativity of streaming butterflies remains poorly understood, with existing methods either neglecting this property or relying on simplistic, scale-variant heuristics. In response, we propose a novel, scale-invariant strength assortativity measure for streaming butterflies, dubbed SISA. By leveraging a combination of reservoir sampling and incremental graph decomposition, SISA enables efficient, real-time computation of strength assortativity on massive, dynamic graphs. Our approach is grounded in a rigorous theoretical framework, guaranteeing accurate, unbiased estimates of strength assortativity even in the presence of severe graph skew. Empirical evaluation on a diverse range of real-world datasets, including social networks, web graphs, and biological networks, demonstrates the efficacy of SISA, yielding a 3-5x speedup over state-of-the-art methods while maintaining a 10-15% improvement in assortativity estimation accuracy. Furthermore, our results reveal intriguing insights into the structural properties of real-world networks, highlighting the importance of scale-invariant strength assortativity in characterizing network resilience and robustness. Overall, SISA constitutes a significant advance in scalable graph processing, enabling researchers and practitioners to better understand and analyze the complex dynamics of massive, streaming graphs.

title: Flexible Pattern Discovery and Analysis
text: Based on the analysis of the proportion of utility in the supporting transactions used in the field of data mining, high utility-occupancy pattern mining (HUOPM) has recently attracted widespread attention. Unlike high-utility pattern mining (HUPM), which involves the enumeration of high-utility (e.g., profitable) patterns, HUOPM aims to find patterns representing a collection of existing transactions. In practical applications, however, not all patterns are used or valuable. For example, a pattern might contain too many items, that is, the pattern might be too specific and therefore lack value for users in real life. To achieve qualified patterns with a flexible length, we constrain the minimum and maximum lengths during the mining process and introduce a novel algorithm for the mining of flexible high utility-occupancy patterns. Our algorithm is referred to as HUOPM+. To ensure the flexibility of the patterns and tighten the upper bound of the utility-occupancy, a strategy called the length upper-bound (LUB) is presented to prune the search space. In addition, a utility-occupancy nested list (UO-nlist) and a frequency-utility-occupancy table (FUO-table) are employed to avoid multiple scans of the database. Evaluation results of the subsequent experiments confirm that the proposed algorithm can effectively control the length of the derived patterns, for both real-world and synthetic datasets. Moreover, it can decrease the execution time and memory consumption.

title: Flexible Pattern Discovery and Analysis
text: The proliferation of data from diverse sources has necessitated the development of versatile pattern discovery techniques capable of handling complex, heterogeneous, and often noisy data. Traditional approaches, reliant on predefined schema or rigid pattern definitions, are ill-equipped to accommodate the dynamic nature of modern data landscapes. In response, we propose a novel framework for flexible pattern discovery and analysis, dubbed FlexPat, which leverages a hybrid approach combining symbolic and sub-symbolic representation learning. By integrating a probabilistic grammar-based pattern language with deep neural networks, FlexPat enables the discovery of intricate patterns across multiple data modalities, including relational, graph, and time-series data. Our framework's flexibility is facilitated by a novel mechanism for adaptive pattern refinement, which iteratively refines pattern definitions based on feedback from the analysis process. Experimental evaluations on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate FlexPat's efficacy in uncovering meaningful patterns, often overlooked by traditional techniques. Notably, our approach achieves a 32% increase in pattern recall and a 25% reduction in false positive rates compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, FlexPat's flexibility enables the discovery of novel patterns, including those exhibiting non-linear relationships and context-dependent behaviors. Our contributions have far-reaching implications for various applications, including data mining, knowledge graph construction, and recommender systems.

title: xFuzz: Machine Learning Guided Cross-Contract Fuzzing
text: Smart contract transactions are increasingly interleaved by cross-contract calls. While many tools have been developed to identify a common set of vulnerabilities, the cross-contract vulnerability is overlooked by existing tools. Cross-contract vulnerabilities are exploitable bugs that manifest in the presence of more than two interacting contracts. Existing methods are however limited to analyze a maximum of two contracts at the same time. Detecting cross-contract vulnerabilities is highly non-trivial. With multiple interacting contracts, the search space is much larger than that of a single contract. To address this problem, we present xFuzz, a machine learning guided smart contract fuzzing framework. The machine learning models are trained with novel features (e.g., word vectors and instructions) and are used to filter likely benign program paths. Comparing with existing static tools, machine learning model is proven to be more robust, avoiding directly adopting manually-defined rules in specific tools. We compare xFuzz with three state-of-the-art tools on 7,391 contracts. xFuzz detects 18 exploitable cross-contract vulnerabilities, of which 15 vulnerabilities are exposed for the first time. Furthermore, our approach is shown to be efficient in detecting non-cross-contract vulnerabilities as well -- using less than 20% time as that of other fuzzing tools, xFuzz detects twice as many vulnerabilities.

title: xFuzz: Machine Learning Guided Cross-Contract Fuzzing
text: The increasing adoption of decentralized applications has led to a surge in the development of smart contracts, which often interact with each other in complex ways. However, the lack of systematic testing methodologies for these interactions renders them vulnerable to unforeseen bugs and security vulnerabilities. Fuzz testing, a widely used technique for identifying bugs, is particularly challenging in this context due to the inherent complexity of contracts and their interactions. To address this challenge, we propose xFuzz, a novel machine learning guided cross-contract fuzzing framework that leverages reinforcement learning to efficiently explore the vast input space of contract interactions. xFuzz incorporates a hierarchical fuzzing strategy that combines both black-box and white-box techniques to generate inputs that maximize code coverage and fault detection. We evaluate xFuzz on a benchmark of 100 popular Ethereum contracts and demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying 23 previously unknown bugs, including 5 critical security vulnerabilities. Our results show that xFuzz achieves a 3x increase in code coverage and a 2x increase in fault detection compared to state-of-the-art fuzzing techniques. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that xFuzz is particularly effective in detecting bugs that arise from complex interactions between contracts, highlighting the importance of cross-contract fuzzing in ensuring the reliability and security of decentralized applications.

title: Time and Memory Efficient Parallel Algorithm for Structural Graph Summaries and two Extensions to Incremental Summarization and $k$-Bisimulation for Long $k$-Chaining
text: We developed a flexible parallel algorithm for graph summarization based on vertex-centric programming and parameterized message passing. The base algorithm supports infinitely many structural graph summary models defined in a formal language. An extension of the parallel base algorithm allows incremental graph summarization. In this paper, we prove that the incremental algorithm is correct and show that updates are performed in time $\mathcal{O}(Δ\cdot d^k)$, where $Δ$ is the number of additions, deletions, and modifications to the input graph, $d$ the maximum degree, and $k$ is the maximum distance in the subgraphs considered. Although the iterative algorithm supports values of $k>1$, it requires nested data structures for the message passing that are memory-inefficient. Thus, we extended the base summarization algorithm by a hash-based messaging mechanism to support a scalable iterative computation of graph summarizations based on $k$-bisimulation for arbitrary $k$. We empirically evaluate the performance of our algorithms using benchmark and real-world datasets. The incremental algorithm almost always outperforms the batch computation. We observe in our experiments that the incremental algorithm is faster even in cases when $50\%$ of the graph database changes from one version to the next. The incremental computation requires a three-layered hash index, which has a low memory overhead of only $8\%$ ($\pm 1\%$). Finally, the incremental summarization algorithm outperforms the batch algorithm even with fewer cores. The iterative parallel $k$-bisimulation algorithm computes summaries on graphs with over $10$M edges within seconds. We show that the algorithm processes graphs of $100+\,$M edges within a few minutes while having a moderate memory consumption of $<150$ GB. For the largest BSBM1B dataset with 1 billion edges, it computes $k=10$ bisimulation in under an hour.

title: Time and Memory Efficient Parallel Algorithm for Structural Graph Summaries and two Extensions to Incremental Summarization and $k$-Bisimulation for Long $k$-Chaining
text: A novel parallel algorithm for graph summarization is presented, grounded in vertex-centric programming and parameterized message passing. This algorithmic framework accommodates a wide range of structural graph summary models, formally defined through a versatile language. An incremental extension of the base algorithm is introduced, facilitating efficient updates to graph summaries. We establish the correctness of this incremental algorithm and demonstrate its time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(Δ\cdot d^k)$, where $Δ$ represents the number of graph modifications, $d$ the maximum degree, and $k$ the maximum distance considered in subgraphs. Although the iterative algorithm supports arbitrary values of $k$, its nested data structures lead to memory inefficiencies. To overcome this limitation, we integrate a hash-based messaging mechanism into the base algorithm, enabling scalable iterative computations of graph summarizations based on $k$-bisimulation for any $k$. Empirical evaluations on benchmark and real-world datasets reveal the incremental algorithm's consistent outperformance of batch computation, even when $50\%$ of the graph database undergoes changes. The incremental approach requires a three-layered hash index, incurring a modest memory overhead of $8\%$ ($\pm 1\%$). Furthermore, the incremental summarization algorithm surpasses the batch algorithm's performance with fewer cores. The iterative parallel $k$-bisimulation algorithm achieves rapid summarization on graphs with over $10$M edges, processing larger graphs of $100+\,$M edges within minutes while maintaining a moderate memory footprint of $<150$ GB. Notably, it computes $k=10$ bisimulation on the massive BSBM1B dataset with 1 billion edges in under an hour.

title: FLACOCO: Fault Localization for Java based on Industry-grade Coverage
text: Fault localization is an essential step in the debugging process. Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) is a popular fault localization family of techniques, utilizing code-coverage to predict suspicious lines of code. In this paper, we present FLACOCO, a new fault localization tool for Java. The key novelty of FLACOCO is that it is built on top of one of the most used and most reliable coverage libraries for Java, JaCoCo. FLACOCO is made available through a well-designed command-line interface and Java API and supports all Java versions. We validate FLACOCO on two use-cases from the automatic program repair domain by reproducing previous scientific experiments. We find it is capable of effectively replacing the state-of-the-art FL library. Overall, we hope that FLACOCO will help research in fault localization as well as industry adoption thanks to being founded on industry-grade code coverage. An introductory video is available at

title: FLACOCO: Fault Localization for Java based on Industry-grade Coverage
text: The increasing complexity of modern software systems has led to a growing need for effective fault localization techniques. Despite significant advances, existing approaches often rely on simplistic assumptions about code structure and testing practices, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios. In the context of Java-based systems, which dominate the industry landscape, the lack of practical and scalable fault localization techniques hinders the efficiency of debugging and maintenance efforts. This paper presents FLACOCO, a novel approach to fault localization that leverages industry-grade code coverage data to identify faulty code regions. By integrating advanced statistical analysis and machine learning techniques, FLACOCO achieves high accuracy and precision in pinpointing faults, even in complex systems with numerous dependencies. Our comprehensive evaluation on a suite of real-world Java projects demonstrates FLACOCO's superiority over state-of-the-art techniques, reducing the average number of lines of code to inspect by 75% and improving debugging efficiency by 30%.

title: Two step clustering for data reduction combining DBSCAN and k-means clustering
text: A novel combination of two widely-used clustering algorithms is proposed here for the detection and reduction of high data density regions. The Density Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) algorithm is used for the detection of high data density regions and the k-means algorithm for reduction. The proposed algorithm iterates while successively decrementing the DBSCAN search radius, allowing for an adaptive reduction factor based on the effective data density. The algorithm is demonstrated for a physics simulation application, where a surrogate model for fusion reactor plasma turbulence is generated with neural networks. A training dataset for the surrogate model is created with a quasilinear gyrokinetics code for turbulent transport calculations in fusion plasmas. The training set consists of model inputs derived from a repository of experimental measurements, meaning there is a potential risk of over-representing specific regions of this input parameter space. By applying the proposed reduction algorithm to this dataset, this study demonstrates that the training dataset can be reduced by a factor ~20 using the proposed algorithm, without a noticeable loss in the surrogate model accuracy. This reduction provides a novel way of analyzing existing high-dimensional datasets for biases and consequently reducing them, which lowers the cost of re-populating that parameter space with higher quality data.

title: Two step clustering for data reduction combining DBSCAN and k-means clustering
text: The proliferation of high-density regions in datasets can lead to biased surrogate models, necessitating the development of effective data reduction strategies. We present a novel hybrid approach that combines the strengths of DBSCAN and k-means clustering algorithms to detect and reduce high-density regions in datasets. Our algorithm iteratively adjusts the DBSCAN search radius to adapt to the underlying data density, thereby ensuring an optimal reduction factor. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in the context of a physics simulation application, where a neural network-based surrogate model is generated for fusion reactor plasma turbulence using a quasilinear gyrokinetics code. By applying our reduction algorithm to the training dataset derived from experimental measurements, we achieve a reduction factor of approximately 20 without compromising the accuracy of the surrogate model. This significant reduction enables the identification and mitigation of biases in high-dimensional datasets, ultimately reducing the cost of repopulating the parameter space with higher quality data. Our approach offers a valuable tool for analyzing and refining existing datasets, thereby enhancing the reliability of surrogate models in various domains.

title: SchemaDB: Structures in Relational Datasets
text: In this paper we introduce the SchemaDB data-set; a collection of relational database schemata in both sql and graph formats. Databases are not commonly shared publicly for reasons of privacy and security, so schemata are not available for study. Consequently, an understanding of database structures in the wild is lacking, and most examples found publicly belong to common development frameworks or are derived from textbooks or engine benchmark designs. SchemaDB contains 2,500 samples of relational schemata found in public repositories which we have standardised to MySQL syntax. We provide our gathering and transformation methodology, summary statistics, and structural analysis, and discuss potential downstream research tasks in several domains.

title: SchemaDB: Structures in Relational Datasets
text: Relational databases are ubiquitous in modern applications, yet their schemas often remain opaque to users, hindering data exploration and integration. To address this, we introduce SchemaDB, a novel system that uncovers hidden structures in relational datasets. By leveraging a combination of data profiling, graph mining, and probabilistic modeling, SchemaDB infers a rich schema graph that captures intricate relationships between attributes. Our experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that SchemaDB outperforms state-of-the-art schema inference methods in terms of accuracy and scalability. Furthermore, we show how SchemaDB's output enables more effective data integration and querying, with applications in data warehousing, business intelligence, and data science.

title: Who, What, Why and How? Towards the Monetary Incentive in Crowd Collaboration: A Case Study of Github's Sponsor Mechanism
text: While many forms of financial support are currently available, there are still many complaints about inadequate financing from software maintainers. In May 2019, GitHub, the world's most active social coding platform, launched the Sponsor mechanism as a step toward more deeply integrating open source development and financial support. This paper collects data on 8,028 maintainers, 13,555 sponsors, and 22,515 sponsorships and conducts a comprehensive analysis. We explore the relationship between the Sponsor mechanism and developers along four dimensions using a combination of qualitative and quantitative analysis, examining why developers participate, how the mechanism affects developer activity, who obtains more sponsorships, and what mechanism flaws developers have encountered in the process of using it. We find a long-tail effect in the act of sponsorship, with most maintainers' expectations remaining unmet, and sponsorship has only a short-term, slightly positive impact on development activity but is not sustainable. While sponsors participate in this mechanism mainly as a means of thanking the developers of OSS that they use, in practice, the social status of developers is the primary influence on the number of sponsorships. We find that both the Sponsor mechanism and open source donations have certain shortcomings and need further improvements to attract more participants.

title: Who, What, Why and How? Towards the Monetary Incentive in Crowd Collaboration: A Case Study of Github's Sponsor Mechanism
text: The advent of crowd collaboration has revolutionized the way software is developed, maintained, and disseminated. One prominent platform facilitating this phenomenon is GitHub, which recently introduced the Sponsor mechanism, allowing users to financially support their favorite open-source projects. Despite its potential, the dynamics underlying this monetary incentive remain poorly understood. This study aims to elucidate the motivations, behaviors, and outcomes of GitHub users participating in the Sponsor mechanism. We conducted a mixed-methods case study, combining quantitative analysis of 10,000+ sponsorships with in-depth interviews of 25 sponsors and maintainers. Our results reveal that sponsors are predominantly motivated by altruism and a desire for reciprocity, rather than self-interested gain. We also find that sponsored projects exhibit increased issue resolution rates, reduced response times, and higher contributor engagement. Furthermore, our analysis uncovers a significant positive correlation between sponsorship amounts and project popularity. However, we also identify potential drawbacks, including the emergence of a 'sponsorship gap' between popular and niche projects. Our findings have important implications for the design and optimization of incentive mechanisms in crowd collaboration platforms, highlighting the need for nuanced strategies that balance individual motivations with collective benefits.

title: Application of canonical augmentation to the atomic substitution problem
text: A common approach for studying a solid solution or disordered system within a periodic ab-initio framework is to create a supercell in which a certain amount of target elements is substituted with other ones. The key to generating supercells is determining how to eliminate symmetry-equivalent structures from the large number of substitution patterns. Although the total number of substitutions is on the order of trillions, only symmetry-inequivalent atomic substitution patterns need to be identified, and their number is far smaller than the total. A straightforward solution would be to classify them after determining all possible patterns, but it is redundant and practically unfeasible. Therefore, to alleviate this drawback, we developed a new formalism based on the {\it canonical augmentation}, and successfully applied it to the atomic substitution problem. Our developed \verb|python| software package, which is called \textsc{SHRY} (\underline{S}uite for \underline{H}igh-th\underline{r}oughput generation of models with atomic substitutions implemented by p\underline{y}thon), enables us to pick up only symmetry-inequivalent structures from the vast number of candidates very efficiently. We demonstrate that the computational time required by our algorithm to find $N$ symmetry-inequivalent structures scales {\it linearly} with $N$ up to $\sim 10^9$. This is the best scaling for such problems.

title: Application of canonical augmentation to the atomic substitution problem
text: The study of solid solutions and disordered systems within a periodic ab-initio framework often employs the creation of supercells, where target elements are substituted with others in a specific arrangement. A crucial step in generating these supercells is the identification of symmetry-inequivalent atomic substitution patterns, thereby eliminating redundant structures from the vast number of possible substitution patterns. Although the total number of substitutions can reach trillions, the number of symmetry-inequivalent patterns is significantly smaller. To address the inefficiency of classifying all possible patterns, we developed a novel formalism based on canonical augmentation and successfully applied it to the atomic substitution problem. Our Python software package, SHRY (Suite for High-throughput generation of models with atomic substitutions implemented by Python), enables the efficient selection of symmetry-inequivalent structures from a vast pool of candidates. Notably, our algorithm exhibits a linear scaling of computational time with the number of symmetry-inequivalent structures, N, up to approximately 10^9, representing the best scaling achieved for this problem.

title: A Taxonomy of Anomalies in Log Data
text: Log data anomaly detection is a core component in the area of artificial intelligence for IT operations. However, the large amount of existing methods makes it hard to choose the right approach for a specific system. A better understanding of different kinds of anomalies, and which algorithms are suitable for detecting them, would support researchers and IT operators. Although a common taxonomy for anomalies already exists, it has not yet been applied specifically to log data, pointing out the characteristics and peculiarities in this domain. In this paper, we present a taxonomy for different kinds of log data anomalies and introduce a method for analyzing such anomalies in labeled datasets. We applied our taxonomy to the three common benchmark datasets Thunderbird, Spirit, and BGL, and trained five state-of-the-art unsupervised anomaly detection algorithms to evaluate their performance in detecting different kinds of anomalies. Our results show, that the most common anomaly type is also the easiest to predict. Moreover, deep learning-based approaches outperform data mining-based approaches in all anomaly types, but especially when it comes to detecting contextual anomalies.

title: A Taxonomy of Anomalies in Log Data
text: The proliferation of logging mechanisms in modern software systems has led to an explosion of log data, making it increasingly challenging to identify and diagnose anomalies. Despite the importance of anomaly detection in log data, there exists a lack of standardized terminology and classification, hindering the development of effective detection techniques. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a comprehensive taxonomy of anomalies in log data. Through a systematic analysis of 1500+ logs from various domains, including cloud computing, web applications, and IoT systems, we identify and categorize 27 distinct anomaly types. Our taxonomy is based on a novel framework that considers the anomaly's manifestation, root cause, and impact on the system. We demonstrate the efficacy of our taxonomy through a case study on a real-world cloud computing platform, where we show that it enables the detection of 95% of anomalies with a reduced false positive rate of 2.5%. Our taxonomy provides a foundation for the development of anomaly detection techniques tailored to specific log data characteristics, facilitating more accurate and efficient diagnosis of system failures.

title: Bitemporal Property Graphs to Organize Evolving Systems
text: This work is a summarized view on the results of a one-year cooperation between Oracle Corp. and the University of Leipzig. The goal was to research the organization of relationships within multi-dimensional time-series data, such as sensor data from the IoT area. We showed in this project that temporal property graphs with some extensions are a prime candidate for this organizational task that combines the strengths of both data models (graph and time-series). The outcome of the cooperation includes four achievements: (1) a bitemporal property graph model, (2) a temporal graph query language, (3) a conception of continuous event detection, and (4) a prototype of a bitemporal graph database that supports the model, language and event detection.

title: Bitemporal Property Graphs to Organize Evolving Systems
text: Evolving systems, such as social networks and knowledge graphs, undergo continuous changes, making it challenging to manage and query their temporal dynamics. Existing property graph models are limited in their ability to capture both valid-time and transaction-time dimensions, leading to fragmented and incomplete representations. This paper introduces Bitemporal Property Graphs (BPGs), a novel data model that integrates both time dimensions, enabling a unified and consistent view of evolving systems. We develop a formal framework for BPGs, including a data model, query language, and indexing techniques. Experimental evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of BPGs in supporting complex temporal queries, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches by up to 3x in query performance and 2x in storage efficiency.

title: Controlling the Correctness of Aggregation Operations During Sessions of Interactive Analytic Queries
text: We present a comprehensive set of conditions and rules to control the correctness of aggregation queries within an interactive data analysis session. The goal is to extend self-service data preparation and BI tools to automatically detect semantically incorrect aggregate queries on analytic tables and views built by using the common analytic operations including filter, project, join, aggregate, union, difference, and pivot. We introduce aggregable properties to describe for any attribute of an analytic table which aggregation functions correctly aggregates the attribute along which sets of dimension attributes. These properties can also be used to formally identify attributes which are summarizable with respect to some aggregation function along a given set of dimension attributes. This is particularly helpful to detect incorrect aggregations of measures obtained through the use of non-distributive aggregation functions like average and count. We extend the notion of summarizability by introducing a new generalized summarizability condition to control the aggregation of attributes after any analytic operation. Finally, we define propagation rules which transform aggregable properties of the query input tables into new aggregable properties for the result tables, preserving summarizability and generalized summarizability.

title: Controlling the Correctness of Aggregation Operations During Sessions of Interactive Analytic Queries
text: We establish a rigorous framework for governing the correctness of aggregation queries within interactive data analysis sessions, thereby enhancing self-service data preparation and business intelligence tools. Specifically, our approach enables the automatic detection of semantically incorrect aggregate queries on analytic tables and views constructed via common operations such as filter, project, join, aggregate, union, difference, and pivot. A key innovation is the introduction of aggregable properties, which describe the aggregation functions that correctly operate on an attribute along specific sets of dimension attributes. These properties also facilitate the formal identification of summarizable attributes with respect to a given aggregation function and dimension attributes, thereby detecting incorrect aggregations of measures derived using non-distributive functions like average and count. We further generalize the notion of summarizability by introducing a novel condition that controls attribute aggregation following any analytic operation. Moreover, we define propagation rules that transform input table aggregable properties into result table properties, preserving summarizability and generalized summarizability.

title: Leveraging Unsupervised Learning to Summarize APIs Discussed in Stack Overflow
text: Automated source code summarization is a task that generates summarized information about the purpose, usage, and--or implementation of methods and classes to support understanding of these code entities. Multiple approaches and techniques have been proposed for supervised and unsupervised learning in code summarization, however, they were mostly focused on generating a summary for a piece of code. In addition, very few works have leveraged unofficial documentation. This paper proposes an automatic and novel approach for summarizing Android API methods discussed in Stack Overflow that we consider as unofficial documentation in this research. Our approach takes the API method's name as an input and generates a natural language summary based on Stack Overflow discussions of that API method. We have conducted a survey that involves 16 Android developers to evaluate the quality of our automatically generated summaries and compare them with the official Android documentation. Our results demonstrate that while developers find the official documentation more useful in general, the generated summaries are also competitive, in particular for offering implementation details, and can be used as a complementary source for guiding developers in software development and maintenance tasks.

title: Leveraging Unsupervised Learning to Summarize APIs Discussed in Stack Overflow
text: The growing complexity of software systems and the proliferation of application programming interfaces (APIs) have led to an explosion of online discussions on platforms like Stack Overflow, where developers seek help and share knowledge. However, the sheer volume of these discussions makes it challenging for developers to locate relevant information, leading to duplicated efforts and decreased productivity. To address this issue, we propose an unsupervised learning approach to automatically summarize APIs discussed in Stack Overflow. Our methodology involves a multi-step pipeline, where we first collect and preprocess a large dataset of API-related questions and answers from Stack Overflow. We then employ a combination of natural language processing and graph-based clustering techniques to identify key concepts and relationships within the data. Finally, we generate concise summaries of each API, highlighting its key features, usage scenarios, and common pitfalls. Our evaluation on a dataset of 10,000 API-related questions shows that our approach significantly outperforms traditional topic modeling techniques, achieving a 32% improvement in summary coherence and a 25% improvement in relevance to the original API documentation. Our results have important implications for the development of more effective API documentation and discovery tools.

title: Semantic Code Search for Smart Contracts
text: Semantic code search technology allows searching for existing code snippets through natural language, which can greatly improve programming efficiency. Smart contracts, programs that run on the blockchain, have a code reuse rate of more than 90%, which means developers have a great demand for semantic code search tools. However, the existing code search models still have a semantic gap between code and query, and perform poorly on specialized queries of smart contracts. In this paper, we propose a Multi-Modal Smart contract Code Search (MM-SCS) model. Specifically, we construct a Contract Elements Dependency Graph (CEDG) for MM-SCS as an additional modality to capture the data-flow and control-flow information of the code. To make the model more focused on the key contextual information, we use a multi-head attention network to generate embeddings for code features. In addition, we use a fine-tuned pretrained model to ensure the model's effectiveness when the training data is small. We compared MM-SCS with four state-of-the-art models on a dataset with 470K (code, docstring) pairs collected from Github and Etherscan. Experimental results show that MM-SCS achieves an MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank) of 0.572, outperforming four state-of-the-art models UNIF, DeepCS, CARLCS-CNN, and TAB-CS by 34.2%, 59.3%, 36.8%, and 14.1%, respectively. Additionally, the search speed of MM-SCS is second only to UNIF, reaching 0.34s/query.

title: Semantic Code Search for Smart Contracts
text: The advent of semantic code search technology has revolutionized the way programmers discover and reuse existing code, significantly enhancing development efficiency. In the realm of smart contracts, which exhibit a remarkable code reuse rate exceeding 90%, the demand for effective semantic code search tools is particularly pronounced. However, current code search models struggle to bridge the semantic gap between code and query, leading to subpar performance on specialized smart contract queries. To address this limitation, we introduce the Multi-Modal Smart contract Code Search (MM-SCS) model, which leverages a Contract Elements Dependency Graph (CEDG) as an additional modality to capture data-flow and control-flow information. By integrating a multi-head attention network to generate contextualized code feature embeddings and fine-tuning a pre-trained model, our approach ensures robustness even with limited training data. Evaluating MM-SCS on a large dataset of 470,000 code-docstring pairs from Github and Etherscan, we demonstrate a significant improvement in Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) to 0.572, surpassing four state-of-the-art models by 34.2%, 59.3%, 36.8%, and 14.1%, respectively. Furthermore, MM-SCS achieves a search speed of 0.34 seconds per query, second only to UNIF.

title: Agility in Software 2.0 -- Notebook Interfaces and MLOps with Buttresses and Rebars
text: Artificial intelligence through machine learning is increasingly used in the digital society. Solutions based on machine learning bring both great opportunities, thus coined "Software 2.0," but also great challenges for the engineering community to tackle. Due to the experimental approach used by data scientists when developing machine learning models, agility is an essential characteristic. In this keynote address, we discuss two contemporary development phenomena that are fundamental in machine learning development, i.e., notebook interfaces and MLOps. First, we present a solution that can remedy some of the intrinsic weaknesses of working in notebooks by supporting easy transitions to integrated development environments. Second, we propose reinforced engineering of AI systems by introducing metaphorical buttresses and rebars in the MLOps context. Machine learning-based solutions are dynamic in nature, and we argue that reinforced continuous engineering is required to quality assure the trustworthy AI systems of tomorrow.

title: Agility in Software 2.0 -- Notebook Interfaces and MLOps with Buttresses and Rebars
text: The pervasive adoption of machine learning in digital society has spawned a new paradigm, dubbed "Software 2.0," which presents both transformative opportunities and formidable engineering challenges. The experimental nature of machine learning development necessitates agility, which is often compromised by the limitations of notebook interfaces and the lack of structured engineering practices. This keynote address examines two pivotal phenomena in machine learning development: notebook interfaces and MLOps. We introduce a novel solution that enables seamless transitions from notebooks to integrated development environments, thereby mitigating inherent weaknesses. Furthermore, we propose a metaphorical framework of buttresses and rebars to reinforce MLOps, ensuring the development of trustworthy AI systems.
