By recognizing the dynamic nature of machine learning-based solutions, we argue that reinforced continuous engineering is essential for quality assurance in AI systems.

title: Code Clone Detection based on Event Embedding and Event Dependency
text: The code clone detection method based on semantic similarity has important value in software engineering tasks (e.g., software evolution, software reuse). Traditional code clone detection technologies pay more attention to the similarity of code at the syntax level, and less attention to the semantic similarity of the code. As a result, candidate codes similar in semantics are ignored. To address this issue, we propose a code clone detection method based on semantic similarity. By treating code as a series of interdependent events that occur continuously, we design a model namely EDAM to encode code semantic information based on event embedding and event dependency. The EDAM model uses the event embedding method to model the execution characteristics of program statements and the data dependence information between all statements. In this way, we can embed the program semantic information into a vector and use the vector to detect codes similar in semantics. Experimental results show that the performance of our EDAM model is superior to state of-the-art open source models for code clone detection.

title: Code Clone Detection based on Event Embedding and Event Dependency
text: Semantic similarity-based code clone detection is crucial in software engineering, particularly in software evolution and reuse. Conventional approaches focus primarily on syntactic similarity, overlooking semantically similar code candidates. This limitation necessitates a novel approach that prioritizes semantic analysis. We introduce EDAM, a model that encodes code semantics by treating code as a sequence of interdependent events. By leveraging event embedding and dependency, EDAM captures the execution characteristics of program statements and data dependence information between them. This enables the embedding of program semantics into a vector, facilitating the detection of semantically similar codes. Our experimental results demonstrate that EDAM outperforms state-of-the-art open-source models in code clone detection, underscoring the efficacy of our semantic similarity-based approach.

title: Schema matching using Gaussian mixture models with Wasserstein distance
text: Gaussian mixture models find their place as a powerful tool, mostly in the clustering problem, but with proper preparation also in feature extraction, pattern recognition, image segmentation and in general machine learning. When faced with the problem of schema matching, different mixture models computed on different pieces of data can maintain crucial information about the structure of the dataset. In order to measure or compare results from mixture models, the Wasserstein distance can be very useful, however it is not easy to calculate for mixture distributions. In this paper we derive one of possible approximations for the Wasserstein distance between Gaussian mixture models and reduce it to linear problem. Furthermore, application examples concerning real world data are shown.

title: Schema matching using Gaussian mixture models with Wasserstein distance
text: Gaussian mixture models have established themselves as a versatile technique, excelling in clustering, feature extraction, pattern recognition, image segmentation, and broader machine learning applications. In schema matching, multiple mixture models computed on disparate data subsets can preserve vital structural information about the dataset. The Wasserstein distance is a valuable metric for evaluating and comparing mixture model outcomes, but its calculation for mixture distributions poses significant challenges. This paper presents an approximation of the Wasserstein distance between Gaussian mixture models, reducing it to a tractable linear problem. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through real-world data applications, showcasing its potential in facilitating meaningful comparisons between mixture models.

title: Enhancing syntax expressiveness in domain-specific modelling
text: Domain-specific modelling helps tame the complexity of today's application domains by formalizing concepts and their relationships in modelling languages. While meta-editors are widely-used frameworks for implementing graphical editors for such modelling languages, they are best suitable for defining {novel} topological notations, i.e., syntaxes where the model layout does not contribute to the model semantics. In contrast, many engineering fields, e.g., railways systems or electrical engineering, use notations that, on the one hand, are standard and, on the other hand, are demanding more expressive power than topological syntaxes. In this paper, we discuss the problem of enhancing the expressiveness of modelling editors towards geometric/positional syntaxes. Several potential solutions are experimentally implemented on the jjodel web-based platform with the aim of identifying challenges and opportunities.

title: Enhancing syntax expressiveness in domain-specific modelling
text: Formalizing domain-specific concepts and relationships through modelling languages has become essential for managing complexity in modern application domains. Meta-editors, widely employed for implementing graphical editors, are well-suited for novel topological notations where layout does not affect semantics. However, many engineering fields, such as railways and electrical engineering, utilize standard notations that require more expressive power, which topological syntaxes cannot provide. This paper addresses the challenge of enhancing modelling editor expressiveness to accommodate geometric and positional syntaxes. We experimentally evaluate potential solutions on the jjodel web-based platform, identifying key challenges and opportunities that can inform future development.

title: Standing on Shoulders or Feet? An Extended Study on the Usage of the MSR Data Papers
text: Context: The establishment of the Mining Software Repositories (MSR) data showcase conference track has encouraged researchers to provide data sets as a basis for further empirical studies. Objective: Examine the usage of data papers published in the MSR proceedings in terms of use frequency, users, and use purpose. Method: Data track papers were collected from the MSR data showcase track and through the manual inspection of older MSR proceedings. The use of data papers was established through manual citation searching followed by reading the citing studies and dividing them into strong and weak citations. Contrary to weak, strong citations truly use the data set of a data paper. Data papers were then manually clustered based on their content, whereas their strong citations were classified by hand according to the knowledge areas of the Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge. A survey study on 108 authors and users of data papers provided further insights regarding motivation and effort in data paper production, encouraging and discouraging factors in data set use, and future desired direction regarding data papers. Results: We found that 65% of the data papers have been used in other studies, with a long-tail distribution in the number of strong citations. Weak citations to data papers usually refer to them as an example. MSR data papers are cited in total less than other MSR papers. A considerable number of the strong citations stem from the teams that authored the data papers. Publications providing Version Control System (VCS) primary and derived data are the most frequent data papers and the most often strongly cited ones. Enhanced developer data papers are the least common ones, and the second least frequently strongly cited. Data paper authors tend to gather data in the context of other research. [...]

title: Standing on Shoulders or Feet? An Extended Study on the Usage of the MSR Data Papers
text: The proliferation of data papers in the Mining Software Repositories (MSR) conference track has facilitated the creation of a valuable resource for empirical software engineering research. This study investigates the utilization patterns of MSR data papers, focusing on their frequency of use, user demographics, and purposes of application. We compiled a comprehensive dataset of MSR data track papers through manual inspection of conference proceedings and subsequent citation analysis. Strong citations, which genuinely utilize the data sets provided, were distinguished from weak citations, which merely reference data papers as examples. The content of data papers was manually clustered, and their strong citations were categorized according to the knowledge areas outlined in the Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge. A survey of 108 data paper authors and users provided additional insights into their motivations, effort, and perceived challenges in data paper creation, as well as their desired future directions for data papers. Our results show that 65% of data papers have been reused in other studies, with a skewed distribution of strong citations. Notably, data papers authored by teams that also contributed to their citation were prevalent. Data papers providing Version Control System (VCS) primary and derived data were the most frequently cited and strongly utilized, whereas enhanced developer data papers were the least common and second least frequently strongly cited. Furthermore, our findings suggest that data paper authors often collect data in the context of other research endeavors, highlighting the need for more targeted data collection efforts.

title: Bounding the Last Mile: Efficient Learned String Indexing
text: We introduce the RadixStringSpline (RSS) learned index structure for efficiently indexing strings. RSS is a tree of radix splines each indexing a fixed number of bytes. RSS approaches or exceeds the performance of traditional string indexes while using 7-70$\times$ less memory. RSS achieves this by using the minimal string prefix to sufficiently distinguish the data unlike most learned approaches which index the entire string. Additionally, the bounded-error nature of RSS accelerates the last mile search and also enables a memory-efficient hash-table lookup accelerator. We benchmark RSS on several real-world string datasets against ART and HOT. Our experiments suggest this line of research may be promising for future memory-intensive database applications.

title: Bounding the Last Mile: Efficient Learned String Indexing
text: The proliferation of large-scale string datasets has exacerbated the need for efficient indexing techniques that facilitate fast lookup and retrieval operations. Traditional approaches, such as trie-based indexing, often suffer from poor space efficiency and limited scalability. In response, learned indexing methods have emerged as a promising solution, leveraging machine learning models to predict the location of strings in a dataset. This work presents a novel learned string indexing approach that achieves state-of-the-art space efficiency and query performance. By incorporating a bounded last-mile retrieval mechanism, our method reduces the average query latency by 3.2x compared to existing learned indexing techniques, while maintaining a space overhead of less than 1.5% on real-world datasets.

title: US-Rule: Discovering Utility-driven Sequential Rules
text: Utility-driven mining is an important task in data science and has many applications in real life. High utility sequential pattern mining (HUSPM) is one kind of utility-driven mining. HUSPM aims to discover all sequential patterns with high utility. However, the existing algorithms of HUSPM can not provide an accurate probability to deal with some scenarios for prediction or recommendation. High-utility sequential rule mining (HUSRM) was proposed to discover all sequential rules with high utility and high confidence. There is only one algorithm proposed for HUSRM, which is not enough efficient. In this paper, we propose a faster algorithm, called US-Rule, to efficiently mine high-utility sequential rules. It utilizes rule estimated utility co-occurrence pruning strategy (REUCP) to avoid meaningless computation. To improve the efficiency on dense and long sequence datasets, four tighter upper bounds (LEEU, REEU, LERSU, RERSU) and their corresponding pruning strategies (LEEUP, REEUP, LERSUP, RERSUP) are proposed. Besides, US-Rule proposes rule estimated utility recomputing pruning strategy (REURP) to deal with sparse datasets. At last, a large number of experiments on different datasets compared to the state-of-the-art algorithm demonstrate that US-Rule can achieve better performance in terms of execution time, memory consumption and scalability.

title: US-Rule: Discovering Utility-driven Sequential Rules
text: The proliferation of sequential data in various domains has spawned a surge of interest in discovering insightful patterns from such data. Existing sequential rule mining approaches primarily focus on frequency-based measures, overlooking the inherent utility associated with each item in the sequence. This oversight leads to the extraction of rules that might not be meaningful or actionable in real-world applications. To bridge this gap, we propose US-Rule, a novel framework for discovering utility-driven sequential rules. US-Rule integrates the concepts of utility theory and sequential pattern mining to extract rules that maximize utility, rather than mere frequency. Our approach employs a novel utility-aware sequence encoding scheme and a tailored search strategy to efficiently explore the vast space of possible rules. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of US-Rule in discovering high-utility rules that are often overlooked by traditional frequency-based approaches. Furthermore, our framework is shown to be robust against noise and variations in the input data, making it a reliable tool for utility-driven decision-making in a wide range of applications, including recommender systems, healthcare, and finance.

title: Anomaly Rule Detection in Sequence Data
text: Analyzing sequence data usually leads to the discovery of interesting patterns and then anomaly detection. In recent years, numerous frameworks and methods have been proposed to discover interesting patterns in sequence data as well as detect anomalous behavior. However, existing algorithms mainly focus on frequency-driven analytic, and they are challenging to be applied in real-world settings. In this work, we present a new anomaly detection framework called DUOS that enables Discovery of Utility-aware Outlier Sequential rules from a set of sequences. In this pattern-based anomaly detection algorithm, we incorporate both the anomalousness and utility of a group, and then introduce the concept of utility-aware outlier sequential rule (UOSR). We show that this is a more meaningful way for detecting anomalies. Besides, we propose some efficient pruning strategies w.r.t. upper bounds for mining UOSR, as well as the outlier detection. An extensive experimental study conducted on several real-world datasets shows that the proposed DUOS algorithm has a better effectiveness and efficiency. Finally, DUOS outperforms the baseline algorithm and has a suitable scalability.

title: Anomaly Rule Detection in Sequence Data
text: Sequence data analysis often uncovers intriguing patterns and anomalies, prompting the development of various frameworks and methods to identify these phenomena. Despite this, existing algorithms predominantly rely on frequency-driven approaches, which struggle to translate to real-world applications. This limitation motivates the introduction of DUOS, a novel anomaly detection framework that extracts utility-aware outlier sequential rules from a collection of sequences. By integrating both anomalousness and utility considerations, our pattern-based approach defines the concept of utility-aware outlier sequential rules (UOSRs). We demonstrate that this paradigm shift yields more meaningful anomaly detection. To facilitate efficient UOSR mining and outlier detection, we propose upper-bound-based pruning strategies. An exhaustive evaluation on multiple real-world datasets reveals that DUOS exhibits superior effectiveness and efficiency compared to baseline algorithms, while also demonstrating suitable scalability.

title: Living-Off-The-Land Command Detection Using Active Learning
text: In recent years, enterprises have been targeted by advanced adversaries who leverage creative ways to infiltrate their systems and move laterally to gain access to critical data. One increasingly common evasive method is to hide the malicious activity behind a benign program by using tools that are already installed on user computers. These programs are usually part of the operating system distribution or another user-installed binary, therefore this type of attack is called "Living-Off-The-Land". Detecting these attacks is challenging, as adversaries may not create malicious files on the victim computers and anti-virus scans fail to detect them. We propose the design of an Active Learning framework called LOLAL for detecting Living-Off-the-Land attacks that iteratively selects a set of uncertain and anomalous samples for labeling by a human analyst. LOLAL is specifically designed to work well when a limited number of labeled samples are available for training machine learning models to detect attacks. We investigate methods to represent command-line text using word-embedding techniques, and design ensemble boosting classifiers to distinguish malicious and benign samples based on the embedding representation. We leverage a large, anonymized dataset collected by an endpoint security product and demonstrate that our ensemble classifiers achieve an average F1 score of 0.96 at classifying different attack classes. We show that our active learning method consistently improves the classifier performance, as more training data is labeled, and converges in less than 30 iterations when starting with a small number of labeled instances.

title: Living-Off-The-Land Command Detection Using Active Learning
text: Advanced attackers often employ Living-Off-The-Land (LOTL) tactics, leveraging existing system tools and binaries to evade detection by traditional signature-based approaches. The lack of distinct malicious patterns and the inherent noise in system calls make LOTL command detection a challenging problem. To tackle this, we propose an active learning framework that selectively queries an oracle to label a subset of system calls, thereby minimizing the labeling effort while maximizing the detection accuracy. Our approach, dubbed LOTL-AL, combines a novel uncertainty-based sampling strategy with a state-of-the-art deep learning model to identify LOTL commands. We evaluate LOTL-AL on a large-scale dataset of system calls collected from a variety of sources, including real-world attack scenarios and benign system activity. Our experimental results demonstrate that LOTL-AL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art LOTL detection methods, achieving an F1-score of 0.93 compared to 0.78 and 0.82 of the baselines. Furthermore, we show that our active learning framework reduces the labeling effort by 60% while maintaining a high detection accuracy. A detailed analysis of the labeled data reveals that LOTL-AL is effective in detecting LOTL commands that involve file system and network interactions. We believe that our approach has the potential to significantly improve the detection capabilities of modern security information and event management systems, thereby reducing the attack surface of modern systems.

title: Mitigating Adversarial Attacks by Distributing Different Copies to Different Users
text: Machine learning models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. In this paper, we consider the scenario where a model is distributed to multiple buyers, among which a malicious buyer attempts to attack another buyer. The malicious buyer probes its copy of the model to search for adversarial samples and then presents the found samples to the victim's copy of the model in order to replicate the attack. We point out that by distributing different copies of the model to different buyers, we can mitigate the attack such that adversarial samples found on one copy would not work on another copy. We observed that training a model with different randomness indeed mitigates such replication to a certain degree. However, there is no guarantee and retraining is computationally expensive. A number of works extended the retraining method to enhance the differences among models. However, a very limited number of models can be produced using such methods and the computational cost becomes even higher. Therefore, we propose a flexible parameter rewriting method that directly modifies the model's parameters. This method does not require additional training and is able to generate a large number of copies in a more controllable manner, where each copy induces different adversarial regions. Experimentation studies show that rewriting can significantly mitigate the attacks while retaining high classification accuracy. For instance, on GTSRB dataset with respect to Hop Skip Jump attack, using attractor-based rewriter can reduce the success rate of replicating the attack to 0.5% while independently training copies with different randomness can reduce the success rate to 6.5%. From this study, we believe that there are many further directions worth exploring.

title: Mitigating Adversarial Attacks by Distributing Different Copies to Different Users
text: The proliferation of deep learning models in security-critical applications has exposed them to an array of adversarial attacks, which can manipulate the input data to compromise the model's integrity. While various defense strategies have been proposed, most of them focus on robustifying the model itself, overlooking the inherent vulnerabilities in the data distribution pipeline. In this context, we explore a novel approach that leverages the distribution of different model copies to different users, thereby increasing the attacker's uncertainty and cost. Our methodology involves generating multiple variants of a given model, each with its unique set of parameters, and distributing them across the user base. We employ a multi-objective optimization framework to ensure that the generated models are not only diverse but also retain their predictive performance on benign inputs. We evaluate the efficacy of our approach against a range of state-of-the-art attacks, including FGSM, PGD, and CW, on multiple benchmark datasets. Our experimental results demonstrate that distributing diverse model copies significantly increases the attacker's error rate, with an average improvement of 23.4% across all attack scenarios. Furthermore, we observe that the attacker's success rate decreases exponentially with the number of model variants, indicating a substantial increase in the attacker's cost. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the trade-offs between model diversity, predictive performance, and robustness, providing valuable insights for practitioners. Our approach offers a promising solution for mitigating adversarial attacks in real-world applications, particularly in scenarios where model updates are frequent, and user populations are diverse. By distributing different model copies to different users, we can create a moving target for attackers, making it increasingly difficult for them to launch successful attacks.

title: Benchmark Static API Call Datasets for Malware Family Classification
text: Nowadays, malware and malware incidents are increasing daily, even with various antivirus systems and malware detection or classification methodologies. Machine learning techniques have been the main focus of the security experts to detect malware and determine their families. Many static, dynamic, and hybrid techniques have been presented for that purpose. In this study, the static analysis technique has been applied to malware samples to extract API calls, which is one of the most used features in machine/deep learning models as it represents the behavior of malware samples. Since the rapid increase and continuous evolution of malware affect the detection capacity of antivirus scanners, recent and updated datasets of malicious software became necessary to overcome this drawback. This paper introduces two new datasets: One with 14,616 samples obtained and compiled from VirusShare and one with 9,795 samples from VirusSample. In addition, benchmark results based on static API calls of malware samples are presented using several machine and deep learning models on these datasets. We believe that these two datasets and benchmark results enable researchers to test and validate their methods and approaches in this field.

title: Benchmark Static API Call Datasets for Malware Family Classification
text: Malware family classification is a crucial task in cybersecurity, enabling the identification of malware strains and informing defense strategies. Static API call analysis has emerged as a prominent approach, leveraging the sequence of API calls made by a malware sample to determine its family affiliation. However, the lack of standardized, publicly available datasets hinders the development and evaluation of effective classification models. To address this gap, we introduce three benchmark datasets for static API call-based malware family classification, comprising 10,000 samples from 25 prominent malware families. Our datasets are constructed using a novel, modular framework that integrates various data sources, including VirusTotal, MalwareBazaar, and manual reverse engineering. We apply a range of feature extraction techniques, including n-gram analysis and graph-based representations, to generate a comprehensive set of features for each sample. Experimental results using popular machine learning algorithms demonstrate the efficacy of our datasets, achieving an average F1-score of 0.93 across five classification models. We also highlight the limitations of existing feature extraction methods and provide insights into the most discriminative API calls for each malware family. Our datasets and findings provide a foundation for advancing the state-of-the-art in malware family classification.

title: Privacy-Preserving Decentralized Exchange Marketplaces
text: Decentralized exchange markets leveraging blockchain have been proposed recently to provide open and equal access to traders, improve transparency and reduce systemic risk of centralized exchanges. However, they compromise on the privacy of traders with respect to their asset ownership, account balance, order details and their identity. In this paper, we present Rialto, a fully decentralized privacy-preserving exchange marketplace with support for matching trade orders, on-chain settlement and market price discovery. Rialto provides confidentiality of order rates and account balances and unlinkability between traders and their trade orders, while retaining the desirable properties of a traditional marketplace like front-running resilience and market fairness. We define formal security notions and present a security analysis of the marketplace. We perform a detailed evaluation of our solution, demonstrate that it scales well and is suitable for a large class of goods and financial instruments traded in modern exchange markets.

title: Privacy-Preserving Decentralized Exchange Marketplaces
text: Decentralized exchange marketplaces have gained popularity as a means to facilitate trustless and censorship-resistant transactions. However, they often compromise on privacy, exposing sensitive user information to malicious actors. To address this limitation, we propose a novel decentralized exchange architecture that leverages secure multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption to enable privacy-preserving trades. Our approach utilizes a decentralized network of nodes, each maintaining a local order book, to facilitate matchmaking and trade execution while keeping user identities and trade details confidential. We evaluate our design through a combination of theoretical analysis and experimental simulations, demonstrating its scalability and resistance to various attack vectors. Our results show that our protocol reduces the privacy leakage by 95% compared to existing decentralized exchange solutions, while incurring an acceptable overhead of 15% in terms of transaction latency.

title: Towards Automated Semantic Grouping in Workflows for Multi-Disciplinary Analysis
text: When designing multidisciplinary tool workflows in visual development environments, researchers and engineers often combine simulation tools which serve a functional purpose and helper tools that merely ensure technical compatibility by, e.g., converting between file formats. If the development environment does not offer native support for such groups of tools, maintainability of the developed workflow quickly deteriorates with an increase in complexity. We present an approach towards automatically identifying such groups of closely related tools in multidisciplinary workflows implemented in RCE by transforming the workflow into a graph and applying graph clustering algorithms to it. Further, we implement this approach and evaluate multiple clustering algorithms. Our results strongly indicate that this approach can yield groups of closely related tools in RCE workflows, but also that solutions to this problem will have to be tailor-made to each specific style of workflow design.

title: Towards Automated Semantic Grouping in Workflows for Multi-Disciplinary Analysis
text: The proliferation of multi-disciplinary analysis has led to an explosion of complex workflows, often comprising hundreds of tasks, which are difficult to comprehend and maintain. A crucial step in workflow comprehension is the identification of semantically related tasks, enabling the abstraction of workflows into higher-level constructs. However, manual grouping is time-consuming and error-prone. We propose a novel approach to automate semantic grouping in workflows using a combination of natural language processing and graph-based clustering techniques. Our methodology involves parsing task descriptions and labels to extract semantic features, followed by graph construction and clustering to identify densely connected components. Evaluation on a dataset of 50 real-world workflows from diverse domains demonstrates that our approach achieves a mean F1-score of 0.87, outperforming existing methods by at least 15%. Our results pave the way for scalable and accurate workflow comprehension, enabling more effective collaboration and knowledge reuse in multi-disciplinary analysis.

title: The Impact of Considering Human Values during Requirements Engineering Activities
text: Human values, or what people hold important in their life, such as freedom, fairness, and social responsibility, often remain unnoticed and unattended during software development. Ignoring values can lead to values violations in software that can result in financial losses, reputation damage, and widespread social and legal implications. However, embedding human values in software is not only non-trivial but also generally an unclear process. Commencing as early as during the Requirements Engineering (RE) activities promises to ensure fit-for-purpose and quality software products that adhere to human values. But what is the impact of considering human values explicitly during early RE activities? To answer this question, we conducted a scenario-based survey where 56 software practitioners contextualised requirements analysis towards a proposed mobile application for the homeless and suggested values-laden software features accordingly. The suggested features were qualitatively analysed. Results show that explicit considerations of values can help practitioners identify applicable values, associate purpose with the features they develop, think outside-the-box, and build connections between software features and human values. Finally, drawing from the results and experiences of this study, we propose a scenario-based values elicitation process -- a simple four-step takeaway as a practical implication of this study.

title: The Impact of Considering Human Values during Requirements Engineering Activities
text: The consideration of human values during requirements engineering (RE) activities is crucial for developing software systems that align with societal norms and user expectations. Despite this, existing RE methodologies often neglect value considerations, leading to systems that can perpetuate biases, discriminate, or infringe upon user privacy. This study investigates the impact of explicitly considering human values during RE activities on the resulting software systems. We conducted a mixed-methods study, comprising a systematic literature review, a survey of 30 RE practitioners, and a controlled experiment with 60 participants. Our results show that explicitly considering human values during RE activities leads to a significant increase in the inclusion of value-related requirements, improved system usability, and enhanced user satisfaction. Furthermore, our study reveals that the consideration of human values reduces the likelihood of bias and discrimination in software systems. We also identify significant challenges and limitations in incorporating value considerations into RE practices, including the need for value-aware RE methodologies and tools. Our findings have important implications for the development of software systems that respect human values and contribute to a more socially responsible software engineering discipline.

title: A Semi-automated Method for Domain-Specific Ontology Creation from Medical Guidelines
text: The automated capturing and summarization of medical consultations has the potential to reduce the administrative burden in healthcare. Consultations are structured conversations that broadly follow a guideline with a systematic examination of predefined observations and symptoms to diagnose and treat well-defined medical conditions. A key component in automated conversation summarization is the matching of the knowledge graph of the consultation transcript with a medical domain ontology for the interpretation of the consultation conversation. Existing general medical ontologies such as SNOMED CT provide a taxonomic view on the terminology, but they do not capture the essence of the guidelines that define consultations. As part of our research on medical conversation summarization, this paper puts forward a semi-automated method for generating an ontological representation of a medical guideline. The method, which takes as input the well-known SNOMED CT nomenclature and a medical guideline, maps the guidelines to a so-called Medical Guideline Ontology (MGO), a machine-processable version of the guideline that can be used for interpreting the conversation during a consultation. We illustrate our approach by discussing the creation of an MGO of the medical condition of ear canal inflammation (Otitis Externa) given the corresponding guideline from a Dutch medical authority.

title: A Semi-automated Method for Domain-Specific Ontology Creation from Medical Guidelines
text: The lack of standardized, domain-specific ontologies hinders the integration and analysis of medical knowledge, leading to inefficient decision-making and poor patient outcomes. Medical guidelines, which capture evidence-based best practices, offer a rich source of domain knowledge for ontology creation. However, manual ontology construction from these guidelines is time-consuming, error-prone, and requires significant domain expertise. We propose a semi-automated method for domain-specific ontology creation from medical guidelines, leveraging natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning (ML) techniques. Our approach involves guideline preprocessing, entity recognition, and relation extraction using a hybrid NLP pipeline. The extracted entities and relations are then used to construct an ontology, which is refined through ML-based clustering and classification. We evaluated our method on a corpus of 50 guidelines from the American Heart Association, achieving an F1-score of 0.92 for entity recognition and 0.85 for relation extraction. The resulting ontology, comprising 350 concepts and 1,200 relations, demonstrates high coherence and consistency with existing biomedical ontologies. Our method reduces the time and effort required for ontology creation by 70%, while maintaining high accuracy and facilitating the integration of medical knowledge from diverse guidelines.

title: Exploring rationality of self awareness in social networking for logical modeling of unintentional insiders
text: Unawareness of privacy risks together with approval seeking motivations make humans enter too much detail into the likes of Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram. To test whether the rationality principle applies, we construct a tool that shows to a user what is known publicly on social networking sites about her. In our experiment, we check whether this revelation changes human behaviour. To extrapolate and generalize, we use the insights gained by practical experimentation. Unaware users can become targeted by attackers. They then become unintentional insiders. We demonstrate this by extending the Isabelle Insider framework to accommodate a formal model of unintentional insiders, an open problem with long standing.

title: Exploring rationality of self awareness in social networking for logical modeling of unintentional insiders
text: The propensity for individuals to overshare personal information on social media platforms, such as Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram, can be attributed to a lack of awareness regarding privacy risks and the desire for approval. This study investigates the rationality principle by developing a tool that discloses publicly available information about a user on these platforms. Through experimentation, we examine whether this revelation prompts behavioral changes. Our findings provide valuable insights, highlighting the risks of uninformed users becoming targeted by attackers and, subsequently, unintentional insiders. We formally model this phenomenon by extending the Isabelle Insider framework, addressing a long-standing open problem in the field.

title: Evaluating Gradient Inversion Attacks and Defenses in Federated Learning
text: Gradient inversion attack (or input recovery from gradient) is an emerging threat to the security and privacy preservation of Federated learning, whereby malicious eavesdroppers or participants in the protocol can recover (partially) the clients' private data. This paper evaluates existing attacks and defenses. We find that some attacks make strong assumptions about the setup. Relaxing such assumptions can substantially weaken these attacks. We then evaluate the benefits of three proposed defense mechanisms against gradient inversion attacks. We show the trade-offs of privacy leakage and data utility of these defense methods, and find that combining them in an appropriate manner makes the attack less effective, even under the original strong assumptions. We also estimate the computation cost of end-to-end recovery of a single image under each evaluated defense. Our findings suggest that the state-of-the-art attacks can currently be defended against with minor data utility loss, as summarized in a list of potential strategies. Our code is available at:

title: Evaluating Gradient Inversion Attacks and Defenses in Federated Learning
text: Federated learning, a decentralized approach to collaborative model training, is vulnerable to gradient inversion attacks, which enable malicious entities to recover clients' private data from shared model updates. This vulnerability compromises the security and privacy of the learning protocol. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of existing gradient inversion attacks and defense mechanisms, revealing that the efficacy of these attacks is often contingent upon strong assumptions about the setup. By relaxing these assumptions, we demonstrate a significant weakening of the attacks. Furthermore, we assess the trade-offs between privacy leakage and data utility for three proposed defense strategies, showcasing that a judicious combination of these methods can effectively mitigate gradient inversion attacks even under stringent conditions. We also quantify the computational cost of end-to-end image recovery under each defense mechanism. Our results indicate that current state-of-the-art attacks can be defended against with minimal data utility loss, and we outline potential strategies to achieve this.

title: Maliva: Using Machine Learning to Rewrite Visualization Queries Under Time Constraints
text: We consider data-visualization systems where a middleware layer translates a frontend request to a SQL query to a backend database to compute visual results. We study the problem of answering a visualization request within a limited time constraint due to the responsiveness requirement. We explore the optimization options of rewriting an original query by adding hints and/or doing approximations so that the total time is within the time constraint. We develop a novel middleware solution called Maliva based on machine learning (ML) techniques. It applies the Markov Decision Process (MDP) model to decide how to rewrite queries and uses training instances to learn an agent to make a sequence of decisions judiciously for an online request. We give a full specification of the technique, including how to construct an MDP model, how to train an agent, and how to use approximating rewrite options. Our experiments on both real and synthetic datasets show that Maliva performs significantly better than a baseline solution that does not do any rewriting, in terms of both the probability of serving requests interactively and query execution time.

title: Maliva: Using Machine Learning to Rewrite Visualization Queries Under Time Constraints
text: The proliferation of data visualization tools has led to an exponential increase in visualization queries, often resulting in performance bottlenecks. In response, database administrators resort to query rewriting, a labor-intensive process that requires domain expertise. We propose Maliva, a machine learning framework that rewrites visualization queries under time constraints, mitigating performance issues while preserving result accuracy. Maliva's core component is a query rewriting engine, powered by a graph neural network (GNN) that learns to identify optimization opportunities from a corpus of visualization queries. Our methodology involves collecting a large dataset of queries, annotating them with performance metrics, and training the GNN to predict optimal rewrite strategies. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that Maliva reduces query execution time by up to 75% while maintaining result accuracy within 5% of the original query. Furthermore, our framework outperforms state-of-the-art query optimization techniques by an average of 32% in terms of query execution time. Maliva's ability to efficiently rewrite visualization queries under time constraints has significant implications for large-scale data analytics and business intelligence applications.

title: Public Data-Assisted Mirror Descent for Private Model Training
text: In this paper, we revisit the problem of using in-distribution public data to improve the privacy/utility trade-offs for differentially private (DP) model training. (Here, public data refers to auxiliary data sets that have no privacy concerns.) We design a natural variant of DP mirror descent, where the DP gradients of the private/sensitive data act as the linear term, and the loss generated by the public data as the mirror map. We show that, for linear regression with feature vectors drawn from a non-isotropic sub-Gaussian distribution, our algorithm, PDA-DPMD (a variant of mirror descent), provides population risk guarantees that are asymptotically better than the best known guarantees under DP (without having access to public data), when the number of public data samples ($n_{\sf pub}$) is sufficiently large. We further show that our algorithm has natural "noise stability" properties that control the variance due to noise added to ensure DP. We demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithm by showing privacy/utility trade-offs on four benchmark datasets (StackOverflow, WikiText-2, CIFAR-10, and EMNIST). We show that our algorithm not only significantly improves over traditional DP-SGD, which does not have access to public data, but to our knowledge is the first to improve over DP-SGD on models that have been pre-trained with public data.

title: Public Data-Assisted Mirror Descent for Private Model Training
text: The incorporation of in-distribution public data offers a promising avenue for enhancing the privacy/utility trade-offs in differentially private (DP) model training. We propose a novel variant of DP mirror descent, wherein the DP gradients of the private/sensitive data comprise the linear term, and the loss generated by the public data serves as the mirror map. Our theoretical analysis reveals that, for linear regression with non-isotropic sub-Gaussian feature vectors, our algorithm, PDA-DPMD, yields asymptotically superior population risk guarantees compared to the state-of-the-art DP methods that do not leverage public data, provided the number of public data samples (n_pub) is sufficiently large. Furthermore, we establish that PDA-DPMD exhibits natural "noise stability" properties, which effectively mitigate the variance introduced by the noise added to ensure DP. Empirical evaluations on four benchmark datasets (StackOverflow, WikiText-2, CIFAR-10, and EMNIST) demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, surpassing traditional DP-SGD and, to our knowledge, marking the first improvement over DP-SGD on pre-trained models utilizing public data.

title: Efficient loading of reduced data ensembles produced at ORNL SNS/HFIR neutron time-of-flight facilities
text: We present algorithmic improvements to the loading operations of certain reduced data ensembles produced from neutron scattering experiments at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) facilities. Ensembles from multiple measurements are required to cover a wide range of the phase space of a sample material of interest. They are stored using the standard NeXus schema on individual HDF5 files. This makes it a scalability challenge, as the number of experiments stored increases in a single ensemble file. The present work follows up on our previous efforts on data management algorithms, to address identified input output (I/O) bottlenecks in Mantid, an open-source data analysis framework used across several neutron science facilities around the world. We reuse an in-memory binary-tree metadata index that resembles data access patterns, to provide a scalable search and extraction mechanism. In addition, several memory operations are refactored and optimized for the current common use cases, ranging most frequently from 10 to 180, and up to 360 separate measurement configurations. Results from this work show consistent speed ups in wall-clock time on the Mantid LoadMD routine, ranging from 19\% to 23\% on average, on ORNL production computing systems. The latter depends on the complexity of the targeted instrument-specific data and the system I/O and compute variability for the shared computational resources available to users of ORNL's Spallation Neutron Source (SNS) and the High Flux Isotope Reactor (HFIR) instruments. Nevertheless, we continue to highlight the need for more research to address reduction challenges as experimental data volumes, user time and processing costs increase.

title: Efficient loading of reduced data ensembles produced at ORNL SNS/HFIR neutron time-of-flight facilities
text: Optimizations to the loading operations of reduced data ensembles, generated from neutron scattering experiments at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) facilities, are presented. These ensembles, comprising multiple measurements, are essential for comprehensively mapping the phase space of sample materials. The standard NeXus schema is employed to store these ensembles on individual HDF5 files, which can lead to scalability issues as the number of stored experiments increases. Building upon our previous research on data management algorithms, we address input/output (I/O) bottlenecks in Mantid, a widely-used open-source data analysis framework for neutron science facilities worldwide. By leveraging an in-memory binary-tree metadata index that mirrors data access patterns, we develop a scalable search and extraction mechanism. Furthermore, memory operations are refactored and optimized for common use cases, encompassing 10 to 180, and up to 360 separate measurement configurations. The resulting enhancements yield consistent wall-clock time speedups of 19% to 23% on average in the Mantid LoadMD routine, as demonstrated on ORNL's production computing systems. The performance variability is attributed to the complexity of instrument-specific data and the shared computational resources available to users of ORNL's Spallation Neutron Source (SNS) and High Flux Isotope Reactor (HFIR) instruments. Despite these improvements, the need for further research into reduction challenges remains pressing, as experimental data volumes, user time, and processing costs continue to escalate.

title: Adversarial Attacks Against Deep Generative Models on Data: A Survey
text: Deep generative models have gained much attention given their ability to generate data for applications as varied as healthcare to financial technology to surveillance, and many more - the most popular models being generative adversarial networks and variational auto-encoders. Yet, as with all machine learning models, ever is the concern over security breaches and privacy leaks and deep generative models are no exception. These models have advanced so rapidly in recent years that work on their security is still in its infancy. In an attempt to audit the current and future threats against these models, and to provide a roadmap for defense preparations in the short term, we prepared this comprehensive and specialized survey on the security and privacy preservation of GANs and VAEs. Our focus is on the inner connection between attacks and model architectures and, more specifically, on five components of deep generative models: the training data, the latent code, the generators/decoders of GANs/ VAEs, the discriminators/encoders of GANs/ VAEs, and the generated data. For each model, component and attack, we review the current research progress and identify the key challenges. The paper concludes with a discussion of possible future attacks and research directions in the field.

title: Adversarial Attacks Against Deep Generative Models on Data: A Survey
text: Deep generative models have emerged as powerful tools for data synthesis, augmentation, and manipulation, with applications in computer vision, natural language processing, and data analytics. However, their vulnerability to adversarial attacks poses a significant threat to their reliability and trustworthiness. Adversarial attacks on deep generative models can compromise the integrity of the generated data, leading to misclassification, misinterpretation, or even exploitation of the generated data for malicious purposes. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the existing literature on adversarial attacks against deep generative models on data. We systematically review various attack methods, including optimization-based, gradient-based, and black-box attacks, and discuss their strengths, limitations, and applicability to different types of generative models. Our analysis reveals that current attacks can be broadly categorized into three categories: input attacks, model inversion attacks, and output attacks. We also identify key challenges and open research directions, including the lack of standardized evaluation metrics, the need for more robust defense mechanisms, and the importance of considering real-world constraints in attack scenarios. Our survey aims to provide a foundation for future research in this area, ultimately contributing to the development of more robust and secure deep generative models.

title: A Blockchain-Enabled Incentivised Framework for Cyber Threat Intelligence Sharing in ICS
text: In recent years Industrial Control Systems (ICS) have been targeted increasingly by sophisticated cyberattacks. Improving ICS security has drawn significant attention in the literature that emphasises the importance of Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) sharing in accelerating detection, mitigation, and prevention of cyberattacks. However, organisations are reluctant to exchange CTI due to fear of exposure, reputational damage, and lack of incentives. Furthermore, there has been limited discussion about the factors influencing participation in sharing CTI about ICS. The existing CTI-sharing platforms rely on centralised trusted architectures that suffer from a single point of failure and risk companies' privacy as the central node maintains CTI details. In this paper, we address the needs of organisations involved in the management and protection of ICS and present a novel framework that facilitates secure, private, and incentivised exchange of CTI related to ICS using blockchain. We propose a new blockchain-enabled framework that facilitates the secure dissemination of CTI data among multiple stakeholders in ICS. We provide the framework design, technical development and evaluate the framework's feasibility in a real-world application environment using practical use-case scenarios. Our proposed design shows a more practical and efficient framework for a CTI sharing network for ICS, including the bestowal and acknowledgment of data privacy, trust barriers, and security issues ingrained in this domain.

title: A Blockchain-Enabled Incentivised Framework for Cyber Threat Intelligence Sharing in ICS
text: The increasing reliance on Industrial Control Systems (ICS) has introduced novel cyber threats, underscoring the need for efficient threat intelligence sharing among stakeholders. Existing solutions often rely on centralized architectures, which are prone to single points of failure, data manipulation, and lack of transparency. To address these limitations, we propose a blockchain-enabled incentivized framework for cyber threat intelligence sharing in ICS. Our framework leverages a decentralized architecture, where stakeholders can share and access threat intelligence in a trustless environment. We incorporate a token-based incentive mechanism, which rewards participants for contributing high-quality intelligence, thereby promoting a collaborative ecosystem. To ensure the integrity and validity of shared intelligence, we employ a reputation-based system, where participants' credibility is evaluated based on the accuracy of their contributions. Our evaluation, conducted on a simulated ICS testbed, demonstrates the efficacy of our framework in facilitating timely and accurate threat intelligence sharing. The results show a significant reduction in mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to respond (MTTR) to cyber threats, with an average improvement of 37.5% and 42.1%, respectively, compared to traditional centralized approaches. Our framework provides a promising solution for enhancing the resilience of ICS against cyber threats, and its decentralized nature makes it adaptable to diverse industrial environments.

title: Conflict-free Collaborative Set Sharing for Distributed Systems
text: Collaborative Data Sharing is widely noticed to be essential for distributed systems. Among several proposed strategies, conflict-free techniques are considered useful for serverless concurrent systems. They aim at making shared data be consistent between peers in such a way that their local data do not become equal at once, but they arrive at the same data eventually when no updates occur in any peer. Although the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT) approach could be used in data sharing as well, it puts restrictions on available operations so as to concurrent updates never cause conflicts. Even for sets, popular operations such as insertion and deletion are not freely used, for example. We propose a novel scheme for Conflict-free Collaborative Set Sharing that allows both insertion and deletion operations. It will provide a new synchronization method for data sharing and gives a fresh insight into designing conflict-free replicated data types. We might consider that this becomes a substitute for CRDTs.

title: Conflict-free Collaborative Set Sharing for Distributed Systems
text: Distributed systems rely heavily on efficient set sharing mechanisms to facilitate collaboration and data exchange among nodes. However, ensuring conflict-free access to shared sets in the presence of concurrent updates and network partitions remains a long-standing challenge. Existing solutions often compromise on either consistency, availability, or partition tolerance, leading to suboptimal performance and scalability. This paper presents a novel conflict-free collaborative set sharing (CFCSS) protocol that strikes a balance between these competing goals. Our approach leverages a combination of vector clocks, operation logging, and a customized version of the Paxos consensus algorithm to ensure strong consistency and high availability in the face of node failures and network partitions. We implement CFCSS in a distributed key-value store and evaluate its performance using a comprehensive benchmark suite. Our experiments demonstrate that CFCSS outperforms state-of-the-art set sharing protocols by up to 35% in terms of throughput and 25% in terms of latency, while maintaining strong consistency and fault tolerance guarantees.

title: Operation-based Collaborative Data Sharing for Distributed Systems
text: Collaborative Data Sharing raises a fundamental issue in distributed systems. Several strategies have been proposed for making shared data consistent between peers in such a way that the shared part of their local data become equal. Most of the proposals rely on state-based semantics. But this suffers from a lack of descriptiveness in conflict-free features of synchronization required for flexible network connections. Recent applications tend to use non-permanent connection with mobile devices or allow temporary breakaways from the system, for example. To settle ourselves in conflict-free data sharing, we propose a novel scheme "Operation-based Collaborative Data Sharing" that enables conflict-free strategies for synchronization based on operational semantics.

title: Operation-based Collaborative Data Sharing for Distributed Systems
text: In distributed systems, collaborative data sharing poses a fundamental challenge, necessitating consistent data synchronization among peers. Existing strategies, largely grounded in state-based semantics, fall short in capturing the nuanced features of conflict-free synchronization essential for flexible network connections. The limitations of these approaches are particularly pronounced in modern applications, where non-permanent connections with mobile devices and temporary system disconnections are increasingly common. To address this shortcoming, we introduce Operation-based Collaborative Data Sharing, a novel scheme that leverages operational semantics to enable conflict-free synchronization strategies, thereby facilitating seamless data sharing in dynamic environments.

title: Software Variants for Hardware Trojan Detection and Resilience in COTS Processors
text: The commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) component based ecosystem provides an attractive system design paradigm due to the drastic reduction in development time and cost compared to custom solutions. However, it brings in a growing concern of trustworthiness arising from the possibility of embedded malicious logic, or hardware Trojans in COTS components. Existing trust-verification approaches are typically not applicable to COTS hardware due to the absence of golden models and the lack of observability of internal signals. In this work, we propose a novel approach for runtime Trojan detection and resilience in untrusted COTS processors through judicious modifications in software. The proposed approach does not rely on any hardware redundancy or architectural modification and hence seamlessly integrates with the COTS-based system design process. Trojan resilience is achieved through the execution of multiple functionally equivalent software variants. We have developed and implemented a solution for compiler-based automatic generation of program variants, metric-guided selection of variants, and their integration in a single executable. To evaluate the proposed approach, we first analyzed the effectiveness of program variants in avoiding the activation of a random pool of Trojans. By implementing several Trojans in an OpenRISC 1000 processor, we analyzed the detectability and resilience during Trojan activation in both single and multiple variants. We also present delay and code size overhead for the automatically generated variants for several programs and discuss future research directions to reduce the overhead.

title: Software Variants for Hardware Trojan Detection and Resilience in COTS Processors
text: The advent of commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) component-based systems has revolutionized system design, offering significant reductions in development time and cost. However, this paradigm shift is accompanied by a growing concern regarding the trustworthiness of COTS components, which may harbor embedded malicious logic or hardware Trojans. The lack of golden models and internal signal observability renders existing trust verification approaches inapplicable to COTS hardware. This paper presents a novel approach to runtime Trojan detection and resilience in untrusted COTS processors, achieved through software modifications that do not require hardware redundancy or architectural alterations, thereby ensuring seamless integration with COTS-based system design. By executing multiple functionally equivalent software variants, Trojan resilience is attained. We have developed a comprehensive solution, encompassing compiler-based automatic variant generation, metric-guided variant selection, and integration into a single executable. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through the analysis of program variants in evading Trojan activation, using an OpenRISC 1000 processor with implanted Trojans. Our results show the detectability and resilience of our approach in both single and multiple variant scenarios, along with an evaluation of the delay and code size overheads for various programs, highlighting avenues for future research to mitigate these overheads.

title: Trusted And Confidential Program Analysis
text: We develop the concept of Trusted and Confidential Program Analysis (TCPA) which enables program certification to be used where previously there was insufficient trust. Imagine a scenario where a producer may not be trusted to certify its own software (perhaps by a foreign regulator), and the producer is unwilling to release its sources and detailed design to any external body. We present a protocol that can, using trusted computing based on encrypted sources, create certification via which all can trust the delivered object code without revealing the unencrypted sources to any party. Furthermore, we describe a realization of TCPA with trusted execution environments (TEE) that enables general and efficient computation. We have implemented the TCPA protocol in a system called TCWasm for web assembly architectures. In our evaluation with 33 benchmark cases, TCWasm managed to finish the analysis with relatively slight overheads.

title: Trusted And Confidential Program Analysis
text: The proliferation of sensitive data in software applications has spurred a pressing need for trusted and confidential program analysis. Existing approaches often rely on either static or dynamic analysis, which are inherently limited by their inability to balance accuracy and performance. We propose a novel hybrid framework that leverages the strengths of both paradigms to provide a comprehensive and efficient analysis of program behavior. Our approach, dubbed "TAPAS," integrates a sophisticated static abstract interpretation with a dynamic symbolic execution engine, ensuring both soundness and precision. We evaluate TAPAS on a diverse set of benchmarks, demonstrating a significant reduction in false positives and negatives compared to state-of-the-art tools. Furthermore, our framework exhibits a marked improvement in scalability, handling large programs with complex control flows. The results of this study have far-reaching implications for the development of secure and reliable software systems.

title: Wiretap Secret Key Agreement Via Secure Omniscience
text: In this paper, we explore the connection between secret key agreement and secure omniscience within the setting of the multiterminal source model with a wiretapper who has side information. While the secret key agreement problem considers the generation of a maximum-rate secret key through public discussion, the secure omniscience problem is concerned with communication protocols for omniscience that minimize the rate of information leakage to the wiretapper. The starting point of our work is a lower bound on the minimum leakage rate for omniscience, $R_{\mathop{\mathrm{L}}}$, in terms of the wiretap secret key capacity, $C_{\mathop{\mathrm{W}}}$. Our interest is in identifying broad classes of sources for which this lower bound is met with equality, in which case we say that there is a duality between secure omniscience and secret key agreement. We show that this duality holds in the case of certain finite linear source (FLS) models, such as two-terminal FLS models and pairwise independent network models on trees with a linear wiretapper. Duality also holds for any FLS model in which $C_{\mathop{\mathrm{W}}}$ is achieved by a perfect linear secret key agreement scheme. We conjecture that the duality in fact holds unconditionally for any FLS model. On the negative side, we give an example of a (non-FLS) source model for which duality does not hold if we limit ourselves to communication-for-omniscience protocols with at most two (interactive) communications. We also address the secure function computation problem and explore the connection between the minimum leakage rate for computing a function and the wiretap secret key capacity.

title: Wiretap Secret Key Agreement Via Secure Omniscience
text: The proliferation of wireless devices has led to a pressing need for secure key agreement protocols that can operate in the presence of an eavesdropping adversary. In this context, wiretap secret key agreement (WSKA) has emerged as a promising approach, wherein two legitimate parties, Alice and Bob, establish a shared secret key over an insecure channel while keeping it concealed from an eavesdropper, Eve. However, existing WSKA protocols often rely on unrealistic assumptions about the channel conditions or Eve's capabilities, limiting their practical applicability. This paper presents a novel WSKA protocol, dubbed Secure Omniscience (SO), which leverages the concept of omniscience to achieve secure key agreement in a more realistic adversarial setting. Specifically, SO exploits the inherent randomness in the wireless channel to generate a shared secret key between Alice and Bob, while ensuring that Eve's uncertainty about the key remains above a certain threshold. Our protocol employs a carefully designed combination of channel probing, error correction, and privacy amplification to achieve this goal. Through a comprehensive security analysis, we demonstrate that SO can achieve a secret key rate of up to 0.5 bits per channel use, even when Eve has access to a significant portion of the channel observations. Furthermore, our protocol remains secure against sophisticated attacks, including those exploiting Eve's knowledge of the channel statistics. We validate the performance of SO through extensive simulations, showcasing its feasibility in realistic wireless environments. Overall, our results contribute to the development of practical WSKA protocols that can effectively counter eavesdropping attacks in modern wireless networks.

title: Quantum-Resistant Cryptography
text: Quantum-resistant cryptography is cryptography that aims to deliver cryptographic functions and protocols that remain secure even if large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computers are built. NIST will soon announce the first selected public-key cryptography algorithms in its Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) standardization which is the most important current effort in the field of quantum-resistant cryptography. This report provides an overview to security experts who do not yet have a deep understanding of quantum-resistant cryptography. It surveys the computational model of quantum computers; the quantum algorithms that affect cryptography the most; the risk of Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computers (CRQCs) being built; the security of symmetric and public-key cryptography in the presence of CRQCs; the NIST PQC standardization effort; the migration to quantum-resistant public-key cryptography; the relevance of Quantum Key Distribution as a complement to conventional cryptography; and the relevance of Quantum Random Number Generators as a complement to current hardware Random Number Generators.

title: Quantum-Resistant Cryptography
text: The advent of quantum computers poses a significant threat to modern public-key cryptography, as Shor's algorithm can efficiently factor large numbers and compute discrete logarithms. In response, we develop and analyze a novel suite of quantum-resistant cryptographic primitives, leveraging the hardness of problems related to ideal lattices and error-correcting codes. Our methodology involves constructing cryptographic schemes that are provably secure against quantum attacks, while maintaining compatibility with existing infrastructure and ensuring acceptable performance overhead. We present a new key encapsulation mechanism, QROM-KEM, which demonstrates a 30% reduction in ciphertext size compared to prior art, while achieving a security level of 128 bits against quantum attacks. Additionally, we provide a thorough evaluation of our schemes on various platforms, including a custom-built quantum simulator, to demonstrate their feasibility and practicality. Our results contribute to the development of a post-quantum cryptographic ecosystem, ensuring the long-term security of communication networks and data storage systems.

title: How to use Persistent Memory in your Database
text: Persistent or Non Volatile Memory (PMEM or NVM) has recently become commercially available under several configurations with different purposes and goals. Despite the attention to the topic, we are not aware of a comprehensive empirical analysis of existing relational database engines under different PMEM configurations. Such a study is important to understand the performance implications of the various hardware configurations and how different DB engines can benefit from them. To this end, we analyze three different engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLServer) under common workloads (TPC-C and TPC-H) with all possible PMEM configurations supported by Intel's Optane NVM devices (PMEM as persistent memory in AppDirect mode and PMEM as volatile memory in Memory mode). Our results paint a complex picture and are not always intuitive due to the many factors involved. Based on our findings, we provide insights on how the different engines behave with PMEM and which configurations and queries perform best. Our results show that using PMEM as persistent storage usually speeds up query execution, but with some caveats as the I/O path is not fully optimized. Additionally, using PMEM in Memory mode does not offer any performance advantage despite the larger volatile memory capacity. Through the extensive coverage of engines and parameters, we provide an important starting point for exploiting PMEM in databases and tuning relational engines to take advantage of this new technology.

title: How to use Persistent Memory in your Database
text: The advent of persistent memory (PM) technologies has sparked significant interest in the database community, promising to revolutionize data storage and retrieval. Despite its potential, the successful integration of PM into database systems remains an open challenge. In particular, the lack of comprehensive guidelines on how to effectively utilize PM in database architectures hinders widespread adoption. To address this gap, we present a systematic study on the optimal use of PM in databases, focusing on the interplay between PM, storage layouts, and query optimization. Our methodology involves a thorough analysis of various PM-enabled database configurations, encompassing different storage layouts, caching strategies, and query patterns. We develop a novel cost model that accurately captures the performance implications of PM on database workloads, and validate our findings through extensive experiments on a realistic benchmark suite. Our results show that a carefully crafted PM-based storage hierarchy can yield significant performance improvements, with average query latencies reduced by up to 43% compared to traditional storage architectures. Furthermore, we identify key factors influencing PM's efficacy, including data access patterns, storage layout, and caching strategies. Our study provides actionable insights for database practitioners, enabling them to unlock the full potential of PM in their systems. By shedding light on the complex interplay between PM and database architectures, our work paves the way for the widespread adoption of PM in the database community.

title: TROLLMAGNIFIER: Detecting State-Sponsored Troll Accounts on Reddit
text: Growing evidence points to recurring influence campaigns on social media, often sponsored by state actors aiming to manipulate public opinion on sensitive political topics. Typically, campaigns are performed through instrumented accounts, known as troll accounts; despite their prominence, however, little work has been done to detect these accounts in the wild. In this paper, we present TROLLMAGNIFIER, a detection system for troll accounts. Our key observation, based on analysis of known Russian-sponsored troll accounts identified by Reddit, is that they show loose coordination, often interacting with each other to further specific narratives. Therefore, troll accounts controlled by the same actor often show similarities that can be leveraged for detection. TROLLMAGNIFIER learns the typical behavior of known troll accounts and identifies more that behave similarly. We train TROLLMAGNIFIER on a set of 335 known troll accounts and run it on a large dataset of Reddit accounts. Our system identifies 1,248 potential troll accounts; we then provide a multi-faceted analysis to corroborate the correctness of our classification. In particular, 66% of the detected accounts show signs of being instrumented by malicious actors (e.g., they were created on the same exact day as a known troll, they have since been suspended by Reddit, etc.). They also discuss similar topics as the known troll accounts and exhibit temporal synchronization in their activity. Overall, we show that using TROLLMAGNIFIER, one can grow the initial knowledge of potential trolls provided by Reddit by over 300%.

title: TROLLMAGNIFIER: Detecting State-Sponsored Troll Accounts on Reddit
text: Recurring influence campaigns on social media, often sponsored by state actors, have been increasingly documented, with the primary goal of manipulating public opinion on sensitive political topics. While instrumented accounts, commonly referred to as troll accounts, play a pivotal role in these campaigns, their detection in real-world settings has received limited attention. This paper presents TROLLMAGNIFIER, a novel detection system designed to identify troll accounts. Our analysis of known Russian-sponsored troll accounts on Reddit reveals a key characteristic: loose coordination, where accounts controlled by the same actor interact with each other to promote specific narratives, exhibiting similarities in behavior that can be leveraged for detection. By learning the typical behavior of known troll accounts, TROLLMAGNIFIER identifies additional accounts that display similar patterns. We train our system on a dataset of 335 known troll accounts and apply it to a large set of Reddit accounts, resulting in the detection of 1,248 potential troll accounts. A comprehensive analysis of these detected accounts reveals a significant proportion (66%) exhibiting signs of malicious instrumentation, such as identical creation dates, subsequent suspension by Reddit, and synchronization of activity. Furthermore, they engage in similar topic discussions and display temporal synchronization, reinforcing the accuracy of our classification. Our results demonstrate that TROLLMAGNIFIER can expand the initial knowledge of potential trolls provided by Reddit by over 300%.

title: Reliability Assessment and Safety Arguments for Machine Learning Components in System Assurance
text: The increasing use of Machine Learning (ML) components embedded in autonomous systems -- so-called Learning-Enabled Systems (LESs) -- has resulted in the pressing need to assure their functional safety. As for traditional functional safety, the emerging consensus within both, industry and academia, is to use assurance cases for this purpose. Typically assurance cases support claims of reliability in support of safety, and can be viewed as a structured way of organising arguments and evidence generated from safety analysis and reliability modelling activities. While such assurance activities are traditionally guided by consensus-based standards developed from vast engineering experience, LESs pose new challenges in safety-critical application due to the characteristics and design of ML models. In this article, we first present an overall assurance framework for LESs with an emphasis on quantitative aspects, e.g., breaking down system-level safety targets to component-level requirements and supporting claims stated in reliability metrics. We then introduce a novel model-agnostic Reliability Assessment Model (RAM) for ML classifiers that utilises the operational profile and robustness verification evidence. We discuss the model assumptions and the inherent challenges of assessing ML reliability uncovered by our RAM and propose solutions to practical use. Probabilistic safety argument templates at the lower ML component-level are also developed based on the RAM. Finally, to evaluate and demonstrate our methods, we not only conduct experiments on synthetic/benchmark datasets but also scope our methods with case studies on simulated Autonomous Underwater Vehicles and physical Unmanned Ground Vehicles.

title: Reliability Assessment and Safety Arguments for Machine Learning Components in System Assurance
