text: The increasing adoption of machine learning (ML) components in safety-critical systems has raised concerns about their reliability and trustworthiness. Despite their potential benefits, ML components can introduce new failure modes and uncertainty, which can compromise system assurance. To address this challenge, we present a systematic approach for assessing the reliability of ML components and constructing safety arguments for their integration into safety-critical systems. Our methodology combines fault injection testing, uncertainty quantification, and Bayesian network modeling to evaluate the reliability of ML components under various operating conditions. We demonstrate the applicability of our approach on a case study involving a convolutional neural network (CNN) used for image classification in an autonomous vehicle system. Our results show that the reliability of the CNN component can be significantly impacted by variations in input data quality, model parameters, and computational resources. We also develop a safety argument framework that incorporates the reliability assessment results, system architecture analysis, and hazard identification to provide a comprehensive safety case for the ML component. Our framework is grounded in the Goal-Based Safety Engineering (GBSE) methodology and is tailored to address the unique challenges of ML-based systems. The proposed approach is evaluated through a series of workshops with industry experts, who validate its effectiveness in supporting system assurance and certification. Our research contributes to the development of rigorous methods for ensuring the reliability and safety of ML components in safety-critical systems, thereby facilitating their widespread adoption.

title: Certified Adversarial Defenses Meet Out-of-Distribution Corruptions: Benchmarking Robustness and Simple Baselines
text: Certified robustness guarantee gauges a model's robustness to test-time attacks and can assess the model's readiness for deployment in the real world. In this work, we critically examine how the adversarial robustness guarantees from randomized smoothing-based certification methods change when state-of-the-art certifiably robust models encounter out-of-distribution (OOD) data. Our analysis demonstrates a previously unknown vulnerability of these models to low-frequency OOD data such as weather-related corruptions, rendering these models unfit for deployment in the wild. To alleviate this issue, we propose a novel data augmentation scheme, FourierMix, that produces augmentations to improve the spectral coverage of the training data. Furthermore, we propose a new regularizer that encourages consistent predictions on noise perturbations of the augmented data to improve the quality of the smoothed models. We find that FourierMix augmentations help eliminate the spectral bias of certifiably robust models enabling them to achieve significantly better robustness guarantees on a range of OOD benchmarks. Our evaluation also uncovers the inability of current OOD benchmarks at highlighting the spectral biases of the models. To this end, we propose a comprehensive benchmarking suite that contains corruptions from different regions in the spectral domain. Evaluation of models trained with popular augmentation methods on the proposed suite highlights their spectral biases and establishes the superiority of FourierMix trained models at achieving better-certified robustness guarantees under OOD shifts over the entire frequency spectrum.

title: Certified Adversarial Defenses Meet Out-of-Distribution Corruptions: Benchmarking Robustness and Simple Baselines
text: The proliferation of deep learning models has led to a surge in research on adversarial robustness, with certified defenses emerging as a promising approach. However, these defenses are typically evaluated solely on their ability to withstand adversarial attacks, overlooking their performance under out-of-distribution (OOD) corruptions. This oversight is particularly concerning, as real-world systems are often exposed to a wide range of unforeseen perturbations. To address this limitation, we present a comprehensive benchmarking study that evaluates the robustness of certified adversarial defenses against OOD corruptions. Our methodology involves augmenting existing adversarial defense benchmarks with a suite of OOD corruption types, including noise, blur, and weather effects. We then assess the performance of several certified defenses, including interval bound propagation and CROWN-IBP, on these corrupted datasets. Our results reveal that even state-of-the-art certified defenses can be brittle under OOD corruptions, often suffering significant performance degradation. Surprisingly, we find that simple baseline models, such as input preprocessing and ensemble methods, can provide competitive robustness to certified defenses under OOD corruptions. These findings underscore the need for a more nuanced understanding of robustness, one that considers both adversarial attacks and OOD corruptions. Our benchmarking framework and results provide a foundation for the development of more comprehensive and reliable robustness evaluation methodologies.

title: MOMO -- Deep Learning-driven classification of external DICOM studies for PACS archivation
text: Patients regularly continue assessment or treatment in other facilities than they began them in, receiving their previous imaging studies as a CD-ROM and requiring clinical staff at the new hospital to import these studies into their local database. However, between different facilities, standards for nomenclature, contents, or even medical procedures may vary, often requiring human intervention to accurately classify the received studies in the context of the recipient hospital's standards. In this study, the authors present MOMO (MOdality Mapping and Orchestration), a deep learning-based approach to automate this mapping process utilizing metadata substring matching and a neural network ensemble, which is trained to recognize the 76 most common imaging studies across seven different modalities. A retrospective study is performed to measure the accuracy that this algorithm can provide. To this end, a set of 11,934 imaging series with existing labels was retrieved from the local hospital's PACS database to train the neural networks. A set of 843 completely anonymized external studies was hand-labeled to assess the performance of our algorithm. Additionally, an ablation study was performed to measure the performance impact of the network ensemble in the algorithm, and a comparative performance test with a commercial product was conducted. In comparison to a commercial product (96.20% predictive power, 82.86% accuracy, 1.36% minor errors), a neural network ensemble alone performs the classification task with less accuracy (99.05% predictive power, 72.69% accuracy, 10.3% minor errors). However, MOMO outperforms either by a large margin in accuracy and with increased predictive power (99.29% predictive power, 92.71% accuracy, 2.63% minor errors).

title: MOMO -- Deep Learning-driven classification of external DICOM studies for PACS archivation
text: The transfer of patients between healthcare facilities often necessitates the exchange of imaging studies, typically via CD-ROM, which then require manual importation and classification into the recipient hospital's database. However, disparities in nomenclature, content, and medical procedures between facilities frequently demand human intervention to ensure accurate categorization. To address this challenge, we introduce MOMO, a deep learning-driven approach that leverages metadata substring matching and a neural network ensemble to automate the mapping process. Trained on a dataset of 11,934 imaging series from a local hospital's PACS database, MOMO is capable of recognizing the 76 most common imaging studies across seven modalities. We evaluate MOMO's performance using a retrospective study and a hand-labeled set of 843 anonymized external studies. An ablation study and comparative performance test with a commercial product are also conducted to assess the efficacy of the neural network ensemble. The results show that while a standalone neural network ensemble achieves 99.05% predictive power, 72.69% accuracy, and 10.3% minor errors, MOMO significantly outperforms both the ensemble and the commercial product (96.20% predictive power, 82.86% accuracy, 1.36% minor errors), demonstrating 99.29% predictive power, 92.71% accuracy, and 2.63% minor errors.

title: A Few-Shot Meta-Learning based Siamese Neural Network using Entropy Features for Ransomware Classification
text: Ransomware defense solutions that can quickly detect and classify different ransomware classes to formulate rapid response plans have been in high demand in recent years. Though the applicability of adopting deep learning techniques to provide automation and self-learning provision has been proven in many application domains, the lack of data available for ransomware (and other malware)samples has been raised as a barrier to developing effective deep learning-based solutions. To address this concern, we propose a few-shot meta-learning based Siamese Neural Network that not only detects ransomware attacks but is able to classify them into different classes. Our proposed model utilizes the entropy feature directly extracted from ransomware binary files to retain more fine-grained features associated with different ransomware signatures. title: A Few-Shot Meta-Learning based Siamese Neural Network using Entropy Features for Ransomware Classification
text: Ransomware attacks have necessitated the development of swift detection and classification systems to facilitate timely response strategies. Despite the demonstrated potential of deep learning in various domains, the scarcity of ransomware and malware samples has hindered the creation of effective deep learning-based solutions. This paper proposes a few-shot meta-learning based Siamese Neural Network to address this challenge, capable of detecting ransomware attacks and categorizing them into distinct classes. By directly extracting entropy features from ransomware binary files, our model preserves fine-grained characteristics associated with diverse ransomware signatures. These features are then utilized to train and optimize the model via a pre-trained network, such as VGG-16, in a meta-learning framework. This approach generates more accurate weight factors, mitigating the bias inherent in models trained on limited samples. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed model, achieving a weighted F1-score exceeding 86%.

title: BERT_SE: A Pre-trained Language Representation Model for Software Engineering
text: The application of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has achieved a high level of relevance in several areas. In the field of software engineering (SE), NLP applications are based on the classification of similar texts (e.g. software requirements), applied in tasks of estimating software effort, selection of human resources, etc. Classifying software requirements has been a complex task, considering the informality and complexity inherent in the texts produced during the software development process. The pre-trained embedding models are shown as a viable alternative when considering the low volume of textual data labeled in the area of software engineering, as well as the lack of quality of these data. Although there is much research around the application of word embedding in several areas, to date, there is no knowledge of studies that have explored its application in the creation of a specific model for the domain of the SE area. Thus, this article presents the proposal for a contextualized embedding model, called BERT_SE, which allows the recognition of specific and relevant terms in the context of SE. The assessment of BERT_SE was performed using the software requirements classification task, demonstrating that this model has an average improvement rate of 13% concerning the BERT_base model, made available by the authors of BERT. title: BERT_SE: A Pre-trained Language Representation Model for Software Engineering
text: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has become increasingly relevant across various domains, with applications in software engineering (SE) relying heavily on text classification, particularly in tasks such as software effort estimation and human resource selection. However, classifying software requirements remains a challenging task due to the inherent informality and complexity of texts generated during software development. The scarcity of high-quality labeled textual data in SE hinders the development of accurate classification models. Pre-trained embedding models offer a promising solution to this problem. Despite extensive research on word embeddings in other areas, there is a notable gap in exploring their application in creating a domain-specific model for SE. This paper proposes BERT_SE, a contextualized embedding model designed to recognize relevant terms in the SE domain. An evaluation of BERT_SE using the software requirements classification task reveals an average improvement of 13% over the BERT_base model. This study contributes to the development of more accurate text classification models in SE, with the code and pre-trained models made publicly available.

title: Stateful Entities: Object-oriented Cloud Applications as Distributed Dataflows
text: Although the cloud has reached a state of robustness, the burden of using its resources falls on the shoulders of programmers who struggle to keep up with ever-growing cloud infrastructure services and abstractions. As a result, state management, scaling, operation, and failure management of scalable cloud applications, require disproportionately more effort than developing the applications' actual business logic. Our vision aims to raise the abstraction level for programming scalable cloud applications by compiling stateful entities -- a programming model enabling imperative transactional programs authored in Python -- into stateful streaming dataflows. We propose a compiler pipeline that analyzes the abstract syntax tree of stateful entities and transforms them into an intermediate representation based on stateful dataflow graphs. It then compiles that intermediate representation into different dataflow engines, leveraging their exactly-once message processing guarantees to prevent state or failure management primitives from "leaking" into the level of the programming model. Preliminary experiments with a proof of concept implementation show that despite program transformation and translation to dataflows, stateful entities can perform at sub-100ms latency even for transactional workloads.

title: Stateful Entities: Object-oriented Cloud Applications as Distributed Dataflows
text: Cloud computing has revolutionized the way applications are designed, deployed, and scaled. However, traditional object-oriented programming (OOP) principles often struggle to cope with the inherently distributed nature of cloud environments. This mismatch leads to complexities in managing consistency, concurrency, and fault tolerance, ultimately hindering the development of scalable and resilient cloud applications. To address this challenge, we propose the concept of Stateful Entities, a novel paradigm that reconciles OOP with distributed dataflows. By explicitly modeling entities as stateful, self-contained units of computation, we enable a seamless integration of object-oriented design principles with the principles of dataflow programming. Our approach leverages a declarative dataflow language to specify entity behavior, which is then compiled into an optimized, distributed execution plan. We evaluate our approach through a prototype implementation, demonstrating significant improvements in scalability, fault tolerance, and development productivity compared to traditional cloud-based OOP frameworks. Furthermore, our results show that Stateful Entities can effectively mitigate consistency and concurrency issues, paving the way for the development of robust, large-scale cloud applications.

title: Collaborative Artificial Intelligence Needs Stronger Assurances Driven by Risks
text: Collaborative AI systems (CAISs) aim at working together with humans in a shared space to achieve a common goal. This critical setting yields hazardous circumstances that could harm human beings. Thus, building such systems with strong assurances of compliance with requirements, domain-specific standards and regulations is of greatest importance. Only few scale impact has been reported so far for such systems since much work remains to manage possible risks. We identify emerging problems in this context and then we report our vision, as well as the progress of our multidisciplinary research team composed of software/systems, and mechatronics engineers to develop a risk-driven assurance process for CAISs.

title: Collaborative Artificial Intelligence Needs Stronger Assurances Driven by Risks
text: Collaborative AI systems (CAISs) operating in shared spaces with humans pose inherent risks to human safety, underscoring the need for stringent compliance with requirements, domain-specific standards, and regulations. Despite their potential, CAISs have yet to achieve widespread impact due to the pressing need to mitigate potential risks. This paper highlights the emerging challenges in this context and outlines the vision and progress of our multidisciplinary research team, comprising software/systems and mechatronics engineers, towards developing a risk-driven assurance process for CAISs, ensuring their safe and reliable operation.

title: ReIGNN: State Register Identification Using Graph Neural Networks for Circuit Reverse Engineering
text: Reverse engineering an integrated circuit netlist is a powerful tool to help detect malicious logic and counteract design piracy. A critical challenge in this domain is the correct classification of data-path and control-logic registers in a design. We present ReIGNN, a novel learning-based register classification methodology that combines graph neural networks (GNNs) with structural analysis to classify the registers in a circuit with high accuracy and generalize well across different designs. GNNs are particularly effective in processing circuit netlists in terms of graphs and leveraging properties of the nodes and their neighborhoods to learn to efficiently discriminate between different types of nodes. Structural analysis can further rectify any registers misclassified as state registers by the GNN by analyzing strongly connected components in the netlist graph. Numerical results on a set of benchmarks show that ReIGNN can achieve, on average, 96.5% balanced accuracy and 97.7% sensitivity across different designs.

title: ReIGNN: State Register Identification Using Graph Neural Networks for Circuit Reverse Engineering
text: The quest for accurate register classification is a pivotal step in reverse-engineering integrated circuit netlists, enabling the detection of malicious logic and combating design piracy. A longstanding challenge in this domain revolves around distinguishing data-path and control-logic registers within a design. This paper proposes ReIGNN, a novel learning-based methodology that synergistically combines graph neural networks (GNNs) with structural analysis to achieve high-accuracy register classification across diverse designs. By representing circuit netlists as graphs, GNNs effectively leverage node properties and neighborhood relationships to discern between node types. Additionally, structural analysis rectifies potential misclassifications by examining strongly connected components in the netlist graph. Empirical evaluations on a benchmark suite demonstrate ReIGNN's efficacy, yielding an average balanced accuracy of 96.5% and sensitivity of 97.7% across various designs.

title: The Price of Differential Privacy under Continual Observation
text: We study the accuracy of differentially private mechanisms in the continual release model. A continual release mechanism receives a sensitive dataset as a stream of $T$ inputs and produces, after receiving each input, an accurate output on the obtained inputs. In contrast, a batch algorithm receives the data as one batch and produces a single output. We provide the first strong lower bounds on the error of continual release mechanisms. In particular, for two fundamental problems that are widely studied and used in the batch model, we show that the worst case error of every continual release algorithm is $\tilde Ω(T^{1/3})$ times larger than that of the best batch algorithm. Previous work shows only a polylogarithimic (in $T$) gap between the worst case error achievable in these two models; further, for many problems, including the summation of binary attributes, the polylogarithmic gap is tight (Dwork et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2010). Our results show that problems closely related to summation -- specifically, those that require selecting the largest of a set of sums -- are fundamentally harder in the continual release model than in the batch model. Our lower bounds assume only that privacy holds for streams fixed in advance (the "nonadaptive" setting). However, we provide matching upper bounds that hold in a model where privacy is required even for adaptively selected streams. This model may be of independent interest.

title: The Price of Differential Privacy under Continual Observation
text: The proliferation of online services that continually collect and process user data has sparked growing concerns about privacy. Differential privacy, a gold standard for privacy protection, provides a robust framework for ensuring that individual-level information remains confidential. However, its implementation in continually observed systems, where data is streamed in over time, remains largely unexplored. In this setting, the traditional approach of applying differential privacy mechanisms to each individual data point independently can result in excessive noise accumulation, rendering the output useless. We investigate the fundamental tradeoffs between privacy and utility in continually observed systems, focusing on the challenging scenario where an adversary has access to the entire observation history. Our methodology revolves around the concept of "privacy budgets," which quantify the total amount of privacy loss incurred over time. We establish a lower bound on the privacy budget required to achieve a given level of utility, demonstrating that it grows logarithmically with the number of observations. This bound is tight, as we provide a novel algorithm that matches it, leveraging a combination of advanced composition theorems and online learning techniques. Our findings have significant implications for the design of continually observed systems, highlighting the need for careful calibration of privacy parameters to balance utility and privacy. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to achieve meaningful utility while maintaining strong privacy guarantees. Ultimately, our work provides a crucial step towards developing practical and private continually observed systems, enabling the responsible collection and processing of sensitive user data.

title: AWESOME: Empowering Scalable Data Science on Social Media Data with an Optimized Tri-Store Data System
text: Modern data science applications increasingly use heterogeneous data sources and analytics. This has led to growing interest in polystore systems, especially analytical polystores. In this work, we focus on emerging multi-data model analytics workloads over social media data that fluidly straddle relational, graph, and text analytics. Instead of a generic polystore, we build a "tri-store" system that is more aware of the underlying data models to better optimize execution to improve scalability and runtime efficiency. We name our system AWESOME (Analytics WorkbEnch for SOcial MEdia). It features a powerful domain-specific language named ADIL. ADIL builds on top of underlying query engines (e.g., SQL and Cypher) and features native data types for succinctly specifying cross-engine queries and NLP operations, as well as automatic in-memory and query optimizations. Using real-world tri-model analytical workloads and datasets, we empirically demonstrate the functionalities of AWESOME for scalable data science over social media data and evaluate its efficiency.

title: AWESOME: Empowering Scalable Data Science on Social Media Data with an Optimized Tri-Store Data System
text: The proliferation of heterogeneous data sources and analytics in modern data science applications has spurred interest in polystore systems, particularly those oriented towards analytical workloads. This research focuses on emerging multi-data model analytics that seamlessly integrate relational, graph, and text analytics over social media data. We propose a "tri-store" system, AWESOME (Analytics WorkbEnch for SOcial MEdia), designed to optimize execution by leveraging awareness of underlying data models, thereby enhancing scalability and runtime efficiency. AWESOME features ADIL, a domain-specific language that builds upon underlying query engines (such as SQL and Cypher) and provides native data types for concisely specifying cross-engine queries and NLP operations. ADIL also incorporates automatic in-memory and query optimizations. Through empirical evaluation using real-world tri-model analytical workloads and datasets, we demonstrate AWESOME's capabilities for scalable data science over social media data and assess its efficiency.

title: Improving Differentially Private SGD via Randomly Sparsified Gradients
text: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) has been widely adopted in deep learning to provide rigorously defined privacy, which requires gradient clipping to bound the maximum norm of individual gradients and additive isotropic Gaussian noise. With analysis of the convergence rate of DP-SGD in a non-convex setting, we identify that randomly sparsifying gradients before clipping and noisification adjusts a trade-off between internal components of the convergence bound and leads to a smaller upper bound when the noise is dominant. Additionally, our theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations show that the trade-off is not trivial but possibly a unique property of DP-SGD, as either canceling noisification or gradient clipping eliminates the trade-off in the bound. This observation is indicative, as it implies DP-SGD has special inherent room for (even simply random) gradient compression. To verify the observation and utilize it, we propose an efficient and lightweight extension using random sparsification (RS) to strengthen DP-SGD. Experiments with various DP-SGD frameworks show that RS can improve performance. Additionally, the produced sparse gradients of RS exhibit advantages in reducing communication cost and strengthening privacy against reconstruction attacks, which are also key problems in private machine learning.

title: Improving Differentially Private SGD via Randomly Sparsified Gradients
text: The incorporation of differential privacy in stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) has become a standard approach in deep learning, relying on gradient clipping and additive isotropic Gaussian noise to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. Our investigation into the convergence rate of DP-SGD in non-convex settings reveals that randomly sparsifying gradients prior to clipping and noisification effectively balances the internal components of the convergence bound, yielding a smaller upper bound when noise dominates. Notably, our theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations demonstrate that this trade-off is a unique property of DP-SGD, as eliminating either noisification or gradient clipping abolishes the trade-off. This insight suggests that DP-SGD possesses inherent potential for gradient compression, which can be leveraged to improve performance. We propose a lightweight extension incorporating random sparsification (RS) to enhance DP-SGD, and experiments with various frameworks demonstrate its efficacy. The sparse gradients generated by RS also offer advantages in reducing communication costs and strengthening privacy against reconstruction attacks, addressing key challenges in private machine learning.

title: Common Bugs in Scratch Programs
text: Bugs in Scratch programs can spoil the fun and inhibit learning success. Many common bugs are the result of recurring patterns of bad code. In this paper we present a collection of common code patterns that typically hint at bugs in Scratch programs, and the LitterBox tool which can automatically detect them. We empirically evaluate how frequently these patterns occur, and how severe their consequences usually are. While fixing bugs inevitably is part of learning, the possibility to identify the bugs automatically provides the potential to support learners

title: Common Bugs in Scratch Programs
text: Block-based programming languages like Scratch have democratized coding for novice programmers, but the lack of systematic analysis of errors in these languages hinders our understanding of the difficulties faced by young learners. We manually analyzed a dataset of 10,000 Scratch programs, identifying a set of 15 common bug patterns that account for over 70% of all errors. Our findings suggest that syntax errors are relatively rare, while semantic errors, particularly those related to event handling and data storage, are more prevalent and often difficult to diagnose.

title: A Survey on Scenario-Based Testing for Automated Driving Systems in High-Fidelity Simulation
text: Automated Driving Systems (ADSs) have seen rapid progress in recent years. To ensure the safety and reliability of these systems, extensive testings are being conducted before their future mass deployment. Testing the system on the road is the closest to real-world and desirable approach, but it is incredibly costly. Also, it is infeasible to cover rare corner cases using such real-world testing. Thus, a popular alternative is to evaluate an ADS's performance in some well-designed challenging scenarios, a.k.a. scenario-based testing. High-fidelity simulators have been widely used in this setting to maximize flexibility and convenience in testing what-if scenarios. Although many works have been proposed offering diverse frameworks/methods for testing specific systems, the comparisons and connections among these works are still missing. To bridge this gap, in this work, we provide a generic formulation of scenario-based testing in high-fidelity simulation and conduct a literature review on the existing works. We further compare them and present the open challenges as well as potential future research directions.

title: A Survey on Scenario-Based Testing for Automated Driving Systems in High-Fidelity Simulation
text: The development of automated driving systems (ADS) has reached a critical stage, where ensuring their reliability and safety is paramount. Scenario-based testing in high-fidelity simulation has emerged as a promising approach to validate ADS performance in diverse, complex, and potentially hazardous scenarios. This survey provides a comprehensive review of the current state-of-the-art in scenario-based testing for ADS in high-fidelity simulation. We systematically analyze 35 relevant papers, published between 2015 and 2022, to identify key trends, challenges, and future research directions. Our analysis reveals that existing approaches focus on scenario modeling, test case generation, and evaluation metrics. However, there is a lack of standardized scenario representations, limited consideration of multimodal sensor data, and inadequate exploration of edge cases. We also observe a growing interest in integrating machine learning and simulation-based testing. Our survey provides a roadmap for researchers and practitioners to develop more effective and efficient scenario-based testing methodologies for ADS in high-fidelity simulation environments.

title: Worst-case Optimal Binary Join Algorithms under General $\ell_p$ Constraints
text: Worst-case optimal join algorithms have so far been studied in two broad contexts -- $(1)$ when we are given input relation sizes [Atserias et al., FOCS 2008, Ngo et al., PODS 2012, Velduizhen et. al, ICDT 2014] $(2)$ when in addition to size, we are given a degree bound on the relation [Abo Khamis et al., PODS 2017]. To the best of our knowledge, this problem has not been studied beyond these two statistics even for the case when input relations have arity (at most) two. In this paper, we present a worst-case optimal join algorithm when are given $\ell_{p}$-norm size bounds on input relations of arity at most two for $p \in (1, 2]$. ($p=1$ corresponds to relation size bounds and $p=\infty$ corresponds to the degree bounds.) The worst-case optimality holds any fixed $p \in (2, \infty)$ as well (as long as the join query graph has large enough girth). Our algorithm is {\em simple}, does not depend on $p$ (or) the $\ell_{p}$-norm bounds and avoids the (large) poly-log factor associated with the best known algorithm PANDA [Abo Khamis et al., PODS 2017] for the size and degree bounds setting of the problem. In this process, we (partially) resolve two open question from [Ngo, 2018 Gems of PODS]. We believe our algorithm has the {\em potential} to pave the way for practical worst-case optimal join algorithms beyond the case of size bounds.

title: Worst-case Optimal Binary Join Algorithms under General $\ell_p$ Constraints
text: The study of worst-case optimal join algorithms has thus far been confined to two primary contexts: instances where input relation sizes are known, and those where both relation sizes and degree bounds are provided. Despite this, the problem remains unexplored beyond these two statistics, even for binary input relations. This paper marks a significant departure from this narrow focus by presenting a worst-case optimal join algorithm that leverages $\ell_{p}$-norm size bounds on input relations of arity at most two, for $p \in (1, 2]$. Notably, this optimality extends to any fixed $p \in (2, \infty)$, given a join query graph with sufficient girth. Our proposed algorithm boasts simplicity, independence from $p$ and the $\ell_{p}$-norm bounds, and avoids the poly-logarithmic factor inherent in the state-of-the-art PANDA algorithm. In doing so, we partially resolve two open questions posed in [Ngo, 2018 Gems of PODS]. We anticipate that our algorithm will pave the way for practical worst-case optimal join algorithms that transcend the limitations of size bounds, thereby expanding the possibilities for efficient query processing.

title: CoviChain: A Blockchain Based COVID-19 Vaccination Passport
text: Vaccination passports are being issued by governments around the world in order to open up their travel and hospitality sectors. Civil liberty campaigners on the other hand argue that such mandatory instruments encroach upon our fundamental right to anonymity, freedom of movement, and are a backdoor to issuing "identity documents" to citizens by their governments. In this paper we present a privacy-preserving framework that uses two-factor authentication to create a unique identifier that can be used to locate a person's vaccination record on a blockchain, but does not store any personal information about them. Our main contribution is the employment of a locality sensitive hashing algorithm over an iris extraction technique, that can be used to authenticate users and anonymously locate vaccination records on the blockchain, without leaking any personally identifiable information to the blockchain. Our proposed system allows for the safe reopening of society, while maintaining the privacy of citizens.

title: CoviChain: A Blockchain Based COVID-19 Vaccination Passport
text: The widespread adoption of vaccination passports by governments aims to revitalize the travel and hospitality industries, but has sparked controversy among civil liberty advocates, who contend that such mandatory measures infringe upon fundamental rights to anonymity and freedom of movement. This paper proposes a privacy-preserving framework that leverages two-factor authentication to generate a unique identifier, enabling the secure retrieval of vaccination records on a blockchain without storing personal information. Our novel approach employs a locality sensitive hashing algorithm in conjunction with iris extraction, facilitating anonymous user authentication and vaccination record retrieval on the blockchain, while ensuring the non-disclosure of personally identifiable information. By providing a secure and privacy-conscious solution, our system enables the safe reopening of society while safeguarding citizens' privacy.

title: A tool to support the investigation and visualization of cyber and/or physical incidents
text: Investigating efficiently the data collected from a system's activity can help to detect malicious attempts and better understand the context behind past incident occurrences. Nowadays, several solutions can be used to monitor system activities to detect probable abnormalities and malfunctions. However, most of these systems overwhelm their users with vast amounts of information, making it harder for them to perceive incident occurrences and their context. Our approach combines a dynamic and intuitive user interface with Machine Learning forecasts to provide an intelligent investigation tool that facilitates the security operator's work. Our system can also act as an enhanced and fully automated decision support mechanism that provides suggestions about possible incident occurrences.

title: A tool to support the investigation and visualization of cyber and/or physical incidents
text: The increasing frequency and complexity of cyber and physical incidents necessitate effective investigation and visualization tools to facilitate swift response and mitigation. This work presents a novel, open-source platform designed to support incident responders in reconstructing and analyzing cyber-physical attack scenarios. Our tool integrates heterogeneous data sources, including network logs, sensor readings, and eyewitness accounts, to provide a unified, interactive visualization of the incident timeline. We employ a graph-based approach to model the incident's causal relationships, enabling users to explore and correlate disparate data elements. Evaluation on real-world incident datasets demonstrates the tool's ability to accelerate incident response by 35% and improve situational awareness among responders by 42%.

title: A Practical Dynamic Programming Approach to Datalog Provenance Computation
text: We establish a translation between a formalism for dynamic programming over hypergraphs and the computation of semiring-based provenance for Datalog programs. The benefit of this translation is a new method for computing provenance for a specific class of semirings. Theoretical and practical optimizations lead to an efficient implementation using \textsc{Soufflé}, a state-of-the-art Datalog interpreter. Experimental results on real-world data suggest this approach to be efficient in practical contexts, even competing with our previous dedicated solutions for computing provenance in annotated graph databases. The cost overhead compared to plain Datalog evaluation is fairly moderate in many cases of interest.

title: A Practical Dynamic Programming Approach to Datalog Provenance Computation
text: This work presents a novel translation between dynamic programming over hypergraphs and semiring-based provenance computation for Datalog programs, yielding a new method for provenance calculation in a specific class of semirings. By applying theoretical and practical optimizations, we achieve an efficient implementation utilizing the state-of-the-art Datalog interpreter, Soufflé. Experimental evaluations on real-world data demonstrate the approach's practical efficiency, often rivaling dedicated solutions for annotated graph databases. Notably, the cost overhead relative to plain Datalog evaluation is moderate in many relevant scenarios.

title: AST-Transformer: Encoding Abstract Syntax Trees Efficiently for Code Summarization
text: Code summarization aims to generate brief natural language descriptions for source code. As source code is highly structured and follows strict programming language grammars, its Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) is often leveraged to inform the encoder about the structural information. However, ASTs are usually much longer than the source code. Current approaches ignore the size limit and simply feed the whole linearized AST into the encoder. To address this problem, we propose AST-Transformer to efficiently encode tree-structured ASTs. Experiments show that AST-Transformer outperforms the state-of-arts by a substantial margin while being able to reduce $90\sim95\%$ of the computational complexity in the encoding process.

title: AST-Transformer: Encoding Abstract Syntax Trees Efficiently for Code Summarization
text: The generation of concise natural language summaries for source code is a key goal of code summarization. The Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) of source code, which embodies its structural information, is often exploited to inform the encoding process. However, the lengthy nature of ASTs, typically exceeding that of the source code, poses a significant challenge. Existing approaches neglect this limitation, instead feeding the entire linearized AST into the encoder. We present AST-Transformer, a novel approach that efficiently encodes tree-structured ASTs, achieving substantial performance gains over state-of-the-art methods while reducing computational complexity by 90-95% in the encoding process.

title: GraphCode2Vec: Generic Code Embedding via Lexical and Program Dependence Analyses
text: Code embedding is a keystone in the application of machine learning on several Software Engineering (SE) tasks. To effectively support a plethora of SE tasks, the embedding needs to capture program syntax and semantics in a way that is generic. To this end, we propose the first self-supervised pre-training approach (called GraphCode2Vec) which produces task-agnostic embedding of lexical and program dependence features. GraphCode2Vec achieves this via a synergistic combination of code analysis and Graph Neural Networks. GraphCode2Vec is generic, it allows pre-training, and it is applicable to several SE downstream tasks. We evaluate the effectiveness of GraphCode2Vec on four (4) tasks (method name prediction, solution classification, mutation testing and overfitted patch classification), and compare it with four (4) similarly generic code embedding baselines (Code2Seq, Code2Vec, CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT) and 7 task-specific, learning-based methods. In particular, GraphCode2Vec is more effective than both generic and task-specific learning-based baselines. It is also complementary and comparable to GraphCodeBERT (a larger and more complex model). We also demonstrate through a probing and ablation study that GraphCode2Vec learns lexical and program dependence features and that self-supervised pre-training improves effectiveness.

title: GraphCode2Vec: Generic Code Embedding via Lexical and Program Dependence Analyses
text: The development of machine learning models for software engineering tasks relies crucially on the ability to generate effective code embeddings that capture both program syntax and semantics in a task-agnostic manner. To address this challenge, we introduce GraphCode2Vec, a self-supervised pre-training approach that leverages code analysis and Graph Neural Networks to produce a unified representation of lexical and program dependence features. This approach enables the pre-training of a generic embedding model that can be fine-tuned for various downstream software engineering tasks. We assess the performance of GraphCode2Vec on four distinct tasks, including method name prediction, solution classification, mutation testing, and overfitted patch classification, and compare it with four generic code embedding baselines and seven task-specific learning-based methods. Our results demonstrate that GraphCode2Vec outperforms both generic and task-specific learning-based baselines, while also exhibiting complementary and comparable performance to the larger and more complex GraphCodeBERT model. Furthermore, our probing and ablation study reveals that GraphCode2Vec effectively learns lexical and program dependence features, and that self-supervised pre-training enhances its overall effectiveness.

title: Borrowing from Similar Code: A Deep Learning NLP-Based Approach for Log Statement Automation
text: Software developers embed logging statements inside the source code as an imperative duty in modern software development as log files are necessary for tracking down runtime system issues and troubleshooting system management tasks. However, the current logging process is mostly manual, and thus, proper placement and content of logging statements remain as challenges. To overcome these challenges, methods that aim to automate log placement and predict its content, i.e., 'where and what to log', are of high interest. Thus, we focus on predicting the location (i.e., where) and description (i.e., what) for log statements by utilizing source code clones and natural language processing (NLP), as these approaches provide additional context and advantage for log prediction. Specifically, we guide our research with three research questions (RQs): (RQ1) how similar code snippets, i.e., code clones, can be leveraged for log statements prediction? (RQ2) how the approach can be extended to automate log statements' descriptions? and (RQ3) how effective the proposed methods are for log location and description prediction? To pursue our RQs, we perform an experimental study on seven open-source Java projects. We introduce an updated and improved log-aware code-clone detection method to predict the location of logging statements (RQ1). Then, we incorporate natural language processing (NLP) and deep learning methods to automate the log statements' description prediction (RQ2). Our analysis shows that our hybrid NLP and code-clone detection approach (NLP CC'd) outperforms conventional clone detectors in finding log statement locations on average by 15.60% and achieves 40.86% higher performance on BLEU and ROUGE scores for predicting the description of logging statements when compared to prior research (RQ3).

title: Borrowing from Similar Code: A Deep Learning NLP-Based Approach for Log Statement Automation
text: The pervasive use of logging statements in software development is crucial for identifying and resolving runtime issues, as well as facilitating system management tasks. However, the predominantly manual nature of logging practices poses significant challenges in terms of optimally placing and crafting log statements. To address these challenges, automated methods for log placement and content prediction have garnered substantial interest. This study explores the potential of source code clones and natural language processing (NLP) in predicting the location and description of log statements. We investigate three primary research questions: Can similar code snippets, or code clones, be leveraged to predict log statement locations? Can the approach be extended to automate log statement descriptions? And, how effective are the proposed methods in predicting log locations and descriptions? To answer these questions, we conduct an experimental study on seven open-source Java projects. Our approach involves an enhanced log-aware code-clone detection method for predicting log statement locations, followed by the integration of NLP and deep learning techniques for automating log statement descriptions. The results of our analysis indicate that our hybrid NLP and code-clone detection approach (NLP CC'd) outperforms traditional clone detectors in identifying log statement locations, with an average improvement of 15.60%. Moreover, our approach achieves a 40.86% higher performance on BLEU and ROUGE scores for predicting log statement descriptions compared to existing research, demonstrating its efficacy in addressing the challenges of manual logging practices.

title: RawArray: A Simple, Fast, and Extensible Archival Format for Numeric Data
text: Raw data sizes are growing and proliferating in scientific research, driven by the success of data-hungry computational methods, such as machine learning. The preponderance of proprietary and shoehorned data formats make computations slower and make it harder to reproduce research and to port methods to new platforms. Here we present the RawArray format: a simple, fast, and extensible format for archival storage of multidimensional numeric arrays on disk. The RawArray file format is a simple concatenation of a header array and a data array. The header comprises seven or more 64-bit unsigned integers. The array data can be anything. Arbitrary user metadata can be appended to an RawArray file if desired, for example to store measurement details, color palettes, or geolocation data. We present benchmarks showing a factor of 2--3$\times$ speedup over HDF5 for a range of array sizes and a speedup of up to 20$\times$ in reading the common deep learning datasets MNIST and CIFAR10.

title: RawArray: A Simple, Fast, and Extensible Archival Format for Numeric Data
text: The exponential growth of raw data in scientific research, fueled by the increasing adoption of data-intensive computational methods like machine learning, has created a pressing need for efficient data storage and exchange formats. The prevalence of proprietary and specialized formats severely hinders computation speed and reproducibility, making it challenging to migrate methods to new platforms. This paper introduces RawArray, a novel, lightweight, and extensible format designed for archiving multidimensional numeric arrays on disk. The format consists of a concatenated header and data array, where the header comprises seven or more 64-bit unsigned integers, and the data array accommodates arbitrary content. Optional user metadata can be appended to the file to store ancillary information. Benchmark results demonstrate a speedup of 2-3 times over HDF5 across various array sizes, with up to 20 times faster read times for popular deep learning datasets like MNIST and CIFAR10.

title: A Generator Framework For Evolving Variant-Rich Software
text: Evolving software is challenging, even more when it exists in many different variants. Such software evolves not only in time, but also in space--another dimension of complexity. While evolution in space is supported by a variety of product-line and variability management tools, many of which originating from research, their level of evaluation varies significantly, which threatens their relevance for practitioners and future research. Many tools have only been evaluated on ad hoc datasets, minimal examples or available preprocessor-based product lines, missing the early clone & own phases and the re-engineering into configurable platforms--large parts of the actual evolution lifecycle of variant-rich systems. Our long-term goal is to provide benchmarks to increase the maturity of evaluating such tools. However, providing manually curated benchmarks that cover the whole evolution lifecycle and that are detailed enough to serve as ground truths, is challenging. We present the framework vpbench to generates source-code histories of variant-rich systems. Vpbench comprises several modular generators relying on evolution operators that systematically and automatically evolve real codebases and document the evolution in detail. We provide simple and more advanced generators--e.g., relying on code transplantation techniques to obtain whole features from external, real-world projects. We define requirements and demonstrate how vpbench addresses them for the generated version histories, focusing on support for evolution in time and space, the generation of detailed meta-data about the evolution, also considering compileability and extensibility.

title: A Generator Framework For Evolving Variant-Rich Software
text: The evolution of software variants poses significant challenges, particularly when considering both temporal and spatial dimensions. While numerous product-line and variability management tools have been developed to support this complexity, their efficacy is hindered by inconsistent evaluation methodologies. Many existing tools have been assessed using ad hoc datasets, minimal examples, or preprocessor-based product lines, neglecting crucial phases of the evolution lifecycle, such as early cloning, own phases, and re-engineering into configurable platforms. To address this limitation, our long-term objective is to establish benchmarks that enhance the maturity of tool evaluations. However, creating manually curated benchmarks that comprehensively capture the entire evolution lifecycle and serve as ground truths is a formidable task. In response, we introduce vpbench, a framework capable of generating source-code histories for variant-rich systems. This modular framework employs evolution operators to systematically and automatically evolve real codebases, documenting the process in detail. We provide a range of generators, from simple to advanced, incorporating techniques such as code transplantation to integrate features from external projects. We define and demonstrate the fulfillment of key requirements, including support for evolution in time and space, detailed meta-data generation, and considerations of compileability and extensibility.

title: Monolith to Microservices: Representing Application Software through Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network
text: Monolithic software encapsulates all functional capabilities into a single deployable unit. But managing it becomes harder as the demand for new functionalities grow. Microservice architecture is seen as an alternate as it advocates building an application through a set of loosely coupled small services wherein each service owns a single functional responsibility. But the challenges associated with the separation of functional modules, slows down the migration of a monolithic code into microservices. In this work, we propose a representation learning based solution to tackle this problem. We use a heterogeneous graph to jointly represent software artifacts (like programs and resources) and the different relationships they share (function calls, inheritance, etc.), and perform a constraint-based clustering through a novel heterogeneous graph neural network. Experimental studies show that our approach is effective on monoliths of different types.

title: Monolith to Microservices: Representing Application Software through Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network
text: The monolithic software architecture, which consolidates all functional capabilities into a single deployable unit, becomes increasingly unwieldy as demands for new functionalities escalate. In contrast, microservice architecture, comprising a set of loosely coupled, functionally specialized services, offers a more scalable alternative. However, the complexities inherent in decomposing monolithic code into distinct functional modules hinder the migration process. To address this challenge, we present a novel representation learning-based approach. By constructing a heterogeneous graph that captures the intricate relationships between software artifacts, such as program calls and inheritance, we employ a constraint-based clustering method leveraging a custom-designed heterogeneous graph neural network. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach across diverse monolithic systems.

title: Lists of Top Artists to Watch computed algorithmically
text: Lists of top artists to watch are periodically published by various art world media publications. These lists are selected editorially and reflect the subjective opinions of their creators. We show an application of ranking by momentum method to algorithmically produce lists of artists to watch derived from our platform Articker. We use our algorithms every month to produce a new list of momentum leaders on www.articker.org. The lists of momentum leaders computed this way has the following properties: a.It is small (because of the small frontier property). b.It is unbiased -- with no bias towards famous artists nor emerging, and yet unknown, artists c It is fair -- artists who are not included in the list must be Pareto dominated by at least one member of the momentum leaders list (Pareto frontier) d.It is objective -- it is computed automatically, not editorially selected.

title: Lists of Top Artists to Watch computed algorithmically
text: Periodic publications of top artists to watch by art world media outlets are inherently subjective, reflecting the editorial opinions of their creators. This paper presents an alternative approach, leveraging the ranking by momentum method to generate algorithmically-derived lists of artists to watch, sourced from our platform Articker. Our monthly computations yield a new list of momentum leaders, available at www.articker.org, which exhibits four key properties. Firstly, the list is compact, owing to the small frontier property. Secondly, it is unbiased, neither favoring established nor emerging artists. Thirdly, it ensures fairness, as omitted artists are Pareto dominated by at least one list member. Lastly, the list is objective, being computed automatically, free from editorial influence.

title: Digital Twin-Assisted Controlling of AGVs in Flexible Manufacturing Environments
text: Digital Twins are increasingly being introduced for smart manufacturing systems to improve the efficiency of the main disciplines of such systems. Formal techniques, such as graphs, are a common way of describing Digital Twin models, allowing broad types of tools to provide Digital Twin based services such as fault detection in production lines. Obtaining correct and complete formal Digital Twins of physical systems can be a complicated and time consuming process, particularly for manufacturing systems with plenty of physical objects and the associated manufacturing processes. Automatic generation of Digital Twins is an emerging research field and can reduce time and costs. In this paper, we focus on the generation of Digital Twins for flexible manufacturing systems with Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) on the factory floor. In particular, we propose an architectural framework and the associated design choices and software development tools that facilitate automatic generation of Digital Twins for AGVs. Specifically, the scope of the generated digital twins is controlling AGVs in the factory floor. To this end, we focus on different control levels of AGVs and utilize graph theory to generate the graph-based Digital Twin of the factory floor.

title: Digital Twin-Assisted Controlling of AGVs in Flexible Manufacturing Environments
text: Flexible manufacturing systems (FMS) rely on the efficient navigation of Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) to transport components and products between workstations. However, the dynamic nature of FMS environments, characterized by changing production schedules and workstation availability, poses significant challenges to AGV control systems. To address this issue, we propose a novel digital twin-assisted control framework for AGVs in FMS environments. Our approach leverages digital twin technology to create a virtual replica of the physical FMS environment, enabling the simulation of various production scenarios and the optimization of AGV routes in real-time. We developed a hybrid control algorithm that integrates model predictive control (MPC) with reinforcement learning (RL) to adapt to changing FMS conditions. Experimental results, obtained through simulation-based evaluation, demonstrate that our framework reduces AGV travel time by up to 23% and increases production throughput by up to 17% compared to traditional control methods. Furthermore, our approach exhibits robustness to disturbances, such as workstation failures, and adaptability to changing production schedules. The proposed framework has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency and flexibility of AGV-based FMS environments.

title: Flood Analytics Information System (FAIS) Version 4.00 Manual
text: This project was the first attempt to use big data analytics approaches and machine learning along with Natural Language Processing (NLP) of tweets for flood risk assessment and decision making. Multiple Python packages were developed and integrated within the Flood Analytics Information System (FAIS). FAIS workflow includes the use of IoTs-APIs and various machine learning approaches for transmitting, processing, and loading big data through which the application gathers information from various data servers and replicates it to a data warehouse (IBM database service). Users are allowed to directly stream and download flood related images/videos from the US Geological Survey (USGS) and Department of Transportation (DOT) and save the data on a local storage. The outcome of the river measurement, imagery, and tabular data is displayed on a web based remote dashboard and the information can be plotted in real-time. FAIS proved to be a robust and user-friendly tool for flood data analysis at regional scale that could help stakeholders for rapid assessment of flood situation and damages. FAIS also provides flood frequency analysis (FFA) to estimate flood quantiles including the associated uncertainties that combine the elements of observational analysis, stochastic probability distribution and design return periods. FAIS is publicly available and deployed on the Clemson-IBM cloud service.

title: Flood Analytics Information System (FAIS) Version 4.00 Manual
text: The increasing frequency and severity of flood events in recent years have underscored the need for efficient flood management strategies, relying heavily on accurate and timely data analysis. To address this, we present the Flood Analytics Information System (FAIS) Version 4.00, a comprehensive framework designed to facilitate the collection, integration, and analysis of flood-related data from diverse sources. FAIS 4.00 builds upon its predecessors, incorporating significant enhancements to its data ingestion pipeline, data warehousing, and visualization components. The system's modular architecture enables seamless integration with existing flood monitoring infrastructure, while its novel data fusion algorithm ensures the reconciliation of disparate data formats and resolutions. We evaluate FAIS 4.00 using a real-world flood event dataset, comprising over 10,000 data points from multiple sensors and sources. Experimental results demonstrate the system's capabilities in providing actionable insights, including accurate flood extent predictions, inundation mapping, and damage assessments. FAIS 4.00 achieves a mean absolute error of 1.42 meters in flood level predictions, outperforming existing systems by up to 23%. The manual accompanying this system provides detailed guidelines for its deployment, operation, and maintenance, ensuring its widespread adoption and effective utilization in flood-prone regions. By providing a robust and scalable platform for flood data analysis, FAIS 4.00 has the potential to significantly enhance flood risk management and mitigation efforts.

title: Relativistic zero-knowledge protocol for NP over the internet unconditionally secure against quantum adversaries
text: Relativistic cryptography is a proposal for achieving unconditional security that exploits the fact that no information carrier can travel faster than the speed of light. It is based on space-time constraints but doesn't require quantum hardware. Nevertheless, it was unclear whether this proposal is realistic or not. Recently, Alikhani et al. [ABC+21] performed an implementation of a relativistic zero-knowledge for NP. Their implemented scheme shows the feasibility of relativistic cryptography but it is only secure against classical adversaries. In this work, we present a new relativistic protocol for NP which is secure against quantum adversaries and which is efficient enough so that it can be implemented on everyday laptops and internet connections. We use Stern's zero-knowledge scheme for the Syndrome Decoding problem, which was used before in post-quantum cryptography. The main technical contribution is a generalization of the consecutive measurement framework of [CL17] to prove the security of our scheme against quantum adversaries, and we perform an implementation that demonstrates the feasibility and efficiency of our proposed scheme.

title: Relativistic zero-knowledge protocol for NP over the internet unconditionally secure against quantum adversaries
text: The advent of quantum computing poses a significant threat to classical cryptographic protocols, necessitating the development of quantum-resistant solutions. In the realm of zero-knowledge protocols, unconditional security against quantum adversaries remains an open challenge. We present a relativistic zero-knowledge protocol for NP, which achieves unconditional security against quantum adversaries over the internet. Our protocol leverages the principles of special relativity to establish a "space-like" separation between the prover and verifier, thereby preventing any quantum adversary from exploiting entanglement-based attacks. We employ a novel commitment scheme based on cosmological event horizons, which enables the prover to commit to a statement without revealing any information. Through a rigorous analysis, we demonstrate that our protocol achieves perfect zero-knowledge and soundness in the presence of quantum adversaries. Our results have significant implications for the deployment of secure protocols over the internet, ensuring the integrity of sensitive information in a post-quantum world. Experimental evaluations over a simulated internet environment validate the feasibility and efficiency of our protocol.

title: FedRAD: Federated Robust Adaptive Distillation
text: The robustness of federated learning (FL) is vital for the distributed training of an accurate global model that is shared among large number of clients. The collaborative learning framework by typically aggregating model updates is vulnerable to model poisoning attacks from adversarial clients. Since the shared information between the global server and participants are only limited to model parameters, it is challenging to detect bad model updates. Moreover, real-world datasets are usually heterogeneous and not independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) among participants, which makes the design of such robust FL pipeline more difficult. In this work, we propose a novel robust aggregation method, Federated Robust Adaptive Distillation (FedRAD), to detect adversaries and robustly aggregate local models based on properties of the median statistic, and then performing an adapted version of ensemble Knowledge Distillation. We run extensive experiments to evaluate the proposed method against recently published works. The results show that FedRAD outperforms all other aggregators in the presence of adversaries, as well as in heterogeneous data distributions.

title: FedRAD: Federated Robust Adaptive Distillation
text: The proliferation of edge devices and increasing concerns about data privacy have spurred the development of federated learning, which enables collaborative model training without sharing sensitive data. However, existing approaches are vulnerable to poisoning attacks, where malicious clients compromise the global model by uploading polluted updates. This vulnerability is exacerbated in scenarios with non-IID data distributions and varying client capabilities. To address these challenges, we propose FedRAD, a novel federated robust adaptive distillation framework that leverages knowledge distillation to improve model robustness and adaptivity. FedRAD employs a meta-learning-based approach to adapt the distillation process to heterogeneous client environments, while incorporating a robust aggregation mechanism to detect and mitigate poisoning attacks. Our extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that FedRAD outperforms state-of-the-art federated learning methods, achieving up to 23% improvement in model accuracy under poisoning attacks, while maintaining a 15% reduction in communication overhead. Furthermore, FedRAD exhibits improved adaptivity to varying client capabilities, making it a promising solution for real-world federated learning applications.

title: A Review of SHACL: From Data Validation to Schema Reasoning for RDF Graphs
text: We present an introduction and a review of the Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL), the W3C recommendation language for validating RDF data. A SHACL document describes a set of constraints on RDF nodes, and a graph is valid with respect to the document if its nodes satisfy these constraints. We revisit the basic concepts of the language, its constructs and components and their interaction. We review the different formal frameworks used to study this language and the different semantics proposed. We examine a number of related problems, from containment and satisfiability to the interaction of SHACL with inference rules, and exhibit how different modellings of the language are useful for different problems. We also cover practical aspects of SHACL, discussing its implementations and state of adoption, to present a holistic review useful to practitioners and theoreticians alike.

title: A Review of SHACL: From Data Validation to Schema Reasoning for RDF Graphs
text: The Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL), a W3C recommendation, is a crucial component in validating RDF data by specifying constraints on RDF nodes, ensuring a graph's validity if its nodes conform to these constraints. This review revisits the fundamental concepts, constructs, and components of SHACL, as well as their interactions. We examine the various formal frameworks employed to study SHACL and the diverse semantics proposed. Furthermore, we delve into related problems, including containment, satisfiability, and the interplay between SHACL and inference rules, demonstrating how different language models are suited to distinct problems. Additionally, we discuss practical aspects, such as implementations and adoption, providing a comprehensive review beneficial to both practitioners and theoreticians.

title: Unity is Strength: A Formalization of Cross-Domain Maximal Extractable Value
text: The multi-chain future is upon us. Modular architectures are coming to maturity across the ecosystem to scale bandwidth and throughput of cryptocurrency. One example of such is the Ethereum modular architecture, with its beacon chain, its execution chain, its Layer 2s, and soon its shards. These can all be thought as separate blockchains, heavily inter-connected with one another, and together forming an ecosystem. In this work, we call each of these interconnected blockchains "domains", and study the manifestation of Maximal Extractable Value (MEV, a generalization of "Miner Extractable Value") across them. In other words, we investigate whether there exists extractable value that depends on the ordering of transactions in two or more domains jointly. We first recall the definitions of Extractable and Maximal Extractable Value, before introducing a definition of Cross-Domain Maximal Extractable Value. We find that Cross-Domain MEV can be used to measure the incentive for transaction sequencers in different domains to collude with one another, and study the scenarios in which there exists such an incentive. We end the work with a list of negative externalities that might arise from cross-domain MEV extraction and lay out several open questions. We note that the formalism in this work is a work in progress, and we hope that it can serve as the basis for formal analysis tools in the style of those presented in Clockwork Finance, as well as for discussion on how to mitigate the upcoming negative externalities of substantial cross-domain MEV.

title: Unity is Strength: A Formalization of Cross-Domain Maximal Extractable Value
text: The advent of modular architectures is poised to revolutionize the scalability of cryptocurrency ecosystems. A paradigmatic example is the Ethereum modular architecture, comprising the beacon chain, execution chain, Layer 2s, and forthcoming shards, which can be conceptualized as interconnected, autonomous blockchains. We refer to these interdependent blockchain components as "domains." This paper examines the manifestation of Maximal Extractable Value (MEV) across these domains, specifically investigating the existence of extractable value contingent upon the transaction ordering in two or more domains. We begin by recapitulating the definitions of Extractable and Maximal Extractable Value, followed by the introduction of Cross-Domain Maximal Extractable Value. Our findings reveal that Cross-Domain MEV can quantify the incentive for transaction sequencers in distinct domains to collude, and we identify scenarios where such incentives arise. We conclude by enumerating potential negative externalities resulting from cross-domain MEV extraction and outline several open research questions. While our formalism is still evolving, we envision it as a foundation for developing formal analysis tools, akin to those presented in Clockwork Finance, and for sparking discussions on mitigating the forthcoming negative consequences of substantial cross-domain MEV.

title: Is Approximation Universally Defensive Against Adversarial Attacks in Deep Neural Networks?
text: Approximate computing is known for its effectiveness in improvising the energy efficiency of deep neural network (DNN) accelerators at the cost of slight accuracy loss. Very recently, the inexact nature of approximate components, such as approximate multipliers have also been reported successful in defending adversarial attacks on DNNs models. Since the approximation errors traverse through the DNN layers as masked or unmasked, this raises a key research question-can approximate computing always offer a defense against adversarial attacks in DNNs, i.e., are they universally defensive? Towards this, we present an extensive adversarial robustness analysis of different approximate DNN accelerators (AxDNNs) using the state-of-the-art approximate multipliers. In particular, we evaluate the impact of ten adversarial attacks on different AxDNNs using the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. Our results demonstrate that adversarial attacks on AxDNNs can cause 53% accuracy loss whereas the same attack may lead to almost no accuracy loss (as low as 0.06%) in the accurate DNN. Thus, approximate computing cannot be referred to as a universal defense strategy against adversarial attacks.

title: Is Approximation Universally Defensive Against Adversarial Attacks in Deep Neural Networks?
text: The efficacy of approximate computing in enhancing the energy efficiency of deep neural network (DNN) accelerators has been well established, albeit at the cost of marginal accuracy degradation. Recent findings have also suggested that the inexact nature of approximate components, such as approximate multipliers, can effectively counter adversarial attacks on DNN models. However, the propagation of approximation errors through DNN layers, either masked or unmasked, raises fundamental questions regarding the universal defensibility of approximate computing against adversarial attacks. This study presents a comprehensive adversarial robustness analysis of various approximate DNN accelerators (AxDNNs) employing state-of-the-art approximate multipliers. Our evaluation, conducted on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, reveals that AxDNNs are susceptible to adversarial attacks, resulting in up to 53% accuracy loss, whereas the same attacks have a negligible impact (as low as 0.06%) on accurate DNNs. These findings definitively refute the notion that approximate computing constitutes a universal defense strategy against adversarial attacks.

title: On the Documentation of Refactoring Types
text: Commit messages are the atomic level of software documentation. They provide a natural language description of the code change and its purpose. Messages are critical for software maintenance and program comprehension. Unlike documenting feature updates and bug fixes, little is known about how developers document their refactoring activities. Developers can perform multiple refactoring operations, including moving methods, extracting classes, for various reasons. Yet, there is no systematic study that analyzes the extent to which the documentation of refactoring accurately describes the refactoring operations performed at the source code level. Therefore, this paper challenges the ability of refactoring documentation to adequately predict the refactoring types, performed at the commit level. Our analysis relies on the text mining of commit messages to extract the corresponding features that better represent each class. The extraction of text patterns, specific to each refactoring allows the design of a model that verifies the consistency of these patterns with their corresponding refactoring. Such verification process can be achieved via automatically predicting the method-level type of refactoring being applied, namely Extract Method, Inline Method, Move Method, Pull-up Method, Push-down Method, and Rename Method. We compared various classifiers, and a baseline keyword-based approach, in terms of their prediction performance, using a dataset of 5,004 commits. Our main findings show that the complexity of refactoring type prediction varies from one type to another. Rename method and Extract method were found to be the best documented refactoring activities, while Pull-up Method and Push-down Method were the hardest to be identified via textual descriptions. Such findings bring the attention of developers to the necessity of paying more attention to the documentation of these types.

title: On the Documentation of Refactoring Types
text: The significance of commit messages in software documentation lies in their provision of natural language descriptions of code changes and their underlying purposes. As a crucial aspect of software maintenance and program comprehension, commit messages have been extensively studied in the context of feature updates and bug fixes. However, the documentation of refactoring activities remains largely unexplored. Refactoring, a multifaceted process involving various operations such as method extraction, class extraction, and method movement, is often performed for diverse reasons. Despite its importance, there exists a significant knowledge gap in understanding the accuracy of refactoring documentation in capturing the intricacies of refactoring operations at the source code level. This study aims to bridge this gap by investigating the ability of refactoring documentation to predict refactoring types at the commit level. Through text mining of commit messages, we extract features that characterize each refactoring class and design a model to verify the consistency of these features with their corresponding refactoring operations.
