Our approach enables the automatic prediction of method-level refactoring types, including Extract Method, Inline Method, Move Method, Pull-up Method, Push-down Method, and Rename Method. An evaluation of various classifiers and a baseline keyword-based approach using a dataset of 5,004 commits reveals that the complexity of refactoring type prediction varies significantly across different types. Notably, Rename Method and Extract Method are found to be the most accurately documented refactoring activities, while Pull-up Method and Push-down Method are the most challenging to identify through textual descriptions. These findings highlight the need for developers to prioritize the documentation of these refactoring types.

title: The Art and Practice of Data Science Pipelines: A Comprehensive Study of Data Science Pipelines In Theory, In-The-Small, and In-The-Large
text: Increasingly larger number of software systems today are including data science components for descriptive, predictive, and prescriptive analytics. The collection of data science stages from acquisition, to cleaning/curation, to modeling, and so on are referred to as data science pipelines. To facilitate research and practice on data science pipelines, it is essential to understand their nature. What are the typical stages of a data science pipeline? How are they connected? Do the pipelines differ in the theoretical representations and that in the practice? Today we do not fully understand these architectural characteristics of data science pipelines. In this work, we present a three-pronged comprehensive study to answer this for the state-of-the-art, data science in-the-small, and data science in-the-large. Our study analyzes three datasets: a collection of 71 proposals for data science pipelines and related concepts in theory, a collection of over 105 implementations of curated data science pipelines from Kaggle competitions to understand data science in-the-small, and a collection of 21 mature data science projects from GitHub to understand data science in-the-large. Our study has led to three representations of data science pipelines that capture the essence of our subjects in theory, in-the-small, and in-the-large.

title: The Art and Practice of Data Science Pipelines: A Comprehensive Study of Data Science Pipelines In Theory, In-The-Small, and In-The-Large
text: Data science pipelines have become a crucial component of modern data-driven systems, enabling the extraction of insights and value from vast amounts of data. Despite their widespread adoption, the design, development, and deployment of data science pipelines remain a complex and multifaceted problem. This comprehensive study aims to provide a thorough understanding of data science pipelines from three distinct perspectives: theoretical foundations, small-scale experimentation, and large-scale industrial deployments. We begin by formalizing the concept of data science pipelines as a sequence of data transformations and model compositions, providing a theoretical framework for pipeline design and optimization. Next, we conduct a series of controlled experiments to evaluate the performance and scalability of various pipeline architectures and components, including data ingestion, feature engineering, and model serving. Finally, we present a large-scale analysis of real-world data science pipelines deployed in industrial settings, examining their design patterns, performance characteristics, and maintenance challenges. Our study reveals several key findings, including the importance of modular pipeline design, the trade-offs between data quality and model complexity, and the need for automated pipeline management and optimization techniques. We also identify significant gaps between theoretical pipeline design and real-world deployments, highlighting areas for future research and development. This work provides a comprehensive understanding of data science pipelines, informing the development of more efficient, scalable, and effective data-driven systems.

title: What Not to Test (for Cyber-Physical Systems)
text: For simulation-based systems, finding a set of test cases with the least cost by exploring multiple goals is a complex task. Domain-specific optimization goals (e.g. maximize output variance) are useful for guiding the rapid selection of test cases via mutation. But evaluating the selected test cases via mutation (that can distinguish the current program from the mutated systems) is a different goal to domain-specific optimizations. While the optimization goals can be used to guide the mutation analysis, that guidance should be viewed as a weak indicator since it can hurt the mutation effectiveness goals by focusing too much on the optimization goals. Based on the above, this paper proposes DoLesS (Domination with Least Squares Approximation) that selects the minimal and effective test cases by averaging over a coarse-grained grid of the information gained from multiple optimizations goals. DoLesS applies an inverted least squares approximation approach to find a minimal set of tests that can distinguish better from worse parts of the optimization goals. When tested on multiple simulation-based systems, DoLesS performs as well or even better as the prior state-of-the-art, while running 80-360 times faster on average (seconds instead of hours).

title: What Not to Test (for Cyber-Physical Systems)
text: The identification of a cost-effective set of test cases for simulation-based systems, tailored to multiple optimization goals, poses a significant challenge. Domain-specific optimization objectives, such as maximizing output variance, can effectively guide the rapid selection of test cases through mutation. However, these objectives diverge from the primary goal of evaluating test cases via mutation, which aims to distinguish the original program from its mutated counterparts. Although optimization goals can inform mutation analysis, their influence should be treated with caution, as an overemphasis on optimization may compromise mutation effectiveness. To address this, we introduce DoLesS (Domination with Least Squares Approximation), a method that selects minimal yet effective test cases by aggregating information from multiple optimization goals across a coarse-grained grid. DoLesS employs an inverted least squares approximation to identify a minimal test set that effectively differentiates between superior and inferior aspects of the optimization goals. Experimental results on multiple simulation-based systems demonstrate that DoLesS performs comparably to, or even surpasses, state-of-the-art approaches, while achieving a significant speedup of 80-360 times on average, reducing evaluation times from hours to seconds.

title: Is RobustBench/AutoAttack a suitable Benchmark for Adversarial Robustness?
text: Recently, RobustBench (Croce et al. 2020) has become a widely recognized benchmark for the adversarial robustness of image classification networks. In its most commonly reported sub-task, RobustBench evaluates and ranks the adversarial robustness of trained neural networks on CIFAR10 under AutoAttack (Croce and Hein 2020b) with l-inf perturbations limited to eps = 8/255. With leading scores of the currently best performing models of around 60% of the baseline, it is fair to characterize this benchmark to be quite challenging. Despite its general acceptance in recent literature, we aim to foster discussion about the suitability of RobustBench as a key indicator for robustness which could be generalized to practical applications. Our line of argumentation against this is two-fold and supported by excessive experiments presented in this paper: We argue that I) the alternation of data by AutoAttack with l-inf, eps = 8/255 is unrealistically strong, resulting in close to perfect detection rates of adversarial samples even by simple detection algorithms and human observers. We also show that other attack methods are much harder to detect while achieving similar success rates. II) That results on low-resolution data sets like CIFAR10 do not generalize well to higher resolution images as gradient-based attacks appear to become even more detectable with increasing resolutions.

title: Is RobustBench/AutoAttack a suitable Benchmark for Adversarial Robustness?
text: Evaluating the robustness of deep neural networks against adversarial attacks is crucial for deploying machine learning models in security-critical applications. Recently, RobustBench, a popular benchmark for adversarial robustness, has been complemented by AutoAttack, a parameter-free attack that adaptively combines existing attacks to improve their effectiveness. While RobustBench/AutoAttack has been widely adopted, its suitability as a benchmark for adversarial robustness has not been thoroughly examined. In this study, we conduct a systematic analysis of RobustBench/AutoAttack's efficacy in evaluating model robustness across diverse architectures, datasets, and threat models. Our methodology involves assessing the benchmark's consistency, reliability, and sensitivity to various factors, such as model capacity, training objectives, and input preprocessing techniques. Our findings suggest that RobustBench/AutoAttack can be overly pessimistic, yielding inaccurate robustness estimates for certain models and datasets. Specifically, we observe that AutoAttack's adaptive nature can lead to overestimation of robustness degradation, while RobustBench's fixed set of attacks may not capture the full spectrum of potential threats. Our results have significant implications for the development of robust machine learning models, highlighting the need for more comprehensive and nuanced evaluation methodologies.

title: A Grounded Theory Based Approach to Characterize Software Attack Surfaces
text: The notion of Attack Surface refers to the critical points on the boundary of a software system which are accessible from outside or contain valuable content for attackers. The ability to identify attack surface components of software system has a significant role in effectiveness of vulnerability analysis approaches. Most prior works focus on vulnerability techniques that use an approximation of attack surfaces and there has not been many attempt to create a comprehensive list of attack surface components. Although limited number of studies have focused on attack surface analysis, they defined attack surface components based on project specific hypotheses to evaluate security risk of specific types of software applications. In this study, we leverage a qualitative analysis approach to empirically identify an extensive list of attack surface components. To this end, we conduct a Grounded Theory (GT) analysis on 1444 previously published vulnerability reports and weaknesses with a team of three software developers and security experts. We extract vulnerability information from two publicly available repositories: 1) Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, and 2) Common Weakness Enumeration. We ask three key questions: where the attacks come from, what they target, and how they emerge, and to help answer these questions we define three core categories for attack surface components: Entry points, Targets, and Mechanisms. We extract attack surface concepts related to each category from collected vulnerability information using the GT analysis and provide a comprehensive categorization that represents attack surface components of software systems from various perspectives. The comparison of the proposed attack surface model with the literature shows in the best case previous works cover only 50% of the attack surface components at network level and only 6.7% of the components at code level.

title: A Grounded Theory Based Approach to Characterize Software Attack Surfaces
text: Attack surface components, situated at the boundary of a software system, encompass critical points that are externally accessible or contain valuable content for potential attackers. Identifying these components is crucial for the efficacy of vulnerability analysis approaches. While prior research has primarily focused on vulnerability techniques that approximate attack surfaces, few attempts have been made to create a comprehensive catalog of attack surface components. Existing studies on attack surface analysis have been project-specific, defining components based on hypotheses tailored to evaluate security risks in particular software applications. This study employs a qualitative analysis approach to empirically derive an exhaustive list of attack surface components. Through a Grounded Theory analysis of 1444 previously published vulnerability reports and weaknesses, conducted by a team of three software developers and security experts, we extracted vulnerability information from the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures and Common Weakness Enumeration repositories. By posing three fundamental questions – where attacks originate, what they target, and how they emerge – we established three core categories for attack surface components: Entry points, Targets, and Mechanisms. Using Grounded Theory analysis, we extracted attack surface concepts related to each category and developed a comprehensive categorization that captures attack surface components from diverse perspectives. Notably, our proposed attack surface model outperforms existing models, with previous works covering at most 50% of attack surface components at the network level and a mere 6.7% at the code level.

title: Systematically reviewing the layered architectural pattern principles and their use to reconstruct software architectures
text: Architectural reconstruction is a reverse engineering activity aiming at recovering the missing decisions on a system. It can help identify the components, within a legacy software application, according to the application's architectural pattern. It is useful to identify architectural technical debt. We are interested in identifying layers within a layered application since the layered pattern is one of the most used patterns to structure large systems. Earlier component reconstruction work focusing on that pattern relied on generic component identification criteria, such as cohesion and coupling. Recent work has identified architectural-pattern specific criteria to identify components within that pattern. However, the architectural-pattern specific criteria that the layered pattern embodies are loosely defined. In this paper, we present a first systematic literature review (SLR) of the literature aiming at inventorying such criteria for layers within legacy applications and grouping them under four principles that embody the fundamental design principles under-lying the architectural pattern. We identify six such criteria in the form of design rules. We also perform a second systematic literature review to synthesize the literature on software architecture reconstruction in the light of these criteria. We report those principles, the rules they encompass, their representation, and their usage in software architecture reconstruction.

title: Systematically reviewing the layered architectural pattern principles and their use to reconstruct software architectures
text: The layered architectural pattern is a widely adopted design principle in software engineering, yet its underlying principles and application in reconstructing software architectures remain poorly understood. Despite its prevalence, the literature lacks a systematic review of the pattern's core tenets and their implications on software architecture reconstruction. This study aims to bridge this gap by conducting a comprehensive review of the layered architectural pattern principles and their use in reconstructing software architectures. We employed a systematic literature review methodology, analyzing 153 primary studies published between 2000 and 2022. Our results show that the layered pattern is often misunderstood, with many architects misapplying its principles or combining them with other patterns in ad-hoc ways. We identify seven key principles underlying the layered pattern, including separation of concerns, abstraction, and hierarchical decomposition. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the pattern is most effective when used in conjunction with other architectural patterns, such as the Model-View-Controller pattern. We also find that the layered pattern's application is largely domain-agnostic, with successful implementations reported in diverse domains, including web development, mobile apps, and enterprise software. Our study's findings provide a foundation for architects to make informed design decisions when reconstructing software architectures using the layered pattern, and highlight areas for future research into its application and limitations.

title: FP-Radar: Longitudinal Measurement and Early Detection of Browser Fingerprinting
text: Browser fingerprinting is a stateless tracking technique that attempts to combine information exposed by multiple different web APIs to create a unique identifier for tracking users across the web. Over the last decade, trackers have abused several existing and newly proposed web APIs to further enhance the browser fingerprint. Existing approaches are limited to detecting a specific fingerprinting technique(s) at a particular point in time. Thus, they are unable to systematically detect novel fingerprinting techniques that abuse different web APIs. In this paper, we propose FP-Radar, a machine learning approach that leverages longitudinal measurements of web API usage on top-100K websites over the last decade, for early detection of new and evolving browser fingerprinting techniques. The results show that FP-Radar is able to early detect the abuse of newly introduced properties of already known (e.g., WebGL, Sensor) and as well as previously unknown (e.g., Gamepad, Clipboard) APIs for browser fingerprinting. To the best of our knowledge, FP-Radar is also the first to detect the abuse of the Visibility API for ephemeral fingerprinting in the wild.

title: FP-Radar: Longitudinal Measurement and Early Detection of Browser Fingerprinting
text: Browser fingerprinting, a technique used to track users online, has raised significant privacy concerns. Despite its pervasiveness, longitudinal studies on fingerprinting prevalence and detection efficacy are scarce. We address this gap by designing FP-Radar, a large-scale, longitudinal measurement framework that monitors browser fingerprinting activities across various websites and browsers. Over a period of 12 months, FP-Radar collected 3.2 million browser fingerprints from 150 popular websites, revealing a significant increase in fingerprinting attempts (35%) and a shift towards more sophisticated techniques. We propose a novel early detection approach, leveraging machine learning and graph-based methods to identify fingerprinting scripts. Our evaluation shows that FP-Radar detects fingerprinting scripts with an accuracy of 92.5%, outperforming existing approaches by 15%. Furthermore, we identify 15 previously unknown fingerprinting scripts, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. Our findings have important implications for browser vendors, policymakers, and users, highlighting the need for more robust countermeasures against browser fingerprinting. FP-Radar is a valuable tool for the community, providing insights into the evolving fingerprinting landscape and enabling the development of more effective defenses.

title: Differential Privacy in Privacy-Preserving Big Data and Learning: Challenge and Opportunity
text: Differential privacy (DP) has become the de facto standard of privacy preservation due to its strong protection and sound mathematical foundation, which is widely adopted in different applications such as big data analysis, graph data process, machine learning, deep learning, and federated learning. Although DP has become an active and influential area, it is not the best remedy for all privacy problems in different scenarios. Moreover, there are also some misunderstanding, misuse, and great challenges of DP in specific applications. In this paper, we point out a series of limits and open challenges of corresponding research areas. Besides, we offer potentially new insights and avenues on combining differential privacy with other effective dimension reduction techniques and secure multiparty computing to clearly define various privacy models.

title: Differential Privacy in Privacy-Preserving Big Data and Learning: Challenge and Opportunity
text: Differential privacy has emerged as a prevalent standard for privacy preservation, owing to its robust protection and rigorous mathematical underpinnings, with applications spanning big data analysis, graph data processing, machine learning, deep learning, and federated learning. Despite its widespread adoption and influence, differential privacy is not a panacea for all privacy concerns across varying scenarios. Furthermore, its implementation is often marred by misconceptions, misuses, and significant challenges in specific contexts. This paper elucidates the limitations and open challenges inherent to these research domains. Additionally, we propose novel perspectives and avenues for integrating differential privacy with dimension reduction techniques and secure multiparty computing, thereby providing a clearer delineation of diverse privacy models.

title: Single-Shot Black-Box Adversarial Attacks Against Malware Detectors: A Causal Language Model Approach
text: Deep Learning (DL)-based malware detectors are increasingly adopted for early detection of malicious behavior in cybersecurity. However, their sensitivity to adversarial malware variants has raised immense security concerns. Generating such adversarial variants by the defender is crucial to improving the resistance of DL-based malware detectors against them. This necessity has given rise to an emerging stream of machine learning research, Adversarial Malware example Generation (AMG), which aims to generate evasive adversarial malware variants that preserve the malicious functionality of a given malware. Within AMG research, black-box method has gained more attention than white-box methods. However, most black-box AMG methods require numerous interactions with the malware detectors to generate adversarial malware examples. Given that most malware detectors enforce a query limit, this could result in generating non-realistic adversarial examples that are likely to be detected in practice due to lack of stealth. In this study, we show that a novel DL-based causal language model enables single-shot evasion (i.e., with only one query to malware detector) by treating the content of the malware executable as a byte sequence and training a Generative Pre-Trained Transformer (GPT). Our proposed method, MalGPT, significantly outperformed the leading benchmark methods on a real-world malware dataset obtained from VirusTotal, achieving over 24.51\% evasion rate. MalGPT enables cybersecurity researchers to develop advanced defense capabilities by emulating large-scale realistic AMG.

title: Single-Shot Black-Box Adversarial Attacks Against Malware Detectors: A Causal Language Model Approach
text: The proliferation of malware detectors has led to a cat-and-mouse game between defenders and attackers, with each side continually adapting to outmaneuver the other. While recent advances in adversarial machine learning have demonstrated the vulnerability of malware detectors to sophisticated evasion techniques, existing methods typically require multiple queries to the target model or access to its internal workings. In reality, such assumptions are often unrealistic, as attackers may only have a single opportunity to probe the system or may face opaque, black-box detectors. To address this limitation, we propose a novel single-shot black-box adversarial attack framework against malware detectors, leveraging a causal language model to generate perturbations that maximize the likelihood of misclassification. Our approach exploits the sequential nature of malware executables, treating them as a sequence of API calls that can be manipulated to deceive the detector. Experimental results on a range of commercial and open-source malware detectors demonstrate the efficacy of our method, achieving an average evasion rate of 84.2% across five distinct datasets. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the perturbations generated by our framework are highly interpretable, often exploiting specific vulnerabilities or weaknesses in the detectors' parsing mechanisms. Our work has significant implications for the development of more robust malware detectors and highlights the need for defenders to reconsider their assumptions about the capabilities of modern attackers.

title: Understanding Performance Problems in Deep Learning Systems
text: Deep learning (DL) has been widely applied to many domains. Unique challenges in engineering DL systems are posed by the programming paradigm shift from traditional systems to DL systems, and performance is one of the challenges. Performance problems (PPs) in DL systems can cause severe consequences such as excessive resource consumption and financial loss. While bugs in DL systems have been extensively investigated, PPs in DL systems have hardly been explored. To bridge this gap, we present the first comprehensive study to i) characterize symptoms, root causes, and introducing and exposing stages of PPs in DL systems developed in TensorFLow and Keras, with 224 PPs collected from 210 StackOverflow posts, and to ii) assess the capability of existing performance analysis approaches in tackling PPs, with a constructed benchmark of 58 PPs in DL systems. Our findings shed light on the implications on developing high-performance DL systems, and detecting and localizing PPs in DL systems. To demonstrate the usefulness of our findings, we develop a static checker Deep-Perf to detect three types of PPs. It has detected 488 new PPs in 130 GitHub projects. 105 and 27 PPs have been confirmed and fixed.

title: Understanding Performance Problems in Deep Learning Systems
text: The advent of deep learning (DL) has precipitated a paradigm shift in system design, introducing unique engineering challenges. Notably, performance issues in DL systems can have severe consequences, including excessive resource consumption and financial loss. Despite extensive research on bug detection in DL systems, performance problems (PPs) have received scant attention. This knowledge gap is addressed through a comprehensive study, wherein we characterize the symptoms, root causes, and introducing and exposing stages of PPs in DL systems developed using TensorFLow and Keras. Our analysis is based on 224 PPs collected from 210 StackOverflow posts and a constructed benchmark of 58 PPs. The study's findings provide insights into the development of high-performance DL systems and the detection and localization of PPs. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of our research by developing a static checker, Deep-Perf, which detects three types of PPs. When applied to 130 GitHub projects, Deep-Perf identified 488 new PPs, with 105 and 27 subsequently confirmed and fixed, respectively.

title: The UniNAS framework: combining modules in arbitrarily complex configurations with argument trees
text: Designing code to be simplistic yet to offer choice is a tightrope walk. Additional modules such as optimizers and data sets make a framework useful to a broader audience, but the added complexity quickly becomes a problem. Framework parameters may apply only to some modules but not others, be mutually exclusive or depend on each other, often in unclear ways. Even so, many frameworks are limited to a few specific use cases. This paper presents the underlying concept of UniNAS, a framework designed to incorporate a variety of Neural Architecture Search approaches. Since they differ in the number of optimizers and networks, hyper-parameter optimization, network designs, candidate operations, and more, a traditional approach can not solve the task. Instead, every module defines its own hyper-parameters and a local tree structure of module requirements. A configuration file specifies which modules are used, their used parameters, and which other modules they use in turn This concept of argument trees enables combining and reusing modules in complex configurations while avoiding many problems mentioned above. Argument trees can also be configured from a graphical user interface so that designing and changing experiments becomes possible without writing a single line of code. title: The UniNAS framework: combining modules in arbitrarily complex configurations with argument trees
text: Balancing simplicity with flexibility is a delicate challenge in code design. While incorporating additional modules, such as optimizers and datasets, can broaden a framework's appeal, the resulting complexity can quickly become overwhelming. A key issue lies in the intricate relationships between framework parameters, which may be module-specific, mutually exclusive, or interdependent in unclear ways. Consequently, many frameworks are limited to a narrow range of use cases. This paper introduces UniNAS, a novel framework designed to accommodate diverse Neural Architecture Search approaches. Given the disparate requirements of these approaches, including varying numbers of optimizers and networks, hyper-parameter optimization strategies, network designs, and candidate operations, a traditional monolithic approach is insufficient. Instead, UniNAS adopts a modular design, where each module defines its own hyper-parameters and a local tree structure of dependencies. A configuration file specifies the modules used, their parameters, and inter-module relationships, enabling the creation of complex configurations while mitigating the aforementioned issues. Furthermore, a graphical user interface allows users to configure argument trees without writing code, making it easier to design and modify experiments.

title: A Privacy-Preserving Platform for Recording COVID-19 Vaccine Passports
text: Digital vaccine passports are one of the main solutions which would allow the restart of travel in a post COVID-19 world. Trust, scalability and security are all key challenges one must overcome in implementing a vaccine passport. Initial approaches attempt to solve this problem by using centralised systems with trusted authorities. However, sharing vaccine passport data between different organisations, regions and countries has become a major challenge. This paper designs a new platform architecture for creating, storing and verifying digital COVID-19 vaccine certifications. The platform makes use of the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) to guarantee there is no single point of failure and allow data to be securely distributed globally. Blockchain and smart contracts are also integrated into the platform to define policies and log access rights to vaccine passport data while ensuring all actions are audited and verifiably immutable. Our proposed platform realises General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) requirements in terms of user consent, data encryption, data erasure and accountability obligations. We assess the scalability and performance of the platform using IPFS and Blockchain test networks.

title: A Privacy-Preserving Platform for Recording COVID-19 Vaccine Passports
text: The widespread adoption of COVID-19 vaccine passports has raised significant concerns about the privacy and security of sensitive health information. Existing solutions rely on centralized repositories or trusted intermediaries, introducing vulnerabilities to data breaches and unauthorized access. We propose a decentralized, privacy-preserving platform for recording and verifying COVID-19 vaccine passports, leveraging homomorphic encryption and secure multi-party computation. Our platform enables individuals to store their vaccination records locally, while allowing authorized parties to verify the authenticity and validity of the records without accessing the underlying data. We implement a prototype using the Paillier cryptosystem and evaluate its performance on a dataset of 10,000 synthetic vaccination records. Our results demonstrate that the platform can efficiently handle large-scale verifications while maintaining the privacy of individual records. Specifically, our experiments show that the verification process takes an average of 350 milliseconds per record, with a throughput of 285 verifications per second. We also conduct a security analysis, demonstrating the platform's resistance to various attacks, including data tampering and unauthorized access. Our approach provides a promising solution for privacy-preserving COVID-19 vaccine passport management.

title: Catch Me If You Can: Blackbox Adversarial Attacks on Automatic Speech Recognition using Frequency Masking
text: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) models are prevalent, particularly in applications for voice navigation and voice control of domestic appliances. The computational core of ASRs are deep neural networks (DNNs) that have been shown to be susceptible to adversarial perturbations; easily misused by attackers to generate malicious outputs. To help test the security and robustnesss of ASRS, we propose techniques that generate blackbox (agnostic to the DNN), untargeted adversarial attacks that are portable across ASRs. This is in contrast to existing work that focuses on whitebox targeted attacks that are time consuming and lack portability. Our techniques generate adversarial attacks that have no human audible difference by manipulating the audio signal using a psychoacoustic model that maintains the audio perturbations below the thresholds of human perception. We evaluate portability and effectiveness of our techniques using three popular ASRs and two input audio datasets using the metrics - Word Error Rate (WER) of output transcription, Similarity to original audio, attack Success Rate on different ASRs and Detection score by a defense system. We found our adversarial attacks were portable across ASRs, not easily detected by a state-of-the-art defense system, and had significant difference in output transcriptions while sounding similar to original audio.

title: Catch Me If You Can: Blackbox Adversarial Attacks on Automatic Speech Recognition using Frequency Masking
text: The widespread adoption of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems in various applications has raised concerns about their vulnerability to adversarial attacks. While recent studies have demonstrated the feasibility of whitebox attacks on ASR systems, the more realistic and challenging problem of blackbox attacks remains largely unexplored. In this context, we investigate the use of frequency masking as a novel technique for crafting blackbox adversarial attacks on ASR systems. Our approach exploits the fact that ASR models are sensitive to perturbations in the frequency domain, allowing an attacker to create malicious audio samples that are imperceptible to human listeners but misclassified by the ASR system. We propose a gradient-free optimization algorithm to efficiently search for effective frequency masks, and demonstrate its efficacy on two popular ASR models. Our experiments show that the proposed attacks can achieve high success rates (>90%) with minimal distortion to the original audio signal, even when the ASR models are trained with adversarial defenses. Furthermore, we find that the frequency masking technique is highly transferable across different ASR models and acoustic conditions, highlighting the urgent need for developing more robust ASR systems that can withstand such attacks.

title: Discovery of Crime Event Sequences with Constricted Spatio-Temporal Sequential Patterns
text: In this article, we introduce a novel type of spatio-temporal sequential patterns called Constricted Spatio-Temporal Sequential (CSTS) patterns and thoroughly analyze their properties. We demonstrate that the set of CSTS patterns is a concise representation of all spatio-temporal sequential patterns that can be discovered in a given dataset. To measure significance of the discovered CSTS patterns we adapt the participation index measure. We also provide CSTS-Miner: an algorithm that discovers all participation index strong CSTS patterns in event data. We experimentally evaluate the proposed algorithms using two crime-related datasets: Pittsburgh Police Incident Blotter Dataset and Boston Crime Incident Reports Dataset. In the experiments, the CSTS-Miner algorithm is compared with the other four state-of-the-art algorithms: STS-Miner, CSTPM, STBFM and CST-SPMiner. As the results of experiments suggest, the proposed algorithm discovers much fewer patterns than the other selected algorithms. Finally, we provide the examples of interesting crime-related patterns discovered by the proposed CSTS-Miner algorithm.

title: Discovery of Crime Event Sequences with Constricted Spatio-Temporal Sequential Patterns
text: Urban crime is a pervasive problem that poses significant threats to public safety and social stability. To combat this issue, law enforcement agencies rely heavily on data-driven approaches to identify and analyze crime patterns. While existing methods focus on spatial or temporal aspects of crime separately, they overlook the complex interplay between these dimensions. This paper proposes a novel framework for discovering crime event sequences with constricted spatio-temporal sequential patterns. We formulate this problem as a constrained sequential pattern mining task and develop an efficient algorithm, CSTSP-Mine, to extract meaningful patterns from large-scale crime datasets. Our approach incorporates a novel constraint-based pruning strategy to reduce the search space and improve computational efficiency. Experimental evaluations on real-world crime datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of CSTSP-Mine in uncovering insightful patterns, such as sequential burglaries in nearby locations within a short time frame. These discoveries can inform proactive policing strategies and enhance crime prevention efforts.

title: GECCO: Constraint-driven Abstraction of Low-level Event Logs
text: Process mining enables the analysis of complex systems using event data recorded during the execution of processes. Specifically, models of these processes can be discovered from event logs, i.e., sequences of events. However, the recorded events are often too fine-granular and result in unstructured models that are not meaningful for analysis. Log abstraction therefore aims to group together events to obtain a higher-level representation of the event sequences. While such a transformation shall be driven by the analysis goal, existing techniques force users to define how the abstraction is done, rather than what the result shall be. In this paper, we propose GECCO, an approach for log abstraction that enables users to impose requirements on the resulting log in terms of constraints. GECCO then groups events so that the constraints are satisfied and the distance to the original log is minimized. Since exhaustive log abstraction suffers from an exponential runtime complexity, GECCO also offers a heuristic approach guided by behavioral dependencies found in the log. We show that the abstraction quality of GECCO is superior to baseline solutions and demonstrate the relevance of considering constraints during log abstraction in real-life settings.

title: GECCO: Constraint-driven Abstraction of Low-level Event Logs
text: The analysis of complex systems via process mining relies on event data, which is often too granular, yielding unstructured models that hinder meaningful analysis. Log abstraction addresses this issue by grouping events to obtain a higher-level representation of event sequences. However, existing techniques require users to specify how abstraction is performed, rather than defining the desired outcome. This paper presents GECCO, a novel approach to log abstraction that allows users to impose constraints on the resulting log, thereby enabling goal-driven abstraction. GECCO groups events to satisfy these constraints while minimizing the distance to the original log. To mitigate the exponential runtime complexity of exhaustive log abstraction, GECCO incorporates a heuristic approach informed by behavioral dependencies in the log. Our evaluation demonstrates the superiority of GECCO's abstraction quality compared to baseline solutions and highlights the importance of considering constraints in real-world log abstraction scenarios.

title: Revisiting Neuron Coverage for DNN Testing: A Layer-Wise and Distribution-Aware Criterion
text: Various deep neural network (DNN) coverage criteria have been proposed to assess DNN test inputs and steer input mutations. The coverage is characterized via neurons having certain outputs, or the discrepancy between neuron outputs. Nevertheless, recent research indicates that neuron coverage criteria show little correlation with test suite quality. In general, DNNs approximate distributions, by incorporating hierarchical layers, to make predictions for inputs. Thus, we champion to deduce DNN behaviors based on its approximated distributions from a layer perspective. A test suite should be assessed using its induced layer output distributions. Accordingly, to fully examine DNN behaviors, input mutation should be directed toward diversifying the approximated distributions. This paper summarizes eight design requirements for DNN coverage criteria, taking into account distribution properties and practical concerns. We then propose a new criterion, NeuraL Coverage (NLC), that satisfies all design requirements. NLC treats a single DNN layer as the basic computational unit (rather than a single neuron) and captures four critical properties of neuron output distributions. Thus, NLC accurately describes how DNNs comprehend inputs via approximated distributions. We demonstrate that NLC is significantly correlated with the diversity of a test suite across a number of tasks (classification and generation) and data formats (image and text). Its capacity to discover DNN prediction errors is promising. Test input mutation guided by NLC results in a greater quality and diversity of exposed erroneous behaviors.

title: Revisiting Neuron Coverage for DNN Testing: A Layer-Wise and Distribution-Aware Criterion
text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) approximate complex distributions through hierarchical layers, enabling predictions for input data. Consequently, evaluating DNN behaviors via approximated distributions at the layer level offers a more comprehensive understanding of their internal workings. Current neuron-centric coverage criteria, which assess test inputs based on neuron outputs or output discrepancies, have been shown to exhibit limited correlation with test suite quality. To address this limitation, we establish eight design requirements for DNN coverage criteria that incorporate distribution properties and practical considerations. We then introduce NeuraL Coverage (NLC), a novel criterion that satisfies all design requirements by treating individual layers as the fundamental computational units. NLC captures four essential properties of neuron output distributions, providing an accurate description of how DNNs process inputs through approximated distributions. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates a significant correlation between NLC and test suite diversity across various tasks (classification and generation) and data formats (image and text). Furthermore, NLC-guided test input mutation yields a higher quality and diversity of exposed erroneous behaviors, highlighting its potential for error discovery.

title: Provably Valid and Diverse Mutations of Real-World Media Data for DNN Testing
text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) often accept high-dimensional media data (e.g., photos, text, and audio) and understand their perceptual content (e.g., a cat). To test DNNs, diverse inputs are needed to trigger mis-predictions. Some preliminary works use byte-level mutations or domain-specific filters (e.g., foggy), whose enabled mutations may be limited and likely error-prone. SOTA works employ deep generative models to generate (infinite) inputs. Also, to keep the mutated inputs perceptually valid (e.g., a cat remains a "cat" after mutation), existing efforts rely on imprecise and less generalizable heuristics. This study revisits two key objectives in media input mutation - perception diversity (DIV) and validity (VAL) - in a rigorous manner based on manifold, a well-developed theory capturing perceptions of high-dimensional media data in a low-dimensional space. We show important results that DIV and VAL inextricably bound each other, and prove that SOTA generative model-based methods fundamentally fail to mutate real-world media data (either sacrificing DIV or VAL). In contrast, we discuss the feasibility of mutating real-world media data with provably high DIV and VAL based on manifold. We concretize the technical solution of mutating media data of various formats (images, audios, text) via a unified manner based on manifold. Specifically, when media data are projected into a low-dimensional manifold, the data can be mutated by walking on the manifold with certain directions and step sizes. When contrasted with the input data, the mutated data exhibit encouraging DIV in the perceptual traits (e.g., lying vs. standing dog) while retaining reasonably high VAL (i.e., a dog remains a dog). We implement our techniques in DEEPWALK for testing DNNs. DEEPWALK outperforms prior methods in testing comprehensiveness and can find more error-triggering inputs with higher quality.

title: Provably Valid and Diverse Mutations of Real-World Media Data for DNN Testing
text: The widespread adoption of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in safety-critical applications has elevated the importance of thoroughly testing these models to ensure their reliability and robustness. However, generating high-quality, realistic test data that can effectively stress DNNs remains a significant challenge. Recent efforts have focused on generating synthetic data through various mutation strategies, but these approaches often lack diversity and fail to capture the intricacies of real-world data distributions. In response, we propose a novel framework for generating provably valid and diverse mutations of real-world media data, specifically targeting image and audio datasets. Our approach leverages a combination of formal methods and machine learning techniques to produce a vast, heterogeneous set of mutated data points that are both realistic and perturbed. We employ a novel, SMT-based constraint solver to ensure the semantic validity of our mutations, which are then diversified through a probabilistic, hierarchical clustering mechanism. Extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in generating high-quality, diverse mutations that can effectively stress DNNs. Notably, our mutated data points are able to expose a significant number of previously unknown errors and inconsistencies in state-of-the-art DNN models, while also improving their overall robustness and generalizability. Furthermore, our approach is shown to be computationally efficient, scalable, and flexible, making it an attractive solution for large-scale DNN testing and validation. We believe our work has important implications for the development of more reliable and trustworthy AI systems, and we provide an open-source implementation of our framework to facilitate further research and adoption.

title: IRShield: A Countermeasure Against Adversarial Physical-Layer Wireless Sensing
text: Wireless radio channels are known to contain information about the surrounding propagation environment, which can be extracted using established wireless sensing methods. Thus, today's ubiquitous wireless devices are attractive targets for passive eavesdroppers to launch reconnaissance attacks. In particular, by overhearing standard communication signals, eavesdroppers obtain estimations of wireless channels which can give away sensitive information about indoor environments. For instance, by applying simple statistical methods, adversaries can infer human motion from wireless channel observations, allowing to remotely monitor premises of victims. In this work, building on the advent of intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRSs), we propose IRShield as a novel countermeasure against adversarial wireless sensing. IRShield is designed as a plug-and-play privacy-preserving extension to existing wireless networks. At the core of IRShield, we design an IRS configuration algorithm to obfuscate wireless channels. We validate the effectiveness with extensive experimental evaluations. In a state-of-the-art human motion detection attack using off-the-shelf Wi-Fi devices, IRShield lowered detection rates to 5% or less.

title: IRShield: A Countermeasure Against Adversarial Physical-Layer Wireless Sensing
text: The proliferation of wireless sensing technology has introduced a new attack vector, where adversaries can manipulate the physical layer to deceive sensors and compromise system integrity. Recent works have demonstrated the feasibility of such attacks, highlighting the need for effective countermeasures. We propose IRShield, a novel defense mechanism that leverages inherent radio frequency (RF) imperfections to detect and mitigate adversarial physical-layer manipulation. IRShield exploits the unique characteristics of wireless channel responses to generate a fingerprint of the legitimate transmitter, enabling the receiver to distinguish between authentic and spoofed signals. Our approach is evaluated using a custom-built testbed, where we demonstrate IRShield's efficacy in detecting attacks with an accuracy of 97.4% and a false positive rate of 2.1%. We also show that IRShield introduces negligible overhead, making it a practical solution for resource-constrained wireless sensing applications. Our findings underscore the potential of IRShield as a robust countermeasure against adversarial physical-layer wireless sensing attacks.

title: A Survey on Concept Drift in Process Mining
text: Concept drift in process mining (PM) is a challenge as classical methods assume processes are in a steady-state, i.e., events share the same process version. We conducted a systematic literature review on the intersection of these areas, and thus, we review concept drift in process mining and bring forward a taxonomy of existing techniques for drift detection and online process mining for evolving environments. Existing works depict that (i) PM still primarily focuses on offline analysis, and (ii) the assessment of concept drift techniques in processes is cumbersome due to the lack of common evaluation protocol, datasets, and metrics.

title: A Survey on Concept Drift in Process Mining
text: Process mining, a discipline predicated on the assumption of steady-state processes, is vulnerable to concept drift, which occurs when events are governed by different process versions. To address this limitation, we undertook a systematic literature review of concept drift in process mining, yielding a comprehensive taxonomy of techniques for detecting drift and enabling online process mining in dynamic environments. Our findings highlight the prevailing focus on offline analysis in process mining, as well as the need for standardized evaluation protocols, datasets, and metrics to assess concept drift in processes, a challenge that currently hinders meaningful technique assessment.

title: Multilingual training for Software Engineering
text: Well-trained machine-learning models, which leverage large amounts of open-source software data, have now become an interesting approach to automating many software engineering tasks. Several SE tasks have all been subject to this approach, with performance gradually improving over the past several years with better models and training methods. More, and more diverse, clean, labeled data is better for training; but constructing good-quality datasets is time-consuming and challenging. Ways of augmenting the volume and diversity of clean, labeled data generally have wide applicability. For some languages (e.g., Ruby) labeled data is less abundant; in others (e.g., JavaScript) the available data maybe more focused on some application domains, and thus less diverse. As a way around such data bottlenecks, we present evidence suggesting that human-written code in different languages (which performs the same function), is rather similar, and particularly preserving of identifier naming patterns; we further present evidence suggesting that identifiers are a very important element of training data for software engineering tasks. We leverage this rather fortuitous phenomenon to find evidence that available multilingual training data (across different languages) can be used to amplify performance. We study this for 3 different tasks: code summarization, code retrieval, and function naming. We note that this data-augmenting approach is broadly compatible with different tasks, languages, and machine-learning models.

title: Multilingual training for Software Engineering
text: The increasing complexity of modern software systems has led to a growing need for software engineers to communicate effectively across linguistic and cultural boundaries. However, the prevalence of English-centric software development resources and tools hinders the participation of non-English speaking developers, resulting in a significant loss of diversity and talent. To address this issue, we explore the potential of multilingual training for software engineering, where models are trained on a diverse set of programming languages and natural languages. We propose a novel framework, PolySE, which leverages a combination of machine translation, code switching, and multitask learning to enable software engineering models to generalize across languages. Our framework is evaluated on a large-scale dataset of open-source software projects, comprising over 100,000 code snippets and 10,000 comments in five languages. Experimental results demonstrate that PolySE outperforms state-of-the-art monolingual models on a range of software engineering tasks, including code completion, bug detection, and comment generation. Notably, our approach achieves a 23% improvement in code completion accuracy for non-English languages, and a 17% increase in bug detection recall for projects with multilingual comments. Our findings suggest that multilingual training can significantly enhance the inclusivity and effectiveness of software engineering tools, paving the way for a more diverse and global software development community.

title: Evaluating Two Approaches to Assessing Student Progress in Cybersecurity Exercises
text: Cybersecurity students need to develop practical skills such as using command-line tools. Hands-on exercises are the most direct way to assess these skills, but assessing students' mastery is a challenging task for instructors. We aim to alleviate this issue by modeling and visualizing student progress automatically throughout the exercise. The progress is summarized by graph models based on the shell commands students typed to achieve discrete tasks within the exercise. We implemented two types of models and compared them using data from 46 students at two universities. To evaluate our models, we surveyed 22 experienced computing instructors and qualitatively analyzed their responses. The majority of instructors interpreted the graph models effectively and identified strengths, weaknesses, and assessment use cases for each model. Based on the evaluation, we provide recommendations to instructors and explain how our graph models innovate teaching and promote further research. The impact of this paper is threefold. First, it demonstrates how multiple institutions can collaborate to share approaches to modeling student progress in hands-on exercises. Second, our modeling techniques generalize to data from different environments to support student assessment, even outside the cybersecurity domain. Third, we share the acquired data and open-source software so that others can use the models in their classes or research.

title: Evaluating Two Approaches to Assessing Student Progress in Cybersecurity Exercises
text: Assessing students' mastery of practical skills, such as command-line tool proficiency, is a significant challenge in cybersecurity education. Hands-on exercises offer the most direct approach to evaluation, but instructors struggle to accurately gauge student progress. To address this issue, we present a novel framework for automated modeling and visualization of student progress throughout hands-on exercises. By analyzing shell commands used to complete discrete tasks, our graph-based models provide a comprehensive summary of student performance. We implemented and compared two model types using data from 46 students across two universities. A survey of 22 experienced computing instructors revealed that the majority effectively interpreted the graph models, identifying strengths, weaknesses, and assessment use cases. Our evaluation yields valuable recommendations for instructors and demonstrates the potential for innovative teaching and further research. This work has a triple impact: it showcases the benefits of multi-institutional collaboration in developing student progress models; it demonstrates the generalizability of our modeling techniques across different environments and domains; and it provides a valuable resource through open-source software and shared data, enabling others to integrate these models into their own teaching and research practices.

title: Cyberphysical Sequencing for Distributed Asset Management with Broad Traceability
text: Cyber-Physical systems (CPS) have complex lifecycles involving multiple stakeholders, and the transparency of both hardware and software components' supply chain is opaque at best. This raises concerns for stakeholders who may not trust that what they receive is what was requested. There is an opportunity to build a cyberphysical titling process offering universal traceability and the ability to differentiate systems based on provenance. Today, RFID tags and barcodes address some of these needs, though they are easily manipulated due to non-linkage with an object or system's intrinsic characteristics. We propose cyberphysical sequencing as a low-cost, light-weight and pervasive means of adding track-and-trace capabilities to any asset that ties a system's physical identity to a unique and invariant digital identifier. CPS sequencing offers benefits similar Digital Twins' for identifying and managing the provenance and identity of an asset throughout its life with far fewer computational and other resources.

title: Cyberphysical Sequencing for Distributed Asset Management with Broad Traceability
text: The lifecycle of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) involves multiple stakeholders and is characterized by opaque supply chains for both hardware and software components, leading to concerns about the authenticity of received systems. This lack of transparency hinders trust among stakeholders, who require assurance that the delivered system matches the requested specifications. To address this challenge, we envision a cyberphysical titling process that provides universal traceability and enables differentiation based on provenance. Existing solutions, such as RFID tags and barcodes, are limited by their susceptibility to manipulation due to the lack of inherent linkage with an object's characteristics. Our proposed cyberphysical sequencing offers a low-cost, lightweight, and pervasive approach to track-and-trace capabilities, linking a system's physical identity to a unique digital identifier. This method provides benefits analogous to Digital Twins, but with significantly reduced computational resources, enabling effective identification and management of asset provenance and identity throughout their lifecycle.

title: Improving the Reliability of Network Intrusion Detection Systems through Dataset Integration
text: This work presents Reliable-NIDS (R-NIDS), a novel methodology for Machine Learning (ML) based Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) that allows ML models to work on integrated datasets, empowering the learning process with diverse information from different datasets. Therefore, R-NIDS targets the design of more robust models, that generalize better than traditional approaches. We also propose a new dataset, called UNK21. It is built from three of the most well-known network datasets (UGR'16, USNW-NB15 and NLS-KDD), each one gathered from its own network environment, with different features and classes, by using a data aggregation approach present in R-NIDS. Following R-NIDS, in this work we propose to build two well-known ML models (a linear and a non-linear one) based on the information of three of the most common datasets in the literature for NIDS evaluation, those integrated in UNK21. The results that the proposed methodology offers show how these two ML models trained as a NIDS solution could benefit from this approach, being able to generalize better when training on the newly proposed UNK21 dataset. Furthermore, these results are carefully analyzed with statistical tools that provide high confidence on our conclusions.

title: Improving the Reliability of Network Intrusion Detection Systems through Dataset Integration
text: This research introduces Reliable-NIDS (R-NIDS), a novel framework designed to enhance the performance of Machine Learning (ML) based Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) by integrating diverse datasets. By leveraging the strengths of multiple datasets, R-NIDS facilitates the development of more robust ML models that generalize better than traditional approaches. To validate this framework, we created UNK21, a comprehensive dataset aggregated from three prominent network datasets (UGR'16, USNW-NB15, and NLS-KDD), each with unique features and classes. We then employed R-NIDS to train two well-established ML models (linear and non-linear) using the integrated UNK21 dataset. The results demonstrate that these models, when trained as a NIDS solution, exhibit improved generalizability compared to traditional approaches. A rigorous statistical analysis of the results provides high confidence in our conclusions, underscoring the effectiveness of R-NIDS in developing more reliable NIDSs.

title: Examining Zero-Shot Vulnerability Repair with Large Language Models
text: Human developers can produce code with cybersecurity bugs. Can emerging 'smart' code completion tools help repair those bugs? In this work, we examine the use of large language models (LLMs) for code (such as OpenAI's Codex and AI21's Jurassic J-1) for zero-shot vulnerability repair. We investigate challenges in the design of prompts that coax LLMs into generating repaired versions of insecure code. This is difficult due to the numerous ways to phrase key information - both semantically and syntactically - with natural languages. We perform a large scale study of five commercially available, black-box, "off-the-shelf" LLMs, as well as an open-source model and our own locally-trained model, on a mix of synthetic, hand-crafted, and real-world security bug scenarios. Our experiments demonstrate that while the approach has promise (the LLMs could collectively repair 100% of our synthetically generated and hand-crafted scenarios), a qualitative evaluation of the model's performance over a corpus of historical real-world examples highlights challenges in generating functionally correct code.

title: Examining Zero-Shot Vulnerability Repair with Large Language Models
text: The discovery of vulnerabilities in software systems poses significant threats to the security and reliability of modern computing infrastructure. Despite advances in automated vulnerability detection, repairing these vulnerabilities often relies on manual intervention, which can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. Recent studies have demonstrated the potential of large language models (LLMs) in generating code for various programming tasks. In this work, we explore the feasibility of leveraging LLMs for zero-shot vulnerability repair, where the model repairs vulnerabilities without prior training on similar examples. Our approach involves fine-tuning a state-of-the-art LLM on a large corpus of open-source code and evaluating its performance on a benchmark of 100 real-world vulnerabilities. Our results show that the LLM can successfully repair 43% of the vulnerabilities, with 75% of the repairs being functionally correct. We also analyze the characteristics of the repaired vulnerabilities and identify key factors that influence the model's performance. Our findings suggest that LLM-based zero-shot vulnerability repair is a promising direction for improving software security, but further research is needed to overcome the current limitations.

title: V2X Misbehavior and Collective Perception Service: Considerations for Standardization
text: Connected and Automated Vehicles use sensors and wireless communication to improve road safety and efficiency. However, attackers may target Vehicle-to-Everything communication. Indeed, an attacker may send authenticated but wrong data to send false location information, alert incorrect events or report a bogus object endangering the safety of other CAVs. Currently, Standardization Development Organizations are working on developing security standards against such attacks. Unfortunately, current standardization efforts do not include misbehavior specifications for advanced V2X services such as Collective Perception yet. This work assesses the security of Collective Perception Messages and proposes inputs for consideration in existing standards.

title: V2X Misbehavior and Collective Perception Service: Considerations for Standardization
text: The proliferation of Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication necessitates rigorous evaluation of misbehavior detection and mitigation strategies to ensure safety and security in intelligent transportation systems. We investigate the Collective Perception Service (CPS), a novel V2X application, and its susceptibility to misbehavior. Through a comprehensive simulation framework, we analyze the impact of various misbehavior types on CPS performance and propose a taxonomy of misbehavior detection techniques. Our results highlight the need for standardized misbehavior detection and mitigation protocols, and we provide guidelines for their integration into V2X communication standards, enabling robust and secure CPS deployments.

title: Analysis of Communication Channels Related to Physical Unclonable Functions
text: Cryptographic algorithms rely on the secrecy of their corresponding keys. On embedded systems with standard CMOS chips, where secure permanent memory such as flash is not available as a key storage, the secret key can be derived from Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) that make use of minuscule manufacturing variations of, for instance, SRAM cells. Since PUFs are affected by environmental changes, the reliable reproduction of the PUF key requires error correction. For silicon PUFs with binary output, errors occur in the form of bitflips within the PUFs response. Modelling the channel as a Binary Symmetric Channel (BSC) with fixed crossover probability $p$ is only a first-order approximation of the real behavior of the PUF response. We propose a more realistic channel model, refered to as the Varying Binary Symmetric Channel (VBSC), which takes into account that the reliability of different PUF response bits may not be equal. We investigate its channel capacity for various scenarios which differ in the channel state information (CSI) present at encoder and decoder. We compare the capacity results for the VBSC for the different CSI cases with reference to the distribution of the bitflip probability according a work by Maes et al.

title: Analysis of Communication Channels Related to Physical Unclonable Functions
text: Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) have emerged as a promising solution for securing resource-constrained devices, leveraging the inherent randomness of their physical properties to generate unique identifiers. However, the security of PUF-based systems relies heavily on the integrity of the communication channels used to access and evaluate these functions. In this context, understanding the characteristics of these channels is crucial to preventing attacks and ensuring the reliability of PUF-based authentication and cryptographic protocols. This work presents a comprehensive analysis of communication channels related to PUFs, focusing on the effects of noise, signal attenuation, and interference on the accuracy and reliability of PUF responses. We employ a combination of theoretical modeling, simulation, and experimental evaluation using a custom-built PUF platform to investigate the impact of channel impairments on PUF-based systems. Our results show that even moderate levels of noise and interference can significantly degrade the performance of PUF-based authentication, and that careful consideration of channel characteristics is necessary to ensure the security and reliability of these systems. Furthermore, we identify key channel parameters that can be leveraged to improve the resilience of PUF-based systems to channel-related attacks. Our findings have important implications for the design and implementation of secure PUF-based systems in real-world applications.

title: Node-wise Hardware Trojan Detection Based on Graph Learning
text: In the fourth industrial revolution, securing the protection of the supply chain has become an ever-growing concern. One such cyber threat is a hardware Trojan (HT), a malicious modification to an IC. HTs are often identified in the hardware manufacturing process, but should be removed earlier, when the design is being specified. Machine learning-based HT detection in gate-level netlists is an efficient approach to identify HTs at the early stage. However, feature-based modeling has limitations in discovering an appropriate set of HT features. We thus propose NHTD-GL in this paper, a novel node-wise HT detection method based on graph learning (GL). Given the formal analysis of HT features obtained from domain knowledge, NHTD-GL bridges the gap between graph representation learning and feature-based HT detection. The experimental results demonstrate that NHTD-GL achieves 0.998 detection accuracy and outperforms state-of-the-art node-wise HT detection methods. NHTD-GL extracts HT features without heuristic feature engineering.

title: Node-wise Hardware Trojan Detection Based on Graph Learning
text: The escalating importance of supply chain security in the fourth industrial revolution has highlighted the need to mitigate cyber threats, particularly hardware Trojans (HTs), which are malicious modifications to integrated circuits (ICs). Although HTs are typically detected during the manufacturing process, early identification during the design specification stage is crucial. Machine learning-based approaches, such as gate-level netlist analysis, have shown promise in detecting HTs at an early stage. However, feature-based modeling is limited in its ability to discover an optimal set of HT features. This paper proposes NHTD-GL, a novel node-wise HT detection method leveraging graph learning (GL) to bridge the gap between graph representation learning and feature-based HT detection. By formally analyzing HT features derived from domain knowledge, NHTD-GL achieves a detection accuracy of 0.998, outperforming state-of-the-art node-wise HT detection methods without relying on heuristic feature engineering.

title: A Game-Theoretic Approach for AI-based Botnet Attack Defence
text: The new generation of botnets leverages Artificial Intelligent (AI) techniques to conceal the identity of botmasters and the attack intention to avoid detection. Unfortunately, there has not been an existing assessment tool capable of evaluating the effectiveness of existing defense strategies against this kind of AI-based botnet attack. In this paper, we propose a sequential game theory model that is capable to analyse the details of the potential strategies botnet attackers and defenders could use to reach Nash Equilibrium (NE). The utility function is computed under the assumption when the attacker launches the maximum number of DDoS attacks with the minimum attack cost while the defender utilises the maximum number of defense strategies with the minimum defense cost. We conduct a numerical analysis based on a various number of defense strategies involved on different (simulated) cloud-band sizes in relation to different attack success rate values. Our experimental results confirm that the success of defense highly depends on the number of defense strategies used according to careful evaluation of attack rates.

title: A Game-Theoretic Approach for AI-based Botnet Attack Defence
text: The escalating threat of botnet attacks has prompted a pressing need for innovative defence strategies, particularly in the realm of AI-powered solutions. Current defence mechanisms often rely on rule-based systems or machine learning algorithms, which can be evaded by sophisticated attackers. To address this limitation, we propose a game-theoretic approach for AI-based botnet attack defence, which models the interactions between attackers and defenders as a dynamic game. Our framework, dubbed "GADBAD," integrates a novel botnet detection algorithm with a strategic decision-making module, enabling defenders to anticipate and respond to attacks proactively. We evaluate GADBAD using a comprehensive dataset of real-world botnet traffic and demonstrate a significant reduction in detection latency and false positive rates compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our approach exhibits robustness against adaptive attackers, who attempt to manipulate the defence system by modifying their attack strategies. Theoretical analysis and simulation results confirm the effectiveness of our game-theoretic approach in improving the resilience of AI-based botnet defence systems.

title: PhishMatch: A Layered Approach for Effective Detection of Phishing URLs
text: Phishing attacks continue to be a significant threat on the Internet. Prior studies show that it is possible to determine whether a website is phishing or not just by analyzing its URL more carefully. A major advantage of the URL based approach is that it can identify a phishing website even before the web page is rendered in the browser, thus avoiding other potential problems such as cryptojacking and drive-by downloads. However, traditional URL based approaches have their limitations. Blacklist based approaches are prone to zero-hour phishing attacks, advanced machine learning based approaches consume high resources, and other approaches send the URL to a remote server which compromises user's privacy. In this paper, we present a layered anti-phishing defense, PhishMatch, which is robust, accurate, inexpensive, and client-side. We design a space-time efficient Aho-Corasick algorithm for exact string matching and n-gram based indexing technique for approximate string matching to detect various cybersquatting techniques in the phishing URL. To reduce false positives, we use a global whitelist and personalized user whitelists. We also determine the context in which the URL is visited and use that information to classify the input URL more accurately. The last component of PhishMatch involves a machine learning model and controlled search engine queries to classify the URL. A prototype plugin of PhishMatch, developed for the Chrome browser, was found to be fast and lightweight. Our evaluation shows that PhishMatch is both efficient and effective.

title: PhishMatch: A Layered Approach for Effective Detection of Phishing URLs
text: The proliferation of phishing attacks on the Internet underscores the need for effective countermeasures. Research has demonstrated that a careful analysis of a website's URL can accurately distinguish between legitimate and phishing sites. The URL-based approach offers a distinct advantage, as it can identify phishing websites before the web page is rendered, thereby mitigating additional threats such as cryptojacking and drive-by downloads. However, traditional URL-based methods have inherent limitations, including susceptibility to zero-hour phishing attacks, high resource consumption, and privacy compromises. This paper presents PhishMatch, a novel, layered anti-phishing defense that addresses these shortcomings. Our approach leverages a space-time efficient Aho-Corasick algorithm for exact string matching and an n-gram based indexing technique for approximate string matching to detect various cybersquatting techniques in phishing URLs. To minimize false positives, we employ a global whitelist and personalized user whitelists, as well as contextual information about the URL visit. The final component of PhishMatch involves a machine learning model and controlled search engine queries to classify the URL. A prototype Chrome browser plugin demonstrates the efficacy and efficiency of PhishMatch, which is both fast and lightweight. Our evaluation confirms that PhishMatch is a robust, accurate, and inexpensive client-side solution.

title: Efficient FPGA-based ECDSA Verification Engine for Permissioned Blockchains
text: As enterprises embrace blockchain technology, many real-world applications have been developed and deployed using permissioned blockchain platforms (access to network is controlled and given to only nodes with known identities). Such blockchain platforms heavily depend on cryptography to provide a layer of trust within the network, thus verification of cryptographic signatures often becomes the bottleneck. The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) is the most commonly used cryptographic scheme in permissioned blockchains. In this paper, we propose an efficient implementation of ECDSA signature verification on an FPGA, in order to improve the performance of permissioned blockchains that aim to use FPGA-based hardware accelerators. We propose several optimizations for modular arithmetic (e.g., custom multipliers and fast modular reduction) and point arithmetic (e.g., reduced number of point double and addition operations, and optimal width NAF representation). Based on these optimized modular and point arithmetic modules, we propose an ECDSA verification engine that can be used by any application for fast verification of ECDSA signatures. We further optimize our ECDSA verification engine for Hyperledger Fabric (one of the most widely used permissioned blockchain platforms) by moving carefully selected operations to a precomputation block, thus simplifying the critical path of ECDSA signature verification. From our implementation on Xilinx Alveo U250 accelerator board with target frequency of 250MHz, our ECDSA verification engine can perform a single verification in $760μs$ resulting in a throughput of 1,315 verifications per second, which is ~2.5x faster than state-of-the-art FPGA-based implementations. Our Hyperledger Fabric-specific ECDSA engine can perform a single verification in $368μs$ with a throughput of 2,717 verifications per second.
