title: Efficient FPGA-based ECDSA Verification Engine for Permissioned Blockchains
text: The increasing adoption of permissioned blockchains in various industries necessitates efficient and secure verification of digital signatures, a crucial component of blockchain transactions. Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) is widely used in permissioned blockchains, but its verification process is computationally intensive, leading to performance bottlenecks. Existing software-based ECDSA verification solutions suffer from high latency and energy consumption, making them unsuitable for resource-constrained environments. This work presents a novel FPGA-based ECDSA verification engine optimized for permissioned blockchains. We exploit the parallelization capabilities of FPGAs to accelerate the ECDSA verification process, achieving significant performance gains. Our proposed architecture comprises a pipelined design with parallelized modular exponentiation and multiplication units, ensuring efficient computation of ECDSA signature verification. We implement our design on a Xilinx Zynq-7000 SoC FPGA, leveraging its ARM Cortex-A9 processor for control logic and the programmable logic fabric for acceleration. Our evaluation demonstrates that our FPGA-based ECDSA verification engine outperforms state-of-the-art software-based solutions by a factor of 15.6x in terms of throughput, while reducing energy consumption by 73%. We also achieve a latency reduction of 12.3x compared to optimized software implementations. Our proposed engine is highly scalable, supporting various elliptic curve parameters and signature formats. We integrate our FPGA-based engine with a permissioned blockchain framework, demonstrating its feasibility in real-world scenarios. The proposed solution has significant implications for the widespread adoption of permissioned blockchains in resource-constrained environments, enabling secure and efficient verification of digital signatures.

title: SHAPr: An Efficient and Versatile Membership Privacy Risk Metric for Machine Learning
text: Data used to train machine learning (ML) models can be sensitive. Membership inference attacks (MIAs), attempting to determine whether a particular data record was used to train an ML model, risk violating membership privacy. ML model builders need a principled definition of a metric to quantify the membership privacy risk of (a) individual training data records, (b) computed independently of specific MIAs, (c) which assesses susceptibility to different MIAs, (d) can be used for different applications, and (e) efficiently. None of the prior membership privacy risk metrics simultaneously meet all these requirements. We present SHAPr, a membership privacy metric based on Shapley values which is a leave-one-out (LOO) technique, originally intended to measure the contribution of a training data record on model utility. We conjecture that contribution to model utility can act as a proxy for memorization, and hence represent membership privacy risk. Using ten benchmark datasets, we show that SHAPr is indeed effective in estimating susceptibility of training data records to MIAs. We also show that, unlike prior work, SHAPr is significantly better in estimating susceptibility to newer, and more effective MIA. We apply SHAPr to evaluate the efficacy of several defenses against MIAs: using regularization and removing high risk training data records. Moreover, SHAPr is versatile: it can be used for estimating vulnerability of different subgroups to MIAs, and inherits applications of Shapley values (e.g., data valuation). We show that SHAPr has an acceptable computational cost (compared to naive LOO), varying from a few minutes for the smallest dataset to ~92 minutes for the largest dataset.

title: SHAPr: An Efficient and Versatile Membership Privacy Risk Metric for Machine Learning
text: The sensitive nature of data employed to train machine learning models renders them vulnerable to membership inference attacks, which aim to determine whether a specific data record was utilized in the training process, thereby compromising membership privacy. A pressing need exists for a principled metric that quantifies the membership privacy risk of individual training data records, independent of specific attacks, and assesses susceptibility to diverse membership inference attacks across various applications. Moreover, this metric should be computationally efficient. Existing membership privacy risk metrics fail to simultaneously satisfy these requirements. This paper introduces SHAPr, a novel membership privacy metric founded on Shapley values, which leverages a leave-one-out technique originally designed to measure the contribution of a training data record to model utility. We hypothesize that this contribution can serve as a proxy for memorization, thereby representing membership privacy risk. Empirical evaluations on ten benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of SHAPr in estimating the susceptibility of training data records to membership inference attacks. Notably, SHAPr outperforms prior work in estimating susceptibility to newer, more effective attacks. We apply SHAPr to evaluate the effectiveness of various defenses against membership inference attacks, including regularization and high-risk data record removal. Furthermore, SHAPr's versatility enables its application to estimating subgroup vulnerability and inherits the broader applications of Shapley values, such as data valuation. Computational cost analysis reveals that SHAPr's execution time ranges from a few minutes for smaller datasets to approximately 92 minutes for larger datasets, making it a practical solution.

title: IMCRYPTO: An In-Memory Computing Fabric for AES Encryption and Decryption
text: This paper proposes IMCRYPTO, an in-memory computing (IMC) fabric for accelerating AES encryption and decryption. IMCRYPTO employs a unified structure to implement encryption and decryption in a single hardware architecture, with combined (Inv)SubBytes and (Inv)MixColumns steps. Because of this step-combination, as well as the high parallelism achieved by multiple units of random-access memory (RAM) and random-access/content-addressable memory (RA/CAM) arrays, IMCRYPTO achieves high throughput encryption and decryption without sacrificing area and power consumption. Additionally, due to the integration of a RISC-V core, IMCRYPTO offers programmability and flexibility. IMCRYPTO improves the throughput per area by a minimum (maximum) of 3.3x (223.1x) when compared to previous ASICs/IMC architectures for AES-128 encryption. Projections show added benefit from emerging technologies of up to 5.3x to the area-delay-power product of IMCRYPTO.

title: IMCRYPTO: An In-Memory Computing Fabric for AES Encryption and Decryption
text: The widespread adoption of cloud computing and the Internet of Things has led to an exponential increase in data being stored and transmitted, prompting a surge in the demand for efficient and secure encryption mechanisms. Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) is a widely used symmetric-key block cipher, but its computational overhead hinders its deployment in resource-constrained environments. To address this challenge, we propose IMCRYPTO, an in-memory computing fabric that accelerates AES encryption and decryption by minimizing data movement and exploiting the inherent parallelism of the encryption algorithm. Our fabric integrates a custom-designed AES accelerator with a 3D-stacked memory architecture, achieving a 3.2x speedup and 2.5x energy reduction compared to state-of-the-art software implementations. Experimental results demonstrate IMCRYPTO's efficacy in securing real-world workloads, including cloud storage and IoT communication, while maintaining a high throughput and low latency.

title: Bridging Pre-trained Models and Downstream Tasks for Source Code Understanding
text: With the great success of pre-trained models, the pretrain-then-finetune paradigm has been widely adopted on downstream tasks for source code understanding. However, compared to costly training a large-scale model from scratch, how to effectively adapt pre-trained models to a new task has not been fully explored. In this paper, we propose an approach to bridge pre-trained models and code-related tasks. We exploit semantic-preserving transformation to enrich downstream data diversity, and help pre-trained models learn semantic features invariant to these semantically equivalent transformations. Further, we introduce curriculum learning to organize the transformed data in an easy-to-hard manner to fine-tune existing pre-trained models. We apply our approach to a range of pre-trained models, and they significantly outperform the state-of-the-art models on tasks for source code understanding, such as algorithm classification, code clone detection, and code search. Our experiments even show that without heavy pre-training on code data, natural language pre-trained model RoBERTa fine-tuned with our lightweight approach could outperform or rival existing code pre-trained models fine-tuned on the above tasks, such as CodeBERT and GraphCodeBERT. This finding suggests that there is still much room for improvement in code pre-trained models.

title: Bridging Pre-trained Models and Downstream Tasks for Source Code Understanding
text: The proliferation of pre-trained language models has revolutionized natural language processing, yet their application to source code understanding remains limited. A major bottleneck is the lack of effective bridging between pre-trained models and downstream tasks, hindering the exploitation of these models' capabilities for code comprehension. This paper tackles this challenge by proposing a novel framework that seamlessly integrates pre-trained models with downstream tasks for source code understanding. Our approach involves task-aware adapter modules that learn to adapt pre-trained models to specific downstream tasks, such as code search, code summarization, and bug detection. We evaluate our framework on a range of downstream tasks and demonstrate significant performance improvements over existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. Notably, our approach enables the effective transfer of knowledge from pre-trained models to downstream tasks, even when limited task-specific training data is available. Our findings have important implications for the development of more accurate and efficient source code understanding tools, ultimately enhancing software development productivity and code quality.

title: Fast and Secure Key Generation with Channel Obfuscation in Slowly Varying Environments
text: The physical-layer secret key generation has emerged as a promising solution for establishing cryptographic keys by leveraging reciprocal and time-varying wireless channels. However, existing approaches suffer from low key generation rates and vulnerabilities under various attacks in slowly varying environments. We propose a new physical-layer secret key generation approach with channel obfuscation, which improves the dynamic property of channel parameters based on random filtering and random antenna scheduling. Our approach makes one party obfuscate the channel to allow the legitimate party to obtain similar dynamic channel parameters yet prevents a third party from inferring the obfuscation information. Our approach allows more random bits to be extracted from the obfuscated channel parameters by a joint design of the K-L transform and adaptive quantization. A testbed implementation shows that our approach, compared to the existing ones that we evaluate, performs the best in generating high entropy bits at a fast rate and a high-security level in slowly varying environments. Specifically, our approach can achieve a significantly faster secret bit generation rate at about $67$ bit/pkt, and the key sequences can pass the randomness tests of the NIST test suite.

title: Fast and Secure Key Generation with Channel Obfuscation in Slowly Varying Environments
text: Secure key generation is a pivotal component in various cryptographic protocols, particularly in wireless communication systems where the environment is subject to variations. Existing methods rely on exploiting the randomness of the wireless channel to generate keys, but they often struggle with slow variations in the environment, leading to compromised security. We address this challenge by proposing a novel approach that leverages channel obfuscation to generate fast and secure keys in slowly varying environments. Our method, dubbed CO-SKG, injects carefully crafted artificial noise into the channel, effectively obscuring the legitimate channel variations and creating a more dynamic environment. This allows for faster key generation while maintaining a high level of security. We theoretically analyze the security of CO-SKG and demonstrate its resilience against various attacks. Through extensive simulations, we show that CO-SKG outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of key generation rate, achieving a speedup of up to 5x in slowly varying environments. Furthermore, our results indicate that CO-SKG is robust against channel estimation errors and can adapt to different environmental conditions. Our approach has significant implications for secure communication systems, enabling fast and reliable key generation in a wide range of scenarios.

title: Characterizing Retweet Bots: The Case of Black Market Accounts
text: Malicious Twitter bots are detrimental to public discourse on social media. Past studies have looked at spammers, fake followers, and astroturfing bots, but retweet bots, which artificially inflate content, are not well understood. In this study, we characterize retweet bots that have been uncovered by purchasing retweets from the black market. We detect whether they are fake or genuine accounts involved in inauthentic activities and what they do in order to appear legitimate. We also analyze their differences from human-controlled accounts. From our findings on the nature and life-cycle of retweet bots, we also point out several inconsistencies between the retweet bots used in this work and bots studied in prior works. Our findings challenge some of the fundamental assumptions related to bots and in particular how to detect them.

title: Characterizing Retweet Bots: The Case of Black Market Accounts
text: The proliferation of malicious Twitter bots undermines the integrity of online public discourse, with retweet bots, in particular, artificially inflating content and remaining poorly understood. While prior research has investigated spammers, fake followers, and astroturfing bots, this study provides an in-depth characterization of retweet bots obtained from the black market. We employ a multifaceted approach to distinguish between fake and genuine accounts engaging in inauthentic activities, and identify the strategies employed to feign legitimacy. A comparative analysis with human-controlled accounts reveals notable differences. Our findings on the nature and lifecycle of retweet bots also highlight discrepancies with previously studied bots, prompting a reevaluation of fundamental assumptions regarding bot detection and characterization.

title: My(o) Armband Leaks Passwords: An EMG and IMU Based Keylogging Side-Channel Attack
text: Wearables that constantly collect various sensor data of their users increase the chances for inferences of unintentional and sensitive information such as passwords typed on a physical keyboard. We take a thorough look at the potential of using electromyographic (EMG) data, a sensor modality which is new to the market but has lately gained attention in the context of wearables for augmented reality (AR), for a keylogging side-channel attack. Our approach is based on neural networks for a between-subject attack in a realistic scenario using the Myo Armband to collect the sensor data. In our approach, the EMG data has proven to be the most prominent source of information compared to the accelerometer and gyroscope, increasing the keystroke detection performance. For our end-to-end approach on raw data, we report a mean balanced accuracy of about 76 % for the keystroke detection and a mean top-3 key accuracy of about 32 % on 52 classes for the key identification on passwords of varying strengths. We have created an extensive dataset including more than 310 000 keystrokes recorded from 37 volunteers, which is available as open access along with the source code used to create the given results.

title: My(o) Armband Leaks Passwords: An EMG and IMU Based Keylogging Side-Channel Attack
text: The proliferation of wearables that continually collect diverse sensor data from their users raises concerns about the inadvertent disclosure of sensitive information, including passwords entered on physical keyboards. This study explores the viability of exploiting electromyographic (EMG) data, a nascent sensor modality gaining traction in augmented reality (AR) wearables, for keylogging side-channel attacks. We employ a neural network-based approach for a between-subject attack in a realistic setting, utilizing the Myo Armband to collect sensor data. Our findings indicate that EMG data constitutes the primary source of information, outperforming accelerometer and gyroscope data, and thereby enhancing keystroke detection performance. Our end-to-end approach on raw data achieves a mean balanced accuracy of approximately 76% for keystroke detection and a mean top-3 key accuracy of around 32% for key identification across 52 classes, encompassing passwords of varying strengths. We contribute an extensive, open-access dataset comprising over 310,000 keystrokes recorded from 37 volunteers, accompanied by the source code used to generate these results.

title: Towards automated verification of multi-party consensus protocols
text: Blockchain technology and related frameworks have recently received extensive attention. Blockchain systems use multi-party consensus protocols to reach agreements on transactions. Hyperledger Fabric framework exposes a multi-party consensus, based on endorsement policy protocol, to reach a consensus on a transaction. In this paper, we define a problem of verification of a blockchain multi-party consensus with probabilistic properties. Further, we propose a verification technique of endorsement policies using statistical model checking and hypothesis testing. We analyze several aspects of the policies, including the ability to assign weights to organizations and the refusal probabilities of organizations. We demonstrate on experiments the work of our verification technique and how one can use experimental results to make the model satisfiable the specification. One can use our technique to design enterprise applications with the Hyperledger Fabric framework.

title: Towards automated verification of multi-party consensus protocols
text: Blockchain systems, relying on multi-party consensus protocols to validate transactions, have garnered significant attention of late. The Hyperledger Fabric framework, in particular, employs an endorsement policy protocol to achieve consensus. This paper tackles the problem of formally verifying the probabilistic properties of blockchain multi-party consensus. We propose a novel verification technique that leverages statistical model checking and hypothesis testing to analyze endorsement policies. Our approach examines various policy aspects, including the assignment of weights to organizations and refusal probabilities. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our technique in rendering the model specification satisfiable. This verification method has significant implications for the design of enterprise applications built upon the Hyperledger Fabric framework.

title: Making Access Control Easy in IoT
text: Secure installation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices requires configuring access control correctly for each device. In order to enable correct configuration the Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) has been developed by Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) to automate the protection of IoT devices by micro-segmentation using dynamic access control lists. The protocol defines a conceptually straightforward method to implement access control upon installation by providing a list of every authorized access for each device. This access control list may contain a few rules or hundreds of rules for each device. As a result, validating these rules is a challenge. In order to make the MUD standard more usable for developers, system integrators, and network operators, we report on an interactive system called MUD-Visualizer that visualizes the files containing these access control rules. We show that, unlike manual analysis, the level of the knowledge and experience does not affect the accuracy of the analysis when MUD-Visualizer is used, indicating that the tool is effective for all participants in our study across knowledge and experience levels.

title: Making Access Control Easy in IoT
text: The Internet of Things (IoT) device installation security hinges on correct access control configuration, a challenge addressed by the Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) protocol developed by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). MUD automates IoT device protection through dynamic access control lists, providing a straightforward method for implementing access control upon installation. However, the resulting access control lists, which can comprise anywhere from a few to hundreds of rules per device, pose a significant validation challenge. To enhance the usability of the MUD standard for developers, system integrators, and network operators, we present MUD-Visualizer, an interactive system that graphically represents the files containing these access control rules. Our study demonstrates that, unlike manual analysis, the accuracy of analysis using MUD-Visualizer is unaffected by the level of knowledge and experience, indicating the tool's effectiveness across diverse user groups.

title: Provisioning Fog Services to 3GPP Subscribers: Authentication and Application Mobility
text: Multi-Access Edge computing (MEC) and Fog computing provide services to subscribers at low latency. There is a need to form a federation among 3GPP MEC and fog to provide better coverage to 3GPP subscribers. This federation gives rise to two issues - third-party authentication and application mobility - for continuous service during handover from 3GPP MEC to fog without re-authentication. In this paper, we propose: 1) a proxy-based state transfer and third-party authentication (PS3A) that uses a transparent proxy to transfer the authentication and application state information, and 2) a token-based state transfer and proxy-based third-party authentication (TSP3A) that uses the proxy to transfer the authentication information and tokens to transfer the application state from 3GPP MEC to the fog. The proxy is kept transparent with virtual counterparts, to avoid any changes to the existing 3GPP MEC and fog architectures. We implemented these solutions on a testbed and results show that PS3A and TSP3A provide authentication within 0.345-2.858s for a 0-100 Mbps proxy load. The results further show that TSP3A provides application mobility while taking 40-52% less time than PS3A using state tokens. TSP3A and PS3A also reduce the service interruption latency by 82.4% and 84.6%, compared to the cloud-based service via tokens and prefetching.

title: Provisioning Fog Services to 3GPP Subscribers: Authentication and Application Mobility
text: The proliferation of Fog Computing has enabled low-latency, proximity-based services for 3GPP subscribers, but provisioning these services while ensuring authentication and application mobility remains a significant challenge. In 3GPP networks, subscribers roam across different cells, necessitating seamless handover of Fog services to maintain quality of experience. We tackle this challenge by proposing a novel provisioning framework that integrates authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA) with application mobility management. Our framework utilizes a decentralized, blockchain-based AAA mechanism to securely authenticate subscribers and authorize Fog service access, while a novel application mobility protocol ensures seamless handover of Fog services during subscriber roaming. We evaluate our framework through a combination of simulation and testbed experiments, demonstrating a 35% reduction in handover latency and a 25% improvement in Fog service availability compared to existing approaches. Furthermore, our framework reduces the signaling overhead by 40% and achieves a 95% reduction in authentication latency. The results demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of our provisioning framework in supporting secure, seamless, and efficient Fog services for 3GPP subscribers. Our work has significant implications for enabling widespread adoption of Fog Computing in 3GPP networks.

title: Design Trade-offs for a Robust Dynamic Hybrid Hash Join (Extended Version)
text: The Join operator, as one of the most expensive and commonly used operators in database systems, plays a substantial role in Database Management System (DBMS) performance. Among the many different Join algorithms studied over the last decades, Hybrid Hash Join (HHJ) has proven to be one of the most efficient and widely-used join algorithms. While the performance of HHJ depends largely on accurate statistics and information about the input relations, it may not always be practical or possible for a system to have such information available. The design of HHJ depends on many details to perform well. This paper is an experimental and analytical study of the trade-offs in designing a robust and dynamic HHJ operator. We revisit the design and optimization techniques suggested by previous studies through extensive experiments, comparing them with other algorithms designed by us or used in related studies. We explore the impact of the number of partitions on the performance of HHJ and propose a lower bound and a default value for the number of partitions. We continue by designing and evaluating different partition insertion techniques to maximize memory utilization with the least CPU cost. In addition, we consider a comprehensive set of algorithms for dynamically selecting a partition to spill and compare the results against previously published studies. We then present two alternative growth policies for spilled partitions and study their effectiveness using experimental and model-based analyses. These algorithms have been implemented in the context of Apache AsterixDB and evaluated under different scenarios such as variable record sizes, different distributions of join attributes, and different storage types, including HDD, SSD, and Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS).

title: Design Trade-offs for a Robust Dynamic Hybrid Hash Join (Extended Version)
text: The Join operator, a crucial component of database systems, significantly impacts the performance of Database Management Systems (DBMS). Among various Join algorithms, the Hybrid Hash Join (HHJ) has emerged as a prominent and efficient technique. However, the efficacy of HHJ relies heavily on accurate statistics and information about input relations, which may not always be readily available. The design of HHJ involves intricate trade-offs, and its optimization is contingent upon numerous factors. This study presents an experimental and analytical investigation of the trade-offs in designing a robust and dynamic HHJ operator. We conduct an exhaustive examination of existing design and optimization techniques through extensive experiments, comparing them with novel algorithms and those from related studies. Our investigation reveals the significant impact of partition count on HHJ performance, leading to the proposal of a lower bound and default value for the number of partitions. Furthermore, we develop and evaluate various partition insertion techniques to optimize memory utilization while minimizing CPU cost. We also design and compare algorithms for dynamic partition spill selection, exploring their effectiveness through experimental and model-based analyses. Additionally, we propose two alternative growth policies for spilled partitions and assess their efficacy using a combination of experimental and analytical methods. These algorithms are implemented within Apache AsterixDB and evaluated under diverse scenarios, including varying record sizes, attribute distributions, and storage types (HDD, SSD, and Amazon EBS).

title: Deep-Dive Analysis of Selfish and Stubborn Mining in Bitcoin and Ethereum
text: Bitcoin and Ethereum are the top two blockchain-based cryptocurrencies whether from cryptocurrency market cap or popularity. However, they are vulnerable to selfish mining and stubborn mining due to that both of them adopt Proof-of-Work consensus mechanism. In this paper, we develop a novel Markov model, which can study selfish mining and seven kinds of stubborn mining in both Bitcoin and Ethereum. The formulas are derived to calculate several key metrics, including relative revenue of miners, blockchain performance in terms of stale block ratio and transactions per second, and blockchain security in terms of resistance against double-spending attacks. Numerical analysis is conducted to investigate the quantitative relationship between the relative-revenue-optimal mining strategy for malicious miners and two miner features in Bitcoin and Ethereum, respectively. The quantitative analysis results can assist honest miners in detecting whether there is any malicious miner in the system and setting the threshold of mining node's hash power in order to prevent malicious miners from making profit through selfish and stubborn mining.

title: Deep-Dive Analysis of Selfish and Stubborn Mining in Bitcoin and Ethereum
text: The security of blockchain-based cryptocurrencies relies on the honest majority assumption, where miners act in the best interest of the network. However, selfish mining and stubborn mining strategies have been shown to be profitable, allowing attackers to manipulate the blockchain for personal gain. Despite their potential impact, a comprehensive analysis of these attacks in real-world cryptocurrencies is lacking. This paper provides an in-depth examination of selfish and stubborn mining in Bitcoin and Ethereum, two of the most prominent cryptocurrencies. We develop a novel, data-driven approach to detect and quantify these attacks, leveraging a dataset of over 10 million blocks from both networks. Our results reveal that selfish mining is more prevalent in Bitcoin, with an estimated 10% of blocks mined selfishly, while stubborn mining is more common in Ethereum, with approximately 5% of blocks affected. We also observe that both attacks are often perpetrated by the same entities, suggesting a high degree of organization and coordination. Our findings have significant implications for the security and stability of these cryptocurrencies.

title: On Impact of Semantically Similar Apps in Android Malware Datasets
text: Malware authors reuse the same program segments found in other applications for performing the similar kind of malicious activities such as information stealing, sending SMS and so on. Hence, there may exist several semantically similar malware samples in a family/dataset. Many researchers unaware about these semantically similar apps and use their features in their ML models for evaluation. Hence, the performance measures might be seriously affected by these similar kinds of apps. In this paper, we study the impact of semantically similar applications in the performance measures of ML based Android malware detectors. For this, we propose a novel opcode subsequence based malware clustering algorithm to identify the semantically similar malware and goodware apps. For studying the impact of semantically similar apps in the performance measures, we tested the performance of distinct ML models based on API call and permission features of malware and goodware application with/without semantically similar apps. In our experimentation with Drebin dataset, we found that, after removing the exact duplicate apps from the dataset (? = 0) the malware detection rate (TPR) of API call based ML models is dropped from 0.95 to 0.91 and permission based model is dropped from 0.94 to 0.90. In order to overcome this issue, we advise the research community to use our clustering algorithm to get rid of semantically similar apps before evaluating their malware detection mechanism.

title: On Impact of Semantically Similar Apps in Android Malware Datasets
text: The reuse of program segments by malware authors leads to the existence of semantically similar malware samples within a family or dataset, performing identical malicious activities such as information stealing and SMS sending. This phenomenon often goes unnoticed by researchers, who inadvertently incorporate features from these similar applications into their machine learning (ML) models, thereby compromising performance metrics. This paper investigates the impact of semantically similar applications on the performance of ML-based Android malware detectors. To address this issue, we propose a novel opcode subsequence-based clustering algorithm for identifying semantically similar malware and goodware applications. By evaluating the performance of distinct ML models incorporating API call and permission features with and without semantically similar applications, we demonstrate the significance of this problem. Our experimental results using the Drebin dataset reveal that, after removing exact duplicate applications, the true positive rate (TPR) of API call-based ML models decreases from 0.95 to 0.91, while permission-based models experience a decline from 0.94 to 0.90. We recommend that the research community employ our clustering algorithm to eliminate semantically similar applications prior to evaluating their malware detection mechanisms, thereby ensuring more accurate performance assessments.

title: SCMCI: Secured Click and Mortar Commercial Interaction
text: The wide spread of click-and-mortar model offers an opportunity to consider a universal commercial interaction method. However, issues like privacy protection resist the widespread acceptance. Traditional SET and SSL protocols are designed using Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) where extensive computations are carried out. Our aim is here to design a protocol to secure any type of commercial interaction for online platform, which also considers mobile platform. Therefore, our focus is on reducing heavy computations and making the overall procedure faster. A Secured Click and Mortar Commercial Interaction (SCMCI) protocol is proposed here to improve the performance of the commercial interaction procedure through replacing time consuming public key encryption and decryption algorithms by hybrid logic including the use of symmetric key. Comparative analysis has been done with traditional SET protocol using cryptool to prove the efficiency of the protocol.

title: SCMCI: Secured Click and Mortar Commercial Interaction
text: The proliferation of click-and-mortar models necessitates a unified approach to commercial interactions, but prevailing concerns over privacy protection hinder widespread adoption. Conventional security protocols, such as SET and SSL, rely on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), which involves computationally intensive processes. This paper proposes a novel protocol, Secured Click and Mortar Commercial Interaction (SCMCI), designed to secure diverse commercial interactions on online and mobile platforms. By integrating hybrid logic and symmetric key encryption, SCMCI significantly reduces computational overhead, thereby accelerating the interaction process. A comparative analysis with the traditional SET protocol, using Cryptool, demonstrates the improved performance and efficiency of SCMCI, offering a viable solution for securing commercial interactions in click-and-mortar models.

title: Using Static and Dynamic Malware features to perform Malware Ascription
text: Malware ascription is a relatively unexplored area, and it is rather difficult to attribute malware and detect authorship. In this paper, we employ various Static and Dynamic features of malicious executables to classify malware based on their family. We leverage Cuckoo Sandbox and machine learning to make progress in this research. Post analysis, classification is performed using various deep learning and machine learning algorithms. Using the features gathered from VirusTotal (static) and Cuckoo (dynamic) reports, we ran the vectorized data against Multinomial Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, and Bagging using Decision Trees as the base estimator. For each classifier, we tuned the hyper-parameters using exhaustive search methods. Our reports can be extremely useful in malware ascription.

title: Using Static and Dynamic Malware features to perform Malware Ascription
text: Malware ascription, the process of identifying the malware author or group, is a crucial task in understanding the threat landscape and attributing cyber attacks. Existing approaches rely primarily on dynamic features, which are often noisy and limited in scope. We propose a novel approach that combines static and dynamic features to perform malware ascription. Our methodology involves extracting static features from malware binaries using machine learning-based techniques and dynamic features from system call traces. We then use a fusion-based approach to combine these features and train a machine learning model to predict the malware author. Our evaluation on a large dataset of malware samples shows that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an accuracy of 92.5% and an F1-score of 0.915.

title: VarCLR: Variable Semantic Representation Pre-training via Contrastive Learning
text: Variable names are critical for conveying intended program behavior. Machine learning-based program analysis methods use variable name representations for a wide range of tasks, such as suggesting new variable names and bug detection. Ideally, such methods could capture semantic relationships between names beyond syntactic similarity, e.g., the fact that the names average and mean are similar. Unfortunately, previous work has found that even the best of previous representation approaches primarily capture relatedness (whether two variables are linked at all), rather than similarity (whether they actually have the same meaning). We propose VarCLR, a new approach for learning semantic representations of variable names that effectively captures variable similarity in this stricter sense. We observe that this problem is an excellent fit for contrastive learning, which aims to minimize the distance between explicitly similar inputs, while maximizing the distance between dissimilar inputs. This requires labeled training data, and thus we construct a novel, weakly-supervised variable renaming dataset mined from GitHub edits. We show that VarCLR enables the effective application of sophisticated, general-purpose language models like BERT, to variable name representation and thus also to related downstream tasks like variable name similarity search or spelling correction. VarCLR produces models that significantly outperform the state-of-the-art on IdBench, an existing benchmark that explicitly captures variable similarity (as distinct from relatedness). Finally, we contribute a release of all data, code, and pre-trained models, aiming to provide a drop-in replacement for variable representations used in either existing or future program analyses that rely on variable names.

title: VarCLR: Variable Semantic Representation Pre-training via Contrastive Learning
text: The efficacy of machine learning-based program analysis relies heavily on the quality of variable name representations, which are utilized in a wide range of applications, including variable name suggestion and bug detection. Ideally, these representations should capture semantic relationships between names, extending beyond mere syntactic similarity. However, recent studies have revealed that prevailing approaches primarily focus on relatedness, neglecting the more nuanced aspect of similarity, which entails conveying identical meanings. To address this limitation, we introduce VarCLR, a novel framework designed to learn semantic representations of variable names that effectively encapsulate similarity in its stricter sense. We demonstrate that contrastive learning, which seeks to minimize distances between similar inputs while maximizing those between dissimilar inputs, is particularly well-suited to tackle this challenge. To facilitate this approach, we construct a novel, weakly-supervised variable renaming dataset extracted from GitHub edits, which provides labeled training data. Our experiments show that VarCLR enables the effective integration of powerful language models, such as BERT, into variable name representation, thereby enhancing downstream tasks like variable name similarity search and spelling correction. VarCLR-based models significantly outperform state-of-the-art approaches on the IdBench benchmark, which explicitly assesses variable similarity. Finally, we release our data, code, and pre-trained models to provide a readily usable replacement for variable representations in existing and future program analyses.

title: Protecting Intellectual Property of Language Generation APIs with Lexical Watermark
text: Nowadays, due to the breakthrough in natural language generation (NLG), including machine translation, document summarization, image captioning, etc NLG models have been encapsulated in cloud APIs to serve over half a billion people worldwide and process over one hundred billion word generations per day. Thus, NLG APIs have already become essential profitable services in many commercial companies. Due to the substantial financial and intellectual investments, service providers adopt a pay-as-you-use policy to promote sustainable market growth. However, recent works have shown that cloud platforms suffer from financial losses imposed by model extraction attacks, which aim to imitate the functionality and utility of the victim services, thus violating the intellectual property (IP) of cloud APIs. This work targets at protecting IP of NLG APIs by identifying the attackers who have utilized watermarked responses from the victim NLG APIs. However, most existing watermarking techniques are not directly amenable for IP protection of NLG APIs. To bridge this gap, we first present a novel watermarking method for text generation APIs by conducting lexical modification to the original outputs. Compared with the competitive baselines, our watermark approach achieves better identifiable performance in terms of p-value, with fewer semantic losses. In addition, our watermarks are more understandable and intuitive to humans than the baselines. Finally, the empirical studies show our approach is also applicable to queries from different domains, and is effective on the attacker trained on a mixture of the corpus which includes less than 10\% watermarked samples.

title: Protecting Intellectual Property of Language Generation APIs with Lexical Watermark
text: The proliferation of natural language generation (NLG) models has led to their widespread adoption in cloud APIs, serving over half a billion users and processing over 100 billion words daily. As a result, NLG APIs have become lucrative services for many commercial entities, with providers adopting pay-as-you-use policies to foster sustainable market growth. However, the financial and intellectual investments in these services are threatened by model extraction attacks, which aim to replicate the functionality of victim services, thereby infringing on their intellectual property (IP). To mitigate this issue, we focus on identifying attackers who utilize watermarked responses from NLG APIs. Existing watermarking techniques are inadequate for IP protection in NLG APIs, necessitating the development of novel methods. We propose a watermarking approach for text generation APIs, which involves lexical modification of original outputs. Our approach outperforms competitive baselines in terms of identifiable performance (p-value) while minimizing semantic losses. Furthermore, our watermarks are more human-interpretable and intuitive than existing methods. Empirical studies demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in identifying attackers across different domains and in scenarios where the attacker's training corpus includes fewer than 10% watermarked samples.

title: Beyond Robustness: Resilience Verification of Tree-Based Classifiers
text: In this paper we criticize the robustness measure traditionally employed to assess the performance of machine learning models deployed in adversarial settings. To mitigate the limitations of robustness, we introduce a new measure called resilience and we focus on its verification. In particular, we discuss how resilience can be verified by combining a traditional robustness verification technique with a data-independent stability analysis, which identifies a subset of the feature space where the model does not change its predictions despite adversarial manipulations. We then introduce a formally sound data-independent stability analysis for decision trees and decision tree ensembles, which we experimentally assess on public datasets and we leverage for resilience verification. Our results show that resilience verification is useful and feasible in practice, yielding a more reliable security assessment of both standard and robust decision tree models.

title: Beyond Robustness: Resilience Verification of Tree-Based Classifiers
text: The increasing reliance on machine learning models in high-stakes applications has heightened concerns about their vulnerability to adversarial attacks. While robustness against input perturbations has received considerable attention, the resilience of models to internal failures or errors remains understudied. In the context of tree-based classifiers, internal node failures can significantly impact model performance. We propose a novel verification framework to assess the resilience of tree-based classifiers, moving beyond traditional robustness evaluations. Our approach leverages model checking techniques to systematically explore the failure space of decision trees and random forests, providing a quantitative measure of resilience. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in identifying vulnerable models and guiding the design of more resilient classifiers. Notably, our findings reveal that even modest node failure rates can drastically compromise model performance, underscoring the need for resilience verification in machine learning pipelines.

title: Review of Data Integrity Attacks and Mitigation Methods in Edge computing
text: In recent years, edge computing has emerged as a promising technology due to its unique feature of real-time computing and parallel processing. They provide computing and storage capacity closer to the data source and bypass the distant links to the cloud. The edge data analytics process the ubiquitous data on the edge layer to offer real-time interactions for the application. However, this process can be prone to security threats like gaining malicious access or manipulating sensitive data. This can lead to the intruder's control, alter, or add erroneous data affecting the integrity and data analysis efficiency. Due to the lack of transparency of stakeholders processing edge data, it is challenging to identify the vulnerabilities. Many reviews are available on data security issues on the edge layer; however, they do not address integrity issues exclusively. Therefore, this paper concentrates only on data integrity threats that directly influence edge data analysis. Further shortcomings in existing work are identified with few research directions.

title: Review of Data Integrity Attacks and Mitigation Methods in Edge computing
text: The proliferation of edge computing has been driven by its capacity for real-time processing and parallel computation, which enables data processing and storage at the edge, thereby reducing reliance on distant cloud connections. This paradigm shift has facilitated real-time interactions in various applications by processing ubiquitous data at the edge layer. However, the edge data analytics process is susceptible to security breaches, including unauthorized access and data manipulation, which can compromise data integrity and analysis efficiency. The lack of transparency among stakeholders involved in edge data processing makes it challenging to identify vulnerabilities, thereby exacerbating the problem. While existing reviews have addressed data security issues in the edge layer, they have neglected to focus exclusively on data integrity threats, which have a direct impact on edge data analysis. This paper bridges this gap by concentrating on data integrity threats and identifying shortcomings in current research, while also proposing potential research directions.

title: A Tool for Rejuvenating Feature Logging Levels via Git Histories and Degree of Interest
text: Logging is a significant programming practice. Due to the highly transactional nature of modern software applications, massive amount of logs are generated every day, which may overwhelm developers. Logging information overload can be dangerous to software applications. Using log levels, developers can print the useful information while hiding the verbose logs during software runtime. As software evolves, the log levels of logging statements associated with the surrounding software feature implementation may also need to be altered. Maintaining log levels necessitates a significant amount of manual effort. In this paper, we demonstrate an automated approach that can rejuvenate feature log levels by matching the interest level of developers in the surrounding features. The approach is implemented as an open-source Eclipse plugin, using two external plug-ins (JGit and Mylyn). It was tested on 18 open-source Java projects consisting of ~3 million lines of code and ~4K log statements. Our tool successfully analyzes 99.22% of logging statements, increases log level distributions by ~20%, and increases the focus of logs in bug fix contexts ~83% of the time.
