title: A Tool for Rejuvenating Feature Logging Levels via Git Histories and Degree of Interest
text: The efficacy of feature logging levels in software systems is crucial for debugging, testing, and maintenance. However, as software evolves, logging levels tend to become stale, leading to a mismatch between the original intentions of the developers and the current system behavior. This mismatch can result in unnecessary logging, performance degradation, and increased maintenance costs. To address this issue, we propose a novel tool that rejuvenates feature logging levels by leveraging Git histories and degree of interest. Our approach combines static analysis of Git commit histories with dynamic analysis of system execution traces to identify logging levels that are no longer aligned with the system's current behavior. We then utilize a degree of interest metric, which quantifies the relevance of each logging statement to the system's functionality, to prioritize logging level adjustments. Our evaluation on a dataset of 15 open-source systems shows that our tool can reduce unnecessary logging by up to 73% while maintaining a high degree of interest in the remaining log statements. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in rejuvenating feature logging levels, leading to improved system performance, reduced maintenance costs, and enhanced debugging capabilities.

title: Staring Down the Digital Fulda Gap Path Dependency as a Cyber Defense Vulnerability
text: Academia, homeland security, defense, and media have accepted the perception that critical infrastructure in a future cyber war cyber conflict is the main gateway for a massive cyber assault on the U.S. The question is not if the assumption is correct or not, the question is instead of how did we arrive at that assumption. The cyber paradigm considers critical infrastructure the primary attack vector for future cyber conflicts. The national vulnerability embedded in critical infrastructure is given a position in the cyber discourse as close to an unquestionable truth as a natural law. The American reaction to Sept. 11, and any attack on U.S. soil, hint to an adversary that attacking critical infrastructure to create hardship for the population could work contrary to the intended softening of the will to resist foreign influence. It is more likely that attacks that affect the general population instead strengthen the will to resist and fight, similar to the British reaction to the German bombing campaign Blitzen in 1940. We cannot rule out attacks that affect the general population, but there are not enough adversarial offensive capabilities to attack all 16 critical infrastructure sectors and gain strategic momentum. An adversary has limited cyberattack capabilities and needs to prioritize cyber targets that are aligned with the overall strategy. Logically, an adversary will focus their OCO on operations that has national security implications and support their military operations by denying, degrading, and confusing the U.S. information environment and U.S. cyber assets.

title: Staring Down the Digital Fulda Gap Path Dependency as a Cyber Defense Vulnerability
text: The Digital Fulda Gap, a concept originating from military strategy, refers to the vulnerability of a system to catastrophic collapse when a single, critical component fails. In the context of computer networks, this concept has been largely overlooked, despite its potential to significantly impact the resilience of modern cyber defenses. We investigate the role of path dependency in exacerbating the Digital Fulda Gap, focusing on the interplay between network topology, routing protocols, and attacker behavior. Our methodology combines graph theory, network simulations, and game-theoretic analysis to model the strategic interactions between attackers and defenders. We develop a novel metric, the Fulda Gap Index (FGI), to quantify the vulnerability of a network to cascading failures. Through a series of experiments on real-world network topologies, we demonstrate that path dependency can amplify the Fulda Gap effect, leading to a significantly increased likelihood of catastrophic network collapse. Our results show that attackers can exploit path dependencies to create targeted, high-impact attacks that compromise critical network infrastructure. Specifically, we find that the FGI is strongly correlated with the efficacy of attack strategies, with networks exhibiting high FGI values being more susceptible to collapse. Furthermore, our game-theoretic analysis reveals that defenders' optimal strategies are often inadequate in the face of path-dependent attacks, highlighting the need for novel defense mechanisms that account for these dynamics. Our work provides a fundamental understanding of the Digital Fulda Gap in computer networks, underscoring the importance of considering path dependency in the design of resilient cyber defenses.

title: ML Attack Models: Adversarial Attacks and Data Poisoning Attacks
text: Many state-of-the-art ML models have outperformed humans in various tasks such as image classification. With such outstanding performance, ML models are widely used today. However, the existence of adversarial attacks and data poisoning attacks really questions the robustness of ML models. For instance, Engstrom et al. demonstrated that state-of-the-art image classifiers could be easily fooled by a small rotation on an arbitrary image. As ML systems are being increasingly integrated into safety and security-sensitive applications, adversarial attacks and data poisoning attacks pose a considerable threat. This chapter focuses on the two broad and important areas of ML security: adversarial attacks and data poisoning attacks.

title: ML Attack Models: Adversarial Attacks and Data Poisoning Attacks
text: Machine learning (ML) models are increasingly vulnerable to attacks that compromise their performance and security. This paper presents a comprehensive study on two primary types of attacks: adversarial attacks, which perturb input data to mislead models, and data poisoning attacks, which manipulate training data to induce erroneous behavior. We develop a novel framework to systematically evaluate the resilience of ML models against these attacks, using a combination of white-box and black-box attack strategies. Our experiments on multiple datasets and models demonstrate that even state-of-the-art defenses can be evaded by sophisticated attacks, highlighting the need for more robust ML models and adaptive defense mechanisms.

title: MDPFuzz: Testing Models Solving Markov Decision Processes
text: The Markov decision process (MDP) provides a mathematical framework for modeling sequential decision-making problems, many of which are crucial to security and safety, such as autonomous driving and robot control. The rapid development of artificial intelligence research has created efficient methods for solving MDPs, such as deep neural networks (DNNs), reinforcement learning (RL), and imitation learning (IL). However, these popular models solving MDPs are neither thoroughly tested nor rigorously reliable. We present MDPFuzz, the first blackbox fuzz testing framework for models solving MDPs. MDPFuzz forms testing oracles by checking whether the target model enters abnormal and dangerous states. During fuzzing, MDPFuzz decides which mutated state to retain by measuring if it can reduce cumulative rewards or form a new state sequence. We design efficient techniques to quantify the "freshness" of a state sequence using Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) and dynamic expectation-maximization (DynEM). We also prioritize states with high potential of revealing crashes by estimating the local sensitivity of target models over states. MDPFuzz is evaluated on five state-of-the-art models for solving MDPs, including supervised DNN, RL, IL, and multi-agent RL. Our evaluation includes scenarios of autonomous driving, aircraft collision avoidance, and two games that are often used to benchmark RL. During a 12-hour run, we find over 80 crash-triggering state sequences on each model. We show inspiring findings that crash-triggering states, though they look normal, induce distinct neuron activation patterns compared with normal states. We further develop an abnormal behavior detector to harden all the evaluated models and repair them with the findings of MDPFuzz to significantly enhance their robustness without sacrificing accuracy.

title: MDPFuzz: Testing Models Solving Markov Decision Processes
text: Sequential decision-making problems, ubiquitous in security- and safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving and robot control, are formally captured by the Markov decision process (MDP) framework. Recent advances in artificial intelligence have yielded efficient solutions for MDPs, including deep neural networks, reinforcement learning, and imitation learning. However, the reliability and robustness of these models remain largely untested and unverified. To address this concern, we introduce MDPFuzz, a novel blackbox fuzz testing framework designed specifically for MDP-solving models. By constructing testing oracles that detect abnormal and hazardous states, MDPFuzz systematically mutates and selects states based on their potential to reduce cumulative rewards or explore novel state sequences. We develop efficient techniques for quantifying state sequence "freshness" using Gaussian mixture models and dynamic expectation-maximization, as well as prioritizing states with high crash-inducing potential by estimating local sensitivity. Our evaluation of five state-of-the-art MDP-solving models across various scenarios, including autonomous driving, aircraft collision avoidance, and benchmark games, reveals over 80 crash-triggering state sequences per model within a 12-hour period. Notably, our analysis reveals distinct neuron activation patterns in crash-inducing states, which appear normal at first glance. By integrating an abnormal behavior detector and leveraging MDPFuzz's findings, we successfully harden and repair the evaluated models, significantly enhancing their robustness without compromising accuracy.

title: Finding Deviated Behaviors of the Compressed DNN Models for Image Classifications
text: Model compression can significantly reduce the sizes of deep neural network (DNN) models, and thus facilitates the dissemination of sophisticated, sizable DNN models, especially for their deployment on mobile or embedded devices. However, the prediction results of compressed models may deviate from those of their original models. To help developers thoroughly understand the impact of model compression, it is essential to test these models to find those deviated behaviors before dissemination. However, this is a non-trivial task because the architectures and gradients of compressed models are usually not available. To this end, we propose DFLARE, a novel, search-based, black-box testing technique to automatically find triggering inputs that result in deviated behaviors in image classification tasks. DFLARE iteratively applies a series of mutation operations to a given seed image, until a triggering input is found. For better efficacy and efficiency, DFLARE models the search problem as Markov Chains and leverages the Metropolis-Hasting algorithm to guide the selection of mutation operators in each iteration. Further, DFLARE utilizes a novel fitness function to prioritize the mutated inputs that either cause large differences between two models' outputs, or trigger previously unobserved models' probability vectors. We evaluated DFLARE on 21 compressed models for image classification tasks with three datasets. The results show that DFLARE outperforms the baseline in terms of efficacy and efficiency. We also demonstrated that the triggering inputs found by DFLARE can be used to repair up to 48.48% deviated behaviors in image classification tasks and further decrease the effectiveness of DFLARE on the repaired models.

title: Finding Deviated Behaviors of the Compressed DNN Models for Image Classifications
text: The burgeoning demand for deploying deep neural network (DNN) models on resource-constrained devices has underscored the significance of model compression. While compression can drastically reduce model sizes, it may also introduce deviations in prediction results compared to the original models. To ensure the reliability of compressed models, it is crucial to identify and rectify these deviations prior to deployment. However, the lack of access to compressed model architectures and gradients renders this task particularly challenging. This paper proposes DFLARE, a novel black-box testing technique that leverages a search-based approach to automatically detect triggering inputs responsible for deviated behaviors in image classification tasks. By modeling the search problem as Markov Chains and employing the Metropolis-Hasting algorithm, DFLARE efficiently guides the selection of mutation operators to iteratively perturb a seed image until a triggering input is found. A custom-designed fitness function prioritizes mutated inputs that either induce large output differences between models or trigger novel probability vectors. Experimental evaluations on 21 compressed models across three datasets demonstrate DFLARE's superior efficacy and efficiency compared to the baseline. Notably, the triggering inputs identified by DFLARE can be utilized to rectify up to 48.48% of deviated behaviors in image classification tasks, thereby further diminishing the effectiveness of DFLARE on repaired models.

title: PAN-DOMAIN: Privacy-preserving Sharing and Auditing of Infection Identifier Matching
text: The spread of COVID-19 has highlighted the need for a robust contact tracing infrastructure that enables infected individuals to have their contacts traced, and followed up with a test. The key entities involved within a contact tracing infrastructure may include the Citizen, a Testing Centre (TC), a Health Authority (HA), and a Government Authority (GA). Typically, these different domains need to communicate with each other about an individual. A common approach is when a citizen discloses his personally identifiable information to both the HA a TC, if the test result comes positive, the information is used by the TC to alert the HA. Along with this, there can be other trusted entities that have other key elements of data related to the citizen. However, the existing approaches comprise severe flaws in terms of privacy and security. Additionally, the aforementioned approaches are not transparent and often being questioned for the efficacy of the implementations. In order to overcome the challenges, this paper outlines the PAN-DOMAIN infrastructure that allows for citizen identifiers to be matched amongst the TA, the HA and the GA. PAN-DOMAIN ensures that the citizen can keep control of the mapping between the trusted entities using a trusted converter, and has access to an audit log.

title: PAN-DOMAIN: Privacy-preserving Sharing and Auditing of Infection Identifier Matching
text: The rapid proliferation of digital contact tracing apps has raised pressing concerns about the privacy and security of sensitive user data, particularly in the context of infection identifier matching. To address this challenge, we propose PAN-DOMAIN, a novel framework for privacy-preserving sharing and auditing of infection identifier matching. Our approach leverages a combination of homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation, and blockchain technology to enable secure and transparent matching of infection identifiers across different domains. We formally prove the security and privacy guarantees of PAN-DOMAIN under a malicious adversary model, demonstrating its resistance to various attacks, including inference attacks and collusion attacks. We implement PAN-DOMAIN using a combination of open-source libraries and conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets, showcasing its scalability and efficiency. Our results demonstrate that PAN-DOMAIN achieves a 3.2x speedup in matching time compared to existing solutions while maintaining a high accuracy of 98.5%. Furthermore, our framework enables real-time auditing and accountability, allowing for the detection of malicious activities with a high degree of precision. PAN-DOMAIN offers a promising solution for privacy-preserving infection identifier matching, enabling the secure and efficient sharing of sensitive data across different domains. Our framework has significant implications for the development of secure and trustworthy digital contact tracing systems, and we believe it can play a vital role in the global response to pandemics and other public health crises.

title: When the Curious Abandon Honesty: Federated Learning Is Not Private
text: In federated learning (FL), data does not leave personal devices when they are jointly training a machine learning model. Instead, these devices share gradients, parameters, or other model updates, with a central party (e.g., a company) coordinating the training. Because data never "leaves" personal devices, FL is often presented as privacy-preserving. Yet, recently it was shown that this protection is but a thin facade, as even a passive, honest-but-curious attacker observing gradients can reconstruct data of individual users contributing to the protocol. In this work, we show a novel data reconstruction attack which allows an active and dishonest central party to efficiently extract user data from the received gradients. While prior work on data reconstruction in FL relies on solving computationally expensive optimization problems or on making easily detectable modifications to the shared model's architecture or parameters, in our attack the central party makes inconspicuous changes to the shared model's weights before sending them out to the users. We call the modified weights of our attack trap weights. Our active attacker is able to recover user data perfectly, i.e., with zero error, even when this data stems from the same class. Recovery comes with near-zero costs: the attack requires no complex optimization objectives. Instead, our attacker exploits inherent data leakage from model gradients and simply amplifies this effect by maliciously altering the weights of the shared model through the trap weights. These specificities enable our attack to scale to fully-connected and convolutional deep neural networks trained with large mini-batches of data. For example, for the high-dimensional vision dataset ImageNet, we perfectly reconstruct more than 50% of the training data points from mini-batches as large as 100 data points.

title: When the Curious Abandon Honesty: Federated Learning Is Not Private
text: Federated learning (FL) has garnered attention for its potential to train machine learning models while maintaining user privacy, as data remains on personal devices and only model updates are shared with a central party. However, recent studies have demonstrated that even passive attackers can reconstruct user data from observed gradients, undermining the purported privacy guarantees. We present a novel data reconstruction attack that enables an active and dishonest central party to extract user data from received gradients with high fidelity. Unlike prior approaches that rely on solving complex optimization problems or making detectable modifications to the model architecture or parameters, our attack involves introducing inconspicuous changes to the shared model's weights, which we term "trap weights." These modifications allow the central party to recover user data with zero error, even when the data belongs to the same class, at near-zero cost and without requiring complex optimization objectives. Our attack exploits inherent data leakage from model gradients, amplifying this effect through malicious weight alterations. We demonstrate the scalability of our attack to fully-connected and convolutional deep neural networks trained with large mini-batches of data. Notably, we achieve perfect reconstruction of over 50% of the training data points from mini-batches of 100 data points on the high-dimensional vision dataset ImageNet.

title: Hyperstyle: A Tool for Assessing the Code Quality of Solutions to Programming Assignments
text: In software engineering, it is not enough to simply write code that only works as intended, even if it is free from vulnerabilities and bugs. Every programming language has a style guide and a set of best practices defined by its community, which help practitioners to build solutions that have a clear structure and therefore are easy to read and maintain. To introduce assessment of code quality into the educational process, we developed a tool called Hyperstyle. To make it reflect the needs of the programming community and at the same time be easily extendable, we built it upon several existing professional linters and code checkers. Hyperstyle supports four programming languages (Python, Java, Kotlin, and Javascript) and can be used as a standalone tool or integrated into a MOOC platform. We have integrated the tool into two educational platforms, Stepik and JetBrains Academy, and it has been used to process about one million submissions every week since May 2021.

title: Hyperstyle: A Tool for Assessing the Code Quality of Solutions to Programming Assignments
text: The assessment of code quality in programming assignments is a crucial aspect of computer science education, as it enables instructors to provide constructive feedback and students to improve their programming skills. However, manual evaluation of code quality is time-consuming and often subjective, which can lead to inconsistent grading and decreased instructor productivity. To address this challenge, we present Hyperstyle, a novel tool for automatically assessing the code quality of solutions to programming assignments. Hyperstyle leverages a combination of static analysis techniques and machine learning algorithms to evaluate various aspects of code quality, including syntax, style, and design. We evaluate Hyperstyle on a dataset of over 10,000 student submissions to programming assignments in Java and Python, and demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying high-quality code with a precision of 0.92 and recall of 0.88. Our results show that Hyperstyle can significantly reduce the time and effort required for manual evaluation, while providing consistent and objective feedback to students.

title: Jigsaw: Large Language Models meet Program Synthesis
text: Large pre-trained language models such as GPT-3, Codex, and Google's language model are now capable of generating code from natural language specifications of programmer intent. We view these developments with a mixture of optimism and caution. On the optimistic side, such large language models have the potential to improve productivity by providing an automated AI pair programmer for every programmer in the world. On the cautionary side, since these large language models do not understand program semantics, they offer no guarantees about quality of the suggested code. In this paper, we present an approach to augment these large language models with post-processing steps based on program analysis and synthesis techniques, that understand the syntax and semantics of programs. Further, we show that such techniques can make use of user feedback and improve with usage. We present our experiences from building and evaluating such a tool jigsaw, targeted at synthesizing code for using Python Pandas API using multi-modal inputs. Our experience suggests that as these large language models evolve for synthesizing code from intent, jigsaw has an important role to play in improving the accuracy of the systems.

title: Jigsaw: Large Language Models meet Program Synthesis
text: Program synthesis, the task of generating executable code from natural language specifications, has seen significant progress in recent years. However, existing approaches are limited by their reliance on hand-crafted grammars, narrow domain knowledge, and small-scale datasets. Meanwhile, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities in understanding and generating human language. We propose Jigsaw, a novel program synthesis framework that leverages the strengths of LLMs to tackle the challenges of program synthesis. By fine-tuning a pre-trained LLM on a large dataset of programming problems, Jigsaw learns to generate syntactically correct and semantically meaningful code. We evaluate Jigsaw on a diverse set of programming tasks, including algorithmic puzzles, data structure implementations, and mathematical computations. Our results show that Jigsaw outperforms state-of-the-art program synthesis approaches by a significant margin, achieving an average accuracy of 84.2% on unseen problems. Furthermore, we demonstrate Jigsaw's ability to generalize to new domains and programming languages, highlighting its potential for real-world applications. Our work opens up new avenues for exploring the intersection of natural language processing and program synthesis, and has implications for the development of more intelligent and autonomous coding tools.

title: Hardware Trojan Insertion in Finalized Layouts: From Methodology to a Silicon Demonstration
text: Owning a high-end semiconductor foundry is a luxury very few companies can afford. Thus, fabless design companies outsource integrated circuit fabrication to third parties. Within foundries, rogue elements may gain access to the customer's layout and perform malicious acts, including the insertion of a hardware trojan (HT). Many works focus on the structure/effects of a HT, while very few have demonstrated the viability of their HTs in silicon. Even fewer disclose how HTs are inserted or the time required for this activity. Our work details, for the first time, how effortlessly a HT can be inserted into a finalized layout by presenting an insertion framework based on the engineering change order flow. For validation, we have built an ASIC prototype in 65nm CMOS technology comprising of four trojaned cryptocores. A side-channel HT is inserted in each core with the intent of leaking the cryptokey over a power channel. Moreover, we have determined that the entire attack can be mounted in a little over one hour. We also show that the attack was successful for all tested samples. Finally, our measurements demonstrate the robustness of our SCT against skews in the manufacturing process.

title: Hardware Trojan Insertion in Finalized Layouts: From Methodology to a Silicon Demonstration
text: The prohibitive cost of high-end semiconductor foundries necessitates that fabless design companies outsource integrated circuit fabrication to third-party vendors, introducing a risk of rogue elements gaining access to sensitive design information. Specifically, malicious actors may insert hardware trojans (HTs) into the design, compromising its security. While numerous studies have investigated the structure and effects of HTs, few have demonstrated the feasibility of implementing these threats in silicon, and even fewer have disclosed the insertion methodology or duration. This work pioneers the development of an HT insertion framework leveraging the engineering change order flow, enabling the effortless insertion of HTs into finalized layouts. We validate our approach by designing and fabricating an ASIC prototype in 65nm CMOS technology, featuring four cryptocores with side-channel HTs designed to leak cryptokeys over the power channel. Notably, our results show that the entire attack can be mounted in under 1.5 hours, with a 100% success rate across all tested samples. Furthermore, our measurements demonstrate the robustness of our side-channel trojan against manufacturing process skews.

title: Thinking Beyond Distributions in Testing Machine Learned Models
text: Testing practices within the machine learning (ML) community have centered around assessing a learned model's predictive performance measured against a test dataset, often drawn from the same distribution as the training dataset. While recent work on robustness and fairness testing within the ML community has pointed to the importance of testing against distributional shifts, these efforts also focus on estimating the likelihood of the model making an error against a reference dataset/distribution. We argue that this view of testing actively discourages researchers and developers from looking into other sources of robustness failures, for instance corner cases which may have severe undesirable impacts. We draw parallels with decades of work within software engineering testing focused on assessing a software system against various stress conditions, including corner cases, as opposed to solely focusing on average-case behaviour. Finally, we put forth a set of recommendations to broaden the view of machine learning testing to a rigorous practice.

title: Thinking Beyond Distributions in Testing Machine Learned Models
text: Machine learning (ML) testing has traditionally focused on evaluating model performance using a test dataset drawn from the same distribution as the training data. However, recent efforts to enhance robustness and fairness have highlighted the importance of testing against distributional shifts. Notwithstanding, these approaches still prioritize estimating error likelihood against a reference dataset or distribution. We contend that this perspective inadvertently overlooks other critical sources of robustness failures, such as corner cases, which can have severe and undesirable consequences. In contrast, software engineering testing has long recognized the value of assessing systems under diverse stress conditions, including corner cases, to move beyond average-case behavior. By drawing on these insights, we propose a set of recommendations to expand the scope of ML testing, embracing a more comprehensive and rigorous approach.

title: LightSync: Ultra Light Client for PoW Blockchains
text: Full nodes in a blockchain network store and verify a copy of the whole blockchain. Unlike full nodes, light clients are low-capacity devices that want to validate certain data on a blockchain. They query the data they want from a full node. If light clients do not verify the data they receive, full nodes might deceive them. SPV, introduced in the Bitcoin paper, is a practical solution to this problem currently used in many PoW blockchains. In SPV, the resources needed to verify a full node's response grow linearly with the blockchain size, making it inefficient over the long run. Another issue with SPV is that the full nodes do not get compensated for the services they provide. In this work, we introduce LightSync, a simple and cost-effective solution for light clients to verify the inclusion of certain data in a PoW blockchain. The resources needed for running LightSync remain constant no matter what the size of the blockchain is. LightSync uses an incentive mechanism that encourages full nodes to participate in the protocol. We perform a thorough analysis of the security of LightSync and discuss the details of deploying it in a real-world environment.

title: LightSync: Ultra Light Client for PoW Blockchains
text: The Proof of Work (PoW) consensus algorithm has been instrumental in securing blockchain networks, but its high computational overhead poses significant challenges for lightweight clients. Existing solutions, such as Simplified Payment Verification (SPV) clients, compromise on security by relying on trusted servers, while others, like Bitcoin-NG, require significant modifications to the underlying blockchain architecture. In this context, we present LightSync, a novel ultra-light client for PoW blockchains that achieves a 99.9% reduction in computational overhead while maintaining the security guarantees of full nodes. LightSync leverages a probabilistic filtering technique, which exploits the statistical properties of PoW to identify and prune unnecessary block verification. We implement LightSync as a modification to the Bitcoin client and evaluate its performance on a testnet. Our results show that LightSync reduces the client's computational overhead from 1.34 GHz to 1.34 MHz, making it feasible to run on resource-constrained devices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that LightSync achieves a verification latency of 10 seconds, comparable to that of full nodes, while maintaining a high level of security. Our findings have significant implications for the widespread adoption of PoW-based blockchains in IoT and mobile devices.

title: Adversarial Machine Learning In Network Intrusion Detection Domain: A Systematic Review
text: Due to their massive success in various domains, deep learning techniques are increasingly used to design network intrusion detection solutions that detect and mitigate unknown and known attacks with high accuracy detection rates and minimal feature engineering. However, it has been found that deep learning models are vulnerable to data instances that can mislead the model to make incorrect classification decisions so-called (adversarial examples). Such vulnerability allows attackers to target NIDSs by adding small crafty perturbations to the malicious traffic to evade detection and disrupt the system's critical functionalities. The problem of deep adversarial learning has been extensively studied in the computer vision domain; however, it is still an area of open research in network security applications. Therefore, this survey explores the researches that employ different aspects of adversarial machine learning in the area of network intrusion detection in order to provide directions for potential solutions. First, the surveyed studies are categorized based on their contribution to generating adversarial examples, evaluating the robustness of ML-based NIDs towards adversarial examples, and defending these models against such attacks. Second, we highlight the characteristics identified in the surveyed research. Furthermore, we discuss the applicability of the existing generic adversarial attacks for the NIDS domain, the feasibility of launching the proposed attacks in real-world scenarios, and the limitations of the existing mitigation solutions.

title: Adversarial Machine Learning In Network Intrusion Detection Domain: A Systematic Review
text: The widespread adoption of deep learning techniques in network intrusion detection systems (NIDSs) has led to improved detection rates and reduced feature engineering efforts. However, deep learning models have been found to be susceptible to adversarial examples, which are crafted to mislead the model into making incorrect classification decisions. This vulnerability can be exploited by attackers to evade detection and disrupt system functionality by introducing subtle perturbations into malicious traffic. While adversarial machine learning has been extensively studied in computer vision, its application to network security remains an open research area. This survey provides a comprehensive review of research that leverages adversarial machine learning in network intrusion detection, identifying potential solutions and future directions. We categorize surveyed studies into three areas: generating adversarial examples, evaluating the robustness of machine learning-based NIDSs, and defending against adversarial attacks. We also highlight key characteristics, discuss the applicability and feasibility of existing attacks in real-world scenarios, and examine the limitations of current mitigation strategies.

title: Test-Time Detection of Backdoor Triggers for Poisoned Deep Neural Networks
text: Backdoor (Trojan) attacks are emerging threats against deep neural networks (DNN). A DNN being attacked will predict to an attacker-desired target class whenever a test sample from any source class is embedded with a backdoor pattern; while correctly classifying clean (attack-free) test samples. Existing backdoor defenses have shown success in detecting whether a DNN is attacked and in reverse-engineering the backdoor pattern in a "post-training" regime: the defender has access to the DNN to be inspected and a small, clean dataset collected independently, but has no access to the (possibly poisoned) training set of the DNN. However, these defenses neither catch culprits in the act of triggering the backdoor mapping, nor mitigate the backdoor attack at test-time. In this paper, we propose an "in-flight" defense against backdoor attacks on image classification that 1) detects use of a backdoor trigger at test-time; and 2) infers the class of origin (source class) for a detected trigger example. The effectiveness of our defense is demonstrated experimentally against different strong backdoor attacks.

title: Test-Time Detection of Backdoor Triggers for Poisoned Deep Neural Networks
text: Backdoor attacks on deep neural networks, where maliciously crafted inputs trigger undesired behavior, pose a significant threat to the trustworthiness of AI systems. Existing detection methods are often limited to identifying poisoned models during training, leaving test-time detection largely unexplored. This paper proposes a novel technique, TriggerSentry, for detecting backdoor triggers at test-time, enabling the identification of compromised models in real-world deployments. Our approach leverages the observation that backdoor triggers often exhibit abnormal activation patterns in the neural network's internal representations. We develop a statistical testing framework to detect such anomalies, using a combination of feature importance metrics and outlier detection algorithms. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets show that TriggerSentry achieves high detection accuracy (95.6% on average) with a low false positive rate (1.2% on average) across various backdoor attack scenarios. Furthermore, our method is robust against evasion attacks and outperforms baseline approaches by a significant margin. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of TriggerSentry in safeguarding deep learning models against backdoor attacks in real-world applications.

title: Alice in Passphraseland: Assessing the Memorability of Familiar Vocabularies for System-Assigned Passphrases
text: Text-based secrets are still the most commonly used authentication mechanism in information systems. IT managers must strike a balance between security and memorability while developing password policies. Initially introduced as more secure authentication keys that people could recall, passphrases are passwords consisting of multiple words. However, when left to the choice of users, they tend to choose predictable natural language patterns in passphrases, resulting in vulnerability to guessing attacks. System-assigned authentication keys can be guaranteed to be secure, but this comes at a cost to memorability. In this study we investigate the memorability of system-assigned passphrases from a familiar vocabulary to the user. The passphrases are generated with the Generative Pre-trained Transformer 2 (GPT-2) model trained on the familiar vocabulary and are readable, pronounceable, sentence like passphrases resembling natural English sentences. Through an online user study with 500 participants on Amazon Mechanical Turk, we test our hypothesis - following a spaced repetition schedule, passphrases as natural English sentences, based on familiar vocabulary are easier to recall than passphrases composed of random common words. As a proof-of-concept, we tested the idea with Amazon Mechanical Turk participants by assigning them GPT-2 generated passphrases based on stories they were familiar with. Contrary to expectations, following a spaced repetition schedule, passphrases as natural English sentences, based on familiar vocabulary performed similarly to system-assigned passphrases based on random common words.

title: Alice in Passphraseland: Assessing the Memorability of Familiar Vocabularies for System-Assigned Passphrases
text: The widespread adoption of passphrase-based authentication has led to a growing concern about the memorability of system-assigned passphrases. While prior research has explored the use of randomly generated passphrases, the efficacy of familiar vocabularies in enhancing memorability remains understudied. This paper bridges this gap by investigating the memorability of system-assigned passphrases derived from familiar vocabularies, inspired by Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. We conducted a large-scale user study with 300 participants, who were assigned passphrases based on either a random word sequence or a sequence of words from a familiar vocabulary (e.g., book titles, song lyrics, or movie quotes). Our results show that participants who received passphrases from familiar vocabularies exhibited significantly better recall rates (84.2% vs. 56.1%) and reported higher confidence in their ability to remember the passphrases. Furthermore, we observed that the memorability of familiar vocabulary-based passphrases is influenced by the level of personal connection to the vocabulary source, with participants who reported a strong connection to the vocabulary exhibiting improved recall rates. Our findings have significant implications for the design of system-assigned passphrase policies, suggesting that the use of familiar vocabularies can improve the usability and security of passphrase-based authentication systems. We conclude by discussing the limitations of our study and outlining avenues for future research.

title: Manas: Mining Software Repositories to Assist AutoML
text: Today deep learning is widely used for building software. A software engineering problem with deep learning is that finding an appropriate convolutional neural network (CNN) model for the task can be a challenge for developers. Recent work on AutoML, more precisely neural architecture search (NAS), embodied by tools like Auto-Keras aims to solve this problem by essentially viewing it as a search problem where the starting point is a default CNN model, and mutation of this CNN model allows exploration of the space of CNN models to find a CNN model that will work best for the problem. These works have had significant success in producing high-accuracy CNN models. There are two problems, however. First, NAS can be very costly, often taking several hours to complete. Second, CNN models produced by NAS can be very complex that makes it harder to understand them and costlier to train them. We propose a novel approach for NAS, where instead of starting from a default CNN model, the initial model is selected from a repository of models extracted from GitHub. The intuition being that developers solving a similar problem may have developed a better starting point compared to the default model. We also analyze common layer patterns of CNN models in the wild to understand changes that the developers make to improve their models. Our approach uses commonly occurring changes as mutation operators in NAS. We have extended Auto-Keras to implement our approach. Our evaluation using 8 top voted problems from Kaggle for tasks including image classification and image regression shows that given the same search time, without loss of accuracy, Manas produces models with 42.9% to 99.6% fewer number of parameters than Auto-Keras' models. Benchmarked on GPU, Manas' models train 30.3% to 641.6% faster than Auto-Keras' models.

title: Manas: Mining Software Repositories to Assist AutoML
text: The rising popularity of Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) has significantly reduced the barriers to machine learning adoption, but the quality of AutoML-generated models often relies on the availability of high-quality datasets and hyperparameter tuning expertise. Meanwhile, software repositories contain a vast amount of knowledge embodied in the collective experience of developers, which remains largely untapped. This paper presents Manas, a novel approach that leverages software repositories to assist AutoML pipelines. By mining open-source software repositories, Manas extracts valuable insights from the development history of machine learning projects, including data preprocessing techniques, feature engineering strategies, and hyperparameter settings. These insights are then used to inform and augment AutoML pipelines, enabling the generation of more accurate and robust models. Our methodology involves a staged approach, where we first develop a data extraction framework to collect relevant information from software repositories, followed by a knowledge graph construction phase that integrates the extracted information into a unified representation. We then design a recommendation engine that leverages this knowledge graph to provide data-driven suggestions for AutoML pipelines. Our experimental evaluation on a dataset of 100 open-source machine learning projects demonstrates that Manas can improve the performance of AutoML-generated models by up to 23% compared to state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that Manas is particularly effective in scenarios where limited domain expertise is available, highlighting its potential to democratize access to machine learning capabilities. Overall, Manas contributes to the development of more effective and efficient AutoML systems by harnessing the collective knowledge embedded in software repositories.

title: A Survey of Verification, Validation and Testing Solutions for Smart Contracts
text: Smart contracts are programs stored on a blockchain that run when predetermined conditions are met. However, designing and implementing a smart contract is not trivial since upon deployment on a blockchain, it is no longer possible to modify it (neither for improving nor for bug fixing). It is only possible by deploying a new version of the smart contract which is costly (deployment cost for the new contract and destruction cost for the old contract). To this end, there are many solutions for testing the smart contracts before their deployment. Since realizing bug-free smart contracts increase the reliability, as well as reduce the cost, testing is an essential activity. In this paper, we group the existing solutions that attempt to tackle smart contract testing into following categories: public test networks, security analysis tools, blockchain emulators and blockchain simulators. Then, we analyze these solutions, categorize them and show what their pros and cons are.

title: A Survey of Verification, Validation and Testing Solutions for Smart Contracts
text: The increasing adoption of blockchain technology has led to a surge in the development of smart contracts, which are self-executing programs that automate various aspects of business logic. However, the lack of rigorous verification, validation, and testing (VV&T) of these contracts poses significant risks, including financial losses and compromised security. To address this concern, we conducted a comprehensive survey of existing VV&T solutions for smart contracts, encompassing a wide range of techniques, including formal verification, runtime verification, testing frameworks, and code analysis tools. Our methodology involved a systematic review of 75 research papers, as well as an analysis of 20 popular smart contract platforms and 15 VV&T tools. Our findings highlight the diversity of VV&T approaches, with strengths and weaknesses varying across different categories. We identify key challenges, including scalability, usability, and the need for standardized testing frameworks. Our survey provides a nuanced understanding of the current state of VV&T for smart contracts, informing future research directions and practitioner decisions.

title: Locally Differentially Private Sparse Vector Aggregation
text: Vector mean estimation is a central primitive in federated analytics. In vector mean estimation, each user $i \in [n]$ holds a real-valued vector $v_i\in [-1, 1]^d$, and a server wants to estimate the mean of all $n$ vectors. Not only so, we would like to protect each individual user's privacy. In this paper, we consider the $k$-sparse version of the vector mean estimation problem, that is, suppose that each user's vector has at most $k$ non-zero coordinates in its $d$-dimensional vector, and moreover, $k \ll d$. In practice, since the universe size $d$ can be very large (e.g., the space of all possible URLs), we would like the per-user communication to be succinct, i.e., independent of or (poly-)logarithmic in the universe size. In this paper, we are the first to show matching upper- and lower-bounds for the $k$-sparse vector mean estimation problem under local differential privacy. Specifically, we construct new mechanisms that achieve asymptotically optimal error as well as succinct communication, either under user-level-LDP or event-level-LDP. We implement our algorithms and evaluate them on synthetic as well as real-world datasets. Our experiments show that we can often achieve one or two orders of magnitude reduction in error in comparison with prior works under typical choices of parameters, while incurring insignificant communication cost.

title: Locally Differentially Private Sparse Vector Aggregation
text: The proliferation of decentralized data collection has heightened concerns about user privacy, particularly in scenarios where sensitive information is aggregated from multiple sources. One promising approach to mitigate these risks is locally differentially private (LDP) sparse vector aggregation, which enables clients to perturb their data locally before transmission, thereby guaranteeing a strong privacy guarantee. Despite its appeal, existing LDP protocols for sparse vector aggregation suffer from high communication overhead and inaccurate aggregation results. To address these limitations, we propose a novel LDP sparse vector aggregation protocol that leverages a combination of random matrix projection and adaptive sampling. Our method, dubbed RMP-AS, achieves a delicate balance between privacy, communication efficiency, and aggregation accuracy. Theoretically, we establish that RMP-AS ensures (ε, δ)-differential privacy while incurring a communication cost of O(d log(d/δ)), a significant improvement over existing protocols. Empirically, our experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that RMP-AS outperforms state-of-the-art protocols in terms of aggregation accuracy, often by a substantial margin. Notably, our protocol is highly versatile and can be seamlessly integrated into various decentralized data collection applications, including federated learning and personalized recommendation systems. We believe that RMP-AS constitutes a significant advancement in the area of LDP sparse vector aggregation, offering a robust and efficient solution for privacy-conscious data aggregation in modern distributed systems.

title: Location Leakage in Federated Signal Maps
text: We consider the problem of predicting cellular network performance (signal maps) from measurements collected by several mobile devices. We formulate the problem within the online federated learning framework: (i) federated learning (FL) enables users to collaboratively train a model, while keeping their training data on their devices; (ii) measurements are collected as users move around over time and are used for local training in an online fashion. We consider an honest-but-curious server, who observes the updates from target users participating in FL and infers their location using a deep leakage from gradients (DLG) type of attack, originally developed to reconstruct training data of DNN image classifiers. We make the key observation that a DLG attack, applied to our setting, infers the average location of a batch of local data, and can thus be used to reconstruct the target users' trajectory at a coarse granularity. We build on this observation to protect location privacy, in our setting, by revisiting and designing mechanisms within the federated learning framework including: tuning the FL parameters for averaging, curating local batches so as to mislead the DLG attacker, and aggregating across multiple users with different trajectories. We evaluate the performance of our algorithms through both analysis and simulation based on real-world mobile datasets, and we show that they achieve a good privacy-utility tradeoff.

title: Location Leakage in Federated Signal Maps
text: Federated signal maps have emerged as a promising approach for collaborative sensing and analytics, enabling the aggregation of local sensor data from numerous devices while preserving user privacy. However, the decentralized nature of this paradigm raises concerns about the potential for location information leakage. In this setting, an adversary can exploit subtle patterns in the aggregated data to infer sensitive location information about individual users. We investigate this threat through a comprehensive study on location leakage in federated signal maps. Our methodology involves developing a novel framework for simulating federated signal map constructions, which we use to generate a large-scale dataset of aggregated sensor readings. We then employ a range of machine learning-based inference attacks to analyze the dataset and quantify the location leakage risk. Our findings suggest that federated signal maps are indeed vulnerable to location leakage, with our attacks achieving high accuracy in inferring user locations even in the presence of strong privacy-preserving mechanisms. Notably, we observe that the leakage risk is exacerbated by the spatial correlation between sensor readings, as well as the heterogeneity of device distributions. We also identify key factors that contribute to the leakage, including the density of devices, the frequency of sensor readings, and the choice of aggregation algorithms. Our results underscore the need for more robust privacy protection mechanisms in federated signal maps and provide valuable insights for designing secure and private collaborative sensing systems.

title: Glue: Adaptively Merging Single Table Cardinality to Estimate Join Query Size
text: Cardinality estimation (CardEst), a central component of the query optimizer, plays a significant role in generating high-quality query plans in DBMS. The CardEst problem has been extensively studied in the last several decades, using both traditional and ML-enhanced methods. Whereas, the hardest problem in CardEst, i.e., how to estimate the join query size on multiple tables, has not been extensively solved. Current methods either reply on independence assumptions or apply techniques with heavy burden, whose performance is still far from satisfactory. Even worse, existing CardEst methods are often designed to optimize one goal, i.e., inference speed or estimation accuracy, which can not adapt to different occasions. In this paper, we propose a very general framework, called Glue, to tackle with these challenges. Its key idea is to elegantly decouple the correlations across different tables and losslessly merge single table CardEst results to estimate the join query size. Glue supports obtaining the single table-wise CardEst results using any existing CardEst method and can process any complex join schema. Therefore, it easily adapts to different scenarios having different performance requirements, i.e., OLTP with fast estimation time or OLAP with high estimation accuracy. Meanwhile, we show that Glue can be seamlessly integrated into the plan search process and is able to support counting distinct number of values. All these properties exhibit the potential advances of deploying Glue in real-world DBMS.

title: Glue: Adaptively Merging Single Table Cardinality to Estimate Join Query Size
text: Optimizing join query performance is crucial in modern data-intensive applications, as it significantly affects query latency and resource utilization. Accurate estimation of join query size is key to this optimization, yet remains a challenging problem due to the inherent complexity of join operations. Existing approaches rely on either sampling-based methods, which can be inaccurate, or detailed statistics, which may not be readily available. We propose Glue, a novel, adaptive approach to estimating join query size by merging single table cardinality estimates. Glue leverages a probabilistic framework to combine individual table cardinalities, effectively capturing the correlations between tables. Our approach is adaptive, as it dynamically adjusts the merging strategy based on the query workload and available statistics. We evaluate Glue using a diverse set of real-world datasets and query workloads, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. Our results show that Glue achieves an average error reduction of 35% compared to sampling-based methods and 22% compared to detailed statistics-based methods. Furthermore, Glue exhibits robustness to varying data distributions and query patterns, making it a reliable choice for real-world applications. We also provide theoretical guarantees on the accuracy of Glue's estimates, further solidifying its position as a valuable tool for join query optimization.

title: SpaceSaving$^\pm$: An Optimal Algorithm for Frequency Estimation and Frequent items in the Bounded Deletion Model
text: In this paper, we propose the first deterministic algorithms to solve the frequency estimation and frequent item problems in the bounded deletion model. We establish the space lower bound for solving the deterministic frequent items problem in the bounded deletion model, and propose the Lazy SpaceSaving$^\pm$ and SpaceSaving$^\pm$ algorithms with optimal space bound. We then develop an efficient implementation of the SpaceSaving$^\pm$ algorithm that minimizes the latency of update operations using novel data structures. The experimental evaluations testify that SpaceSaving$^\pm$ has accurate frequency estimations and achieves very high recall and precision across different data distributions while using minimal space. Our analysis and experiments clearly demonstrate that SpaceSaving$^\pm$ provides more accurate estimations using the same space as the state of the art protocols for applications with up to 93% of items deleted. Moreover, motivated by prior work, we propose Dyadic SpaceSaving$^\pm$, the first deterministic quantile approximation sketch in the bounded deletion model.

title: SpaceSaving$^\pm$: An Optimal Algorithm for Frequency Estimation and Frequent items in the Bounded Deletion Model
text: We introduce a suite of deterministic algorithms for solving the frequency estimation and frequent item problems in the bounded deletion model, a milestone not previously achieved. Our theoretical contributions include establishing a lower bound on the space complexity of deterministic frequent item algorithms in this model and presenting the Lazy SpaceSaving$^\pm$ and SpaceSaving$^\pm$ algorithms, which achieve optimal space efficiency. Furthermore, we develop a latency-optimized implementation of SpaceSaving$^\pm$ that leverages novel data structures to minimize update operation latency. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the accuracy and high recall and precision of SpaceSaving$^\pm$ across diverse data distributions, all while occupying minimal space. Notably, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art protocols in terms of estimation accuracy when up to 93% of items are deleted, while utilizing the same space. Additionally, we extend our work to propose Dyadic SpaceSaving$^\pm$, the first deterministic quantile approximation sketch in the bounded deletion model, inspired by prior research.

title: Defending against Model Stealing via Verifying Embedded External Features
text: Obtaining a well-trained model involves expensive data collection and training procedures, therefore the model is a valuable intellectual property. Recent studies revealed that adversaries can `steal' deployed models even when they have no training samples and can not get access to the model parameters or structures. Currently, there were some defense methods to alleviate this threat, mostly by increasing the cost of model stealing. In this paper, we explore the defense from another angle by verifying whether a suspicious model contains the knowledge of defender-specified \emph{external features}. Specifically, we embed the external features by tempering a few training samples with style transfer. We then train a meta-classifier to determine whether a model is stolen from the victim. This approach is inspired by the understanding that the stolen models should contain the knowledge of features learned by the victim model. We examine our method on both CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our method is effective in detecting different types of model stealing simultaneously, even if the stolen model is obtained via a multi-stage stealing process. title: Defending against Model Stealing via Verifying Embedded External Features
text: The intellectual property value of a well-trained model is heightened by the costly data collection and training procedures involved in its development. Recent findings have demonstrated that adversaries can successfully "steal" deployed models, even in the absence of training samples and model parameter or structure access. While existing defense strategies primarily focus on increasing the cost of model stealing, this paper explores an alternative approach, namely, verifying the presence of defender-specified external features in a suspicious model. To achieve this, we employ style transfer to temper a few training samples, thereby embedding the external features, and subsequently train a meta-classifier to determine whether a model has been stolen from the victim. This approach is grounded in the understanding that stolen models should inherit the knowledge of features learned by the victim model. We evaluate our method on both CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets, and our experimental results show its effectiveness in detecting various types of model stealing, including those involving multi-stage stealing processes.

title: BDFA: A Blind Data Adversarial Bit-flip Attack on Deep Neural Networks
text: Adversarial bit-flip attack (BFA) on Neural Network weights can result in catastrophic accuracy degradation by flipping a very small number of bits. A major drawback of prior bit flip attack techniques is their reliance on test data. This is frequently not possible for applications that contain sensitive or proprietary data. In this paper, we propose Blind Data Adversarial Bit-flip Attack (BDFA), a novel technique to enable BFA without any access to the training or testing data. This is achieved by optimizing for a synthetic dataset, which is engineered to match the statistics of batch normalization across different layers of the network and the targeted label. Experimental results show that BDFA could decrease the accuracy of ResNet50 significantly from 75.96\% to 13.94\% with only 4 bits flips.

title: BDFA: A Blind Data Adversarial Bit-flip Attack on Deep Neural Networks
text: Neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial bit-flip attacks (BFAs) that compromise their accuracy by manipulating a minimal number of weight bits. Existing BFA techniques, however, rely on access to test data, which is often infeasible for applications involving sensitive or proprietary information. We address this limitation by introducing Blind Data Adversarial Bit-flip Attack (BDFA), a novel approach that enables BFA without requiring access to training or testing data. BDFA optimizes a synthetic dataset that mirrors the statistical properties of batch normalization across network layers and targeted labels. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of BDFA, which reduces the accuracy of ResNet50 from 75.96% to 13.94% with a mere 4-bit flip.

title: Decision-based Black-box Attack Against Vision Transformers via Patch-wise Adversarial Removal
text: Vision transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated impressive performance and stronger adversarial robustness compared to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). On the one hand, ViTs' focus on global interaction between individual patches reduces the local noise sensitivity of images. On the other hand, the neglect of noise sensitivity differences between image regions by existing decision-based attacks further compromises the efficiency of noise compression, especially for ViTs. Therefore, validating the black-box adversarial robustness of ViTs when the target model can only be queried still remains a challenging problem. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the limitations of existing decision-based attacks from the perspective of noise sensitivity difference between regions of the image, and propose a new decision-based black-box attack against ViTs, termed Patch-wise Adversarial Removal (PAR). PAR divides images into patches through a coarse-to-fine search process and compresses the noise on each patch separately. PAR records the noise magnitude and noise sensitivity of each patch and selects the patch with the highest query value for noise compression. In addition, PAR can be used as a noise initialization method for other decision-based attacks to improve the noise compression efficiency on both ViTs and CNNs without introducing additional calculations. Extensive experiments on three datasets demonstrate that PAR achieves a much lower noise magnitude with the same number of queries.

title: Decision-based Black-box Attack Against Vision Transformers via Patch-wise Adversarial Removal
text: Vision transformers have achieved state-of-the-art performance in various computer vision tasks, yet their vulnerability to adversarial attacks remains a pressing concern. Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of black-box attacks against vision transformers, but these attacks often rely on gradient-based optimization or exhaustive search, limiting their practicality. We propose a novel decision-based black-box attack, Patch-wise Adversarial Removal (PAR), which targets vision transformers by selectively removing patches from the input image. PAR iteratively identifies the most informative regions in the image and removes them until the model's confidence in the predicted class drops below a certain threshold. Our attack exploits the Transformer's attention mechanism, which enables it to focus on the most relevant regions, making it more susceptible to patch removal. We evaluate PAR on several vision transformers, including DeiT, Swin Transformer, and ViT, and demonstrate its effectiveness in reducing the models' accuracy on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 datasets. Notably, PAR achieves higher success rates and requires fewer queries compared to existing black-box attacks. We also analyze the transferability of PAR across different models and datasets, providing insights into the vulnerability of vision transformers to patch-wise adversarial removal. Our findings have significant implications for the development of robust vision transformers and the design of more effective defenses against black-box attacks.

title: Control Parameters Considered Harmful: Detecting Range Specification Bugs in Drone Configuration Modules via Learning-Guided Search
text: In order to support a variety of missions and deal with different flight environments, drone control programs typically provide configurable control parameters. However, such a flexibility introduces vulnerabilities. One such vulnerability, referred to as range specification bugs, has been recently identified. The vulnerability originates from the fact that even though each individual parameter receives a value in the recommended value range, certain combinations of parameter values may affect the drone physical stability. In this paper we develop a novel learning-guided search system to find such combinations, that we refer to as incorrect configurations. Our system applies metaheuristic search algorithms mutating configurations to detect the configuration parameters that have values driving the drone to unstable physical states. To guide the mutations, our system leverages a machine learning predictor as the fitness evaluator. Finally, by utilizing multi-objective optimization, our system returns the feasible ranges based on the mutation search results. Because in our system the mutations are guided by a predictor, evaluating the parameter configurations does not require realistic/simulation executions. Therefore, our system supports a comprehensive and yet efficient detection of incorrect configurations. We have carried out an experimental evaluation of our system. The evaluation results show that the system successfully reports potentially incorrect configurations, of which over 85% lead to actual unstable physical states.

title: Control Parameters Considered Harmful: Detecting Range Specification Bugs in Drone Configuration Modules via Learning-Guided Search
text: Configurable control parameters in drone control programs enable adaptability to diverse missions and environmental conditions, but this flexibility can also introduce vulnerabilities. A recently identified vulnerability, termed range specification bugs, arises from the fact that although individual parameters are set within recommended value ranges, certain combinations of parameter values can compromise drone physical stability. This paper presents a novel learning-guided search system designed to detect such incorrect configurations. Our system employs metaheuristic search algorithms to mutate configurations and identify parameter values that drive the drone to unstable physical states. A machine learning predictor serves as the fitness evaluator, guiding the mutations. By applying multi-objective optimization, our system derives feasible value ranges from the search results. Notably, the predictor-based guidance eliminates the need for realistic or simulated executions to evaluate parameter configurations, enabling comprehensive and efficient detection of incorrect configurations. Experimental evaluation of our system reveals that it successfully identifies potentially incorrect configurations, with over 85% of these leading to actual unstable physical states, validating its effectiveness in supporting drone control program reliability.

title: Private Robust Estimation by Stabilizing Convex Relaxations
text: We give the first polynomial time and sample $(ε, δ)$-differentially private (DP) algorithm to estimate the mean, covariance and higher moments in the presence of a constant fraction of adversarial outliers. Our algorithm succeeds for families of distributions that satisfy two well-studied properties in prior works on robust estimation: certifiable subgaussianity of directional moments and certifiable hypercontractivity of degree 2 polynomials. Our recovery guarantees hold in the "right affine-invariant norms": Mahalanobis distance for mean, multiplicative spectral and relative Frobenius distance guarantees for covariance and injective norms for higher moments. Prior works obtained private robust algorithms for mean estimation of subgaussian distributions with bounded covariance. For covariance estimation, ours is the first efficient algorithm (even in the absence of outliers) that succeeds without any condition-number assumptions. Our algorithms arise from a new framework that provides a general blueprint for modifying convex relaxations for robust estimation to satisfy strong worst-case stability guarantees in the appropriate parameter norms whenever the algorithms produce witnesses of correctness in their run. We verify such guarantees for a modification of standard sum-of-squares (SoS) semidefinite programming relaxations for robust estimation. Our privacy guarantees are obtained by combining stability guarantees with a new "estimate dependent" noise injection mechanism in which noise scales with the eigenvalues of the estimated covariance. We believe this framework will be useful more generally in obtaining DP counterparts of robust estimators. Independently of our work, Ashtiani and Liaw [AL21] also obtained a polynomial time and sample private robust estimation algorithm for Gaussian distributions.

title: Private Robust Estimation by Stabilizing Convex Relaxations
text: We present the first polynomial-time algorithm that achieves (ε, δ)-differential privacy while estimating the mean, covariance, and higher moments in the presence of a constant fraction of adversarial outliers. This algorithm succeeds for distribution families that exhibit certifiable subgaussianity of directional moments and certifiable hypercontractivity of degree 2 polynomials, two properties well-established in prior robust estimation research. Our recovery guarantees are provided in affine-invariant norms, specifically the Mahalanobis distance for mean estimation, multiplicative spectral and relative Frobenius distances for covariance estimation, and injective norms for higher moments. Notably, our algorithm is the first to efficiently estimate covariance without condition-number assumptions, even in the absence of outliers. This achievement is enabled by a novel framework that modifies convex relaxations for robust estimation to ensure strong worst-case stability guarantees in appropriate parameter norms, provided the algorithms produce correctness witnesses during execution. We demonstrate the efficacy of this framework by adapting standard sum-of-squares semidefinite programming relaxations for robust estimation. Furthermore, we develop an "estimate-dependent" noise injection mechanism, where noise scales with the estimated covariance's eigenvalues, to establish our privacy guarantees. This framework has broader implications for developing differentially private counterparts of robust estimators. Concurrently, Ashtiani and Liaw [AL21] have also proposed a polynomial-time and sample private robust estimation algorithm, albeit restricted to Gaussian distributions.

title: Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles
text: A membership inference attack allows an adversary to query a trained machine learning model to predict whether or not a particular example was contained in the model's training dataset. These attacks are currently evaluated using average-case "accuracy" metrics that fail to characterize whether the attack can confidently identify any members of the training set. We argue that attacks should instead be evaluated by computing their true-positive rate at low (e.g., <0.1%) false-positive rates, and find most prior attacks perform poorly when evaluated in this way. To address this we develop a Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) that carefully combines multiple ideas from the literature. Our attack is 10x more powerful at low false-positive rates, and also strictly dominates prior attacks on existing metrics.

title: Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles
text: Differential privacy has been widely adopted as a gold standard for privacy preservation, but its robustness against membership inference attacks remains understudied. We revisit the fundamental limits of membership inference from first principles, providing a rigorous characterization of the attack's feasibility. By formulating the problem as a hypothesis testing task, we derive a novel, model-agnostic bound on the attack's accuracy in terms of the privacy parameter ε and the data distribution's Rényi entropy. Our analysis reveals that, even in the absence of auxiliary information, membership inference attacks can be highly effective, especially when the target model is overparameterized. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on real-world datasets, demonstrating the vulnerability of differentially private models to membership inference attacks and highlighting the need for more robust privacy mechanisms.

title: IntelliTC: Automating Type Changes in IntelliJ IDEA
text: Developers often change types of program elements. Such refactoring often involves updating not only the type of the element itself, but also the API of all type-dependent references in the code, thus it is tedious and time-consuming. Despite type changes being more frequent than renamings, just a few current IDE tools provide partially-automated support only for a small set of hard-coded types. Researchers have recently proposed a data-driven approach to inferring API rewrite rules for type change patterns in Java using code commits history. In this paper, we build upon these recent advances and introduce IntelliTC - a tool to perform Java type change refactoring. We implemented it as a plugin for IntelliJ IDEA, a popular Java IDE developed by JetBrains. We present 3 different ways of providing support for such a refactoring from the standpoint of the user experience: Classic mode, Suggested Refactoring, and Inspection mode. To evaluate these modalities of using IntelliTC, we surveyed 22 experienced software developers. They positively rated the usefulness of the tool. The source code and distribution of the plugin are available on GitHub: A demonstration video is on YouTube:

title: IntelliTC: Automating Type Changes in IntelliJ IDEA
text: The proliferation of Integrated Development Environments (IDEs) has significantly improved the productivity of software developers, but type-related refactorings remain a tedious and error-prone task. IntelliJ IDEA, a popular IDE, offers limited automation for type changes, relying on manual interventions that can lead to inconsistencies and bugs. To address this limitation, we present IntelliTC, a novel approach for automating type changes in IntelliJ IDEA. Our system leverages a combination of static analysis, type inference, and machine learning to identify and apply type changes accurately. We formulate the type change problem as a constraint satisfaction problem and develop a solver that minimizes the number of changes while ensuring type safety. Our evaluation on a dataset of 150 open-source projects reveals that IntelliTC achieves an accuracy of 93.4% in identifying correct type changes, outperforming existing tools by 21.1%. Furthermore, our user study with 25 professional developers shows that IntelliTC reduces the time spent on type changes by 63.2% and decreases the number of type-related errors by 51.9%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of IntelliTC in automating type changes, making it a valuable tool for developers and improving the overall quality of software development.

title: BlockGC: A Joint Learning Framework for Account Identity Inference on Blockchain with Graph Contrast
text: Blockchain technology has the characteristics of decentralization, traceability and tamper proof, which creates a reliable decentralized transaction mode, further accelerating the development of the blockchain platforms. However, with the popularization of various financial applications, security problems caused by blockchain digital assets, such as money laundering, illegal fundraising and phishing fraud, are constantly on the rise. Therefore, financial security has become an important issue in the blockchain ecosystem, and identifying the types of accounts in blockchain (e.g. miners, phishing accounts, Ponzi contracts, etc.) is of great significance in risk assessment and market supervision. In this paper, we construct an account interaction graph using raw blockchain data in a graph perspective, and proposes a joint learning framework for account identity inference on blockchain with graph contrast.
