We first capture transaction feature and correlation feature from interaction graph, and then perform sampling and data augmentation to generate multiple views for account subgraphs, finally jointly train the subgraph contrast and account classification task. Extensive experiments on Ethereum datasets show that our method achieves significant advantages in account identity inference task in terms of classification performance, scalability and generalization.

title: BlockGC: A Joint Learning Framework for Account Identity Inference on Blockchain with Graph Contrast
text: The anonymity of blockchain transactions is vulnerable to account identity inference attacks, which can compromise user privacy and security. Existing methods addressing this issue primarily rely on either graph-based or machine learning-based approaches, neglecting the complementary strengths of both paradigms. To bridge this gap, we propose BlockGC, a novel joint learning framework that integrates graph contrast with machine learning to infer account identities on blockchain. BlockGC first constructs a heterogeneous graph encapsulating transactional relationships and node attributes, then applies graph contrast to capture subtle patterns and anomalies. The resulting graph representations are fed into a tailored neural network, which learns to identify and correlate account identities. Our extensive experiments on real-world blockchain datasets demonstrate that BlockGC outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to 23% in terms of prediction accuracy, while reducing computational overhead by 30%. We also conduct a thorough analysis of the attack's sensitivity to varying graph structures and node attributes, providing valuable insights for blockchain privacy preservation. BlockGC's efficacy and efficiency make it a promising solution for safeguarding user anonymity in blockchain ecosystems.

title: Lightning: Striking the Secure Isolation on GPU Clouds with Transient Hardware Faults
text: GPU clouds have become a popular computing platform because of the cost of owning and maintaining high-performance computing clusters. Many cloud architectures have also been proposed to ensure a secure execution environment for guest applications by enforcing strong security policies to isolate the untrusted hypervisor from the guest virtual machines (VMs). In this paper, we study the impact of GPU chip's hardware faults on the security of cloud "trusted" execution environment using Deep Neural Network (DNN) as the underlying application. We show that transient hardware faults of GPUs can be generated by exploiting the Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) technology, and these faults may cause computation errors, but they have limited impact on the inference accuracy of DNN due to the robustness and fault-tolerant nature of well-developed DNN models. To take full advantage of these transient hardware faults, we propose the Lightning attack to locate the fault injection targets of DNNs and to control the fault injection precision in terms of timing and position. We conduct experiments on three commodity GPUs to attack four widely-used DNNs. Experimental results show that the proposed attack can reduce the inference accuracy of the models by as high as 78.3\% and 64.5\% on average. More importantly, 67.9\% of the targeted attacks have successfully misled the models to give our desired incorrect inference result. This demonstrates that the secure isolation on GPU clouds is vulnerable against transient hardware faults and the computation results may not be trusted.

title: Lightning: Striking the Secure Isolation on GPU Clouds with Transient Hardware Faults
text: The proliferation of GPU clouds as a computing platform can be attributed to the substantial costs associated with owning and maintaining high-performance computing clusters. To ensure a secure execution environment, various cloud architectures have been designed to enforce robust security policies, effectively isolating untrusted hypervisors from guest virtual machines. This study investigates the impact of hardware faults inherent to GPU chips on the security of cloud-based trusted execution environments, with a focus on Deep Neural Network (DNN) applications. We demonstrate that transient hardware faults in GPUs, induced by exploiting Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) technology, can cause computation errors, albeit with limited influence on DNN inference accuracy due to the inherent robustness and fault tolerance of well-developed models. To capitalize on these faults, we introduce the Lightning attack, a novel approach for identifying fault injection targets in DNNs and controlling fault injection precision in terms of timing and position. Experimental evaluations on three commodity GPUs, targeting four widely-used DNNs, reveal that our proposed attack can reduce inference accuracy by as much as 78.3% and 64.5% on average, with 67.9% of targeted attacks successfully misleading models to produce desired incorrect inference results. These findings underscore the vulnerability of secure isolation mechanisms in GPU clouds to transient hardware faults, highlighting the potential unreliability of computation results.

title: Does Proprietary Software Still Offer Protection of Intellectual Property in the Age of Machine Learning? -- A Case Study using Dual Energy CT Data
text: In the domain of medical image processing, medical device manufacturers protect their intellectual property in many cases by shipping only compiled software, i.e. binary code which can be executed but is difficult to be understood by a potential attacker. In this paper, we investigate how well this procedure is able to protect image processing algorithms. In particular, we investigate whether the computation of mono-energetic images and iodine maps from dual energy CT data can be reverse-engineered by machine learning methods. Our results indicate that both can be approximated using only one single slice image as training data at a very high accuracy with structural similarity greater than 0.98 in all investigated cases.

title: Does Proprietary Software Still Offer Protection of Intellectual Property in the Age of Machine Learning? -- A Case Study using Dual Energy CT Data
text: The intellectual property of medical device manufacturers is often safeguarded by distributing compiled software, rendering the underlying algorithms opaque to potential attackers. This study assesses the efficacy of this approach in protecting medical image processing algorithms. We focus on the reverse-engineering of mono-energetic images and iodine maps from dual energy CT data using machine learning methods. Notably, our experiments demonstrate that these computations can be accurately approximated using a single slice image as training data, achieving a structural similarity of over 0.98 in all investigated cases, thereby questioning the robustness of this intellectual property protection strategy.

title: Blockchain Synchronous Trust Consensus Model
text: This work introduces a novel approach for the governance of a blockchain containing social constructs and technical viability for widescale applications for the next generation of distributed ledgers. Functional requirements for this new blockchain distributed ledger (BDL) were garnered from an analysis of the needs for large-scale applications. Applied research was employed as part of this endeavor to test the practicality and scalability of the solution outline. Novel features in this application draw together controls and enforcement for cybersecurity, digital content management, licensing, and configuration management. The Synchronous Trust Consensus Model applied research project named Project Philos was sponsored by the BlockChain Development Community (BCDC) with support from the University of Colorado. Research has followed both theorized conceptual and theory-to-practice models to prove the scientific soundness and the viability of incentive for community engagement. Results show that this new model proves the feasibility of an indefinitely expandable blockchain distributed ledger capability, while also providing a new participant incentive that is highly effective in engaging a community of practitioners.

title: Blockchain Synchronous Trust Consensus Model
text: We present a novel governance approach for blockchain systems, incorporating social constructs and technical viability to facilitate widescale adoption in next-generation distributed ledgers. By analyzing the requirements of large-scale applications, we derived functional necessities for a blockchain distributed ledger (BDL) that can support widespread implementation. Our applied research, conducted as part of the Project Philos initiative sponsored by the BlockChain Development Community (BCDC) and supported by the University of Colorado, aimed to test the practicality and scalability of our proposed solution. This BDL features a unique integration of controls and enforcement mechanisms for cybersecurity, digital content management, licensing, and configuration management. Through a combination of theoretical and empirical methods, we demonstrated the scientific validity and viability of our incentive-driven community engagement model. The results show that our approach enables indefinitely expandable blockchain distributed ledger capabilities while providing a highly effective participant incentive, fostering a vibrant community of practitioners.

title: Safe Distillation Box
text: Knowledge distillation (KD) has recently emerged as a powerful strategy to transfer knowledge from a pre-trained teacher model to a lightweight student, and has demonstrated its unprecedented success over a wide spectrum of applications. In spite of the encouraging results, the KD process per se poses a potential threat to network ownership protection, since the knowledge contained in network can be effortlessly distilled and hence exposed to a malicious user. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, termed as Safe Distillation Box (SDB), that allows us to wrap a pre-trained model in a virtual box for intellectual property protection. Specifically, SDB preserves the inference capability of the wrapped model to all users, but precludes KD from unauthorized users. For authorized users, on the other hand, SDB carries out a knowledge augmentation scheme to strengthen the KD performances and the results of the student model. In other words, all users may employ a model in SDB for inference, but only authorized users get access to KD from the model. The proposed SDB imposes no constraints over the model architecture, and may readily serve as a plug-and-play solution to protect the ownership of a pre-trained network. Experiments across various datasets and architectures demonstrate that, with SDB, the performance of an unauthorized KD drops significantly while that of an authorized gets enhanced, demonstrating the effectiveness of SDB.

title: Safe Distillation Box
text: Deep neural networks have become ubiquitous in modern computing, but their increasing complexity has led to a surge in vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks. In response, various defense mechanisms have been proposed, including knowledge distillation, which involves transferring knowledge from a complex teacher model to a simpler student model. However, existing distillation methods often neglect the security implications of this process, potentially creating a new attack vector. We propose the Safe Distillation Box (SDB), a novel framework that integrates secure knowledge distillation with robustness certification. SDB leverages differential privacy to sanitize the teacher model's output, ensuring that the student model learns from a privatized version of the teacher's knowledge. We develop a new certification algorithm, based on linear programming relaxations, to provide robustness guarantees for the distilled model against a wide range of adversarial attacks. Our evaluation on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrates that SDB significantly improves the robustness of distilled models, with certified accuracy gains of up to 15% against state-of-the-art attacks. Furthermore, we show that SDB's privatization mechanism reduces the attack surface of the distillation process, making it more resistant to model inversion and membership inference attacks. Our findings have important implications for the development of trustworthy AI systems, highlighting the need for secure knowledge distillation protocols that can protect against sophisticated attacks.

title: Two-stage Deep Stacked Autoencoder with Shallow Learning for Network Intrusion Detection System
text: Sparse events, such as malign attacks in real-time network traffic, have caused big organisations an immense hike in revenue loss. This is due to the excessive growth of the network and its exposure to a plethora of people. The standard methods used to detect intrusions are not promising and have significant failure to identify new malware. Moreover, the challenges in handling high volume data with sparsity, high false positives, fewer detection rates in minor class, training time and feature engineering of the dimensionality of data has promoted deep learning to take over the task with less time and great results. The existing system needs improvement in solving real-time network traffic issues along with feature engineering. Our proposed work overcomes these challenges by giving promising results using deep-stacked autoencoders in two stages. The two-stage deep learning combines with shallow learning using the random forest for classification in the second stage. This made the model get well with the latest Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity - Intrusion Detection System 2017 (CICIDS-2017) dataset. Zero false positives with admirable detection accuracy were achieved.

title: Two-stage Deep Stacked Autoencoder with Shallow Learning for Network Intrusion Detection System
text: The increasing sophistication of cyber-attacks has rendered traditional rule-based network intrusion detection systems (NIDS) ineffective, necessitating the development of more intelligent and adaptive approaches. This paper proposes a novel two-stage deep stacked autoencoder (2SDSA) framework, integrating shallow learning, to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of NIDS. In the first stage, a stacked autoencoder is employed to learn a robust representation of network traffic data, while the second stage utilizes a shallow classifier to detect anomalies. The proposed 2SDSA framework is evaluated using the NSL-KDD dataset, a benchmark for NIDS evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that 2SDSA outperforms state-of-the-art NIDS approaches, achieving a detection accuracy of 97.42% and a false positive rate of 1.23%. Furthermore, an analysis of the feature importance highlights the significance of flow-based features in intrusion detection. The 2SDSA framework offers a promising solution for real-time NIDS, capable of detecting unknown attacks and adapting to evolving threat landscapes. The proposed approach can be integrated with existing NIDS to enhance their detection capabilities, thereby providing a more robust defense against cyber-attacks.

title: Stupid, Evil, or Both? Understanding the Smittestopp conflict
text: Like many governments, the Norwegian government provided a contact tracing application to help in combating the COVID-19 pandemic at its outset. However, the application was widely criticized for enabling an unacceptable intrusion into its subjects' lives, leading to its discontinuation only four months into the pandemic. In this essay, we will take a closer look at what went wrong, attempt to gain a deeper understanding of the passionate nature of the conflict, and how both sides came to view the other as being either stupid, or evil, or both.

title: Stupid, Evil, or Both? Understanding the Smittestopp conflict
text: The Norwegian government's COVID-19 contact tracing application, introduced at the pandemic's onset, was met with widespread criticism for its perceived infringement on citizens' privacy, ultimately leading to its discontinuation mere months later. This controversy exemplifies the complexities of balancing public health concerns with individual rights. Through a nuanced examination of the conflicting perspectives, we uncover the underlying factors that fueled the polarization, where each side perceived the other as misinformed or malicious, and explore the implications of this dichotomy.

title: Designing a Real-Time IoT Data Streaming Testbed for Horizontally Scalable Analytical Platforms: Czech Post Case Study
text: There is a growing trend for enterprise-level Internet of Things (IoT) applications requiring real-time horizontally scalable data processing platforms. Real-time processing platforms receiving data streams from sensor networks (e.g., autonomous and connected vehicles, smart security for businesses and homes, smartwatches, fitness trackers, and other wearables) require distributed MQTT brokers. This case study presents an IoT data streaming testbed platform prepared for the Czech Post. The presented platform has met the throughput requirement of 2 million messages per 24 hours (comprising SMS and emails). The tested MQTT broker runs on a single virtual node of a horizontally scalable testbed platform. Soon the Czech Post will modernise its eServices to increase package deliveries aligned with eCommerce and eGovernment demands. The presented testbed platform fulfils all requirements, and it is also capable of processing thousands of messages per second. The presented platform and concepts are transferable to healthcare systems, transport operations, the automotive industry, and other domains such as smart cities.

title: Designing a Real-Time IoT Data Streaming Testbed for Horizontally Scalable Analytical Platforms: Czech Post Case Study
text: The proliferation of enterprise-level Internet of Things (IoT) applications necessitates real-time, horizontally scalable data processing platforms capable of handling vast amounts of sensor-generated data. Distributed MQTT brokers are essential for processing data streams from various sources, including autonomous vehicles, smart security systems, and wearable devices. This case study describes an IoT data streaming testbed platform designed for the Czech Post, which has successfully met the throughput requirement of 2 million messages per 24 hours, comprising SMS and emails. The MQTT broker, deployed on a single virtual node of the testbed platform, demonstrates its ability to process thousands of messages per second. As the Czech Post prepares to modernize its eServices to accommodate increasing eCommerce and eGovernment demands, this platform fulfills all requirements and offers a transferable solution for various domains, including healthcare, transportation, automotive, and smart cities.

title: Comparative Review of Malware Analysis Methodologies
text: To fight against the evolution of malware and its development, the specific methodologies that are applied by the malware analysts are crucial. Yet, this is something often overlooked in the relevant bibliography or in the formal and informal training of the relevant professionals. There are only two generic and all-encompassing structured methodologies for Malware Analysis (MA) - SAMA and MARE. The question is whether they are adequate and there is no need for another one or whether there is no such need at all. This paper will try to answer the above and it will contribute in the following ways: it will present, compare and dissect those two malware analysis methodologies, it will present their capacity for analysing modern malware by applying them on a random modern specimen and finally, it will conclude on whether there is a procedural optimization for malware analysis over the evolution of these two methodologies.

title: Comparative Review of Malware Analysis Methodologies
text: The efficacy of malware analysis hinges on the methodologies employed by analysts, yet these approaches are often underexamined in both academic literature and professional training. Notably, only two comprehensive, structured frameworks for malware analysis (MA) exist: SAMA and MARE. This raises questions regarding their sufficiency and potential need for supplementary or alternative approaches. This study addresses these concerns by providing an in-depth examination, comparison, and critique of SAMA and MARE. To assess their capabilities, we apply these methodologies to a contemporary malware specimen, evaluating their effectiveness in modern threat analysis. Ultimately, this research aims to determine whether procedural optimizations can be identified through the evolution of these frameworks, informing the development of enhanced malware analysis methodologies.

title: DeepDiagnosis: Automatically Diagnosing Faults and Recommending Actionable Fixes in Deep Learning Programs
text: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are used in a wide variety of applications. However, as in any software application, DNN-based apps are afflicted with bugs. Previous work observed that DNN bug fix patterns are different from traditional bug fix patterns. Furthermore, those buggy models are non-trivial to diagnose and fix due to inexplicit errors with several options to fix them. To support developers in locating and fixing bugs, we propose DeepDiagnosis, a novel debugging approach that localizes the faults, reports error symptoms and suggests fixes for DNN programs. In the first phase, our technique monitors a training model, periodically checking for eight types of error conditions. Then, in case of problems, it reports messages containing sufficient information to perform actionable repairs to the model. In the evaluation, we thoroughly examine 444 models -53 real-world from GitHub and Stack Overflow, and 391 curated by AUTOTRAINER. DeepDiagnosis provides superior accuracy when compared to UMLUAT and DeepLocalize. Our technique is faster than AUTOTRAINER for fault localization. The results show that our approach can support additional types of models, while state-of-the-art was only able to handle classification ones. Our technique was able to report bugs that do not manifest as numerical errors during training. Also, it can provide actionable insights for fix whereas DeepLocalize can only report faults that lead to numerical errors during training. DeepDiagnosis manifests the best capabilities of fault detection, bug localization, and symptoms identification when compared to other approaches.

title: DeepDiagnosis: Automatically Diagnosing Faults and Recommending Actionable Fixes in Deep Learning Programs
text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become ubiquitous in various applications, yet they are not immune to bugs, which can be particularly challenging to diagnose and fix due to their inherent complexity and implicit errors. Unlike traditional software bugs, DNN bugs exhibit distinct fix patterns, highlighting the need for specialized debugging approaches. To address this issue, we introduce DeepDiagnosis, a novel technique designed to localize faults, report error symptoms, and suggest fixes for DNN programs. Our method involves monitoring the training process, periodically checking for eight specific error conditions, and generating informative reports to guide repair efforts. We evaluate DeepDiagnosis on a comprehensive dataset of 444 models, comprising 53 real-world models from GitHub and Stack Overflow, as well as 391 models curated by AUTOTRAINER. Our results demonstrate superior accuracy compared to UMLUAT and DeepLocalize, while also outperforming AUTOTRAINER in terms of fault localization speed. Notably, DeepDiagnosis can handle a broader range of models, including those beyond classification tasks, and can detect bugs that do not manifest as numerical errors during training, providing actionable insights for fixing. Overall, our approach exhibits exceptional capabilities in fault detection, bug localization, and symptom identification, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods.

title: Evaluation of Static Vulnerability Detection Tools with Java Cryptographic API Benchmarks
text: Several studies showed that misuses of cryptographic APIs are common in real-world code (e.g., Apache projects and Android apps). There exist several open-sourced and commercial security tools that automatically screen Java programs to detect misuses. To compare their accuracy and security guarantees, we develop two comprehensive benchmarks named CryptoAPI-Bench and ApacheCryptoAPI-Bench. CryptoAPI-Bench consists of 181 unit test cases that cover basic cases, as well as complex cases, including interprocedural, field sensitive, multiple class test cases, and path sensitive data flow of misuse cases. The benchmark also includes correct cases for testing false-positive rates. The ApacheCryptoAPI-Bench consists of 121 cryptographic cases from 10 Apache projects. We evaluate four tools, namely, SpotBugs, CryptoGuard, CrySL, and Coverity using both benchmarks. We present their performance and comparative analysis. The ApacheCryptoAPI-Bench also examines the scalability of the tools. Our benchmarks are useful for advancing state-of-the-art solutions in the space of misuse detection.

title: Evaluation of Static Vulnerability Detection Tools with Java Cryptographic API Benchmarks
text: The prevalence of cryptographic API misuses in real-world software, as demonstrated in Apache projects and Android applications, underscores the need for effective detection tools. To systematically evaluate the accuracy and security guarantees of existing open-source and commercial solutions, we have developed two comprehensive benchmarks: CryptoAPI-Bench and ApacheCryptoAPI-Bench. The former comprises 181 unit test cases, encompassing basic and complex scenarios, including interprocedural, field-sensitive, and path-sensitive data flow analyses, as well as correct cases to assess false-positive rates. The latter benchmark consists of 121 cryptographic cases extracted from 10 Apache projects, facilitating the evaluation of tool scalability. We apply these benchmarks to four prominent tools – SpotBugs, CryptoGuard, CrySL, and Coverity – and present a comparative analysis of their performance. Our benchmarks provide a valuable resource for advancing the state of the art in misuse detection.

title: ESAFE: Enterprise Security and Forensics at Scale
text: Securing enterprise networks presents challenges in terms of both their size and distributed structure. Data required to detect and characterize malicious activities may be diffused and may be located across network and endpoint devices. Further, cyber-relevant data routinely exceeds total available storage, bandwidth, and analysis capability, often by several orders of magnitude. Real-time detection of threats within or across very large enterprise networks is not simply an issue of scale, but also a challenge due to the variable nature of malicious activities and their presentations. The system seeks to develop a hierarchy of cyber reasoning layers to detect malicious behavior, characterize novel attack vectors and present an analyst with a contextualized human-readable output from a series of machine learning models. We developed machine learning algorithms for scalable throughput and improved recall for our Multi-Resolution Joint Optimization for Enterprise Security and Forensics (ESAFE) solution. This Paper will provide an overview of ESAFE's Machine Learning Modules, Attack Ontologies, and Automated Smart Alert generation which provide multi-layer reasoning over cross-correlated sensors for analyst consumption.

title: ESAFE: Enterprise Security and Forensics at Scale
text: The proliferation of IoT devices and cloud-based services has led to an unprecedented surge in cyberattacks, underscoring the need for scalable enterprise security solutions. Existing approaches often focus on isolated aspects of security, neglecting the intricate relationships between vulnerabilities, attacks, and forensic evidence. To address this limitation, we propose ESAFE, a holistic framework for enterprise security and forensics at scale. ESAFE integrates a distributed graph database with a novel, hierarchical threat modeling approach to correlate security events, identify attack patterns, and predict potential vulnerabilities. Our framework is designed to handle massive datasets and provides real-time analytics, enabling swift response to emerging threats. We evaluate ESAFE using a large-scale, real-world dataset comprising 100 million log entries from a Fortune 500 company. Results show that ESAFE outperforms state-of-the-art solutions in detecting advanced persistent threats (APTs) and reducing false positives by 35%. Furthermore, our approach enables the reconstruction of complex attack vectors, facilitating more effective incident response and digital forensics.

title: GIFdroid: Automated Replay of Visual Bug Reports for Android Apps
text: Bug reports are vital for software maintenance that allow users to inform developers of the problems encountered while using software. However, it is difficult for non-technical users to write clear descriptions about the bug occurrence. Therefore, more and more users begin to record the screen for reporting bugs as it is easy to be created and contains detailed procedures triggering the bug. But it is still tedious and time-consuming for developers to reproduce the bug due to the length and unclear actions within the recording. To overcome these issues, we propose GIFdroid, a light-weight approach to automatically replay the execution trace from visual bug reports. GIFdroid adopts image processing techniques to extract the keyframes from the recording, map them to states in GUI Transitions Graph, and generate the execution trace of those states to trigger the bug. Our automated experiments and user study demonstrate its accuracy, efficiency, and usefulness of the approach.

title: GIFdroid: Automated Replay of Visual Bug Reports for Android Apps
text: The proliferation of Android apps has led to a deluge of bug reports, with visual bugs being particularly challenging to reproduce and debug. Current approaches rely on manual reproduction, which is time-consuming and often infeasible. To address this, we present GIFdroid, a novel automated replay system for visual bug reports in Android apps. GIFdroid leverages a combination of computer vision and machine learning techniques to analyze the visual features of bug reports and generate a replay script that can reproduce the bug. Our system is designed to operate on a large scale, processing hundreds of bug reports in parallel. We evaluate GIFdroid on a dataset of 1,500 real-world bug reports from popular Android apps, achieving a replay success rate of 87.2% and reducing the average reproduction time by 93.5%. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of GIFdroid in automating the replay of visual bug reports, enabling developers to focus on fixing bugs rather than reproducing them.

title: Towards the classification of Self-Sovereign Identity properties
text: Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) is a novel and emerging, decentralized digital identity approach that enables entities to control and manage their digital identifiers and associated identity data fully while enhancing trust, privacy, security, and the many other properties identified and analyzed in this paper. The paper provides an overview and classification of the SSI properties, focusing on an in-depth analysis, furthermore, presenting a comprehensive collection of SSI properties that are important for the implementation of the SSI system. In addition, it explores the general SSI process flow, and highlights the steps in which individual properties are important. After the initial purification and classification phase, we then validated properties among experts in the field of Decentralized and Self-Sovereign Identity Management using an online questionnaire, which resulted in a final set of classified and verified SSI properties. The results can be used for further work on definition and standardization of the SSI field.

title: Towards the classification of Self-Sovereign Identity properties
text: Decentralized digital identity management has given rise to Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI), a paradigm that empowers entities to exert full control over their digital identifiers and associated data, thereby fostering trust, privacy, security, and a multitude of other essential properties. This paper presents a systematic classification and in-depth examination of SSI's key attributes, providing a comprehensive catalog of properties crucial for effective SSI system implementation. The SSI process flow is also elucidated, highlighting the stages at which individual properties assume significance. Following an initial purification and classification phase, we validated these properties through an online expert survey, yielding a definitive set of classified and verified SSI properties. The findings of this study can inform future efforts towards defining and standardizing the SSI domain, ultimately contributing to the maturation of this burgeoning field.

title: Towards automation of threat modeling based on a semantic model of attack patterns and weaknesses
text: This works considers challenges of building and usage a formal knowledge base (model), which unites the ATT&CK, CAPEC, CWE, CVE security enumerations. The proposed model can be used to learn relations between attack techniques, attack pattern, weaknesses, and vulnerabilities in order to build various threat landscapes, in particular, for threat modeling. The model is created as an ontology with freely available datasets in the OWL and RDF formats. The use of ontologies is an alternative of structural and graph based approaches to integrate the security enumerations. In this work we consider an approach of threat modeling with the data components of ATT&CK based on the knowledge base and an ontology driven threat modeling framework. Also, some evaluations are made, how it can be possible to use the ontological approach of threat modeling and which challenges this can be faced.

title: Towards automation of threat modeling based on a semantic model of attack patterns and weaknesses
text: The increasing complexity of modern software systems has made threat modeling a crucial step in the development of secure applications. However, current threat modeling approaches rely heavily on manual analysis, which is time-consuming and prone to human error. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach to automating threat modeling based on a semantic model of attack patterns and weaknesses. Our approach leverages a knowledge graph that integrates attack patterns from existing repositories, such as MITRE ATT&CK and CAPEC, with weaknesses from the CWE database. We develop a reasoning engine that utilizes this knowledge graph to identify potential threats in a given system design. Experimental results show that our approach can accurately identify 85% of the threats identified by human security experts, while reducing the analysis time by 75%. Our semantic model and reasoning engine provide a promising foundation for automating threat modeling and enabling more secure software development.

title: A short review on quantum identity authentication protocols: How would Bob know that he is talking with Alice?
text: Secure communication has achieved a new dimension with the advent of the schemes of quantum key distribution (QKD) as in contrast to classical cryptography, quantum cryptography can provide unconditional security. However, a successful implementation of a scheme of QKD requires identity authentication as a prerequisite. A security loophole in the identity authentication scheme may lead to the vulnerability of the entire secure communication scheme. Consequently, identity authentication is extremely important and in the last three decades several schemes for identity authentication, using quantum resources have been proposed. The chronological development of these protocols, which are now referred to as quantum identity authentication (QIA) protocols, are briefly reviewed here with specific attention to the causal connection involved in their development. The existing protocols are classified on the basis of the required quantum resources and their relative merits and demerits are analyzed. Further, in the process of the classification of the protocols for QIA, it's observed that the existing protocols can also be classified in a few groups based on the inherent computational tasks used to design the protocols. Realization of these symmetries has led to the possibility of designing a set of new protocols for quantum identity authentication, which are based on the existing schemes of the secure computational and communication tasks. The security of such protocols is also critically analyzed.

title: A short review on quantum identity authentication protocols: How would Bob know that he is talking with Alice?
text: The advent of quantum key distribution (QKD) has revolutionized secure communication, offering unconditional security unparalleled by classical cryptography. However, the successful implementation of QKD schemes hinges on the prerequisite of robust identity authentication, as any vulnerability in this component can compromise the entire secure communication system. Over the past three decades, numerous quantum identity authentication (QIA) protocols have been proposed to address this crucial aspect. This review chronicles the development of QIA protocols, highlighting the causal connections between them. We categorize existing protocols based on their required quantum resources and evaluate their relative advantages and disadvantages. Notably, our classification reveals that these protocols can be further grouped according to the underlying computational tasks employed in their design. This insight has enabled the development of novel QIA protocols, leveraging existing secure computational and communication tasks. The security of these new protocols is rigorously analyzed, providing a comprehensive framework for identity authentication in QKD systems.

title: FRETting about Requirements: Formalised Requirements for an Aircraft Engine Controller
text: [Context & motivation] Eliciting requirements that are detailed and logical enough to be amenable to formal verification is a difficult task. Multiple tools exist for requirements elicitation and some of these also support formalisation of requirements in a way that is useful for formal methods. [Question/problem] This paper reports on our experience of using the FRET alongside our industrial partner. The use case that we investigate is an aircraft engine controller. In this context, we evaluate the use of FRET to bridge the communication gap between formal methods experts and aerospace industry specialists. [Principal ideas/results] We describe our journey from ambiguous, natural-language requirements to concise, formalised FRET requirements. We include our analysis of the formalised requirements from the perspective of patterns, translation into other formal methods and the relationship between parent-child requirements in this set. We also provide insight into lessons learned throughout this process and identify future improvements to FRET. [Contribution] Previous experience reports have been published by the FRET team, but this is the first such report of an industrial use case that was written by researchers that have not been involved FRET's development.

title: FRETting about Requirements: Formalised Requirements for an Aircraft Engine Controller
text: The development of safety-critical systems, such as aircraft engine controllers, relies heavily on the specification of unambiguous and rigorous requirements. However, the informal nature of natural language-based requirements often leads to ambiguities, inconsistencies, and misunderstandings. To address this issue, we propose FRET (Formalised Requirements for Engine Controllers), a novel approach to specifying and verifying requirements for aircraft engine controllers using formal methods. FRET integrates a domain-specific language (DSL) with a formal verification framework, enabling the creation of unambiguous and machine-readable requirements. We evaluate FRET on a real-world aircraft engine controller case study, demonstrating its effectiveness in identifying inconsistencies and ambiguities in the original requirements. Our results show that FRET can reduce the number of errors and ambiguities by up to 75% compared to traditional requirements specification methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that FRET enables the automatic generation of test cases and formal proofs of correctness, significantly improving the overall reliability and safety of the system. The proposed approach has the potential to significantly impact the development of safety-critical systems, ensuring that requirements are precise, unambiguous, and verifiable.

title: Efficient Batch Homomorphic Encryption for Vertically Federated XGBoost
text: More and more orgainizations and institutions make efforts on using external data to improve the performance of AI services. To address the data privacy and security concerns, federated learning has attracted increasing attention from both academia and industry to securely construct AI models across multiple isolated data providers. In this paper, we studied the efficiency problem of adapting widely used XGBoost model in real-world applications to vertical federated learning setting. State-of-the-art vertical federated XGBoost frameworks requires large number of encryption operations and ciphertext transmissions, which makes the model training much less efficient than training XGBoost models locally. To bridge this gap, we proposed a novel batch homomorphic encryption method to cut the cost of encryption-related computation and transmission in nearly half. This is achieved by encoding the first-order derivative and the second-order derivative into a single number for encryption, ciphertext transmission, and homomorphic addition operations. The sum of multiple first-order derivatives and second-order derivatives can be simultaneously decoded from the sum of encoded values. We are motivated by the batch idea in the work of BatchCrypt for horizontal federated learning, and design a novel batch method to address the limitations of allowing quite few number of negative numbers. The encode procedure of the proposed batch method consists of four steps, including shifting, truncating, quantizing and batching, while the decoding procedure consists of de-quantization and shifting back. The advantages of our method are demonstrated through theoretical analysis and extensive numerical experiments.

title: Efficient Batch Homomorphic Encryption for Vertically Federated XGBoost
text: Vertically federated learning has emerged as a promising approach for collaborative model training across organizations, preserving data privacy and confidentiality. However, the computational overhead and communication costs of existing secure protocols hinder their adoption in real-world applications. In this context, homomorphic encryption (HE) has been identified as a key enabler for privacy-preserving machine learning, but its application to vertically federated XGBoost, a widely used gradient boosting framework, remains an open challenge. We propose an efficient batch homomorphic encryption scheme tailored for vertically federated XGBoost, which significantly reduces the computational overhead and communication costs associated with secure model training. Our scheme leverages a novel combination of lattice-based cryptography and optimized data encoding techniques, allowing for efficient batch encryption and decryption of model updates. We also develop a novel secure aggregation protocol that ensures the confidentiality and integrity of model parameters during the federated learning process. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed scheme achieves a significant reduction in computational overhead (up to 75%) and communication costs (up to 90%) compared to state-of-the-art HE-based approaches, while maintaining the accuracy and convergence guarantees of the XGBoost algorithm. Furthermore, our scheme is scalable and adaptable to varying network conditions and participant numbers, making it a viable solution for real-world vertically federated learning applications. Our work paves the way for the widespread adoption of HE-based secure protocols in vertically federated machine learning, enabling data-driven collaborations across organizations while preserving data confidentiality and privacy.

title: Cyber-Security Investment in the Context of Disruptive Technologies: Extension of the Gordon-Loeb Model
text: Cyber-security breaches inflict significant costs on organizations. Hence, the development of an information-systems defense capability through cyber-security investment is a prerequisite. The question of how to determine the optimal amount to invest in cyber-security has been widely investigated in the literature. In this respect, the Gordon-Loeb model and its extensions received wide-scale acceptance. However, such models predominantly rely on restrictive assumptions that are not adapted for analyzing dynamic aspects of cyber-security investment. Yet, understanding such dynamic aspects is a key feature for studying cyber-security investment in the context of a fast-paced and continuously evolving technological landscape. We propose an extension of the Gordon-Loeb model by considering multi-period and relaxing the assumption of a continuous security-breach probability function. Such theoretical adaptations enable to capture dynamic aspects of cyber-security investment such as the advent of a disruptive technology and its investment consequences. Such a proposed extension of the Gordon-Loeb model gives room for a hypothetical decrease of the optimal level of cyber-security investment, due to a potential technological shift. While we believe our framework should be generalizable across the cyber-security milieu, we illustrate our approach in the context of critical-infrastructure protection, where security-cost reductions related to risk events are of paramount importance as potential losses reach unaffordable proportions. Moreover, despite the fact that some technologies are considered as disruptive and thus promising for critical-infrastructure protection, their effects on cyber-security investment have been discussed little.

title: Cyber-Security Investment in the Context of Disruptive Technologies: Extension of the Gordon-Loeb Model
text: Cyber-security breaches pose substantial financial burdens on organizations, underscoring the imperative of developing a robust defense capability through strategic investment. Determining the optimal investment level has been a longstanding concern in the literature, with the Gordon-Loeb model and its variants receiving widespread acceptance. However, these models rely heavily on restrictive assumptions that fail to capture the dynamic aspects of cyber-security investment, which are crucial in the context of rapidly evolving technological landscapes. To address this limitation, we propose an extension of the Gordon-Loeb model that incorporates multi-period analysis and relaxes the assumption of a continuous security-breach probability function. This adaptation enables the capture of dynamic investment aspects, such as the emergence of disruptive technologies and their consequences on investment strategies. Our extended framework suggests that the optimal level of cyber-security investment may decrease in response to a technological shift, underscoring the need for nuanced investment decisions. We demonstrate the applicability of our approach in the context of critical-infrastructure protection, where risk-event cost reductions are vital due to the potentially catastrophic consequences of security breaches. Furthermore, our work sheds light on the underexplored impact of disruptive technologies on cyber-security investment in this domain.

title: Dependability Engineering in Isabelle
text: In this paper, we introduce a process of formal system development supported by interactive theorem proving in a dedicated Isabelle framework. This Isabelle Infrastructure framework implements specification and verification in a cyclic process supported by attack tree analysis closely inter-connected with formal refinement of the specification. The process is cyclic: in a repeated iteration the refinement adds more detail to the system specification. It is a known hard problem how to find the next refinement step: this problem is addressed by the attack based analysis using Kripke structures and CTL logic. We call this cyclic process the Refinement-Risk cycle (RR-cycle). It has been developed for security and privacy of IoT healthcare systems initially but is more generally applicable for safety as well, that is, dependability in general. In this paper, we present the extensions to the Isabelle Infrastructure framework implementing a formal notion of property preserving refinement interleaved with attack tree analysis for the RR-cycle. The process is illustrated on the specification development and privacy analysis of the mobile Corona-virus warning app.

title: Dependability Engineering in Isabelle
text: Formal verification of dependability properties in safety-critical systems is an open challenge, particularly when considering the complexity of modern software and hardware architectures. In response, we present a rigorous, proof-based approach to dependability engineering in the Isabelle theorem prover. Our methodology leverages Isabelle's higher-order logic to formally model and verify fault-tolerant systems, focusing on the compositional verification of fault trees and error propagation analysis. We demonstrate the applicability of our approach through a case study on a representative aerospace system, where we formally derive and verify dependability metrics, including reliability, availability, and maintainability. Our results show that the proposed methodology can effectively handle the complexity of real-world systems, yielding trustworthy dependability assessments and facilitating the identification of critical fault paths. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive evaluation of our approach, including a comparison with state-of-the-art model checking techniques, highlighting the benefits of our proof-based methodology in terms of scalability, expressiveness, and assurance.

title: On anti-stochastic properties of unlabeled graphs
text: We study vulnerability of a uniformly distributed random graph to an attack by an adversary who aims for a global change of the distribution while being able to make only a local change in the graph. We call a graph property $A$ anti-stochastic if the probability that a random graph $G$ satisfies $A$ is small but, with high probability, there is a small perturbation transforming $G$ into a graph satisfying $A$. While for labeled graphs such properties are easy to obtain from binary covering codes, the existence of anti-stochastic properties for unlabeled graphs is not so evident. If an admissible perturbation is either the addition or the deletion of one edge, we exhibit an anti-stochastic property that is satisfied by a random unlabeled graph of order $n$ with probability $(2+o(1))/n^2$, which is as small as possible. We also express another anti-stochastic property in terms of the degree sequence of a graph. This property has probability $(2+o(1))/(n\ln n)$, which is optimal up to factor of 2.

title: On anti-stochastic properties of unlabeled graphs
text: The study of unlabeled graphs has garnered significant attention in recent years due to their prevalence in various domains, including social networks, biological systems, and cryptography. A fundamental challenge in this context is the development of techniques that can effectively distinguish between structurally similar graphs. In this regard, stochastic properties have been widely exploited as a means of characterizing graph structure. However, the reliance on stochasticity can be limiting, particularly in scenarios where adversarial actors may intentionally manipulate graph structure to evade detection. This paper presents a novel framework for analyzing anti-stochastic properties of unlabeled graphs, which are defined as properties that are invariant under stochastic perturbations. We propose a rigorous methodology based on spectral graph theory and higher-order graph motifs to identify and quantify anti-stochastic properties. Through an extensive evaluation on a range of real-world and synthetic graph datasets, we demonstrate that our approach can effectively detect and distinguish between structurally similar graphs, even in the presence of significant stochastic noise. Our findings have important implications for graph-based anomaly detection and adversarial graph analysis in various domains.

title: Segment and Complete: Defending Object Detectors against Adversarial Patch Attacks with Robust Patch Detection
text: Object detection plays a key role in many security-critical systems. Adversarial patch attacks, which are easy to implement in the physical world, pose a serious threat to state-of-the-art object detectors. Developing reliable defenses for object detectors against patch attacks is critical but severely understudied. In this paper, we propose Segment and Complete defense (SAC), a general framework for defending object detectors against patch attacks through detection and removal of adversarial patches. We first train a patch segmenter that outputs patch masks which provide pixel-level localization of adversarial patches. We then propose a self adversarial training algorithm to robustify the patch segmenter. In addition, we design a robust shape completion algorithm, which is guaranteed to remove the entire patch from the images if the outputs of the patch segmenter are within a certain Hamming distance of the ground-truth patch masks. Our experiments on COCO and xView datasets demonstrate that SAC achieves superior robustness even under strong adaptive attacks with no reduction in performance on clean images, and generalizes well to unseen patch shapes, attack budgets, and unseen attack methods. Furthermore, we present the APRICOT-Mask dataset, which augments the APRICOT dataset with pixel-level annotations of adversarial patches. We show SAC can significantly reduce the targeted attack success rate of physical patch attacks. Our code is available at

title: Segment and Complete: Defending Object Detectors against Adversarial Patch Attacks with Robust Patch Detection
text: Object detectors, a cornerstone of computer vision, are vulnerable to adversarial patch attacks, which can mislead detectors by adding a small, specially crafted patch to the input image. These attacks pose a significant threat to a wide range of applications, from autonomous driving to surveillance systems. Existing defenses against patch attacks primarily focus on improving the robustness of the detector itself, often at the cost of computational efficiency. In contrast, we propose a novel, two-stage approach that detects and removes adversarial patches before feeding the image into the detector. Our Segment and Complete method first identifies suspicious regions in the input image using a patch detection network, and then reconstructs the original image by inpainting the detected regions. We evaluate our approach on various object detection architectures and datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness against a range of patch attack strategies. Our results show that Segment and Complete significantly improves the robustness of object detectors, reducing the attack success rate by up to 75%, while maintaining a high detection accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, we analyze the robustness of our approach against adaptive attacks, where the attacker has knowledge of our defense mechanism, and demonstrate its resilience under such scenarios. Our findings have important implications for the development of secure and reliable object detection systems in the presence of adversarial patch attacks.

title: SoK: Anti-Facial Recognition Technology
text: The rapid adoption of facial recognition (FR) technology by both government and commercial entities in recent years has raised concerns about civil liberties and privacy. In response, a broad suite of so-called "anti-facial recognition" (AFR) tools has been developed to help users avoid unwanted facial recognition. The set of AFR tools proposed in the last few years is wide-ranging and rapidly evolving, necessitating a step back to consider the broader design space of AFR systems and long-term challenges. This paper aims to fill that gap and provides the first comprehensive analysis of the AFR research landscape. Using the operational stages of FR systems as a starting point, we create a systematic framework for analyzing the benefits and tradeoffs of different AFR approaches. We then consider both technical and social challenges facing AFR tools and propose directions for future research in this field.

title: SoK: Anti-Facial Recognition Technology
text: The proliferation of facial recognition technology in both public and private sectors has sparked intense debate about individual privacy and civil liberties. As a countermeasure, a diverse array of anti-facial recognition tools has emerged, purported to enable users to evade unwanted facial scrutiny. However, the rapid evolution and expanding scope of these tools warrant a thorough examination of the overarching design space and long-term implications of anti-facial recognition systems. This study provides a comprehensive survey of the research landscape, articulating a systematic framework for evaluating the efficacy and tradeoffs of disparate anti-facial recognition approaches, anchored in the operational stages of facial recognition systems. We also elucidate the technical and social hurdles confronting these tools, outlining potential avenues for future research in this burgeoning field.

title: Building Usable Witness Encryption
text: Witness encryption using multilinear maps was first proposed in 2013, and has continued to evolve since. In this paper, we build on an open-source multilinear map implementation by Carmer and Malozemoff of the graded encoding scheme CLT13 with asymmetric modifications. Using this map, we created the world's first ciphertext encoded with a candidate witness encryption scheme. Finally, using a reduction from Sudoku to Exact Cover, we encrypted the private key to a Bitcoin wallet with 22,700 Satoshi using a Sudoku.

title: Building Usable Witness Encryption
text: We extend the concept of witness encryption, initially introduced in 2013, by leveraging an open-source implementation of the CLT13 graded encoding scheme with asymmetric modifications, courtesy of Carmer and Malozemoff. This enables the construction of the first ciphertext encoded with a candidate witness encryption scheme. Furthermore, we demonstrate the scheme's feasibility by encrypting a private Bitcoin wallet key, valued at 22,700 Satoshi, using a reduction from Sudoku to Exact Cover.

title: Efficient Checking of Temporal Compliance Rules Over Business Process Event Logs
text: Verifying temporal compliance rules, such as a rule stating that an inquiry must be answered within a time limit, is a recurrent operation in the realm of business process compliance. In this setting, a typical use case is one where a manager seeks to retrieve all cases where a temporal rule is violated, given an event log recording the execution of a process over a time period. Existing approaches for checking temporal rules require a full scan of the log. Such approaches are unsuitable for interactive use when the log is large and the set of compliance rules is evolving. This paper proposes an approach to evaluate temporal compliance rules in sublinear time by pre-computing a data structure that summarizes the temporal relations between activities in a log. The approach caters for a wide range of temporal compliance patterns and supports incremental updates. Our evaluation on twenty real-life logs shows that our data structure allows for real-time checking of a large set of compliance rules.

title: Efficient Checking of Temporal Compliance Rules Over Business Process Event Logs
text: Temporal compliance rules, which dictate constraints on the timing of process activities, are a crucial aspect of business process compliance. A common scenario involves identifying instances of non-compliance, given an event log capturing process execution over time. Conventional methods for verifying temporal rules necessitate a complete log scan, rendering them impractical for interactive applications with large logs and dynamic rule sets. This research presents a novel approach that enables sublinear-time evaluation of temporal compliance rules by pre-computing a data structure encapsulating temporal relationships between activities within a log. This approach accommodates a diverse range of temporal compliance patterns and supports incremental updates. Empirical evaluation on twenty real-world logs demonstrates that our data structure facilitates real-time compliance checking for a large set of rules, thereby addressing the limitations of existing methods.

title: Process Mining-Driven Analysis of the COVID19 Impact on the Vaccinations of Victorian Patients
text: Process mining is a discipline sitting between data mining and process science, whose goal is to provide theoretical methods and software tools to analyse process execution data, known as event logs. Although process mining was originally conceived to facilitate business process management activities, research studies have shown the benefit of leveraging process mining tools in different contexts, including healthcare. However, applying process mining tools to analyse healthcare process execution data is not straightforward. In this paper, we report the analysis of an event log recording more than 30 million events capturing the general practice healthcare processes of more than one million patients in Victoria--Australia--over five years. Our analysis allowed us to understand benefits and limitations of the state-of-the-art process mining techniques when dealing with highly variable processes and large data-sets. While we provide solutions to the identified limitations, the overarching goal of this study was to detect differences between the patients` health services utilization pattern observed in 2020--during the COVID-19 pandemic and mandatory lock-downs --and the one observed in the prior four years, 2016 to 2019. By using a combination of process mining techniques and traditional data mining, we were able to demonstrate that vaccinations in Victoria did not drop drastically--as other interactions did. On the contrary, we observed a surge of influenza and pneumococcus vaccinations in 2020, contradicting research findings of similar studies conducted in different geographical areas.

title: Process Mining-Driven Analysis of the COVID19 Impact on the Vaccinations of Victorian Patients
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly disrupted healthcare systems worldwide, with vaccination programs being particularly affected. In Victoria, Australia, the vaccination process has been severely impacted, leading to delays and inefficiencies. To better understand the impact of COVID-19 on vaccination processes, we propose a process mining-driven approach to analyze the vaccination data of Victorian patients. We leverage the MIMIC-IV dataset, which contains electronic health records of patients in Victoria, and apply process mining techniques to reconstruct the vaccination processes. Our methodology involves extracting event logs from the MIMIC-IV dataset, which are then used to construct process models using the ProM framework. We apply conformance checking and enhancement techniques to identify deviations and inefficiencies in the vaccination process. Our results show that the COVID-19 pandemic has significantly increased the cycle time of vaccination processes, with an average delay of 34.7 days. We also identify bottlenecks in the process, including delays in vaccine administration and inadequate staffing. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the pandemic has led to a significant increase in process variability, with 23.1% of patients experiencing deviations from the standard vaccination process. Our findings have important implications for healthcare policymakers and practitioners, highlighting the need for process improvements and resource reallocation to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 on vaccination programs. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of process mining in analyzing and improving healthcare processes, particularly in the context of pandemic response.

title: Differentially Private Ensemble Classifiers for Data Streams
text: Learning from continuous data streams via classification/regression is prevalent in many domains. Adapting to evolving data characteristics (concept drift) while protecting data owners' private information is an open challenge. We present a differentially private ensemble solution to this problem with two distinguishing features: it allows an \textit{unbounded} number of ensemble updates to deal with the potentially never-ending data streams under a fixed privacy budget, and it is \textit{model agnostic}, in that it treats any pre-trained differentially private classification/regression model as a black-box. Our method outperforms competitors on real-world and simulated datasets for varying settings of privacy, concept drift, and data distribution.

title: Differentially Private Ensemble Classifiers for Data Streams
text: Classifying and regressing continuous data streams is a ubiquitous task across various domains, yet adapting to concept drift while preserving data privacy remains an unresolved issue. We propose a novel, differentially private ensemble approach that tackles this challenge by accommodating an unlimited number of updates within a fixed privacy budget, thereby catering to infinite data streams. Furthermore, our method is model-agnostic, treating any pre-trained, differentially private classification or regression model as a black box. Experimental results on real-world and simulated datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our approach under diverse settings of privacy, concept drift, and data distribution.

title: OPTT: Optimal Piecewise Transformation Technique for Analyzing Numerical Data under Local Differential Privacy
text: Privacy preserving data analysis (PPDA) has received increasing attention due to a great variety of applications. Local differential privacy (LDP), as an emerging standard that is suitable for PPDA, has been widely deployed into various real-world scenarios to analyze massive data while protecting against many forms of privacy breach. In this study, we are mainly concerned with piecewise transformation technique (PTT) for analyzing numerical data under local differential privacy. We provide a principled framework for PTT in the context of LDP, based on which PTT is studied systematically. As a result, we show that (1) many members in PTTs are asymptotically optimal when used to obtain an unbiased estimator for mean of numerical data, and (2) for a given privacy budget, there is PTT that reaches the theoretical low bound with respect to variance. Next, we prove by studying two classes of PTTs in detail that (1) there do not exist optimal PTTs compared to the well-used technique, i.e., Duchi's scheme, in terms of the consistency noisy variance, (2) on the other hand, one has the ability to find a great number of PTTs that are consistently more optimal than the latter with regard to the worst-case noisy variance, which is never reported so far. When we are restricted to consider only the high privacy level, enough PTTs turn out to be optimal than the well-known Laplace mechanism. Lastly, we prove that for a family of PTTs, the correspondingly theoretical low bound of noisy variance follows $O(ε^{-2})$ when considering the high privacy level.

title: OPTT: Optimal Piecewise Transformation Technique for Analyzing Numerical Data under Local Differential Privacy
text: The proliferation of sensitive numerical data has necessitated the development of privacy-preserving techniques for analysis. Local differential privacy (LDP) has emerged as a promising paradigm, enabling clients to perturb their data locally before sharing it with an untrusted aggregator. However, existing LDP mechanisms often compromise on utility, particularly when dealing with skewed or heterogeneous distributions. We propose OPTT, a novel Optimal Piecewise Transformation Technique that achieves a superior tradeoff between privacy and utility for numerical data analysis under LDP. OPTT partitions the data domain into disjoint intervals and applies a customized perturbation mechanism to each segment, carefully calibrating the noise levels to minimize information loss. By adaptively adjusting the partition boundaries and noise scales, OPTT optimizes the privacy-utility frontier, outperforming state-of-the-art LDP techniques. Our theoretical analysis establishes the privacy guarantees of OPTT, demonstrating that it satisfies (ε, δ)-LDP. We also provide a thorough empirical evaluation, using a range of real-world datasets and analytical tasks, including mean and variance estimation, frequency analysis, and outlier detection. The results show that OPTT consistently outperforms existing LDP mechanisms, often by a significant margin, while maintaining strong privacy guarantees. Notably, OPTT's flexibility and adaptability enable it to effectively handle diverse data distributions, including those with heavy tails or multimodal structures. Our technique has far-reaching implications for various applications, such as smart metering, location-based services, and personalized recommendation systems, where sensitive numerical data is increasingly prevalent. By providing a robust and efficient framework for private numerical data analysis, OPTT has the potential to significantly impact the development of privacy-preserving data analytics.

title: Justifying the Dependability and Security of Business-Critical Blockchain-based Applications
text: In the industry, blockchains are increasingly used as the backbone of product and process traceability. Blockchain-based traceability participates in the demonstration of product and/or process compliance with existing safety standards or quality criteria. In this perspective, services and applications built on top of blockchains are business-critical applications, because an intended failure or corruption of the system can lead to an important reputation loss regarding the products or the processes involved. The development of a blockchain-based business-critical application must be then conducted carefully, requiring a thorough justification of its dependability and security. To this end, this paper encourages an engineering perspective rooted in well-understood tools and concepts borrowed from the engineering of safety-critical systems. Concretely, we use a justification framework, called CAE (Claim, Argument, Evidence), by following an approach based on assurance cases, in order to provide convincing arguments that a business-critical blockchain-based application is dependable and secure. The application of this approach is sketched with a case study based on the blockchain HYPERLEDGER FABRIC.

title: Justifying the Dependability and Security of Business-Critical Blockchain-based Applications
text: The increasing adoption of blockchain technology in industry has led to its widespread use as a foundation for product and process traceability, enabling the demonstration of compliance with safety standards and quality criteria. As blockchain-based applications assume a business-critical role, their failure or corruption can result in significant reputational damage to products and processes. Consequently, the development of such applications demands a rigorous approach to ensure their dependability and security. This paper advocates for an engineering perspective grounded in established tools and concepts from the safety-critical systems domain. Specifically, we employ the Claim, Argument, Evidence (CAE) justification framework, rooted in assurance cases, to provide robust arguments for the dependability and security of business-critical blockchain-based applications. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through a case study using the Hyperledger Fabric blockchain platform, highlighting its potential to instill confidence in the reliability of these critical systems.

title: How Not to Protect Your IP -- An Industry-Wide Break of IEEE 1735 Implementations
text: Modern hardware systems are composed of a variety of third-party Intellectual Property (IP) cores to implement their overall functionality. Since hardware design is a globalized process involving various (untrusted) stakeholders, a secure management of the valuable IP between authors and users is inevitable to protect them from unauthorized access and modification. To this end, the widely adopted IEEE standard 1735-2014 was created to ensure confidentiality and integrity. In this paper, we outline structural weaknesses in IEEE 1735 that cannot be fixed with cryptographic solutions (given the contemporary hardware design process) and thus render the standard inherently insecure. We practically demonstrate the weaknesses by recovering the private keys of IEEE 1735 implementations from major Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tool vendors, namely Intel, Xilinx, Cadence, Siemens, Microsemi, and Lattice, while results on a seventh case study are withheld. As a consequence, we can decrypt, modify, and re-encrypt all allegedly protected IP cores designed for the respective tools, thus leading to an industry-wide break. As part of this analysis, we are the first to publicly disclose three RSA-based white-box schemes that are used in real-world products and present cryptanalytical attacks for all of them, finally resulting in key recovery.

title: How Not to Protect Your IP -- An Industry-Wide Break of IEEE 1735 Implementations
text: The IEEE 1735 standard for encrypting intellectual property (IP) in electronic design automation (EDA) is widely adopted across the semiconductor industry. Despite its purported security guarantees, we demonstrate that implementations of IEEE 1735 by major EDA vendors are vulnerable to a devastating key recovery attack. Our attack exploits a previously unknown vulnerability in the standard's encryption scheme, which stems from an insufficiently secure pseudorandom number generator. We developed a custom fuzz testing framework to systematically analyze the encryption implementations of seven prominent EDA vendors, including Synopsys, Cadence, and Mentor Graphics. Our results show that all vendors' implementations are susceptible to our attack, allowing an attacker to recover the IP encryption key with minimal computational effort. We successfully extracted sensitive IP from encrypted designs, including a commercial system-on-chip (SoC) and a proprietary GPU architecture. The implications of our findings are severe, as they undermine the trustworthiness of the entire EDA ecosystem. We notify the affected vendors and provide recommendations for remediation. Our work highlights the need for rigorous security audits in the EDA industry and underscores the importance of proactive vulnerability disclosure.

title: A Qualitative Study on the Sources, Impacts, and Mitigation Strategies of Flaky Tests
text: Test flakiness forms a major testing concern. Flaky tests manifest non-deterministic outcomes that cripple continuous integration and lead developers to investigate false alerts. Industrial reports indicate that on a large scale, the accrual of flaky tests breaks the trust in test suites and entails significant computational cost. To alleviate this, practitioners are constrained to identify flaky tests and investigate their impact. To shed light on such mitigation mechanisms, we interview 14 practitioners with the aim to identify (i) the sources of flakiness within the testing ecosystem, (ii) the impacts of flakiness, (iii) the measures adopted by practitioners when addressing flakiness, and (iv) the automation opportunities for these measures. Our analysis shows that, besides the tests and code, flakiness stems from interactions between the system components, the testing infrastructure, and external factors. We also highlight the impact of flakiness on testing practices and product quality and show that the adoption of guidelines together with a stable infrastructure are key measures in mitigating the problem.

title: A Qualitative Study on the Sources, Impacts, and Mitigation Strategies of Flaky Tests
text: Flaky tests, which exhibit intermittent pass or fail behavior, are a pervasive issue in software testing, causing wasted resources, delayed releases, and decreased confidence in automated testing. Despite their prevalence, the root causes and consequences of flaky tests are not well understood. This qualitative study aims to fill this knowledge gap by investigating the sources, impacts, and mitigation strategies of flaky tests through a mixed-methods approach. We conducted 22 semi-structured interviews with experienced software developers and testers from 15 companies, and analyzed 1,500 flaky test reports from three open-source projects. Our findings identify 13 sources of flakiness, including infrastructure issues, concurrency problems, and test data dependencies. We also uncover significant impacts on testing efficiency, developer morale, and product quality. Furthermore, we distill 10 mitigation strategies, such as test refactoring, parallelization, and result caching, which are currently employed by practitioners to alleviate flakiness. Our study provides actionable insights for software practitioners, researchers, and managers to better understand and address the flaky test problem in their organizations.

title: Automated Side Channel Analysis of Media Software with Manifold Learning
text: The prosperous development of cloud computing and machine learning as a service has led to the widespread use of media software to process confidential media data. This paper explores an adversary's ability to launch side channel analyses (SCA) against media software to reconstruct confidential media inputs. Recent advances in representation learning and perceptual learning inspired us to consider the reconstruction of media inputs from side channel traces as a cross-modality manifold learning task that can be addressed in a unified manner with an autoencoder framework trained to learn the mapping between media inputs and side channel observations. We further enhance the autoencoder with attention to localize the program points that make the primary contribution to SCA, thus automatically pinpointing information-leakage points in media software. We also propose a novel and highly effective defensive technique called perception blinding that can perturb media inputs with perception masks and mitigate manifold learning-based SCA.
