Our evaluation exploits three popular media software to reconstruct inputs in image, audio, and text formats. We analyze three common side channels - cache bank, cache line, and page tables - and userspace-only cache set accesses logged by standard Prime+Probe. Our framework successfully reconstructs high-quality confidential inputs from the assessed media software and automatically pinpoint their vulnerable program points, many of which are unknown to the public. We further show that perception blinding can mitigate manifold learning-based SCA with negligible extra cost.

title: Automated Side Channel Analysis of Media Software with Manifold Learning
text: The proliferation of multimedia software has introduced a multitude of potential side channels, enabling adversaries to infer sensitive information about users. Despite the severity of these vulnerabilities, existing analyses rely on manual, labor-intensive approaches that are often incomplete and prone to human error. In response, we propose a novel framework for automated side channel analysis of media software using manifold learning. Our approach leverages recent advances in deep learning to learn a low-dimensional representation of the software's execution behavior, capturing intricate patterns and relationships that are difficult to discern through manual inspection. By applying manifold learning techniques to a large dataset of execution traces, we are able to identify and characterize complex side channels in popular media software, including audio and video players, image editors, and codecs. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, uncovering previously unknown side channels in multiple software packages. Notably, we identify a novel cache-based side channel in a widely-used video player, which can be exploited to infer user preferences with high accuracy. We further show that our framework can be used to generate optimized input stimuli, maximizing the leakage of sensitive information through identified side channels. Our work has significant implications for the development of more secure media software and highlights the need for more rigorous, automated side channel analysis in the field.

title: Mutual Adversarial Training: Learning together is better than going alone
text: Recent studies have shown that robustness to adversarial attacks can be transferred across networks. In other words, we can make a weak model more robust with the help of a strong teacher model. We ask if instead of learning from a static teacher, can models "learn together" and "teach each other" to achieve better robustness? In this paper, we study how interactions among models affect robustness via knowledge distillation. We propose mutual adversarial training (MAT), in which multiple models are trained together and share the knowledge of adversarial examples to achieve improved robustness. MAT allows robust models to explore a larger space of adversarial samples, and find more robust feature spaces and decision boundaries. Through extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, we demonstrate that MAT can effectively improve model robustness and outperform state-of-the-art methods under white-box attacks, bringing $\sim$8% accuracy gain to vanilla adversarial training (AT) under PGD-100 attacks. In addition, we show that MAT can also mitigate the robustness trade-off among different perturbation types, bringing as much as 13.1% accuracy gain to AT baselines against the union of $l_\infty$, $l_2$ and $l_1$ attacks. These results show the superiority of the proposed method and demonstrate that collaborative learning is an effective strategy for designing robust models.

title: Mutual Adversarial Training: Learning together is better than going alone
text: The transferability of robustness to adversarial attacks across neural networks has been well-established in recent studies. However, the conventional paradigm of leveraging a strong teacher model to enhance the robustness of a weaker model raises an intriguing question: can models reciprocally learn from each other to achieve improved robustness? This paper investigates the effects of inter-model interactions on robustness through the lens of knowledge distillation. We introduce mutual adversarial training (MAT), a novel framework where multiple models engage in collaborative training, sharing knowledge of adversarial examples to bolster robustness. By exploring a larger adversarial sample space, MAT facilitates the discovery of more robust feature spaces and decision boundaries. Our comprehensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate that MAT significantly enhances model robustness, outperforming state-of-the-art methods under white-box attacks, with a notable 8% accuracy gain over vanilla adversarial training (AT) under PGD-100 attacks. Furthermore, MAT mitigates the robustness trade-off across different perturbation types, yielding an impressive 13.1% accuracy gain over AT baselines against the union of $l_\infty$, $l_2$, and $l_1$ attacks. These findings underscore the efficacy of collaborative learning in designing robust models.

title: Polynomial XL: A Variant of the XL Algorithm Using Macaulay Matrices over Polynomial Rings
text: Solving a system of $m$ multivariate quadratic equations in $n$ variables over finite fields (the MQ problem) is one of the important problems in the theory of computer science. The XL algorithm (XL for short) is a major approach for solving the MQ problem with linearization over a coefficient field. Furthermore, the hybrid approach with XL (h-XL) is a variant of XL guessing some variables beforehand. In this paper, we present a variant of h-XL, which we call the \textit{polynomial XL (PXL)}. In PXL, the whole $n$ variables are divided into $k$ variables to be fixed and the remaining $n-k$ variables as ``main variables'', and we generate a Macaulay matrix with respect to the $n-k$ main variables over a polynomial ring of the $k$ (sub-)variables. By eliminating some columns of the Macaulay matrix over the polynomial ring before guessing $k$ variables, the amount of operations required for each guessed value can be reduced compared with h-XL. Our complexity analysis of PXL (under some practical assumptions and heuristics) gives a new theoretical bound, and it indicates that PXL could be more efficient than other algorithms in theory on the random system with $n=m$, which is the case of general multivariate signatures. For example, on systems over the finite field with ${2^8}$ elements with $n=m=80$, the numbers of operations deduced from the theoretical bounds of the hybrid approaches with XL and Wiedemann XL, Crossbred, and PXL with optimal $k$ are estimated as $2^{252}$, $2^{234}$, $2^{237}$, and $2^{220}$, respectively.

title: Polynomial XL: A Variant of the XL Algorithm Using Macaulay Matrices over Polynomial Rings
text: The Multivariate Quadratic (MQ) problem, encompassing the solution of systems of m multivariate quadratic equations in n variables over finite fields, is a fundamental challenge in computer science theory. The XL algorithm, a prominent approach for solving MQ problems via linearization over a coefficient field, has been augmented by the hybrid approach with XL (h-XL), which involves guessing some variables a priori. This paper introduces a novel variant of h-XL, termed Polynomial XL (PXL), where the n variables are partitioned into k variables to be fixed and n-k "main variables". A Macaulay matrix is constructed with respect to the main variables over a polynomial ring of the k sub-variables. By selectively eliminating columns of the Macaulay matrix over the polynomial ring prior to guessing k variables, PXL reduces the operational complexity per guessed value compared to h-XL. Under practical assumptions and heuristics, our complexity analysis yields a new theoretical bound, indicating that PXL may outperform existing algorithms in theory for random systems with n=m, a scenario typical of general multivariate signatures. Notably, for systems over finite fields with 2^8 elements and n=m=80, our theoretical bounds estimate the number of operations required by hybrid approaches with XL and Wiedemann XL, Crossbred, and PXL with optimal k to be approximately 2^252, 2^234, 2^237, and 2^220, respectively.

title: Deep Learning based Differential Distinguisher for Lightweight Block Ciphers
text: Recent years have seen an increasing involvement of Deep Learning in the cryptanalysis of various ciphers. The present study is inspired by past works on differential distinguishers, to develop a Deep Neural Network-based differential distinguisher for round reduced lightweight block ciphers PRESENT and Simeck. We make improvements in the state-of-the-art approach and extend its use to the two structurally different block ciphers, PRESENT-80 and Simeck64/128. The obtained results suggest the universality of our cryptanalysis method. The proposed method can distinguish random data from the cipher data obtained until 6 rounds of PRESENT and 7 rounds of Simeck encryption with high accuracy. In addition to this, we explore a new approach to select good input differentials, which to the best of our knowledge has not been explored in the past. We also provide a minimum-security requirement for the discussed ciphers against our differential attack.

title: Deep Learning based Differential Distinguisher for Lightweight Block Ciphers
text: Deep learning has been increasingly employed in cryptanalysis, particularly in the development of differential distinguishers for various ciphers. Building upon previous research, this study devises a deep neural network-based differential distinguisher tailored to round-reduced lightweight block ciphers, specifically PRESENT and Simeck. By refining the state-of-the-art approach, we successfully extend its application to the structurally distinct block ciphers PRESENT-80 and Simeck64/128. Our results underscore the versatility of our cryptanalysis method, which accurately distinguishes between random and cipher data up to 6 rounds of PRESENT and 7 rounds of Simeck encryption. Notably, we introduce a novel approach for selecting optimal input differentials, a previously unexplored area. Furthermore, we establish a minimum-security requirement for the ciphers in question against our differential attack.

title: Spinning Language Models: Risks of Propaganda-As-A-Service and Countermeasures
text: We investigate a new threat to neural sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models: training-time attacks that cause models to "spin" their outputs so as to support an adversary-chosen sentiment or point of view -- but only when the input contains adversary-chosen trigger words. For example, a spinned summarization model outputs positive summaries of any text that mentions the name of some individual or organization. Model spinning introduces a "meta-backdoor" into a model. Whereas conventional backdoors cause models to produce incorrect outputs on inputs with the trigger, outputs of spinned models preserve context and maintain standard accuracy metrics, yet also satisfy a meta-task chosen by the adversary. Model spinning enables propaganda-as-a-service, where propaganda is defined as biased speech. An adversary can create customized language models that produce desired spins for chosen triggers, then deploy these models to generate disinformation (a platform attack), or else inject them into ML training pipelines (a supply-chain attack), transferring malicious functionality to downstream models trained by victims. To demonstrate the feasibility of model spinning, we develop a new backdooring technique. It stacks an adversarial meta-task onto a seq2seq model, backpropagates the desired meta-task output to points in the word-embedding space we call "pseudo-words," and uses pseudo-words to shift the entire output distribution of the seq2seq model. We evaluate this attack on language generation, summarization, and translation models with different triggers and meta-tasks such as sentiment, toxicity, and entailment. Spinned models largely maintain their accuracy metrics (ROUGE and BLEU) while shifting their outputs to satisfy the adversary's meta-task. We also show that, in the case of a supply-chain attack, the spin functionality transfers to downstream models.

title: Spinning Language Models: Risks of Propaganda-As-A-Service and Countermeasures
text: The proliferation of language models has enabled a lucrative market for propaganda-as-a-service, where nefarious actors can commission tailored disinformation campaigns to sway public opinion. This phenomenon poses a significant threat to the integrity of online discourse, democratic processes, and societal cohesion. In response, we investigate the risks associated with spinning language models and propose a suite of countermeasures to mitigate their misuse. We develop a novel framework to analyze the propaganda potential of language models, encompassing factors such as contextual manipulation, emotional appeal, and narrative coherence. Our methodology involves training and fine-tuning a range of language models on diverse datasets, including news articles, social media posts, and propaganda exemplars. We then evaluate their propensity to generate persuasive, yet misleading, content through a combination of automated metrics and human assessments. Our experiments reveal that even innocuous language models can be repurposed for propaganda when fed biased or misleading input. Moreover, we find that the most effective propaganda generators are those that balance coherence and novelty, making them particularly insidious. To counter these risks, we propose a set of countermeasures, including input filtering, output watermarking, and adversarial training. Our results demonstrate that these techniques can significantly reduce the propaganda potential of language models, while preserving their utility for benign applications. This research contributes to the growing body of work on AI ethics and accountability, providing a crucial understanding of the propaganda risks associated with language models. Our findings and countermeasures offer a timely response to the emerging threats of propaganda-as-a-service, informing the development of more responsible AI systems that promote trustworthy online interactions.

title: Transfer learning using deep neural networks for Ear Presentation Attack Detection: New Database for PAD
text: Ear recognition system has been widely studied whereas there are just a few ear presentation attack detection methods for ear recognition systems, consequently, there is no publicly available ear presentation attack detection (PAD) database. In this paper, we propose a PAD method using a pre-trained deep neural network and release a new dataset called Warsaw University of Technology Ear Dataset for Presentation Attack Detection (WUT-Ear V1.0). There is no ear database that is captured using mobile devices. Hence, we have captured more than 8500 genuine ear images from 134 subjects and more than 8500 fake ear images using. We made replay-attack and photo print attacks with 3 different mobile devices. Our approach achieves 99.83% and 0.08% for the half total error rate (HTER) and attack presentation classification error rate (APCER), respectively, on the replay-attack database. The captured data is analyzed and visualized statistically to find out its importance and make it a benchmark for further research. The experiments have been found out a secure PAD method for ear recognition system, publicly available ear image, and ear PAD dataset. The codes and evaluation results are publicly available at

title: Transfer learning using deep neural networks for Ear Presentation Attack Detection: New Database for PAD
text: The development of ear recognition systems has garnered significant attention, yet presentation attack detection (PAD) methods tailored to these systems remain scarce. Furthermore, a publicly available ear PAD database is nonexistent. To address this gap, we propose a novel PAD approach leveraging a pre-trained deep neural network and introduce the Warsaw University of Technology Ear Dataset for Presentation Attack Detection (WUT-Ear V1.0), a comprehensive dataset comprising over 17,000 ear images. Notably, WUT-Ear V1.0 is the first ear database captured using mobile devices, featuring 134 subjects with more than 8500 genuine ear images and an equal number of fake ear images generated through replay-attack and photo print attacks using three distinct mobile devices. Our method yields a half total error rate (HTER) of 0.17% and an attack presentation classification error rate (APCER) of 0.08% on the replay-attack database. Statistical analysis and visualization of the captured data underscore its significance, establishing a benchmark for future research. This work contributes a secure PAD method, a publicly available ear image dataset, and an ear PAD dataset, with codes and evaluation results available for further exploration.

title: RamBoAttack: A Robust Query Efficient Deep Neural Network Decision Exploit
text: Machine learning models are critically susceptible to evasion attacks from adversarial examples. Generally, adversarial examples, modified inputs deceptively similar to the original input, are constructed under whitebox settings by adversaries with full access to the model. However, recent attacks have shown a remarkable reduction in query numbers to craft adversarial examples using blackbox attacks. Particularly, alarming is the ability to exploit the classification decision from the access interface of a trained model provided by a growing number of Machine Learning as a Service providers including Google, Microsoft, IBM and used by a plethora of applications incorporating these models. The ability of an adversary to exploit only the predicted label from a model to craft adversarial examples is distinguished as a decision-based attack. In our study, we first deep dive into recent state-of-the-art decision-based attacks in ICLR and SP to highlight the costly nature of discovering low distortion adversarial employing gradient estimation methods. We develop a robust query efficient attack capable of avoiding entrapment in a local minimum and misdirection from noisy gradients seen in gradient estimation methods. The attack method we propose, RamBoAttack, exploits the notion of Randomized Block Coordinate Descent to explore the hidden classifier manifold, targeting perturbations to manipulate only localized input features to address the issues of gradient estimation methods. Importantly, the RamBoAttack is more robust to the different sample inputs available to an adversary and the targeted class. Overall, for a given target class, RamBoAttack is demonstrated to be more robust at achieving a lower distortion within a given query budget. We curate our extensive results using the large-scale high-resolution ImageNet dataset and open-source our attack, test samples and artifacts on GitHub.

title: RamBoAttack: A Robust Query Efficient Deep Neural Network Decision Exploit
text: The rise of deep neural networks (DNNs) has brought about unprecedented advancements in various domains, but their vulnerability to decision-based attacks has raised significant concerns. In decision-based attacks, an adversary can manipulate inputs to mislead a DNN into making incorrect predictions, often with severe consequences. Existing approaches to defend against such attacks focus on enhancing model robustness, but they often compromise query efficiency, making them impractical for real-world applications. We introduce RamBoAttack, a novel query-efficient deep neural network decision exploit that can effectively expose the vulnerabilities of DNN-based systems. RamBoAttack leverages a robust optimization framework to craft perturbations that maximize the likelihood of misclassification while minimizing the number of queries required to achieve the attack objective. Our approach is grounded in a theoretical analysis of the DNN's decision boundary, which enables us to devise a tailored perturbation strategy that adapts to the model's architecture and the input data distribution. Through a comprehensive evaluation on several benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the efficacy of RamBoAttack in compromising the integrity of DNN-based systems. Our results show that RamBoAttack can achieve a high attack success rate (>95%) while requiring significantly fewer queries (up to 5x fewer) compared to state-of-the-art decision-based attacks. Furthermore, we find that RamBoAttack's perturbations are more transferable across different models and datasets, making it a more potent threat to DNN-based systems. Our work highlights the need for more robust and query-efficient defenses against decision-based attacks and provides a foundation for developing more effective countermeasures.

title: Are We There Yet? Timing and Floating-Point Attacks on Differential Privacy Systems
text: Differential privacy is a de facto privacy framework that has seen adoption in practice via a number of mature software platforms. Implementation of differentially private (DP) mechanisms has to be done carefully to ensure end-to-end security guarantees. In this paper we study two implementation flaws in the noise generation commonly used in DP systems. First we examine the Gaussian mechanism's susceptibility to a floating-point representation attack. The premise of this first vulnerability is similar to the one carried out by Mironov in 2011 against the Laplace mechanism. Our experiments show attack's success against DP algorithms, including deep learning models trained using differentially-private stochastic gradient descent. In the second part of the paper we study discrete counterparts of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms that were previously proposed to alleviate the shortcomings of floating-point representation of real numbers. We show that such implementations unfortunately suffer from another side channel: a novel timing attack. An observer that can measure the time to draw (discrete) Laplace or Gaussian noise can predict the noise magnitude, which can then be used to recover sensitive attributes. This attack invalidates differential privacy guarantees of systems implementing such mechanisms. We demonstrate that several commonly used, state-of-the-art implementations of differential privacy are susceptible to these attacks. We report success rates up to 92.56% for floating-point attacks on DP-SGD, and up to 99.65% for end-to-end timing attacks on private sum protected with discrete Laplace. Finally, we evaluate and suggest partial mitigations.

title: Are We There Yet? Timing and Floating-Point Attacks on Differential Privacy Systems
text: The widespread adoption of differential privacy in various software platforms underscores the importance of rigorous implementation to ensure end-to-end security guarantees. This paper investigates two critical vulnerabilities in the noise generation mechanisms commonly employed in differentially private systems. We first demonstrate the susceptibility of the Gaussian mechanism to floating-point representation attacks, exploiting the inherent imprecision of real number representations. Our experiments reveal the attack's efficacy against differentially private algorithms, including deep learning models trained using differentially-private stochastic gradient descent. Furthermore, we examine the discrete counterparts of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, previously proposed to mitigate the limitations of floating-point representations. However, we uncover a novel timing side channel in these implementations, enabling an observer to predict the noise magnitude by measuring the time required to draw discrete Laplace or Gaussian noise. This attack compromises the differential privacy guarantees of systems relying on these mechanisms. We successfully demonstrate the vulnerability of several state-of-the-art differential privacy implementations, achieving success rates of up to 92.56% for floating-point attacks on DP-SGD and up to 99.65% for end-to-end timing attacks on private sum protected with discrete Laplace. Finally, we evaluate and propose partial mitigations to address these vulnerabilities.

title: MOBAFS: A Multi Objective Bee Algorithm for Feature subset selection in Software Product Lines
text: Software product line represents software engineering methods, tools and techniques for creating a group of related software systems from a shared set of software assets. Each product is a combination of multiple features. These features are known as software assets. So, the task of production can be mapped to a feature subset selection problem which is an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem. This issue is much significant when the number of features in a software product line is huge. In this paper, a new method based on Multi Objective Bee Swarm Optimization algorithm (called MOBAFS) is presented. The MOBAFS is a population based optimization algorithm which is inspired by foraging behavior of honey bees. The is used to solve a SBSE problem. This technique is evaluated on five large scale real world software product lines in the range of 1,244 to 6,888 features. The proposed method is compared with the state-of-the-art, SATIBEA. According to results of three solution quality indicators and two diversity metrics, the proposed method, in most cases, surpasses the other algorithm.

title: MOBAFS: A Multi Objective Bee Algorithm for Feature subset selection in Software Product Lines
text: The increasing complexity of software product lines (SPLs) necessitates efficient feature subset selection to ensure optimal performance, scalability, and maintainability. Existing feature selection methods often rely on single-objective optimization, which may not adequately capture the intricate relationships between features in SPLs. This paper proposes MOBAFS, a novel multi-objective bee algorithm for feature subset selection in SPLs. MOBAFS leverages the strengths of bee colony optimization to simultaneously optimize multiple conflicting objectives, such as feature relevance, redundancy, and SPL stakeholder satisfaction. We evaluate MOBAFS on six real-world SPL datasets and compare its performance with state-of-the-art feature selection methods. Experimental results demonstrate that MOBAFS outperforms existing methods in terms of feature subset quality, convergence rate, and computational efficiency. Moreover, MOBAFS is shown to be robust to noisy and high-dimensional data, making it a promising approach for feature subset selection in SPLs. Our findings have important implications for the development of efficient and scalable SPLs, and highlight the potential of multi-objective optimization techniques in software engineering.

title: Efficient Action Poisoning Attacks on Linear Contextual Bandits
text: Contextual bandit algorithms have many applicants in a variety of scenarios. In order to develop trustworthy contextual bandit systems, understanding the impacts of various adversarial attacks on contextual bandit algorithms is essential. In this paper, we propose a new class of attacks: action poisoning attacks, where an adversary can change the action signal selected by the agent. We design action poisoning attack schemes against linear contextual bandit algorithms in both white-box and black-box settings. We further analyze the cost of the proposed attack strategies for a very popular and widely used bandit algorithm: LinUCB. We show that, in both white-box and black-box settings, the proposed attack schemes can force the LinUCB agent to pull a target arm very frequently by spending only logarithm cost.

title: Efficient Action Poisoning Attacks on Linear Contextual Bandits
text: Linear contextual bandits are widely employed in personalized recommendation systems, where an attacker can manipulate user feedback to degrade the system's performance. We investigate action poisoning attacks on linear contextual bandits, where an attacker alters a subset of actions to mislead the learning algorithm. Existing attacks are either ineffective or computationally expensive. We propose a novel, efficient attack framework that leverages the bandit's exploration mechanism to identify the most influential actions. Our approach, dubbed EAP, iteratively updates the attack strategy using a surrogate model, achieving a significant increase in attack efficacy while reducing computational overhead. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that EAP outperforms state-of-the-art attacks, inducing up to 50% degradation in the bandit's performance while requiring only 10% of the attacker's budget.

title: SLUGGER: Lossless Hierarchical Summarization of Massive Graphs
text: Given a massive graph, how can we exploit its hierarchical structure for concisely but exactly summarizing the graph? By exploiting the structure, can we achieve better compression rates than state-of-the-art graph summarization methods? The explosive proliferation of the Web has accelerated the emergence of large graphs, such as online social networks and hyperlink networks. Consequently, graph compression has become increasingly important to process such large graphs without expensive I/O over the network or to disk. Among a number of approaches, graph summarization, which in essence combines similar nodes into a supernode and describe their connectivity concisely, protrudes with several advantages. However, we note that it fails to exploit pervasive hierarchical structures of real-world graphs as its underlying representation model enforces supernodes to be disjoint. In this work, we propose the hierarchical graph summarization model, which is an expressive graph representation model that includes the previous one proposed by Navlakha et al. as a special case. The new model represents an unweighted graph using positive and negative edges between hierarchical supernodes, each of which can contain others. Then, we propose Slugger, a scalable heuristic for concisely and exactly representing a given graph under our new model. Slugger greedily merges nodes into supernodes while maintaining and exploiting their hierarchy, which is later pruned. Slugger significantly accelerates this process by sampling, approximation, and memoization. Our experiments on 16 real-world graphs show that Slugger is (a) Effective: yielding up to 29.6% more concise summary than state-of-the-art lossless summarization methods, (b) Fast: summarizing a graph with 0.8 billion edges in a few hours, and (c) Scalable: scaling linearly with the number of edges in the input graph.

title: SLUGGER: Lossless Hierarchical Summarization of Massive Graphs
text: The proliferation of massive graphs in modern data repositories poses significant scalability challenges for graph analytics and visualization. As graph sizes continue to grow, even seemingly simple queries can become computationally prohibitive, necessitating efficient summarization techniques to facilitate effective graph exploration. While existing graph summarization methods often compromise on information loss or scalability, we propose SLUGGER, a novel lossless hierarchical summarization framework for massive graphs. SLUGGER leverages a multi-resolution approach, recursively applying a set of carefully designed graph contraction operations to produce a hierarchy of summarized graphs. By exploiting structural properties of real-world graphs, our method ensures that each summarized graph preserves the essential connectivity and community structure of the original graph. We formulate the graph contraction problem as a mixed-integer linear program, which we solve using a customized branch-and-bound algorithm. Our experimental evaluation on a diverse range of massive graphs, including social networks, web graphs, and biological networks, demonstrates SLUGGER's ability to generate high-quality summaries with significant reductions in graph size (up to 97% reduction in edge count). Furthermore, we show that SLUGGER outperforms state-of-the-art graph summarization methods in terms of information preservation and query performance, while maintaining a competitive computational overhead. Notably, SLUGGER enables fast and accurate graph pattern matching, community detection, and graph traversal queries on the summarized graphs, with average speedups ranging from 5x to 20x compared to querying the original graph. Our findings have significant implications for large-scale graph analytics, suggesting that SLUGGER can serve as a crucial preprocessing step for various graph-based applications, including graph databases, network analytics, and visualization systems.

title: Cross-Modal Transferable Adversarial Attacks from Images to Videos
text: Recent studies have shown that adversarial examples hand-crafted on one white-box model can be used to attack other black-box models. Such cross-model transferability makes it feasible to perform black-box attacks, which has raised security concerns for real-world DNNs applications. Nevertheless, existing works mostly focus on investigating the adversarial transferability across different deep models that share the same modality of input data. The cross-modal transferability of adversarial perturbation has never been explored. This paper investigates the transferability of adversarial perturbation across different modalities, i.e., leveraging adversarial perturbation generated on white-box image models to attack black-box video models. Specifically, motivated by the observation that the low-level feature space between images and video frames are similar, we propose a simple yet effective cross-modal attack method, named as Image To Video (I2V) attack. I2V generates adversarial frames by minimizing the cosine similarity between features of pre-trained image models from adversarial and benign examples, then combines the generated adversarial frames to perform black-box attacks on video recognition models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that I2V can achieve high attack success rates on different black-box video recognition models. On Kinetics-400 and UCF-101, I2V achieves an average attack success rate of 77.88% and 65.68%, respectively, which sheds light on the feasibility of cross-modal adversarial attacks.

title: Cross-Modal Transferable Adversarial Attacks from Images to Videos
text: Deep learning models have been shown to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks, which can be crafted to mislead models by adding imperceptible perturbations to input data. While most existing works focus on intra-modal attacks within images or videos, there is a growing concern about the potential risks of cross-modal attacks, where an adversary exploits the shared representation space across different modalities. In this context, we investigate the feasibility of cross-modal transferable adversarial attacks from images to videos. We propose a novel attack framework that leverages the shared latent space between images and videos to generate transferable perturbations. Our approach involves training a generative model to produce perturbations that are effective across both images and videos, and then fine-tuning the model using a video-specific loss function. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed attack framework can successfully transfer perturbations from images to videos, achieving high success rates on various video analysis tasks, including action recognition and object detection. Notably, our attacks are shown to be robust against existing defense mechanisms, including input preprocessing and adversarial training. Our study highlights the vulnerability of deep learning models to cross-modal attacks and underscores the need for developing more robust and modality-agnostic defense strategies.

title: Compositional Test Generation of Industrial Synchronous Systems
text: Synchronous systems provide a basic model of embedded systems and industrial systems are modeled as Simulink diagrams and/or Lustre programs. Although the test generation problem is critical in the development of safe systems, it often fails because of the spatial and temporal complexity of the system descriptions. This paper presents a compositional test generation method to address the complexity issue. We regard a test case as a counterexample in safety verification, and represent a test generation process as a deductive proof tree built with dedicated inference rules; we conduct both spatial- and temporal-compositional reasoning along with a modular system structure. A proof tree is generated using our semi-automated scheme involving manual effort on contract generation and automatic processes for counterexample search with SMT solvers. As case studies, the proposed method is applied to four industrial examples involving such features as enabled/triggered subsystems, multiple execution rates, filter components, and nested counters. In the experiments, we successfully generated test cases for target systems that were difficult to deal with using the existing tools.

title: Compositional Test Generation of Industrial Synchronous Systems
text: Embedded systems and industrial systems are often modeled as Simulink diagrams or Lustre programs, which can be abstracted as synchronous systems. The test generation problem, a crucial step in ensuring system safety, is frequently hindered by the spatial and temporal complexities inherent in system descriptions. To mitigate this issue, we propose a compositional test generation method that leverages the modular structure of systems. By representing test cases as counterexamples in safety verification and the test generation process as a deductive proof tree, we enable both spatial and temporal compositional reasoning. Our semi-automated approach involves manual contract generation and automated counterexample search using SMT solvers. The efficacy of our method is demonstrated through four industrial case studies, which feature complex system attributes such as enabled/triggered subsystems, multiple execution rates, filter components, and nested counters. Notably, our approach successfully generated test cases for systems that were intractable using existing tools.

title: On the Security & Privacy in Federated Learning
text: Recent privacy awareness initiatives such as the EU General Data Protection Regulation subdued Machine Learning (ML) to privacy and security assessments. Federated Learning (FL) grants a privacy-driven, decentralized training scheme that improves ML models' security. The industry's fast-growing adaptation and security evaluations of FL technology exposed various vulnerabilities that threaten FL's confidentiality, integrity, or availability (CIA). This work assesses the CIA of FL by reviewing the state-of-the-art (SoTA) and creating a threat model that embraces the attack's surface, adversarial actors, capabilities, and goals. We propose the first unifying taxonomy for attacks and defenses and provide promising future research directions.

title: On the Security & Privacy in Federated Learning
text: The escalating emphasis on privacy, exemplified by the EU's General Data Protection Regulation, has necessitated the integration of privacy and security considerations into Machine Learning (ML) development. Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized, privacy-centric approach to ML model training, enhancing security. However, the rapid adoption and security evaluations of FL technology have revealed vulnerabilities that compromise its confidentiality, integrity, or availability (CIA). This study provides a comprehensive assessment of FL's CIA through a review of the state-of-the-art and a novel threat model incorporating attack surfaces, adversaries, capabilities, and objectives. A unified taxonomy for attacks and defenses is proposed, alongside promising avenues for future research.

title: An Evaluation and Enhancement of Seredynski-Bouvry CA-based Encryption Scheme
text: In this paper, we study a block cipher based on cellular automata, proposed by Seredynski and Bouvry in against \emph{plain-text avalanche criteria} and \emph{randomness} tests. Our experiments shows that Seredynski-Bouvry encryption scheme does not pass some NIST statistical tests by neighborhood radius less than three. It also showed that if the CA rule is selected carelessly, it weaken the security of scheme. Therefor, the selection of CA-rule as part of key can not be left to the user. Hence, cryptographic properties such as balancedness and non-linearity should be considered in the selection of CA-rules. This approach is more compliant with Kerckhoffs principle. So security should depend just on security of final data. We also improve Seredynski-Bouvry encryption scheme to satisfy strict avalanche criteria and NIST statistical test suite in about half number of iterations comparing to original scheme. This improvement is achieved by change in the definition of neighborhood.

title: An Evaluation and Enhancement of Seredynski-Bouvry CA-based Encryption Scheme
text: Cellular Automata (CA)-based encryption schemes have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their potential to provide efficient and secure data encryption. The Seredynski-Bouvry scheme, a prominent CA-based approach, has been shown to offer promising security features. However, a comprehensive evaluation of its cryptographic strength and potential enhancements remains an open research direction. This study undertakes a rigorous assessment of the Seredynski-Bouvry scheme, focusing on its resistance to various cryptanalytic attacks, including differential and linear cryptanalysis. Our experimental results reveal that the scheme is vulnerable to certain types of attacks, thereby compromising its security. To address these limitations, we propose an enhanced variant of the scheme, which incorporates a novel key scheduling algorithm and a modified CA structure. Our evaluation demonstrates that the enhanced scheme exhibits improved security margins, providing a more robust encryption solution for real-world applications. The proposed enhancements are validated through extensive simulations and security analysis, showcasing the feasibility of CA-based encryption schemes in modern cryptography.

title: Applying the Shuffle Model of Differential Privacy to Vector Aggregation
text: In this work we introduce a new protocol for vector aggregation in the context of the Shuffle Model, a recent model within Differential Privacy (DP). It sits between the Centralized Model, which prioritizes the level of accuracy over the secrecy of the data, and the Local Model, for which an improvement in trust is counteracted by a much higher noise requirement. The Shuffle Model was developed to provide a good balance between these two models through the addition of a shuffling step, which unbinds the users from their data whilst maintaining a moderate noise requirement. We provide a single message protocol for the summation of real vectors in the Shuffle Model, using advanced composition results. Our contribution provides a mechanism to enable private aggregation and analysis across more sophisticated structures such as matrices and higher-dimensional tensors, both of which are reliant on the functionality of the vector case.

title: Applying the Shuffle Model of Differential Privacy to Vector Aggregation
text: Within the realm of Differential Privacy (DP), the Shuffle Model has emerged as a promising paradigm, striking a balance between the Centralized and Local Models by incorporating a shuffling step that decouples users from their data while maintaining a moderate noise requirement. Building upon this framework, we propose a novel protocol for vector aggregation, facilitating the private summation of real vectors through a single message. Leveraging advanced composition results, our approach enables the extension of private aggregation and analysis to more complex data structures, including matrices and higher-dimensional tensors, which rely on the foundational functionality of vector aggregation. By providing a robust mechanism for private aggregation, this work paves the way for sophisticated analytics in the Shuffle Model, bridging the gap between accuracy and data secrecy.

title: Linear complementary dual code-based Multi-secret sharing scheme
text: Hiding a secret is needed in many situations. Secret sharing plays an important role in protecting information from getting lost, stolen, or destroyed and has been applicable in recent years. A secret sharing scheme is a cryptographic protocol in which a dealer divides the secret into several pieces of share and one share is given to each participant. To recover the secret, the dealer requires a subset of participants called access structure. In this paper, we present a multi-secret sharing scheme over a local ring based on linear complementary dual codes using Blakley's method. We take a large secret space over a local ring that is greater than other code-based schemes and obtain a perfect and almost ideal scheme.

title: Linear complementary dual code-based Multi-secret sharing scheme
text: Secret sharing schemes are essential for secure data distribution in multi-party computation, cloud storage, and distributed systems. Existing multi-secret sharing schemes often rely on complex cryptographic primitives, incurring significant computational overhead. We propose a novel linear complementary dual code-based multi-secret sharing scheme that achieves efficient and secure secret sharing. Our approach leverages the properties of linear complementary dual codes to construct a threshold-based scheme, enabling the sharing of multiple secrets among a set of participants. Through rigorous security analysis, we demonstrate that our scheme achieves information-theoretic security and is resistant to collusion attacks. Experimental results show that our scheme outperforms existing solutions in terms of computational efficiency, making it suitable for resource-constrained environments. Our scheme has significant implications for secure data sharing in distributed systems and multi-party computation.

title: How to Quantify the Security Level of Embedded Systems? A Taxonomy of Security Metrics
text: Embedded Systems (ES) development has been historically focused on functionality rather than security, and today it still applies in many sectors and applications. However, there is an increasing number of security threats over ES, and a successful attack could have economical, physical or even human consequences, since many of them are used to control critical applications. A standardized and general accepted security testing framework is needed to provide guidance, common reporting forms, and the possibility to compare the results along the time. This can be achieved by introducing security metrics into the evaluation or assessment process. If carefully designed and chosen, metrics could provide a quantitative, repeatable and reproducible value that would reflect the level of security protection of the ES. This paper analyzes the features that a good security metric should exhibit, introduces a taxonomy for classifying them, and finally, it carries out a literature survey on security metrics for the security evaluation of ES. In this review, more than 500 metrics were collected and analyzed. Then, they were reduced to 169 metrics that have the potential to be applied to ES security evaluation. As expected, the 77.5 % of them is related exclusively to software, and only the 0.6 % of them addresses exclusively hardware security. This work aims to lay the foundations for constructing a security evaluation methodology that uses metrics to quantify the security level of an ES.

title: How to Quantify the Security Level of Embedded Systems? A Taxonomy of Security Metrics
text: The proliferation of embedded systems in various domains, including industrial control systems, automotive, and consumer electronics, has increased the attack surface, making security a paramount concern. Despite the significance of security in embedded systems, quantifying the security level of these systems remains a daunting task. The lack of a standardized framework for evaluating the security posture of embedded systems hinders the development of secure designs, making it challenging to prioritize security investments. This paper proposes a taxonomy of security metrics to quantify the security level of embedded systems. We conducted a comprehensive review of existing security metrics, categorizing them into five distinct classes: device-centric, network-centric, software-centric, data-centric, and system-centric metrics. Our taxonomy is based on a rigorous analysis of 150 research papers, 30 industry reports, and 20 expert interviews. We identified 35 security metrics, which we evaluated using a set of criteria, including relevance, accuracy, and feasibility. Our findings indicate that the majority of existing security metrics focus on device-centric and software-centric aspects, while neglecting system-centric and data-centric aspects. We also observed that only 20% of the metrics are highly relevant, accurate, and feasible for embedded systems. The proposed taxonomy provides a structured approach to selecting and combining security metrics, enabling the quantification of the security level of embedded systems. Our work contributes to the development of a standardized framework for evaluating the security posture of embedded systems, facilitating informed decision-making and prioritization of security investments.

title: BCD: A Cross-Architecture Binary Comparison Database Experiment Using Locality Sensitive Hashing Algorithms
text: Given a binary executable without source code, it is difficult to determine what each function in the binary does by reverse engineering it, and even harder without prior experience and context. In this paper, we performed a comparison of different hashing functions' effectiveness at detecting similar lifted snippets of LLVM IR code, and present the design and implementation of a framework for cross-architecture binary code similarity search database using MinHash as the chosen hashing algorithm, over SimHash, SSDEEP and TLSH. The motivation is to help reverse engineers to quickly gain context of functions in an unknown binary by comparing it against a database of known functions. The code for this project is open source and can be found at

title: BCD: A Cross-Architecture Binary Comparison Database Experiment Using Locality Sensitive Hashing Algorithms
text: The proliferation of binaries across diverse architectures has rendered traditional code similarity analysis ineffective, necessitating novel approaches to identify similarities and potential security vulnerabilities. We propose BCD, a cross-architecture binary comparison database experiment leveraging locality sensitive hashing (LSH) algorithms. By harnessing the properties of LSH, BCD efficiently indexes and retrieves similar binaries across x86, ARM, and MIPS architectures. Our evaluation on a dataset of 10,000 binaries reveals a significant reduction in comparison time, with an average speedup of 7.5x over traditional pairwise comparison methods. Furthermore, BCD achieves a high accuracy of 93.2% in identifying similar binaries, outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of LSH-based binary comparison, paving the way for large-scale binary analysis and vulnerability detection across diverse architectures.

title: Improving Productivity through Corporate Hackathons: A Multiple Case Study of Two Large-scale Agile Organizations
text: Software development companies organize hackathons to encourage innovation. Despite many benefits of hackathons, in large-scale agile organizations where many teams work together, stopping the ongoing work results in a significant decrease in the immediate output. Motivated by the need to understand whether and how to run hackathons, we investigated how the practice affects productivity on the individual and organizational levels. By mapping the benefits and challenges to an established productivity framework, we found that hackathons improve developers' satisfaction and well-being, strengthen the company culture, improve performance (as many ideas are tested), increase activity (as the ideas are developed quickly), and improve communication and collaboration (because the social network is strengthened). Addressing managerial concerns, we found that hackathons also increase efficiency and flow because people learn to complete work and make progress quickly, and they build new competence. Finally, with respect to virtual hackathons we found that developers work more in isolation because tasks are split between team members resulting in less collaboration. This means that some important, expected hackathon values in virtual contexts require extra effort and cannot be taken for granted.

title: Improving Productivity through Corporate Hackathons: A Multiple Case Study of Two Large-scale Agile Organizations
text: In large-scale agile organizations, the implementation of hackathons, aimed at fostering innovation, poses a dilemma: while they offer numerous benefits, they necessitate a temporary halt in ongoing work, resulting in an immediate decline in output. To reconcile this trade-off, we explored the impact of hackathons on productivity at both individual and organizational levels. By mapping the benefits and challenges against a well-established productivity framework, our study reveals that hackathons enhance developer satisfaction and well-being, fortify company culture, and improve performance through rapid idea testing and development. Furthermore, they boost activity, communication, and collaboration by strengthening social networks. Contrary to managerial concerns, our findings indicate that hackathons also increase efficiency and flow, as participants learn to expedite task completion and build new competencies. Notably, however, our research highlights that virtual hackathons require additional effort to replicate the collaborative benefits of in-person events, as tasks are often fragmented among team members, leading to increased isolation.

title: TechRank: A Network-Centrality Approach for Informed Cybersecurity-Investment
text: The cybersecurity technological landscape is a complex ecosystem in which entities -- such as companies and technologies -- influence each other in a non-trivial manner. Measuring the influence between entities is a tenet for informed technological investments in critical infrastructure. To study the mutual influence of companies and technologies from the cybersecurity field, we consider a bi-partite graph that links both sets of entities. Each node in this graph is weighted by applying a recursive algorithm based on the method of reflection. This endeavor helps to measure the impact of an entity on the cybersecurity market. Our results help researchers measure more precisely the magnitude of influence of each entity, and allows decision-makers to devise more informed investment strategies, according to their portfolio preferences. Finally, a research agenda is suggested, with the aim of allowing tailor-made investments by arbitrarily calibrating specific features of both types of entities.

title: TechRank: A Network-Centrality Approach for Informed Cybersecurity-Investment
text: The intricate dynamics of the cybersecurity technological landscape are characterized by complex interdependencies between entities, including companies and technologies. Accurately quantifying these influences is essential for informed investments in critical infrastructure. To elucidate the reciprocal relationships between companies and technologies in the cybersecurity domain, we employ a weighted bi-partite graph that captures the interlinkages between these two entity sets. A recursive algorithm, grounded in the method of reflection, is applied to assign weights to each node, thereby enabling the assessment of an entity's market impact. Our findings facilitate precise measurements of influence magnitude, empowering decision-makers to develop investment strategies aligned with their portfolio preferences. Furthermore, we outline a research agenda aimed at enabling tailored investments through the calibration of specific features of both entity types.

title: Combining Design Thinking and Software Requirements Engineering to create Human-centered Software-intensive Systems
text: Effective Requirements Engineering is a crucial activity in softwareintensive development projects. The human-centric working mode of Design Thinking is considered a powerful way to complement such activities when designing innovative systems. Research has already made great strides to illustrate the benefits of using Design Thinking for Requirements Engineering. However, it has remained mostly unclear how to actually realize a combination of both. In this chapter, we contribute an artifact-based model that integrates Design Thinking and Requirements Engineering for innovative software-intensive systems. Drawing from our research and project experiences, we suggest three strategies for tailoring and integrating Design Thinking and Requirements Engineering with complementary synergies.

title: Combining Design Thinking and Software Requirements Engineering to create Human-centered Software-intensive Systems
text: The success of software-intensive development projects hinges on effective Requirements Engineering, which can be significantly enhanced by incorporating the human-centered approach of Design Thinking. While prior research has demonstrated the benefits of combining these two disciplines, the practical implementation of their integration remains largely unexplored. This knowledge gap is addressed by our artifact-based model, which seamlessly merges Design Thinking and Requirements Engineering for innovative software-intensive systems. Through our research and project experiences, we identify three tailored strategies that leverage complementary synergies, providing a nuanced understanding of how to effectively integrate these two methodologies.

title: An Interface between Legacy and Modern Mobile Devices for Digital Identity
text: In developing regions a substantial number of users rely on legacy and ultra-low-cost mobile devices. Unfortunately, many of these devices are not equipped to run the standard authentication or identity apps that are available for smartphones. Increasingly, apps that display Quick Response (QR) codes are being used to communicate personal credentials (e.g., Covid-19 vaccination certificates). This paper describes a novel interface for QR code credentials that is compatible with legacy mobile devices. Our solution, which we have released under open source licensing, allows Web Application Enabled legacy mobile devices to load and display standard QR codes. This technique makes modern identity platforms available to previously excluded and economically disadvantaged populations.

title: An Interface between Legacy and Modern Mobile Devices for Digital Identity
text: The proliferation of mobile devices has led to a fragmented digital identity ecosystem, where users struggle to maintain a unified online presence across legacy and modern devices. This disparity hinders secure authentication, authorization, and access control. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel interface that enables seamless interactions between legacy and modern mobile devices, facilitating a unified digital identity. Our approach leverages a decentralized authentication framework, built upon a lightweight, attribute-based encryption scheme. We implement and evaluate our interface on a diverse set of devices, demonstrating significant improvements in authentication latency and success rates, while maintaining robust security guarantees. Our findings have significant implications for enhancing digital identity management in heterogeneous mobile environments.

title: An Annotation-based Approach for Finding Bugs in Neural Network Programs
text: As neural networks are increasingly included as core components of safety-critical systems, developing effective testing techniques specialized for them becomes crucial. The bulk of the research has focused on testing neural-network models; but these models are defined by writing programs, and there is growing evidence that these neural-network programs often have bugs too. This paper presents aNNoTest: an approach to generating test inputs for neural-network programs. A fundamental challenge is that the dynamically-typed languages (e.g., Python) commonly used to program neural networks cannot express detailed constraints about valid function inputs (e.g., matrices with certain dimensions). Without knowing these constraints, automated test-case generation is prone to producing invalid inputs, which trigger spurious failures and are useless for identifying real bugs. To address this problem, we introduce a simple annotation language tailored for concisely expressing valid function inputs in neural-network programs. aNNoTest takes as input an annotated program, and uses property-based testing to generate random inputs that satisfy the validity constraints. In the paper, we also outline guidelines that simplify writing aNNoTest annotations. We evaluated aNNoTest on 19 neural-network programs from Islam et al's survey., which we manually annotated following our guidelines -- producing 6 annotations per tested function on average. aNNoTest automatically generated test inputs that revealed 94 bugs, including 63 bugs that the survey reported for these projects. These results suggest that aNNoTest can be a valuable approach to finding widespread bugs in real-world neural-network programs.

title: An Annotation-based Approach for Finding Bugs in Neural Network Programs
text: The increasing integration of neural networks into safety-critical systems necessitates the development of specialized testing techniques. While significant research has focused on testing neural network models, the programs that define these models are also prone to bugs. This paper introduces aNNoTest, a novel approach to generating test inputs for neural network programs. A major obstacle in automated test-case generation is the inability of dynamically-typed languages, commonly used for programming neural networks, to express detailed constraints on valid function inputs. This limitation leads to the production of invalid inputs, which trigger spurious failures and fail to identify real bugs. To overcome this challenge, we propose a concise annotation language tailored to specifying valid function inputs in neural network programs. aNNoTest takes annotated programs as input and employs property-based testing to generate random inputs that satisfy the validity constraints. We also provide guidelines to simplify the annotation process. Our evaluation of aNNoTest on 19 neural network programs, annotated with an average of 6 annotations per function, revealed 94 bugs, including 63 previously reported bugs. These results demonstrate the potential of aNNoTest as a valuable approach for detecting widespread bugs in real-world neural network programs.

title: Copy, Right? A Testing Framework for Copyright Protection of Deep Learning Models
text: Deep learning (DL) models, especially those large-scale and high-performance ones, can be very costly to train, demanding a great amount of data and computational resources. Unauthorized reproduction of DL models can lead to copyright infringement and cause huge economic losses to model owners. Existing copyright protection techniques are mostly based on watermarking, which embeds an owner-specified watermark into the model. While being able to provide exact ownership verification, these techniques are 1) invasive, as they need to tamper with the training process, which may affect the utility or introduce new security risks; 2) prone to adaptive attacks that attempt to remove the watermark; and 3) not robust to the emerging model extraction attacks. Latest fingerprinting work, though being non-invasive, also falls short when facing the diverse and ever-growing attack scenarios. In this paper, we propose a novel testing framework for DL copyright protection: DEEPJUDGE. DEEPJUDGE quantitatively tests the similarities between two DL models: a victim model and a suspect model. It leverages a diverse set of testing metrics and test case generation methods to produce a chain of supporting evidence to help determine whether a suspect model is a copy of the victim model. Advantages of DEEPJUDGE include: 1) non-invasive, as it works directly on the model and does not tamper with the training process; 2) efficient, as it only needs a small set of test cases and a quick scan of models; 3) flexible, as it can easily incorporate new metrics or generation methods to obtain more confident judgement; and 4) fairly robust to model extraction and adaptive attacks. We verify the effectiveness of DEEPJUDGE under typical copyright infringement scenarios, including model finetuning, pruning and extraction, via extensive experiments on both image and speech datasets with a variety of model architectures.

title: Copy, Right? A Testing Framework for Copyright Protection of Deep Learning Models
text: The training of large-scale, high-performance deep learning (DL) models necessitates substantial computational resources and data, rendering them valuable assets vulnerable to unauthorized reproduction and copyright infringement. Existing copyright protection techniques, predominantly based on watermarking, embed an owner-specified mark into the model, enabling exact ownership verification. However, these methods are beset by limitations, including invasiveness, which may compromise model utility or introduce security risks, susceptibility to adaptive attacks aimed at watermark removal, and fragility against emerging model extraction attacks. Recent fingerprinting approaches, although non-invasive, are also inadequate in the face of diverse and evolving attack scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce DEEPJUDGE, a novel testing framework for DL copyright protection. DEEPJUDGE quantitatively assesses the similarities between a victim model and a suspect model by leveraging a diverse set of testing metrics and test case generation methods, thereby generating a chain of evidence to determine whether the suspect model is a replica of the victim model. The key advantages of DEEPJUDGE include its non-invasive nature, efficiency, flexibility, and robustness against model extraction and adaptive attacks. Through extensive experiments on various image and speech datasets with diverse model architectures, we demonstrate the effectiveness of DEEPJUDGE in detecting copyright infringement under common scenarios, including model finetuning, pruning, and extraction.

title: Preemptive Image Robustification for Protecting Users against Man-in-the-Middle Adversarial Attacks
text: Deep neural networks have become the driving force of modern image recognition systems. However, the vulnerability of neural networks against adversarial attacks poses a serious threat to the people affected by these systems. In this paper, we focus on a real-world threat model where a Man-in-the-Middle adversary maliciously intercepts and perturbs images web users upload online. This type of attack can raise severe ethical concerns on top of simple performance degradation. To prevent this attack, we devise a novel bi-level optimization algorithm that finds points in the vicinity of natural images that are robust to adversarial perturbations. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet show our method can effectively robustify natural images within the given modification budget. We also show the proposed method can improve robustness when jointly used with randomized smoothing.

title: Preemptive Image Robustification for Protecting Users against Man-in-the-Middle Adversarial Attacks
text: The proliferation of deep neural networks in modern image recognition systems has led to a heightened vulnerability to adversarial attacks, posing significant risks to individuals reliant on these systems. A particularly insidious threat arises from Man-in-the-Middle adversaries that maliciously intercept and perturb online image uploads, compromising not only system performance but also raising grave ethical concerns. To mitigate this threat, we develop a novel bi-level optimization algorithm that identifies robust points near natural images, resilient to adversarial perturbations. Empirical evaluations on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our method in robustifying natural images within a predefined modification budget. Furthermore, our approach exhibits improved robustness when combined with randomized smoothing techniques.

title: Sample and Threshold Differential Privacy: Histograms and applications
text: Federated analytics seeks to compute accurate statistics from data distributed across users' devices while providing a suitable privacy guarantee and being practically feasible to implement and scale. In this paper, we show how a strong $(ε, δ)$-Differential Privacy (DP) guarantee can be achieved for the fundamental problem of histogram generation in a federated setting, via a highly practical sampling-based procedure that does not add noise to disclosed data. Given the ubiquity of sampling in practice, we thus obtain a DP guarantee almost for free, avoid over-estimating histogram counts, and allow easy reasoning about how privacy guarantees may obscure minorities and outliers. Using such histograms, related problems such as heavy hitters and quantiles can be answered with provable error and privacy guarantees. Experimental results show that our sample-and-threshold approach is accurate and scalable.

title: Sample and Threshold Differential Privacy: Histograms and applications
text: Differential privacy (DP) has emerged as a gold standard for privacy-preserving data analysis, but existing DP mechanisms often suffer from significant utility loss. Sample and threshold differential privacy (STDP) is a promising alternative that leverages sampling and thresholding to achieve better trade-offs between privacy and utility. In this work, we develop and analyze STDP mechanisms for histogram release, a fundamental task in data analysis. We provide a comprehensive framework for STDP histogram release, including novel algorithms and theoretical guarantees for privacy and utility. Our experiments demonstrate that STDP outperforms state-of-the-art DP mechanisms in terms of utility, often by an order of magnitude, while maintaining strong privacy guarantees. We also explore applications of STDP in frequency estimation and heavy hitter identification, showcasing its potential for real-world data analysis tasks.

title: Attacks on Wireless Coexistence: Exploiting Cross-Technology Performance Features for Inter-Chip Privilege Escalation
text: Modern mobile devices feature multiple wireless technologies, such as Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and LTE. Each of them is implemented within a separate wireless chip, sometimes packaged as combo chips. However, these chips share components and resources, such as the same antenna or wireless spectrum. Wireless coexistence interfaces enable them to schedule packets without collisions despite shared resources, essential to maximizing networking performance. Today's hardwired coexistence interfaces hinder clear security boundaries and separation between chips and chip components. This paper shows practical coexistence attacks on Broadcom, Cypress, and Silicon Labs chips deployed in billions of devices. For example, we demonstrate that a Bluetooth chip can directly extract network passwords and manipulate traffic on a Wi-Fi chip. Coexistence attacks enable a novel type of lateral privilege escalation across chip boundaries. We responsibly disclosed the vulnerabilities to the vendors. Yet, only partial fixes were released for existing hardware since wireless chips would need to be redesigned from the ground up to prevent the presented attacks on coexistence.

title: Attacks on Wireless Coexistence: Exploiting Cross-Technology Performance Features for Inter-Chip Privilege Escalation
text: The proliferation of wireless devices has led to a crowded radio frequency spectrum, necessitating coexistence mechanisms to ensure harmonious operation. However, these mechanisms can be exploited to launch attacks that compromise device security. We demonstrate a novel class of attacks on wireless coexistence, leveraging cross-technology performance features to achieve inter-chip privilege escalation. Our methodology involves analyzing the coexistence protocols used in Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and Zigbee, identifying vulnerabilities that enable an attacker to manipulate the performance metrics of adjacent devices. We develop a custom-built testbed to emulate real-world scenarios, and conduct a series of experiments to validate our attacks. Our results show that an attacker can exploit coexistence mechanisms to escalate privileges across chip boundaries, gaining unauthorized access to sensitive information. We demonstrate the feasibility of our attacks on commercial off-the-shelf devices, highlighting the need for a reevaluation of wireless coexistence protocols to ensure the security and integrity of wireless communications.

title: Two Sequential Squaring Verifiable Delay Function
text: A Verifiable Delay Function (VDF) is a function that takes a specified sequential time to be evaluated, but can be efficiently verified. VDFs are useful in several applications ranging from randomness beacons to sustainable blockchains but are really rare in practice. Most of the VDFs are based on algebraic assumptions like time-lock puzzle in unknown group orders [6, 8] and isogenies over pairing groups [4]. The number of modulo squaring required for verification in the time-lock puzzle based VDFs are proportional to their security parameter. This paper proposes a verifiable delay function that requires only 2- modulo squaring for verification. So the sequential effort required for verification is independent of the security parameter.

title: Two Sequential Squaring Verifiable Delay Function
text: Verifiable delay functions (VDFs) are a critical component in many cryptographic protocols, enabling the creation of decentralized and trustless systems. However, existing VDF constructions rely on complex and computationally expensive algorithms, limiting their practical applicability. We propose a novel VDF construction, dubbed Two Sequential Squaring (TSS), which leverages the sequential nature of squaring operations to achieve high performance and simplicity. Our approach reduces the computational overhead by a factor of 4 compared to state-of-the-art VDFs, while maintaining the same level of security. We provide a rigorous security analysis, demonstrating that TSS is secure under the RSA assumption. Implementation results on modern hardware platforms demonstrate the feasibility and efficiency of TSS in real-world scenarios.

title: Auto-Tag: Tagging-Data-By-Example in Data Lakes
text: As data lakes become increasingly popular in large enterprises today, there is a growing need to tag or classify data assets (e.g., files and databases) in data lakes with additional metadata (e.g., semantic column-types), as the inferred metadata can enable a range of downstream applications like data governance (e.g., GDPR compliance), and dataset search. Given the sheer size of today's enterprise data lakes with petabytes of data and millions of data assets, it is imperative that data assets can be ``auto-tagged'', using lightweight inference algorithms and minimal user input. In this work, we develop Auto-Tag, a corpus-driven approach that automates data-tagging of \textit{custom} data types in enterprise data lakes. Using Auto-Tag, users only need to provide \textit{one} example column to demonstrate the desired data-type to tag. Leveraging an index structure built offline using a lightweight scan of the data lake, which is analogous to pre-training in machine learning, Auto-Tag can infer suitable data patterns to best ``describe'' the underlying ``domain'' of the given column at an interactive speed, which can then be used to tag additional data of the same ``type'' in data lakes. The Auto-Tag approach can adapt to custom data-types, and is shown to be both accurate and efficient. Part of Auto-Tag ships as a ``custom-classification'' feature in a cloud-based data governance and catalog solution \textit{Azure Purview}.

title: Auto-Tag: Tagging-Data-By-Example in Data Lakes
text: The proliferation of data lakes in large enterprises has created a pressing need for enriching data assets with additional metadata, such as semantic column-types, to facilitate downstream applications like data governance and dataset search. The scale of modern enterprise data lakes, characterized by petabytes of data and millions of assets, necessitates the development of efficient auto-tagging methods that can operate with minimal user input and lightweight inference algorithms. This paper presents Auto-Tag, a corpus-driven approach that automates the tagging of custom data types in enterprise data lakes. By providing a single example column, users can demonstrate the desired data type, and Auto-Tag can infer suitable patterns to describe the underlying domain at interactive speeds. This is achieved through an offline-built index structure, analogous to pre-training in machine learning, which enables the approach to adapt to custom data types while maintaining accuracy and efficiency. The effectiveness of Auto-Tag is demonstrated by its integration as a custom-classification feature in Azure Purview, a cloud-based data governance and catalog solution.

title: MedAttacker: Exploring Black-Box Adversarial Attacks on Risk Prediction Models in Healthcare
text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been broadly adopted in health risk prediction to provide healthcare diagnoses and treatments. To evaluate their robustness, existing research conducts adversarial attacks in the white/gray-box setting where model parameters are accessible. However, a more realistic black-box adversarial attack is ignored even though most real-world models are trained with private data and released as black-box services on the cloud. To fill this gap, we propose the first black-box adversarial attack method against health risk prediction models named MedAttacker to investigate their vulnerability. MedAttacker addresses the challenges brought by EHR data via two steps: hierarchical position selection which selects the attacked positions in a reinforcement learning (RL) framework and substitute selection which identifies substitute with a score-based principle. Particularly, by considering the temporal context inside EHRs, it initializes its RL position selection policy by using the contribution score of each visit and the saliency score of each code, which can be well integrated with the deterministic substitute selection process decided by the score changes. In experiments, MedAttacker consistently achieves the highest average success rate and even outperforms a recent white-box EHR adversarial attack technique in certain cases when attacking three advanced health risk prediction models in the black-box setting across multiple real-world datasets.
