In addition, based on the experiment results we include a discussion on defending EHR adversarial attacks.

title: MedAttacker: Exploring Black-Box Adversarial Attacks on Risk Prediction Models in Healthcare
text: The widespread adoption of deep neural networks (DNNs) in health risk prediction has sparked concerns about their robustness, particularly in the face of adversarial attacks. While existing research has focused on white-box and gray-box attacks, where model parameters are accessible, the more realistic scenario of black-box attacks, common in real-world cloud-based services with private data, has been largely overlooked. This knowledge gap is addressed by our proposed black-box adversarial attack method, MedAttacker, designed to assess the vulnerability of health risk prediction models. MedAttacker tackles the challenges inherent in Electronic Health Records (EHRs) through a two-pronged approach: hierarchical position selection, which leverages reinforcement learning to identify attack positions, and substitute selection, which employs a score-based principle to determine substitutes. By incorporating temporal context within EHRs, MedAttacker initializes its policy using contribution and saliency scores, seamlessly integrating with the deterministic substitute selection process. Our experimental results demonstrate MedAttacker's superior performance, achieving the highest average success rate and, in some cases, outperforming a recent white-box EHR adversarial attack technique when targeting three advanced health risk prediction models across multiple real-world datasets. Furthermore, our findings inform a discussion on strategies for defending against EHR adversarial attacks.

title: A Note on the Post-Quantum Security of (Ring) Signatures
text: This work revisits the security of classical signatures and ring signatures in a quantum world. For (ordinary) signatures, we focus on the arguably preferable security notion of blind-unforgeability recently proposed by Alagic et al. (Eurocrypt'20). We present two short signature schemes achieving this notion: one is in the quantum random oracle model, assuming quantum hardness of SIS; and the other is in the plain model, assuming quantum hardness of LWE with super-polynomial modulus. Prior to this work, the only known blind-unforgeable schemes are Lamport's one-time signature and the Winternitz one-time signature, and both of them are in the quantum random oracle model. For ring signatures, the recent work by Chatterjee et al. (Crypto'21) proposes a definition trying to capture adversaries with quantum access to the signer. However, it is unclear if their definition, when restricted to the classical world, is as strong as the standard security notion for ring signatures. They also present a construction that only partially achieves (even) this seeming weak definition, in the sense that the adversary can only conduct superposition attacks over the messages, but not the rings. We propose a new definition that does not suffer from the above issue. Our definition is an analog to the blind-unforgeability in the ring signature setting. Moreover, assuming the quantum hardness of LWE, we construct a compiler converting any blind-unforgeable (ordinary) signatures to a ring signature satisfying our definition.

title: A Note on the Post-Quantum Security of (Ring) Signatures
text: The advent of large-scale quantum computers poses an imminent threat to the security of classical public-key cryptosystems, necessitating a thorough examination of the post-quantum security of existing cryptographic constructions. In this regard, digital signatures are a crucial primitive, and their security in the post-quantum era is of paramount importance. This work focuses on the security of ring signatures, a type of digital signature that enables a signer to anonymously authenticate a message on behalf of a group of users. We investigate the post-quantum security of two prominent ring signature schemes, namely, the ring signature scheme of Rivest et al. and the lattice-based ring signature scheme of Bai et al. Our analysis is grounded in the quantum random oracle model, which provides a more realistic assessment of the security of these schemes against quantum adversaries. Through a careful examination of the underlying mathematical structures, we demonstrate that the Rivest et al. scheme is vulnerable to a quantum attack, thereby rendering it insecure in the post-quantum era. In contrast, we show that the Bai et al. scheme is secure against quantum attacks, assuming the hardness of the shortest vector problem in ideal lattices. Our findings have significant implications for the design and deployment of post-quantum secure ring signature schemes, highlighting the need for a more nuanced understanding of the interplay between cryptography and quantum computing.

title: Anomaly Detection in Blockchain Networks: A Comprehensive Survey
text: Over the past decade, blockchain technology has attracted a huge attention from both industry and academia because it can be integrated with a large number of everyday applications of modern information and communication technologies (ICT). Peer-to-peer (P2P) architecture of blockchain enhances these applications by providing strong security and trust-oriented guarantees, such as immutability, verifiability, and decentralization. Despite these incredible features that blockchain technology brings to these ICT applications, recent research has indicated that the strong guarantees are not sufficient enough and blockchain networks may still be prone to various security, privacy, and reliability issues. In order to overcome these issues, it is important to identify the anomalous behaviour within the actionable time frame. In this article, we provide an in-depth survey regarding integration of anomaly detection models in blockchain technology. For this, we first discuss how anomaly detection can aid in ensuring security of blockchain based applications. Then, we demonstrate certain fundamental evaluation metrics and key requirements that can play a critical role while developing anomaly detection models for blockchain. Afterwards, we present a thorough survey of various anomaly detection models from the perspective of each layer of blockchain. Finally, we conclude the article by highlighting certain important challenges alongside discussing how they can serve as future research directions for new researchers in the field.

title: Anomaly Detection in Blockchain Networks: A Comprehensive Survey
text: Blockchain technology has garnered significant interest from both industry and academia over the past decade, owing to its potential to integrate with various modern information and communication technologies (ICT) applications. The peer-to-peer architecture of blockchain enhances these applications by providing robust security and trust-oriented guarantees, including immutability, verifiability, and decentralization. However, recent research has revealed that despite these benefits, blockchain networks remain vulnerable to diverse security, privacy, and reliability issues. To address these concerns, timely identification of anomalous behavior is crucial. This article provides a comprehensive survey on the integration of anomaly detection models in blockchain technology, exploring how these models can enhance the security of blockchain-based applications. We discuss key evaluation metrics and requirements for developing effective anomaly detection models for blockchain, followed by a thorough examination of various models from the perspective of each blockchain layer. Finally, we highlight significant challenges and potential future research directions, providing a roadmap for new researchers in the field.

title: CryptoEval: Evaluating the Risk of Cryptographic Misuses in Android Apps with Data-Flow Analysis
text: The misunderstanding and incorrect configurations of cryptographic primitives have exposed severe security vulnerabilities to attackers. Due to the pervasiveness and diversity of cryptographic misuses, a comprehensive and accurate understanding of how cryptographic misuses can undermine the security of an Android app is critical to the subsequent mitigation strategies but also challenging. Although various approaches have been proposed to detect cryptographic misuse in Android apps, studies have yet to focus on estimating the security risks of cryptographic misuse. To address this problem, we present an extensible framework for deciding the threat level of cryptographic misuse in Android apps. Firstly, we propose a general and unified specification for representing cryptographic misuses to make our framework extensible and develop adapters to unify the detection results of the state-of-the-art cryptographic misuse detectors, resulting in an adapter-based detection tool chain for a more comprehensive list of cryptographic misuses. Secondly, we employ a misuse-originating data-flow analysis to connect each cryptographic misuse to a set of data-flow sinks in an app, based on which we propose a quantitative data-flow-driven metric for assessing the overall risk of the app introduced by cryptographic misuses. To make the per-app assessment more useful for app vetting at the app-store level, we apply unsupervised learning to predict and classify the top risky threats to guide more efficient subsequent mitigation. In the experiments on an instantiated implementation of the framework, we evaluate the accuracy of our detection and the effect of data-flow-driven risk assessment of our framework. Our empirical study on over 40,000 apps and the analysis of popular apps reveal important security observations on the real threats of cryptographic misuse in Android apps.

title: CryptoEval: Evaluating the Risk of Cryptographic Misuses in Android Apps with Data-Flow Analysis
text: The prevalence of cryptographic misuses in Android apps has significant security implications, as they can be exploited by attackers to compromise app security. A thorough understanding of the security risks associated with cryptographic misuses is essential for devising effective mitigation strategies. While various approaches have been proposed to detect cryptographic misuses, the estimation of security risks posed by these misuses remains an understudied area. This paper addresses this knowledge gap by introducing a flexible framework for evaluating the threat level of cryptographic misuses in Android apps. Our framework is designed to be extensible, with a unified specification for representing cryptographic misuses and adapters to integrate the output of state-of-the-art detection tools. We also develop a data-flow-driven metric to quantify the overall risk posed by cryptographic misuses, which involves tracing the flow of data from misuse sources to sinks within an app. Furthermore, we apply unsupervised learning to identify and prioritize high-risk threats, facilitating more efficient app vetting at the app-store level. An empirical evaluation of our framework on a large dataset of over 40,000 apps reveals critical security insights into the real-world threats posed by cryptographic misuses in Android apps. Our findings highlight the importance of considering the security risks associated with cryptographic misuses in the development and vetting of Android apps.

title: Programming with Neural Surrogates of Programs
text: Surrogates, models that mimic the behavior of programs, form the basis of a variety of development workflows. We study three surrogate-based design patterns, evaluating each in case studies on a large-scale CPU simulator. With surrogate compilation, programmers develop a surrogate that mimics the behavior of a program to deploy to end-users in place of the original program. Surrogate compilation accelerates the CPU simulator under study by $1.6\times$. With surrogate adaptation, programmers develop a surrogate of a program then retrain that surrogate on a different task. Surrogate adaptation decreases the simulator's error by up to $50\%$. With surrogate optimization, programmers develop a surrogate of a program, optimize input parameters of the surrogate, then plug the optimized input parameters back into the original program. Surrogate optimization finds simulation parameters that decrease the simulator's error by $5\%$ compared to the error induced by expert-set parameters. In this paper we formalize this taxonomy of surrogate-based design patterns. We further describe the programming methodology common to all three design patterns. Our work builds a foundation for the emerging class of workflows based on programming with surrogates of programs.

title: Programming with Neural Surrogates of Programs
text: The advent of neural program analysis has led to a proliferation of techniques for reasoning about program behavior using learned models. However, the majority of these approaches focus on analyzing existing programs rather than synthesizing new ones. We propose a novel paradigm, Programming with Neural Surrogates of Programs (PNSP), which leverages learned models as first-class citizens in the programming process. In PNSP, neural networks are trained to surrogate complex programs, capturing their input-output behavior and latent structure. These surrogates are then used as building blocks for constructing new programs, allowing developers to compose and manipulate them using familiar programming abstractions. We develop a theoretical framework for PNSP, providing guarantees on the correctness and efficiency of the synthesized programs. Our methodology is evaluated on a range of programming tasks, including program repair and synthesis, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art techniques. Notably, our approach achieves a 3x reduction in synthesis time while maintaining a 95% correctness rate on a benchmark suite of programming challenges. The PNSP framework has far-reaching implications for the development of more efficient, intelligent, and human-centered programming tools.

title: An Optimized Quantum Implementation of ISD on Scalable Quantum Resources
text: The security of code based constructions is usually assessed by Information Set Decoding (ISD) algorithms. In the quantum setting, amplitude amplification yields an asymptotic square root gain over the classical analogue. However, it is still unclear whether a real quantum circuit could yield actual improvements or suffer an enormous overhead due to its implementation. This leads to different considerations of these quantum attacks in the security analysis of code based proposals. In this work we clarify this doubt by giving the first quantum circuit design of the fully-fledged ISD procedure, an implementation in the quantum simulation library Qibo as well as precise estimates of its complexities. We show that against common belief, Prange's ISD algorithm can be implemented rather efficiently on a quantum computer, namely with only a logarithmic overhead in circuit depth compared to a classical implementation. As another major contribution, we leverage the idea of classical co-processors to design hybrid classical-quantum trade-offs, that allow to tailor the necessary qubits to any available amount, while still providing quantum speedups. Interestingly, when constraining the width of the circuit instead of its depth we are able to overcome previous optimality results on constraint quantum search.

title: An Optimized Quantum Implementation of ISD on Scalable Quantum Resources
text: The increasing complexity of cryptographic primitives has necessitated the development of quantum computers capable of efficiently solving problems intractable for classical computers. The Ideal Sponge Downsampling (ISD) problem, a crucial component in the security analysis of cryptographic hash functions, is one such problem. However, existing quantum implementations of ISD are often limited by their resource requirements, hindering their scalability. This paper presents an optimized quantum implementation of ISD that leverages scalable quantum resources, enabling the solution of large problem instances. Our approach employs a novel combination of quantum circuit synthesis and optimization techniques, resulting in a significant reduction in quantum gate count and circuit depth. We demonstrate the efficacy of our implementation on a range of problem sizes, achieving a speedup of up to 4.5x over existing state-of-the-art implementations. Furthermore, our implementation is highly parallelizable, making it amenable to large-scale quantum computing architectures. The implications of our work are twofold: firstly, it enables the security analysis of cryptographic hash functions on larger problem sizes, and secondly, it showcases the potential of scalable quantum resources in solving complex computational problems.

title: Nalin: Learning from Runtime Behavior to Find Name-Value Inconsistencies in Jupyter Notebooks
text: Variable names are important to understand and maintain code. If a variable name and the value stored in the variable do not match, then the program suffers from a name-value inconsistency, which is due to one of two situations that developers may want to fix: Either a correct value is referred to through a misleading name, which negatively affects code understandability and maintainability, or the correct name is bound to a wrong value, which may cause unexpected runtime behavior. Finding name-value inconsistencies is hard because it requires an understanding of the meaning of names and knowledge about the values assigned to a variable at runtime. This paper presents Nalin, a technique to automatically detect name-value inconsistencies. The approach combines a dynamic analysis that tracks assignments of values to names with a neural machine learning model that predicts whether a name and a value fit together. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to formulate the problem of finding coding issues as a classification problem over names and runtime values. We apply Nalin to 106,652 real-world Python programs, where meaningful names are particularly important due to the absence of statically declared types. Our results show that the classifier detects name-value inconsistencies with high accuracy, that the warnings reported by Nalin have a precision of 80% and a recall of 76% w.r.t. a ground truth created in a user study, and that our approach complements existing techniques for finding coding issues.

title: Nalin: Learning from Runtime Behavior to Find Name-Value Inconsistencies in Jupyter Notebooks
text: Jupyter notebooks have become a de facto standard for data science and scientific computing, fostering reproducibility and collaboration. However, their dynamic nature and lack of explicit type systems make them prone to name-value inconsistencies, where variable names and their associated values are mismatched. These inconsistencies can lead to incorrect results, wasted computational resources, and decreased productivity. Current approaches to detecting such inconsistencies rely on static analysis or user-defined annotations, which are often incomplete, imprecise, or cumbersome. We propose Nalin, a novel approach that leverages runtime behavior to identify name-value inconsistencies in Jupyter notebooks. Nalin employs a hybrid methodology combining program analysis, machine learning, and visualization techniques. It first extracts execution traces from Jupyter notebooks and constructs a graph-based representation of variable interactions. Then, it applies a graph neural network to learn patterns and anomalies in these interactions, predicting potential inconsistencies. Finally, Nalin visualizes the predicted inconsistencies, enabling users to inspect and correct them. Our evaluation on a diverse set of 150 Jupyter notebooks from various domains demonstrates Nalin's effectiveness in detecting name-value inconsistencies, achieving an F1-score of 0.93 and outperforming state-of-the-art static analysis tools. We also show that Nalin can reduce the time spent on debugging by an average of 35%. Furthermore, our user study involving 20 data scientists reveals that Nalin's visualization component enhances their understanding of variable interactions and facilitates the correction of inconsistencies. Nalin's ability to learn from runtime behavior makes it a promising approach for improving the reliability and productivity of data science workflows.

title: Parallel Batch-Dynamic $k$d-Trees
text: $k$d-trees are widely used in parallel databases to support efficient neighborhood/similarity queries. Supporting parallel updates to $k$d-trees is therefore an important operation. In this paper, we present BDL-tree, a parallel, batch-dynamic implementation of a $k$d-tree that allows for efficient parallel $k$-NN queries over dynamically changing point sets. BDL-trees consist of a log-structured set of $k$d-trees which can be used to efficiently insert or delete batches of points in parallel with polylogarithmic depth. Specifically, given a BDL-tree with $n$ points, each batch of $B$ updates takes $O(B\log^2{(n+B)})$ amortized work and $O(\log(n+B)\log\log{(n+B)})$ depth (parallel time). We provide an optimized multicore implementation of BDL-trees. Our optimizations include parallel cache-oblivious $k$d-tree construction and parallel bloom filter construction. Our experiments on a 36-core machine with two-way hyper-threading using a variety of synthetic and real-world datasets show that our implementation of BDL-tree achieves a self-relative speedup of up to $34.8\times$ ($28.4\times$ on average) for batch insertions, up to $35.5\times$ ($27.2\times$ on average) for batch deletions, and up to $46.1\times$ ($40.0\times$ on average) for $k$-nearest neighbor queries. In addition, it achieves throughputs of up to 14.5 million updates/second for batch-parallel updates and 6.7 million queries/second for $k$-NN queries. We compare to two baseline $k$d-tree implementations and demonstrate that BDL-trees achieve a good tradeoff between the two baseline options for implementing batch updates.

title: Parallel Batch-Dynamic $k$d-Trees
text: The increasing prevalence of large-scale datasets has necessitated the development of efficient indexing structures capable of handling massive amounts of data. The $k$d-tree, a classic data structure, has been widely employed for organizing and querying high-dimensional datasets. However, its sequential nature renders it unsuitable for modern parallel computing architectures. To address this limitation, we present Parallel Batch-Dynamic $k$d-Trees, a novel indexing framework that leverages parallelism to accelerate batch-oriented operations on dynamic datasets. Our approach exploits the inherent parallelism in batch operations by partitioning the dataset into smaller, independent chunks, and processing them concurrently across multiple threads. We devise a novel parallelization strategy that minimizes inter-thread communication and ensures load balancing, thereby maximizing the benefits of parallelism. Furthermore, we propose an efficient method for dynamically updating the index in response to insertions, deletions, and modifications, ensuring the integrity and consistency of the data structure. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that our Parallel Batch-Dynamic $k$d-Trees outperform state-of-the-art sequential and parallel indexing techniques by up to 12.5x and 3.2x, respectively, in terms of query response time. Additionally, our approach exhibits superior scalability, with near-linear speedup as the number of threads increases. These results underscore the potential of our framework to accelerate data-intensive applications, such as similarity search, clustering, and data mining, in domains like computer vision, robotics, and scientific computing.

title: Report on A Formally-Founded Model-Based Approach to Engineer Self-Adaptive Systems
text: Self-adaptive systems manage themselves to deal with uncertainties that can only be resolved during operation. A common approach to realize self-adaptation is by adding a feedback loop to the system that monitors the system and adapts it to realize a set of adaptation goals. ActivFORMS (Active FORmal Models for Self-adaptation) provides an end-to-end approach for engineering self-adaptive systems. ActivFORMS relies on feedback loops that consists of formally verified models that are directly deployed and executed at runtime to realize self-adaptation. At runtime, the approach relies on statistical verification techniques that allow efficient analysis of the possible options for adaptation. Further, ActivFORMS supports on-the-fly changes of adaptation goals and updates of the verified models to to meet the new goals. ActivFORMSi provides a tool-supported instance of ActivFORMS. The approach has been validates using an IoT application for building security monitoring. This report provides complementary material to the paper ``ActivFORMS: A Formally-Founded Model-Based Approach to Engineer Self-Adaptive Systems'' [Weyns and Iftikhar 2019].

title: Report on A Formally-Founded Model-Based Approach to Engineer Self-Adaptive Systems
text: Uncertainties inherent to operational contexts necessitate self-adaptive systems that can manage themselves dynamically. A prevalent strategy for achieving self-adaptation involves incorporating a feedback loop that continuously monitors the system and adjusts it to fulfill a set of predefined adaptation objectives. ActivFORMS offers a comprehensive engineering approach for developing self-adaptive systems, leveraging feedback loops comprising formally verified models that are directly deployed and executed at runtime. During operation, the approach utilizes statistical verification techniques to efficiently analyze adaptation options, enabling swift decision-making. Notably, ActivFORMS accommodates on-the-fly adjustments to adaptation goals and updates to verified models, ensuring seamless adaptation to changing requirements. A tool-supported instance of ActivFORMS, ActivFORMSi, has been successfully validated through an IoT-based building security monitoring application. This report serves as supplementary material to the original paper "ActivFORMS: A Formally-Founded Model-Based Approach to Engineer Self-Adaptive Systems" [Weyns and Iftikhar 2019].

title: Secure Routine: A Routine-Based Algorithm for Drivers Identification
text: The introduction of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) in transportation systems leads to several advantages (efficiency of transport, mobility, traffic management). However, it may bring some drawbacks in terms of increasing security challenges, also related to human behaviour. As an example , in the last decades attempts to characterize drivers' behaviour have been mostly targeted. This paper presents Secure Routine, a paradigm that uses driver's habits to driver identification and, in particular, to distinguish the vehicle's owner from other drivers. We evaluate Secure Routine in combination with other three existing research works based on machine learning techniques. Results are measured using well-known metrics and show that Secure Routine outperforms the compared works.

title: Secure Routine: A Routine-Based Algorithm for Drivers Identification
text: The increasing reliance on vehicle-based services has created a pressing need for robust driver identification mechanisms. Existing approaches, relying on biometric or behavioral features, often suffer from limitations in terms of accuracy, scalability, and privacy. This work proposes Secure Routine, a novel algorithm that leverages routine-based driver identification, exploiting the unique patterns of drivers' regular activities. Our approach employs a combination of GPS, accelerometer, and gyroscope data to model drivers' routines, and subsequently, identifies them through a machine learning-based classification framework. Experimental evaluation on a large-scale dataset of 500 drivers shows that Secure Routine achieves an accuracy of 94.2% and outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to 12.5%.

title: Graph Pattern Matching in GQL and SQL/PGQ
text: As graph databases become widespread, JTC1 -- the committee in joint charge of information technology standards for the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) -- has approved a project to create GQL, a standard property graph query language. This complements a project to extend SQL with a new part, SQL/PGQ, which specifies how to define graph views over an SQL tabular schema, and to run read-only queries against them. Both projects have been assigned to the ISO/IEC JTC1 SC32 working group for Database Languages, WG3, which continues to maintain and enhance SQL as a whole. This common responsibility helps enforce a policy that the identical core of both PGQ and GQL is a graph pattern matching sub-language, here termed GPML. The WG3 design process is also analyzed by an academic working group, part of the Linked Data Benchmark Council (LDBC), whose task is to produce a formal semantics of these graph data languages, which complements their standard specifications. This paper, written by members of WG3 and LDBC, presents the key elements of the GPML of SQL/PGQ and GQL in advance of the publication of these new standards.

title: Graph Pattern Matching in GQL and SQL/PGQ
text: The proliferation of graph-structured data in diverse domains has spurred the development of query languages specifically designed to handle graph patterns. Among these, Graph Query Language (GQL) and SQL/PGQ have emerged as prominent alternatives. Despite their widespread adoption, the expressiveness and performance of these languages in graph pattern matching remain inadequately understood. This study undertakes a comprehensive investigation of graph pattern matching in GQL and SQL/PGQ, focusing on their capabilities to handle complex patterns, scalability, and query optimization. We devise a novel benchmark suite, comprising 25 graph patterns with varying complexity, and evaluate the performance of GQL and SQL/PGQ on a large-scale graph dataset. Our experimental results reveal that GQL outperforms SQL/PGQ in matching complex patterns, whereas SQL/PGQ demonstrates superior scalability for large graphs. We also identify key optimization opportunities in both languages, including the impact of indexing and caching on query performance. Furthermore, our analysis of language features and syntax reveals that GQL's declarative nature and SQL/PGQ's procedural approach influence their pattern matching capabilities. Our findings provide valuable insights for query optimization and language design, ultimately contributing to the advancement of graph query languages.

title: Rise of Distributed Deep Learning Training in the Big Model Era: From a Software Engineering Perspective
text: Deep learning (DL) has become a key component of modern software. In the "big model" era, the rich features of DL-based software substantially rely on powerful DL models, e.g., BERT, GPT-3, and the recently emerging GPT-4, which are trained on the powerful cloud with large datasets. Hence, training effective DL models has become a vital stage in the whole software lifecycle. When training deep learning models, especially those big models, developers need to parallelize and distribute the computation and memory resources amongst multiple devices in the training process, which is known as distributed deep learning training, or distributed training for short. However, the unique challenges that developers encounter in distributed training process have not been studied in the software engineering community. Given the increasingly heavy dependence of current DL-based software on distributed training, this paper aims to fill in the knowledge gap and presents the first comprehensive study on developers' issues in distributed training. To this end, we analyze 1,131 real-world developers' issues about using these frameworks reported on Stack Overflow and GitHub. We construct a fine-grained taxonomy consisting of 30 categories regarding the fault symptoms and summarize common fix patterns for different symptoms. Based on the results, we suggest actionable implications on research avenues that can potentially facilitate the distributed training to develop DL-based software, such as focusing on the frequent and common fix patterns when designing testing or debugging tools, developing efficient testing and debugging techniques for communication configuration along with the synthesis of network configuration analysis, designing new multi-device checkpoint-and-replay techniques to help reproduction, and designing serverless APIs for cloud platforms.

title: Rise of Distributed Deep Learning Training in the Big Model Era: From a Software Engineering Perspective
text: The advent of big models has revolutionized the landscape of deep learning, with models boasting billions of parameters becoming the norm. However, the scale and complexity of these models pose significant challenges to their training, necessitating the development of distributed deep learning training systems. In response, the software engineering community has risen to the challenge, proposing a plethora of frameworks, libraries, and tools to facilitate the efficient training of big models. Despite this, the software engineering aspects of distributed deep learning training remain understudied, with a dearth of empirical investigations into the design, development, and deployment of these systems. This paper addresses this knowledge gap by presenting a comprehensive study of distributed deep learning training from a software engineering perspective. We conducted a mixed-methods investigation, comprising a systematic literature review, a survey of 150 deep learning practitioners, and a case study of three popular open-source distributed deep learning frameworks. Our study reveals that the development of distributed deep learning training systems is a complex, multidisciplinary endeavor, requiring careful consideration of scalability, communication overhead, and fault tolerance. We identify several key challenges, including the need for more efficient communication protocols, improved support for heterogeneous hardware, and better integration with existing software development workflows. Our findings also highlight the importance of software engineering best practices, such as modularity, abstraction, and testing, in ensuring the reliability and maintainability of distributed deep learning training systems. Finally, we propose a set of guidelines and recommendations for the design and development of distributed deep learning training systems, with implications for both research and practice in the field.

title: Boosting the Capability of Intelligent Vulnerability Detection by Training in a Human-Learning Manner
text: Due to its powerful automatic feature extraction, deep learning (DL) has been widely used in source code vulnerability detection. However, although it performs well on artificial datasets, its performance is not satisfactory when detecting real-world vulnerabilities due to the high complexity of real-world samples. In this paper, we propose to train DL-based vulnerability detection models in a human-learning manner, that is, start with the simplest samples and then gradually transition to difficult knowledge. Specifically, we design a novel framework (Humer) that can enhance the detection ability of DL-based vulnerability detectors. To validate the effectiveness of Humer, we select five state-of-the-art DL-based vulnerability detection models (TokenCNN, VulDeePecker, StatementGRU, ASTGRU, and Devign) to complete our evaluations. Through the results, we find that the use of Humer can increase the F1 of these models by an average of 10.5%. Moreover, Humer can make the model detect up to 16.7% more real-world vulnerabilities. Meanwhile, we also conduct a case study to uncover vulnerabilities from real-world open source products by using these enhanced DL-based vulnerability detectors. Through the results, we finally discover 281 unreported vulnerabilities in NVD, of which 98 have been silently patched by vendors in the latest version of corresponding products, but 159 still exist in the products.

title: Boosting the Capability of Intelligent Vulnerability Detection by Training in a Human-Learning Manner
text: The discovery of software vulnerabilities is a crucial aspect of cybersecurity, yet existing automated detection methods often struggle to keep pace with the increasing complexity of modern software systems. Inspired by the human learning process, we propose a novel approach to intelligent vulnerability detection that leverages a cognitive training framework to enhance the capability of machine learning models. By mimicking the way humans learn from experience and adapt to new situations, our approach enables the model to learn from a diverse set of vulnerability examples and generalize to unseen scenarios. We design a multi-stage training pipeline that incorporates a cognitive module, which simulates human-like reasoning and decision-making processes, to iteratively refine the model's detection capabilities. Experimental results on a large-scale dataset of real-world vulnerabilities demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 32% increase in detection accuracy and a 25% reduction in false positives. Furthermore, we observe that our model is more resilient to adversarial attacks and better equipped to handle novel vulnerability types. Our findings have important implications for the development of more effective and efficient vulnerability detection systems, and highlight the potential of cognitive-inspired machine learning techniques in cybersecurity applications.

title: SparseFed: Mitigating Model Poisoning Attacks in Federated Learning with Sparsification
text: Federated learning is inherently vulnerable to model poisoning attacks because its decentralized nature allows attackers to participate with compromised devices. In model poisoning attacks, the attacker reduces the model's performance on targeted sub-tasks (e.g. classifying planes as birds) by uploading "poisoned" updates. In this report we introduce \algoname{}, a novel defense that uses global top-k update sparsification and device-level gradient clipping to mitigate model poisoning attacks. We propose a theoretical framework for analyzing the robustness of defenses against poisoning attacks, and provide robustness and convergence analysis of our algorithm. To validate its empirical efficacy we conduct an open-source evaluation at scale across multiple benchmark datasets for computer vision and federated learning.

title: SparseFed: Mitigating Model Poisoning Attacks in Federated Learning with Sparsification
text: Decentralized learning paradigms, such as federated learning, are susceptible to model poisoning attacks, wherein malicious participants can degrade the model's performance on specific sub-tasks by uploading manipulated updates. To counter this threat, we propose \algoname{}, a novel defense mechanism that leverages global top-k update sparsification and device-level gradient clipping. We establish a theoretical framework for assessing the robustness of defenses against poisoning attacks and provide a comprehensive analysis of our algorithm's robustness and convergence properties. Empirical evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets for computer vision and federated learning demonstrate the efficacy of \algoname{} in mitigating model poisoning attacks.

title: Quantifying and Understanding Adversarial Examples in Discrete Input Spaces
text: Modern classification algorithms are susceptible to adversarial examples--perturbations to inputs that cause the algorithm to produce undesirable behavior. In this work, we seek to understand and extend adversarial examples across domains in which inputs are discrete, particularly across new domains, such as computational biology. As a step towards this goal, we formalize a notion of synonymous adversarial examples that applies in any discrete setting and describe a simple domain-agnostic algorithm to construct such examples. We apply this algorithm across multiple domains--including sentiment analysis and DNA sequence classification--and find that it consistently uncovers adversarial examples. We seek to understand their prevalence theoretically and we attribute their existence to spurious token correlations, a statistical phenomenon that is specific to discrete spaces. Our work is a step towards a domain-agnostic treatment of discrete adversarial examples analogous to that of continuous inputs.

title: Quantifying and Understanding Adversarial Examples in Discrete Input Spaces
text: Adversarial examples, perturbations that induce undesirable behavior in classification algorithms, have been extensively studied in continuous input domains. However, their implications in discrete input domains, particularly in emerging areas like computational biology, remain largely unexplored. We bridge this gap by introducing a notion of synonymous adversarial examples applicable to any discrete setting and propose a simple, domain-agnostic algorithm for their construction. Our approach is validated across multiple domains, including sentiment analysis and DNA sequence classification, where it consistently reveals adversarial examples. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that the prevalence of these examples can be attributed to spurious token correlations, a statistical phenomenon inherent to discrete spaces. Our research paves the way for a unified treatment of discrete adversarial examples, mirroring the progress made in continuous input domains.

title: Weakly Supervised Text-to-SQL Parsing through Question Decomposition
text: Text-to-SQL parsers are crucial in enabling non-experts to effortlessly query relational data. Training such parsers, by contrast, generally requires expertise in annotating natural language (NL) utterances with corresponding SQL queries. In this work, we propose a weak supervision approach for training text-to-SQL parsers. We take advantage of the recently proposed question meaning representation called QDMR, an intermediate between NL and formal query languages. Given questions, their QDMR structures (annotated by non-experts or automatically predicted), and the answers, we are able to automatically synthesize SQL queries that are used to train text-to-SQL models. We test our approach by experimenting on five benchmark datasets. Our results show that the weakly supervised models perform competitively with those trained on annotated NL-SQL data. Overall, we effectively train text-to-SQL parsers, while using zero SQL annotations.

title: Weakly Supervised Text-to-SQL Parsing through Question Decomposition
text: The development of text-to-SQL parsers has facilitated non-expert access to relational data querying. Conversely, parser training typically relies on expert annotation of natural language utterances with corresponding SQL queries. This work presents a weak supervision approach to alleviate this annotation bottleneck. Leveraging the question meaning representation (QDMR) as an intermediate between natural language and formal query languages, we synthesize SQL queries from questions, their QDMR structures, and answers. This enables the training of text-to-SQL models without requiring expert SQL annotations. Experimental results on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that our weakly supervised models achieve competitive performance with models trained on annotated NL-SQL data, effectively eliminating the need for SQL annotations altogether.

title: Interpolated Joint Space Adversarial Training for Robust and Generalizable Defenses
text: Adversarial training (AT) is considered to be one of the most reliable defenses against adversarial attacks. However, models trained with AT sacrifice standard accuracy and do not generalize well to novel attacks. Recent works show generalization improvement with adversarial samples under novel threat models such as on-manifold threat model or neural perceptual threat model. However, the former requires exact manifold information while the latter requires algorithm relaxation. Motivated by these considerations, we exploit the underlying manifold information with Normalizing Flow, ensuring that exact manifold assumption holds. Moreover, we propose a novel threat model called Joint Space Threat Model (JSTM), which can serve as a special case of the neural perceptual threat model that does not require additional relaxation to craft the corresponding adversarial attacks. Under JSTM, we develop novel adversarial attacks and defenses. The mixup strategy improves the standard accuracy of neural networks but sacrifices robustness when combined with AT. To tackle this issue, we propose the Robust Mixup strategy in which we maximize the adversity of the interpolated images and gain robustness and prevent overfitting. Our experiments show that Interpolated Joint Space Adversarial Training (IJSAT) achieves good performance in standard accuracy, robustness, and generalization in CIFAR-10/100, OM-ImageNet, and CIFAR-10-C datasets. IJSAT is also flexible and can be used as a data augmentation method to improve standard accuracy and combine with many existing AT approaches to improve robustness.

title: Interpolated Joint Space Adversarial Training for Robust and Generalizable Defenses
text: The robustness of deep neural networks against adversarial attacks remains a pressing concern, with adversarial training (AT) being a widely recognized defense mechanism. However, AT-learned models often compromise on standard accuracy and exhibit poor generalizability to novel attacks. Recent studies have demonstrated improved generalization capabilities by incorporating adversarial samples under novel threat models, such as the on-manifold and neural perceptual threat models. Nevertheless, these approaches rely on exact manifold information or algorithm relaxation, respectively. To address these limitations, we leverage Normalizing Flow to capture the underlying manifold information, thereby ensuring the validity of the exact manifold assumption. Furthermore, we introduce the Joint Space Threat Model (JSTM), a novel paradigm that generalizes the neural perceptual threat model without requiring additional relaxation for crafting adversarial attacks. Within the JSTM framework, we develop novel attacks and defenses, including the Robust Mixup strategy, which maximizes the adversity of interpolated images to achieve a balance between robustness and standard accuracy. Our experiments on CIFAR-10/100, OM-ImageNet, and CIFAR-10-C datasets demonstrate that Interpolated Joint Space Adversarial Training (IJSAT) excels in standard accuracy, robustness, and generalization. Notably, IJSAT can be seamlessly integrated as a data augmentation method to enhance standard accuracy and combined with existing AT approaches to bolster robustness.

title: Pool-Party: Exploiting Browser Resource Pools as Side-Channels for Web Tracking
text: We identify class of covert channels in browsers that are not mitigated by current defenses, which we call "pool-party" attacks. Pool-party attacks allow sites to create covert channels by manipulating limited-but-unpartitioned resource pools. These class of attacks have been known, but in this work we show that they are both more prevalent, more practical for exploitation, and allow exploitation in more ways, than previously identified. These covert channels have sufficient bandwidth to pass cookies and identifiers across site boundaries under practical and real-world conditions. We identify pool-party attacks in all popular browsers, and show they are practical cross-site tracking techniques (i.e., attacks take 0.6s in Chrome and Edge, and 7s in Firefox and Tor Browser). In this paper we make the following contributions: first, we describe pool-party covert channel attacks that exploit limits in application-layer resource pools in browsers. Second, we demonstrate that pool-party attacks are practical, and can be used to track users in all popular browsers; we also share open source implementations of the attack and evaluate them through a representative web crawl. Third, we show that in Gecko based-browsers (including the Tor Browser) pool-party attacks can also be used for cross-profile tracking (e.g., linking user behavior across normal and private browsing sessions). Finally, we discuss possible mitigation strategies and defenses

title: Pool-Party: Exploiting Browser Resource Pools as Side-Channels for Web Tracking
text: Beneath the surface of current browser security defenses lies a class of covert channels, which we term "pool-party" attacks, that remain unmitigated. These attacks capitalize on the manipulation of limited-but-unpartitioned resource pools, allowing sites to establish covert communication channels. Our research reveals that pool-party attacks are more widespread, exploitable, and versatile than previously acknowledged. Notably, these covert channels possess sufficient bandwidth to facilitate the transmission of cookies and identifiers across site boundaries under realistic conditions. We have identified pool-party attacks in all popular browsers, demonstrating their feasibility as cross-site tracking techniques with surprisingly low latency (0.6 seconds in Chrome and Edge, and 7 seconds in Firefox and Tor Browser). This paper makes three primary contributions: (1) a comprehensive description of pool-party covert channel attacks that exploit limitations in application-layer resource pools; (2) a demonstration of their practicality and effectiveness in tracking users across all popular browsers, accompanied by open-source implementations and a web crawl-based evaluation; and (3) the discovery that, in Gecko-based browsers, including the Tor Browser, pool-party attacks can also enable cross-profile tracking, linking user behavior across normal and private browsing sessions. Finally, we discuss potential mitigation strategies and defenses to counter these attacks.

title: Graph-based hierarchical record clustering for unsupervised entity resolution
text: Here we study the problem of matched record clustering in unsupervised entity resolution. We build upon a state-of-the-art probabilistic framework named the Data Washing Machine (DWM). We introduce a graph-based hierarchical 2-step record clustering method (GDWM) that first identifies large, connected components or, as we call them, soft clusters in the matched record pairs using a graph-based transitive closure algorithm utilized in the DWM. That is followed by breaking down the discovered soft clusters into more precise entity clusters in a hierarchical manner using an adapted graph-based modularity optimization method. Our approach provides several advantages over the original implementation of the DWM, mainly a significant speed-up, increased precision, and overall increased F1 scores. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach using experiments on multiple synthetic datasets. Our results also provide evidence of the utility of graph theory-based algorithms despite their sparsity in the literature on unsupervised entity resolution.

title: Graph-based hierarchical record clustering for unsupervised entity resolution
text: Entity resolution, the process of identifying and merging duplicate records referring to the same real-world entity, is a fundamental problem in data integration and cleaning. Despite significant advances, existing approaches often struggle with large, heterogeneous datasets, where entities exhibit complex relationships and varying degrees of similarity. This paper presents a novel, graph-based hierarchical record clustering approach for unsupervised entity resolution. By modeling records as nodes in a graph, we leverage structural and attribute-based similarities to identify densely connected clusters, which are then recursively merged to form a hierarchical representation of the data. Experimental evaluation on four benchmark datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of precision, recall, and F1-score. Notably, our approach achieves a 12% improvement in F1-score on the challenging Cora dataset, showcasing its robustness in handling noisy and ambiguous data. The proposed method's efficiency and scalability make it a promising solution for large-scale entity resolution tasks.

title: Probabilistic Counting in Uncertain Spatial Databases using Generating Functions
text: Location data is inherently uncertain for many reasons including 1) imprecise location measurements, 2) obsolete observations that are often interpolated, and 3) deliberate obfuscation to preserve location privacy. What makes handling uncertainty data challenging is the exponentially large number of possible worlds, which lies in O(2^N), for a database having N uncertain objects as it has been shown that general query processing in uncertain spatial data is NP-hard. Many applications using spatial data require counting the number of spatial objects within a region. An example is the k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) query: Asking if an object A is a kNN of another object Q is equivalent to asking whether no more than k-1 objects are located inside the circle centered at Q having a radius equal to the distance between Q and A. For this problem of counting uncertain objects within a region, an efficient solution based on Generating Functions has been proposed and successfully used in many applications, including range-count queries, kNN queries, distance ranking queries, and reverse kNN queries. This spatial gem describes the generating function technique for probabilistic counting and provides examples and implementation details.

title: Probabilistic Counting in Uncertain Spatial Databases using Generating Functions
text: Uncertainty is an inherent characteristic of location data, stemming from imprecise measurements, outdated observations, and intentional obfuscation for privacy preservation. The challenge in processing uncertain data lies in the exponential growth of possible worlds, with a complexity of O(2^N) for a database containing N uncertain objects, rendering general query processing NP-hard. Counting the number of spatial objects within a region is a fundamental operation in many applications, exemplified by the k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) query. This query can be reduced to counting objects within a circular region, where the radius is determined by the distance between the query point and the object in question. To address this problem, a Generating Functions-based approach has been proposed, offering an efficient solution for probabilistic counting in uncertain spatial data. This technique has been successfully applied to various query types, including range-count, kNN, distance ranking, and reverse kNN queries. This spatial gem provides a detailed exposition of the generating function technique, accompanied by illustrative examples and implementation guidance.

title: Quantum commitments and signatures without one-way functions
text: In the classical world, the existence of commitments is equivalent to the existence of one-way functions. In the quantum setting, on the other hand, commitments are not known to imply one-way functions, but all known constructions of quantum commitments use at least one-way functions. Are one-way functions really necessary for commitments in the quantum world? In this work, we show that non-interactive quantum commitments (for classical messages) with computational hiding and statistical binding exist if pseudorandom quantum states exist. Pseudorandom quantum states are sets of quantum states that are efficiently generated but their polynomially many copies are computationally indistinguishable from the same number of copies of Haar random states [Ji, Liu, and Song, CRYPTO 2018]. It is known that pseudorandom quantum states exist even if $\BQP=\QMA$ (relative to a quantum oracle) [Kretschmer, TQC 2021], which means that pseudorandom quantum states can exist even if no quantum-secure classical cryptographic primitive exists. Our result therefore shows that quantum commitments can exist even if no quantum-secure classical cryptographic primitive exists. In particular, quantum commitments can exist even if no quantum-secure one-way function exists. In this work, we also consider digital signatures, which are other fundamental primitives in cryptography. We show that one-time secure digital signatures with quantum public keys exist if pseudorandom quantum states exist. In the classical setting, the existence of digital signatures is equivalent to the existence of one-way functions. Our result, on the other hand, shows that quantum signatures can exist even if no quantum-secure classical cryptographic primitive (including quantum-secure one-way functions) exists.

title: Quantum commitments and signatures without one-way functions
text: The existence of one-way functions is a fundamental assumption in cryptography, underpinning the security of various primitives, including commitments and signatures. However, constructing one-way functions from scratch has proven to be a challenging task, and their existence is still unproven. This has led researchers to investigate alternative approaches that avoid relying on one-way functions. In this context, quantum cryptography offers a promising avenue, as it enables the creation of secure primitives based on the principles of quantum mechanics rather than computational assumptions. We present a quantum commitment scheme and a quantum signature scheme that do not rely on one-way functions. Our constructions leverage the power of quantum entanglement and superposition to achieve security. The commitment scheme uses a novel encoding technique that exploits the no-cloning theorem to ensure binding and hiding properties. The signature scheme employs a quantum version of the Fiat-Shamir heuristic, combined with a clever use of entangled measurements to achieve security against adaptive attacks. We rigorously analyze the security of our schemes in the quantum random oracle model, providing detailed proofs of their correctness and security. Our results demonstrate that, contrary to previous beliefs, one-way functions are not essential for constructing secure commitments and signatures. This opens up new possibilities for post-quantum cryptography, where the existence of one-way functions is uncertain. Furthermore, our schemes offer improved efficiency and scalability compared to classical counterparts, making them attractive for real-world applications. Our work paves the way for further research into quantum-based cryptographic primitives, which could lead to a new generation of secure and efficient cryptographic protocols.

title: Does Fully Homomorphic Encryption Need Compute Acceleration?
text: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) allows arbitrarily complex computations on encrypted data without ever needing to decrypt it, thus enabling us to maintain data privacy on third-party systems. Unfortunately, sustaining deep computations with FHE requires a periodic noise reduction step known as bootstrapping. The cost of the bootstrapping operation is one of the primary barriers to the wide-spread adoption of FHE. In this paper, we present an in-depth architectural analysis of the bootstrapping step in FHE. First, we observe that secure implementations of bootstrapping exhibit a low arithmetic intensity (<1 Op/byte), require large caches (>100 MB), and are heavily bound by the main memory bandwidth. Consequently, we demonstrate that existing workloads observe marginal performance gains from the design of bespoke high-throughput arithmetic units tailored to FHE. Second, we propose several cache-friendly algorithmic optimizations that improve the throughput in FHE bootstrapping by enabling up to 3.2x higher arithmetic intensity and 4.6x lower memory bandwidth. Our optimizations apply to a wide range of structurally similar computations such as private evaluation and training of machine learning models. Finally, we incorporate these optimizations into an architectural tool which, given a cache size, memory subsystem, the number of functional units and a desired security level, selects optimal cryptosystem parameters to maximize the bootstrapping throughput. Our optimized bootstrapping implementation represents a best-case scenario for compute acceleration of FHE. We show that despite these optimizations, bootstrapping continues to be bottlenecked by main memory bandwidth. We propose new research directions to address the underlying memory bottleneck. In summary, our answer to the titular question is: yes, but only after addressing the memory bottleneck!

title: Does Fully Homomorphic Encryption Need Compute Acceleration?
text: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) has emerged as a promising approach to enable secure computation on sensitive data in untrusted environments. However, the computational overhead associated with FHE schemes has hindered their widespread adoption. A natural question arises: can compute acceleration mitigate the performance bottleneck of FHE? To investigate this, we conduct a comprehensive study on the interplay between FHE and compute acceleration. We focus on the CKKS scheme, a state-of-the-art FHE scheme that supports efficient homomorphic computations. We implement CKKS on various hardware platforms, including CPU, GPU, and FPGA, and evaluate their performance on a range of benchmark datasets. Our results show that, while compute acceleration can significantly improve the performance of CKKS, the speedup is highly dependent on the specific acceleration platform and the characteristics of the input data. Notably, we observe that GPU acceleration yields the most significant speedup for large datasets, whereas FPGA acceleration is more effective for smaller datasets. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the memory bandwidth and cache hierarchy of the acceleration platform play critical roles in determining the performance of CKKS. We also develop a theoretical model to predict the performance of CKKS on different acceleration platforms, which is validated by our experimental results. Our findings have important implications for the design and deployment of FHE-based systems. Specifically, our study suggests that a careful consideration of the acceleration platform and input data characteristics is essential to optimize the performance of FHE schemes. Furthermore, our results highlight the need for further research on optimizing FHE schemes for emerging compute acceleration platforms, such as quantum computers and neuromorphic chips.

title: What can Data-Centric AI Learn from Data and ML Engineering?
text: Data-centric AI is a new and exciting research topic in the AI community, but many organizations already build and maintain various "data-centric" applications whose goal is to produce high quality data. These range from traditional business data processing applications (e.g., "how much should we charge each of our customers this month?") to production ML systems such as recommendation engines. The fields of data and ML engineering have arisen in recent years to manage these applications, and both include many interesting novel tools and processes. In this paper, we discuss several lessons from data and ML engineering that could be interesting to apply in data-centric AI, based on our experience building data and ML platforms that serve thousands of applications at a range of organizations.

title: What can Data-Centric AI Learn from Data and ML Engineering?
text: The proliferation of data-centric applications across various organizations has led to the emergence of data and machine learning engineering as distinct fields, dedicated to managing these systems. These applications, encompassing traditional business data processing and production machine learning systems like recommendation engines, share the common objective of generating high-quality data. Through our experience in developing data and machine learning platforms that support thousands of applications across diverse organizations, we have distilled valuable lessons that can be fruitfully applied to the burgeoning field of data-centric AI. This paper presents these insights, highlighting the novel tools and processes that can be leveraged to advance data-centric AI research and practice.

title: Detecting Audio Adversarial Examples with Logit Noising
text: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems are vulnerable to audio adversarial examples that attempt to deceive ASR systems by adding perturbations to benign speech signals. Although an adversarial example and the original benign wave are indistinguishable to humans, the former is transcribed as a malicious target sentence by ASR systems. Several methods have been proposed to generate audio adversarial examples and feed them directly into the ASR system (over-line). Furthermore, many researchers have demonstrated the feasibility of robust physical audio adversarial examples(over-air). To defend against the attacks, several studies have been proposed. However, deploying them in a real-world situation is difficult because of accuracy drop or time overhead. In this paper, we propose a novel method to detect audio adversarial examples by adding noise to the logits before feeding them into the decoder of the ASR. We show that carefully selected noise can significantly impact the transcription results of the audio adversarial examples, whereas it has minimal impact on the transcription results of benign audio waves. Based on this characteristic, we detect audio adversarial examples by comparing the transcription altered by logit noising with its original transcription. The proposed method can be easily applied to ASR systems without any structural changes or additional training. The experimental results show that the proposed method is robust to over-line audio adversarial examples as well as over-air audio adversarial examples compared with state-of-the-art detection methods.

title: Detecting Audio Adversarial Examples with Logit Noising
text: The proliferation of deep learning models in audio processing tasks has introduced a new attack vector: audio adversarial examples. These maliciously crafted inputs can manipulate model outputs, posing significant security risks in applications such as voice assistants and audio classification systems. Existing detection methods, primarily designed for image domains, often fail to generalize to audio due to the distinct characteristics of audio signals. To address this challenge, we propose Logit Noising, a novel approach for detecting audio adversarial examples. Our method injects noise into the logit layer of a neural network, effectively perturbing the model's output probabilities. This noise injection enables the distinction between legitimate and adversarial inputs, as the latter exhibit increased sensitivity to logit perturbations. We evaluate Logit Noising on a range of audio datasets, including SpeechCommands and AudioSet, using state-of-the-art audio adversarial attacks. Our results demonstrate that Logit Noising significantly outperforms existing detection methods, achieving an average detection rate of 93.5% on unseen attacks. Furthermore, we show that our approach is robust to various attack strategies, including white-box and black-box scenarios. The proposed method provides a promising direction for securing audio processing systems against adversarial threats, with potential applications in multiple domains, including audio forensics and cybersecurity.

title: Comments on "A Privacy-Preserving Online Ride-Hailing System Without Involving a Third Trusted Server"
text: Recently, Xie et al. (IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security, vol. 16, pp. 3068-3081, 2021) proposed a privacy-preserving Online Ride-Hailing (ORH) protocol that does not make use of a trusted third-party server. The primary goal of such privacy-preserving ORH protocols is to ensure the privacy of riders' and drivers' location data w.r.t. the ORH Service Provider (SP). In this note, we demonstrate a passive attack by the SP in the protocol of Xie et al. that enables it to completely recover the location of the rider as well as that of the responding drivers in each and every ride request query.

title: Comments on "A Privacy-Preserving Online Ride-Hailing System Without Involving a Third Trusted Server"
text: Recent online ride-hailing systems prioritizing user privacy have relied on trusted third-party servers, which can be vulnerable to data breaches and single points of failure. A recent proposal, "A Privacy-Preserving Online Ride-Hailing System Without Involving a Third Trusted Server," claimed to eliminate this reliance. However, we identify critical flaws in their design, compromising user privacy and system security. Through a thorough security analysis, we demonstrate that their protocol is susceptible to replay attacks and lacks robustness against malicious riders. We propose concrete countermeasures to mitigate these vulnerabilities, emphasizing the need for rigorous security proofs in privacy-preserving systems.

title: A Novel Model for Vulnerability Analysis through Enhanced Directed Graphs and Quantitative Metrics
text: Industrial components are of high importance because they control critical infrastructures that form the lifeline of modern societies. However, the rapid evolution of industrial components, together with the new paradigm of Industry 4.0, and the new connectivity features that will be introduced by the 5G technology, all increase the likelihood of security incidents. These incidents are caused by the vulnerabilities present in these devices. In addition, although international standards define tasks to assess vulnerabilities, they do not specify any particular method. Having a secure design is important, but is also complex, costly, and an extra factor to manage during the lifespan of the device. This paper presents a model to analyze the known vulnerabilities of industrial components over time. The proposed model is based on two main elements: a directed graph representation of the internal structure of the component, and a set of quantitative metrics that are based on international security standards; such as, the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). This model is applied throughout the entire lifespan of a device to track vulnerabilities, identify new requirements, root causes, and test cases. The proposed model also helps to prioritize patching activities. To test its potential, the proposed model is applied to the OpenPLC project. The results show that most of the root causes of these vulnerabilities are related to memory buffer operations and are concentrated in the \textit{libssl} library. Consequently, new requirements and test cases were generated from the obtained data.

title: A Novel Model for Vulnerability Analysis through Enhanced Directed Graphs and Quantitative Metrics
text: The reliability of modern societies hinges on the secure operation of industrial components, which control critical infrastructures. The confluence of rapid technological advancements, the Industry 4.0 paradigm, and the imminent introduction of 5G connectivity features has increased the likelihood of security breaches in these devices. Vulnerabilities inherent to these components are the primary cause of such incidents. Although international standards outline tasks for vulnerability assessment, they fail to specify a standardized method. Ensuring secure design is crucial but complex, costly, and adds an extra layer of complexity to device management. This paper proposes a novel model for analyzing known vulnerabilities in industrial components over time. The model relies on a directed graph representation of the component's internal structure and a set of quantitative metrics grounded in international security standards, including the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). By applying this model throughout a device's lifespan, vulnerabilities can be tracked, new requirements identified, root causes pinpointed, and test cases generated. The model also facilitates the prioritization of patching activities. To demonstrate its efficacy, the proposed model is applied to the OpenPLC project, revealing that most root causes of vulnerabilities are linked to memory buffer operations and are concentrated in the libssl library. This analysis yields new requirements and test cases, underscoring the model's potential in enhancing industrial component security.

title: Proof of Steak
text: We introduce Proof-of-Steak (PoS) as a fundamental net-zero block generation technique, often accompanied by Non-Frangipane Tokens. Genesis cut is gradually heated and minted (using the appropriate sauce), enabling the miners to redirect the extracted gold and the dissipated heat into the furnace, hence enabling the first fully-circular economy ever built using blockchain technology, utilising tamper-evident steak haché. In this paper we present the basic ingredients for building Proof-of-Steak, assessing its global impact, and opportunities to save the world and beyond!

title: Proof of Steak
text: We present Proof of Steak, a novel consensus protocol that leverages game-theoretic incentives to secure decentralized systems. By formalizing the notion of "steak" as a scarce, desirable resource, we create an environment where rational actors prioritize consensus participation over selfish behavior. Through a combination of cryptographic commitments and economically-incentivized verification, our protocol achieves 33% higher throughput and 25% lower latency compared to existing proof-of-work-based systems, while maintaining equivalent security guarantees in the presence of Byzantine faults.

title: A Structured Analysis of Information Security Incidents in the Maritime Sector
text: Cyber attacks in the maritime sector can have a major impact on world economy. However, the severity of this threat can be underestimated because many attacks remain unknown or unnoticed. We present an overview about publicly known cyber incidents in the maritime sector from the past 20 years. In total, we found 90 publicly reported attacks and 15 proof of concepts. Furthermore, we interviewed five IT security experts from the maritime sector. The interviews put the results of our research in perspective and confirm that our view is comprehensive. However, the interviewees highlight that there is a high dark figure of unreported incidents and argue that threat information sharing may potentially be helpful for attack prevention. From these results, we extract threats for players in the maritime sector.

title: A Structured Analysis of Information Security Incidents in the Maritime Sector
text: The maritime sector's increasing reliance on digital technologies has heightened its vulnerability to information security incidents, posing significant risks to global trade, economic stability, and human life. Despite this, there exists a dearth of systematic studies on maritime cybersecurity incidents. This paper addresses this gap by conducting a structured analysis of 154 reported incidents between 2015 and 2020, leveraging a custom-built taxonomy and a mixed-methods approach. Our findings reveal that phishing and unauthorized access are the most prevalent incident types, while human error and inadequate security measures are the primary contributing factors. Furthermore, we identify a significant increase in incident frequency and severity over the studied period, highlighting the need for sector-specific cybersecurity frameworks and proactive threat mitigation strategies. Our research provides a crucial understanding of the maritime sector's information security landscape, informing the development of targeted risk management and incident response strategies.

title: One Size Fits All: A Conceptual Data Model for Any Approach to Terminology
text: In this paper, we want to speculate about the possibility to model all the currently known/proposed approaches to terminology into a single schema. We will use the Entity-Relationship (ER) diagram as our tool for the conceptual data model of the problem and to express the associations between the objects of the study. We will analyse the onomasiological and semasiological approaches, the ontoterminology paradigm, and the frame-based model, and we will draw the consequences in terms of the conceptual data model. The result of this discussion will be used as the basis of the next step of the data organization in terms of standardized terminological records and Linked Data.

title: One Size Fits All: A Conceptual Data Model for Any Approach to Terminology
text: This study explores the feasibility of integrating disparate approaches to terminology into a unified framework. Employing the Entity-Relationship diagram as a conceptual data modeling tool, we examine the interrelationships between key objects of study. A comprehensive analysis of onomasiological and semasiological approaches, the ontoterminology paradigm, and frame-based models informs the development of a conceptual data model. The implications of this investigation will serve as the foundation for subsequent data organization efforts, ultimately culminating in the creation of standardized terminological records and Linked Data.

title: From Anecdote to Evidence: The Relationship Between Personality and Need for Cognition of Developers
text: There is considerable anecdotal evidence suggesting that software engineers enjoy engaging in solving puzzles and other cognitive efforts. A tendency to engage in and enjoy effortful thinking is referred to as a person's 'need for cognition.' In this article we study the relationship between software engineers' personality traits and their need for cognition. Through a large-scale sample study of 483 respondents we collected data to capture the six 'bright' personality traits of the HEXACO model of personality, and three `dark' personality traits. Data were analyzed using several methods including a multiple Bayesian linear regression analysis. The results indicate that ca. 33% of variation in developers' need for cognition can be explained by personality traits. The Bayesian analysis suggests four traits to be of particular interest in predicting need for cognition: openness to experience, conscientiousness, honesty-humility, and emotionality. Further, we also find that need for cognition of software engineers is, on average, higher than in the general population, based on a comparison with prior studies. Given the importance of human factors for software engineers' performance in general, and problem solving skills in particular, our findings suggest several implications for recruitment, working behavior, and teaming.

title: From Anecdote to Evidence: The Relationship Between Personality and Need for Cognition of Developers
text: Research suggests that software engineers tend to derive enjoyment from puzzle-solving and other cognitively demanding activities, a propensity known as the "need for cognition". This study examines the relationship between software engineers' personality traits and their need for cognition.
