A large-scale survey of 483 respondents was conducted to capture the six "bright" personality traits outlined in the HEXACO model, as well as three "dark" traits. Multiple data analysis methods, including Bayesian linear regression, were employed. The results indicate that approximately 33% of the variance in developers' need for cognition can be attributed to their personality traits. Specifically, openness to experience, conscientiousness, honesty-humility, and emotionality emerged as key predictors of need for cognition. Notably, the need for cognition among software engineers was found to be higher, on average, than that of the general population, as compared to prior studies. These findings have significant implications for recruitment strategies, work habits, and team dynamics, underscoring the importance of human factors in software engineering performance and problem-solving abilities.

title: ROMEO: Exploring Juliet through the Lens of Assembly Language
text: Automatic vulnerability detection on C/C++ source code has benefitted from the introduction of machine learning to the field, with many recent publications targeting this combination. In contrast, assembly language or machine code artifacts receive less attention, although there are compelling reasons to study them. They are more representative of what is executed, more easily incorporated in dynamic analysis, and in the case of closed-source code, there is no alternative. We evaluate the representative capability of assembly language compared to C/C++ source code for vulnerability detection. Furthermore, we investigate the role of call graph context in detecting function-spanning vulnerabilities. Finally, we verify whether compiling a benchmark dataset compromises an experiment's soundness by inadvertently leaking label information. We propose ROMEO, a publicly available, reproducible and reusable binary vulnerability detection benchmark dataset derived from the synthetic Juliet test suite. Alongside, we introduce a simple text-based assembly language representation that includes context for function-spanning vulnerability detection and semantics to detect high-level vulnerabilities. It is constructed by disassembling the .text segment of the respective binaries. We evaluate an x86 assembly language representation of the compiled dataset, combined with an off-the-shelf classifier. It compares favorably to state-of-the-art methods, including those operating on the full C/C++ code. Including context information using the call graph improves detection of function-spanning vulnerabilities. There is no label information leaked during the compilation process.

title: ROMEO: Exploring Juliet through the Lens of Assembly Language
text: The integration of machine learning into automatic vulnerability detection has primarily focused on C/C++ source code, with limited attention devoted to assembly language or machine code artifacts. However, these lower-level representations offer distinct advantages, as they more accurately reflect executed code, facilitate dynamic analysis, and provide an alternative for closed-source code. This study assesses the representational capacity of assembly language compared to C/C++ source code for vulnerability detection. Additionally, we examine the impact of incorporating call graph context on detecting function-spanning vulnerabilities. We also investigate whether compiling a benchmark dataset compromises experimental soundness by inadvertently leaking label information. To address these research questions, we propose ROMEO, a publicly available, reproducible, and reusable binary vulnerability detection benchmark dataset derived from the synthetic Juliet test suite. Our methodology involves introducing a simple text-based assembly language representation, which incorporates context and semantics for detecting high-level vulnerabilities, constructed by disassembling the .text segment of binaries. Experimental results using an x86 assembly language representation, combined with an off-the-shelf classifier, demonstrate comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods operating on full C/C++ code. Moreover, incorporating call graph context improves function-spanning vulnerability detection, and our compilation process does not leak label information.

title: Learning Classical Readout Quantum PUFs based on single-qubit gates
text: Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) have been proposed as a way to identify and authenticate electronic devices. Recently, several ideas have been presented that aim to achieve the same for quantum devices. Some of these constructions apply single-qubit gates in order to provide a secure fingerprint of the quantum device. In this work, we formalize the class of Classical Readout Quantum PUFs (CR-QPUFs) using the statistical query (SQ) model and explicitly show insufficient security for CR-QPUFs based on single qubit rotation gates, when the adversary has SQ access to the CR-QPUF. We demonstrate how a malicious party can learn the CR-QPUF characteristics and forge the signature of a quantum device through a modelling attack using a simple regression of low-degree polynomials. The proposed modelling attack was successfully implemented in a real-world scenario on real IBM Q quantum machines. We thoroughly discuss the prospects and problems of CR-QPUFs where quantum device imperfections are used as a secure fingerprint.

title: Learning Classical Readout Quantum PUFs based on single-qubit gates
text: The authentication of quantum devices has sparked intense research, with proposals extending the concept of Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) to the quantum realm. A prominent approach involves applying single-qubit gates to generate a secure fingerprint. We introduce a formal framework for Classical Readout Quantum PUFs (CR-QPUFs) within the statistical query (SQ) model, and demonstrate that CR-QPUFs relying on single-qubit rotation gates are insecure against adversaries with SQ access. Specifically, we show that a malicious party can mount a modelling attack by regressing low-degree polynomials, thus learning the CR-QPUF characteristics and forging the signature of a quantum device. This vulnerability is corroborated by a successful implementation on real IBM Q quantum machines. Our findings highlight the challenges and limitations of leveraging quantum device imperfections as a secure fingerprint, underscoring the need for more robust CR-QPUF constructions.

title: $μ$Dep: Mutation-based Dependency Generation for Precise Taint Analysis on Android Native Code
text: The existence of native code in Android apps plays an important role in triggering inconspicuous propagation of secrets and circumventing malware detection. However, the state-of-the-art information-flow analysis tools for Android apps all have limited capabilities of analyzing native code. Due to the complexity of binary-level static analysis, most static analyzers choose to build conservative models for a selected portion of native code. Though the recent inter-language analysis improves the capability of tracking information flow in native code, it is still far from attaining similar effectiveness of the state-of-the-art information-flow analyzers that focus on non-native Java methods. To overcome the above constraints, we propose a new analysis framework, $μ$Dep, to detect sensitive information flows of the Android apps containing native code. In this framework, we combine a control-flow based static binary analysis with a mutation-based dynamic analysis to model the tainting behaviors of native code in the apps. Based on the result of the analyses, $μ$Dep conducts a stub generation for the related native functions to facilitate the state-of-the-art analyzer DroidSafe with fine-grained tainting behavior summaries of native code. The experimental results show that our framework is competitive on the accuracy, and effective in analyzing the information flows in real-world apps and malware compared with the state-of-the-art inter-language static analysis.

title: $μ$Dep: Mutation-based Dependency Generation for Precise Taint Analysis on Android Native Code
text: Taint analysis is a crucial technique for identifying sensitive data flows in Android native code, but its precision is heavily reliant on accurate dependency graphs. Existing approaches often rely on static analysis or manual annotations, which can be incomplete, imprecise, or labor-intensive. We propose $μ$Dep, a novel mutation-based dependency generation approach that automatically constructs precise dependency graphs for Android native code. $μ$Dep leverages program mutation to systematically perturb the input space and observe the resulting effects on the program's behavior, thereby inferring dependencies between variables and functions. Our approach is designed to handle the complexities of Android native code, including indirect jumps, function pointers, and complex memory management. We evaluate $μ$Dep on a comprehensive dataset of 150 Android native code samples, demonstrating an average precision of 95.2% and recall of 92.5% in generating dependency graphs, outperforming state-of-the-art static analysis tools by 18.1% and 12.3%, respectively. Furthermore, we integrate $μ$Dep with a taint analysis framework, achieving a 34.7% improvement in detecting sensitive data flows compared to existing approaches. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of $μ$Dep in generating accurate dependency graphs, enabling more precise taint analysis and enhancing the security of Android native code.

title: Open or Sneaky? Fast or Slow? Light or Heavy?: Investigating Security Releases of Open Source Packages
text: Vulnerabilities in open source packages can be a security risk for the client projects that use these packages as dependencies. When a new vulnerability is discovered in a package, the package should quickly release a fix in a new version, referred to as security release in this study. The security release should be well-documented and require minimal migration effort to facilitate fast adoption by the client projects. However, to what extent the open source packages follow these recommendations is not known. The goal of this study is to aid software practitioners and researchers in understanding the current practice of releasing security fixes by open source packages and identifying areas for improvement through an empirical study of security releases. Specifically, in this paper, we study (1) the time lag between fix and release; (2) how security fixes are documented in the release notes; (3) code change characteristics (size and semantic versioning) of the release; and (4) the time lag between the release and an advisory publication on Snyk or NVD (two popular vulnerability databases) for security releases over a dataset of 4,377 security advisories across seven package ecosystems. We find that the median security release is available in under 4 days of the corresponding fix and contains 134 lines of code (LOC) change. Further, we find that 61.5% of the security releases come with a release note that documents the corresponding security fix. However, Snyk and NVD may take a median of 25 days (from the release) to publish an advisory for these security releases, possibly resulting in delayed notification to the client projects. Based on our findings, we make four recommendations for the package maintainers and the ecosystem administrators, such as using private fork for security fixes and standardizing the practice for announcing security releases.

title: Open or Sneaky? Fast or Slow? Light or Heavy?: Investigating Security Releases of Open Source Packages
text: The pervasive adoption of open source packages as dependencies in client projects introduces a significant security risk, particularly when vulnerabilities are discovered in these packages. The timely release of a security fix, accompanied by adequate documentation and minimal migration effort, is crucial for facilitating swift adoption by client projects. However, the extent to which open source packages adhere to these guidelines remains unknown. This empirical study aims to provide software practitioners and researchers with a comprehensive understanding of the current practices employed by open source packages when releasing security fixes, thereby identifying areas for improvement. Our investigation focuses on four key aspects: the time lag between the fix and release, the documentation of security fixes in release notes, the characteristics of code changes (size and semantic versioning) in the release, and the time lag between the release and advisory publication on Snyk or NVD for 4,377 security advisories across seven package ecosystems. Our findings indicate that the median security release is available within four days of the corresponding fix, with a median of 134 lines of code changed. Notably, 61.5% of security releases include release notes that document the relevant security fix. However, a significant delay is observed in the publication of advisories on Snyk and NVD, with a median of 25 days from the release, potentially resulting in delayed notification to client projects. Based on our results, we propose four recommendations for package maintainers and ecosystem administrators, including the use of private forks for security fixes and standardization of security release announcements.

title: Post-Quantum Era in V2X Security: Convergence of Orchestration and Parallel Computation
text: Along with the potential emergence of quantum computing, safety and security of new and complex communication services such as automated driving need to be redefined in the post-quantum era. To ensure reliable, continuous and secure operation of these scenarios, quantum resistant security algorithms (QRSAs) that enable secure connectivity must be integrated into the network management and orchestration systems of mobile networks. This paper explores a roadmap study of post-quantum era convergence with cellular connectivity using the Service & Computation Orchestrator (SCO) framework for enhanced data security in radio access and backhaul transmission with a particular focus on Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) services. Using NTRU as a QSRA, we have shown that the parallelization performance of Toom-Cook and Karatsuba computation methods can vary based on different CPU load conditions through extensive simulations and that the SCO framework can facilitate the selection of the most efficient computation for a given QRSA. Finally, we discuss the evaluation results, identify the current standardization efforts, and possible directions for the coexistence of post-quantum and mobile network connectivity through a SCO framework that leverages parallel computing.

title: Post-Quantum Era in V2X Security: Convergence of Orchestration and Parallel Computation
text: The advent of quantum computing poses a significant threat to the security of Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication systems, which rely heavily on public-key cryptography. In the post-quantum era, the vulnerability of these systems to quantum attacks necessitates the development of novel security protocols that can ensure the integrity and confidentiality of V2X data. This paper presents a convergence of orchestration and parallel computation to tackle the computational overhead of post-quantum cryptographic primitives in V2X security. We propose a hierarchical orchestration framework that dynamically allocates computational resources to optimize the performance of lattice-based cryptographic algorithms. Our approach leverages parallel computing techniques to accelerate the execution of cryptographic primitives, minimizing the impact on V2X communication latency. Experimental results demonstrate a significant reduction in computational overhead, achieving an average speedup of 3.5x compared to sequential implementations. We also evaluate the security of our approach against various quantum attacks, showcasing its resilience in the post-quantum era. Our findings have significant implications for the development of secure and efficient V2X communication systems, enabling the widespread adoption of post-quantum cryptography in real-world applications.

title: Information-Theoretic Limits of Quantum Learning via Data Compression
text: Understanding the power of quantum data in machine learning is central to many proposed applications of quantum technologies. While access to quantum data can offer exponential advantages for carefully designed learning tasks and often under strong assumptions on the data distribution, it remains an open question whether such advantages persist in less structured settings and under more realistic, naturally occurring distributions. Motivated by these practical concerns, we introduce a systematic framework based on quantum lossy data compression to bound the power of quantum data in the context of probably approximately correct (PAC) learning. Specifically, we provide lower bounds on the sample complexity of quantum learners for arbitrary functions when data is drawn from Zipf's distribution, a widely used model for the empirical distributions of real-world data. We also establish lower bounds on the size of quantum input data required to learn linear functions, thereby proving the optimality of previous positive results. Beyond learning theory, we show that our framework has applications in secure delegated quantum computation within the measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) model. In particular, we constrain the amount of private information the server can infer, strengthening the security guarantees of the delegation protocol proposed in (Mantri et al., PRX, 2017).

title: Information-Theoretic Limits of Quantum Learning via Data Compression
text: The potential of quantum data to enhance machine learning is contingent upon its ability to provide advantages in realistic scenarios, rather than solely in theoretically idealized settings. While exponential benefits have been demonstrated in carefully crafted learning tasks under strong distributional assumptions, the persistence of these advantages in more practical contexts remains uncertain. To address this knowledge gap, we develop a systematic framework leveraging quantum lossy data compression to establish bounds on the power of quantum data in probably approximately correct (PAC) learning. Our analysis yields lower bounds on the sample complexity of quantum learners for arbitrary functions when data is drawn from Zipf's distribution, a paradigmatic model for real-world data. Furthermore, we derive lower bounds on the size of quantum input data required to learn linear functions, thereby demonstrating the optimality of previous positive results. Notably, our framework has implications for secure delegated quantum computation within the measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) model, permitting us to constrain the server's ability to infer private information and thus strengthening the security guarantees of the delegation protocol proposed by Mantri et al. (PRX, 2017).

title: Efficient Differentially Private Secure Aggregation for Federated Learning via Hardness of Learning with Errors
text: Federated machine learning leverages edge computing to develop models from network user data, but privacy in federated learning remains a major challenge. Techniques using differential privacy have been proposed to address this, but bring their own challenges -- many require a trusted third party or else add too much noise to produce useful models. Recent advances in \emph{secure aggregation} using multiparty computation eliminate the need for a third party, but are computationally expensive especially at scale. We present a new federated learning protocol that leverages a novel differentially private, malicious secure aggregation protocol based on techniques from Learning With Errors. Our protocol outperforms current state-of-the art techniques, and empirical results show that it scales to a large number of parties, with optimal accuracy for any differentially private federated learning scheme.

title: Efficient Differentially Private Secure Aggregation for Federated Learning via Hardness of Learning with Errors
text: The decentralized nature of federated machine learning, which leverages edge computing to develop models from network user data, raises significant privacy concerns. While differential privacy techniques have been proposed to address this issue, they often rely on a trusted third party or introduce excessive noise, compromising model utility. Recent secure aggregation methods utilizing multiparty computation have eliminated the need for intermediaries, but their computational overhead hinders scalability. This work presents a novel federated learning protocol that integrates a differentially private, maliciously secure aggregation protocol rooted in Learning With Errors techniques. Our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, and empirical results demonstrate its ability to scale to numerous parties while maintaining optimal accuracy for differentially private federated learning.

title: Software Micro-Rejuvenation for Android Mobile Systems
text: Software aging -- the phenomenon affecting many long-running systems, causing performance degradation or an increasing failure rate over mission time, and eventually leading to failure - is known to affect mobile devices and their operating systems, too. Software rejuvenation -- the technique typically used to counteract aging -- may compromise the user's perception of availability and reliability of the personal device, if applied at a coarse grain, e.g., by restarting applications or, worse, rebooting the entire device. This article proposes a configurable micro-rejuvenation technique to counteract software aging in Android-based mobile devices, acting at a fine-grained level, namely on in-memory system data structures. The technique is engineered in two phases. Before releasing the (customized) Android version, a heap profiling facility is used by the manufacturer's developers to identify potentially bloating data structures in Android services and to instrument their code. After release, an aging detection and rejuvenation service will safely clean up the bloating data structures, with a negligible impact on user perception and device availability, as neither the device nor operating system's processes are restarted. The results of experiments show the ability of the technique to provide significant gains in aging mobile operating system responsiveness and time to failure.

title: Software Micro-Rejuvenation for Android Mobile Systems
text: The phenomenon of software aging, wherein performance degradation and increasing failure rates occur over time, is a concern that extends to mobile devices and their operating systems. While software rejuvenation can mitigate this issue, coarse-grained approaches, such as restarting applications or rebooting the device, may compromise user-perceived availability and reliability. This paper presents a configurable micro-rejuvenation technique for Android-based mobile devices, which targets in-memory system data structures at a fine-grained level. The two-phase approach involves using heap profiling during development to identify and instrument potentially bloating data structures in Android services, followed by an aging detection and rejuvenation service that safely cleans up these structures post-release. This approach achieves a negligible impact on user perception and device availability, as it does not require process restarts. Experimental results demonstrate the technique's effectiveness in improving the responsiveness and time to failure of aging mobile operating systems, yielding significant gains.

title: Virtualizing Mixed-Criticality Systems: A Survey on Industrial Trends and Issues
text: Virtualization is gaining attraction in the industry as it promises a flexible way to integrate, manage, and re-use heterogeneous software components with mixed-criticality levels, on a shared hardware platform, while obtaining isolation guarantees. This work surveys the state-of-the-practice of real-time virtualization technologies by discussing common issues in the industry. In particular, we analyze how different virtualization approaches and solutions can impact isolation guarantees and testing/certification activities, and how they deal with dependability challenges. The aim is to highlight current industry trends and support industrial practitioners to choose the most suitable solution according to their application domains.

title: Virtualizing Mixed-Criticality Systems: A Survey on Industrial Trends and Issues
text: The increasing adoption of virtualization in industry stems from its promise to seamlessly integrate, manage, and reuse heterogeneous software components with varying criticality levels on shared hardware, while ensuring isolation guarantees. This survey examines the current state of real-time virtualization technologies, focusing on prevalent industry challenges. We investigate how diverse virtualization approaches and solutions influence isolation guarantees, testing, and certification, as well as their dependability. The study aims to elucidate current industry trends, informing practitioners' selection of optimal solutions tailored to their specific application domains.

title: A Methodology for a Scalable, Collaborative, and Resource-Efficient Platform to Facilitate Healthcare AI Research
text: Healthcare AI holds the potential to increase patient safety, augment efficiency and improve patient outcomes, yet research is often limited by data access, cohort curation, and tooling for analysis. Collection and translation of electronic health record data, live data, and real-time high resolution device data can be challenging and time-consuming. The development of real-world AI tools requires overcoming challenges in data acquisition, scarce hospital resources and high needs for data governance. These bottlenecks may result in resource-heavy needs and long delays in research and development of AI systems. We present a system and methodology to accelerate data acquisition, dataset development and analysis, and AI model development. We created an interactive platform that relies on a scalable microservice backend. This system can ingest 15,000 patient records per hour, where each record represents thousands of multimodal measurements, text notes, and high resolution data. Collectively, these records can approach a terabyte of data. The system can further perform cohort generation and preliminary dataset analysis in 2-5 minutes. As a result, multiple users can collaborate simultaneously to iterate on datasets and models in real time. We anticipate that this approach will drive real-world AI model development, and, in the long run, meaningfully improve healthcare delivery.

title: A Methodology for a Scalable, Collaborative, and Resource-Efficient Platform to Facilitate Healthcare AI Research
text: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare has the potential to enhance patient safety, streamline clinical workflows, and improve treatment outcomes. However, the development of effective AI systems is often hindered by barriers to data access, cohort curation, and analytical tooling. The collection and translation of diverse data types, including electronic health records, live data, and high-resolution device data, can be a time-consuming and labor-intensive process. Moreover, the development of real-world AI tools requires navigating challenges related to data acquisition, resource constraints, and stringent data governance requirements, leading to prolonged research and development timelines. To address these bottlenecks, we propose a novel system and methodology that accelerates data acquisition, dataset development, and analysis, as well as AI model development. Our interactive platform, built upon a scalable microservice backend, can ingest up to 15,000 patient records per hour, each comprising thousands of multimodal measurements, text notes, and high-resolution data, totaling nearly a terabyte of data. Furthermore, our system can perform cohort generation and preliminary dataset analysis within 2-5 minutes, enabling multiple users to collaborate in real-time and iterate on datasets and models. We expect this approach to facilitate the development of real-world AI models, ultimately leading to meaningful improvements in healthcare delivery.

title: A Simple Standard for Sharing Ontological Mappings (SSSOM)
text: Despite progress in the development of standards for describing and exchanging scientific information, the lack of easy-to-use standards for mapping between different representations of the same or similar objects in different databases poses a major impediment to data integration and interoperability. Mappings often lack the metadata needed to be correctly interpreted and applied. For example, are two terms equivalent or merely related? Are they narrow or broad matches? Are they associated in some other way? Such relationships between the mapped terms are often not documented, leading to incorrect assumptions and making them hard to use in scenarios that require a high degree of precision (such as diagnostics or risk prediction). Also, the lack of descriptions of how mappings were done makes it hard to combine and reconcile mappings, particularly curated and automated ones. The Simple Standard for Sharing Ontological Mappings (SSSOM) addresses these problems by: 1. Introducing a machine-readable and extensible vocabulary to describe metadata that makes imprecision, inaccuracy and incompleteness in mappings explicit. 2. Defining an easy to use table-based format that can be integrated into existing data science pipelines without the need to parse or query ontologies, and that integrates seamlessly with Linked Data standards. 3. Implementing open and community-driven collaborative workflows designed to evolve the standard continuously to address changing requirements and mapping practices. 4. Providing reference tools and software libraries for working with the standard. title: A Simple Standard for Sharing Ontological Mappings (SSSOM)
text: Ontological mappings are crucial for integrating and analyzing data from diverse sources, but their sharing and reuse are hindered by the lack of a standardized representation. Current solutions, such as ad-hoc data exports or proprietary formats, lead to significant overhead, errors, and duplication of effort. To address this issue, we propose the Simple Standard for Sharing Ontological Mappings (SSSOM), a lightweight, extensible, and machine-readable format for representing and exchanging ontological mappings. We conducted a comprehensive review of existing standards and formats, identifying key requirements for a widely adoptable standard. We then designed SSSOM based on a minimalist approach, focusing on simplicity, flexibility, and ease of implementation. SSSOM is built around a core data model comprising four essential components: ontology metadata, mapping tables, term annotations, and provenance information. This design enables efficient serialization and deserialization, supports various data formats, and facilitates integration with existing tools and workflows. To evaluate SSSOM's effectiveness, we implemented a suite of tools and performed a series of experiments using real-world ontologies and mappings. Our results show that SSSOM can reduce the size of mapping data by up to 90% compared to existing formats, while maintaining compatibility with popular ontology editors and reasoners. Furthermore, our evaluation demonstrates that SSSOM-enabled tools can significantly improve the performance and accuracy of ontology-based data integration tasks. The SSSOM specification, implementation, and evaluation datasets are publicly available, providing a foundation for widespread adoption and further development. By establishing a simple, standardized format for sharing ontological mappings, SSSOM has the potential to streamline data integration, enable large-scale ontology-based applications, and foster collaboration across diverse research communities.

title: Differentially Private Data Publication with Multi-level Data Utility
text: Conventional private data publication mechanisms aim to retain as much data utility as possible while ensuring sufficient privacy protection on sensitive data. Such data publication schemes implicitly assume that all data analysts and users have the same data access privilege levels. However, it is not applicable for the scenario that data users often have different levels of access to the same data, or different requirements of data utility. The multi-level privacy requirements for different authorization levels pose new challenges for private data publication. Traditional PPDP mechanisms only publish one perturbed and private data copy satisfying some privacy guarantee to provide relatively accurate analysis results. To find a good tradeoff between privacy preservation level and data utility itself is a hard problem, let alone achieving multi-level data utility on this basis. In this paper, we address this challenge in proposing a novel framework of data publication with compressive sensing supporting multi-level utility-privacy tradeoffs, which provides differential privacy. Specifically, we resort to compressive sensing (CS) method to project a $n$-dimensional vector representation of users' data to a lower $m$-dimensional space, and then add deliberately designed noise to satisfy differential privacy. Then, we selectively obfuscate the measurement vector under compressive sensing by adding linearly encoded noise, and provide different data reconstruction algorithms for users with different authorization levels. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that ML-DPCS yields multi-level of data utility for specific users at different authorization levels.

title: Differentially Private Data Publication with Multi-level Data Utility
text: The prevailing paradigm in private data publication prioritizes balancing data utility with privacy protection, implicitly assuming uniform access privileges among data analysts and users. However, this assumption is untenable in scenarios where users exhibit varying levels of access to the same data, necessitating distinct requirements for data utility. This disparity in authorization levels introduces novel challenges for private data publication, as traditional privacy-preserving data publication (PPDP) mechanisms only provide a single perturbed data copy that satisfies a certain privacy guarantee, yielding relatively accurate analysis results. The quest for an optimal tradeoff between privacy preservation and data utility is already a formidable problem; incorporating multi-level data utility exacerbates this challenge. This paper presents a novel framework for data publication that leverages compressive sensing to support multi-level utility-privacy tradeoffs, ensuring differential privacy. By projecting users' data from an n-dimensional vector space to a lower m-dimensional space using compressive sensing, and subsequently adding noise to satisfy differential privacy, we enable selective obfuscation of the measurement vector through linearly encoded noise. This facilitates the provision of distinct data reconstruction algorithms tailored to users with varying authorization levels. Our comprehensive experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework, ML-DPCS, successfully yields multi-level data utility for specific users at different authorization levels.

title: Simultaneous execution of quantum circuits on current and near-future NISQ systems
text: In the NISQ era, multi-programming of quantum circuits (QC) helps to improve the throughput of quantum computation. Although the crosstalk, which is a major source of noise on NISQ processors, may cause performance degradation of concurrent execution of multiple QCs, its characterization cost grows quadratically in processor size. To address these challenges, we introduce palloq (parallel allocation of QCs) for improving the performance of quantum multi-programming on NISQ processors while paying attention to the combination of QCs in parallel execution and their layout on the quantum processor, and reducing unwanted interference between QCs caused by crosstalk. We also propose a software-based crosstalk detection protocol that efficiently and successfully characterizes the hardware's suitability for multi-programming. We found a trade-off between the success rate and execution time of the multi-programming. This would be attractive not only to quantum computer service but also to users around the world who want to run algorithms of suitable scale on NISQ processors that have recently attracted great attention and are being enthusiastically investigated.

title: Simultaneous execution of quantum circuits on current and near-future NISQ systems
text: The concurrent execution of multiple quantum circuits (QCs) on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) processors can enhance computational throughput, but crosstalk, a dominant noise source, can compromise performance. Characterizing crosstalk, however, incurs a quadratic cost in processor size, hindering its mitigation. We present palloq, a framework that optimizes QC allocation for NISQ multi-programming by jointly considering QC combinations, processor layout, and crosstalk-induced interference reduction. Moreover, we develop a software-based crosstalk detection protocol that efficiently assesses hardware suitability for multi-programming. Our results reveal a trade-off between success rate and execution time, indicating that palloq can benefit not only quantum computing services but also users seeking to execute scalable algorithms on NISQ processors, which have garnered significant attention and are being actively explored. By addressing the crosstalk challenge, palloq enables more efficient and reliable multi-programming on NISQ processors.

title: QuISP: a Quantum Internet Simulation Package
text: We present an event-driven simulation package called QuISP for large-scale quantum networks built on top of the OMNeT++ discrete event simulation framework. Although the behavior of quantum networking devices have been revealed by recent research, it is still an open question how they will work in networks of a practical size. QuISP is designed to simulate large-scale quantum networks to investigate their behavior under realistic, noisy and heterogeneous configurations. The protocol architecture we propose enables studies of different choices for error management and other key decisions. Our confidence in the simulator is supported by comparing its output to analytic results for a small network. A key reason for simulation is to look for emergent behavior when large numbers of individually characterized devices are combined. QuISP can handle thousands of qubits in dozens of nodes on a laptop computer, preparing for full Quantum Internet simulation. This simulator promotes the development of protocols for larger and more complex quantum networks.

title: QuISP: a Quantum Internet Simulation Package
text: Large-scale quantum networks pose significant simulation challenges, particularly in capturing the intricacies of device behavior under realistic, noisy, and heterogeneous conditions. To address this, we introduce QuISP, a scalable event-driven simulation package built upon the OMNeT++ discrete event simulation framework. QuISP is designed to investigate the behavior of large-scale quantum networks, enabling the exploration of diverse error management strategies and key architectural decisions. The simulator's validity is substantiated by comparisons with analytical results for small-scale networks. A primary motivation for simulation is the discovery of emergent behavior arising from the interaction of numerous characterized devices. Notably, QuISP can efficiently simulate thousands of qubits across dozens of nodes on a laptop computer, paving the way for comprehensive Quantum Internet simulations. By facilitating the development of protocols for larger, more complex quantum networks, QuISP has the potential to significantly advance the field.

title: A code-based hybrid signcryption scheme
text: A key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) that takes as input an arbitrary string, i.e., a tag, is known as tag-KEM, while a scheme that combines signature and encryption is called signcryption. In this paper, we present a code-based signcryption tag-KEM scheme. We utilize a code-based signature and an IND-CCA2 (adaptive chosen ciphertext attack) secure version of McEliece's encryption scheme. The proposed scheme uses an equivalent subcode as a public code for the receiver, making the NPcompleteness of the subcode equivalence problem to be one of our main security assumptions. We then base the signcryption tag-KEM to design a code-based hybrid signcryption scheme. A hybrid scheme deploys asymmetric- as well as symmetric-key encryption. We give security analyses of both our schemes in the standard model and prove that they are secure against IND-CCA2 (indistinguishability under adaptive chosen ciphertext attack) and SUF-CMA (strong existential unforgeability under chosen message attack).

title: A code-based hybrid signcryption scheme
text: The proliferation of decentralized systems and applications has created an urgent need for efficient and secure signcryption schemes that can simultaneously provide confidentiality, authenticity, and non-repudiation. Existing schemes, however, often suffer from high computational overhead, large ciphertext sizes, or vulnerability to quantum attacks. To address these limitations, we propose a code-based hybrid signcryption scheme that leverages the hardness of the syndrome decoding problem and the learning parity with noise problem. Our scheme combines a lattice-based digital signature with a code-based encryption algorithm, ensuring high security and efficiency. We provide a rigorous security analysis, demonstrating that our scheme is secure against adaptive chosen-ciphertext attacks and existential forgery attacks in the quantum random oracle model. Our implementation results show that our scheme achieves a 30% reduction in computational overhead and a 25% decrease in ciphertext size compared to existing state-of-the-art schemes, making it a promising solution for resource-constrained devices and real-time applications.

title: Better Pay Attention Whilst Fuzzing
text: Fuzzing is one of the prevailing methods for vulnerability detection. However, even state-of-the-art fuzzing methods become ineffective after some period of time, i.e., the coverage hardly improves as existing methods are ineffective to focus the attention of fuzzing on covering the hard-to-trigger program paths. In other words, they cannot generate inputs that can break the bottleneck due to the fundamental difficulty in capturing the complex relations between the test inputs and program coverage. In particular, existing fuzzers suffer from the following main limitations: 1) lacking an overall analysis of the program to identify the most "rewarding" seeds, and 2) lacking an effective mutation strategy which could continuously select and mutates the more relevant "bytes" of the seeds. In this work, we propose an approach called ATTuzz to address these two issues systematically. First, we propose a lightweight dynamic analysis technique which estimates the "reward" of covering each basic block and selects the most rewarding seeds accordingly. Second, we mutate the selected seeds according to a neural network model which predicts whether a certain "rewarding" block will be covered given certain mutation on certain bytes of a seed. The model is a deep learning model equipped with attention mechanism which is learned and updated periodically whilst fuzzing. Our evaluation shows that ATTuzz significantly outperforms 5 state-of-the-art grey-box fuzzers on 13 popular real-world programs at achieving higher edge coverage and finding new bugs. In particular, ATTuzz achieved 2X edge coverage and 4X bugs detected than AFL over 24-hour runs. Moreover, ATTuzz persistently improves the edge coverage in the long run, i.e., achieving 50% more coverage than AFL in 5 days.

title: Better Pay Attention Whilst Fuzzing
text: The efficacy of fuzzing in vulnerability detection is hindered by its tendency to plateau, failing to meaningfully improve coverage over time. This stagnation stems from the inability of existing methods to effectively focus on hard-to-trigger program paths, owing to the inherent complexity of relationships between test inputs and program coverage. Specifically, current fuzzers are limited by their inability to conduct comprehensive program analysis, identify the most promising seeds, and develop an effective mutation strategy that selectively targets and mutates relevant seed bytes. To address these limitations, we introduce ATTuzz, a novel approach that systematically tackles these challenges. Our method employs a lightweight dynamic analysis technique to estimate the reward of covering each basic block, informing the selection of the most rewarding seeds. Additionally, we utilize a neural network model, equipped with an attention mechanism, to predict the likelihood of covering a rewarding block given specific mutations on certain seed bytes. This model is periodically updated during fuzzing, enabling adaptive refinement. Our evaluation demonstrates that ATTuzz significantly outperforms five state-of-the-art grey-box fuzzers on 13 real-world programs, achieving higher edge coverage and detecting more bugs. Notably, ATTuzz surpasses AFL, achieving 2X edge coverage and 4X bug detection over 24-hour runs, and persistently improving coverage, with a 50% increase over AFL in 5 days.

title: MuxLink: Circumventing Learning-Resilient MUX-Locking Using Graph Neural Network-based Link Prediction
text: Logic locking has received considerable interest as a prominent technique for protecting the design intellectual property from untrusted entities, especially the foundry. Recently, machine learning (ML)-based attacks have questioned the security guarantees of logic locking, and have demonstrated considerable success in deciphering the secret key without relying on an oracle, hence, proving to be very useful for an adversary in the fab. Such ML-based attacks have triggered the development of learning-resilient locking techniques. The most advanced state-of-the-art deceptive MUX-based locking (D-MUX) and the symmetric MUX-based locking techniques have recently demonstrated resilience against existing ML-based attacks. Both defense techniques obfuscate the design by inserting key-controlled MUX logic, ensuring that all the secret inputs to the MUXes are equiprobable. In this work, we show that these techniques primarily introduce local and limited changes to the circuit without altering the global structure of the design. By leveraging this observation, we propose a novel graph neural network (GNN)-based link prediction attack, MuxLink, that successfully breaks both the D-MUX and symmetric MUX-locking techniques, relying only on the underlying structure of the locked design, i.e., in an oracle-less setting. Our trained GNN model learns the structure of the given circuit and the composition of gates around the non-obfuscated wires, thereby generating meaningful link embeddings that help decipher the secret inputs to the MUXes. The proposed MuxLink achieves key prediction accuracy and precision up to 100% on D-MUX and symmetric MUX-locked ISCAS-85 and ITC-99 benchmarks, fully unlocking the designs. We open-source MuxLink [1].

title: MuxLink: Circumventing Learning-Resilient MUX-Locking Using Graph Neural Network-based Link Prediction
text: The proliferation of machine learning (ML)-based attacks has compromised the security of logic locking, a technique designed to safeguard design intellectual property from untrusted entities, particularly foundries. These attacks have successfully deciphered secret keys without relying on oracles, rendering them a formidable tool for adversaries in the fabrication process. In response, researchers have developed learning-resilient locking techniques, including deceptive MUX-based locking (D-MUX) and symmetric MUX-based locking, which obfuscate designs by inserting key-controlled MUX logic and ensuring equiprobable secret inputs to MUXes. However, we observe that these techniques primarily introduce localized, limited changes to the circuit without altering its global structure. Exploiting this insight, we propose MuxLink, a novel graph neural network (GNN)-based link prediction attack that successfully breaches both D-MUX and symmetric MUX-locking techniques in an oracle-less setting. By learning the structure of the locked design and the composition of gates around non-obfuscated wires, our trained GNN model generates meaningful link embeddings that facilitate the deciphering of secret inputs to MUXes. Notably, MuxLink achieves 100% key prediction accuracy and precision on D-MUX and symmetric MUX-locked ISCAS-85 and ITC-99 benchmarks, fully unlocking the designs. Our open-source implementation of MuxLink provides a valuable resource for the research community.

title: Blockchain Developments and Innovations
text: Blockchain has received expanding interest from various domains. Institutions, enterprises, governments, and agencies are interested in Blockchain potential to augment their software systems. The unique requirements and characteristics of Blockchain platforms raise new challenges involving extensive enhancement to conventional software development processes to meet the needs of these domains. Software engineering approaches supporting Blockchain-oriented developments have been slow to materialize, despite proposals in the literature, and they have yet to be objectively analyzed. A critical appraisal of these innovations is crucial to identify their respective strengths and weaknesses. We present an analytical evaluation of several prominent Blockchain-oriented methods through a comprehensive, criteria-based evaluation framework. The results can be used for comparing, adapting, and developing a new generation of Blockchain-oriented software development processes and innovations.

title: Blockchain Developments and Innovations
text: The advent of blockchain technology has sparked a plethora of innovations, transforming the way we approach decentralized systems, security, and trust. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of recent blockchain developments and innovations, focusing on the convergence of distributed ledger technology, cryptography, and software engineering. We systematically analyze 150 research articles, patent filings, and open-source projects, identifying key trends, challenges, and opportunities in the field. Our methodology involves a multi-dimensional assessment of blockchain systems, encompassing scalability, security, usability, and interoperability. The findings reveal a significant shift towards hybrid blockchain architectures, decentralized identity management, and smart contract optimization. Furthermore, we highlight the emergence of novel consensus protocols, such as proof of stake and delegated Byzantine fault tolerance, which promise to enhance the overall efficiency and sustainability of blockchain networks.

title: In-Kernel Control-Flow Integrity on Commodity OSes using ARM Pointer Authentication
text: This paper presents an in-kernel, hardware-based control-flow integrity (CFI) protection, called PAL, that utilizes ARM's Pointer Authentication (PA). It provides three important benefits over commercial, state-of-the-art PA-based CFIs like iOS's: 1) enhancing CFI precision via automated refinement techniques, 2) addressing hindsight problems of PA for in kernel uses such as preemptive hijacking and brute-forcing attacks, and 3) assuring the algorithmic or implementation correctness via post validation. PAL achieves these goals in an OS-agnostic manner, so could be applied to commodity OSes like Linux and FreeBSD. The precision of the CFI protection can be adjusted for better performance or improved for better security with minimal engineering efforts if a user opts in to. Our evaluation shows that PAL incurs negligible performance overhead: e.g., <1% overhead for Apache benchmark and 3~5% overhead for Linux perf benchmark on the latest Mac mini (M1). Our post-validation approach helps us ensure the security invariant required for the safe uses of PA inside the kernel, which also reveals new attack vectors on the iOS kernel. PAL as well as the CFI-protected kernels will be open sourced.

title: In-Kernel Control-Flow Integrity on Commodity OSes using ARM Pointer Authentication
text: Control-Flow Integrity (CFI) is a crucial security mechanism for defending against code-reuse attacks, yet its adoption on commodity operating systems remains limited due to performance and compatibility concerns. We present a novel approach to in-kernel CFI on ARM-based systems, leveraging the ARMv8.3-A Pointer Authentication (PA) extension to efficiently enforce control-flow constraints. Our method, dubbed KPA-CFI, integrates PA-based CFI checks into the Linux kernel, providing comprehensive protection for kernel code and data. We implement KPA-CFI on a commodity ARMv8.3-A platform and evaluate its performance using a range of microbenchmarks and real-world workloads. Our results show that KPA-CFI incurs an average overhead of 1.47% on kernel execution time, making it a viable solution for practical deployment. Furthermore, we demonstrate KPA-CFI's effectiveness in preventing code-reuse attacks, including return-oriented programming and jump-oriented programming, using a custom-built attack framework. Our work provides a significant step towards widespread adoption of CFI on commodity OSes, and paves the way for further research into hardware-assisted security mechanisms.

title: The Interaction between Inputs and Configurations fed to Software Systems: an Empirical Study
text: Widely used software systems such as video encoders are by necessity highly configurable, with hundreds or even thousands of options to choose from. Their users often have a hard time finding suitable values for these options (i.e. finding a proper configuration of the software system) to meet their goals for the tasks at hand, e.g. compress a video down to a certain size. One dimension of the problem is of course that performance depends on the input data: a video as input to an encoder like x264 or a file system fed to a tool like xz. To achieve good performance, users should therefore take into account both dimensions of (1) software variability and (2) input data. In this problem-statement paper, we conduct a large study over 8 configurable systems that quantifies the existing interactions between input data and configurations of software systems. The results exhibit that (1) inputs fed to software systems interact with their configuration options in non monotonous ways, significantly impacting their performance properties (2) tuning a software system for its input data makes it possible to multiply its performance by up to ten (3) input variability can jeopardize the relevance of performance predictive models for a field deployment.

title: The Interaction between Inputs and Configurations fed to Software Systems: an Empirical Study
text: Configurable software systems, such as video encoders, often present users with an overwhelming number of options to tailor their behavior to specific tasks, like compressing a video to a target size. However, finding an optimal configuration that balances performance and objectives is a daunting task. The complexity of this problem is twofold, as performance is influenced by both software variability and input data characteristics. This paper presents a large-scale study examining the intricate relationships between input data and configuration options in eight configurable systems, including x264 and xz. Our findings reveal that input data and software configurations interact in complex, non-monotonic ways, significantly affecting performance properties. Moreover, we demonstrate that tuning a software system to its input data can yield up to a tenfold performance improvement. Furthermore, our study highlights the vulnerability of performance predictive models to input variability, which can compromise their relevance in real-world deployments.

title: MMO: Meta Multi-Objectivization for Software Configuration Tuning
text: Software configuration tuning is essential for optimizing a given performance objective (e.g., minimizing latency). Yet, due to the software's intrinsically complex configuration landscape and expensive measurement, there has been a rather mild success, particularly in preventing the search from being trapped in local optima. To address this issue, in this paper we take a different perspective. Instead of focusing on improving the optimizer, we work on the level of optimization model and propose a meta multi-objectivization (MMO) model that considers an auxiliary performance objective (e.g., throughput in addition to latency). What makes this model distinct is that we do not optimize the auxiliary performance objective, but rather use it to make similarly-performing while different configurations less comparable (i.e. Pareto nondominated to each other), thus preventing the search from being trapped in local optima. Importantly, by designing a new normalization method, we show how to effectively use the MMO model without worrying about its weight -- the only yet highly sensitive parameter that can affect its effectiveness. Experiments on 22 cases from 11 real-world software systems/environments confirm that our MMO model with the new normalization performs better than its state-of-the-art single-objective counterparts on 82% cases while achieving up to 2.09x speedup. For 68% of the cases, the new normalization also enables the MMO model to outperform the instance when using it with the normalization from our prior FSE work under pre-tuned best weights, saving a great amount of resources which would be otherwise necessary to find a good weight. We also demonstrate that the MMO model with the new normalization can consolidate recent model-based tuning tools on 68% of the cases with up to 1.22x speedup in general.

title: MMO: Meta Multi-Objectivization for Software Configuration Tuning
text: Software configuration tuning is a crucial step in ensuring optimal performance, scalability, and reliability of complex systems. However, this task is often hindered by the inherent complexity of modern software systems, which are typically characterized by numerous interacting parameters, conflicting objectives, and uncertain environmental conditions. Traditional configuration tuning approaches, such as manual experimentation, grid search, and genetic algorithms, are often inadequate in handling these complexities, leading to suboptimal solutions and wasted resources. To address these challenges, we propose MMO, a novel Meta Multi-Objectivization framework for software configuration tuning. MMO leverages the concept of multi-objectivization to transform the original single-objective optimization problem into a set of interconnected multi-objective sub-problems. This allows MMO to effectively handle conflicting objectives, explore the vast configuration space more efficiently, and adapt to changing environmental conditions. The meta-layer of MMO incorporates a Bayesian optimization strategy to dynamically adjust the weights of the sub-problems, ensuring a balanced exploration of the Pareto front. We evaluate MMO on a diverse set of software systems, including a cloud-based e-commerce platform, a distributed database, and a real-time video processing pipeline. Our results show that MMO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art configuration tuning approaches, achieving up to 35% improvement in overall system performance, 28% reduction in resource utilization, and 20% increase in reliability. Furthermore, MMO demonstrates robustness in handling noisy and uncertain data, and adaptability in responding to changing system conditions. Our findings have significant implications for the development of autonomous, self-optimizing software systems that can efficiently operate in dynamic and uncertain environments.

title: Sherman: A Write-Optimized Distributed B+Tree Index on Disaggregated Memory
text: Memory disaggregation architecture physically separates CPU and memory into independent components, which are connected via high-speed RDMA networks, greatly improving resource utilization of databases. However, such an architecture poses unique challenges to data indexing in databases due to limited RDMA semantics and near-zero computation power at memory-side. Existing indexes supporting disaggregated memory either suffer from low write performance, or require hardware modification. This paper presents Sherman, a write-optimized distributed B+Tree index on disaggregated memory that delivers high performance with commodity RDMA NICs. Sherman combines RDMA hardware features and RDMA-friendly software techniques to boost index write performance from three angles. First, to reduce round trips, Sherman coalesces dependent RDMA commands by leveraging in-order delivery property of RDMA. Second, to accelerate concurrent accesses, Sherman introduces a hierarchical lock that exploits on-chip memory of RDMA NICs. Finally, to mitigate write amplification, Sherman tailors the data structure layout of B+Tree with a two-level version mechanism. Our evaluation shows that, Sherman is one order of magnitude faster in terms of both throughput and 99th percentile latency on typical write-intensive workloads, compared with state-of-the-art designs.

title: Sherman: A Write-Optimized Distributed B+Tree Index on Disaggregated Memory
text: The proliferation of disaggregated memory architectures has necessitated the redesign of traditional indexing data structures to fully leverage their capabilities. B+Trees, a staple in database indexing, are particularly ill-suited for these environments due to their read-heavy nature. We propose Sherman, a write-optimized distributed B+Tree index tailored to disaggregated memory systems. By decoupling the index's logical and physical structures, Sherman enables efficient write operations by minimizing remote memory accesses and leveraging the aggregate bandwidth of the dis-aggregated memory pool. Our approach employs a novel combination of tree rebalancing and data migration techniques to maintain a balanced index while adapting to shifting workload patterns. Experimental evaluations on a 64-node disaggregated memory cluster demonstrate Sherman's ability to achieve up to 3.5x higher write throughput and 2.2x lower write latency compared to state-of-the-art indexing solutions. Additionally, Sherman exhibits improved scalability and resilience in the face of node failures, making it an attractive solution for modern data-intensive applications.

title: Right-hand side decoding of Gabidulin code and applications
text: We discuss the decoding of Gabidulin and interleaved Gabidulin codes. We give the full presentation of a decoding algorithm for Gabidulin codes, which as Loidreau's seminal algorithm consists in localizing errors in the spirit of Berlekamp-Welch algorithm for Reed-Solomon codes. On the other hand, this algorithm consists in acting on codewords on the right while Loidreau's algorithm considers an action on the left. This right-hand side decoder was already introduced by the authors in a previous work for cryptanalytic applications. We give here a generalised version which applies to the case of non-full length Gabidulin codes. Finally, we show that this algorithm turns out to provide a very clear and natural approach for the decoding of interleaved Gabidulin codes.

title: Right-hand side decoding of Gabidulin code and applications
text: Gabidulin codes are a class of rank-metric codes that have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their applications in cryptography and coding theory. Decoding Gabidulin codes is a challenging problem, and existing approaches have limited efficiency. This paper presents a novel right-hand side (RHS) decoding algorithm for Gabidulin codes, which achieves improved performance compared to existing methods. Our approach exploits the structure of Gabidulin codes to reduce the decoding problem to a linear system, which is then solved using a probabilistic algorithm. Experimental results demonstrate that our RHS decoding algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of decoding speed and error correction capability. We also explore applications of our algorithm in cryptographic primitives, such as digital signatures and public-key encryption schemes, and demonstrate its potential in enhancing their security and efficiency.

title: Speeding up enclave transitions for IO-intensive applications
text: Process-based confidential computing enclaves such as Intel SGX can be used to protect the confidentiality and integrity of workloads, without the overhead of virtualisation. However, they introduce a notable performance overhead, especially when it comes to transitions in and out of the enclave context. Such overhead makes the use of enclaves impractical for running IO-intensive applications, such as network packet processing or biological sequence analysis. We build on earlier approaches to improve the IO performance of work-loads in Intel SGX enclaves and propose the SGX-Bundler library, which helps reduce the cost of both individual single enclave transitions well as of the total number of enclave transitions in trusted applications running in Intel SGX enclaves. We describe the implementation of the SGX-Bundler library, evaluate its performance and demonstrate its practicality using the case study of Open vSwitch, a widely used software switch implementation.

title: Speeding up enclave transitions for IO-intensive applications
text: The proliferation of confidential computing has led to widespread adoption of trusted execution environments (TEEs) in various domains. However, frequent transitions between the enclave and the untrusted host environment, necessary for IO operations, significantly degrade performance in IO-intensive applications. This bottleneck is exacerbated by the overhead of entering and exiting the enclave, which can reach up to 10,000 cycles. To mitigate this issue, we propose a novel optimization technique, dubbed ETrans, which leverages a combination of batching, caching, and asynchronous processing to minimize enclave transitions. Our evaluation on a suite of IO-intensive workloads demonstrates that ETrans reduces the average transition overhead by 73%, resulting in a 34% increase in overall system throughput. Furthermore, we observe that ETrans achieves a 95% reduction in tail latency, making it particularly suited for latency-critical applications.

title: Answering Queries with Negation over Existential Rules
text: Ontology-based query answering with existential rules is well understood and implemented for positive queries, in particular conjunctive queries. The situation changes drastically for queries with negation, where there is no agreed-upon semantics or standard implementation. Stratification, as used for Datalog, is not enough for existential rules, since the latter still admit multiple universal models that can differ on negative queries. We therefore propose universal core models as a basis for a meaningful (non-monotonic) semantics for queries with negation. Since cores are hard to compute, we identify syntactic descriptions of queries that can equivalently be answered over other types of models. This leads to fragments of queries with negation that can safely be evaluated by current chase implementations. We establish new techniques to estimate how the core model differs from other universal models, and we incorporate our findings into a new reasoning approach for existential rules with negation.

title: Answering Queries with Negation over Existential Rules
text: The proliferation of existential rules in knowledge bases has enabled the representation of complex relationships and constraints, but querying these knowledge bases remains a challenging task, particularly when negation is involved. Previous approaches have relied on rewriting queries into disjunctive normal form or using iterative rewriting, which can lead to exponential blowup or incomplete results. We propose a novel approach to answering queries with negation over existential rules, leveraging a combination of chase-based and resolution-based techniques. Our method first applies the chase to saturate the knowledge base, and then employs a resolution-based algorithm to compute the answers. We establish the correctness and completeness of our approach, and provide an experimental evaluation demonstrating its efficiency and scalability on real-world datasets. Notably, our approach can handle queries with negation over recursive rules, a case not addressed by previous methods.

title: Randomized Response Mechanisms for Differential Privacy Data Analysis: Bounds and Applications
text: Randomized response, as a basic building-block for differentially private mechanism, has given rise to great interest and found various potential applications in science communities. In this work, we are concerned with three-elements randomized response (RR$_{3}$) along with relevant applications to the analysis of weighted bipartite graph upon differentially private guarantee. We develop a principled framework for estimating statistics produced by RR$_{3}$-based mechanisms, and then prove the corresponding estimations to be unbiased. At the same time, we study in detail several fundamental and significant members in RR$_{3}$ family, and derive the closed-form solutions to unbiased estimations. Next, we show potential applications of several RR$_{3}$-based mechanisms into the estimation of average degree and average weighted value on weighted bipartite graph when requiring local differential privacy guarantee. In the meantime, we determine the lower bounds for choice of relevant parameters by minimizing variance of statistics in order to design optimal RR$_{3}$-based local differential private mechanisms, with which we optimize previous protocols in the literature and put forward a version that achieves the tight bound. Last but most importantly, we observe that in the analysis of relational data such as weighted bipartite graph, a portion of privacy budget in local differential private mechanism is sometimes "consumed" by mechanism itself accidentally, resulting to a more stronger privacy guarantee than we would get by simply sequential compositions.

title: Randomized Response Mechanisms for Differential Privacy Data Analysis: Bounds and Applications
text: The widespread adoption of data-driven decision making has created an unprecedented need for privacy-preserving data analysis techniques. Differential privacy has emerged as a gold standard for privacy guarantees, but its implementation often comes at the cost of utility. Randomized response mechanisms offer a promising approach to achieving differential privacy, but their theoretical foundations and practical applicability require further exploration. This work provides a comprehensive analysis of randomized response mechanisms for differential privacy data analysis. We establish novel bounds on the privacy-utility tradeoff, demonstrating that certain mechanisms can achieve near-optimal privacy guarantees while maintaining acceptable data utility. Our theoretical results are complemented by an empirical evaluation of various mechanisms on real-world datasets, showcasing their feasibility in practice. Notably, our findings indicate that a judicious choice of mechanism parameters can result in significant improvements in data utility, even at high privacy budgets. We also demonstrate the applicability of our mechanisms to a variety of data analysis tasks, including frequency estimation and heavy hitter identification. Furthermore, we provide a thorough comparison of our approach with existing state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the advantages and limitations of each. Our contributions have far-reaching implications for the development of privacy-preserving data analysis pipelines, enabling organizations to extract insights from sensitive data while maintaining the trust of their users. By providing a rigorous framework for designing and evaluating randomized response mechanisms, this work paves the way for widespread adoption of differential privacy in real-world applications.

title: INRU: A Quasigroup Based Lightweight Block Cipher
text: In this paper, we propose a quasigroup based block cipher design. The round functions of the encryption and decryption algorithms use quasigroup based string transformations. We show the robustness of the design against the standard differential, linear and algebraic cryptanalytic attacks. We also provide detailed statistical analysis using NIST test suite in CBC, CFB, OFB, and CTR modes of operation. We compare the statistical experimental results with the AES-128 in the same setup and conclude that the randomizing ability of our algorithm is equivalent to that of AES-128.

title: INRU: A Quasigroup Based Lightweight Block Cipher
text: We present a novel block cipher design founded on quasigroup-based string transformations, which are integrated into the round functions of both encryption and decryption algorithms. Our design exhibits robust resistance against differential, linear, and algebraic cryptanalytic attacks. A comprehensive statistical analysis, utilizing the NIST test suite, is conducted in various modes of operation, including CBC, CFB, OFB, and CTR. Notably, our algorithm's randomization capabilities are demonstrated to be on par with those of AES-128, as evidenced by comparative experimental results.

title: Phishing in Organizations: Findings from a Large-Scale and Long-Term Study
text: In this paper, we present findings from a large-scale and long-term phishing experiment that we conducted in collaboration with a partner company. Our experiment ran for 15 months during which time more than 14,000 study participants (employees of the company) received different simulated phishing emails in their normal working context. We also deployed a reporting button to the company's email client which allowed the participants to report suspicious emails they received. We measured click rates for phishing emails, dangerous actions such as submitting credentials, and reported suspicious emails. The results of our experiment provide three types of contributions. First, some of our findings support previous literature with improved ecological validity. One example of such results is good effectiveness of warnings on emails. Second, some of our results contradict prior literature and common industry practices. Surprisingly, we find that embedded training during simulated phishing exercises, as commonly deployed in the industry today, does not make employees more resilient to phishing, but instead it can have unexpected side effects that can make employees even more susceptible to phishing. And third, we report new findings. In particular, we are the first to demonstrate that using the employees as a collective phishing detection mechanism is practical in large organizations. Our results show that such crowd-sourcing allows fast detection of new phishing campaigns, the operational load for the organization is acceptable, and the employees remain active over long periods of time.

title: Phishing in Organizations: Findings from a Large-Scale and Long-Term Study
text: A large-scale, long-term phishing experiment was conducted in collaboration with a partner company, involving over 14,000 employees who received simulated phishing emails in their normal working context over a 15-month period. A reporting button was integrated into the company's email client, enabling participants to report suspicious emails. The experiment yielded valuable insights into click rates, dangerous actions such as credential submission, and reported suspicious emails. The results make three significant contributions to the field. Firstly, our findings reaffirm previous literature with enhanced ecological validity, including the effectiveness of email warnings. Secondly, our results challenge existing literature and industry practices, revealing that embedded training during simulated phishing exercises does not enhance employee resilience to phishing, but instead may have unintended consequences that increase susceptibility. Finally, we present novel findings, notably demonstrating the feasibility of leveraging employees as a collective phishing detection mechanism in large organizations. Our results show that this crowd-sourced approach facilitates rapid detection of new phishing campaigns, imposes an acceptable operational load, and sustains employee engagement over extended periods.

title: TCUDB: Accelerating Database with Tensor Processors
text: The emergence of novel hardware accelerators has powered the tremendous growth of machine learning in recent years. These accelerators deliver incomparable performance gains in processing high-volume matrix operators, particularly matrix multiplication, a core component of neural network training and inference. In this work, we explored opportunities of accelerating database systems using NVIDIA's Tensor Core Units (TCUs). We present TCUDB, a TCU-accelerated query engine processing a set of query operators including natural joins and group-by aggregates as matrix operators within TCUs. Matrix multiplication was considered inefficient in the past; however, this strategy has remained largely unexplored in conventional GPU-based databases, which primarily rely on vector or scalar processing. We demonstrate the significant performance gain of TCUDB in a range of real-world applications including entity matching, graph query processing, and matrix-based data analytics. TCUDB achieves up to 288x speedup compared to a baseline GPU-based query engine.

title: TCUDB: Accelerating Database with Tensor Processors
text: With the proliferation of data-intensive applications, traditional databases struggle to keep pace with the increasing computational demands. The advent of Tensor Processors (TPUs) offers a promising solution, as they excel in matrix-based computations. We present TCUDB, a novel database architecture that leverages TPUs to accelerate query processing. By offloading computationally expensive operations, such as joins and aggregations, to TPUs, TCUDB achieves significant performance gains. Our design incorporates a TPU-aware query optimizer, which dynamically schedules queries to maximize TPU utilization. Experimental results on a real-world dataset demonstrate that TCUDB outperforms state-of-the-art databases by up to 5.2x in query execution time, while maintaining comparable energy efficiency. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that TCUDB's performance benefits are most pronounced for complex queries with high arithmetic intensity. These findings underscore the potential of TPUs in accelerating database workloads and paving the way for future research in this area.

title: Real-time SIL Emulation Architecture for Cooperative Automated Vehicles
