text: The development of safety applications for Connected Automated Vehicles requires testing in many different scenarios. However, the recreation of test scenarios for evaluating safety applications is a very challenging task. This is mainly due to the randomness in communication, difficulty in recreating vehicle movements precisely, and safety concerns for certain scenarios. We propose to develop a standalone Remote Vehicle Emulator that can reproduce V2V messages of remote vehicles from simulations or previous tests. This is expected to accelerate the development cycle significantly. Remote Vehicle Emulator is a unique and easily configurable emulation cum simulation setup to allow Software in the Loop (SIL) testing of connected vehicle applications realistically and safely. It will help in tailoring numerous test scenarios, expediting algorithm development and validation, and increasing the probability of finding failure modes. This, in turn, will help improve the quality of safety applications while saving testing time and reducing cost.

title: Real-time SIL Emulation Architecture for Cooperative Automated Vehicles
text: The proliferation of safety-critical applications in Connected Automated Vehicles necessitates rigorous testing across a diverse range of scenarios. However, recreating these scenarios for evaluation purposes poses significant challenges, primarily due to the inherent randomness of communication, the precision required in recreating vehicle movements, and the safety concerns associated with certain scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose the development of a standalone Remote Vehicle Emulator capable of reproducing V2V messages from simulations or previous tests. This emulator is designed to facilitate realistic and safe Software in the Loop testing of connected vehicle applications, enabling the rapid creation of numerous test scenarios and expediting algorithm development and validation. By increasing the likelihood of detecting failure modes, the Remote Vehicle Emulator is expected to improve the quality of safety applications while reducing testing time and costs.

title: A Game-Theoretical Self-Adaptation Framework for Securing Software-Intensive Systems
text: The increasing prevalence of security attacks on software-intensive systems calls for new, effective methods for detecting and responding to these attacks. As one promising approach, game theory provides analytical tools for modeling the interaction between the system and the adversarial environment and designing reliable defense. In this paper, we propose an approach for securing software-intensive systems using a rigorous game-theoretical framework. First, a self-adaptation framework is deployed on a component-based software intensive system, which periodically monitors the system for anomalous behaviors. A learning-based method is proposed to detect possible on-going attacks on the system components and predict potential threats to components. Then, an algorithm is designed to automatically build a \emph{Bayesian game} based on the system architecture (of which some components might have been compromised) once an attack is detected, in which the system components are modeled as independent players in the game. Finally, an optimal defensive policy is computed by solving the Bayesian game to achieve the best system utility, which amounts to minimizing the impact of the attack. We conduct two sets of experiments on two general benchmark tasks for security domain. Moreover, we systematically present a case study on a real-world water treatment testbed, i.e. the Secure Water Treatment System. Experiment results show the applicability and the effectiveness of our approach.

title: A Game-Theoretical Self-Adaptation Framework for Securing Software-Intensive Systems
text: Software-intensive systems are increasingly vulnerable to security threats, owing to their inherent complexity and dynamic nature. Traditional security approaches often rely on static analysis and manual configuration, which can be insufficient to counter sophisticated attacks. This paper proposes a novel game-theoretical self-adaptation framework for securing software-intensive systems, which leverages the principles of game theory to dynamically adapt security mechanisms in response to evolving threats. Our framework, termed GAMESec, models the interaction between the system and potential attackers as a dynamic game, wherein the system strives to maximize its security posture while the attackers aim to compromise it. GAMESec employs a hybrid approach, combining model-driven engineering with machine learning techniques, to analyze system behavior and detect potential vulnerabilities. The framework then uses game-theoretical algorithms to select and deploy optimal security countermeasures, taking into account the attacker's likely strategies and the system's resource constraints. Through a comprehensive evaluation on a realistic case study, we demonstrate that GAMESec significantly improves the security posture of software-intensive systems, reducing the attack surface by up to 37% and minimizing the mean time to detect and respond to threats by 62%. Our results also show that GAMESec outperforms existing adaptive security approaches, showcasing its effectiveness in dynamic and uncertain environments. The proposed framework has far-reaching implications for the development of secure and resilient software-intensive systems, enabling them to stay ahead of evolving cyber threats.

title: D-LNBot: A Scalable, Cost-Free and Covert Hybrid Botnet on Bitcoin's Lightning Network
text: While various covert botnets were proposed in the past, they still lack complete anonymization for their servers/botmasters or suffer from slow communication between the botmaster and the bots. In this paper, we first propose a new generation hybrid botnet that covertly and efficiently communicates over Bitcoin Lightning Network (LN), called LNBot. Exploiting various anonymity features of LN, we show the feasibility of a scalable two-layer botnet which completely anonymizes the identity of the botmaster. In the first layer, the botmaster anonymously sends the commands to the command and control (C&C) servers through regular LN payments. Specifically, LNBot allows botmaster's commands to be sent in the form of surreptitious multi-hop LN payments, where the commands are either encoded with the payments or attached to the payments to provide covert communications. In the second layer, C&C servers further relay those commands to the bots in their mini-botnets to launch any type of attacks to victim machines. We further improve on this design by introducing D-LNBot; a distributed version of LNBot that generates its C&C servers by infecting users on the Internet and forms the C&C connections by opening channels to the existing nodes on LN. In contrary to the LNBot, the whole botnet formation phase is distributed and the botmaster is never involved in the process. By utilizing Bitcoin's Testnet and the new message attachment feature of LN, we show that D-LNBot can be run for free and commands are propagated faster to all the C&C servers compared to LNBot. We presented proof-of-concept implementations for both LNBot and D-LNBot on the actual LN and extensively analyzed their delay and cost performance. Finally, we also provide and discuss a list of potential countermeasures to detect LNBot and D-LNBot activities and minimize their impacts.

title: D-LNBot: A Scalable, Cost-Free and Covert Hybrid Botnet on Bitcoin's Lightning Network
text: The proliferation of decentralized systems has given rise to novel threats, including the emergence of botnets that exploit blockchain-based networks. The Lightning Network, a second-layer scaling solution for Bitcoin, has recently gained popularity, but its security against botnet attacks remains largely unexplored. In this context, we present D-LNBot, a scalable, cost-free, and covert hybrid botnet that leverages the Lightning Network's decentralized architecture to launch distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, spam, and other malicious activities. To develop D-LNBot, we conducted a thorough analysis of the Lightning Network's protocol and identified vulnerabilities that enable the creation of a botnet without incurring significant operational costs. We designed a novel, hierarchical architecture that combines the advantages of centralized and decentralized botnets, allowing for efficient command and control, as well as robustness against takedowns. Our approach utilizes a custom-built, Python-based implementation of the Lightning Network protocol to create a network of compromised nodes that can be remotely controlled to launch attacks. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of D-LNBot in launching large-scale DDoS attacks against target nodes on the Lightning Network. Our results show that D-LNBot can achieve a significant amplification of attack traffic, with a peak bandwidth of 10 Gbps, while maintaining a low operational cost of approximately 0.01 BTC per day. Furthermore, we evaluate the detectability of D-LNBot and find that it can evade state-of-the-art botnet detection techniques, including those based on machine learning and graph analysis. Our work highlights the need for more robust security measures to prevent the abuse of decentralized systems and underscores the importance of proactive threat modeling in the context of blockchain-based networks.

title: A study on the Morris Worm
text: The Morris worm was one of the first worms spread via the internet. It was spread on November 2, 1988, and changed how computer security was viewed by computer professionals as well as general public. Since its inception the Morris worm has been studied extensively from the security point of view and is still a point of interest. This paper summarizes the effects, impacts, and lessons learned from the episode. There are other copies of this paper present. However, I recommend using the arXiv version only.

title: A study on the Morris Worm
text: The Morris Worm, launched in 1988, remains one of the most significant cyber threats in history, infecting an estimated 6,000 machines. This study conducts a thorough analysis of the worm's propagation mechanisms, exploiting vulnerabilities in sendmail, finger, and rsh. Our approach combines static and dynamic code analysis, network simulations, and historic traffic data to recreate the worm's spread. Our findings reveal that the worm's exponential growth was primarily fueled by the sendmail exploit, while its eventual containment was largely due to the rapid deployment of patches and firewalls.

title: Public key cryptography based on twisted dihedral group algebras
text: In this paper, we propose to use a twisted dihedral group algebra for public-key cryptography. For this, we introduce a new $2$-cocycle $α_λ$ to twist the dihedral group algebra. Using the ambient space $\mathbb{F}^{α_λ} D_{2n}$, we then introduce a key exchange protocol and present an analysis of its security. Moreover, we explore the properties of the resulting twisted algebra $\mathbb{F}^{α_λ}D_{2n}$, exploiting them to enhance our key exchange protocol. We also introduce a probabilistic public-key scheme derived from our key-exchange protocol and obtain a key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) by applying a well-known generic transformation to our public-key scheme. Finally, we present a proof-of-concept implementation of the resulting key encapsulation mechanism.

title: Public key cryptography based on twisted dihedral group algebras
text: The limited scalability and quantum vulnerability of existing public key cryptosystems have sparked a quest for alternative mathematical foundations. This work explores the unconventional realm of twisted dihedral group algebras, yielding a novel public key encryption scheme. Our approach leverages the rich structure of these algebras to construct a key exchange protocol and a digital signature scheme. We provide a rigorous security analysis, demonstrating the scheme's resistance to quantum attacks and its ability to thwart certain classical attacks. Implementations in software and hardware validate the scheme's feasibility, showcasing competitive performance and key sizes comparable to state-of-the-art cryptosystems.

title: Quantifying Cybersecurity Effectiveness of Dynamic Network Diversity
text: The deployment of monoculture software stacks can have devastating consequences because a single attack can compromise all of the vulnerable computers in cyberspace. This one-vulnerability-affects-all phenomenon will continue until after software stacks are diversified, which is well recognized by the research community. However, existing studies mainly focused on investigating the effectiveness of software diversity at the building-block level (e.g., whether two independent implementations indeed exhibit independent vulnerabilities); the effectiveness of enforcing network-wide software diversity is little understood, despite its importance in possibly helping justify investment in software diversification. As a first step towards ultimately tackling this problem, we propose a systematic framework for modeling and quantifying the cybersecurity effectiveness of network diversity, including a suite of cybersecurity metrics. We also present an agent-based simulation to empirically demonstrate the usefulness of the framework. We draw a number of insights, including the surprising result that proactive diversity is effective under very special circumstances, but reactive-adaptive diversity is much more effective in most cases.

title: Quantifying Cybersecurity Effectiveness of Dynamic Network Diversity
text: The widespread adoption of monoculture software stacks poses a significant threat to cybersecurity, as a single vulnerability can compromise entire networks. The importance of diversifying software stacks to mitigate this risk is well established, yet existing research has primarily focused on the effectiveness of diversity at the component level. In contrast, the impact of network-wide software diversity on cybersecurity remains poorly understood, despite its critical role in justifying investment in diversification strategies. To address this knowledge gap, we develop a systematic framework for modeling and quantifying the cybersecurity benefits of network diversity, encompassing a range of metrics. We validate our framework using an agent-based simulation, which reveals that proactive diversity measures are only effective under specific circumstances, whereas reactive-adaptive diversity strategies demonstrate significantly greater efficacy in most scenarios.

title: HyObscure: Hybrid Obscuring for Privacy-Preserving Data Publishing
text: Minimizing privacy leakage while ensuring data utility is a critical problem to data holders in a privacy-preserving data publishing task. Most prior research concerns only with one type of data and resorts to a single obscuring method, \eg, obfuscation or generalization, to achieve a privacy-utility tradeoff, which is inadequate for protecting real-life heterogeneous data and is hard to defend ever-growing machine learning based inference attacks. This work takes a pilot study on privacy-preserving data publishing when both generalization and obfuscation operations are employed for heterogeneous data protection. To this end, we first propose novel measures for privacy and utility quantification and formulate the hybrid privacy-preserving data obscuring problem to account for the joint effect of generalization and obfuscation. We then design a novel hybrid protection mechanism called HyObscure, to cross-iteratively optimize the generalization and obfuscation operations for maximum privacy protection under a certain utility guarantee. The convergence of the iterative process and the privacy leakage bound of HyObscure are also provided in theory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HyObscure significantly outperforms a variety of state-of-the-art baseline methods when facing various inference attacks under different scenarios. HyObscure also scales linearly to the data size and behaves robustly with varying key parameters.

title: HyObscure: Hybrid Obscuring for Privacy-Preserving Data Publishing
text: The pursuit of optimal privacy-utility tradeoffs in data publishing is hindered by the limitations of current approaches, which typically focus on a single data type and rely on a solitary obscuring method, such as obfuscation or generalization. This narrow scope renders them inadequate for safeguarding real-life heterogeneous data against increasingly sophisticated machine learning-based inference attacks. This study pioneers a comprehensive investigation into the application of hybrid generalization and obfuscation operations for heterogeneous data protection. We introduce novel metrics for quantifying privacy and utility, and formulate a hybrid privacy-preserving data obscuring problem that accounts for the synergistic effects of these operations. Our proposed HyObscure mechanism iteratively optimizes generalization and obfuscation to achieve maximal privacy protection while ensuring a specified utility threshold. Theoretical guarantees are provided for the convergence of this iterative process and the resulting privacy leakage bound. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that HyObscure outperforms state-of-the-art methods in thwarting various inference attacks across diverse scenarios, while exhibiting linear scalability and robustness with respect to key parameters.

title: Tracing Text Provenance via Context-Aware Lexical Substitution
text: Text content created by humans or language models is often stolen or misused by adversaries. Tracing text provenance can help claim the ownership of text content or identify the malicious users who distribute misleading content like machine-generated fake news. There have been some attempts to achieve this, mainly based on watermarking techniques. Specifically, traditional text watermarking methods embed watermarks by slightly altering text format like line spacing and font, which, however, are fragile to cross-media transmissions like OCR. Considering this, natural language watermarking methods represent watermarks by replacing words in original sentences with synonyms from handcrafted lexical resources (e.g., WordNet), but they do not consider the substitution's impact on the overall sentence's meaning. Recently, a transformer-based network was proposed to embed watermarks by modifying the unobtrusive words (e.g., function words), which also impair the sentence's logical and semantic coherence. Besides, one well-trained network fails on other different types of text content. To address the limitations mentioned above, we propose a natural language watermarking scheme based on context-aware lexical substitution (LS). Specifically, we employ BERT to suggest LS candidates by inferring the semantic relatedness between the candidates and the original sentence. Based on this, a selection strategy in terms of synchronicity and substitutability is further designed to test whether a word is exactly suitable for carrying the watermark signal. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, under both objective and subjective metrics, our watermarking scheme can well preserve the semantic integrity of original sentences and has a better transferability than existing methods. Besides, the proposed LS approach outperforms the state-of-the-art approach on the Stanford Word Substitution Benchmark.

title: Tracing Text Provenance via Context-Aware Lexical Substitution
text: Text provenance, the process of tracing the origin and evolution of textual data, is a crucial task in digital forensic analysis, plagiarism detection, and intellectual property protection. However, the increasing prevalence of AI-generated content and sophisticated editing tools has rendered traditional provenance techniques ineffective. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach, Context-Aware Lexical Substitution (CALS), which leverages the subtle linguistic patterns and contextual inconsistencies introduced during the editing process to trace the provenance of text. Our methodology involves a two-stage framework: (1) lexical substitution, where we identify and substitute suspicious words with their synonyms, and (2) context-aware analysis, which examines the resulting text's coherence, fluency, and semantic consistency. We develop a set of features that capture the contextual differences between the original and substituted texts, including syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic markers. These features are then fed into a machine learning model to predict the likelihood of textual manipulation. Extensive experiments on a large-scale dataset of edited texts demonstrate the efficacy of CALS in tracing text provenance. Our approach achieves a significant improvement over state-of-the-art methods, with an average accuracy of 87.3% in detecting edited texts and 81.5% in identifying the specific editing operations. Furthermore, our framework is robust against adversarial attacks, such as paraphrasing and word substitution, and can generalize well to unseen editing styles and domains. The proposed CALS approach has significant implications for digital forensic analysis, intellectual property protection, and the detection of AI-generated content.

title: Does a Face Mask Protect my Privacy?: Deep Learning to Predict Protected Attributes from Masked Face Images
text: Contactless and efficient systems are implemented rapidly to advocate preventive methods in the fight against the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite the positive benefits of such systems, there is potential for exploitation by invading user privacy. In this work, we analyse the privacy invasiveness of face biometric systems by predicting privacy-sensitive soft-biometrics using masked face images. We train and apply a CNN based on the ResNet-50 architecture with 20,003 synthetic masked images and measure the privacy invasiveness. Despite the popular belief of the privacy benefits of wearing a mask among people, we show that there is no significant difference to privacy invasiveness when a mask is worn. In our experiments we were able to accurately predict sex (94.7%),race (83.1%) and age (MAE 6.21 and RMSE 8.33) from masked face images. Our proposed approach can serve as a baseline utility to evaluate the privacy-invasiveness of artificial intelligence systems that make use of privacy-sensitive information. We open-source all contributions for re-producibility and broader use by the research community.

title: Does a Face Mask Protect my Privacy?: Deep Learning to Predict Protected Attributes from Masked Face Images
text: The rapid deployment of contactless systems to combat COVID-19 has sparked concerns about their potential to compromise user privacy. This study investigates the privacy implications of face biometric systems, focusing on the prediction of privacy-sensitive soft-biometrics from masked face images. We utilize a ResNet-50-based convolutional neural network trained on a dataset of 20,003 synthetic masked images to assess privacy invasiveness. Contrary to the popular assumption that mask-wearing enhances privacy, our results reveal no significant difference in privacy invasiveness when a mask is worn. Specifically, our model achieves high accuracy in predicting sex (94.7%), race (83.1%), and age (MAE 6.21, RMSE 8.33) from masked face images. Our approach provides a baseline utility for evaluating the privacy-invasiveness of AI systems that leverage sensitive information, and we make our contributions open-source to facilitate reproducibility and broader adoption by the research community.

title: Service Oriented Architecture in Enterprise Application
text: At present organizations try to achieve competitive advantages using information technology (IT). Organizations not only use Information technology to manage their internal operations but also to collaborate with their customers and suppliers. For these organizations use enterprise applications. Also, organizations expect IT to address their shifting needs in on demand environment. So currently IT face challenges in integrating the various system into a function that can address the organization's on-demand needs and span over the organizational boundaries. Now Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) imagine as an architectural framework that addresses the issues on previous enterprise applications. This paper represents the Service-Oriented Architecture in Enterprise Applications. The enterprise application gives a brief idea about enterprise applications. Afterward, this paper addresses the main problems faced by enterprise applications on the evolution of enterprise applications and the needs of service-oriented architecture in enterprise applications. Afterward, discuss Service Oriented Architecture and challenges on Service Oriented Architecture.

title: Service Oriented Architecture in Enterprise Application
text: The proliferation of disparate systems and data silos in modern enterprises has necessitated the adoption of Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) to facilitate integration, reuse, and scalability. Despite its promise, SOA's effectiveness in enterprise application development remains understudied. This paper presents a comprehensive examination of SOA's role in enhancing the maintainability, flexibility, and performance of enterprise applications. We conducted a mixed-methods study, combining a systematic review of 35 SOA-based enterprise systems with a case study of a large-scale SOA implementation in a Fortune 500 company. Our results show that SOA-based systems exhibit improved modularity, reduced coupling, and enhanced reusability, leading to a 35% reduction in maintenance costs and a 25% increase in system responsiveness. However, we also identify key challenges, including service granularity, interface complexity, and governance, which can hinder SOA's adoption. Our findings provide actionable insights for practitioners and inform the development of more effective SOA-based enterprise application architectures.

title: MissMarple : A Novel Socio-inspired Feature-transfer Learning Deep Network for Image Splicing Detection
text: In this paper we propose a novel socio-inspired convolutional neural network (CNN) deep learning model for image splicing detection. Based on the premise that learning from the detection of coarsely spliced image regions can improve the detection of visually imperceptible finely spliced image forgeries, the proposed model referred to as, MissMarple, is a twin CNN network involving feature-transfer learning. Results obtained from training and testing the proposed model using the benchmark datasets like Columbia splicing, WildWeb, DSO1 and a proposed dataset titled AbhAS consisting of realistic splicing forgeries revealed improvement in detection accuracy over the existing deep learning models.

title: MissMarple : A Novel Socio-inspired Feature-transfer Learning Deep Network for Image Splicing Detection
text: We introduce MissMarple, a socio-inspired convolutional neural network (CNN) deep learning model tailored for image splicing detection, which leverages the insight that detecting coarsely spliced regions can enhance the identification of imperceptible finely spliced forgeries. This twin CNN architecture incorporates feature-transfer learning, enabling the model to capture nuanced patterns. Evaluations on benchmark datasets, including Columbia Splicing, WildWeb, DSO1, and our newly introduced AbhAS dataset featuring realistic splicing forgeries, demonstrate significant improvements in detection accuracy compared to existing deep learning models.

title: Academic Storage Cluster
text: Decentralized storage is still rarely used in an academic and educational environment, although it offers better availability than conventional systems. It still happens that data is not available at a certain time due to heavy load or maintenance on university servers. A decentralized solution can help keep the data available and distribute the load among several peers. In our experiment, we created a cluster of containers in Docker to evaluate a private IPFS cluster for an academic data store focusing on availability, GET/PUT performance, and storage needs. As sample data, we used PDF files to analyze the data transport in our peer-to-peer network with Wireshark. We found that a bandwidth of at least 100 kbit/s is required for IPFS to function but recommend at least 1000 kbit/s for smooth operation. Also, the hard disk and memory size should be adapted to the data. Other limiting factors such as CPU power and delay in the internet connection did not affect the operation of the IPFS cluster.

title: Academic Storage Cluster
text: Massive-scale data storage and retrieval have become crucial components of modern academic institutions, necessitating efficient and scalable storage solutions. Existing storage systems often fail to meet the unique demands of academic environments, where data is typically characterized by high variability in size, access patterns, and retention periods. This paper presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of the Academic Storage Cluster (ASC), a novel storage architecture tailored to the specific requirements of academic settings. ASC leverages a hybrid approach, combining the benefits of distributed file systems, object stores, and erasure coding to provide a scalable, fault-tolerant, and cost-effective storage solution. Our evaluation, conducted on a 100-node cluster, demonstrates that ASC outperforms state-of-the-art storage systems in terms of throughput, latency, and storage efficiency. Notably, ASC achieves a 32% reduction in storage costs and a 25% increase in data retrieval speeds compared to traditional HDFS-based solutions. The ASC prototype has been successfully deployed at a large research university, serving over 500 users and storing in excess of 10 PB of data.

title: Characterizing the Program Expressive Power of Existential Rule Languages
text: Existential rule languages are a family of ontology languages that have been widely used in ontology-mediated query answering (OMQA). However, for most of them, the expressive power of representing domain knowledge for OMQA, known as the program expressive power, is not well-understood yet. In this paper, we establish a number of novel characterizations for the program expressive power of several important existential rule languages, including tuple-generating dependencies (TGDs), linear TGDs, as well as disjunctive TGDs. The characterizations employ natural model-theoretic properties, and automata-theoretic properties sometimes, which thus provide powerful tools for identifying the definability of domain knowledge for OMQA in these languages.

title: Characterizing the Program Expressive Power of Existential Rule Languages
text: Existential rule languages have emerged as a prominent paradigm for knowledge representation and reasoning in artificial intelligence and databases. Despite their widespread adoption, the program expressive power of these languages remains poorly understood. This paper provides a comprehensive characterization of the program expressive power of existential rule languages, examining their ability to simulate various computational models. We employ a novel methodology combining proof-theoretic and model-theoretic techniques to establish that existential rule languages can simulate nondeterministic Turing machines, yet are incapable of simulating deterministic Turing machines. Our results have significant implications for the design and optimization of rule-based systems, shedding light on their fundamental limitations and potential applications.

title: EXT-TAURUM P2T: an Extended Secure CAN-FD Architecture for Road Vehicles
text: The automobile industry is no longer relying on pure mechanical systems; instead, it benefits from advanced Electronic Control Units (ECUs) in order to provide new and complex functionalities in the effort to move toward fully connected cars. However, connected cars provide a dangerous playground for hackers. Vehicles are becoming increasingly vulnerable to cyber attacks as they come equipped with more connected features and control systems. This situation may expose strategic assets in the automotive value chain. In this scenario, the Controller Area Network (CAN) is the most widely used communication protocol in the automotive domain. However, this protocol lacks encryption and authentication. Consequently, any malicious/hijacked node can cause catastrophic accidents and financial loss. Starting from the analysis of the vulnerability connected to the CAN communication protocol in the automotive domain, this paper proposes EXT-TAURUM P2T a new low-cost secure CAN-FD architecture for the automotive domain implementing secure communication among ECUs, a novel key provisioning strategy, intelligent throughput management, and hardware signature mechanisms. The proposed architecture has been implemented, resorting to a commercial Multi-Protocol Vehicle Interface module, and the obtained results experimentally demonstrate the approach's feasibility.

title: EXT-TAURUM P2T: an Extended Secure CAN-FD Architecture for Road Vehicles
text: The Controller Area Network with Flexible Data-rate (CAN-FD) has become a de facto standard for in-vehicle communication in modern road vehicles, but its security limitations have raised concerns about the integrity of safety-critical systems. Recent studies have demonstrated the feasibility of injecting malicious messages into CAN-FD buses, highlighting the need for robust security countermeasures. To address this issue, we present EXT-TAURUM P2T, an extended secure CAN-FD architecture for road vehicles. Our approach combines a lightweight cryptographic scheme with a novel protocol for Trust Anchor establishment and message authentication. We employ a hybrid encryption method, leveraging the strengths of both symmetric and asymmetric cryptography to minimize computational overhead. The Trust Anchor is established through a secure out-of-band channel, ensuring the authenticity of onboard devices. Our evaluation demonstrates that EXT-TAURUM P2T incurs a latency overhead of less than 10% compared to unsecured CAN-FD, while providing robust protection against message injection and replay attacks. We also conduct a comprehensive security analysis, including formal verification and penetration testing, to validate the effectiveness of our architecture. EXT-TAURUM P2T offers a promising solution for securing next-generation vehicle networks, enabling the widespread adoption of connected and autonomous vehicles.

title: Using the DELPHI Method for Model for Role Assignment in the Software Industry
text: Over the past two decades, there has been a growing interest in modeling the elements that need to be considered when assigning people to roles in software projects, as evidenced by the number of available publications related to the topic. However, for the most part, these studies, have taken only a partial approach to the issue. Some have focused on the target roles competency profile, while others have tried to understand the preferences of software developers for activities linked to certain roles and the relationship between these preferences and the candidates personal traits, to mention only two examples. Our research aims to find elements that can be integrated into an allocation model that complements current approaches by including competencies, personal traits, and project team building theories. To do so we performed an experts consultation exercise using the DELPHI method; which allowed us to validate a set of patterns related to different candidates personal traits, and the link between the teams motivational motors and their roles within the software development.

title: Using the DELPHI Method for Model for Role Assignment in the Software Industry
text: The software industry relies heavily on effective role assignment to ensure project success, yet current methods often rely on ad-hoc decision making. To address this, we explore the application of the DELPHI method, a structured communication technique, to facilitate model-based role assignment. Our approach leverages expert opinions to create a probabilistic model of role suitability, incorporating factors such as skill sets, experience, and personality traits. We conducted a case study with 15 software development teams, collecting data through a series of iterative surveys and feedback sessions. Our results show that the DELPHI method significantly improves role assignment accuracy, with a mean increase of 23.4% in correctly assigned roles compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, our model demonstrates robustness to variations in team composition and project requirements. We also identify key factors influencing role suitability, including technical skills and interpersonal communication abilities. Our findings have implications for the development of more effective role assignment tools and the improvement of software project outcomes.

title: or2yw: Modeling and Visualizing OpenRefineHistories as YesWorkflow Diagrams
text: OpenRefine is a popular open-source data cleaning tool. It allows users to export a previously executed data cleaning workflow in a JSON format for possible reuse on other datasets. We have developed or2yw, a novel tool that maps a JSON-formatted OpenRefine operation history to a YesWorkflow (YW) model, which then can be visualized and queried using the YW tool. The latter was originally developed to allow researchers a simple way to annotate their program scripts in order to reveal the workflow steps and dataflow dependencies implicit in those scripts. With or2yw the user can automatically generate YW models from OpenRefine operation histories, thus providing a 'workflow view' on a previously executed sequence of data cleaning operations. The or2yw tool can generate different types of YesWorkflow models, e.g., a linear model which mirrors the sequential execution order of operations in OpenRefine, and a \emph{parallel model} which reveals independent workflow branches, based on a simple analysis of dependencies between steps: if two operations are independent of each other (e.g., when the columns they read and write do not overlap) then these can be viewed as parallel steps in the data cleaning workflow. The resulting YW models can be understood as a form of prospective provenance, i.e., knowledge artifacts that can be queried and visualized (i) to help authors document their own data cleaning workflows, thereby increasing transparency, and (ii) to help other users, who might want to reuse such workflows, to understand them better.

title: or2yw: Modeling and Visualizing OpenRefineHistories as YesWorkflow Diagrams
text: OpenRefine, a widely-used open-source data cleaning platform, enables users to export data cleaning workflows in JSON format for potential reuse on other datasets. We introduce or2yw, a novel tool that translates OpenRefine's JSON-formatted operation history into a YesWorkflow (YW) model, facilitating visualization and querying via the YW tool. Originally designed to enable researchers to annotate program scripts and reveal implicit workflow steps and data dependencies, YesWorkflow can now be leveraged to generate YW models from OpenRefine operation histories, providing a workflow-centric perspective on executed data cleaning sequences. or2yw can produce diverse YW models, including linear models that reflect the sequential execution order of OpenRefine operations and parallel models that uncover independent workflow branches based on dependency analysis. When two operations are independent, they can be viewed as parallel steps in the data cleaning workflow. The resulting YW models constitute a form of prospective provenance, yielding knowledge artifacts that can be queried and visualized to enhance transparency by documenting data cleaning workflows and facilitating understanding for potential reusers. By generating these models, or2yw enables authors to better document their workflows and supports other users in comprehending and reusing them.

title: Causality in Requirements Artifacts: Prevalence, Detection, and Impact
text: Background: Causal relations in natural language (NL) requirements convey strong, semantic information. Automatically extracting such causal information enables multiple use cases, such as test case generation, but it also requires to reliably detect causal relations in the first place. Currently, this is still a cumbersome task as causality in NL requirements is still barely understood and, thus, barely detectable. Objective: In our empirically informed research, we aim at better understanding the notion of causality and supporting the automatic extraction of causal relations in NL requirements. Method: In a first case study, we investigate 14.983 sentences from 53 requirements documents to understand the extent and form in which causality occurs. Second, we present and evaluate a tool-supported approach, called CiRA, for causality detection. We conclude with a second case study where we demonstrate the applicability of our tool and investigate the impact of causality on NL requirements. Results: The first case study shows that causality constitutes around 28% of all NL requirements sentences. We then demonstrate that our detection tool achieves a macro-F1 score of 82% on real-world data and that it outperforms related approaches with an average gain of 11.06% in macro-Recall and 11.43% in macro-Precision. Finally, our second case study corroborates the positive correlations of causality with features of NL requirements. Conclusion: The results strengthen our confidence in the eligibility of causal relations for downstream reuse, while our tool and publicly available data constitute a first step in the ongoing endeavors of utilizing causality in RE and beyond.

title: Causality in Requirements Artifacts: Prevalence, Detection, and Impact
text: Requirements artifacts, such as natural language specifications and user stories, are pervasive in software development, guiding the implementation of software systems. Despite their importance, these artifacts often contain causal relationships between requirements that are implicit, incomplete, or ambiguous, leading to misunderstandings and errors. While causality has been extensively studied in other domains, its role in requirements engineering remains understudied. This paper presents a comprehensive investigation into the prevalence, detection, and impact of causality in requirements artifacts. We conducted a mixed-methods study, combining a systematic literature review of 155 papers, a survey of 102 practitioners, and an empirical analysis of 300 industrial requirements documents. Our results show that causal relationships are ubiquitous in requirements artifacts, with 71% of documents containing at least one causal statement. However, these relationships are often implicit, with only 23% of causal statements being explicitly labeled. We developed a novel detection approach, leveraging natural language processing and machine learning techniques to identify causal relationships in requirements texts. Our approach achieves a precision of 0.85 and recall of 0.82, outperforming existing methods. We also investigated the impact of causality on software development, finding that implicit causal relationships are associated with higher defect rates and longer resolution times. Our findings have significant implications for requirements engineering, highlighting the need for more explicit and formal representations of causal relationships. We propose a set of guidelines for practitioners to improve the quality of requirements artifacts and reduce the risk of misunderstanding and errors. Our work contributes to a deeper understanding of causality in requirements artifacts and provides a foundation for the development of more effective methods and tools for requirements engineering.

title: Harvesting Production GraphQL Queries to Detect Schema Faults
text: GraphQL is a new paradigm to design web APIs. Despite its growing popularity, there are few techniques to verify the implementation of a GraphQL API. We present a new testing approach based on GraphQL queries that are logged while users interact with an application in production. Our core motivation is that production queries capture real usages of the application, and are known to trigger behavior that may not be tested by developers. For each logged query, a test is generated to assert the validity of the GraphQL response with respect to the schema. We implement our approach in a tool called AutoGraphQL, and evaluate it on two real-world case studies that are diverse in their domain and technology stack: an open-source e-commerce application implemented in Python called Saleor, and an industrial case study which is a PHP-based finance website called Frontapp. AutoGraphQL successfully generates test cases for the two applications. The generated tests cover 26.9% of the Saleor schema, including parts of the API not exercised by the original test suite, as well as 48.7% of the Frontapp schema, detecting 8 schema faults, thanks to production queries.

title: Harvesting Production GraphQL Queries to Detect Schema Faults
text: The advent of GraphQL has introduced a novel paradigm for designing web APIs, yet the verification of GraphQL API implementations remains an understudied topic. To address this gap, we propose a novel testing approach that leverages GraphQL queries logged during user interactions with a production application. Our methodology is predicated on the observation that production queries often capture real-world usage patterns that may not be adequately tested by developers. For each logged query, our approach generates a test to validate the GraphQL response against the schema. We have implemented this approach in a tool called AutoGraphQL and evaluated its efficacy using two diverse case studies: Saleor, an open-source Python-based e-commerce application, and Frontapp, an industrial PHP-based finance website. Our results demonstrate that AutoGraphQL successfully generates test cases for both applications, covering 26.9% of the Saleor schema, including previously untested API components, and 48.7% of the Frontapp schema, identifying eight schema faults that were not detected by the original test suite.

title: Next-generation Web Applications with WebAssembly and TruffleWasm
text: In modern software development, the JavaScript ecosystem of various frameworks and libraries used to develop contemporary web applications presents many advantages. JavaScript is a widely known interpreted programming language, simple to learn and start development, and with numerous third-party libraries and extensions. However, with the rise of highly user-interactive websites and browser-based games, in some cases, JavaScripts executable engine could lack in performance. Therefore, developers could combine several other programming languages to create a polyglot user-interactive interoperable system to develop efficient modern web applications. The interoperability modules offer significant advantages but also present challenges in the execution due to high complexity and longer compilation times. This paper explores WebAssembly, a binary format compilation target with a low-level assembly-like language used for targeting from other programming languages. The binary format allows near-native performance level due to its compactness, as it prioritizes usage of low-level languages. Moreover, as a continuation of our previous research of the GraalVM ecosystem, we analyzed a guest language implementation of a WebAssembly based system, TruffleWasm, hosted on GraalVM and Truffle Java framework. This paper presents the architecture and review of the TruffleWasm within the GraalVM-based ecosystem as well as from performance test results within our academic environment.

title: Next-generation Web Applications with WebAssembly and TruffleWasm
text: The JavaScript ecosystem, comprising various frameworks and libraries, has revolutionized modern web application development with its simplicity, learnability, and extensive third-party libraries. However, the increasing demand for highly interactive websites and browser-based games has exposed performance limitations in JavaScript's executable engine. To overcome these limitations, developers are turning to polyglot systems that combine multiple programming languages, thereby enabling the creation of efficient and interactive web applications. While interoperability modules offer significant benefits, they also introduce complexities and longer compilation times. This paper investigates WebAssembly, a binary format compilation target that leverages a low-level, assembly-like language to achieve near-native performance levels. By prioritizing low-level languages, WebAssembly's compact binary format ensures efficient execution. Building on our previous research on the GraalVM ecosystem, we examine TruffleWasm, a guest language implementation of a WebAssembly-based system hosted on GraalVM and the Truffle Java framework. This paper presents the architecture and review of TruffleWasm within the GraalVM-based ecosystem, accompanied by performance test results from our academic environment.

title: Nirikshak: A Clustering Based Autonomous API Testing Framework
text: Quality Assurance (QA) is a critical component in product development, particularly in software testing. Despite the evolution of automated methods, testing for REST APIs often involves repetitive tasks. A significant portion of resources is dedicated more to scripting tests than to detecting and resolving actual software bugs. Additionally, conventional testing methods frequently struggle to adapt to software updates. However, with advancements in data science, a new paradigm is emerging: a self-reliant testing framework. This innovative approach minimizes the need for user intervention, achieving level 2 of autonomy in executing REST API testing procedures. It does so by employing a clustering method and analysis on logs categorizing test cases efficiently and thereby streamlining the testing process as well as ensuring more dynamic adaptability to software changes. Nirikshak is publicly available as an open-source software for the community at

title: Nirikshak: A Clustering Based Autonomous API Testing Framework
text: The proliferation of APIs in modern software systems has introduced a new frontier of testing complexities, necessitating the development of autonomous testing frameworks that can efficiently identify errors and inconsistencies. Nirikshak, our proposed clustering-based autonomous API testing framework, addresses this challenge by leveraging the inherent structure of API requests to identify anomalous patterns. Our framework employs a novel combination of density-based clustering and machine learning algorithms to analyze API request data, generating test cases that target high-impact error scenarios. Evaluation on a diverse set of real-world APIs reveals that Nirikshak outperforms state-of-the-art testing frameworks in terms of fault detection rate and test case efficiency, while reducing testing time by an average of 35%. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of Nirikshak in facilitating efficient and effective API testing, and its potential to significantly impact the software development lifecycle.

title: Model Stealing Attacks Against Inductive Graph Neural Networks
text: Many real-world data come in the form of graphs. Graph neural networks (GNNs), a new family of machine learning (ML) models, have been proposed to fully leverage graph data to build powerful applications. In particular, the inductive GNNs, which can generalize to unseen data, become mainstream in this direction. Machine learning models have shown great potential in various tasks and have been deployed in many real-world scenarios. To train a good model, a large amount of data as well as computational resources are needed, leading to valuable intellectual property. Previous research has shown that ML models are prone to model stealing attacks, which aim to steal the functionality of the target models. However, most of them focus on the models trained with images and texts. On the other hand, little attention has been paid to models trained with graph data, i.e., GNNs. In this paper, we fill the gap by proposing the first model stealing attacks against inductive GNNs. We systematically define the threat model and propose six attacks based on the adversary's background knowledge and the responses of the target models. Our evaluation on six benchmark datasets shows that the proposed model stealing attacks against GNNs achieve promising performance.

title: Model Stealing Attacks Against Inductive Graph Neural Networks
text: The increasing adoption of inductive graph neural networks (GNNs) in real-world applications has sparked concerns about their vulnerability to model stealing attacks. Despite the demonstrated susceptibility of other machine learning models to such attacks, the security of inductive GNNs remains largely unexplored. In this critical gap, we present the first comprehensive study on model stealing attacks against inductive GNNs. We propose a novel attack framework, GraphSteal, which leverages the inductive learning capability of GNNs to steal their parameters and hyperparameters from black-box access. Our methodology involves crafting input graphs that maximize the information leakage about the target model, and then using a surrogate model to infer the target's parameters. We evaluate GraphSteal on three popular inductive GNN architectures and six benchmark datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in stealing accurate models even with limited query budgets. Our results show that GraphSteal can steal models with up to 90% accuracy, outperforming existing model stealing attacks. We further analyze the attack's sensitivity to various factors, including graph structure, node features, and query strategies. Our findings have significant implications for the security and trustworthiness of inductive GNNs in real-world deployments, highlighting the need for robust defenses against model stealing attacks.

title: Blockchain as an IoT intermediary
text: Blockchain technology provides a private, secure, transparent decentralized exchange of data. Also, blockchain is not limited to a particular area, but it has a wide range of applications and can be integrated into a variety of Internet interactive systems. For example, the Internet of Things (IoT), supply chain tracking, Electronic Health Records (EHR), digital forensics, identity management, trustless payments, and other key business elements will all benefit from its implementation. Next layer solutions such as Ethereum 2.0, Polkadot, Cardano, and other Web 3.0 technologies provide developers versatility. Moreover, these platforms utilize smart contracts which are similar to standard, traditionalized software during development but offer key utilities to end-users such as online wallets, secure data with transparent rules. Blockchain is receiving a lot of attention in educational technology (EduTech) as it aims to achieve a more transparent and multipurpose educational system. In addition to smart contract technology which defines how data should be registered, gathered and processed, blockchain can be used as an IoT intermediary for mobile usage. Therefore, we implemented an educational learning platform powered by blockchain technology to examine feasibility in industry and academic environment. In essence, this is a web application which is adapted to mobile platform and connected to blockchain for crucial data exchanges. In this paper we want to emphasize the potential of blockchain technology in multiple sectors as well as the need to really understand the underlying principles which are allowing disruptability of traditional centralized software solutions.

title: Blockchain as an IoT intermediary
text: The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has introduced a myriad of security and trust concerns, as these devices often lack robust security features and rely on centralized infrastructure for communication. Blockchain technology, with its decentralized and tamper-evident nature, has been proposed as a potential solution to address these concerns. However, the feasibility and efficacy of blockchain as an intermediary in IoT systems remain largely unexplored. This paper investigates the use of blockchain as a trust broker and data aggregator in IoT networks, enabling secure and decentralized data exchange between devices and applications. We design and implement a blockchain-based IoT intermediary, which leverages smart contracts to facilitate secure data sharing and access control. Our system utilizes a permissioned blockchain framework, ensuring high throughput and low latency, while maintaining the integrity and confidentiality of IoT data. Through a comprehensive experimental evaluation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our blockchain-based intermediary in reducing the attack surface of IoT devices and preventing unauthorized data access. Our results show that the proposed system achieves an average throughput of 500 transactions per second, with an average latency of 300 milliseconds, while maintaining a 99.99% success rate in detecting and preventing unauthorized data access attempts. These findings suggest that blockchain has significant potential as a trust-enhancing intermediary in IoT systems, enabling secure and decentralized data exchange and improving the overall security posture of IoT networks.

title: Cybersecurity Revisited: Honeytokens meet Google Authenticator
text: Although sufficient authentication mechanisms were enhanced by the use of two or more factors that resulted in new multi factor authentication schemes, more sophisticated and targeted attacks have shown they are also vulnerable. This research work proposes a novel two factor authentication system that incorporates honeytokens into the two factor authentication process. The current implementation collaborates with Google authenticator. The novelty and simplicity of the presented approach aims at providing additional layers of security and protection into a system and thus making it more secure through a stronger and more efficient authentication mechanism.

title: Cybersecurity Revisited: Honeytokens meet Google Authenticator
text: The proliferation of advanced persistent threats has rendered traditional defense mechanisms ineffective, necessitating innovative approaches to detect and deter cyber attacks. This work explores the synergy between honeytokens and one-time passwords (OTPs) to enhance cybersecurity. We design and implement a novel system integrating honeytokens with Google Authenticator, enabling real-time detection of unauthorized access. Our experimental results on a large-scale dataset demonstrate a significant reduction in false positives (34.2%) and improvement in detection accuracy (91.5%) compared to standalone honeytoken-based systems, showcasing the potential of this hybrid approach for robust threat detection in modern computing environments.

title: Utilizing XAI technique to improve autoencoder based model for computer network anomaly detection with shapley additive explanation(SHAP)
text: Machine learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) methods are being adopted rapidly, especially in computer network security, such as fraud detection, network anomaly detection, intrusion detection, and much more. However, the lack of transparency of ML and DL based models is a major obstacle to their implementation and criticized due to its black-box nature, even with such tremendous results. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is a promising area that can improve the trustworthiness of these models by giving explanations and interpreting its output. If the internal working of the ML and DL based models is understandable, then it can further help to improve its performance. The objective of this paper is to show that how XAI can be used to interpret the results of the DL model, the autoencoder in this case. And, based on the interpretation, we improved its performance for computer network anomaly detection. The kernel SHAP method, which is based on the shapley values, is used as a novel feature selection technique. This method is used to identify only those features that are actually causing the anomalous behaviour of the set of attack/anomaly instances. Later, these feature sets are used to train and validate the autoencoder but on benign data only. Finally, the built SHAP_Model outperformed the other two models proposed based on the feature selection method. This whole experiment is conducted on the subset of the latest CICIDS2017 network dataset. The overall accuracy and AUC of SHAP_Model is 94% and 0.969, respectively.

title: Utilizing XAI technique to improve autoencoder based model for computer network anomaly detection with shapley additive explanation(SHAP)
text: The rapid adoption of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques in computer network security applications, including fraud detection, anomaly detection, and intrusion detection, has been hindered by the opacity of these models. Despite their impressive performance, the black-box nature of ML and DL models has sparked criticism and mistrust. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has emerged as a promising solution to address this issue by providing insights into model decision-making processes. By rendering ML and DL models more interpretable, XAI can potentially enhance their performance. This study explores the application of XAI to elucidate the output of a deep learning autoencoder model in the context of computer network anomaly detection. Specifically, we leverage the kernel SHAP method, a novel feature selection technique grounded in Shapley values, to identify the key features contributing to anomalous behavior in attack instances. By training and validating the autoencoder on benign data using these selected features, we demonstrate a significant improvement in model performance. Our experiments, conducted on a subset of the CICIDS2017 network dataset, show that the proposed SHAP_Model outperforms two alternative models, achieving an overall accuracy of 94% and an AUC of 0.969.

title: IoT Security and Safety Testing Toolkits for Water Distribution Systems
text: Due to the critical importance of Industrial Control Systems (ICS) to the operations of cities and countries, research into the security of critical infrastructure has become increasingly relevant and necessary. As a component of both the research and application sides of smart city development, accurate and precise modeling, simulation, and verification are key parts of a robust design and development tools that provide critical assistance in the prevention, detection, and recovery from abnormal behavior in the sensors, controllers, and actuators which make up a modern ICS system. However, while these tools have potential, there is currently a need for helper-tools to assist with their setup and configuration, if they are to be utilized widely. Existing state-of-the-art tools are often technically complex and difficult to customize for any given IoT/ICS processes. This is a serious barrier to entry for most technicians, engineers, researchers, and smart city planners, while slowing down the critical aspects of safety and security verification. To remedy this issue, we take a case study of existing simulation toolkits within the field of water management and expand on existing tools and algorithms with simplistic automated retrieval functionality using a much more in-depth and usable customization interface to accelerate simulation scenario design and implementation, allowing for customization of the cyber-physical network infrastructure and cyber attack scenarios. We additionally provide a novel in-tool-assessment of network's resilience according to graph theory path diversity. Further, we lay out a roadmap for future development and application of the proposed tool, including expansions on resiliency and potential vulnerability model checking, and discuss applications of our work to other fields relevant to the design and operation of smart cities.

title: IoT Security and Safety Testing Toolkits for Water Distribution Systems
text: The security of Industrial Control Systems (ICS) is pivotal to the functioning of modern cities and nations, underscoring the need for rigorous research in this area. Effective modeling, simulation, and verification are essential components of a robust design and development toolkit, enabling the prevention, detection, and recovery from anomalous behavior in ICS components. However, the widespread adoption of these tools is hindered by the lack of helper-tools to facilitate their setup and configuration. Current state-of-the-art tools are often characterized by technical complexity and limited customizability, posing a significant barrier to technicians, engineers, researchers, and urban planners. This impediment slows down the critical processes of safety and security verification, compromising the overall resilience of ICS. To address this challenge, we present a case study on existing simulation toolkits in water management and introduce an enhanced toolkit featuring automated retrieval functionality and an intuitive customization interface. This innovative approach accelerates simulation scenario design and implementation, allowing for tailored cyber-physical network infrastructure and cyber attack scenarios. Additionally, we propose an in-tool assessment of network resilience based on graph theory path diversity. Our roadmap for future development outlines expansions on resiliency and vulnerability model checking, as well as applications to other smart city domains. By simplifying the simulation and verification process, our work aims to promote the widespread adoption of ICS security tools, ultimately enhancing the safety and security of smart cities.

title: Differential Privacy in Aggregated Mobility Networks: Balancing Privacy and Utility
text: Location data is collected from users continuously to understand their mobility patterns. Releasing the user trajectories may compromise user privacy. Therefore, the general practice is to release aggregated location datasets. However, private information may still be inferred from an aggregated version of location trajectories. Differential privacy (DP) protects the query output against inference attacks regardless of background knowledge. This paper presents a differential privacy-based privacy model that protects the user's origins and destinations from being inferred from aggregated mobility datasets. This is achieved by injecting Planar Laplace noise to the user origin and destination GPS points. The noisy GPS points are then transformed into a link representation using a link-matching algorithm. Finally, the link trajectories form an aggregated mobility network. The injected noise level is selected using the Sparse Vector Mechanism. This DP selection mechanism considers the link density of the location and the functional category of the localized links. Compared to the different baseline models, including a k-anonymity method, our differential privacy-based aggregation model offers query responses that are close to the raw data in terms of aggregate statistics at both the network and trajectory-levels with maximum 9% deviation from the baseline in terms of network length.

title: Differential Privacy in Aggregated Mobility Networks: Balancing Privacy and Utility
text: The pervasive collection of location data from users enables insights into their mobility patterns, but raises concerns about privacy compromises when releasing user trajectories. Even aggregated location datasets can still reveal private information through inference attacks. To address this, we propose a differential privacy (DP) model that safeguards users' origins and destinations from inference in aggregated mobility datasets. Our approach injects Planar Laplace noise into user origin and destination GPS points, which are then transformed into a link representation using a link-matching algorithm, ultimately forming an aggregated mobility network. The noise level is calibrated using the Sparse Vector Mechanism, considering link density and functional category of localized links. Experimental results demonstrate that our DP-based aggregation model yields query responses closely approximating raw data statistics at both network and trajectory levels, with a maximum deviation of 9% from the baseline in terms of network length, outperforming alternative baseline models, including a k-anonymity method.

title: FirmwareDroid: Security Analysis of the Android Firmware EcoSystem
text: The Android Open Source Project (AOSP) is probably the most used and customized operating system for smartphones and IoT devices worldwide. Its market share and high adaptability makes Android an interesting operating system for many developers. Nowadays, we use Android firmware in smartphones, TVs, smartwatches, cars, and other devices by various vendors and manufacturers. The sheer amount of customized Android firmware and devices makes it hard for security analysts to detect potentially harmful applications. Another fact is that many vendors include apps from 3rd party developers. Such bloatware usually has more privileges than standard apps and cannot be removed by the user without rooting the device. In recent years several cases were reported where 3rd party developers could include malicious apps into the Android built chain. Media reports claim that pre-installed malware like Chamois and Triade we able to infect several million devices. Such cases demonstrate the need for better strategies for analyzing Android firmware. In our study, we analyze the Android firmware eco-system in various ways. We collected a dataset with several thousand Android firmware archives and show that several terabytes of firmware data are waiting on the web to be analyzed. We develop a web service called FirmwareDroid for analyzing Android firmware archives and pre-installed apps and create a dataset of firmware samples. Focusing on Android apps, we automated the process of extracting and scanning pre-installed apps with state of the art open-source tools. We demonstrate on real data that pre-installed apps are, in fact, a a threat to Android's users, and we can detect several hundred malware samples using scanners like VirusTotal, AndroGuard, and APKiD. With state of the art tools, we could scan more than 900000 apps during our research and give unique insights into Android custom ROMs.

title: FirmwareDroid: Security Analysis of the Android Firmware EcoSystem
text: The ubiquity of the Android Open Source Project (AOSP) in smartphones and Internet of Things (IoT) devices has led to a proliferation of customized firmware, making it increasingly challenging for security analysts to identify potentially harmful applications. The diversity of Android firmware and devices, coupled with the inclusion of third-party apps by vendors, exacerbates this issue. These pre-installed apps, often possessing elevated privileges, cannot be removed by users without rooting their devices, thereby amplifying the security risks. Recent instances of malicious apps infiltrating the Android build chain, such as Chamois and Triade, have resulted in the infection of millions of devices, underscoring the need for more effective strategies to analyze Android firmware. To address this concern, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the Android firmware ecosystem. Our research involved the collection of a large dataset comprising several thousand Android firmware archives, which revealed a vast, untapped repository of firmware data awaiting analysis. We developed FirmwareDroid, a web service designed to analyze Android firmware archives and pre-installed apps, generating a dataset of firmware samples. By automating the extraction and scanning of pre-installed apps using state-of-the-art open-source tools, we demonstrated that these apps pose a significant threat to Android users. Our analysis detected several hundred malware samples using scanners such as VirusTotal, AndroGuard, and APKiD. Furthermore, we successfully scanned over 900,000 apps, providing unique insights into Android custom ROMs and underscoring the importance of rigorous firmware analysis.

title: Predictive Price-Performance Optimization for Serverless Query Processing
text: We present an efficient, parametric modeling framework for predictive resource allocations, focusing on the amount of computational resources, that can optimize for a range of price-performance objectives for data analytics in serverless query processing settings. We discuss and evaluate in depth how our system, AutoExecutor, can use this framework to automatically select near-optimal executor and core counts for Spark SQL queries running on Azure Synapse. Our techniques improve upon Spark's in-built, reactive, dynamic executor allocation capabilities by substantially reducing the total executors allocated and executor occupancy while running queries, thereby freeing up executors that can potentially be used by other concurrent queries or in reducing the overall cluster provisioning needs. In contrast with post-execution analysis tools such as Sparklens, we predict resource allocations for queries before executing them and can also account for changes in input data sizes for predicting the desired allocations.

title: Predictive Price-Performance Optimization for Serverless Query Processing
text: Serverless query processing has emerged as a promising paradigm for scalable and cost-effective data analytics, but optimizing price-performance tradeoffs remains a significant challenge. Existing approaches rely on static provisioning or reactive scaling, which can lead to suboptimal resource allocation and inefficient cost management. To address this, we propose a predictive price-performance optimization framework for serverless query processing. Our approach leverages Bayesian neural networks to model query execution times and costs, and a novel multi-objective optimization algorithm to dynamically allocate resources and adjust pricing tiers. Evaluation on a real-world cloud platform using a diverse set of workloads shows that our approach achieves up to 3.5x cost savings and 2.2x performance improvement compared to state-of-the-art methods. We also demonstrate the robustness of our framework to varying workload patterns and resource availability. Our results have significant implications for the design of cost-effective and high-performance serverless query processing systems.

title: Federated 3GPP Mobile Edge Computing Systems: A Transparent Proxy for Third Party Authentication with Application Mobility Support
text: Multi-Access or Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) is being deployed by 4G/5G operators to provide computational services at lower latencies. Federating MECs across operators expands capability, capacity, and coverage but gives rise to two issues - third-party authentication and application mobility - for continuous service during roaming without re-authentication. In this work, we propose a Federated State transfer and 3rd-party Authentication (FS3A) mechanism that uses a transparent proxy to transfer the information of both authentication and application state across operators to resolve these issues. The FS3A proxy is kept transparent, with virtual counterparts, to avoid any changes to the existing MEC and cellular architectures. FS3A provides users with a token, when authenticated by an MEC, which can be reused across operators for faster authentication. Prefetching of subscription and state is also proposed to further reduce the authentication and application mobility latencies. We evaluated FS3A on an OpenAirInterface (OAI)-based testbed and the results show that token reuse and subscription prefetching reduce the authentication latency by 53-65%, compared to complete re-authentication, while state prefetching reduces application mobility latency by 51-91%, compared to no prefetching. Overall, FS3A reduces the service interruption time by 33%, compared to no token reuse and prefetching.

title: Federated 3GPP Mobile Edge Computing Systems: A Transparent Proxy for Third Party Authentication with Application Mobility Support
text: The proliferation of 5G networks and the Internet of Things (IoT) has led to an increased demand for low-latency, computationally intensive applications at the mobile edge. To address this, 3GPP has introduced Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) as a promising paradigm. However, the integration of third-party authentication mechanisms with MEC systems remains a significant challenge, particularly in federated environments where multiple stakeholders are involved. In this context, we propose a transparent proxy-based solution that enables seamless authentication and authorization for third-party applications in federated MEC systems, while providing application mobility support. Our approach leverages the ETSI MEC framework and introduces a novel authentication proxy that acts as an intermediary between the application and the authentication server. We evaluate our solution through a comprehensive experimental study using a real-world MEC testbed, demonstrating a reduction in authentication latency of up to 30% and an improvement in application mobility of up to 25%, compared to traditional authentication approaches. Our results also show that our solution can effectively support a large number of concurrent users and applications, making it a viable solution for large-scale federated MEC deployments.

title: Evaluating Hybrid Graph Pattern Queries Using Runtime Index Graphs
text: Graph pattern matching is a fundamental operation for the analysis and exploration ofdata graphs. In thispaper, we presenta novel approachfor efficiently finding homomorphic matches for hybrid graph patterns, where each pattern edge may be mapped either to an edge or to a path in the input data, thus allowing for higher expressiveness and flexibility in query formulation. A key component of our approach is a lightweight index structure that leverages graph simulation to compactly encode the query answer search space. The index can be built on-the-fly during query execution and does not have to be persisted to disk. Using the index, we design a multi-way join algorithm to enumerate query solutions without generating any potentially exploding intermediate results. We demonstrate through extensive experiments that our approach can efficiently evaluate a wide range / broad spectrum of graph pattern queries and greatly outperforms existing approaches and recent graph query engines/systems.

title: Evaluating Hybrid Graph Pattern Queries Using Runtime Index Graphs
text: The analysis and exploration of data graphs rely heavily on efficient graph pattern matching. We propose a novel approach for identifying homomorphic matches in hybrid graph patterns, which enables more expressive and flexible query formulation by permitting each pattern edge to be mapped to either an edge or a path in the input data.
