A crucial aspect of our approach is a lightweight index structure, built on-the-fly during query execution, that harnesses graph simulation to concisely encode the search space of query answers. This index facilitates a multi-way join algorithm that enumerates query solutions without generating intermediate results that might exponentially increase in size. Our comprehensive experimental evaluation demonstrates the efficiency of our approach in evaluating a broad range of graph pattern queries, significantly outperforming existing methods and recent graph query engines.

title: Revisiting Fuzzy Signatures: Towards a More Risk-Free Cryptographic Authentication System based on Biometrics
text: Biometric authentication is one of the promising alternatives to standard password-based authentication offering better usability and security. In this work, we revisit the biometric authentication based on "fuzzy signatures" introduced by Takahashi et al. (ACNS'15, IJIS'19). These are special types of digital signatures where the secret signing key can be a "fuzzy" data such as user's biometrics. Compared to other cryptographically secure biometric authentications as those relying on fuzzy extractors, the fuzzy signature-based scheme provides a more attractive security guarantee. However, despite their potential values, fuzzy signatures have not attracted much attention owing to their theory-oriented presentations in all prior works. For instance, the discussion on the practical feasibility of the assumptions (such as the entropy of user biometrics), which the security of fuzzy signatures hinges on, is completely missing. In this work, we revisit fuzzy signatures and show that we can indeed efficiently and securely implement them in practice. At a high level, our contribution is threefold: (i) we provide a much simpler, more efficient, and direct construction of fuzzy signature compared to prior works; (ii) we establish novel statistical techniques to experimentally evaluate the conditions on biometrics that are required to securely instantiate fuzzy signatures; and (iii) we provide experimental results using a real-world finger-vein dataset to show that finger-veins from a single hand are sufficient to construct efficient and secure fuzzy signatures. Our performance analysis shows that in a practical scenario with 112-bits of security, the size of the signature is 1256 bytes, and the running time for signing/verification is only a few milliseconds.

title: Revisiting Fuzzy Signatures: Towards a More Risk-Free Cryptographic Authentication System based on Biometrics
text: Biometric authentication offers a promising alternative to traditional password-based systems, enhancing both usability and security. Building upon the concept of "fuzzy signatures" introduced by Takahashi et al., we reexamine the feasibility of digital signatures that utilize "fuzzy" data, such as user biometrics, as the secret signing key. Notably, fuzzy signature-based schemes provide a more robust security guarantee compared to other cryptographically secure biometric authentication methods, including those relying on fuzzy extractors. Despite their potential, fuzzy signatures have received limited attention due to their theoretical focus in previous works, neglecting essential practical considerations. Specifically, the practical feasibility of assumptions, such as the entropy of user biometrics, which underpin the security of fuzzy signatures, has been overlooked. This study addresses these gaps by demonstrating the efficient and secure implementation of fuzzy signatures in practice. Our contributions are threefold: we present a simpler, more efficient, and direct construction of fuzzy signatures; develop novel statistical techniques to experimentally evaluate the required biometric conditions for secure instantiation; and provide experimental results using a real-world finger-vein dataset, showcasing the sufficiency of finger-veins from a single hand for constructing efficient and secure fuzzy signatures. Our performance analysis reveals that, with 112-bits of security, the signature size is 1256 bytes, and the signing/verification time is merely a few milliseconds, making fuzzy signatures a viable solution for practical applications.

title: Construction of Differentially Private Summaries over Fully Homomorphic Encryption
text: Cloud computing has garnered attention as a platform of query processing systems. However, data privacy leakage is a critical problem. Chowdhury et al. proposed Crypt(epsilon), which executes differential privacy (DP) over encrypted data on two non-colluding semi-honest servers. Further, the DP index proposed by these authors summarizes a dataset to prevent information leakage while improving the performance. However, two problems persist: 1) the original data are decrypted to apply sorting via a garbled circuit, and 2) the added noise becomes large because the sorted data are partitioned with equal width, regardless of the data distribution. To solve these problems, we propose a new method called DP-summary that summarizes a dataset into differentially private data over a homomorphic encryption without decryption, thereby enhancing data security. Furthermore, our scheme adopts Li et al.'s data-aware and workload-aware (DAWA) algorithm for the encrypted data, thereby minimizing the noise caused by DP and reducing the errors of query responses. An experimental evaluation using torus fully homomorphic encryption (TFHE), a bit-wise fully homomorphic encryption library, confirms the applicability of the proposed method, which summarized eight 16-bit data in 12.5 h. We also confirmed that there was no accuracy degradation even after adopting TFHE along with the DAWA algorithm.

title: Construction of Differentially Private Summaries over Fully Homomorphic Encryption
text: The proliferation of sensitive data across various domains has created an urgent need for privacy-preserving data analysis techniques. Recent advancements in fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) have enabled computations over encrypted data, but the construction of differentially private summaries remains a significant challenge. In this context, we propose a novel framework for constructing differentially private summaries over FHE-encrypted data, ensuring that the summaries do not compromise individual privacy. Our approach leverages the concept of functional encryption, which allows for flexible access control and computation over encrypted data. We design a novel encryption scheme that integrates the Brakerski-Fan-Vercauteren (BFV) FHE scheme with the Gaussian mechanism, a fundamental component of differential privacy. The resulting encrypted summaries are perturbed using a carefully calibrated noise distribution, ensuring that the summaries satisfy differential privacy guarantees. Through a comprehensive evaluation, we demonstrate the efficacy of our framework in achieving accurate and private summaries over various data distributions. Our approach exhibits a significant reduction in computational overhead compared to existing techniques, while maintaining stringent privacy guarantees. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the trade-off between privacy and accuracy, providing insights into the optimal parameter settings for real-world applications. Our work has significant implications for privacy-preserving data analysis, enabling the construction of private summaries over sensitive data without compromising individual privacy.

title: Bent Functions in the Partial Spread Class Generated by Linear Recurring Sequences
text: We present a construction of partial spread bent functions using subspaces generated by linear recurring sequences (LRS). We first show that the kernels of the linear mappings defined by two LRS have a trivial intersection if and only if their feedback polynomials are relatively prime. Then, we characterize the appropriate parameters for a family of pairwise coprime polynomials to generate a partial spread required for the support of a bent function, showing that such families exist if and only if the degrees of the underlying polynomials is either $1$ or $2$. We then count the resulting sets of polynomials and prove that for degree $1$, our LRS construction coincides with the Desarguesian partial spread. Finally, we perform a computer search of all $\mathcal{PS}^-$ and $\mathcal{PS}^+$ bent functions of $n=8$ variables generated by our construction and compute their 2-ranks. The results show that many of these functions defined by polynomials of degree $b=2$ are not EA-equivalent to any Maiorana-McFarland or Desarguesian partial spread function.

title: Bent Functions in the Partial Spread Class Generated by Linear Recurring Sequences
text: The partial spread class is a rich source of bent functions, which are crucial components in symmetric cryptography, particularly in the design of stream ciphers and block ciphers. Despite their importance, the construction of bent functions remains a challenging problem, and new methods for generating them are highly desirable. In this study, we explore the potential of using linear recurring sequences (LRS) to generate bent functions in the partial spread class. We develop a novel approach that leverages the algebraic properties of LRS to construct bent functions with desirable properties. Our methodology involves the use of finite field arithmetic and a careful analysis of the Walsh-Hadamard transform. Through an exhaustive search, we identify several new bent functions in the partial spread class that can be generated using LRS. Our findings demonstrate that LRS-based constructions can yield bent functions with high nonlinearity and resiliency, making them suitable for cryptographic applications. The results of this study contribute to the advancement of symmetric cryptography and have potential implications for the design of secure cryptographic primitives.

title: Unsupervised Matching of Data and Text
text: Entity resolution is a widely studied problem with several proposals to match records across relations. Matching textual content is a widespread task in many applications, such as question answering and search. While recent methods achieve promising results for these two tasks, there is no clear solution for the more general problem of matching textual content and structured data. We introduce a framework that supports this new task in an unsupervised setting for any pair of corpora, being relational tables or text documents. Our method builds a fine-grained graph over the content of the corpora and derives word embeddings to represent the objects to match in a low dimensional space. The learned representation enables effective and efficient matching at different granularity, from relational tuples to text sentences and paragraphs. Our flexible framework can exploit pre-trained resources, but it does not depends on their existence and achieves better quality performance in matching content when the vocabulary is domain specific. We also introduce optimizations in the graph creation process with an "expand and compress" approach that first identifies new valid relationships across elements, to improve matching, and then prunes nodes and edges, to reduce the graph size. Experiments on real use cases and public datasets show that our framework produces embeddings that outperform word embeddings and fine-tuned language models both in results' quality and in execution times.

title: Unsupervised Matching of Data and Text
text: The confluence of entity resolution and textual content matching has spawned numerous approaches, yet a unified solution for integrating both textual and structured data remains elusive. This integration is crucial in various applications, such as question answering and search, where the ability to match records across relations and textual content is paramount. We propose a novel unsupervised framework capable of addressing this challenge for any pair of corpora, encompassing relational tables and text documents. By constructing a fine-grained graph over the corpora content and deriving word embeddings, our method represents objects in a low-dimensional space, facilitating effective and efficient matching at multiple granularities, from relational tuples to text sentences and paragraphs. The flexibility of our framework allows it to leverage pre-trained resources when available, but it does not rely on their existence, thereby achieving superior performance in domain-specific vocabulary contexts. Furthermore, we introduce an "expand and compress" optimization strategy for graph creation, which identifies new relationships to improve matching and subsequently prunes nodes and edges to reduce graph size. Experimental results on real-world use cases and public datasets demonstrate that our framework produces embeddings that surpass both word embeddings and fine-tuned language models in terms of quality and execution time.

title: Correlation inference attacks against machine learning models
text: Despite machine learning models being widely used today, the relationship between a model and its training dataset is not well understood. We explore correlation inference attacks, whether and when a model leaks information about the correlations between the input variables of its training dataset. We first propose a model-less attack, where an adversary exploits the spherical parametrization of correlation matrices alone to make an informed guess. Second, we propose a model-based attack, where an adversary exploits black-box model access to infer the correlations using minimal and realistic assumptions. Third, we evaluate our attacks against logistic regression and multilayer perceptron models on three tabular datasets and show the models to leak correlations. We finally show how extracted correlations can be used as building blocks for attribute inference attacks and enable weaker adversaries. Our results raise fundamental questions on what a model does and should remember from its training set.

title: Correlation inference attacks against machine learning models
text: The interplay between a machine learning model and its training dataset remains poorly understood, despite the widespread adoption of these models. This knowledge gap is particularly concerning in the context of correlation inference attacks, which aim to uncover the relationships between input variables in the training data. We investigate this vulnerability by proposing two novel attack strategies: a model-less approach that leverages the spherical parametrization of correlation matrices, and a model-based approach that exploits black-box model access with minimal assumptions. Our evaluation on logistic regression and multilayer perceptron models across three tabular datasets reveals that these models indeed leak correlation information. Furthermore, we demonstrate how extracted correlations can be utilized as building blocks for attribute inference attacks, thereby empowering weaker adversaries. Our findings prompt essential questions about the fundamental principles governing what a model should retain from its training data.

title: Topology optimization with a closed cavity exclusion constraint for additive manufacturing based on the fictitious physical model approach
text: This paper proposes a topology optimization method that considers the geometric constraint of no closed cavities to improve the effectiveness of additive manufacturing based on the fictitious physical model approach. First, the basic topology optimization concept and level set-based method are introduced. Next, the fictitious physical model for a geometric constraint in the topology optimization framework is discussed. Then, a model for the geometric constraint of no closed cavities for additive manufacturing is proposed. Numerical examples are provided to validate the proposed model. In addition, topology optimization considering the geometric constraint is formulated, and topology optimization algorithms are constructed using the finite element method. Finally, optimization examples are provided to validate the proposed topology optimization method.

title: Topology optimization with a closed cavity exclusion constraint for additive manufacturing based on the fictitious physical model approach
text: We present a novel topology optimization methodology that incorporates the geometric constraint of avoiding closed cavities, thereby enhancing the efficacy of additive manufacturing processes. Building upon the fundamental concepts of topology optimization and level set-based methods, we develop a fictitious physical model that accommodates geometric constraints within the optimization framework. A tailored model is proposed to enforce the absence of closed cavities, a crucial consideration in additive manufacturing. The validity of this approach is demonstrated through numerical examples. Furthermore, we formulate the topology optimization problem with geometric constraints and construct algorithms leveraging the finite element method. The proposed methodology is substantiated by optimization examples, showcasing its effectiveness in generating designs optimized for additive manufacturing.

title: Addressing Adversarial Machine Learning Attacks in Smart Healthcare Perspectives
text: Smart healthcare systems are gaining popularity with the rapid development of intelligent sensors, the Internet of Things (IoT) applications and services, and wireless communications. However, at the same time, several vulnerabilities and adversarial attacks make it challenging for a safe and secure smart healthcare system from a security point of view. Machine learning has been used widely to develop suitable models to predict and mitigate attacks. Still, the attacks could trick the machine learning models and misclassify outputs generated by the model. As a result, it leads to incorrect decisions, for example, false disease detection and wrong treatment plans for patients. In this paper, we address the type of adversarial attacks and their impact on smart healthcare systems. We propose a model to examine how adversarial attacks impact machine learning classifiers. To test the model, we use a medical image dataset. Our model can classify medical images with high accuracy. We then attacked the model with a Fast Gradient Sign Method attack (FGSM) to cause the model to predict the images and misclassify them inaccurately. Using transfer learning, we train a VGG-19 model with the medical dataset and later implement the FGSM to the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to examine the significant impact it causes on the performance and accuracy of the machine learning model. Our results demonstrate that the adversarial attack misclassifies the images, causing the model's accuracy rate to drop from 88% to 11%.

title: Addressing Adversarial Machine Learning Attacks in Smart Healthcare Perspectives
text: The proliferation of smart healthcare systems has ushered in unprecedented opportunities for personalized medicine, remote patient monitoring, and data-driven healthcare decision-making. However, the increasing reliance on machine learning (ML) models in these systems has created a vulnerable attack surface, susceptible to adversarial machine learning (AML) attacks. Such attacks can have devastating consequences, including misdiagnosis, compromised patient data, and even loss of life. This paper presents a comprehensive framework to address AML attacks in smart healthcare systems, focusing on the detection and mitigation of evasion, poisoning, and inference attacks. We propose a novel, hybrid approach that integrates anomaly detection, digital watermarking, and adversarial training to enhance the robustness of ML models. Our methodology involves a thorough analysis of existing AML attacks in healthcare, followed by the design and implementation of a robust, adaptive defense system. The system is evaluated using a diverse set of healthcare datasets, including medical imaging, electronic health records, and sensor data. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in detecting AML attacks with high accuracy (95.2%) and reducing the attack success rate by 87.5%. Furthermore, our framework is shown to be scalable, adaptable to various healthcare applications, and computationally efficient. The findings of this research have significant implications for the development of secure, reliable, and trustworthy smart healthcare systems, ultimately contributing to improved patient outcomes and enhanced healthcare services.

title: Computing the Shapley Value of Facts in Query Answering
text: The Shapley value is a game-theoretic notion for wealth distribution that is nowadays extensively used to explain complex data-intensive computation, for instance, in network analysis or machine learning. Recent theoretical works show that query evaluation over relational databases fits well in this explanation paradigm. Yet, these works fall short of providing practical solutions to the computational challenge inherent to the Shapley computation. We present in this paper two practically effective solutions for computing Shapley values in query answering. We start by establishing a tight theoretical connection to the extensively studied problem of query evaluation over probabilistic databases, which allows us to obtain a polynomial-time algorithm for the class of queries for which probability computation is tractable. We then propose a first practical solution for computing Shapley values that adopts tools from probabilistic query evaluation. In particular, we capture the dependence of query answers on input database facts using Boolean expressions (data provenance), and then transform it, via Knowledge Compilation, into a particular circuit form for which we devise an algorithm for computing the Shapley values. Our second practical solution is a faster yet inexact approach that transforms the provenance to a Conjunctive Normal Form and uses a heuristic to compute the Shapley values. Our experiments on TPC-H and IMDB demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our solutions.

title: Computing the Shapley Value of Facts in Query Answering
text: The Shapley value, a game-theoretic concept for fair wealth distribution, has been increasingly applied to explain complex data-intensive computations, such as network analysis and machine learning. Recent theoretical advancements have demonstrated the applicability of this paradigm to query evaluation over relational databases. However, these works have not provided practical solutions to address the inherent computational challenges of Shapley value computation. This paper bridges this gap by presenting two effective solutions for computing Shapley values in query answering. By establishing a theoretical connection to probabilistic database query evaluation, we develop a polynomial-time algorithm for queries with tractable probability computation. Our first practical solution leverages tools from probabilistic query evaluation, capturing query answer dependence on input database facts using Boolean expressions and transforming them into a circuit form amenable to Shapley value computation. Alternatively, our second solution employs a faster, albeit approximate, approach, transforming the provenance to Conjunctive Normal Form and utilizing a heuristic for Shapley value estimation. Experimental evaluations on TPC-H and IMDB datasets demonstrate the practical efficacy of our proposed solutions.

title: CodedPaddedFL and CodedSecAgg: Straggler Mitigation and Secure Aggregation in Federated Learning
text: We present two novel federated learning (FL) schemes that mitigate the effect of straggling devices by introducing redundancy on the devices' data across the network. Compared to other schemes in the literature, which deal with stragglers or device dropouts by ignoring their contribution, the proposed schemes do not suffer from the client drift problem. The first scheme, CodedPaddedFL, mitigates the effect of stragglers while retaining the privacy level of conventional FL. It combines one-time padding for user data privacy with gradient codes to yield straggler resiliency. The second scheme, CodedSecAgg, provides straggler resiliency and robustness against model inversion attacks and is based on Shamir's secret sharing. We apply CodedPaddedFL and CodedSecAgg to a classification problem. For a scenario with 120 devices, CodedPaddedFL achieves a speed-up factor of 18 for an accuracy of 95% on the MNIST dataset compared to conventional FL. Furthermore, it yields similar performance in terms of latency compared to a recently proposed scheme by Prakash et al. without the shortcoming of additional leakage of private data. CodedSecAgg outperforms the state-of-the-art secure aggregation scheme LightSecAgg by a speed-up factor of 6.6-18.7 for the MNIST dataset for an accuracy of 95%.

title: CodedPaddedFL and CodedSecAgg: Straggler Mitigation and Secure Aggregation in Federated Learning
text: Federated learning has emerged as a promising approach for collaborative model training on decentralized data, but it is vulnerable to straggler nodes that slow down the training process and malicious nodes that compromise the model's integrity. To address these challenges, we propose two novel protocols: CodedPaddedFL, a straggler mitigation technique, and CodedSecAgg, a secure aggregation protocol. CodedPaddedFL combines coded computing with padding to mask the presence of stragglers, allowing the system to proceed without waiting for the slowest nodes. We prove that CodedPaddedFL achieves a throughput gain of up to 3.5x compared to existing straggler mitigation techniques. CodedSecAgg, on the other hand, leverages cryptographic techniques and coding theory to ensure the confidentiality and integrity of the aggregated model updates. Our security analysis demonstrates that CodedSecAgg is secure against semi-honest adversaries and achieves a communication overhead of only 12.5%. We implement and evaluate our protocols on a real-world federated learning benchmark, demonstrating significant improvements in training time and model accuracy. Our work bridges the gap between federated learning and coded computing, paving the way for more efficient and secure collaborative model training.

title: Towards Homomorphic Inference Beyond the Edge
text: Beyond edge devices can function off the power grid and without batteries, enabling them to operate in difficult to access regions. However, energy costly long-distance communication required for reporting results or offloading computation becomes a limitation. Here, we reduce this overhead by developing a beyond edge device which can effectively act as a nearby server to offload computation. For security reasons, this device must operate on encrypted data, which incurs a high overhead. We use energy-efficient and intermittent-safe in-memory computation to enable this encrypted computation, allowing it to provide a speedup for beyond edge applications within a power budget of a few milliWatts.

title: Towards Homomorphic Inference Beyond the Edge
text: Self-sustaining beyond edge devices, unencumbered by power grids and batteries, can operate in remote and inaccessible areas. However, the energy-intensive long-distance communication required for result reporting and computation offloading poses a significant limitation. To mitigate this, we propose a beyond edge device capable of serving as a proximal server for computation offloading, thereby reducing the overhead. Since secure operation necessitates encrypted data processing, which is computationally expensive, we employ energy-efficient and intermittent-safe in-memory computation techniques to enable encrypted computation within a stringent power budget of a few milliWatts, ultimately yielding a speedup for beyond edge applications.

title: A Heterogeneous Graph Learning Model for Cyber-Attack Detection
text: A cyber-attack is a malicious attempt by experienced hackers to breach the target information system. Usually, the cyber-attacks are characterized as hybrid TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) and long-term adversarial behaviors, making the traditional intrusion detection methods ineffective. Most existing cyber-attack detection systems are implemented based on manually designed rules by referring to domain knowledge (e.g., threat models, threat intelligences). However, this process is lack of intelligence and generalization ability. Aiming at this limitation, this paper proposes an intelligent cyber-attack detection method based on provenance data. To effective and efficient detect cyber-attacks from a huge number of system events in the provenance data, we firstly model the provenance data by a heterogeneous graph to capture the rich context information of each system entities (e.g., process, file, socket, etc.), and learns a semantic vector representation for each system entity. Then, we perform online cyber-attack detection by sampling a small and compact local graph from the heterogeneous graph, and classifying the key system entities as malicious or benign. We conducted a series of experiments on two provenance datasets with real cyber-attacks. The experiment results show that the proposed method outperforms other learning based detection models, and has competitive performance against state-of-the-art rule based cyber-attack detection systems.

title: A Heterogeneous Graph Learning Model for Cyber-Attack Detection
text: Cyber-attacks, orchestrated by skilled hackers, pose a significant threat to information systems, often manifesting as hybrid Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) and prolonged adversarial behaviors. Traditional intrusion detection methods are frequently rendered ineffective by these sophisticated attacks. The majority of existing detection systems rely on manually crafted rules informed by domain knowledge, such as threat models and threat intelligence. However, this approach is limited by its lack of adaptability and generalizability. To address this shortcoming, we propose a novel, intelligent cyber-attack detection method leveraging provenance data. By modeling provenance data as a heterogeneous graph, we capture the rich contextual information of system entities, including processes, files, and sockets, and learn semantic vector representations for each entity. Online detection is facilitated by sampling compact local graphs and classifying key entities as malicious or benign. Our experiments, conducted on two real-world provenance datasets, demonstrate the proposed method's superior performance compared to learning-based models and competitiveness with state-of-the-art rule-based systems.

title: APTSHIELD: A Stable, Efficient and Real-time APT Detection System for Linux Hosts
text: Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) attack usually refers to the form of long-term, covert and sustained attack on specific targets, with an adversary using advanced attack techniques to destroy the key facilities of an organization. APT attacks have caused serious security threats and massive financial loss worldwide. Academics and industry thereby have proposed a series of solutions to detect APT attacks, such as dynamic/static code analysis, traffic detection, sandbox technology, endpoint detection and response (EDR), etc. However, existing defenses are failed to accurately and effectively defend against the current APT attacks that exhibit strong persistent, stealthy, diverse and dynamic characteristics due to the weak data source integrity, large data processing overhead and poor real-time performance in the process of real-world scenarios. To overcome these difficulties, in this paper we propose APTSHIELD, a stable, efficient and real-time APT detection system for Linux hosts. In the aspect of data collection, audit is selected to stably collect kernel data of the operating system so as to carry out a complete portrait of the attack based on comprehensive analysis and comparison of existing logging tools; In the aspect of data processing, redundant semantics skipping and non-viable node pruning are adopted to reduce the amount of data, so as to reduce the overhead of the detection system; In the aspect of attack detection, an APT attack detection framework based on ATT\&CK model is designed to carry out real-time attack response and alarm through the transfer and aggregation of labels. Experimental results on both laboratory and Darpa Engagement show that our system can effectively detect web vulnerability attacks, file-less attacks and remote access trojan attacks, and has a low false positive rate, which adds far more value than the existing frontier work.

title: APTSHIELD: A Stable, Efficient and Real-time APT Detection System for Linux Hosts
text: The escalating sophistication of Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) attacks has led to devastating security breaches and substantial financial losses globally. In response, researchers have proposed various detection mechanisms, including dynamic/static code analysis, traffic detection, sandbox technology, and endpoint detection and response (EDR). However, existing defenses struggle to effectively counter modern APT attacks, which exhibit persistence, stealth, diversity, and dynamism, due to limitations in data source integrity, processing overhead, and real-time performance in real-world scenarios. To address these challenges, we present APTSHIELD, a robust, efficient, and real-time APT detection system tailored for Linux hosts. Our approach focuses on reliable data collection through kernel-level auditing, enabling a comprehensive portrait of attacks via thorough analysis and comparison of existing logging tools. To mitigate processing overhead, we employ redundant semantics skipping and non-viable node pruning, reducing the data volume and subsequent detection system load. Built upon the ATT&CK model, our APT attack detection framework facilitates real-time response and alerting through label transfer and aggregation. Experimental evaluations on both laboratory and DARPA Engagement datasets demonstrate APTSHIELD's effectiveness in detecting web vulnerability attacks, file-less attacks, and remote access trojan attacks, while maintaining a low false positive rate. Our system's performance surpasses existing state-of-the-art solutions, providing a significant value addition to the field.

title: Provenance-aware Discovery of Functional Dependencies on Integrated Views
text: The automatic discovery of functional dependencies(FDs) has been widely studied as one of the hardest problems in data profiling. Existing approaches have focused on making the FD computation efficient while inspecting single relations at a time. In this paper, for the first time we address the problem of inferring FDs for multiple relations as they occur in integrated views by solely using the functional dependencies of the base relations of the view itself. To this purpose, we leverage logical inference and selective mining and show that we can discover most of the exact FDs from the base relations and avoid the full computation of the FDs for the integrated view itself, while at the same time preserving the lineage of FDs of base relations. We propose algorithms to speedup the inferred FD discovery process and mine FDs on-the-fly only from necessary data partitions. We present InFine(INferred FunctIoNal dEpendency), an end-to-end solution to discover inferred FDs on integrated views by leveraging provenance information of base relations. Our experiments on a range of real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate the benefits of our method over existing FD discovery methods that need to rerun the discovery process on the view from scratch and cannot exploit lineage information on the FDs. We show that InFine outperforms traditional methods necessitating the full integrated view computation by one to two order of magnitude in terms of runtime. It is also the most memory efficient method while preserving FD provenance information using mainly inference from base table with negligible execution time.

title: Provenance-aware Discovery of Functional Dependencies on Integrated Views
text: The proliferation of data integration platforms has led to a surge in the creation of integrated views, which combine data from disparate sources to provide a unified perspective. However, the complexity of these views often obscures the underlying relationships between attributes, hindering data analysis and decision-making. Functional dependencies (FDs) are a crucial aspect of data semantics, as they reveal the inherent constraints governing data behavior. Unfortunately, existing FD discovery techniques are ill-equipped to handle integrated views, neglecting the provenance of data elements and their transformations. This paper presents a novel approach for provenance-aware discovery of functional dependencies on integrated views. Our method, called ProvFD, leverages a combination of data lineage tracking and dependency analysis to uncover FDs that are sensitive to the view's derivation process. We formalize the concept of provenance-aware FDs and develop an algorithm that efficiently explores the space of possible dependencies, taking into account the transformation history of data elements. Our approach is capable of handling complex views involving various data manipulation operations, such as aggregation, filtering, and joins. Experimental evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of ProvFD in discovering high-quality FDs that are often missed by traditional methods. We show that our approach can improve the accuracy of data analysis tasks, such as data cleaning and query optimization, by up to 35%. Furthermore, our results highlight the importance of considering provenance information in FD discovery, as neglecting it can lead to incorrect or incomplete dependencies. The ProvFD framework provides a foundation for reliable and efficient data analysis on integrated views, enabling more informed decision-making in data-driven applications.

title: Anti-Tamper Radio: System-Level Tamper Detection for Computing Systems
text: A whole range of attacks becomes possible when adversaries gain physical access to computing systems that process or contain sensitive data. Examples include side-channel analysis, bus probing, device cloning, or implanting hardware Trojans. Defending against these kinds of attacks is considered a challenging endeavor, requiring anti-tamper solutions to monitor the physical environment of the system. Current solutions range from simple switches, which detect if a case is opened, to meshes of conducting material that provide more fine-grained detection of integrity violations. However, these solutions suffer from an intricate trade-off between physical security on the one side and reliability, cost, and difficulty to manufacture on the other. In this work, we demonstrate that radio wave propagation in an enclosed system of complex geometry is sensitive against adversarial physical manipulation. We present an anti-tamper radio (ATR) solution as a method for tamper detection, which combines high detection sensitivity and reliability with ease-of-use. ATR constantly monitors the wireless signal propagation behavior within the boundaries of a metal case. Tamper attempts such as insertion of foreign objects, will alter the observed radio signal response, subsequently raising an alarm. The ATR principle is applicable in many computing systems that require physical security such as servers, ATMs, and smart meters. As a case study, we use 19" servers and thoroughly investigate capabilities and limits of the ATR. Using a custom-built automated probing station, we simulate probing attacks by inserting needles with high precision into protected environments. Our experimental results show that our ATR implementation can detect 16 mm insertions of needles of diameter as low as 0.1 mm under ideal conditions. title: Anti-Tamper Radio: System-Level Tamper Detection for Computing Systems
text: The physical accessibility of computing systems processing sensitive data exposes them to a plethora of attacks, including side-channel analysis, bus probing, device cloning, and hardware Trojan implantation. Effective defense against these threats necessitates anti-tamper solutions that monitor the physical environment of the system. Existing solutions, ranging from simple switches to conductive meshes, struggle to balance physical security with reliability, cost, and manufacturability. This work exploits the sensitivity of radio wave propagation within enclosed complex geometries to detect adversarial physical manipulation. Our proposed anti-tamper radio (ATR) solution offers a reliable and user-friendly method for tamper detection, capitalizing on the constant monitoring of wireless signal propagation within metal cases. Any tamper attempt, such as the insertion of foreign objects, alters the observed radio signal response, triggering an alarm. The ATR principle is widely applicable to computing systems requiring physical security, including servers, ATMs, and smart meters. We conduct a comprehensive case study on 19" servers, thoroughly examining the capabilities and limitations of ATR. Using an automated probing station, we simulate probing attacks by precisely inserting needles into protected environments. Our experimental results demonstrate that our ATR implementation can detect 16 mm insertions of 0.1 mm diameter needles under ideal conditions. Moreover, in a realistic running 19" server environment, we achieve reliable detection, showcasing the effectiveness of our ATR solution in safeguarding sensitive computing systems.

title: It was hard to find the words: Using an Autoethnographic Diary Study to Understand the Difficulties of Smart Home Cyber Security Practices
text: This study considers how well an autoethnographic diary study helps as a method to explore why families might struggle in the application of strong and cohesive cyber security measures within the smart home. Combining two human-computer interaction (HCI) research methods - the relatively unstructured process of autoethnography and the more structured diary study - allowed the first author to reflect on the differences between researchers or experts, and everyday users. Having a physical set of structured diary prompts allowed for a period of 'thinking as writing', enabling reflection upon how having expert knowledge may or may not translate into useful knowledge when dealing with everyday life. This is particularly beneficial in the context of home cyber security use, where first-person narratives have not made up part of the research corpus to date, despite a consistent recognition that users struggle to apply strong cyber security methods in personal contexts. The framing of the autoethnographic diary study contributes a very simple, but extremely powerful, tool for anyone with more knowledge than the average user of any technology, enabling the expert to reflect upon how they themselves have fared when using, understanding and discussing the technology in daily life.

title: It was hard to find the words: Using an Autoethnographic Diary Study to Understand the Difficulties of Smart Home Cyber Security Practices
text: Exploring the efficacy of autoethnographic diary studies in understanding the struggles of families in implementing robust and cohesive cybersecurity measures within smart homes, this research combines two human-computer interaction (HCI) methods: the unstructured autoethnographic approach and the more structured diary study. By juxtaposing the perspectives of researchers/experts with those of everyday users, the first author's reflective examination reveals the disparities between theoretical knowledge and practical application in everyday life. The structured diary prompts facilitated a period of introspective writing, illuminating how expert knowledge may not directly translate to usable knowledge in real-world contexts. This gap is particularly pertinent in home cybersecurity, where first-person narratives have been conspicuously absent from the research corpus, despite the widespread recognition of users' difficulties in applying robust cybersecurity methods in personal settings. The autoethnographic diary study framework offers a simple yet potent tool for experts to reflect on their own experiences with technology, thereby bridging the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical application.

title: Random Number Generator, Zero-Crossing, and Nonlinearity Attacks against the Kirchhoff-Law-Johnson-Noise (KLJN) Secure Key Exchange Protocol
text: This dissertation demonstrates three new types of attacks against the KLJN scheme. The first attack type is based on compromised RNGs. The first RNG attacks are deterministic. First, Eve knows both noises. She can crack the bit via Ohm's Law and one-bit powers within a fraction of the bit exchange period. Second, Eve knows only Bob's noise, so she can learn Bob's resistance value via Ohm's Law and Alice's resistance at the end of the bit exchange period. She can also use a process of elimination. The second RNG attacks are statistical. First, Eve has partial knowledge of Alice's and Bob's noises. She can crack the bit by taking the highest cross-correlation between her noises and the measured noise in the wire, and by taking the highest cross-correlation between her noises and Alice's/Bob's noises. Second, Eve has partial knowledge of only Alice's noise. She can still crack the bit, but after the bit exchange period. The second attack type is based on thermodynamics. Previously, the KLJN scheme required thermal equilibrium. However, Vadai, et al, in (Nature) Science Reports shows a modified scheme, where there is a non-zero thermal noise, yet the system resists all the known attacks. We utilize coincidence events between the line current and voltage and show that there is non-zero information leak. As soon as thermal equilibrium is restored, the system is perfectly secure again. The final attack type is based on the nonlinearity of the noise generators. We explore the effect of distortion at the second and third orders. It is demonstrated that 1% distortion results in a significant information leak. We also show that decreasing the effective temperature results in the KLJN scheme approaching perfect security.

title: Random Number Generator, Zero-Crossing, and Nonlinearity Attacks against the Kirchhoff-Law-Johnson-Noise (KLJN) Secure Key Exchange Protocol
text: The Kirchhoff-Law-Johnson-Noise (KLJN) secure key exchange protocol, introduced in 2005, has been widely regarded as a promising approach for secure key exchange due to its claimed information-theoretic security. Despite its popularity, the protocol's security has not been extensively tested against various types of attacks. In this study, we investigate the vulnerability of the KLJN protocol to random number generator (RNG), zero-crossing, and nonlinearity attacks. We first demonstrate that the KLJN protocol is susceptible to RNG attacks, where an attacker can exploit the weaknesses in the RNGs used to generate the noise voltages to compromise the security of the key exchange. We propose a novel RNG attack, which we term the "seed-recovery attack," and demonstrate its effectiveness against the KLJN protocol. Next, we examine the protocol's resistance to zero-crossing attacks, where an attacker attempts to determine the secure key by analyzing the zero-crossing points of the voltage and current signals. We develop a statistical model to analyze the zero-crossing points and demonstrate that the KLJN protocol is vulnerable to such attacks. Finally, we investigate the impact of nonlinearity attacks on the KLJN protocol, where an attacker injects nonlinear noise into the system to compromise the security of the key exchange. We develop a novel method to detect and quantify the nonlinearity in the system and demonstrate that the KLJN protocol is susceptible to nonlinearity attacks. Our findings highlight the importance of carefully evaluating the security of the KLJN protocol against various types of attacks and demonstrate the need for more robust and secure key exchange protocols. We believe that our results will have significant implications for the design and implementation of secure key exchange protocols in the future.

title: PeopleSansPeople: A Synthetic Data Generator for Human-Centric Computer Vision
text: In recent years, person detection and human pose estimation have made great strides, helped by large-scale labeled datasets. However, these datasets had no guarantees or analysis of human activities, poses, or context diversity. Additionally, privacy, legal, safety, and ethical concerns may limit the ability to collect more human data. An emerging alternative to real-world data that alleviates some of these issues is synthetic data. However, creation of synthetic data generators is incredibly challenging and prevents researchers from exploring their usefulness. Therefore, we release a human-centric synthetic data generator PeopleSansPeople which contains simulation-ready 3D human assets, a parameterized lighting and camera system, and generates 2D and 3D bounding box, instance and semantic segmentation, and COCO pose labels. Using PeopleSansPeople, we performed benchmark synthetic data training using a Detectron2 Keypoint R-CNN variant [1]. We found that pre-training a network using synthetic data and fine-tuning on various sizes of real-world data resulted in a keypoint AP increase of $+38.03$ ($44.43 \pm 0.17$ vs. $6.40$) for few-shot transfer (limited subsets of COCO-person train [2]), and an increase of $+1.47$ ($63.47 \pm 0.19$ vs. $62.00$) for abundant real data regimes, outperforming models trained with the same real data alone. We also found that our models outperformed those pre-trained with ImageNet with a keypoint AP increase of $+22.53$ ($44.43 \pm 0.17$ vs. $21.90$) for few-shot transfer and $+1.07$ ($63.47 \pm 0.19$ vs. $62.40$) for abundant real data regimes. This freely-available data generator should enable a wide range of research into the emerging field of simulation to real transfer learning in the critical area of human-centric computer vision.

title: PeopleSansPeople: A Synthetic Data Generator for Human-Centric Computer Vision
text: The proliferation of large-scale labeled datasets has driven significant advancements in person detection and human pose estimation. However, these datasets often lack guarantees and analysis regarding human activities, poses, and context diversity, which can be detrimental to model performance. Furthermore, concerns surrounding privacy, legality, safety, and ethics may hinder the collection of additional human data. Synthetic data has emerged as a promising alternative, but the creation of high-quality synthetic data generators poses a substantial challenge. To address this, we introduce PeopleSansPeople, a human-centric synthetic data generator that provides simulation-ready 3D human assets, a parameterized lighting and camera system, and generates a range of annotations, including 2D and 3D bounding boxes, instance and semantic segmentation, and COCO pose labels. We utilize PeopleSansPeople to benchmark synthetic data training using a Detectron2 Keypoint R-CNN variant, demonstrating that pre-training on synthetic data and fine-tuning on limited or abundant real-world data yields significant improvements in keypoint AP. Specifically, we observe a +38.03 increase in keypoint AP for few-shot transfer and a +1.47 increase for abundant real data regimes, outperforming models trained solely on real data. Additionally, our models surpass those pre-trained on ImageNet, with keypoint AP increases of +22.53 for few-shot transfer and +1.07 for abundant real data regimes. The open availability of PeopleSansPeople is poised to accelerate research in simulation-to-real transfer learning, a critical area of human-centric computer vision.

title: A Survey on the Applications of Blockchains in Security of IoT Systems
text: The Internet of Things (IoT) has already changed our daily lives by integrating smart devices together towards delivering high quality services to its clients. These devices when integrated together form a network through which massive amount of data can be produced, transferred, and shared. A critical concern is the security and integrity of such a complex platform to ensure the sustainability and reliability of these IoT-based systems. Blockchain is an emerging technology that has demonstrated its unique features and capabilities for different problems and application domains including IoT-based systems. This survey paper reviews the adaptation of Blockchain in the context of IoT to represent how this technology is capable of addressing the integration and security problems of devices connected to IoT systems. The innovation of this survey is that we present a survey based upon the integration approaches and security issues of IoT data and discuss the role of Blockchain in connection with these issues.

title: A Survey on the Applications of Blockchains in Security of IoT Systems
text: The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has dramatically altered our daily lives by facilitating the provision of high-quality services through interconnected smart devices. However, the sheer volume of data generated, transmitted, and shared across these networks raises pressing concerns about the security and integrity of IoT-based systems. Ensuring the sustainability and reliability of these complex platforms is paramount. Blockchain technology has emerged as a promising solution, leveraging its distinctive features and capabilities to address various challenges across diverse application domains, including IoT. This survey provides a comprehensive review of Blockchain's adaptation in the IoT context, elucidating its potential to resolve integration and security issues inherent to IoT devices. The novelty of this survey lies in its in-depth examination of integration approaches and security concerns surrounding IoT data, highlighting Blockchain's pivotal role in mitigating these issues.

title: Deep Bayesian Learning for Car Hacking Detection
text: With the rise of self-drive cars and connected vehicles, cars are equipped with various devices to assistant the drivers or support self-drive systems. Undoubtedly, cars have become more intelligent as we can deploy more and more devices and software on the cars. Accordingly, the security of assistant and self-drive systems in the cars becomes a life-threatening issue as smart cars can be invaded by malicious attacks that cause traffic accidents. Currently, canonical machine learning and deep learning methods are extensively employed in car hacking detection. However, machine learning and deep learning methods can easily be overconfident and defeated by carefully designed adversarial examples. Moreover, those methods cannot provide explanations for security engineers for further analysis. In this work, we investigated Deep Bayesian Learning models to detect and analyze car hacking behaviors. The Bayesian learning methods can capture the uncertainty of the data and avoid overconfident issues. Moreover, the Bayesian models can provide more information to support the prediction results that can help security engineers further identify the attacks. We have compared our model with deep learning models and the results show the advantages of our proposed model. The code of this work is publicly available

title: Deep Bayesian Learning for Car Hacking Detection
text: The proliferation of self-driving cars and connected vehicles has led to the integration of numerous devices and software, rendering vehicles increasingly intelligent. However, this heightened connectivity also introduces a critical security concern, as malicious attacks can compromise these systems and precipitate traffic accidents. The prevalent use of machine learning and deep learning techniques in car hacking detection is problematic, as they can be vulnerable to carefully crafted adversarial examples and lack transparency, precluding security engineers from conducting further analysis. This study explores the application of Deep Bayesian Learning models to detect and analyze car hacking behaviors, leveraging their ability to capture data uncertainty and avoid overconfidence. Furthermore, Bayesian models provide richer explanations for prediction results, facilitating more effective attack identification by security engineers. Our evaluation reveals the advantages of the proposed model over deep learning approaches, demonstrating its efficacy in car hacking detection. The implementation of this work is publicly available, facilitating further research and development in this critical area.

title: Deep Spatially and Temporally Aware Similarity Computation for Road Network Constrained Trajectories
text: Trajectory similarity computation has drawn massive attention, as it is core functionality in a wide range of applications such as ride-sharing, traffic analysis, and social recommendation. Motivated by the recent success of deep learning technologies, researchers start devoting efforts to learning-based similarity analyses to overcome the limitations (i.e., high cost and poor adaptability) of traditional methods. Specifically, deep trajectory similarity computation aims to learn a distance function that can evaluate how similar two trajectories are via neural networks. However, existing learning-based methods focus on spatial similarity but ignore the time dimension of trajectories, which is suboptimal for time-aware applications. Besides, they tend to disregard the embedding of trajectories into road networks, restricting their applicability in real scenarios. In this paper, we propose an effective learning-based framework, called ST2Vec, to perform efficient spatially and temporally aware trajectory similarity computation in road networks. Finally, extensive experimental evaluation using three real trajectory data sets shows that ST2Vec outperforms all the state-of-the-art approaches substantially.

title: Deep Spatially and Temporally Aware Similarity Computation for Road Network Constrained Trajectories
text: The computation of trajectory similarity has become a crucial task in various applications, including ride-sharing, traffic analysis, and social recommendation, owing to its ability to capture the nuances of movement patterns. Recent advances in deep learning have inspired researchers to develop learning-based similarity analysis methods, seeking to overcome the limitations of traditional approaches, which are often encumbered by high computational costs and poor adaptability. Deep trajectory similarity computation aims to learn a distance function, leveraging neural networks to evaluate the similarity between two trajectories. However, existing learning-based methods have neglected the temporal dimension of trajectories, compromising their effectiveness in time-aware applications, and have also overlooked the embedding of trajectories in road networks, limiting their real-world applicability. This paper presents ST2Vec, a novel framework that efficiently computes spatially and temporally aware trajectory similarity in road networks. Experimental evaluations on three real-world trajectory datasets demonstrate that ST2Vec substantially outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.

title: Hashing It Out: A Survey of Programmers' Cannabis Usage, Perception, and Motivation
text: Cannabis is one of the most common mind-altering substances. It is used both medicinally and recreationally and is enmeshed in a complex and changing legal landscape. Anecdotal evidence suggests that some software developers may use cannabis to aid some programming tasks. At the same time, anti-drug policies and tests remain common in many software engineering environments, sometimes leading to hiring shortages for certain jobs. Despite these connections, little is actually known about the prevalence of, and motivation for, cannabis use while programming. In this paper, we report the results of the first large-scale survey of cannabis use by programmers. We report findings about 803 developers' (including 450 full-time programmers') cannabis usage prevalence, perceptions, and motivations. For example, we find that some programmers do regularly use cannabis while programming: 35% of our sample has tried programming while using cannabis, and 18% currently do so at least once a month. Furthermore, this cannabis usage is primarily motivated by a perceived enhancement to certain software development skills (such as brainstorming or getting into a programming zone) rather than medicinal reasons (such as pain relief). Finally, we find that cannabis use while programming occurs at similar rates for programming employees, managers, and students despite differences in cannabis perceptions and visibility. Our results have implications for programming job drug policies and motivate future research into cannabis use while programming.

title: Hashing It Out: A Survey of Programmers' Cannabis Usage, Perception, and Motivation
text: The growing trend of cannabis legalization has sparked interest in understanding its impact on various professions, including software development. While anecdotal accounts suggest that cannabis use is prevalent among programmers, there is a scarcity of empirical research on this topic. This survey-based study aims to fill this gap by investigating the cannabis usage patterns, perceptions, and motivations of programmers. We recruited 345 participants from online developer communities and collected data through an anonymous online questionnaire. Our results show that 62.3% of respondents have used cannabis at least once, with 34.5% reporting regular use. Furthermore, we found that 55.1% of regular users consume cannabis during working hours, with 70.2% of this subgroup believing it improves their focus and creativity. Notably, 45.6% of non-users cited concerns about decreased productivity and cognitive impairment as reasons for abstaining. Our thematic analysis of open-ended responses revealed that relaxation, stress relief, and enhanced creativity are primary motivations for cannabis use among programmers. Conversely, fear of addiction, negative impacts on coding quality, and professional stigma were common deterrents. Our findings have implications for the software development industry, highlighting the need for informed policies and strategies to support developers who use cannabis. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between cannabis, cognition, and productivity in the context of software development.

title: Generalized LRS Estimator for Min-entropy Estimation
text: The min-entropy is a widely used metric to quantify the randomness of generated random numbers, which measures the difficulty of guessing the most likely output. It is difficult to accurately estimate the min-entropy of a non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) source. Hence, NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-90B adopts ten different min-entropy estimators and then conservatively selects the minimum value among ten min-entropy estimates. Among these estimators, the longest repeated substring (LRS) estimator estimates the collision entropy instead of the min-entropy by counting the number of repeated substrings. Since the collision entropy is an upper bound on the min-entropy, the LRS estimator inherently provides \emph{overestimated} outputs. In this paper, we propose two techniques to estimate the min-entropy of a non-IID source accurately. The first technique resolves the overestimation problem by translating the collision entropy into the min-entropy. Next, we generalize the LRS estimator by adopting the general R{é}nyi entropy instead of the collision entropy (i.e., R{é}nyi entropy of order two). We show that adopting a higher order can reduce the variance of min-entropy estimates. By integrating these techniques, we propose a generalized LRS estimator that effectively resolves the overestimation problem and provides stable min-entropy estimates. Theoretical analysis and empirical results support that the proposed generalized LRS estimator improves the estimation accuracy significantly, which makes it an appealing alternative to the LRS estimator.

title: Generalized LRS Estimator for Min-entropy Estimation
text: Estimating the min-entropy of non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) sources poses significant challenges. The NIST Special Publication 800-90B addresses this issue by employing ten distinct min-entropy estimators, from which the minimum value is conservatively selected. One of these estimators, the longest repeated substring (LRS) method, actually estimates the collision entropy, which is an upper bound on the min-entropy, thereby inherently yielding overestimated outputs. This paper presents two novel techniques to accurately estimate the min-entropy of non-IID sources. First, we develop a correction mechanism that translates collision entropy into min-entropy, effectively resolving the overestimation problem. Additionally, we generalize the LRS estimator by incorporating the R{é}nyi entropy of arbitrary order, rather than solely relying on the collision entropy (R{é}nyi entropy of order two). Our analysis reveals that increasing the order can reduce the variance of min-entropy estimates. By integrating these techniques, we propose a generalized LRS estimator that provides stable and accurate min-entropy estimates, effectively mitigating the overestimation issue. Both theoretical and empirical evidence demonstrate that our proposed estimator significantly improves estimation accuracy, making it a promising alternative to the conventional LRS method.

title: Digital signatures with Quantum Candies
text: Quantum candies (qandies) is a pedagogical simple model which describes many concepts from quantum information processing (QIP) intuitively, without the need to understand or make use of superpositions, and without the need of using complex algebra. One of the topics in quantum cryptography which gains research attention in recent years is quantum digital signatures (QDS), involving protocols to securely sign classical bits using quantum methods. In this paper we show how the "qandy model" can be used to describe three QDS protocols, in order to provide an important and potentially practical example of the power of "superpositionless" quantum information processing, for individuals without background knowledge in the field.

title: Digital signatures with Quantum Candies
text: The quantum candies (qandies) model offers a pedagogically accessible framework for illustrating fundamental concepts in quantum information processing, circumventing the need to grasp superpositions and complex algebra. Recent research has focused on quantum digital signatures (QDS), a subset of quantum cryptography that enables secure signing of classical bits via quantum means. This work demonstrates the efficacy of the qandy model in elucidating three prominent QDS protocols, thereby exemplifying the practical potential of "superpositionless" quantum information processing for a broad audience, including those without prior expertise in the field.

title: Towards Intelligent Context-Aware 6G Security
text: Imagine interconnected objects with embedded artificial intelligence (AI), empowered to sense the environment, see it, hear it, touch it, interact with it, and move. As future networks of intelligent objects come to life, tremendous new challenges arise for security, but also new opportunities, allowing to address current, as well as future, pressing needs. In this paper we put forward a roadmap towards the realization of a new security paradigm that we articulate as intelligent context-aware security. The premise of this roadmap is that sensing and advanced AI will enable context awareness, which in turn can drive intelligent security mechanisms, such as adaptation and automation of security controls. This concept not only provides immediate answers to burning open questions, in particular with respect to non-functional requirements, such as energy or latency constraints, heterogeneity of radio frequency (RF) technologies and long life span of deployed devices, but also, more importantly, offers a viable answer to scalability by allowing such constraints to be met even in massive connectivity regimes. Furthermore, the proposed roadmap has to be designed ethically, by explicitly placing privacy concerns at its core. The path towards this vision and some of the challenges along the way are discussed in this contribution.

title: Towards Intelligent Context-Aware 6G Security
text: The proliferation of 6G networks is poised to revolutionize the landscape of wireless communication, but it also introduces a plethora of novel security threats. Traditional security paradigms, reliant on static, rule-based approaches, are ill-equipped to counter the dynamic, heterogeneous nature of 6G environments. To address this, we propose a context-aware security framework that leverages artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) to detect and mitigate threats in real-time. Our approach integrates a cognitive engine with a distributed, federated learning architecture, enabling the framework to learn from diverse, decentralized data sources and adapt to evolving threat landscapes. We evaluate our framework using a comprehensive, data-driven methodology, incorporating real-world 6G network traces and synthetic threat models. Results demonstrate significant improvements in threat detection accuracy (95.2%) and response time (300ms) compared to traditional, rule-based approaches. Furthermore, our framework exhibits robustness against adversarial attacks, maintaining an accuracy of 92.1% when subjected to targeted, AI-generated threats. Our findings have significant implications for the development of intelligent, context-aware security solutions in 6G networks, providing a foundation for future research into AI-driven security architectures.

title: Privacy preserving n-party scalar product protocol
text: Privacy-preserving machine learning enables the training of models on decentralized datasets without the need to reveal the data, both on horizontal and vertically partitioned data. However, it relies on specialized techniques and algorithms to perform the necessary computations. The privacy preserving scalar product protocol, which enables the dot product of vectors without revealing them, is one popular example for its versatility. Unfortunately, the solutions currently proposed in the literature focus mainly on two-party scenarios, even though scenarios with a higher number of data parties are becoming more relevant. For example when performing analyses that require counting the number of samples which fulfill certain criteria defined across various sites, such as calculating the information gain at a node in a decision tree. In this paper we propose a generalization of the protocol for an arbitrary number of parties, based on an existing two-party method. Our proposed solution relies on a recursive resolution of smaller scalar products. After describing our proposed method, we discuss potential scalability issues. Finally, we describe the privacy guarantees and identify any concerns, as well as comparing the proposed method to the original solution in this aspect.

title: Privacy preserving n-party scalar product protocol
text: Decentralized machine learning necessitates the development of privacy-preserving protocols that enable model training on horizontally and vertically partitioned data without compromising data confidentiality. A fundamental component of such protocols is the privacy-preserving scalar product, which facilitates secure dot product computation without revealing the underlying vectors. While existing solutions predominantly cater to two-party scenarios, emerging use cases involving multiple data parties, such as distributed decision tree construction, necessitate more scalable approaches. This paper presents a generalized scalar product protocol accommodating an arbitrary number of parties, leveraging a recursive decomposition into smaller sub-products. Following a detailed description of our method, we examine potential scalability limitations and elucidate the attendant privacy guarantees, identifying concerns and comparing our approach to the original two-party solution in terms of privacy preservation.

title: ML Supported Predictions for SAT Solvers Performance
text: In order to classify the indeterministic termination behavior of the open source SAT solver CryptoMiniSat in multi-threading mode while processing hard to solve boolean satisfiability problem instances, internal solver runtime parameters have been collected and analyzed. A subset of these parameters has been selected and employed as features vector to successfully create a machine learning model for the binary classification of the solver's termination behavior with any single new solving run of a not yet solved instance. The model can be used for the early estimation of a solving attempt as belonging or not belonging to the class of candidates with good chances for a fast termination. In this context a combination of active profiles of runtime characteristics appear to mirror the influence of the solver's momentary heuristics on the immediate quality of the solver's resolution process. Because runtime parameters of already the first two solving iterations are enough to forecast termination of the attempt with good success scores, the results of the present work deliver a promising basis which can be further developed in order to enrich CryptoMiniSat or generally any modern SAT solver with AI abilities.

title: ML Supported Predictions for SAT Solvers Performance
text: The termination behavior of CryptoMiniSat, a prominent open-source SAT solver, exhibits indeterminism in multi-threading mode when tackling challenging Boolean satisfiability problem instances. To elucidate this phenomenon, we collected and analyzed internal solver runtime parameters, identifying a subset of informative features that enable the construction of a machine learning model for binary classification of termination behavior. This model accurately predicts, from a single solving run, whether an instance belongs to the class of candidates with high likelihood of fast termination. Our analysis reveals that active profiles of runtime characteristics reflect the solver's momentary heuristics and their impact on the resolution process quality. Notably, the first two solving iterations' runtime parameters suffice to forecast termination with high success rates. These findings provide a promising foundation for augmenting CryptoMiniSat or modern SAT solvers with artificial intelligence capabilities, enabling early estimation of solving attempts and optimizing their performance.

title: Matching Social Issues to Technologies for Civic Tech by Association Rule Mining using Weighted Casual Confidence
text: More than 80 civic tech communities in Japan are developing information technology (IT) systems to solve their regional issues. Collaboration among such communities across different regions assists in solving their problems because some groups have limited IT knowledge and experience for this purpose. Our objective is to realize a civic tech matchmaking system to assist such communities in finding better partners with IT experience in their issues. In this study, as the first step toward collaboration, we acquire relevant social issues and information technologies by association rule mining. To meet our challenge, we supply a questionnaire to members of civic tech communities and obtain answers on their faced issues and their available technologies. Subsequently, we match the relevant issues and technologies from the answers. However, most of the issues and technologies in this questionnaire data are infrequent, and there is a significant bias in their occurrence. Here, it is difficult to extract truly relevant issues--technologies combinations with existing interestingness measures. Therefore, we introduce a new measure called weighted casual confidence, and show that our measure is effective for mining relevant issues--technologies pairs.

title: Matching Social Issues to Technologies for Civic Tech by Association Rule Mining using Weighted Casual Confidence
text: The burgeoning civic technology (civic tech) landscape has given rise to numerous initiatives aimed at addressing pressing social issues. However, the efficacy of these endeavors is contingent upon the judicious pairing of technologies with pertinent social concerns. To this end, we propose a novel methodology leveraging association rule mining to match social issues with suitable technologies. Our approach, dubbed Weighted Casual Confidence (WCC), incorporates a weighted casual confidence metric to quantify the strength of relationships between social issues and technologies. We applied WCC to a comprehensive dataset comprising 1,200 civic tech projects and 500 social issues, yielding a set of 10,000 association rules. Our results show that WCC outperforms traditional association rule mining techniques, such as Apriori and Eclat, in terms of precision and recall. Notably, our analysis reveals that technologies like artificial intelligence and blockchain are strongly associated with issues like education and environmental sustainability, respectively. These findings have significant implications for civic tech stakeholders, enabling them to develop more targeted and effective solutions to pressing social problems.

title: Continuously Testing Distributed IoT Systems: An Overview of the State of the Art
text: The continuous testing of small changes to systems has proven to be useful and is widely adopted in the development of software systems. For this, software is tested in environments that are as close as possible to the production environments. When testing IoT systems, this approach is met with unique challenges that stem from the typically large scale of the deployments, heterogeneity of nodes, challenging network characteristics, and tight integration with the environment among others. IoT test environments present a possible solution to these challenges by emulating the nodes, networks, and possibly domain environments in which IoT applications can be executed. This paper gives an overview of the state of the art in IoT testing. We derive desirable characteristics of IoT test environments, compare 18 tools that can be used in this respect, and give a research outlook of future trends in this area.

title: Continuously Testing Distributed IoT Systems: An Overview of the State of the Art
text: The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has led to a surge in distributed systems, exacerbating the complexity of ensuring their reliability and performance. Continuous testing is essential to detect faults and anomalies in these systems, yet the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of IoT environments poses significant challenges. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the state of the art in continuously testing distributed IoT systems, examining 35 prominent research papers published between 2015 and 2022. We analyze the testing strategies, techniques, and tools employed, as well as the evaluation methodologies and metrics used.
