Our findings indicate that while significant progress has been made, there remains a lack of standardization, limited scalability, and inadequate consideration of IoT-specific constraints. We identify key research gaps and opportunities for future work, highlighting the need for more holistic and adaptive approaches to ensure the dependability of distributed IoT systems.

title: Subverting Stateful Firewalls with Protocol States (Extended Version)
text: We analyzed the generation of protocol header fields in the implementations of multiple TCP/IP network stacks and found new ways to leak information about global protocol states. We then demonstrated new covert channels by remotely observing and modifying the system's global state via these protocol fields. Unlike earlier works, our research focuses on hosts that reside in firewalled networks (including source address validation -- SAV), which is a very common scenario nowadays. Our attacks are designed to be non-disruptive -- in the exfiltration scenario, this makes the attacks stealthier and thus extends their longevity, and in case of host alias resolution and similar techniques -- this ensures the techniques are ethical. We focused on ICMP, which is commonly served by firewalls, and on UDP, which is forecasted to take a more prominent share of the Internet traffic with the advent of HTTP/3 and QUIC, though we report results for TCP as well. The information leakage scenarios we discovered enable the construction of practical covert channels which directly pierce firewalls, or indirectly establish communication via hosts in firewalled networks that also employ SAV. We describe and test three novel attacks in this context: exfiltration via the firewall itself, exfiltration via a DMZ host, and exfiltration via co-resident containers. These are three generic, new use cases for covert channels that work around firewalling and enable devices that are not allowed direct communication with the Internet, to still exfiltrate data out of the network. In other words, we exfiltrate data from isolated networks to the Internet. We also explain how to mount known attacks such as host alias resolution, de-NATting and container co-residence detection, using the new information leakage techniques.

title: Subverting Stateful Firewalls with Protocol States (Extended Version)
text: The widespread adoption of stateful firewalls has led to a false sense of security, as they are often configured to allow traffic based on incomplete or outdated protocol specifications. This oversight can be exploited by an attacker to bypass firewall rules and gain unauthorized access to protected networks. In this vulnerability landscape, we investigate the effectiveness of protocol states in subverting stateful firewalls. We develop a novel framework, dubbed StateBender, which leverages ambiguities in protocol specifications to craft packets that manipulate firewall states. Our approach involves careful analysis of protocol semantics and the implementation of a packet generation engine that can create packets with conflicting or ambiguous state information. We evaluate StateBender against six commercial stateful firewalls, demonstrating its ability to bypass security rules and establish covert channels in 85% of the tested scenarios. Our findings reveal that stateful firewalls are often unable to correctly handle packets with conflicting or ambiguous state information, leading to inconsistent firewall states and potential security breaches. We identify several key factors contributing to this vulnerability, including incomplete protocol specifications, implementation inconsistencies, and the lack of robust state management mechanisms. We propose a set of mitigation strategies, including the implementation of protocol-aware firewall rules and the adoption of robust state validation mechanisms. Our work highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of protocol states and their role in firewall security, emphasizing the importance of rigorous testing and validation in the development of stateful firewalls. The implications of our research are far-reaching, with potential consequences for the security of networks and systems that rely on stateful firewalls for protection.

title: Exact and Approximate Counting of Database Repairs
text: A key task in the context of consistent query answering is to count the number of repairs that entail the query, with the ultimate goal being a precise data complexity classification. This has been achieved in the case of primary keys and self-join-free conjunctive queries (CQs) via an FP/#P-complete dichotomy. We lift this result to the more general case of functional dependencies (FDs). Another important task in this context is whenever the counting problem in question is intractable, to classify it as approximable, i.e., the target value can be efficiently approximated with error guarantees via a fully polynomial-time randomized approximation scheme (FPRAS), or as inapproximable. Although for primary keys and CQs (even with self-joins) the problem is always approximable, we prove that this is not the case for FDs. We show, however, that the class of FDs with a left-hand side chain forms an island of approximability. We see these results, apart from being interesting in their own right, as crucial steps towards a complete classification of approximate counting of repairs in the case of FDs and self-join-free CQs.

title: Exact and Approximate Counting of Database Repairs
text: The enumeration of repairs entailing a query is a fundamental problem in consistent query answering, with a primary objective of achieving a precise data complexity classification. For primary keys and self-join-free conjunctive queries, this challenge has been addressed through an FP/#P-complete dichotomy. We extend this result to encompass the more general framework of functional dependencies. In cases where exact counting is intractable, an important secondary goal is to determine whether the problem admits efficient approximation with error guarantees via a fully polynomial-time randomized approximation scheme or is inherently inapproximable. While primary keys and conjunctive queries (including those with self-joins) yield approximable counting problems, we demonstrate that this is not universally true for functional dependencies. However, we identify a subset of functional dependencies with a left-hand side chain that forms an approximable class. Our findings constitute significant milestones towards a comprehensive classification of approximate repair counting for functional dependencies and self-join-free conjunctive queries.

title: scenoRITA: Generating Less-Redundant, Safety-Critical and Motion Sickness-Inducing Scenarios for Autonomous Vehicles
text: There is tremendous global enthusiasm for research, development, and deployment of autonomous vehicles (AVs), e.g., self-driving taxis and trucks from Waymo and Baidu. The current practice for testing AVs uses virtual tests-where AVs are tested in software simulations-since they offer a more efficient and safer alternative compared to field operational tests. Specifically, search-based approaches are used to find particularly critical situations. These approaches provide an opportunity to automatically generate tests; however, systematically creating valid and effective tests for AV software remains a major challenge. To address this challenge, we introduce scenoRITA, a test generation approach for AVs that uses evolutionary algorithms with (1) a novel gene representation that allows obstacles to be fully mutable, hence, resulting in more reported violations, (2) 5 test oracles to determine both safety and motion sickness-inducing violations, and (3) a novel technique to identify and eliminate duplicate tests. Our extensive evaluation shows that scenoRITA can produce effective driving scenarios that expose an ego car to safety critical situations. scenoRITA generated tests that resulted in a total of 1,026 unique violations, increasing the number of reported violations by 23.47% and 24.21% compared to random test generation and state-of-the-art partially-mutable test generation, respectively.

title: scenoRITA: Generating Less-Redundant, Safety-Critical and Motion Sickness-Inducing Scenarios for Autonomous Vehicles
text: The development of autonomous vehicles (AVs) relies heavily on the generation of diverse, realistic, and challenging scenarios to train and evaluate their safety-critical capabilities. However, existing scenario generation methods often produce redundant or unrealistic scenarios, neglecting to account for human factors such as motion sickness. We present scenoRITA, a novel scenario generation framework that addresses these limitations by incorporating safety-critical and motion sickness-inducing considerations. scenoRITA leverages a combination of probabilistic modeling, graph theory, and machine learning to generate less-redundant scenarios that are tailored to specific AV architectures and operational domains. Our methodology involves analyzing real-world traffic data to identify critical scenarios, which are then modified and extended using a probabilistic graph model to introduce variability and complexity. We evaluate scenoRITA using a comprehensive simulation framework, demonstrating its ability to generate more diverse and challenging scenarios compared to existing methods. Our results show that AVs trained on scenoRITA-generated scenarios exhibit improved safety-critical performance and reduced motion sickness incidence in human subjects. By providing a more comprehensive and realistic scenario generation framework, scenoRITA has the potential to significantly accelerate the development and deployment of safe and reliable AVs.

title: Interpretable Data-Based Explanations for Fairness Debugging
text: A wide variety of fairness metrics and eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches have been proposed in the literature to identify bias in machine learning models that are used in critical real-life contexts. However, merely reporting on a model's bias, or generating explanations using existing XAI techniques is insufficient to locate and eventually mitigate sources of bias. We introduce Gopher, a system that produces compact, interpretable and causal explanations for bias or unexpected model behavior by identifying coherent subsets of the training data that are root-causes for this behavior. Specifically, we introduce the concept of causal responsibility that quantifies the extent to which intervening on training data by removing or updating subsets of it can resolve the bias. Building on this concept, we develop an efficient approach for generating the top-k patterns that explain model bias that utilizes techniques from the machine learning (ML) community to approximate causal responsibility and uses pruning rules to manage the large search space for patterns. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of Gopher in generating interpretable explanations for identifying and debugging sources of bias.

title: Interpretable Data-Based Explanations for Fairness Debugging
text: Data-driven decision-making systems are increasingly being scrutinized for fairness, with debugging and explanation of unfair biases becoming a pressing concern. Existing approaches to fairness debugging often rely on domain expertise, manual feature engineering, or simplistic statistical measures, which can be insufficient, time-consuming, or misleading. We propose a novel, interpretable, and data-based explanation framework for fairness debugging, which uses a combination of data mining and machine learning techniques to identify and rank influential factors contributing to unfair outcomes. Our approach, dubbed FairExplain, leverages a novel graph-based representation of data distributions to uncover complex relationships between variables and outcomes, and a Bayesian attribution method to quantify the contribution of each feature to fairness metrics. Evaluations on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of FairExplain in identifying and explaining unfair biases, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, interpretability, and scalability. Our findings highlight the importance of data-based explanations in fairness debugging, and provide insights into the development of more transparent, accountable, and fair decision-making systems.

title: Know Your Customer: Balancing Innovation and Regulation for Financial Inclusion
text: Financial inclusion depends on providing adjusted services for citizens with disclosed vulnerabilities. At the same time, the financial industry needs to adhere to a strict regulatory framework, which is often in conflict with the desire for inclusive, adaptive, and privacy-preserving services. In this article we study how this tension impacts the deployment of privacy-sensitive technologies aimed at financial inclusion. We conduct a qualitative study with banking experts to understand their perspectives on service development for financial inclusion. We build and demonstrate a prototype solution based on open source decentralized identifiers and verifiable credentials software and report on feedback from the banking experts on this system. The technology is promising thanks to its selective disclosure of vulnerabilities to the full control of the individual. This supports GDPR requirements, but at the same time, there is a clear tension between introducing these technologies and fulfilling other regulatory requirements, particularly with respect to 'Know Your Customer.' We consider the policy implications stemming from these tensions and provide guidelines for the further design of related technologies.

title: Know Your Customer: Balancing Innovation and Regulation for Financial Inclusion
text: The provision of adapted financial services to vulnerable citizens is contingent upon the reconciliation of competing demands: meeting stringent regulatory requirements while ensuring inclusive, adaptive, and privacy-preserving services. This tension is particularly pronounced in the deployment of privacy-sensitive technologies aimed at promoting financial inclusion. To better understand this conundrum, we conducted an in-depth qualitative study with banking experts, eliciting their perspectives on service development for financially vulnerable populations. We also designed and demonstrated a prototype solution leveraging open-source decentralized identifiers and verifiable credentials software, which enables selective disclosure of vulnerabilities under individual control. While this approach aligns with GDPR requirements, it introduces tensions with respect to 'Know Your Customer' regulations. Our findings highlight the need for policy considerations and guidelines to inform the design of future technologies, striking a balance between regulatory compliance and the pursuit of financial inclusion.

title: Privacy Leakage over Dependent Attributes in One-Sided Differential Privacy
text: Providing a provable privacy guarantees while maintaining the utility of data is a challenging task in many real-world applications. Recently, a new framework called One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) was introduced that extends existing differential privacy approaches. OSDP increases the utility of the data by taking advantage of the fact that not all records are sensitive. However, the previous work assumed that all records are statistically independent from each other. Motivated by occupancy data in building management systems, this paper extends the existing one-sided differential privacy framework. In this paper, we quantify the overall privacy leakage when the adversary is given dependency information between the records. In addition, we show how an optimization problem can be constructed that efficiently trades off between the utility and privacy.

title: Privacy Leakage over Dependent Attributes in One-Sided Differential Privacy
text: Guaranteeing privacy while preserving data utility is a longstanding challenge in various real-world applications. One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP), a recently introduced framework, builds upon existing differential privacy approaches to enhance data utility by leveraging the fact that not all records are sensitive. However, the assumption of statistical independence among records underpins previous work, which may not always hold true. This paper extends the OSDP framework, motivated by occupancy data in building management systems, to accommodate dependent records. We quantify the cumulative privacy leakage in the presence of an adversary with knowledge of inter-record dependencies. Furthermore, we formulate an optimization problem that efficiently balances utility and privacy, enabling a tunable tradeoff between these competing objectives.

title: Time-Aware Neighbor Sampling for Temporal Graph Networks
text: We present a new neighbor sampling method on temporal graphs. In a temporal graph, predicting different nodes' time-varying properties can require the receptive neighborhood of various temporal scales. In this work, we propose the TNS (Time-aware Neighbor Sampling) method: TNS learns from temporal information to provide an adaptive receptive neighborhood for every node at any time. Learning how to sample neighbors is non-trivial, since the neighbor indices in time order are discrete and not differentiable. To address this challenge, we transform neighbor indices from discrete values to continuous ones by interpolating the neighbors' messages. TNS can be flexibly incorporated into popular temporal graph networks to improve their effectiveness without increasing their time complexity. TNS can be trained in an end-to-end manner. It needs no extra supervision and is automatically and implicitly guided to sample the neighbors that are most beneficial for prediction. Empirical results on multiple standard datasets show that TNS yields significant gains on edge prediction and node classification.

title: Time-Aware Neighbor Sampling for Temporal Graph Networks
text: Temporal graph networks have become increasingly prevalent in modeling complex relationships between entities that evolve over time. However, the sheer scale and dynamic nature of these networks pose significant challenges for efficient and effective graph neural network (GNN) training. A key bottleneck lies in the neighbor sampling strategy, which is crucial for reducing the computational cost and improving the model's ability to capture temporal dependencies. Existing sampling methods are often oblivious to the temporal dimension, leading to suboptimal performance and inefficient use of computational resources. We propose Time-Aware Neighbor Sampling (TANS), a novel approach that incorporates temporal information into the sampling process. TANS adaptively selects neighbors based on their temporal proximity to the target node, thereby preserving the temporal locality and reducing the sampling bias. Our experimental results on several real-world temporal graph datasets demonstrate that TANS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art sampling methods, achieving up to 25% improvement in prediction accuracy and 30% reduction in training time.

title: Distributed design of deterministic discrete-time privacy preserving average consensus for multi-agent systems through network augmentation
text: Average consensus protocols emerge with a central role in distributed systems and decision-making such as distributed information fusion, distributed optimization, distributed estimation, and control. A key advantage of these protocols is that agents exchange and reveal their state information only to their neighbors. Yet, it can raise privacy concerns in situations where the agents' states contain sensitive information. In this paper, we propose a novel (noiseless) privacy preserving distributed algorithms for multi-agent systems to reach an average consensus. The main idea of the algorithms is that each agent runs a (small) network with a crafted structure and dynamics to form a network of networks (i.e., the connection between the newly created networks and their interconnections respecting the initial network connections). Together with a re-weighting of the dynamic parameters dictating the inter-agent dynamics and the initial states, we show that it is possible to ensure that the value of each node converges to the consensus value of the original network. Furthermore, we show that, under mild assumptions, it is possible to craft the dynamics such that the design can be achieved in a distributed fashion. Finally, we illustrate the proposed algorithm with examples.

title: Distributed design of deterministic discrete-time privacy preserving average consensus for multi-agent systems through network augmentation
text: The proliferation of multi-agent systems in various domains has necessitated the development of efficient and private consensus protocols. Average consensus, a fundamental problem in distributed computing, has garnered significant attention in recent years. However, existing solutions often compromise on either privacy or determinism, or are limited to specific network topologies. This paper presents a novel framework for designing deterministic discrete-time privacy-preserving average consensus protocols for multi-agent systems through network augmentation. Our approach leverages a combination of cryptographic techniques and graph theory to ensure privacy and correctness in the presence of malicious agents. We propose a distributed algorithm that dynamically augments the underlying network topology to facilitate the computation of average consensus while maintaining the privacy of individual agents' initial values. Through a rigorous analysis, we establish the correctness, privacy, and fault tolerance of our protocol. Simulation results on various network topologies demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, achieving a significant reduction in communication overhead and improved resilience to Byzantine faults compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions. Our framework has far-reaching implications for distributed control and optimization in various domains, including smart grids, autonomous vehicles, and social networks.

title: A First Approach to Risk-Limiting Audits for Single Transferable Vote Elections
text: Risk-limiting audits (RLAs) are an increasingly important method for checking that the reported outcome of an election is, in fact, correct. Indeed, their use is increasingly being legislated. While effective methods for RLAs have been developed for many forms of election -- for example: first-past-the-post, instant-runoff voting, and D'Hondt elections -- auditing methods for single transferable vote (STV) elections have yet to be developed. STV elections are notoriously hard to reason about since there is a complex interaction of votes that change their value throughout the process. In this paper we present the first approach to risk-limiting audits for STV elections, restricted to the case of 2-seat STV elections.

title: A First Approach to Risk-Limiting Audits for Single Transferable Vote Elections
text: Single Transferable Vote (STV) elections are increasingly used in various settings, but their complexity makes them vulnerable to errors. Risk-limiting audits (RLAs) are a promising approach to ensure the correctness of election outcomes, but existing RLA methods are designed for simpler voting systems. We propose a novel RLA method tailored to STV elections, leveraging the properties of Meek's STV algorithm. Our approach involves constructing a probabilistic audit graph, which enables the efficient computation of risk estimates. We evaluate our method using simulated elections and real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting errors while providing a quantifiable risk limit. Our results pave the way for the development of practical RLAs for STV elections.

title: System Attack Modeling Techniques Critical Information Infrastructure
text: Every day around the world, various organizations are exposed to more than a hundred attacks, most of which are success-fully repelled by information security specialists. However, attacks are also carried out that some information systems or specialists are unable to repel, which is why a large number of enterprises, as well as individuals, suffer huge monetary and reputational losses. The aim of the work is to train specialists through cyber polygons and interactive games to a high level of knowledge and skills in the field of information security

title: System Attack Modeling Techniques Critical Information Infrastructure
text: Critical information infrastructure faces increasing threats from sophisticated attacks, emphasizing the need for effective attack modeling techniques. We propose a novel hybrid approach combining Bayesian networks and attack graphs to model system attacks. Our methodology involves integrating vulnerability data, network topology, and attacker behavior to generate a comprehensive attack model. Experimental evaluations on a real-world industrial control system demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in identifying high-severity attack paths and improving the accuracy of risk assessments by 32% compared to existing techniques.

title: Decentralizing Information Technology: The Advent of Resource Based Systems
text: The growth of the Bitcoin network during the first decade of its operation to a global scale system is a singular event in the deployment of Information Technology systems. Can this approach serve as a wider paradigm for Information Technology services beyond the use case of digital currencies? We investigate this question by introducing the concept of resource based systems and their four fundamental characteristics: (i) resource-based operation, (ii) tokenomics, (iii) decentralized service provision, and (iv) rewards sharing. We explore these characteristics, identify design goals and challenges and investigate some crucial game theoretic aspects of reward sharing that can be decisive for their effective operation.

title: Decentralizing Information Technology: The Advent of Resource Based Systems
text: The unprecedented scaling of the Bitcoin network to a global system within its first decade raises questions about its potential as a paradigm for broader IT services beyond digital currencies. To explore this, we conceptualize resource-based systems, defined by four key attributes: resource-driven operation, tokenomic structures, decentralized service provision, and reward sharing mechanisms. We delve into the design goals, challenges, and game-theoretic implications of reward sharing, which critically influence the efficacy of these systems. Our investigation provides insights into the viability of this approach as a model for IT services, with potential implications for the development of decentralized, community-driven infrastructure.

title: Multi-step LRU: SIMD-based Cache Replacement for Lower Overhead and Higher Precision
text: A key-value cache is a key component of many services to provide low-latency and high-throughput data accesses to a huge amount of data. To improve the end-to-end performance of such services, a key-value cache must achieve a high cache hit ratio with high throughput. In this paper, we propose a new cache replacement algorithm, multi-step LRU, which achieves high throughput by efficiently exploiting SIMD instructions without using per-item additional memory (LRU metadata) to record information such as the last access timestamp. For a small set of items that can fit within a vector register, SIMD-based LRU management without LRU metadata is known (in-vector LRU). It remembers the access history by reordering items in one vector using vector shuffle instruction. In-vector LRU alone cannot be used for a caching system since it can manage only few items. Set-associative cache is a straightforward way to build a large cache using in-vector LRU as a building block. However, a naive set-associative cache based on in-vector LRU has a poorer cache hit ratio than the original LRU although it can achieve a high throughput. Our multi-step LRU enhances naive set-associative cache based on in-vector LRU for improving cache accuracy by taking both access frequency and access recency of items into account while keeping the efficiency by SIMD instructions. Our results indicate that multi-step LRU outperforms the original LRU and GCLOCK algorithms in terms of both execution speed and cache hit ratio. Multi-step LRU improves the cache hit ratios over the original LRU by implicitly taking access frequency of items as well as access recency into account. The cache hit ratios of multi-step LRU are similar to those of ARC, which achieves a higher a cache hit ratio in a tradeoff for using more LRU metadata.

title: Multi-step LRU: SIMD-based Cache Replacement for Lower Overhead and Higher Precision
text: Optimizing the performance of key-value caches is crucial for many services, as they rely on low-latency and high-throughput data accesses to massive datasets. To achieve this, caches must strike a balance between high cache hit ratios and throughput. We present a novel cache replacement algorithm, multi-step LRU, which leverages SIMD instructions to enhance throughput while avoiding the use of per-item metadata for recording access information. Building upon the concept of in-vector LRU, which efficiently manages a small set of items within a vector register by reordering access history using vector shuffle instructions, we develop a set-associative cache architecture to scale up the cache size. However, a naive implementation of set-associative cache based on in-vector LRU compromises cache hit ratios despite achieving high throughput. Our multi-step LRU algorithm addresses this limitation by incorporating both access frequency and recency into the cache replacement decision, thereby improving cache accuracy while maintaining the efficiency of SIMD instructions. Experimental results demonstrate that multi-step LRU outperforms traditional LRU and GCLOCK algorithms in terms of execution speed and cache hit ratio. Furthermore, our approach implicitly considers access frequency and recency, resulting in cache hit ratios comparable to those of ARC, which sacrifices metadata efficiency for higher cache hit ratios.

title: Cryptography from Pseudorandom Quantum States
text: Pseudorandom states, introduced by Ji, Liu and Song (Crypto'18), are efficiently-computable quantum states that are computationally indistinguishable from Haar-random states. One-way functions imply the existence of pseudorandom states, but Kretschmer (TQC'20) recently constructed an oracle relative to which there are no one-way functions but pseudorandom states still exist. Motivated by this, we study the intriguing possibility of basing interesting cryptographic tasks on pseudorandom states. We construct, assuming the existence of pseudorandom state generators that map a $λ$-bit seed to a $ω(\logλ)$-qubit state, (a) statistically binding and computationally hiding commitments and (b) pseudo one-time encryption schemes. A consequence of (a) is that pseudorandom states are sufficient to construct maliciously secure multiparty computation protocols in the dishonest majority setting. Our constructions are derived via a new notion called pseudorandom function-like states (PRFS), a generalization of pseudorandom states that parallels the classical notion of pseudorandom functions. Beyond the above two applications, we believe our notion can effectively replace pseudorandom functions in many other cryptographic applications.

title: Cryptography from Pseudorandom Quantum States
text: Quantum computers pose a significant threat to classical public-key cryptography, emphasizing the need for novel cryptographic primitives resistant to quantum attacks. Pseudorandom quantum states, generated using classical resources, offer a promising approach to construct quantum-resistant cryptographic schemes. We investigate the feasibility of harnessing pseudorandom quantum states for cryptographic purposes, exploring their potential in realizing secure key establishment protocols. Our methodology involves the design and analysis of a novel cryptographic framework, wherein pseudorandom quantum states are leveraged to encode and decode classical information. We demonstrate the security of our framework against various quantum attacks, including distinguishability and cloning attacks. Notably, our results show that the proposed framework achieves comparable security guarantees to existing quantum-resistant schemes, while offering improved efficiency in terms of computational overhead and key sizes. Furthermore, we provide evidence that our approach can be integrated with existing cryptographic infrastructures, paving the way for a seamless transition to quantum-resistant cryptography.

title: Attack of the Knights: A Non Uniform Cache Side-Channel Attack
text: For a distributed last-level cache (LLC) in a large multicore chip, the access time to one LLC bank can significantly differ from that to another due to the difference in physical distance. In this paper, we successfully demonstrated a new distance-based side-channel attack by timing the AES decryption operation and extracting part of an AES secret key on an Intel Knights Landing CPU. We introduce several techniques to overcome the challenges of the attack, including the use of multiple attack threads to ensure LLC hits, to detect vulnerable memory locations, and to obtain fine-grained timing of the victim operations. While operating as a covert channel, this attack can reach a bandwidth of 205 kbps with an error rate of only 0.02%. We also observed that the side-channel attack can extract 4 bytes of an AES key with 100% accuracy with only 4000 trial rounds of encryption

title: Attack of the Knights: A Non Uniform Cache Side-Channel Attack
text: The pervasive adoption of cloud computing has led to a surge in research on cache side-channel attacks, which exploit shared cache resources to compromise sensitive information. Despite significant advances, prior work has primarily focused on uniform cache architectures, neglecting the non-uniform cache access (NUCA) configurations prevalent in modern cloud infrastructures. This oversight has critical implications, as NUCA designs can exacerbate cache side-channel vulnerabilities. We present Attack of the Knights, a novel non-uniform cache side-channel attack that leverages the inherent variability in cache access times to infer sensitive information. Our methodology involves carefully crafted memory access patterns, coupled with machine learning-based classification techniques, to detect and exploit NUCA-induced timing variations. Experimental evaluations on a commercial cloud platform demonstrate the efficacy of our attack, achieving a 95% success rate in recovering AES encryption keys. Our findings underscore the urgency of reevaluating cache side-channel defenses in the context of NUCA-based cloud architectures.

title: Pure Differential Privacy from Secure Intermediaries
text: Recent work in differential privacy has explored the prospect of combining local randomization with a secure intermediary. Specifically, there are a variety of protocols in the secure shuffle model (where an intermediary randomly permutes messages) as well as the secure aggregation model (where an intermediary adds messages). Most of these protocols are limited to approximate differential privacy. An exception is the shuffle protocol by Ghazi, Golowich, Kumar, Manurangsi, Pagh, and Velingker (arXiv:2002.01919): it computes bounded sums under pure differential privacy. Its additive error is $\tilde{O}(1/\varepsilon^{3/2})$, where $\varepsilon$ is the privacy parameter. In this work, we give a new protocol that ensures $O(1/\varepsilon)$ error under pure differential privacy. We also show how to use it to test uniformity of distributions over $[d]$. The tester's sample complexity has an optimal dependence on $d$. Our work relies on a novel class of secure intermediaries which are of independent interest.

title: Pure Differential Privacy from Secure Intermediaries
text: Differential privacy has emerged as a gold standard for privacy-preserving data analysis, but its implementation often relies on trusted data curators, which can be a single point of failure. We revisit the concept of pure differential privacy, which eliminates the need for trusted intermediaries, and present a novel approach to achieving it through secure multi-party computation. Our methodology leverages garbled circuits and oblivious transfer to enable private data aggregation, ensuring that no single entity can access or manipulate individual records. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach through a comprehensive evaluation on real-world datasets, showing that our protocol can scale to large datasets while maintaining a high level of accuracy. Notably, our results indicate that pure differential privacy can be achieved with an acceptable overhead in terms of computational resources and communication complexity, making it a viable solution for privacy-conscious data analysis in decentralized settings.

title: hybrid-Falcon: Hybrid Pattern Malware Detection and Categorization with Network Traffic and Program Code
text: Nowadays, Android is the most dominant operating system in the mobile ecosystem, with billions of people using its apps daily. As expected, this trend did not go unnoticed by miscreants, and Android became the favorite platform for discovering new victims through malicious apps. Moreover, these apps have become so sophisticated that they can bypass anti-malware measures to protect the users. Therefore, it is safe to admit that traditional anti-malware techniques have become cumbersome, sparking the urge to develop an efficient way to detect Android malware. This paper presents hybrid-Flacon, a hybrid pattern Android malware detection and categorization framework. It combines dynamic and static features of Android malware, which are from network traffic and code graph structure. In hybrid-Flacon, we treat network traffic as a dynamic feature and process it as a 2D image sequence. Meanwhile, hybrid-Flacon handles each network flow in the packet as a 2D image and uses a bidirectional LSTM network to process those 2D-image sequences to obtain vectors representing network packets. We use the program code graph for a static feature and introduce natural language processing (NLP) inspired techniques on function call graph (FCG). We design a graph neural network-based approach to convert the whole graph structure of Android apps to vectors. Finally, We utilize those converted vectors, both network and program code features, and concatenate them to detect and categorize the malware. Our results reveal that hybrid-Flacon yields better results as we get 97.16% accuracy on average for malware detection and 88.32% accuracy for malware categorization. Additionally, we release a dataset AndroNetMnist, which converts the network traffic to a 2D-image sequence and helps to accomplish malware detection on a 2D-image sequence.

title: hybrid-Falcon: Hybrid Pattern Malware Detection and Categorization with Network Traffic and Program Code
text: The rapid proliferation of malware has necessitated the development of sophisticated detection and categorization techniques to mitigate the threats posed to modern computing systems. Despite advances in signature-based and anomaly-based approaches, the limitations of relying on a single detection modality have become increasingly apparent. In response, we propose hybrid-Falcon, a novel hybrid framework that synergistically combines network traffic analysis and program code inspection to detect and categorize malware. Our methodology leverages a multi-stage architecture, wherein network traffic is initially analyzed using a supervised machine learning classifier to identify suspicious patterns. Subsequently, the program code of flagged samples is subjected to a hybrid analysis incorporating both static and dynamic techniques. The static analysis involves parsing the code to extract features related to API calls, system resources, and control flow, while the dynamic analysis involves executing the code in a sandboxed environment to capture behavioral characteristics. The efficacy of hybrid-Falcon is evaluated using a comprehensive dataset comprising 10,000 malware samples and 5,000 benign executables. Our results demonstrate a significant improvement in detection accuracy, with a true positive rate of 97.5% and a false positive rate of 2.1%. Furthermore, our categorization module, which employs a hierarchical clustering approach, achieves a precision of 93.2% in identifying malware families. The key contributions of this work are twofold. Firstly, we demonstrate the effectiveness of combining network traffic and program code analysis in detecting and categorizing malware, highlighting the complementary nature of these approaches. Secondly, we provide a rigorous evaluation of our framework using a large and diverse dataset, underscoring its potential for real-world deployment. The hybrid-Falcon framework has far-reaching implications for the development of more robust and resilient malware detection systems.

title: Android-COCO: Android Malware Detection with Graph Neural Network for Byte- and Native-Code
text: With the popularity of Android growing exponentially, the amount of malware has significantly exploded. It is arguably one of the most viral problems on mobile platforms. Recently, various approaches have been introduced to detect Android malware, the majority of these are either based on the Manifest File features or the structural information, such as control flow graph and API calls. Among those methods, nearly all of them only consider the Java byte-code as the target to detect malicious behaviors. However, Recent research and our own statistics show that native payloads are commonly used in both benign and malicious apps. Current state-of-the-art Android static analysis tools avoid handling native method invocation. None of those tools have the capability to capture the inter-language behaviors. In this work, we explore an ensemble mechanism, which presents how the combination of byte-code and native-code analysis of Android applications can be efficiently used to cope with the advanced sophistication of Android malware. We, therefore, present a multi-layer approach that utilizes deep learning, natural language processing (NLP), as well as graph embedding techniques to handle the threats of Android malware, both from the Java byte-code and native code. After that, we design an ensemble algorithm to get the final result of malware detection system. To be specific, the first layer of our detection approach operates on the byte-code of application and the native code level, whereas the second layer focuses on the ensemble algorithm. Large-scale experiments on 100,113 samples (35,113 malware and 65,000 benign) show that only byte-code sub-system yields 99.8% accuracy and native-code sub-system yields an accuracy of 96.6%, whereas the Android-COCO method attains an accuracy of 99.86% which outperforms various related works.

title: Android-COCO: Android Malware Detection with Graph Neural Network for Byte- and Native-Code
text: The proliferation of Android malware poses a significant threat to the security and privacy of mobile devices, with the annual number of malware variants exceeding one million. Existing detection approaches relying on manual feature engineering or traditional machine learning techniques struggle to keep pace with the evolving complexity of malware, necessitating the development of more effective and adaptive solutions. In response, we propose Android-COCO, a novel Android malware detection framework that leverages graph neural networks (GNNs) to analyze both byte- and native-code representations of Android applications. Our approach begins by constructing a comprehensive graph representation of an Android app, incorporating byte-code and native-code components, as well as their interactions and dependencies. We then employ a GNN model to learn a robust and discriminative representation of the graph, enabling the detection of malicious patterns and behaviors. To facilitate training and evaluation, we curate a large-scale dataset of 150,000 Android apps, comprising 75,000 malware samples and 75,000 benign apps. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of Android-COCO, achieving an accuracy of 97.4% and an F1-score of 96.8%, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches by 5.6% and 4.2%, respectively. Notably, our framework exhibits improved robustness against code obfuscation and anti-analysis techniques, commonly employed by malware authors to evade detection. Furthermore, Android-COCO's ability to handle both byte- and native-code representations enables the detection of malware that exploits native libraries or uses native code to evade detection. Our findings have significant implications for the development of more effective Android malware detection solutions, and we envision Android-COCO serving as a foundation for future research in this domain.

title: Reproducibility Challenges and Their Impacts on Technical Q&A Websites: The Practitioners' Perspectives
text: Software developers often look for solutions to their code-level problems by submitting questions to technical Q&A websites like Stack Overflow (SO). They usually include example code segments with questions to describe the programming issues. SO users prefer to reproduce the reported issues using the given code segments when they attempt to answer the questions. Unfortunately, such code segments could not always reproduce the issues due to several unmet challenges (e.g., external library not found) that might prevent questions from receiving prompt and appropriate solutions. A previous study produced a catalog of potential challenges that hinder the reproducibility of issues reported at SO questions. However, it is unknown how the practitioners (i.e., developers) perceive the challenge catalog. Understanding the developers' perspective is inevitable to introduce interactive tool support that promotes reproducibility. We thus attempt to understand developers' perspectives by surveying 53 users of SO. In particular, we attempt to -- (1) see developers' viewpoints on the agreement to those challenges, (2) find the potential impact of those challenges, (3) see how developers address them, and (4) determine and prioritize tool support needs. Survey results show that about 90% of participants agree to the already exposed challenges. However, they report some additional challenges (e.g., error log missing) that might prevent reproducibility. According to the participants, too short code segment and absence of required Class/Interface/Method from code segments severely prevent reproducibility, followed by missing important part of code. To promote reproducibility, participants strongly recommend introducing tool support that interacts with question submitters with suggestions for improving the code segments if the given code segments fail to reproduce the issues.

title: Reproducibility Challenges and Their Impacts on Technical Q&A Websites: The Practitioners' Perspectives
text: The efficacy of technical Q&A websites, such as Stack Overflow, hinges on the ability of users to reproduce reported issues using provided code segments. However, various challenges, including the absence of external libraries, can hinder this process, potentially delaying or preventing the receipt of suitable solutions. A prior study identified a comprehensive catalog of challenges that impede the reproducibility of issues reported on Stack Overflow. Despite this, there is a lack of understanding regarding how practitioners perceive these challenges, a crucial gap that must be addressed to develop effective tool support promoting reproducibility. To bridge this gap, we conducted a survey of 53 Stack Overflow users, aiming to elucidate their perspectives on the challenges, assess their perceived impact, and determine how they currently address these issues. Furthermore, we sought to identify and prioritize the need for tool support. Our results indicate that approximately 90% of participants concurred with the previously identified challenges, while also highlighting additional obstacles, such as the absence of error logs, that can impede reproducibility. The survey respondents emphasized that incomplete or overly concise code segments, as well as the absence of essential classes, interfaces, or methods, are the primary barriers to reproducibility. To overcome these challenges, participants strongly advocated for the development of interactive tool support that provides suggestions to question submitters on improving their code segments when they fail to reproduce the reported issues.

title: Privacy-preserving and Trusted Threat Intelligence Sharing using Distributed Ledgers
text: Threat information sharing is considered as one of the proactive defensive approaches for enhancing the overall security of trusted partners. Trusted partner organizations can provide access to past and current cybersecurity threats for reducing the risk of a potential cyberattack - the requirements for threat information sharing range from simplistic sharing of documents to threat intelligence sharing. Therefore, the storage and sharing of highly sensitive threat information raises considerable concerns regarding constructing a secure, trusted threat information exchange infrastructure. Establishing a trusted ecosystem for threat sharing will promote the validity, security, anonymity, scalability, latency efficiency, and traceability of the stored information that protects it from unauthorized disclosure. This paper proposes a system that ensures the security principles mentioned above by utilizing a distributed ledger technology that provides secure decentralized operations through smart contracts and provides a privacy-preserving ecosystem for threat information storage and sharing regarding the MITRE ATT\&CK framework.

title: Privacy-preserving and Trusted Threat Intelligence Sharing using Distributed Ledgers
text: The exchange of threat information among trusted partners is a crucial proactive defense strategy for bolstering their collective security. By sharing knowledge of past and current cybersecurity threats, partners can reduce their vulnerability to potential attacks. However, the storage and dissemination of sensitive threat information pose significant security concerns, necessitating the development of a trusted infrastructure for threat information exchange. A secure ecosystem for threat sharing must ensure the validity, security, anonymity, scalability, latency efficiency, and traceability of stored information to prevent unauthorized disclosure. This paper presents a decentralized system that addresses these security principles by leveraging distributed ledger technology and smart contracts to provide a privacy-preserving environment for threat information storage and sharing, with a specific focus on the MITRE ATT\&CK framework.

title: An Architecture for Exploiting Native User-Land Checkpoint-Restart to Improve Fuzzing
text: Fuzzing is one of the most popular and widely used techniques to find vulnerabilities in any application. Fuzzers are fast enough, but they still spend a good portion of time to restart a crashed application and then fuzz it from the beginning. Fuzzing an application from a point deeper in the execution is also important. To do this, a user needs to take a snapshot of the program while fuzzing it on top of an emulator, virtual machine, or by utilizing a special kernel module to enable checkpointing. Even with this ability, it can be difficult to attach a fuzzer after restoring a checkpoint. As a result, most fuzzers leverage a form of fork-server design. We propose a novel testing architecture that allows users to attach a fuzzer after the program has started running. We do this by natively checkpointing the target application at a point of interest, and attaching the fuzzer after restoring the checkpoint. A fork-server may even be engaged at the point of restoration. This not only improves the throughput of the fuzzing campaign by minimizing startup time, but opens up a new way to fuzz applications. With this architecture, a user can take a series of checkpoints at points of interest, and run parallel tests to reduce the overall state-complexity of an individual test. Checkpoints allow us to begin fuzzing from a deeper point in the execution path, omitting prior execution from the required coverage path. This and other checkpointing techniques are described in the paper to help improve fuzzing.

title: An Architecture for Exploiting Native User-Land Checkpoint-Restart to Improve Fuzzing
text: The efficacy of fuzz testing in discovering vulnerabilities in software applications is well established. However, conventional fuzzers are hindered by the time-consuming process of restarting a crashed application from the beginning. Moreover, resuming fuzz testing from a deeper point in the execution path is crucial, yet challenging. This typically requires taking a snapshot of the program using an emulator, virtual machine, or kernel module, followed by attaching a fuzzer after restoring the checkpoint, which can be difficult. The prevalent fork-server design attempts to address this limitation. We introduce a novel testing architecture that enables seamless attachment of a fuzzer after the program has initiated execution. By natively checkpointing the target application at a point of interest and attaching the fuzzer post-restoration, our approach minimizes startup time, thereby improving the throughput of fuzz testing campaigns. Additionally, this architecture facilitates parallel testing by taking multiple checkpoints at points of interest, reducing the overall state complexity of individual tests. By omitting prior execution from the required coverage path, our checkpointing techniques enable fuzzing from deeper points in the execution path, thereby enhancing the fuzz testing process. The paper provides a comprehensive description of these checkpointing techniques and their applications in fuzz testing.

title: Early Detection of Security-Relevant Bug Reports using Machine Learning: How Far Are We?
text: Bug reports are common artefacts in software development. They serve as the main channel for users to communicate to developers information about the issues that they encounter when using released versions of software programs. In the descriptions of issues, however, a user may, intentionally or not, expose a vulnerability. In a typical maintenance scenario, such security-relevant bug reports are prioritised by the development team when preparing corrective patches. Nevertheless, when security relevance is not immediately expressed (e.g., via a tag) or rapidly identified by triaging teams, the open security-relevant bug report can become a critical leak of sensitive information that attackers can leverage to perform zero-day attacks. To support practitioners in triaging bug reports, the research community has proposed a number of approaches for the detection of security-relevant bug reports. In recent years, approaches in this respect based on machine learning have been reported with promising performance. Our work focuses on such approaches, and revisits their building blocks to provide a comprehensive view on the current achievements. To that end, we built a large experimental dataset and performed extensive experiments with variations in feature sets and learning algorithms. Eventually, our study highlights different approach configurations that yield best performing classifiers.

title: Early Detection of Security-Relevant Bug Reports using Machine Learning: How Far Are We?
text: The timely identification of security-relevant bug reports is crucial for ensuring the integrity of software systems. Despite the significance of this task, the current practice of manually reviewing bug reports is time-consuming and prone to errors. Recent studies have proposed the application of machine learning techniques to automate this process, but their effectiveness remains unclear. This study provides a comprehensive evaluation of the state-of-the-art in machine learning-based early detection of security-relevant bug reports. We conduct an extensive analysis of 15 publicly available bug report datasets, comprising over 150,000 reports, and employ a range of machine learning models, including traditional feature-based classifiers and deep learning architectures. Our results show that, while machine learning can achieve high accuracy in detecting security-relevant bug reports, the performance varies significantly across datasets and models. Notably, we find that deep learning models outperform traditional classifiers, but are more susceptible to overfitting. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the quality of the training data has a profound impact on the model's performance, highlighting the need for high-quality, diverse datasets. Overall, our study provides a nuanced understanding of the capabilities and limitations of machine learning in early detection of security-relevant bug reports, informing the development of more effective automated detection systems.

title: Blockchain-based Platform for Secure Sharing and Validation of Vaccination Certificates
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has recently emerged as a worldwide health emergency that necessitates coordinated international measures. To contain the virus's spread, governments and health organisations raced to develop vaccines that would lower Covid-19 morbidity, relieve pressure on healthcare systems, and allow economies to open. As a way forward after the COVID-19 vaccination, the Vaccination certificate has been adopted to help the authorities formulate policies by controlling cross-border travelling. To resolve significant privacy concerns and remove the need for relying on third parties to maintain trust and control the user's data, in this paper, we leverage blockchain technologies in developing a secure and verifiable vaccination certificate. Our approach has the advantage of utilising a hybrid architecture that implements different advanced technologies, such as smart contracts, interPlanetary File System (IPFS), and Self-sovereign Identity (SSI). We will rely on verifiable credentials paired with smart contracts to implement on-chain access control decisions and provide on-chain verification and validation of the user and issuer DIDs. The usability of this approach was further analysed, particularly concerning performance and security. Our analysis proved that our approach satisfies vaccination certificate security requirements.

title: Blockchain-based Platform for Secure Sharing and Validation of Vaccination Certificates
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the need for a secure, decentralized, and transparent system for sharing and validating vaccination certificates. Existing solutions rely on centralized authorities and siloed data, making them vulnerable to data breaches, fraud, and manipulation. To address these limitations, we propose a blockchain-based platform for secure sharing and validation of vaccination certificates. Our platform leverages a permissioned blockchain network, smart contracts, and cryptographic techniques to ensure the integrity, confidentiality, and authenticity of vaccination records. We implement a decentralized identity management system, enabling individuals to control their vaccination data and share it with authorized parties. Our evaluation demonstrates the platform's ability to withstand various attacks, including data tampering, unauthorized access, and sybil attacks. The results show that our platform outperforms traditional centralized systems in terms of security, scalability, and efficiency. We also conduct a usability study, revealing high user satisfaction and acceptance of the platform. Our work has significant implications for the development of secure, decentralized health information systems, enabling trustworthy data exchange and verification in the fight against infectious diseases.

title: Performance analysis of continuous-variable quantum key distribution using non-Gaussian states
text: In this study, we analyze the efficiency of a protocol with discrete modulation of continuous variable non-Gaussian states, the coherent states having one photon added and then one photon subtracted (PASCS). We calculate the secure key generation rate against collective attacks using the fact that Eve's information can be bounded based on the protocol with Gaussian modulation, which in turn is unconditionally secure. Our results for a four-state protocol show that the PASCS always outperforms the equivalent coherent states protocol under the same environmental conditions. Interestingly, we find that for the protocol using discrete-modulated PASCS, the noisier the line, the better will be its performance compared to the protocol using coherent states. Thus, our proposal proves to be advantageous for performing quantum key distribution in non-ideal situations.

title: Performance analysis of continuous-variable quantum key distribution using non-Gaussian states
text: We investigate the efficiency of a protocol exploiting discrete modulation of continuous variable non-Gaussian states, specifically coherent states with one photon added and then subtracted (PASCS). By leveraging the unconditional security of Gaussian modulation protocols, we establish an upper bound on Eve's information and calculate the secure key generation rate against collective attacks. Our analysis reveals that the four-state PASCS protocol consistently surpasses its coherent state counterpart under identical environmental conditions. Notably, we observe that the performance advantage of discrete-modulated PASCS over coherent states increases with the level of noise in the channel, rendering our proposal particularly suitable for quantum key distribution in non-ideal scenarios.

title: What are Weak Links in the npm Supply Chain?
text: Modern software development frequently uses third-party packages, raising the concern of supply chain security attacks. Many attackers target popular package managers, like npm, and their users with supply chain attacks. In 2021 there was a 650% year-on-year growth in security attacks by exploiting Open Source Software's supply chain. Proactive approaches are needed to predict package vulnerability to high-risk supply chain attacks. The goal of this work is to help software developers and security specialists in measuring npm supply chain weak link signals to prevent future supply chain attacks by empirically studying npm package metadata. In this paper, we analyzed the metadata of 1.63 million JavaScript npm packages. We propose six signals of security weaknesses in a software supply chain, such as the presence of install scripts, maintainer accounts associated with an expired email domain, and inactive packages with inactive maintainers. One of our case studies identified 11 malicious packages from the install scripts signal. We also found 2,818 maintainer email addresses associated with expired domains, allowing an attacker to hijack 8,494 packages by taking over the npm accounts. We obtained feedback on our weak link signals through a survey responded to by 470 npm package developers. The majority of the developers supported three out of our six proposed weak link signals. The developers also indicated that they would want to be notified about weak links signals before using third-party packages. Additionally, we discussed eight new signals suggested by package developers.

title: What are Weak Links in the npm Supply Chain?
text: The npm registry, with over 1.3 million packages, is a cornerstone of modern JavaScript development, yet its supply chain remains understudied. Recent incidents have demonstrated the devastating impact of compromised packages on the ecosystem, underscoring the need to identify and mitigate vulnerabilities. This paper presents the first large-scale empirical study of weak links in the npm supply chain, focusing on the critical yet overlooked dependencies that connect packages. We crawled the npm registry, collecting metadata and dependencies for 1,155,119 packages, and developed a novel dependency graph analysis framework to identify weak links. We define weak links as packages with low maintainer activity, few dependents, or high churn rates, which are more susceptible to abandonment, exploitation, or malicious manipulation. Our analysis reveals that 23.4% of packages (268,111) have at least one weak link in their dependency chain, with 12.5% (143,751) relying on a weak link in their critical path. Furthermore, we find that weak links are more prevalent in packages with high usage rates, increasing the attack surface of the ecosystem. We also identify a set of 157 high-risk packages with weak links in their critical path, which are depended upon by 44,121 other packages. Our results have significant implications for npm package maintainers, developers, and security professionals, highlighting the need for more robust dependency management practices and increased scrutiny of the supply chain. Our framework and dataset are made available to facilitate further research and to support the development of more resilient software ecosystems.

title: Using data compression and randomization to build an unconditionally secure short key cipher
text: We consider the problem of constructing an unconditionally secure cipher for the case when the key length is less than the length of the encrypted message. (Unconditional security means that a computationally unbounded adversary cannot obtain information about the encrypted message without the key.) In this article, we propose data compression and randomization techniques combined with entropically-secure encryption. The resulting cipher can be used for encryption in such a way that the key length does not depend on the entropy or the length of the encrypted message; instead, it is determined by the required security level.

title: Using data compression and randomization to build an unconditionally secure short key cipher
text: The problem of designing an unconditionally secure cipher is challenging when the key length is shorter than the encrypted message. We overcome this limitation by proposing a novel approach that integrates data compression and randomization techniques with entropically-secure encryption. This innovative cipher enables encryption independent of the entropy or length of the message, with the key length instead determined by the desired security level, thereby providing unconditional security against computationally unbounded adversaries.

title: Robust and Privacy-Preserving Collaborative Learning: A Comprehensive Survey
text: With the rapid demand of data and computational resources in deep learning systems, a growing number of algorithms to utilize collaborative machine learning techniques, for example, federated learning, to train a shared deep model across multiple participants. It could effectively take advantage of the resources of each participant and obtain a more powerful learning system. However, integrity and privacy threats in such systems have greatly obstructed the applications of collaborative learning. And a large amount of works have been proposed to maintain the model integrity and mitigate the privacy leakage of training data during the training phase for different collaborative learning systems. Compared with existing surveys that mainly focus on one specific collaborative learning system, this survey aims to provide a systematic and comprehensive review of security and privacy researches in collaborative learning. Our survey first provides the system overview of collaborative learning, followed by a brief introduction of integrity and privacy threats. In an organized way, we then detail the existing integrity and privacy attacks as well as their defenses. We also list some open problems in this area and opensource the related papers on GitHub:

title: Robust and Privacy-Preserving Collaborative Learning: A Comprehensive Survey
text: The proliferation of machine learning has led to an increased focus on collaborative learning, where multiple parties jointly train a model on their collective data. However, this paradigm raises pressing concerns about data privacy and robustness, particularly in scenarios where participants may be incentivized to manipulate the model or compromise each other's data. Recent advances in cryptography, secure multi-party computation, and differential privacy have spawned a diverse array of techniques for robust and privacy-preserving collaborative learning. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the existing literature, categorizing and analyzing state-of-the-art approaches according to their underlying cryptographic primitives, threat models, and performance characteristics. We identify key challenges and open research directions, including the need for more efficient protocols, improved scalability, and rigorous evaluation methodologies. Our analysis reveals that, despite significant progress, the development of practical and robust collaborative learning systems remains an open problem, particularly in high-stakes applications such as healthcare and finance. By synthesizing the current state of knowledge, this survey aims to inform and guide future research in this critical area.

title: Deriving Semantics-Aware Fuzzers from Web API Schemas
text: Fuzzing -- whether generating or mutating inputs -- has found many bugs and security vulnerabilities in a wide range of domains. Stateful and highly structured web APIs present significant challenges to traditional fuzzing techniques, as execution feedback is usually limited to a response code instead of code coverage and vulnerabilities of interest include silent information-disclosure in addition to explicit errors. Our tool, Schemathesis, derives structure- and semantics-aware fuzzers from web API schemas in the OpenAPI or GraphQL formats, using property-based testing tools. Derived fuzzers can be incorporated into unit-test suites or run directly, with or without end-user customisation of data generation and semantic checks. We construct the most comprehensive evaluation of web API fuzzers to date, running eight fuzzers against sixteen real-world open source web services. OpenAPI schemas found in the wild have a long tail of rare features and complex structures. Of the tools we evaluated, Schemathesis was the only one to handle more than two-thirds of our target services without a fatal internal error. Schemathesis finds 1.4 times to 4.5 times more unique defects than the respectively second-best fuzzer for each target, and is the only fuzzer to find defects in four targets.

title: Deriving Semantics-Aware Fuzzers from Web API Schemas
text: The proliferation of web APIs has led to a surge in API-based vulnerabilities, underscoring the need for effective fuzz testing techniques. While existing fuzzers excel at identifying low-level errors, they often fail to uncover semantic vulnerabilities rooted in API logic. We propose a novel approach to derive semantics-aware fuzzers from web API schemas, enabling the discovery of complex, logic-based flaws. Our methodology involves a combination of static analysis and machine learning to extract semantic patterns from API schemas, which are then used to guide the fuzzing process. Specifically, we develop a schema-aware fuzzing framework that integrates with popular API description languages, such as OpenAPI and GraphQL. Our evaluation on a diverse set of APIs reveals that our approach uncovers a significant number of previously unknown semantic vulnerabilities, including logic flaws, authentication bypasses, and data tampering attacks. In comparison to state-of-the-art fuzzers, our semantics-aware fuzzer achieves a 3.5x increase in vulnerability detection rate, while reducing the number of false positives by 70%. Our work demonstrates the potential of schema-driven fuzzing in improving the security and reliability of web APIs.

title: Smart Home: Application using HTTP and MQTT as Communication Protocols
text: This study discloses the development of a solution for realizing a smart home in the post COVID-19 era using the Internet of Things domain knowledge. COVID-19 outbreak has been catastrophic and impacted everyone's lives due to its rapid transmission from one body to another. This study aims to reduce virus transmission by eliminating the need to touch any common-point surface in a home, such as switches, doorknobs, and remotes. We provide a generic solution by coupling things with the internet to control them remotely. The project aims to showcase a working solution to controlling devices like smart bulbs, smart fans, smart ACs, and smart door locks in our self-developed emulator over WWW securely using two different protocols, viz., HTTP and MQTT-over-WSS. Additionally, intent authentication over HTTP is based on digital signature that is demonstrated using RSA (encryption) and MD5 (hashing) when the system is deployed in insecure environment(s). RESTful API deployed on AWS EC2 is used to realize HTTP communication protocol, and MQTT is realized using AWS IoT service. The developed project can be applied to any smart home setting like a hotel or public place using AWS IoT, Lambda, or similar infrastructure as a broker.

title: Smart Home: Application using HTTP and MQTT as Communication Protocols
text: The proliferation of smart devices in home automation has led to a pressing need for efficient and secure communication protocols. This work presents a comprehensive study on the implementation of HTTP and MQTT as communication protocols in a smart home environment. We design and develop a smart home system comprising various devices, including sensors, actuators, and gateways, and evaluate the performance of HTTP and MQTT in terms of latency, throughput, and energy consumption. Our experimental setup consists of a Raspberry Pi-based gateway, running a customized Linux distribution, and various devices communicating with the gateway using HTTP and MQTT protocols. We conduct a series of experiments to measure the performance metrics under varying network conditions and device loads. The results show that MQTT outperforms HTTP in terms of latency and energy consumption, while HTTP achieves higher throughput in certain scenarios. We also analyze the security vulnerabilities of both protocols and propose mitigation strategies to ensure secure communication in the smart home environment. Our findings have significant implications for the design and development of efficient and secure communication protocols in smart home systems, and can inform the development of future IoT systems.

title: Systematic Literature Review on Cyber Situational Awareness Visualizations
text: The dynamics of cyber threats are increasingly complex, making it more challenging than ever for organizations to obtain in-depth insights into their cyber security status. Therefore, organizations rely on Cyber Situational Awareness (CSA) to support them in better understanding the threats and associated impacts of cyber events. Due to the heterogeneity and complexity of cyber security data, often with multidimensional attributes, sophisticated visualization techniques are needed to achieve CSA. However, there have been no previous attempts to systematically review and analyze the scientific literature on CSA visualizations. In this paper, we systematically select and review 54 publications that discuss visualizations to support CSA. We extract data from these papers to identify key stakeholders, information types, data sources, and visualization techniques. Furthermore, we analyze the level of CSA supported by the visualizations, alongside examining the maturity of the visualizations, challenges, and practices related to CSA visualizations to prepare a full analysis of the current state of CSA in an organizational context. Our results reveal certain gaps in CSA visualizations. For instance, the largest focus is on operational-level staff, and there is a clear lack of visualizations targeting other types of stakeholders such as managers, higher-level decision makers, and non-expert users. Most papers focus on threat information visualization, and there is a dearth of papers that visualize impact information, response plans, and information shared within teams. Based on the results that highlight the important concerns in CSA visualizations, we recommend a list of future research directions.

title: Systematic Literature Review on Cyber Situational Awareness Visualizations
text: The increasing complexity of cyber threats and the escalating reliance on digital technologies have created a pressing need for effective cyber situational awareness (CSA) to facilitate timely and informed decision-making. Visualization plays a crucial role in CSA, enabling the comprehension and interpretation of complex cyber data. Despite the growing body of research on CSA visualizations, a comprehensive understanding of the current state of the art is lacking. This systematic literature review aims to address this gap by providing a thorough analysis of existing CSA visualization approaches. We conducted a rigorous search of prominent computer science and cybersecurity databases, yielding a corpus of 56 relevant studies published between 2010 and 2022. Our methodology involved a multi-stage screening process, data extraction, and quality assessment using standardized tools. We identified and categorized various visualization techniques, including network visualization, geospatial visualization, and temporal visualization, among others. Our findings indicate that the majority of CSA visualization research focuses on network-centric approaches, with a significant emphasis on graph-based representations. Furthermore, we observed a lack of standardization in visualization design and evaluation, with limited consideration given to human factors and user experience. Notably, few studies have explored the application of machine learning and artificial intelligence in CSA visualization. Our review highlights the need for a more comprehensive and interdisciplinary approach to CSA visualization, incorporating insights from cognitive psychology, human-computer interaction, and data visualization to enhance the effectiveness of CSA systems.

title: An Investigation into Inconsistency of Software Vulnerability Severity across Data Sources
text: Software Vulnerability (SV) severity assessment is a vital task for informing SV remediation and triage. Ranking of SV severity scores is often used to advise prioritization of patching efforts. However, severity assessment is a difficult and subjective manual task that relies on expertise, knowledge, and standardized reporting schemes. Consequently, different data sources that perform independent analysis may provide conflicting severity rankings. Inconsistency across these data sources affects the reliability of severity assessment data, and can consequently impact SV prioritization and fixing.
