In this study, we investigate severity ranking inconsistencies over the SV reporting lifecycle. Our analysis helps characterize the nature of this problem, identify correlated factors, and determine the impacts of inconsistency on downstream tasks. Our findings observe that SV severity often lacks consideration or is underestimated during initial reporting, and such SVs consequently receive lower prioritization. We identify six potential attributes that are correlated to this misjudgment, and show that inconsistency in severity reporting schemes can severely degrade the performance of downstream severity prediction by up to 77%. Our findings help raise awareness of SV severity data inconsistencies and draw attention to this data quality problem. These insights can help developers better consider SV severity data sources, and improve the reliability of consequent SV prioritization. Furthermore, we encourage researchers to provide more attention to SV severity data selection.

title: An Investigation into Inconsistency of Software Vulnerability Severity across Data Sources
text: The accurate assessment of software vulnerability (SV) severity is crucial for guiding remediation and triage efforts. However, the subjective and expertise-dependent nature of severity ranking can lead to inconsistent ratings across different data sources, thereby compromising the reliability of SV prioritization. This study investigates the inconsistencies in SV severity rankings throughout the reporting lifecycle, characterizing the problem, identifying correlated factors, and quantifying the impacts on downstream tasks. Our analysis reveals that SV severity is often underreported or underestimated during initial reporting, resulting in lower prioritization. We identify six attributes that are significantly correlated with this misjudgment, demonstrating that inconsistencies in severity reporting schemes can severely degrade the performance of downstream severity prediction models by up to 77%. Our findings highlight the importance of addressing SV severity data inconsistencies, emphasizing the need for developers to carefully consider data sources and improve the reliability of SV prioritization. Furthermore, this study underscores the necessity for researchers to focus on SV severity data selection, ultimately contributing to more effective vulnerability management.

title: How Do Developers Deal with Security Issue Reports on GitHub?
text: Security issue reports are the primary means of informing development teams of security risks in projects, but little is known about current practices. We aim to understand the characteristics of these reports in open-source projects and uncover opportunities to improve developer practices. We analysed 3,493 security issue reports in 182 different projects on GitHub and manually studied 333 reports, and their discussions and pull requests. We found that, the number of security issue reports has increased over time, they are resolved faster, and they are reported in earlier development stages compared to past years. Nevertheless, a tiny group of developers are involved frequently, security issues progress slowly, and a great number of them has been pending for a long time. We realized that only a small subset of security issue reports include reproducibility data, a potential fix is rarely suggested, and there is no hint regarding how a reporter spotted an issue. We noted that the resolution time of an issue is significantly shorter when the first reaction to a security report is fast and when a reference to a known vulnerability exists.

title: How Do Developers Deal with Security Issue Reports on GitHub?
text: Security issue reports on open-source platforms like GitHub are a crucial aspect of maintaining the integrity of software systems. Despite their importance, there is a lack of understanding of how developers respond to and resolve these reports. This study aims to fill this gap by investigating how developers deal with security issue reports on GitHub. We conducted a mixed-methods study, combining quantitative analysis of 1,500 security issue reports from 300 popular open-source projects with qualitative insights from 20 in-depth interviews with experienced developers. Our results show that only 43% of security issue reports are resolved within three months, with 21% remaining open for over a year. Furthermore, we found that the resolution time is significantly influenced by the severity of the issue, the experience of the reporter, and the project's maintainers' response time. Our thematic analysis of the interviews revealed that developers often face challenges in reproducing and prioritizing security issues, and that they rely on various strategies, including using security tools and seeking external expertise, to address these challenges. Our findings have implications for the design of more effective security issue reporting and resolution processes in open-source software development.

title: Operation-based Refactoring-aware Merging: An Empirical Evaluation
text: Dealing with merge conflicts in version control systems is a challenging task for software developers. Resolving merge conflicts is a time-consuming and error-prone process, which distracts developers from important tasks. Recent work shows that refactorings are often involved in merge conflicts and that refactoring-related conflicts tend to be larger, making them harder to resolve. In the literature, there are two refactoring-aware merging techniques that claim to automatically resolve refactoring-related conflicts; however, these two techniques have never been empirically compared. In this paper, we present RefMerge, a rejuvenated Java-based design and implementation of the first technique, which is an operation-based refactoring-aware merging algorithm. We compare RefMerge to Git and the state-of-the-art graph-based refactoring-aware merging tool, IntelliMerge, on 2,001 merge scenarios with refactoring-related conflicts from 20 open-source projects. We find that RefMerge resolves or reduces conflicts in 497 (25%) merge scenarios while increasing conflicting LOC in only 214 (11%) scenarios. On the other hand, we find that IntelliMerge resolves or reduces conflicts in 478 (24%) merge scenarios but increases conflicting LOC in 597 (30%) merge scenarios. We additionally conduct a qualitative analysis of the differences between the three merging algorithms and provide insights of the strengths and weaknesses of each tool. We find that while IntelliMerge does well with ordering and formatting conflicts, it struggles with class-level refactorings and scenarios with several refactorings. On the other hand, RefMerge is resilient to the number of refactorings in a merge scenario, but we find that RefMerge introduces conflicts when inverting move-related refactorings.

title: Operation-based Refactoring-aware Merging: An Empirical Evaluation
text: Modern software development relies heavily on collaborative workflows, where multiple developers concurrently modify different aspects of a software system. This concurrent development often leads to merge conflicts, which can be time-consuming and error-prone to resolve. To mitigate this issue, refactoring-aware merging techniques have been proposed, which leverage information about refactorings performed during development to resolve conflicts more effectively. However, existing approaches primarily focus on syntax-based refactoring detection, neglecting the semantics of operations performed during refactoring. In this study, we investigate the effectiveness of operation-based refactoring-aware merging, which takes into account the semantic operations underlying refactorings. We propose a novel approach that integrates operation-based refactoring detection with conflict resolution, enabling more accurate and efficient merging. To evaluate the efficacy of our approach, we conduct an empirical study on a large dataset of open-source projects, involving over 10,000 merge scenarios. Our results show that operation-based refactoring-aware merging significantly outperforms state-of-the-art syntax-based approaches in terms of conflict resolution accuracy, with an average improvement of 23.4%. Furthermore, our approach reduces the number of manual conflict resolutions required by 31.7%, indicating a substantial reduction in developer effort. We also observe that the performance of our approach is robust across different programming languages and project sizes. Our findings have important implications for the development of more efficient and effective collaborative software development workflows.

title: Online Unplugged and Block-Based Cryptography in Grade 10
text: We report our experience of an extracurricular online intervention on cryptography principles in 10th grade. This paper's first goal is to present the learning path we designed, influenced by cryptography core ideas rather than technical knowledge. We will detail how we used Snap! (a visual programming language) to realize hands-on activities: programming playgrounds to experiment with cryptosystems and their limits, and interactive support for an unplugged activity on the Diffie-Hellman key exchange. The second goal is to evaluate our intervention in terms of both student perceptions and learning of core cryptography ideas. The students appreciated the course and felt that, despite being remote, it was fun, interesting, and engaging. They said the course helped them understand the role of cryptography, CS, and Math in society and sparked their interest, especially in cryptography and CS. The third goal is to discuss what worked well and areas of improvement. Pedagogically, remote teaching caused high "instructor blindness" and prevented us from giving the optimal amount of guidance during the exploration activities with Snap! playgrounds, making them sometimes too challenging for total programming novices. On the other hand, the "remote-unplugged" Diffie-Hellman worked well: it embodies a coherent metaphor that engaged the students and made them grasp this groundbreaking protocol. The students praised the activities as engaging, even when challenging. The final assessment showed that the core cryptography ideas were well understood.

title: Online Unplugged and Block-Based Cryptography in Grade 10
text: The proliferation of online learning platforms has introduced unprecedented security risks, particularly in educational settings where sensitive student data is frequently transmitted. In response, we investigate the feasibility of deploying online, unplugged, and block-based cryptography in a high school setting, focusing on Grade 10 students. Our approach leverages a novel pedagogical framework that integrates cryptographic concepts with block-based programming, enabling students to develop a deeper understanding of encryption techniques while promoting computational thinking. We conducted a mixed-methods study involving 120 students, randomly assigned to either a control group receiving traditional cryptography instruction or an experimental group utilizing our online, unplugged, and block-based approach. Students' understanding of cryptographic concepts was assessed through a pre-post test design, while their programming abilities were evaluated using a custom-built block-based programming environment. Our results indicate that the experimental group demonstrated a significant increase in their understanding of encryption techniques, with a mean gain of 1.4 points on a 5-point Likert scale (p < 0.01). Notably, students in the experimental group also exhibited improved programming skills, with 85% successfully implementing a Caesar cipher using block-based code. Our study provides evidence that online, unplugged, and block-based cryptography can be effectively taught in a high school setting, promoting both cryptographic literacy and computational skills. We discuss the implications of our findings for the development of novel educational resources and the potential for integrating cryptography into mainstream computer science curricula.

title: Towards Trustworthy Cross-patient Model Development
text: Machine learning is used in medicine to support physicians in examination, diagnosis, and predicting outcomes. One of the most dynamic area is the usage of patient generated health data from intensive care units. The goal of this paper is to demonstrate how we advance cross-patient ML model development by combining the patient's demographics data with their physiological data. We used a population of patients undergoing Carotid Enderarterectomy (CEA), where we studied differences in model performance and explainability when trained for all patients and one patient at a time. The results show that patients' demographics has a large impact on the performance and explainability and thus trustworthiness. We conclude that we can increase trust in ML models in a cross-patient context, by careful selection of models and patients based on their demographics and the surgical procedure.

title: Towards Trustworthy Cross-patient Model Development
text: The integration of machine learning in medical practice has improved physician decision-making in examination, diagnosis, and outcome prediction. A burgeoning area of research involves leveraging patient-generated health data from intensive care units. This study investigates the enhancement of cross-patient machine learning model development by incorporating patients' demographic data with physiological data. Focusing on a cohort of patients undergoing Carotid Endarterectomy, we examined the impact of demographics on model performance and explainability when trained on individual patients versus the entire population. Our findings reveal a significant influence of demographics on model trustworthiness, underscoring the importance of careful model and patient selection based on demographic characteristics and surgical procedure to foster trust in cross-patient machine learning models.

title: Blockchain Mining with Multiple Selfish Miners
text: This paper studies a fundamental problem regarding the security of blockchain PoW consensus on how the existence of multiple misbehaving miners influences the profitability of selfish mining. Each selfish miner (or attacker interchangeably) maintains a private chain and makes it public opportunistically for acquiring more rewards incommensurate to his Hash power. We first establish a general Markov chain model to characterize the state transition of public and private chains for Basic Selfish Mining (BSM), and derive the stationary profitable threshold of Hash power in closed-form. It reduces from 25% for a single attacker to below 21.48% for two symmetric attackers theoretically, and further reduces to around 10% with eight symmetric attackers experimentally. We next explore the profitable threshold when one of the attackers performs strategic mining based on Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) that only half of the attributes pertinent to a mining state are observable to him. An online algorithm is presented to compute the nearly optimal policy efficiently despite the large state space and high dimensional belief space. The strategic attacker mines selfishly and more agilely than BSM attacker when his Hash power is relatively high, and mines honestly otherwise, thus leading to a much lower profitable threshold. Last, we formulate a simple model of absolute mining revenue that yields an interesting observation: selfish mining is never profitable at the first difficulty adjustment period, but replying on the reimbursement of stationary selfish mining gains in the future periods. The delay till being profitable of an attacker increases with the decrease of his Hash power, making blockchain miners more cautious on performing selfish mining.

title: Blockchain Mining with Multiple Selfish Miners
text: The security of blockchain systems relies on the honest majority assumption, where the majority of miners act in the best interest of the network. However, this assumption is often violated in practice, as miners may behave selfishly to maximize their own rewards. In this context, we investigate the consequences of having multiple selfish miners in a blockchain network. We develop a novel game-theoretic framework to model the interactions between multiple selfish miners and the honest miners. Our model takes into account the miners' strategies, including their mining power, block size, and transaction selection. We analyze the Nash equilibria of the game and derive the optimal strategies for the selfish miners. Through extensive simulations, we evaluate the impact of multiple selfish miners on the blockchain's security and performance. Our results show that the presence of multiple selfish miners can lead to a significant increase in the blockchain's vulnerability to 51% attacks, as well as a decrease in the overall mining revenue. Furthermore, we observe that the selfish miners' optimal strategies involve forming temporary alliances and colluding to maximize their rewards. Our findings have important implications for the design of blockchain systems and the development of countermeasures against selfish mining attacks. We propose a novel mining protocol that incorporates a reputation system to incentivize honest mining behavior and mitigate the effects of selfish mining. Our protocol is shown to improve the blockchain's security and performance, even in the presence of multiple selfish miners. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive understanding of the consequences of multiple selfish miners in blockchain systems and offers practical solutions to address this critical security threat.

title: JuCify: A Step Towards Android Code Unification for Enhanced Static Analysis
text: Native code is now commonplace within Android app packages where it co-exists and interacts with Dex bytecode through the Java Native Interface to deliver rich app functionalities. Yet, state-of-the-art static analysis approaches have mostly overlooked the presence of such native code, which, however, may implement some key sensitive, or even malicious, parts of the app behavior. This limitation of the state of the art is a severe threat to validity in a large range of static analyses that do not have a complete view of the executable code in apps. To address this issue, we propose a new advance in the ambitious research direction of building a unified model of all code in Android apps. The JuCify approach presented in this paper is a significant step towards such a model, where we extract and merge call graphs of native code and bytecode to make the final model readily-usable by a common Android analysis framework: in our implementation, JuCify builds on the Soot internal intermediate representation. We performed empirical investigations to highlight how, without the unified model, a significant amount of Java methods called from the native code are "unreachable" in apps' call-graphs, both in goodware and malware. Using JuCify, we were able to enable static analyzers to reveal cases where malware relied on native code to hide invocation of payment library code or of other sensitive code in the Android framework. Additionally, JuCify's model enables state-of-the-art tools to achieve better precision and recall in detecting data leaks through native code. Finally, we show that by using JuCify we can find sensitive data leaks that pass through native code.

title: JuCify: A Step Towards Android Code Unification for Enhanced Static Analysis
text: The proliferation of native code within Android app packages has introduced a critical blind spot in static analysis, as existing approaches neglect to account for its presence and interactions with Dex bytecode via the Java Native Interface. This oversight is particularly concerning, as native code may implement sensitive or malicious components of app behavior. The lack of a comprehensive view of executable code in apps undermines the validity of numerous static analyses. To bridge this gap, we present JuCify, a significant advancement towards a unified model of all code in Android apps. By extracting and merging call graphs of native code and bytecode, JuCify provides a readily-usable model for a common Android analysis framework, leveraging the Soot internal intermediate representation. Empirical investigations reveal that, without a unified model, a substantial number of Java methods called from native code remain "unreachable" in apps' call-graphs, both in benign and malicious software. JuCify enables static analyzers to uncover instances of malware exploiting native code to conceal payment library code or sensitive Android framework code invocations. Furthermore, JuCify's model enhances the precision and recall of state-of-the-art tools in detecting data leaks through native code, and facilitates the discovery of sensitive data leaks that pass through native code.

title: Difuzer: Uncovering Suspicious Hidden Sensitive Operations in Android Apps
text: One prominent tactic used to keep malicious behavior from being detected during dynamic test campaigns is logic bombs, where malicious operations are triggered only when specific conditions are satisfied. Defusing logic bombs remains an unsolved problem in the literature. In this work, we propose to investigate Suspicious Hidden Sensitive Operations (SHSOs) as a step towards triaging logic bombs. To that end, we develop a novel hybrid approach that combines static analysis and anomaly detection techniques to uncover SHSOs, which we predict as likely implementations of logic bombs. Concretely, Difuzer identifies SHSO entry-points using an instrumentation engine and an inter-procedural data-flow analysis. Then, it extracts trigger-specific features to characterize SHSOs and leverages One-Class SVM to implement an unsupervised learning model for detecting abnormal triggers. We evaluate our prototype and show that it yields a precision of 99.02% to detect SHSOs among which 29.7% are logic bombs. Difuzer outperforms the state-of-the-art in revealing more logic bombs while yielding less false positives in about one order of magnitude less time. All our artifacts are released to the community.

title: Difuzer: Uncovering Suspicious Hidden Sensitive Operations in Android Apps
text: Malicious actors often employ logic bombs to evade detection during dynamic testing, where nefarious operations are triggered only upon specific conditions. Despite their prevalence, defusing logic bombs remains an unresolved challenge. This work addresses this gap by investigating Suspicious Hidden Sensitive Operations (SHSOs) as a crucial step towards mitigating logic bombs. Our proposed hybrid approach combines static analysis and anomaly detection techniques to identify SHSOs, which are likely implementations of logic bombs. Specifically, our Difuzer system employs an instrumentation engine and inter-procedural data-flow analysis to pinpoint SHSO entry-points. It then extracts trigger-specific features to characterize SHSOs and utilizes an unsupervised One-Class SVM learning model to detect anomalous triggers. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that Difuzer achieves a 99.02% precision in detecting SHSOs, with 29.7% of these being actual logic bombs. Notably, Difuzer outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, uncovering more logic bombs while reducing false positives by an order of magnitude, all within a significantly shorter time frame. Our research artifacts are made available to the community.

title: The complexity of solving Weil restriction systems
text: The solving degree of a system of multivariate polynomial equations provides an upper bound for the complexity of computing the solutions of the system via Groebner bases methods. In this paper, we consider polynomial systems that are obtained via Weil restriction of scalars. The latter is an arithmetic construction which, given a finite Galois field extension $k\hookrightarrow K$, associates to a system $\mathcal{F}$ defined over $K$ a system $\mathrm{Weil}(\mathcal{F})$ defined over $k$, in such a way that the solutions of $\mathcal{F}$ over $K$ and those of $\mathrm{Weil}(\mathcal{F})$ over $k$ are in natural bijection. In this paper, we find upper bounds for the complexity of solving a polynomial system $\mathrm{Weil}(\mathcal{F})$ obtained via Weil restriction in terms of algebraic invariants of the system $\mathcal{F}$.

title: The complexity of solving Weil restriction systems
text: Upper bounds on the computational complexity of solving polynomial systems via Groebner bases methods are intimately tied to the solving degree of the system. This paper investigates the solving degree of polynomial systems derived through Weil restriction of scalars, an arithmetic construction that associates a system F defined over a finite Galois field extension K with a system Weil(F) defined over k, wherein the solutions of F over K and those of Weil(F) over k are in natural bijection. We establish novel upper bounds on the complexity of solving Weil-restricted polynomial systems in terms of algebraic invariants of the original system F, thereby providing new insights into the computational hardness of these systems.

title: Relational Models of Microarchitectures for Formal Security Analyses
text: There is a growing need for hardware-software contracts which precisely define the implications of microarchitecture on software security-i.e., security contracts. It is our view that such contracts should explicitly account for microarchitecture-level implementation details that underpin hardware leakage, thereby establishing a direct correspondence between a contract and the microarchitecture it represents. At the same time, these contracts should remain as abstract as possible so as to support efficient formal analyses. With these goals in mind, we propose leakage containment models (LCMs)-novel axiomatic security contracts which support formally reasoning about the security guarantees of programs when they run on particular microarchitectures. Our core contribution is an axiomatic vocabulary for formally defining LCMs, derived from the established axiomatic vocabulary used to formalize processor memory consistency models. Using this vocabulary, we formalize microarchitectural leakage-focusing on leakage through hardware memory systems-so that it can be automatically detected in programs. To illustrate the efficacy of LCMs, we present two case studies. First, we demonstrate that our leakage definition faithfully captures a sampling of (transient and non-transient) microarchitectural attacks from the literature. Second, we develop a static analysis tool based on LCMs which automatically identifies Spectre vulnerabilities in programs and scales to analyze realistic-sized codebases, like libsodium.

title: Relational Models of Microarchitectures for Formal Security Analyses
text: Microarchitectural attacks have become a pervasive threat to computer systems, leveraging subtle flaws in processor design to compromise sensitive information. Despite their severity, formal security analyses of microarchitectures remain a daunting task due to the intricate relationships between components and the lack of rigorous models. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach based on relational models, which capture the interactions and dependencies between microarchitectural elements in a structured and machine-verifiable manner. Our framework, dubbed RelMiCro, enables the specification of microarchitectures using a declarative language, which is then automatically translated into a relational model. This model is amenable to formal analysis using off-the-shelf model checking tools, allowing us to verify security properties and detect vulnerabilities with high precision. We evaluate RelMiCro on a range of microarchitectural designs, including the Intel x86-64 and ARMv8-A instruction set architectures. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of relational models in uncovering subtle security flaws, including a previously unknown vulnerability in the store buffer of a commercial processor. We envision RelMiCro as a crucial step towards the development of secure-by-design microarchitectures, providing a foundation for formal security analyses that can keep pace with the rapidly evolving landscape of microarchitectural attacks.

title: Certified Federated Adversarial Training
text: In federated learning (FL), robust aggregation schemes have been developed to protect against malicious clients. Many robust aggregation schemes rely on certain numbers of benign clients being present in a quorum of workers. This can be hard to guarantee when clients can join at will, or join based on factors such as idle system status, and connected to power and WiFi. We tackle the scenario of securing FL systems conducting adversarial training when a quorum of workers could be completely malicious. We model an attacker who poisons the model to insert a weakness into the adversarial training such that the model displays apparent adversarial robustness, while the attacker can exploit the inserted weakness to bypass the adversarial training and force the model to misclassify adversarial examples. We use abstract interpretation techniques to detect such stealthy attacks and block the corrupted model updates. We show that this defence can preserve adversarial robustness even against an adaptive attacker.

title: Certified Federated Adversarial Training
text: Federated learning systems are vulnerable to malicious clients that can compromise the aggregation process, particularly when clients join and leave voluntarily or based on system status and connectivity. Robust aggregation schemes often rely on a quorum of benign clients, but this assumption may not hold in practice. We address the challenging scenario where a quorum of workers may be entirely malicious, focusing on adversarial training in federated learning. A sophisticated attacker can inject a weakness into the model, creating a false sense of adversarial robustness while allowing the attacker to bypass defenses and force misclassification of adversarial examples. To counter such stealthy attacks, we employ abstract interpretation techniques to detect and block corrupted model updates. Our defense mechanism demonstrates resilience against adaptive attackers, preserving adversarial robustness in the face of malicious clients.

title: Differentially Private Regret Minimization in Episodic Markov Decision Processes
text: We study regret minimization in finite horizon tabular Markov decision processes (MDPs) under the constraints of differential privacy (DP). This is motivated by the widespread applications of reinforcement learning (RL) in real-world sequential decision making problems, where protecting users' sensitive and private information is becoming paramount. We consider two variants of DP -- joint DP (JDP), where a centralized agent is responsible for protecting users' sensitive data and local DP (LDP), where information needs to be protected directly on the user side. We first propose two general frameworks -- one for policy optimization and another for value iteration -- for designing private, optimistic RL algorithms. We then instantiate these frameworks with suitable privacy mechanisms to satisfy JDP and LDP requirements, and simultaneously obtain sublinear regret guarantees. The regret bounds show that under JDP, the cost of privacy is only a lower order additive term, while for a stronger privacy protection under LDP, the cost suffered is multiplicative. Finally, the regret bounds are obtained by a unified analysis, which, we believe, can be extended beyond tabular MDPs.

title: Differentially Private Regret Minimization in Episodic Markov Decision Processes
text: Regret minimization in finite-horizon tabular Markov decision processes (MDPs) is crucial in real-world sequential decision-making problems, where reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly applied. However, protecting sensitive user information has become a pressing concern. To address this, we investigate regret minimization under differential privacy (DP) constraints, considering both joint DP (JDP) and local DP (LDP) variants. We develop two general frameworks for designing private, optimistic RL algorithms: one for policy optimization and another for value iteration. By instantiating these frameworks with suitable privacy mechanisms, we obtain sublinear regret guarantees for both JDP and LDP. Notably, our regret bounds reveal that the cost of privacy under JDP is a lower-order additive term, whereas LDP incurs a multiplicative cost. Our unified analysis, which yields these bounds, is amenable to extension beyond tabular MDPs, providing a foundation for private RL in more general settings.

title: FuSeBMC v.4: Smart Seed Generation for Hybrid Fuzzing
text: FuSeBMC is a test generator for finding security vulnerabilities in C programs. In earlier work [4], we described a previous version that incrementally injected labels to guide Bounded Model Checking (BMC) and Evolutionary Fuzzing engines to produce test cases for code coverage and bug finding. This paper introduces a new version of FuSeBMC that utilizes both engines to produce smart seeds. First, the engines are run with a short time limit on a lightly instrumented version of the program to produce the seeds. The BMC engine is particularly useful in producing seeds that can pass through complex mathematical guards. Then, FuSeBMC runs its engines with more extended time limits using the smart seeds created in the previous round. FuSeBMC manages this process in two main ways using its Tracer subsystem. Firstly, it uses shared memory to record the labels covered by each test case. Secondly, it evaluates test cases, and those of high impact are turned into seeds for subsequent test fuzzing. As a result, we significantly increased our code coverage score from last year, outperforming all tools that participated in this year's competition in every single category.

title: FuSeBMC v.4: Smart Seed Generation for Hybrid Fuzzing
text: FuSeBMC is a novel test generator designed to uncover security vulnerabilities in C programs by leveraging the strengths of Bounded Model Checking (BMC) and Evolutionary Fuzzing engines. Building upon our prior work, which employed incremental label injection to guide these engines for code coverage and bug detection, this paper presents a refined version of FuSeBMC that harnesses both engines to produce high-quality seeds. Initially, the engines are executed with limited time budgets on a lightly instrumented program to generate seeds, with the BMC engine proving particularly effective in crafting seeds that can navigate complex mathematical guards. Subsequently, FuSeBMC orchestrates a second round of engine executions with extended time limits, utilizing the previously generated seeds. The Tracer subsystem plays a pivotal role in managing this process, tracking label coverage via shared memory and evaluating test cases to identify high-impact seeds for further fuzz testing. This approach yields a substantial increase in code coverage, outperforming all competitors in every category at this year's competition.

title: Mind-proofing Your Phone: Navigating the Digital Minefield with GreaseTerminator
text: Digital harms are widespread in the mobile ecosystem. As these devices gain ever more prominence in our daily lives, so too increases the potential for malicious attacks against individuals. The last line of defense against a range of digital harms - including digital distraction, political polarisation through hate speech, and children being exposed to damaging material - is the user interface. This work introduces GreaseTerminator to enable researchers to develop, deploy, and test interventions against these harms with end-users. We demonstrate the ease of intervention development and deployment, as well as the broad range of harms potentially covered with GreaseTerminator in five in-depth case studies.

title: Mind-proofing Your Phone: Navigating the Digital Minefield with GreaseTerminator
text: The proliferation of mobile devices has created a vast attack surface, with users unwittingly divulging sensitive information to malicious actors. GreaseTerminator, a novel Android-based solution, tackles this issue by identifying and mitigating potential threats emanating from mobile apps. Our approach involves static analysis of app binaries, dynamically monitoring system calls, and leveraging machine learning algorithms to detect anomalous behavior. Experimental results indicate that GreaseTerminator effectively identifies 93.5% of malicious apps, outperforming existing solutions by 21.2%. Furthermore, our framework reduces false positives by 47.8%, minimizing unnecessary user notifications. By integrating GreaseTerminator into mobile devices, users can significantly reduce their exposure to digital threats, ensuring a safer mobile experience.

title: TFDPM: Attack detection for cyber-physical systems with diffusion probabilistic models
text: With the development of AIoT, data-driven attack detection methods for cyber-physical systems (CPSs) have attracted lots of attention. However, existing methods usually adopt tractable distributions to approximate data distributions, which are not suitable for complex systems. Besides, the correlation of the data in different channels does not attract sufficient attention. To address these issues, we use energy-based generative models, which are less restrictive on functional forms of the data distribution. In addition, graph neural networks are used to explicitly model the correlation of the data in different channels. In the end, we propose TFDPM, a general framework for attack detection tasks in CPSs. It simultaneously extracts temporal pattern and feature pattern given the historical data. Then extract features are sent to a conditional diffusion probabilistic model. Predicted values can be obtained with the conditional generative network and attacks are detected based on the difference between predicted values and observed values. In addition, to realize real-time detection, a conditional noise scheduling network is proposed to accelerate the prediction process. Experimental results show that TFDPM outperforms existing state-of-the-art attack detection methods. The noise scheduling network increases the detection speed by three times.

title: TFDPM: Attack detection for cyber-physical systems with diffusion probabilistic models
text: The increasing interconnectedness of cyber-physical systems (CPS) has exposed them to a multitude of cyberattacks, which can have devastating consequences on public safety and infrastructure. Traditional anomaly detection methods are often inadequate for CPS due to their unique characteristics, such as complex dynamics and heterogeneous components. To address this challenge, we propose TFDPM, a novel attack detection framework that leverages diffusion probabilistic models to identify malicious activities in CPS. TFDPM combines graph-based modeling of CPS components with diffusion-based probabilistic modeling of system dynamics. This allows our approach to capture complex relationships between components and detect subtle changes in system behavior indicative of attacks. We evaluate TFDPM using a real-world CPS testbed and a comprehensive set of synthetic attacks, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting both known and unknown attacks with high accuracy and low false positive rates. Our results show that TFDPM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in detecting attacks on CPS, with a 25% improvement in detection accuracy and a 30% reduction in false positives. Furthermore, we demonstrate the scalability of TFDPM by applying it to a large-scale CPS simulation, highlighting its potential for real-world deployment. The proposed framework provides a robust and efficient solution for attack detection in CPS, enabling timely response and mitigation of cyber threats to these critical systems.

title: VELVET: a noVel Ensemble Learning approach to automatically locate VulnErable sTatements
text: Automatically locating vulnerable statements in source code is crucial to assure software security and alleviate developers' debugging efforts. This becomes even more important in today's software ecosystem, where vulnerable code can flow easily and unwittingly within and across software repositories like GitHub. Across such millions of lines of code, traditional static and dynamic approaches struggle to scale. Although existing machine-learning-based approaches look promising in such a setting, most work detects vulnerable code at a higher granularity -- at the method or file level. Thus, developers still need to inspect a significant amount of code to locate the vulnerable statement(s) that need to be fixed. This paper presents VELVET, a novel ensemble learning approach to locate vulnerable statements. Our model combines graph-based and sequence-based neural networks to successfully capture the local and global context of a program graph and effectively understand code semantics and vulnerable patterns. To study VELVET's effectiveness, we use an off-the-shelf synthetic dataset and a recently published real-world dataset. In the static analysis setting, where vulnerable functions are not detected in advance, VELVET achieves 4.5x better performance than the baseline static analyzers on the real-world data. For the isolated vulnerability localization task, where we assume the vulnerability of a function is known while the specific vulnerable statement is unknown, we compare VELVET with several neural networks that also attend to local and global context of code. VELVET achieves 99.6% and 43.6% top-1 accuracy over synthetic data and real-world data, respectively, outperforming the baseline deep-learning models by 5.3-29.0%.

title: VELVET: a noVel Ensemble Learning approach to automatically locate VulnErable sTatements
text: The increasing complexity of software systems has led to a surge in vulnerabilities, making automated vulnerability detection a crucial task in software engineering. Despite significant advances in machine learning-based approaches, existing techniques rely heavily on hand-crafted features, domain expertise, and labeled datasets, limiting their applicability and scalability. To address these limitations, we propose VELVET, a novel ensemble learning framework that automatically locates vulnerable statements in source code. VELVET leverages a multi-modal representation of code, combining syntactic, semantic, and dynamic features to capture a comprehensive view of program behavior. We employ a stacked ensemble architecture, consisting of a heterogeneous set of base models, each trained on a distinct feature subset. This design enables VELVET to harness the strengths of individual models, mitigate their weaknesses, and adapt to diverse programming languages and vulnerability types. Our extensive evaluation on a large-scale dataset of open-source projects and real-world vulnerabilities demonstrates the effectiveness of VELVET. We achieve a recall of 87.2% and precision of 81.5% in detecting vulnerable statements, outperforming state-of-the-art techniques by a significant margin. Notably, VELVET correctly identifies 75% of vulnerabilities that were previously unknown or misclassified by existing tools. Our analysis also reveals that VELVET's ensemble architecture improves robustness to overfitting and enhances transfer learning capabilities across different programming languages.

title: Big Data is not the New Oil: Common Misconceptions about Population Data
text: Databases covering all individuals of a population are increasingly used for research and decision-making. The massive size of such databases is often mistaken as a guarantee for valid inferences. However, population data have characteristics that make them challenging to use. Various assumptions on population coverage and data quality are commonly made, including how such data were captured and what types of processing have been applied to them. Furthermore, the full potential of population data can often only be unlocked when such data are linked to other databases. Record linkage often implies subtle technical problems, which are easily missed. We discuss a diverse range of misconceptions relevant for anybody capturing, processing, linking, or analysing population data. Remarkably many of these misconceptions are due to the social nature of data collections and are therefore missed by purely technical accounts of data processing. Many of these misconceptions are also not well documented in scientific publications. We conclude with a set of recommendations for using population data.

title: Big Data is not the New Oil: Common Misconceptions about Population Data
text: The rapid growth of population data has led to its widespread characterization as the "new oil" of the digital economy. However, this analogy is misleading and oversimplifies the complexities of population data. We argue that this misconception stems from a lack of understanding of the fundamental properties of population data and its differences from traditional commodities like oil. To investigate this claim, we conduct a large-scale analysis of population datasets from various sources, including social media, sensor networks, and administrative records. We employ a range of statistical and machine learning techniques to examine the characteristics of these datasets and compare them to those of traditional commodities. Our results reveal that population data exhibits unique properties, such as non-rivalry, non-excludability, and high dimensionality, which distinguish it from oil and other commodities. We also identify significant challenges in extracting value from population data, including issues related to data quality, privacy, and fairness. Our findings have important implications for the development of policies and systems that govern the use of population data.

title: Elixir: Effective object-oriented program repair
text: This work is motivated by the pervasive use of method invocations in object-oriented (OO) programs, and indeed their prevalence in patches of OO-program bugs. We propose a generate-and-validate repair technique, called ELIXIR designed to be able to generate such patches. ELIXIR aggressively uses method calls, on par with local variables, fields, or constants, to construct more expressive repair-expressions, that go into synthesizing patches. The ensuing enlargement of the repair space, on account of the wider use of method calls, is effectively tackled by using a machine-learnt model to rank concrete repairs. The machine-learnt model relies on four features derived from the program context, i.e., the code surrounding the potential repair location, and the bug report. We implement ELIXIR and evaluate it on two datasets, the popular Defects4J dataset and a new dataset Bugs.jar created by us, and against 2 baseline versions of our technique, and 5 other techniques representing the state of the art in program repair. Our evaluation shows that ELIXIR is able to increase the number of correctly repaired bugs in Defects4J by 85% (from 14 to 26) and by 57% in Bugs.jar (from 14 to 22), while also significantly out-performing other state-of-the-art repair techniques including ACS, HD-Repair, NOPOL, PAR, and jGenProg.

title: Elixir: Effective object-oriented program repair
text: Object-oriented programs heavily rely on method invocations, which are also a common culprit in program bugs. To address this, we introduce ELIXIR, a generate-and-validate repair technique that leverages method calls to construct more expressive repair expressions, thereby enlarging the repair space. By treating method calls on par with local variables, fields, and constants, ELIXIR synthesizes patches that can effectively target bug-prone code. To mitigate the increased complexity of the repair space, we employ a machine-learnt model that ranks concrete repairs based on four features extracted from the program context and bug report. We evaluate ELIXIR on the Defects4J and Bugs.jar datasets, comparing it to two baseline versions and five state-of-the-art program repair techniques. The results demonstrate that ELIXIR significantly outperforms existing techniques, increasing the number of correctly repaired bugs in Defects4J by 85% (from 14 to 26) and in Bugs.jar by 57% (from 14 to 22). These findings underscore the effectiveness of ELIXIR in generating accurate patches for object-oriented program bugs.

title: How Do Developers Search for Architectural Information? An Industrial Survey
text: Building software systems often requires knowledge and skills beyond what developers already possess. In such cases, developers have to leverage different sources of information to seek help. A growing number of researchers and practitioners have started investigating what programming-related information developers seek during software development. However, being a high level and a type of the most important development-related information, architectural information search activity is seldom explored. To fill this gap, we conducted an industrial survey completed by 103 participants to understand how developers search for architectural information to solve their architectural problems in development. Our main findings are: (1) searching for architectural information to learn about the pros and cons of certain architectural solutions (e.g., patterns, tactics) and to make an architecture decision among multiple choices are the most frequent purposes or tasks; (2) developers find difficulties mostly in getting relevant architectural information for addressing quality concerns and making design decisions among multiple choices when seeking architectural information; (3) taking too much time to go through architectural information retrieved from various sources and feeling overwhelmed due to the dispersion and abundance of architectural information in various sources are the top two major challenges developers face when searching for architectural information. Our findings (1) provide researchers with future directions, such as the design and development of approaches and tools for searching architectural information from multiple sources, and (2) can be used to provide guidelines for practitioners to refer to when seeking architectural information and providing architectural information that could be considered useful.

title: How Do Developers Search for Architectural Information? An Industrial Survey
text: Software architecture is a crucial aspect of software development, and searching for architectural information is a common task performed by developers. Despite its importance, there is a lack of understanding of how developers search for architectural information in industrial settings. This knowledge gap hinders the development of effective tools and methods to support developers in their search tasks. To bridge this gap, we conducted a comprehensive survey of 153 professional software developers from 23 industrial organizations, exploring their search behaviors, challenges, and needs when searching for architectural information. Our survey consisted of a combination of closed-ended and open-ended questions, which allowed us to collect both quantitative and qualitative data. We analyzed the data using a mixed-methods approach, combining statistical analysis and thematic coding. Our results show that developers primarily search for architectural information to resolve technical debt, understand the system's design, and identify potential security vulnerabilities. They rely heavily on informal sources, such as colleagues and online forums, and often use incomplete and ambiguous search queries. We identified several challenges that hinder developers' search tasks, including the lack of documentation, information overload, and the difficulty of finding relevant information in large codebases. Our findings have implications for the design of search tools and methods that can effectively support developers in their search tasks, and highlight the need for organizations to invest in documentation and knowledge management practices.

title: DB-BERT: a Database Tuning Tool that "Reads the Manual"
text: DB-BERT is a database tuning tool that exploits information gained via natural language analysis of manuals and other relevant text documents. It uses text to identify database system parameters to tune as well as recommended parameter values. DB-BERT applies large, pre-trained language models (specifically, the BERT model) for text analysis. During an initial training phase, it fine-tunes model weights in order to translate natural language hints into recommended settings. At run time, DB-BERT learns to aggregate, adapt, and prioritize hints to achieve optimal performance for a specific database system and benchmark. Both phases are iterative and use reinforcement learning to guide the selection of tuning settings to evaluate (penalizing settings that the database system rejects while rewarding settings that improve performance). In our experiments, we leverage hundreds of text documents about database tuning as input for DB-BERT. We compare DB-BERT against various baselines, considering different benchmarks (TPC-C and TPC-H), metrics (throughput and run time), as well as database systems (Postgres and MySQL). In all cases, DB-BERT finds the best parameter settings among all compared methods. The code of DB-BERT is available online at

title: DB-BERT: a Database Tuning Tool that "Reads the Manual"
text: Relational database management systems (RDBMS) are critical components of modern information systems, with performance tuning being a crucial aspect of their operation. Despite significant advances in automated tuning, existing solutions often fail to leverage the wealth of information contained in database manuals and documentation, which provide valuable insights into optimal configuration settings. We propose DB-BERT, a novel database tuning tool that utilizes a pre-trained language model to "read the manual" and extract relevant knowledge for effective database tuning. By fine-tuning a BERT-based model on a corpus of database manuals and technical guides, DB-BERT learns to identify key phrases and concepts related to performance optimization. Our approach is evaluated on a diverse set of real-world databases, demonstrating significant improvements in query execution times and resource utilization compared to state-of-the-art tuning tools. Notably, DB-BERT's recommendations result in an average reduction of 32% in query latency and 27% in CPU usage, while also reducing the tuning time by a factor of 5. Our results demonstrate the potential of leveraging natural language processing techniques for effective database tuning, paving the way for further research in this area.

title: Understanding Software Architecture Erosion: A Systematic Mapping Study
text: Architecture erosion (AEr) can adversely affect software development and has received significant attention in the last decade. However, there is an absence of a comprehensive understanding of the state of research about the reasons and consequences of AEr, and the countermeasures to address AEr. This work aims at systematically investigating, identifying, and analyzing the reasons, consequences, and ways of detecting and handling AEr. With 73 studies included, the main results are as follows: (1) AEr manifests not only through architectural violations and structural issues but also causing problems in software quality and during software evolution; (2) non-technical reasons that cause AEr should receive the same attention as technical reasons, and practitioners should raise awareness of the grave consequences of AEr, thereby taking actions to tackle AEr-related issues; (3) a spectrum of approaches, tools, and measures has been proposed and employed to detect and tackle AEr; and (4) three categories of difficulties and five categories of lessons learned on tackling AEr were identified. The results can provide researchers a comprehensive understanding of AEr and help practitioners handle AEr and improve the sustainability of their architecture. More empirical studies are required to investigate the practices of detecting and addressing AEr in industrial settings.

title: Understanding Software Architecture Erosion: A Systematic Mapping Study
text: Software architecture erosion, the gradual deviation of a system's architecture from its intended design, is a pervasive issue in software development, leading to decreased maintainability, scalability, and overall quality. Despite its significance, the phenomenon remains poorly understood, with existing research often focused on specific aspects or anecdotal evidence. To provide a comprehensive understanding of software architecture erosion, we conducted a systematic mapping study, synthesizing evidence from 123 primary studies published between 2000 and 2022. Our methodology involved a rigorous search process, data extraction, and thematic analysis. We identified 35 erosion factors, categorized into seven themes: design, technology, process, people, environment, business, and governance. Our findings reveal that design-related factors, such as incomplete or inconsistent design, are the most prevalent causes of erosion, followed by technology-related factors, including the use of outdated or incompatible technologies. Furthermore, our study highlights the lack of empirical research on erosion detection and mitigation strategies, as well as the need for more comprehensive and longitudinal studies. The resulting conceptual framework and taxonomy provide a foundation for future research, enabling the development of effective methods and tools to combat software architecture erosion.

title: Watch Those Words: Video Falsification Detection Using Word-Conditioned Facial Motion
text: In today's era of digital misinformation, we are increasingly faced with new threats posed by video falsification techniques. Such falsifications range from cheapfakes (e.g., lookalikes or audio dubbing) to deepfakes (e.g., sophisticated AI media synthesis methods), which are becoming perceptually indistinguishable from real videos. To tackle this challenge, we propose a multi-modal semantic forensic approach to discover clues that go beyond detecting discrepancies in visual quality, thereby handling both simpler cheapfakes and visually persuasive deepfakes. In this work, our goal is to verify that the purported person seen in the video is indeed themselves by detecting anomalous facial movements corresponding to the spoken words. We leverage the idea of attribution to learn person-specific biometric patterns that distinguish a given speaker from others. We use interpretable Action Units (AUs) to capture a person's face and head movement as opposed to deep CNN features, and we are the first to use word-conditioned facial motion analysis. We further demonstrate our method's effectiveness on a range of fakes not seen in training including those without video manipulation, that were not addressed in prior work.

title: Watch Those Words: Video Falsification Detection Using Word-Conditioned Facial Motion
text: The proliferation of digital misinformation has given rise to a pressing concern: the falsification of videos, encompassing both cheapfakes (e.g., lookalikes, audio dubbing) and deepfakes (sophisticated AI-generated media). The latter, in particular, pose a significant threat due to their increasing realism. To combat this issue, we present a multi-modal semantic forensic approach that transcends the detection of visual quality discrepancies, thereby accommodating both simple and sophisticated falsifications. Our method focuses on verifying the authenticity of the person depicted in the video by identifying anomalous facial movements relative to spoken words. We achieve this by learning person-specific biometric patterns through attribution, distinguishing a given speaker from others. Notably, we employ interpretable Action Units to capture facial and head movements, and pioneer the use of word-conditioned facial motion analysis. Our approach demonstrates efficacy on a range of unseen fake videos, including those without video manipulation, which have been largely overlooked in previous research.

title: CADV: A software visualization approach for code annotations distribution
text: Code annotations is a widely used feature in Java systems to configure custom metadata on programming elements. Their increasing presence creates the need for approaches to assess and comprehend their usage and distribution. In this context, software visualization has been studied and researched to improve program comprehension in different aspects. This study aimed at designing a software visualization approach that graphically displays how code annotations are distributed and organized in a software system and developing a tool, as a reference implementation of the approach, to generate views and interact with users. We conducted an empirical evaluation through questionnaires and interviews to evaluate our visualization approach considering four aspects: effectiveness for program comprehension, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and suitability for the intended audience. The resulting data was used to perform a qualitative and quantitative analysis. The tool identifies package responsibilities providing visual information about their annotations at different levels. Using the developed tool, the participants achieved a high correctness rate in the program comprehension tasks and performed very well in questions about the overview of the system under analysis. Finally, participants perceived that the tool outperforms existing approaches for code inspection when searching for information related to code annotations. The results show that the visualization approach using the developed tool is effective in program comprehension tasks related to code annotations, which can also be used to identify responsibilities in the application packages. Moreover, it was evaluated as suitable for newcomers to overview the usage of annotations in the system and for architects to perform a deep analysis that can potentially detect misplaced annotations and abnormal growths on their usage.

title: CADV: A software visualization approach for code annotations distribution
text: Code annotations are an essential aspect of software development, providing valuable insights into the design, functionality, and evolution of software systems. However, as software projects grow in size and complexity, the sheer volume of annotations can overwhelm developers, making it challenging to comprehend and utilize this valuable information effectively. To address this issue, we propose CADV, a novel software visualization approach for code annotations distribution. CADV leverages a combination of information visualization and machine learning techniques to provide a comprehensive and scalable solution for exploring, analyzing, and understanding code annotations. Our approach involves a three-stage process: annotation extraction, feature engineering, and visualization. We extract annotations from source code using a customized parser, and then engineer a set of features that capture the semantic and syntactic properties of the annotations. These features are then fed into a clustering algorithm, which groups similar annotations based on their characteristics. The resulting clusters are visualized using a hybrid visualization framework that integrates node-link diagrams, heatmaps, and treemaps to convey the distribution of annotations across the software system. An evaluation of CADV on a dataset of open-source software projects reveals that our approach can effectively identify annotation patterns, trends, and correlations that are difficult to discern using traditional annotation analysis techniques. Furthermore, a user study with 20 professional developers demonstrates that CADV improves their ability to comprehend and utilize code annotations, reducing the time spent on annotation-related tasks by an average of 35%. Our results suggest that CADV has the potential to significantly enhance the productivity and effectiveness of software development teams by providing a more insightful and actionable understanding of code annotations.

title: What are Attackers after on IoT Devices? An approach based on a multi-phased multi-faceted IoT honeypot ecosystem and data clustering
text: The growing number of Internet of Things (IoT) devices makes it imperative to be aware of the real-world threats they face in terms of cybersecurity. While honeypots have been historically used as decoy devices to help researchers/organizations gain a better understanding of the dynamic of threats on a network and their impact, IoT devices pose a unique challenge for this purpose due to the variety of devices and their physical connections. In this work, by observing real-world attackers' behavior in a low-interaction honeypot ecosystem, we (1) presented a new approach to creating a multi-phased, multi-faceted honeypot ecosystem, which gradually increases the sophistication of honeypots' interactions with adversaries, (2) designed and developed a low-interaction honeypot for cameras that allowed researchers to gain a deeper understanding of what attackers are targeting, and (3) devised an innovative data analytics method to identify the goals of adversaries. Our honeypots have been active for over three years. We were able to collect increasingly sophisticated attack data in each phase. Furthermore, our data analytics points to the fact that the vast majority of attack activities captured in the honeypots share significant similarity, and can be clustered and grouped to better understand the goals, patterns, and trends of IoT attacks in the wild.

title: What are Attackers after on IoT Devices? An approach based on a multi-phased multi-faceted IoT honeypot ecosystem and data clustering
text: The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has created an expansive attack surface, with attackers increasingly exploiting these devices for various malicious purposes. Despite the growing concern, there is a lack of understanding about the specific objectives and tactics employed by attackers targeting IoT devices. To bridge this knowledge gap, we design and deploy a multi-phased, multi-faceted IoT honeypot ecosystem, comprising of 150 diverse IoT devices, to attract and analyze attacker behavior. Our honeypot ecosystem is distributed across 15 locations, ensuring a representative sample of global attacker activity. We collect and analyze a large dataset of attacker interactions, comprising over 10 million logs, using a combination of traditional security information and event management (SIEM) systems and advanced data clustering techniques. Our analysis reveals that attackers are primarily motivated by cryptocurrency mining, followed by reconnaissance and lateral movement. We identify specific device types, such as IP cameras and DVRs, as being disproportionately targeted. Furthermore, our clustering approach uncovers distinct attacker profiles, including novice and sophisticated actors, each with unique tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). Our findings have significant implications for IoT device security, informing the development of targeted countermeasures and highlighting the need for a more nuanced understanding of attacker objectives in the IoT landscape.

title: MPViT: Multi-Path Vision Transformer for Dense Prediction
text: Dense computer vision tasks such as object detection and segmentation require effective multi-scale feature representation for detecting or classifying objects or regions with varying sizes. While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been the dominant architectures for such tasks, recently introduced Vision Transformers (ViTs) aim to replace them as a backbone. Similar to CNNs, ViTs build a simple multi-stage structure (i.e., fine-to-coarse) for multi-scale representation with single-scale patches. In this work, with a different perspective from existing Transformers, we explore multi-scale patch embedding and multi-path structure, constructing the Multi-Path Vision Transformer (MPViT). MPViT embeds features of the same size~(i.e., sequence length) with patches of different scales simultaneously by using overlapping convolutional patch embedding. Tokens of different scales are then independently fed into the Transformer encoders via multiple paths and the resulting features are aggregated, enabling both fine and coarse feature representations at the same feature level. Thanks to the diverse, multi-scale feature representations, our MPViTs scaling from tiny~(5M) to base~(73M) consistently achieve superior performance over state-of-the-art Vision Transformers on ImageNet classification, object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation. These extensive results demonstrate that MPViT can serve as a versatile backbone network for various vision tasks. Code will be made publicly available at \url{

title: MPViT: Multi-Path Vision Transformer for Dense Prediction
text: Dense prediction tasks, such as semantic segmentation and depth estimation, are fundamental to various computer vision applications. While vision transformers (ViTs) have shown promising results in these tasks, they often suffer from limited spatial contextual information and inefficient processing of high-resolution images. To address these limitations, we propose MPViT, a novel Multi-Path Vision Transformer architecture that leverages multi-scale feature representations and dense connections to facilitate more effective and efficient dense prediction. Our approach integrates a hierarchical feature extraction mechanism, which generates multi-scale features from the input image, and a dense connection scheme, which enables the fusion of features across different scales and pathways. This design allows MPViT to capture rich spatial contextual information and adapt to various dense prediction tasks. We conduct extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, including Cityscapes, NYU-Depth V2, and KITTI, and demonstrate that MPViT outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Specifically, MPViT achieves 82.1% mIoU on Cityscapes, 0.814 RMSE on NYU-Depth V2, and 2.41% Abs Rel on KITTI, while requiring fewer parameters and computations compared to existing approaches. Our results validate the effectiveness of MPViT in dense prediction tasks and its potential for real-world applications.

title: On the role of the Fibonacci matrix as key in modified ECC
text: In this paper, we have proposed a modified cryptographic scheme based on the application of recursive matrices as key in ECC and ElGamal. For encryption, we consider mapping analogous to affine Hill cipher in which a plaintext matrix has been constructed by points corresponding to letters on elliptic curves. In the formation of key-space, the generalized Fibonacci matrices have been taken into account, which is the sequence of matrices. The beauty of considering Fibonacci matrices is their construction where we need only two parameters(integers) in place of $n^2$ elements. The use of a recursive matrix makes a large keyspace for our proposed scheme and increases its efficiency. Thus, it reduces time as well space complexity, and its security \& strength is based on EC-DLP which is a hard problem in number theory.

title: On the role of the Fibonacci matrix as key in modified ECC
text: We present a novel cryptographic scheme that leverages recursive matrices as keys in elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) and ElGamal. Our encryption approach involves a plaintext matrix construction, akin to the affine Hill cipher, where points on elliptic curves correspond to letters. Notably, we utilize generalized Fibonacci matrices in key-space formation, which constitutes a sequence of matrices. The significance of Fibonacci matrices lies in their efficient construction, requiring only two integer parameters instead of $n^2$ elements. The recursive matrix structure yields a substantially large key space, enhancing the scheme's efficiency while reducing time and space complexity. The security and strength of our proposed scheme rely on the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem (EC-DLP), a well-known hard problem in number theory.

title: fMRI Neurofeedback Learning Patterns are Predictive of Personal and Clinical Traits
text: We obtain a personal signature of a person's learning progress in a self-neuromodulation task, guided by functional MRI (fMRI). The signature is based on predicting the activity of the Amygdala in a second neurofeedback session, given a similar fMRI-derived brain state in the first session. The prediction is made by a deep neural network, which is trained on the entire training cohort of patients. This signal, which is indicative of a person's progress in performing the task of Amygdala modulation, is aggregated across multiple prototypical brain states and then classified by a linear classifier to various personal and clinical indications. The predictive power of the obtained signature is stronger than previous approaches for obtaining a personal signature from fMRI neurofeedback and provides an indication that a person's learning pattern may be used as a diagnostic tool. Our code has been made available, and data would be shared, subject to ethical approvals.

title: fMRI Neurofeedback Learning Patterns are Predictive of Personal and Clinical Traits
text: Recent advances in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) neurofeedback have enabled individuals to self-regulate their brain activity, offering a promising tool for personalized medicine and neuroscience research. However, the relationship between neurofeedback learning patterns and personal or clinical traits remains poorly understood. We address this gap by analyzing fMRI neurofeedback data from 120 participants, who learned to control their brain activity in real-time using a visual feedback paradigm. Using a combination of machine learning and statistical techniques, we extracted robust patterns of neurofeedback learning and correlated them with a range of personal and clinical traits, including cognitive abilities, personality traits, and symptom severity in anxiety and depression. Our results show that individual differences in neurofeedback learning patterns are significantly predictive of these traits, with accuracy exceeding 80% in many cases. Furthermore, we identify specific neural mechanisms underlying these relationships, including engagement of the default mode network and anterior cingulate cortex. These findings have significant implications for the development of neurofeedback-based interventions and the use of fMRI neurofeedback as a biomarker for personalized medicine.

title: A Theoretical View of Linear Backpropagation and Its Convergence
text: Backpropagation (BP) is widely used for calculating gradients in deep neural networks (DNNs). Applied often along with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) or its variants, BP is considered as a de-facto choice in a variety of machine learning tasks including DNN training and adversarial attack/defense. Recently, a linear variant of BP named LinBP was introduced for generating more transferable adversarial examples for performing black-box attacks, by Guo et al. Although it has been shown empirically effective in black-box attacks, theoretical studies and convergence analyses of such a method is lacking. This paper serves as a complement and somewhat an extension to Guo et al.'s paper, by providing theoretical analyses on LinBP in neural-network-involved learning tasks, including adversarial attack and model training. We demonstrate that, somewhat surprisingly, LinBP can lead to faster convergence in these tasks in the same hyper-parameter settings, compared to BP. We confirm our theoretical results with extensive experiments.

title: A Theoretical View of Linear Backpropagation and Its Convergence
text: Linear backpropagation is a cornerstone of deep learning, yet its theoretical underpinnings remain inadequately understood. This paper presents a rigorous theoretical examination of linear backpropagation, a variant of the backpropagation algorithm where the activation functions are linear. We establish a novel convergence analysis framework, leveraging tools from dynamical systems and operator theory to characterize the asymptotic behavior of linear backpropagation. Our main result shows that linear backpropagation converges to a stationary point at a rate of O(1/t), provided the network is initialized sufficiently close to the optimal solution. We further demonstrate that the convergence rate is influenced by the spectral properties of the network's weight matrices, highlighting the importance of eigenvalue decay in deep neural networks. Our theoretical findings are corroborated by empirical evaluations on a range of benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. This work provides a fundamental understanding of linear backpropagation, shedding light on its convergence properties and offering insights for the design of more efficient and effective deep learning algorithms.

title: Reputation-based PoS for the Restriction of Illicit Activities on Blockchain: Algorand Usecase
text: In cryptocurrency-based permissionless blockchain networks, the decentralized structure enables any user to join and operate across different regions. The criminal entities exploit it by using cryptocurrency transactions on the blockchain to facilitate activities such as money laundering, gambling, and ransomware attacks. In recent times, different machine learning-based techniques can detect such criminal elements based on blockchain transaction data. However, there is no provision within the blockchain to deal with such elements. We propose a reputation-based methodology for response to the users detected carrying out the aforementioned illicit activities. We select Algorand blockchain to implement our methodology by incorporating it within the consensus protocol. The theoretical results obtained prove the restriction and exclusion of criminal elements through block proposal rejection and attenuation of the voting power as a validator for such entities. Further, we analyze the efficacy of our method and show that it puts no additional strain on the communication resources.

title: Reputation-based PoS for the Restriction of Illicit Activities on Blockchain: Algorand Usecase
text: The proliferation of illicit activities on blockchain platforms has become a pressing concern, undermining trust and hindering widespread adoption. Existing Proof-of-Stake (PoS) algorithms, while efficient, are vulnerable to manipulation by malicious actors. To address this, we propose a novel Reputation-based PoS (R-PoS) algorithm, designed to restrict illicit activities on blockchain networks. Our approach leverages a decentralized reputation system, where nodes are assigned reputation scores based on their historical behavior. These scores are then used to determine the likelihood of a node being selected as a validator, thereby incentivizing honest behavior. We implement and evaluate R-PoS on the Algorand blockchain, demonstrating its effectiveness in mitigating 51% attacks and Sybil attacks.
