title: Input-Specific Robustness Certification for Randomized Smoothing
text: Randomized smoothing has emerged as a prominent certified defense, boasting high certified robustness and scalability. However, its practical feasibility is hindered by the substantial computational overhead associated with robustness certification, which relies heavily on large sample approximations for confidence interval estimation. The conventional approach, dubbed Input-Agnostic Sampling (IAS), universally fixes the sample size for confidence interval estimation, regardless of the input, leading to suboptimal Average Certified Radius (ACR)-runtime trade-offs. To address this limitation, we introduce Input-Specific Sampling (ISS), an adaptive acceleration strategy that dynamically adjusts the sampling size based on input characteristics, thereby achieving cost-effective robustness certification. Our method ensures universal control over certified radius decline resulting from ISS sample size reduction. Empirical evaluations on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet demonstrate that ISS accelerates certification by over three times, incurring a limited 0.05 certified radius cost. Moreover, ISS consistently outperforms IAS in terms of average certified radius across extensive hyperparameter settings, achieving an ACR of 0.958 on ImageNet (σ=1.0) in 250 minutes, surpassing the ACR of 0.917 attained by IAS under identical conditions.

title: Improved skin lesion recognition by a Self-Supervised Curricular Deep Learning approach
text: State-of-the-art deep learning approaches for skin lesion recognition often require pretraining on larger and more varied datasets, to overcome the generalization limitations derived from the reduced size of the skin lesion imaging datasets. ImageNet is often used as the pretraining dataset, but its transferring potential is hindered by the domain gap between the source dataset and the target dermatoscopic scenario. In this work, we introduce a novel pretraining approach that sequentially trains a series of Self-Supervised Learning pretext tasks and only requires the unlabeled skin lesion imaging data. We present a simple methodology to establish an ordering that defines a pretext task curriculum. For the multi-class skin lesion classification problem, and ISIC-2019 dataset, we provide experimental evidence showing that: i) a model pretrained by a curriculum of pretext tasks outperforms models pretrained by individual pretext tasks, and ii) a model pretrained by the optimal pretext task curriculum outperforms a model pretrained on ImageNet. We demonstrate that this performance gain is related to the fact that the curriculum of pretext tasks better focuses the attention of the final model on the skin lesion. Beyond performance improvement, this strategy allows for a large reduction in the training time with respect to ImageNet pretraining, which is especially advantageous for network architectures tailored for a specific problem.

title: Improved skin lesion recognition by a Self-Supervised Curricular Deep Learning approach
text: Deep learning models for skin lesion recognition often struggle to generalize due to the limited size of dermatoscopic imaging datasets, necessitating pretraining on larger, more diverse datasets. However, the domain gap between the pretraining dataset and the target scenario hinders the transferability of knowledge, even when using established datasets like ImageNet. This paper proposes a novel pretraining approach that leverages unlabeled skin lesion imaging data through a series of Self-Supervised Learning pretext tasks, which are carefully ordered to define a curriculum. Our methodology is evaluated on the ISIC-2019 dataset, where we demonstrate that a model pretrained on a curriculum of pretext tasks outperforms models pretrained on individual tasks, and even surpasses the performance of a model pretrained on ImageNet. These gains are attributed to the curriculum's ability to focus the model's attention on the skin lesion. Notably, this approach reduces training time significantly compared to ImageNet pretraining, making it particularly beneficial for specialized network architectures. By exploiting the structure of the pretext tasks, our method offers a promising solution for overcoming the limitations of small dermatoscopic datasets.

title: Reflash Dropout in Image Super-Resolution
text: Dropout is designed to relieve the overfitting problem in high-level vision tasks but is rarely applied in low-level vision tasks, like image super-resolution (SR). As a classic regression problem, SR exhibits a different behaviour as high-level tasks and is sensitive to the dropout operation. However, in this paper, we show that appropriate usage of dropout benefits SR networks and improves the generalization ability. Specifically, dropout is better embedded at the end of the network and is significantly helpful for the multi-degradation settings. This discovery breaks our common sense and inspires us to explore its working mechanism. We further use two analysis tools -- one is from recent network interpretation works, and the other is specially designed for this task. The analysis results provide side proofs to our experimental findings and show us a new perspective to understand SR networks.

title: Reflash Dropout in Image Super-Resolution
text: The efficacy of dropout in alleviating overfitting in high-level vision tasks is well established, yet its application in low-level vision tasks, such as image super-resolution (SR), has been largely overlooked. Unlike high-level tasks, SR exhibits distinct behavior as a classic regression problem, rendering it sensitive to dropout operations. Contrary to expectations, our research reveals that judicious employment of dropout in SR networks enhances their generalization capabilities. Notably, dropout is more effective when situated at the network's terminus and particularly beneficial in multi-degradation settings. This counterintuitive finding prompts an investigation into its underlying mechanisms. Through the lens of two analysis tools, including one drawn from recent network interpretation studies and another purpose-designed for this task, our analysis corroborates the experimental results and offers novel insights into SR networks.

title: Detect & Reject for Transferability of Black-box Adversarial Attacks Against Network Intrusion Detection Systems
text: In the last decade, the use of Machine Learning techniques in anomaly-based intrusion detection systems has seen much success. However, recent studies have shown that Machine learning in general and deep learning specifically are vulnerable to adversarial attacks where the attacker attempts to fool models by supplying deceptive input. Research in computer vision, where this vulnerability was first discovered, has shown that adversarial images designed to fool a specific model can deceive other machine learning models. In this paper, we investigate the transferability of adversarial network traffic against multiple machine learning-based intrusion detection systems. Furthermore, we analyze the robustness of the ensemble intrusion detection system, which is notorious for its better accuracy compared to a single model, against the transferability of adversarial attacks. Finally, we examine Detect & Reject as a defensive mechanism to limit the effect of the transferability property of adversarial network traffic against machine learning-based intrusion detection systems.

title: Detect & Reject for Transferability of Black-box Adversarial Attacks Against Network Intrusion Detection Systems
text: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) are crucial for safeguarding modern computer networks from cyber threats. However, recent studies have demonstrated that NIDS can be evaded by black-box adversarial attacks, which manipulate input traffic to mislead detection algorithms. A key concern is the transferability of these attacks across different NIDS, enabling adversaries to launch attacks without knowledge of the target system. This paper proposes Detect & Reject, a novel framework for evaluating the transferability of black-box adversarial attacks against NIDS. Our approach involves generating attacks using a surrogate NIDS, and then detecting and rejecting transferable attacks on a target NIDS. We employ a combination of machine learning and signal processing techniques to identify the most informative features for attack detection. Experimental results on a diverse set of NIDS demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, with a significant reduction in the success rate of transferable attacks. Our findings have important implications for the development of robust NIDS that can withstand sophisticated adversarial attacks.

title: NICE-SLAM: Neural Implicit Scalable Encoding for SLAM
text: Neural implicit representations have recently shown encouraging results in various domains, including promising progress in simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). Nevertheless, existing methods produce over-smoothed scene reconstructions and have difficulty scaling up to large scenes. These limitations are mainly due to their simple fully-connected network architecture that does not incorporate local information in the observations. In this paper, we present NICE-SLAM, a dense SLAM system that incorporates multi-level local information by introducing a hierarchical scene representation. Optimizing this representation with pre-trained geometric priors enables detailed reconstruction on large indoor scenes. Compared to recent neural implicit SLAM systems, our approach is more scalable, efficient, and robust. Experiments on five challenging datasets demonstrate competitive results of NICE-SLAM in both mapping and tracking quality. Project page:

title: NICE-SLAM: Neural Implicit Scalable Encoding for SLAM
text: Recent advances in neural implicit representations have demonstrated potential in various domains, with notable progress in simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). However, existing methods are limited by their tendency to produce over-smoothed scene reconstructions and struggle to scale to large scenes, primarily due to the simplicity of their fully-connected network architecture, which neglects local information in observations. We propose NICE-SLAM, a dense SLAM system that addresses these limitations by incorporating multi-level local information through a hierarchical scene representation. By optimizing this representation with pre-trained geometric priors, we achieve detailed reconstructions of large indoor scenes. Our approach exhibits improved scalability, efficiency, and robustness compared to recent neural implicit SLAM systems, as demonstrated by competitive results in both mapping and tracking quality across five challenging datasets.

title: Can Deep Neural Networks be Converted to Ultra Low-Latency Spiking Neural Networks?
text: Spiking neural networks (SNNs), that operate via binary spikes distributed over time, have emerged as a promising energy efficient ML paradigm for resource-constrained devices. However, the current state-of-the-art (SOTA) SNNs require multiple time steps for acceptable inference accuracy, increasing spiking activity and, consequently, energy consumption. SOTA training strategies for SNNs involve conversion from a non-spiking deep neural network (DNN). In this paper, we determine that SOTA conversion strategies cannot yield ultra low latency because they incorrectly assume that the DNN and SNN pre-activation values are uniformly distributed. We propose a new training algorithm that accurately captures these distributions, minimizing the error between the DNN and converted SNN. The resulting SNNs have ultra low latency and high activation sparsity, yielding significant improvements in compute efficiency. In particular, we evaluate our framework on image recognition tasks from CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets on several VGG and ResNet architectures. We obtain top-1 accuracy of 64.19% with only 2 time steps on the CIFAR-100 dataset with ~159.2x lower compute energy compared to an iso-architecture standard DNN. Compared to other SOTA SNN models, our models perform inference 2.5-8x faster (i.e., with fewer time steps).

title: Can Deep Neural Networks be Converted to Ultra Low-Latency Spiking Neural Networks?
text: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) have gained prominence as an energy-efficient machine learning paradigm for resource-constrained devices, owing to their binary spike-based operation. However, current state-of-the-art (SOTA) SNNs require multiple time steps to achieve acceptable inference accuracy, thereby increasing spiking activity and energy consumption. A key limitation of SOTA SNN training strategies lies in their conversion from non-spiking deep neural networks (DNNs), which relies on the flawed assumption of uniform distributions for DNN and SNN pre-activation values. This paper presents a novel training algorithm that accurately models these distributions, thereby minimizing the error between the DNN and converted SNN. The resulting SNNs exhibit ultra-low latency and high activation sparsity, leading to significant improvements in compute efficiency. We evaluate our framework on image recognition tasks from the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets using various VGG and ResNet architectures, achieving a top-1 accuracy of 64.19% with only 2 time steps on the CIFAR-100 dataset, while reducing compute energy by ~159.2x compared to an iso-architecture standard DNN. Notably, our models perform inference 2.5-8x faster than other SOTA SNN models.

title: Multi-modal 3D Human Pose Estimation with 2D Weak Supervision in Autonomous Driving
text: 3D human pose estimation (HPE) in autonomous vehicles (AV) differs from other use cases in many factors, including the 3D resolution and range of data, absence of dense depth maps, failure modes for LiDAR, relative location between the camera and LiDAR, and a high bar for estimation accuracy. Data collected for other use cases (such as virtual reality, gaming, and animation) may therefore not be usable for AV applications. This necessitates the collection and annotation of a large amount of 3D data for HPE in AV, which is time-consuming and expensive. In this paper, we propose one of the first approaches to alleviate this problem in the AV setting. Specifically, we propose a multi-modal approach which uses 2D labels on RGB images as weak supervision to perform 3D HPE. The proposed multi-modal architecture incorporates LiDAR and camera inputs with an auxiliary segmentation branch. On the Waymo Open Dataset, our approach achieves a 22% relative improvement over camera-only 2D HPE baseline, and 6% improvement over LiDAR-only model. Finally, careful ablation studies and parts based analysis illustrate the advantages of each of our contributions.

title: Multi-modal 3D Human Pose Estimation with 2D Weak Supervision in Autonomous Driving
text: The ability to accurately estimate 3D human pose from visual data is crucial for autonomous driving systems to anticipate and respond to pedestrian behavior. Existing approaches rely on large-scale 3D pose datasets, which are time-consuming and expensive to annotate. We propose a novel multi-modal 3D human pose estimation framework that leverages 2D weak supervision from autonomous driving datasets, eliminating the need for explicit 3D annotations. Our approach integrates a 2D pose estimator with a depth-aware 3D pose regressor, which is trained using a combination of 2D keypoints and depth maps from stereo cameras. We evaluate our method on the KITTI and Cityscapes datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance in 3D pose estimation with a mean average precision of 75.1% and 72.5%, respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in real-world autonomous driving scenarios, where accurate 3D pose estimation enables the vehicle to better understand pedestrian intentions and trajectories. Our framework has significant implications for the development of more advanced and safe autonomous driving systems.

title: Scaling Open-Vocabulary Image Segmentation with Image-Level Labels
text: We design an open-vocabulary image segmentation model to organize an image into meaningful regions indicated by arbitrary texts. Recent works (CLIP and ALIGN), despite attaining impressive open-vocabulary classification accuracy with image-level caption labels, are unable to segment visual concepts with pixels. We argue that these models miss an important step of visual grouping, which organizes pixels into groups before learning visual-semantic alignments. We propose OpenSeg to address the above issue while still making use of scalable image-level supervision of captions. First, it learns to propose segmentation masks for possible organizations. Then it learns visual-semantic alignments by aligning each word in a caption to one or a few predicted masks. We find the mask representations are the key to support learning image segmentation from captions, making it possible to scale up the dataset and vocabulary sizes. OpenSeg significantly outperforms the recent open-vocabulary method of LSeg by +19.9 mIoU on PASCAL dataset, thanks to its scalability.

title: Scaling Open-Vocabulary Image Segmentation with Image-Level Labels
text: The task of open-vocabulary image segmentation, where a model must identify and segment objects of unseen classes, remains a significant challenge in computer vision. Existing approaches often rely on pixel-level annotations, which are time-consuming and expensive to collect. In this work, we investigate the use of image-level labels, a weaker form of supervision, to scale open-vocabulary image segmentation. We propose a novel framework that leverages a large-scale image dataset with image-level labels to learn a class-agnostic segmentation model. Our approach involves a two-stage training process, where we first learn a representation that captures object semantics and then fine-tune the model on a small set of Open Images Dataset (OID) classes. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on OID, outperforming existing methods that rely on stronger supervision. Moreover, we show that our model can effectively generalize to unseen classes, achieving a 15.5% increase in mIoU on the held-out classes.

title: Recur, Attend or Convolve? On Whether Temporal Modeling Matters for Cross-Domain Robustness in Action Recognition
text: Most action recognition models today are highly parameterized, and evaluated on datasets with appearance-wise distinct classes. It has also been shown that 2D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) tend to be biased toward texture rather than shape in still image recognition tasks, in contrast to humans. Taken together, this raises suspicion that large video models partly learn spurious spatial texture correlations rather than to track relevant shapes over time to infer generalizable semantics from their movement. A natural way to avoid parameter explosion when learning visual patterns over time is to make use of recurrence. Biological vision consists of abundant recurrent circuitry, and is superior to computer vision in terms of domain shift generalization. In this article, we empirically study whether the choice of low-level temporal modeling has consequences for texture bias and cross-domain robustness. In order to enable a light-weight and systematic assessment of the ability to capture temporal structure, not revealed from single frames, we provide the Temporal Shape (TS) dataset, as well as modified domains of Diving48 allowing for the investigation of spatial texture bias in video models. The combined results of our experiments indicate that sound physical inductive bias such as recurrence in temporal modeling may be advantageous when robustness to domain shift is important for the task.

title: Recur, Attend or Convolve? On Whether Temporal Modeling Matters for Cross-Domain Robustness in Action Recognition
text: The prevailing action recognition models rely heavily on parameterization and are typically evaluated on datasets comprising appearance-wise distinct classes. Furthermore, recent findings have demonstrated that 2D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) exhibit a bias towards texture rather than shape in still image recognition tasks, diverging from human perception. This phenomenon raises concerns that large video models may be learning spurious spatial texture correlations rather than tracking relevant shapes over time to infer generalizable semantics from their movement. To mitigate the risk of parameter explosion when learning visual patterns over time, incorporating recurrence into the modeling process presents a viable solution. Notably, biological vision relies extensively on recurrent circuitry and exhibits superior domain shift generalization capabilities compared to computer vision. This study empirically investigates the implications of low-level temporal modeling choices on texture bias and cross-domain robustness. To facilitate a lightweight and systematic evaluation of temporal structure capture, we introduce the Temporal Shape (TS) dataset and modified domains of Diving48, enabling the assessment of spatial texture bias in video models. Our experimental results collectively suggest that incorporating sound physical inductive bias, such as recurrence in temporal modeling, can be advantageous when domain shift robustness is crucial for the task.

title: Multimodal Personality Recognition using Cross-Attention Transformer and Behaviour Encoding
text: Personality computing and affective computing have gained recent interest in many research areas. The datasets for the task generally have multiple modalities like video, audio, language and bio-signals. In this paper, we propose a flexible model for the task which exploits all available data. The task involves complex relations and to avoid using a large model for video processing specifically, we propose the use of behaviour encoding which boosts performance with minimal change to the model. Cross-attention using transformers has become popular in recent times and is utilised for fusion of different modalities. Since long term relations may exist, breaking the input into chunks is not desirable, thus the proposed model processes the entire input together. title: Multimodal Personality Recognition using Cross-Attention Transformer and Behaviour Encoding
text: The burgeoning fields of personality computing and affective computing necessitate the development of robust models capable of harnessing the richness of multimodal datasets, comprising video, audio, language, and bio-signals. We introduce a flexible framework that effectively integrates all available data, bypassing the limitations of modality-specific models. By leveraging behaviour encoding, we enhance performance while minimizing model complexity, particularly for video processing. Furthermore, we employ cross-attention mechanisms using transformers to fuse modalities, capturing complex relationships. Notably, our approach processes entire inputs holistically, eschewing chunk-based processing that may disrupt long-term dependencies. Experimental results underscore the significance of each of these contributions, demonstrating the efficacy of our proposed model.

title: Fine-grained Multi-Modal Self-Supervised Learning
text: Multi-Modal Self-Supervised Learning from videos has been shown to improve model's performance on various downstream tasks. However, such Self-Supervised pre-training requires large batch sizes and a large amount of computation resources due to the noise present in the uncurated data. This is partly due to the fact that the prevalent training scheme is trained on coarse-grained setting, in which vectors representing the whole video clips or natural language sentences are used for computing similarity. Such scheme makes training noisy as part of the video clips can be totally not correlated with the other-modality input such as text description. In this paper, we propose a fine-grained multi-modal self-supervised training scheme that computes the similarity between embeddings at finer-scale (such as individual feature map embeddings and embeddings of phrases), and uses attention mechanisms to reduce noisy pairs' weighting in the loss function. We show that with the proposed pre-training scheme, we can train smaller models, with smaller batch-size and much less computational resources to achieve downstream tasks performances comparable to State-Of-The-Art, for tasks including action recognition and text-image retrievals.

title: Fine-grained Multi-Modal Self-Supervised Learning
text: The efficacy of multi-modal self-supervised learning from videos has been well established in enhancing model performance across various downstream tasks. However, a major hindrance to its widespread adoption lies in the requirement for substantial computational resources and large batch sizes, primarily due to the noise inherent in uncurated data. This limitation stems from the prevalent coarse-grained training scheme, which computes similarity using vectors representing entire video clips or natural language sentences. This approach introduces noise, as certain video segments may be unrelated to corresponding text descriptions. To address this, we introduce a fine-grained multi-modal self-supervised training scheme that calculates similarity at a finer scale, leveraging individual feature map embeddings and phrase embeddings. We incorporate attention mechanisms to mitigate the impact of noisy pairs on the loss function. Our proposed scheme enables the training of smaller models with reduced batch sizes and computational resources, achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art models in downstream tasks such as action recognition and text-image retrieval.

title: Maximum Entropy on Erroneous Predictions (MEEP): Improving model calibration for medical image segmentation
text: Modern deep neural networks achieved remarkable progress in medical image segmentation tasks. However, it has recently been observed that they tend to produce overconfident estimates, even in situations of high uncertainty, leading to poorly calibrated and unreliable models. In this work we introduce Maximum Entropy on Erroneous Predictions (MEEP), a training strategy for segmentation networks which selectively penalizes overconfident predictions, focusing only on misclassified pixels. Our method is agnostic to the neural architecture, does not increase model complexity and can be coupled with multiple segmentation loss functions. We benchmark the proposed strategy in two challenging segmentation tasks: white matter hyperintensity lesions in magnetic resonance images (MRI) of the brain, and atrial segmentation in cardiac MRI. The experimental results demonstrate that coupling MEEP with standard segmentation losses leads to improvements not only in terms of model calibration, but also in segmentation quality.

title: Maximum Entropy on Erroneous Predictions (MEEP): Improving model calibration for medical image segmentation
text: Deep neural networks have achieved impressive performance in medical image segmentation tasks, but recent studies have revealed that they often produce overconfident predictions, even when uncertainty is high, resulting in poorly calibrated and unreliable models. To address this issue, we propose Maximum Entropy on Erroneous Predictions (MEEP), a training strategy that selectively penalizes overconfident predictions by focusing on misclassified pixels. Notably, MEEP is architecture-agnostic, does not increase model complexity, and can be combined with various segmentation loss functions. We evaluate MEEP on two challenging segmentation tasks: white matter hyperintensity lesions in brain MRI and atrial segmentation in cardiac MRI. Our results show that integrating MEEP with standard segmentation losses leads to significant improvements in both model calibration and segmentation quality, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

title: SAMCNet for Spatial-configuration-based Classification: A Summary of Results
text: The goal of spatial-configuration-based classification is to build a classifier to distinguish two classes (e.g., responder, non-responder) based on the spatial arrangements (e.g., spatial interactions between different point categories) given multi-category point data from two classes. This problem is important for generating hypotheses in medical pathology towards discovering new immunotherapies for cancer treatment as well as for other applications in biomedical research and microbial ecology. This problem is challenging due to an exponential number of category subsets which may vary in the strength of spatial interactions. Most prior efforts on using human selected spatial association measures may not be sufficient for capturing the relevant (e.g., surrounded by) spatial interactions which may be of biological significance. In addition, the related deep neural networks are limited to category pairs and do not explore larger subsets of point categories. To overcome these limitations, we propose a Spatial-interaction Aware Multi-Category deep neural Network (SAMCNet) architecture and contribute novel local reference frame characterization and point pair prioritization layers for spatial-configuration-based classification. Extensive experimental results on multiple cancer datasets show that the proposed architecture provides higher prediction accuracy over baseline methods.

title: SAMCNet for Spatial-configuration-based Classification: A Summary of Results
text: Spatial-configuration-based classification seeks to develop a classifier that distinguishes between two classes, such as responders and non-responders, based on the spatial arrangements of multi-category point data. This problem has significant implications for medical pathology, particularly in the discovery of new immunotherapies for cancer treatment, as well as biomedical research and microbial ecology. The challenge lies in the exponential number of category subsets, which can exhibit varying strengths of spatial interactions. Previous approaches relying on human-selected spatial association measures may not capture biologically significant spatial interactions, such as surrounding patterns. Moreover, existing deep neural networks are limited to category pairs and fail to explore larger point category subsets. We propose the Spatial-interaction Aware Multi-Category deep neural Network (SAMCNet) architecture, which incorporates novel local reference frame characterization and point pair prioritization layers. Our extensive experiments on multiple cancer datasets demonstrate that SAMCNet achieves higher prediction accuracy compared to baseline methods, highlighting its potential for advancing spatial-configuration-based classification.

title: Electromagnetic Side-Channel Attack Resilience against PRESENT Lightweight Block Cipher
text: Lightweight cryptography is a novel diversion from conventional cryptography that targets internet-of-things (IoT) platform due to resource constraints. In comparison, it offers smaller cryptographic primitives such as shorter key sizes, block sizes and lesser energy drainage. The main focus can be seen in algorithm developments in this emerging subject. Thus, verification is carried out based upon theoretical (mathematical) proofs mostly. Among the few available side-channel analysis studies found in literature, the highest percentage is taken by power attacks. PRESENT is a promising lightweight block cipher to be included in IoT devices in the near future. Thus, the emphasis of this paper is on lightweight cryptology, and our investigation shows unavailability of a correlation electromagnetic analysis (CEMA) of it. Hence, in an effort to fill in this research gap, we opted to investigate the capabilities of CEMA against the PRESENT algorithm. This work aims to determine the probability of secret key leakage with a minimum number of electromagnetic (EM) waveforms possible. The process initially started from a simple EM analysis (SEMA) and gradually enhanced up to a CEMA. This paper presents our methodology in attack modelling, current results that indicate a probability of leaking seven bytes of the key and upcoming plans for optimisation. In addition, introductions to lightweight cryptanalysis and theories of EMA are also included.

title: Electromagnetic Side-Channel Attack Resilience against PRESENT Lightweight Block Cipher
text: The widespread adoption of resource-constrained devices in the Internet of Things (IoT) has led to a surge in the use of lightweight block ciphers, such as PRESENT, to provide confidentiality and integrity guarantees. However, these ciphers are vulnerable to electromagnetic (EM) side-channel attacks, which exploit the correlation between the cipher's power consumption or electromagnetic radiation and the secret key. EM attacks pose a significant threat to the security of IoT devices, especially in scenarios where physical access to the device is possible. In this context, we investigate the resilience of PRESENT against EM side-channel attacks. We employ a novel approach that combines machine learning techniques with signal processing methods to analyze the EM traces of a PRESENT implementation on a 32-bit microcontroller. Our methodology involves collecting EM traces for different key values, followed by feature extraction and selection, and finally, training a classifier to predict the secret key. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach using metrics such as guessing entropy and success rate. Our experimental results demonstrate that PRESENT is vulnerable to EM side-channel attacks, with a success rate of over 90% using a single EM trace. Furthermore, we show that the attack's efficiency can be improved by incorporating domain-specific knowledge and optimizing the feature extraction step. Our findings highlight the need for EM side-channel attack countermeasures in lightweight block ciphers, and our proposed methodology provides a framework for evaluating the resilience of such ciphers against EM attacks.

title: Leveraging Synthetic Data in Object Detection on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
text: Acquiring data to train deep learning-based object detectors on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) is expensive, time-consuming and may even be prohibited by law in specific environments. On the other hand, synthetic data is fast and cheap to access. In this work, we explore the potential use of synthetic data in object detection from UAVs across various application environments. For that, we extend the open-source framework DeepGTAV to work for UAV scenarios. We capture various large-scale high-resolution synthetic data sets in several domains to demonstrate their use in real-world object detection from UAVs by analyzing multiple training strategies across several models. Furthermore, we analyze several different data generation and sampling parameters to provide actionable engineering advice for further scientific research. The DeepGTAV framework is available at

title: Leveraging Synthetic Data in Object Detection on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
text: The high cost, time-consuming nature, and potential legal restrictions associated with acquiring data for training deep learning-based object detectors on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have hindered their widespread adoption. In contrast, synthetic data offers a rapid and inexpensive alternative. This study investigates the viability of synthetic data for object detection in various UAV application environments. To this end, we modified the open-source DeepGTAV framework to accommodate UAV scenarios, generating large-scale, high-resolution synthetic datasets across multiple domains. Our analysis of different training strategies and models reveals the effectiveness of synthetic data in real-world UAV object detection tasks. Furthermore, we examine the impact of various data generation and sampling parameters, providing valuable insights for future research and engineering applications.

title: Human Activity Recognition on wrist-worn accelerometers using self-supervised neural networks
text: Measures of Activity of Daily Living (ADL) are an important indicator of overall health but difficult to measure in-clinic. Automated and accurate human activity recognition (HAR) using wrist-worn accelerometers enables practical and cost efficient remote monitoring of ADL. Key obstacles in developing high quality HAR is the lack of large labeled datasets and the performance loss when applying models trained on small curated datasets to the continuous stream of heterogeneous data in real-life. In this work we design a self-supervised learning paradigm to create a robust representation of accelerometer data that can generalize across devices and subjects. We demonstrate that this representation can separate activities of daily living and achieve strong HAR accuracy (on multiple benchmark datasets) using very few labels. We also propose a segmentation algorithm which can identify segments of salient activity and boost HAR accuracy on continuous real-life data.

title: Human Activity Recognition on wrist-worn accelerometers using self-supervised neural networks
text: Human activity recognition (HAR) using wrist-worn accelerometers has gained significant attention in recent years due to its potential applications in health monitoring and personalized feedback. Despite advances in deep learning, most HAR systems rely on labor-intensive annotated datasets, limiting their scalability and generalizability. This paper proposes a self-supervised neural network approach for HAR on wrist-worn accelerometers, eliminating the need for labeled data. Our method leverages a contrastive loss function to learn representations from unlabeled accelerometer data, which are then fine-tuned for activity recognition. Experiments on a large-scale dataset comprising 10,000 hours of data from 100 participants demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming traditional supervised methods by 5.5% in terms of F1-score. Furthermore, our model exhibits improved robustness to sensor orientation and noise, making it a promising solution for real-world HAR applications.

title: Randomize the Future: Asymptotically Optimal Locally Private Frequency Estimation Protocol for Longitudinal Data
text: Longitudinal data tracking under Local Differential Privacy (LDP) is a challenging task. Baseline solutions that repeatedly invoke a protocol designed for one-time computation lead to linear decay in the privacy or utility guarantee with respect to the number of computations. To avoid this, the recent approach of Erlingsson et al. (2020) exploits the potential sparsity of user data that changes only infrequently. Their protocol targets the fundamental problem of frequency estimation protocol for longitudinal binary data, with $\ell_\infty$ error of $O ( (1 / ε) \cdot (\log d)^{3 / 2} \cdot k \cdot \sqrt{ n \cdot \log ( d / β) } )$, where $ε$ is the privacy budget, $d$ is the number of time periods, $k$ is the maximum number of changes of user data, and $β$ is the failure probability. Notably, the error bound scales polylogarithmically with $d$, but linearly with $k$. In this paper, we break through the linear dependence on $k$ in the estimation error. Our new protocol has error $O ( (1 / ε) \cdot (\log d) \cdot \sqrt{ k \cdot n \cdot \log ( d / β) } )$, matching the lower bound up to a logarithmic factor. The protocol is an online one, that outputs an estimate at each time period. The key breakthrough is a new randomizer for sequential data, FutureRand, with two key features. The first is a composition strategy that correlates the noise across the non-zero elements of the sequence. The second is a pre-computation technique which, by exploiting the symmetry of input space, enables the randomizer to output the results on the fly, without knowing future inputs. Our protocol closes the error gap between existing online and offline algorithms.

title: Randomize the Future: Asymptotically Optimal Locally Private Frequency Estimation Protocol for Longitudinal Data
text: Longitudinal data tracking under Local Differential Privacy (LDP) poses a significant challenge, as naive approaches that repeatedly invoke a one-time computation protocol suffer from a linear degradation in privacy or utility guarantees with respect to the number of computations. A recent approach by Erlingsson et al. (2020) leverages the sparsity of user data, which changes infrequently, to address the fundamental problem of frequency estimation for longitudinal binary data. Their protocol achieves an $\ell_\infty$ error of $O ( (1 / ε) \cdot (\log d)^{3 / 2} \cdot k \cdot \sqrt{ n \cdot \log ( d / β) } )$, where $ε$ is the privacy budget, $d$ is the number of time periods, $k$ is the maximum number of changes, and $β$ is the failure probability. Notably, the error bound exhibits polylogarithmic scaling with $d$, but linear scaling with $k$. This paper presents a breakthrough in frequency estimation, overcoming the linear dependence on $k$ in the estimation error. Our novel protocol achieves an error of $O ( (1 / ε) \cdot (\log d) \cdot \sqrt{ k \cdot n \cdot \log ( d / β) } )$, effectively matching the lower bound up to a logarithmic factor. The online protocol outputs an estimate at each time period, enabled by our innovative randomizer, FutureRand, which features a composition strategy correlating noise across non-zero sequence elements and a pre-computation technique exploiting input space symmetry to generate results on the fly without knowledge of future inputs. This advance closes the error gap between existing online and offline algorithms.

title: Adversarial Attacks against Windows PE Malware Detection: A Survey of the State-of-the-Art
text: Malware has been one of the most damaging threats to computers that span across multiple operating systems and various file formats. To defend against ever-increasing and ever-evolving malware, tremendous efforts have been made to propose a variety of malware detection that attempt to effectively and efficiently detect malware so as to mitigate possible damages as early as possible. Recent studies have shown that, on the one hand, existing ML and DL techniques enable superior solutions in detecting newly emerging and previously unseen malware. However, on the other hand, ML and DL models are inherently vulnerable to adversarial attacks in the form of adversarial examples. In this paper, we focus on malware with the file format of portable executable (PE) in the family of Windows operating systems, namely Windows PE malware, as a representative case to study the adversarial attack methods in such adversarial settings. To be specific, we start by first outlining the general learning framework of Windows PE malware detection based on ML/DL and subsequently highlighting three unique challenges of performing adversarial attacks in the context of Windows PE malware. Then, we conduct a comprehensive and systematic review to categorize the state-of-the-art adversarial attacks against PE malware detection, as well as corresponding defenses to increase the robustness of Windows PE malware detection. Finally, we conclude the paper by first presenting other related attacks against Windows PE malware detection beyond the adversarial attacks and then shedding light on future research directions and opportunities. In addition, a curated resource list of adversarial attacks and defenses for Windows PE malware detection is also available at

title: Adversarial Attacks against Windows PE Malware Detection: A Survey of the State-of-the-Art
text: The pervasive menace of malware necessitates the development of effective detection strategies that can counter its relentless evolution. While machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques have demonstrated superior performance in detecting novel and unseen malware, these models are inherently susceptible to adversarial attacks, which can compromise their efficacy. Focusing on Windows portable executable (PE) malware, this study delves into the adversarial attack methods pertinent to this context. We first establish a general learning framework for Windows PE malware detection using ML/DL, highlighting three unique challenges associated with adversarial attacks in this domain. A comprehensive review of state-of-the-art adversarial attacks against PE malware detection is then conducted, categorizing these attacks and corresponding defensive strategies aimed at enhancing the robustness of Windows PE malware detection. The paper concludes by discussing additional attacks beyond adversarial attacks and outlining future research directions and opportunities. Notably, the study's findings underscore the need for more resilient Windows PE malware detection systems capable of withstanding sophisticated threats. The proliferation of malware necessitates continued innovation in detection strategies, and this research contributes to the ongoing quest for more effective and robust malware defense mechanisms.

title: A Multi-Objective Degree-Based Network Anonymization Approach
text: Enormous amounts of data collected from social networks or other online platforms are being published for the sake of statistics, marketing, and research, among other objectives. The consequent privacy and data security concerns have motivated the work on degree-based data anonymization. We propose and study a new multi-objective anonymization approach that generalizes the known degree anonymization problem and attempts at improving it as a more realistic model for data security/privacy. Our suggested model guarantees a convenient privacy level based on modifying the degrees in a way that respects some given local restrictions, per node, such that the total modifications at the global level (in the whole graph/network) are bounded by some given value. The corresponding multi-objective graph realization approach is solved using Integer Linear Programming to obtain the best possible solutions. Our experimental studies provide empirical evidence of the effectiveness of the new approach; by specifically showing that the introduced anonymization algorithm has a negligible effect on the way nodes are clustered, thereby preserving valuable network information while significantly improving data privacy.

title: A Multi-Objective Degree-Based Network Anonymization Approach
text: The rapid growth of online social networks and the increasing reliance on networked systems have heightened concerns about privacy and anonymity. Network anonymization has emerged as a crucial technique to protect sensitive information by modifying the network structure while preserving its essential properties. However, existing anonymization methods often focus on a single objective, such as k-anonymity or l-diversity, which may not comprehensively address the complex requirements of real-world networks. We propose a novel multi-objective degree-based network anonymization approach that simultaneously optimizes multiple conflicting objectives, including anonymity, utility, and scalability. Our approach leverages a graph-based representation and a hybrid optimization algorithm to identify the optimal anonymization strategy. Experimental results on several real-world networks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving a better trade-off between anonymity and utility compared to state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, our approach achieves an average improvement of 23% in anonymity and 17% in utility on the Facebook network dataset. The proposed approach has significant implications for the development of privacy-preserving network analysis and mining techniques.

title: Robust and Precise Facial Landmark Detection by Self-Calibrated Pose Attention Network
text: Current fully-supervised facial landmark detection methods have progressed rapidly and achieved remarkable performance. However, they still suffer when coping with faces under large poses and heavy occlusions for inaccurate facial shape constraints and insufficient labeled training samples. In this paper, we propose a semi-supervised framework, i.e., a Self-Calibrated Pose Attention Network (SCPAN) to achieve more robust and precise facial landmark detection in challenging scenarios. To be specific, a Boundary-Aware Landmark Intensity (BALI) field is proposed to model more effective facial shape constraints by fusing boundary and landmark intensity field information. Moreover, a Self-Calibrated Pose Attention (SCPA) model is designed to provide a self-learned objective function that enforces intermediate supervision without label information by introducing a self-calibrated mechanism and a pose attention mask. We show that by integrating the BALI fields and SCPA model into a novel self-calibrated pose attention network, more facial prior knowledge can be learned and the detection accuracy and robustness of our method for faces with large poses and heavy occlusions have been improved. The experimental results obtained for challenging benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in the literature.

title: Robust and Precise Facial Landmark Detection by Self-Calibrated Pose Attention Network
text: The performance of fully-supervised facial landmark detection methods has improved significantly, yet they still struggle with faces exhibiting large poses and heavy occlusions due to inadequate facial shape constraints and limited labeled training data. To address these limitations, we introduce a semi-supervised framework, namely the Self-Calibrated Pose Attention Network (SCPAN), which achieves more robust and accurate facial landmark detection in challenging scenarios. By integrating a Boundary-Aware Landmark Intensity (BALI) field, we effectively model facial shape constraints by combining boundary and landmark intensity field information. Furthermore, our Self-Calibrated Pose Attention (SCPA) model provides a self-learned objective function, enabling intermediate supervision without label information through a self-calibrated mechanism and pose attention mask. The proposed SCPAN framework leverages these components to learn more facial prior knowledge, resulting in improved detection accuracy and robustness for faces with large poses and heavy occlusions. Experimental results on challenging benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing state-of-the-art methods.

title: MVDG: A Unified Multi-view Framework for Domain Generalization
text: To generalize the model trained in source domains to unseen target domains, domain generalization (DG) has recently attracted lots of attention. Since target domains can not be involved in training, overfitting source domains is inevitable. As a popular regularization technique, the meta-learning training scheme has shown its ability to resist overfitting. However, in the training stage, current meta-learning-based methods utilize only one task along a single optimization trajectory, which might produce a biased and noisy optimization direction. Beyond the training stage, overfitting could also cause unstable prediction in the test stage. In this paper, we propose a novel multi-view DG framework to effectively reduce the overfitting in both the training and test stage. Specifically, in the training stage, we develop a multi-view regularized meta-learning algorithm that employs multiple optimization trajectories to produce a suitable optimization direction for model updating. We also theoretically show that the generalization bound could be reduced by increasing the number of tasks in each trajectory. In the test stage, we utilize multiple augmented images to yield a multi-view prediction to alleviate unstable prediction, which significantly promotes model reliability. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets validate that our method can find a flat minimum to enhance generalization and outperform several state-of-the-art approaches.

title: MVDG: A Unified Multi-view Framework for Domain Generalization
text: Domain generalization (DG) has garnered significant attention in recent years, as it enables models trained on source domains to generalize to unseen target domains. However, the absence of target domains during training inevitably leads to overfitting on the source domains. Meta-learning has emerged as a promising regularization technique to mitigate overfitting, but current meta-learning-based methods are limited by their reliance on a single task along a single optimization trajectory, which can result in biased and noisy optimization directions. Furthermore, overfitting can also cause unstable predictions during testing. To address these limitations, we propose a novel multi-view DG framework that effectively reduces overfitting in both training and testing stages. Our approach employs a multi-view regularized meta-learning algorithm that leverages multiple optimization trajectories to produce a robust optimization direction for model updating, and we theoretically demonstrate that increasing the number of tasks in each trajectory can tighten the generalization bound. Additionally, we utilize multiple augmented images to generate a multi-view prediction, thereby alleviating unstable predictions and enhancing model reliability. Our extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method can converge to a flat minimum, thereby improving generalization and outperforming state-of-the-art approaches.

title: Flakify: A Black-Box, Language Model-based Predictor for Flaky Tests
text: Software testing assures that code changes do not adversely affect existing functionality. However, a test case can be flaky, i.e., passing and failing across executions, even for the same version of the source code. Flaky test cases introduce overhead to software development as they can lead to unnecessary attempts to debug production or testing code. The state-of-the-art ML-based flaky test case predictors rely on pre-defined sets of features that are either project-specific, require access to production code, which is not always available to software test engineers. Therefore, in this paper, we propose Flakify, a black-box, language model-based predictor for flaky test cases. Flakify relies exclusively on the source code of test cases, thus not requiring to (a) access to production code (black-box), (b) rerun test cases, (c) pre-define features. To this end, we employed CodeBERT, a pre-trained language model, and fine-tuned it to predict flaky test cases using the source code of test cases. We evaluated Flakify on two publicly available datasets (FlakeFlagger and IDoFT) for flaky test cases and compared our technique with the FlakeFlagger approach using two different evaluation procedures: cross-validation and per-project validation. Flakify achieved high F1-scores on both datasets using cross-validation and per-project validation, and surpassed FlakeFlagger by 10 and 18 percentage points in terms of precision and recall, respectively, when evaluated on the FlakeFlagger dataset, thus reducing the cost bound to be wasted on unnecessarily debugging test cases and production code by the same percentages. Flakify also achieved significantly higher prediction results when used to predict test cases on new projects, suggesting better generalizability over FlakeFlagger. Our results further show that a black-box version of FlakeFlagger is not a viable option for predicting flaky test cases.

title: Flakify: A Black-Box, Language Model-based Predictor for Flaky Tests
text: The assurance of software quality relies heavily on rigorous testing, but the presence of flaky test cases, which exhibit inconsistent pass or fail outcomes despite identical source code versions, can hinder this process. The resultant debugging efforts can lead to unnecessary overhead in software development. Existing machine learning-based predictors of flaky test cases rely on predefined feature sets that are often project-specific or require access to production code, which may not always be available to software test engineers. To address these limitations, we present Flakify, a novel, black-box predictor that leverages a language model to identify flaky test cases solely based on their source code. By employing CodeBERT, a pre-trained language model fine-tuned for this task, Flakify eliminates the need for access to production code, test reruns, or feature engineering. Our evaluation of Flakify on two publicly available datasets (FlakeFlagger and IDoFT) demonstrates its effectiveness, with high F1-scores achieved through cross-validation and per-project validation. Notably, Flakify outperforms the FlakeFlagger approach by 10 and 18 percentage points in terms of precision and recall, respectively, on the FlakeFlagger dataset, thereby reducing the cost associated with unnecessary debugging by the same margins. Furthermore, Flakify exhibits better generalizability when applied to new projects, and our results suggest that a black-box adaptation of FlakeFlagger is not a viable alternative for predicting flaky test cases.

title: Revisiting Transformation Invariant Geometric Deep Learning: An Initial Representation Perspective
text: Deep neural networks have achieved great success in the last decade. When designing neural networks to handle the ubiquitous geometric data such as point clouds and graphs, it is critical that the model can maintain invariance towards various transformations such as translation, rotation, and scaling. Most existing graph neural network (GNN) approaches can only maintain permutation-invariance, failing to guarantee invariance with respect to other transformations. Besides GNNs, other works design sophisticated transformation-invariant layers, which are computationally expensive and difficult to be extended. In this paper, we revisit why general neural networks cannot maintain transformation invariance. Our findings show that transformation-invariant and distance-preserving initial point representations are sufficient to achieve transformation invariance rather than needing sophisticated neural layer designs. Motivated by these findings, we propose Transformation Invariant Neural Networks (TinvNN), a straightforward and general plug-in for geometric data. Specifically, we realize transformation invariant and distance-preserving initial point representations by modifying multi-dimensional scaling and feed the representations into existing neural networks. We prove that TinvNN can strictly guarantee transformation invariance, being general and flexible enough to be combined with the existing neural networks. Extensive experimental results on point cloud analysis and combinatorial optimization demonstrate the effectiveness and general applicability of our method. We also extend our method into equivariance cases. Based on the results, we advocate that TinvNN should be considered as an essential baseline for further studies of transformation-invariant geometric deep learning.

title: Revisiting Transformation Invariant Geometric Deep Learning: An Initial Representation Perspective
text: The success of deep learning in computer vision is largely attributed to the ability of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to exploit translational equivariance, yet their vulnerability to other geometric transformations remains a major concern. Recent attempts to incorporate transformation invariance into deep neural networks have focused on imposing constraints on the learned representations, often at the cost of increased computational complexity and reduced model expressiveness. We revisit this problem from an initial representation perspective, arguing that the choice of input representation plays a crucial role in the development of transformation-invariant geometric deep learning models. By leveraging the mathematical framework of group theory, we propose a novel family of transformation-invariant initial representations, dubbed GIFT (Group-Invariant Feature Templates), which can be seamlessly integrated into existing CNN architectures. Our extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and STL-10, demonstrate that GIFT-based models achieve state-of-the-art performance in terms of transformation invariance, while maintaining competitive accuracy and computational efficiency. Notably, our approach outperforms existing methods by significant margins on challenging tasks such as rotation-invariant image classification and object recognition under severe viewpoint changes. Our findings suggest that a careful reconsideration of the input representation can have a profound impact on the development of robust and efficient geometric deep learning models.

title: Statistical Feature-based Personal Information Detection in Mobile Network Traffic
text: With the popularity of smartphones, mobile applications (apps) have penetrated the daily life of people. Although apps provide rich functionalities, they also access a large amount of personal information simultaneously. As a result, privacy concerns are raised. To understand what personal information the apps collect, many solutions are presented to detect privacy leaks in apps. Recently, the traffic monitoring-based privacy leak detection method has shown promising performance and strong scalability. However, it still has some shortcomings. Firstly, it suffers from detecting the leakage of personal information with obfuscation. Secondly, it cannot discover the privacy leaks of undefined type. Aiming at solving the above problems, a new personal information detection method based on traffic monitoring is proposed in this paper. In this paper, statistical features of personal information are designed to depict the occurrence patterns of personal information in the traffic, including local patterns and global patterns. Then a detector is trained based on machine learning algorithms to discover potential personal information with similar patterns. Since the statistical features are independent of the value and type of personal information, the trained detector is capable of identifying various types of privacy leaks and obfuscated privacy leaks. As far as we know, this is the first work that detects personal information based on statistical features. Finally, the experimental results show that the proposed method could achieve better performance than the state-of-the-art.

title: Statistical Feature-based Personal Information Detection in Mobile Network Traffic
text: The pervasive use of smartphones has led to mobile applications (apps) becoming an integral part of daily life, providing rich functionalities while simultaneously accessing copious amounts of personal information. This dichotomy has sparked concerns regarding privacy. To mitigate these concerns, numerous solutions have been proposed to detect privacy leaks in apps, with traffic monitoring-based methods demonstrating promising performance and scalability. However, these approaches still exhibit shortcomings, particularly in detecting leaks of obfuscated personal information and identifying privacy leaks of undefined types. This paper proposes a novel personal information detection method based on traffic monitoring, which addresses these limitations. By designing statistical features that capture the occurrence patterns of personal information in traffic, including local and global patterns, we train a machine learning-based detector to identify potential personal information exhibiting similar patterns. The independence of these statistical features from the value and type of personal information enables the detector to identify various types of privacy leaks, including obfuscated ones. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first approach to leverage statistical features for personal information detection. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art solutions.

title: Learning Hierarchical Attention for Weakly-supervised Chest X-Ray Abnormality Localization and Diagnosis
text: We consider the problem of abnormality localization for clinical applications. While deep learning has driven much recent progress in medical imaging, many clinical challenges are not fully addressed, limiting its broader usage. While recent methods report high diagnostic accuracies, physicians have concerns trusting these algorithm results for diagnostic decision-making purposes because of a general lack of algorithm decision reasoning and interpretability. One potential way to address this problem is to further train these models to localize abnormalities in addition to just classifying them. However, doing this accurately will require a large amount of disease localization annotations by clinical experts, a task that is prohibitively expensive to accomplish for most applications. In this work, we take a step towards addressing these issues by means of a new attention-driven weakly supervised algorithm comprising a hierarchical attention mining framework that unifies activation- and gradient-based visual attention in a holistic manner. Our key algorithmic innovations include the design of explicit ordinal attention constraints, enabling principled model training in a weakly-supervised fashion, while also facilitating the generation of visual-attention-driven model explanations by means of localization cues. On two large-scale chest X-ray datasets (NIH ChestX-ray14 and CheXpert), we demonstrate significant localization performance improvements over the current state of the art while also achieving competitive classification performance. title: Learning Hierarchical Attention for Weakly-supervised Chest X-Ray Abnormality Localization and Diagnosis
text: Abnormality localization is a critical challenge in medical imaging, where the lack of transparency in deep learning-based decision-making processes hinders their widespread adoption in clinical applications. Despite achieving high diagnostic accuracies, existing methods fail to provide interpretable results, leading to concerns among physicians regarding the trustworthiness of algorithm-driven diagnoses. A promising approach to address this limitation is to equip models with the capability to localize abnormalities in addition to classification. However, this requires a substantial amount of disease localization annotations from clinical experts, a resource-intensive task that is often impractical. To overcome this hurdle, we propose a novel attention-driven weakly supervised algorithm that integrates activation- and gradient-based visual attention within a hierarchical attention mining framework. Our approach introduces explicit ordinal attention constraints, enabling principled model training in a weakly-supervised setting while generating visual-attention-driven explanations through localization cues. Evaluations on two large-scale chest X-ray datasets (NIH ChestX-ray14 and CheXpert) demonstrate significant improvements in localization performance over the current state of the art, accompanied by competitive classification performance.

title: A Random Point Initialization Approach to Image Segmentation with Variational Level-sets
text: Image segmentation is an essential component in many image processing and computer vision tasks. The primary goal of image segmentation is to simplify an image for easier analysis, and there are two broad approaches for achieving this: edge based methods, which extract the boundaries of specific known objects, and region based methods, which partition the image into regions that are statistically homogeneous. One of the more prominent edge finding methods, known as the level set method, evolves a zero-level contour in the image plane with gradient descent until the contour has converged to the object boundaries. While the classical level set method and its variants have proved successful in segmenting real images, they are susceptible to becoming stuck in noisy regions of the image plane without a priori knowledge of the image and they are unable to provide details beyond object outer boundary locations. We propose a modification to the variational level set image segmentation method that can quickly detect object boundaries by making use of random point initialization. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by comparing the performance of our method on real images to that of the prominent Canny Method.

title: A Random Point Initialization Approach to Image Segmentation with Variational Level-sets
text: Image segmentation, a fundamental step in image processing and computer vision, aims to simplify images for efficient analysis. This process can be approached through either edge-based methods, which extract object boundaries, or region-based methods, which partition images into statistically homogeneous regions. The level set method, a prominent edge-finding technique, iteratively evolves a zero-level contour in the image plane using gradient descent until convergence to object boundaries. Despite the success of classical level set methods and their variants in segmenting real-world images, they are prone to stagnation in noisy regions without a priori knowledge of the image, and are limited to identifying object outer boundaries. We introduce a modified variational level set image segmentation method that leverages random point initialization to rapidly detect object boundaries. Through comparative experiments on real images, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving performance comparable to the widely-used Canny Method.

title: Dual Path Structural Contrastive Embeddings for Learning Novel Objects
text: Learning novel classes from a very few labeled samples has attracted increasing attention in machine learning areas. Recent research on either meta-learning based or transfer-learning based paradigm demonstrates that gaining information on a good feature space can be an effective solution to achieve favorable performance on few-shot tasks. In this paper, we propose a simple but effective paradigm that decouples the tasks of learning feature representations and classifiers and only learns the feature embedding architecture from base classes via the typical transfer-learning training strategy. To maintain both the generalization ability across base and novel classes and discrimination ability within each class, we propose a dual path feature learning scheme that effectively combines structural similarity with contrastive feature construction. In this way, both inner-class alignment and inter-class uniformity can be well balanced, and result in improved performance. Experiments on three popular benchmarks show that when incorporated with a simple prototype based classifier, our method can still achieve promising results for both standard and generalized few-shot problems in either an inductive or transductive inference setting.

title: Dual Path Structural Contrastive Embeddings for Learning Novel Objects
text: The ability to recognize and learn novel objects is a fundamental challenge in computer vision, particularly in scenarios where limited labeled data is available. Recent advances in contrastive learning have shown promise in this regard, but existing methods often struggle to effectively capture structural information and suffer from over-smoothing issues. We propose Dual Path Structural Contrastive Embeddings (DP-SCE), a novel approach that addresses these limitations by incorporating dual path encoders to separately capture local and global structural features. Our method leverages a contrastive loss function that encourages the alignment of embeddings from both paths, while also maintaining their distinctiveness. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DP-SCE, achieving state-of-the-art performance in few-shot object recognition tasks. Specifically, our approach outperforms existing methods by an average of 5.2% on the CIFAR-FS dataset and 3.8% on the mini-ImageNet dataset. Ablation studies further validate the importance of the dual path architecture and contrastive loss function in capturing robust and discriminative embeddings for novel objects.

title: DENSE: Data-Free One-Shot Federated Learning
text: One-shot Federated Learning (FL) has recently emerged as a promising approach, which allows the central server to learn a model in a single communication round. Despite the low communication cost, existing one-shot FL methods are mostly impractical or face inherent limitations, \eg a public dataset is required, clients' models are homogeneous, and additional data/model information need to be uploaded. To overcome these issues, we propose a novel two-stage \textbf{D}ata-fre\textbf{E} o\textbf{N}e-\textbf{S}hot federated l\textbf{E}arning (DENSE) framework, which trains the global model by a data generation stage and a model distillation stage. DENSE is a practical one-shot FL method that can be applied in reality due to the following advantages: (1) DENSE requires no additional information compared with other methods (except the model parameters) to be transferred between clients and the server; (2) DENSE does not require any auxiliary dataset for training; (3) DENSE considers model heterogeneity in FL, \ie different clients can have different model architectures. Experiments on a variety of real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method.For example, DENSE outperforms the best baseline method Fed-ADI by 5.08\% on CIFAR10 dataset.

title: DENSE: Data-Free One-Shot Federated Learning
text: Federated Learning (FL) has made significant strides with the emergence of one-shot approaches, which enable the central server to learn a model in a single communication round, thereby minimizing communication costs. However, existing one-shot FL methods are often encumbered by limitations, including the requirement for public datasets, homogeneous client models, and the need for additional data or model information uploads. To address these constraints, we introduce a novel two-stage framework, dubbed DENSE, which leverages data generation and model distillation to train the global model. This practical one-shot FL approach offers several advantages, including the absence of additional information requirements beyond model parameters, no need for auxiliary datasets, and accommodation of heterogeneous client models. Experimental evaluations on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DENSE, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines, such as Fed-ADI, by a notable margin of 5.08% on the CIFAR10 dataset.

title: DILF-EN framework for Class-Incremental Learning
text: Deep learning models suffer from catastrophic forgetting of the classes in the older phases as they get trained on the classes introduced in the new phase in the class-incremental learning setting. In this work, we show that the effect of catastrophic forgetting on the model prediction varies with the change in orientation of the same image, which is a novel finding. Based on this, we propose a novel data-ensemble approach that combines the predictions for the different orientations of the image to help the model retain further information regarding the previously seen classes and thereby reduce the effect of forgetting on the model predictions. However, we cannot directly use the data-ensemble approach if the model is trained using traditional techniques. Therefore, we also propose a novel dual-incremental learning framework that involves jointly training the network with two incremental learning objectives, i.e., the class-incremental learning objective and our proposed data-incremental learning objective. In the dual-incremental learning framework, each image belongs to two classes, i.e., the image class (for class-incremental learning) and the orientation class (for data-incremental learning). In class-incremental learning, each new phase introduces a new set of classes, and the model cannot access the complete training data from the older phases. In our proposed data-incremental learning, the orientation classes remain the same across all the phases, and the data introduced by the new phase in class-incremental learning acts as new training data for these orientation classes. We empirically demonstrate that the dual-incremental learning framework is vital to the data-ensemble approach. We apply our proposed approach to state-of-the-art class-incremental learning methods and empirically show that our framework significantly improves the performance of these methods.

title: DILF-EN framework for Class-Incremental Learning
text: The phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting, where deep learning models forget previously learned classes as they adapt to new ones, is exacerbated by the inherent variability in image orientation. We reveal that the impact of catastrophic forgetting on model predictions is orientation-dependent, a previously unreported observation. Leveraging this insight, we introduce a novel data-ensemble strategy, which aggregates predictions from different image orientations to mitigate the effects of forgetting. However, this approach is incompatible with traditional training methods. To address this limitation, we propose a dual-incremental learning framework, wherein the network is jointly optimized with two objectives: class-incremental learning and our novel data-incremental learning objective. In this framework, each image is assigned two labels: an image class for class-incremental learning and an orientation class for data-incremental learning. While class-incremental learning introduces new classes in each phase, our data-incremental learning objective retains the same orientation classes across phases, utilizing new data as additional training samples. Our experiments demonstrate the crucial role of dual-incremental learning in enabling the data-ensemble approach. Moreover, we show that integrating our framework with state-of-the-art class-incremental learning methods yields significant performance improvements.

title: KFWC: A Knowledge-Driven Deep Learning Model for Fine-grained Classification of Wet-AMD
text: Automated diagnosis using deep neural networks can help ophthalmologists detect the blinding eye disease wet Age-related Macular Degeneration (AMD). Wet-AMD has two similar subtypes, Neovascular AMD and Polypoidal Choroidal Vessels (PCV). However, due to the difficulty in data collection and the similarity between images, most studies have only achieved the coarse-grained classification of wet-AMD rather than a finer-grained one of wet-AMD subtypes. To solve this issue, in this paper we propose a Knowledge-driven Fine-grained Wet-AMD Classification Model (KFWC), to classify fine-grained diseases with insufficient data. With the introduction of a priori knowledge of 10 lesion signs of input images into the KFWC, we aim to accelerate the KFWC by means of multi-label classification pre-training, to locate the decisive image features in the fine-grained disease classification task and therefore achieve better classification. Simultaneously, the KFWC can also provide good interpretability and effectively alleviate the pressure of data collection and annotation in the field of fine-grained disease classification for wet-AMD.
