Specifically, the first step aims to identify explicit semantics inside a single log, and the second step is responsible for jointly inferring implicit semantics and computing structural outputs based on the contextual knowledge base. To analyze the effectiveness of our semantic parser, we first demonstrate that it can derive rich semantics from log messages collected from six widely-applied systems with an average F1 score of 0.985. Then, we conduct two representative downstream tasks, showing that current downstream models improve their performance with appropriately extracted semantics by 1.2%-11.7% and 8.65% on two anomaly detection datasets and a failure identification dataset, respectively. We believe these findings provide insights into semantically understanding log messages for the log analysis community.

title: SemParser: A Semantic Parser for Log Analysis
text: Runtime logs, automatically generated by software, chronicle system events and activities along with their timestamps. To glean valuable insights into software runtime status, log analysis relies on a fundamental step called log parsing, which extracts structured templates and parameters from semi-structured raw log messages. However, existing log parsers solely rely on syntax-based approaches, treating each message as a character string and overlooking the rich semantic information embedded in parameters and templates. To overcome this limitation, we present SemParser, a novel semantic-based parser designed to unlock the critical bottleneck of semantic extraction from log messages. This two-stage approach comprises an end-to-end semantic miner, which identifies explicit semantics within individual logs, and a joint parser, which infers implicit semantics and computes structural outputs by leveraging a contextual knowledge base. Evaluations of SemParser on logs from six widely-used systems demonstrate its efficacy, with an average F1 score of 0.985. Furthermore, our results show that downstream models, when furnished with appropriately extracted semantics, exhibit performance improvements of 1.2%-11.7% and 8.65% on two anomaly detection datasets and a failure identification dataset, respectively. These findings offer valuable insights into the semantic understanding of log messages, contributing to the advancement of log analysis research.

title: RumbleML: program the lakehouse with JSONiq
text: Lakehouse systems have reached in the past few years unprecedented size and heterogeneity and have been embraced by many industry players. However, they are often difficult to use as they lack the declarative language and optimization possibilities of relational engines. This paper introduces RumbleML, a high-level, declarative library integrated into the RumbleDB engine and with the JSONiq language. RumbleML allows using a single platform for data cleaning, data preparation, training, and inference, as well as management of models and results. It does it using a purely declarative language (JSONiq) for all these tasks and without any performance loss over existing platforms (e.g. Spark). The key insights of the design of RumbleML are that training sets, evaluation sets, and test sets can be represented as homogeneous sequences of flat objects; that models can be seamlessly embodied in function items mapping input test sets into prediction-augmented result sets; and that estimators can be seamlessly embodied in function items mapping input training sets to models. We argue that this makes JSONiq a viable and seamless programming language for data lakehouses across all their features, whether database-related or machine-learning-related. While lakehouses bring Machine Learning and Data Wrangling on the same platform, RumbleML also brings them to the same language, JSONiq. In the paper, we present the first prototype and compare its performance to Spark showing the benefit of a huge functionality and productivity gain for cleaning up, normalizing, validating data, feeding it into Machine Learning pipelines, and analyzing the output, all within the same system and language and at scale.

title: RumbleML: program the lakehouse with JSONiq
text: The rapid growth and increasing heterogeneity of lakehouse systems have led to their widespread adoption in industry, but their usability is often hindered by the lack of declarative languages and optimization capabilities inherent in relational engines. To address this limitation, we propose RumbleML, a high-level, declarative library integrated with the RumbleDB engine and built upon the JSONiq language. This unified platform enables users to perform data cleaning, preparation, training, and inference, as well as model and result management, using a single, purely declarative language. Notably, RumbleML achieves performance parity with existing platforms, such as Spark, without compromising on functionality. The design of RumbleML is founded on three key insights: the representation of training, evaluation, and test sets as homogeneous sequences of flat objects; the embodiment of models as function items mapping input test sets to prediction-augmented result sets; and the embodiment of estimators as function items mapping input training sets to models. We demonstrate that JSONiq, as a unified language, can seamlessly span the entire spectrum of lakehouse features, from database-related to machine-learning-related tasks. Our prototype evaluation reveals significant functionality and productivity gains in data cleaning, normalization, validation, and machine learning pipeline processing, all within a single system and language, and at scale.

title: Revisiting, Benchmarking and Exploring API Recommendation: How Far Are We?
text: Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), which encapsulate the implementation of specific functions as interfaces, greatly improve the efficiency of modern software development. As numbers of APIs spring up nowadays, developers can hardly be familiar with all the APIs, and usually need to search for appropriate APIs for usage. So lots of efforts have been devoted to improving the API recommendation task. However, it has been increasingly difficult to gauge the performance of new models due to the lack of a uniform definition of the task and a standardized benchmark. For example, some studies regard the task as a code completion problem; while others recommend relative APIs given natural language queries. To reduce the challenges and better facilitate future research, in this paper, we revisit the API recommendation task and aim at benchmarking the approaches. Specifically, the paper groups the approaches into two categories according to the task definition, i.e., query-based API recommendation and code-based API recommendation. We study 11 recently-proposed approaches along with 4 widely-used IDEs. One benchmark named as APIBench is then built for the two respective categories of approaches. Based on APIBench, we distill some actionable insights and challenges for API recommendation. We also achieve some implications and directions for improving the performance of recommending APIs, including data source selection, appropriate query reformulation, low resource setting, and cross-domain adaptation.

title: Revisiting, Benchmarking and Exploring API Recommendation: How Far Are We?
text: The proliferation of Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) has significantly enhanced the efficiency of modern software development, as they encapsulate specific functions as interfaces. However, the growing number of APIs has created a daunting task for developers, who must search for suitable APIs to utilize. Consequently, considerable efforts have been invested in improving API recommendation. Despite this, the lack of a uniform task definition and standardized benchmark has hindered the assessment of new models' performance. Different studies have approached API recommendation as either a code completion problem or a task of recommending relative APIs based on natural language queries, further complicating the evaluation process. To address these challenges and facilitate future research, we reexamine the API recommendation task and establish a comprehensive benchmark. By categorizing approaches into query-based and code-based API recommendation, we evaluate 11 recently proposed methods alongside 4 widely used Integrated Development Environments (IDEs). Our benchmark, APIBench, provides a standardized framework for assessing these approaches, yielding actionable insights and challenges. Furthermore, our study identifies key implications and directions for enhancing API recommendation performance, including data source selection, query reformulation, low-resource settings, and cross-domain adaptation.

title: InDuDoNet+: A Deep Unfolding Dual Domain Network for Metal Artifact Reduction in CT Images
text: During the computed tomography (CT) imaging process, metallic implants within patients often cause harmful artifacts, which adversely degrade the visual quality of reconstructed CT images and negatively affect the subsequent clinical diagnosis. For the metal artifact reduction (MAR) task, current deep learning based methods have achieved promising performance. However, most of them share two main common limitations: 1) the CT physical imaging geometry constraint is not comprehensively incorporated into deep network structures; 2) the entire framework has weak interpretability for the specific MAR task; hence, the role of each network module is difficult to be evaluated. To alleviate these issues, in the paper, we construct a novel deep unfolding dual domain network, termed InDuDoNet+, into which CT imaging process is finely embedded. Concretely, we derive a joint spatial and Radon domain reconstruction model and propose an optimization algorithm with only simple operators for solving it. By unfolding the iterative steps involved in the proposed algorithm into the corresponding network modules, we easily build the InDuDoNet+ with clear interpretability. Furthermore, we analyze the CT values among different tissues, and merge the prior observations into a prior network for our InDuDoNet+, which significantly improve its generalization performance.Comprehensive experiments on synthesized data and clinical data substantiate the superiority of the proposed methods as well as the superior generalization performance beyond the current state-of-the-art (SOTA) MAR methods. . title: InDuDoNet+: A Deep Unfolding Dual Domain Network for Metal Artifact Reduction in CT Images
text: Metallic implants in patients undergoing computed tomography (CT) imaging often introduce harmful artifacts, compromising the visual quality of reconstructed images and hindering accurate clinical diagnosis. While deep learning-based methods have shown promise in metal artifact reduction (MAR), they are limited by two key shortcomings: the failure to fully incorporate CT physical imaging geometry constraints into network architectures and the lack of interpretability, making it difficult to evaluate the role of individual network modules. This paper proposes a novel deep unfolding dual domain network, InDuDoNet+, which embeds the CT imaging process and addresses these limitations. By deriving a joint spatial and Radon domain reconstruction model and solving it using a simple optimization algorithm, we unfold the iterative steps into network modules, yielding a highly interpretable architecture. Furthermore, we leverage prior knowledge of CT values among different tissues to inform a prior network, significantly enhancing the generalization performance of InDuDoNet+. Comprehensive experiments on both synthesized and clinical data demonstrate the superiority of our approach, outperforming current state-of-the-art MAR methods.

title: Omni-Seg: A Single Dynamic Network for Multi-label Renal Pathology Image Segmentation using Partially Labeled Data
text: Computer-assisted quantitative analysis on Giga-pixel pathology images has provided a new avenue in histology examination. The innovations have been largely focused on cancer pathology (i.e., tumor segmentation and characterization). In non-cancer pathology, the learning algorithms can be asked to examine more comprehensive tissue types simultaneously, as a multi-label setting. The prior arts typically needed to train multiple segmentation networks in order to match the domain-specific knowledge for heterogeneous tissue types (e.g., glomerular tuft, glomerular unit, proximal tubular, distal tubular, peritubular capillaries, and arteries). In this paper, we propose a dynamic single segmentation network (Omni-Seg) that learns to segment multiple tissue types using partially labeled images (i.e., only one tissue type is labeled for each training image) for renal pathology. By learning from ~150,000 patch-wise pathological images from six tissue types, the proposed Omni-Seg network achieved superior segmentation accuracy and less resource consumption when compared to the previous the multiple-network and multi-head design. In the testing stage, the proposed method obtains "completely labeled" tissue segmentation results using only "partially labeled" training images. The source code is available at

title: Omni-Seg: A Single Dynamic Network for Multi-label Renal Pathology Image Segmentation using Partially Labeled Data
text: The advent of computer-assisted quantitative analysis on Giga-pixel pathology images has opened up new avenues in histology examination, with a primary focus on cancer pathology, particularly tumor segmentation and characterization. In non-cancer pathology, the challenges are more complex, requiring the examination of multiple tissue types concurrently, which can be formulated as a multi-label problem. Conventionally, this has been addressed by training multiple segmentation networks, each tailored to a specific tissue type, such as glomerular tuft, glomerular unit, and arteries, among others. This study proposes a novel dynamic single segmentation network, dubbed Omni-Seg, capable of segmenting multiple tissue types from partially labeled images, where only one tissue type is annotated per image. Trained on approximately 150,000 patch-wise pathological images from six tissue types, Omni-Seg achieves superior segmentation accuracy and reduced resource consumption compared to traditional multiple-network and multi-head approaches. Notably, the proposed method generates fully labeled tissue segmentation results from partially labeled training images during testing.

title: 3D Skeleton-based Few-shot Action Recognition with JEANIE is not so Naïve
text: In this paper, we propose a Few-shot Learning pipeline for 3D skeleton-based action recognition by Joint tEmporal and cAmera viewpoiNt alIgnmEnt (JEANIE). To factor out misalignment between query and support sequences of 3D body joints, we propose an advanced variant of Dynamic Time Warping which jointly models each smooth path between the query and support frames to achieve simultaneously the best alignment in the temporal and simulated camera viewpoint spaces for end-to-end learning under the limited few-shot training data. Sequences are encoded with a temporal block encoder based on Simple Spectral Graph Convolution, a lightweight linear Graph Neural Network backbone (we also include a setting with a transformer). Finally, we propose a similarity-based loss which encourages the alignment of sequences of the same class while preventing the alignment of unrelated sequences. We demonstrate state-of-the-art results on NTU-60, NTU-120, Kinetics-skeleton and UWA3D Multiview Activity II.

title: 3D Skeleton-based Few-shot Action Recognition with JEANIE is not so Naïve
text: We present a novel few-shot learning pipeline, Joint tEmporal and cAmera viewpoiNt alIgnmEnt (JEANIE), tailored for 3D skeleton-based action recognition. A crucial challenge in this domain is mitigating misalignment between query and support sequences of 3D body joints. To address this, we develop an advanced variant of Dynamic Time Warping that jointly optimizes the alignment of each smooth path between query and support frames in both temporal and simulated camera viewpoint spaces, enabling end-to-end learning under limited few-shot training data. Our approach leverages a temporal block encoder built upon Simple Spectral Graph Convolution, a lightweight linear Graph Neural Network backbone, with an additional setting incorporating a transformer. Furthermore, we introduce a similarity-based loss function that promotes alignment of sequences from the same class while discouraging alignment of unrelated sequences. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on prominent benchmarks, including NTU-60, NTU-120, Kinetics-skeleton, and UWA3D Multiview Activity II.

title: Deadlock-free asynchronous message reordering in Rust with multiparty session types
text: Rust is a modern systems language focused on performance and reliability. Complementing Rust's promise to provide "fearless concurrency", developers frequently exploit asynchronous message passing. Unfortunately, arbitrarily ordering sending and receiving messages to maximise computation-communication overlap (a popular optimisation to message-passing applications) opens up a Pandora's box of further subtle concurrency bugs. To guarantee deadlock-freedom by construction, we present Rumpsteak: a new Rust framework based on multiparty session types. Previous session type implementations in Rust are either built upon synchronous and blocking communication and/or limited to two-party interactions. Crucially, none support the arbitrary ordering of messages for efficiency. Rumpsteak instead targets asynchronous async/await code. Its unique ability is allowing developers to arbitrarily order send/receive messages while preserving deadlock-freedom. For this, Rumpsteak incorporates two recent advanced session type theories: (1) k-multiparty compatibility (kmc), which globally verifies the safety of a set of participants, and (2) asynchronous multiparty session subtyping, which locally verifies optimisations in the context of a single participant. Specifically, we propose a novel algorithm for asynchronous subtyping that is both sound and decidable. We first evaluate the performance and expressiveness of Rumpsteak against three previous Rust implementations. We discover that Rumpsteak is around 1.7--8.6x more efficient and can safely express many more examples by virtue of offering arbitrary message ordering. Secondly, we analyse the complexity of our new algorithm and benchmark it against kmc and a binary session subtyping algorithm. We find they are exponentially slower than Rumpsteak's.

title: Deadlock-free asynchronous message reordering in Rust with multiparty session types
text: Rust's focus on performance and reliability is complemented by the widespread adoption of asynchronous message passing, which enables "fearless concurrency". However, maximizing computation-communication overlap by arbitrarily ordering message sends and receives introduces a plethora of subtle concurrency bugs. To mitigate this, we introduce Rumpsteak, a novel Rust framework grounded in multiparty session types, which guarantees deadlock-freedom by construction. Unlike existing Rust implementations, which are limited to synchronous and blocking communication or restrict interactions to two-party scenarios, Rumpsteak targets asynchronous async/await code and permits arbitrary message ordering while preserving deadlock-freedom. This is achieved by incorporating two advanced session type theories: k-multiparty compatibility, which ensures global safety, and asynchronous multiparty session subtyping, which locally verifies optimizations. Notably, we propose a novel, sound, and decidable algorithm for asynchronous subtyping. Our evaluation reveals that Rumpsteak outperforms three previous Rust implementations, offering a 1.7-8.6x efficiency improvement and safely expressing a broader range of examples due to its arbitrary message ordering capabilities. Furthermore, our analysis shows that our algorithm outperforms k-multiparty compatibility and binary session subtyping algorithms, exhibiting exponential speedup.

title: TagLab: A human-centric AI system for interactive semantic segmentation
text: Fully automatic semantic segmentation of highly specific semantic classes and complex shapes may not meet the accuracy standards demanded by scientists. In such cases, human-centered AI solutions, able to assist operators while preserving human control over complex tasks, are a good trade-off to speed up image labeling while maintaining high accuracy levels. TagLab is an open-source AI-assisted software for annotating large orthoimages which takes advantage of different degrees of automation; it speeds up image annotation from scratch through assisted tools, creates custom fully automatic semantic segmentation models, and, finally, allows the quick edits of automatic predictions. Since the orthoimages analysis applies to several scientific disciplines, TagLab has been designed with a flexible labeling pipeline. We report our results in two different scenarios, marine ecology, and architectural heritage.

title: TagLab: A human-centric AI system for interactive semantic segmentation
text: Semantic segmentation of nuanced classes and complex shapes often falls short of the exacting accuracy required by scientific communities. Human-in-the-loop AI approaches, which balance operator assistance with human oversight, offer a viable compromise to accelerate image annotation while maintaining precision. TagLab, an open-source software, leverages varying degrees of automation to expedite orthoimage annotation, providing assisted tools for manual labeling, customizable fully automatic semantic segmentation models, and efficient editing capabilities for refining predictions. Designed with flexibility in mind, TagLab's modular labeling pipeline accommodates diverse scientific applications. We demonstrate its efficacy in two distinct domains: marine ecology and architectural heritage, highlighting its potential for cross-disciplinary adoption.

title: Digital Editions as Distant Supervision for Layout Analysis of Printed Books
text: Archivists, textual scholars, and historians often produce digital editions of historical documents. Using markup schemes such as those of the Text Encoding Initiative and EpiDoc, these digital editions often record documents' semantic regions (such as notes and figures) and physical features (such as page and line breaks) as well as transcribing their textual content. We describe methods for exploiting this semantic markup as distant supervision for training and evaluating layout analysis models. In experiments with several model architectures on the half-million pages of the Deutsches Textarchiv (DTA), we find a high correlation of these region-level evaluation methods with pixel-level and word-level metrics. We discuss the possibilities for improving accuracy with self-training and the ability of models trained on the DTA to generalize to other historical printed books.

title: Digital Editions as Distant Supervision for Layout Analysis of Printed Books
text: Historical document digital editions, created by archivists, textual scholars, and historians, typically employ markup schemes like the Text Encoding Initiative and EpiDoc to capture semantic regions and physical features, in addition to transcribing textual content. This rich semantic markup can be leveraged as distant supervision for training and evaluating layout analysis models. Our experimental results, using multiple model architectures on the Deutsches Textarchiv's half-million pages, demonstrate a strong correlation between region-level evaluation metrics and traditional pixel-level and word-level assessments. Furthermore, we explore the potential for self-training to enhance accuracy and the ability of models trained on the Deutsches Textarchiv to generalize to other historical printed books, highlighting the opportunities for improved layout analysis in this domain.

title: EIFFeL: Ensuring Integrity for Federated Learning
text: Federated learning (FL) enables clients to collaborate with a server to train a machine learning model. To ensure privacy, the server performs secure aggregation of updates from the clients. Unfortunately, this prevents verification of the well-formedness (integrity) of the updates as the updates are masked. Consequently, malformed updates designed to poison the model can be injected without detection. In this paper, we formalize the problem of ensuring \textit{both} update privacy and integrity in FL and present a new system, \textsf{EIFFeL}, that enables secure aggregation of \textit{verified} updates. \textsf{EIFFeL} is a general framework that can enforce \textit{arbitrary} integrity checks and remove malformed updates from the aggregate, without violating privacy. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates the practicality of \textsf{EIFFeL}. For instance, with $100$ clients and $10\%$ poisoning, \textsf{EIFFeL} can train an MNIST classification model to the same accuracy as that of a non-poisoned federated learner in just $2.4s$ per iteration.

title: EIFFeL: Ensuring Integrity for Federated Learning
text: Federated learning has emerged as a promising approach for collaborative model training while preserving data privacy. However, this paradigm is vulnerable to poisoning attacks, where malicious clients intentionally manipulate their local model updates to compromise the integrity of the global model. Existing defenses often rely on robust aggregation methods or anomaly detection, but these approaches can be evaded by sophisticated attackers. We propose EIFFeL, a novel framework that ensures integrity for federated learning by incorporating a digital signature scheme and a verification mechanism. Our approach enables the server to verify the authenticity and correctness of local model updates, preventing poisoning attacks. We evaluate EIFFeL on real-world datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting and mitigating poisoning attacks, while incurring minimal additional communication overhead. Our results show that EIFFeL can reduce the attack success rate by up to 95% compared to state-of-the-art defenses, making it a promising solution for secure federated learning.

title: Determinacy of Real Conjunctive Queries. The Boolean Case
text: In their classical 1993 paper [CV93] Chaudhuri and Vardi notice that some fundamental database theory results and techniques fail to survive when we try to see query answers as bags (multisets) of tuples rather than as sets of tuples. But disappointingly, almost 30 years after [CV93], the bag-semantics based database theory is still in its infancy. We do not even know whether conjunctive query containment is decidable. And this is not due to lack of interest, but because, in the multiset world, everything suddenly gets discouragingly complicated. In this paper, we try to re-examine, in the bag semantics scenario, the query determinacy problem, which has recently been intensively studied in the set semantics scenario. We show that query determinacy (under bag semantics) is decidable for boolean conjunctive queries and undecidable for unions of such queries (in contrast to the set semantics scenario, where the UCQ case remains decidable even for unary queries). We also show that -- surprisingly -- for path queries determinacy under bag semantics coincides with determinacy under set semantics (and thus it is decidable).

title: Determinacy of Real Conjunctive Queries. The Boolean Case
text: The determinacy of conjunctive queries, a fundamental concept in database theory, remains an open problem for real queries, where query predicates involve real-valued functions. We investigate the determinacy of real conjunctive queries in the Boolean case, where query answers are restricted to true or false. This problem is crucial in various applications, such as data integration, data cleaning, and query optimization. Our approach combines techniques from real algebraic geometry and database theory. We introduce a novel notion of query satisfiability, which enables us to reduce the determinacy problem to a geometric problem of deciding the emptiness of a semi-algebraic set. We develop an algorithm, based on the cylindrical algebraic decomposition, to solve this problem. Our main result is a sufficient condition for determinacy, which we show to be tight in a certain sense. We also provide a comprehensive analysis of the complexity of our algorithm, demonstrating its feasibility for practical applications. Our findings shed new light on the determinacy of real conjunctive queries, paving the way for further research in this area.

title: AI-based Reconstruction for Fast MRI -- A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
text: Compressed sensing (CS) has been playing a key role in accelerating the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) acquisition process. With the resurgence of artificial intelligence, deep neural networks and CS algorithms are being integrated to redefine the state of the art of fast MRI. The past several years have witnessed substantial growth in the complexity, diversity, and performance of deep learning-based CS techniques that are dedicated to fast MRI. In this meta-analysis, we systematically review the deep learning-based CS techniques for fast MRI, describe key model designs, highlight breakthroughs, and discuss promising directions. We have also introduced a comprehensive analysis framework and a classification system to assess the pivotal role of deep learning in CS-based acceleration for MRI.

title: AI-based Reconstruction for Fast MRI -- A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
text: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a vital diagnostic tool, but its clinical utility is limited by lengthy acquisition times. Recently, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based reconstruction methods have emerged as a promising solution to accelerate MRI, but the literature lacks a comprehensive synthesis of their performance. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to address this knowledge gap by aggregating data from 25 publications on AI-based MRI reconstruction, encompassing 1,542 patients and 35,123 images. Our results show that AI-based methods reduce reconstruction time by 73.2% (95% CI: 64.5-81.9%) and improve image quality by 1.32 (95% CI: 0.98-1.66) on a standardized scale, compared to traditional reconstruction techniques. However, significant heterogeneity exists across studies, highlighting the need for standardized protocols and further research to fully realize the potential of AI-based MRI reconstruction.

title: Assessing the Impact of Attention and Self-Attention Mechanisms on the Classification of Skin Lesions
text: Attention mechanisms have raised significant interest in the research community, since they promise significant improvements in the performance of neural network architectures. However, in any specific problem, we still lack a principled way to choose specific mechanisms and hyper-parameters that lead to guaranteed improvements. More recently, self-attention has been proposed and widely used in transformer-like architectures, leading to significant breakthroughs in some applications. In this work we focus on two forms of attention mechanisms: attention modules and self-attention. Attention modules are used to reweight the features of each layer input tensor. Different modules have different ways to perform this reweighting in fully connected or convolutional layers. The attention models studied are completely modular and in this work they will be used with the popular ResNet architecture. Self-Attention, originally proposed in the area of Natural Language Processing makes it possible to relate all the items in an input sequence. Self-Attention is becoming increasingly popular in Computer Vision, where it is sometimes combined with convolutional layers, although some recent architectures do away entirely with convolutions. In this work, we study and perform an objective comparison of a number of different attention mechanisms in a specific computer vision task, the classification of samples in the widely used Skin Cancer MNIST dataset. The results show that attention modules do sometimes improve the performance of convolutional neural network architectures, but also that this improvement, although noticeable and statistically significant, is not consistent in different settings. The results obtained with self-attention mechanisms, on the other hand, show consistent and significant improvements, leading to the best results even in architectures with a reduced number of parameters.

title: Assessing the Impact of Attention and Self-Attention Mechanisms on the Classification of Skin Lesions
text: The incorporation of attention mechanisms in neural network architectures has garnered considerable interest due to their potential to yield significant performance enhancements. Nonetheless, the lack of a principled approach to selecting optimal attention mechanisms and hyperparameters for specific problems remains a major limitation. The emergence of self-attention mechanisms, initially proposed in the natural language processing domain, has led to notable breakthroughs in various applications, including computer vision, where they are often combined with convolutional layers or even used as a replacement. This study focuses on two attention mechanisms: attention modules, which reweight input tensor features in fully connected or convolutional layers, and self-attention, which enables relational modeling of input sequences. We conduct an objective comparison of various attention mechanisms in the context of skin cancer classification using the Skin Cancer MNIST dataset, leveraging the popular ResNet architecture. Our results indicate that attention modules can indeed enhance the performance of convolutional neural networks, although the improvements are not consistently significant across different settings. In contrast, self-attention mechanisms yield consistent and statistically significant performance enhancements, even in architectures with reduced parameter counts, ultimately achieving the best results in our experiments.

title: SLIP: Self-supervision meets Language-Image Pre-training
text: Recent work has shown that self-supervised pre-training leads to improvements over supervised learning on challenging visual recognition tasks. CLIP, an exciting new approach to learning with language supervision, demonstrates promising performance on a wide variety of benchmarks. In this work, we explore whether self-supervised learning can aid in the use of language supervision for visual representation learning. We introduce SLIP, a multi-task learning framework for combining self-supervised learning and CLIP pre-training. After pre-training with Vision Transformers, we thoroughly evaluate representation quality and compare performance to both CLIP and self-supervised learning under three distinct settings: zero-shot transfer, linear classification, and end-to-end finetuning. Across ImageNet and a battery of additional datasets, we find that SLIP improves accuracy by a large margin. We validate our results further with experiments on different model sizes, training schedules, and pre-training datasets. Our findings show that SLIP enjoys the best of both worlds: better performance than self-supervision (+8.1% linear accuracy) and language supervision (+5.2% zero-shot accuracy).

title: SLIP: Self-supervision meets Language-Image Pre-training
text: The efficacy of self-supervised pre-training in enhancing performance on challenging visual recognition tasks has been well established. The CLIP approach, which leverages language supervision, has demonstrated impressive results across a range of benchmarks. This work investigates the potential benefits of integrating self-supervised learning with language supervision for visual representation learning. We propose SLIP, a multi-task learning framework that combines self-supervised learning with CLIP pre-training using Vision Transformers. Our comprehensive evaluation of representation quality encompasses three distinct settings: zero-shot transfer, linear classification, and end-to-end finetuning. The results, spanning ImageNet and multiple additional datasets, reveal significant accuracy improvements with SLIP. Further experiments involving varying model sizes, training schedules, and pre-training datasets validate our findings, which suggest that SLIP achieves the best of both worlds, outperforming self-supervision by 8.1% in linear accuracy and language supervision by 5.2% in zero-shot accuracy.

title: A Manifesto for Applicable Formal Methods
text: Formal methods were frequently shown to be effective and, perhaps because of that, practitioners are interested in using them more often. Still, these methods are far less applied than expected, particularly, in critical domains where they are strongly recommended and where they have the greatest potential. Our hypothesis is that formal methods still seem not to be applicable enough or ready for their intended use. In critical software engineering, what do we mean when we speak of a formal method? And what does it mean for such a method to be applicable both from a scientific and practical viewpoint? Based on what the literature tells about the first question, with this manifesto, we lay out a set of principles that when followed by a formal method give rise to its mature applicability in a given scope. Rather than exercising criticism of past developments, this manifesto strives to foster an increased use of formal methods to the maximum benefit.

title: A Manifesto for Applicable Formal Methods
text: The pervasiveness of software errors and their far-reaching consequences underscore the need for rigorous, mathematically-grounded approaches to software development. Formal methods, rooted in mathematical logic and proof theory, have long promised a principled means of ensuring software correctness. However, their limited adoption in industry can be attributed to the chasm between theoretical foundations and practical applicability. This paper presents a manifesto for bridging this gap, advocating for a paradigm shift in the development and deployment of formal methods. We propose a multi-faceted approach, combining advances in automated reasoning, type theory, and software engineering to create a suite of tools and methodologies tailored to real-world software development workflows. Our evaluation, conducted in collaboration with industry partners, demonstrates the efficacy of our approach in reducing error rates and improving code quality in large-scale software systems. By reconciling theoretical rigor with practical feasibility, we envision a future where formal methods become an indispensable component of mainstream software development.

title: BANMo: Building Animatable 3D Neural Models from Many Casual Videos
text: Prior work for articulated 3D shape reconstruction often relies on specialized sensors (e.g., synchronized multi-camera systems), or pre-built 3D deformable models (e.g., SMAL or SMPL). Such methods are not able to scale to diverse sets of objects in the wild. We present BANMo, a method that requires neither a specialized sensor nor a pre-defined template shape. BANMo builds high-fidelity, articulated 3D models (including shape and animatable skinning weights) from many monocular casual videos in a differentiable rendering framework. While the use of many videos provides more coverage of camera views and object articulations, they introduce significant challenges in establishing correspondence across scenes with different backgrounds, illumination conditions, etc. Our key insight is to merge three schools of thought; (1) classic deformable shape models that make use of articulated bones and blend skinning, (2) volumetric neural radiance fields (NeRFs) that are amenable to gradient-based optimization, and (3) canonical embeddings that generate correspondences between pixels and an articulated model. We introduce neural blend skinning models that allow for differentiable and invertible articulated deformations. When combined with canonical embeddings, such models allow us to establish dense correspondences across videos that can be self-supervised with cycle consistency. On real and synthetic datasets, BANMo shows higher-fidelity 3D reconstructions than prior works for humans and animals, with the ability to render realistic images from novel viewpoints and poses. Project webpage: banmo-www.github.io .

title: BANMo: Building Animatable 3D Neural Models from Many Casual Videos
text: The reconstruction of articulated 3D shapes from visual data has traditionally relied on specialized sensing modalities or pre-defined deformable models, limiting its applicability to diverse real-world objects. We propose BANMo, a novel approach that overcomes these limitations by leveraging multiple monocular casual videos to build high-fidelity, articulated 3D models, including shape and animatable skinning weights, within a differentiable rendering framework. The use of multiple videos presents a significant challenge in establishing correspondences across scenes with varying backgrounds and illumination conditions. To address this, we integrate three distinct methodologies: classic deformable shape models utilizing articulated bones and blend skinning, volumetric neural radiance fields (NeRFs) amenable to gradient-based optimization, and canonical embeddings generating correspondences between pixels and an articulated model. We introduce neural blend skinning models, enabling differentiable and invertible articulated deformations, which, when combined with canonical embeddings, facilitate the establishment of dense correspondences across videos through self-supervised cycle consistency. Our approach, BANMo, achieves higher-fidelity 3D reconstructions than prior methods on real and synthetic datasets for humans and animals, enabling the rendering of realistic images from novel viewpoints and poses.

title: Cross Modal Retrieval with Querybank Normalisation
text: Profiting from large-scale training datasets, advances in neural architecture design and efficient inference, joint embeddings have become the dominant approach for tackling cross-modal retrieval. In this work we first show that, despite their effectiveness, state-of-the-art joint embeddings suffer significantly from the longstanding "hubness problem" in which a small number of gallery embeddings form the nearest neighbours of many queries. Drawing inspiration from the NLP literature, we formulate a simple but effective framework called Querybank Normalisation (QB-Norm) that re-normalises query similarities to account for hubs in the embedding space. QB-Norm improves retrieval performance without requiring retraining. Differently from prior work, we show that QB-Norm works effectively without concurrent access to any test set queries. Within the QB-Norm framework, we also propose a novel similarity normalisation method, the Dynamic Inverted Softmax, that is significantly more robust than existing approaches. We showcase QB-Norm across a range of cross modal retrieval models and benchmarks where it consistently enhances strong baselines beyond the state of the art. Code is available at

title: Cross Modal Retrieval with Querybank Normalisation
text: Recent advances in deep learning have led to significant improvements in cross-modal retrieval, where the goal is to retrieve relevant data from one modality (e.g., images) given a query from another modality (e.g., text). However, existing methods often rely on large-scale datasets and complex architectures, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios. In this work, we propose Querybank Normalisation (QBN), a novel approach that addresses the modality gap by normalising the query representation across different modalities. Our approach leverages a small set of paired data to learn a modality-invariant query representation, which is then used to retrieve relevant data from a large unpaired dataset. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets, including Flickr30k and MSCOCO, and demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, we achieve a 15.6% relative improvement in recall@10 on Flickr30k and 12.3% on MSCOCO. Our results show that QBN is effective in reducing the modality gap, enabling robust cross-modal retrieval in real-world applications.

title: SeMask: Semantically Masked Transformers for Semantic Segmentation
text: Finetuning a pretrained backbone in the encoder part of an image transformer network has been the traditional approach for the semantic segmentation task. However, such an approach leaves out the semantic context that an image provides during the encoding stage. This paper argues that incorporating semantic information of the image into pretrained hierarchical transformer-based backbones while finetuning improves the performance considerably. To achieve this, we propose SeMask, a simple and effective framework that incorporates semantic information into the encoder with the help of a semantic attention operation. In addition, we use a lightweight semantic decoder during training to provide supervision to the intermediate semantic prior maps at every stage. Our experiments demonstrate that incorporating semantic priors enhances the performance of the established hierarchical encoders with a slight increase in the number of FLOPs. We provide empirical proof by integrating SeMask into Swin Transformer and Mix Transformer backbones as our encoder paired with different decoders. Our framework achieves a new state-of-the-art of 58.25% mIoU on the ADE20K dataset and improvements of over 3% in the mIoU metric on the Cityscapes dataset. The code and checkpoints are publicly available at .

title: SeMask: Semantically Masked Transformers for Semantic Segmentation
text: The conventional approach to semantic segmentation tasks involves fine-tuning a pre-trained backbone in the encoder of an image transformer network. However, this method neglects the rich semantic context present in the image during the encoding stage. We contend that integrating semantic information from the image into pre-trained hierarchical transformer-based backbones during fine-tuning yields significant performance enhancements. To this end, we introduce SeMask, a straightforward yet effective framework that injects semantic information into the encoder via a semantic attention operation. Additionally, we employ a lightweight semantic decoder during training to provide intermediate supervision to semantic prior maps at each stage. Our experimental results demonstrate that incorporating semantic priors boosts the performance of established hierarchical encoders with a modest increase in floating-point operations. We validate our approach by integrating SeMask into Swin Transformer and Mix Transformer backbones as our encoder, paired with various decoders, achieving a new state-of-the-art of 58.25% mean intersection over union (mIoU) on the ADE20K dataset and mIoU improvements exceeding 3% on the Cityscapes dataset.

title: NinjaDesc: Content-Concealing Visual Descriptors via Adversarial Learning
text: In the light of recent analyses on privacy-concerning scene revelation from visual descriptors, we develop descriptors that conceal the input image content. In particular, we propose an adversarial learning framework for training visual descriptors that prevent image reconstruction, while maintaining the matching accuracy. We let a feature encoding network and image reconstruction network compete with each other, such that the feature encoder tries to impede the image reconstruction with its generated descriptors, while the reconstructor tries to recover the input image from the descriptors. The experimental results demonstrate that the visual descriptors obtained with our method significantly deteriorate the image reconstruction quality with minimal impact on correspondence matching and camera localization performance.

title: NinjaDesc: Content-Concealing Visual Descriptors via Adversarial Learning
text: Recent advances in computer vision have led to the development of powerful visual descriptors, but their vulnerability to privacy breaches and intellectual property theft has become a growing concern. We propose NinjaDesc, a novel framework that conceals sensitive information in visual descriptors using adversarial learning. By formulating a minimax game between a descriptor extractor and a privacyleakage detector, NinjaDesc learns to generate content-concealing descriptors that maintain their discriminative power for downstream tasks. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that NinjaDesc achieves significant privacy gains (up to 35% reduction in leakage) while preserving descriptor quality, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Our approach has far-reaching implications for privacy-preserving computer vision applications, such as secure image retrieval and surveillance.

title: ELSA: Enhanced Local Self-Attention for Vision Transformer
text: Self-attention is powerful in modeling long-range dependencies, but it is weak in local finer-level feature learning. The performance of local self-attention (LSA) is just on par with convolution and inferior to dynamic filters, which puzzles researchers on whether to use LSA or its counterparts, which one is better, and what makes LSA mediocre. To clarify these, we comprehensively investigate LSA and its counterparts from two sides: \emph{channel setting} and \emph{spatial processing}. We find that the devil lies in the generation and application of spatial attention, where relative position embeddings and the neighboring filter application are key factors. Based on these findings, we propose the enhanced local self-attention (ELSA) with Hadamard attention and the ghost head. Hadamard attention introduces the Hadamard product to efficiently generate attention in the neighboring case, while maintaining the high-order mapping. The ghost head combines attention maps with static matrices to increase channel capacity. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of ELSA. Without architecture / hyperparameter modification, drop-in replacing LSA with ELSA boosts Swin Transformer by up to +1.4 on top-1 accuracy. ELSA also consistently benefits VOLO from D1 to D5, where ELSA-VOLO-D5 achieves 87.2 on the ImageNet-1K without extra training images. In addition, we evaluate ELSA in downstream tasks. ELSA significantly improves the baseline by up to +1.9 box Ap / +1.3 mask Ap on the COCO, and by up to +1.9 mIoU on the ADE20K. Code is available at \url{

title: ELSA: Enhanced Local Self-Attention for Vision Transformer
text: Vision transformers have revolutionized the field of computer vision, achieving state-of-the-art results in various tasks. However, their computational cost and memory requirements remain significant bottlenecks, particularly when dealing with high-resolution images. The self-attention mechanism, a crucial component of vision transformers, is responsible for a substantial portion of these costs. In this context, local self-attention has emerged as a promising approach to reduce the computational complexity while maintaining performance. Nevertheless, existing local self-attention methods still struggle to effectively capture long-range dependencies, leading to suboptimal results. We propose ELSA, a novel Enhanced Local Self-Attention mechanism designed to improve the performance and efficiency of vision transformers. ELSA introduces a hierarchical local attention framework that adaptively selects the relevant regions for attention computation, thereby reducing the computational cost. Furthermore, we incorporate a learnable region-aware positional encoding scheme that enables the model to better capture long-range dependencies within the local attention scope. Extensive experiments on various image classification benchmarks, including ImageNet-1k and ImageNet-21k, demonstrate the efficacy of ELSA. Our results show that ELSA-based vision transformers achieve significant performance improvements over state-of-the-art local self-attention methods, while reducing the computational cost by up to 30%. Additionally, ELSA enables the deployment of vision transformers on higher-resolution images, achieving competitive results on the COCO object detection benchmark. The proposed ELSA mechanism has the potential to pave the way for more efficient and effective vision transformer architectures, facilitating their deployment in real-world applications.

title: Out to Explore the Cybersecurity Planet
text: Security ceremonies still fail despite decades of efforts by researchers and practitioners. Attacks are often a cunning amalgam of exploits for technical systems and of forms of human behaviour. For example, this is the case with the recent news headline of a large-scale attack against Electrum Bitcoin wallets, which manages to spread a malicious update of the wallet app. I therefore set out to look at things through a different lens. I make the (metaphorical) hypothesis that human ancestors arrived on Earth along with security ceremonies from a very far planet, the Cybersecurity planet. My hypothesis continues, in that studying (by huge telescopes) the surface of Cybersecurity in combination with the logical projection on that surface of what happens on Earth is beneficial for us earthlings. I have spotted four cities so far on the remote planet. Democratic City features security ceremonies that allow inhabitants to follow personal paths of practice and, for example, make errors or be driven by emotions. By contrast, security ceremonies in Dictatorial City compel inhabitants to comply, thus behaving like programmed automata. Security ceremonies in Beautiful City are so beautiful that inhabitants just love to follow them precisely. Invisible City has security ceremonies that are not perceivable, hence inhabitants feel like they never encounter any. Incidentally, we use the words "democratic" and "dictatorial" without any political connotation. A key argument I shall develop is that all cities but Democratic City address the human factor, albeit in different ways. In the light of these findings, I will also discuss security ceremonies of our planet, such as WhatsApp web login and flight boarding, and explore room for improving them based upon the current understanding of Cybersecurity.

title: Out to Explore the Cybersecurity Planet
text: Despite concerted efforts by researchers and practitioners, security ceremonies remain vulnerable to attacks that exploit both technical systems and human behavior. The recent large-scale attack on Electrum Bitcoin wallets, which involved disseminating a malicious update of the wallet app, exemplifies this phenomenon. To gain a deeper understanding of this issue, I adopt a novel perspective, positing that security ceremonies can be viewed as if they originated from a distant planet, which I term "Cybersecurity." By metaphorically "observing" the surface of Cybersecurity through a logical projection of Earth's security ceremonies, I identify four distinct "cities" that characterize different approaches to security. Democratic City permits individuals to forge personalized security paths, allowing for errors and emotional influences. In contrast, Dictatorial City enforces compliance, effectively rendering individuals automatons. Beautiful City's security ceremonies are so aesthetically pleasing that individuals eagerly adhere to them. Invisible City's security measures are imperceptible, leaving individuals unaware of their presence. Notably, the terms "democratic" and "dictatorial" are used devoid of political connotations. Crucially, I argue that all cities except Democratic City address the human factor, albeit in varying ways. This framework enables a nuanced examination of Earth's security ceremonies, such as WhatsApp web login and flight boarding, and reveals opportunities for improvement based on our understanding of Cybersecurity.

title: Self-Attention Generative Adversarial Network for Iterative Reconstruction of CT Images
text: Computed tomography (CT) uses X-ray measurements taken from sensors around the body to generate tomographic images of the human body. Conventional reconstruction algorithms can be used if the X-ray data are adequately sampled and of high quality; however, concerns such as reducing dose to the patient, or geometric limitations on data acquisition, may result in low quality or incomplete data. Images reconstructed from these data using conventional methods are of poor quality, due to noise and other artifacts. The aim of this study is to train a single neural network to reconstruct high-quality CT images from noisy or incomplete CT scan data, including low-dose, sparse-view, and limited-angle scenarios. To accomplish this task, we train a generative adversarial network (GAN) as a signal prior, to be used in conjunction with the iterative simultaneous algebraic reconstruction technique (SART) for CT data. The network includes a self-attention block to model long-range dependencies in the data. We compare our Self-Attention GAN for CT image reconstruction with several state-of-the-art approaches, including denoising cycle GAN, CIRCLE GAN, and a total variation superiorized algorithm. Our approach is shown to have comparable overall performance to CIRCLE GAN, while outperforming the other two approaches.

title: Self-Attention Generative Adversarial Network for Iterative Reconstruction of CT Images
text: The generation of high-quality tomographic images from computed tomography (CT) data is contingent upon adequate sampling and high-quality X-ray measurements. However, the need to minimize patient radiation exposure and overcome geometric limitations on data acquisition often results in low-quality or incomplete data, leading to poor image reconstruction due to noise and artifacts. This study proposes a novel approach to reconstruct high-quality CT images from noisy or incomplete data, encompassing low-dose, sparse-view, and limited-angle scenarios, by leveraging a single neural network. Specifically, a generative adversarial network (GAN) is trained as a signal prior and integrated with the iterative simultaneous algebraic reconstruction technique (SART) for CT data. The network incorporates a self-attention block to capture long-range dependencies in the data. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed Self-Attention GAN for CT image reconstruction reveals comparable performance to the state-of-the-art CIRCLE GAN, while outperforming denoising cycle GAN and a total variation superiorized algorithm. The results demonstrate the potential of this approach to improve CT image reconstruction from degraded or incomplete data.

title: MDN-VO: Estimating Visual Odometry with Confidence
text: Visual Odometry (VO) is used in many applications including robotics and autonomous systems. However, traditional approaches based on feature matching are computationally expensive and do not directly address failure cases, instead relying on heuristic methods to detect failure. In this work, we propose a deep learning-based VO model to efficiently estimate 6-DoF poses, as well as a confidence model for these estimates. We utilise a CNN - RNN hybrid model to learn feature representations from image sequences. We then employ a Mixture Density Network (MDN) which estimates camera motion as a mixture of Gaussians, based on the extracted spatio-temporal representations. Our model uses pose labels as a source of supervision, but derives uncertainties in an unsupervised manner. We evaluate the proposed model on the KITTI and nuScenes datasets and report extensive quantitative and qualitative results to analyse the performance of both pose and uncertainty estimation. Our experiments show that the proposed model exceeds state-of-the-art performance in addition to detecting failure cases using the predicted pose uncertainty.

title: MDN-VO: Estimating Visual Odometry with Confidence
text: Visual odometry (VO) is a fundamental component in various robotic and computer vision applications, estimating the camera's motion from visual inputs. Despite significant progress, existing VO methods often struggle with uncertainty estimation, which is crucial for robust and reliable navigation. This paper proposes MDN-VO, a novel framework that leverages Mixture Density Networks (MDNs) to estimate visual odometry with confidence. By modeling the uncertainty of VO predictions using a mixture of Gaussians, MDN-VO provides a probabilistic representation of the camera's motion. Our approach is trained end-to-end using a robust loss function that incorporates both pose and uncertainty estimates. Experimental results on the KITTI and TUM-VI benchmarks demonstrate that MDN-VO outperforms state-of-the-art VO methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, particularly in scenarios with significant occlusions, textureless regions, or motion blur. Furthermore, our framework provides well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, enabling more informed decision-making in downstream applications. The code and models will be made publicly available to facilitate further research in this area.

title: Multi-Camera Sensor Fusion for Visual Odometry using Deep Uncertainty Estimation
text: Visual Odometry (VO) estimation is an important source of information for vehicle state estimation and autonomous driving. Recently, deep learning based approaches have begun to appear in the literature. However, in the context of driving, single sensor based approaches are often prone to failure because of degraded image quality due to environmental factors, camera placement, etc. To address this issue, we propose a deep sensor fusion framework which estimates vehicle motion using both pose and uncertainty estimations from multiple on-board cameras. We extract spatio-temporal feature representations from a set of consecutive images using a hybrid CNN - RNN model. We then utilise a Mixture Density Network (MDN) to estimate the 6-DoF pose as a mixture of distributions and a fusion module to estimate the final pose using MDN outputs from multi-cameras. We evaluate our approach on the publicly available, large scale autonomous vehicle dataset, nuScenes. The results show that the proposed fusion approach surpasses the state-of-the-art, and provides robust estimates and accurate trajectories compared to individual camera-based estimations.

title: Multi-Camera Sensor Fusion for Visual Odometry using Deep Uncertainty Estimation
text: Estimating precise camera motion from visual inputs is crucial for various applications, including robotics, autonomous driving, and virtual reality. However, existing visual odometry (VO) methods often struggle to accurately handle complex scenarios, such as dynamic scenes, varying lighting conditions, and multi-camera setups. To address these limitations, we propose a novel multi-camera sensor fusion framework that leverages deep uncertainty estimation for robust VO. Our approach combines the strengths of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) to model both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties in camera motion estimation. We design a hierarchical fusion module that aggregates features from multiple cameras, while explicitly reasoning about the uncertainty associated with each camera's estimate. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art VO approaches, achieving a significant reduction in translational and rotational errors. We also show that our uncertainty estimates effectively capture the ambiguity in camera motion, enabling robust and informed decision-making in real-world applications.

title: A Rationale-Based Classification of MISRA C Guidelines
text: MISRA C is the most authoritative language subset for the C programming language that is a de facto standard in several industry sectors where safety and security are of paramount importance. While MISRA C is currently encoded in 175 guidelines (coding rules and directives), it does not coincide with them: proper adoption of MISRA C requires embracing its preventive approach (as opposed to the "bug finding" approach) and a documented development process where justifiable non-compliances are authorized and recorded as deviations. MISRA C guidelines are classified along several axes in the official MISRA documents. In this paper, we add to these an orthogonal classification that associates guidelines with their main rationale. The advantages of this new classification are illustrated for different kinds of projects, including those not (yet) having MISRA compliance among their objectives.

title: A Rationale-Based Classification of MISRA C Guidelines
text: The MISRA C guidelines are a widely adopted set of coding standards for ensuring the safety and security of critical software systems. While these guidelines provide valuable insights, their informal presentation hinders their systematic analysis and automated enforcement. This paper proposes a rationale-based classification of MISRA C guidelines, which categorizes each guideline according to its underlying safety and security concerns. We employ a rigorous methodology, involving a thorough examination of the guidelines and their associated rationales, as well as a survey of expert opinions. Our classification framework comprises six categories, including memory safety, data integrity, and error handling, among others. The results show that 85% of the guidelines can be classified into three primary categories, indicating a strong correlation between the guidelines and their underlying concerns. This work provides a foundation for the development of more effective and efficient verification tools, and paves the way for the creation of more reliable and secure software systems.

title: Dense Out-of-Distribution Detection by Robust Learning on Synthetic Negative Data
text: Standard machine learning is unable to accommodate inputs which do not belong to the training distribution. The resulting models often give rise to confident incorrect predictions which may lead to devastating consequences. This problem is especially demanding in the context of dense prediction since input images may be only partially anomalous. Previous work has addressed dense out-of-distribution detection by discriminative training with respect to off-the-shelf negative datasets. However, real negative data are unlikely to cover all modes of the entire visual world. To this end, we extend this approach by generating synthetic negative patches along the border of the inlier manifold. We leverage a jointly trained normalizing flow due to coverage-oriented learning objective and the capability to generate samples at different resolutions. We detect anomalies according to a principled information-theoretic criterion which can be consistently applied through training and inference. The resulting models set the new state of the art on benchmarks for out-of-distribution detection in road-driving scenes and remote sensing imagery, in spite of minimal computational overhead.

title: Dense Out-of-Distribution Detection by Robust Learning on Synthetic Negative Data
text: The inability of standard machine learning models to accommodate inputs that deviate from the training distribution can lead to overconfident misclassifications, which can have catastrophic consequences. This limitation is particularly problematic in dense prediction tasks, where images may exhibit only partial anomalies. Existing approaches to dense out-of-distribution detection have relied on discriminative training using off-the-shelf negative datasets, but these datasets are unlikely to capture the full spectrum of visual anomalies. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that generates synthetic negative patches along the boundary of the inlier manifold using a jointly trained normalizing flow. This approach enables coverage-oriented learning and flexible sampling at multiple resolutions. Furthermore, we introduce an information-theoretic criterion for anomaly detection that can be consistently applied throughout training and inference. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks for out-of-distribution detection in road-driving scenes and remote sensing imagery, while incurring minimal computational overhead.

title: Software Engineering Education Knowledge Versus Industrial Needs
text: Contribution: Determine and analyze the gap between software practitioners' education outlined in the 2014IEEE/ACM Software Engineering Education Knowledge (SEEK) and industrial needs pointed by Wikipedia articles referenced in Stack Overflow (SO) posts. Background: Previous work has uncovered deficiencies in the coverage of computer fundamentals, people skills, software processes, and human-computer interaction, suggesting rebalancing. Research Questions: 1) To what extent are developers' needs, in terms of Wikipedia articles referenced in SO posts, covered by the SEEK knowledge units? 2) How does the popularity of Wikipedia articles relate to their SEEK coverage? 3) What areas of computing knowledge can be better covered by the SEEK knowledge units? 4) Why are Wikipedia articles covered by the SEEK knowledge units cited on SO? Methodology: Wikipedia articles were systematically collected from SO posts. The most cited were manually mapped to the SEEK knowledge units, assessed according to their degree of coverage. Articles insufficiently covered by the SEEK were classified by hand using the 2012 ACM Computing Classification System. A sample of posts referencing sufficiently covered articles was manually analyzed. A survey was conducted on software practitioners to validate the study findings. Findings: SEEK appears to cover sufficiently computer science fundamentals, software design and mathematical concepts, but less so areas like the World Wide Web, software engineering components, and computer graphics. Developers seek advice, best practices and explanations about software topics, and code review assistance. Future SEEK models and the computing education could dive deeper in information systems, design, testing, security, and soft skills.

title: Software Engineering Education Knowledge Versus Industrial Needs
text: The software engineering education landscape has undergone significant changes in recent years, with a growing emphasis on preparing students for the demands of industrial practice. However, there is a persistent concern that the knowledge and skills imparted in academic programs may not align with the needs of the software industry. To investigate this gap, we conducted a large-scale study involving 157 software engineering educators and 235 industry professionals from 15 countries. We employed a mixed-methods approach, combining surveys, interviews, and focus groups to gather data on the knowledge and skills perceived as essential by both academics and practitioners. Our analysis reveals a significant mismatch between the software engineering education knowledge and industrial needs. While educators emphasize theoretical foundations and technical skills, industry professionals prioritize soft skills, such as communication, teamwork, and adaptability. The study also highlights a lack of emphasis on emerging areas like artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and data science in software engineering curricula. Furthermore, our results show that industry professionals are more likely to value practical experience and project-based learning, whereas educators tend to focus on theoretical aspects of software engineering. The findings of this study have important implications for software engineering education, suggesting a need for academia to rebalance its focus towards industry-relevant skills and knowledge. We propose a framework for integrating industrial needs into software engineering curricula, emphasizing the importance of collaboration between academia and industry to ensure that graduates are better prepared for the demands of professional practice. Our study contributes to the ongoing debate on the relevance and effectiveness of software engineering education, providing insights for educators, policymakers, and industry stakeholders seeking to bridge the gap between academic knowledge and industrial needs.

title: Faster Deep Ensemble Averaging for Quantification of DNA Damage from Comet Assay Images With Uncertainty Estimates
text: Several neurodegenerative diseases involve the accumulation of cellular DNA damage. Comet assays are a popular way of estimating the extent of DNA damage. Current literature on the use of deep learning to quantify DNA damage presents an empirical approach to hyper-parameter optimization and does not include uncertainty estimates. Deep ensemble averaging is a standard approach to estimating uncertainty but it requires several iterations of network training, which makes it time-consuming. Here we present an approach to quantify the extent of DNA damage that combines deep learning with a rigorous and comprehensive method to optimize the hyper-parameters with the help of statistical tests. We also use an architecture that allows for a faster computation of deep ensemble averaging and performs statistical tests applicable to networks using transfer learning. We applied our approach to a comet assay dataset with more than 1300 images and achieved an $R^2$ of 0.84, where the output included the confidence interval for each prediction. The proposed architecture is an improvement over the current approaches since it speeds up the uncertainty estimation by 30X while being statistically more rigorous.

title: Faster Deep Ensemble Averaging for Quantification of DNA Damage from Comet Assay Images With Uncertainty Estimates
text: Neurodegenerative diseases are often characterized by the accumulation of cellular DNA damage, which can be estimated using comet assays. Despite the growing application of deep learning in DNA damage quantification, existing approaches rely on empirical hyper-parameter optimization and neglect uncertainty estimates. Conventional uncertainty estimation methods, such as deep ensemble averaging, are computationally expensive, requiring multiple network training iterations. This study presents a novel approach that integrates deep learning with rigorous statistical testing for hyper-parameter optimization. Our architecture enables efficient computation of deep ensemble averaging, leveraging transfer learning, and facilitates statistical testing for uncertainty estimation. When applied to a comet assay dataset comprising over 1300 images, our approach achieved an R^2 of 0.84, providing confidence intervals for each prediction. Notably, our proposed architecture accelerates uncertainty estimation by a factor of 30, while ensuring statistical rigor, thereby improving upon current methods.

title: Impact of class imbalance on chest x-ray classifiers: towards better evaluation practices for discrimination and calibration performance
text: This work aims to analyze standard evaluation practices adopted by the research community when assessing chest x-ray classifiers, particularly focusing on the impact of class imbalance in such appraisals. Our analysis considers a comprehensive definition of model performance, covering not only discriminative performance but also model calibration, a topic of research that has received increasing attention during the last years within the machine learning community. Firstly, we conducted a literature study to analyze common scientific practices and confirmed that: (1) even when dealing with highly imbalanced datasets, the community tends to use metrics that are dominated by the majority class; and (2) it is still uncommon to include calibration studies for chest x-ray classifiers, albeit its importance in the context of healthcare. Secondly, we perform a systematic experiment on two major chest x-ray datasets to explore the behavior of several performance metrics under different class ratios and show that widely adopted metrics can conceal the performance in the minority class. Finally, we recommend the inclusion of complementary metrics to better reflect the system's performance in such scenarios. Our study indicates that current evaluation practices adopted by the research community for chest x-ray computer-aided diagnosis systems may not reflect their performance in real clinical scenarios, and suggest alternatives to improve this situation.

title: Impact of class imbalance on chest x-ray classifiers: towards better evaluation practices for discrimination and calibration performance
text: The widespread adoption of deep learning in medical imaging has led to a surge in the development of chest X-ray classifiers, with many recent studies reporting high accuracy on benchmark datasets. However, these datasets often exhibit severe class imbalance, which can significantly impact the reliability of performance estimates. Despite this, the effect of class imbalance on chest X-ray classifiers has received scant attention, and evaluation practices remain largely unchanged. We investigate the impact of class imbalance on the discrimination and calibration performance of chest X-ray classifiers. We conduct a large-scale study on three popular benchmark datasets, using a range of state-of-the-art architectures and class imbalance mitigation strategies. Our results show that even modest levels of class imbalance can lead to substantial overestimation of performance, with some models exhibiting accuracy inflation of up to 20%. Furthermore, we observe that commonly used evaluation metrics, such as the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, are inadequate for capturing calibration performance in imbalanced settings. In response, we propose a novel evaluation framework that incorporates both discrimination and calibration metrics, providing a more comprehensive understanding of model performance. Our findings have significant implications for the development and deployment of chest X-ray classifiers in real-world clinical settings, highlighting the need for more nuanced evaluation practices that account for class imbalance.

title: SoK: Privacy-preserving Deep Learning with Homomorphic Encryption
text: Outsourced computation for neural networks allows users access to state of the art models without needing to invest in specialized hardware and know-how. The problem is that the users lose control over potentially privacy sensitive data. With homomorphic encryption (HE) computation can be performed on encrypted data without revealing its content. In this systematization of knowledge, we take an in-depth look at approaches that combine neural networks with HE for privacy preservation. We categorize the changes to neural network models and architectures to make them computable over HE and how these changes impact performance. We find numerous challenges to HE based privacy-preserving deep learning such as computational overhead, usability, and limitations posed by the encryption schemes.

title: SoK: Privacy-preserving Deep Learning with Homomorphic Encryption
text: The proliferation of deep learning models in cloud-based services has sparked concerns about the privacy of sensitive user data. Homomorphic encryption (HE) offers a promising solution, enabling computations on encrypted data without decryption.
