title: Generalized Wasserstein Dice Loss, Test-time Augmentation, and Transformers for the BraTS 2021 challenge
text: The segmentation of brain tumors from multi-modal Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) data poses a significant challenge in medical image computation, primarily due to the variability in scanner and imaging protocols. To address this issue, we investigate strategies for enhancing model robustness without compromising inference time. Our approach involves identifying a robust ensemble of models trained with diverse losses, optimizers, and data splits. Notably, we explore the integration of a transformer within the U-Net architecture's bottleneck. Although the transformer-based model slightly underperforms the baseline U-Net on average, the generalized Wasserstein Dice loss consistently yields superior results. Furthermore, we employ an efficient test-time augmentation strategy to facilitate rapid and robust inference. Our final ensemble, comprising seven 3D U-Nets with test-time augmentation, achieves an average Dice score of 89.4% and an average Hausdorff 95% distance of 10.0 mm on the BraTS 2021 testing dataset.

title: Fight Perturbations with Perturbations: Defending Adversarial Attacks via Neuron Influence
text: The vulnerabilities of deep learning models towards adversarial attacks have attracted increasing attention, especially when models are deployed in security-critical domains. Numerous defense methods, including reactive and proactive ones, have been proposed for model robustness improvement. Reactive defenses, such as conducting transformations to remove perturbations, usually fail to handle large perturbations. The proactive defenses that involve retraining, suffer from the attack dependency and high computation cost. In this paper, we consider defense methods from the general effect of adversarial attacks that take on neurons inside the model. We introduce the concept of neuron influence, which can quantitatively measure neurons' contribution to correct classification. Then, we observe that almost all attacks fool the model by suppressing neurons with larger influence and enhancing those with smaller influence. Based on this, we propose \emph{Neuron-level Inverse Perturbation} (NIP), a novel defense against general adversarial attacks. It calculates neuron influence from benign examples and then modifies input examples by generating inverse perturbations that can in turn strengthen neurons with larger influence and weaken those with smaller influence.

title: Fight Perturbations with Perturbations: Defending Adversarial Attacks via Neuron Influence
text: Deep neural networks have been shown to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks, which can mislead models by adding carefully crafted perturbations to the input data. Existing defense strategies often rely on detecting or removing these perturbations, but we propose a novel approach that leverages perturbations to fight perturbations. Our method, dubbed Neuron Influence Defense (NID), identifies influential neurons that contribute significantly to the model's predictions and adaptively perturbs their activations to counteract the effects of adversarial attacks. We formulate the defense as a bi-level optimization problem, where the outer level optimizes the perturbations to the influential neurons and the inner level computes the optimal response of the model to the perturbed activations. Experimental results on benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, demonstrate that NID outperforms state-of-the-art defenses against various types of attacks, including FGSM, PGD, and CW attacks, while maintaining a high level of accuracy on clean data. Our approach provides a new perspective on defending against adversarial attacks and has significant implications for the design of robust neural networks.

title: CatchBackdoor: Backdoor Detection via Critical Trojan Neural Path Fuzzing
text: The success of deep neural networks (DNNs) in real-world applications has benefited from abundant pre-trained models. However, the backdoored pre-trained models can pose a significant trojan threat to the deployment of downstream DNNs. Numerous backdoor detection methods have been proposed but are limited to two aspects: (1) high sensitivity on trigger size, especially on stealthy attacks (i.e., blending attacks and defense adaptive attacks); (2) rely heavily on benign examples for reverse engineering. To address these challenges, we empirically observed that trojaned behaviors triggered by various trojan attacks can be attributed to the trojan path, composed of top-$k$ critical neurons with more significant contributions to model prediction changes. Motivated by it, we propose CatchBackdoor, a detection method against trojan attacks. Based on the close connection between trojaned behaviors and trojan path to trigger errors, CatchBackdoor starts from the benign path and gradually approximates the trojan path through differential fuzzing. We then reverse triggers from the trojan path, to trigger errors caused by diverse trojaned attacks. Extensive experiments on MINST, CIFAR-10, and a-ImageNet datasets and 7 models (LeNet, ResNet, and VGG) demonstrate the superiority of CatchBackdoor over the state-of-the-art methods, in terms of (1) \emph{effective} - it shows better detection performance, especially on stealthy attacks ($\sim$ $\times$ 2 on average); (2) \emph{extensible} - it is robust to trigger size and can conduct detection without benign examples.

title: CatchBackdoor: Backdoor Detection via Critical Trojan Neural Path Fuzzing
text: Backdoor attacks have emerged as a severe threat to the security and trustworthiness of deep neural networks (DNNs), where an attacker injects a Trojan into the model to manipulate its behavior. Despite recent advances in backdoor detection, existing methods often rely on manual feature engineering, are limited to specific types of backdoors, or require expensive retraining. In this context, we propose CatchBackdoor, a novel approach that leverages critical Trojan neural path fuzzing to detect backdoors in DNNs. Our method identifies the most critical neurons and paths in the Trojan-infected model and applies fuzz testing to perturb the inputs, thereby exposing the backdoor behavior. We formulate the fuzzing process as a Markov decision process and employ reinforcement learning to optimize the exploration strategy. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of CatchBackdoor, achieving an average detection rate of 95.2% and outperforming state-of-the-art methods by up to 15.4%. Notably, our approach is model-agnostic, requiring no modifications to the target model or access to its training data. We further analyze the security implications of our findings, highlighting the potential for CatchBackdoor to be integrated into the development pipeline to ensure the reliability of DNN-based systems.

title: A Triangular Fuzzy based Multicriteria Decision Making Approach for Assessing Security Risks in 5G Networks
text: The emerging 5G network is a new global wireless standard after 1G, 2G, 3G, and 4G networks. In comparison to 4G, it has lower latency, larger capacity, and more bandwidth. These network upgrades will have a profound impact on how people throughout the world live and work. The current research investigates mechanisms to protect the 5G networks to meet resilience requirements and to minimize the damage from attacks that do occur. The main contribution of this paper includes: (1) Improving the current 5G security testbed by orchestrating the security services using the OSM and Open stack, Integrating the FlexRan with the testbed components to control and manage the eNodeB, and implementing some real-time security experiments to test and validate the testbed. (2) Develop an intelligent fuzzy method to improve the accuracy of the current Vulnerability Assessment Approach (VAA) using a new approach that integrates the Triangular Fuzzy Numbers (TFNs) and a multi-criteria decision-making technique to find the attack graph paths where the attack most probably will propagate in the 5G network.

title: A Triangular Fuzzy based Multicriteria Decision Making Approach for Assessing Security Risks in 5G Networks
text: The fifth generation of wireless networks (5G) is poised to revolutionize the telecommunications landscape, but it also brings unprecedented security risks. As 5G networks increasingly rely on software-defined and virtualized architectures, the attack surface expands, making risk assessment a crucial task. Traditional security risk assessment methods, however, are often inadequate for 5G networks due to their complexity, dynamicity, and inherent uncertainties. To address this challenge, we propose a novel triangular fuzzy-based multicriteria decision-making approach for assessing security risks in 5G networks. Our approach leverages triangular fuzzy numbers to model the uncertainty and imprecision inherent in security risk assessments, and integrates multiple criteria decision analysis to evaluate the risks from different perspectives. We evaluate our approach using a real-world 5G network testbed and demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying high-risk attack vectors and prioritizing security investments. The results show that our approach outperforms traditional risk assessment methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, and provides a comprehensive and nuanced understanding of security risks in 5G networks.

title: Virtuoso: Video-based Intelligence for real-time tuning on SOCs
text: Efficient and adaptive computer vision systems have been proposed to make computer vision tasks, such as image classification and object detection, optimized for embedded or mobile devices. These solutions, quite recent in their origin, focus on optimizing the model (a deep neural network, DNN) or the system by designing an adaptive system with approximation knobs. In spite of several recent efforts, we show that existing solutions suffer from two major drawbacks. First, the system does not consider energy consumption of the models while making a decision on which model to run. Second, the evaluation does not consider the practical scenario of contention on the device, due to other co-resident workloads. In this work, we propose an efficient and adaptive video object detection system, Virtuoso, which is jointly optimized for accuracy, energy efficiency, and latency. Underlying Virtuoso is a multi-branch execution kernel that is capable of running at different operating points in the accuracy-energy-latency axes, and a lightweight runtime scheduler to select the best fit execution branch to satisfy the user requirement. To fairly compare with Virtuoso, we benchmark 15 state-of-the-art or widely used protocols, including Faster R-CNN (FRCNN), YOLO v3, SSD, EfficientDet, SELSA, MEGA, REPP, FastAdapt, and our in-house adaptive variants of FRCNN+, YOLO+, SSD+, and EfficientDet+ (our variants have enhanced efficiency for mobiles). With this comprehensive benchmark, Virtuoso has shown superiority to all the above protocols, leading the accuracy frontier at every efficiency level on NVIDIA Jetson mobile GPUs. Specifically, Virtuoso has achieved an accuracy of 63.9%, which is more than 10% higher than some of the popular object detection models, FRCNN at 51.1%, and YOLO at 49.5%.

title: Virtuoso: Video-based Intelligence for real-time tuning on SOCs
text: The proliferation of multimedia applications on System-on-Chip (SoC) architectures has led to an unprecedented demand for efficient video processing. Existing approaches rely on static, offline profiling-based tuning, which often fails to capture dynamic workload variations, resulting in suboptimal system performance and power consumption. To address this limitation, we propose Virtuoso, a novel video-based intelligence framework for real-time tuning on SOCs. Virtuoso leverages computer vision techniques to analyze video frames and infer workload characteristics, enabling dynamic optimization of SoC resources. Our framework consists of two primary components: a lightweight, real-time video analytics module that extracts relevant features from video frames, and a machine learning-based tuning engine that adapts SoC configuration parameters to optimize performance and power consumption. We evaluate Virtuoso on a range of video workloads, including 4K video encoding, object detection, and video conferencing, on a heterogeneous SoC platform. Experimental results demonstrate that Virtuoso achieves an average of 23.4% improvement in frames per second and 17.1% reduction in power consumption compared to state-of-the-art, offline profiling-based approaches. Furthermore, Virtuoso adapts quickly to workload variations, maintaining an average response time of 12.5ms. Our findings suggest that Virtuoso is a promising solution for real-time tuning on SoCs, enabling efficient video processing in emerging applications such as autonomous vehicles, smart surveillance, and augmented reality.

title: Multi-Scale Feature Fusion: Learning Better Semantic Segmentation for Road Pothole Detection
text: This paper presents a novel pothole detection approach based on single-modal semantic segmentation. It first extracts visual features from input images using a convolutional neural network. A channel attention module then reweighs the channel features to enhance the consistency of different feature maps. Subsequently, we employ an atrous spatial pyramid pooling module (comprising of atrous convolutions in series, with progressive rates of dilation) to integrate the spatial context information. This helps better distinguish between potholes and undamaged road areas. Finally, the feature maps in the adjacent layers are fused using our proposed multi-scale feature fusion module. This further reduces the semantic gap between different feature channel layers. Extensive experiments were carried out on the Pothole-600 dataset to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. The quantitative comparisons suggest that our method achieves the state-of-the-art (SoTA) performance on both RGB images and transformed disparity images, outperforming three SoTA single-modal semantic segmentation networks.

title: Multi-Scale Feature Fusion: Learning Better Semantic Segmentation for Road Pothole Detection
text: Road pothole detection is a critical task in autonomous driving and infrastructure maintenance, where accurate semantic segmentation is essential. Existing approaches often struggle to capture diverse pothole characteristics, leading to subpar performance. We propose Multi-Scale Feature Fusion (MSFF), a novel framework that integrates multi-scale contextual information to learn better semantic segmentation for road pothole detection. MSFF leverages a pyramid pooling module to extract features at different scales, which are then fused using a gated attention mechanism. This allows the model to selectively emphasize relevant features and capture complex pothole patterns. We evaluate MSFF on a large dataset of road images and demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, achieving a mean IoU of 84.2% and outperforming the best baseline by 5.1%. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our multi-scale feature fusion strategy, and visualizations reveal improved segmentation accuracy, particularly for small and irregularly-shaped potholes.

title: SimViT: Exploring a Simple Vision Transformer with sliding windows
text: Although vision Transformers have achieved excellent performance as backbone models in many vision tasks, most of them intend to capture global relations of all tokens in an image or a window, which disrupts the inherent spatial and local correlations between patches in 2D structure. In this paper, we introduce a simple vision Transformer named SimViT, to incorporate spatial structure and local information into the vision Transformers. Specifically, we introduce Multi-head Central Self-Attention(MCSA) instead of conventional Multi-head Self-Attention to capture highly local relations. The introduction of sliding windows facilitates the capture of spatial structure. Meanwhile, SimViT extracts multi-scale hierarchical features from different layers for dense prediction tasks. Extensive experiments show the SimViT is effective and efficient as a general-purpose backbone model for various image processing tasks. Especially, our SimViT-Micro only needs 3.3M parameters to achieve 71.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1k dataset, which is the smallest size vision Transformer model by now. title: SimViT: Exploring a Simple Vision Transformer with sliding windows
text: The prevailing vision Transformers, despite their excellent performance in various vision tasks, often overlook the inherent spatial and local correlations between patches in 2D structures by focusing on capturing global relations among all tokens in an image or window. To address this limitation, we propose SimViT, a novel vision Transformer architecture that effectively incorporates spatial structure and local information. Our approach replaces conventional Multi-head Self-Attention with Multi-head Central Self-Attention (MCSA), which enables the capture of highly local relations. Additionally, we employ sliding windows to facilitate the modeling of spatial structure. SimViT also extracts multi-scale hierarchical features from different layers, making it suitable for dense prediction tasks. Our extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of SimViT as a general-purpose backbone model, with our smallest model, SimViT-Micro, achieving 71.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1k with only 3.3M parameters, the smallest size vision Transformer model to date.

title: Fine-Tuning Data Structures for Analytical Query Processing
text: We introduce a framework for automatically choosing data structures to support efficient computation of analytical workloads. Our contributions are twofold. First, we introduce a novel low-level intermediate language that can express the algorithms behind various query processing paradigms such as classical joins, groupjoin, and in-database machine learning engines. This language is designed around the notion of dictionaries, and allows for a more fine-grained choice of its low-level implementation. Second, the cost model for alternative implementations is automatically inferred by combining machine learning and program reasoning. The dictionary cost model is learned using a regression model trained over the profiling dataset of dictionary operations on a given hardware architecture. The program cost model is inferred using static program analysis. Our experimental results show the effectiveness of the trained cost model on micro benchmarks. Furthermore, we show that the performance of the code generated by our framework either outperforms or is on par with the state-of-the-art analytical query engines and a recent in-database machine learning framework.

title: Fine-Tuning Data Structures for Analytical Query Processing
text: The proliferation of data-intensive applications has catapulted query processing to the forefront of database research. As data volumes continue to escalate, traditional indexing schemes and query optimizers are increasingly inadequate, precipitating a paradigm shift towards analytical query processing. This paper presents a systematic investigation into fine-tuning data structures for optimal analytical query performance. We propose a novel framework that synergistically integrates adaptive indexing, data partitioning, and query rewriting to minimize query latency and maximize throughput. Our approach leverages statistical modeling and machine learning to dynamically optimize data structure configurations in response to query workloads and data distributions. Experimental evaluations using real-world datasets and query benchmarks demonstrate that our fine-tuned data structures achieve significant performance gains, with average query response times reduced by 43% and throughput increased by 27% compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, our framework exhibits robustness and adaptability in the face of diverse query patterns and data characteristics, underscoring its potential for widespread adoption in modern data analytics pipelines.

title: Invertible Network for Unpaired Low-light Image Enhancement
text: Existing unpaired low-light image enhancement approaches prefer to employ the two-way GAN framework, in which two CNN generators are deployed for enhancement and degradation separately. However, such data-driven models ignore the inherent characteristics of transformation between the low and normal light images, leading to unstable training and artifacts. Here, we propose to leverage the invertible network to enhance low-light image in forward process and degrade the normal-light one inversely with unpaired learning. The generated and real images are then fed into discriminators for adversarial learning. In addition to the adversarial loss, we design various loss functions to ensure the stability of training and preserve more image details. Particularly, a reversibility loss is introduced to alleviate the over-exposure problem. Moreover, we present a progressive self-guided enhancement process for low-light images and achieve favorable performance against the SOTAs.

title: Invertible Network for Unpaired Low-light Image Enhancement
text: Low-light image enhancement is a challenging task due to the inherent noise and loss of details in dark regions. Existing methods often rely on paired training data, which is difficult to obtain, or require manual parameter tuning. We propose an invertible network for unpaired low-light image enhancement, which leverages the invertible property to effectively learn the mapping between low-light and normal-light images without paired supervision. Our network consists of a series of invertible blocks, each composed of a coupling layer and an affine coupling layer, allowing for efficient and flexible feature learning. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of visual quality, PSNR, and SSIM, while requiring minimal manual tuning. Additionally, we show that our invertible network can be easily adapted to other image-to-image translation tasks, such as image denoising and deraining.

title: Ultrasound Speckle Suppression and Denoising using MRI-derived Normalizing Flow Priors
text: Ultrasonography offers an inexpensive, widely-accessible and compact medical imaging solution. However, compared to other imaging modalities such as CT and MRI, ultrasound images notoriously suffer from strong speckle noise, which originates from the random interference of sub-wavelength scattering. This deteriorates ultrasound image quality and makes interpretation challenging. We here propose a new unsupervised ultrasound speckle reduction and image denoising method based on maximum-a-posteriori estimation with deep generative priors that are learned from high-quality MRI images. To model the generative tissue reflectivity prior, we exploit normalizing flows, which in recent years have shown to be very powerful in modeling signal priors across a variety of applications. To facilitate generaliation, we factorize the prior and train our flow model on patches from the NYU fastMRI (fully-sampled) dataset. This prior is then used for inference in an iterative denoising scheme. We first validate the utility of our learned priors on noisy MRI data (no prior domain shift), and then turn to evaluating performance on both simulated and in-vivo ultrasound images from the PICMUS and CUBDL datasets. The results show that the method outperforms other (unsupervised) ultrasound denoising methods (NLM and OBNLM) both quantitatively and qualitatively.

title: Ultrasound Speckle Suppression and Denoising using MRI-derived Normalizing Flow Priors
text: Ultrasound imaging is a ubiquitous diagnostic tool, but its widespread adoption is hindered by the presence of speckle noise, which degrades image quality and hampers accurate interpretation. Current denoising techniques rely on handcrafted filters or deep learning models that require extensive training datasets, often unavailable in clinical settings. We propose a novel approach that leverages normalizing flow priors derived from Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) data to suppress speckle noise and denoise ultrasound images. By exploiting the anatomical similarities between MRI and ultrasound modalities, our method can effectively capture the underlying tissue structures and separate them from speckle noise. Our framework consists of a normalizing flow model, trained on MRI images, which is used to regularize a variational optimization problem for ultrasound denoising. Experimental results on a dataset of 200 ultrasound images demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art denoising methods, achieving a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) improvement of 2.5 dB and a structural similarity index (SSIM) increase of 0.15. Furthermore, our method is computationally efficient, requiring only 10% of the parameters compared to deep learning-based approaches. These findings suggest that our MRI-derived normalizing flow priors can effectively suppress speckle noise and denoise ultrasound images, paving the way for improved diagnostic accuracy in clinical settings.

title: The Curse of Zero Task Diversity: On the Failure of Transfer Learning to Outperform MAML and their Empirical Equivalence
text: Recently, it has been observed that a transfer learning solution might be all we need to solve many few-shot learning benchmarks -- thus raising important questions about when and how meta-learning algorithms should be deployed. In this paper, we seek to clarify these questions by proposing a novel metric -- the diversity coefficient -- to measure the diversity of tasks in a few-shot learning benchmark. We hypothesize that the diversity coefficient of the few-shot learning benchmark is predictive of whether meta-learning solutions will succeed or not. Using the diversity coefficient, we show that the MiniImagenet benchmark has zero diversity. This novel insight contextualizes claims that transfer learning solutions are better than meta-learned solutions. Specifically, we empirically find that a diversity coefficient of zero correlates with a high similarity between transfer learning and Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) learned solutions in terms of meta-accuracy (at meta-test time). Therefore, we conjecture meta-learned solutions have the same meta-test performance as transfer learning when the diversity coefficient is zero. Our work provides the first test of whether diversity correlates with meta-learning success.

title: The Curse of Zero Task Diversity: On the Failure of Transfer Learning to Outperform MAML and their Empirical Equivalence
text: The ability to learn across tasks has been a long-standing goal in machine learning, with transfer learning and meta-learning emerging as popular approaches. However, the recent proliferation of task-agnostic models has led to an overlooked yet crucial consideration: the diversity of tasks. We investigate the hitherto unexplored phenomenon of zero task diversity, where models are trained and evaluated on identical tasks. Through a rigorous empirical study, we reveal a surprising failure of transfer learning to outperform model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) in this scenario. Our findings demonstrate that, despite their differing formulations, transfer learning and MAML converge to empirically equivalent solutions when task diversity is absent. We attribute this equivalence to the overparameterization of modern deep networks, which enables them to memorize the training task. Our results have significant implications for the design of task-agnostic models, highlighting the need to carefully consider task diversity in both training and evaluation. Furthermore, we provide a set of recommendations for practitioners to mitigate the curse of zero task diversity and develop more robust models that generalize across diverse tasks.

title: Does MAML Only Work via Feature Re-use? A Data Centric Perspective
text: Recent work has suggested that a good embedding is all we need to solve many few-shot learning benchmarks. Furthermore, other work has strongly suggested that Model Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) also works via this same method - by learning a good embedding. These observations highlight our lack of understanding of what meta-learning algorithms are doing and when they work. In this work, we provide empirical results that shed some light on how meta-learned MAML representations function. In particular, we identify three interesting properties: 1) In contrast to previous work, we show that it is possible to define a family of synthetic benchmarks that result in a low degree of feature re-use - suggesting that current few-shot learning benchmarks might not have the properties needed for the success of meta-learning algorithms; 2) meta-overfitting occurs when the number of classes (or concepts) are finite, and this issue disappears once the task has an unbounded number of concepts (e.g., online learning); 3) more adaptation at meta-test time with MAML does not necessarily result in a significant representation change or even an improvement in meta-test performance - even when training on our proposed synthetic benchmarks. Finally, we suggest that to understand meta-learning algorithms better, we must go beyond tracking only absolute performance and, in addition, formally quantify the degree of meta-learning and track both metrics together. Reporting results in future work this way will help us identify the sources of meta-overfitting more accurately and help us design more flexible meta-learning algorithms that learn beyond fixed feature re-use. Finally, we conjecture the core challenge of re-thinking meta-learning is in the design of few-shot learning data sets and benchmarks - rather than in the algorithms, as suggested by previous work.

title: Does MAML Only Work via Feature Re-use? A Data Centric Perspective
text: Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) has emerged as a prominent approach to few-shot learning, demonstrating remarkable success in various computer vision tasks. Despite its widespread adoption, the underlying mechanisms driving MAML's effectiveness remain poorly understood. Recent studies have suggested that MAML's success can be attributed to its ability to learn reusable features across tasks. However, this perspective overlooks the critical role of data in shaping the learning process. In this study, we adopt a data-centric perspective to investigate whether MAML's performance is primarily due to feature re-use or if there are other factors at play. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of MAML's behavior on a range of few-shot image classification benchmarks, including mini-ImageNet, CIFAR-FS, and FC100. Our methodology involves carefully controlling for various data-related factors, such as class similarity, data augmentation, and sample quality, to isolate their impact on MAML's performance. We employ a combination of visualization techniques, including t-SNE and feature importance analysis, to gain insights into the learned representations. Our findings suggest that while feature re-use does play a role in MAML's success, it is not the sole driving factor. We observe that MAML's performance is strongly correlated with the quality and diversity of the training data, as well as the similarity between the meta-training and meta-testing classes. Moreover, we find that data augmentation strategies can significantly impact MAML's ability to adapt to new tasks. Our results have important implications for the design of MAML-based systems, highlighting the need to consider data-centric factors in addition to model architecture and optimization strategies.

title: Reconstructing Compact Building Models from Point Clouds Using Deep Implicit Fields
text: While three-dimensional (3D) building models play an increasingly pivotal role in many real-world applications, obtaining a compact representation of buildings remains an open problem. In this paper, we present a novel framework for reconstructing compact, watertight, polygonal building models from point clouds. Our framework comprises three components: (a) a cell complex is generated via adaptive space partitioning that provides a polyhedral embedding as the candidate set; (b) an implicit field is learned by a deep neural network that facilitates building occupancy estimation; (c) a Markov random field is formulated to extract the outer surface of a building via combinatorial optimization. We evaluate and compare our method with state-of-the-art methods in generic reconstruction, model-based reconstruction, geometry simplification, and primitive assembly. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world point clouds have demonstrated that, with our neural-guided strategy, high-quality building models can be obtained with significant advantages in fidelity, compactness, and computational efficiency. Our method also shows robustness to noise and insufficient measurements, and it can directly generalize from synthetic scans to real-world measurements. The source code of this work is freely available at

title: Reconstructing Compact Building Models from Point Clouds Using Deep Implicit Fields
text: The proliferation of 3D point cloud data has created opportunities for automated building modeling, but existing methods often struggle to balance accuracy and compactness. We propose a novel approach to reconstructing compact building models from point clouds using deep implicit fields. Our method leverages the expressive power of implicit neural representations to encode shape and topology, enabling the recovery of detailed, watertight models from noisy and incomplete input data. By formulating the reconstruction problem as a variational optimization, we are able to jointly infer building shape, topology, and semantic labels from the point cloud. Experiments on the Paris-rue-Madame and Semantic3D datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of model compactness and accuracy, achieving a 30% reduction in polygon count while maintaining a mean intersection-over-union score of 0.85. Furthermore, our method is computationally efficient, requiring only a fraction of the memory and computation required by existing techniques. These results have significant implications for urban planning, architecture, and computer-aided design applications, where compact, accurate building models are essential.

title: SoK: A Study of the Security on Voice Processing Systems
text: As the use of Voice Processing Systems (VPS) continues to become more prevalent in our daily lives through the increased reliance on applications such as commercial voice recognition devices as well as major text-to-speech software, the attacks on these systems are increasingly complex, varied, and constantly evolving. With the use cases for VPS rapidly growing into new spaces and purposes, the potential consequences regarding privacy are increasingly more dangerous. In addition, the growing number and increased practicality of over-the-air attacks have made system failures much more probable. In this paper, we will identify and classify an arrangement of unique attacks on voice processing systems. Over the years research has been moving from specialized, untargeted attacks that result in the malfunction of systems and the denial of services to more general, targeted attacks that can force an outcome controlled by an adversary. The current and most frequently used machine learning systems and deep neural networks, which are at the core of modern voice processing systems, were built with a focus on performance and scalability rather than security. Therefore, it is critical for us to reassess the developing voice processing landscape and to identify the state of current attacks and defenses so that we may suggest future developments and theoretical improvements.

title: SoK: A Study of the Security on Voice Processing Systems
text: The widespread adoption of voice-controlled devices has led to a surge in voice processing systems, which have become an attractive target for malicious actors. Despite their increasing popularity, the security of these systems remains understudied, with existing research focusing primarily on individual components rather than the system as a whole. This paper presents a comprehensive study of the security of voice processing systems, examining the entire pipeline from audio input to output. Our study employs a mixed-methods approach, combining a systematic literature review of 135 papers with interviews from 20 industry experts and a thorough analysis of 15 popular voice processing systems. We identify 35 unique vulnerabilities across the systems, including 15 previously unknown attacks. Our findings indicate that the majority of systems fail to implement adequate security measures, with 80% of systems vulnerable to audio tampering attacks and 60% susceptible to unauthorized access. We also discovered a lack of standardization in security practices, with many systems relying on proprietary solutions that hinder interoperability and transparency. Our research highlights the need for a standardized security framework for voice processing systems and provides a foundation for future research in this area. By shedding light on the security risks associated with voice processing systems, this study aims to inform the development of more secure and trustworthy systems, ultimately protecting users from potential attacks.

title: Fast and Scalable Computation of the Forward and Inverse Discrete Periodic Radon Transform
text: The Discrete Periodic Radon Transform (DPRT) has been extensively used in applications that involve image reconstructions from projections. This manuscript introduces a fast and scalable approach for computing the forward and inverse DPRT that is based on the use of: (i) a parallel array of fixed-point adder trees, (ii) circular shift registers to remove the need for accessing external memory components when selecting the input data for the adder trees, (iii) an image block-based approach to DPRT computation that can fit the proposed architecture to available resources, and (iv) fast transpositions that are computed in one or a few clock cycles that do not depend on the size of the input image. As a result, for an $N\times N$ image ($N$ prime), the proposed approach can compute up to $N^{2}$ additions per clock cycle. Compared to previous approaches, the scalable approach provides the fastest known implementations for different amounts of computational resources. For example, for a $251\times 251$ image, for approximately $25\%$ fewer flip-flops than required for a systolic implementation, we have that the scalable DPRT is computed 36 times faster. For the fastest case, we introduce optimized architectures that can compute the DPRT and its inverse in just $2N+\left\lceil \log_{2}N\right\rceil+1$ and $2N+3\left\lceil \log_{2}N\right\rceil+B+2$ cycles respectively, where $B$ is the number of bits used to represent each input pixel. On the other hand, the scalable DPRT approach requires more 1-bit additions than for the systolic implementation and provides a trade-off between speed and additional 1-bit additions. All of the proposed DPRT architectures were implemented in VHDL and validated using an FPGA implementation.

title: Fast and Scalable Computation of the Forward and Inverse Discrete Periodic Radon Transform
text: The discrete periodic Radon transform (DPRT) has emerged as a crucial tool in various image processing and computer vision applications, including feature extraction, image reconstruction, and shape analysis. Despite its importance, the computation of the forward and inverse DPRT remains a significant computational bottleneck, hindering its widespread adoption. Existing methods suffer from high computational complexity, limiting their applicability to large images and high-dimensional datasets. To address this limitation, we propose a novel algorithm for fast and scalable computation of the forward and inverse DPRT. Our approach leverages the periodicity of the Radon transform and exploits the inherent structure of the underlying convolutional operator. By decomposing the DPRT into a series of carefully crafted convolutional layers, we reduce the computational complexity from O(n^3) to O(n^2 log n), where n is the image size. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through extensive experiments on various image datasets, showcasing significant speedups over existing state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, our algorithm achieves an average speedup of 10x for the forward DPRT and 15x for the inverse DPRT on large images. Furthermore, we establish the theoretical correctness of our algorithm and provide bounds on the approximation error. The proposed algorithm has far-reaching implications for various computer vision applications, including feature extraction, image denoising, and shape analysis. We demonstrate the applicability of our approach in these domains, achieving state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets. Our work paves the way for the widespread adoption of the DPRT in real-world applications, where computational efficiency and scalability are critical.

title: Fast 2D Convolutions and Cross-Correlations Using Scalable Architectures
text: The manuscript describes fast and scalable architectures and associated algorithms for computing convolutions and cross-correlations. The basic idea is to map 2D convolutions and cross-correlations to a collection of 1D convolutions and cross-correlations in the transform domain. This is accomplished through the use of the Discrete Periodic Radon Transform (DPRT) for general kernels and the use of SVD-LU decompositions for low-rank kernels. The approach uses scalable architectures that can be fitted into modern FPGA and Zynq-SOC devices. Based on different types of available resources, for $P\times P$ blocks, 2D convolutions and cross-correlations can be computed in just $O(P)$ clock cycles up to $O(P^2)$ clock cycles. Thus, there is a trade-off between performance and required numbers and types of resources. We provide implementations of the proposed architectures using modern programmable devices (Virtex-7 and Zynq-SOC). Based on the amounts and types of required resources, we show that the proposed approaches significantly outperform current methods.

title: Fast 2D Convolutions and Cross-Correlations Using Scalable Architectures
text: The proliferation of deep neural networks in computer vision has led to an unprecedented demand for efficient 2D convolution and cross-correlation computations. Despite their widespread adoption, existing hardware-accelerated implementations often struggle to scale with increasing image sizes and filter complexities. This limitation stems from the inherent memory-bound nature of these operations, which hinders their parallelization on modern architectures. To address this bottleneck, we propose a novel, scalable architecture that leverages a hybrid data layout and a bespoke memory hierarchy to minimize data movement and maximize parallelism. Our approach, dubbed ScalConv, achieves a 3.2x speedup over state-of-the-art GPU implementations on large-scale image processing tasks, while maintaining a 2.5x reduction in memory bandwidth utilization. Experimental results on various convolutional neural network models demonstrate the efficacy of ScalConv in accelerating object detection, image segmentation, and feature extraction tasks.

title: Stealthy Attack on Algorithmic-Protected DNNs via Smart Bit Flipping
text: Recently, deep neural networks (DNNs) have been deployed in safety-critical systems such as autonomous vehicles and medical devices. Shortly after that, the vulnerability of DNNs were revealed by stealthy adversarial examples where crafted inputs -- by adding tiny perturbations to original inputs -- can lead a DNN to generate misclassification outputs. To improve the robustness of DNNs, some algorithmic-based countermeasures against adversarial examples have been introduced thereafter. In this paper, we propose a new type of stealthy attack on protected DNNs to circumvent the algorithmic defenses: via smart bit flipping in DNN weights, we can reserve the classification accuracy for clean inputs but misclassify crafted inputs even with algorithmic countermeasures. To fool protected DNNs in a stealthy way, we introduce a novel method to efficiently find their most vulnerable weights and flip those bits in hardware. Experimental results show that we can successfully apply our stealthy attack against state-of-the-art algorithmic-protected DNNs.

title: Stealthy Attack on Algorithmic-Protected DNNs via Smart Bit Flipping
text: The increasing deployment of deep neural networks (DNNs) in safety-critical systems, such as autonomous vehicles and medical devices, has exposed their vulnerability to stealthy adversarial examples. These crafted inputs, generated by introducing minute perturbations to original inputs, can prompt DNNs to produce misclassification outputs. In response, various algorithmic countermeasures have been developed to enhance DNN robustness. However, we demonstrate that protected DNNs remain susceptible to a novel type of stealthy attack, wherein strategic bit flipping in DNN weights enables the preservation of classification accuracy for clean inputs while inducing misclassifications for crafted inputs, even in the presence of algorithmic defenses. We propose an efficient method for identifying the most vulnerable weights in protected DNNs and flipping the corresponding bits in hardware, thereby successfully evading state-of-the-art algorithmic protections, as validated by our experimental results.

title: Semantic Clustering based Deduction Learning for Image Recognition and Classification
text: The paper proposes a semantic clustering based deduction learning by mimicking the learning and thinking process of human brains. Human beings can make judgments based on experience and cognition, and as a result, no one would recognize an unknown animal as a car. Inspired by this observation, we propose to train deep learning models using the clustering prior that can guide the models to learn with the ability of semantic deducing and summarizing from classification attributes, such as a cat belonging to animals while a car pertaining to vehicles. %Specifically, if an image is labeled as a cat, then the model is trained to learn that "this image is totally not any random class that is the outlier of animal". The proposed approach realizes the high-level clustering in the semantic space, enabling the model to deduce the relations among various classes during the learning process. In addition, the paper introduces a semantic prior based random search for the opposite labels to ensure the smooth distribution of the clustering and the robustness of the classifiers. The proposed approach is supported theoretically and empirically through extensive experiments. We compare the performance across state-of-the-art classifiers on popular benchmarks, and the generalization ability is verified by adding noisy labeling to the datasets. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach.

title: Semantic Clustering based Deduction Learning for Image Recognition and Classification
text: The proliferation of deep learning models in image recognition and classification has led to remarkable advances, yet the underlying mechanisms of these models remain poorly understood. In particular, the lack of transparency in complex neural networks hinders the identification of crucial features driving classification decisions. To address this limitation, we propose Semantic Clustering based Deduction Learning (SCDL), a novel framework that distills interpretable knowledge from deep models. SCDL integrates semantic clustering with deduction learning to uncover latent patterns in the feature space, enabling the discovery of meaningful clusters that align with human-perceived semantics. Our approach leverages a dual-branch architecture, where a clustering module groups features based on their semantic similarity, and a deduction module learns to predict class labels from these clusters. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets (CIFAR-10, ImageNet), we demonstrate that SCDL outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, while providing valuable insights into the decision-making process of deep models. Notably, our framework achieves a 3.5% increase in accuracy on ImageNet compared to a ResNet-50 baseline, while reducing the number of parameters by 25%. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that SCDL-derived clusters are highly correlated with object parts and attributes, offering a promising direction for explainable AI research.

title: Cyberattack Detection in Large-Scale Smart Grids using Chebyshev Graph Convolutional Networks
text: As a highly complex and integrated cyber-physical system, modern power grids are exposed to cyberattacks. False data injection attacks (FDIAs), specifically, represent a major class of cyber threats to smart grids by targeting the measurement data's integrity. Although various solutions have been proposed to detect those cyberattacks, the vast majority of the works have ignored the inherent graph structure of the power grid measurements and validated their detectors only for small test systems with less than a few hundred buses. To better exploit the spatial correlations of smart grid measurements, this paper proposes a deep learning model for cyberattack detection in large-scale AC power grids using Chebyshev Graph Convolutional Networks (CGCN). By reducing the complexity of spectral graph filters and making them localized, CGCN provides a fast and efficient convolution operation to model the graph structural smart grid data. We numerically verify that the proposed CGCN based detector surpasses the state-of-the-art model by 7.86 in detection rate and 9.67 in false alarm rate for a large-scale power grid with 2848 buses. It is notable that the proposed approach detects cyberattacks under 4 milliseconds for a 2848-bus system, which makes it a good candidate for real-time detection of cyberattacks in large systems.

title: Cyberattack Detection in Large-Scale Smart Grids using Chebyshev Graph Convolutional Networks
text: The modern power grid, a sophisticated cyber-physical system, is vulnerable to cyberattacks, with false data injection attacks (FDIAs) posing a significant threat to smart grid integrity. Existing solutions for detecting these attacks have largely overlooked the inherent graph structure of power grid measurements, instead validating their detectors on small test systems with fewer than a few hundred buses. This paper addresses this limitation by proposing a deep learning model that leverages the spatial correlations of smart grid measurements in large-scale AC power grids using Chebyshev Graph Convolutional Networks (CGCN). By reducing the complexity of spectral graph filters and localizing them, CGCN enables fast and efficient convolution operations to model graph-structured smart grid data. Our numerical results demonstrate that the proposed CGCN-based detector outperforms the state-of-the-art model, achieving a 7.86% improvement in detection rate and a 9.67% reduction in false alarm rate for a large-scale power grid with 2848 buses. Notably, our approach detects cyberattacks in under 4 milliseconds for a 2848-bus system, making it a promising solution for real-time detection in large systems.

title: An Experimental Evaluation and Investigation of Waves of Misery in R-trees
text: Waves of misery is a phenomenon where spikes of many node splits occur over short periods of time in tree indexes. Waves of misery negatively affect the performance of tree indexes in insertion-heavy workloads.Waves of misery have been first observed in the context of the B-tree, where these waves cause unpredictable index performance. In particular, the performance of search and index-update operations deteriorate when a wave of misery takes place, but is more predictable between the waves. This paper investigates the presence or lack of waves of misery in several R-tree variants, and studies the extent of which these waves impact the performance of each variant. Interestingly, although having poorer query performance, the Linear and Quadratic R-trees are found to be more resilient to waves of misery than both the Hilbert and R*-trees. This paper presents several techniques to reduce the impact in performance of the waves of misery for the Hilbert and R*-trees. One way to eliminate waves of misery is to force node splits to take place at regular times before nodes become full to achieve deterministic performance. The other way is that upon splitting a node, do not split it evenly but rather at different node utilization factors. This allows leaf nodes not to fill at the same pace. We study the impact of two new techniques to mitigate waves of misery after the tree index has been constructed, namely Regular Elective Splits (RES, for short) and Unequal Random Splits (URS, for short). Our experimental investigation highlights the trade-offs in performance of the introduced techniques and the pros and cons of each technique.

title: An Experimental Evaluation and Investigation of Waves of Misery in R-trees
text: The phenomenon of waves of misery, characterized by bursts of node splits over brief periods, significantly degrades the performance of tree indexes in insertion-intensive workloads. This issue was first identified in the context of B-trees, where it yields unpredictable index performance. Specifically, search and index-update operations exhibit deteriorated performance during waves of misery, but display more predictable behavior between these events. This study examines the prevalence and impact of waves of misery in various R-tree variants, revealing that Linear and Quadratic R-trees, despite their poorer query performance, exhibit greater resilience to waves of misery compared to Hilbert and R*-trees. To mitigate the performance degradation caused by waves of misery in Hilbert and R*-trees, we propose two techniques: Regular Elective Splits (RES) and Unequal Random Splits (URS). RES involves forcing node splits at regular intervals, prior to node saturation, to achieve deterministic performance. URS, on the other hand, involves uneven node splitting at varying utilization factors, allowing leaf nodes to fill at different rates. Our experimental evaluation highlights the trade-offs in performance associated with these techniques, as well as their respective advantages and disadvantages, in the context of mitigating waves of misery in pre-constructed tree indexes.

title: Gradient Leakage Attack Resilient Deep Learning
text: Gradient leakage attacks are considered one of the wickedest privacy threats in deep learning as attackers covertly spy gradient updates during iterative training without compromising model training quality, and yet secretly reconstruct sensitive training data using leaked gradients with high attack success rate. Although deep learning with differential privacy is a defacto standard for publishing deep learning models with differential privacy guarantee, we show that differentially private algorithms with fixed privacy parameters are vulnerable against gradient leakage attacks. This paper investigates alternative approaches to gradient leakage resilient deep learning with differential privacy (DP). First, we analyze existing implementation of deep learning with differential privacy, which use fixed noise variance to injects constant noise to the gradients in all layers using fixed privacy parameters. Despite the DP guarantee provided, the method suffers from low accuracy and is vulnerable to gradient leakage attacks. Second, we present a gradient leakage resilient deep learning approach with differential privacy guarantee by using dynamic privacy parameters. Unlike fixed-parameter strategies that result in constant noise variance, different dynamic parameter strategies present alternative techniques to introduce adaptive noise variance and adaptive noise injection which are closely aligned to the trend of gradient updates during differentially private model training. Finally, we describe four complementary metrics to evaluate and compare alternative approaches.

title: Gradient Leakage Attack Resilient Deep Learning
text: Deep learning models trained with differential privacy guarantees are susceptible to gradient leakage attacks, which compromise the privacy of sensitive training data despite preserving model training quality. While differentially private algorithms with fixed privacy parameters are widely adopted for publishing deep learning models, we reveal their vulnerability to such attacks. This study explores alternative approaches to developing gradient leakage resilient deep learning models with differential privacy guarantees. We critically examine existing implementations of differentially private deep learning, which inject constant noise into gradients across all layers using fixed privacy parameters, and find that they suffer from low accuracy and vulnerability to gradient leakage attacks. In response, we propose a novel approach that leverages dynamic privacy parameters to introduce adaptive noise variance and injection, closely tied to the trend of gradient updates during differentially private model training. This adaptive strategy enhances the resilience of deep learning models to gradient leakage attacks while maintaining differential privacy guarantees. We further establish four complementary metrics to evaluate and compare the efficacy of alternative approaches in mitigating gradient leakage attacks.

title: DSRGAN: Detail Prior-Assisted Perceptual Single Image Super-Resolution via Generative Adversarial Networks
text: The generative adversarial network (GAN) is successfully applied to study the perceptual single image superresolution (SISR). However, the GAN often tends to generate images with high frequency details being inconsistent with the real ones. Inspired by conventional detail enhancement algorithms, we propose a novel prior knowledge, the detail prior, to assist the GAN in alleviating this problem and restoring more realistic details. The proposed method, named DSRGAN, includes a well designed detail extraction algorithm to capture the most important high frequency information from images. Then, two discriminators are utilized for supervision on image-domain and detail-domain restorations, respectively. The DSRGAN merges the restored detail into the final output via a detail enhancement manner. The special design of DSRGAN takes advantages from both the model-based conventional algorithm and the data-driven deep learning network. Experimental results demonstrate that the DSRGAN outperforms the state-of-the-art SISR methods on perceptual metrics and achieves comparable results in terms of fidelity metrics simultaneously. Following the DSRGAN, it is feasible to incorporate other conventional image processing algorithms into a deep learning network to form a model-based deep SISR.

title: DSRGAN: Detail Prior-Assisted Perceptual Single Image Super-Resolution via Generative Adversarial Networks
text: Single image super-resolution (SISR) remains a fundamental problem in computer vision, where the goal is to recover a high-resolution (HR) image from a low-resolution (LR) input. Despite significant progress, existing methods often struggle to effectively preserve details and textures in the reconstructed HR images. In this work, we propose DSRGAN, a novel generative adversarial network (GAN) framework that incorporates a detail prior-assisted perceptual loss to tackle this challenge. Specifically, our approach involves jointly training a generator network to reconstruct HR images and a discriminator network to distinguish between real and generated HR images. The key innovation lies in the incorporation of a detail prior module, which captures and refines local texture patterns in the LR image, and a perceptual loss function that encourages the generator to produce HR images with realistic textures and details. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of DSRGAN over state-of-the-art methods, achieving significant improvements in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and visual quality. Furthermore, our ablation studies validate the effectiveness of the detail prior-assisted perceptual loss in preserving details and textures in the reconstructed HR images.

title: Network-Aware 5G Edge Computing for Object Detection: Augmenting Wearables to "See" More, Farther and Faster
text: Advanced wearable devices are increasingly incorporating high-resolution multi-camera systems. As state-of-the-art neural networks for processing the resulting image data are computationally demanding, there has been growing interest in leveraging fifth generation (5G) wireless connectivity and mobile edge computing for offloading this processing to the cloud. To assess this possibility, this paper presents a detailed simulation and evaluation of 5G wireless offloading for object detection within a powerful, new smart wearable called VIS4ION, for the Blind-and-Visually Impaired (BVI). The current VIS4ION system is an instrumented book-bag with high-resolution cameras, vision processing and haptic and audio feedback. The paper considers uploading the camera data to a mobile edge cloud to perform real-time object detection and transmitting the detection results back to the wearable. To determine the video requirements, the paper evaluates the impact of video bit rate and resolution on object detection accuracy and range. A new street scene dataset with labeled objects relevant to BVI navigation is leveraged for analysis. The vision evaluation is combined with a detailed full-stack wireless network simulation to determine the distribution of throughputs and delays with real navigation paths and ray-tracing from new high-resolution 3D models in an urban environment. For comparison, the wireless simulation considers both a standard 4G-Long Term Evolution (LTE) carrier and high-rate 5G millimeter-wave (mmWave) carrier. The work thus provides a thorough and realistic assessment of edge computing with mmWave connectivity in an application with both high bandwidth and low latency requirements.

title: Network-Aware 5G Edge Computing for Object Detection: Augmenting Wearables to "See" More, Farther and Faster
text: The proliferation of high-resolution multi-camera systems in advanced wearable devices has created a pressing need for efficient processing of the resulting image data. Recent advances in fifth-generation (5G) wireless connectivity and mobile edge computing have sparked interest in offloading computationally demanding neural networks to the cloud. This paper presents a comprehensive simulation and evaluation of 5G wireless offloading for object detection in VIS4ION, a novel smart wearable designed for the Blind-and-Visually Impaired (BVI). The VIS4ION system, comprising an instrumented book-bag with high-resolution cameras, vision processing, and haptic and audio feedback, is assessed for uploading camera data to a mobile edge cloud for real-time object detection, with detection results transmitted back to the wearable. The impact of video bit rate and resolution on object detection accuracy and range is evaluated using a new street scene dataset with labeled objects relevant to BVI navigation. A detailed full-stack wireless network simulation, incorporating real navigation paths and ray-tracing from high-resolution 3D models in an urban environment, is conducted to determine the distribution of throughputs and delays. Both standard 4G-Long Term Evolution (LTE) and high-rate 5G millimeter-wave (mmWave) carriers are considered, providing a thorough and realistic assessment of edge computing with mmWave connectivity in an application requiring high bandwidth and low latency.

title: FMViz: Visualizing Tests Generated by AFL at the Byte-level
text: Software fuzzing is a strong testing technique that has become the de facto approach for automated software testing and software vulnerability detection in the industry. The random nature of fuzzing makes monitoring and understanding the behavior of fuzzers difficult. In this paper, we report the development of Fuzzer Mutation Visualizer (FMViz), a tool that focuses on visualizing byte-level mutations in fuzzers. In particular, FMViz extends American Fuzzy Lop (AFL) to visualize the generated test inputs and highlight changes between consecutively generated seeds as a fuzzing campaign progresses. The overarching goal of our tool is to help developers and students comprehend the inner-workings of the AFL fuzzer better. In this paper, we present the architecture of FMViz, discuss a sample case study of it, and outline the future work. FMViz is open-source and publicly available at

title: FMViz: Visualizing Tests Generated by AFL at the Byte-level
text: The increasing adoption of fuzz testing in software development has led to a surge in the generation of test cases, making it challenging to comprehend and analyze the testing process. American Fuzzy Lop (AFL) is a popular fuzz testing tool that generates a vast number of tests, but its output lacks visual representation, hindering the understanding of test case generation and fault localization. To address this limitation, we propose FMViz, a novel visualization framework that represents AFL-generated tests at the byte level. FMViz utilizes a combination of sequence alignment and dimensionality reduction techniques to create a 2D visualization of test cases, enabling the identification of patterns and correlations among them. Our evaluation on several real-world programs demonstrates that FMViz effectively reveals the underlying structure of the test suite, facilitating the discovery of redundant and ineffective tests. Furthermore, FMViz-assisted analysis improves the fault localization capabilities of AFL, resulting in a 32% reduction in the number of test cases required to identify bugs.

title: "We do not appreciate being experimented on": Developer and Researcher Views on the Ethics of Experiments on Open-Source Projects
text: A tenet of open source software development is to accept contributions from users-developers (typically after appropriate vetting). But should this also include interventions done as part of research on open source development? Following an incident in which buggy code was submitted to the Linux kernel to see whether it would be caught, we conduct a survey among open source developers and empirical software engineering researchers to see what behaviors they think are acceptable. This covers two main issues: the use of publicly accessible information, and conducting active experimentation. The survey had 224 respondents. The results indicate that open-source developers are largely open to research, provided it is done transparently. In other words, many would agree to experiments on open-source projects if the subjects were notified and provided informed consent, and in special cases also if only the project leaders agree. While researchers generally hold similar opinions, they sometimes fail to appreciate certain nuances that are important to developers. Examples include observing license restrictions on publishing open-source code and safeguarding the code. Conversely, researchers seem to be more concerned than developers about privacy issues. Based on these results, it is recommended that open source repositories and projects address use for research in their access guidelines, and that researchers take care to ask permission also when not formally required to do so. We note too that the open source community wants to be heard, so professional societies and IRBs should consult with them when formulating ethics codes.

title: "We do not appreciate being experimented on": Developer and Researcher Views on the Ethics of Experiments on Open-Source Projects
text: The ethos of open source software development emphasizes the importance of accepting contributions from user-developers, but a crucial question arises: should this inclusivity extend to interventions conducted in the context of research on open source development? This inquiry is motivated by a recent incident in which intentionally faulty code was submitted to the Linux kernel to test the efficacy of its vetting process. To elucidate the boundaries of acceptable behavior, we conducted a comprehensive survey among 224 open source developers and empirical software engineering researchers, focusing on two primary aspects: the utilization of publicly accessible information and the conduct of active experimentation. Our findings indicate that open source developers are generally receptive to research initiatives, provided they are characterized by transparency and informed consent. Specifically, many developers are willing to accept experiments on open source projects, contingent upon the notification and consent of subjects, and in certain cases, the approval of project leaders. While researchers tend to share similar opinions, they often overlook nuances crucial to developers, such as adhering to license restrictions and ensuring code safeguarding. Conversely, researchers exhibit greater concern for privacy issues. Our study underscores the need for open source repositories and projects to establish guidelines for research use, and for researchers to seek permission even when not formally required. Moreover, our results highlight the open source community's desire for a voice in the formulation of ethics codes, emphasizing the importance of consultation between professional societies, IRBs, and the open source community.

title: Pseudocylindrical Convolutions for Learned Omnidirectional Image Compression
text: Although equirectangular projection (ERP) is a convenient form to store omnidirectional images (also known as 360-degree images), it is neither equal-area nor conformal, thus not friendly to subsequent visual communication. In the context of image compression, ERP will over-sample and deform things and stuff near the poles, making it difficult for perceptually optimal bit allocation. In conventional 360-degree image compression, techniques such as region-wise packing and tiled representation are introduced to alleviate the over-sampling problem, achieving limited success. In this paper, we make one of the first attempts to learn deep neural networks for omnidirectional image compression. We first describe parametric pseudocylindrical representation as a generalization of common pseudocylindrical map projections. A computationally tractable greedy method is presented to determine the (sub)-optimal configuration of the pseudocylindrical representation in terms of a novel proxy objective for rate-distortion performance. We then propose pseudocylindrical convolutions for 360-degree image compression. Under reasonable constraints on the parametric representation, the pseudocylindrical convolution can be efficiently implemented by standard convolution with the so-called pseudocylindrical padding. To demonstrate the feasibility of our idea, we implement an end-to-end 360-degree image compression system, consisting of the learned pseudocylindrical representation, an analysis transform, a non-uniform quantizer, a synthesis transform, and an entropy model. Experimental results on $19,790$ omnidirectional images show that our method achieves consistently better rate-distortion performance than the competing methods. Moreover, the visual quality by our method is significantly improved for all images at all bitrates.

title: Pseudocylindrical Convolutions for Learned Omnidirectional Image Compression
text: Omnidirectional images have gained popularity in various applications, including virtual reality, robotics, and computer vision. However, their high-resolution and spherical nature pose significant challenges for efficient compression. Traditional image compression techniques are not well-suited for omnidirectional images, resulting in suboptimal compression ratios and visual artifacts. Recently, learned image compression methods have demonstrated promising results for perspective images, but their extension to omnidirectional images remains an open problem. We propose pseudocylindrical convolutions, a novel neural network architecture that effectively captures the spherical structure of omnidirectional images. Our approach projects the spherical image onto a pseudocylindrical surface, allowing for the application of standard convolutional neural networks. We integrate this projection into a learned compression framework, incorporating a rate-distortion optimization objective to balance compression ratio and visual quality. Experimental results on several omnidirectional image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. We achieve an average bitrate reduction of 23.5% compared to traditional compression methods, while maintaining similar or improved visual quality. Additionally, our method outperforms existing learned compression techniques adapted for omnidirectional images by 12.2% in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio. Our pseudocylindrical convolutions provide a new direction for learned omnidirectional image compression, enabling more efficient and visually appealing compression of these complex images.

title: An Ensemble of Pre-trained Transformer Models For Imbalanced Multiclass Malware Classification
text: Classification of malware families is crucial for a comprehensive understanding of how they can infect devices, computers, or systems. Thus, malware identification enables security researchers and incident responders to take precautions against malware and accelerate mitigation. API call sequences made by malware are widely utilized features by machine and deep learning models for malware classification as these sequences represent the behavior of malware. However, traditional machine and deep learning models remain incapable of capturing sequence relationships between API calls. On the other hand, the transformer-based models process sequences as a whole and learn relationships between API calls due to multi-head attention mechanisms and positional embeddings. Our experiments demonstrate that the transformer model with one transformer block layer surpassed the widely used base architecture, LSTM. Moreover, BERT or CANINE, pre-trained transformer models, outperformed in classifying highly imbalanced malware families according to evaluation metrics, F1-score, and AUC score. Furthermore, the proposed bagging-based random transformer forest (RTF), an ensemble of BERT or CANINE, has reached the state-of-the-art evaluation scores on three out of four datasets, particularly state-of-the-art F1-score of 0.6149 on one of the commonly used benchmark dataset.

title: An Ensemble of Pre-trained Transformer Models For Imbalanced Multiclass Malware Classification
text: Malware classification is a crucial task in cybersecurity, with the majority of existing approaches focusing on binary classification or multiclass classification with balanced datasets. However, real-world malware datasets often exhibit severe class imbalance, which can degrade the performance of machine learning models. To address this challenge, we propose an ensemble method that leverages multiple pre-trained transformer models for imbalanced multiclass malware classification. Our approach combines the strengths of various transformer architectures, including BERT, RoBERTa, and XLNet, to capture diverse representations of malware samples. We employ a novel weighted voting scheme that takes into account the class distribution and the performance of each individual model on different classes. Experimental results on a large-scale, imbalanced malware dataset demonstrate that our ensemble method achieves significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, with an F1-score of 0.933 compared to 0.854 for the best individual model. We also conduct an in-depth analysis of the importance of each transformer model in the ensemble and the impact of different weighting strategies on the classification performance. Our findings have important implications for the development of robust and accurate malware classification systems in real-world scenarios.

title: Motion Illusions Generated Using Predictive Neural Networks Also Fool Humans
text: Why do we sometimes perceive static images as if they were moving? Visual motion illusions enjoy a sustained popularity, yet there is no definitive answer to the question of why they work. Here we present evidence in favor of the hypothesis that illusory motion is a side effect of the predictive abilities of the brain. We present a generative model, the Evolutionary Illusion GENerator (EIGen), that creates new visual motion illusions based on a video predictive neural network. We confirm that the constructed illusions are effective on human participants through a psychometric survey. Our results support the hypothesis that illusory motion might be the consequence of perceiving the brain's own predictions rather than perceiving raw visual input from the eyes. The philosophical motivation of this paper is to call attention to the untapped potential of "motivated failures", ways for artificial systems to fail as biological systems fail, as a worthy outlet for Artificial Intelligence and Artificial Life research.

title: Motion Illusions Generated Using Predictive Neural Networks Also Fool Humans
text: The human visual system's susceptibility to motion illusions has fascinated researchers for centuries, with recent advances in computer vision enabling the creation of sophisticated stimuli to study these phenomena. This work explores the potential of predictive neural networks to generate motion illusions that deceive humans, leveraging their ability to learn complex patterns in visual data. We propose a novel framework that utilizes a predictive neural network to synthesize motion patterns, which are then used to create illusions of motion in static images. Our approach is validated through a series of psychophysical experiments, where human participants are asked to classify the direction of motion in images generated by our model. The results show a significant proportion of incorrect classifications, indicating that the generated motion illusions effectively fool human observers. Furthermore, we find that the patterns of errors are similar to those observed in traditional motion illusions, suggesting that our model taps into the same underlying visual mechanisms. These findings have implications for the development of more realistic computer-generated imagery and a deeper understanding of human visual perception.

title: Artifact Reduction in Fundus Imaging using Cycle Consistent Adversarial Neural Networks
text: Fundus images are very useful in identifying various ophthalmic disorders. However, due to the presence of artifacts, the visibility of the retina is severely affected. This may result in misdiagnosis of the disorder which may lead to more complicated problems.
