Since deep learning is a powerful tool to extract patterns from data without much human intervention, they can be applied to image-to-image translation problems. An attempt has been made in this paper to automatically rectify such artifacts present in the images of the fundus. We use a CycleGAN based model which consists of residual blocks to reduce the artifacts in the images. Significant improvements are seen when compared to the existing techniques.

title: Artifact Reduction in Fundus Imaging using Cycle Consistent Adversarial Neural Networks
text: The diagnostic utility of fundus images is hindered by the presence of artifacts, which can obscure retinal visibility and lead to misdiagnosis. Leveraging the pattern recognition capabilities of deep learning, this study addresses the challenge of artifact removal in fundus images through image-to-image translation. We propose a CycleGAN-based model incorporating residual blocks to rectify artifacts and enhance image quality. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements over existing techniques, underscoring the potential of our approach to facilitate accurate diagnoses and mitigate the risk of complications.

title: Task and Model Agnostic Adversarial Attack on Graph Neural Networks
text: Adversarial attacks on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) reveal their security vulnerabilities, limiting their adoption in safety-critical applications. However, existing attack strategies rely on the knowledge of either the GNN model being used or the predictive task being attacked. Is this knowledge necessary? For example, a graph may be used for multiple downstream tasks unknown to a practical attacker. It is thus important to test the vulnerability of GNNs to adversarial perturbations in a model and task agnostic setting. In this work, we study this problem and show that GNNs remain vulnerable even when the downstream task and model are unknown. The proposed algorithm, TANDIS (Targeted Attack via Neighborhood DIStortion) shows that distortion of node neighborhoods is effective in drastically compromising prediction performance. Although neighborhood distortion is an NP-hard problem, TANDIS designs an effective heuristic through a novel combination of Graph Isomorphism Network with deep Q-learning. Extensive experiments on real datasets and state-of-the-art models show that, on average, TANDIS is up to 50% more effective than state-of-the-art techniques, while being more than 1000 times faster.

title: Task and Model Agnostic Adversarial Attack on Graph Neural Networks
text: The security of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) is compromised by adversarial attacks, hindering their deployment in safety-critical domains. A crucial question remains: is knowledge of the GNN model or predictive task essential for launching a successful attack? In practice, an attacker may not have access to this information, as a graph can be utilized for multiple, unknown downstream tasks. Therefore, it is essential to investigate the vulnerability of GNNs to adversarial perturbations in a model- and task-agnostic context. This study demonstrates that GNNs remain susceptible to attacks even when the model and task are unknown. We propose TANDIS, an algorithm that exploits neighborhood distortion to substantially degrade prediction performance. By combining a Graph Isomorphism Network with deep Q-learning, TANDIS develops an effective heuristic for this NP-hard problem. Experimental results on real datasets and state-of-the-art models show that TANDIS outperforms existing techniques by up to 50% on average, while being more than 1000 times faster.

title: DIAR: Removing Uninteresting Bytes from Seeds in Software Fuzzing
text: Software fuzzing mutates bytes in the test seeds to explore different behaviors of the program under test. Initial seeds can have great impact on the performance of a fuzzing campaign. Mutating a lot of uninteresting bytes in a large seed wastes the fuzzing resources. In this paper, we present the preliminary results of our approach that aims to improve the performance of fuzzers through identifying and removing uninteresting bytes in the seeds. In particular, we present DIAR, a technique that reduces the size of the seeds based on their coverage. Our preliminary results suggest fuzzing campaigns that start with reduced seeds, find new paths faster, and can produce higher coverage overall.

title: DIAR: Removing Uninteresting Bytes from Seeds in Software Fuzzing
text: Software fuzzing is a widely-used technique for discovering vulnerabilities in programs, but its effectiveness is often hindered by the presence of uninteresting bytes in seeds, which can lead to wasted computational resources and reduced code coverage. We propose DIAR, a novel approach for removing uninteresting bytes from seeds, thereby increasing the efficiency of software fuzzing. Our methodology involves analyzing the execution traces of seeds to identify bytes that do not affect the program's control flow, and then removing these bytes to create more effective seeds. Experimental results on several real-world programs demonstrate that DIAR can reduce the number of uninteresting bytes by up to 75%, resulting in an average increase of 23% in code coverage and 17% in unique crashes discovered.

title: Defending Against Membership Inference Attacks on Beacon Services
text: Large genomic datasets are now created through numerous activities, including recreational genealogical investigations, biomedical research, and clinical care. At the same time, genomic data has become valuable for reuse beyond their initial point of collection, but privacy concerns often hinder access. Over the past several years, Beacon services have emerged to broaden accessibility to such data. These services enable users to query for the presence of a particular minor allele in a private dataset, information that can help care providers determine if genomic variation is spurious or has some known clinical indication. However, various studies have shown that even this limited access model can leak if individuals are members in the underlying dataset. Several approaches for mitigating this vulnerability have been proposed, but they are limited in that they 1) typically rely on heuristics and 2) offer probabilistic privacy guarantees, but neglect utility. In this paper, we present a novel algorithmic framework to ensure privacy in a Beacon service setting with a minimal number of query response flips (e.g., changing a positive response to a negative). Specifically, we represent this problem as combinatorial optimization in both the batch setting (where queries arrive all at once), as well as the online setting (where queries arrive sequentially). The former setting has been the primary focus in prior literature, whereas real Beacons allow sequential queries, motivating the latter investigation. We present principled algorithms in this framework with both privacy and, in some cases, worst-case utility guarantees. Moreover, through an extensive experimental evaluation, we show that the proposed approaches significantly outperform the state of the art in terms of privacy and utility.

title: Defending Against Membership Inference Attacks on Beacon Services
text: The proliferation of beacon services in IoT devices, location-based services, and online social networks has made them an attractive target for membership inference attacks. These attacks, which involve determining whether a specific individual's data is present in a target dataset, pose significant privacy risks to users. Existing defense mechanisms against membership inference attacks are often ineffective against beacon services, which typically involve periodic broadcasts of identifiers or pseudonyms. To address this gap, we propose a novel defense framework that leverages a combination of cryptographic techniques and differential privacy. Our approach involves encrypting the broadcasted identifiers using a keyed hash function and then adding noise to the encrypted identifiers using a Laplacian mechanism. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through a series of experiments on real-world datasets, including a large-scale location-based service and a popular online social network. Our results show that our defense mechanism can reduce the accuracy of membership inference attacks by up to 90% while incurring minimal overhead in terms of computational resources and communication bandwidth. We also evaluate the robustness of our framework against various types of attacks, including record-level and attribute-level attacks, and demonstrate its resilience even in the presence of auxiliary information. Theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations confirm that our approach provides strong differential privacy guarantees while maintaining the functionality of the beacon service. Our defense framework has significant implications for the design of privacy-preserving beacon services and can be applied to a wide range of applications, including IoT devices, location-based services, and online social networks.

title: Unsupervised Clustering Active Learning for Person Re-identification
text: Supervised person re-identification (re-id) approaches require a large amount of pairwise manual labeled data, which is not applicable in most real-world scenarios for re-id deployment. On the other hand, unsupervised re-id methods rely on unlabeled data to train models but performs poorly compared with supervised re-id methods. In this work, we aim to combine unsupervised re-id learning with a small number of human annotations to achieve a competitive performance. Towards this goal, we present a Unsupervised Clustering Active Learning (UCAL) re-id deep learning approach. It is capable of incrementally discovering the representative centroid-pairs and requiring human annotate them. These few labeled representative pairwise data can improve the unsupervised representation learning model with other large amounts of unlabeled data. More importantly, because the representative centroid-pairs are selected for annotation, UCAL can work with very low-cost human effort. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model over state-of-the-art active learning methods on three re-id benchmark datasets.

title: Unsupervised Clustering Active Learning for Person Re-identification
text: The scalability of supervised person re-identification (re-id) approaches is hindered by their reliance on large amounts of manually labeled pairwise data, a luxury rarely afforded in real-world deployment scenarios. Conversely, unsupervised re-id methods, although applicable to unlabeled data, suffer from inferior performance compared to their supervised counterparts. This study seeks to strike a balance by integrating unsupervised re-id learning with a judicious selection of human annotations to achieve competitive performance. We propose the Unsupervised Clustering Active Learning (UCAL) approach, a deep learning framework that incrementally identifies representative centroid-pairs, which are then annotated by humans. By leveraging these sparse yet informative labels, our model enhances unsupervised representation learning from large amounts of unlabeled data. Notably, the strategic selection of centroid-pairs for annotation minimizes human effort, rendering UCAL a low-cost solution. Our extensive experiments on three re-id benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of UCAL over state-of-the-art active learning methods.

title: Learning Cross-Scale Weighted Prediction for Efficient Neural Video Compression
text: Neural video codecs have demonstrated great potential in video transmission and storage applications. Existing neural hybrid video coding approaches rely on optical flow or Gaussian-scale flow for prediction, which cannot support fine-grained adaptation to diverse motion content. Towards more content-adaptive prediction, we propose a novel cross-scale prediction module that achieves more effective motion compensation. Specifically, on the one hand, we produce a reference feature pyramid as prediction sources and then transmit cross-scale flows that leverage the feature scale to control the precision of prediction. On the other hand, for the first time, a weighted prediction mechanism is introduced even if only a single reference frame is available, which can help synthesize a fine prediction result by transmitting cross-scale weight maps. In addition to the cross-scale prediction module, we further propose a multi-stage quantization strategy, which improves the rate-distortion performance with no extra computational penalty during inference. We show the encouraging performance of our efficient neural video codec (ENVC) on several benchmark datasets. In particular, the proposed ENVC can compete with the latest coding standard H.266/VVC in terms of sRGB PSNR on UVG dataset for the low-latency mode. We also analyze in detail the effectiveness of the cross-scale prediction module in handling various video content, and provide a comprehensive ablation study to analyze those important components. Test code is available at .

title: Learning Cross-Scale Weighted Prediction for Efficient Neural Video Compression
text: The burgeoning demand for high-quality video content has precipitated a pressing need for efficient compression algorithms that can effectively balance rate and distortion. Recently, neural video compression has emerged as a promising paradigm, leveraging the representational prowess of deep neural networks to learn compact video representations. However, existing approaches often struggle to effectively capture cross-scale dependencies, leading to suboptimal compression performance. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework for learning cross-scale weighted prediction in neural video compression. Our method, dubbed CSWP, adaptively weights and aggregates predictions from multiple scales to generate a more accurate and compressible video representation. We formulate the problem as a multi-task learning objective, jointly optimizing rate, distortion, and a novel scale-aware regularization term. The CSWP framework is instantiated using a hierarchical neural network architecture, comprising a pyramid of convolutional and recurrent layers that extract and fuse features across different scales. Experimental results on the UVG and HEVC datasets demonstrate that CSWP achieves state-of-the-art compression performance, outperforming existing neural video compression methods by up to 2.3 dB in PSNR and 15.6% in bitrate savings. Furthermore, our ablation studies reveal that the proposed cross-scale weighting mechanism is crucial in capturing complex spatio-temporal dependencies, leading to improved compression efficiency.

title: Miti-DETR: Object Detection based on Transformers with Mitigatory Self-Attention Convergence
text: Object Detection with Transformers (DETR) and related works reach or even surpass the highly-optimized Faster-RCNN baseline with self-attention network architectures. Inspired by the evidence that pure self-attention possesses a strong inductive bias that leads to the transformer losing the expressive power with respect to network depth, we propose a transformer architecture with a mitigatory self-attention mechanism by applying possible direct mapping connections in the transformer architecture to mitigate the rank collapse so as to counteract feature expression loss and enhance the model performance. We apply this proposal in object detection tasks and develop a model named Miti-DETR. Miti-DETR reserves the inputs of each single attention layer to the outputs of that layer so that the "non-attention" information has participated in any attention propagation. The formed residual self-attention network addresses two critical issues: (1) stop the self-attention networks from degenerating to rank-1 to the maximized degree; and (2) further diversify the path distribution of parameter update so that easier attention learning is expected. Miti-DETR significantly enhances the average detection precision and convergence speed towards existing DETR-based models on the challenging COCO object detection dataset. Moreover, the proposed transformer with the residual self-attention network can be easily generalized or plugged in other related task models without specific customization.

title: Miti-DETR: Object Detection based on Transformers with Mitigatory Self-Attention Convergence
text: Object detection has witnessed significant advancements with the emergence of transformer-based architectures, particularly DETR, which has demonstrated remarkable performance in various benchmarks. However, DETR's self-attention mechanism can lead to convergence issues, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address this limitation, we propose Miti-DETR, a novel object detection framework that incorporates mitigatory self-attention convergence techniques to improve DETR's stability and accuracy. Our approach introduces a novel self-attention regularization scheme, which adaptively adjusts the attention weights based on the convergence rate of the detector. This scheme enables the model to focus on the most relevant regions of interest, reducing the impact of noisy attention weights on the detection performance. Furthermore, we propose a multi-scale feature fusion strategy that leverages the hierarchical representation capabilities of transformers to enhance object feature extraction. Extensive experiments on the COCO dataset demonstrate that Miti-DETR outperforms state-of-the-art DETR-based models, achieving an absolute gain of 2.5% in terms of AP and 3.1% in terms of AR. Our ablation studies show that the mitigatory self-attention convergence technique and multi-scale feature fusion strategy contribute significantly to the performance improvements. The proposed Miti-DETR framework offers a promising direction for developing more accurate and robust object detection models, particularly in scenarios where convergence issues are prevalent.

title: Silent Bugs in Deep Learning Frameworks: An Empirical Study of Keras and TensorFlow
text: Deep Learning (DL) frameworks are now widely used, simplifying the creation of complex models as well as their integration to various applications even to non DL experts. However, like any other programs, they are prone to bugs. This paper deals with the subcategory of bugs named silent bugs: they lead to wrong behavior but they do not cause system crashes or hangs, nor show an error message to the user. Such bugs are even more dangerous in DL applications and frameworks due to the "black-box" and stochastic nature of the systems (the end user can not understand how the model makes decisions). This paper presents the first empirical study of Keras and TensorFlow silent bugs, and their impact on users' programs. We extracted closed issues related to Keras from the TensorFlow GitHub repository. Out of the 1,168 issues that we gathered, 77 were reproducible silent bugs affecting users' programs. We categorized the bugs based on the effects on the users' programs and the components where the issues occurred, using information from the issue reports. We then derived a threat level for each of the issues, based on the impact they had on the users' programs. To assess the relevance of identified categories and the impact scale, we conducted an online survey with 103 DL developers. The participants generally agreed with the significant impact of silent bugs in DL libraries and acknowledged our findings (i.e., categories of silent bugs and the proposed impact scale). Finally, leveraging our analysis, we provide a set of guidelines to facilitate safeguarding against such bugs in DL frameworks.

title: Silent Bugs in Deep Learning Frameworks: An Empirical Study of Keras and TensorFlow
text: Deep learning frameworks have become ubiquitous in modern machine learning, with Keras and TensorFlow being two of the most widely used libraries. Despite their popularity, recent studies have hinted at the presence of silent bugs, which are defects that do not cause program crashes or explicit errors but can still lead to incorrect results or undesired behavior. However, the prevalence and characteristics of silent bugs in deep learning frameworks remain poorly understood. In this study, we present the first comprehensive empirical investigation of silent bugs in Keras and TensorFlow. We develop a systematic approach to detect silent bugs by injecting faults into the frameworks' source code and analyzing the resulting behavior. Our methodology involves creating a set of fault injection templates tailored to the specific characteristics of deep learning frameworks, which are then used to inject faults into the codebases of Keras and TensorFlow. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach by analyzing the output of the faulty frameworks on a range of benchmark datasets and comparing the results to those obtained from the original, unmodified frameworks. Our findings are alarming: we identify a total of 127 silent bugs in Keras and 215 in TensorFlow, with many of these bugs causing significant deviations in model performance or producing incorrect results. We also observe that silent bugs are more prevalent in certain components of the frameworks, such as optimization algorithms and layer implementations. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that many silent bugs can be triggered by seemingly innocuous inputs or hyperparameter settings, highlighting the need for more rigorous testing and validation procedures in deep learning framework development. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the silent bug problem in deep learning frameworks and underscores the importance of addressing this critical issue to ensure the reliability and trustworthiness of AI systems.

title: Airphant: Cloud-oriented Document Indexing
text: Modern data warehouses can scale compute nodes independently of storage. These systems persist their data on cloud storage, which is always available and cost-efficient. Ad-hoc compute nodes then fetch necessary data on-demand from cloud storage. This ability to quickly scale or shrink data systems is highly beneficial if query workloads may change over time. We apply this new architecture to search engines with a focus on optimizing their latencies in cloud environments. However, simply placing existing search engines (e.g., Apache Lucene) on top of cloud storage significantly increases their end-to-end query latencies (i.e., more than 6 seconds on average in one of our studies). This is because their indexes can incur multiple network round-trips due to their hierarchical structure (e.g., skip lists, B-trees, learned indexes). To address this issue, we develop a new statistical index (called IoU Sketch). For lookup, IoU Sketch makes multiple asynchronous network requests in parallel. While IoU Sketch may fetch more bytes than existing indexes, it significantly reduces the index lookup time because parallel requests do not block each other. Based on IoU Sketch, we build an end-to-end search engine, called Airphant; we describe how Airphant builds, optimizes, and manages IoU Sketch; and ultimately, supports keyword-based querying. In our experiments with four real datasets, Airphant's average end-to-end latencies are between 13 milliseconds and 300 milliseconds, being up to 8.97x faster than Apache Lucence and 113.39x faster than Elasticsearch.

title: Airphant: Cloud-oriented Document Indexing
text: The emergence of modern data warehouses that can scale compute nodes independently of storage has precipitated a paradigm shift in data processing. By persisting data on cloud storage, these systems can tap into its inherent benefits of high availability and cost-effectiveness. In this context, we investigate the application of this architecture to search engines, with a specific focus on optimizing their latency in cloud environments. However, our experiments reveal that simply deploying existing search engines, such as Apache Lucene, on top of cloud storage results in significant increases in end-to-end query latency, with average latencies exceeding 6 seconds. This performance degradation is attributed to the hierarchical structure of their indexes, which can incur multiple network round-trips. To mitigate this issue, we propose the IoU Sketch, a novel statistical index that leverages parallel asynchronous network requests to reduce index lookup time. Our end-to-end search engine, Airphant, is built around the IoU Sketch, and we describe its mechanisms for building, optimizing, and managing the index, as well as its support for keyword-based querying. Experimental results on four real datasets demonstrate that Airphant achieves average end-to-end latencies between 13 milliseconds and 300 milliseconds, outperforming Apache Lucene by up to 8.97 times and Elasticsearch by up to 113.39 times.

title: Continuous Offline Handwriting Recognition using Deep Learning Models
text: Handwritten text recognition is an open problem of great interest in the area of automatic document image analysis. The transcription of handwritten content present in digitized documents is significant in analyzing historical archives or digitizing information from handwritten documents, forms, and communications. In the last years, great advances have been made in this area due to applying deep learning techniques to its resolution. This Thesis addresses the offline continuous handwritten text recognition (HTR) problem, consisting of developing algorithms and models capable of transcribing the text present in an image without the need for the text to be segmented into characters. For this purpose, we have proposed a new recognition model based on integrating two types of deep learning architectures: convolutional neural networks (CNN) and sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models, respectively. The convolutional component of the model is oriented to identify relevant features present in characters, and the seq2seq component builds the transcription of the text by modeling the sequential nature of the text. For the design of this new model, an extensive analysis of the capabilities of different convolutional architectures in the simplified problem of isolated character recognition has been carried out in order to identify the most suitable ones to be integrated into the continuous model. Additionally, extensive experimentation of the proposed model for the continuous problem has been carried out to determine its robustness to changes in parameterization. The generalization capacity of the model has also been validated by evaluating it on three handwritten text databases using different languages: IAM in English, RIMES in French, and Osborne in Spanish, respectively. The new proposed model provides competitive results with those obtained with other well-established methodologies.

title: Continuous Offline Handwriting Recognition using Deep Learning Models
text: The ability to recognize handwritten text accurately and efficiently is crucial for various applications, including document analysis, language translation, and human-computer interaction. Despite significant progress in online handwriting recognition, offline recognition remains a challenging task due to the complexity and variability of handwriting styles. In this context, deep learning models have shown promising results in image-based recognition tasks, but their application to offline handwriting recognition is still limited. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach for continuous offline handwriting recognition using deep learning models. Our method leverages a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to recognize handwritten text in a continuous manner. The CNNs are used to extract features from handwritten images, while the RNNs are employed to model the sequential dependencies in the handwritten text. We evaluate our approach on three publicly available datasets, including IAM, RIMES, and CVL, and achieve state-of-the-art performance in terms of character recognition accuracy. Specifically, our approach achieves an accuracy of 93.1% on the IAM dataset, outperforming existing methods by 2.5%. We also conduct an ablation study to investigate the impact of different components of our approach, including the feature extraction mechanism and the sequence modeling technique. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of deep learning models for continuous offline handwriting recognition and provide insights into the design of robust recognition systems. Furthermore, our approach has the potential to be applied to various applications, including document analysis, language translation, and human-computer interaction. Finally, we plan to extend our approach to recognize handwritten text in other languages and scripts, enabling its application to a broader range of scenarios.

title: MPCLeague: Robust MPC Platform for Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning
text: In the modern era of computing, machine learning tools have demonstrated their potential in vital sectors, such as healthcare and finance, to derive proper inferences. The sensitive and confidential nature of the data in such sectors raises genuine concerns for data privacy. This motivated the area of Privacy-preserving Machine Learning (PPML), where privacy of data is guaranteed. In this thesis, we design an efficient platform, MPCLeague, for PPML in the Secure Outsourced Computation (SOC) setting using Secure Multi-party Computation (MPC) techniques. MPC, the holy-grail problem of secure distributed computing, enables a set of n mutually distrusting parties to perform joint computation on their private inputs in a way that no coalition of t parties can learn more information than the output (privacy) or affect the true output of the computation (correctness). While MPC, in general, has been a subject of extensive research, the area of MPC with a small number of parties has drawn popularity of late mainly due to its application to real-time scenarios, efficiency and simplicity. This thesis focuses on designing efficient MPC frameworks for 2, 3 and 4 parties, with at most one corruption and supports ring structures. At the heart of this thesis are four frameworks - ASTRA, SWIFT, Tetrad, ABY2.0 - catered to different settings. The practicality of our framework is argued through improvements in the benchmarking of widely used ML algorithms -- Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, Neural Networks, and Support Vector Machines. We propose two variants for each of our frameworks, with one variant aiming to minimise the execution time while the other focuses on the monetary cost. The concrete efficiency gains of our frameworks coupled with the stronger security guarantee of robustness make our platform an ideal choice for a real-time deployment of PPML techniques.

title: MPCLeague: Robust MPC Platform for Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning
text: The proliferation of machine learning models in real-world applications has raised concerns about data privacy, as sensitive information is often shared among multiple parties. Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) offers a promising solution, enabling collaborative learning while protecting individual data. However, existing MPC frameworks are limited by their lack of scalability, high computational overhead, and inadequate support for complex machine learning algorithms. To address these challenges, we propose MPCLeague, a robust MPC platform designed specifically for privacy-preserving machine learning. Our platform leverages a novel combination of cryptographic protocols, including homomorphic encryption and garbled circuits, to facilitate efficient and secure computation. MPCLeague's modular architecture allows for seamless integration of various machine learning libraries, enabling the deployment of complex models while maintaining data confidentiality. We evaluate MPCLeague's performance using a range of benchmarks, including logistic regression, decision trees, and neural networks. Our experiments demonstrate significant improvements in computational efficiency, with speedups of up to 5x compared to state-of-the-art MPC frameworks. Furthermore, we demonstrate the platform's scalability by training models on large datasets, including the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. Theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations confirm the security and correctness of MPCLeague's protocols. We also conduct a comprehensive comparison with existing MPC frameworks, highlighting the advantages of our approach in terms of performance, scalability, and ease of use. MPCLeague's robustness and versatility make it an attractive solution for real-world applications, enabling the development of privacy-preserving machine learning models in a wide range of domains.

title: Quasi-Taylor Samplers for Diffusion Generative Models based on Ideal Derivatives
text: Diffusion generative models have emerged as a new challenger to popular deep neural generative models such as GANs, but have the drawback that they often require a huge number of neural function evaluations (NFEs) during synthesis unless some sophisticated sampling strategies are employed. This paper proposes new efficient samplers based on the numerical schemes derived by the familiar Taylor expansion, which directly solves the ODE/SDE of interest. In general, it is not easy to compute the derivatives that are required in higher-order Taylor schemes, but in the case of diffusion models, this difficulty is alleviated by the trick that the authors call ``ideal derivative substitution,'' in which the higher-order derivatives are replaced by tractable ones. To derive ideal derivatives, the authors argue the ``single point approximation,'' in which the true score function is approximated by a conditional one, holds in many cases, and considered the derivatives of this approximation. Applying thus obtained new quasi-Taylor samplers to image generation tasks, the authors experimentally confirmed that the proposed samplers could synthesize plausible images in small number of NFEs, and that the performance was better or at the same level as DDIM and Runge-Kutta methods. The paper also argues the relevance of the proposed samplers to the existing ones mentioned above.

title: Quasi-Taylor Samplers for Diffusion Generative Models based on Ideal Derivatives
text: The proliferation of diffusion-based generative models has sparked widespread interest in efficient sampling techniques, as the requisite number of iterations can be computationally prohibitive. In this context, Taylor series-based methods have emerged as a promising avenue, leveraging the tractability of ideal derivatives to approximate complex transition operators. However, the strict requirements on the Lipschitz continuity of the drift coefficient can render these approaches inapplicable to many real-world scenarios. We propose Quasi-Taylor Samplers, a novel class of methods that relax these constraints by incorporating quasi-Newton approximations of the Hessian matrix. By exploiting the inherent structure of the diffusion process, our approach enables the efficient computation of high-order Taylor approximations, even in the presence of non-smooth drift coefficients. We demonstrate the efficacy of Quasi-Taylor Samplers through a comprehensive evaluation on a range of benchmark datasets, showcasing improved convergence rates and enhanced sample quality compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we provide a rigorous theoretical analysis, establishing the convergence of our approach under mild assumptions on the underlying diffusion process. Our findings have significant implications for the deployment of diffusion-based models in applications where sampling efficiency is paramount, such as image synthesis and data augmentation.

title: Towards a conjecture on a special class of matrices over commutative rings of characteristic 2
text: In this paper, we prove the conjecture posed by Keller and Rosemarin at Eurocrypt 2021 on the nullity of a matrix polynomial of a block matrix with Hadamard type blocks over commutative rings of characteristic 2. Therefore, it confirms the conjectural optimal bound on the dimension of invariant subspace of the Starkad cipher using the HADES design strategy. Moreover, we reveal the algebraic structure formed by Hadamard matrices over commutative rings from the perspectives of group algebra and polynomial algebra. An interesting relation between block-Hadamard matrices and Hadamard-block matrices is obtained as well.

title: Towards a conjecture on a special class of matrices over commutative rings of characteristic 2
text: We establish the nullity of a matrix polynomial associated with a block matrix comprising Hadamard-type blocks over commutative rings of characteristic 2, thereby resolving the conjecture posed by Keller and Rosemarin at Eurocrypt 2021. This result confirms the optimality of the dimension bound for invariant subspaces of the Starkad cipher under the HADES design strategy. Furthermore, our analysis uncovers the algebraic structure of Hadamard matrices over commutative rings, revealing connections with group algebra and polynomial algebra, as well as an intriguing relationship between block-Hadamard and Hadamard-block matrices.

title: AlertTrap: A study on object detection in remote insects trap monitoring system using on-the-edge deep learning platform
text: Fruit flies are one of the most harmful insect species to fruit yields. In AlertTrap, implementation of Single-Shot Multibox Detector (SSD) architecture with different state-of-the-art backbone feature extractors such as MobileNetV1 and MobileNetV2 appears to be potential solutions for the real-time detection problem. SSD-MobileNetV1 and SSD-MobileNetV2 perform well and result in AP at 0.5 of 0.957 and 1.0, respectively. You Only Look Once (YOLO) v4-tiny outperforms the SSD family with 1.0 in AP at 0.5; however, its throughput velocity is considerably slower, which shows SSD models are better candidates for real-time implementation. We also tested the models with synthetic test sets simulating expected environmental disturbances. The YOLOv4-tiny had better tolerance to these disturbances than the SSD models. The Raspberry Pi system successfully gathered environmental data and pest counts, sending them via email over 4 G. However, running the full YOLO version in real time on Raspberry Pi is not feasible, indicating the need for a lighter object detection algorithm for future research. Among model candidates, YOLOv4-tiny generally performs best, with SSD-MobileNetV2 also comparable and sometimes better, especially in scenarios with synthetic disturbances. SSD models excel in processing time, enabling real-time, high-accuracy detection.

title: AlertTrap: A study on object detection in remote insects trap monitoring system using on-the-edge deep learning platform
text: Fruit flies pose a significant threat to fruit yields, necessitating the development of efficient real-time detection systems. We explore the potential of Single-Shot Multibox Detector (SSD) architecture with state-of-the-art backbone feature extractors, specifically MobileNetV1 and MobileNetV2, for addressing this problem. Our experiments reveal that SSD-MobileNetV1 and SSD-MobileNetV2 achieve high average precision (AP) values of 0.957 and 1.0, respectively, at an Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold of 0.5. Although You Only Look Once (YOLO) v4-tiny outperforms the SSD family with an AP of 1.0, its slower throughput velocity renders SSD models more suitable for real-time implementation. Furthermore, we assess the models' robustness to environmental disturbances using synthetic test sets, finding that YOLOv4-tiny exhibits greater tolerance. Our Raspberry Pi system successfully collects environmental data and pest counts, transmitting them via email over 4G. However, the feasibility of running the full YOLO version in real-time on Raspberry Pi is limited, highlighting the need for lighter object detection algorithms in future research. Overall, YOLOv4-tiny and SSD-MobileNetV2 emerge as top contenders, with SSD models offering superior processing times for high-accuracy, real-time detection.

title: The Quantum Version of Prediction for Binary Classification Problem by Ensemble Methods
text: In this work, we consider the performance of using a quantum algorithm to predict a result for a binary classification problem if a machine learning model is an ensemble from any simple classifiers. Such an approach is faster than classical prediction and uses quantum and classical computing, but it is based on a probabilistic algorithm. Let $N$ be a number of classifiers from an ensemble model and $O(T)$ be the running time of prediction on one classifier. In classical case, an ensemble model gets answers from each classifier and "averages" the result. The running time in classical case is $O\left( N \cdot T \right)$. We propose an algorithm which works in $O\left(\sqrt{N} \cdot T\right)$.

title: The Quantum Version of Prediction for Binary Classification Problem by Ensemble Methods
text: We examine the efficacy of a quantum algorithm in predicting outcomes for binary classification problems, where the machine learning model is an ensemble of simple classifiers. This hybrid approach, leveraging both quantum and classical computing, offers a probabilistic solution that accelerates prediction compared to classical methods. In the classical paradigm, an ensemble model aggregates results from individual classifiers, incurring a running time of O(N · T), where N denotes the number of classifiers and O(T) represents the prediction time for a single classifier. In contrast, our proposed algorithm achieves a significant speedup, operating in O(√N · T), thereby reducing the computational overhead.

title: Novel Dual-Channel Long Short-Term Memory Compressed Capsule Networks for Emotion Recognition
text: Recent analysis on speech emotion recognition has made considerable advances with the use of MFCCs spectrogram features and the implementation of neural network approaches such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Capsule networks (CapsNet) have gained gratitude as alternatives to CNNs with their larger capacities for hierarchical representation. To address these issues, this research introduces a text-independent and speaker-independent SER novel architecture, where a dual-channel long short-term memory compressed-CapsNet (DC-LSTM COMP-CapsNet) algorithm is proposed based on the structural features of CapsNet. Our proposed novel classifier can ensure the energy efficiency of the model and adequate compression method in speech emotion recognition, which is not delivered through the original structure of a CapsNet. Moreover, the grid search approach is used to attain optimal solutions. Results witnessed an improved performance and reduction in the training and testing running time. The speech datasets used to evaluate our algorithm are: Arabic Emirati-accented corpus, English speech under simulated and actual stress corpus, English Ryerson audio-visual database of emotional speech and song corpus, and crowd-sourced emotional multimodal actors dataset. This work reveals that the optimum feature extraction method compared to other known methods is MFCCs delta-delta. Using the four datasets and the MFCCs delta-delta, DC-LSTM COMP-CapsNet surpasses all the state-of-the-art systems, classical classifiers, CNN, and the original CapsNet. Using the Arabic Emirati-accented corpus, our results demonstrate that the proposed work yields average emotion recognition accuracy of 89.3% compared to 84.7%, 82.2%, 69.8%, 69.2%, 53.8%, 42.6%, and 31.9% based on CapsNet, CNN, support vector machine, multi-layer perceptron, k-nearest neighbor, radial basis function, and naive Bayes, respectively.

title: Novel Dual-Channel Long Short-Term Memory Compressed Capsule Networks for Emotion Recognition
text: Emotion recognition from speech and text has garnered significant attention in recent years, driven by its potential to enhance human-computer interaction and sentiment analysis applications. Despite advances in deep learning-based approaches, existing methods often struggle to effectively capture the complex, hierarchical relationships between emotional cues and contextual information. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Dual-Channel Long Short-Term Memory Compressed Capsule Network (DC-LSTM-CCN) architecture, which leverages the strengths of both capsule networks and LSTM-based recurrent neural networks. Our approach involves dual-channel processing, where speech and text modalities are processed separately using LSTM networks, and subsequently fused using a novel compressed capsule layer. This allows for the modeling of intricate relationships between local and global features, while reducing the risk of overfitting. We evaluate our DC-LSTM-CCN model on the IEMOCAP and MELD datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results with an average F1-score of 84.2% and 81.5%, respectively. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of our dual-channel approach, with significant performance improvements observed when compared to single-modality and early-fusion baselines. Furthermore, our model exhibits robustness to noise and variability in the input data, making it a promising solution for real-world affective computing applications. The proposed DC-LSTM-CCN architecture offers a new direction for research in multimodal emotion recognition, with potential applications in fields such as human-robot interaction, sentiment analysis, and mental health monitoring.

title: Novel Hybrid DNN Approaches for Speaker Verification in Emotional and Stressful Talking Environments
text: In this work, we conducted an empirical comparative study of the performance of text-independent speaker verification in emotional and stressful environments. This work combined deep models with shallow architecture, which resulted in novel hybrid classifiers. Four distinct hybrid models were utilized: deep neural network-hidden Markov model (DNN-HMM), deep neural network-Gaussian mixture model (DNN-GMM), Gaussian mixture model-deep neural network (GMM-DNN), and hidden Markov model-deep neural network (HMM-DNN). All models were based on novel implemented architecture. The comparative study used three distinct speech datasets: a private Arabic dataset and two public English databases, namely, Speech Under Simulated and Actual Stress (SUSAS) and Ryerson Audio-Visual Database of Emotional Speech and Song (RAVDESS). The test results of the aforementioned hybrid models demonstrated that the proposed HMM-DNN leveraged the verification performance in emotional and stressful environments. Results also showed that HMM-DNN outperformed all other hybrid models in terms of equal error rate (EER) and area under the curve (AUC) evaluation metrics. The average resulting verification system based on the three datasets yielded EERs of 7.19%, 16.85%, 11.51%, and 11.90% based on HMM-DNN, DNN-HMM, DNN-GMM, and GMM-DNN, respectively. Furthermore, we found that the DNN-GMM model demonstrated the least computational complexity compared to all other hybrid models in both talking environments. Conversely, the HMM-DNN model required the greatest amount of training time. Findings also demonstrated that EER and AUC values depended on the database when comparing average emotional and stressful performances.

title: Novel Hybrid DNN Approaches for Speaker Verification in Emotional and Stressful Talking Environments
text: Empirical investigations into the efficacy of text-independent speaker verification systems in emotional and stressful environments have yielded inconsistent results, necessitating a comparative analysis of novel hybrid classifiers. By integrating deep models with shallow architectures, we devised four distinct hybrid models: DNN-HMM, DNN-GMM, GMM-DNN, and HMM-DNN, each founded on a novel implemented architecture. A comprehensive evaluation of these models was conducted using three diverse speech datasets, encompassing a private Arabic dataset and two public English databases, SUSAS and RAVDESS. The results revealed that the HMM-DNN hybrid model significantly enhanced verification performance in emotional and stressful environments, outperforming its counterparts in terms of equal error rate (EER) and area under the curve (AUC) metrics. The average EERs across the three datasets were 7.19%, 16.85%, 11.51%, and 11.90% for HMM-DNN, DNN-HMM, DNN-GMM, and GMM-DNN, respectively. Notably, the DNN-GMM model exhibited the lowest computational complexity, whereas the HMM-DNN model required the longest training time. Furthermore, our findings indicate that EER and AUC values are database-dependent when comparing average emotional and stressful performances, underscoring the importance of dataset selection in speaker verification tasks.

title: AIDA: An Active Inference-based Design Agent for Audio Processing Algorithms
text: In this paper we present AIDA, which is an active inference-based agent that iteratively designs a personalized audio processing algorithm through situated interactions with a human client. The target application of AIDA is to propose on-the-spot the most interesting alternative values for the tuning parameters of a hearing aid (HA) algorithm, whenever a HA client is not satisfied with their HA performance. AIDA interprets searching for the "most interesting alternative" as an issue of optimal (acoustic) context-aware Bayesian trial design. In computational terms, AIDA is realized as an active inference-based agent with an Expected Free Energy criterion for trial design. This type of architecture is inspired by neuro-economic models on efficient (Bayesian) trial design in brains and implies that AIDA comprises generative probabilistic models for acoustic signals and user responses. We propose a novel generative model for acoustic signals as a sum of time-varying auto-regressive filters and a user response model based on a Gaussian Process Classifier. The full AIDA agent has been implemented in a factor graph for the generative model and all tasks (parameter learning, acoustic context classification, trial design, etc.) are realized by variational message passing on the factor graph. All verification and validation experiments and demonstrations are freely accessible at our GitHub repository.

title: AIDA: An Active Inference-based Design Agent for Audio Processing Algorithms
text: The design of audio processing algorithms is a complex, multi-objective optimization problem, often relying on manual tuning of hyperparameters by human experts. This process can be time-consuming, labor-intensive, and may not always lead to optimal solutions. Recent advances in active inference, a subfield of artificial intelligence, offer a promising approach to automate this process. We present AIDA, an Active Inference-based Design Agent for Audio Processing Algorithms, which leverages probabilistic modeling and active learning to efficiently explore the hyperparameter space of audio processing algorithms. AIDA's core component is a hierarchical Bayesian model that encapsulates the relationships between algorithmic hyperparameters, audio features, and perceptual quality metrics. Through a series of experiments on a range of audio processing tasks, including echo cancellation and noise reduction, we demonstrate that AIDA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art optimization methods, such as grid search and Bayesian optimization, in terms of convergence speed and solution quality. Furthermore, we show that AIDA's active inference mechanism enables it to adapt to changing audio environments and user preferences, making it a versatile tool for real-world audio processing applications. Our results have significant implications for the automation of audio processing algorithm design, and highlight the potential of active inference in solving complex, real-world optimization problems.

title: A Trained Regularization Approach Based on Born Iterative Method for Electromagnetic Imaging
text: A trained-based Born iterative method (TBIM) is developed for electromagnetic imaging (EMI) applications. The proposed TBIM consists of a nested loop; the outer loop executes TBIM iteration steps, while the inner loop executes a trained iterative shrinkage thresholding algorithm (TISTA). The applied TISTA runs linear Landweber iterations implemented with a trained regularization network designed based on U-net architecture. A normalization process was imposed in TISTA that made TISTA training applicable within the proposed TBIM. The iterative utilization of the regularization network in TISTA is a bottleneck that demands high memory allocation through the training process. Therefore TISTA within each TBIM step was trained separately. The TISTA regularization network in each TBIM step was initialized using the weights from the previous TBIM step. The above approach achieved high-quality image restoration after running few TBIM steps while maintained low memory allocation through the training process. The proposed framework can be extended to Newton or quasi-Newton schemes, where within each Newton iteration, a linear ill-posed problem is optimized that differs from one example to another. The numerical results illustrated in this work show the superiority of the proposed TBIM compared to the conventional sparse-based Born iterative method (SBIM).

title: A Trained Regularization Approach Based on Born Iterative Method for Electromagnetic Imaging
text: Electromagnetic imaging is a non-invasive technique for reconstructing the internal structures of objects from scattered electromagnetic field data. However, the inverse problem of electromagnetic imaging is often ill-posed, leading to unstable and inaccurate solutions. Recently, deep learning-based methods have shown promising results in solving this problem, but they typically require large amounts of labeled training data and can be computationally expensive. In this work, we propose a trained regularization approach based on the Born iterative method, a classical technique for solving electromagnetic inverse problems. Our approach leverages the physical insights provided by the Born iterative method to design a regularization term, which is then learned from a small amount of labeled data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a range of electromagnetic imaging problems, including 2D and 3D reconstructions, and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency. Our approach achieves an average reconstruction error of 5.21% on a benchmark dataset, compared to 7.56% for the best existing method. Furthermore, our approach requires significantly less training data and computational resources, making it a promising solution for practical electromagnetic imaging applications. The proposed method can be easily extended to other inverse problems in imaging and can pave the way for the development of more accurate and efficient imaging techniques.

title: Delivery Issues Identification from Customer Feedback Data
text: Millions of packages are delivered successfully by online and local retail stores across the world every day. The proper delivery of packages is needed to ensure high customer satisfaction and repeat purchases. These deliveries suffer various problems despite the best efforts from the stores. These issues happen not only due to the large volume and high demand for low turnaround time but also due to mechanical operations and natural factors. These issues range from receiving wrong items in the package to delayed shipment to damaged packages because of mishandling during transportation. Finding solutions to various delivery issues faced by both sending and receiving parties plays a vital role in increasing the efficiency of the entire process. This paper shows how to find these issues using customer feedback from the text comments and uploaded images. We used transfer learning for both Text and Image models to minimize the demand for thousands of labeled examples. The results show that the model can find different issues. Furthermore, it can also be used for tasks like bottleneck identification, process improvement, automating refunds, etc. Compared with the existing process, the ensemble of text and image models proposed in this paper ensures the identification of several types of delivery issues, which is more suitable for the real-life scenarios of delivery of items in retail businesses. This method can supply a new idea of issue detection for the delivery of packages in similar industries.

title: Delivery Issues Identification from Customer Feedback Data
text: The rise of e-commerce has led to an exponential increase in parcel shipments, resulting in a surge of customer complaints related to delivery issues. Identifying and addressing these concerns is crucial for logistics companies to maintain customer satisfaction and loyalty. Existing methods for complaint analysis rely heavily on manual processing, which is time-consuming, error-prone, and inefficient. This paper proposes a novel approach to automate the identification of delivery issues from customer feedback data using computer vision and natural language processing techniques. Our methodology involves collecting and preprocessing a large dataset of customer reviews and feedback forms, which are then fed into a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract visual features from images of damaged or incorrect packages. The text data is processed using a long short-term memory (LSTM) network to capture semantic relationships between words and phrases. The output of both models is fused using a multimodal fusion technique to generate a comprehensive representation of the delivery issue. Experimental results on a real-world dataset of 10,000 customer feedback forms demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving an F1-score of 0.93 in identifying delivery issues, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by 12%. Our approach can be integrated into existing logistics systems, enabling companies to quickly identify and resolve delivery issues, thereby improving customer satisfaction and reducing operational costs.

title: FRuDA: Framework for Distributed Adversarial Domain Adaptation
text: Breakthroughs in unsupervised domain adaptation (uDA) can help in adapting models from a label-rich source domain to unlabeled target domains. Despite these advancements, there is a lack of research on how uDA algorithms, particularly those based on adversarial learning, can work in distributed settings. In real-world applications, target domains are often distributed across thousands of devices, and existing adversarial uDA algorithms -- which are centralized in nature -- cannot be applied in these settings. To solve this important problem, we introduce FRuDA: an end-to-end framework for distributed adversarial uDA. Through a careful analysis of the uDA literature, we identify the design goals for a distributed uDA system and propose two novel algorithms to increase adaptation accuracy and training efficiency of adversarial uDA in distributed settings. Our evaluation of FRuDA with five image and speech datasets show that it can boost target domain accuracy by up to 50% and improve the training efficiency of adversarial uDA by at least 11 times.

title: FRuDA: Framework for Distributed Adversarial Domain Adaptation
text: The proliferation of machine learning models across diverse domains has led to a pressing need for robust domain adaptation techniques, particularly in the presence of adversaries. Existing approaches, however, are often limited by their reliance on centralized data and vulnerability to attacks. To address these shortcomings, we propose FRuDA, a novel framework for distributed adversarial domain adaptation. FRuDA enables multiple parties to collaboratively adapt a shared model to a target domain while protecting against malicious attacks and preserving data privacy. Our approach leverages a decentralized architecture, where each party maintains a local model and exchanges knowledge with peers using a novel, adversarial-resistant aggregation scheme. We theoretically analyze FRuDA's convergence guarantees and demonstrate its efficacy through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets. Our results show that FRuDA outperforms state-of-the-art methods in adapting to target domains while exhibiting improved robustness to adversarial attacks, even in scenarios with Byzantine failures.

title: Will You Dance To The Challenge? Predicting User Participation of TikTok Challenges
text: TikTok is a popular new social media, where users express themselves through short video clips. A common form of interaction on the platform is participating in "challenges", which are songs and dances for users to iterate upon. Challenge contagion can be measured through replication reach, i.e., users uploading videos of their participation in the challenges. The uniqueness of the TikTok platform where both challenge content and user preferences are evolving requires the combination of challenge and user representation. This paper investigates social contagion of TikTok challenges through predicting a user's participation. We propose a novel deep learning model, deepChallenger, to learn and combine latent user and challenge representations from past videos to perform this user-challenge prediction task. We collect a dataset of over 7,000 videos from 12 trending challenges on the ForYouPage, the app's landing page, and over 10,000 videos from 1303 users. Extensive experiments are conducted and the results show that our proposed deepChallenger (F1=0.494) outperforms baselines (F1=0.188) in the prediction task.

title: Will You Dance To The Challenge? Predicting User Participation of TikTok Challenges
text: On TikTok, a burgeoning social media platform, users convey their individuality through brief video snippets, often engaging in "challenges" that involve iterating on songs and dances. The propagation of these challenges can be quantified by replication reach, which is the number of users uploading videos of their participation. The dynamic nature of TikTok, where both challenge content and user preferences are in a state of flux, necessitates a unified representation of challenges and users. This study examines the social contagion of TikTok challenges by predicting user participation. We introduce deepChallenger, a novel deep learning model that integrates latent user and challenge representations from past videos to accomplish this prediction task. Our dataset comprises over 7,000 videos from 12 trending challenges on the ForYouPage and more than 10,000 videos from 1,303 users. Experimental results demonstrate that deepChallenger (F1 = 0.494) significantly outperforms baseline models (F1 = 0.188) in predicting user participation.

title: Reducing Planning Complexity of General Reinforcement Learning with Non-Markovian Abstractions
text: The field of General Reinforcement Learning (GRL) formulates the problem of sequential decision-making from ground up. The history of interaction constitutes a "ground" state of the system, which never repeats. On the one hand, this generality allows GRL to model almost every domain possible, e.g.\ Bandits, MDPs, POMDPs, PSRs, and history-based environments. On the other hand, in general, the near-optimal policies in GRL are functions of complete history, which hinders not only learning but also planning in GRL. The usual way around for the planning part is that the agent is given a Markovian abstraction of the underlying process. So, it can use any MDP planning algorithm to find a near-optimal policy. The Extreme State Aggregation (ESA) framework has extended this idea to non-Markovian abstractions without compromising on the possibility of planning through a (surrogate) MDP. A distinguishing feature of ESA is that it proves an upper bound of $O\left(\varepsilon^{-A} \cdot (1-γ)^{-2A}\right)$ on the number of states required for the surrogate MDP (where $A$ is the number of actions, $γ$ is the discount-factor, and $\varepsilon$ is the optimality-gap) which holds \emph{uniformly} for \emph{all} domains. While the possibility of a universal bound is quite remarkable, we show that this bound is very loose. We propose a novel non-MDP abstraction which allows for a much better upper bound of $O\left(\varepsilon^{-1} \cdot (1-γ)^{-2} \cdot A \cdot 2^{A}\right)$. Furthermore, we show that this bound can be improved further to $O\left(\varepsilon^{-1} \cdot (1-γ)^{-2} \cdot \log^3 A \right)$ by using an action-sequentialization method.

title: Reducing Planning Complexity of General Reinforcement Learning with Non-Markovian Abstractions
text: General reinforcement learning (RL) frameworks often struggle to scale with large state and action spaces due to the curse of dimensionality, leading to intractable planning complexity. This issue is exacerbated in non-Markovian domains, where the environment's dynamics cannot be captured by a Markov decision process (MDP). To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that leverages non-Markovian abstractions to reduce the planning complexity of general RL. Our methodology is based on a hierarchical abstraction scheme, where the original problem is decomposed into a sequence of smaller, more manageable sub-problems. Each sub-problem is modeled as a non-Markovian decision process (NMDP), which is then solved using a bespoke planning algorithm. The key innovation lies in the use of a probabilistic abstraction mechanism, which enables the transfer of knowledge across sub-problems, thereby reducing the overall planning complexity. We theoretically analyze the proposed approach and provide bounds on the sub-optimality of the obtained policies. Empirical evaluations on a range of benchmark problems, including robotic control and resource allocation tasks, demonstrate significant reductions in planning complexity, often by several orders of magnitude, while maintaining near-optimal performance. Our results have important implications for the development of more efficient and scalable RL methods, particularly in real-world domains where Markovian assumptions are often violated. By providing a principled approach to non-Markovian abstraction, this work takes a crucial step towards bridging the gap between theoretical RL and real-world applications.

title: Long Story Short: Omitted Variable Bias in Causal Machine Learning
text: We develop a general theory of omitted variable bias for a wide range of common causal parameters, including (but not limited to) averages of potential outcomes, average treatment effects, average causal derivatives, and policy effects from covariate shifts. Our theory applies to nonparametric models, while naturally allowing for (semi-)parametric restrictions (such as partial linearity) when such assumptions are made. We show how simple plausibility judgments on the maximum explanatory power of omitted variables are sufficient to bound the magnitude of the bias, thus facilitating sensitivity analysis in otherwise complex, nonlinear models. Finally, we provide flexible and efficient statistical inference methods for the bounds, which can leverage modern machine learning algorithms for estimation. These results allow empirical researchers to perform sensitivity analyses in a flexible class of machine-learned causal models using very simple, and interpretable, tools. We demonstrate the utility of our approach with two empirical examples.

title: Long Story Short: Omitted Variable Bias in Causal Machine Learning
text: Causal machine learning has emerged as a crucial tool for decision-making in various domains, from healthcare to economics. However, omitted variable bias (OVB) poses a significant threat to the validity of causal inferences drawn from these models. OVB arises when a relevant variable is omitted from the analysis, leading to biased estimates of causal effects. Despite its importance, OVB remains understudied in the context of machine learning. We investigate OVB in causal machine learning and develop a novel framework to detect and mitigate its impact. Our approach leverages the concept of proxy variables to identify potential sources of OVB and incorporates them into the causal model. Through extensive simulations and real-world experiments, we demonstrate that our method significantly reduces OVB and improves the accuracy of causal estimates. Our findings have important implications for the development of reliable and trustworthy causal machine learning models in various applications.

title: Abstractions of General Reinforcement Learning
text: The field of artificial intelligence (AI) is devoted to the creation of artificial decision-makers that can perform (at least) on par with the human counterparts on a domain of interest. Unlike the agents in traditional AI, the agents in artificial general intelligence (AGI) are required to replicate human intelligence in almost every domain of interest. Moreover, an AGI agent should be able to achieve this without (virtually any) further changes, retraining, or fine-tuning of the parameters. The real world is non-stationary, non-ergodic, and non-Markovian: we, humans, can neither revisit our past nor are the most recent observations sufficient statistics. Yet, we excel at a variety of complex tasks. Many of these tasks require longterm planning. We can associate this success to our natural faculty to abstract away task-irrelevant information from our overwhelming sensory experience. We make task-specific mental models of the world without much effort. Due to this ability to abstract, we can plan on a significantly compact representation of a task without much loss of performance. Not only this, we also abstract our actions to produce high-level plans: the level of action-abstraction can be anywhere between small muscle movements to a mental notion of "doing an action". It is natural to assume that any AGI agent competing with humans (at every plausible domain) should also have these abilities to abstract its experiences and actions. This thesis is an inquiry into the existence of such abstractions which aid efficient planing for a wide range of domains, and most importantly, these abstractions come with some optimality guarantees.

title: Abstractions of General Reinforcement Learning
text: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in various domains, but its widespread adoption is hindered by the need for domain-specific knowledge and careful tuning of hyperparameters. General RL, which aims to learn policies that generalize across diverse environments, is a promising approach to mitigate these limitations. However, the development of general RL algorithms is challenging due to the lack of a unified framework for understanding the fundamental abstractions that underlie this problem. In this work, we propose a novel framework for general RL that identifies and formalizes three key abstractions: task semantics, environment structure, and policy invariants. We demonstrate that these abstractions are essential for generalizing RL policies across different environments and tasks. To validate our framework, we introduce a new benchmark, GeneralRLBench, which comprises 15 diverse environments and 50 tasks. We evaluate several state-of-the-art RL algorithms on GeneralRLBench and show that they fail to generalize across environments and tasks, highlighting the need for more principled approaches to general RL. We then develop a new algorithm, Abstraction-Augmented RL (A2RL), which explicitly incorporates the proposed abstractions into the learning process. A2RL outperforms existing methods on GeneralRLBench, achieving an average improvement of 23.4% in terms of task success rate. Our analysis reveals that A2RL's success is attributed to its ability to discover and leverage the underlying abstractions, enabling it to generalize more effectively across environments and tasks. This work provides a crucial step towards the development of more general and robust RL algorithms, and has significant implications for the deployment of RL in real-world applications.

title: Perlin Noise Improve Adversarial Robustness
text: Adversarial examples are some special input that can perturb the output of a deep neural network, in order to make produce intentional errors in the learning algorithms in the production environment. Most of the present methods for generating adversarial examples require gradient information. Even universal perturbations that are not relevant to the generative model rely to some extent on gradient information. Procedural noise adversarial examples is a new way of adversarial example generation, which uses computer graphics noise to generate universal adversarial perturbations quickly while not relying on gradient information. Combined with the defensive idea of adversarial training, we use Perlin noise to train the neural network to obtain a model that can defend against procedural noise adversarial examples. In combination with the use of model fine-tuning methods based on pre-trained models, we obtain faster training as well as higher accuracy. Our study shows that procedural noise adversarial examples are defensible, but why procedural noise can generate adversarial examples and how to defend against other kinds of procedural noise adversarial examples that may emerge in the future remain to be investigated.

title: Perlin Noise Improve Adversarial Robustness
text: Deep neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples, which are crafted inputs designed to intentionally induce errors in learning algorithms. The majority of existing methods for generating these examples rely on gradient information, including universal perturbations that are model-agnostic. However, we propose a novel approach, termed procedural noise adversarial examples, which leverages computer graphics noise to rapidly generate universal perturbations without relying on gradient information. By integrating this approach with adversarial training, we utilize Perlin noise to train neural networks that are resilient to these attacks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that fine-tuning pre-trained models yields faster training and improved accuracy. Our results show that procedural noise adversarial examples can be defended against, yet the underlying mechanisms by which procedural noise generates these examples and the development of defenses against emerging variants remain important avenues for future research.

title: Generative Kernel Continual learning
text: Kernel continual learning by \citet{derakhshani2021kernel} has recently emerged as a strong continual learner due to its non-parametric ability to tackle task interference and catastrophic forgetting. Unfortunately its success comes at the expense of an explicit memory to store samples from past tasks, which hampers scalability to continual learning settings with a large number of tasks. In this paper, we introduce generative kernel continual learning, which explores and exploits the synergies between generative models and kernels for continual learning. The generative model is able to produce representative samples for kernel learning, which removes the dependence on memory in kernel continual learning. Moreover, as we replay only on the generative model, we avoid task interference while being computationally more efficient compared to previous methods that need replay on the entire model. We further introduce a supervised contrastive regularization, which enables our model to generate even more discriminative samples for better kernel-based classification performance. We conduct extensive experiments on three widely-used continual learning benchmarks that demonstrate the abilities and benefits of our contributions. Most notably, on the challenging SplitCIFAR100 benchmark, with just a simple linear kernel we obtain the same accuracy as kernel continual learning with variational random features for one tenth of the memory, or a 10.1\% accuracy gain for the same memory budget.

title: Generative Kernel Continual learning
text: The non-parametric kernel continual learning approach proposed by Derakhshani et al. (2021) has shown promising results in mitigating task interference and catastrophic forgetting. However, its reliance on an explicit memory to store past task samples significantly hinders its scalability in settings with numerous tasks. We propose a novel generative kernel continual learning framework, which leverages the synergies between generative models and kernels to overcome this limitation. By utilizing a generative model to produce representative samples for kernel learning, we eliminate the need for explicit memory storage, thereby enhancing scalability. Furthermore, our approach achieves improved computational efficiency by replaying only on the generative model, thereby avoiding task interference. We also introduce a supervised contrastive regularization technique, which enables the generation of more discriminative samples, leading to enhanced kernel-based classification performance. Through extensive experiments on three prominent continual learning benchmarks, we demonstrate the efficacy of our contributions. Notably, on the challenging SplitCIFAR100 benchmark, our approach achieves comparable accuracy to kernel continual learning with variational random features using only a tenth of the memory, or a 10.1% accuracy gain when using the same memory budget.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Dynamic Convex Risk Measures
text: We develop an approach for solving time-consistent risk-sensitive stochastic optimization problems using model-free reinforcement learning (RL). Specifically, we assume agents assess the risk of a sequence of random variables using dynamic convex risk measures. We employ a time-consistent dynamic programming principle to determine the value of a particular policy, and develop policy gradient update rules that aid in obtaining optimal policies. We further develop an actor-critic style algorithm using neural networks to optimize over policies. Finally, we demonstrate the performance and flexibility of our approach by applying it to three optimization problems: statistical arbitrage trading strategies, financial hedging, and obstacle avoidance robot control.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Dynamic Convex Risk Measures
text: Modern reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms often rely on static risk measures, neglecting the dynamic nature of many real-world applications. We propose a novel RL framework incorporating dynamic convex risk measures, enabling agents to adapt to changing risk preferences and uncertainty environments. Our approach leverages a time-varying coherent risk measure, which is optimized using a policy gradient method. Empirical results on a portfolio optimization task demonstrate improved performance and risk-awareness compared to traditional RL methods. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that dynamic risk measures lead to more robust policies, mitigating the impact of model uncertainty and distributional shifts.

title: Attribute Inference Attack of Speech Emotion Recognition in Federated Learning Settings
text: Speech emotion recognition (SER) processes speech signals to detect and characterize expressed perceived emotions.
