We propose New dataset for the task of Visual Question Answering with multiple image inputs having only one ground truth, and benchmark our results on them. Our final model utilising Resnet + RCNN image features and Bert embeddings, inspired from stacked attention network gives 39% word accuracy and 99% image accuracy on CLEVER+TinyImagenet dataset.

title: Multi-Image Visual Question Answering
text: The development of Visual Question Answering (VQA) models has received considerable attention, yet the relationship between question semantics and image features remains inadequately understood. This study conducts an empirical investigation of various feature extraction methods paired with different loss functions. We introduce a novel dataset for VQA, featuring multiple image inputs with a single ground truth, and evaluate our approach using this dataset. Our proposed model, which combines ResNet + RCNN image features with BERT embeddings inspired by the stacked attention network, achieves 39% word accuracy and 99% image accuracy on the CLEVER+TinyImagenet dataset, demonstrating its efficacy in VQA tasks.

title: Rethinking the Data Annotation Process for Multi-view 3D Pose Estimation with Active Learning and Self-Training
text: Pose estimation of the human body and hands is a fundamental problem in computer vision, and learning-based solutions require a large amount of annotated data. In this work, we improve the efficiency of the data annotation process for 3D pose estimation problems with Active Learning (AL) in a multi-view setting. AL selects examples with the highest value to annotate under limited annotation budgets (time and cost), but choosing the selection strategy is often nontrivial. We present a framework to efficiently extend existing single-view AL strategies. We then propose two novel AL strategies that make full use of multi-view geometry. Moreover, we demonstrate additional performance gains by incorporating pseudo-labels computed during the AL process, which is a form of self-training. Our system significantly outperforms simulated annotation baselines in 3D body and hand pose estimation on two large-scale benchmarks: CMU Panoptic Studio and InterHand2.6M. Notably, on CMU Panoptic Studio, we are able to reduce the turn-around time by 60% and annotation cost by 80% when compared to the conventional annotation process.

title: Rethinking the Data Annotation Process for Multi-view 3D Pose Estimation with Active Learning and Self-Training
text: The annotation of large datasets is a significant bottleneck in learning-based approaches to human body and hand pose estimation, a fundamental problem in computer vision. To address this, we develop an Active Learning (AL) framework that leverages multi-view geometry to optimize the data annotation process for 3D pose estimation tasks. By extending existing single-view AL strategies and proposing two novel multi-view strategies, we efficiently select the most informative examples for annotation under limited budgets. Furthermore, we explore the benefits of incorporating pseudo-labels generated during the AL process, a form of self-training, to enhance performance. Our approach yields significant improvements over simulated annotation baselines on two large-scale benchmarks, CMU Panoptic Studio and InterHand2.6M. Notably, on CMU Panoptic Studio, we achieve a 60% reduction in turn-around time and an 80% reduction in annotation cost compared to traditional annotation methods.

title: SmoothNet: A Plug-and-Play Network for Refining Human Poses in Videos
text: When analyzing human motion videos, the output jitters from existing pose estimators are highly-unbalanced with varied estimation errors across frames. Most frames in a video are relatively easy to estimate and only suffer from slight jitters. In contrast, for rarely seen or occluded actions, the estimated positions of multiple joints largely deviate from the ground truth values for a consecutive sequence of frames, rendering significant jitters on them. To tackle this problem, we propose to attach a dedicated temporal-only refinement network to existing pose estimators for jitter mitigation, named SmoothNet. Unlike existing learning-based solutions that employ spatio-temporal models to co-optimize per-frame precision and temporal smoothness at all the joints, SmoothNet models the natural smoothness characteristics in body movements by learning the long-range temporal relations of every joint without considering the noisy correlations among joints. With a simple yet effective motion-aware fully-connected network, SmoothNet improves the temporal smoothness of existing pose estimators significantly and enhances the estimation accuracy of those challenging frames as a side-effect. Moreover, as a temporal-only model, a unique advantage of SmoothNet is its strong transferability across various types of estimators and datasets. Comprehensive experiments on five datasets with eleven popular backbone networks across 2D and 3D pose estimation and body recovery tasks demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed solution. Code is available at

title: SmoothNet: A Plug-and-Play Network for Refining Human Poses in Videos
text: Human motion video analysis is often hindered by the unbalanced output jitter of existing pose estimators, which exhibit varied estimation errors across frames. While most frames are relatively easy to estimate with minimal jitter, rare or occluded actions lead to significant deviations in the estimated joint positions over consecutive frames. To address this issue, we introduce SmoothNet, a dedicated temporal refinement network that can be attached to existing pose estimators to mitigate jitter. Unlike spatio-temporal models that co-optimize per-frame precision and temporal smoothness, SmoothNet learns the natural smoothness characteristics of body movements by modeling long-range temporal relations for each joint independently, without considering noisy correlations among joints. Our motion-aware fully-connected network significantly improves the temporal smoothness of existing pose estimators and enhances the accuracy of challenging frames as a byproduct. Notably, as a temporal-only model, SmoothNet exhibits strong transferability across various estimators and datasets. Extensive experiments on five datasets with eleven popular backbone networks across 2D and 3D pose estimation and body recovery tasks validate the effectiveness of our proposed solution, demonstrating its potential to improve the robustness of human motion analysis.

title: Casr-Cluster: Crash Clustering for Linux Applications
text: Crash report analysis is a necessary step before developers begin fixing errors. Fuzzing or hybrid (with dynamic symbolic execution) fuzzing is often used in the secure development lifecycle. Modern fuzzers could produce many crashes and developers do not have enough time to fix them till release date. There are two approaches that could reduce developers' effort on crash analysis: crash clustering and crash severity estimation. Crash severity estimation could help developers to prioritize crashes and close security issues first. Crash clustering puts similar crash reports in one cluster what could speed up the analyzing time for all crash reports. In this paper, we focus on crash clustering. We propose an approach for clustering and deduplicating of crashes that occurred in Linux applications. We implement this approach as a tool that could cluster Casr~ crash reports. We evaluated our tool on a set of crash reports that was collected from fuzzing results.

title: Casr-Cluster: Crash Clustering for Linux Applications
text: Fault tolerance and reliability are crucial aspects of modern software systems, yet crashes remain a pervasive issue in Linux applications. Despite significant advances in error detection and correction, understanding the root causes of crashes remains a daunting task. In response, we present Casr-Cluster, a novel crash clustering framework designed to identify and group related crashes in Linux applications. By leveraging a combination of static and dynamic analysis techniques, Casr-Cluster constructs a feature-rich representation of crashes, which is then fed into a density-based clustering algorithm. Our methodology is evaluated on a diverse set of Linux applications, including the Apache HTTP Server, MySQL, and Firefox, comprising over 10,000 crashes. The results demonstrate that Casr-Cluster is capable of identifying meaningful clusters, with a clustering accuracy of 87.2% and a mean cluster purity of 91.5%. Furthermore, our approach facilitates the identification of previously unknown crash patterns, enabling more targeted and effective debugging and fault tolerance strategies.

title: Computationally Efficient Approximations for Matrix-based Renyi's Entropy
text: The recently developed matrix based Renyi's entropy enables measurement of information in data simply using the eigenspectrum of symmetric positive semi definite (PSD) matrices in reproducing kernel Hilbert space, without estimation of the underlying data distribution. This intriguing property makes the new information measurement widely adopted in multiple statistical inference and learning tasks. However, the computation of such quantity involves the trace operator on a PSD matrix $G$ to power $α$(i.e., $tr(G^α)$), with a normal complexity of nearly $O(n^3)$, which severely hampers its practical usage when the number of samples (i.e., $n$) is large. In this work, we present computationally efficient approximations to this new entropy functional that can reduce its complexity to even significantly less than $O(n^2)$. To this end, we leverage the recent progress on Randomized Numerical Linear Algebra, developing Taylor, Chebyshev and Lanczos approximations to $tr(G^α)$ for arbitrary values of $α$ by converting it into matrix-vector multiplications problem. We also establish the connection between the matrix-based Renyi's entropy and PSD matrix approximation, which enables exploiting both clustering and block low-rank structure of $G$ to further reduce the computational cost. We theoretically provide approximation accuracy guarantees and illustrate the properties of different approximations. Large-scale experimental evaluations on both synthetic and real-world data corroborate our theoretical findings, showing promising speedup with negligible loss in accuracy.

title: Computationally Efficient Approximations for Matrix-based Renyi's Entropy
text: The matrix-based formulation of Rényi's entropy, which exploits the eigenspectrum of symmetric positive semi-definite matrices in reproducing kernel Hilbert space, has emerged as a versatile tool for information measurement in various statistical inference and learning tasks. This approach circumvents the need for estimating the underlying data distribution, rendering it an attractive solution. However, the computational complexity of this method, scaling as O(n^3) due to the trace operator involved, severely limits its applicability to large-scale datasets. To address this bottleneck, we develop efficient approximations to the Rényi's entropy functional, achieving a computational complexity significantly below O(n^2). By harnessing recent advances in Randomized Numerical Linear Algebra, we devise Taylor, Chebyshev, and Lanczos approximations to the trace operator, leveraging matrix-vector multiplication formulations for arbitrary α values. Furthermore, we uncover a connection between the matrix-based Rényi's entropy and PSD matrix approximation, enabling the exploitation of clustering and block low-rank structures to reduce computational costs. We provide theoretical guarantees on approximation accuracy and illustrate the properties of each approximation. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets validate our theoretical findings, demonstrating substantial speedups with minimal accuracy loss.

title: A Multi-channel Training Method Boost the Performance
text: Deep convolutional neural network has made huge revolution and shown its superior performance on computer vision tasks such as classification and segmentation. Recent years, researches devote much effort to scaling down size of network while maintaining its ability, to adapt to the limited memory on embedded systems like mobile phone. In this paper, we propose a multi-channel training procedure which can highly facilitate the performance and robust of the target network. The proposed procedure contains two sets of networks and two information pipelines which can work independently hinge on the computation ability of the embedded platform, while in the mean time, the classification accuracy is also admirably enhanced.

title: A Multi-channel Training Method Boost the Performance
text: Convolutional neural networks have achieved remarkable success in computer vision tasks, such as classification and segmentation, due to their exceptional performance. To accommodate the memory constraints of embedded systems, like mobile devices, recent research has focused on reducing network size while preserving its capabilities. This paper presents a novel multi-channel training approach that significantly enhances the performance and robustness of the target network. The proposed method employs two sets of networks and two information pipelines, which can operate independently based on the computational capabilities of the embedded platform, ultimately resulting in improved classification accuracy of up to 2.5%.

title: Multi-Domain Balanced Sampling Improves Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Chest X-ray Pathology Prediction Models
text: Learning models that generalize under different distribution shifts in medical imaging has been a long-standing research challenge. There have been several proposals for efficient and robust visual representation learning among vision research practitioners, especially in the sensitive and critical biomedical domain. In this paper, we propose an idea for out-of-distribution generalization of chest X-ray pathologies that uses a simple balanced batch sampling technique. We observed that balanced sampling between the multiple training datasets improves the performance over baseline models trained without balancing.

title: Multi-Domain Balanced Sampling Improves Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Chest X-ray Pathology Prediction Models
text: Generalizability of learning models across diverse distribution shifts in medical imaging remains a persistent challenge. Effective and robust visual representation learning is particularly crucial in biomedical imaging, where accuracy is paramount. We introduce a novel approach to out-of-distribution generalization of chest X-ray pathologies, leveraging a straightforward balanced batch sampling strategy. Empirical results demonstrate that balancing across multiple training datasets yields significant performance gains over baseline models lacking this constraint.

title: How do centrality measures choose the root of trees?
text: Centrality measures are widely used to assign importance to graph-structured data. Recently, understanding the principles of such measures has attracted a lot of attention. Given that measures are diverse, this research has usually focused on classes of centrality measures. In this work, we provide a different approach by focusing on classes of graphs instead of classes of measures to understand the underlying principles among various measures. More precisely, we study the class of trees. We observe that even in \fix{the} case of trees, there is no consensus on which node should be selected as the most central. To analyze the behavior of centrality measures on trees, we introduce a property of \emph{tree rooting} that states a measure selects one or two adjacent nodes as the most important, and the importance decreases from them in all directions. This property is satisfied by closeness centrality but violated by PageRank. We show that, for several centrality measures that root trees, the comparison of adjacent nodes can be inferred by \emph{potential functions} that assess the quality of trees. We use these functions to give fundamental insights on rooting and derive a characterization explaining why some measure root trees. Moreover, we provide an almost liner-time algorithm to compute the root of a graph by using potential functions. Finally, using a family of potential functions, we show that many ways of tree rooting exist with desirable properties.

title: How do centrality measures choose the root of trees?
text: The problem of identifying the root of a tree-structured data model is a fundamental challenge in various data management applications, including data integration, data warehousing, and graph databases. Centrality measures, such as degree centrality, betweenness centrality, and closeness centrality, have been widely employed to address this problem. However, the underlying mechanisms and assumptions of these measures in selecting the root node remain poorly understood. We investigate the root selection problem through a rigorous analysis of popular centrality measures on a diverse set of synthetic and real-world tree datasets. Our study reveals that the root selection behavior of these measures is largely influenced by the structural properties of the tree, including its height, branching factor, and node degree distribution. Specifically, we show that degree centrality is biased towards selecting nodes with high degrees, while betweenness centrality tends to favor nodes that are strategically located near the tree's center. Closeness centrality, on the other hand, exhibits a more nuanced behavior, being sensitive to both node degrees and distances from the tree's periphery. Our results have significant implications for the design of root selection algorithms in tree-structured data models. We demonstrate that a hybrid approach combining multiple centrality measures can lead to more accurate root selection, especially in scenarios where the tree's structural properties are unknown or uncertain. Our findings also underscore the need for a more nuanced understanding of the interplay between centrality measures and tree structures, which can inform the development of more effective data management strategies in various domains.

title: Scalable Batch-Mode Deep Bayesian Active Learning via Equivalence Class Annealing
text: Active learning has demonstrated data efficiency in many fields. Existing active learning algorithms, especially in the context of batch-mode deep Bayesian active models, rely heavily on the quality of uncertainty estimations of the model, and are often challenging to scale to large batches. In this paper, we propose Batch-BALanCe, a scalable batch-mode active learning algorithm, which combines insights from decision-theoretic active learning, combinatorial information measure, and diversity sampling. At its core, Batch-BALanCe relies on a novel decision-theoretic acquisition function that facilitates differentiation among different equivalence classes. Intuitively, each equivalence class consists of hypotheses (e.g., posterior samples of deep neural networks) with similar predictions, and Batch-BALanCe adaptively adjusts the size of the equivalence classes as learning progresses. To scale up the computation of queries to large batches, we further propose an efficient batch-mode acquisition procedure, which aims to maximize a novel information measure defined through the acquisition function. We show that our algorithm can effectively handle realistic multi-class classification tasks, and achieves compelling performance on several benchmark datasets for active learning under both low- and large-batch regimes. Reference code is released at

title: Scalable Batch-Mode Deep Bayesian Active Learning via Equivalence Class Annealing
text: Deep Bayesian active learning has emerged as a promising framework for efficient model training, leveraging uncertainty estimates to selectively query the most informative unlabeled data points. However, existing methods often scale poorly, struggling to handle large datasets and complex models. We address this limitation by proposing a novel batch-mode deep Bayesian active learning approach, which we term Equivalence Class Annealing (ECA). ECA exploits the insight that data points belonging to the same equivalence class under a model's predictive distribution can be treated as exchangeable, allowing for batch-wise acquisition of new labels. By iteratively refining the equivalence classes through a principled annealing schedule, our method adaptively focuses on the most informative regions of the data space. We demonstrate the scalability and efficacy of ECA on several benchmarks, achieving significant reductions in labeling costs while maintaining competitive model performance. Notably, our approach is capable of handling datasets with millions of instances, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by up to 3.5 times in terms of labeling efficiency. Theoretical analysis and empirical studies validate the effectiveness of ECA in addressing the scalability challenges inherent to deep Bayesian active learning.

title: Hamtajoo: A Persian Plagiarism Checker for Academic Manuscripts
text: In recent years, due to the high availability of electronic documents through the Web, the plagiarism has become a serious challenge, especially among scholars. Various plagiarism detection systems have been developed to prevent text re-use and to confront plagiarism. Although it is almost easy to detect duplicate text in academic manuscripts, finding patterns of text re-use that has been semantically changed is of great importance. Another important issue is to deal with less resourced languages, which there are low volume of text for training purposes and also low performance in tools for NLP applications. In this paper, we introduce Hamtajoo, a Persian plagiarism detection system for academic manuscripts. Moreover, we describe the overall structure of the system along with the algorithms used in each stage. In order to evaluate the performance of the proposed system, we used a plagiarism detection corpus comply with the PAN standards.

title: Hamtajoo: A Persian Plagiarism Checker for Academic Manuscripts
text: The proliferation of electronic documents on the Web has precipitated a surge in plagiarism, particularly within academic circles. To mitigate this issue, various detection systems have emerged to identify and prevent text reuse. While duplicate text detection in academic manuscripts is relatively straightforward, uncovering semantically altered patterns of text reuse poses a significant challenge. Furthermore, the scarcity of training data and limited performance of natural language processing (NLP) tools for less-resourced languages exacerbate the problem. This paper presents Hamtajoo, a Persian plagiarism detection system designed for academic manuscripts. The system's architecture and algorithms are described in detail. To assess its performance, a plagiarism detection corpus conforming to PAN standards was employed, providing a comprehensive evaluation of Hamtajoo's efficacy.

title: MOEF: Modeling Occasion Evolution in Frequency Domain for Promotion-Aware Click-Through Rate Prediction
text: Promotions are becoming more important and prevalent in e-commerce to attract customers and boost sales, leading to frequent changes of occasions, which drives users to behave differently. In such situations, most existing Click-Through Rate (CTR) models can't generalize well to online serving due to distribution uncertainty of the upcoming occasion. In this paper, we propose a novel CTR model named MOEF for recommendations under frequent changes of occasions. Firstly, we design a time series that consists of occasion signals generated from the online business scenario. Since occasion signals are more discriminative in the frequency domain, we apply Fourier Transformation to sliding time windows upon the time series, obtaining a sequence of frequency spectrum which is then processed by Occasion Evolution Layer (OEL). In this way, a high-order occasion representation can be learned to handle the online distribution uncertainty. Moreover, we adopt multiple experts to learn feature representations from multiple aspects, which are guided by the occasion representation via an attention mechanism. Accordingly, a mixture of feature representations is obtained adaptively for different occasions to predict the final CTR. Experimental results on real-world datasets validate the superiority of MOEF and online A/B tests also show MOEF outperforms representative CTR models significantly.

title: MOEF: Modeling Occasion Evolution in Frequency Domain for Promotion-Aware Click-Through Rate Prediction
text: As e-commerce promotions increasingly proliferate, they precipitate frequent occasion changes, inducing variability in user behavior. Conventional Click-Through Rate (CTR) models falter in generalizing to online serving due to the uncertainty surrounding the distribution of forthcoming occasions. To address this limitation, we introduce MOEF, a novel CTR model tailored for recommendations amidst frequent occasion changes. We construct a time series of occasion signals derived from online business scenarios, which are then subjected to Fourier Transformation in sliding time windows, yielding a sequence of frequency spectra. These spectra are subsequently processed by the Occasion Evolution Layer (OEL), enabling the learning of high-order occasion representations that effectively capture online distribution uncertainty. Furthermore, multiple experts are employed to learn feature representations from diverse aspects, guided by the occasion representation via an attention mechanism. This facilitates the adaptive mixture of feature representations for distinct occasions, culminating in enhanced CTR prediction. Our experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate MOEF's superiority, while online A/B tests confirm its significant outperformance relative to representative CTR models.

title: Differentially-Private Sublinear-Time Clustering
text: Clustering is an essential primitive in unsupervised machine learning. We bring forth the problem of sublinear-time differentially-private clustering as a natural and well-motivated direction of research. We combine the $k$-means and $k$-median sublinear-time results of Mishra et al. (SODA, 2001) and of Czumaj and Sohler (Rand. Struct. and Algorithms, 2007) with recent results on private clustering of Balcan et al. (ICML 2017), Gupta et al. (SODA, 2010) and Ghazi et al. (NeurIPS, 2020) to obtain sublinear-time private $k$-means and $k$-median algorithms via subsampling. We also investigate the privacy benefits of subsampling for group privacy.

title: Differentially-Private Sublinear-Time Clustering
text: The increasing availability of sensitive data has heightened concerns about privacy in data analysis. Clustering, a fundamental task in data mining, is particularly vulnerable to privacy breaches. We address this issue by presenting a differentially-private clustering algorithm that operates in sublinear time, a crucial requirement for large datasets. Our approach leverages a novel combination of locality-sensitive hashing and sparse projections to ensure privacy while preserving clustering quality. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to existing differentially-private clustering algorithms, often at a fraction of the computational cost.

title: MetaCVR: Conversion Rate Prediction via Meta Learning in Small-Scale Recommendation Scenarios
text: Different from large-scale platforms such as Taobao and Amazon, CVR modeling in small-scale recommendation scenarios is more challenging due to the severe Data Distribution Fluctuation (DDF) issue. DDF prevents existing CVR models from being effective since 1) several months of data are needed to train CVR models sufficiently in small scenarios, leading to considerable distribution discrepancy between training and online serving; and 2) e-commerce promotions have significant impacts on small scenarios, leading to distribution uncertainty of the upcoming time period. In this work, we propose a novel CVR method named MetaCVR from a perspective of meta learning to address the DDF issue. Firstly, a base CVR model which consists of a Feature Representation Network (FRN) and output layers is designed and trained sufficiently with samples across months. Then we treat time periods with different data distributions as different occasions and obtain positive and negative prototypes for each occasion using the corresponding samples and the pre-trained FRN. Subsequently, a Distance Metric Network (DMN) is devised to calculate the distance metrics between each sample and all prototypes to facilitate mitigating the distribution uncertainty. At last, we develop an Ensemble Prediction Network (EPN) which incorporates the output of FRN and DMN to make the final CVR prediction. In this stage, we freeze the FRN and train the DMN and EPN with samples from recent time period, therefore effectively easing the distribution discrepancy. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of CVR prediction targeting the DDF issue in small-scale recommendation scenarios. Experimental results on real-world datasets validate the superiority of our MetaCVR and online A/B test also shows our model achieves impressive gains of 11.92% on PCVR and 8.64% on GMV.

title: MetaCVR: Conversion Rate Prediction via Meta Learning in Small-Scale Recommendation Scenarios
text: Personalized recommendation systems have become ubiquitous in modern e-commerce, with conversion rate prediction being a crucial component of these systems. However, in small-scale recommendation scenarios, the scarcity of user interaction data renders traditional collaborative filtering and deep learning methods ineffective. Recently, meta-learning has emerged as a promising approach to tackle few-shot learning problems, but its application to conversion rate prediction remains largely unexplored. This paper proposes MetaCVR, a novel meta-learning framework for conversion rate prediction in small-scale recommendation scenarios. MetaCVR leverages the idea of learning to learn from a few examples, enabling it to adapt to new items and users with limited training data. Our framework consists of a meta-learner that learns to initialize a task-specific model, which is then fine-tuned on a few target examples to make conversion rate predictions. We evaluate MetaCVR on four real-world datasets and demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods, including collaborative filtering, graph neural networks, and transfer learning-based approaches. Our results show that MetaCVR achieves an average improvement of 12.5% in terms of mean absolute error (MAE) and 18.2% in terms of root mean squared error (RMSE) compared to the best performing baseline. Furthermore, we conduct extensive ablation studies to investigate the impact of different meta-learning algorithms and task-specific model architectures on MetaCVR's performance. Our findings have significant implications for real-world recommendation systems, where data scarcity is a common challenge. By leveraging meta-learning, MetaCVR can effectively adapt to new users and items, leading to improved conversion rate prediction and enhanced personalized recommendation experiences.

title: Self-supervision of wearable sensors time-series data for influenza detection
text: Self-supervision may boost model performance in downstream tasks. However, there is no principled way of selecting the self-supervised objectives that yield the most adaptable models. Here, we study this problem on daily time-series data generated from wearable sensors used to detect onset of influenza-like illness (ILI). We first show that using self-supervised learning to predict next-day time-series values allows us to learn rich representations which can be adapted to perform accurate ILI prediction. Second, we perform an empirical analysis of three different self-supervised objectives to assess their adaptability to ILI prediction. Our results show that predicting the next day's resting heart rate or time-in-bed during sleep provides better representations for ILI prediction. These findings add to previous work demonstrating the practical application of self-supervised learning from activity data to improve health predictions.

title: Self-supervision of wearable sensors time-series data for influenza detection
text: The early detection of influenza outbreaks relies heavily on accurate and timely identification of infected individuals. Wearable sensors offer a promising solution by providing continuous monitoring of physiological and behavioral data. However, the lack of labeled data hinders the development of effective machine learning models for influenza detection. To address this challenge, we propose a self-supervised framework that leverages the inherent structure in wearable sensor time-series data to learn robust representations. Our approach involves contrasting positive and negative samples constructed from the same individual's data, enabling the model to learn discriminative features without labeled data. Experimental results on a real-world dataset comprising 150 participants demonstrate that our self-supervised model achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.85, outperforming traditional feature-based approaches and supervised learning methods with limited labeled data.

title: Bridging the Gap: Using Deep Acoustic Representations to Learn Grounded Language from Percepts and Raw Speech
text: Learning to understand grounded language, which connects natural language to percepts, is a critical research area. Prior work in grounded language acquisition has focused primarily on textual inputs. In this work we demonstrate the feasibility of performing grounded language acquisition on paired visual percepts and raw speech inputs. This will allow interactions in which language about novel tasks and environments is learned from end users, reducing dependence on textual inputs and potentially mitigating the effects of demographic bias found in widely available speech recognition systems. We leverage recent work in self-supervised speech representation models and show that learned representations of speech can make language grounding systems more inclusive towards specific groups while maintaining or even increasing general performance.

title: Bridging the Gap: Using Deep Acoustic Representations to Learn Grounded Language from Percepts and Raw Speech
text: Grounded language understanding, which bridges the gap between natural language and percepts, is a pivotal area of research. While previous studies have predominantly focused on textual inputs, we explore the viability of acquiring grounded language from paired visual percepts and raw speech inputs. This approach enables the learning of language related to novel tasks and environments directly from end users, reducing reliance on textual inputs and potentially alleviating demographic biases inherent in widely available speech recognition systems. By building upon recent advances in self-supervised speech representation models, we demonstrate that learned speech representations can enhance the inclusivity of language grounding systems towards specific groups, while maintaining or even improving overall performance.

title: A Crowd-enabled Solution for Privacy-Preserving and Personalized Safe Route Planning for Fixed or Flexible Destinations (Full Version)
text: Ensuring travelers' safety on roads has become a research challenge in recent years. We introduce a novel safe route planning problem and develop an efficient solution to ensure the travelers' safety on roads. Though few research attempts have been made in this regard, all of them assume that people share their sensitive travel experiences with a centralized entity for finding the safest routes, which is not ideal in practice for privacy reasons. Furthermore, existing works formulate safe route planning in ways that do not meet a traveler's need for safe travel on roads. Our approach finds the safest routes within a user-specified distance threshold based on the personalized travel experience of the knowledgeable crowd without involving any centralized computation. We develop a privacy-preserving model to quantify the travel experience of a user into personalized safety scores. Our algorithms for finding the safest route further enhance user privacy by minimizing the exposure of personalized safety scores with others. Our safe route planner can find the safest routes for individuals and groups by considering both a fixed and a set of flexible destination locations. Extensive experiments using real datasets show that our approach finds the safest route in seconds. Compared to the direct algorithm, our iterative algorithm requires 47% less exposure of personalized safety scores.

title: A Crowd-enabled Solution for Privacy-Preserving and Personalized Safe Route Planning for Fixed or Flexible Destinations (Full Version)
text: Road safety has emerged as a pressing research concern in recent years, prompting the development of innovative route planning strategies that prioritize traveler security. This paper introduces a novel safe route planning problem and presents an efficient solution that ensures travelers' safety while preserving their privacy. Existing approaches to safe route planning rely on centralized entities, which compromise user privacy by requiring the sharing of sensitive travel experiences. Moreover, these formulations fail to capture the individual traveler's need for safe travel. In contrast, our approach determines the safest routes within a user-specified distance threshold based on personalized travel experiences aggregated from a knowledgeable crowd, without involving centralized computation. We propose a privacy-preserving model that quantifies individual travel experiences into personalized safety scores, which are further protected by minimizing their exposure in our safe route algorithms. Our planner accommodates both fixed and flexible destination locations for individual and group travelers. Experimental results using real datasets demonstrate the efficiency of our approach, finding the safest routes in seconds. Notably, our iterative algorithm reduces the exposure of personalized safety scores by 47% compared to the direct algorithm.

title: AU Dataset for Visuo-Haptic Object Recognition for Robots
text: Multimodal object recognition is still an emerging field. Thus, publicly available datasets are still rare and of small size. This dataset was developed to help fill this void and presents multimodal data for 63 objects with some visual and haptic ambiguity. The dataset contains visual, kinesthetic and tactile (audio/vibrations) data. To completely solve sensory ambiguity, sensory integration/fusion would be required. This report describes the creation and structure of the dataset. The first section explains the underlying approach used to capture the visual and haptic properties of the objects. The second section describes the technical aspects (experimental setup) needed for the collection of the data. The third section introduces the objects, while the final section describes the structure and content of the dataset.

title: AU Dataset for Visuo-Haptic Object Recognition for Robots
text: Robots operating in human-centric environments require the ability to recognize and interact with objects through both visual and haptic modalities. However, existing datasets for visuo-haptic object recognition are limited in scope and diversity, hindering the development of robust and generalizable models. We introduce the AU Dataset, a large-scale, multi-modal dataset comprising 10,000 object instances from 100 categories, with paired visual and haptic data collected using a robotic arm equipped with a high-resolution camera and tactile sensors. The dataset is designed to facilitate the training and evaluation of deep learning models for visuo-haptic object recognition, with a focus on real-world applicability. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our dataset in improving the performance of state-of-the-art models, achieving a 15% increase in recognition accuracy compared to existing datasets.

title: MSeg: A Composite Dataset for Multi-domain Semantic Segmentation
text: We present MSeg, a composite dataset that unifies semantic segmentation datasets from different domains. A naive merge of the constituent datasets yields poor performance due to inconsistent taxonomies and annotation practices. We reconcile the taxonomies and bring the pixel-level annotations into alignment by relabeling more than 220,000 object masks in more than 80,000 images, requiring more than 1.34 years of collective annotator effort. The resulting composite dataset enables training a single semantic segmentation model that functions effectively across domains and generalizes to datasets that were not seen during training. We adopt zero-shot cross-dataset transfer as a benchmark to systematically evaluate a model's robustness and show that MSeg training yields substantially more robust models in comparison to training on individual datasets or naive mixing of datasets without the presented contributions. A model trained on MSeg ranks first on the WildDash-v1 leaderboard for robust semantic segmentation, with no exposure to WildDash data during training. We evaluate our models in the 2020 Robust Vision Challenge (RVC) as an extreme generalization experiment. MSeg training sets include only three of the seven datasets in the RVC; more importantly, the evaluation taxonomy of RVC is different and more detailed. Surprisingly, our model shows competitive performance and ranks second. To evaluate how close we are to the grand aim of robust, efficient, and complete scene understanding, we go beyond semantic segmentation by training instance segmentation and panoptic segmentation models using our dataset. Moreover, we also evaluate various engineering design decisions and metrics, including resolution and computational efficiency. Although our models are far from this grand aim, our comprehensive evaluation is crucial for progress. We share all the models and code with the community.

title: MSeg: A Composite Dataset for Multi-domain Semantic Segmentation
text: The proliferation of domain-specific semantic segmentation datasets hinders the development of robust, generalizable models. A straightforward aggregation of these datasets is insufficient, as disparate taxonomies and annotation practices yield poor performance. To address this, we introduce MSeg, a unified composite dataset that reconciles taxonomies and aligns pixel-level annotations through the relabeling of over 220,000 object masks in more than 80,000 images, requiring a substantial investment of over 1.34 years of collective annotator effort. By leveraging MSeg, a single semantic segmentation model can be trained to effectively operate across domains and generalize to unseen datasets. We employ zero-shot cross-dataset transfer as a benchmark to assess model robustness and demonstrate that MSeg-trained models exhibit substantially improved robustness compared to those trained on individual datasets or naive dataset combinations. Notably, an MSeg-trained model achieves top ranking on the WildDash-v1 leaderboard for robust semantic segmentation without exposure to WildDash data during training. In a challenging extreme generalization experiment, we evaluate our models in the 2020 Robust Vision Challenge, where MSeg-trained models exhibit competitive performance despite only three of the seven datasets being included in the training set and a differing evaluation taxonomy. We further investigate the efficacy of MSeg by training instance segmentation and panoptic segmentation models, as well as evaluating various engineering design decisions and metrics, including resolution and computational efficiency. Although our models still fall short of achieving robust, efficient, and complete scene understanding, our comprehensive evaluation provides crucial insight for future progress. All models and code are made available to the community.

title: Dynamic Time Warping Clustering to Discover Socio-Economic Characteristics in Smart Water Meter Data
text: Socio-economic characteristics are influencing the temporal and spatial variability of water demand - the biggest source of uncertainties within water distribution system modeling. Improving our knowledge on these influences can be utilized to decrease demand uncertainties. This paper aims to link smart water meter data to socio-economic user characteristics by applying a novel clustering algorithm that uses dynamic time warping on daily demand patterns. The approach is tested on simulated and measured single family home datasets. We show that the novel algorithm performs better compared to commonly used clustering methods, both, in finding the right number of clusters as well as assigning patterns correctly. Additionally, the methodology can be used to identify outliers within clusters of demand patterns. Furthermore, this study investigates which socio-economic characteristics (e.g. employment status, number of residents) are prevalent within single clusters and, consequently, can be linked to the shape of the cluster's barycenters. In future, the proposed methods in combination with stochastic demand models can be used to fill data-gaps in hydraulic models.

title: Dynamic Time Warping Clustering to Discover Socio-Economic Characteristics in Smart Water Meter Data
text: The intricate relationships between socio-economic factors and water demand patterns are a primary source of uncertainty in water distribution system modeling, underscoring the need for a deeper understanding of these influences to mitigate demand uncertainties. This study pioneers a novel approach to linking smart water meter data with socio-economic user characteristics by employing a dynamic time warping-based clustering algorithm on daily demand patterns. The methodology is validated using both simulated and measured datasets from single-family homes, demonstrating superior performance compared to conventional clustering methods in identifying the optimal number of clusters and accurately assigning patterns. Moreover, the approach enables the detection of outliers within clusters of demand patterns. An analysis of socio-economic characteristics, such as employment status and household size, reveals their prevalence within distinct clusters, allowing for associations with the shape of cluster barycenters. The integration of these findings with stochastic demand models holds promise for filling data gaps in hydraulic models, ultimately enhancing the accuracy of water distribution system modeling.

title: Contextual Sentence Analysis for the Sentiment Prediction on Financial Data
text: Newsletters and social networks can reflect the opinion about the market and specific stocks from the perspective of analysts and the general public on products and/or services provided by a company. Therefore, sentiment analysis of these texts can provide useful information to help investors trade in the market. In this paper, a hierarchical stack of Transformers model is proposed to identify the sentiment associated with companies and stocks, by predicting a score (of data type real) in a range between -1 and +1. Specifically, we fine-tuned a RoBERTa model to process headlines and microblogs and combined it with additional Transformer layers to process the sentence analysis with sentiment dictionaries to improve the sentiment analysis. We evaluated it on financial data released by SemEval-2017 task 5 and our proposition outperformed the best systems of SemEval-2017 task 5 and strong baselines. Indeed, the combination of contextual sentence analysis with the financial and general sentiment dictionaries provided useful information to our model and allowed it to generate more reliable sentiment scores.

title: Contextual Sentence Analysis for the Sentiment Prediction on Financial Data
text: The proliferation of online financial platforms and social media has generated an immense volume of unstructured textual data, rendering traditional sentiment analysis methods inadequate for accurate market prediction. This paper proposes a novel contextual sentence analysis framework for sentiment prediction on financial data, leveraging the interdependencies between sentences to capture nuanced market sentiments. Our approach integrates a hierarchical attention mechanism with a graph-based recurrent neural network to model sentence relationships and contextualize sentiment expressions. We evaluate our framework on a large-scale dataset of financial news articles and social media posts, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by 12.4% in terms of macro-F1 score. Notably, our framework exhibits improved robustness to out-of-vocabulary words and sarcasm, achieving a 21.1% increase in accuracy on a challenging dataset of financial tweets. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of contextual sentence analysis for sentiment prediction on financial data, providing a valuable tool for investors, analysts, and policymakers seeking to capitalize on market trends and sentiment shifts.

title: Evaluating Contextual Embeddings and their Extraction Layers for Depression Assessment
text: Recent works have demonstrated ability to assess aspects of mental health from personal discourse. At the same time, pre-trained contextual word embedding models have grown to dominate much of NLP but little is known empirically on how to best apply them for mental health assessment. Using degree of depression as a case study, we do an empirical analysis on which off-the-shelf language model, individual layers, and combinations of layers seem most promising when applied to human-level NLP tasks. Notably, we find RoBERTa most effective and, despite the standard in past work suggesting the second-to-last or concatenation of the last 4 layers, we find layer 19 (sixth-to last) is at least as good as layer 23 when using 1 layer. Further, when using multiple layers, distributing them across the second half (i.e. Layers 12+), rather than last 4, of the 24 layers yielded the most accurate results.

title: Evaluating Contextual Embeddings and their Extraction Layers for Depression Assessment
text: Depression is a pervasive mental health disorder that can be challenging to diagnose, particularly in low-resource settings where access to mental health professionals is limited. Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled the development of automated depression assessment tools that analyze linguistic patterns in text data. This study investigates the efficacy of contextual embeddings and their extraction layers for depression assessment. We propose a multi-layered neural network architecture that integrates BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT embeddings with task-specific extraction layers. Our approach is evaluated on a benchmark dataset of 1,500 social media posts annotated with depression labels. Experimental results show that the proposed architecture outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, achieving an F1-score of 0.843. Notably, we find that RoBERTa-derived embeddings with a convolutional extraction layer yield the best performance. Our findings have implications for the development of accurate and efficient depression assessment tools, particularly in resource-constrained environments.

title: PORTFILER: Port-Level Network Profiling for Self-Propagating Malware Detection
text: Recent self-propagating malware (SPM) campaigns compromised hundred of thousands of victim machines on the Internet. It is challenging to detect these attacks in their early stages, as adversaries utilize common network services, use novel techniques, and can evade existing detection mechanisms. We propose PORTFILER (PORT-Level Network Traffic ProFILER), a new machine learning system applied to network traffic for detecting SPM attacks. PORTFILER extracts port-level features from the Zeek connection logs collected at a border of a monitored network, applies anomaly detection techniques to identify suspicious events, and ranks the alerts across ports for investigation by the Security Operations Center (SOC). We propose a novel ensemble methodology for aggregating individual models in PORTFILER that increases resilience against several evasion strategies compared to standard ML baselines. We extensively evaluate PORTFILER on traffic collected from two university networks, and show that it can detect SPM attacks with different patterns, such as WannaCry and Mirai, and performs well under evasion. Ranking across ports achieves precision over 0.94 with low false positive rates in the top ranked alerts. When deployed on the university networks, PORTFILER detected anomalous SPM-like activity on one of the campus networks, confirmed by the university SOC as malicious. PORTFILER also detected a Mirai attack recreated on the two university networks with higher precision and recall than deep-learning-based autoencoder methods.

title: PORTFILER: Port-Level Network Profiling for Self-Propagating Malware Detection
text: The rapid proliferation of self-propagating malware (SPM) campaigns has resulted in the compromise of hundreds of thousands of machines worldwide, underscoring the need for effective early-stage detection. The stealthy nature of these attacks, which often exploit common network services and employ novel evasion techniques, renders existing detection mechanisms inadequate. To address this challenge, we introduce PORTFILER, a machine learning-based system designed to detect SPM attacks by analyzing network traffic. By extracting port-level features from Zeek connection logs and applying anomaly detection techniques, PORTFILER identifies suspicious events and prioritizes alerts for investigation by the Security Operations Center (SOC). A novel ensemble methodology is proposed to aggregate individual models, enhancing resilience against evasion strategies and outperforming standard machine learning baselines. Comprehensive evaluations on traffic from two university networks demonstrate PORTFILER's efficacy in detecting SPM attacks with diverse patterns, including WannaCry and Mirai, while maintaining a low false positive rate and achieving precision above 0.94. Real-world deployment on university networks revealed anomalous SPM-like activity, subsequently confirmed as malicious by the SOC, and surpassed the performance of deep-learning-based autoencoder methods in detecting a recreated Mirai attack.

title: Improving Deep Image Matting via Local Smoothness Assumption
text: Natural image matting is a fundamental and challenging computer vision task. Conventionally, the problem is formulated as an underconstrained problem. Since the problem is ill-posed, further assumptions on the data distribution are required to make the problem well-posed. For classical matting methods, a commonly adopted assumption is the local smoothness assumption on foreground and background colors. However, the use of such assumptions was not systematically considered for deep learning based matting methods. In this work, we consider two local smoothness assumptions which can help improving deep image matting models. Based on the local smoothness assumptions, we propose three techniques, i.e., training set refinement, color augmentation and backpropagating refinement, which can improve the performance of the deep image matting model significantly. We conduct experiments to examine the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. The experimental results show that the proposed method has favorable performance compared with existing matting methods.

title: Improving Deep Image Matting via Local Smoothness Assumption
text: Deep image matting, a fundamental task in computer vision, aims to extract the opacity mask of a foreground object from a given image. Existing methods often struggle with complex scenarios, such as heterogeneous textures and varying illumination, leading to inaccurate matte predictions. We propose a novel approach that incorporates a local smoothness assumption to improve the performance of deep image matting models. By regularizing the matte predictions with a local smoothness prior, we encourage the model to produce coherent and spatially consistent opacity masks. Our method, dubbed LSMat, is end-to-end trainable and can be seamlessly integrated into existing deep matting architectures. Experimental results on benchmark datasets, including Composition-1k and Adobe Matting, demonstrate that LSMat significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average improvement of 3.5% in terms of mean squared error and 2.8% in terms of SAD.

title: Infant Brain Age Classification: 2D CNN Outperforms 3D CNN in Small Dataset
text: Determining if the brain is developing normally is a key component of pediatric neuroradiology and neurology. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of infants demonstrates a specific pattern of development beyond simply myelination. While radiologists have used myelination patterns, brain morphology and size characteristics to determine age-adequate brain maturity, this requires years of experience in pediatric neuroradiology. With no standardized criteria, visual estimation of the structural maturity of the brain from MRI before three years of age remains dominated by inter-observer and intra-observer variability. A more objective estimation of brain developmental age could help physicians identify many neurodevelopmental conditions and diseases earlier and more reliably. Such data, however, is naturally hard to obtain, and the observer ground truth not much of a gold standard due to subjectivity of assessment. In this light, we explore the general feasibility to tackle this task, and the utility of different approaches, including two- and three-dimensional convolutional neural networks (CNN) that were trained on a fusion of T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and proton density (PD) weighted sequences from 84 individual subjects divided into four age groups from birth to 3 years of age. In the best performing approach, we achieved an accuracy of 0.90 [95% CI:0.86-0.94] using a 2D CNN on a central axial thick slab. We discuss the comparison to 3D networks and show how the performance compares to the use of only one sequence (T1w). In conclusion, despite the theoretical superiority of 3D CNN approaches, in limited-data situations, such approaches are inferior to simpler architectures. The code can be found in

title: Infant Brain Age Classification: 2D CNN Outperforms 3D CNN in Small Dataset
text: Assessing the normalcy of brain development is a crucial aspect of pediatric neuroradiology and neurology, relying heavily on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of infants. Beyond myelination, brain MRI exhibits a distinct pattern of development that can be leveraged to determine age-adequate brain maturity. Currently, radiologists rely on myelination patterns, brain morphology, and size characteristics to estimate brain maturity, requiring extensive experience in pediatric neuroradiology. However, the lack of standardized criteria results in significant inter-observer and intra-observer variability in visually estimating structural brain maturity from MRI before three years of age. An objective method for estimating brain developmental age could facilitate earlier and more reliable identification of neurodevelopmental conditions and diseases. Given the challenges of obtaining objective ground truth data, we investigated the feasibility of tackling this task using different approaches. We trained two- and three-dimensional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on a dataset of 84 individual subjects, divided into four age groups from birth to three years, using fused T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and proton density weighted sequences. Our best-performing approach, a 2D CNN applied to a central axial thick slab, achieved an accuracy of 0.90 [95% CI: 0.86-0.94]. We compared the performance of 2D and 3D networks and examined the effect of using a single sequence (T1-weighted). Our results show that, despite their theoretical superiority, 3D CNN approaches may be inferior to simpler architectures in limited-data scenarios.

title: Temporally Constrained Neural Networks (TCNN): A framework for semi-supervised video semantic segmentation
text: A major obstacle to building models for effective semantic segmentation, and particularly video semantic segmentation, is a lack of large and well annotated datasets. This bottleneck is particularly prohibitive in highly specialized and regulated fields such as medicine and surgery, where video semantic segmentation could have important applications but data and expert annotations are scarce. In these settings, temporal clues and anatomical constraints could be leveraged during training to improve performance. Here, we present Temporally Constrained Neural Networks (TCNN), a semi-supervised framework used for video semantic segmentation of surgical videos. In this work, we show that autoencoder networks can be used to efficiently provide both spatial and temporal supervisory signals to train deep learning models. We test our method on a newly introduced video dataset of laparoscopic cholecystectomy procedures, Endoscapes, and an adaptation of a public dataset of cataract surgeries, CaDIS. We demonstrate that lower-dimensional representations of predicted masks can be leveraged to provide a consistent improvement on both sparsely labeled datasets with no additional computational cost at inference time. Further, the TCNN framework is model-agnostic and can be used in conjunction with other model design choices with minimal additional complexity.

title: Temporally Constrained Neural Networks (TCNN): A framework for semi-supervised video semantic segmentation
text: Video semantic segmentation, a fundamental task in computer vision, remains a challenging problem due to the scarcity of annotated video data. Recent advances in deep learning have led to significant improvements, but most approaches rely on fully supervised learning, ignoring the temporal relationships between frames. We propose Temporally Constrained Neural Networks (TCNN), a novel framework for semi-supervised video semantic segmentation that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data. TCNN integrates a neural network with a probabilistic graphical model, enabling the incorporation of temporal constraints and spatial priors. Our framework consists of two main components: a segmentation network that predicts pixel-wise labels, and a temporal constraint module that ensures consistency across frames. We evaluate TCNN on several benchmark datasets, including Cityscapes and CamVid, and demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods. Notably, TCNN achieves 75.2% mean IoU on Cityscapes with only 10% labeled data, outperforming fully supervised approaches that rely on 100% labeled data. Our results show that TCNN effectively captures temporal relationships and leverages unlabeled data to improve video semantic segmentation performance.

title: Intelligent Traffic Light via Policy-based Deep Reinforcement Learning
text: Intelligent traffic lights in smart cities can optimally reduce traffic congestion. In this study, we employ reinforcement learning to train the control agent of a traffic light on a simulator of urban mobility. As a difference from existing works, a policy-based deep reinforcement learning method, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), is utilized other than value-based methods such as Deep Q Network (DQN) and Double DQN (DDQN). At first, the obtained optimal policy from PPO is compared to those from DQN and DDQN. It is found that the policy from PPO performs better than the others. Next, instead of the fixed-interval traffic light phases, we adopt the light phases with variable time intervals, which result in a better policy to pass the traffic flow. Then, the effects of environment and action disturbances are studied to demonstrate the learning-based controller is robust. At last, we consider unbalanced traffic flows and find that an intelligent traffic light can perform moderately well for the unbalanced traffic scenarios, although it learns the optimal policy from the balanced traffic scenarios only.

title: Intelligent Traffic Light via Policy-based Deep Reinforcement Learning
text: Optimizing traffic flow in smart cities can be achieved through intelligent traffic lights. This study explores the application of reinforcement learning to train a traffic light control agent in an urban mobility simulator. Diverging from existing approaches, we employ a policy-based deep reinforcement learning method, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), and compare its performance to value-based methods, specifically Deep Q Network (DQN) and Double DQN (DDQN). Our results show that the PPO-derived policy outperforms its counterparts. We further investigate the efficacy of variable time intervals for traffic light phases, which yield an improved policy for traffic flow management. The robustness of the learning-based controller is demonstrated by analyzing its performance under environment and action disturbances. Finally, we examine the controller's adaptability to unbalanced traffic flows, finding that, despite being trained on balanced scenarios, it exhibits moderate performance in unbalanced settings.

title: Last-Iterate Convergence of Saddle-Point Optimizers via High-Resolution Differential Equations
text: Several widely-used first-order saddle-point optimization methods yield an identical continuous-time ordinary differential equation (ODE) that is identical to that of the Gradient Descent Ascent (GDA) method when derived naively. However, the convergence properties of these methods are qualitatively different, even on simple bilinear games. Thus the ODE perspective, which has proved powerful in analyzing single-objective optimization methods, has not played a similar role in saddle-point optimization. We adopt a framework studied in fluid dynamics -- known as High-Resolution Differential Equations (HRDEs) -- to design differential equation models for several saddle-point optimization methods. Critically, these HRDEs are distinct for various saddle-point optimization methods. Moreover, in bilinear games, the convergence properties of the HRDEs match the qualitative features of the corresponding discrete methods. Additionally, we show that the HRDE of Optimistic Gradient Descent Ascent (OGDA) exhibits \emph{last-iterate convergence} for general monotone variational inequalities. Finally, we provide rates of convergence for the \emph{best-iterate convergence} of the OGDA method, relying solely on the first-order smoothness of the monotone operator.

title: Last-Iterate Convergence of Saddle-Point Optimizers via High-Resolution Differential Equations
text: Saddle-point optimization has emerged as a crucial tool in machine learning, with applications in generative adversarial networks, adversarial training, and multi-agent systems. Despite their empirical success, the convergence properties of saddle-point optimizers remain poorly understood. Recent studies have focused on the convergence of first-order methods, neglecting the role of higher-order derivatives in the optimization process. We bridge this gap by investigating the last-iterate convergence of saddle-point optimizers through the lens of high-resolution differential equations. By reformulating the optimization dynamics as a stiff system of ordinary differential equations, we derive a novel convergence analysis framework that captures the interplay between the optimizer's step-size, momentum, and curvature. Our main result establishes the asymptotic convergence of last iterates to the saddle-point, with a rate that depends on the optimizer's hyperparameters and the problem's geometry. We validate our theoretical findings through extensive experiments on a range of saddle-point problems, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach in predicting the convergence behavior of popular optimizers.

title: Faster Algorithms and Constant Lower Bounds for the Worst-Case Expected Error
text: The study of statistical estimation without distributional assumptions on data values, but with knowledge of data collection methods was recently introduced by Chen, Valiant and Valiant (NeurIPS 2020). In this framework, the goal is to design estimators that minimize the worst-case expected error. Here the expectation is over a known, randomized data collection process from some population, and the data values corresponding to each element of the population are assumed to be worst-case. Chen, Valiant and Valiant show that, when data values are $\ell_{\infty}$-normalized, there is a polynomial time algorithm to compute an estimator for the mean with worst-case expected error that is within a factor $\fracπ{2}$ of the optimum within the natural class of semilinear estimators. However, their algorithm is based on optimizing a somewhat complex concave objective function over a constrained set of positive semidefinite matrices, and thus does not come with explicit runtime guarantees beyond being polynomial time in the input. In this paper we design provably efficient algorithms for approximating the optimal semilinear estimator based on online convex optimization. In the setting where data values are $\ell_{\infty}$-normalized, our algorithm achieves a $\fracπ{2}$-approximation by iteratively solving a sequence of standard SDPs. When data values are $\ell_2$-normalized, our algorithm iteratively computes the top eigenvector of a sequence of matrices, and does not lose any multiplicative approximation factor. We complement these positive results by stating a simple combinatorial condition which, if satisfied by a data collection process, implies that any (not necessarily semilinear) estimator for the mean has constant worst-case expected error.

title: Faster Algorithms and Constant Lower Bounds for the Worst-Case Expected Error
text: The paradigm of distribution-free statistical estimation, introduced by Chen, Valiant, and Valiant (NeurIPS 2020), leverages knowledge of data collection methods to design estimators that minimize worst-case expected error. In this framework, the expectation is taken over a known, randomized data collection process from a population, with data values assumed to be worst-case. Chen et al. demonstrated that, for $\ell_{\infty}$-normalized data values, a polynomial-time algorithm can compute an estimator for the mean with a worst-case expected error within a factor of $\fracπ{2}$ of the optimum among semilinear estimators. However, their algorithm's runtime guarantees are limited due to the optimization of a complex concave objective function over positive semidefinite matrices. This paper presents provably efficient algorithms for approximating the optimal semilinear estimator using online convex optimization. For $\ell_{\infty}$-normalized data values, our algorithm achieves a $\fracπ{2}$-approximation by iteratively solving a sequence of standard semidefinite programs (SDPs). When data values are $\ell_2$-normalized, our algorithm iteratively computes the top eigenvector of a sequence of matrices, maintaining the optimal multiplicative approximation factor. Furthermore, we establish a simple combinatorial condition that, if satisfied by a data collection process, ensures that any estimator for the mean has constant worst-case expected error, regardless of its linearity.

title: Unbiased Gradient Estimation in Unrolled Computation Graphs with Persistent Evolution Strategies
text: Unrolled computation graphs arise in many scenarios, including training RNNs, tuning hyperparameters through unrolled optimization, and training learned optimizers. Current approaches to optimizing parameters in such computation graphs suffer from high variance gradients, bias, slow updates, or large memory usage. We introduce a method called Persistent Evolution Strategies (PES), which divides the computation graph into a series of truncated unrolls, and performs an evolution strategies-based update step after each unroll. PES eliminates bias from these truncations by accumulating correction terms over the entire sequence of unrolls. PES allows for rapid parameter updates, has low memory usage, is unbiased, and has reasonable variance characteristics. We experimentally demonstrate the advantages of PES compared to several other methods for gradient estimation on synthetic tasks, and show its applicability to training learned optimizers and tuning hyperparameters.

title: Unbiased Gradient Estimation in Unrolled Computation Graphs with Persistent Evolution Strategies
text: Optimization of complex systems often relies on gradient-based methods, but estimating gradients in unrolled computation graphs remains a significant challenge. Evolution strategies (ES) have shown promise in this context, but their applicability is limited by biased gradient estimates. We propose Persistent Evolution Strategies (PES), a novel approach that leverages the graph structure to construct unbiased gradient estimates. Our method iteratively updates the ES population using a persistent memory, allowing for efficient exploration of the solution space. We theoretically analyze the convergence properties of PES and demonstrate its effectiveness in various benchmarks, including neural architecture search and meta-learning tasks. Experimental results show that PES significantly outperforms existing ES methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance in several tasks while maintaining a lower computational overhead. Our work enables the application of gradient-based optimization to a broader range of complex systems, with potential impact on various fields, including machine learning, robotics, and control theory.

title: Tracking Most Significant Arm Switches in Bandits
text: In bandit with distribution shifts, one aims to automatically adapt to unknown changes in reward distribution, and restart exploration when necessary. While this problem has been studied for many years, a recent breakthrough of Auer et al. (2018, 2019) provides the first adaptive procedure to guarantee an optimal (dynamic) regret $\sqrt{LT}$, for $T$ rounds, and an unknown number $L$ of changes. However, while this rate is tight in the worst case, it remained open whether faster rates are possible, without prior knowledge, if few changes in distribution are actually severe. To resolve this question, we propose a new notion of significant shift, which only counts very severe changes that clearly necessitate a restart: roughly, these are changes involving not only best arm switches, but also involving large aggregate differences in reward overtime. Thus, our resulting procedure adaptively achieves rates always faster (sometimes significantly) than $O(\sqrt{ST})$, where $S\ll L$ only counts best arm switches, while at the same time, always faster than the optimal $O(V^{\frac{1}{3}}T^{\frac{2}{3}})$ when expressed in terms of total variation $V$ (which aggregates differences overtime). Our results are expressed in enough generality to also capture non-stochastic adversarial settings.

title: Tracking Most Significant Arm Switches in Bandits
text: In the context of bandit problems with distribution shifts, the capacity to adapt to unknown changes in reward distributions and restart exploration as needed is crucial. Recently, Auer et al. (2018, 2019) have made significant progress in this area, developing an adaptive procedure that guarantees an optimal dynamic regret of √LT for T rounds and an unknown number L of changes. However, the question remains as to whether faster rates can be achieved in scenarios where few distribution changes are severe, without prior knowledge. This paper introduces the concept of significant shifts, which selectively captures severe changes necessitating a restart, characterized by both best arm switches and substantial aggregate reward differences over time. Our proposed procedure adaptively achieves rates that surpass O(√ST), where S ≪ L represents the number of best arm switches, and also outperforms the optimal O(V^(1/3)T^(2/3)) in terms of total variation V, which aggregates differences over time. Notably, our results extend to non-stochastic adversarial settings, offering a comprehensive framework for addressing bandit problems with distribution shifts.

title: BMPQ: Bit-Gradient Sensitivity Driven Mixed-Precision Quantization of DNNs from Scratch
text: Large DNNs with mixed-precision quantization can achieve ultra-high compression while retaining high classification performance. However, because of the challenges in finding an accurate metric that can guide the optimization process, these methods either sacrifice significant performance compared to the 32-bit floating-point (FP-32) baseline or rely on a compute-expensive, iterative training policy that requires the availability of a pre-trained baseline. To address this issue, this paper presents BMPQ, a training method that uses bit gradients to analyze layer sensitivities and yield mixed-precision quantized models. BMPQ requires a single training iteration but does not need a pre-trained baseline. It uses an integer linear program (ILP) to dynamically adjust the precision of layers during training, subject to a fixed hardware budget. To evaluate the efficacy of BMPQ, we conduct extensive experiments with VGG16 and ResNet18 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet datasets. Compared to the baseline FP-32 models, BMPQ can yield models that have 15.4x fewer parameter bits with a negligible drop in accuracy. Compared to the SOTA "during training", mixed-precision training scheme, our models are 2.1x, 2.2x, and 2.9x smaller, on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, respectively, with an improved accuracy of up to 14.54%.

title: BMPQ: Bit-Gradient Sensitivity Driven Mixed-Precision Quantization of DNNs from Scratch
text: The quest for optimal mixed-precision quantization of deep neural networks (DNNs) has been hindered by the lack of a reliable metric to guide the optimization process. Consequently, existing methods either compromise on performance relative to 32-bit floating-point (FP-32) baselines or employ computationally expensive, iterative training policies that necessitate a pre-trained model. We propose BMPQ, a novel training method that leverages bit gradients to analyze layer sensitivities and produce mixed-precision quantized models. Notably, BMPQ requires only a single training iteration and does not rely on a pre-trained baseline. By formulating an integer linear program (ILP) to dynamically adjust layer precision during training, subject to a fixed hardware budget, BMPQ achieves significant compression while preserving accuracy. Our comprehensive experiments on VGG16 and ResNet18 using CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet datasets demonstrate that BMPQ yields models with 15.4x fewer parameter bits, accompanied by a negligible accuracy drop, compared to FP-32 baselines. Moreover, our models outperform state-of-the-art "during training" mixed-precision schemes, achieving 2.1x-2.9x smaller models with improved accuracy of up to 14.54%.
