title: MedShift: identifying shift data for medical dataset curation
text: Detecting data variance between internal and external sources is a pivotal step in curating high-quality datasets, yet existing methods for identifying shift or variance in data are limited. The lack of effective approaches to learn dense representations of datasets and the difficulties of sharing private data across medical institutions hinder progress in this area. To address these challenges, we introduce MedShift, a unified pipeline for detecting top-level shift samples and facilitating medical data curation. Our approach involves training anomaly detectors for each class of the internal dataset in an unsupervised manner, which are then applied to the external dataset without data exchange. The resulting anomaly scores identify shift data, and clustering these scores by class enables quantification of the external dataset's shiftness. We further evaluate shiftness by training a multi-class classifier on the internal dataset and measuring its performance variance on the external dataset, iteratively removing the group with the highest anomaly score for each class. Additionally, we adapt a dataset quality metric to inspect distribution differences across multiple medical sources. Experiments on musculoskeletal radiographs and chest X-rays from multiple external sources demonstrate the efficacy of MedShift in helping medical centers curate high-quality datasets more efficiently.

title: Free-Viewpoint RGB-D Human Performance Capture and Rendering
text: Capturing and faithfully rendering photo-realistic humans from novel views is a fundamental problem for AR/VR applications. While prior work has shown impressive performance capture results in laboratory settings, it is non-trivial to achieve casual free-viewpoint human capture and rendering for unseen identities with high fidelity, especially for facial expressions, hands, and clothes. To tackle these challenges we introduce a novel view synthesis framework that generates realistic renders from unseen views of any human captured from a single-view and sparse RGB-D sensor, similar to a low-cost depth camera, and without actor-specific models. We propose an architecture to create dense feature maps in novel views obtained by sphere-based neural rendering, and create complete renders using a global context inpainting model. Additionally, an enhancer network leverages the overall fidelity, even in occluded areas from the original view, producing crisp renders with fine details. We show that our method generates high-quality novel views of synthetic and real human actors given a single-stream, sparse RGB-D input. It generalizes to unseen identities, and new poses and faithfully reconstructs facial expressions. Our approach outperforms prior view synthesis methods and is robust to different levels of depth sparsity.

title: Free-Viewpoint RGB-D Human Performance Capture and Rendering
text: The faithful rendering of photorealistic humans from arbitrary viewpoints is a long-standing challenge in augmented and virtual reality applications. Despite impressive performance capture results in controlled laboratory environments, achieving casual free-viewpoint human capture and rendering for unseen identities with high fidelity, particularly for facial expressions, hands, and clothing, remains a significant hurdle. This paper presents a novel view synthesis framework that addresses these challenges by generating realistic renders from unseen views of any human captured using a single-view, sparse RGB-D sensor, without relying on actor-specific models. Our approach leverages sphere-based neural rendering to create dense feature maps in novel views, which are then completed using a global context inpainting model. An enhancer network is also employed to refine the overall fidelity, even in occluded areas, producing crisp renders with fine details. Experimental results demonstrate that our method generates high-quality novel views of synthetic and real human actors from single-stream, sparse RGB-D input, generalizing to unseen identities, new poses, and faithfully reconstructing facial expressions, while outperforming prior view synthesis methods and exhibiting robustness to varying levels of depth sparsity.

title: SPViT: Enabling Faster Vision Transformers via Soft Token Pruning
text: Recently, Vision Transformer (ViT) has continuously established new milestones in the computer vision field, while the high computation and memory cost makes its propagation in industrial production difficult. Pruning, a traditional model compression paradigm for hardware efficiency, has been widely applied in various DNN structures. Nevertheless, it stays ambiguous on how to perform exclusive pruning on the ViT structure. Considering three key points: the structural characteristics, the internal data pattern of ViTs, and the related edge device deployment, we leverage the input token sparsity and propose a computation-aware soft pruning framework, which can be set up on vanilla Transformers of both flatten and CNN-type structures, such as Pooling-based ViT (PiT). More concretely, we design a dynamic attention-based multi-head token selector, which is a lightweight module for adaptive instance-wise token selection. We further introduce a soft pruning technique, which integrates the less informative tokens generated by the selector module into a package token that will participate in subsequent calculations rather than being completely discarded. Our framework is bound to the trade-off between accuracy and computation constraints of specific edge devices through our proposed computation-aware training strategy. Experimental results show that our framework significantly reduces the computation cost of ViTs while maintaining comparable performance on image classification. Moreover, our framework can guarantee the identified model to meet resource specifications of mobile devices and FPGA, and even achieve the real-time execution of DeiT-T on mobile platforms. For example, our method reduces the latency of DeiT-T to 26 ms (26%$\sim $41% superior to existing works) on the mobile device with 0.25%$\sim $4% higher top-1 accuracy on ImageNet.

title: SPViT: Enabling Faster Vision Transformers via Soft Token Pruning
text: Vision Transformers (ViT) have revolutionized the field of computer vision, achieving state-of-the-art results in various tasks. However, their high computational complexity and memory requirements hinder their deployment on resource-constrained devices. Recent efforts have focused on pruning techniques to reduce the number of parameters and computations, but these methods often suffer from significant accuracy drops or require expensive retraining. To address this limitation, we propose SPViT, a novel soft token pruning approach that enables faster Vision Transformers without sacrificing accuracy. SPViT introduces a soft pruning mask, learned during training, to selectively eliminate redundant tokens in the self-attention mechanism. This approach allows for efficient token pruning without modifying the model architecture or requiring retraining. We further propose a dynamic pruning schedule, which adaptively adjusts the pruning ratio during inference, ensuring a better trade-off between speed and accuracy. Extensive experiments on various vision benchmarks, including ImageNet, COCO, and CIFAR-10, demonstrate the effectiveness of SPViT. Our approach achieves an average speedup of 2.3x on GPU and 4.1x on CPU compared to the baseline ViT model, while maintaining a negligible accuracy drop of 0.5%. Notably, SPViT outperforms state-of-the-art pruning methods, including weight pruning and knowledge distillation, in terms of both speed and accuracy. The proposed method has significant implications for real-world vision applications, enabling the deployment of Vision Transformers on resource-constrained devices while preserving their remarkable performance.

title: GPU-accelerated Faster Mean Shift with euclidean distance metrics
text: Handling clustering problems are important in data statistics, pattern recognition and image processing. The mean-shift algorithm, a common unsupervised algorithms, is widely used to solve clustering problems. However, the mean-shift algorithm is restricted by its huge computational resource cost. In previous research[10], we proposed a novel GPU-accelerated Faster Mean-shift algorithm, which greatly speed up the cosine-embedding clustering problem. In this study, we extend and improve the previous algorithm to handle Euclidean distance metrics. Different from conventional GPU-based mean-shift algorithms, our algorithm adopts novel Seed Selection & Early Stopping approaches, which greatly increase computing speed and reduce GPU memory consumption. In the simulation testing, when processing a 200K points clustering problem, our algorithm achieved around 3 times speedup compared to the state-of-the-art GPU-based mean-shift algorithms with optimized GPU memory consumption. Moreover, in this study, we implemented a plug-and-play model for faster mean-shift algorithm, which can be easily deployed. (Plug-and-play model is available:

title: GPU-accelerated Faster Mean Shift with euclidean distance metrics
text: Mean Shift clustering is a popular density-based algorithm widely employed in computer vision applications, including object tracking, image segmentation, and feature space analysis. However, its cubic computational complexity hinders its applicability to large datasets. Recent efforts have focused on developing faster variants, yet these approaches often compromise on accuracy or rely on approximate distance metrics. In this work, we present a GPU-accelerated Faster Mean Shift algorithm that leverages the Euclidean distance metric, maintaining the accuracy of the original algorithm while achieving significant speedups. Our approach exploits the massively parallel architecture of modern GPUs to accelerate the most computationally intensive steps of the algorithm. Experimental results on various benchmark datasets demonstrate that our GPU-accelerated implementation achieves speedups of up to 35x compared to the CPU-based implementation, while maintaining identical clustering results. We further evaluate the effectiveness of our approach in real-world computer vision applications, including image segmentation and object tracking, showcasing its potential for large-scale data analysis.

title: Non-Reference Quality Monitoring of Digital Images using Gradient Statistics and Feedforward Neural Networks
text: Digital images contain a lot of redundancies, therefore, compressions are applied to reduce the image size without the loss of reasonable image quality. The same become more prominent in the case of videos that contains image sequences and higher compression ratios are achieved in low throughput networks. Assessment of the quality of images in such scenarios becomes of particular interest. Subjective evaluation in most of the scenarios becomes infeasible so objective evaluation is preferred. Among the three objective quality measures, full-reference and reduced-reference methods require an original image in some form to calculate the quality score which is not feasible in scenarios such as broadcasting or IP video. Therefore, a non-reference quality metric is proposed to assess the quality of digital images which calculates luminance and multiscale gradient statistics along with mean subtracted contrast normalized products as features to train a Feedforward Neural Network with Scaled Conjugate Gradient. The trained network has provided good regression and R2 measures and further testing on LIVE Image Quality Assessment database release-2 has shown promising results. Pearson, Kendall, and Spearman's correlation are calculated between predicted and actual quality scores and their results are comparable to the state-of-the-art systems. Moreover, the proposed metric is computationally faster than its counterparts and can be used for the quality assessment of image sequences.

title: Non-Reference Quality Monitoring of Digital Images using Gradient Statistics and Feedforward Neural Networks
text: The inherent redundancies in digital images necessitate compression to reduce storage requirements while preserving acceptable image quality, a concern that is amplified in video sequences transmitted over low-throughput networks. In such scenarios, evaluating image quality becomes crucial. While subjective assessment is often infeasible, objective methods are preferred. Notably, full-reference and reduced-reference approaches require access to the original image, rendering them impractical for applications like broadcasting or IP video. This limitation motivates the development of a non-reference quality metric, which we propose. Our approach extracts luminance and multiscale gradient statistics, along with mean-subtracted contrast-normalized products, as features to train a feedforward neural network using the scaled conjugate gradient algorithm. The trained network demonstrates strong regression performance and R2 measures. Evaluation on the LIVE Image Quality Assessment database (release 2) yields promising results. Correlation analysis between predicted and actual quality scores, using Pearson, Kendall, and Spearman's coefficients, indicates performance comparable to state-of-the-art systems. Furthermore, our proposed metric offers a computational advantage over existing methods, making it suitable for quality assessment of image sequences.

title: Two Sparsities Are Better Than One: Unlocking the Performance Benefits of Sparse-Sparse Networks
text: In principle, sparse neural networks should be significantly more efficient than traditional dense networks. Neurons in the brain exhibit two types of sparsity; they are sparsely interconnected and sparsely active. These two types of sparsity, called weight sparsity and activation sparsity, when combined, offer the potential to reduce the computational cost of neural networks by two orders of magnitude. Despite this potential, today's neural networks deliver only modest performance benefits using just weight sparsity, because traditional computing hardware cannot efficiently process sparse networks. In this article we introduce Complementary Sparsity, a novel technique that significantly improves the performance of dual sparse networks on existing hardware. We demonstrate that we can achieve high performance running weight-sparse networks, and we can multiply those speedups by incorporating activation sparsity. Using Complementary Sparsity, we show up to 100X improvement in throughput and energy efficiency performing inference on FPGAs. We analyze scalability and resource tradeoffs for a variety of kernels typical of commercial convolutional networks such as ResNet-50 and MobileNetV2. Our results with Complementary Sparsity suggest that weight plus activation sparsity can be a potent combination for efficiently scaling future AI models.

title: Two Sparsities Are Better Than One: Unlocking the Performance Benefits of Sparse-Sparse Networks
text: The prospect of sparse neural networks has long been touted as a means to drastically enhance efficiency relative to traditional dense networks. Inspired by the brain's sparse interconnectivity and activity patterns, the dual application of weight sparsity and activation sparsity theoretically offers a two-order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost. However, current neural networks only marginally benefit from weight sparsity due to the inefficiencies of traditional computing hardware in processing sparse networks. This paper presents Complementary Sparsity, a novel approach that significantly boosts the performance of dual sparse networks on existing hardware. By leveraging both weight and activation sparsity, we demonstrate substantial speedups in throughput and energy efficiency, achieving up to 100-fold improvements during inference on FPGAs. A thorough analysis of scalability and resource tradeoffs is conducted for various kernels characteristic of commercial convolutional networks, such as ResNet-50 and MobileNetV2. Our findings suggest that the synergy of weight and activation sparsity holds considerable promise for efficiently scaling future AI models.

title: Leveraging Trust for Joint Multi-Objective and Multi-Fidelity Optimization
text: In the pursuit of efficient optimization of expensive-to-evaluate systems, this paper investigates a novel approach to Bayesian multi-objective and multi-fidelity (MOMF) optimization. Traditional optimization methods, while effective, often encounter prohibitively high costs in multi-dimensional optimizations of one or more objectives. Multi-fidelity approaches offer potential remedies by utilizing multiple, less costly information sources, such as low-resolution simulations. However, integrating these two strategies presents a significant challenge. We suggest the innovative use of a trust metric to support simultaneous optimization of multiple objectives and data sources. Our method modifies a multi-objective optimization policy to incorporate the trust gain per evaluation cost as one objective in a Pareto optimization problem, enabling simultaneous MOMF at lower costs. We present and compare two MOMF optimization methods: a holistic approach selecting both the input parameters and the trust parameter jointly, and a sequential approach for benchmarking. Through benchmarks on synthetic test functions, our approach is shown to yield significant cost reductions - up to an order of magnitude compared to pure multi-objective optimization. Furthermore, we find that joint optimization of the trust and objective domains outperforms addressing them in sequential manner. We validate our results using the use case of optimizing laser-plasma acceleration simulations, demonstrating our method's potential in Pareto optimization of high-cost black-box functions. Implementing these methods in existing Bayesian frameworks is simple, and they can be readily extended to batch optimization. With their capability to handle various continuous or discrete fidelity dimensions, our techniques offer broad applicability in solving simulation problems in fields such as plasma physics and fluid dynamics.

title: Leveraging Trust for Joint Multi-Objective and Multi-Fidelity Optimization
text: Optimization problems in real-world applications often involve multiple conflicting objectives and varying levels of fidelity, necessitating the development of efficient multi-objective and multi-fidelity optimization methods. However, existing approaches typically focus on either objective or fidelity, neglecting the intricate relationships between them. In this context, trust, a notion rooted in human decision-making, can be leveraged to facilitate joint optimization. We propose a novel trust-based framework, which integrates principles from multi-objective optimization, surrogate-assisted optimization, and Bayesian optimization to efficiently navigate the complex landscape of joint optimization. Our approach, dubbed TrustMOFO, models the trustworthiness of each objective and fidelity level using Gaussian processes, allowing for adaptive weighing and selection of objectives and fidelities during optimization. We demonstrate the efficacy of TrustMOFO on a range of benchmark problems, showcasing significant improvements in terms of convergence speed and solution quality compared to state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our approach excels in situations where objectives exhibit strong correlations or fidelities have varying levels of accuracy. Furthermore, we provide a rigorous theoretical analysis, establishing convergence guarantees and bounds on the regret of TrustMOFO. Our work has far-reaching implications for various domains, including engineering design, resource allocation, and machine learning, where joint optimization of multiple objectives and fidelities is crucial.

title: Does CLIP Benefit Visual Question Answering in the Medical Domain as Much as it Does in the General Domain?
text: Contrastive Language--Image Pre-training (CLIP) has shown remarkable success in learning with cross-modal supervision from extensive amounts of image--text pairs collected online. Thus far, the effectiveness of CLIP has been investigated primarily in general-domain multimodal problems. This work evaluates the effectiveness of CLIP for the task of Medical Visual Question Answering (MedVQA). To this end, we present PubMedCLIP, a fine-tuned version of CLIP for the medical domain based on PubMed articles. Our experiments are conducted on two MedVQA benchmark datasets and investigate two MedVQA methods, MEVF (Mixture of Enhanced Visual Features) and QCR (Question answering via Conditional Reasoning). For each of these, we assess the merits of visual representation learning using PubMedCLIP, the original CLIP, and state-of-the-art MAML (Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning) networks pre-trained only on visual data. We open source the code for our MedVQA pipeline and pre-training PubMedCLIP. CLIP and PubMedCLIP achieve improvements in comparison to MAML's visual encoder. PubMedCLIP achieves the best results with gains in the overall accuracy of up to 3%. Individual examples illustrate the strengths of PubMedCLIP in comparison to the previously widely used MAML networks. Visual representation learning with language supervision in PubMedCLIP leads to noticeable improvements for MedVQA. Our experiments reveal distributional differences in the two MedVQA benchmark datasets that have not been imparted in previous work and cause different back-end visual encoders in PubMedCLIP to exhibit different behavior on these datasets. Moreover, we witness fundamental performance differences of VQA in general versus medical domains.

title: Does CLIP Benefit Visual Question Answering in the Medical Domain as Much as it Does in the General Domain?
text: The success of Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) in learning from large-scale online image-text pairs has primarily been demonstrated in general-domain multimodal settings. However, its effectiveness in specialized domains remains largely unexplored. This study investigates the applicability of CLIP to Medical Visual Question Answering (MedVQA), a task that requires accurate understanding of medical images and texts. We introduce PubMedCLIP, a fine-tuned variant of CLIP tailored to the medical domain using PubMed articles. Experiments on two MedVQA benchmark datasets examine the performance of PubMedCLIP, the original CLIP, and state-of-the-art MAML networks pre-trained solely on visual data, in conjunction with two MedVQA methods: MEVF and QCR. Our results show that both CLIP and PubMedCLIP outperform MAML's visual encoder, with PubMedCLIP achieving the highest overall accuracy, yielding up to 3% improvement. Notably, visual representation learning with language supervision in PubMedCLIP leads to significant enhancements in MedVQA. Furthermore, our analysis reveals previously unreported distributional differences between the two MedVQA datasets, which affect the performance of different visual encoders in PubMedCLIP. Our findings also highlight fundamental performance disparities between general-domain and medical VQA tasks.

title: Forensic Issues and Techniques to Improve Security in SSD with Flex Capacity Feature
text: Over-provisioning technology is typically introduced as a means to improve the performance of storage systems, such as databases. The over-provisioning area is both hidden and difficult for normal users to access. This paper focuses on attack models for such hidden areas. Malicious hackers use advanced over-provisioning techniques that vary capacity according to workload, and as such, our focus is on attack models that use variable over-provisioning technology. According to these attack models, it is possible to scan for invalid blocks containing original data or malware code that is hidden in the over-provisioning area. In this paper, we outline the different forensic processes performed for each memory cell type of the over-provisioning area and disclose security enhancement techniques that increase immunity to these attack models. This leads to a discussion of forensic possibilities and countermeasures for SSDs that can change the over-provisioning area. We also present information-hiding attacks and information-exposing attacks on the invalidation area of the SSD. Our research provides a good foundation upon which the performance and security of SSD-based databases can be further improved.

title: Forensic Issues and Techniques to Improve Security in SSD with Flex Capacity Feature
text: The proliferation of Solid-State Drives (SSDs) with Flex Capacity feature has introduced new challenges in digital forensics, as the dynamic allocation of spare cells and metadata rewriting mechanisms can compromise the integrity of forensic evidence. The lack of standardized forensic tools and procedures for SSDs with Flex Capacity further exacerbates the issue. To address these concerns, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the Flex Capacity feature and its implications on digital forensics. We develop a novel forensic framework that incorporates advanced techniques for data carving, metadata reconstruction, and anomaly detection. Our methodology involves experiments on a range of SSDs with varying capacities and firmware versions, as well as simulations of real-world scenarios using custom-built testbeds. The results show that our framework can effectively recover deleted data, identify tampered metadata, and detect anomalies in SSDs with Flex Capacity. Furthermore, we identify several previously unknown vulnerabilities in popular SSD firmware, which can be exploited by attackers to conceal evidence. Our findings have significant implications for the development of robust forensic tools and procedures for SSDs with Flex Capacity, and contribute to the advancement of digital forensics research in the context of emerging storage technologies.

title: Improving Depth Estimation using Location Information
text: The ability to accurately estimate depth information is crucial for many autonomous applications to recognize the surrounded environment and predict the depth of important objects. One of the most recently used techniques is monocular depth estimation where the depth map is inferred from a single image. This paper improves the self-supervised deep learning techniques to perform accurate generalized monocular depth estimation. The main idea is to train the deep model to take into account a sequence of the different frames, each frame is geotagged with its location information. This makes the model able to enhance depth estimation given area semantics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model to improve depth estimation results. The model is trained in a realistic environment and the results show improvements in the depth map after adding the location data to the model training phase.

title: Improving Depth Estimation using Location Information
text: Estimating depth from a single RGB image is a fundamental problem in computer vision, with applications in robotics, autonomous driving, and augmented reality. While recent deep learning methods have achieved impressive results, they often struggle to accurately estimate depth in scenes with complex geometry or lacking distinctive features. In this work, we explore the use of location information, such as GPS coordinates and orientation, to improve depth estimation. We propose a novel architecture that incorporates location-aware features into a state-of-the-art depth estimation model. Our approach leverages a graph-based method to fuse location information with visual features, enabling the model to better understand scene geometry and context. Experimental results on the KITTI and NYUv2 datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods, particularly in scenarios with limited texture or repetitive patterns, achieving a relative improvement of 12.5% in root mean squared error.

title: Resource-Efficient and Delay-Aware Federated Learning Design under Edge Heterogeneity
text: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a popular technique for distributing machine learning across wireless edge devices. We examine FL under two salient properties of contemporary networks: device-server communication delays and device computation heterogeneity. Our proposed StoFedDelAv algorithm incorporates a local-global model combiner into the FL synchronization step. We theoretically characterize the convergence behavior of StoFedDelAv and obtain the optimal combiner weights, which consider the global model delay and expected local gradient error at each device. We then formulate a network-aware optimization problem which tunes the minibatch sizes of the devices to jointly minimize energy consumption and machine learning training loss, and solve the non-convex problem through a series of convex approximations. Our simulations reveal that StoFedDelAv outperforms the current art in FL, evidenced by the obtained improvements in optimization objective.

title: Resource-Efficient and Delay-Aware Federated Learning Design under Edge Heterogeneity
text: Federated learning has become a prominent approach for decentralized machine learning in wireless edge networks, where device-server communication delays and computation heterogeneity are inherent properties. To address these challenges, we develop StoFedDelAv, an algorithm that integrates a local-global model combiner into the synchronization step. We provide theoretical guarantees for the convergence behavior of StoFedDelAv, deriving optimal combiner weights that account for global model delay and expected local gradient error at each device. Furthermore, we formulate a network-aware optimization problem to jointly minimize energy consumption and training loss by tuning device minibatch sizes, and solve it using a series of convex approximations. Simulation results demonstrate the superiority of StoFedDelAv over state-of-the-art federated learning methods, as measured by improvements in the optimization objective.

title: RELDEC: Reinforcement Learning-Based Decoding of Moderate Length LDPC Codes
text: In this work we propose RELDEC, a novel approach for sequential decoding of moderate length low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. The main idea behind RELDEC is that an optimized decoding policy is subsequently obtained via reinforcement learning based on a Markov decision process (MDP). In contrast to our previous work, where an agent learns to schedule only a single check node (CN) within a group (cluster) of CNs per iteration, in this work we train the agent to schedule all CNs in a cluster, and all clusters in every iteration. That is, in each learning step of RELDEC an agent learns to schedule CN clusters sequentially depending on a reward associated with the outcome of scheduling a particular cluster. We also modify the state space representation of the MDP, enabling RELDEC to be suitable for larger block length LDPC codes than those studied in our previous work. Furthermore, to address decoding under varying channel conditions, we propose agile meta-RELDEC (AM-RELDEC) that employs meta-reinforcement learning. The proposed RELDEC scheme significantly outperforms standard flooding and random sequential decoding for a variety of LDPC codes, including codes designed for 5G new radio.

title: RELDEC: Reinforcement Learning-Based Decoding of Moderate Length LDPC Codes
text: Low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes have emerged as a crucial component in modern communication systems, offering exceptional error correction capabilities. However, their decoding complexity remains a major bottleneck, particularly for moderate length codes. Traditional belief propagation (BP) and its variants suffer from high computational overhead, while more efficient algorithms often compromise on decoding performance. This paper introduces RELDEC, a novel reinforcement learning (RL) framework for decoding moderate length LDPC codes. By formulating the decoding process as a Markov decision process, RELDEC leverages RL to learn an optimal policy for navigating the decoding trellis. Our approach exploits the inherent structural properties of LDPC codes to reduce the state and action spaces, ensuring tractability and scalability. Experimental results demonstrate that RELDEC outperforms state-of-the-art decoding algorithms, including offset min-sum and normalized min-sum, in terms of block error rate (BLER) and decoding latency. Notably, RELDEC achieves a 25% reduction in BLER and a 30% reduction in decoding time compared to offset min-sum for a (1024, 512) LDPC code. Our findings have significant implications for the development of efficient and reliable LDPC decoding schemes, particularly in resource-constrained communication systems.

title: AET-SGD: Asynchronous Event-triggered Stochastic Gradient Descent
text: Communication cost is the main bottleneck for the design of effective distributed learning algorithms. Recently, event-triggered techniques have been proposed to reduce the exchanged information among compute nodes and thus alleviate the communication cost. However, most existing event-triggered approaches only consider heuristic event-triggered thresholds. They also ignore the impact of computation and network delay, which play an important role on the training performance. In this paper, we propose an Asynchronous Event-triggered Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) framework, called AET-SGD, to i) reduce the communication cost among the compute nodes, and ii) mitigate the impact of the delay. Compared with baseline event-triggered methods, AET-SGD employs a linear increasing sample size event-triggered threshold, and can significantly reduce the communication cost while keeping good convergence performance. We implement AET-SGD and evaluate its performance on multiple representative data sets, including MNIST, FashionMNIST, KMNIST and CIFAR10. The experimental results validate the correctness of the design and show a significant communication cost reduction from 44x to 120x, compared to the state of the art. Our results also show that AET-SGD can resist large delay from the straggler nodes while obtaining a decent performance and a desired speedup ratio.

title: AET-SGD: Asynchronous Event-triggered Stochastic Gradient Descent
text: Distributed stochastic gradient descent (SGD) has become a cornerstone of modern machine learning, enabling the training of large-scale models on vast datasets. However, its synchronous nature, where all nodes wait for the slowest node to update, can lead to significant communication overhead and straggler effects. Asynchronous SGD methods alleviate this issue but often compromise on convergence guarantees. Meanwhile, event-triggered control strategies have been successfully applied in other domains to reduce communication costs. We propose AET-SGD, an asynchronous event-triggered stochastic gradient descent algorithm that leverages the benefits of both approaches. In AET-SGD, each node updates its model parameters independently, and triggers communication with the parameter server only when the local gradient norm exceeds a specified threshold. We provide a rigorous convergence analysis, showing that AET-SGD converges to a stationary point of the non-convex objective function at a rate of O(1/√T), matching the convergence rate of synchronous SGD. Experiments on various deep learning models and datasets demonstrate that AET-SGD achieves significant speedups over synchronous SGD, while maintaining comparable model accuracy. AET-SGD offers a promising solution for large-scale distributed machine learning, where communication efficiency and model accuracy are crucial.

title: SPIDER: Searching Personalized Neural Architecture for Federated Learning
text: Federated learning (FL) is an efficient learning framework that assists distributed machine learning when data cannot be shared with a centralized server due to privacy and regulatory restrictions. Recent advancements in FL use predefined architecture-based learning for all the clients. However, given that clients' data are invisible to the server and data distributions are non-identical across clients, a predefined architecture discovered in a centralized setting may not be an optimal solution for all the clients in FL. Motivated by this challenge, in this work, we introduce SPIDER, an algorithmic framework that aims to Search Personalized neural architecture for federated learning. SPIDER is designed based on two unique features: (1) alternately optimizing one architecture-homogeneous global model (Supernet) in a generic FL manner and one architecture-heterogeneous local model that is connected to the global model by weight sharing-based regularization (2) achieving architecture-heterogeneous local model by a novel neural architecture search (NAS) method that can select optimal subnet progressively using operation-level perturbation on the accuracy value as the criterion. Experimental results demonstrate that SPIDER outperforms other state-of-the-art personalization methods, and the searched personalized architectures are more inference efficient.

title: SPIDER: Searching Personalized Neural Architecture for Federated Learning
text: The federated learning (FL) paradigm enables distributed machine learning in scenarios where data sharing with a centralized server is prohibited by privacy and regulatory constraints. While recent FL advancements rely on predefined architecture-based learning for all clients, the assumption of a universally optimal architecture is problematic, given that client data remains opaque to the server and exhibits non-identical distributions. This challenge motivates the development of SPIDER, an algorithmic framework designed to search for personalized neural architectures tailored to FL. SPIDER operates on two key principles: (1) alternating optimization of a homogeneous global model (Supernet) in a standard FL setting and a heterogeneous local model connected via weight sharing-based regularization, and (2) employing a novel neural architecture search (NAS) method that progressively selects optimal subnets based on operation-level perturbation of the accuracy metric. Our experimental results show that SPIDER surpasses state-of-the-art personalization methods, yielding more inference-efficient, personalized architectures.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning with Chance-constrained Model Predictive Control
text: Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) problems often demand that agents behave safely by obeying a set of designed constraints. We address the challenge of safe RL by coupling a safety guide based on model predictive control (MPC) with a modified policy gradient framework in a linear setting with continuous actions. The guide enforces safe operation of the system by embedding safety requirements as chance constraints in the MPC formulation. The policy gradient training step then includes a safety penalty which trains the base policy to behave safely. We show theoretically that this penalty allows for a provably safe optimal base policy and illustrate our method with a simulated linearized quadrotor experiment.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning with Chance-constrained Model Predictive Control
text: Reinforcement learning (RL) agents often operate in uncertainty-prone environments, necessitating careful consideration of safety constraints to prevent catastrophic failures. This paper presents a novel approach to safe RL by integrating chance-constrained model predictive control (CC-MPC) with RL. We formulate a probabilistic model of the environment and leverage CC-MPC to compute a sequence of actions that satisfy constraints with high probability. Our method, Safe-Ctrl, iteratively refines the model and adjusts the control policy to balance exploration and exploitation while ensuring safety. Experiments in simulated robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate that Safe-Ctrl significantly outperforms state-of-the-art safe RL methods, achieving higher rewards while satisfying constraints with probability guarantees.

title: PriFit: Learning to Fit Primitives Improves Few Shot Point Cloud Segmentation
text: We present PriFit, a semi-supervised approach for label-efficient learning of 3D point cloud segmentation networks. PriFit combines geometric primitive fitting with point-based representation learning. Its key idea is to learn point representations whose clustering reveals shape regions that can be approximated well by basic geometric primitives, such as cuboids and ellipsoids. The learned point representations can then be re-used in existing network architectures for 3D point cloud segmentation, and improves their performance in the few-shot setting. According to our experiments on the widely used ShapeNet and PartNet benchmarks, PriFit outperforms several state-of-the-art methods in this setting, suggesting that decomposability into primitives is a useful prior for learning representations predictive of semantic parts. We present a number of ablative experiments varying the choice of geometric primitives and downstream tasks to demonstrate the effectiveness of the method.

title: PriFit: Learning to Fit Primitives Improves Few Shot Point Cloud Segmentation
text: Point cloud segmentation remains a challenging task, especially in few-shot settings where annotated data is scarce. Existing methods often rely on complex neural networks that struggle to generalize to new scenes and objects. In contrast, we propose PriFit, a novel approach that learns to fit primitives to point clouds, enabling efficient and effective segmentation. Our key insight is that many objects can be represented as a combination of simple geometric primitives, such as planes and spheres. By learning to fit these primitives, PriFit can accurately segment point clouds with a small number of annotated examples. We evaluate PriFit on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation methods. Notably, PriFit achieves an average IoU gain of 10.3% on the ScanObjectNN dataset, while reducing the number of model parameters by 75%. These results suggest that PriFit's primitive-based approach is a promising direction for few-shot point cloud segmentation.

title: Improving Nonparametric Classification via Local Radial Regression with an Application to Stock Prediction
text: For supervised classification problems, this paper considers estimating the query's label probability through local regression using observed covariates. Well-known nonparametric kernel smoother and $k$-nearest neighbor ($k$-NN) estimator, which take label average over a ball around the query, are consistent but asymptotically biased particularly for a large radius of the ball. To eradicate such bias, local polynomial regression (LPoR) and multiscale $k$-NN (MS-$k$-NN) learn the bias term by local regression around the query and extrapolate it to the query itself. However, their theoretical optimality has been shown for the limit of the infinite number of training samples. For correcting the asymptotic bias with fewer observations, this paper proposes a \emph{local radial regression (LRR)} and its logistic regression variant called \emph{local radial logistic regression~(LRLR)}, by combining the advantages of LPoR and MS-$k$-NN. The idea is quite simple: we fit the local regression to observed labels by taking only the radial distance as the explanatory variable and then extrapolate the estimated label probability to zero distance. The usefulness of the proposed method is shown theoretically and experimentally. We prove the convergence rate of the $L^2$ risk for LRR with reference to MS-$k$-NN, and our numerical experiments, including real-world datasets of daily stock indices, demonstrate that LRLR outperforms LPoR and MS-$k$-NN.

title: Improving Nonparametric Classification via Local Radial Regression with an Application to Stock Prediction
text: This study investigates the estimation of query label probabilities in supervised classification problems using local regression on observed covariates. While nonparametric kernel smoothers and k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) estimators are consistent, they exhibit asymptotic bias, particularly when the radius of the ball around the query is large. To mitigate this bias, local polynomial regression (LPoR) and multiscale k-NN (MS-k-NN) employ local regression to learn the bias term and extrapolate it to the query. However, their theoretical optimality is established only in the limit of infinite training samples. We propose a novel approach, local radial regression (LRR), and its logistic variant, local radial logistic regression (LRLR), which combines the strengths of LPoR and MS-k-NN to correct asymptotic bias with fewer observations. By fitting local regression to observed labels using radial distance as the sole explanatory variable and extrapolating to zero distance, we achieve improved estimation. Theoretical analysis and experimental results, including daily stock index datasets, demonstrate the effectiveness of LRLR, outperforming LPoR and MS-k-NN, with a proven convergence rate of the L2 risk for LRR relative to MS-k-NN.

title: Source Feature Compression for Object Classification in Vision-Based Underwater Robotics
text: New efficient source feature compression solutions are proposed based on a two-stage Walsh-Hadamard Transform (WHT) for Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-based object classification in underwater robotics. The object images are firstly transformed by WHT following a two-stage process. The transform-domain tensors have large values concentrated in the upper left corner of the matrices in the RGB channels. By observing this property, the transform-domain matrix is partitioned into inner and outer regions. Consequently, two novel partitioning methods are proposed in this work: (i) fixing the size of inner and outer regions; and (ii) adjusting the size of inner and outer regions adaptively per image. The proposals are evaluated with an underwater object dataset captured from the Raritan River in New Jersey, USA. It is demonstrated and verified that the proposals reduce the training time effectively for learning-based underwater object classification task and increase the accuracy compared with the competing methods. The object classification is an essential part of a vision-based underwater robot that can sense the environment and navigate autonomously. Therefore, the proposed method is well-suited for efficient computer vision-based tasks in underwater robotics applications.

title: Source Feature Compression for Object Classification in Vision-Based Underwater Robotics
text: Object classification is a vital task in vision-based underwater robotics, enabling autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) to recognize and interact with their environment. However, the high-dimensional feature spaces inherent to underwater images pose significant computational and storage challenges. To address this, we investigate source feature compression (SFC) as a means to reduce the dimensionality of feature representations while preserving classification performance. Our approach leverages a novel combination of feature selection and transformation techniques, applied directly to the output of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). We evaluate SFC on a comprehensive dataset of underwater images, comprising 10,000 instances across 20 object classes. Experimental results demonstrate that SFC achieves a compression ratio of up to 75% while maintaining a classification accuracy of 92.5%, outperforming state-of-the-art dimensionality reduction methods. Furthermore, we show that SFC enables real-time object classification on resource-constrained AUVs, with a speedup of 3.2x compared to uncompressed feature representations. Our findings have significant implications for the development of efficient and effective vision-based underwater robotic systems.

title: A Blockchain-based Data Governance Framework with Privacy Protection and Provenance for e-Prescription
text: Real-world applications in healthcare and supply chain domains produce, exchange, and share data in a multi-stakeholder environment. Data owners want to control their data and privacy in such settings. On the other hand, data consumers demand methods to understand when, how, and who produced the data. These requirements necessitate data governance frameworks that guarantee data provenance, privacy protection, and consent management. We introduce a decentralized data governance framework based on blockchain technology and proxy re-encryption to let data owners control and track their data through privacy-enhancing and consent management mechanisms. Besides, our framework allows the data consumers to understand data lineage through a blockchain-based provenance mechanism. We have used Digital e-prescription as the use case since it has multiple stakeholders and sensitive data while enabling the medical fraternity to manage patients' prescription data, involving patients as data owners, doctors and pharmacists as data consumers. Our proof-of-concept implementation and evaluation results based on CosmWasm, Ethereum, and pyUmbral PRE show that the proposed decentralized system guarantees transparency, privacy, and trust with minimal overhead.

title: A Blockchain-based Data Governance Framework with Privacy Protection and Provenance for e-Prescription
text: Electronic prescription systems have transformed the healthcare industry, but they also raise concerns about data privacy, integrity, and provenance. The lack of transparency and accountability in existing systems can lead to unauthorized data access, tampering, and misuse. To address these challenges, we propose a blockchain-based data governance framework for e-prescription systems that ensures privacy protection and provenance. Our framework utilizes a permissioned blockchain network to store and manage electronic prescriptions, enabling secure, transparent, and tamper-evident data sharing among authorized stakeholders. We employ a combination of attribute-based encryption and zero-knowledge proofs to protect patient data while enabling selective access and verification. Furthermore, we incorporate a provenance mechanism that tracks data origin, modifications, and accesses, ensuring accountability and trustworthiness. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility and efficiency of our framework, achieving an average transaction throughput of 150 tx/s and a latency of 3.2 seconds. Our approach has the potential to significantly enhance the security, transparency, and reliability of e-prescription systems, ultimately improving patient care and trust in the healthcare ecosystem.

title: Online Allocation Problem with Two-sided Resource Constraints
text: In this paper, we investigate the online allocation problem of maximizing the overall revenue subject to both lower and upper bound constraints. Compared to the extensively studied online problems with only resource upper bounds, the two-sided constraints affect the prospects of resource consumption more severely. As a result, only limited violations of constraints or pessimistic competitive bounds could be guaranteed. To tackle the challenge, we define a measure of feasibility $ξ^*$ to evaluate the hardness of this problem, and estimate this measurement by an optimization routine with theoretical guarantees. We propose an online algorithm adopting a constructive framework, where we initialize a threshold price vector using the estimation, then dynamically update the price vector and use it for decision-making at each step. It can be shown that the proposed algorithm is $\big(1-O(\frac{\varepsilon}{ξ^*-\varepsilon})\big)$ or $\big(1-O(\frac{\varepsilon}{ξ^*-\sqrt{\varepsilon}})\big)$ competitive with high probability for $ξ^*$ known or unknown respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first result establishing a nearly optimal competitive algorithm for solving two-sided constrained online allocation problems with a high probability of feasibility.

title: Online Allocation Problem with Two-sided Resource Constraints
text: The online allocation problem with both lower and upper bound constraints on resource consumption poses a significant challenge, as it exacerbates the uncertainty of resource utilization compared to the extensively studied problems with only upper bounds. Consequently, existing approaches can merely guarantee limited constraint violations or pessimistic competitive bounds. To address this issue, we introduce a measure of feasibility, denoted by $ξ^*$, to quantify the problem's hardness and develop an optimization routine to estimate it with theoretical guarantees. Our proposed online algorithm leverages a constructive framework, where an initial threshold price vector is set based on the estimation, and then dynamically updated to inform decision-making at each step. We theoretically demonstrate that our algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of $\big(1-O(\frac{\varepsilon}{ξ^*-\varepsilon})\big)$ or $\big(1-O(\frac{\varepsilon}{ξ^*-\sqrt{\varepsilon}})\big)$ with high probability, depending on whether $ξ^*$ is known or unknown. Notably, this is the first result to establish a nearly optimal competitive algorithm for two-sided constrained online allocation problems with a high probability of feasibility.

title: Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
text: Knowledge distillation, a technique recently gaining popularity for enhancing model generalization in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), operates under the assumption that both teacher and student models are trained on identical data distributions. However, its effect on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) is less than satisfactory since the graph topology and node attributes are prone to evolve, thereby leading to the issue of distribution shift. In this paper, we tackle this challenge by simultaneously training a group of graph neural networks in an online distillation fashion, where the group knowledge plays a role as a dynamic virtual teacher and the structure changes in graph neural networks are effectively captured. To improve the distillation performance, two types of knowledge are transferred among the students to enhance each other: local knowledge reflecting information in the graph topology and node attributes, and global knowledge reflecting the prediction over classes. We transfer the global knowledge with KL-divergence as the vanilla knowledge distillation does, while exploiting the complicated structure of the local knowledge with an efficient adversarial cyclic learning framework. Extensive experiments verified the effectiveness of our proposed online adversarial distillation approach. The code is published at

title: Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
text: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for graph-structured data, achieving state-of-the-art performance in various applications. However, their vulnerability to adversarial attacks raises concerns about their reliability in real-world scenarios. Knowledge distillation, which involves transferring knowledge from a teacher model to a student model, has been shown to improve the robustness of neural networks against adversarial attacks. Nevertheless, existing knowledge distillation methods for GNNs are limited to offline settings, where the teacher and student models are trained simultaneously. In this work, we propose an online adversarial knowledge distillation framework for GNNs, where the teacher model is updated dynamically during the training process to adapt to the student's progress. Our approach leverages a min-max optimization strategy, where the teacher model generates adversarial samples to challenge the student, and the student model learns to defend against these attacks. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that our online adversarial knowledge distillation framework significantly improves the robustness of GNNs against various types of attacks, outperforming existing defense mechanisms. Additionally, our approach yields improved performance on clean data, suggesting its potential as a regularizer for GNNs.

title: LINDA: Unsupervised Learning to Interpolate in Natural Language Processing
text: Despite the success of mixup in data augmentation, its applicability to natural language processing (NLP) tasks has been limited due to the discrete and variable-length nature of natural languages. Recent studies have thus relied on domain-specific heuristics and manually crafted resources, such as dictionaries, in order to apply mixup in NLP. In this paper, we instead propose an unsupervised learning approach to text interpolation for the purpose of data augmentation, to which we refer as "Learning to INterpolate for Data Augmentation" (LINDA), that does not require any heuristics nor manually crafted resources but learns to interpolate between any pair of natural language sentences over a natural language manifold. After empirically demonstrating the LINDA's interpolation capability, we show that LINDA indeed allows us to seamlessly apply mixup in NLP and leads to better generalization in text classification both in-domain and out-of-domain.

title: LINDA: Unsupervised Learning to Interpolate in Natural Language Processing
text: The ability to interpolate between exemplar inputs is a crucial aspect of human intelligence, yet current natural language processing (NLP) models often struggle to generalize beyond their training data. We propose LINDA, a novel unsupervised learning framework that enables NLP models to interpolate in latent space, effectively generating novel sentences that combine characteristics of the input exemplars. LINDA leverages a conditional variational autoencoder to learn a smooth, continuous representation of language, which is then used to interpolate between input sentences. We evaluate LINDA on a range of NLP tasks, including text classification, sentiment analysis, and machine translation, demonstrating significant improvements in generalization performance compared to state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, our framework allows for controllable generation of novel sentences, enabling fine-grained exploration of the latent space. Our findings have important implications for developing more robust and flexible NLP models that can effectively generalize to unseen data.

title: A Moment in the Sun: Solar Nowcasting from Multispectral Satellite Data using Self-Supervised Learning
text: Solar energy is now the cheapest form of electricity in history. Unfortunately, significantly increasing the grid's fraction of solar energy remains challenging due to its variability, which makes balancing electricity's supply and demand more difficult. While thermal generators' ramp rate -- the maximum rate that they can change their output -- is finite, solar's ramp rate is essentially infinite. Thus, accurate near-term solar forecasting, or nowcasting, is important to provide advance warning to adjust thermal generator output in response to solar variations to ensure a balanced supply and demand. To address the problem, this paper develops a general model for solar nowcasting from abundant and readily available multispectral satellite data using self-supervised learning. Specifically, we develop deep auto-regressive models using convolutional neural networks (CNN) and long short-term memory networks (LSTM) that are globally trained across multiple locations to predict raw future observations of the spatio-temporal data collected by the recently launched GOES-R series of satellites. Our model estimates a location's future solar irradiance based on satellite observations, which we feed to a regression model trained on smaller site-specific solar data to provide near-term solar photovoltaic (PV) forecasts that account for site-specific characteristics. We evaluate our approach for different coverage areas and forecast horizons across 25 solar sites and show that our approach yields errors close to that of a model using ground-truth observations.

title: A Moment in the Sun: Solar Nowcasting from Multispectral Satellite Data using Self-Supervised Learning
text: The unprecedented affordability of solar energy has sparked widespread adoption, yet its integration into the grid remains hindered by the challenge of balancing supply and demand amidst its inherent variability. The finite ramp rate of thermal generators necessitates accurate near-term solar forecasting, or nowcasting, to enable timely adjustments in response to solar fluctuations. Leveraging the abundant and readily available multispectral satellite data from the GOES-R series, this study develops a generalizable model for solar nowcasting using self-supervised learning. We propose a deep auto-regressive framework combining convolutional neural networks (CNN) and long short-term memory networks (LSTM), trained globally across multiple locations to predict future raw observations of spatio-temporal data. By estimating location-specific future solar irradiance from satellite observations and feeding it into a regression model trained on site-specific solar data, our approach generates near-term solar photovoltaic (PV) forecasts that account for local characteristics. Evaluating our model across 25 solar sites and varying coverage areas and forecast horizons, we demonstrate errors comparable to those achieved using ground-truth observations, highlighting the potential of our approach to facilitate seamless grid integration of solar energy.

title: Exploiting Fine-grained Face Forgery Clues via Progressive Enhancement Learning
text: With the rapid development of facial forgery techniques, forgery detection has attracted more and more attention due to security concerns. Existing approaches attempt to use frequency information to mine subtle artifacts under high-quality forged faces. However, the exploitation of frequency information is coarse-grained, and more importantly, their vanilla learning process struggles to extract fine-grained forgery traces. To address this issue, we propose a progressive enhancement learning framework to exploit both the RGB and fine-grained frequency clues. Specifically, we perform a fine-grained decomposition of RGB images to completely decouple the real and fake traces in the frequency space. Subsequently, we propose a progressive enhancement learning framework based on a two-branch network, combined with self-enhancement and mutual-enhancement modules. The self-enhancement module captures the traces in different input spaces based on spatial noise enhancement and channel attention. The Mutual-enhancement module concurrently enhances RGB and frequency features by communicating in the shared spatial dimension. The progressive enhancement process facilitates the learning of discriminative features with fine-grained face forgery clues. Extensive experiments on several datasets show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art face forgery detection methods.

title: Exploiting Fine-grained Face Forgery Clues via Progressive Enhancement Learning
text: The proliferation of facial forgery techniques has heightened security concerns, prompting increased attention to forgery detection. While existing approaches leverage frequency information to uncover subtle artifacts in high-quality forged faces, they suffer from coarse-grained exploitation and ineffective learning processes that struggle to extract fine-grained forgery traces. We propose a novel progressive enhancement learning framework that capitalizes on both RGB and fine-grained frequency cues. By decomposing RGB images to decouple real and fake traces in the frequency space, we enable a two-branch network with self-enhancement and mutual-enhancement modules. The former captures traces in different input spaces via spatial noise enhancement and channel attention, while the latter concurrently enhances RGB and frequency features through shared spatial dimension communication. This progressive enhancement process facilitates the learning of discriminative features with fine-grained face forgery cues. Our method demonstrates superior performance to state-of-the-art face forgery detection methods across multiple datasets, underscoring its efficacy in detecting facial forgeries.

title: Quaternion-based dynamic mode decomposition for background modeling in color videos
text: Scene Background Initialization (SBI) is one of the challenging problems in computer vision. Dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) is a recently proposed method to robustly decompose a video sequence into the background model and the corresponding foreground part. However, this method needs to convert the color image into the grayscale image for processing, which leads to the neglect of the coupling information between the three channels of the color image. In this study, we propose a quaternion-based DMD (Q-DMD), which extends the DMD by quaternion matrix analysis, so as to completely preserve the inherent color structure of the color image and the color video. We exploit the standard eigenvalues of the quaternion matrix to compute its spectral decomposition and calculate the corresponding Q-DMD modes and eigenvalues. The results on the publicly available benchmark datasets prove that our Q-DMD outperforms the exact DMD method, and experiment results also demonstrate that the performance of our approach is comparable to that of the state-of-the-art ones.

title: Quaternion-based dynamic mode decomposition for background modeling in color videos
text: Background modeling in color videos is a fundamental task in computer vision, enabling applications such as object detection, tracking, and surveillance. Traditional methods, however, often struggle with complex scenes, varying illumination, and multimodal backgrounds. To address these challenges, we propose a novel quaternion-based dynamic mode decomposition (qDMD) approach for background modeling in color videos. Our method leverages the quaternion algebra to jointly encode color and spatial information, enabling the extraction of robust and meaningful features from video data. By applying qDMD to a sequence of video frames, we can efficiently separate the background from the foreground, even in the presence of complex motions and varying lighting conditions. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and robustness. Notably, our method achieves a 15% improvement in F-measure on the CDnet 2014 dataset, showcasing its potential for real-world applications.

title: Siamese Network with Interactive Transformer for Video Object Segmentation
text: Semi-supervised video object segmentation (VOS) refers to segmenting the target object in remaining frames given its annotation in the first frame, which has been actively studied in recent years. The key challenge lies in finding effective ways to exploit the spatio-temporal context of past frames to help learn discriminative target representation of current frame. In this paper, we propose a novel Siamese network with a specifically designed interactive transformer, called SITVOS, to enable effective context propagation from historical to current frames. Technically, we use the transformer encoder and decoder to handle the past frames and current frame separately, i.e., the encoder encodes robust spatio-temporal context of target object from the past frames, while the decoder takes the feature embedding of current frame as the query to retrieve the target from the encoder output. To further enhance the target representation, a feature interaction module (FIM) is devised to promote the information flow between the encoder and decoder. Moreover, we employ the Siamese architecture to extract backbone features of both past and current frames, which enables feature reuse and is more efficient than existing methods. Experimental results on three challenging benchmarks validate the superiority of SITVOS over state-of-the-art methods.

title: Siamese Network with Interactive Transformer for Video Object Segmentation
text: Video object segmentation, a fundamental task in computer vision, involves separating objects of interest from the background in a video sequence. Despite significant progress, existing approaches often struggle with segmenting objects undergoing complex motions, deformation, or occlusion. To address these challenges, we propose a novel architecture that integrates a Siamese network with an interactive transformer, dubbed Siamese Interactive Transformer (SIT). Our SIT model leverages the strengths of both components: the Siamese network extracts robust feature representations from the video frames, while the interactive transformer captures long-range dependencies and contextual information between objects. During training, we employ a multi-task loss function that combines a segmentation loss with a motion prediction loss, encouraging the model to learn motion-aware features. Experimental results on the DAVIS-2017 and YouTube-VOS benchmarks demonstrate that SIT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a mean IoU of 84.2% and 76.5%, respectively. Notably, our model exhibits improved performance on challenging scenarios, such as occlusion and fast motion, where traditional approaches often fail. Our findings suggest that the proposed SIT architecture provides a promising direction for advancing video object segmentation capabilities.

title: LatteGAN: Visually Guided Language Attention for Multi-Turn Text-Conditioned Image Manipulation
text: Text-guided image manipulation tasks have recently gained attention in the vision-and-language community. While most of the prior studies focused on single-turn manipulation, our goal in this paper is to address the more challenging multi-turn image manipulation (MTIM) task. Previous models for this task successfully generate images iteratively, given a sequence of instructions and a previously generated image. However, this approach suffers from under-generation and a lack of generated quality of the objects that are described in the instructions, which consequently degrades the overall performance. To overcome these problems, we present a novel architecture called a Visually Guided Language Attention GAN (LatteGAN). Here, we address the limitations of the previous approaches by introducing a Visually Guided Language Attention (Latte) module, which extracts fine-grained text representations for the generator, and a Text-Conditioned U-Net discriminator architecture, which discriminates both the global and local representations of fake or real images. Extensive experiments on two distinct MTIM datasets, CoDraw and i-CLEVR, demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of the proposed model.

title: LatteGAN: Visually Guided Language Attention for Multi-Turn Text-Conditioned Image Manipulation
text: The vision-and-language community has witnessed a surge of interest in text-guided image manipulation tasks, with a notable emphasis on single-turn manipulation. However, we tackle the more intricate problem of multi-turn image manipulation (MTIM), where a sequence of instructions guides the iterative refinement of an image. Existing models have successfully generated images incrementally, but they often succumb to under-generation and compromised quality of objects described in the instructions, ultimately hindering overall performance. Our proposed LatteGAN architecture addresses these limitations by incorporating a Visually Guided Language Attention (Latte) module, which extracts nuanced text representations for the generator, and a Text-Conditioned U-Net discriminator, which assesses both global and local representations of real and fake images. Comprehensive experiments on the CoDraw and i-CLEVR datasets demonstrate the superior performance of LatteGAN, establishing it as a state-of-the-art model for MTIM tasks.

title: Deep-CNN based Robotic Multi-Class Under-Canopy Weed Control in Precision Farming
text: Smart weeding systems to perform plant-specific operations can contribute to the sustainability of agriculture and the environment. Despite monumental advances in autonomous robotic technologies for precision weed management in recent years, work on under-canopy weeding in fields is yet to be realized. A prerequisite of such systems is reliable detection and classification of weeds to avoid mistakenly spraying and, thus, damaging the surrounding plants. Real-time multi-class weed identification enables species-specific treatment of weeds and significantly reduces the amount of herbicide use. Here, our first contribution is the first adequately large realistic image dataset \textit{AIWeeds} (one/multiple kinds of weeds in one image), a library of about 10,000 annotated images of flax, and the 14 most common weeds in fields and gardens taken from 20 different locations in North Dakota, California, and Central China. Second, we provide a full pipeline from model training with maximum efficiency to deploying the TensorRT-optimized model onto a single board computer. Based on \textit{AIWeeds} and the pipeline, we present a baseline for classification performance using five benchmark CNN models. Among them, MobileNetV2, with both the shortest inference time and lowest memory consumption, is the qualified candidate for real-time applications. Finally, we deploy MobileNetV2 onto our own compact autonomous robot \textit{SAMBot} for real-time weed detection. The 90\% test accuracy realized in previously unseen scenes in flax fields (with a row spacing of 0.2-0.3 m), with crops and weeds, distortion, blur, and shadows, is a milestone towards precision weed control in the real world.
