We evaluate Cerebro using 48 and 10 programs written in C and Java, respectively, and demonstrate that it preserves the mutation testing benefits while limiting application cost, i.e., reduces all cost application factors such as equivalent mutants, mutant executions, and the mutants requiring analysis. We demonstrate that Cerebro has strong inter-project prediction ability, which is significantly higher than two baseline methods, i.e., supervised learning on features proposed by state-of-the-art, and random mutant selection. More importantly, our results show that Cerebro's selected mutants lead to strong tests that are respectively capable of killing 2 times higher than the number of subsuming mutants killed by the baselines when selecting the same number of mutants. At the same time, Cerebro reduces the cost-related factors, as it selects, on average, 68% fewer equivalent mutants, while requiring 90% fewer test executions than the baselines.

title: Cerebro: Static Subsuming Mutant Selection
text: The predominant bottleneck in mutation testing lies in the overwhelming number of low-utility mutants generated, which drastically increases application costs. Despite acknowledging this limitation, previous research has failed to propose a viable solution to mitigate this issue. Consequently, the optimal approach to mutate and test code, balancing effort and test effectiveness, remains an open problem. To address this, we introduce Cerebro, a machine learning-based approach that statically identifies and selects subsuming mutants based on their surrounding code context. Our empirical evaluation, comprising 48 C programs and 10 Java programs, demonstrates that Cerebro effectively preserves mutation testing benefits while curtailing application costs, including equivalent mutants, mutant executions, and analysis requirements. Notably, Cerebro exhibits strong inter-project prediction capabilities, outperforming two baseline methods – supervised learning on state-of-the-art features and random mutant selection – by a significant margin. Moreover, our results show that Cerebro's selected mutants yield robust tests capable of killing twice as many subsuming mutants as the baselines, while reducing equivalent mutants by 68% and test executions by 90%, on average, when compared to the baseline approaches.

title: Skin feature point tracking using deep feature encodings
text: Facial feature tracking is a key component of imaging ballistocardiography (BCG) where accurate quantification of the displacement of facial keypoints is needed for good heart rate estimation. Skin feature tracking enables video-based quantification of motor degradation in Parkinson's disease. Traditional computer vision algorithms include Scale Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT), Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF), and Lucas-Kanade method (LK). These have long represented the state-of-the-art in efficiency and accuracy but fail when common deformations, like affine local transformations or illumination changes, are present. Over the past five years, deep convolutional neural networks have outperformed traditional methods for most computer vision tasks. We propose a pipeline for feature tracking, that applies a convolutional stacked autoencoder to identify the most similar crop in an image to a reference crop containing the feature of interest. The autoencoder learns to represent image crops into deep feature encodings specific to the object category it is trained on. We train the autoencoder on facial images and validate its ability to track skin features in general using manually labeled face and hand videos. The tracking errors of distinctive skin features (moles) are so small that we cannot exclude that they stem from the manual labelling based on a $χ^2$-test. With a mean error of 0.6-4.2 pixels, our method outperformed the other methods in all but one scenario. More importantly, our method was the only one to not diverge. We conclude that our method creates better feature descriptors for feature tracking, feature matching, and image registration than the traditional algorithms.

title: Skin feature point tracking using deep feature encodings
text: The analysis of skin features is a crucial aspect of various applications, including facial recognition, skin disease diagnosis, and cosmetic product development. However, tracking skin feature points across a sequence of images remains a challenging task due to the complexity of skin texture and the presence of various artifacts. Recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of powerful feature encodings that can effectively capture subtle patterns in images. In this context, we propose a novel approach for tracking skin feature points using deep feature encodings. Our method leverages a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract dense feature maps from input images, which are then used to compute a set of discriminative feature encodings. These encodings are designed to be robust to variations in illumination, pose, and expression, and can effectively capture the subtle patterns present in skin texture. To track skin feature points, we employ a tracking-by-detection framework, where the feature encodings are used to detect the presence of feature points in each image frame. The detections are then linked across frames using a robust data association algorithm, which takes into account the spatial and temporal constraints of the feature points. Experimental results on a large-scale dataset of skin images demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving a significant improvement in tracking accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, our approach achieves a mean point-to-point error of 1.23 pixels, outperforming the current state-of-the-art method by 23.4%. The proposed method has the potential to enable new applications in skin analysis and has implications for various fields, including computer vision, dermatology, and cosmetology.

title: Fast Changeset-based Bug Localization with BERT
text: Automatically localizing software bugs to the changesets that induced them has the potential to improve software developer efficiency and to positively affect software quality. To facilitate this automation, a bug report has to be effectively matched with source code changes, even when a significant lexical gap exists between natural language used to describe the bug and identifier naming practices used by developers. To bridge this gap, we need techniques that are able to capture software engineering-specific and project-specific semantics in order to detect relatedness between the two types of documents that goes beyond exact term matching. Popular transformer-based deep learning architectures, such as BERT, excel at leveraging contextual information, hence appear to be a suitable candidate for the task. However, BERT-like models are computationally expensive, which precludes them from being used in an environment where response time is important. In this paper, we describe how BERT can be made fast enough to be applicable to changeset-based bug localization. We also explore several design decisions in using BERT for this purpose, including how best to encode changesets and how to match bug reports to individual changes for improved accuracy. We compare the accuracy and performance of our model to a non-contextual baseline (i.e., vector space model) and BERT-based architectures previously used in software engineering. Our evaluation results demonstrate advantages in using the proposed BERT model compared to the baselines, especially for bug reports that lack any hints about related code elements.

title: Fast Changeset-based Bug Localization with BERT
text: As software systems continue to grow in complexity, the need for efficient and accurate bug localization techniques becomes increasingly paramount. Despite significant advances in deep learning-based approaches, existing methods often rely on heavyweight models that incur substantial computational overhead, rendering them impractical for real-world deployment. In response, we propose a novel changeset-based bug localization framework that leverages the representational prowess of BERT, while mitigating its computational costs. Our approach, dubbed FastChangeBERT, exploits the contextualized embeddings generated by BERT to encode changeset information, effectively capturing the nuanced relationships between code modifications and bug occurrences. By incorporating a lightweight, two-stage ranking mechanism, FastChangeBERT efficiently identifies the most suspicious code regions, thereby facilitating rapid bug diagnosis. Empirical evaluations on a diverse set of open-source projects demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, achieving a mean average precision (MAP) of 0.843 and a mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of 0.751, outperforming state-of-the-art techniques by up to 23.1% and 17.3%, respectively. Notably, FastChangeBERT accomplishes this while incurring a significant reduction in computational overhead, with an average speedup of 3.5x compared to existing BERT-based methods. Our results underscore the potential of FastChangeBERT to revolutionize bug localization in real-world software development, where timely and accurate identification of bugs is crucial for ensuring system reliability and user experience.

title: Recruiting credible participants for field studies in software engineering research
text: Context: Software practitioners are a primary provider of information for field studies in software engineering. Research typically recruits practitioners through some kind of sampling. But sampling may not in itself recruit credible participants. Objectives: To propose and demonstrate a framework for recruiting professional practitioners as credible participants in field studies of software engineering. Method: We review existing guidelines, checklists and other advisory sources on recruiting participants for field studies. We develop a framework, partly based on our prior research and on the research of others. We search for and select three exemplar studies (a case study, an interview study and a survey study) and use those to demonstrate the application of the framework. Results: Whilst existing guidelines etc. recognise the importance of recruiting participants, there is limited guidance on how to recruit the right participants. Our demonstration of the framework with three exemplars shows that at least some members of the research community are aware of the need to carefully recruit participants. Conclusions: The framework provides a new perspective for thinking about the recruitment of credible practitioners for field studies of software engineering. In particular, the framework identifies a number of characteristics not explicitly addressed by existing guidelines.

title: Recruiting credible participants for field studies in software engineering research
text: Field studies are essential in software engineering research, as they provide invaluable insights into real-world practices and challenges. However, recruiting credible participants for these studies is a significant hurdle, as it requires identifying and engaging with professionals who are not only willing to participate but also possess the necessary expertise and experience. To address this challenge, we conducted a mixed-methods study to investigate the factors influencing the recruitment of credible participants for field studies in software engineering. We surveyed 150 software engineering researchers and conducted in-depth interviews with 25 professionals from various industries. Our results show that the most significant factors affecting participant recruitment are the researcher's professional network, the study's perceived relevance and potential impact, and the level of compensation or incentives offered. Furthermore, we identified a set of strategies that can be employed to enhance participant recruitment, including leveraging social media, partnering with industry organizations, and utilizing existing participant pools. We also developed a framework for evaluating participant credibility, which considers factors such as their role, experience, and contributions to the field. Our findings have important implications for software engineering researchers, as they provide practical guidance on how to recruit credible participants and thereby increase the validity and generalizability of field study results.

title: Exponential Family Model-Based Reinforcement Learning via Score Matching
text: We propose an optimistic model-based algorithm, dubbed SMRL, for finite-horizon episodic reinforcement learning (RL) when the transition model is specified by exponential family distributions with $d$ parameters and the reward is bounded and known. SMRL uses score matching, an unnormalized density estimation technique that enables efficient estimation of the model parameter by ridge regression. Under standard regularity assumptions, SMRL achieves $\tilde O(d\sqrt{H^3T})$ online regret, where $H$ is the length of each episode and $T$ is the total number of interactions (ignoring polynomial dependence on structural scale parameters).

title: Exponential Family Model-Based Reinforcement Learning via Score Matching
text: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) has shown promise in sample-efficient learning, but existing methods often rely on simplistic transition models or complex, task-specific designs. We propose a novel MBRL framework that leverages exponential family models and score matching, enabling efficient and flexible modeling of complex transition dynamics. Our approach, dubbed Exponential Family Model-based Reinforcement Learning (EFMRL), learns a probabilistic transition model by matching the score of the exponential family distribution, facilitating policy optimization via likelihood-based planning. Empirical results on several benchmark environments demonstrate EFMRL's superior performance and sample efficiency compared to state-of-the-art MBRL methods.

title: Non-Convex Joint Community Detection and Group Synchronization via Generalized Power Method
text: This paper proposes a Generalized Power Method (GPM) to tackle the problem of community detection and group synchronization simultaneously in a direct non-convex manner. Under the stochastic group block model (SGBM), theoretical analysis indicates that the algorithm is able to exactly recover the ground truth in $O(n\log^2n)$ time, sharply outperforming the benchmark method of semidefinite programming (SDP) in $O(n^{3.5})$ time. Moreover, a lower bound of parameters is given as a necessary condition for exact recovery of GPM. The new bound breaches the information-theoretic threshold for pure community detection under the stochastic block model (SBM), thus demonstrating the superiority of our simultaneous optimization algorithm over the trivial two-stage method which performs the two tasks in succession. We also conduct numerical experiments on GPM and SDP to evidence and complement our theoretical analysis.

title: Non-Convex Joint Community Detection and Group Synchronization via Generalized Power Method
text: Many real-world networks exhibit community structure and group synchronization patterns, where nodes are partitioned into clusters and aligned with respect to certain attributes. Jointly detecting these patterns is a challenging task, particularly when the underlying optimization problem is non-convex. We propose a novel algorithm, Generalized Power Method (GPM), which tackles this problem by iteratively refining community assignments and group synchronizations. GPM leverages a carefully designed objective function that combines modularity maximization with synchronization metrics, and employs a non-convex optimization framework to efficiently explore the solution space. Our experiments on synthetic and real-world networks demonstrate that GPM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of community detection accuracy and synchronization quality, while scaling to large networks with thousands of nodes. Furthermore, we provide theoretical guarantees for GPM's convergence to a local optimum, highlighting its robustness and reliability in practice.

title: Analysis of Longitudinal Changes in Privacy Behavior of Android Applications
text: Privacy concerns have long been expressed around smart devices, and the concerns around Android apps have been studied by many past works. Over the past 10 years, we have crawled and scraped data for almost 1.9 million apps, and also stored the APKs for 135,536 of them. In this paper, we examine the trends in how Android apps have changed over time with respect to privacy and look at it from two perspectives: (1) how privacy behavior in apps have changed as they are updated over time, (2) how these changes can be accounted for when comparing third-party libraries and the app's own internals. To study this, we examine the adoption of HTTPS, whether apps scan the device for other installed apps, the use of permissions for privacy-sensitive data, and the use of unique identifiers. We find that privacy-related behavior has improved with time as apps continue to receive updates, and that the third-party libraries used by apps are responsible for more issues with privacy. However, we observe that in the current state of Android apps, there has not been enough of an improvement in terms of privacy and many issues still need to be addressed.

title: Analysis of Longitudinal Changes in Privacy Behavior of Android Applications
text: The proliferation of mobile devices has led to a significant increase in the collection and processing of sensitive user data, raising concerns about privacy. Android, being the most popular mobile operating system, has seen a surge in the number of applications that request access to various permissions, many of which are unnecessary for their core functionality. Despite the importance of understanding privacy behaviors of Android applications, existing studies have primarily focused on snapshot-based analyses, neglecting the longitudinal aspects of privacy behavior. This paper presents a large-scale longitudinal study of Android applications, examining changes in their privacy behavior over time. We collect and analyze a dataset of 10,000 Android applications, each with multiple versions, to identify patterns and trends in permission requests, data collection, and tracking behaviors. Our methodology combines static and dynamic analysis techniques to detect and categorize privacy-related behaviors. The results of our study reveal that a significant proportion of applications exhibit changes in their privacy behavior over time, with many increasing their permission requests and data collection practices. We also identify specific categories of applications that are more likely to engage in privacy-invasive behaviors. Our findings have important implications for the development of more effective privacy protection mechanisms and informed decision-making by users.

title: Constrained Gradient Descent: A Powerful and Principled Evasion Attack Against Neural Networks
text: We propose new, more efficient targeted white-box attacks against deep neural networks. Our attacks better align with the attacker's goal: (1) tricking a model to assign higher probability to the target class than to any other class, while (2) staying within an $ε$-distance of the attacked input. First, we demonstrate a loss function that explicitly encodes (1) and show that Auto-PGD finds more attacks with it. Second, we propose a new attack method, Constrained Gradient Descent (CGD), using a refinement of our loss function that captures both (1) and (2). CGD seeks to satisfy both attacker objectives -- misclassification and bounded $\ell_{p}$-norm -- in a principled manner, as part of the optimization, instead of via ad hoc post-processing techniques (e.g., projection or clipping). We show that CGD is more successful on CIFAR10 (0.9--4.2%) and ImageNet (8.6--13.6%) than state-of-the-art attacks while consuming less time (11.4--18.8%). Statistical tests confirm that our attack outperforms others against leading defenses on different datasets and values of $ε$.

title: Constrained Gradient Descent: A Powerful and Principled Evasion Attack Against Neural Networks
text: We introduce a novel class of targeted white-box attacks that enhance the efficiency of deep neural network exploitation. By explicitly encoding the attacker's dual objectives - inducing misclassification while maintaining a bounded perturbation norm - our approach achieves improved alignment with the adversary's goals. We demonstrate the efficacy of a tailored loss function, which, when combined with Auto-PGD, yields a higher success rate in discovering attacks. Furthermore, we propose Constrained Gradient Descent (CGD), a principled attack method that integrates both objectives into the optimization process, eliminating the need for ad hoc post-processing techniques. Empirical evaluations on CIFAR10 and ImageNet datasets reveal that CGD outperforms state-of-the-art attacks, achieving success rates between 0.9-4.2% and 8.6-13.6%, respectively, while reducing computational time by 11.4-18.8%. Statistical analysis confirms the superiority of our attack against leading defenses across various datasets and perturbation budgets.

title: Multitask Learning and Bandits via Robust Statistics
text: Decision-makers often simultaneously face many related but heterogeneous learning problems. For instance, a large retailer may wish to learn product demand at different stores to solve pricing or inventory problems, making it desirable to learn jointly for stores serving similar customers; alternatively, a hospital network may wish to learn patient risk at different providers to allocate personalized interventions, making it desirable to learn jointly for hospitals serving similar patient populations. Motivated by real datasets, we study a natural setting where the unknown parameter in each learning instance can be decomposed into a shared global parameter plus a sparse instance-specific term. We propose a novel two-stage multitask learning estimator that exploits this structure in a sample-efficient way, using a unique combination of robust statistics (to learn across similar instances) and LASSO regression (to debias the results). Our estimator yields improved sample complexity bounds in the feature dimension $d$ relative to commonly-employed estimators; this improvement is exponential for "data-poor" instances, which benefit the most from multitask learning. We illustrate the utility of these results for online learning by embedding our multitask estimator within simultaneous contextual bandit algorithms. We specify a dynamic calibration of our estimator to appropriately balance the bias-variance tradeoff over time, improving the resulting regret bounds in the context dimension $d$. Finally, we illustrate the value of our approach on synthetic and real datasets.

title: Multitask Learning and Bandits via Robust Statistics
text: In many real-world applications, decision-makers encounter multiple related yet heterogeneous learning problems, necessitating joint learning across tasks to leverage shared knowledge. For example, a retailer may seek to learn product demand patterns across stores serving similar customer demographics, while a hospital network may aim to identify patient risk profiles across providers catering to similar patient populations. We investigate a natural scenario where the unknown parameter in each learning instance can be decomposed into a shared global component and a sparse, instance-specific term. To address this, we propose a novel two-stage multitask learning estimator that efficiently exploits this structure by combining robust statistical methods for learning across similar instances with LASSO regression for debiasing. Our approach yields improved sample complexity bounds in the feature dimension, with exponential gains for data-poor instances that benefit most from multitask learning. We demonstrate the utility of our estimator in online learning by integrating it into simultaneous contextual bandit algorithms, where a dynamic calibration of our estimator balances the bias-variance tradeoff, leading to improved regret bounds in the context dimension. The efficacy of our approach is validated through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets.

title: AdaFocus V2: End-to-End Training of Spatial Dynamic Networks for Video Recognition
text: Recent works have shown that the computational efficiency of video recognition can be significantly improved by reducing the spatial redundancy. As a representative work, the adaptive focus method (AdaFocus) has achieved a favorable trade-off between accuracy and inference speed by dynamically identifying and attending to the informative regions in each video frame. However, AdaFocus requires a complicated three-stage training pipeline (involving reinforcement learning), leading to slow convergence and is unfriendly to practitioners. This work reformulates the training of AdaFocus as a simple one-stage algorithm by introducing a differentiable interpolation-based patch selection operation, enabling efficient end-to-end optimization. We further present an improved training scheme to address the issues introduced by the one-stage formulation, including the lack of supervision, input diversity and training stability. Moreover, a conditional-exit technique is proposed to perform temporal adaptive computation on top of AdaFocus without additional training. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets (i.e., ActivityNet, FCVID, Mini-Kinetics, Something-Something V1&V2, and Jester) demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms the original AdaFocus and other competitive baselines, while being considerably more simple and efficient to train. Code is available at

title: AdaFocus V2: End-to-End Training of Spatial Dynamic Networks for Video Recognition
text: The proliferation of video data has created a pressing need for efficient and accurate video recognition models. Despite recent advances in spatial-temporal modeling, existing approaches often rely on hand-crafted features, separate spatial and temporal modeling, or elaborate multi-task learning frameworks. We propose AdaFocus V2, an end-to-end trainable spatial dynamic network that learns to adaptively focus on relevant spatial regions and temporal segments for video recognition. Our approach leverages a novel attention-based mechanism to dynamically modulate the spatial and temporal receptive fields of the network, allowing it to selectively emphasize informative regions and frames. We train AdaFocus V2 using a novel curriculum learning strategy that gradually increases the difficulty of the training data, promoting the network to learn increasingly complex spatial-temporal patterns. Experiments on four benchmark video recognition datasets demonstrate that AdaFocus V2 achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing methods by an average of 3.2% in terms of accuracy. Notably, AdaFocus V2 reduces the computational cost of video recognition by 25.6% compared to the closest competing approach, making it a promising solution for real-world video analysis applications.

title: TAGPerson: A Target-Aware Generation Pipeline for Person Re-identification
text: Nowadays, real data in person re-identification (ReID) task is facing privacy issues, e.g., the banned dataset DukeMTMC-ReID. Thus it becomes much harder to collect real data for ReID task. Meanwhile, the labor cost of labeling ReID data is still very high and further hinders the development of the ReID research. Therefore, many methods turn to generate synthetic images for ReID algorithms as alternatives instead of real images. However, there is an inevitable domain gap between synthetic and real images. In previous methods, the generation process is based on virtual scenes, and their synthetic training data can not be changed according to different target real scenes automatically. To handle this problem, we propose a novel Target-Aware Generation pipeline to produce synthetic person images, called TAGPerson. Specifically, it involves a parameterized rendering method, where the parameters are controllable and can be adjusted according to target scenes. In TAGPerson, we extract information from target scenes and use them to control our parameterized rendering process to generate target-aware synthetic images, which would hold a smaller gap to the real images in the target domain. In our experiments, our target-aware synthetic images can achieve a much higher performance than the generalized synthetic images on MSMT17, i.e. 47.5% vs. 40.9% for rank-1 accuracy. We will release this toolkit\footnote{\noindent Code is available at \href{ for the ReID community to generate synthetic images at any desired taste.

title: TAGPerson: A Target-Aware Generation Pipeline for Person Re-identification
text: Person re-identification (re-ID) has become a crucial component in various surveillance and forensic applications, where the goal is to associate individuals across non-overlapping camera views. Existing re-ID methods typically rely on learning a shared feature space for all individuals, which can be suboptimal due to the inherent variability in human appearance and pose. To address this limitation, we propose TAGPerson, a novel target-aware generation pipeline that synthesizes personalized features for each individual, effectively capturing their unique characteristics. Our approach leverages a two-stage framework, where a generative adversarial network (GAN) is first employed to generate diverse and realistic person images conditioned on the target identity. Subsequently, a re-ID network is trained to learn a target-aware representation by exploiting the generated images as auxiliary training data. Extensive experiments on popular re-ID benchmarks, including Market-1501 and DukeMTMC-reID, demonstrate the effectiveness of TAGPerson, with significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our approach achieves a 4.3% boost in rank-1 accuracy and a 5.6% increase in mAP on Market-1501, while requiring only a fraction of the training data. The proposed pipeline offers a promising direction for robust person re-ID, particularly in scenarios where limited data is available or high variability in appearance is present.

title: Efficient Quantum Voting with Information-Theoretic Security
text: Ensuring security and integrity of elections constitutes an important challenge with wide-ranging societal implications. Classically, security guarantees can be ensured based on computational complexity, which may be challenged by quantum computers. We show that the use of quantum networks can enable information-theoretic security for the desirable aspects of a distributed voting scheme in a resource-efficient manner. In our approach, ballot information is encoded in quantum states that enable an exponential reduction in communication complexity compared to classical communication. In addition, we provide an efficient and secure anonymous queuing protocol based on a distributed secure sum. As a result, our scheme only requires modest quantum memories with size scaling logarithmically with the number of voters. This intrinsic efficiency together with certain noise-robustness of our protocol paves the way for its physical implementation in realistic quantum networks.

title: Efficient Quantum Voting with Information-Theoretic Security
text: The integrity and security of elections pose a significant challenge with far-reaching societal consequences. While classical security guarantees rely on computational complexity, the advent of quantum computers may undermine these assurances. We demonstrate that leveraging quantum networks can provide information-theoretic security for key aspects of distributed voting systems, achieving this goal with remarkable resource efficiency. By encoding ballot information in quantum states, our approach reduces communication complexity exponentially compared to classical methods. Furthermore, we develop an efficient and secure anonymous queuing protocol based on distributed secure sum, which requires only modest quantum memories that scale logarithmically with the number of voters. The intrinsic efficiency and robustness of our protocol to noise make it a viable candidate for implementation in realistic quantum networks.

title: Robust Convergence in Federated Learning through Label-wise Clustering
text: Non-IID dataset and heterogeneous environment of the local clients are regarded as a major issue in Federated Learning (FL), causing a downturn in the convergence without achieving satisfactory performance. In this paper, we propose a novel Label-wise clustering algorithm that guarantees the trainability among geographically dispersed heterogeneous local clients, by selecting only the local models trained with a dataset that approximates into uniformly distributed class labels, which is likely to obtain faster minimization of the loss and increment the accuracy among the FL network. Through conducting experiments on the suggested six common non-IID scenarios, we empirically show that the vanilla FL aggregation model is incapable of gaining robust convergence generating biased pre-trained local models and drifting the local weights to mislead the trainability in the worst case. Moreover, we quantitatively estimate the expected performance of the local models before training, which offers a global server to select the optimal clients, saving additional computational costs. Ultimately, in order to gain resolution of the non-convergence in such non-IID situations, we design clustering algorithms based on local input class labels, accommodating the diversity and assorting clients that could lead the overall system to attain the swift convergence as global training continues. Our paper shows that proposed Label-wise clustering demonstrates prompt and robust convergence compared to other FL algorithms when local training datasets are non-IID or coexist with IID through multiple experiments.

title: Robust Convergence in Federated Learning through Label-wise Clustering
text: The federated learning (FL) paradigm is often hindered by the non-independently and identically distributed (non-IID) nature of local client datasets and the heterogeneity of client environments, leading to convergence issues and subpar performance. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel label-wise clustering algorithm that ensures trainability among geographically dispersed heterogeneous clients by selectively aggregating local models trained on datasets with approximately uniform class label distributions. This approach is likely to accelerate loss minimization and improve accuracy across the FL network. Through a comprehensive evaluation of six common non-IID scenarios, we demonstrate that the conventional FL aggregation model fails to achieve robust convergence, resulting in biased pre-trained local models and divergent local weights. Moreover, we provide a quantitative estimate of local model performance prior to training, enabling the global server to select optimal clients and reduce computational overhead. By designing clustering algorithms that account for local input class labels, we can accommodate diversity and assort clients, leading to swift convergence as global training progresses. Our experiments show that the proposed label-wise clustering algorithm outperforms other FL algorithms in terms of convergence speed and robustness, even in the presence of both non-IID and IID local training datasets.

title: Nested Nonparametric Instrumental Variable Regression
text: Several causal parameters in short panel data models are functionals of a nested nonparametric instrumental variable regression (nested NPIV). Recent examples include mediated, time varying, and long term treatment effects identified using proxy variables. In econometrics, examples arise in triangular simultaneous equations and hedonic price systems. However, it appears that explicit mean square convergence rates for nested NPIV are unknown, preventing inference on some of these parameters with generic machine learning. A major challenge is compounding ill posedness due to the nested inverse problems. To limit how ill posedness compounds, we introduce two techniques: relative well posedness, and multiple robustness to ill posedness. With these techniques, we provide explicit mean square rates for nested NPIV and efficient inference for recently identified causal parameters. Our nonasymptotic analysis accommodates neural networks, random forests, and reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. It extends to causal functions, e.g. heterogeneous long term treatment effects.

title: Nested Nonparametric Instrumental Variable Regression
text: The estimation of various causal parameters in short panel data models relies on nested nonparametric instrumental variable regression (nested NPIV), encompassing mediated, time-varying, and long-term treatment effects identified through proxy variables. In econometrics, triangular simultaneous equations and hedonic price systems exemplify such applications. Despite this, explicit mean square convergence rates for nested NPIV have remained unknown, hindering inference on these parameters using generic machine learning approaches. The primary obstacle lies in the compounding ill-posedness resulting from the nested inverse problems. To mitigate this issue, we propose two novel techniques: relative well-posedness and multiple robustness to ill-posedness. By leveraging these techniques, we establish explicit mean square rates for nested NPIV and facilitate efficient inference for recently identified causal parameters. Our non-asymptotic analysis encompasses neural networks, random forests, and reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, and extends to causal functions, including heterogeneous long-term treatment effects.

title: Beta-VAE Reproducibility: Challenges and Extensions
text: $β$-VAE is a follow-up technique to variational autoencoders that proposes special weighting of the KL divergence term in the VAE loss to obtain disentangled representations. Unsupervised learning is known to be brittle even on toy datasets and a meaningful, mathematically precise definition of disentanglement remains difficult to find. Here we investigate the original $β$-VAE paper and add evidence to the results previously obtained indicating its lack of reproducibility. We also further expand the experimentation of the models and include further more complex datasets in the analysis. We also implement an FID scoring metric for the $β$-VAE model and conclude a qualitative analysis of the results obtained. We end with a brief discussion on possible future investigations that can be conducted to add more robustness to the claims.

title: Beta-VAE Reproducibility: Challenges and Extensions
text: The Beta-VAE, a popular variant of the Variational Autoencoder, has been widely adopted in representation learning due to its flexibility in balancing reconstruction accuracy and latent space regularization. However, recent studies have raised concerns about the reproducibility of Beta-VAE results, highlighting the need for a systematic investigation. We conduct a large-scale reproducibility study on Beta-VAE, evaluating 15 publicly available implementations across 5 datasets. Our results reveal significant discrepancies in performance, attributed to differences in hyperparameter tuning, optimization algorithms, and architectural variations. We propose a set of extensions, including a novel hyperprior learning scheme and a regularization term, which improve the reproducibility and robustness of Beta-VAE. Our findings provide a more nuanced understanding of the Beta-VAE's strengths and limitations, and offer practical guidelines for its reliable deployment in real-world applications.

title: Multimodal perception for dexterous manipulation
text: Humans usually perceive the world in a multimodal way that vision, touch, sound are utilised to understand surroundings from various dimensions. These senses are combined together to achieve a synergistic effect where the learning is more effectively than using each sense separately. For robotics, vision and touch are two key senses for the dexterous manipulation. Vision usually gives us apparent features like shape, color, and the touch provides local information such as friction, texture, etc. Due to the complementary properties between visual and tactile senses, it is desirable for us to combine vision and touch for a synergistic perception and manipulation. Many researches have been investigated about multimodal perception such as cross-modal learning, 3D reconstruction, multimodal translation with vision and touch. Specifically, we propose a cross-modal sensory data generation framework for the translation between vision and touch, which is able to generate realistic pseudo data. By using this cross-modal translation method, it is desirable for us to make up inaccessible data, helping us to learn the object's properties from different views. Recently, the attention mechanism becomes a popular method either in visual perception or in tactile perception. We propose a spatio-temporal attention model for tactile texture recognition, which takes both spatial features and time dimension into consideration. Our proposed method not only pays attention to the salient features in each spatial feature, but also models the temporal correlation in the through the time. The obvious improvement proves the efficiency of our selective attention mechanism. The spatio-temporal attention method has potential in many applications such as grasping, recognition, and multimodal perception.

title: Multimodal perception for dexterous manipulation
text: Dexterous manipulation of objects is a hallmark of human intelligence, requiring the seamless integration of visual, tactile, and proprioceptive feedback. Despite significant advances in robotic arms and grippers, current systems struggle to generalize to novel objects and scenarios, often relying on simplified models or explicit programming. We propose a multimodal perception framework that leverages the complementary strengths of vision, touch, and proprioception to enable dexterous manipulation in unstructured environments. Our approach combines a high-resolution tactile sensor with a stereo camera and proprioceptive joint encoders to create a rich, multimodal representation of the manipulation scene. We develop a novel, hierarchical neural network architecture that integrates these modalities, learning to predict object properties, grasp affordances, and manipulation outcomes from large-scale, real-world datasets. Through extensive experiments on a robotic arm platform, we demonstrate significant improvements in grasping and manipulation success rates, particularly for novel, unseen objects. Notably, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art, vision-only methods by 23.4% on a challenging grasping benchmark, while also exhibiting improved robustness to sensor noise and occlusion. Furthermore, we show that our multimodal framework enables the robot to adapt to new objects and scenarios through online learning, achieving a 45.1% improvement in manipulation success rate after only 50 trials. These results suggest that multimodal perception is a crucial component of dexterous manipulation, and that our approach provides a promising foundation for the development of more capable, autonomous robotic systems.

title: DeepAdversaries: Examining the Robustness of Deep Learning Models for Galaxy Morphology Classification
text: With increased adoption of supervised deep learning methods for processing and analysis of cosmological survey data, the assessment of data perturbation effects (that can naturally occur in the data processing and analysis pipelines) and the development of methods that increase model robustness are increasingly important. In the context of morphological classification of galaxies, we study the effects of perturbations in imaging data. In particular, we examine the consequences of using neural networks when training on baseline data and testing on perturbed data. We consider perturbations associated with two primary sources: 1) increased observational noise as represented by higher levels of Poisson noise and 2) data processing noise incurred by steps such as image compression or telescope errors as represented by one-pixel adversarial attacks. We also test the efficacy of domain adaptation techniques in mitigating the perturbation-driven errors. We use classification accuracy, latent space visualizations, and latent space distance to assess model robustness. Without domain adaptation, we find that processing pixel-level errors easily flip the classification into an incorrect class and that higher observational noise makes the model trained on low-noise data unable to classify galaxy morphologies. On the other hand, we show that training with domain adaptation improves model robustness and mitigates the effects of these perturbations, improving the classification accuracy by 23% on data with higher observational noise. Domain adaptation also increases by a factor of ~2.3 the latent space distance between the baseline and the incorrectly classified one-pixel perturbed image, making the model more robust to inadvertent perturbations.

title: DeepAdversaries: Examining the Robustness of Deep Learning Models for Galaxy Morphology Classification
text: As the application of supervised deep learning methods to cosmological survey data becomes more widespread, it is essential to investigate the impact of data perturbations on model performance and develop strategies to enhance model robustness. This study focuses on the effects of perturbations in imaging data on morphological galaxy classification. We examine the consequences of training neural networks on baseline data and testing on perturbed data, considering two primary sources of perturbations: increased observational noise, simulated by augmenting Poisson noise levels, and data processing noise, modeled using one-pixel adversarial attacks. To mitigate perturbation-driven errors, we evaluate the effectiveness of domain adaptation techniques. Our assessment metrics include classification accuracy, latent space visualizations, and latent space distance. Without domain adaptation, our results show that processing pixel-level errors can readily induce misclassification, and higher observational noise renders models trained on low-noise data incapable of accurately classifying galaxy morphologies. In contrast, we demonstrate that domain adaptation significantly improves model robustness, yielding a 23% increase in classification accuracy on data with higher observational noise. Furthermore, domain adaptation enhances the latent space distance between the baseline and incorrectly classified one-pixel perturbed images by a factor of approximately 2.3, thereby increasing the model's resilience to inadvertent perturbations.

title: Time-Incremental Learning from Data Using Temporal Logics
text: Real-time and human-interpretable decision-making in cyber-physical systems is a significant but challenging task, which usually requires predictions of possible future events from limited data. In this paper, we introduce a time-incremental learning framework: given a dataset of labeled signal traces with a common time horizon, we propose a method to predict the label of a signal that is received incrementally over time, referred to as prefix signal. Prefix signals are the signals that are being observed as they are generated, and their time length is shorter than the common horizon of signals. We present a novel decision-tree based approach to generate a finite number of Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications from the given dataset, and construct a predictor based on them. Each STL specification, as a binary classifier of time-series data, captures the temporal properties of the dataset over time. The predictor is constructed by assigning time-variant weights to the STL formulas. The weights are learned by using neural networks, with the goal of minimizing the misclassification rate for the prefix signals defined over the given dataset. The learned predictor is used to predict the label of a prefix signal, by computing the weighted sum of the robustness of the prefix signal with respect to each STL formula. The effectiveness and classification performance of our algorithm are evaluated on an urban-driving and a naval-surveillance case studies.

title: Time-Incremental Learning from Data Using Temporal Logics
text: Real-time decision-making in cyber-physical systems poses a significant challenge, particularly when predicting future events from limited data. To address this, we develop a time-incremental learning framework that leverages a dataset of labeled signal traces with a common time horizon. Our approach focuses on predicting the label of a signal received incrementally over time, referred to as a prefix signal, which is characterized by its shorter time length compared to the common horizon. We propose a novel decision-tree-based method to generate a finite set of Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications from the dataset, each capturing the temporal properties of the data over time. These STL specifications serve as binary classifiers of time-series data. By constructing a predictor based on these specifications, we assign time-variant weights learned through neural networks to minimize the misclassification rate for prefix signals defined over the dataset. The predictor's performance is evaluated by computing the weighted sum of the robustness of the prefix signal with respect to each STL formula. We demonstrate the effectiveness and classification performance of our algorithm through two case studies: urban driving and naval surveillance. Our results highlight the potential of this approach for real-time, human-interpretable decision-making in cyber-physical systems.

title: Ensemble Recognition in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces through Aggregated Measurements
text: In this paper, we study the problem of learning dynamical properties of ensemble systems from their collective behaviors using statistical approaches in reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Specifically, we provide a framework to identify and cluster multiple ensemble systems through computing the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between their aggregated measurements in an RKHS, without any prior knowledge of the system dynamics of ensembles. Then, leveraging the gradient flow of the newly proposed notion of aggregated Markov parameters, we present a systematic framework to recognize and identify an ensemble systems using their linear approximations. Finally, we demonstrate that the proposed approaches can be extended to cluster multiple unknown ensembles in RKHS using their aggregated measurements. Numerical experiments show that our approach is reliable and robust to ensembles with different types of system dynamics.

title: Ensemble Recognition in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces through Aggregated Measurements
text: Recognition tasks in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) often rely on individual measurements, which can be noisy or incomplete. We propose an ensemble recognition framework that aggregates multiple measurements to improve the accuracy and robustness of classification. By leveraging the reproducing property of RKHS, we develop a novel aggregation scheme that combines the strengths of individual measurements. Our approach is theoretically grounded in the theory of RKHS and is shown to be consistent and asymptotically efficient. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, achieving state-of-the-art performance in recognizing patterns in high-dimensional data. Furthermore, our approach is computationally efficient and can be parallelized, making it scalable to large datasets. The proposed framework has implications for various applications, including computer vision, natural language processing, and bioinformatics.

title: Improving Prediction of Cognitive Performance using Deep Neural Networks in Sparse Data
text: Cognition in midlife is an important predictor of age-related mental decline and statistical models that predict cognitive performance can be useful for predicting decline. However, existing models struggle to capture complex relationships between physical, sociodemographic, psychological and mental health factors that effect cognition. Using data from an observational, cohort study, Midlife in the United States (MIDUS), we modeled a large number of variables to predict executive function and episodic memory measures. We used cross-sectional and longitudinal outcomes with varying sparsity, or amount of missing data. Deep neural network (DNN) models consistently ranked highest in all of the cognitive performance prediction tasks, as assessed with root mean squared error (RMSE) on out-of-sample data. RMSE differences between DNN and other model types were statistically significant (T(8) = -3.70; p < 0.05). The interaction effect between model type and sparsity was significant (F(9)=59.20; p < 0.01), indicating the success of DNNs can partly be attributed to their robustness and ability to model hierarchical relationships between health-related factors. Our findings underscore the potential of neural networks to model clinical datasets and allow better understanding of factors that lead to cognitive decline.

title: Improving Prediction of Cognitive Performance using Deep Neural Networks in Sparse Data
text: Cognitive performance prediction is a crucial task in various fields, including education, neuroscience, and human-computer interaction. Despite recent advances, existing approaches struggle to accurately predict cognitive performance, especially when dealing with sparse data. This limitation is primarily attributed to the lack of effective feature extraction and modeling techniques. To address this challenge, we propose a novel deep neural network architecture that leverages sparse autoencoders and graph convolutional networks to improve cognitive performance prediction. Our approach is designed to effectively capture complex patterns in sparse data and incorporate domain knowledge from cognitive science. We evaluate our method on a large-scale dataset of cognitive tasks and demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, achieving a mean absolute error reduction of 23.4% and a Pearson correlation coefficient increase of 0.17. Furthermore, we conduct an ablation study to investigate the contribution of each component in our architecture, providing insights into the effectiveness of our approach. Our findings have important implications for the development of personalized cognitive training systems and highlight the potential of deep learning techniques in cognitive performance prediction.

title: FRIDA -- Generative Feature Replay for Incremental Domain Adaptation
text: We tackle the novel problem of incremental unsupervised domain adaptation (IDA) in this paper. We assume that a labeled source domain and different unlabeled target domains are incrementally observed with the constraint that data corresponding to the current domain is only available at a time. The goal is to preserve the accuracies for all the past domains while generalizing well for the current domain. The IDA setup suffers due to the abrupt differences among the domains and the unavailability of past data including the source domain. Inspired by the notion of generative feature replay, we propose a novel framework called Feature Replay based Incremental Domain Adaptation (FRIDA) which leverages a new incremental generative adversarial network (GAN) called domain-generic auxiliary classification GAN (DGAC-GAN) for producing domain-specific feature representations seamlessly. For domain alignment, we propose a simple extension of the popular domain adversarial neural network (DANN) called DANN-IB which encourages discriminative domain-invariant and task-relevant feature learning. Experimental results on Office-Home, Office-CalTech, and DomainNet datasets confirm that FRIDA maintains superior stability-plasticity trade-off than the literature.

title: FRIDA -- Generative Feature Replay for Incremental Domain Adaptation
text: Incremental unsupervised domain adaptation (IDA) poses a unique challenge when a labeled source domain and multiple unlabeled target domains are observed sequentially, with each domain's data available only at a time. The primary objective is to preserve performance on all previous domains while adapting to the current domain. The IDA setup is complicated by the abrupt domain shifts and the unavailability of past data, including the source domain. Building upon the concept of generative feature replay, we introduce Feature Replay based Incremental Domain Adaptation (FRIDA), a novel framework that utilizes a domain-generic auxiliary classification GAN (DGAC-GAN) to generate domain-specific feature representations incrementally. To facilitate domain alignment, we propose DANN-IB, a simple extension of the popular domain adversarial neural network (DANN), which promotes discriminative and task-relevant feature learning that is both domain-invariant and adaptive. The efficacy of FRIDA is demonstrated through experiments on the Office-Home, Office-CalTech, and DomainNet datasets, showcasing its ability to maintain a superior stability-plasticity trade-off compared to existing methods.

title: Quantum Merkle Trees
text: Committing to information is a central task in cryptography, where a party (typically called a prover) stores a piece of information (e.g., a bit string) with the promise of not changing it. This information can be accessed by another party (typically called the verifier), who can later learn the information and verify that it was not meddled with. Merkle trees are a well-known construction for doing so in a succinct manner, in which the verifier can learn any part of the information by receiving a short proof from the honest prover. Despite its significance in classical cryptography, there was no quantum analog of the Merkle tree. A direct generalization using the Quantum Random Oracle Model (QROM) does not seem to be secure. In this work, we propose the quantum Merkle tree. It is based on what we call the Quantum Haar Random Oracle Model (QHROM). In QHROM, both the prover and the verifier have access to a Haar random quantum oracle $G$ and its inverse. Using the quantum Merkle tree, we propose a succinct quantum argument for the Gap-$k$-Local-Hamiltonian problem. Assuming the Quantum PCP conjecture is true, this succinct argument extends to all of QMA. This work raises a number of interesting open research problems.

title: Quantum Merkle Trees
text: The fundamental cryptographic task of committing to information, wherein a prover stores a piece of data with the guarantee of its integrity, is crucial in various cryptographic protocols. In this setting, a verifier can access the committed information and verify its authenticity at a later stage. Merkle trees provide a succinct solution for this problem in the classical realm, enabling the verifier to learn any part of the information via a short proof from the honest prover. However, a quantum analogue of Merkle trees has been elusive, and a direct extension using the Quantum Random Oracle Model (QROM) appears to be insecure. We overcome this challenge by introducing the quantum Merkle tree, which relies on the Quantum Haar Random Oracle Model (QHROM). In QHROM, both the prover and verifier have access to a Haar random quantum oracle G and its inverse. Our quantum Merkle tree construction gives rise to a succinct quantum argument for the Gap-k-Local-Hamiltonian problem, and assuming the Quantum PCP conjecture, this argument extends to all of QMA. This work opens up several intriguing avenues for future research.

title: Brain Tumor Classification by Cascaded Multiscale Multitask Learning Framework Based on Feature Aggregation
text: Brain tumor analysis in MRI images is a significant and challenging issue because misdiagnosis can lead to death. Diagnosis and evaluation of brain tumors in the early stages increase the probability of successful treatment. However, the complexity and variety of tumors, shapes, and locations make their segmentation and classification complex. In this regard, numerous researchers have proposed brain tumor segmentation and classification methods. This paper presents an approach that simultaneously segments and classifies brain tumors in MRI images using a framework that contains MRI image enhancement and tumor region detection. Eventually, a network based on a multitask learning approach is proposed. Subjective and objective results indicate that the segmentation and classification results based on evaluation metrics are better or comparable to the state-of-the-art.

title: Brain Tumor Classification by Cascaded Multiscale Multitask Learning Framework Based on Feature Aggregation
text: The accurate classification of brain tumors from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is crucial for effective treatment planning and patient outcomes. Existing approaches often struggle to capture the inherent heterogeneity and complexity of brain tumors, leading to suboptimal performance. This work proposes a novel cascaded multiscale multitask learning framework that integrates feature aggregation to improve brain tumor classification. Our approach leverages a hierarchical feature extraction strategy, combining local and global features from multiple scales, and jointly optimizes multiple related tasks to improve robustness. Experimental results on a large MRI dataset demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average accuracy of 93.5% and a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 0.87. Our framework offers a promising solution for reliable brain tumor classification, enabling more accurate diagnosis and treatment.

title: Multi-Head Deep Metric Learning Using Global and Local Representations
text: Deep Metric Learning (DML) models often require strong local and global representations, however, effective integration of local and global features in DML model training is a challenge. DML models are often trained with specific loss functions, including pairwise-based and proxy-based losses. The pairwise-based loss functions leverage rich semantic relations among data points, however, they often suffer from slow convergence during DML model training. On the other hand, the proxy-based loss functions often lead to significant speedups in convergence during training, while the rich relations among data points are often not fully explored by the proxy-based losses. In this paper, we propose a novel DML approach to address these challenges. The proposed DML approach makes use of a hybrid loss by integrating the pairwise-based and the proxy-based loss functions to leverage rich data-to-data relations as well as fast convergence. Furthermore, the proposed DML approach utilizes both global and local features to obtain rich representations in DML model training. Finally, we also use the second-order attention for feature enhancement to improve accurate and efficient retrieval. In our experiments, we extensively evaluated the proposed DML approach on four public benchmarks, and the experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieved state-of-the-art performance on all benchmarks.

title: Multi-Head Deep Metric Learning Using Global and Local Representations
text: The success of Deep Metric Learning (DML) models hinges on the effective integration of local and global representations, yet combining these features during training poses a significant challenge. Traditional pairwise-based and proxy-based loss functions have been employed, each with its limitations: pairwise-based losses capture rich semantic relationships among data points but are plagued by slow convergence, while proxy-based losses expedite convergence at the cost of underutilizing these relationships. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hybrid DML approach that synergistically combines pairwise-based and proxy-based losses, thereby leveraging both data-to-data relations and fast convergence. By incorporating both global and local features, our approach yields rich representations during training. Additionally, we employ second-order attention for feature enhancement to improve the accuracy and efficiency of retrieval. Extensive experiments on four public benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance on all benchmarks with notable improvements over existing methods.

title: 360° Optical Flow using Tangent Images
text: Omnidirectional 360° images have found many promising and exciting applications in computer vision, robotics and other fields, thanks to their increasing affordability, portability and their 360° field of view. The most common format for storing, processing and visualising 360° images is equirectangular projection (ERP). However, the distortion introduced by the nonlinear mapping from 360° image to ERP image is still a barrier that holds back ERP images from being used as easily as conventional perspective images. This is especially relevant when estimating 360° optical flow, as the distortions need to be mitigated appropriately. In this paper, we propose a 360° optical flow method based on tangent images. Our method leverages gnomonic projection to locally convert ERP images to perspective images, and uniformly samples the ERP image by projection to a cubemap and regular icosahedron vertices, to incrementally refine the estimated 360° flow fields even in the presence of large rotations. Our experiments demonstrate the benefits of our proposed method both quantitatively and qualitatively.

title: 360° Optical Flow using Tangent Images
text: Estimating 360° optical flow from omnidirectional images is a challenging task due to the unique projection model and self-occlusions inherent to these representations. Existing approaches typically rely on spherical or cylindrical projections, which can lead to distortion and information loss. We propose a novel method that leverages tangent images, a recently introduced representation that preserves the original image resolution and enables efficient processing. Our approach first extracts tangent images from the input omnidirectional images and then computes optical flow using a deep neural network. The network is trained on a large synthetic dataset generated using a custom-built simulator, which models various scenarios and camera motions. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches in terms of average endpoint error and angular error. Furthermore, our method achieves real-time performance on high-resolution images, making it suitable for various computer vision applications, including robotics, surveillance, and virtual reality.

title: Adaptive Client Sampling in Federated Learning via Online Learning with Bandit Feedback
text: Due to the high cost of communication, federated learning (FL) systems need to sample a subset of clients that are involved in each round of training. As a result, client sampling plays an important role in FL systems as it affects the convergence rate of optimization algorithms used to train machine learning models. Despite its importance, there is limited work on how to sample clients effectively. In this paper, we cast client sampling as an online learning task with bandit feedback, which we solve with an online stochastic mirror descent (OSMD) algorithm designed to minimize the sampling variance. We then theoretically show how our sampling method can improve the convergence speed of federated optimization algorithms over the widely used uniform sampling. Through both simulated and real data experiments, we empirically illustrate the advantages of the proposed client sampling algorithm over uniform sampling and existing online learning-based sampling strategies. The proposed adaptive sampling procedure is applicable beyond the FL problem studied here and can be used to improve the performance of stochastic optimization procedures such as stochastic gradient descent and stochastic coordinate descent.

title: Adaptive Client Sampling in Federated Learning via Online Learning with Bandit Feedback
text: Federated learning has emerged as a prominent paradigm for collaborative model training across decentralized devices, preserving data privacy and mitigating communication overhead. However, the inherent heterogeneity in client resources and data distributions often leads to inefficient client selection, resulting in suboptimal model performance and convergence. In this context, adaptive client sampling strategies have been proposed to dynamically select the most informative clients for training. Despite their promise, existing methods rely on simplistic heuristics or offline optimization, neglecting the online nature of federated learning. We propose an adaptive client sampling framework that leverages online learning with bandit feedback to dynamically adapt to the changing client population and data distributions. Our approach models the client selection problem as a multi-armed bandit, where each client is an arm with unknown reward distribution. We develop an online algorithm that balances exploration and exploitation, achieving a regret bound of O(T^2/3) under mild assumptions. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 23% improvement in model accuracy while reducing communication overhead by 34%.

title: Closer Look at the Transferability of Adversarial Examples: How They Fool Different Models Differently
text: Deep neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples (AEs), which have adversarial transferability: AEs generated for the source model can mislead another (target) model's predictions. However, the transferability has not been understood in terms of to which class target model's predictions were misled (i.e., class-aware transferability). In this paper, we differentiate the cases in which a target model predicts the same wrong class as the source model ("same mistake") or a different wrong class ("different mistake") to analyze and provide an explanation of the mechanism. We find that (1) AEs tend to cause same mistakes, which correlates with "non-targeted transferability"; however, (2) different mistakes occur even between similar models, regardless of the perturbation size. Furthermore, we present evidence that the difference between same mistakes and different mistakes can be explained by non-robust features, predictive but human-uninterpretable patterns: different mistakes occur when non-robust features in AEs are used differently by models. Non-robust features can thus provide consistent explanations for the class-aware transferability of AEs.

title: Closer Look at the Transferability of Adversarial Examples: How They Fool Different Models Differently
text: The vulnerability of deep neural networks to adversarial examples has sparked widespread concern, yet the transferability of these examples across different models remains poorly understood. While prior work has demonstrated that adversarial examples can be transferable, the underlying mechanisms driving this phenomenon are unclear. This study investigates the transferability of adversarial examples, focusing on how they deceive different models differently. We generate adversarial examples using three state-of-the-art attack methods and evaluate their transferability across seven diverse neural network architectures. Our analysis reveals that the transferability of adversarial examples is largely dependent on the model's decision boundary and the attack method used. Specifically, we find that attacks exploiting model-specific vulnerabilities are less transferable, whereas those targeting more generalizable features are more likely to succeed across different models. Our results provide new insights into the nature of adversarial examples, highlighting the need for more robust and model-agnostic defense strategies.

title: Super-Efficient Super Resolution for Fast Adversarial Defense at the Edge
text: Autonomous systems are highly vulnerable to a variety of adversarial attacks on Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). Training-free model-agnostic defenses have recently gained popularity due to their speed, ease of deployment, and ability to work across many DNNs. To this end, a new technique has emerged for mitigating attacks on image classification DNNs, namely, preprocessing adversarial images using super resolution -- upscaling low-quality inputs into high-resolution images. This defense requires running both image classifiers and super resolution models on constrained autonomous systems. However, super resolution incurs a heavy computational cost. Therefore, in this paper, we investigate the following question: Does the robustness of image classifiers suffer if we use tiny super resolution models? To answer this, we first review a recent work called Super-Efficient Super Resolution (SESR) that achieves similar or better image quality than prior art while requiring 2x to 330x fewer Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) operations. We demonstrate that despite being orders of magnitude smaller than existing models, SESR achieves the same level of robustness as significantly larger networks. Finally, we estimate end-to-end performance of super resolution-based defenses on a commercial Arm Ethos-U55 micro-NPU. Our findings show that SESR achieves nearly 3x higher FPS than a baseline while achieving similar robustness.

title: Super-Efficient Super Resolution for Fast Adversarial Defense at the Edge
text: The susceptibility of autonomous systems to adversarial attacks on Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) has spurred the development of training-free, model-agnostic defenses that offer rapid deployment and versatility across multiple DNNs. A promising technique for mitigating attacks on image classification DNNs involves preprocessing adversarial images using super resolution, which upscales low-quality inputs into high-resolution images. However, this defense approach incurs a substantial computational cost, particularly when running both image classifiers and super resolution models on resource-constrained autonomous systems. This paper examines the trade-off between model size and robustness in super resolution-based defenses, asking whether the use of tiny super resolution models compromises the robustness of image classifiers. We build upon recent work on Super-Efficient Super Resolution (SESR), which achieves comparable or superior image quality to prior art while reducing Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) operations by 2x to 330x. Our results demonstrate that SESR, despite being orders of magnitude smaller than existing models, maintains the same level of robustness as larger networks. Furthermore, we evaluate the end-to-end performance of super resolution-based defenses on a commercial Arm Ethos-U55 micro-NPU, showing that SESR achieves nearly 3x higher frames per second (FPS) than the baseline while maintaining similar robustness.

title: Federated Learning for Cross-block Oil-water Layer Identification
text: Cross-block oil-water layer(OWL) identification is essential for petroleum development. Traditional methods are greatly affected by subjective factors due to depending mainly on the human experience. AI-based methods have promoted the development of OWL identification. However, because of the significant geological differences across blocks and the severe long-tailed distribution(class imbalanced), the identification effects of existing artificial intelligence(AI) models are limited. In this paper, we address this limitation by proposing a dynamic fusion-based federated learning(FL) for OWL identification. To overcome geological differences, we propose a dynamic weighted strategy to fuse models and train a general OWL identification model. In addition, an F1 score-based re-weighting scheme is designed and a novel loss function is derived theoretically to solve the data long-tailed problem. Further, a geological knowledge-based mask-attention mechanism is proposed to enhance model feature extraction. To our best knowledge, this is the first work to identify OWL using FL. We evaluate the proposed approach with an actual well logging dataset from the oil field and a public 3W dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly out-performs other AI methods.

title: Federated Learning for Cross-block Oil-water Layer Identification
text: Accurate cross-block oil-water layer (OWL) identification is crucial for efficient petroleum development, but traditional methods are often hindered by subjective biases stemming from human experience. The advent of AI-based methods has improved OWL identification, yet existing models struggle to generalize across blocks due to significant geological differences and severe class imbalance. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel dynamic fusion-based federated learning (FL) framework for OWL identification. This approach incorporates a dynamic weighted strategy to fuse models and train a generalizable OWL identification model, thereby mitigating geological differences. Furthermore, we design an F1 score-based re-weighting scheme and derive a novel loss function to address the long-tailed distribution problem. A geological knowledge-based mask-attention mechanism is also introduced to enhance feature extraction. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first FL-based OWL identification approach. Experimental evaluation using real-world well logging and public 3W datasets demonstrates that our approach significantly outperforms existing AI methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance in OWL identification.

title: Feature-context driven Federated Meta-Learning for Rare Disease Prediction
text: Millions of patients suffer from rare diseases around the world. However, the samples of rare diseases are much smaller than those of common diseases. In addition, due to the sensitivity of medical data, hospitals are usually reluctant to share patient information for data fusion citing privacy concerns. These challenges make it difficult for traditional AI models to extract rare disease features for the purpose of disease prediction. In this paper, we overcome this limitation by proposing a novel approach for rare disease prediction based on federated meta-learning. To improve the prediction accuracy of rare diseases, we design an attention-based meta-learning (ATML) approach which dynamically adjusts the attention to different tasks according to the measured training effect of base learners. Additionally, a dynamic-weight based fusion strategy is proposed to further improve the accuracy of federated learning, which dynamically selects clients based on the accuracy of each local model. Experiments show that with as few as five shots, our approach out-performs the original federated meta-learning algorithm in accuracy and speed. Compared with each hospital's local model, the proposed model's average prediction accuracy increased by 13.28%.
