title: Feature-context driven Federated Meta-Learning for Rare Disease Prediction
text: Rare diseases pose significant challenges for machine learning models due to their inherent rarity, leading to limited and imbalanced data availability. Federated learning has emerged as a promising approach to address this issue by leveraging decentralized data from multiple sources. However, existing federated learning methods often fail to capture the complex relationships between features and context in rare disease data. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel feature-context driven federated meta-learning framework for rare disease prediction. Our approach integrates feature extraction, context-aware modeling, and meta-learning to adapt to new, unseen diseases with limited labeled data. We evaluate our method on a real-world rare disease dataset and demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art federated learning and meta-learning baselines, achieving an average AUC-ROC of 0.85 across five rare disease categories. Notably, our approach exhibits robustness to class imbalance and outperforms traditional machine learning methods by up to 15%. Our results have important implications for rare disease diagnosis and personalized medicine, highlighting the potential of federated meta-learning in harnessing decentralized data for improved disease prediction.

title: Adaptivity and Non-stationarity: Problem-dependent Dynamic Regret for Online Convex Optimization
text: We investigate online convex optimization in non-stationary environments and choose dynamic regret as the performance measure, defined as the difference between cumulative loss incurred by the online algorithm and that of any feasible comparator sequence. Let $T$ be the time horizon and $P_T$ be the path length that essentially reflects the non-stationarity of environments, the state-of-the-art dynamic regret is $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T(1+P_T)})$. Although this bound is proved to be minimax optimal for convex functions, in this paper, we demonstrate that it is possible to further enhance the guarantee for some easy problem instances, particularly when online functions are smooth. Specifically, we introduce novel online algorithms that can exploit smoothness and replace the dependence on $T$ in dynamic regret with problem-dependent quantities: the variation in gradients of loss functions, the cumulative loss of the comparator sequence, and the minimum of these two terms. These quantities are at most $\mathcal{O}(T)$ while could be much smaller in benign environments. Therefore, our results are adaptive to the intrinsic difficulty of the problem, since the bounds are tighter than existing results for easy problems and meanwhile safeguard the same rate in the worst case. Notably, our proposed algorithms can achieve favorable dynamic regret with only one gradient per iteration, sharing the same gradient query complexity as the static regret minimization methods. To accomplish this, we introduce the collaborative online ensemble framework. The proposed framework employs a two-layer online ensemble to handle non-stationarity, and uses optimistic online learning and further introduces crucial correction terms to enable effective collaboration within the meta-base two layers, thereby attaining adaptivity. We believe the framework can be useful for broader problems.

title: Adaptivity and Non-stationarity: Problem-dependent Dynamic Regret for Online Convex Optimization
text: The dynamic regret metric has emerged as a crucial performance measure for online convex optimization algorithms in non-stationary environments, where the underlying problem instance changes over time. However, existing dynamic regret bounds typically rely on strong assumptions about the problem's variability, such as a fixed number of breakpoints or a known upper bound on the total variation. In many real-world applications, these assumptions are unrealistic, and the algorithm's adaptivity to the unknown problem variation becomes a critical aspect. We introduce a novel, problem-dependent dynamic regret metric that captures the algorithm's ability to adapt to the underlying non-stationarity. Our approach leverages the local norm of the comparator sequence, which allows us to decouple the algorithm's performance from the problem's variability. We propose a novel online algorithm, Adaptive Gradient (AG), that exploits this new metric to achieve problem-dependent dynamic regret bounds. AG dynamically adjusts its step-size and regularization based on the observed local norm, enabling it to adapt to the changing problem landscape. Our theoretical analysis establishes that AG achieves a near-optimal problem-dependent dynamic regret bound, which scales with the local norm of the comparator sequence. We further demonstrate the efficacy of AG through an extensive set of experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its adaptivity to various types of non-stationarity. Notably, AG outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in scenarios with unknown or time-varying problem variation. Our work provides a significant step towards developing online convex optimization algorithms that can effectively adapt to complex, real-world environments.

title: On the Overlooked Significance of Underutilized Contextual Features in Recent News Recommendation Models
text: Personalized news recommendation aims to provide attractive articles for readers by predicting their likelihood of clicking on a certain article. To accurately predict this probability, plenty of studies have been proposed that actively utilize content features of articles, such as words, categories, or entities. However, we observed that the articles' contextual features, such as CTR (click-through-rate), popularity, or freshness, were either neglected or underutilized recently. To prove that this is the case, we conducted an extensive comparison between recent deep-learning models and naive contextual models that we devised and surprisingly discovered that the latter easily outperforms the former. Furthermore, our analysis showed that the recent tendency to apply overly sophisticated deep-learning operations to contextual features was actually hindering the recommendation performance. From this knowledge, we design a purposefully simple contextual module that can boost the previous news recommendation models by a large margin.

title: On the Overlooked Significance of Underutilized Contextual Features in Recent News Recommendation Models
text: Predicting the likelihood of a user engaging with a news article is a crucial aspect of personalized news recommendation systems. While numerous studies have leveraged article content features, such as words, categories, and entities, to improve prediction accuracy, contextual features like click-through rate, popularity, and freshness have been largely overlooked or underutilized in recent years. Our comprehensive comparative analysis reveals that naive contextual models outperform state-of-the-art deep learning models, suggesting that the complexity of deep learning operations may actually hinder recommendation performance. This finding is attributed to the tendency to over-engineer contextual features, which can lead to decreased performance. By designing a deliberately simple contextual module, we demonstrate a significant boost in performance, highlighting the importance of contextual features in news recommendation systems.

title: Variational Learning for the Inverted Beta-Liouville Mixture Model and Its Application to Text Categorization
text: The finite invert Beta-Liouville mixture model (IBLMM) has recently gained some attention due to its positive data modeling capability. Under the conventional variational inference (VI) framework, the analytically tractable solution to the optimization of the variational posterior distribution cannot be obtained, since the variational object function involves evaluation of intractable moments. With the recently proposed extended variational inference (EVI) framework, a new function is proposed to replace the original variational object function in order to avoid intractable moment computation, so that the analytically tractable solution of the IBLMM can be derived in an elegant way. The good performance of the proposed approach is demonstrated by experiments with both synthesized data and a real-world application namely text categorization.

title: Variational Learning for the Inverted Beta-Liouville Mixture Model and Its Application to Text Categorization
text: The inverted beta-Liouville mixture model is a powerful probabilistic framework for modeling complex distributions, but its inference remains a challenging task. We propose a variational learning approach to approximate the posterior distribution of the model parameters, leveraging a novel evidence lower bound that incorporates a beta-Liouville prior. Our method enables efficient inference and learning of the model from data. We apply our approach to text categorization, where the inverted beta-Liouville mixture model is used to capture the underlying topic structures. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance in terms of topic coherence and document classification accuracy. Furthermore, our approach provides interpretable results, allowing for the extraction of meaningful topics and their relationships.

title: DeepHAM: A Global Solution Method for Heterogeneous Agent Models with Aggregate Shocks
text: An efficient, reliable, and interpretable global solution method, the Deep learning-based algorithm for Heterogeneous Agent Models (DeepHAM), is proposed for solving high dimensional heterogeneous agent models with aggregate shocks. The state distribution is approximately represented by a set of optimal generalized moments. Deep neural networks are used to approximate the value and policy functions, and the objective is optimized over directly simulated paths. In addition to being an accurate global solver, this method has three additional features. First, it is computationally efficient in solving complex heterogeneous agent models, and it does not suffer from the curse of dimensionality. Second, it provides a general and interpretable representation of the distribution over individual states, which is crucial in addressing the classical question of whether and how heterogeneity matters in macroeconomics. Third, it solves the constrained efficiency problem as easily as it solves the competitive equilibrium, which opens up new possibilities for studying optimal monetary and fiscal policies in heterogeneous agent models with aggregate shocks.

title: DeepHAM: A Global Solution Method for Heterogeneous Agent Models with Aggregate Shocks
text: This study presents the Deep learning-based algorithm for Heterogeneous Agent Models (DeepHAM), a novel solution method that efficiently and reliably solves high-dimensional heterogeneous agent models subject to aggregate shocks. By approximating the state distribution using a set of optimal generalized moments, DeepHAM leverages deep neural networks to estimate value and policy functions, optimizing the objective over directly simulated paths. Notably, this approach offers three key advantages. It achieves computational efficiency in solving complex models, circumventing the curse of dimensionality. Additionally, it provides a general and interpretable representation of the distribution over individual states, shedding light on the role of heterogeneity in macroeconomics. Furthermore, DeepHAM can seamlessly solve constrained efficiency problems, facilitating the exploration of optimal monetary and fiscal policies in heterogeneous agent models with aggregate shocks.

title: Background-aware Classification Activation Map for Weakly Supervised Object Localization
text: Weakly supervised object localization (WSOL) relaxes the requirement of dense annotations for object localization by using image-level classification masks to supervise its learning process. However, current WSOL methods suffer from excessive activation of background locations and need post-processing to obtain the localization mask. This paper attributes these issues to the unawareness of background cues, and propose the background-aware classification activation map (B-CAM) to simultaneously learn localization scores of both object and background with only image-level labels. In our B-CAM, two image-level features, aggregated by pixel-level features of potential background and object locations, are used to purify the object feature from the object-related background and to represent the feature of the pure-background sample, respectively. Then based on these two features, both the object classifier and the background classifier are learned to determine the binary object localization mask. Our B-CAM can be trained in end-to-end manner based on a proposed stagger classification loss, which not only improves the objects localization but also suppresses the background activation. Experiments show that our B-CAM outperforms one-stage WSOL methods on the CUB-200, OpenImages and VOC2012 datasets.

title: Background-aware Classification Activation Map for Weakly Supervised Object Localization
text: Weakly supervised object localization, which aims to identify object locations using only image-level labels, remains a challenging task due to the inherent ambiguity of the annotation. Existing methods often struggle to distinguish between object and background regions, leading to inaccurate localization results. To address this issue, we propose a novel Background-aware Classification Activation Map (BCAM) approach that effectively disentangles object and background features. Our method leverages a two-stream architecture, where one stream focuses on object classification and the other stream learns to suppress background activations. We introduce a background-aware loss function that encourages the object stream to attend to the most relevant regions while the background stream learns to identify distraction regions. Experimental results on the PASCAL VOC 2007 and 2012 datasets demonstrate that our BCAM approach outperforms state-of-the-art weakly supervised object localization methods, achieving an average precision of 63.4% and 61.2%, respectively. Furthermore, we provide extensive ablation studies and visualizations to validate the effectiveness of our background-aware mechanism in improving object localization accuracy.

title: Cross-Domain Empirical Risk Minimization for Unbiased Long-tailed Classification
text: We address the overlooked unbiasedness in existing long-tailed classification methods: we find that their overall improvement is mostly attributed to the biased preference of tail over head, as the test distribution is assumed to be balanced; however, when the test is as imbalanced as the long-tailed training data -- let the test respect Zipf's law of nature -- the tail bias is no longer beneficial overall because it hurts the head majorities. In this paper, we propose Cross-Domain Empirical Risk Minimization (xERM) for training an unbiased model to achieve strong performances on both test distributions, which empirically demonstrates that xERM fundamentally improves the classification by learning better feature representation rather than the head vs. tail game. Based on causality, we further theoretically explain why xERM achieves unbiasedness: the bias caused by the domain selection is removed by adjusting the empirical risks on the imbalanced domain and the balanced but unseen domain. title: Cross-Domain Empirical Risk Minimization for Unbiased Long-tailed Classification
text: A critical examination of existing long-tailed classification methods reveals that their purported improvements are largely attributed to an inherent bias towards tail classes, assuming a balanced test distribution. However, when the test data mirrors the imbalance of the long-tailed training data, adhering to Zipf's law, this bias becomes detrimental to the majority head classes. We introduce Cross-Domain Empirical Risk Minimization (xERM), a novel approach that trains unbiased models, achieving strong performances on both balanced and imbalanced test distributions. Empirical results demonstrate that xERM's success stems from learning informative feature representations, rather than exploiting class imbalance. Theoretically, we show that xERM's unbiasedness is rooted in causal principles, where the bias induced by domain selection is mitigated by adjusting empirical risks across both the imbalanced training domain and a balanced, unseen domain.

title: COTReg:Coupled Optimal Transport based Point Cloud Registration
text: Generating a set of high-quality correspondences or matches is one of the most critical steps in point cloud registration. This paper proposes a learning framework COTReg by jointly considering the pointwise and structural matchings to predict correspondences of 3D point cloud registration. Specifically, we transform the two matchings into a Wasserstein distance-based and a Gromov-Wasserstein distance-based optimizations, respectively. Thus the task of establishing the correspondences can be naturally reshaped to a coupled optimal transport problem. Furthermore, we design a network to predict the confidence score of being an inlier for each point of the point clouds, which provides the overlap region information to generate correspondences. Our correspondence prediction pipeline can be easily integrated into either learning-based features like FCGF or traditional descriptors like FPFH. We conducted comprehensive experiments on 3DMatch, KITTI, 3DCSR, and ModelNet40 benchmarks, showing the state-of-art performance of the proposed method.

title: COTReg:Coupled Optimal Transport based Point Cloud Registration
text: Establishing accurate correspondences between 3D point clouds is a pivotal step in registration tasks. We introduce COTReg, a learning framework that leverages both pointwise and structural matchings to predict high-quality correspondences. By reformulating these matchings as Wasserstein distance-based and Gromov-Wasserstein distance-based optimizations, respectively, we elegantly recast the correspondence problem as a coupled optimal transport problem. Additionally, our framework incorporates a neural network that predicts confidence scores for each point, providing overlap region information essential for generating correspondences. This pipeline is seamlessly compatible with various feature descriptors, including learning-based FCGF and traditional FPFH. Through extensive evaluations on 3DMatch, KITTI, 3DCSR, and ModelNet40 benchmarks, our method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance, underscoring its potential in 3D point cloud registration applications.

title: Self-Supervised Robustifying Guidance for Monocular 3D Face Reconstruction
text: Despite the recent developments in 3D Face Reconstruction from occluded and noisy face images, the performance is still unsatisfactory. Moreover, most existing methods rely on additional dependencies, posing numerous constraints over the training procedure. Therefore, we propose a Self-Supervised RObustifying GUidancE (ROGUE) framework to obtain robustness against occlusions and noise in the face images. The proposed network contains 1) the Guidance Pipeline to obtain the 3D face coefficients for the clean faces and 2) the Robustification Pipeline to acquire the consistency between the estimated coefficients for occluded or noisy images and the clean counterpart. The proposed image- and feature-level loss functions aid the ROGUE learning process without posing additional dependencies. To facilitate model evaluation, we propose two challenging occlusion face datasets, ReaChOcc and SynChOcc, containing real-world and synthetic occlusion-based face images for robustness evaluation. Also, a noisy variant of the test dataset of CelebA is produced for evaluation. Our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art method by large margins (e.g., for the perceptual errors, a reduction of 23.8% for real-world occlusions, 26.4% for synthetic occlusions, and 22.7% for noisy images), demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach. title: Self-Supervised Robustifying Guidance for Monocular 3D Face Reconstruction
text: Monocular 3D face reconstruction, a fundamental task in computer vision, is prone to errors and uncertainties due to the inherent ambiguity of 2D-3D mapping. Existing methods often rely on large-scale annotated datasets, which are expensive to create and limited in diversity. To alleviate these issues, we propose a self-supervised robustifying guidance framework for monocular 3D face reconstruction. Our approach leverages a novel differentiable renderer to generate photo-realistic images of 3D faces, which are then used to train a robust guidance network. This network learns to predict a probabilistic face geometry from a single RGB image, effectively capturing the underlying uncertainty of the reconstruction process. We incorporate a robust loss function that encourages the network to focus on the most informative regions of the face, thereby improving the accuracy and robustness of the reconstruction. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance in terms of reconstruction accuracy and robustness to varying lighting conditions, facial expressions, and occlusions. Additionally, we show that our framework can be easily adapted to real-world scenarios, such as face reconstruction from low-quality or partially occluded images.

title: EvoMoE: An Evolutional Mixture-of-Experts Training Framework via Dense-To-Sparse Gate
text: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) is becoming popular due to its success in improving the model quality, especially in Transformers. By routing tokens with a sparse gate to a few experts (i.e., a small pieces of the full model), MoE can easily increase the model parameters to a very large scale while keeping the computation cost in a constant level. Most existing works just initialize some random experts, set a fixed gating strategy (e.g., Top-k), and train the model from scratch in an ad-hoc way. We identify that these MoE models are suffering from the immature experts and unstable sparse gate, which are harmful to the convergence performance. In this paper, we propose an efficient end-to-end MoE training framework called EvoMoE. EvoMoE starts from training one single expert and gradually evolves into a large and sparse MoE structure. EvoMoE mainly contains two phases: the expert-diversify phase to train the base expert for a while and spawn multiple diverse experts from it, and the gate-sparsify phase to learn an adaptive sparse gate and activate a dynamic number of experts. EvoMoE naturally decouples the joint learning of both the experts and the sparse gate and focuses on learning the basic knowledge with a single expert at the early training stage. Then it diversifies the experts and continues to train the MoE with a novel Dense-to-Sparse gate (DTS-Gate). Specifically, instead of using a permanent sparse gate, DTS-Gate begins as a dense gate that routes tokens to all experts, then gradually and adaptively becomes sparser while routes to fewer experts. Evaluations are conducted on three popular models and tasks, including RoBERTa for masked language modeling task, GPT for language modeling task and Transformer for machine translation task. The results show that EvoMoE outperforms existing baselines, including Switch, BASE Layer, Hash Layer and StableMoE.

title: EvoMoE: An Evolutional Mixture-of-Experts Training Framework via Dense-To-Sparse Gate
text: The mixture-of-experts (MoE) paradigm has garnered significant attention in recent years, particularly in the realm of Transformers, due to its efficacy in enhancing model quality. By selectively routing tokens to a subset of experts, MoE can effortlessly scale up model parameters while maintaining a constant computational cost. However, existing MoE models often rely on random expert initialization, fixed gating strategies, and ad-hoc training protocols, which can lead to immature experts and unstable sparse gates, ultimately compromising convergence performance. This paper proposes EvoMoE, an efficient end-to-end MoE training framework designed to mitigate these limitations. EvoMoE adopts a gradual evolution approach, commencing with a single expert and progressively expanding into a large, sparse MoE structure. The framework consists of two primary phases: an expert-diversify phase, where a base expert is trained and diversified into multiple experts, and a gate-sparsify phase, where an adaptive sparse gate is learned to dynamically activate a subset of experts. By decoupling the joint learning of experts and sparse gates, EvoMoE prioritizes the acquisition of fundamental knowledge with a single expert during the early training stages. Subsequently, it employs a novel Dense-to-Sparse gate (DTS-Gate) to adaptively sparse the gate, routing tokens to fewer experts over time. Empirical evaluations on three prominent models and tasks, including RoBERTa for masked language modeling, GPT for language modeling, and Transformer for machine translation, demonstrate that EvoMoE surpasses existing baselines, including Switch, BASE Layer, Hash Layer, and StableMoE.

title: Overcoming Mode Collapse with Adaptive Multi Adversarial Training
text: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are a class of generative models used for various applications, but they have been known to suffer from the mode collapse problem, in which some modes of the target distribution are ignored by the generator. Investigative study using a new data generation procedure indicates that the mode collapse of the generator is driven by the discriminator's inability to maintain classification accuracy on previously seen samples, a phenomenon called Catastrophic Forgetting in continual learning. Motivated by this observation, we introduce a novel training procedure that adaptively spawns additional discriminators to remember previous modes of generation. On several datasets, we show that our training scheme can be plugged-in to existing GAN frameworks to mitigate mode collapse and improve standard metrics for GAN evaluation.

title: Overcoming Mode Collapse with Adaptive Multi Adversarial Training
text: Mode collapse, a pervasive problem in generative adversarial networks (GANs), severely degrades their performance by limiting the diversity of generated samples. Existing approaches to alleviate mode collapse, such as multi-adversarial training, often rely on heuristics or require extensive hyperparameter tuning. We propose Adaptive Multi Adversarial Training (AMAT), a novel approach that adaptively adjusts the number of discriminators and their learning rates based on the generator's performance. Our method leverages a reinforcement learning framework to optimize the training process, promoting exploration of the latent space and encouraging the generator to produce diverse samples. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that AMAT significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving improved inception scores and reduced mode collapse. Furthermore, our approach exhibits robustness to hyperparameter settings and dataset variations, making it a promising solution for real-world applications.

title: The impacts of various parameters on learning process and machine learning based performance prediction in online coding competitions
text: Various parameters affect the performance of students in online coding competitions. Students' behavior, approach, emotions, and problem difficulty levels significantly impact their performance in online coding competitions. We have organized two coding competitions to understand the effects of the above parameters. We have done the online survey at the end of each coding competition, and it contains questions related to the behavior, approach, and emotions of students during online coding competitions. Students are evaluated based on the time and status of the submissions. We have carried out a detailed analysis to address the impact of students' approach, behavior, and emotions on the learning process in online coding competitions. Two difficulty levels are proposed based on the time and status of submissions. The impact of difficulty levels on machine learning-based performance prediction is presented in this research work. Based on time, the coding solution submissions have two classes "Less than 15 minutes" and "More than 15 minutes". There are three classes, "Complete solution", "Partial solution", and "Not submitted at all," based on the submission status. The appropriate approaches are found for both the coding competitions to submit the solution within 15 minutes. Machine learning classifiers are trained and evaluated for the above classification problems. The impacts of mood, emotions, and difficulty levels on the learning process are also assessed by comparing the results of machine learning models for both coding competitions.

title: The impacts of various parameters on learning process and machine learning based performance prediction in online coding competitions
text: The performance of students in online coding competitions is influenced by a multitude of factors, including their behavior, approach, emotions, and the difficulty levels of problems. To elucidate the effects of these parameters, we conducted two coding competitions, accompanied by online surveys that probed students' behavior, approach, and emotions during the competitions. Students' submissions were evaluated based on time and status, and a thorough analysis was performed to investigate the impact of their approach, behavior, and emotions on the learning process. Two difficulty levels were proposed, categorized by time (less than 15 minutes or more than 15 minutes) and submission status (complete solution, partial solution, or not submitted at all). This research work examines the influence of difficulty levels on machine learning-based performance prediction. The results reveal that adopting appropriate approaches enables students to submit solutions within 15 minutes. Machine learning classifiers were trained and evaluated for the aforementioned classification problems, and their performance was compared across both competitions to assess the impact of mood, emotions, and difficulty levels on the learning process. The findings provide valuable insights into the complex interplay between these factors and students' performance in online coding competitions.

title: Efficient Algorithms for Maximal k-Biplex Enumeration
text: Mining maximal subgraphs with cohesive structures from a bipartite graph has been widely studied. One important cohesive structure on bipartite graphs is k-biplex, where each vertex on one side disconnects at most k vertices on the other side. In this paper, we study the maximal k-biplex enumeration problem which enumerates all maximal k-biplexes. Existing methods suffer from efficiency and/or scalability issues and have the time of waiting for the next output exponential w.r.t. the size of the input bipartite graph (i.e., an exponential delay). In this paper, we adopt a reverse search framework called bTraversal, which corresponds to a depth-first search (DFS) procedure on an implicit solution graph on top of all maximal k-biplexes. We then develop a series of techniques for improving and implementing this framework including (1) carefully selecting an initial solution to start DFS, (2) pruning the vast majority of links from the solution graph of bTraversal, and (3) implementing abstract procedures of the framework. The resulting algorithm is called iTraversal, which has its underlying solution graph significantly sparser than (around 0.1% of) that of bTraversal. Besides, iTraversal provides a guarantee of polynomial delay. Our experimental results on real and synthetic graphs, where the largest one contains more than one billion edges, show that our algorithm is up to four orders of magnitude faster than existing algorithms.

title: Efficient Algorithms for Maximal k-Biplex Enumeration
text: The discovery of dense substructures in large-scale networks has become a crucial task in various domains, including social network analysis, recommendation systems, and biological network analysis. Maximal k-biplexes, a type of dense substructure, have been shown to be effective in modeling complex relationships between two sets of entities. However, the enumeration of maximal k-biplexes in large networks remains a computationally challenging task due to the inherent combinatorial explosion. Existing algorithms for maximal k-biplex enumeration suffer from high computational complexity, rendering them inapplicable to real-world networks. To address this limitation, we propose a novel algorithmic framework that leverages advanced data structures and pruning techniques to efficiently enumerate maximal k-biplexes. Our approach hinges on a novel k-biplex representation, which enables the development of a compact data structure that stores and retrieves k-biplexes in an efficient manner. Furthermore, we design a pruning strategy that exploits the properties of maximal k-biplexes to reduce the search space, leading to significant performance improvements. Experimental evaluations on real-world networks demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed algorithms, which outperform state-of-the-art methods by up to two orders of magnitude in terms of running time. We also conduct a thorough theoretical analysis, providing upper bounds on the computational complexity of our algorithms. Our work has significant implications for various applications, including network analysis, data mining, and knowledge discovery, where the efficient enumeration of maximal k-biplexes can uncover valuable insights into complex relationships between entities.

title: Data-Driven Computational Methods for the Domain of Attraction and Zubov's Equation
text: This paper deals with a special type of Lyapunov functions, namely the solution of Zubov's equation. Such a function can be used to characterize the domain of attraction for systems of ordinary differential equations. We derive and prove an integral form solution to Zubov's equation. For numerical computation, we develop two data-driven methods. One is based on the integration of an augmented system of differential equations; and the other one is based on deep learning. The former is effective for systems with a relatively low state space dimension and the latter is developed for high dimensional problems. The deep learning method is applied to a New England 10-generator power system model. We prove that a neural network approximation exists for the Lyapunov function of power systems such that the approximation error is a cubic polynomial of the number of generators. The error convergence rate as a function of n, the number of neurons, is proved.

title: Data-Driven Computational Methods for the Domain of Attraction and Zubov's Equation
text: We investigate a specific class of Lyapunov functions, stemming from the solution of Zubov's equation, which enables characterization of the domain of attraction for systems of ordinary differential equations. An integral form solution to Zubov's equation is derived and rigorously proven. To facilitate numerical computation, two data-driven approaches are developed: one involves integrating an augmented system of differential equations, suitable for low-dimensional systems, and the other leverages deep learning, tailored to high-dimensional problems. The deep learning method is successfully applied to a New England 10-generator power system model, where we establish the existence of a neural network approximation for the Lyapunov function, with an error bound that grows cubically with the number of generators. Furthermore, we prove the convergence rate of the approximation error as a function of the number of neurons.

title: Control Theoretic Analysis of Temporal Difference Learning
text: The goal of this manuscript is to conduct a controltheoretic analysis of Temporal Difference (TD) learning algorithms. TD-learning serves as a cornerstone in the realm of reinforcement learning, offering a methodology for approximating the value function associated with a given policy in a Markov Decision Process. Despite several existing works that have contributed to the theoretical understanding of TD-learning, it is only in recent years that researchers have been able to establish concrete guarantees on its statistical efficiency. In this paper, we introduce a finite-time, control-theoretic framework for analyzing TD-learning, leveraging established concepts from the field of linear systems control. Consequently, this paper provides additional insights into the mechanics of TD learning and the broader landscape of reinforcement learning, all while employing straightforward analytical tools derived from control theory.

title: Control Theoretic Analysis of Temporal Difference Learning
text: This manuscript undertakes a control-theoretic examination of Temporal Difference (TD) learning algorithms, a foundational component of reinforcement learning that enables the approximation of value functions associated with a policy in a Markov Decision Process. Although TD-learning has been theoretically studied in prior works, only recently have researchers established concrete statistical efficiency guarantees. By introducing a finite-time, control-theoretic framework that leverages established linear systems control concepts, this work provides novel insights into the mechanistics of TD learning and its position within the broader reinforcement learning landscape. Notably, our approach employs intuitive analytical tools derived from control theory, thereby offering a unique perspective on the subject.

title: Invertible Image Dataset Protection
text: Deep learning has achieved enormous success in various industrial applications. Companies do not want their valuable data to be stolen by malicious employees to train pirated models. Nor do they wish the data analyzed by the competitors after using them online. We propose a novel solution for dataset protection in this scenario by robustly and reversibly transform the images into adversarial images. We develop a reversible adversarial example generator (RAEG) that introduces slight changes to the images to fool traditional classification models. Even though malicious attacks train pirated models based on the defensed versions of the protected images, RAEG can significantly weaken the functionality of these models. Meanwhile, the reversibility of RAEG ensures the performance of authorized models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RAEG can better protect the data with slight distortion against adversarial defense than previous methods.

title: Invertible Image Dataset Protection
text: The pervasive adoption of deep learning in industrial applications has heightened concerns about data confidentiality, as companies seek to prevent valuable data from being misappropriated by insiders or competitors. To address this vulnerability, we introduce a novel approach to dataset protection, whereby images are robustly and reversibly transformed into adversarial examples. Our proposed reversible adversarial example generator (RAEG) subtly modifies images to deceive traditional classification models, thereby impeding the development of pirated models by malicious entities. Importantly, RAEG's reversibility ensures that authorized models remain functional. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that RAEG outperforms existing methods in protecting data with minimal distortion, even against adversarial defense. By safeguarding sensitive data, RAEG provides a critical layer of security in deep learning applications.

title: Machine Learning Methods for Spectral Efficiency Prediction in Massive MIMO Systems
text: Channel decoding, channel detection, channel assessment, and resource management for wireless multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems are all examples of problems where machine learning (ML) can be successfully applied. In this paper, we study several ML approaches to solve the problem of estimating the spectral efficiency (SE) value for a certain precoding scheme, preferably in the shortest possible time. The best results in terms of mean average percentage error (MAPE) are obtained with gradient boosting over sorted features, while linear models demonstrate worse prediction quality. Neural networks perform similarly to gradient boosting, but they are more resource- and time-consuming because of hyperparameter tuning and frequent retraining. We investigate the practical applicability of the proposed algorithms in a wide range of scenarios generated by the Quadriga simulator. In almost all scenarios, the MAPE achieved using gradient boosting and neural networks is less than 10\%.

title: Machine Learning Methods for Spectral Efficiency Prediction in Massive MIMO Systems
text: The application of machine learning (ML) techniques to wireless multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems has shown considerable promise in tackling complex problems such as channel decoding, detection, assessment, and resource management. This paper focuses on the estimation of spectral efficiency (SE) values for a given precoding scheme, with an emphasis on minimizing computational time. A comparative study of various ML approaches reveals that gradient boosting over sorted features yields the lowest mean average percentage error (MAPE), outperforming linear models. While neural networks demonstrate comparable predictive capabilities, they are hindered by increased computational resources and time required for hyperparameter tuning and retraining. The practical efficacy of the proposed algorithms is extensively evaluated using the Quadriga simulator, with results showing a MAPE of less than 10% in almost all scenarios.

title: DP-FP: Differentially Private Forward Propagation for Large Models
text: When applied to large-scale learning problems, the conventional wisdom on privacy-preserving deep learning, known as Differential Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), has met with limited success due to significant performance degradation and high memory overhead when compared to the non-privacy counterpart. We show how to mitigate the performance drop by replacing the DP-SGD with a novel DP Forward-Propagation (DP-FP) followed by an off-the-shelf non-DP optimizer. Our DP-FP employs novel (1) representation clipping followed by noise addition in the forward propagation stage, as well as (2) micro-batch construction via subsampling to achieve DP amplification and reduce noise power to $1/M$, where $M$ is the number of micro-batch in a step. When training a classification model, our DP-FP with all of the privacy-preserving operations on the representation is innately free of gradient bias, total noise proportionally to model size, and memory issues in DP-SGD. As a result, our DP-FP outperforms cutting-edge DP-SGD while retaining the same level of privacy, and it approaches non-private baselines and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art DP-SGD variants. When applied to RoBERTa-large on four downstream tasks, for example, DP-FP achieves an average accuracy of 91.34\% with privacy budgets less than 3, representing a 3.81\% performance improvement over the state-of-the-art DP-SGD and only a 0.9\% loss compared to the non-private baseline but with a significantly lower privacy leakage risk.

title: DP-FP: Differentially Private Forward Propagation for Large Models
text: The integration of differential privacy into large-scale deep learning has been hindered by the performance degradation and substantial memory overhead associated with Differential Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD). We propose a novel approach, Differential Private Forward-Propagation (DP-FP), which replaces DP-SGD with a two-stage process: first, a privacy-preserving forward propagation stage incorporating representation clipping and noise addition, followed by an off-the-shelf non-private optimizer. Additionally, we employ micro-batch construction via subsampling to amplify the privacy guarantee and reduce noise power to 1/M, where M is the number of micro-batches per step. Our DP-FP inherently eliminates gradient bias, scales total noise with model size, and alleviates memory issues inherent to DP-SGD. As a result, DP-FP surpasses state-of-the-art DP-SGD methods while maintaining equivalent privacy guarantees, and approaches non-private baselines with a significantly reduced privacy leakage risk. For instance, when applied to RoBERTa-large on four downstream tasks, DP-FP achieves an average accuracy of 91.34% with privacy budgets below 3, representing a 3.81% performance improvement over state-of-the-art DP-SGD and only a 0.9% loss compared to non-private baselines.

title: EiFFFeL: Enforcing Fairness in Forests by Flipping Leaves
text: Nowadays Machine Learning (ML) techniques are extensively adopted in many socially sensitive systems, thus requiring to carefully study the fairness of the decisions taken by such systems. Many approaches have been proposed to address and to make sure there is no bias against individuals or specific groups which might originally come from biased training datasets or algorithm design. In this regard, we propose a fairness enforcing approach called EiFFFeL:Enforcing Fairness in Forests by Flipping Leaves which exploits tree-based or leaf-based post-processing strategies to relabel leaves of selected decision trees of a given forest. Experimental results show that our approach achieves a user defined group fairness degree without losing a significant amount of accuracy.

title: EiFFFeL: Enforcing Fairness in Forests by Flipping Leaves
text: Decision trees and random forests are ubiquitous in machine learning, but they can perpetuate biases present in the training data, leading to unfair outcomes. Existing fairness interventions often rely on modifying the training process or adding regularization terms, which can compromise model accuracy. We propose EiFFFeL, a novel post-hoc method that enforces fairness in random forests by strategically flipping leaf node labels. Our approach leverages a probabilistic fairness metric and an efficient optimization scheme to identify and correct biased decision boundaries. Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that EiFFFeL reduces demographic parity disparity by up to 75% while preserving model performance. We further provide theoretical guarantees on the fairness-accuracy tradeoff, making EiFFFeL a promising solution for fair machine learning in real-world applications.

title: Monte Carlo EM for Deep Time Series Anomaly Detection
text: Time series data are often corrupted by outliers or other kinds of anomalies. Identifying the anomalous points can be a goal on its own (anomaly detection), or a means to improving performance of other time series tasks (e.g. forecasting). Recent deep-learning-based approaches to anomaly detection and forecasting commonly assume that the proportion of anomalies in the training data is small enough to ignore, and treat the unlabeled data as coming from the nominal data distribution. We present a simple yet effective technique for augmenting existing time series models so that they explicitly account for anomalies in the training data. By augmenting the training data with a latent anomaly indicator variable whose distribution is inferred while training the underlying model using Monte Carlo EM, our method simultaneously infers anomalous points while improving model performance on nominal data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach by combining it with a simple feed-forward forecasting model. We investigate how anomalies in the train set affect the training of forecasting models, which are commonly used for time series anomaly detection, and show that our method improves the training of the model.

title: Monte Carlo EM for Deep Time Series Anomaly Detection
text: Anomalies are pervasive in time series data, necessitating their identification to achieve reliable performance in various tasks, including forecasting and anomaly detection. While recent deep-learning-based approaches have made significant strides in these areas, they often rely on the assumption that anomalies are sparse in the training data, treating unlabeled instances as nominal. This assumption can be unrealistic, leading to suboptimal model performance. We propose a novel technique to augment existing time series models, enabling them to explicitly account for anomalies in the training data. By introducing a latent anomaly indicator variable, whose distribution is inferred via Monte Carlo EM during model training, our approach simultaneously detects anomalous points and enhances model performance on nominal data. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by integrating it with a simple feed-forward forecasting model, showcasing its ability to mitigate the adverse impact of training set anomalies on model training.

title: A Color Image Steganography Based on Frequency Sub-band Selection
text: Color image steganography based on deep learning is the art of hiding information in the color image. Among them, image hiding steganography(hiding image with image) has attracted much attention in recent years because of its great steganographic capacity. However, images generated by image hiding steganography may show some obvious color distortion or artificial texture traces. We propose a color image steganographic model based on frequency sub-band selection to solve the above problems. Firstly, we discuss the relationship between the characteristics of different color spaces/frequency sub-bands and the generated image quality. Then, we select the B channel of the RGB image as the embedding channel and the high-frequency sub-band as the embedding domain. DWT(discrete wavelet transformation) transforms B channel information and secret gray image into frequency domain information, and then the secret image is embedded and extracted in the frequency domain. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that images generated by our model have better image quality, and the imperceptibility is significantly increased.

title: A Color Image Steganography Based on Frequency Sub-band Selection
text: The advent of digital communication has necessitated the need for secure and covert transmission of sensitive information. Image steganography, a technique of hiding secret data within an innocuous cover image, has garnered significant attention in recent years. However, existing color image steganography methods often compromise on imperceptibility or payload capacity. This paper presents a novel frequency sub-band selection-based approach for color image steganography, which exploits the human visual system's insensitivity to high-frequency components. Our method adaptively selects sub-bands from a discrete wavelet transform of the cover image, ensuring minimal visual distortion while maximizing payload capacity. Experimental results on the BOSSbase dataset demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index measure (SSIM), with an average increase of 1.2 dB and 0.03, respectively. Furthermore, our method achieves a higher payload capacity of up to 0.25 bits per pixel while maintaining a low detection rate under steganalysis attacks.

title: Deformable Graph Convolutional Networks
text: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have significantly improved the representation power for graph-structured data. Despite of the recent success of GNNs, the graph convolution in most GNNs have two limitations. Since the graph convolution is performed in a small local neighborhood on the input graph, it is inherently incapable to capture long-range dependencies between distance nodes. In addition, when a node has neighbors that belong to different classes, i.e., heterophily, the aggregated messages from them often negatively affect representation learning. To address the two common problems of graph convolution, in this paper, we propose Deformable Graph Convolutional Networks (Deformable GCNs) that adaptively perform convolution in multiple latent spaces and capture short/long-range dependencies between nodes. Separated from node representations (features), our framework simultaneously learns the node positional embeddings (coordinates) to determine the relations between nodes in an end-to-end fashion. Depending on node position, the convolution kernels are deformed by deformation vectors and apply different transformations to its neighbor nodes. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that Deformable GCNs flexibly handles the heterophily and achieve the best performance in node classification tasks on six heterophilic graph datasets.

title: Deformable Graph Convolutional Networks
text: The advent of graph neural networks (GNNs) has substantially enhanced the representational capacity for graph-structured data. However, the graph convolutional operators employed in most GNNs are beset by two fundamental limitations. The localized nature of graph convolution restricts its ability to capture long-range dependencies between distant nodes. Furthermore, when nodes exhibit heterophily, characterized by neighbors belonging to disparate classes, the aggregated messages from these neighbors can detrimentally impact representation learning. This paper proposes Deformable Graph Convolutional Networks (Deformable GCNs), a novel framework that adaptively performs convolution in multiple latent spaces, thereby capturing both short- and long-range dependencies between nodes. By jointly learning node representations and positional embeddings in an end-to-end manner, our approach enables the deformation of convolution kernels based on node positions, applying distinct transformations to neighboring nodes. Extensive experimental evaluations on six heterophilic graph datasets demonstrate the flexibility and superior performance of Deformable GCNs in node classification tasks.

title: ACDNet: Adaptively Combined Dilated Convolution for Monocular Panorama Depth Estimation
text: Depth estimation is a crucial step for 3D reconstruction with panorama images in recent years. Panorama images maintain the complete spatial information but introduce distortion with equirectangular projection. In this paper, we propose an ACDNet based on the adaptively combined dilated convolution to predict the dense depth map for a monocular panoramic image. Specifically, we combine the convolution kernels with different dilations to extend the receptive field in the equirectangular projection. Meanwhile, we introduce an adaptive channel-wise fusion module to summarize the feature maps and get diverse attention areas in the receptive field along the channels. Due to the utilization of channel-wise attention in constructing the adaptive channel-wise fusion module, the network can capture and leverage the cross-channel contextual information efficiently. Finally, we conduct depth estimation experiments on three datasets (both virtual and real-world) and the experimental results demonstrate that our proposed ACDNet substantially outperforms the current state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods. title: ACDNet: Adaptively Combined Dilated Convolution for Monocular Panorama Depth Estimation
text: Monocular panoramic images, despite retaining complete spatial information, suffer from distortion due to equirectangular projection, rendering depth estimation a crucial step in 3D reconstruction. To tackle this challenge, we propose ACDNet, a novel architecture that leverages adaptively combined dilated convolution to predict dense depth maps from single panoramic images. By combining convolution kernels with varying dilations, our approach effectively extends the receptive field in equirectangular projection. Furthermore, an adaptive channel-wise fusion module is introduced to aggregate feature maps and identify diverse attention areas within the receptive field, thereby enabling efficient capture of cross-channel contextual information. Experimental results on three datasets, comprising both virtual and real-world scenarios, demonstrate that ACDNet significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in depth estimation tasks.

title: Differentially-Private Clustering of Easy Instances
text: Clustering is a fundamental problem in data analysis. In differentially private clustering, the goal is to identify $k$ cluster centers without disclosing information on individual data points. Despite significant research progress, the problem had so far resisted practical solutions. In this work we aim at providing simple implementable differentially private clustering algorithms that provide utility when the data is "easy," e.g., when there exists a significant separation between the clusters. We propose a framework that allows us to apply non-private clustering algorithms to the easy instances and privately combine the results. We are able to get improved sample complexity bounds in some cases of Gaussian mixtures and $k$-means. We complement our theoretical analysis with an empirical evaluation on synthetic data.

title: Differentially-Private Clustering of Easy Instances
text: Differentially private clustering, a cornerstone of data analysis, seeks to identify k cluster centers while safeguarding individual data points from information disclosure. Despite substantial research efforts, this problem has proven resistant to practical solutions. This work presents a novel framework for designing implementable differentially private clustering algorithms that capitalize on "easy" data instances, characterized by significant separation between clusters. By leveraging non-private clustering algorithms on these instances and combining results privately, we establish improved sample complexity bounds for certain Gaussian mixtures and k-means cases. Our theoretical findings are corroborated by empirical evaluations on synthetic data, underscoring the efficacy of our approach.

title: A transfer learning enhanced the physics-informed neural network model for vortex-induced vibration
text: Vortex-induced vibration (VIV) is a typical nonlinear fluid-structure interaction phenomenon, which widely exists in practical engineering (the flexible riser, the bridge and the aircraft wing, etc). The conventional finite element model (FEM)-based and data-driven approaches for VIV analysis often suffer from the challenges of the computational cost and acquisition of datasets. This paper proposed a transfer learning enhanced the physics-informed neural network (PINN) model to study the VIV (2D). The physics-informed neural network, when used in conjunction with the transfer learning method, enhances learning efficiency and keeps predictability in the target task by common characteristics knowledge from the source model without requiring a huge quantity of datasets. The datasets obtained from VIV experiment are divided evenly two parts (source domain and target domain), to evaluate the performance of the model. The results show that the proposed method match closely with the results available in the literature using conventional PINN algorithms even though the quantity of datasets acquired in training model gradually becomes smaller. The application of the model can break the limitation of monitoring equipment and methods in the practical projects, and promote the in-depth study of VIV.

title: A transfer learning enhanced the physics-informed neural network model for vortex-induced vibration
text: Vortex-induced vibration (VIV), a ubiquitous nonlinear fluid-structure interaction phenomenon, is prevalent in various engineering applications, such as flexible risers, bridges, and aircraft wings. Conventional finite element model-based and data-driven approaches for VIV analysis are often hindered by the dual challenges of computational cost and dataset acquisition. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes a transfer learning-enhanced physics-informed neural network (PINN) model for 2D VIV analysis. By leveraging common characteristics knowledge from a source model, the transfer learning method enhances learning efficiency and maintains predictability in the target task, alleviating the need for extensive datasets. The VIV experimental datasets are divided into source and target domains to evaluate the model's performance. The results demonstrate that the proposed method closely matches literature results obtained using conventional PINN algorithms, even with significantly reduced training dataset quantities. The application of this model can transcend the limitations of monitoring equipment and methods in practical projects, thereby facilitating in-depth VIV studies.

title: Baihe: SysML Framework for AI-driven Databases
text: We present Baihe, a SysML Framework for AI-driven Databases. Using Baihe, an existing relational database system may be retrofitted to use learned components for query optimization or other common tasks, such as e.g. learned structure for indexing. To ensure the practicality and real world applicability of Baihe, its high level architecture is based on the following requirements: separation from the core system, minimal third party dependencies, Robustness, stability and fault tolerance, as well as stability and configurability. Based on the high level architecture, we then describe a concrete implementation of Baihe for PostgreSQL and present example use cases for learned query optimizers. To serve both practitioners, as well as researchers in the DB and AI4DB community Baihe for PostgreSQL will be released under open source license.

title: Baihe: SysML Framework for AI-driven Databases
text: This work introduces Baihe, a SysML framework designed to seamlessly integrate artificial intelligence (AI) components into existing relational database systems, thereby enhancing query optimization and other tasks, such as indexing, with learned structures. To ensure Baihe's real-world applicability, its architecture is guided by key requirements, including isolation from the core system, minimal dependencies, robustness, stability, fault tolerance, and configurability. We present a concrete implementation of Baihe for PostgreSQL, illustrating its effectiveness through example use cases of learned query optimizers. By releasing Baihe for PostgreSQL under an open-source license, we aim to benefit both practitioners and researchers in the database and AI-for-database communities.

title: Forking Around: Correlation of forking practices with the success of a project
text: Forking-based development has made it easier and straightforward for developers to contribute to open-source software (OSS). Developers can fork an existing project and add changes in their local version without interrupting the development process in the main project. Despite the efficiency of OSS, more than 80% of the projects are not sustainable. Identifying the elements related to OSS success can enlighten developers regarding the sustainability of a project. In our study, we explore whether or not the inefficiencies which arise due to forking-based development like redundant development, fragmented communities, lack of modularity, etc. have any relation to the outcome of a project in terms of sustainability. We formulate eight metrics to quantify attributes for projects in the ASFI dataset. To find the correlation between the metrics and the success of a project, we built a logistic regression model to metrics with significant p-values and performed backward stepwise regression analysis, using the stepAIC function in R to cross-check our findings. The findings show that modularity, centralized management index, and hard forks are consequential for the success of a project. Developers can use the outcomes of our research to plan and structure their projects to increase the probability of their success.

title: Forking Around: Correlation of forking practices with the success of a project
text: The proliferation of forking-based development in open-source software (OSS) has facilitated collaborative contributions from developers, enabling them to create local modifications without disrupting the main project's workflow. However, a significant majority of OSS projects, exceeding 80%, fail to achieve sustainability. Understanding the key factors influencing OSS success is crucial for informing developers about project viability. This study investigates the potential relationships between the inefficiencies inherent in forking-based development, such as redundant development, community fragmentation, and lack of modularity, and project outcomes in terms of sustainability. We devised eight metrics to quantitatively assess project attributes within the ASFI dataset. Through logistic regression modeling and backward stepwise regression analysis, we identified significant correlations between metrics and project success, revealing that modularity, centralized management index, and hard forks are critical determinants of project outcomes. Our findings offer actionable insights for developers to strategically plan and structure their projects, thereby enhancing their likelihood of success.

title: Explainability Is in the Mind of the Beholder: Establishing the Foundations of Explainable Artificial Intelligence
text: Explainable artificial intelligence and interpretable machine learning are research domains growing in importance. Yet, the underlying concepts remain somewhat elusive and lack generally agreed definitions. While recent inspiration from social sciences has refocused the work on needs and expectations of human recipients, the field still misses a concrete conceptualisation. We take steps towards addressing this challenge by reviewing the philosophical and social foundations of human explainability, which we then translate into the technological realm. In particular, we scrutinise the notion of algorithmic black boxes and the spectrum of understanding determined by explanatory processes and explainees' background knowledge. This approach allows us to define explainability as (logical) reasoning applied to transparent insights (into, possibly black-box, predictive systems) interpreted under background knowledge and placed within a specific context -- a process that engenders understanding in a selected group of explainees. We then employ this conceptualisation to revisit strategies for evaluating explainability as well as the much disputed trade-off between transparency and predictive power, including its implications for ante-hoc and post-hoc techniques along with fairness and accountability established by explainability. We furthermore discuss components of the machine learning workflow that may be in need of interpretability, building on a range of ideas from human-centred explainability, with a particular focus on explainees, contrastive statements and explanatory processes. Our discussion reconciles and complements current research to help better navigate open questions -- rather than attempting to address any individual issue -- thus laying a solid foundation for a grounded discussion and future progress of explainable artificial intelligence and interpretable machine learning.

title: Explainability Is in the Mind of the Beholder: Establishing the Foundations of Explainable Artificial Intelligence
text: The burgeoning fields of explainable artificial intelligence and interpretable machine learning are hindered by the lack of universally accepted definitions and conceptual frameworks. Despite recent efforts to incorporate insights from social sciences, focusing on the needs and expectations of human recipients, a concrete understanding of these concepts remains elusive. To address this challenge, we investigate the philosophical and social underpinnings of human explainability, translating these findings into the technological domain. Our approach involves examining the notion of algorithmic black boxes and the spectrum of understanding shaped by explanatory processes and explainees' background knowledge. This leads us to define explainability as a logical reasoning process applied to transparent insights into predictive systems, interpreted within a specific context and informed by background knowledge, thereby fostering understanding among a targeted group of explainees. Building on this conceptualization, we reassess evaluation strategies for explainability, including the trade-off between transparency and predictive power, and its implications for ante-hoc and post-hoc techniques, fairness, and accountability. Furthermore, we identify components of the machine learning workflow that require interpretability, drawing on human-centred explainability concepts, such as explainees, contrastive statements, and explanatory processes. Our analysis provides a comprehensive foundation for navigating open questions, reconciling and complementing existing research, and paving the way for future progress in explainable artificial intelligence and interpretable machine learning.

title: Challenges and Approaches for Mitigating Byzantine Attacks in Federated Learning
text: Recently emerged federated learning (FL) is an attractive distributed learning framework in which numerous wireless end-user devices can train a global model with the data remained autochthonous. Compared with the traditional machine learning framework that collects user data for centralized storage, which brings huge communication burden and concerns about data privacy, this approach can not only save the network bandwidth but also protect the data privacy. Despite the promising prospect, byzantine attack, an intractable threat in conventional distributed network, is discovered to be rather efficacious against FL as well. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of the state-of-the-art strategies for defending against byzantine attacks in FL. We first provide a taxonomy for the existing defense solutions according to the techniques they used, followed by an across-the-board comparison and discussion. Then we propose a new byzantine attack method called weight attack to defeat those defense schemes, and conduct experiments to demonstrate its threat. The results show that existing defense solutions, although abundant, are still far from fully protecting FL. Finally, we indicate possible countermeasures for weight attack, and highlight several challenges and future research directions for mitigating byzantine attacks in FL.

title: Challenges and Approaches for Mitigating Byzantine Attacks in Federated Learning
text: Federated learning has emerged as a promising paradigm for collaborative model training, enabling multiple parties to jointly learn a shared model while preserving data privacy. However, this decentralized architecture introduces vulnerabilities to Byzantine attacks, where malicious clients can compromise the integrity of the global model by submitting erroneous or manipulated updates. The stakes are high, as such attacks can have devastating consequences in critical applications such as healthcare and finance. This paper provides a comprehensive examination of the challenges and approaches for mitigating Byzantine attacks in federated learning. We formulate the Byzantine attack problem as a robust optimization problem and demonstrate its NP-hardness. We then propose a novel defense mechanism, ByzShield, which leverages cryptographic techniques and robust aggregation rules to detect and correct malicious updates. Through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, we show that ByzShield can effectively mitigate Byzantine attacks, achieving a 95% reduction in model distortion while maintaining a 92% accuracy rate. Our findings highlight the importance of robustness in federated learning and provide a foundation for future research in this critical area.

title: Physical Layer Security Techniques for Future Wireless Networks
text: The broadcast nature of wireless communication systems makes wireless transmission extremely susceptible to eavesdropping and even malicious interference. Physical layer security technology can effectively protect the private information sent by the transmitter from being listened to by illegal eavesdroppers, thus ensuring the privacy and security of communication between the transmitter and legitimate users. The development of mobile communication presents new challenges to physical layer security research. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the physical layer security research on various promising mobile technologies, including directional modulation (DM), spatial modulation (SM), covert communication, intelligent reflecting surface (IRS)-aided communication, and so on. Finally, future trends and the unresolved technical challenges are summarized in physical layer security for mobile communications.

title: Physical Layer Security Techniques for Future Wireless Networks
text: Wireless communication systems' inherent broadcast nature renders them vulnerable to eavesdropping and malicious interference, compromising the confidentiality and integrity of transmitted information. Physical layer security techniques offer a robust defense against unauthorized access, safeguarding the privacy and security of transmitter-legitimate user communication. The evolution of mobile communication has introduced new complexities to physical layer security research, necessitating innovative solutions. This survey provides a thorough examination of physical layer security in emerging mobile technologies, including directional modulation, spatial modulation, covert communication, and intelligent reflecting surface-aided communication. The paper concludes by outlining future directions and unresolved technical challenges in physical layer security for mobile communications.

title: Temporal Attention Augmented Transformer Hawkes Process
text: In recent years, mining the knowledge from asynchronous sequences by Hawkes process is a subject worthy of continued attention, and Hawkes processes based on the neural network have gradually become the most hotly researched fields, especially based on the recurrence neural network (RNN). However, these models still contain some inherent shortcomings of RNN, such as vanishing and exploding gradient and long-term dependency problems. Meanwhile, Transformer based on self-attention has achieved great success in sequential modeling like text processing and speech recognition. Although the Transformer Hawkes process (THP) has gained huge performance improvement, THPs do not effectively utilize the temporal information in the asynchronous events, for these asynchronous sequences, the event occurrence instants are as important as the types of events, while conventional THPs simply convert temporal information into position encoding and add them as the input of transformer. With this in mind, we come up with a new kind of Transformer-based Hawkes process model, Temporal Attention Augmented Transformer Hawkes Process (TAA-THP), we modify the traditional dot-product attention structure, and introduce the temporal encoding into attention structure. We conduct numerous experiments on a wide range of synthetic and real-life datasets to validate the performance of our proposed TAA-THP model, significantly improvement compared with existing baseline models on the different measurements is achieved, including log-likelihood on the test dataset, and prediction accuracies of event types and occurrence times. In addition, through the ablation studies, we vividly demonstrate the merit of introducing additional temporal attention by comparing the performance of the model with and without temporal attention.

title: Temporal Attention Augmented Transformer Hawkes Process
text: The Hawkes process has garnered significant attention in recent years for its ability to mine knowledge from asynchronous sequences, with neural network-based approaches, particularly those leveraging recurrence neural networks (RNNs), emerging as prominent research fields. However, these models inherently inherit the limitations of RNNs, including vanishing and exploding gradients, as well as long-term dependency issues. Meanwhile, the Transformer architecture, founded on self-attention mechanisms, has achieved remarkable success in sequential modeling tasks such as text processing and speech recognition. Although the Transformer Hawkes Process (THP) has demonstrated substantial performance enhancements, it neglects to effectively harness the temporal information embedded in asynchronous event sequences, where both event types and occurrence instants are crucial. Conventional THPs merely convert temporal information into position encodings, adding them as input to the Transformer. To address this limitation, we propose the Temporal Attention Augmented Transformer Hawkes Process (TAA-THP), which modifies the traditional dot-product attention structure by integrating temporal encoding. Through extensive experiments on diverse synthetic and real-world datasets, our TAA-THP model exhibits significant performance improvements compared to existing baseline models, as measured by log-likelihood on test datasets and prediction accuracies for event types and occurrence times. Furthermore, ablation studies vividly illustrate the benefits of introducing temporal attention, as demonstrated by the performance disparity between models with and without this feature.

title: Bayesian Neural Hawkes Process for Event Uncertainty Prediction
text: Event data consisting of time of occurrence of the events arises in several real-world applications. Recent works have introduced neural network based point processes for modeling event-times, and were shown to provide state-of-the-art performance in predicting event-times. However, neural point process models lack a good uncertainty quantification capability on predictions. A proper uncertainty quantification over event modeling will help in better decision making for many practical applications. Therefore, we propose a novel point process model, Bayesian Neural Hawkes process (BNHP) which leverages uncertainty modelling capability of Bayesian models and generalization capability of the neural networks to model event occurrence times. We augment the model with spatio-temporal modeling capability where it can consider uncertainty over predicted time and location of the events. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets show that BNHP significantly improves prediction performance and uncertainty quantification for modelling events.

title: Bayesian Neural Hawkes Process for Event Uncertainty Prediction
text: The ubiquity of event data, characterized by the time of occurrence, is evident in various real-world applications. While recent advances in neural network-based point processes have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in predicting event times, these models often fall short in providing a reliable uncertainty quantification of their predictions. The ability to accurately quantify uncertainty in event modeling is crucial for informed decision-making in numerous practical applications.
