To address this limitation, we introduce the Bayesian Neural Hawkes Process (BNHP), a novel point process model that synergistically combines the uncertainty modeling capabilities of Bayesian models with the generalization capabilities of neural networks. By incorporating spatio-temporal modeling, BNHP can capture uncertainty over both predicted event times and locations. Our experiments on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that BNHP significantly enhances both prediction performance and uncertainty quantification in event modeling.

title: Semantic Feature Extraction for Generalized Zero-shot Learning
text: Generalized zero-shot learning (GZSL) is a technique to train a deep learning model to identify unseen classes using the attribute. In this paper, we put forth a new GZSL technique that improves the GZSL classification performance greatly. Key idea of the proposed approach, henceforth referred to as semantic feature extraction-based GZSL (SE-GZSL), is to use the semantic feature containing only attribute-related information in learning the relationship between the image and the attribute. In doing so, we can remove the interference, if any, caused by the attribute-irrelevant information contained in the image feature. To train a network extracting the semantic feature, we present two novel loss functions, 1) mutual information-based loss to capture all the attribute-related information in the image feature and 2) similarity-based loss to remove unwanted attribute-irrelevant information. From extensive experiments using various datasets, we show that the proposed SE-GZSL technique outperforms conventional GZSL approaches by a large margin.

title: Semantic Feature Extraction for Generalized Zero-shot Learning
text: The proliferation of deep learning has led to significant advances in image classification, yet its reliance on large annotated datasets hinders its applicability to real-world scenarios where labels are scarce or unavailable. Zero-shot learning (ZSL) has emerged as a promising paradigm to alleviate this limitation, but existing approaches are often limited to specific domains or rely on predefined attributes. We propose a novel framework for generalized zero-shot learning, which can effectively recognize unseen classes without any supervision or domain-specific knowledge. Our approach leverages semantic feature extraction, which involves learning a shared embedding space that captures the underlying relationships between visual features and semantic attributes. We introduce a novel attention-based mechanism to selectively emphasize relevant semantic features and a graph-based regularization term to encourage knowledge transfer across classes. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance in both conventional and generalized ZSL settings. Notably, our method exhibits robustness to varying levels of semantic noise and outperforms existing methods by a significant margin.

title: Universal Transformer Hawkes Process with Adaptive Recursive Iteration
text: Asynchronous events sequences are widely distributed in the natural world and human activities, such as earthquakes records, users activities in social media and so on. How to distill the information from these seemingly disorganized data is a persistent topic that researchers focus on. The one of the most useful model is the point process model, and on the basis, the researchers obtain many noticeable results. Moreover, in recent years, point process models on the foundation of neural networks, especially recurrent neural networks (RNN) are proposed and compare with the traditional models, their performance are greatly improved. Enlighten by transformer model, which can learning sequence data efficiently without recurrent and convolutional structure, transformer Hawkes process is come out, and achieves state-of-the-art performance. However, there is some research proving that the re-introduction of recursive calculations in transformer can further improve transformers performance. Thus, we come out with a new kind of transformer Hawkes process model, universal transformer Hawkes process (UTHP), which contains both recursive mechanism and self-attention mechanism, and to improve the local perception ability of the model, we also introduce convolutional neural network (CNN) in the position-wise-feed-forward part. We conduct experiments on several datasets to validate the effectiveness of UTHP and explore the changes after the introduction of the recursive mechanism. These experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that the performance of our proposed new model has a certain improvement compared with the previous state-of-the-art models.

title: Universal Transformer Hawkes Process with Adaptive Recursive Iteration
text: Self-exciting point processes have garnered significant attention in modeling complex event sequences, where the occurrence of past events triggers the likelihood of future events. However, existing methods often struggle to capture the intricate temporal dependencies and non-linear patterns inherent in these sequences. To address this limitation, we propose the Universal Transformer Hawkes Process with Adaptive Recursive Iteration (UTHP-ARI), a novel framework that integrates the strengths of transformer architectures and Hawkes processes. UTHP-ARI leverages the self-attention mechanism to model complex event interactions, while the recursive iteration scheme adaptively refines the event representations by recursively applying the transformer encoder. This allows our model to capture long-range dependencies and identify subtle patterns in the data. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive learning rate scheduler that dynamically adjusts the iteration depth based on the convergence rate of the model, ensuring efficient computation and robustness to overfitting. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets, including social media, financial transactions, and healthcare records, demonstrate the superior performance of UTHP-ARI in predicting event sequences and estimating the underlying intensity functions. Notably, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to 15% in terms of log-likelihood and mean absolute error, while exhibiting improved interpretability and robustness. Theoretical analysis and ablation studies provide insights into the efficacy of the adaptive recursive iteration scheme and the role of self-attention in modeling event dependencies. The proposed UTHP-ARI framework has far-reaching implications for applications in event forecasting, anomaly detection, and recommender systems.

title: GPS: A Policy-driven Sampling Approach for Graph Representation Learning
text: Graph representation learning has drawn increasing attention in recent years, especially for learning the low dimensional embedding at both node and graph level for classification and recommendations tasks. To enable learning the representation on the large-scale graph data in the real world, numerous research has focused on developing different sampling strategies to facilitate the training process. Herein, we propose an adaptive Graph Policy-driven Sampling model (GPS), where the influence of each node in the local neighborhood is realized through the adaptive correlation calculation. Specifically, the selections of the neighbors are guided by an adaptive policy algorithm, contributing directly to the message aggregation, node embedding updating, and graph level readout steps. We then conduct comprehensive experiments against baseline methods on graph classification tasks from various perspectives. Our proposed model outperforms the existing ones by 3%-8% on several vital benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art performance in real-world datasets.

title: GPS: A Policy-driven Sampling Approach for Graph Representation Learning
text: The proliferation of graph-structured data has spurred significant interest in graph representation learning, particularly for node and graph-level embeddings in classification and recommendation tasks. To tackle the challenge of scaling graph representation learning to large real-world datasets, researchers have explored various sampling strategies to expedite training. This paper presents an adaptive Graph Policy-driven Sampling model (GPS), which leverages adaptive correlation calculations to capture the influence of each node within its local neighborhood. The GPS model incorporates an adaptive policy algorithm to guide neighbor selection, directly informing message aggregation, node embedding updates, and graph-level readout. Through comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate that GPS outperforms baseline methods by 3%-8% on multiple benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art performance on real-world datasets in graph classification tasks.

title: Two-phase training mitigates class imbalance for camera trap image classification with CNNs
text: By leveraging deep learning to automatically classify camera trap images, ecologists can monitor biodiversity conservation efforts and the effects of climate change on ecosystems more efficiently. Due to the imbalanced class-distribution of camera trap datasets, current models are biased towards the majority classes. As a result, they obtain good performance for a few majority classes but poor performance for many minority classes. We used two-phase training to increase the performance for these minority classes. We trained, next to a baseline model, four models that implemented a different versions of two-phase training on a subset of the highly imbalanced Snapshot Serengeti dataset. Our results suggest that two-phase training can improve performance for many minority classes, with limited loss in performance for the other classes. We find that two-phase training based on majority undersampling increases class-specific F1-scores up to 3.0%. We also find that two-phase training outperforms using only oversampling or undersampling by 6.1% in F1-score on average. Finally, we find that a combination of over- and undersampling leads to a better performance than using them individually.

title: Two-phase training mitigates class imbalance for camera trap image classification with CNNs
text: The automation of camera trap image classification using deep learning has significant potential to enhance the efficiency of biodiversity conservation and climate change monitoring efforts. However, the inherent class imbalance in camera trap datasets leads to biased models that excel in majority classes but struggle with minority classes. To address this limitation, we explored the application of two-phase training on a subset of the highly imbalanced Snapshot Serengeti dataset. Our experiments involved training a baseline model alongside four variants of two-phase training models. The results demonstrate that two-phase training can effectively improve performance for multiple minority classes with minimal compromise on performance for other classes. Notably, majority undersampling-based two-phase training yields up to 3.0% increases in class-specific F1-scores. Moreover, our findings show that two-phase training outperforms oversampling or undersampling alone by 6.1% on average in terms of F1-score, with a combination of over- and undersampling yielding the best performance.

title: Syntactic Vs. Semantic similarity of Artificial and Real Faults in Mutation Testing Studies
text: Fault seeding is typically used in controlled studies to evaluate and compare test techniques. Central to these techniques lies the hypothesis that artificially seeded faults involve some form of realistic properties and thus provide realistic experimental results. In an attempt to strengthen realism, a recent line of research uses advanced machine learning techniques, such as deep learning and Natural Language Processing (NLP), to seed faults that look like (syntactically) real ones, implying that fault realism is related to syntactic similarity. This raises the question of whether seeding syntactically similar faults indeed results in semantically similar faults and more generally whether syntactically dissimilar faults are far away (semantically) from the real ones. We answer this question by employing 4 fault-seeding techniques (PiTest - a popular mutation testing tool, IBIR - a tool with manually crafted fault patterns, DeepMutation - a learning-based fault seeded framework and CodeBERT - a novel mutation testing tool that use code embeddings) and demonstrate that syntactic similarity does not reflect semantic similarity. We also show that 60%, 47%, 43%, and 7% of the real faults of Defects4J V2 are semantically resembled by CodeBERT, PiTest, IBIR, and DeepMutation faults. We then perform an objective comparison between the techniques and find that CodeBERT and PiTest have similar fault detection capabilities that subsume IBIR and DeepMutation, and that IBIR is the most cost-effective technique. Moreover, the overall fault detection of PiTest, CodeBERT, IBIR, and DeepMutation was, on average, 54%, 53%, 37%, and 7%.

title: Syntactic Vs. Semantic similarity of Artificial and Real Faults in Mutation Testing Studies
text: The validity of fault seeding in evaluating test techniques relies on the assumption that artificially introduced faults exhibit realistic properties, thereby generating reliable experimental outcomes. Recent research has leveraged advanced machine learning techniques, such as deep learning and Natural Language Processing (NLP), to generate faults that mimic real ones syntactically, implying a correlation between fault realism and syntactic similarity. However, this raises fundamental questions regarding the relationship between syntactic and semantic similarity in fault seeding. Specifically, does seeding syntactically similar faults yield semantically similar ones, and conversely, do syntactically dissimilar faults deviate significantly from real ones semantically? To address these questions, we employ four distinct fault-seeding techniques – PiTest, IBIR, DeepMutation, and CodeBERT – and demonstrate that syntactic similarity does not necessarily imply semantic similarity. Our analysis reveals that 60%, 47%, 43%, and 7% of real faults in Defects4J V2 are semantically mirrored by CodeBERT, PiTest, IBIR, and DeepMutation faults, respectively. Furthermore, our objective comparison of the techniques shows that CodeBERT and PiTest exhibit comparable fault detection capabilities, subsuming IBIR and DeepMutation, while IBIR proves to be the most cost-effective approach. Notably, the average fault detection rates for PiTest, CodeBERT, IBIR, and DeepMutation are 54%, 53%, 37%, and 7%, respectively.

title: Spatial Distribution Patterns of Clownfish in Recirculating Aquaculture Systems
text: Successful aquaculture systems can reduce the pressure and help secure the most diverse and productive Red Sea coral reef ecosystem to maintain a healthy and functional ecosystem within a sustainable blue economy. Interestingly, recirculating aquaculture systems are currently emerging in fish farm production practices. On the other hand, monitoring and detecting fish behaviors provide essential information on fish welfare and contribute to an intelligent production in global aquaculture. This work proposes an efficient approach to analyze the spatial distribution status and motion patterns of juvenile clownfish \textit{(Amphiprion bicinctus)} maintained in aquaria at three stocking densities (1, 5, and 10 individuals/aquarium). The estimated displacement is crucial in assessing the dispersion and velocity to express the clownfish's spatial distribution and movement behavior in a recirculating aquaculture system. Indeed, we aim to compute the velocity, magnitude, and turning angle using an optical flow method to assist aquaculturists in efficiently monitoring and identifying fish behavior. We test the system design on a database containing two days of video streams of juvenile clownfish maintained in aquaria. The proposed displacement estimation reveals good performance in measuring clownfish's motion and dispersion characteristics leading to assessing the potential signs of stress behaviors. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed technique for quantifying variation in clownfish activity levels between recordings taken in the morning and afternoon at different stocking densities. It provides practical baseline support for online predicting and monitoring feeding behavior in ornamental fish aquaculture.

title: Spatial Distribution Patterns of Clownfish in Recirculating Aquaculture Systems
text: The preservation of the Red Sea coral reef ecosystem, one of the most biodiverse and productive ecosystems, relies heavily on the development of sustainable aquaculture systems. Recirculating aquaculture systems, a promising approach in fish farm production, can benefit from the integration of advanced monitoring and detection techniques to ensure optimal fish welfare and intelligent production. This study presents an efficient method for analyzing the spatial distribution and motion patterns of juvenile clownfish (Amphiprion bicinctus) in aquaria at varying stocking densities (1, 5, and 10 individuals/aquarium). By estimating displacement, we can assess the dispersion and velocity of clownfish, providing valuable insights into their spatial distribution and movement behavior in recirculating aquaculture systems. Our approach employs an optical flow method to compute velocity, magnitude, and turning angle, facilitating the efficient monitoring and identification of fish behavior. Evaluation of our system on a database of two-day video streams of juvenile clownfish demonstrates its effectiveness in measuring motion and dispersion characteristics, enabling the detection of potential signs of stress behaviors. Furthermore, our technique reveals significant differences in clownfish activity levels between morning and afternoon recordings at varying stocking densities, providing practical support for online prediction and monitoring of feeding behavior in ornamental fish aquaculture.

title: Designing the Topology of Graph Neural Networks: A Novel Feature Fusion Perspective
text: In recent years, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown superior performance on diverse real-world applications. To improve the model capacity, besides designing aggregation operations, GNN topology design is also very important. In general, there are two mainstream GNN topology design manners. The first one is to stack aggregation operations to obtain the higher-level features but easily got performance drop as the network goes deeper. Secondly, the multiple aggregation operations are utilized in each layer which provides adequate and independent feature extraction stage on local neighbors while are costly to obtain the higher-level information. To enjoy the benefits while alleviating the corresponding deficiencies of these two manners, we learn to design the topology of GNNs in a novel feature fusion perspective which is dubbed F$^2$GNN. To be specific, we provide a feature fusion perspective in designing GNN topology and propose a novel framework to unify the existing topology designs with feature selection and fusion strategies. Then we develop a neural architecture search method on top of the unified framework which contains a set of selection and fusion operations in the search space and an improved differentiable search algorithm. The performance gains on eight real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of F$^2$GNN. We further conduct experiments to show that F$^2$GNN can improve the model capacity while alleviating the deficiencies of existing GNN topology design manners, especially alleviating the over-smoothing problem, by utilizing different levels of features adaptively.

title: Designing the Topology of Graph Neural Networks: A Novel Feature Fusion Perspective
text: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for graph-structured data analysis, achieving state-of-the-art performance in various applications. However, the design of GNN architectures remains largely driven by heuristics and trial-and-error, leading to suboptimal performance and limited interpretability. In particular, the topology of GNNs, which defines the interaction between nodes and features, plays a crucial role in capturing complex relationships in graph data, but its optimization has received scant attention. We propose a novel feature fusion perspective to design the topology of GNNs, which views the graph as a heterogeneous information network and leverages feature fusion techniques to optimize the node and feature interactions. Our approach, dubbed TopoFusion, formulates the topology design problem as a bilevel optimization problem, where the upper level optimizes the feature fusion weights and the lower level optimizes the GNN parameters. We develop an efficient algorithm to solve this problem, which involves alternating between feature fusion weight updates and GNN parameter updates. Experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of TopoFusion, achieving significant performance improvements over state-of-the-art GNN architectures. Notably, our approach leads to more interpretable models, as the optimized topology provides insights into the importance of different features and node interactions. Furthermore, TopoFusion is flexible and can be applied to various GNN architectures, making it a promising tool for graph-structured data analysis. Our work provides a new perspective on GNN design, highlighting the importance of topology optimization for improved performance and interpretability.

title: Res2NetFuse: A Novel Res2Net-based Fusion Method for Infrared and Visible Images
text: The fusion of visible light and infrared images has garnered significant attention in the field of imaging due to its pivotal role in various applications, including surveillance, remote sensing, and medical imaging. Therefore, this paper introduces a novel fusion framework using Res2Net architecture, capturing features across diverse receptive fields and scales for effective extraction of global and local features. Our methodology is structured into three fundamental components: the first part involves the Res2Net-based encoder, followed by the second part, which encompasses the fusion layer, and finally, the third part, which comprises the decoder. The encoder based on Res2Net is utilized for extracting multi-scale features from the input image. Simultaneously, with a single image as input, we introduce a pioneering training strategy tailored for a Res2Net-based encoder. We further enhance the fusion process with a novel strategy based on the attention model, ensuring precise reconstruction by the decoder for the fused image. Experimental results unequivocally showcase our method's unparalleled fusion performance, surpassing existing techniques, as evidenced by rigorous subjective and objective evaluations.

title: Res2NetFuse: A Novel Res2Net-based Fusion Method for Infrared and Visible Images
text: Image fusion, which combines visible light and infrared images, has become a crucial technique in various imaging applications, including surveillance, remote sensing, and medical imaging. This paper presents a novel fusion framework that leverages the Res2Net architecture to capture features across diverse receptive fields and scales, enabling effective extraction of both global and local features. The proposed methodology consists of three integral components: a Res2Net-based encoder for extracting multi-scale features from the input image, a fusion layer, and a decoder. Notably, we introduce a novel training strategy tailored for the Res2Net-based encoder, which accepts a single image as input. Furthermore, an attention-based strategy is incorporated to enhance the fusion process, ensuring precise reconstruction of the fused image by the decoder. Extensive subjective and objective evaluations demonstrate the superior fusion performance of our method, outperforming existing techniques with a significant margin. The proposed framework exhibits great potential for applications where image fusion plays a critical role.

title: Altitude Optimization of UAV Base Stations from Satellite Images Using Deep Neural Network
text: It is expected that unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) will play a vital role in future communication systems. Optimum positioning of UAVs, serving as base stations, can be done through extensive field measurements or ray tracing simulations when the 3D model of the region of interest is available. In this paper, we present an alternative approach to optimize UAV base station altitude for a region. The approach is based on deep learning; specifically, a 2D satellite image of the target region is input to a deep neural network to predict path loss distributions for different UAV altitudes. The predicted path distributions are used to calculate the coverage in the region; and the optimum altitude, maximizing the coverage, is determined. The neural network is designed and trained to produce multiple path loss distributions in a single inference; thus, it is not necessary to train a separate network for each altitude.

title: Altitude Optimization of UAV Base Stations from Satellite Images Using Deep Neural Network
text: The increasing demand for reliable wireless communication in remote or disaster-stricken areas has driven the development of Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) base stations. However, optimizing the altitude of these UAVs to ensure maximum coverage and minimal interference remains a crucial challenge. In this context, we propose a novel approach that leverages satellite images and deep neural networks to determine the optimal altitude of UAV base stations. Our method involves training a convolutional neural network (CNN) on a dataset of satellite images with corresponding UAV altitude and coverage information. The CNN learns to predict the optimal altitude of the UAV based on the satellite image features. Experimental results using a dataset of 1000 satellite images demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional optimization methods, achieving an average increase in coverage area of 23.7% and a reduction in interference of 17.3%. Our findings have significant implications for the deployment of UAV base stations in a variety of scenarios, including search and rescue operations and rural area networks.

title: Active Learning of Quantum System Hamiltonians yields Query Advantage
text: Hamiltonian learning is an important procedure in quantum system identification, calibration, and successful operation of quantum computers. Through queries to the quantum system, this procedure seeks to obtain the parameters of a given Hamiltonian model and description of noise sources. Standard techniques for Hamiltonian learning require careful design of queries and $O(ε^{-2})$ queries in achieving learning error $ε$ due to the standard quantum limit. With the goal of efficiently and accurately estimating the Hamiltonian parameters within learning error $ε$ through minimal queries, we introduce an active learner that is given an initial set of training examples and the ability to interactively query the quantum system to generate new training data. We formally specify and experimentally assess the performance of this Hamiltonian active learning (HAL) algorithm for learning the six parameters of a two-qubit cross-resonance Hamiltonian on four different superconducting IBM Quantum devices. Compared with standard techniques for the same problem and a specified learning error, HAL achieves up to a $99.8\%$ reduction in queries required, and a $99.1\%$ reduction over the comparable non-adaptive learning algorithm. Moreover, with access to prior information on a subset of Hamiltonian parameters and given the ability to select queries with linearly (or exponentially) longer system interaction times during learning, HAL can exceed the standard quantum limit and achieve Heisenberg (or super-Heisenberg) limited convergence rates during learning.

title: Active Learning of Quantum System Hamiltonians yields Query Advantage
text: Characterizing the Hamiltonian of a quantum system is a fundamental task in quantum physics, with applications in quantum simulation, metrology, and information processing. However, determining the Hamiltonian from experimental measurements is a challenging problem, particularly when the system's dimensionality is large. Active learning, where the learning algorithm adaptively selects the most informative experiments, has been proposed as a promising approach to tackle this challenge. In this context, we investigate the query complexity of active learning for Hamiltonian characterization and demonstrate a significant query advantage over passive learning methods. Our approach leverages a novel combination of Bayesian experimental design and probabilistic Hamiltonian learning, allowing us to efficiently explore the vast space of possible Hamiltonians. We show that, by actively selecting the most informative measurements, our algorithm can achieve a quadratic reduction in the number of queries required to achieve a target accuracy, compared to passive learning methods. This improvement is robust to various sources of noise and imperfections in the experimental setup. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a range of quantum systems, including spin chains and harmonic oscillators. Our results have significant implications for the experimental characterization of quantum systems, enabling faster and more efficient Hamiltonian learning. Furthermore, our methodology provides a framework for integrating active learning with probabilistic modeling, opening up new avenues for advancing the state-of-the-art in quantum system characterization.

title: Onsite Non-Line-of-Sight Imaging via Online Calibrations
text: There has been an increasing interest in deploying non-line-of-sight (NLOS) imaging systems for recovering objects behind an obstacle. Existing solutions generally pre-calibrate the system before scanning the hidden objects. Onsite adjustments of the occluder, object and scanning pattern require re-calibration. We present an online calibration technique that directly decouples the acquired transients at onsite scanning into the LOS and hidden components. We use the former to directly (re)calibrate the system upon changes of scene/obstacle configurations, scanning regions, and scanning patterns whereas the latter for hidden object recovery via spatial, frequency or learning based techniques. Our technique avoids using auxiliary calibration apparatus such as mirrors or checkerboards and supports both laboratory validations and real-world deployments.

title: Onsite Non-Line-of-Sight Imaging via Online Calibrations
text: Non-line-of-sight (NLoS) imaging has garnered significant attention in computer vision due to its potential applications in fields like robotics, surveillance, and healthcare. However, existing approaches often rely on extensive offline calibration procedures, limiting their practicality in real-world scenarios. We propose a novel onsite NLoS imaging framework that leverages online calibrations to estimate the hidden scene's geometry and reflectance. By fusing transient responses from a laser scanner and a camera, our approach enables high-fidelity imaging of objects outside the direct line of sight. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in various environments, achieving a mean angular error of 2.5° and a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 25.3 dB. These findings pave the way for the development of more practical and versatile NLoS imaging systems.

title: Mutation Testing in Evolving Systems: Studying the relevance of mutants to code evolution
text: When software evolves, opportunities for introducing faults appear. Therefore, it is important to test the evolved program behaviors during each evolution cycle. We conduct an exploratory study to investigate the properties of commit-relevant mutants, i.e., the test elements of commit-aware mutation testing, by offering a general definition and an experimental approach to identify them. We thus, aim at investigating the prevalence, location, comparative advantages of commit-aware mutation testing over time (i.e., the program evolution) and the predictive power of several commit-related features to understand the essential properties for its best-effort application case. Our approach utilizes the impact of mutants and the effects of one mutant on another in capturing and analyzing the implicit interactions between the changed and unchanged code parts. The study analyses millions of mutants (over 10 million), 288 commits, five (5) different open-source software projects involving over 68,213 CPU days of computation and sets a ground truth where we perform our analysis. Our analysis shows that commit-relevant mutants are located mainly outside of program commit change (81%), while an effective selection of commit-relevant mutants can reduce the number of mutants by up to 93%. In addition, we demonstrate that commit relevant mutation testing is significantly more effective and efficient than state-of-the-art baselines. Our analysis of the predictive power of mutants and commit-related features in predicting commit-relevant mutants found that most proxy features do not reliably predict commit-relevant mutants. This empirical study highlights the properties of commit-relevant mutants and demonstrates the importance of identifying and selecting commit-relevant mutants when testing evolving software systems.

title: Mutation Testing in Evolving Systems: Studying the relevance of mutants to code evolution
text: The rapid pace of software evolution necessitates the development of robust testing strategies that can keep up with the dynamic nature of modern software systems. Mutation testing, a popular technique for evaluating the effectiveness of test suites, has been largely overlooked in the context of evolving systems. This oversight is particularly concerning, as the relevance of mutants to code evolution remains unknown. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a large-scale empirical study investigating the relevance of mutants to code evolution in three open-source systems with diverse evolution patterns. We employed a novel mutation testing framework, EvoMut, which incorporates evolutionary information to guide the mutation process. Our methodology involved analyzing over 10,000 mutants, tracing their evolution across 500 commits, and correlating mutant behavior with code changes, developer intentions, and test suite effectiveness. Our findings indicate that a significant proportion of mutants (62%) become irrelevant due to code evolution, with the majority of these (71%) being removed or modified within a short period (≤ 10 commits). Furthermore, we discovered that mutants related to changed functionality are more likely to remain relevant, whereas those related to refactored code are more likely to become obsolete. Our results have significant implications for the development of mutation testing strategies tailored to evolving systems, highlighting the need for adaptive mutation testing approaches that take into account the dynamic nature of software evolution. By providing insights into the relevance of mutants to code evolution, our study lays the foundation for more efficient and effective testing of evolving software systems.

title: Fine-Tuning Transformers: Vocabulary Transfer
text: Transformers are responsible for the vast majority of recent advances in natural language processing. The majority of practical natural language processing applications of these models are typically enabled through transfer learning. This paper studies if corpus-specific tokenization used for fine-tuning improves the resulting performance of the model. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate that such tokenization combined with the initialization and fine-tuning strategy for the vocabulary tokens speeds up the transfer and boosts the performance of the fine-tuned model. We call this aspect of transfer facilitation vocabulary transfer.

title: Fine-Tuning Transformers: Vocabulary Transfer
text: Pre-trained transformers have revolutionized natural language processing, but their vocabulary is often limited to the training dataset. We address this limitation by proposing a novel fine-tuning approach that enables vocabulary transfer across datasets. Our method leverages masked language modeling to adapt the transformer's vocabulary to the target dataset, while preserving its linguistic knowledge. Experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the performance of transformer-based models on out-of-vocabulary words, achieving state-of-the-art results in several cases.

title: A Statistical Analysis of Polyak-Ruppert Averaged Q-learning
text: We study Q-learning with Polyak-Ruppert averaging in a discounted Markov decision process in synchronous and tabular settings. Under a Lipschitz condition, we establish a functional central limit theorem for the averaged iteration $\bar{\boldsymbol{Q}}_T$ and show that its standardized partial-sum process converges weakly to a rescaled Brownian motion. The functional central limit theorem implies a fully online inference method for reinforcement learning. Furthermore, we show that $\bar{\boldsymbol{Q}}_T$ is the regular asymptotically linear (RAL) estimator for the optimal Q-value function $\boldsymbol{Q}^*$ that has the most efficient influence function. We present a nonasymptotic analysis for the $\ell_{\infty}$ error, $\mathbb{E}\|\bar{\boldsymbol{Q}}_T-\boldsymbol{Q}^*\|_{\infty}$, showing that it matches the instance-dependent lower bound for polynomial step sizes. Similar results are provided for entropy-regularized Q-learning without the Lipschitz condition.

title: A Statistical Analysis of Polyak-Ruppert Averaged Q-learning
text: Off-policy reinforcement learning algorithms, such as Q-learning, often suffer from high variance, hindering their applicability in real-world scenarios. Polyak-Ruppert averaging has been proposed as a variance reduction technique, but its effectiveness in Q-learning remains unclear. We investigate the statistical properties of Polyak-Ruppert averaged Q-learning and provide a comprehensive analysis of its convergence and bias-variance tradeoff. Through a combination of theoretical derivations and empirical evaluations, we show that the averaged algorithm achieves a better bias-variance tradeoff than its non-averaged counterpart, leading to improved performance in various environments. Furthermore, we establish a finite-sample error bound for the averaged algorithm, providing insights into its robustness to hyperparameter choices. Our findings have significant implications for the design of efficient off-policy reinforcement learning algorithms.

title: Isotuning With Applications To Scale-Free Online Learning
text: We extend and combine several tools of the literature to design fast, adaptive, anytime and scale-free online learning algorithms. Scale-free regret bounds must scale linearly with the maximum loss, both toward large losses and toward very small losses. Adaptive regret bounds demonstrate that an algorithm can take advantage of easy data and potentially have constant regret. We seek to develop fast algorithms that depend on as few parameters as possible, in particular they should be anytime and thus not depend on the time horizon. Our first and main tool, isotuning, is a generalization of the idea of designing adaptive learning rates that balance the trade-off of the regret. We provide a simple and versatile theorem that can be applied to a wide range of settings, and competes with the best balancing in hindsight within a factor 2. The second tool is an online correction, which allows us to obtain centered bounds for many algorithms, to prevent the regret bounds from being vacuous when the domain is overly large or only partially constrained. The last tool, null updates, prevents the algorithm from performing overly large updates, which could result in unbounded regret, or even invalid updates. We develop a general theory to combine all these tools and apply it to several standard algorithms. In particular, we (almost entirely) restore the adaptivity to small losses of FTRL for unbounded domains, design and prove scale-free adaptive guarantees for a variant of Mirror Descent (at least when the Bregman divergence is convex in its second argument), extend Adapt-ML-Prod to scale-free guarantees, and provide several additional contributions about Prod, AdaHedge, BOA and Soft-Bayes.

title: Isotuning With Applications To Scale-Free Online Learning
text: The proliferation of online learning platforms has necessitated the development of efficient algorithms capable of handling large-scale datasets. However, existing approaches often struggle to accommodate the inherent scale-free nature of these datasets, leading to suboptimal performance. This paper tackles this challenge by introducing Isotuning, a novel online learning framework that leverages the isotropic properties of scale-free networks to adapt to changing data distributions. Isotuning is grounded in the concept of isotropic regularization, which promotes smoothness along all directions in the parameter space. By incorporating this regularization scheme into an online learning framework, we develop an algorithm that can effectively navigate the intricate structure of scale-free networks. Theoretically, we establish the convergence guarantees of Isotuning under mild assumptions, demonstrating its robustness to noisy and non-stationary data. Empirically, we evaluate Isotuning on a range of benchmark datasets, including social networks, recommender systems, and online advertising platforms. Our results show that Isotuning outperforms state-of-the-art online learning algorithms, achieving significant improvements in terms of predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. Notably, Isotuning exhibits remarkable adaptability to concept drift, maintaining its performance even when faced with sudden changes in the data distribution. The implications of our work are far-reaching, with potential applications in various domains, including personalized recommendation, sentiment analysis, and online anomaly detection. As online learning continues to play an increasingly vital role in modern data-driven systems, the development of Isotuning represents a crucial step towards harnessing the full potential of scale-free networks. Ultimately, our work underscores the importance of isotropic regularization in online learning and paves the way for further research into the interplay between network structure and machine learning algorithms.

title: Modified DDPG car-following model with a real-world human driving experience with CARLA simulator
text: In the autonomous driving field, fusion of human knowledge into Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) is often based on the human demonstration recorded in a simulated environment. This limits the generalization and the feasibility of application in real-world traffic. We propose a two-stage DRL method to train a car-following agent, that modifies the policy by leveraging the real-world human driving experience and achieves performance superior to the pure DRL agent. Training a DRL agent is done within CARLA framework with Robot Operating System (ROS). For evaluation, we designed different driving scenarios to compare the proposed two-stage DRL car-following agent with other agents. After extracting the "good" behavior from the human driver, the agent becomes more efficient and reasonable, which makes this autonomous agent more suitable for Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) traffic.

title: Modified DDPG car-following model with a real-world human driving experience with CARLA simulator
text: Autonomous driving systems often rely on human demonstrations recorded in simulated environments to integrate human knowledge into Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). However, this approach can compromise generalizability and real-world applicability. To address this limitation, we propose a two-stage DRL method that modifies the policy by incorporating real-world human driving experience, outperforming pure DRL agents. Within the CARLA framework and utilizing Robot Operating System (ROS), we train a car-following agent and evaluate its performance in various driving scenarios, comparing it to other agents. By extracting desirable behavior from human drivers, our agent exhibits improved efficiency and rationality, rendering it more suitable for Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) in real-world traffic scenarios.

title: HPRN: Holistic Prior-embedded Relation Network for Spectral Super-Resolution
text: Spectral super-resolution (SSR) refers to the hyperspectral image (HSI) recovery from an RGB counterpart. Due to the one-to-many nature of the SSR problem, a single RGB image can be reprojected to many HSIs. The key to tackle this ill-posed problem is to plug into multi-source prior information such as the natural spatial context-prior of RGB images, deep feature-prior or inherent statistical-prior of HSIs, etc., so as to effectively alleviate the degree of ill-posedness. However, most current approaches only consider the general and limited priors in their customized convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which leads to the inability to guarantee the confidence and fidelity of reconstructed spectra. In this paper, we propose a novel holistic prior-embedded relation network (HPRN) to integrate comprehensive priors to regularize and optimize the solution space of SSR. Basically, the core framework is delicately assembled by several multi-residual relation blocks (MRBs) that fully facilitate the transmission and utilization of the low-frequency content prior of RGBs. Innovatively, the semantic prior of RGB inputs is introduced to mark category attributes, and a semantic-driven spatial relation module (SSRM) is invented to perform the feature aggregation of clustered similar range for refining recovered characteristics. Additionally, we develop a transformer-based channel relation module (TCRM), which breaks the habit of employing scalars as the descriptors of channel-wise relations in the previous deep feature-prior, and replaces them with certain vectors to make the mapping function more robust and smoother. In order to maintain the mathematical correlation and spectral consistency between hyperspectral bands, the second-order prior constraints (SOPC) are incorporated into the loss function to guide the HSI reconstruction.

title: HPRN: Holistic Prior-embedded Relation Network for Spectral Super-Resolution
text: Spectral super-resolution, which involves recovering hyperspectral images from their RGB counterparts, is inherently an ill-posed problem due to its one-to-many nature. To address this challenge, it is essential to harness the power of multi-source prior information, including the natural spatial context-prior of RGB images, deep feature-priors, and inherent statistical-priors of hyperspectral images. However, current approaches often rely on limited and general priors embedded in customized convolutional neural networks, which can compromise the confidence and fidelity of the reconstructed spectra. This paper presents a novel holistic prior-embedded relation network (HPRN) that integrates comprehensive priors to regularize and optimize the solution space of spectral super-resolution. The core framework consists of multi-residual relation blocks that effectively transmit and utilize the low-frequency content prior of RGB images. Furthermore, we introduce a semantic prior to categorize attributes and develop a semantic-driven spatial relation module to aggregate features and refine recovered characteristics. A transformer-based channel relation module is also proposed, which replaces scalar descriptors with vector representations to enhance the robustness and smoothness of the mapping function. To ensure mathematical correlation and spectral consistency between hyperspectral bands, we incorporate second-order prior constraints into the loss function, thus guiding the hyperspectral image reconstruction process. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed HPRN in recovering high-fidelity hyperspectral images from RGB counterparts.

title: IoT Security Challenges and Mitigations: An Introduction
text: The use of IoT in society is perhaps already ubiquitous, with a vast attack surface offering multiple opportunities for malicious actors. This short paper first presents an introduction to IoT and its security issues, including an overview of IoT layer models and topologies, IoT standardisation efforts and protocols. The focus then moves to IoT vulnerabilities and specific suggestions for mitigations. This work's intended audience are those relatively new to IoT though with existing network-related knowledge. It is concluded that device resource constraints and a lack of IoT standards are significant issues. Research opportunities exist to develop efficient IoT IDS and energy-saving cryptography techniques lightweight enough to reasonably deploy. The need for standardised protocols and channel-based security solutions is clear, underpinned by legislative directives to ensure high standards that prevent cost-cutting on the device manufacturing side.

title: IoT Security Challenges and Mitigations: An Introduction
text: The pervasive integration of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in modern society has created a vast and vulnerable attack surface, susceptible to exploitation by malicious entities. This concise study provides an introductory examination of IoT security concerns, encompassing an overview of layer models and topologies, standardization efforts, and protocols. The discussion subsequently shifts to IoT vulnerabilities and proposes mitigation strategies. Intended for readers with a background in network-related knowledge but new to IoT, this work highlights the significant challenges posed by device resource constraints and the lack of standardization. Opportunities for future research include the development of efficient IoT intrusion detection systems and lightweight, energy-saving cryptographic techniques. The need for standardized protocols and channel-based security solutions is underscored, necessitating legislative directives to ensure high security standards and prevent cost-cutting compromises during device manufacturing.

title: Time Series Data Mining Algorithms Towards Scalable and Real-Time Behavior Monitoring
text: In recent years, there have been unprecedented technological advances in sensor technology, and sensors have become more affordable than ever. Thus, sensor-driven data collection is increasingly becoming an attractive and practical option for researchers around the globe. Such data is typically extracted in the form of time series data, which can be investigated with data mining techniques to summarize behaviors of a range of subjects including humans and animals. While enabling cheap and mass collection of data, continuous sensor data recording results in datasets which are big in size and volume, which are challenging to process and analyze with traditional techniques in a timely manner. Such collected sensor data is typically extracted in the form of time series data. There are two main approaches in the literature, namely, shape-based classification and feature-based classification. Shape-based classification determines the best class according to a distance measure. Feature-based classification, on the other hand, measures properties of the time series and finds the best class according to the set of features defined for the time series. In this dissertation, we demonstrate that neither of the two techniques will dominate for some problems, but that some combination of both might be the best. In other words, on a single problem, it might be possible that one of the techniques is better for one subset of the behaviors, and the other technique is better for another subset of behaviors. We introduce a hybrid algorithm to classify behaviors, using both shape and feature measures, in weakly labeled time series data collected from sensors to quantify specific behaviors performed by the subject. We demonstrate that our algorithm can robustly classify real, noisy, and complex datasets, based on a combination of shape and features, and tested our proposed algorithm on real-world datasets.

title: Time Series Data Mining Algorithms Towards Scalable and Real-Time Behavior Monitoring
text: The proliferation of IoT devices and sensors has led to an explosion of time series data, offering unprecedented opportunities for monitoring and analyzing complex behaviors in various domains, such as healthcare, finance, and transportation. However, the sheer volume and velocity of this data pose significant challenges to traditional data mining approaches, necessitating the development of scalable and real-time algorithms for behavior monitoring. In response, we propose a novel framework for time series data mining that leverages a combination of distributed computing, parallel processing, and approximate query techniques to achieve efficient and accurate behavior monitoring. Our approach, termed RealMonitor, consists of three primary components: (1) a distributed data ingestion module that handles high-volume time series data streams, (2) a parallelized feature extraction module that computes behavioral patterns and anomalies, and (3) an approximate query module that enables fast and flexible querying of monitored behaviors. We evaluate RealMonitor on four large-scale time series datasets, demonstrating its ability to process millions of data points in real-time while maintaining a high degree of accuracy. Our experimental results show that RealMonitor achieves significant performance gains over existing state-of-the-art algorithms, reducing processing times by up to 75% while maintaining a mean average precision of 92%. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of RealMonitor in a real-world scenario, where it is deployed to monitor the behavior of patients with chronic diseases, enabling early detection of abnormal patterns and improved healthcare outcomes. The contributions of this work are threefold: (1) a novel distributed framework for time series data mining, (2) a set of parallelized algorithms for feature extraction and anomaly detection, and (3) a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed approach on large-scale datasets. Our findings have significant implications for the development of scalable and real-time behavior monitoring systems, enabling new applications in domains such as smart healthcare, finance, and transportation.

title: Universal Online Learning with Bounded Loss: Reduction to Binary Classification
text: We study universal consistency of non-i.i.d. processes in the context of online learning. A stochastic process is said to admit universal consistency if there exists a learner that achieves vanishing average loss for any measurable response function on this process. When the loss function is unbounded, Blanchard et al. showed that the only processes admitting strong universal consistency are those taking a finite number of values almost surely. However, when the loss function is bounded, the class of processes admitting strong universal consistency is much richer and its characterization could be dependent on the response setting (Hanneke). In this paper, we show that this class of processes is independent from the response setting thereby closing an open question (Hanneke, Open Problem 3). Specifically, we show that the class of processes that admit universal online learning is the same for binary classification as for multiclass classification with countable number of classes. Consequently, any output setting with bounded loss can be reduced to binary classification. Our reduction is constructive and practical. Indeed, we show that the nearest neighbor algorithm is transported by our construction. For binary classification on a process admitting strong universal learning, we prove that nearest neighbor successfully learns at least all finite unions of intervals.

title: Universal Online Learning with Bounded Loss: Reduction to Binary Classification
text: The notion of universal consistency is explored in the context of online learning for non-i.i.d. processes. A process is said to exhibit universal consistency if a learner can be devised to attain vanishing average loss for any measurable response function defined on that process. In the unbounded loss function regime, Blanchard et al. demonstrated that strong universal consistency is only achievable for processes taking a finite number of values almost surely. However, in the bounded loss function setting, the class of processes admitting strong universal consistency is more extensive and, as observed by Hanneke, its characterization may depend on the response setting. This paper resolves an open question (Hanneke, Open Problem 3) by establishing that the class of processes admitting universal online learning is, in fact, response-setting-independent. Specifically, we show that the classes of processes exhibiting universal online learning for binary classification and multiclass classification with a countable number of classes are equivalent. This implies that any bounded-loss output setting can be reduced to binary classification. Our reduction is constructive and practical, as exemplified by the transportation of the nearest neighbor algorithm. Furthermore, for binary classification on processes admitting strong universal learning, we prove that the nearest neighbor algorithm successfully learns all finite unions of intervals.

title: Implementation of Convolutional Neural Network Architecture on 3D Multiparametric Magnetic Resonance Imaging for Prostate Cancer Diagnosis
text: Prostate cancer is one of the most common causes of cancer deaths in men. There is a growing demand for noninvasively and accurately diagnostic methods that facilitate the current standard prostate cancer risk assessment in clinical practice. Still, developing computer-aided classification tools in prostate cancer diagnostics from multiparametric magnetic resonance images continues to be a challenge. In this work, we propose a novel deep learning approach for automatic classification of prostate lesions in the corresponding magnetic resonance images by constructing a two-stage multimodal multi-stream convolutional neural network (CNN)-based architecture framework. Without implementing sophisticated image preprocessing steps or third-party software, our framework achieved the classification performance with the area under a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve value of 0.87. The result outperformed most of the submitted methods and shared the highest value reported by the PROSTATEx Challenge organizer. Our proposed CNN-based framework reflects the potential of assisting medical image interpretation in prostate cancer and reducing unnecessary biopsies.

title: Implementation of Convolutional Neural Network Architecture on 3D Multiparametric Magnetic Resonance Imaging for Prostate Cancer Diagnosis
text: The accurate diagnosis of prostate cancer, a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in men, remains a significant clinical challenge. The development of non-invasive diagnostic methods that can augment the current standard of care is increasingly important. Despite the potential of multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) in prostate cancer diagnostics, the creation of reliable computer-aided classification tools remains an open problem. This study presents a novel deep learning approach to automatic lesion classification in mpMRI, employing a two-stage multimodal multi-stream convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture. Notably, our framework achieves a high classification performance, with an area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve of 0.87, without relying on sophisticated image preprocessing or third-party software. This outcome surpasses most submitted methods and matches the highest reported value in the PROSTATEx Challenge, highlighting the potential of our CNN-based framework to enhance medical image interpretation and reduce unnecessary biopsies in prostate cancer diagnosis.

title: On the Instability of Relative Pose Estimation and RANSAC's Role
text: In this paper we study the numerical instabilities of the 5- and 7-point problems for essential and fundamental matrix estimation in multiview geometry. In both cases we characterize the ill-posed world scenes where the condition number for epipolar estimation is infinite. We also characterize the ill-posed instances in terms of the given image data. To arrive at these results, we present a general framework for analyzing the conditioning of minimal problems in multiview geometry, based on Riemannian manifolds. Experiments with synthetic and real-world data then reveal a striking conclusion: that Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC) in Structure-from-Motion (SfM) does not only serve to filter out outliers, but RANSAC also selects for well-conditioned image data, sufficiently separated from the ill-posed locus that our theory predicts. Our findings suggest that, in future work, one could try to accelerate and increase the success of RANSAC by testing only well-conditioned image data.

title: On the Instability of Relative Pose Estimation and RANSAC's Role
text: The multiview geometry community has long recognized the numerical instabilities inherent to the 5- and 7-point problems in essential and fundamental matrix estimation. This work provides a rigorous characterization of the ill-posed world scenes that give rise to infinite condition numbers in epipolar estimation, as well as the corresponding ill-posed instances in terms of image data. Our approach leverages a novel framework for analyzing the conditioning of minimal problems in multiview geometry, grounded in Riemannian manifolds. Experimental validation using synthetic and real-world data reveals a surprising insight: Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC) in Structure-from-Motion (SfM) not only filters outliers but also implicitly selects for well-conditioned image data, avoiding the ill-posed regions predicted by our theory. These findings have significant implications for future work, suggesting that RANSAC performance could be improved by prioritizing well-conditioned image data.

title: Private Rank Aggregation in Central and Local Models
text: In social choice theory, (Kemeny) rank aggregation is a well-studied problem where the goal is to combine rankings from multiple voters into a single ranking on the same set of items. Since rankings can reveal preferences of voters (which a voter might like to keep private), it is important to aggregate preferences in such a way to preserve privacy. In this work, we present differentially private algorithms for rank aggregation in the pure and approximate settings along with distribution-independent utility upper and lower bounds. In addition to bounds in the central model, we also present utility bounds for the local model of differential privacy.

title: Private Rank Aggregation in Central and Local Models
text: Rank aggregation, a fundamental problem in social choice theory, seeks to combine multiple voter rankings into a single ranking over the same item set. However, as individual rankings can inadvertently disclose voter preferences, there is a pressing need to develop aggregation methods that safeguard privacy. This study presents novel, differentially private algorithms for rank aggregation in both pure and approximate settings, accompanied by distribution-independent utility bounds. Furthermore, we derive bounds for both the central and local models of differential privacy, providing a comprehensive examination of privacy-preserving rank aggregation.

title: Gendered Differences in Face Recognition Accuracy Explained by Hairstyles, Makeup, and Facial Morphology
text: Media reports have accused face recognition of being ''biased'', ''sexist'' and ''racist''. There is consensus in the research literature that face recognition accuracy is lower for females, who often have both a higher false match rate and a higher false non-match rate. However, there is little published research aimed at identifying the cause of lower accuracy for females. For instance, the 2019 Face Recognition Vendor Test that documents lower female accuracy across a broad range of algorithms and datasets also lists ''Analyze cause and effect'' under the heading ''What we did not do''. We present the first experimental analysis to identify major causes of lower face recognition accuracy for females on datasets where previous research has observed this result. Controlling for equal amount of visible face in the test images mitigates the apparent higher false non-match rate for females. Additional analysis shows that makeup-balanced datasets further improves females to achieve lower false non-match rates. Finally, a clustering experiment suggests that images of two different females are inherently more similar than of two different males, potentially accounting for a difference in false match rates.

title: Gendered Differences in Face Recognition Accuracy Explained by Hairstyles, Makeup, and Facial Morphology
text: Face recognition systems have become ubiquitous in various applications, including security, surveillance, and social media. Despite their widespread adoption, recent studies have revealed significant gendered differences in face recognition accuracy, with females often being misclassified at higher rates than males. However, the underlying causes of these disparities remain poorly understood. This study investigates the role of hairstyles, makeup, and facial morphology in explaining gendered differences in face recognition accuracy. We collect a large-scale dataset of 10,000 facial images, annotated with Hairstyle, Makeup, and Facial Morphology features, and evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art face recognition models on this dataset. Our results show that hairstyles and makeup significantly contribute to the gender gap in face recognition accuracy, with females wearing makeup being misclassified at a rate 25% higher than females without makeup. Furthermore, we find that facial morphology features, such as nose shape and facial symmetry, also play a significant role in gendered differences. Our findings have important implications for the development of more inclusive and equitable face recognition systems, and highlight the need for more diverse and representative datasets.

title: MetaGraspNet_v0: A Large-Scale Benchmark Dataset for Vision-driven Robotic Grasping via Physics-based Metaverse Synthesis
text: There has been increasing interest in smart factories powered by robotics systems to tackle repetitive, laborious tasks. One impactful yet challenging task in robotics-powered smart factory applications is robotic grasping: using robotic arms to grasp objects autonomously in different settings. Robotic grasping requires a variety of computer vision tasks such as object detection, segmentation, grasp prediction, pick planning, etc. While significant progress has been made in leveraging of machine learning for robotic grasping, particularly with deep learning, a big challenge remains in the need for large-scale, high-quality RGBD datasets that cover a wide diversity of scenarios and permutations. To tackle this big, diverse data problem, we are inspired by the recent rise in the concept of metaverse, which has greatly closed the gap between virtual worlds and the physical world. Metaverses allow us to create digital twins of real-world manufacturing scenarios and to virtually create different scenarios from which large volumes of data can be generated for training models. In this paper, we present MetaGraspNet: a large-scale benchmark dataset for vision-driven robotic grasping via physics-based metaverse synthesis. The proposed dataset contains 100,000 images and 25 different object types and is split into 5 difficulties to evaluate object detection and segmentation model performance in different grasping scenarios. We also propose a new layout-weighted performance metric alongside the dataset for evaluating object detection and segmentation performance in a manner that is more appropriate for robotic grasp applications compared to existing general-purpose performance metrics. Our benchmark dataset is available open-source on Kaggle, with the first phase consisting of detailed object detection, segmentation, layout annotations, and a layout-weighted performance metric script.

title: MetaGraspNet_v0: A Large-Scale Benchmark Dataset for Vision-driven Robotic Grasping via Physics-based Metaverse Synthesis
text: The proliferation of robotics systems in smart factories has highlighted the significance of robotic grasping, a task that entails autonomous object manipulation in diverse settings. Effective robotic grasping relies on a range of computer vision tasks, including object detection, segmentation, and grasp prediction. Although machine learning, particularly deep learning, has made substantial strides in robotic grasping, the lack of large-scale, high-quality RGBD datasets that capture a wide spectrum of scenarios and permutations remains a major hurdle. Inspired by the concept of metaverse, which has bridged the gap between virtual and physical worlds, we propose a novel approach to tackle this data challenge. By creating digital twins of real-world manufacturing scenarios, we can generate vast amounts of data for model training. This paper introduces MetaGraspNet, a large-scale benchmark dataset for vision-driven robotic grasping, synthesized using physics-based metaverse techniques. Comprising 100,000 images and 25 object types, the dataset is divided into five difficulty levels to assess object detection and segmentation model performance in varying grasping scenarios. We also propose a layout-weighted performance metric, tailored to evaluate object detection and segmentation performance in a manner more suited to robotic grasp applications than traditional metrics. The open-source dataset, available on Kaggle, includes detailed object detection, segmentation, and layout annotations, as well as a script for the proposed performance metric.

title: An additive graphical model for discrete data
text: We introduce a nonparametric graphical model for discrete node variables based on additive conditional independence. Additive conditional independence is a three way statistical relation that shares similar properties with conditional independence by satisfying the semi-graphoid axioms. Based on this relation we build an additive graphical model for discrete variables that does not suffer from the restriction of a parametric model such as the Ising model. We develop an estimator of the new graphical model via the penalized estimation of the discrete version of the additive precision operator and establish the consistency of the estimator under the ultrahigh-dimensional setting. Along with these methodological developments, we also exploit the properties of discrete random variables to uncover a deeper relation between additive conditional independence and conditional independence than previously known. The new graphical model reduces to a conditional independence graphical model under certain sparsity conditions. We conduct simulation experiments and analysis of an HIV antiretroviral therapy data set to compare the new method with existing ones.

title: An additive graphical model for discrete data
text: By leveraging additive conditional independence, a three-way statistical relation that satisfies the semi-graphoid axioms, we propose a nonparametric graphical model for discrete node variables that overcomes the limitations of parametric models, such as the Ising model. Our approach involves estimating the discrete additive precision operator using penalized estimation, and we establish the consistency of this estimator in ultrahigh-dimensional settings. Furthermore, we uncover a previously unknown connection between additive conditional independence and conditional independence, which is rooted in the properties of discrete random variables. Notably, our graphical model reduces to a conditional independence graphical model under certain sparsity conditions. We validate our method through comprehensive simulation experiments and a real-world analysis of an HIV antiretroviral therapy data set, comparing its performance to existing approaches. Our findings demonstrate the potential of this novel graphical model to uncover complex dependencies in discrete variables.

title: WaCoDiS: Automated Earth Observation Data Processing within an Event-Driven Architecture for Water Monitoring
text: To ensure an efficient and environmentally friendly water resource management, water management associations need means for efficient water monitoring as well as novel strategies to reduce the pollution of surface and ground water. Traditionally, water management associations operate large sensor networks to suffice their needs for hydrological and meteorological measurement data to monitor and model physical processes within catchments. Implementing a comprehensive monitoring system often suffers from sparse coverage of in-situ data. Due to the evolvement of the Copernicus satellite platforms, the broader availability of satellite data provides a great potential for deriving complementary information from Earth Observation data. Although the number of satellite data platforms that provide online processing environments is growing, it is still a big challenge to integrate those platforms into traditional workflows of users from environmental domains such as hydrology. Thus, in this paper, we introduce a software architecture to facilitate the generation of Earth Observation information targeted towards hydrology. The presented WaCoDiS System comprises several microservices as well standardized interfaces that enable a platform-independent processing of satellite data. First, we discuss the contribution of Earth Observation data to water monitoring and derive several challenges regarding the facilitation of satellite data processing. We then describe our system design with a brief overview about the different system components which form an automated processing pipeline. The suitability of our system is proven as part of a pre-operational deployment for a German water management association. In addition, we demonstrate how our system is capable of integrating satellite data platforms, using the Copernicus Data and Exploitation Platform - Deutschland (CODE-DE) as a reference example.

title: WaCoDiS: Automated Earth Observation Data Processing within an Event-Driven Architecture for Water Monitoring
text: The proliferation of earth observation (EO) satellites has generated unprecedented volumes of data, necessitating efficient processing and analysis to support timely decision-making in water monitoring applications. Traditional processing pipelines, however, are often cumbersome, inflexible, and prone to bottlenecks, hindering the timely dissemination of actionable insights. To address these limitations, we present WaCoDiS, a novel event-driven architecture designed to automate EO data processing for water monitoring. WaCoDiS leverages a microservices-based design, wherein modular components are orchestrated to process EO data in response to specific events, such as sensor activations or data ingestions. This approach enables real-time processing, reduces latency, and enhances fault tolerance. We employ a data-driven methodology, utilizing machine learning algorithms to classify water bodies and detect anomalies, and integrate domain-specific knowledge to contextualize results. Our evaluation, conducted on a large-scale EO dataset, demonstrates WaCoDiS's efficacy in reducing processing times by up to 75% compared to traditional batch-processing approaches. Moreover, WaCoDiS's event-driven paradigm enables the system to respond to changing environmental conditions, such as flood events, with an average response time of 30 minutes. We also observe a significant improvement in accuracy, with WaCoDiS achieving a mean absolute error of 0.12 in water body classification, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. The WaCoDiS framework offers a scalable, flexible, and efficient solution for automating EO data processing in water monitoring applications. Our findings have important implications for the development of real-time decision support systems, enabling timely responses to water-related emergencies and improving the overall resilience of water management systems.

title: StyleGAN-V: A Continuous Video Generator with the Price, Image Quality and Perks of StyleGAN2
text: Videos show continuous events, yet most $-$ if not all $-$ video synthesis frameworks treat them discretely in time. In this work, we think of videos of what they should be $-$ time-continuous signals, and extend the paradigm of neural representations to build a continuous-time video generator. For this, we first design continuous motion representations through the lens of positional embeddings. Then, we explore the question of training on very sparse videos and demonstrate that a good generator can be learned by using as few as 2 frames per clip. After that, we rethink the traditional image + video discriminators pair and design a holistic discriminator that aggregates temporal information by simply concatenating frames' features. This decreases the training cost and provides richer learning signal to the generator, making it possible to train directly on 1024$^2$ videos for the first time. We build our model on top of StyleGAN2 and it is just ${\approx}5\%$ more expensive to train at the same resolution while achieving almost the same image quality. Moreover, our latent space features similar properties, enabling spatial manipulations that our method can propagate in time. We can generate arbitrarily long videos at arbitrary high frame rate, while prior work struggles to generate even 64 frames at a fixed rate. Our model is tested on four modern 256$^2$ and one 1024$^2$-resolution video synthesis benchmarks. In terms of sheer metrics, it performs on average ${\approx}30\%$ better than the closest runner-up.
