title: StyleGAN-V: A Continuous Video Generator with the Price, Image Quality and Perks of StyleGAN2
text: We reconceptualize videos as time-continuous signals, deviating from the prevailing discrete treatment in most video synthesis frameworks. To this end, we develop a continuous-time video generator grounded in neural representations. Our approach begins with the design of continuous motion representations leveraging positional embeddings. We also investigate the feasibility of training on sparse videos, demonstrating that a robust generator can be learned from as few as 2 frames per clip. Furthermore, we overhaul the traditional image-video discriminator paradigm by introducing a holistic discriminator that aggregates temporal information through feature concatenation. This innovative discriminator reduces training costs while providing a richer learning signal to the generator, enabling direct training on 1024² videos for the first time. Built upon StyleGAN2, our model incurs only a 5% additional training cost at the same resolution, while maintaining comparable image quality. Moreover, our latent space exhibits similar properties, facilitating spatial manipulations that can be temporally propagated. Our model can generate arbitrarily long videos at arbitrary high frame rates, unlike prior work, which struggles to produce even 64 frames at a fixed rate. Evaluation on five modern video synthesis benchmarks (four at 256² and one at 1024² resolution) reveals an average improvement of approximately 30% over the closest competitor.

title: Intersection focused Situation Coverage-based Verification and Validation Framework for Autonomous Vehicles Implemented in CARLA
text: Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) i.e., self-driving cars, operate in a safety critical domain, since errors in the autonomous driving software can lead to huge losses. Statistically, road intersections which are a part of the AVs operational design domain (ODD), have some of the highest accident rates. Hence, testing AVs to the limits on road intersections and assuring their safety on road intersections is pertinent, and thus the focus of this paper. We present a situation coverage-based (SitCov) AV-testing framework for the verification and validation (V&V) and safety assurance of AVs, developed in an open-source AV simulator named CARLA. The SitCov AV-testing framework focuses on vehicle-to-vehicle interaction on a road intersection under different environmental and intersection configuration situations, using situation coverage criteria for automatic test suite generation for safety assurance of AVs. We have developed an ontology for intersection situations, and used it to generate a situation hyperspace i.e., the space of all possible situations arising from that ontology. For the evaluation of our SitCov AV-testing framework, we have seeded multiple faults in our ego AV, and compared situation coverage based and random situation generation. We have found that both generation methodologies trigger around the same number of seeded faults, but the situation coverage-based generation tells us a lot more about the weaknesses of the autonomous driving algorithm of our ego AV, especially in edge-cases. Our code is publicly available online, anyone can use our SitCov AV-testing framework and use it or build further on top of it. This paper aims to contribute to the domain of V&V and development of AVs, not only from a theoretical point of view, but also from the viewpoint of an open-source software contribution and releasing a flexible/effective tool for V&V and development of AVs.

title: Intersection focused Situation Coverage-based Verification and Validation Framework for Autonomous Vehicles Implemented in CARLA
text: Ensuring the safety and reliability of Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) is paramount, as software errors can have devastating consequences. Road intersections, a critical component of the operational design domain (ODD), are notorious for their high accident rates. Consequently, rigorous testing and validation of AVs in these scenarios is crucial. This paper presents a novel situation coverage-based (SitCov) testing framework for the verification, validation, and safety assurance of AVs, developed within the open-source CARLA simulator. The SitCov framework focuses on vehicle-to-vehicle interactions at road intersections, leveraging situation coverage criteria to automatically generate test suites that guarantee safety assurance. To this end, we have developed an intersection situation ontology, which enables the creation of a situation hyperspace encompassing all possible scenarios. In evaluating our framework, we injected multiple faults into our ego AV and compared situation coverage-based and random situation generation. Our results show that both approaches trigger a similar number of faults, but the situation coverage-based method provides invaluable insights into the weaknesses of the autonomous driving algorithm, particularly in edge cases. We release our code publicly, allowing the community to utilize and build upon our SitCov framework, thereby contributing to the advancement of AV development and verification from both theoretical and practical perspectives.

title: Parallelized and Randomized Adversarial Imitation Learning for Safety-Critical Self-Driving Vehicles
text: Self-driving cars and autonomous driving research has been receiving considerable attention as major promising prospects in modern artificial intelligence applications. According to the evolution of advanced driver assistance system (ADAS), the design of self-driving vehicle and autonomous driving systems becomes complicated and safety-critical. In general, the intelligent system simultaneously and efficiently activates ADAS functions. Therefore, it is essential to consider reliable ADAS function coordination to control the driving system, safely. In order to deal with this issue, this paper proposes a randomized adversarial imitation learning (RAIL) algorithm. The RAIL is a novel derivative-free imitation learning method for autonomous driving with various ADAS functions coordination; and thus it imitates the operation of decision maker that controls autonomous driving with various ADAS functions. The proposed method is able to train the decision maker that deals with the LIDAR data and controls the autonomous driving in multi-lane complex highway environments. The simulation-based evaluation verifies that the proposed method achieves desired performance.

title: Parallelized and Randomized Adversarial Imitation Learning for Safety-Critical Self-Driving Vehicles
text: Safety-critical self-driving vehicles rely on robust and efficient imitation learning algorithms to mimic human driving behavior. However, existing approaches are often limited by their sequential nature, susceptibility to adversarial attacks, and lack of exploration in complex scenarios. We propose a novel parallelized and randomized adversarial imitation learning framework, tailored to safety-critical self-driving vehicles. Our approach leverages parallel computing to accelerate the learning process, while incorporating randomization techniques to improve exploration and robustness. We introduce a novel adversarial loss function that simulates diverse attack scenarios, enabling the learned policy to generalize better to unseen situations. Experimental results on a large-scale autonomous driving dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art imitation learning algorithms in terms of driving safety, efficiency, and adaptability. Notably, our approach achieves a 37% reduction in collision rate and a 25% improvement in driving smoothness compared to the best baseline method.

title: Shallow decision trees for explainable $k$-means clustering
text: A number of recent works have employed decision trees for the construction of explainable partitions that aim to minimize the $k$-means cost function. These works, however, largely ignore metrics related to the depths of the leaves in the resulting tree, which is perhaps surprising considering how the explainability of a decision tree depends on these depths. To fill this gap in the literature, we propose an efficient algorithm that takes into account these metrics. In experiments on 16 datasets, our algorithm yields better results than decision-tree clustering algorithms such as the ones presented in , , and , typically achieving lower or equivalent costs with considerably shallower trees. We also show, through a simple adaptation of existing techniques, that the problem of building explainable partitions induced by binary trees for the $k$-means cost function does not admit an $(1+ε)$-approximation in polynomial time unless $P=NP$, which justifies the quest for approximation algorithms and/or heuristics.

title: Shallow decision trees for explainable $k$-means clustering
text: The increasing adoption of clustering algorithms in high-stakes applications has heightened the need for explainability, a requirement often at odds with the pursuit of accuracy. In response, we present a novel approach to $k$-means clustering that leverages shallow decision trees to provide interpretable insights into cluster assignments. By training a decision tree to mimic the clustering behavior of a traditional $k$-means model, we create an explainable proxy that approximates the original cluster boundaries. Our methodology, which we term ShallowTree, involves iteratively refining the decision tree using a novel objective function that balances fidelity to the original clusters with tree simplicity. Empirical evaluations on a suite of benchmark datasets demonstrate that ShallowTree achieves comparable clustering performance to traditional $k$-means while providing meaningful feature importance scores and visualizable decision boundaries. Moreover, our approach is shown to be more effective than existing explainable clustering methods in high-dimensional settings, highlighting its potential for real-world applications.

title: Sequential memory improves sample and memory efficiency in Episodic Control
text: State of the art deep reinforcement learning algorithms are sample inefficient due to the large number of episodes they require to achieve asymptotic performance. Episodic Reinforcement Learning (ERL) algorithms, inspired by the mammalian hippocampus, typically use extended memory systems to bootstrap learning from past events to overcome this sample-inefficiency problem. However, such memory augmentations are often used as mere buffers, from which isolated past experiences are drawn to learn from in an offline fashion (e.g., replay). Here, we demonstrate that including a bias in the acquired memory content derived from the order of episodic sampling improves both the sample and memory efficiency of an episodic control algorithm. We test our Sequential Episodic Control (SEC) model in a foraging task to show that storing and using integrated episodes as event sequences leads to faster learning with fewer memory requirements as opposed to a standard ERL benchmark, Model-Free Episodic Control, that buffers isolated events only. We also study the effect of memory constraints and forgetting on the sequential and non-sequential version of the SEC algorithm. Furthermore, we discuss how a hippocampal-like fast memory system could bootstrap slow cortical and subcortical learning subserving habit formation in the mammalian brain.

title: Sequential memory improves sample and memory efficiency in Episodic Control
text: The limitations of deep reinforcement learning algorithms in terms of sample efficiency have been well-documented, requiring a large number of episodes to attain asymptotic performance. Episodic Reinforcement Learning (ERL) algorithms, inspired by the mammalian hippocampus, have been proposed to mitigate this issue by leveraging extended memory systems to bootstrap learning from past events. However, existing approaches often utilize these memory augmentations as mere buffers, drawing isolated past experiences in an offline manner to facilitate learning. We challenge this paradigm by introducing a bias in the acquired memory content derived from the order of episodic sampling, significantly enhancing both sample and memory efficiency in an episodic control algorithm. Our Sequential Episodic Control (SEC) model, evaluated in a foraging task, demonstrates faster learning with reduced memory requirements compared to the standard ERL benchmark, Model-Free Episodic Control, which buffers isolated events only. We also investigate the impact of memory constraints and forgetting on both sequential and non-sequential versions of the SEC algorithm, and discuss the potential for a hippocampal-like fast memory system to bootstrap slow cortical and subcortical learning subserving habit formation in the mammalian brain.

title: Distance-Aware Private Set Intersection
text: Private set intersection (PSI) allows two mutually untrusting parties to compute an intersection of their sets, without revealing information about items that are not in the intersection. This work introduces a PSI variant called distance-aware PSI (DA-PSI) for sets whose elements lie in a metric space. DA-PSI returns pairs of items that are within a specified distance threshold of each other. This paper puts forward DA-PSI constructions for two metric spaces: (i) Minkowski distance of order 1 over the set of integers (i.e., for integers $a$ and $b$, their distance is $|a-b|$); and (ii) Hamming distance over the set of binary strings of length $\ell$. In the Minkowski DA-PSI protocol, the communication complexity scales logarithmically in the distance threshold and linearly in the set size. In the Hamming DA-PSI protocol, the communication volume scales quadratically in the distance threshold and is independent of the dimensionality of string length $\ell$. Experimental results with real applications confirm that DA-PSI provides more effective matching at lower cost than naive solutions.

title: Distance-Aware Private Set Intersection
text: Private set intersection (PSI) enables two parties to compute the intersection of their sets without revealing any additional information. However, existing PSI protocols neglect the spatial relationships between elements, which is essential in many real-world applications, such as location-based services and genomic data analysis. We propose Distance-Aware Private Set Intersection (DA-PSI), a novel protocol that incorporates distance metrics into the PSI computation while maintaining privacy. Our approach leverages a combination of homomorphic encryption and garbled circuits to enable efficient and secure computation of the intersection, along with the distances between elements. We formally prove the security of DA-PSI in the semi-honest model and demonstrate its practicality through experiments on real-world datasets. Our results show that DA-PSI outperforms state-of-the-art PSI protocols in terms of computational overhead and communication complexity, particularly for large datasets. Furthermore, we illustrate the utility of DA-PSI in a location-based service application, where it enables the identification of nearby points of interest while preserving user privacy.

title: Nonconvex Stochastic Scaled-Gradient Descent and Generalized Eigenvector Problems
text: Motivated by the problem of online canonical correlation analysis, we propose the \emph{Stochastic Scaled-Gradient Descent} (SSGD) algorithm for minimizing the expectation of a stochastic function over a generic Riemannian manifold. SSGD generalizes the idea of projected stochastic gradient descent and allows the use of scaled stochastic gradients instead of stochastic gradients. In the special case of a spherical constraint, which arises in generalized eigenvector problems, we establish a nonasymptotic finite-sample bound of $\sqrt{1/T}$, and show that this rate is minimax optimal, up to a polylogarithmic factor of relevant parameters. On the asymptotic side, a novel trajectory-averaging argument allows us to achieve local asymptotic normality with a rate that matches that of Ruppert-Polyak-Juditsky averaging. We bring these ideas together in an application to online canonical correlation analysis, deriving, for the first time in the literature, an optimal one-time-scale algorithm with an explicit rate of local asymptotic convergence to normality. Numerical studies of canonical correlation analysis are also provided for synthetic data.

title: Nonconvex Stochastic Scaled-Gradient Descent and Generalized Eigenvector Problems
text: Optimization problems involving nonconvex objectives and stochastic gradients are ubiquitous in machine learning, yet the development of efficient and effective algorithms for such problems remains an active area of research. In this context, we investigate the Nonconvex Stochastic Scaled-Gradient Descent (NSSGD) algorithm, which leverages a scaled gradient approach to tackle the challenges of nonconvexity and stochasticity. We focus on the application of NSSGD to Generalized Eigenvector Problems (GEPs), which encompass a broad range of machine learning tasks, including canonical correlation analysis and multi-view learning. Theoretically, we establish the convergence of NSSGD to a stationary point of the GEP objective, and provide a characterization of the algorithm's stability and robustness. Empirically, we demonstrate the superior performance of NSSGD compared to existing stochastic gradient methods on a range of benchmark GEP datasets, including those with noisy and corrupted data. Our results have important implications for the development of scalable and reliable machine learning algorithms in the presence of nonconvexity and uncertainty.

title: Disentanglement and Generalization Under Correlation Shifts
text: Correlations between factors of variation are prevalent in real-world data. Exploiting such correlations may increase predictive performance on noisy data; however, often correlations are not robust (e.g., they may change between domains, datasets, or applications) and models that exploit them do not generalize when correlations shift. Disentanglement methods aim to learn representations which capture different factors of variation in latent subspaces. A common approach involves minimizing the mutual information between latent subspaces, such that each encodes a single underlying attribute. However, this fails when attributes are correlated. We solve this problem by enforcing independence between subspaces conditioned on the available attributes, which allows us to remove only dependencies that are not due to the correlation structure present in the training data. We achieve this via an adversarial approach to minimize the conditional mutual information (CMI) between subspaces with respect to categorical variables. We first show theoretically that CMI minimization is a good objective for robust disentanglement on linear problems. We then apply our method on real-world datasets based on MNIST and CelebA, and show that it yields models that are disentangled and robust under correlation shift, including in weakly supervised settings.

title: Disentanglement and Generalization Under Correlation Shifts
text: Real-world data often exhibits correlations between factors of variation, which can be leveraged to enhance predictive performance in noisy settings. However, these correlations are frequently non-robust, varying across domains, datasets, or applications, and models that rely on them may not generalize when correlations shift. Disentanglement techniques aim to learn representations that capture distinct factors of variation in separate latent subspaces. A common approach involves minimizing the mutual information between subspaces to encode individual attributes. Nevertheless, this strategy fails when attributes are correlated. To address this limitation, we propose an adversarial method that enforces independence between subspaces conditioned on available attributes, effectively removing dependencies not attributed to the correlation structure in the training data. We theoretically demonstrate that minimizing conditional mutual information (CMI) is a suitable objective for robust disentanglement in linear problems. Empirical evaluations on MNIST and CelebA datasets show that our approach yields disentangled and robust models under correlation shift, even in weakly supervised settings.

title: A Simple Baseline for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation with Pre-trained Vision-language Model
text: Recently, open-vocabulary image classification by vision language pre-training has demonstrated incredible achievements, that the model can classify arbitrary categories without seeing additional annotated images of that category. However, it is still unclear how to make the open-vocabulary recognition work well on broader vision problems. This paper targets open-vocabulary semantic segmentation by building it on an off-the-shelf pre-trained vision-language model, i.e., CLIP. However, semantic segmentation and the CLIP model perform on different visual granularity, that semantic segmentation processes on pixels while CLIP performs on images. To remedy the discrepancy in processing granularity, we refuse the use of the prevalent one-stage FCN based framework, and advocate a two-stage semantic segmentation framework, with the first stage extracting generalizable mask proposals and the second stage leveraging an image based CLIP model to perform open-vocabulary classification on the masked image crops which are generated in the first stage. Our experimental results show that this two-stage framework can achieve superior performance than FCN when trained only on COCO Stuff dataset and evaluated on other datasets without fine-tuning. Moreover, this simple framework also surpasses previous state-of-the-arts of zero-shot semantic segmentation by a large margin: +29.5 hIoU on the Pascal VOC 2012 dataset, and +8.9 hIoU on the COCO Stuff dataset. With its simplicity and strong performance, we hope this framework to serve as a baseline to facilitate future research. The code are made publicly available at~\url{

title: A Simple Baseline for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation with Pre-trained Vision-language Model
text: The paradigm of open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, where a model is tasked with assigning semantic labels to pixels in an image, has garnered significant attention in recent years. Despite its promise, this setup poses unique challenges, particularly when dealing with unseen classes during inference. Recent attempts have focused on developing complex architectures and training protocols to tackle this problem. However, we argue that the community lacks a simple, yet effective baseline to serve as a starting point for further research. To this end, we propose a surprisingly effective baseline approach that leverages pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) for open-vocabulary semantic segmentation. Our method, dubbed VLM-Seg, exploits the semantic knowledge embedded in VLMs to generate high-quality pseudo-labels for unseen classes. These pseudo-labels are then used to fine-tune a standard segmentation network, enabling it to generalize to novel categories. We conduct extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, including COCO-Stuff, ADE20K, and Pascal-Context, demonstrating that VLM-Seg outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a new benchmark on COCO-Stuff. Notably, our approach achieves this performance without requiring additional annotations, complex architectural modifications, or computationally expensive training protocols. We hope that VLM-Seg will serve as a simple, effective, and widely adopted baseline for open-vocabulary semantic segmentation research, facilitating further innovation in this area.

title: Multivariate Trend Filtering for Lattice Data
text: We study a multivariate version of trend filtering, called Kronecker trend filtering or KTF, for the case in which the design points form a lattice in $d$ dimensions. KTF is a natural extension of univariate trend filtering (Steidl et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2009; Tibshirani, 2014), and is defined by minimizing a penalized least squares problem whose penalty term sums the absolute (higher-order) differences of the parameter to be estimated along each of the coordinate directions. The corresponding penalty operator can be written in terms of Kronecker products of univariate trend filtering penalty operators, hence the name Kronecker trend filtering. Equivalently, one can view KTF in terms of an $\ell_1$-penalized basis regression problem where the basis functions are tensor products of falling factorial functions, a piecewise polynomial (discrete spline) basis that underlies univariate trend filtering. This paper is a unification and extension of the results in Sadhanala et al. (2016, 2017). We develop a complete set of theoretical results that describe the behavior of $k^{\mathrm{th}}$ order Kronecker trend filtering in $d$ dimensions, for every $k \geq 0$ and $d \geq 1$. This reveals a number of interesting phenomena, including the dominance of KTF over linear smoothers in estimating heterogeneously smooth functions, and a phase transition at $d=2(k+1)$, a boundary past which (on the high dimension-to-smoothness side) linear smoothers fail to be consistent entirely. We also leverage recent results on discrete splines from Tibshirani (2020), in particular, discrete spline interpolation results that enable us to extend the KTF estimate to any off-lattice location in constant-time (independent of the size of the lattice $n$).

title: Multivariate Trend Filtering for Lattice Data
text: Trend filtering, a fundamental task in data analysis, becomes increasingly challenging when dealing with lattice-structured data, commonly encountered in computer vision, material science, and social networks. The existing literature primarily focuses on univariate trend filtering, leaving a significant gap in tackling multivariate lattice data. This paper bridges this gap by introducing a novel framework for multivariate trend filtering on lattice data, leveraging the intrinsic spatial dependencies and correlations present in the data. Our approach relies on a hierarchical Bayesian model, which decomposes the multivariate signal into a trend component and a residual component. We formulate the trend component as a multivariate Gaussian Markov random field, incorporating the lattice structure, and the residual component as a multivariate Gaussian distribution. To facilitate efficient inference, we develop a bespoke variational inference algorithm, exploiting the conditional conjugacy of the model. Through an extensive empirical evaluation on synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate the superior performance of our method compared to state-of-the-art algorithms, achieving significant improvements in terms of mean squared error and mean absolute error. Notably, our approach exhibits robustness to noise and outliers, and is capable of handling high-dimensional lattice data. Furthermore, we showcase the versatility of our framework by applying it to various application domains, including image denoising, material property prediction, and social network analysis. Theoretical analysis reveals that our algorithm enjoys a near-optimal convergence rate, and we provide guarantees on the model's consistency and asymptotic normality. Our work contributes to the development of a new generation of trend filtering algorithms, tailored to the complexities of lattice-structured data, and paves the way for further research in this area.

title: Video Reconstruction from a Single Motion Blurred Image using Learned Dynamic Phase Coding
text: Video reconstruction from a single motion-blurred image is a challenging problem, which can enhance the capabilities of existing cameras. Recently, several works addressed this task using conventional imaging and deep learning. Yet, such purely-digital methods are inherently limited, due to direction ambiguity and noise sensitivity. Some works proposed to address these limitations using non-conventional image sensors, however, such sensors are extremely rare and expensive. To circumvent these limitations with simpler means, we propose a hybrid optical-digital method for video reconstruction that requires only simple modifications to existing optical systems. We use a learned dynamic phase-coding in the lens aperture during the image acquisition to encode the motion trajectories, which serve as prior information for the video reconstruction process. The proposed computational camera generates a sharp frame burst of the scene at various frame rates from a single coded motion-blurred image, using an image-to-video convolutional neural network. We present advantages and improved performance compared to existing methods, using both simulations and a real-world camera prototype. We extend our optical coding also to video frame interpolation and present robust and improved results for noisy videos.

title: Video Reconstruction from a Single Motion Blurred Image using Learned Dynamic Phase Coding
text: The reconstruction of videos from a single motion-blurred image poses a significant challenge, with the potential to augment the capabilities of conventional cameras. While recent studies have employed deep learning and traditional imaging techniques to tackle this problem, they are inherently limited by direction ambiguity and noise sensitivity. Alternative approaches leveraging non-conventional image sensors have been proposed to mitigate these limitations, but their rare availability and high cost hinder widespread adoption. We propose a hybrid optical-digital method that circumvents these limitations using simple modifications to existing optical systems. By incorporating learned dynamic phase-coding in the lens aperture during image acquisition, we encode motion trajectories, which serve as prior information for video reconstruction. Our computational camera generates sharp frame bursts of the scene at various frame rates from a single coded motion-blurred image using an image-to-video convolutional neural network. We demonstrate the advantages and improved performance of our approach through simulations and a real-world camera prototype, and further extend our optical coding to video frame interpolation, achieving robust and improved results for noisy videos.

title: Frame invariance and scalability of neural operators for partial differential equations
text: Partial differential equations (PDEs) play a dominant role in the mathematical modeling of many complex dynamical processes. Solving these PDEs often requires prohibitively high computational costs, especially when multiple evaluations must be made for different parameters or conditions. After training, neural operators can provide PDEs solutions significantly faster than traditional PDE solvers. In this work, invariance properties and computational complexity of two neural operators are examined for transport PDE of a scalar quantity. Neural operator based on graph kernel network (GKN) operates on graph-structured data to incorporate nonlocal dependencies. Here we propose a modified formulation of GKN to achieve frame invariance. Vector cloud neural network (VCNN) is an alternate neural operator with embedded frame invariance which operates on point cloud data. GKN-based neural operator demonstrates slightly better predictive performance compared to VCNN. However, GKN requires an excessively high computational cost that increases quadratically with the increasing number of discretized objects as compared to a linear increase for VCNN.

title: Frame invariance and scalability of neural operators for partial differential equations
text: The mathematical modeling of complex dynamical processes frequently relies on partial differential equations (PDEs), whose solution often comes at a prohibitively high computational cost, particularly when multiple evaluations are required for varying parameters or conditions. Neural operators, after training, can provide significantly faster PDE solutions compared to traditional solvers. This study investigates the invariance properties and computational complexity of two neural operators for transport PDEs of scalar quantities. Specifically, we examine a graph kernel network (GKN) based neural operator, which operates on graph-structured data to capture nonlocal dependencies, and propose a modified formulation to achieve frame invariance. In contrast, the vector cloud neural network (VCNN) is an alternative neural operator that inherently embeds frame invariance and operates on point cloud data. Our results show that the GKN-based neural operator exhibits slightly better predictive performance than VCNN, but at the cost of a quadratically increasing computational burden with the number of discretized objects, whereas VCNN's computational cost increases linearly.

title: Gas Gauge: A Security Analysis Tool for Smart Contract Out-of-Gas Vulnerabilities
text: In recent years we have witnessed a dramatic increase in the adoption and application of smart contracts in a variety of contexts such as decentralized finance, supply chain management, and identity management. However, a critical stumbling block to the further adoption of smart contracts is their security. A particularly widespread class of security vulnerabilities that afflicts Ethereum smart contracts is the gas limit denial of service(DoS) on a contract via unbounded operations. These vulnerabilities result in a failed transaction with an out-of-gas error and are often present in contracts containing loops whose bounds are affected by end-user input. Note that such vulnerabilities differ from gas limit DoS on the network via block stuffing. Therefore, we present Gas Gauge, a tool aimed at detecting Out-of-Gas DoS vulnerabilities in Ethereum smart contracts. Gas Gauge consists of three major components: the Detection, Identification, and Correction Phases. The Detection Phase consists of an accurate static analysis approach that finds and summarizes all the loops in a smart contract. The Identification Phase uses a white-box fuzzing approach to generate a set of inputs that causes the contract to run out of gas. The Correction Phase uses static analysis and run-time verification to predict the maximum loop bounds consistent with allowable gas usage and suggest appropriate repairs to the user of the tool. Each part of the tool can be used separately for different purposes or all together to detect, identify and help repair the contracts vulnerable to Out-of-Gas DoS vulnerabilities. Gas Gauge was tested on 1,000 real-world solidity smart contracts deployed on the Ethereum Mainnet. The results were compared to seven state-of-the-art static and symbolic tools, and it was empirically demonstrated that Gas Gauge is far more effective than competing state-of-the-art tools.

title: Gas Gauge: A Security Analysis Tool for Smart Contract Out-of-Gas Vulnerabilities
text: The proliferation of smart contracts across diverse domains, including decentralized finance, supply chain management, and identity management, has been hindered by the pressing concern of security. A pervasive class of vulnerabilities affecting Ethereum smart contracts is the gas limit denial of service (DoS) via unbounded operations, which culminates in failed transactions with out-of-gas errors. This phenomenon often arises in contracts featuring loops whose bounds are susceptible to end-user input manipulation. It is essential to distinguish these vulnerabilities from gas limit DoS attacks on the network via block stuffing. To mitigate this issue, we introduce Gas Gauge, a comprehensive tool designed to detect Out-of-Gas DoS vulnerabilities in Ethereum smart contracts. Gas Gauge comprises three primary components: the Detection, Identification, and Correction Phases. The Detection Phase employs an accurate static analysis methodology to identify and summarize all loops present in a smart contract. The Identification Phase leverages white-box fuzzing to generate a set of inputs that trigger the contract to exhaust its gas allocation. The Correction Phase combines static analysis and run-time verification to predict the maximum loop bounds consistent with permissible gas usage and provide targeted repair suggestions to the user. Each component can be utilized independently for specific purposes or collectively to detect, identify, and facilitate the repair of contracts vulnerable to Out-of-Gas DoS vulnerabilities. We evaluated Gas Gauge on a dataset of 1,000 real-world Solidity smart contracts deployed on the Ethereum Mainnet, comparing its performance to seven state-of-the-art static and symbolic tools. Our empirical results demonstrate that Gas Gauge significantly outperforms its competitors in detecting Out-of-Gas DoS vulnerabilities.

title: Deep Graph Clustering via Dual Correlation Reduction
text: Deep graph clustering, which aims to reveal the underlying graph structure and divide the nodes into different groups, has attracted intensive attention in recent years. However, we observe that, in the process of node encoding, existing methods suffer from representation collapse which tends to map all data into the same representation. Consequently, the discriminative capability of the node representation is limited, leading to unsatisfied clustering performance. To address this issue, we propose a novel self-supervised deep graph clustering method termed Dual Correlation Reduction Network (DCRN) by reducing information correlation in a dual manner. Specifically, in our method, we first design a siamese network to encode samples. Then by forcing the cross-view sample correlation matrix and cross-view feature correlation matrix to approximate two identity matrices, respectively, we reduce the information correlation in the dual-level, thus improving the discriminative capability of the resulting features. Moreover, in order to alleviate representation collapse caused by over-smoothing in GCN, we introduce a propagation regularization term to enable the network to gain long-distance information with the shallow network structure. Extensive experimental results on six benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed DCRN against the existing state-of-the-art methods.

title: Deep Graph Clustering via Dual Correlation Reduction
text: Graph clustering is a fundamental problem in machine learning and data mining, with numerous applications in social network analysis, recommender systems, and bioinformatics. Despite its importance, existing graph clustering methods often struggle with high-dimensional graph data, suffering from issues of scalability, interpretability, and robustness. Recently, deep learning-based approaches have shown promise in addressing these limitations, but most existing methods rely on complex architectures and meticulous hyperparameter tuning. In this work, we propose a novel deep graph clustering framework, Dual Correlation Reduction (DCR), which leverages the dual perspectives of graph structure and node features to reduce correlation and enhance clustering quality. Our approach is built upon a carefully designed graph neural network architecture, which integrates a dual-correlation reduction module to minimize the correlation between node features and graph structure. We evaluate DCR on a range of benchmark datasets, demonstrating its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in terms of clustering performance, scalability, and robustness to noise and outliers. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into the effectiveness of DCR, establishing connections to traditional graph clustering objectives and providing guarantees on the quality of the learned clusters.

title: Working mechanism of Eternalblue and its application in ransomworm
text: After the leaking of exploit Eternalblue, some ransomworms utilizing this exploit have been developed to sweep over the world in recent years. Ransomworm is a global growing threat as it blocks users' access to their files unless a ransom is paid by victims. Wannacry and Notpetya are two of those ransomworms which are responsible for the loss of millions of dollar, from crippling U.K. national systems to shutting down a Honda Motor Company in Japan. Many dynamic analytic papers on Wannacry were published, however, static analytic papers about Wannacry were limited. Our aim is to present readers an systematic knowledge about exploit Eternalblue, from a high\textendash leveled semantic view to the code details. Specifically, the working mechanism of Eternalblue, the reverse engineering analysis of Eternalblue in Wannacry, and the comparison with the Metasploit's Eternalblue exploit are presented. The key finding of our analysis is that the code remains almost the same when Eternalblue is transplanted into Wannacry, which indicates its potential for signatures and thus detection.

title: Working mechanism of Eternalblue and its application in ransomworm
text: The Eternalblue exploit, leveraging a remote code execution vulnerability in Windows SMBv1, has been instrumental in the propagation of notorious ransomware such as WannaCry, NotPetya, and Bad Rabbit. Despite its significance, the underlying working mechanism of Eternalblue remains poorly understood, hindering the development of effective countermeasures. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of Eternalblue's inner workings, revealing the crucial role of the srvnet.sys driver in enabling the exploit's reliability and stealthiness. Through a combination of static and dynamic analysis, we reverse-engineer the exploit's payload, uncovering the clever use of SMB transactional operations to bypass Windows memory protections. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of Eternalblue as a ransomworm, showcasing its potential to self-replicate and encrypt files on compromised systems. Our findings have significant implications for the development of robust defenses against Eternalblue-based attacks, and highlight the need for a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between operating system internals and exploit techniques.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Communication Networks: Context, Use Cases and Opportunities
text: Graph neural networks (GNN) have shown outstanding applications in many fields where data is fundamentally represented as graphs (e.g., chemistry, biology, recommendation systems). In this vein, communication networks comprise many fundamental components that are naturally represented in a graph-structured manner (e.g., topology, configurations, traffic flows). This position article presents GNNs as a fundamental tool for modeling, control and management of communication networks. GNNs represent a new generation of data-driven models that can accurately learn and reproduce the complex behaviors behind real networks. As a result, such models can be applied to a wide variety of networking use cases, such as planning, online optimization, or troubleshooting. The main advantage of GNNs over traditional neural networks lies in its unprecedented generalization capabilities when applied to other networks and configurations unseen during training, which is a critical feature for achieving practical data-driven solutions for networking. This article comprises a brief tutorial on GNNs and their possible applications to communication networks. To showcase the potential of this technology, we present two use cases with state-of-the-art GNN models respectively applied to wired and wireless networks. Lastly, we delve into the key open challenges and opportunities yet to be explored in this novel research area.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Communication Networks: Context, Use Cases and Opportunities
text: The burgeoning field of graph neural networks (GNNs) has demonstrated remarkable efficacy in domains where data is inherently graph-structured, such as chemistry, biology, and recommendation systems. Similarly, communication networks comprise various fundamental components that lend themselves naturally to graph-based representation, including topology, configurations, and traffic flows. This position article advocates for the adoption of GNNs as a foundational tool for modeling, control, and management of communication networks. By accurately capturing the intricate behaviors underlying real-world networks, GNNs can be effectively applied to a broad range of networking scenarios, including planning, online optimization, and troubleshooting. A key advantage of GNNs over traditional neural networks lies in their exceptional generalizability to unseen networks and configurations, a critical feature for realizing practical data-driven solutions in networking. This article provides a concise tutorial on GNNs and their applications to communication networks, accompanied by two case studies showcasing state-of-the-art GNN models applied to wired and wireless networks. Finally, we discuss the outstanding challenges and opportunities that remain to be explored in this emerging research area, highlighting the vast potential of GNNs in communication networks.

title: A sampling-based approach for efficient clustering in large datasets
text: We propose a simple and efficient clustering method for high-dimensional data with a large number of clusters. Our algorithm achieves high-performance by evaluating distances of datapoints with a subset of the cluster centres. Our contribution is substantially more efficient than k-means as it does not require an all to all comparison of data points and clusters. We show that the optimal solutions of our approximation are the same as in the exact solution. However, our approach is considerably more efficient at extracting these clusters compared to the state-of-the-art. We compare our approximation with the exact k-means and alternative approximation approaches on a series of standardised clustering tasks. For the evaluation, we consider the algorithmic complexity, including number of operations to convergence, and the stability of the results.

title: A sampling-based approach for efficient clustering in large datasets
text: High-dimensional data with numerous clusters necessitate an efficient clustering method to mitigate computational complexity. Our proposed algorithm leveraging a subset of cluster centers to evaluate datapoint distances achieves high performance while reducing computational overhead. By circumventing the need for all-to-all comparisons between data points and clusters, our method exhibits substantial efficiency gains over traditional k-means. We theoretically demonstrate that the optimal solutions obtained through our approximation converge to those of the exact solution. Empirical evaluations on standardized clustering tasks further confirm the superiority of our approach, outperforming state-of-the-art alternatives in terms of algorithmic complexity and result stability.

title: Deep Learning meets Liveness Detection: Recent Advancements and Challenges
text: Facial biometrics has been recently received tremendous attention as a convenient replacement for traditional authentication systems. Consequently, detecting malicious attempts has found great significance, leading to extensive studies in face anti-spoofing~(FAS),i.e., face presentation attack detection. Deep feature learning and techniques, as opposed to hand-crafted features, have promised a dramatic increase in the FAS systems' accuracy, tackling the key challenges of materializing the real-world application of such systems. Hence, a new research area dealing with the development of more generalized as well as accurate models is increasingly attracting the attention of the research community and industry. In this paper, we present a comprehensive survey on the literature related to deep-feature-based FAS methods since 2017. To shed light on this topic, a semantic taxonomy based on various features and learning methodologies is represented. Further, we cover predominant public datasets for FAS in chronological order, their evolutional progress, and the evaluation criteria (both intra-dataset and inter-dataset). Finally, we discuss the open research challenges and future directions.

title: Deep Learning meets Liveness Detection: Recent Advancements and Challenges
text: The proliferation of deep fake videos and manipulated media has underscored the pressing need for robust liveness detection systems. Recent years have witnessed a surge in the adoption of deep learning techniques for liveness detection, leveraging advances in computer vision and machine learning. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the recent advancements and challenges in this domain. We survey state-of-the-art deep learning architectures, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), employed for liveness detection. Our analysis reveals that while these models have achieved impressive results on benchmark datasets, they are vulnerable to sophisticated attacks and suffer from poor generalizability. We also identify key challenges and open issues, including the lack of diverse and large-scale datasets, inadequate evaluation metrics, and the need for explainability and interpretability in liveness detection models. Our findings highlight the urgent need for more robust, efficient, and reliable liveness detection systems that can effectively counter emerging threats.

title: DeePN$^2$: A deep learning-based non-Newtonian hydrodynamic model
text: A long standing problem in the modeling of non-Newtonian hydrodynamics of polymeric flows is the availability of reliable and interpretable hydrodynamic models that faithfully encode the underlying micro-scale polymer dynamics. The main complication arises from the long polymer relaxation time, the complex molecular structure and heterogeneous interaction. DeePN$^2$, a deep learning-based non-Newtonian hydrodynamic model, has been proposed and has shown some success in systematically passing the micro-scale structural mechanics information to the macro-scale hydrodynamics for suspensions with simple polymer conformation and bond potential. The model retains a multi-scaled nature by mapping the polymer configurations into a set of symmetry-preserving macro-scale features. The extended constitutive laws for these macro-scale features can be directly learned from the kinetics of their micro-scale counterparts. In this paper, we develop DeePN$^2$ using more complex micro-structural models. We show that DeePN$^2$ can faithfully capture the broadly overlooked viscoelastic differences arising from the specific molecular structural mechanics without human intervention.

title: DeePN$^2$: A deep learning-based non-Newtonian hydrodynamic model
text: Simulating complex fluid dynamics is a long-standing challenge in various fields, including computer-aided engineering, animation, and robotics. Traditional Newtonian models often struggle to capture the non-linear behavior of non-Newtonian fluids, which exhibit varying viscosity in response to stress. Recently, deep learning has shown promise in modeling complex physical phenomena. We propose DeePN$^2$, a novel deep learning-based approach for simulating non-Newtonian hydrodynamics. Our method leverages a hybrid architecture combining a physics-informed neural network (PINN) with a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN). The PINN component ensures physical consistency, while the cGAN component captures the complex, non-linear relationships between fluid properties and flow behavior. We validate DeePN$^2$ on a range of benchmark problems, demonstrating improved accuracy and robustness compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our approach successfully predicts the dynamics of non-Newtonian fluids in various scenarios, including shear-thinning and shear-thickening behaviors. DeePN$^2$ has the potential to revolutionize the simulation of complex fluid flows, enabling breakthroughs in fields such as soft robotics, biomedical engineering, and materials science.

title: Learning Spatially-Adaptive Squeeze-Excitation Networks for Image Synthesis and Image Recognition
text: Learning light-weight yet expressive deep networks in both image synthesis and image recognition remains a challenging problem. Inspired by a more recent observation that it is the data-specificity that makes the multi-head self-attention (MHSA) in the Transformer model so powerful, this paper proposes to extend the widely adopted light-weight Squeeze-Excitation (SE) module to be spatially-adaptive to reinforce its data specificity, as a convolutional alternative of the MHSA, while retaining the efficiency of SE and the inductive basis of convolution. It presents two designs of spatially-adaptive squeeze-excitation (SASE) modules for image synthesis and image recognition respectively. For image synthesis tasks, the proposed SASE is tested in both low-shot and one-shot learning tasks. It shows better performance than prior arts. For image recognition tasks, the proposed SASE is used as a drop-in replacement for convolution layers in ResNets and achieves much better accuracy than the vanilla ResNets, and slightly better than the MHSA counterparts such as the Swin-Transformer and Pyramid-Transformer in the ImageNet-1000 dataset, with significantly smaller models.

title: Learning Spatially-Adaptive Squeeze-Excitation Networks for Image Synthesis and Image Recognition
text: The pursuit of lightweight yet expressive deep networks for image synthesis and recognition remains a formidable challenge. Recent studies have revealed that the data-specificity of multi-head self-attention (MHSA) in Transformer models underlies their remarkable performance. Building upon this insight, we propose a spatially-adaptive extension of the widely adopted Squeeze-Excitation (SE) module, offering a convolutional alternative to MHSA that preserves efficiency and inductive basis. We introduce two novel designs of spatially-adaptive squeeze-excitation (SASE) modules, tailored for image synthesis and recognition tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our SASE module outperforms prior arts in low-shot and one-shot learning tasks for image synthesis. Furthermore, when integrated into ResNets as a drop-in replacement for convolution layers, our SASE module achieves significant accuracy gains over vanilla ResNets and competitive performance with MHSA-based models, such as Swin-Transformer and Pyramid-Transformer, on the ImageNet-1000 dataset, while maintaining a smaller model size.

title: AutoFITS: Automatic Feature Engineering for Irregular Time Series
text: A time series represents a set of observations collected over time. Typically, these observations are captured with a uniform sampling frequency (e.g. daily). When data points are observed in uneven time intervals the time series is referred to as irregular or intermittent. In such scenarios, the most common solution is to reconstruct the time series to make it regular, thus removing its intermittency. We hypothesise that, in irregular time series, the time at which each observation is collected may be helpful to summarise the dynamics of the data and improve forecasting performance. We study this idea by developing a novel automatic feature engineering framework, which focuses on extracting information from this point of view, i.e., when each instance is collected. We study how valuable this information is by integrating it in a time series forecasting workflow and investigate how it compares to or complements state-of-the-art methods for regular time series forecasting. In the end, we contribute by providing a novel framework that tackles feature engineering for time series from an angle previously vastly ignored. We show that our approach has the potential to further extract more information about time series that significantly improves forecasting performance.

title: AutoFITS: Automatic Feature Engineering for Irregular Time Series
text: Time series data, comprising observations collected at varying time intervals, often exhibit irregular or intermittent patterns when sampling frequencies are non-uniform. Conventionally, these irregularities are addressed by reconstructing the time series to achieve regularity. However, we propose that the timing of individual observations itself may possess valuable information for summarizing data dynamics and enhancing forecasting performance. To investigate this notion, we introduce a novel automatic feature engineering framework that extracts insights from the timing of data collection. By integrating this framework into a time series forecasting workflow, we assess the incremental value of timing-based features and their potential to complement or surpass state-of-the-art methods tailored for regular time series. Our research contributes a fresh perspective on feature engineering for time series, previously overlooked, and demonstrates the potential to significantly improve forecasting accuracy by leveraging timing-based information. Experimental results validate the efficacy of our approach, underscoring its potential to uncover new insights in time series analysis.

title: Explanation by Automated Reasoning Using the Isabelle Infrastructure Framework
text: In this paper, we propose the use of interactive theorem proving for explainable machine learning. After presenting our proposition, we illustrate it on the dedicated application of explaining security attacks using the Isabelle Infrastructure framework and its process of dependability engineering. This formal framework and process provides the logics for specification and modeling. Attacks on security of the system are explained by specification and proofs in the Isabelle Infrastructure framework. Existing case studies of dependability engineering in Isabelle are used as feasibility studies to illustrate how different aspects of explanations are covered by the Isabelle Infrastructure framework.

title: Explanation by Automated Reasoning Using the Isabelle Infrastructure Framework
text: We advocate for the integration of interactive theorem proving into explainable machine learning, leveraging its formal foundations to elucidate complex security attacks. To demonstrate this approach, we utilize the Isabelle Infrastructure framework, which provides a rigorous process for dependability engineering. By specifying and modeling system security within this framework, we can formally explain attacks through logical proofs. Case studies in dependability engineering, established within Isabelle, serve as feasibility tests, showcasing the framework's capacity to cover diverse explanatory aspects.

title: Active Learning-Based Optimization of Scientific Experimental Design
text: Active learning (AL) is a machine learning algorithm that can achieve greater accuracy with fewer labeled training instances, for having the ability to ask oracles to label the most valuable unlabeled data chosen iteratively and heuristically by query strategies. Scientific experiments nowadays, though becoming increasingly automated, are still suffering from human involvement in the designing process and the exhaustive search in the experimental space. This article performs a retrospective study on a drug response dataset using the proposed AL scheme comprised of the matrix factorization method of alternating least square (ALS) and deep neural networks (DNN). This article also proposes an AL query strategy based on expected loss minimization. As a result, the retrospective study demonstrates that scientific experimental design, instead of being manually set, can be optimized by AL, and the proposed query strategy ELM sampling shows better experimental performance than other ones such as random sampling and uncertainty sampling.

title: Active Learning-Based Optimization of Scientific Experimental Design
text: Machine learning algorithms, such as active learning (AL), have demonstrated the potential to achieve superior accuracy with limited labeled training data by selectively querying oracles to annotate the most informative unlabeled instances. Despite increasing automation, scientific experiments still rely heavily on human intuition in designing experiments and exhaustively searching the experimental space. This study applies an AL framework, combining matrix factorization via alternating least squares (ALS) and deep neural networks (DNN), to a drug response dataset, and introduces a novel query strategy based on expected loss minimization (ELM). Our retrospective analysis reveals that AL can effectively optimize experimental design, outperforming manual approaches. Notably, the proposed ELM sampling strategy exhibits superior performance compared to random sampling and uncertainty sampling, underscoring the potential of AL to streamline scientific experimentation.

title: Application of Hierarchical Temporal Memory Theory for Document Categorization
text: The current work intends to study the performance of the Hierarchical Temporal Memory(HTM) theory for automated classification of text as well as documents. HTM is a biologically inspired theory based on the working principles of the human neocortex. The current study intends to provide an alternative framework for document categorization using the Spatial Pooler learning algorithm in the HTM Theory. As HTM accepts only a stream of binary data as input, Latent Semantic Indexing(LSI) technique is used for extracting the top features from the input and converting them into binary format. The Spatial Pooler algorithm converts the binary input into sparse patterns with similar input text having overlapping spatial patterns making it easy for classifying the patterns into categories. The results obtained prove that HTM theory, although is in its nascent stages, performs at par with most of the popular machine learning based classifiers.

title: Application of Hierarchical Temporal Memory Theory for Document Categorization
text: This study investigates the efficacy of the Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM) theory in automated text and document classification. Inspired by the neocortex's functioning principles, HTM offers a novel framework for document categorization, leveraging the Spatial Pooler learning algorithm. To accommodate HTM's binary input requirement, Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI) is employed to extract top features from input data and convert them into a binary format. The Spatial Pooler algorithm subsequently transforms these binary inputs into sparse patterns, where similar input texts exhibit overlapping spatial patterns, facilitating classification into categories. Our results demonstrate that, despite being in its early stages, HTM theory performs competitively with established machine learning-based classifiers, highlighting its potential as a viable alternative for document classification tasks.

title: Anomaly Detection in Cyber-Physical Systems: Reconstruction of a Prediction Error Feature Space
text: Cyber-physical systems are infrastructures that use digital information such as network communications and sensor readings to control entities in the physical world. Many cyber-physical systems in airports, hospitals and nuclear power plants are regarded as critical infrastructures since a disruption of its normal functionality can result in negative consequences for the society. In the last few years, some security solutions for cyber-physical systems based on artificial intelligence have been proposed. Nevertheless, knowledge domain is required to properly setup and train artificial intelligence algorithms. Our work proposes a novel anomaly detection framework based on error space reconstruction, where genetic algorithms are used to perform hyperparameter optimization of machine learning methods. The proposed method achieved an F1-score of 87.89% in the SWaT dataset.

title: Anomaly Detection in Cyber-Physical Systems: Reconstruction of a Prediction Error Feature Space
text: Cyber-physical systems (CPS) are increasingly vulnerable to sophisticated attacks, necessitating the development of robust anomaly detection methods. Traditional approaches rely on manual feature engineering, which can be time-consuming and prone to errors. We propose a novel approach that reconstructs a prediction error feature space from CPS sensor data, enabling effective anomaly detection without explicit feature engineering. Our method leverages a deep autoencoder to learn a compressed representation of normal system behavior, and subsequently, identifies anomalies as deviations from this learned model. Experimental evaluations on two real-world CPS datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, achieving a 23% improvement in detection accuracy and a 35% reduction in false positives compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our results have significant implications for enhancing the security and reliability of CPS.

title: ReSplit: Improving the Structure of Jupyter Notebooks by Re-Splitting Their Cells
text: Jupyter notebooks represent a unique format for programming - a combination of code and Markdown with rich formatting, separated into individual cells. We propose to perceive a Jupyter Notebook cell as a simplified and raw version of a programming function. Similar to functions, Jupyter cells should strive to contain singular, self-contained actions. At the same time, research shows that real-world notebooks fail to do so and suffer from the lack of proper structure. To combat this, we propose ReSplit, an algorithm for an automatic re-splitting of cells in Jupyter notebooks. The algorithm analyzes definition-usage chains in the notebook and consists of two parts - merging and splitting the cells. We ran the algorithm on a large corpus of notebooks to evaluate its performance and its overall effect on notebooks, and evaluated it by human experts: we showed them several notebooks in their original and the re-split form. In 29.5% of cases, the re-split notebook was selected as the preferred way of perceiving the code. We analyze what influenced this decision and describe several individual cases in detail.

title: ReSplit: Improving the Structure of Jupyter Notebooks by Re-Splitting Their Cells
text: Jupyter notebooks, a distinctive blend of code and Markdown, comprise individual cells that can be conceptualized as simplified, raw programming functions. Like functions, these cells ideally encapsulate singular, self-contained actions. However, empirical studies reveal that real-world notebooks often deviate from this ideal, suffering from structural deficiencies. To address this, we introduce ReSplit, an algorithm designed to automatically re-split Jupyter notebook cells. By analyzing definition-usage chains within notebooks, ReSplit consists of two complementary stages: cell merging and splitting. We assessed the algorithm's performance on a large corpus of notebooks and evaluated its impact through human expert review, presenting them with original and re-split notebooks. Notably, 29.5% of experts preferred the re-split format, which we attribute to specific factors discussed in detail. We also provide in-depth analyses of individual cases, shedding light on the implications of ReSplit for improving notebook structure and readability.

title: PINNs for the Solution of the Hyperbolic Buckley-Leverett Problem with a Non-convex Flux Function
text: The displacement of two immiscible fluids is a common problem in fluid flow in porous media. Such a problem can be posed as a partial differential equation (PDE) in what is commonly referred to as a Buckley-Leverett (B-L) problem. The B-L problem is a non-linear hyperbolic conservation law that is known to be notoriously difficult to solve using traditional numerical methods. Here, we address the forward hyperbolic B-L problem with a nonconvex flux function using physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). The contributions of this paper are twofold. First, we present a PINN approach to solve the hyperbolic B-L problem by embedding the Oleinik entropy condition into the neural network residual. We do not use a diffusion term (artificial viscosity) in the residual-loss, but we rely on the strong form of the PDE. Second, we use the Adam optimizer with residual-based adaptive refinement (RAR) algorithm to achieve an ultra-low loss without weighting. Our solution method can accurately capture the shock-front and produce an accurate overall solution. We report a L2 validation error of 2 x 10-2 and a L2 loss of 1x 10-6. The proposed method does not require any additional regularization or weighting of losses to obtain such accurate solution.

title: PINNs for the Solution of the Hyperbolic Buckley-Leverett Problem with a Non-convex Flux Function
text: The Buckley-Leverett problem, a fundamental model in porous media flow, has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its relevance to various applications, including oil recovery and contaminant transport. However, its solution remains a challenging task, especially when considering non-convex flux functions, which are often encountered in realistic scenarios. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising approach for solving forward and inverse problems involving nonlinear partial differential equations. In this context, we explore the application of PINNs to the hyperbolic Buckley-Leverett problem with a non-convex flux function. We propose a novel formulation that leverages the automatic differentiation capabilities of deep learning frameworks to enforce the nonlinear flux condition, ensuring a more accurate and efficient solution. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of PINNs in capturing the complex behavior of the Buckley-Leverett problem, even in the presence of non-convex flux functions. We achieve a high degree of accuracy, with relative L2 errors of less than 2%, and outperform traditional numerical methods in terms of computational efficiency. The proposed approach also provides a promising framework for solving more general nonlinear hyperbolic problems, and its extension to multi-phase flow and reactive transport systems is discussed.

title: Recent Trends in Artificial Intelligence-inspired Electronic Thermal Management
text: The rise of computation-based methods in thermal management has gained immense attention in recent years due to the ability of deep learning to solve complex 'physics' problems, which are otherwise difficult to be approached using conventional techniques. Thermal management is required in electronic systems to keep them from overheating and burning, enhancing their efficiency and lifespan. For a long time, numerical techniques have been employed to aid in the thermal management of electronics. However, they come with some limitations. To increase the effectiveness of traditional numerical approaches and address the drawbacks faced in conventional approaches, researchers have looked at using artificial intelligence at various stages of the thermal management process. The present study discusses in detail, the current uses of deep learning in the domain of 'electronic' thermal management.

title: Recent Trends in Artificial Intelligence-inspired Electronic Thermal Management
text: The advent of computation-driven approaches in thermal management has garnered significant interest in recent years, leveraging the capabilities of deep learning to tackle intricate problems in thermal physics that conventional methods struggle to address. Effective thermal management is crucial in electronic systems to prevent overheating, enhance efficiency, and prolong lifespan. While numerical techniques have long been employed to facilitate thermal management, they are hindered by limitations. To augment traditional numerical approaches and overcome their drawbacks, researchers have explored the integration of artificial intelligence across various stages of thermal management. This study provides a comprehensive examination of the current applications of deep learning in electronic thermal management, highlighting its potential to revolutionize the field.

title: A Graph Attention Learning Approach to Antenna Tilt Optimization
text: 6G will move mobile networks towards increasing levels of complexity. To deal with this complexity, optimization of network parameters is key to ensure high performance and timely adaptivity to dynamic network environments. The optimization of the antenna tilt provides a practical and cost-efficient method to improve coverage and capacity in the network. Previous methods based on Reinforcement Learning (RL) have shown great promise for tilt optimization by learning adaptive policies outperforming traditional tilt optimization methods. However, most existing RL methods are based on single-cell features representation, which fails to fully characterize the agent state, resulting in suboptimal performance. Also, most of such methods lack scalability, due to state-action explosion, and generalization ability. In this paper, we propose a Graph Attention Q-learning (GAQ) algorithm for tilt optimization. GAQ relies on a graph attention mechanism to select relevant neighbors information, improve the agent state representation, and update the tilt control policy based on a history of observations using a Deep Q-Network (DQN). We show that GAQ efficiently captures important network information and outperforms standard DQN with local information by a large margin. In addition, we demonstrate its ability to generalize to network deployments of different sizes and densities.

title: A Graph Attention Learning Approach to Antenna Tilt Optimization
text: Wireless networks rely on careful antenna tilt configuration to ensure optimal coverage, capacity, and quality of service. However, the intricate relationships between antenna tilts, surrounding environment, and network performance make manual optimization a daunting task, even for experienced engineers. Recent advances in graph attention learning have shown promise in tackling complex optimization problems, but their application to antenna tilt optimization remains largely unexplored. This paper bridges this gap by introducing a novel graph attention learning approach to antenna tilt optimization. We represent the wireless network as a graph, where nodes denote antennas and edges capture their interactions. Our model learns to attend to relevant nodes and edges, identifying the most critical antenna tilts that impact network performance. Through extensive simulations, we evaluate our approach on a range of scenarios, demonstrating significant improvements in network throughput (up to 23%), coverage (up to 17%), and signal quality (up to 12%) compared to state-of-the-art optimization techniques. Furthermore, our approach exhibits robustness to varying environmental conditions and network topologies. These findings have significant implications for the automation of antenna tilt optimization, enabling wireless networks to dynamically adapt to changing demands and environments.

title: The SAMME.C2 algorithm for severely imbalanced multi-class classification
text: Classification predictive modeling involves the accurate assignment of observations in a dataset to target classes or categories. There is an increasing growth of real-world classification problems with severely imbalanced class distributions. In this case, minority classes have much fewer observations to learn from than those from majority classes. Despite this sparsity, a minority class is often considered the more interesting class yet developing a scientific learning algorithm suitable for the observations presents countless challenges. In this article, we suggest a novel multi-class classification algorithm specialized to handle severely imbalanced classes based on the method we refer to as SAMME.C2. It blends the flexible mechanics of the boosting techniques from SAMME algorithm, a multi-class classifier, and Ada.C2 algorithm, a cost-sensitive binary classifier designed to address highly class imbalances. Not only do we provide the resulting algorithm but we also establish scientific and statistical formulation of our proposed SAMME.C2 algorithm. Through numerical experiments examining various degrees of classifier difficulty, we demonstrate consistent superior performance of our proposed model.

title: The SAMME.C2 algorithm for severely imbalanced multi-class classification
text: The assignment of observations to target classes or categories is a fundamental task in classification predictive modeling. In many real-world applications, however, class distributions are severely imbalanced, with minority classes possessing significantly fewer observations than their majority counterparts. Despite this limitation, minority classes often hold greater interest, yet devising a learning algorithm capable of effectively leveraging these sparse observations poses substantial challenges. To address this issue, we propose a novel multi-class classification algorithm, SAMME.C2, which integrates the flexibility of boosting techniques from the SAMME algorithm with the cost-sensitive approach of Ada.C2, a binary classifier designed to tackle high class imbalances. We provide a rigorous formulation of SAMME.C2, accompanied by a comprehensive evaluation through numerical experiments, which demonstrate its consistent superior performance across various levels of classifier difficulty.

title: Label Distributionally Robust Losses for Multi-class Classification: Consistency, Robustness and Adaptivity
text: We study a family of loss functions named label-distributionally robust (LDR) losses for multi-class classification that are formulated from distributionally robust optimization (DRO) perspective, where the uncertainty in the given label information are modeled and captured by taking the worse case of distributional weights. The benefits of this perspective are several fold: (i) it provides a unified framework to explain the classical cross-entropy (CE) loss and SVM loss and their variants, (ii) it includes a special family corresponding to the temperature-scaled CE loss, which is widely adopted but poorly understood; (iii) it allows us to achieve adaptivity to the uncertainty degree of label information at an instance level. Our contributions include: (1) we study both consistency and robustness by establishing top-$k$ ($\forall k\geq 1$) consistency of LDR losses for multi-class classification, and a negative result that a top-$1$ consistent and symmetric robust loss cannot achieve top-$k$ consistency simultaneously for all $k\geq 2$; (2) we propose a new adaptive LDR loss that automatically adapts the individualized temperature parameter to the noise degree of class label of each instance; (3) we demonstrate stable and competitive performance for the proposed adaptive LDR loss on 7 benchmark datasets under 6 noisy label and 1 clean settings against 13 loss functions, and on one real-world noisy dataset. title: Label Distributionally Robust Losses for Multi-class Classification: Consistency, Robustness and Adaptivity
text: The proliferation of multi-class classification models in real-world applications has highlighted the need for robustness to label distribution shifts, a ubiquitous phenomenon where the test distribution diverges from the training distribution. Existing approaches, such as label smoothing and mixup, have been shown to be inadequate in addressing this issue, often sacrificing consistency for robustness.
