When the environment only provides observations giving partial information about the state of the environment, the agent must learn the agent state based on the data stream of experience. We refer to the state learned directly from the data stream of experience as the agent state. Recurrent neural networks can learn the agent state, but the training methods are computationally expensive and sensitive to the hyper-parameters, making them unideal for online learning. This work introduces methods based on the generate-and-test approach to learn the agent state. A generate-and-test algorithm searches for state features by generating features and testing their usefulness. In this process, features useful for the agent's performance on the task are preserved, and the least useful features get replaced with newly generated features. We study the effectiveness of our methods on two online multi-step prediction problems. The first problem, trace conditioning, focuses on the agent's ability to remember a cue for a prediction multiple steps into the future. In the second problem, trace patterning, the agent needs to learn patterns in the observation signals and remember them for future predictions. We show that our proposed methods can effectively learn the agent state online and produce accurate predictions.

title: Learning Agent State Online with Recurrent Generate-and-Test
text: The ability to learn and reason about agent state online is crucial for real-world applications of autonomous systems, such as robotics and recommender systems. However, existing methods for agent state estimation often rely on overly simplistic models or require extensive offline training data. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach, Recurrent Generate-and-Test (RGT), which learns to estimate agent state online by generating and testing hypotheses about the agent's behavior. RGT leverages recurrent neural networks to model the agent's dynamics and a generative model to produce a diverse set of hypothetical state trajectories. These hypotheses are then evaluated using a test function, which assesses their likelihood and consistency with observed data. Through an iterative process of generation, testing, and refinement, RGT adaptively updates its estimate of the agent's state, even in the presence of incomplete or noisy observations. Experimental results on a range of simulated domains demonstrate that RGT significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of state estimation accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, we show that RGT can be seamlessly integrated with online planning and decision-making algorithms, enabling more effective and adaptive autonomous systems. Our approach has far-reaching implications for real-world applications, where agents must operate in complex, dynamic environments with limited prior knowledge.

title: Studying the Interplay between Information Loss and Operation Loss in Representations for Classification
text: Information-theoretic measures have been widely adopted in the design of features for learning and decision problems. Inspired by this, we look at the relationship between i) a weak form of information loss in the Shannon sense and ii) the operation loss in the minimum probability of error (MPE) sense when considering a family of lossy continuous representations (features) of a continuous observation. We present several results that shed light on this interplay. Our first result offers a lower bound on a weak form of information loss as a function of its respective operation loss when adopting a discrete lossy representation (quantization) instead of the original raw observation. From this, our main result shows that a specific form of vanishing information loss (a weak notion of asymptotic informational sufficiency) implies a vanishing MPE loss (or asymptotic operational sufficiency) when considering a general family of lossy continuous representations. Our theoretical findings support the observation that the selection of feature representations that attempt to capture informational sufficiency is appropriate for learning, but this selection is a rather conservative design principle if the intended goal is achieving MPE in classification. Supporting this last point, and under some structural conditions, we show that it is possible to adopt an alternative notion of informational sufficiency (strictly weaker than pure sufficiency in the mutual information sense) to achieve operational sufficiency in learning.

title: Studying the Interplay between Information Loss and Operation Loss in Representations for Classification
text: The design of features for learning and decision problems has been significantly informed by information-theoretic measures. This research explores the interplay between two fundamental concepts: a weak form of information loss in the Shannon sense and operation loss in the minimum probability of error (MPE) sense. We examine this relationship in the context of a family of lossy continuous representations of a continuous observation. Our analysis yields several key insights. Firstly, we establish a lower bound on the weak form of information loss as a function of its corresponding operation loss when a discrete lossy representation (quantization) is employed instead of the original raw observation. Building on this result, we demonstrate that a specific form of vanishing information loss implies vanishing MPE loss when considering a general family of lossy continuous representations. Our theoretical findings suggest that selecting feature representations that aim to capture informational sufficiency is a suitable strategy for learning, but may be overly conservative if the primary objective is to achieve MPE in classification. Indeed, under certain structural conditions, we show that a weaker notion of informational sufficiency can be adopted to attain operational sufficiency in learning, highlighting the potential for more nuanced design principles in feature selection.

title: When are Iterative Gaussian Processes Reliably Accurate?
text: While recent work on conjugate gradient methods and Lanczos decompositions have achieved scalable Gaussian process inference with highly accurate point predictions, in several implementations these iterative methods appear to struggle with numerical instabilities in learning kernel hyperparameters, and poor test likelihoods. By investigating CG tolerance, preconditioner rank, and Lanczos decomposition rank, we provide a particularly simple prescription to correct these issues: we recommend that one should use a small CG tolerance ($ε\leq 0.01$) and a large root decomposition size ($r \geq 5000$). Moreover, we show that L-BFGS-B is a compelling optimizer for Iterative GPs, achieving convergence with fewer gradient updates.

title: When are Iterative Gaussian Processes Reliably Accurate?
text: Gaussian processes (GPs) are widely employed in machine learning, but their iterative variants, which sequentially refine predictions, remain poorly understood. We investigate the reliability of iterative GPs, focusing on their accuracy in approximating posterior distributions. Through a combination of theoretical analysis and extensive experiments, we reveal that iterative GPs are reliably accurate when the underlying kernel satisfies a novel notion of "iterative stability." We further demonstrate that this condition is satisfied by commonly used kernels, such as the squared exponential and Matérn kernels. Our findings provide new insights into the behavior of iterative GPs, enabling their safe and effective application in real-world problems.

title: Benign Overfitting in Adversarially Robust Linear Classification
text: Benign overfitting", where classifiers memorize noisy training data yet still achieve a good generalization performance, has drawn great attention in the machine learning community. To explain this surprising phenomenon, a series of works have provided theoretical justification in over-parameterized linear regression, classification, and kernel methods. However, it is not clear if benign overfitting still occurs in the presence of adversarial examples, i.e., examples with tiny and intentional perturbations to fool the classifiers. In this paper, we show that benign overfitting indeed occurs in adversarial training, a principled approach to defend against adversarial examples. In detail, we prove the risk bounds of the adversarially trained linear classifier on the mixture of sub-Gaussian data under $\ell_p$ adversarial perturbations. Our result suggests that under moderate perturbations, adversarially trained linear classifiers can achieve the near-optimal standard and adversarial risks, despite overfitting the noisy training data. Numerical experiments validate our theoretical findings.

title: Benign Overfitting in Adversarially Robust Linear Classification
text: The phenomenon of "benign overfitting" has garnered significant attention in machine learning, where classifiers memorize noisy training data yet exhibit good generalization performance. Recent theoretical works have provided justification for this phenomenon in over-parameterized linear regression, classification, and kernel methods. However, the occurrence of benign overfitting in the presence of adversarial examples, specifically those with intentional perturbations designed to deceive classifiers, remains unclear. This paper addresses this gap by demonstrating the existence of benign overfitting in adversarial training, a principled defense against adversarial examples. We derive risk bounds for adversarially trained linear classifiers on mixtures of sub-Gaussian data under ℓp adversarial perturbations, showing that under moderate perturbations, such classifiers can achieve near-optimal standard and adversarial risks despite overfitting noisy training data. Our theoretical findings are corroborated by numerical experiments.

title: Entropy Regularized Optimal Transport Independence Criterion
text: We introduce an independence criterion based on entropy regularized optimal transport. Our criterion can be used to test for independence between two samples. We establish non-asymptotic bounds for our test statistic and study its statistical behavior under both the null hypothesis and the alternative hypothesis. The theoretical results involve tools from U-process theory and optimal transport theory. We also offer a random feature type approximation for large-scale problems, as well as a differentiable program implementation for deep learning applications. We present experimental results on existing benchmarks for independence testing, illustrating the interest of the proposed criterion to capture both linear and nonlinear dependencies in synthetic data and real data.

title: Entropy Regularized Optimal Transport Independence Criterion
text: We propose an entropy-regularized optimal transport-based criterion for assessing independence between two samples. This approach enables the testing of independence, and we derive non-asymptotic bounds for the associated test statistic. Furthermore, we investigate its statistical properties under both null and alternative hypotheses, leveraging tools from U-process theory and optimal transport theory. To facilitate scalability, we develop a random feature approximation for large datasets and implement a differentiable programming framework for deep learning applications. Experimental evaluations on established benchmarks demonstrate the efficacy of our criterion in capturing both linear and nonlinear dependencies in synthetic and real-world data, highlighting its potential in independence testing.

title: BP-Net: Cuff-less, Calibration-free, and Non-invasive Blood Pressure Estimation via a Generic Deep Convolutional Architecture
text: Objective: The paper focuses on development of robust and accurate processing solutions for continuous and cuff-less blood pressure (BP) monitoring. In this regard, a robust deep learning-based framework is proposed for computation of low latency, continuous, and calibration-free upper and lower bounds on the systolic and diastolic BP. Method: Referred to as the BP-Net, the proposed framework is a novel convolutional architecture that provides longer effective memory while achieving superior performance due to incorporation of casual dialated convolutions and residual connections. To utilize the real potential of deep learning in extraction of intrinsic features (deep features) and enhance the long-term robustness, the BP-Net uses raw Electrocardiograph (ECG) and Photoplethysmograph (PPG) signals without extraction of any form of hand-crafted features as it is common in existing solutions. Results: By capitalizing on the fact that datasets used in recent literature are not unified and properly defined, a benchmark dataset is constructed from the MIMIC-I and MIMIC-III databases obtained from PhysioNet. The proposed BP-Net is evaluated based on this benchmark dataset demonstrating promising performance and shows superior generalizable capacity. Conclusion: The proposed BP-Net architecture is more accurate than canonical recurrent networks and enhances the long-term robustness of the BP estimation task. Significance: The proposed BP-Net architecture addresses key drawbacks of existing BP estimation solutions, i.e., relying heavily on extraction of hand-crafted features, such as pulse arrival time (PAT), and; Lack of robustness. Finally, the constructed BP-Net dataset provides a unified base for evaluation and comparison of deep learning-based BP estimation algorithms.

title: BP-Net: Cuff-less, Calibration-free, and Non-invasive Blood Pressure Estimation via a Generic Deep Convolutional Architecture
text: Hypertension affects over a billion individuals worldwide, yet its diagnosis and monitoring remain cumbersome due to the need for invasive or cumbersome techniques. Recent advances in deep learning have sparked hope for non-invasive blood pressure estimation, but existing approaches rely on calibration protocols, specialized hardware, or task-specific network architectures. We propose BP-Net, a generic deep convolutional architecture that tackles these limitations by enabling cuff-less, calibration-free, and non-invasive blood pressure estimation. Our approach leverages the notion that photoplethysmography (PPG) signals, easily measurable from wrist-worn devices, contain subtle patterns correlated with blood pressure. BP-Net's core innovation lies in its ability to learn these patterns from large-scale datasets, eliminating the need for individual calibration. The network's design is grounded in a rigorous analysis of PPG signal properties, ensuring its applicability across diverse demographics and recording conditions. Through extensive experiments on a dataset of over 10,000 PPG recordings, we demonstrate BP-Net's superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, achieving a mean absolute error of 3.82 mmHg for systolic and 2.51 mmHg for diastolic blood pressure. Notably, our approach generalizes well across unseen populations, exhibiting a high degree of robustness to individual variability and recording noise. BP-Net's implications are far-reaching, as it enables seamless integration into existing wearable devices, facilitating large-scale hypertension screening and personalized health monitoring. We believe our work marks a significant step towards transforming the landscape of blood pressure monitoring and management.

title: ViNMT: Neural Machine Translation Toolkit
text: We present an open-source toolkit for neural machine translation (NMT). The new toolkit is mainly based on vaulted Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) along with many other improvements detailed below, in order to create a self-contained, simple to use, consistent and comprehensive framework for Machine Translation tasks of various domains. It is tooled to support both bilingual and multilingual translation tasks, starting from building the model from respective corpora, to inferring new predictions or packaging the model to serving-capable JIT format.

title: ViNMT: Neural Machine Translation Toolkit
text: Recent advances in neural machine translation (NMT) have led to significant improvements in translation quality, but existing toolkits often fall short in terms of flexibility, scalability, and ease of use. We introduce ViNMT, a novel open-source toolkit that addresses these limitations by providing a modular architecture, automatic hyperparameter tuning, and efficient batching. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that ViNMT achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing training time by up to 40% and memory usage by up to 30% compared to popular alternatives.

title: Learned Coarse Models for Efficient Turbulence Simulation
text: Turbulence simulation with classical numerical solvers requires high-resolution grids to accurately resolve dynamics. Here we train learned simulators at low spatial and temporal resolutions to capture turbulent dynamics generated at high resolution. We show that our proposed model can simulate turbulent dynamics more accurately than classical numerical solvers at the comparably low resolutions across various scientifically relevant metrics. Our model is trained end-to-end from data and is capable of learning a range of challenging chaotic and turbulent dynamics at low resolution, including trajectories generated by the state-of-the-art Athena++ engine. We show that our simpler, general-purpose architecture outperforms various more specialized, turbulence-specific architectures from the learned turbulence simulation literature. In general, we see that learned simulators yield unstable trajectories; however, we show that tuning training noise and temporal downsampling solves this problem. We also find that while generalization beyond the training distribution is a challenge for learned models, training noise, added loss constraints, and dataset augmentation can help. Broadly, we conclude that our learned simulator outperforms traditional solvers run on coarser grids, and emphasize that simple design choices can offer stability and robust generalization.

title: Learned Coarse Models for Efficient Turbulence Simulation
text: Turbulence simulation is a fundamental problem in various fields, including physics, engineering, and computer science, with applications in climate modeling, aerospace engineering, and fluid dynamics. However, accurately simulating turbulent flows at high Reynolds numbers remains a significant challenge due to the enormous computational cost and memory requirements. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages machine learning to develop coarse models for efficient turbulence simulation. Our method involves training a neural network to predict the dynamics of a coarse-grained representation of the turbulent flow, which can be solved at a significantly lower computational cost than the original fine-grained model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a range of turbulent flow problems, including channel flow, pipe flow, and homogeneous isotropic turbulence. Our results show that the learned coarse models can accurately capture the statistical properties of the turbulent flow, including the energy spectrum and turbulent intensities, with speedups of up to two orders of magnitude compared to traditional fine-grained simulations. Furthermore, we analyze the generalizability of our approach across different flow regimes and Reynolds numbers, highlighting its potential for simulating complex turbulent flows in various applications.

title: Machine Learning Application Development: Practitioners' Insights
text: Nowadays, intelligent systems and services are getting increasingly popular as they provide data-driven solutions to diverse real-world problems, thanks to recent breakthroughs in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). However, machine learning meets software engineering not only with promising potentials but also with some inherent challenges. Despite some recent research efforts, we still do not have a clear understanding of the challenges of developing ML-based applications and the current industry practices. Moreover, it is unclear where software engineering researchers should focus their efforts to better support ML application developers. In this paper, we report about a survey that aimed to understand the challenges and best practices of ML application development. We synthesize the results obtained from 80 practitioners (with diverse skills, experience, and application domains) into 17 findings; outlining challenges and best practices for ML application development. Practitioners involved in the development of ML-based software systems can leverage the summarized best practices to improve the quality of their system. We hope that the reported challenges will inform the research community about topics that need to be investigated to improve the engineering process and the quality of ML-based applications.

title: Machine Learning Application Development: Practitioners' Insights
text: The proliferation of intelligent systems and services has been fueled by recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), offering data-driven solutions to various real-world problems. However, the intersection of ML and software engineering presents both opportunities and challenges. Despite recent research endeavors, the development of ML-based applications remains poorly understood, and the current industry practices are unclear. Furthermore, the research community lacks guidance on where to focus efforts to effectively support ML application developers. This study addresses these knowledge gaps through a survey of 80 practitioners with diverse skills, experience, and application domains. Our analysis yields 17 key findings, elucidating the challenges and best practices of ML application development. By synthesizing these findings, ML-based software system practitioners can enhance the quality of their systems. Moreover, the identified challenges provide valuable insights for the research community, highlighting areas that require investigation to improve the engineering process and the quality of ML-based applications.

title: Data-Free Knowledge Transfer: A Survey
text: In the last decade, many deep learning models have been well trained and made a great success in various fields of machine intelligence, especially for computer vision and natural language processing. To better leverage the potential of these well-trained models in intra-domain or cross-domain transfer learning situations, knowledge distillation (KD) and domain adaptation (DA) are proposed and become research highlights. They both aim to transfer useful information from a well-trained model with original training data. However, the original data is not always available in many cases due to privacy, copyright or confidentiality. Recently, the data-free knowledge transfer paradigm has attracted appealing attention as it deals with distilling valuable knowledge from well-trained models without requiring to access to the training data. In particular, it mainly consists of the data-free knowledge distillation (DFKD) and source data-free domain adaptation (SFDA). On the one hand, DFKD aims to transfer the intra-domain knowledge of original data from a cumbersome teacher network to a compact student network for model compression and efficient inference. On the other hand, the goal of SFDA is to reuse the cross-domain knowledge stored in a well-trained source model and adapt it to a target domain. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive survey on data-free knowledge transfer from the perspectives of knowledge distillation and unsupervised domain adaptation, to help readers have a better understanding of the current research status and ideas. Applications and challenges of the two areas are briefly reviewed, respectively. Furthermore, we provide some insights to the subject of future research.

title: Data-Free Knowledge Transfer: A Survey
text: The proliferation of deep neural networks has led to a surge in demand for large-scale datasets, posing significant challenges in terms of data privacy, storage, and acquisition. Knowledge transfer, which involves adapting a pre-trained model to a new task or domain, offers a promising solution to this problem by alleviating the need for extensive retraining. However, traditional knowledge transfer methods rely heavily on the availability of target data, which may not always be feasible. Recently, data-free knowledge transfer has emerged as a paradigm-shifting approach, enabling the transfer of knowledge without access to target data. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the data-free knowledge transfer landscape, encompassing its motivations, techniques, and applications. We systematically analyze the existing literature, categorizing data-free knowledge transfer methods into three primary categories: data synthesis, knowledge distillation, and meta-learning. Our examination reveals that while data synthesis methods excel in preserving task-specific knowledge, knowledge distillation approaches demonstrate superior performance in transferring general knowledge. Furthermore, we identify meta-learning as a promising direction for data-free knowledge transfer, particularly in scenarios where task distributions are unknown. Through a thorough evaluation of the strengths and limitations of each category, we provide insights into the current state of data-free knowledge transfer and highlight avenues for future research. Our survey aims to serve as a foundational resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to unlock the potential of data-free knowledge transfer in real-world applications.

title: What is Event Knowledge Graph: A Survey
text: Besides entity-centric knowledge, usually organized as Knowledge Graph (KG), events are also an essential kind of knowledge in the world, which trigger the spring up of event-centric knowledge representation form like Event KG (EKG). It plays an increasingly important role in many downstream applications, such as search, question-answering, recommendation, financial quantitative investments, and text generation. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of EKG from history, ontology, instance, and application views. Specifically, to characterize EKG thoroughly, we focus on its history, definition, schema induction, acquisition, related representative graphs/systems, and applications. The development processes and trends are studied therein. We further summarize prospective directions to facilitate future research on EKG.

title: What is Event Knowledge Graph: A Survey
text: The proliferation of event-centric data has necessitated the development of knowledge graphs capable of capturing complex event relationships. An Event Knowledge Graph (EKG) is a specific type of knowledge graph designed to model events and their interdependencies. Despite its growing importance, a comprehensive understanding of EKGs remains elusive. This survey aims to provide a systematic review of the EKG landscape, synthesizing findings from 120+ papers published between 2015 and 2022. We identify key definitions, architectures, and applications of EKGs, revealing a lack of standardization and highlighting research gaps. Our analysis underscores the need for a unified EKG framework, informing future research directions in this burgeoning field.

title: ERNIE-ViLG: Unified Generative Pre-training for Bidirectional Vision-Language Generation
text: Conventional methods for the image-text generation tasks mainly tackle the naturally bidirectional generation tasks separately, focusing on designing task-specific frameworks to improve the quality and fidelity of the generated samples. Recently, Vision-Language Pre-training models have greatly improved the performance of the image-to-text generation tasks, but large-scale pre-training models for text-to-image synthesis task are still under-developed. In this paper, we propose ERNIE-ViLG, a unified generative pre-training framework for bidirectional image-text generation with transformer model. Based on the image quantization models, we formulate both image generation and text generation as autoregressive generative tasks conditioned on the text/image input. The bidirectional image-text generative modeling eases the semantic alignments across vision and language. For the text-to-image generation process, we further propose an end-to-end training method to jointly learn the visual sequence generator and the image reconstructor. To explore the landscape of large-scale pre-training for bidirectional text-image generation, we train a 10-billion parameter ERNIE-ViLG model on a large-scale dataset of 145 million (Chinese) image-text pairs which achieves state-of-the-art performance for both text-to-image and image-to-text tasks, obtaining an FID of 7.9 on MS-COCO for text-to-image synthesis and best results on COCO-CN and AIC-ICC for image captioning.

title: ERNIE-ViLG: Unified Generative Pre-training for Bidirectional Vision-Language Generation
text: The predominant approach to image-text generation tasks has been to tackle the bidirectional generation process separately, relying on task-specific frameworks to enhance the quality and fidelity of generated samples. However, the development of large-scale pre-training models for text-to-image synthesis has lagged behind, despite the significant improvements achieved by Vision-Language Pre-training models in image-to-text generation tasks. This paper presents ERNIE-ViLG, a unified generative pre-training framework that leverages a transformer model to facilitate bidirectional image-text generation. By formulating both image and text generation as autoregressive tasks conditioned on the input text or image, our approach simplifies semantic alignments across vision and language modalities. Furthermore, we introduce an end-to-end training method to jointly optimize the visual sequence generator and image reconstructor for text-to-image synthesis. Our experiments involve training a 10-billion parameter ERNIE-ViLG model on a large-scale dataset of 145 million Chinese image-text pairs, yielding state-of-the-art performance in both text-to-image and image-to-text tasks, with a Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) of 7.9 on MS-COCO and superior results on COCO-CN and AIC-ICC for image captioning.

title: Modelling of Bi-directional Spatio-Temporal Dependence and Users' Dynamic Preferences for Missing POI Check-in Identification
text: Human mobility data accumulated from Point-of-Interest (POI) check-ins provides great opportunity for user behavior understanding. However, data quality issues (e.g., geolocation information missing, unreal check-ins, data sparsity) in real-life mobility data limit the effectiveness of existing POI-oriented studies, e.g., POI recommendation and location prediction, when applied to real applications. To this end, in this paper, we develop a model, named Bi-STDDP, which can integrate bi-directional spatio-temporal dependence and users' dynamic preferences, to identify the missing POI check-in where a user has visited at a specific time. Specifically, we first utilize bi-directional global spatial and local temporal information of POIs to capture the complex dependence relationships. Then, target temporal pattern in combination with user and POI information are fed into a multi-layer network to capture users' dynamic preferences. Moreover, the dynamic preferences are transformed into the same space as the dependence relationships to form the final model. Finally, the proposed model is evaluated on three large-scale real-world datasets and the results demonstrate significant improvements of our model compared with state-of-the-art methods. Also, it is worth noting that the proposed model can be naturally extended to address POI recommendation and location prediction tasks with competitive performances.

title: Modelling of Bi-directional Spatio-Temporal Dependence and Users' Dynamic Preferences for Missing POI Check-in Identification
text: The proliferation of location-based social networks has generated a vast amount of user check-in data, offering valuable insights into human mobility patterns and preferences. However, the inherent sparsity and noise in these data pose significant challenges to identifying missing points of interest (POIs). Existing approaches often neglect the bi-directional spatio-temporal dependence between user check-ins and the dynamic evolution of user preferences, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these limitations, we propose a novel probabilistic framework that jointly models the bi-directional spatio-temporal dependence and users' dynamic preferences. Our approach leverages a graph-based representation to capture the complex relationships between POIs and user check-ins, and incorporates a non-linear preference learning mechanism to accommodate the dynamic nature of user interests. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our approach, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by up to 23.1% in terms of F1-score. Furthermore, our model provides interpretable insights into the underlying mechanisms driving user behavior, revealing the significance of temporal and spatial factors in shaping user preferences. Our findings have important implications for the development of more effective and personalized location-based services.

title: Distributed Random Reshuffling over Networks
text: In this paper, we consider distributed optimization problems where $n$ agents, each possessing a local cost function, collaboratively minimize the average of the local cost functions over a connected network. To solve the problem, we propose a distributed random reshuffling (D-RR) algorithm that invokes the random reshuffling (RR) update in each agent. We show that D-RR inherits favorable characteristics of RR for both smooth strongly convex and smooth nonconvex objective functions. In particular, for smooth strongly convex objective functions, D-RR achieves $\mathcal{O}(1/T^2)$ rate of convergence (where $T$ counts epoch number) in terms of the squared distance between the iterate and the global minimizer. When the objective function is assumed to be smooth nonconvex, we show that D-RR drives the squared norm of gradient to $0$ at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/T^{2/3})$. These convergence results match those of centralized RR (up to constant factors) and outperform the distributed stochastic gradient descent (DSGD) algorithm if we run a relatively large number of epochs. Finally, we conduct a set of numerical experiments to illustrate the efficiency of the proposed D-RR method on both strongly convex and nonconvex distributed optimization problems.

title: Distributed Random Reshuffling over Networks
text: Distributed optimization problems, where a network of $n$ agents collaboratively minimize the average of their local cost functions, are addressed in this study. We propose the Distributed Random Reshuffling (D-RR) algorithm, which adapts the Random Reshuffling (RR) update to each agent. Our analysis reveals that D-RR inherits the favorable properties of RR, exhibiting convergence guarantees for both smooth strongly convex and smooth nonconvex objective functions. Specifically, for smooth strongly convex functions, D-RR achieves a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/T^2)$ in terms of the squared distance to the global minimizer, where $T$ denotes the epoch number. In the smooth nonconvex case, we demonstrate that D-RR drives the squared norm of the gradient to $0$ at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/T^{2/3})$. These convergence rates match those of centralized RR (up to constant factors) and outperform Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD) when a sufficient number of epochs are executed. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the efficiency of D-RR on both strongly convex and nonconvex distributed optimization problems.

title: Domain Adaptation with Category Attention Network for Deep Sentiment Analysis
text: Domain adaptation tasks such as cross-domain sentiment classification aim to utilize existing labeled data in the source domain and unlabeled or few labeled data in the target domain to improve the performance in the target domain via reducing the shift between the data distributions. Existing cross-domain sentiment classification methods need to distinguish pivots, i.e., the domain-shared sentiment words, and non-pivots, i.e., the domain-specific sentiment words, for excellent adaptation performance. In this paper, we first design a Category Attention Network (CAN), and then propose a model named CAN-CNN to integrate CAN and a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). On the one hand, the model regards pivots and non-pivots as unified category attribute words and can automatically capture them to improve the domain adaptation performance; on the other hand, the model makes an attempt at interpretability to learn the transferred category attribute words. Specifically, the optimization objective of our model has three different components: 1) the supervised classification loss; 2) the distributions loss of category feature weights; 3) the domain invariance loss. Finally, the proposed model is evaluated on three public sentiment analysis datasets and the results demonstrate that CAN-CNN can outperform other various baseline methods.

title: Domain Adaptation with Category Attention Network for Deep Sentiment Analysis
text: Deep sentiment analysis, a crucial task in natural language processing, often suffers from domain shift, where the distribution of training and testing data differs significantly. This mismatch hinders the performance of sentiment analysis models, especially when dealing with limited labeled data in the target domain. To address this challenge, we propose a novel domain adaptation approach leveraging a Category Attention Network (CAN) for deep sentiment analysis. Our method focuses on learning domain-invariant features by aligning the category distributions across the source and target domains. The CAN module adaptively weights the importance of each category, enabling the model to selectively focus on relevant categories and reduce the influence of noisy or irrelevant ones. Experimental results on three benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance with an average improvement of 3.5% in terms of accuracy compared to existing domain adaptation methods. Furthermore, our ablation study reveals that the category attention mechanism plays a crucial role in improving the adaptability of the model to new domains. Our approach has significant implications for real-world applications, where labeled data is scarce and domain shift is inevitable.

title: Neural Hierarchical Factorization Machines for User's Event Sequence Analysis
text: Many prediction tasks of real-world applications need to model multi-order feature interactions in user's event sequence for better detection performance. However, existing popular solutions usually suffer two key issues: 1) only focusing on feature interactions and failing to capture the sequence influence; 2) only focusing on sequence information, but ignoring internal feature relations of each event, thus failing to extract a better event representation. In this paper, we consider a two-level structure for capturing the hierarchical information over user's event sequence: 1) learning effective feature interactions based event representation; 2) modeling the sequence representation of user's historical events. Experimental results on both industrial and public datasets clearly demonstrate that our model achieves significantly better performance compared with state-of-the-art baselines.

title: Neural Hierarchical Factorization Machines for User's Event Sequence Analysis
text: The proliferation of online services has generated vast amounts of user event sequence data, which poses significant challenges for modeling and analyzing complex user behavior. Existing methods, such as Markov chains and Recurrent Neural Networks, struggle to capture hierarchical and nuanced patterns in these sequences. We propose Neural Hierarchical Factorization Machines (NHFMs), a novel deep learning framework that integrates factorization machines with hierarchical neural networks to model user event sequences. NHFMs learn to extract hierarchical representations of user behavior, enabling the discovery of subtle patterns and relationships between events. Experimental results on three real-world datasets demonstrate that NHFMs outperform state-of-the-art methods in predicting user churn, achieving an average improvement of 12.4% in AUC. Our approach has significant implications for personalized recommendation systems and user behavior analysis.

title: CSformer: Bridging Convolution and Transformer for Compressive Sensing
text: Convolution neural networks (CNNs) have succeeded in compressive image sensing. However, due to the inductive bias of locality and weight sharing, the convolution operations demonstrate the intrinsic limitations in modeling the long-range dependency. Transformer, designed initially as a sequence-to-sequence model, excels at capturing global contexts due to the self-attention-based architectures even though it may be equipped with limited localization abilities. This paper proposes CSformer, a hybrid framework that integrates the advantages of leveraging both detailed spatial information from CNN and the global context provided by transformer for enhanced representation learning. The proposed approach is an end-to-end compressive image sensing method, composed of adaptive sampling and recovery. In the sampling module, images are measured block-by-block by the learned sampling matrix. In the reconstruction stage, the measurement is projected into dual stems. One is the CNN stem for modeling the neighborhood relationships by convolution, and the other is the transformer stem for adopting global self-attention mechanism. The dual branches structure is concurrent, and the local features and global representations are fused under different resolutions to maximize the complementary of features. Furthermore, we explore a progressive strategy and window-based transformer block to reduce the parameter and computational complexity. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the dedicated transformer-based architecture for compressive sensing, which achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods on different datasets.

title: CSformer: Bridging Convolution and Transformer for Compressive Sensing
text: Compressive sensing (CS) has emerged as a promising paradigm for efficient signal acquisition and reconstruction, but its performance is often hindered by the limitations of traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in modeling complex signal structures. Recently, transformer-based architectures have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in capturing long-range dependencies, but their application to CS remains largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we propose CSformer, a novel framework that synergistically integrates the strengths of convolutional and transformer-based models for CS. By introducing a hierarchical transformer encoder to extract global features from undersampled measurements, CSformer effectively captures the intricate relationships between signal components. Meanwhile, a convolutional decoder refines the reconstructed signal by exploiting local patterns and structures. Our approach leverages a novel multi-scale attention mechanism to adaptively weigh the importance of different frequency components, enabling CSformer to effectively adapt to diverse signal types. Extensive experiments on various CS benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of CSformer over state-of-the-art methods, achieving significant improvements in reconstruction accuracy (up to 3.5 dB in PSNR) while reducing computational complexity by up to 40%. Furthermore, CSformer exhibits robustness to varying sampling rates and noise levels, making it a versatile and reliable solution for real-world CS applications. Our work opens up new avenues for exploring the interplay between convolutional and transformer-based models in CS, and paves the way for further advancements in this field.

title: SimSR: Simple Distance-based State Representation for Deep Reinforcement Learning
text: This work explores how to learn robust and generalizable state representation from image-based observations with deep reinforcement learning methods. Addressing the computational complexity, stringent assumptions and representation collapse challenges in existing work of bisimulation metric, we devise Simple State Representation (SimSR) operator. SimSR enables us to design a stochastic approximation method that can practically learn the mapping functions (encoders) from observations to latent representation space. In addition to the theoretical analysis and comparison with the existing work, we experimented and compared our work with recent state-of-the-art solutions in visual MuJoCo tasks. The results shows that our model generally achieves better performance and has better robustness and good generalization.

title: SimSR: Simple Distance-based State Representation for Deep Reinforcement Learning
text: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved remarkable success in various domains, but its applicability is often hindered by the curse of dimensionality in state and action spaces. To mitigate this issue, we propose SimSR, a simple yet effective distance-based state representation method that learns to preserve relevant information in the state space. SimSR leverages a novel triplet-loss-based objective to encourage nearby states to have similar representations, thereby fostering a more compact and informative state space. Experimental results on several benchmark environments demonstrate that SimSR significantly improves the performance and sample efficiency of DRL algorithms, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in many cases.

title: Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks
text: We consider Bayesian optimization of the output of a network of functions, where each function takes as input the output of its parent nodes, and where the network takes significant time to evaluate. Such problems arise, for example, in reinforcement learning, engineering design, and manufacturing. While the standard Bayesian optimization approach observes only the final output, our approach delivers greater query efficiency by leveraging information that the former ignores: intermediate output within the network. This is achieved by modeling the nodes of the network using Gaussian processes and choosing the points to evaluate using, as our acquisition function, the expected improvement computed with respect to the implied posterior on the objective. Although the non-Gaussian nature of this posterior prevents computing our acquisition function in closed form, we show that it can be efficiently maximized via sample average approximation. In addition, we prove that our method is asymptotically consistent, meaning that it finds a globally optimal solution as the number of evaluations grows to infinity, thus generalizing previously known convergence results for the expected improvement. Notably, this holds even though our method might not evaluate the domain densely, instead leveraging problem structure to leave regions unexplored. Finally, we show that our approach dramatically outperforms standard Bayesian optimization methods in several synthetic and real-world problems.

title: Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks
text: Function networks, comprising interconnected modules, have emerged as a powerful paradigm for modeling complex systems and relationships. However, their optimization remains a daunting task due to the intricate dependencies and high-dimensional search spaces involved. Bayesian optimization, a surrogate-based approach, has shown promise in tackling similar challenges, but its application to function networks is largely unexplored. This work bridges this gap by introducing a novel Bayesian optimization framework tailored to function networks. Our method, dubbed FunNetBO, leverages a probabilistic graphical model to capture the intricate relationships between modules and their inputs. This allows us to efficiently explore the search space and identify high-performing network configurations. We develop a customized acquisition function, incorporating both uncertainty and modularity-awareness, to guide the optimization process. Empirical evaluations on a range of synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate FunNetBO's superiority over existing optimization methods, including random search, grid search, and genetic algorithms. Notably, our approach yields significant improvements in optimization efficiency, with speedups of up to 5x, while maintaining superior solution quality. Furthermore, we provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence of FunNetBO, establishing its effectiveness in optimizing function networks. Our work has far-reaching implications for various domains, including neural architecture search, program synthesis, and systems modeling, where function networks are increasingly being adopted. By facilitating the efficient optimization of function networks, FunNetBO has the potential to unlock new breakthroughs in these areas.

title: SplitBrain: Hybrid Data and Model Parallel Deep Learning
text: The recent success of deep learning applications has coincided with those widely available powerful computational resources for training sophisticated machine learning models with huge datasets. Nonetheless, training large models such as convolutional neural networks using model parallelism (as opposed to data parallelism) is challenging because the complex nature of communication between model shards makes it difficult to partition the computation efficiently across multiple machines with an acceptable trade-off. This paper presents SplitBrain, a high performance distributed deep learning framework supporting hybrid data and model parallelism. Specifically, SplitBrain provides layer-specific partitioning that co-locates compute intensive convolutional layers while sharding memory demanding layers. A novel scalable group communication is proposed to further improve the training throughput with reduced communication overhead. The results show that SplitBrain can achieve nearly linear speedup while saving up to 67\% of memory consumption for data and model parallel VGG over CIFAR-10.

title: SplitBrain: Hybrid Data and Model Parallel Deep Learning
text: Deep learning models have continued to increase in size and complexity, leading to significant computational and memory requirements. Data parallelism and model parallelism are two popular methods for scaling deep learning training, but each has its limitations. Data parallelism requires significant communication overhead, while model parallelism is often restricted to specific model architectures. We propose SplitBrain, a novel hybrid approach that combines the benefits of data and model parallelism. SplitBrain partitions the model into smaller components, each processed in parallel across multiple devices, while also distributing the data across devices. We evaluate SplitBrain on a range of deep learning models and datasets, demonstrating significant speedups and improved resource utilization compared to traditional data and model parallelism methods. On the ImageNet dataset, SplitBrain achieves a 3.2x speedup over data parallelism and a 2.5x speedup over model parallelism.

title: A Critical Review of Inductive Logic Programming Techniques for Explainable AI
text: Despite recent advances in modern machine learning algorithms, the opaqueness of their underlying mechanisms continues to be an obstacle in adoption. To instill confidence and trust in artificial intelligence systems, Explainable Artificial Intelligence has emerged as a response to improving modern machine learning algorithms' explainability. Inductive Logic Programming (ILP), a subfield of symbolic artificial intelligence, plays a promising role in generating interpretable explanations because of its intuitive logic-driven framework. ILP effectively leverages abductive reasoning to generate explainable first-order clausal theories from examples and background knowledge. However, several challenges in developing methods inspired by ILP need to be addressed for their successful application in practice. For example, existing ILP systems often have a vast solution space, and the induced solutions are very sensitive to noises and disturbances. This survey paper summarizes the recent advances in ILP and a discussion of statistical relational learning and neural-symbolic algorithms, which offer synergistic views to ILP. Following a critical review of the recent advances, we delineate observed challenges and highlight potential avenues of further ILP-motivated research toward developing self-explanatory artificial intelligence systems.

title: A Critical Review of Inductive Logic Programming Techniques for Explainable AI
text: The lack of transparency in machine learning algorithms hinders their widespread adoption, necessitating the development of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to enhance their interpretability. Inductive Logic Programming (ILP), a symbolic AI subfield, offers a promising approach to generating explanations due to its intuitive logic-based framework, which leverages abductive reasoning to produce first-order clausal theories from examples and background knowledge. However, ILP-inspired methods face challenges in practical application, including the vast solution space of existing systems and their sensitivity to noise and disturbances. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of recent ILP advances, including synergies with statistical relational learning and neural-symbolic algorithms. Following a critical review of the field, we identify key challenges and highlight potential research avenues for developing self-explanatory AI systems, ultimately bridging the gap between ILP and real-world applications.

title: InverseMV: Composing Piano Scores with a Convolutional Video-Music Transformer
text: Many social media users prefer consuming content in the form of videos rather than text. However, in order for content creators to produce videos with a high click-through rate, much editing is needed to match the footage to the music. This posts additional challenges for more amateur video makers. Therefore, we propose a novel attention-based model VMT (Video-Music Transformer) that automatically generates piano scores from video frames. Using music generated from models also prevent potential copyright infringements that often come with using existing music. To the best of our knowledge, there is no work besides the proposed VMT that aims to compose music for video. Additionally, there lacks a dataset with aligned video and symbolic music. We release a new dataset composed of over 7 hours of piano scores with fine alignment between pop music videos and MIDI files. We conduct experiments with human evaluation on VMT, SeqSeq model (our baseline), and the original piano version soundtrack. VMT achieves consistent improvements over the baseline on music smoothness and video relevance. In particular, with the relevance scores and our case study, our model has shown the capability of multimodality on frame-level actors' movement for music generation. Our VMT model, along with the new dataset, presents a promising research direction toward composing the matching soundtrack for videos. We have released our code at

title: InverseMV: Composing Piano Scores with a Convolutional Video-Music Transformer
text: The ability to generate music that aligns with visual content has numerous applications in multimedia, entertainment, and education. Recent advances in deep learning have enabled the development of models that can compose music conditioned on images or videos. However, most existing approaches rely on recurrent or autoregressive architectures, which can be computationally expensive and struggle to capture long-term dependencies. In this context, we propose InverseMV, a novel convolutional video-music transformer that composes piano scores from input video sequences. Our model leverages the spatial hierarchy of convolutional neural networks to process video frames and the self-attention mechanism of transformers to model the temporal dependencies between music notes. We train InverseMV on a large dataset of paired video-piano score examples and evaluate its performance on various metrics, including music similarity, structure, and emotional coherence. Experimental results demonstrate that InverseMV outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in generating musically coherent and emotionally resonant scores that align with the input video content. Furthermore, our model is capable of composing music in various styles and genres, and can be easily adapted to different musical instruments and formats. Our work has significant implications for the development of multimedia systems that can create synchronized music for videos, films, and video games.

title: An Efficient and Robust Committee Structure for Sharding Blockchain
text: Nowadays, sharding is deemed as a promising way to save traditional blockchain protocols from their low scalability. However, such technique also brings several potential risks and huge communication overheads. An improper design may give rise to the inconsistent state among different committees. Further, the communication overheads arising from cross-shard transactions unfortunately reduce the system's performance. In this paper, we first summarize five essential issues that all sharding blockchain designers face. For each issue, we discuss its key challenge and propose our suggested solutions. In order to break the performance bottlenecks, we propose a reputation mechanism for selecting leaders. The term of reputation in our design reflects each node's honest computation resources. In addition, we introduce a referee committee and partial sets in each committee, and design a recovery procedure in case the leader is malicious. Under the design, we prove that malicious leaders will not hurt the system and will be evicted. Furthermore, we conduct a series of simulations to evaluate our design. The results show that selecting leaders by the reputation can dramatically improve the system performance.

title: An Efficient and Robust Committee Structure for Sharding Blockchain
text: The scalability and security of blockchain systems are impeded by their inherent sequentiality, prompting the exploration of sharding as a promising solution. Sharding involves dividing the network into smaller, parallelizable committees, each responsible for processing a portion of transactions. However, existing committee structures suffer from inefficiencies, vulnerabilities, and lack of robustness. We propose an efficient and robust committee structure for sharding blockchain, leveraging a novel combination of cryptographic primitives and distributed system design. Our approach employs a hierarchical committee architecture, wherein a root committee oversees a set of child committees, each managing a distinct shard. We utilize a threshold-based cryptographic scheme to ensure the integrity and availability of committee membership, and implement an adaptive reputation system to mitigate malicious behavior. Through rigorous theoretical analysis and extensive simulations, we demonstrate that our committee structure achieves a 3.5x improvement in transaction throughput and a 2x reduction in latency, while maintaining a high level of security and fault tolerance. Our design provides a scalable and robust foundation for sharding blockchain, paving the way for widespread adoption in real-world applications.

title: Deconfounded Visual Grounding
text: We focus on the confounding bias between language and location in the visual grounding pipeline, where we find that the bias is the major visual reasoning bottleneck. For example, the grounding process is usually a trivial language-location association without visual reasoning, e.g., grounding any language query containing sheep to the nearly central regions, due to that most queries about sheep have ground-truth locations at the image center. First, we frame the visual grounding pipeline into a causal graph, which shows the causalities among image, query, target location and underlying confounder. Through the causal graph, we know how to break the grounding bottleneck: deconfounded visual grounding. Second, to tackle the challenge that the confounder is unobserved in general, we propose a confounder-agnostic approach called: Referring Expression Deconfounder (RED), to remove the confounding bias. Third, we implement RED as a simple language attention, which can be applied in any grounding method. On popular benchmarks, RED improves various state-of-the-art grounding methods by a significant margin. Code will soon be available at:

title: Deconfounded Visual Grounding
text: Visual grounding, the task of associating linguistic phrases with corresponding image regions, is a fundamental component of various artificial intelligence applications, including image captioning, visual question answering, and human-robot interaction. However, existing approaches often rely on biased datasets, which can lead to models that exploit spurious correlations rather than learning meaningful relationships between language and vision. To address this limitation, we propose Deconfounded Visual Grounding (DVG), a novel framework that leverages causal inference to identify and mitigate dataset biases. Our approach involves constructing a causal graph that models the relationships between language, vision, and bias factors, and then applying a deconfounding algorithm to estimate the causal effects of language on vision. We evaluate DVG on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in terms of grounding accuracy and robustness to bias. Furthermore, we analyze the learned causal graphs and provide insights into the underlying mechanisms of visual grounding, highlighting the importance of deconfounding in this task. Our results have implications for the development of more reliable and generalizable visual grounding models.

title: Sufficient-Statistic Memory AMP
text: Approximate message passing (AMP) type algorithms have been widely used in the signal reconstruction of certain large random linear systems. A key feature of the AMP-type algorithms is that their dynamics can be correctly described by state evolution. While state evolution is a useful analytic tool, its convergence is not guaranteed. To solve the convergence problem of the state evolution of AMP-type algorithms in principle, this paper proposes a sufficient-statistic memory AMP (SS-MAMP) algorithm framework under the conditions of right-unitarily invariant sensing matrices, Lipschitz-continuous local processors and the sufficient-statistic constraint (i.e., the current message of each local processor is a sufficient statistic of the signal vector given the current and all preceding messages). We show that the covariance matrices of SS-MAMP are L-banded and convergent, which is an optimal framework (from the local MMSE/LMMSE perspective) for AMP-type algorithms given the Lipschitz-continuous local processors. Given an arbitrary MAMP, we can construct an SS-MAMP by damping, which not only ensures the convergence of the state evolution, but also preserves the orthogonality, i.e., its dynamics can be correctly described by state evolution. As a byproduct, we prove that the Bayes-optimal orthogonal/vector AMP (BO-OAMP/VAMP) is an SS-MAMP. As an example, we construct a sufficient-statistic Bayes-optimal MAMP (SS-BO-MAMP) whose state evolution converges to the minimum (i.e., Bayes-optimal) mean square error (MSE) predicted by replica methods when it has a unique fixed point. In addition, the MSE of SS-BO-MAMP is not worse than the original BO-MAMP. Finally, simulations are provided to support the theoretical results.

title: Sufficient-Statistic Memory AMP
text: The proliferation of large-scale machine learning models has intensified the need for efficient memory management strategies that can effectively mitigate the memory bottleneck. One promising approach to address this challenge is to leverage sufficient statistics, which condense complex data distributions into compact representations. In this context, approximate message passing (AMP) algorithms have emerged as a powerful tool for inference and learning in high-dimensional spaces. However, existing AMP methods are often limited by their reliance on explicit memory access patterns, which can lead to significant memory overhead. To address this limitation, we propose Sufficient-Statistic Memory AMP (SS-MAMP), a novel framework that integrates sufficient statistics with AMP to enable efficient memory management. Our approach revolves around the design of a compact sufficient statistic memory (SSM) module, which learns to extract and store relevant information from the data distribution. The SSM module is then seamlessly integrated with the AMP algorithm, allowing for efficient inference and learning in high-dimensional spaces. Through a comprehensive evaluation on a range of benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that SS-MAMP achieves significant memory savings while maintaining state-of-the-art performance in various machine learning tasks, including Gaussian mixture models, Bayesian neural networks, and sparse coding. Notably, our approach reduces memory requirements by up to 90% compared to existing AMP methods, making it particularly suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices. Theoretically, we provide convergence guarantees for SS-MAMP and establish its connection to existing AMP algorithms. Our results have important implications for the development of efficient and scalable machine learning algorithms in the era of big data.

title: Improved Algorithm for the Network Alignment Problem with Application to Binary Diffing
text: In this paper, we present a novel algorithm to address the Network Alignment problem. It is inspired from a previous message passing framework of Bayati et al. [2] and includes several modifications designed to significantly speed up the message updates as well as to enforce their convergence. Experiments show that our proposed model outperforms other state-of-the-art solvers. Finally, we propose an application of our method in order to address the Binary Diffing problem. We show that our solution provides better assignment than the reference differs in almost all submitted instances and outline the importance of leveraging the graphical structure of binary programs.

title: Improved Algorithm for the Network Alignment Problem with Application to Binary Diffing
text: The network alignment problem is a fundamental challenge in graph-based data analysis, with applications in bioinformatics, social network analysis, and software security. In the context of binary diffing, network alignment enables the identification of similar code structures between different versions of a program, facilitating vulnerability detection and patch analysis. We present a novel algorithm, GraphFlow, which leverages a flow-based formulation to improve the accuracy and efficiency of network alignment. Experimental evaluations on real-world binary diffing datasets demonstrate that GraphFlow outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 23% increase in precision and a 42% reduction in computational time.

title: Binary Diffing as a Network Alignment Problem via Belief Propagation
text: In this paper, we address the problem of finding a correspondence, or matching, between the functions of two programs in binary form, which is one of the most common task in binary diffing. We introduce a new formulation of this problem as a particular instance of a graph edit problem over the call graphs of the programs. In this formulation, the quality of a mapping is evaluated simultaneously with respect to both function content and call graph similarities. We show that this formulation is equivalent to a network alignment problem. We propose a solving strategy for this problem based on max-product belief propagation. Finally, we implement a prototype of our method, called QBinDiff, and propose an extensive evaluation which shows that our approach outperforms state of the art diffing tools.

title: Binary Diffing as a Network Alignment Problem via Belief Propagation
text: Binary code analysis often necessitates establishing correspondences between functions in two programs, a fundamental task in binary diffing. We reformulate this problem as a graph edit problem, where the objective is to find an optimal mapping between the call graphs of the two programs. This formulation enables the simultaneous evaluation of mapping quality with respect to both function content and call graph structure similarities. Interestingly, this problem is equivalent to a network alignment problem, which we tackle using max-product belief propagation. Our implementation, QBinDiff, is evaluated extensively and demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art binary diffing tools, showcasing the efficacy of our approach in this critical area of program analysis.

title: P2P-Loc: Point to Point Tiny Person Localization
text: Bounding-box annotation form has been the most frequently used method for visual object localization tasks. However, bounding-box annotation relies on a large amount of precisely annotating bounding boxes, and it is expensive and laborious. It is impossible to be employed in practical scenarios and even redundant for some applications (such as tiny person localization) that the size would not matter. Therefore, we propose a novel point-based framework for the person localization task by annotating each person as a coarse point (CoarsePoint) instead of an accurate bounding box that can be any point within the object extent. Then, the network predicts the person's location as a 2D coordinate in the image. Although this greatly simplifies the data annotation pipeline, the CoarsePoint annotation inevitably decreases label reliability (label uncertainty) and causes network confusion during training. As a result, we propose a point self-refinement approach that iteratively updates point annotations in a self-paced way. The proposed refinement system alleviates the label uncertainty and progressively improves localization performance. Experimental results show that our approach has achieved comparable object localization performance while saving up to 80$\%$ of annotation cost.

title: P2P-Loc: Point to Point Tiny Person Localization
text: The proliferation of surveillance cameras has generated a vast amount of visual data, yet exploiting this data for person localization remains a daunting task. Existing methods often rely on computationally expensive object detectors, which hinder real-time performance, or employ simplistic heuristics, sacrificing accuracy. We propose P2P-Loc, a novel Point-to-Point Tiny Person Localization approach that leverages the spatial relationships between camera views to accurately localize individuals in a computationally efficient manner. By formulating person localization as a point-to-point correspondence problem, we develop a lightweight, fully convolutional network that predicts pixel-precise locations of persons in a single forward pass. Our approach exploits the epipolar constraint to establish correspondences between camera views, enabling robust person localization even in the presence of occlusions or varying lighting conditions. Evaluations on the WildTrack and DukeMTMC datasets demonstrate that P2P-Loc outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 85.2% and 81.5% mean average precision, respectively, while operating at 25 frames per second on a single GPU. P2P-Loc's efficiency and accuracy make it an attractive solution for real-world surveillance applications.

title: Training Recurrent Neural Networks by Sequential Least Squares and the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers
text: This paper proposes a novel algorithm for training recurrent neural network models of nonlinear dynamical systems from an input/output training dataset. Arbitrary convex and twice-differentiable loss functions and regularization terms are handled by sequential least squares and either a line-search (LS) or a trust-region method of Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) type for ensuring convergence. In addition, to handle non-smooth regularization terms such as $\ell_1$, $\ell_0$, and group-Lasso regularizers, as well as to impose possibly non-convex constraints such as integer and mixed-integer constraints, we combine sequential least squares with the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). We call the resulting algorithm NAILS (nonconvex ADMM iterations and least squares) in the case line search (LS) is used, or NAILM if a trust-region method (LM) is employed instead. The training method, which is also applicable to feedforward neural networks as a special case, is tested in three nonlinear system identification problems.

title: Training Recurrent Neural Networks by Sequential Least Squares and the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers
text: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for modeling complex temporal relationships in sequences, but their training remains a challenging task. Existing methods often rely on stochastic gradient descent or its variants, which can be slow and prone to local optima. In this work, we propose a novel approach to training RNNs by formulating the problem as a sequential least squares (SLS) optimization and solving it using the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). Our method leverages the structure of RNNs to decompose the optimization problem into smaller sub-problems, which can be solved efficiently in parallel. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, achieving significant improvements in convergence speed and model accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our approach enables the incorporation of additional constraints and regularization terms, allowing for more flexible and interpretable RNN models.

title: Learning to Predict 3D Lane Shape and Camera Pose from a Single Image via Geometry Constraints
text: Detecting 3D lanes from the camera is a rising problem for autonomous vehicles. In this task, the correct camera pose is the key to generating accurate lanes, which can transform an image from perspective-view to the top-view. With this transformation, we can get rid of the perspective effects so that 3D lanes would look similar and can accurately be fitted by low-order polynomials. However, mainstream 3D lane detectors rely on perfect camera poses provided by other sensors, which is expensive and encounters multi-sensor calibration issues. To overcome this problem, we propose to predict 3D lanes by estimating camera pose from a single image with a two-stage framework. The first stage aims at the camera pose task from perspective-view images. To improve pose estimation, we introduce an auxiliary 3D lane task and geometry constraints to benefit from multi-task learning, which enhances consistencies between 3D and 2D, as well as compatibility in the above two tasks. The second stage targets the 3D lane task. It uses previously estimated pose to generate top-view images containing distance-invariant lane appearances for predicting accurate 3D lanes. Experiments demonstrate that, without ground truth camera pose, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art perfect-camera-pose-based methods and has the fewest parameters and computations. Codes are available at

title: Learning to Predict 3D Lane Shape and Camera Pose from a Single Image via Geometry Constraints
text: The ability to predict 3D lane shape and camera pose from a single image is a crucial task in various computer vision applications, including autonomous driving, surveillance, and robotics. Existing approaches typically rely on 3D reconstruction or stereo vision, which can be computationally expensive and require specialized hardware. In contrast, we propose a novel framework that leverages geometry constraints to learn a deep neural network capable of predicting 3D lane shape and camera pose from a single RGB image. Our approach exploits the intrinsic geometric relationships between lane markings, road surfaces, and camera perspectives, which are often overlooked in traditional methods. Specifically, we design a multi-task loss function that incorporates both lane shape and camera pose predictions, while enforcing geometric constraints such as vanishing points, lane orientation, and camera calibration. Experimental results on the KITTI and Cityscapes datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of lane shape accuracy and camera pose estimation, with a 15% improvement in lane shape error and a 20% reduction in camera pose error compared to the best-performing baseline. Our approach has significant implications for the development of more efficient and accurate computer vision systems, particularly in resource-constrained environments.

title: Sparse LiDAR Assisted Self-supervised Stereo Disparity Estimation
text: Deep stereo matching has made significant progress in recent years. However, state-of-the-art methods are based on expensive 4D cost volume, which limits their use in real-world applications. To address this issue, 3D correlation maps and iterative disparity updates have been proposed. Regarding that in real-world platforms, such as self-driving cars and robots, the Lidar is usually installed. Thus we further introduce the sparse Lidar point into the iterative updates, which alleviates the burden of network updating the disparity from zero states. Furthermore, we propose training the network in a self-supervised way so that it can be trained on any captured data for better generalization ability. Experiments and comparisons show that the presented method is effective and achieves comparable results with related methods.

title: Sparse LiDAR Assisted Self-supervised Stereo Disparity Estimation
text: Estimating accurate stereo disparities from images is a fundamental problem in computer vision, with applications in robotics, autonomous driving, and augmented reality. However, traditional stereo methods rely on dense correspondences, which can be challenging to obtain, especially in scenes with limited texture or repetitive patterns. We propose a novel self-supervised stereo disparity estimation approach that leverages sparse LiDAR points as a regularization cue. Our method, trained on a large dataset of stereo images and sparse LiDAR points, learns to predict accurate disparities by minimizing a photometric loss, a smoothness term, and a LiDAR-based regularization term. Experimental results on the KITTI benchmark demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised stereo methods, achieving a 15% reduction in bad pixel ratio and a 20% increase in accuracy at 3-pixel disparity threshold.
