title: Conditional Generative Data-free Knowledge Distillation
text: Knowledge distillation has made remarkable achievements in model compression. However, most existing methods require the original training data, which is usually unavailable due to privacy and security issues. In this paper, we propose a conditional generative data-free knowledge distillation (CGDD) framework for training lightweight networks without any training data. This method realizes efficient knowledge distillation based on conditional image generation. Specifically, we treat the preset labels as ground truth to train a conditional generator in a semi-supervised manner. The trained generator can produce specified classes of training images. For training the student network, we force it to extract the knowledge hidden in teacher feature maps, which provide crucial cues for the learning process. Moreover, an adversarial training framework for promoting distillation performance is constructed by designing several loss functions. This framework helps the student model to explore larger data space. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we conduct extensive experiments on different datasets. Compared with other data-free works, our work obtains state-of-the-art results on CIFAR100, Caltech101, and different versions of ImageNet datasets. The codes will be released.

title: Conditional Generative Data-free Knowledge Distillation
text: Deep neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art performance in various computer vision tasks, but their large size and computational complexity hinder their deployment on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation, which involves transferring knowledge from a pre-trained teacher network to a smaller student network, has emerged as a promising solution. However, most distillation methods require access to the original training data, which may not always be available due to privacy or storage constraints. To address this limitation, we propose Conditional Generative Data-free Knowledge Distillation (CGD-KD), a novel method that distills knowledge from a teacher network to a student network without requiring the original training data. Our approach leverages a conditional generative model to synthesize samples that mimic the teacher's output, which are then used to train the student network. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that CGD-KD achieves comparable performance to traditional distillation methods that require access to the original data, while reducing the storage and computational requirements. Furthermore, our method is flexible and can be adapted to various computer vision tasks, including image classification, object detection, and segmentation.

title: Modeling Mask Uncertainty in Hyperspectral Image Reconstruction
text: Recently, hyperspectral imaging (HSI) has attracted increasing research attention, especially for the ones based on a coded aperture snapshot spectral imaging (CASSI) system. Existing deep HSI reconstruction models are generally trained on paired data to retrieve original signals upon 2D compressed measurements given by a particular optical hardware mask in CASSI, during which the mask largely impacts the reconstruction performance and could work as a "model hyperparameter" governing on data augmentations. This mask-specific training style will lead to a hardware miscalibration issue, which sets up barriers to deploying deep HSI models among different hardware and noisy environments. To address this challenge, we introduce mask uncertainty for HSI with a complete variational Bayesian learning treatment and explicitly model it through a mask decomposition inspired by real hardware. Specifically, we propose a novel Graph-based Self-Tuning (GST) network to reason uncertainties adapting to varying spatial structures of masks among different hardware. Moreover, we develop a bilevel optimization framework to balance HSI reconstruction and uncertainty estimation, accounting for the hyperparameter property of masks. Extensive experimental results and model discussions validate the effectiveness (over 33/30 dB) of the proposed GST method under two miscalibration scenarios and demonstrate a highly competitive performance compared with the state-of-the-art well-calibrated methods. Our code and pre-trained model are available at

title: Modeling Mask Uncertainty in Hyperspectral Image Reconstruction
text: Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) has garnered significant research interest, particularly in the context of coded aperture snapshot spectral imaging (CASSI) systems. However, existing deep HSI reconstruction models rely on paired data and are typically trained with a specific optical hardware mask, which can significantly impact reconstruction performance and effectively function as a model hyperparameter governing data augmentations. This mask-specific training approach can lead to hardware miscalibration issues, hindering the deployment of deep HSI models across different hardware and noisy environments. To overcome this limitation, we propose a variational Bayesian learning framework that explicitly models mask uncertainty, inspired by real hardware decomposition. Our approach involves a novel Graph-based Self-Tuning (GST) network that adapts to varying spatial structures of masks among different hardware, reasoning uncertainties through a bilevel optimization framework that balances HSI reconstruction and uncertainty estimation, accounting for the hyperparameter property of masks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our GST method, achieving over 33/30 dB performance under two miscalibration scenarios, and show competitive performance compared to well-calibrated state-of-the-art methods.

title: Robust Entropy-regularized Markov Decision Processes
text: Stochastic and soft optimal policies resulting from entropy-regularized Markov decision processes (ER-MDP) are desirable for exploration and imitation learning applications. Motivated by the fact that such policies are sensitive with respect to the state transition probabilities, and the estimation of these probabilities may be inaccurate, we study a robust version of the ER-MDP model, where the stochastic optimal policies are required to be robust with respect to the ambiguity in the underlying transition probabilities. Our work is at the crossroads of two important schemes in reinforcement learning (RL), namely, robust MDP and entropy regularized MDP. We show that essential properties that hold for the non-robust ER-MDP and robust unregularized MDP models also hold in our settings, making the robust ER-MDP problem tractable. We show how our framework and results can be integrated into different algorithmic schemes including value or (modified) policy iteration, which would lead to new robust RL and inverse RL algorithms to handle uncertainties. Analyses on computational complexity and error propagation under conventional uncertainty settings are also provided.

title: Robust Entropy-regularized Markov Decision Processes
text: The pursuit of stochastic and soft optimal policies in entropy-regularized Markov decision processes (ER-MDP) is driven by their potential in exploration and imitation learning. However, the sensitivity of these policies to state transition probabilities, which are often inaccurately estimated, underscores the need for a robust ER-MDP framework. This work converges two significant reinforcement learning (RL) paradigms: robust MDP and entropy-regularized MDP. We demonstrate that crucial properties inherent to non-robust ER-MDP and robust unregularized MDP models are preserved in our robust ER-MDP formulation, rendering the problem tractable. Our framework enables the development of novel robust RL and inverse RL algorithms, capable of handling uncertainties, through integration with value or (modified) policy iteration schemes. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of computational complexity and error propagation under conventional uncertainty settings, elucidating the robustness of our approach.

title: Weakly Supervised Change Detection Using Guided Anisotropic Difusion
text: Large scale datasets created from crowdsourced labels or openly available data have become crucial to provide training data for large scale learning algorithms. While these datasets are easier to acquire, the data are frequently noisy and unreliable, which is motivating research on weakly supervised learning techniques. In this paper we propose original ideas that help us to leverage such datasets in the context of change detection. First, we propose the guided anisotropic diffusion (GAD) algorithm, which improves semantic segmentation results using the input images as guides to perform edge preserving filtering. We then show its potential in two weakly-supervised learning strategies tailored for change detection. The first strategy is an iterative learning method that combines model optimisation and data cleansing using GAD to extract the useful information from a large scale change detection dataset generated from open vector data. The second one incorporates GAD within a novel spatial attention layer that increases the accuracy of weakly supervised networks trained to perform pixel-level predictions from image-level labels. Improvements with respect to state-of-the-art are demonstrated on 4 different public datasets.

title: Weakly Supervised Change Detection Using Guided Anisotropic Difusion
text: The proliferation of large-scale datasets derived from crowdsourced labels or openly available data has fueled the development of large-scale learning algorithms. However, the noisy and unreliable nature of these datasets necessitates the exploration of weakly supervised learning techniques. This paper contributes novel approaches to harnessing such datasets in the context of change detection. We introduce the guided anisotropic diffusion (GAD) algorithm, which enhances semantic segmentation results by leveraging input images as guides for edge-preserving filtering. We then demonstrate the efficacy of GAD in two weakly supervised learning strategies tailored for change detection. The first involves an iterative learning method that integrates model optimization and data cleansing using GAD to extract valuable information from a large-scale change detection dataset generated from open vector data. The second incorporates GAD within a novel spatial attention layer, boosting the accuracy of weakly supervised networks trained on image-level labels for pixel-level predictions. Our approaches yield significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on four public datasets.

title: Processing Images from Multiple IACTs in the TAIGA Experiment with Convolutional Neural Networks
text: Extensive air showers created by high-energy particles interacting with the Earth atmosphere can be detected using imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (IACTs). The IACT images can be analyzed to distinguish between the events caused by gamma rays and by hadrons and to infer the parameters of the event such as the energy of the primary particle. We use convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to analyze Monte Carlo-simulated images from the telescopes of the TAIGA experiment. The analysis includes selection of the images corresponding to the showers caused by gamma rays and estimating the energy of the gamma rays. We compare performance of the CNNs using images from a single telescope and the CNNs using images from two telescopes as inputs.

title: Processing Images from Multiple IACTs in the TAIGA Experiment with Convolutional Neural Networks
text: High-energy particles interacting with the Earth's atmosphere produce extensive air showers, which can be detected using imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (IACTs). The images captured by IACTs can be exploited to differentiate between gamma-ray and hadron-induced events, and to reconstruct the primary particle's energy. In this study, we leverage convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to analyze Monte Carlo-simulated images from the TAIGA experiment's telescopes. Our approach involves gamma-ray event selection and energy estimation. Notably, we investigate the performance of CNNs utilizing single-telescope images versus those incorporating images from two telescopes as inputs, shedding light on the optimal configuration for maximizing detection accuracy.

title: Separation of Scales and a Thermodynamic Description of Feature Learning in Some CNNs
text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are powerful tools for compressing and distilling information. Their scale and complexity, often involving billions of inter-dependent parameters, render direct microscopic analysis difficult. Under such circumstances, a common strategy is to identify slow variables that average the erratic behavior of the fast microscopic variables. Here, we identify a similar separation of scales occurring in fully trained finitely over-parameterized deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and fully connected networks (FCNs). Specifically, we show that DNN layers couple only through the second moment (kernels) of their activations and pre-activations. Moreover, the latter fluctuates in a nearly Gaussian manner. For infinite width DNNs, these kernels are inert, while for finite ones they adapt to the data and yield a tractable data-aware Gaussian Process. The resulting thermodynamic theory of deep learning yields accurate predictions in various settings. In addition, it provides new ways of analyzing and understanding DNNs in general.

title: Separation of Scales and a Thermodynamic Description of Feature Learning in Some CNNs
text: The intricacies of deep neural networks (DNNs) render direct analysis challenging due to their massive scale and intricate parameter dependencies. To circumvent this obstacle, a common approach is to isolate slow variables that encapsulate the averaged behavior of fast microscopic variables. Our research reveals a similar scale separation phenomenon in fully trained, finitely over-parameterized deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and fully connected networks (FCNs). We demonstrate that DNN layers interact solely through the second moment of their activations and pre-activations, which exhibit near-Gaussian fluctuations. In the infinite width limit, these kernels become inert, whereas for finite networks, they adapt to the data, yielding a tractable, data-aware Gaussian Process. The ensuing thermodynamic theory of deep learning affords accurate predictions across various settings and provides novel avenues for analyzing and understanding DNNs.

title: Efficient Single Image Super-Resolution Using Dual Path Connections with Multiple Scale Learning
text: Deep convolutional neural networks have been demonstrated to be effective for SISR in recent years. On the one hand, residual connections and dense connections have been used widely to ease forward information and backward gradient flows to boost performance. However, current methods use residual connections and dense connections separately in most network layers in a sub-optimal way. On the other hand, although various networks and methods have been designed to improve computation efficiency, save parameters, or utilize training data of multiple scale factors for each other to boost performance, it either do super-resolution in HR space to have a high computation cost or can not share parameters between models of different scale factors to save parameters and inference time. To tackle these challenges, we propose an efficient single image super-resolution network using dual path connections with multiple scale learning named as EMSRDPN. By introducing dual path connections inspired by Dual Path Networks into EMSRDPN, it uses residual connections and dense connections in an integrated way in most network layers. Dual path connections have the benefits of both reusing common features of residual connections and exploring new features of dense connections to learn a good representation for SISR. To utilize the feature correlation of multiple scale factors, EMSRDPN shares all network units in LR space between different scale factors to learn shared features and only uses a separate reconstruction unit for each scale factor, which can utilize training data of multiple scale factors to help each other to boost performance, meanwhile which can save parameters and support shared inference for multiple scale factors to improve efficiency. Experiments show EMSRDPN achieves better performance and comparable or even better parameter and inference efficiency over SOTA methods.

title: Efficient Single Image Super-Resolution Using Dual Path Connections with Multiple Scale Learning
text: Single image super-resolution (SISR) has witnessed significant progress in recent years, driven by the proliferation of deep learning techniques. However, existing methods often struggle to balance the trade-off between reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency, particularly when dealing with large images. To address this limitation, we propose a novel SISR framework that leverages dual path connections with multiple scale learning, enabling efficient and accurate image upscaling. Our approach, dubbed DPSR, consists of two parallel branches: a detail-preserving path and a scale-aware path. The former focuses on extracting high-frequency details from the input image, while the latter learns to adapt to different scales and resolutions. The two branches are connected through a series of dual path connections, allowing for efficient feature fusion and reuse. Furthermore, we introduce a multi-scale learning strategy that enables our model to learn from images at varying resolutions, improving its robustness and adaptability. Extensive experimental evaluations on benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of DPSR. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM), outperforming existing methods by a significant margin. Notably, DPSR reduces the computational cost by up to 40% compared to existing deep learning-based methods, making it more suitable for real-world applications. Ablation studies and visual results further validate the effectiveness of our dual path connections and multi-scale learning strategy. Overall, DPSR offers a promising solution for efficient and accurate SISR, with potential applications in various fields, including computer vision, robotics, and graphics.

title: InfoNeRF: Ray Entropy Minimization for Few-Shot Neural Volume Rendering
text: We present an information-theoretic regularization technique for few-shot novel view synthesis based on neural implicit representation. The proposed approach minimizes potential reconstruction inconsistency that happens due to insufficient viewpoints by imposing the entropy constraint of the density in each ray. In addition, to alleviate the potential degenerate issue when all training images are acquired from almost redundant viewpoints, we further incorporate the spatially smoothness constraint into the estimated images by restricting information gains from a pair of rays with slightly different viewpoints. The main idea of our algorithm is to make reconstructed scenes compact along individual rays and consistent across rays in the neighborhood. The proposed regularizers can be plugged into most of existing neural volume rendering techniques based on NeRF in a straightforward way. Despite its simplicity, we achieve consistently improved performance compared to existing neural view synthesis methods by large margins on multiple standard benchmarks.

title: InfoNeRF: Ray Entropy Minimization for Few-Shot Neural Volume Rendering
text: We introduce a novel information-theoretic regularization strategy for few-shot novel view synthesis, leveraging neural implicit representations to mitigate reconstruction inconsistencies arising from limited viewpoints. By imposing an entropy constraint on the density along each ray, our approach reduces inconsistencies in the reconstructed scene. Furthermore, to prevent degeneracy issues that occur when training images are acquired from highly correlated viewpoints, we incorporate a spatial smoothness constraint, restricting information gains between adjacent rays with slightly different viewpoints. This encourages compactness along individual rays and consistency across neighboring rays. Our regularizers seamlessly integrate with existing neural volume rendering techniques based on NeRF, yielding substantial performance improvements over state-of-the-art neural view synthesis methods across multiple benchmarks.

title: A Theoretical Understanding of Gradient Bias in Meta-Reinforcement Learning
text: Gradient-based Meta-RL (GMRL) refers to methods that maintain two-level optimisation procedures wherein the outer-loop meta-learner guides the inner-loop gradient-based reinforcement learner to achieve fast adaptations. In this paper, we develop a unified framework that describes variations of GMRL algorithms and points out that existing stochastic meta-gradient estimators adopted by GMRL are actually \textbf{biased}. Such meta-gradient bias comes from two sources: 1) the compositional bias incurred by the two-level problem structure, which has an upper bound of $\mathcal{O}\big(Kα^{K}\hatσ_{\text{In}}|τ|^{-0.5}\big)$ \emph{w.r.t.} inner-loop update step $K$, learning rate $α$, estimate variance $\hatσ^{2}_{\text{In}}$ and sample size $|τ|$, and 2) the multi-step Hessian estimation bias $\hatΔ_{H}$ due to the use of autodiff, which has a polynomial impact $\mathcal{O}\big((K-1)(\hatΔ_{H})^{K-1}\big)$ on the meta-gradient bias. We study tabular MDPs empirically and offer quantitative evidence that testifies our theoretical findings on existing stochastic meta-gradient estimators. Furthermore, we conduct experiments on Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma and Atari games to show how other methods such as off-policy learning and low-bias estimator can help fix the gradient bias for GMRL algorithms in general.

title: A Theoretical Understanding of Gradient Bias in Meta-Reinforcement Learning
text: Meta-reinforcement learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for adapting to diverse tasks and environments, leveraging shared knowledge across episodes to improve performance. However, recent studies have hinted at a pervasive issue: gradient bias, wherein the meta-objective's optimization process is skewed towards a subset of tasks, compromising overall adaptability. Despite its significance, a comprehensive theoretical understanding of gradient bias in meta-reinforcement learning remains elusive. This work addresses this gap by providing a rigorous analysis of gradient bias, characterizing its manifestations and underlying causes. We develop a novel framework, built upon information-theoretic and game-theoretic tools, to quantify and bound the bias. Our key findings reveal that gradient bias arises from an interplay between task similarity, meta-objective design, and optimization dynamics. Moreover, we demonstrate that bias can be mitigated through carefully crafted regularization schemes and task sampling strategies. Our theoretical insights are supported by empirical evaluations on benchmark meta-reinforcement learning environments, showcasing the potential for significant performance improvements.

title: Relational Experience Replay: Continual Learning by Adaptively Tuning Task-wise Relationship
text: Continual learning is a promising machine learning paradigm to learn new tasks while retaining previously learned knowledge over streaming training data. Till now, rehearsal-based methods, keeping a small part of data from old tasks as a memory buffer, have shown good performance in mitigating catastrophic forgetting for previously learned knowledge. However, most of these methods typically treat each new task equally, which may not adequately consider the relationship or similarity between old and new tasks. Furthermore, these methods commonly neglect sample importance in the continual training process and result in sub-optimal performance on certain tasks. To address this challenging problem, we propose Relational Experience Replay (RER), a bi-level learning framework, to adaptively tune task-wise relationships and sample importance within each task to achieve a better `stability' and `plasticity' trade-off. As such, the proposed method is capable of accumulating new knowledge while consolidating previously learned old knowledge during continual learning. Extensive experiments conducted on three publicly available datasets (i.e., CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet) show that the proposed method can consistently improve the performance of all baselines and surpass current state-of-the-art methods.

title: Relational Experience Replay: Continual Learning by Adaptively Tuning Task-wise Relationship
text: Continual learning, where a model learns from a stream of tasks without forgetting previous knowledge, remains a significant challenge in machine learning. A key obstacle is the inherent imbalance between tasks, causing catastrophic forgetting as the model adapts to new tasks. We propose Relational Experience Replay (RER), a novel approach that tackles this issue by adaptively tuning task-wise relationships in the experience replay buffer. RER dynamically adjusts the sampling probability of each task based on its relative importance, measured by the model's uncertainty and performance on that task. This allows the model to focus on tasks where it is least confident, thereby mitigating forgetting. We evaluate RER on a range of continual learning benchmarks, including permuted MNIST, CIFAR-100, and 20 Newsgroups. Our results show that RER consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 15% improvement in average accuracy across tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that RER is robust to task order and dataset size variations, making it a promising approach for real-world continual learning applications.

title: Virtualization over Multiprocessor System-on-Chip: an Enabling Paradigm for Industrial IoT
text: The next-generation Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) inherently requires smart devices featuring rich connectivity, local intelligence, and autonomous behavior. Emerging Multiprocessor System-on-Chip (MPSoC) platforms along with comprehensive support for virtualization will represent two key building blocks for smart devices in future IIoT edge infrastructures. We review representative existing solutions, highlighting the aspects that are most relevant for integration in IIoT solutions. From the analysis, we derive a reference architecture for a general virtualization-ready edge IIoT node. We then analyze the implications and benefits for a concrete use case scenario and identify the crucial research challenges to be faced to bridge the gap towards full support for virtualization-ready IIoT nodes

title: Virtualization over Multiprocessor System-on-Chip: an Enabling Paradigm for Industrial IoT
text: The proliferation of Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) devices necessitates efficient and scalable system architectures to accommodate diverse workloads. We propose a novel virtualization paradigm over Multiprocessor System-on-Chip (MPSoC) to address this challenge. Our approach exploits the heterogeneous computing capabilities of MPSoC to create multiple virtual machines, each optimized for specific IIoT applications. We develop a custom hypervisor, leveraging the OpenMP framework, to efficiently manage resource allocation and communication between virtual machines. Experimental evaluations on a Xilinx Zynq-7000 SoC demonstrate improved resource utilization, enhanced security, and reduced latency compared to traditional monolithic architectures. Our results underscore the potential of virtualization over MPSoC to revolutionize IIoT system design.

title: Disjoint Contrastive Regression Learning for Multi-Sourced Annotations
text: Large-scale datasets are important for the development of deep learning models. Such datasets usually require a heavy workload of annotations, which are extremely time-consuming and expensive. To accelerate the annotation procedure, multiple annotators may be employed to label different subsets of the data. However, the inconsistency and bias among different annotators are harmful to the model training, especially for qualitative and subjective tasks.To address this challenge, in this paper, we propose a novel contrastive regression framework to address the disjoint annotations problem, where each sample is labeled by only one annotator and multiple annotators work on disjoint subsets of the data. To take account of both the intra-annotator consistency and inter-annotator inconsistency, two strategies are employed.Firstly, a contrastive-based loss is applied to learn the relative ranking among different samples of the same annotator, with the assumption that the ranking of samples from the same annotator is unanimous. Secondly, we apply the gradient reversal layer to learn robust representations that are invariant to different annotators. Experiments on the facial expression prediction task, as well as the image quality assessment task, verify the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

title: Disjoint Contrastive Regression Learning for Multi-Sourced Annotations
text: The proliferation of crowdsourced and multi-sourced annotations has led to a surge in noisy and conflicting labels, hindering the performance of machine learning models. Existing approaches to handle label noise often rely on complex noise modeling or expensive annotation correction procedures. In contrast, we propose Disjoint Contrastive Regression Learning (DCRL), a novel framework that leverages the inherent disparities between multiple annotation sources to improve model robustness. DCRL combines contrastive learning with regression-based modeling to identify and separate noisy labels from accurate ones. Our approach does not require explicit noise modeling or annotation correction, making it computationally efficient and scalable. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of DCRL in improving model performance and robustness, especially in scenarios with high label noise rates. Notably, DCRL outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to 12% in terms of mean absolute error on a real-world dataset with multi-sourced annotations. Our analysis reveals that DCRL effectively captures the underlying patterns and inconsistencies across annotation sources, leading to more reliable and accurate predictions.

title: Representation Learning via Consistent Assignment of Views to Clusters
text: We introduce Consistent Assignment for Representation Learning (CARL), an unsupervised learning method to learn visual representations by combining ideas from self-supervised contrastive learning and deep clustering. By viewing contrastive learning from a clustering perspective, CARL learns unsupervised representations by learning a set of general prototypes that serve as energy anchors to enforce different views of a given image to be assigned to the same prototype. Unlike contemporary work on contrastive learning with deep clustering, CARL proposes to learn the set of general prototypes in an online fashion, using gradient descent without the necessity of using non-differentiable algorithms or K-Means to solve the cluster assignment problem. CARL surpasses its competitors in many representations learning benchmarks, including linear evaluation, semi-supervised learning, and transfer learning.

title: Representation Learning via Consistent Assignment of Views to Clusters
text: The proliferation of multi-view data has created a pressing need for effective representation learning strategies. Existing approaches often rely on ad-hoc view combination methods, neglecting the inherent structural relationships between views. We propose a novel framework, Consistent Assignment of Views to Clusters (CAVC), which learns representations by identifying consistent clusters across views. CAVC employs a probabilistic clustering model to assign views to clusters, encouraging consistent assignments via a novel consistency regularizer. Our approach is theoretically grounded, with provable guarantees on the quality of the learned representations. Empirically, CAVC outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several benchmarks, including multi-view image and text datasets. Moreover, our analysis reveals that CAVC's consistent assignments lead to improved robustness against view corruption and missing data.

title: Robustness and risk management via distributional dynamic programming
text: In dynamic programming (DP) and reinforcement learning (RL), an agent learns to act optimally in terms of expected long-term return by sequentially interacting with its environment modeled by a Markov decision process (MDP). More generally in distributional reinforcement learning (DRL), the focus is on the whole distribution of the return, not just its expectation. Although DRL-based methods produced state-of-the-art performance in RL with function approximation, they involve additional quantities (compared to the non-distributional setting) that are still not well understood. As a first contribution, we introduce a new class of distributional operators, together with a practical DP algorithm for policy evaluation, that come with a robust MDP interpretation. Indeed, our approach reformulates through an augmented state space where each state is split into a worst-case substate and a best-case substate, whose values are maximized by safe and risky policies respectively. Finally, we derive distributional operators and DP algorithms solving a new control task: How to distinguish safe from risky optimal actions in order to break ties in the space of optimal policies?

title: Robustness and risk management via distributional dynamic programming
text: Machine learning models are increasingly being deployed in high-stakes applications, where robustness and risk management are paramount. However, existing methods often rely on simplistic assumptions about the underlying data distributions, which can lead to brittle performance and catastrophic failures. To address this, we propose a novel framework for robustness and risk management via distributional dynamic programming. By modeling the distribution over possible outcomes and explicitly accounting for uncertainty, our approach enables the derivation of robust policies that minimize risk and maximize reward. We develop a theoretical foundation for our method, providing bounds on the suboptimality of the learned policies and characterizing the tradeoffs between robustness and performance. Empirically, we evaluate our approach on a range of benchmarks, including autonomous driving and financial portfolio optimization, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness and risk management compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Our results have important implications for the development of reliable and trustworthy AI systems in high-consequence domains.

title: Adversarial Learning for Incentive Optimization in Mobile Payment Marketing
text: Many payment platforms hold large-scale marketing campaigns, which allocate incentives to encourage users to pay through their applications. To maximize the return on investment, incentive allocations are commonly solved in a two-stage procedure. After training a response estimation model to estimate the users' mobile payment probabilities (MPP), a linear programming process is applied to obtain the optimal incentive allocation. However, the large amount of biased data in the training set, generated by the previous biased allocation policy, causes a biased estimation. This bias deteriorates the performance of the response model and misleads the linear programming process, dramatically degrading the performance of the resulting allocation policy. To overcome this obstacle, we propose a bias correction adversarial network. Our method leverages the small set of unbiased data obtained under a full-randomized allocation policy to train an unbiased model and then uses it to reduce the bias with adversarial learning. Offline and online experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches and significantly improves the performance of the resulting allocation policy in a real-world marketing campaign.

title: Adversarial Learning for Incentive Optimization in Mobile Payment Marketing
text: The optimal allocation of incentives in large-scale marketing campaigns is crucial for payment platforms to maximize their return on investment. A prevalent approach to solving this problem involves a two-stage procedure, where a response estimation model is first trained to predict users' mobile payment probabilities, and then a linear programming process is applied to determine the optimal incentive allocation. However, this approach is often hindered by the presence of biased data in the training set, which is typically generated by previous biased allocation policies. This bias can significantly deteriorate the performance of the response model and subsequently mislead the linear programming process, resulting in suboptimal allocation policies. We propose a bias correction adversarial network to address this issue. By leveraging a small set of unbiased data obtained under a full-randomized allocation policy, our method trains an unbiased model and reduces bias through adversarial learning. Both offline and online experiments demonstrate the superiority of our approach, which significantly improves the performance of the resulting allocation policy in a real-world marketing campaign.

title: Facial-Sketch Synthesis: A New Challenge
text: This paper aims to conduct a comprehensive study on facial-sketch synthesis (FSS). However, due to the high costs of obtaining hand-drawn sketch datasets, there lacks a complete benchmark for assessing the development of FSS algorithms over the last decade. We first introduce a high-quality dataset for FSS, named FS2K, which consists of 2,104 image-sketch pairs spanning three types of sketch styles, image backgrounds, lighting conditions, skin colors, and facial attributes. FS2K differs from previous FSS datasets in difficulty, diversity, and scalability and should thus facilitate the progress of FSS research. Second, we present the largest-scale FSS investigation by reviewing 89 classical methods, including 25 handcrafted feature-based facial-sketch synthesis approaches, 29 general translation methods, and 35 image-to-sketch approaches. Besides, we elaborate comprehensive experiments on the existing 19 cutting-edge models. Third, we present a simple baseline for FSS, named FSGAN. With only two straightforward components, i.e., facial-aware masking and style-vector expansion, FSGAN surpasses the performance of all previous state-of-the-art models on the proposed FS2K dataset by a large margin. Finally, we conclude with lessons learned over the past years and point out several unsolved challenges. Our code is available at

title: Facial-Sketch Synthesis: A New Challenge
text: Facial-sketch synthesis (FSS) has garnered significant attention in recent years, yet the lack of a comprehensive benchmark has hindered the assessment of algorithmic developments. To address this limitation, we introduce FS2K, a high-quality dataset comprising 2,104 image-sketch pairs that exhibit diverse sketch styles, image backgrounds, lighting conditions, skin colors, and facial attributes. Notably, FS2K surpasses existing FSS datasets in terms of difficulty, diversity, and scalability, thereby providing a robust platform for evaluating FSS algorithms. We conduct an exhaustive review of 89 classical methods, including handcrafted feature-based, general translation, and image-to-sketch approaches, as well as 19 state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, we propose a simple yet effective baseline, FSGAN, which leverages facial-aware masking and style-vector expansion to achieve superior performance on the FS2K dataset, outperforming existing models by a significant margin. Our study provides valuable insights into the lessons learned and unresolved challenges in FSS research, paving the way for future advancements in this field.

title: Mythological Medical Machine Learning: Boosting the Performance of a Deep Learning Medical Data Classifier Using Realistic Physiological Models
text: Objective: To determine if a realistic, but computationally efficient model of the electrocardiogram can be used to pre-train a deep neural network (DNN) with a wide range of morphologies and abnormalities specific to a given condition - T-wave Alternans (TWA) as a result of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, or PTSD - and significantly boost performance on a small database of rare individuals. Approach: Using a previously validated artificial ECG model, we generated 180,000 artificial ECGs with or without significant TWA, with varying heart rate, breathing rate, TWA amplitude, and ECG morphology. A DNN, trained on over 70,000 patients to classify 25 different rhythms, was modified the output layer to a binary class (TWA or no-TWA, or equivalently, PTSD or no-PTSD), and transfer learning was performed on the artificial ECG. In a final transfer learning step, the DNN was trained and cross-validated on ECG from 12 PTSD and 24 controls for all combinations of using the three databases. Main results: The best performing approach (AUROC = 0.77, Accuracy = 0.72, F1-score = 0.64) was found by performing both transfer learning steps, using the pre-trained arrhythmia DNN, the artificial data and the real PTSD-related ECG data. Removing the artificial data from training led to the largest drop in performance. Removing the arrhythmia data from training provided a modest, but significant, drop in performance. The final model showed no significant drop in performance on the artificial data, indicating no overfitting. Significance: In healthcare, it is common to only have a small collection of high-quality data and labels, or a larger database with much lower quality (and less relevant) labels. The paradigm presented here, involving model-based performance boosting, provides a solution through transfer learning on a large realistic artificial database, and a partially relevant real database.

title: Mythological Medical Machine Learning: Boosting the Performance of a Deep Learning Medical Data Classifier Using Realistic Physiological Models
text: This study explores the feasibility of leveraging a computationally efficient and realistic electrocardiogram (ECG) model to pre-train a deep neural network (DNN) for the detection of T-wave Alternans (TWA), a hallmark of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). We generated a large database of 180,000 artificial ECGs, encompassing a wide range of morphologies and abnormalities, and used these data to fine-tune a DNN previously trained on over 70,000 patients to classify 25 different cardiac rhythms. The output layer was adapted to dichotomously classify ECGs as exhibiting TWA or not. Transfer learning was performed on this artificial ECG database, followed by a second transfer learning step on a small dataset of 12 PTSD patients and 24 controls. Our results demonstrate that the best-performing approach (AUROC = 0.77, Accuracy = 0.72, F1-score = 0.64) involves performing both transfer learning steps, utilizing the pre-trained arrhythmia DNN, artificial data, and real PTSD-related ECG data. Notably, the exclusion of artificial data from training resulted in the largest decline in performance, while the removal of arrhythmia data led to a modest yet significant decrease. The final model exhibited no significant performance degradation on artificial data, indicating the absence of overfitting. This paradigm has significant implications for healthcare, where high-quality data and labels are often scarce, and larger databases may contain lower-quality or less relevant labels. By harnessing transfer learning on a large, realistic artificial database and a partially relevant real database, our approach offers a promising solution to boost model performance in such scenarios.

title: GANISP: a GAN-assisted Importance SPlitting Probability Estimator
text: Designing manufacturing processes with high yield and strong reliability relies on effective methods for rare event estimation. Genealogical importance splitting reduces the variance of rare event probability estimators by iteratively selecting and replicating realizations that are headed towards a rare event. The replication step is difficult when applied to deterministic systems where the initial conditions of the offspring realizations need to be modified. Typically, a random perturbation is applied to the offspring to differentiate their trajectory from the parent realization. However, this random perturbation strategy may be effective for some systems while failing for others, preventing variance reduction in the probability estimate. This work seeks to address this limitation using a generative model such as a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to generate perturbations that are consistent with the attractor of the dynamical system. The proposed GAN-assisted Importance SPlitting method (GANISP) improves the variance reduction for the system targeted. An implementation of the method is available in a companion repository (

title: GANISP: a GAN-assisted Importance SPlitting Probability Estimator
text: Estimating rare events in manufacturing processes is crucial for ensuring high yield and reliability, but existing methods often struggle to accurately quantify these events. Genealogical importance splitting offers a promising approach, as it reduces the variance of rare event probability estimators by iteratively selecting and replicating realizations that are likely to culminate in a rare event. However, a key challenge arises in deterministic systems, where the initial conditions of the replicated realizations must be modified to differentiate their trajectories from the parent realization. Traditional random perturbation strategies often prove ineffective, leading to inconsistent variance reduction in probability estimates. This study addresses this limitation by utilizing a generative model, specifically a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), to generate perturbations that are consistent with the attractor of the dynamical system. The resulting GAN-assisted Importance Splitting method (GANISP) demonstrates improved variance reduction for the targeted system.

title: Speedup deep learning models on GPU by taking advantage of efficient unstructured pruning and bit-width reduction
text: This work is focused on the pruning of some convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and improving theirs efficiency on graphic processing units (GPU) by using a direct sparse algorithm. The Nvidia deep neural network (cuDnn) library is the most effective implementations of deep learning (DL) algorithms for GPUs. GPUs are the most commonly used accelerators for deep learning computations. One of the most common techniques for improving the efficiency of CNN models is weight pruning and quantization. There are two main types of pruning: structural and non-structural. The first enables much easier acceleration on many type of accelerators, but with this type it is difficult to achieve a sparsity level and accuracy as high as that obtained with the second type. Non-structural pruning with retraining can generate a weight tensors up to 90% or more of sparsity in some deep CNN models. In this article the pruning algorithm is presented which makes it possible to achieve high sparsity levels without accuracy drop. In the next stage the linear and non-linear quantization is adapted for further time and footprint reduction. This paper is an extended of previously published paper concerning effective pruning techniques and present real models pruned with high sparsities and reduced precision which can achieve better performance than the CuDnn library.

title: Speedup deep learning models on GPU by taking advantage of efficient unstructured pruning and bit-width reduction
text: Deep neural networks have become ubiquitous in various applications, but their computational intensity and memory requirements hinder their deployment on resource-constrained devices. While Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) have emerged as a promising platform for accelerating deep learning workloads, the memory bandwidth and compute resources of even the most advanced GPUs are often overwhelmed by the sheer size of modern neural networks. To alleviate this bottleneck, we propose a novel approach that combines efficient unstructured pruning and bit-width reduction to significantly reduce the memory footprint and computation required for deep learning inference on GPUs. Our method leverages a novel importance scoring function to identify and prune redundant connections in the network, followed by a bit-width reduction scheme that minimizes the precision of the remaining weights while maintaining accuracy. We evaluate our approach on a range of benchmark datasets and neural architectures, demonstrating speedups of up to 4.2x and 2.5x on NVIDIA V100 and A100 GPUs, respectively, while incurring minimal accuracy losses. Moreover, our method achieves superior compression ratios and speedups compared to existing state-of-the-art pruning and quantization techniques. Our work has significant implications for deploying deep learning models on resource-constrained devices, enabling real-time inference and paving the way for widespread adoption in Edge AI applications.

title: Uniform-in-Phase-Space Data Selection with Iterative Normalizing Flows
text: Improvements in computational and experimental capabilities are rapidly increasing the amount of scientific data that is routinely generated. In applications that are constrained by memory and computational intensity, excessively large datasets may hinder scientific discovery, making data reduction a critical component of data-driven methods. Datasets are growing in two directions: the number of data points and their dimensionality. Whereas dimension reduction typically aims at describing each data sample on lower-dimensional space, the focus here is on reducing the number of data points. A strategy is proposed to select data points such that they uniformly span the phase-space of the data. The algorithm proposed relies on estimating the probability map of the data and using it to construct an acceptance probability. An iterative method is used to accurately estimate the probability of the rare data points when only a small subset of the dataset is used to construct the probability map. Instead of binning the phase-space to estimate the probability map, its functional form is approximated with a normalizing flow. Therefore, the method naturally extends to high-dimensional datasets. The proposed framework is demonstrated as a viable pathway to enable data-efficient machine learning when abundant data is available. title: Uniform-in-Phase-Space Data Selection with Iterative Normalizing Flows
text: When training machine learning models, it is often crucial to select a representative subset of data that accurately captures the underlying distribution. However, existing data selection methods frequently rely on heuristics or ad-hoc techniques, leading to suboptimal performance and a lack of interpretability. We propose a novel approach, Uniform-in-Phase-Space Data Selection with Iterative Normalizing Flows (UPI-DS), which leverages the expressive power of normalizing flows to model the underlying data distribution. By iteratively refining the flow-based model, UPI-DS identifies a diverse and representative subset of data points that uniformly cover the phase space. We theoretically show that UPI-DS converges to the optimal data selection solution under mild assumptions. Empirically, we evaluate UPI-DS on a range of datasets and demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in terms of model performance, robustness, and computational efficiency. Notably, UPI-DS achieves a 15% increase in accuracy on average, while reducing the required number of data points by 30%. We also provide visualizations of the learned phase space, offering insights into the selection process and facilitating interpretability. Our approach has far-reaching implications for efficient and effective machine learning, particularly in applications where data is scarce or expensive to obtain.

title: Advanced Drone Swarm Security by Using Blockchain Governance Game
text: This research contributes to the security design of an advanced smart drone swarm network based on a variant of the Blockchain Governance Game (BGG), which is the theoretical game model to predict the moments of security actions before attacks, and the Strategic Alliance for Blockchain Governance Game (SABGG), which is one of the BGG variants which has been adapted to construct the best strategies to take preliminary actions based on strategic alliance for protecting smart drones in a blockchain-based swarm network. Smart drones are artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled drones which are capable of being operated autonomously without having any command center. Analytically tractable solutions from the SABGG allow us to estimate the moments of taking preliminary actions by delivering the optimal accountability of drones for preventing attacks. This advanced secured swarm network within AI-enabled drones is designed by adapting the SABGG model. This research helps users to develop a new network-architecture-level security of a smart drone swarm which is based on a decentralized network.

title: Advanced Drone Swarm Security by Using Blockchain Governance Game
text: We propose a novel security framework for an advanced smart drone swarm network, grounded in a variant of the Blockchain Governance Game (BGG) and its extension, the Strategic Alliance for Blockchain Governance Game (SABGG). The SABGG model enables the construction of optimal strategies for proactive security measures, leveraging strategic alliances to safeguard AI-enabled drones in a blockchain-based swarm network. These autonomous drones, capable of operating independently without a central command center, can be protected via analytically tractable solutions derived from the SABGG, which provide optimal accountability and facilitate timely preliminary actions against potential attacks. By adapting the SABGG model, we design a decentralized network architecture that ensures a robust security framework for smart drone swarms. This research contributes to the development of a novel network-architecture-level security paradigm, enhancing the overall security posture of AI-enabled drone swarms in decentralized networks.

title: Accurate and Real-time 3D Pedestrian Detection Using an Efficient Attentive Pillar Network
text: Efficiently and accurately detecting people from 3D point cloud data is of great importance in many robotic and autonomous driving applications. This fundamental perception task is still very challenging due to (i) significant deformations of human body pose and gesture over time and (ii) point cloud sparsity and scarcity for pedestrian class objects. Recent efficient 3D object detection approaches rely on pillar features to detect objects from point cloud data. However, these pillar features do not carry sufficient expressive representations to deal with all the aforementioned challenges in detecting people. To address this shortcoming, we first introduce a stackable Pillar Aware Attention (PAA) module for enhanced pillar features extraction while suppressing noises in the point clouds. By integrating multi-point-channel-pooling, point-wise, channel-wise, and task-aware attention into a simple module, the representation capabilities are boosted while requiring little additional computing resources. We also present Mini-BiFPN, a small yet effective feature network that creates bidirectional information flow and multi-level cross-scale feature fusion to better integrate multi-resolution features. Our proposed framework, namely PiFeNet, has been evaluated on three popular large-scale datasets for 3D pedestrian Detection, i.e. KITTI, JRDB, and nuScenes achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on KITTI Bird-eye-view (BEV) and JRDB and very competitive performance on nuScenes. Our approach has inference speed of 26 frame-per-second (FPS), making it a real-time detector. The code for our PiFeNet is available at

title: Accurate and Real-time 3D Pedestrian Detection Using an Efficient Attentive Pillar Network
text: Pedestrian detection in 3D point clouds is a crucial task in various applications, including autonomous driving, robotics, and surveillance. Despite significant progress in recent years, existing methods often struggle to achieve high accuracy in real-time, particularly in scenarios with dense pedestrian clusters and varying lighting conditions. To address these challenges, we propose an efficient attentive pillar network (EAPN) that leverages a novel attention mechanism to selectively focus on relevant regions in the point cloud, reducing computational overhead while improving detection accuracy. Our approach first converts the point cloud into a pillar representation, which is then fed into a backbone network to extract features. The attentive module, comprising a self-attention mechanism and a sparse attention mechanism, adaptively adjusts the feature weights to highlight pedestrian-related regions. Finally, a detection head predicts 3D bounding boxes and confidence scores. Extensive experiments on the KITTI and nuScenes datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of EAPN, achieving state-of-the-art performance with an average precision of 94.1% and 92.5%, respectively, while maintaining a real-time inference speed of 30 frames per second on a single GPU. Additionally, our ablation study reveals the significant contributions of the attentive module to the overall performance, showcasing the importance of adaptive feature weighting in 3D pedestrian detection.

title: Polynomial-Time Key Recovery Attack on the Lau-Tan Cryptosystem Based on Gabidulin Codes
text: This paper presents a key recovery attack on the cryptosystem proposed by Lau and Tan in a talk at ACISP 2018. The Lau-Tan cryptosystem uses Gabidulin codes as the underlying decodable code. To hide the algebraic structure of Gabidulin codes, the authors chose a matrix of column rank $n$ to mix with a generator matrix of the secret Gabidulin code. The other part of the public key, however, reveals crucial information about the private key. Our analysis shows that the problem of recovering the private key can be reduced to solving a multivariate linear system over the base field, rather than solving a multivariate quadratic system as claimed by the authors. Solving the linear system for any nonzero solution permits us to recover the private key. Apparently, this attack costs polynomial time, and therefore completely breaks the cryptosystem.

title: Polynomial-Time Key Recovery Attack on the Lau-Tan Cryptosystem Based on Gabidulin Codes
text: We demonstrate a polynomial-time key recovery attack on the Lau-Tan cryptosystem, which leverages Gabidulin codes as its underlying decodable code. The authors' attempt to obscure the algebraic structure of Gabidulin codes involves mixing a generator matrix of the secret code with a matrix of column rank $n$. However, our investigation reveals that the remaining public key component inadvertently discloses critical information about the private key. By reducing the key recovery problem to a multivariate linear system over the base field, rather than the purported multivariate quadratic system, we can efficiently recover the private key by solving for any nonzero solution. This attack has profound implications, as it fundamentally compromises the security of the Lau-Tan cryptosystem.

title: Shift-Equivariant Similarity-Preserving Hypervector Representations of Sequences
text: Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC), also known as Vector-Symbolic Architectures (VSA), is a promising framework for the development of cognitive architectures and artificial intelligence systems, as well as for technical applications and emerging neuromorphic and nanoscale hardware. HDC/VSA operate with hypervectors, i.e., distributed vector representations of large fixed dimension (usually > 1000). One of the key ingredients of HDC/VSA are the methods for encoding data of various types (from numeric scalars and vectors to graphs) into hypervectors. In this paper, we propose an approach for the formation of hypervectors of sequences that provides both an equivariance with respect to the shift of sequences and preserves the similarity of sequences with identical elements at nearby positions. Our methods represent the sequence elements by compositional hypervectors and exploit permutations of hypervectors for representing the order of sequence elements. We experimentally explored the proposed representations using a diverse set of tasks with data in the form of symbolic strings. Although our approach is feature-free as it forms the hypervector of a sequence from the hypervectors of its symbols at their positions, it demonstrated the performance on a par with the methods that apply various features, such as subsequences. The proposed techniques were designed for the HDC/VSA model known as Sparse Binary Distributed Representations. However, they can be adapted to hypervectors in formats of other HDC/VSA models, as well as for representing sequences of types other than symbolic strings.

title: Shift-Equivariant Similarity-Preserving Hypervector Representations of Sequences
text: Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC), also referred to as Vector-Symbolic Architectures (VSA), has emerged as a versatile framework for developing cognitive architectures, artificial intelligence systems, and technical applications, particularly in the realm of neuromorphic and nanoscale hardware. A crucial aspect of HDC/VSA lies in the encoding of diverse data types, including numeric scalars, vectors, and graphs, into high-dimensional vectors (hypervectors) typically exceeding 1000 dimensions. This paper presents a novel approach for generating hypervectors of sequences, which simultaneously exhibits equivariance under sequence shifts and preserves the similarity of sequences with identical elements at adjacent positions. Our method leverages compositional hypervectors to represent sequence elements and exploits hypervector permutations to encode the order of sequence elements. Experimental evaluations, performed on a diverse range of tasks involving symbolic string data, demonstrate that our feature-free approach, which forms hypervectors from constituent symbol hypervectors, achieves performance comparable to methods incorporating features such as subsequences. Although designed for Sparse Binary Distributed Representations, a prominent HDC/VSA model, our techniques can be adapted for hypervectors in other HDC/VSA formats, as well as for representing sequences of non-symbolic string types.

title: BTS: An Accelerator for Bootstrappable Fully Homomorphic Encryption
text: Homomorphic encryption (HE) enables the secure offloading of computations to the cloud by providing computation on encrypted data (ciphertexts). HE is based on noisy encryption schemes in which noise accumulates as more computations are applied to the data. The limited number of operations applicable to the data prevents practical applications from exploiting HE. Bootstrapping enables an unlimited number of operations or fully HE (FHE) by refreshing the ciphertext. Unfortunately, bootstrapping requires a significant amount of additional computation and memory bandwidth as well. Prior works have proposed hardware accelerators for computation primitives of FHE. However, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first to propose a hardware FHE accelerator that supports bootstrapping as a first-class citizen. In particular, we propose BTS - Bootstrappable, Technologydriven, Secure accelerator architecture for FHE. We identify the challenges of supporting bootstrapping in the accelerator and analyze the off-chip memory bandwidth and computation required. In particular, given the limitations of modern memory technology, we identify the HE parameter sets that are efficient for FHE acceleration. Based on the insights gained from our analysis, we propose BTS, which effectively exploits the parallelism innate in HE operations by arranging a massive number of processing elements in a grid. We present the design and microarchitecture of BTS, including a network-on-chip design that exploits a deterministic communication pattern. BTS shows 5,556x and 1,306x improved execution time on ResNet-20 and logistic regression over a CPU, with a chip area of 373.6mm^2 and up to 163.2W of power.

title: BTS: An Accelerator for Bootstrappable Fully Homomorphic Encryption
text: The advent of homomorphic encryption (HE) has enabled secure outsourcing of computations to the cloud, allowing operations to be performed directly on encrypted data. However, the inherent noise accumulation in HE schemes limits the number of applicable operations, hindering its practical adoption. To overcome this constraint, bootstrapping techniques have been developed to enable an unlimited number of operations, effectively realizing fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). Nevertheless, bootstrapping incurs significant computational and memory bandwidth overhead. Recent studies have explored hardware accelerators for FHE computation primitives, but none have specifically addressed the integration of bootstrapping as a primary concern. This paper proposes BTS, a novel Bootstrappable, Technology-driven, Secure accelerator architecture designed to support FHE with built-in bootstrapping capabilities. We identify and analyze the key challenges associated with bootstrapping in hardware accelerators, including off-chip memory bandwidth and computational requirements. Our analysis reveals the optimal HE parameter sets for efficient FHE acceleration, given modern memory technology limitations. The BTS architecture is designed to leverage the inherent parallelism in HE operations, featuring a grid-based arrangement of numerous processing elements and a deterministic network-on-chip design. Our results demonstrate significant performance improvements, with a 5,556x and 1,306x speedup in execution time for ResNet-20 and logistic regression, respectively, compared to CPU-based implementations, while occupying a chip area of 373.6mm^2 and consuming up to 163.2W of power.

title: REST API Fuzzing by Coverage Level Guided Blackbox Testing
text: With the growth of web applications, REST APIs have become the primary communication method between services. In order to ensure system reliability and security, software quality can be assured by effective testing methods. Black box fuzz testing is one of the effective methods to perform tests on a large scale. However, conventional black box fuzz testing generates random data without judging the quality of the input. We implement a black box fuzz testing method for REST APIs. It resolves the issues of blind mutations without knowing the effectiveness by Test Coverage Level feedback. We also enhance the mutation strategies by reducing the testing complexity for REST APIs, generating more appropriate test cases to cover possible paths. We evaluate our method by testing two large open-source projects and 89 bugs are reported and confirmed. In addition, we find 351 bugs from 64 remote API services in APIs.guru. The work is in

title: REST API Fuzzing by Coverage Level Guided Blackbox Testing
text: The widespread adoption of RESTful APIs has led to a surge in vulnerabilities, making automated testing a crucial aspect of API security. Existing blackbox fuzzing techniques often rely on simplistic input mutation strategies, neglecting the complexities of modern APIs. We propose a novel approach, Coverage Level Guided Blackbox Testing (CLGBT), which leverages code coverage analysis to guide the fuzzing process. CLGBT prioritizes inputs based on their potential to increase code coverage, targeting uncovered regions of the API implementation. Our approach integrates with popular fuzzing frameworks, enabling seamless adoption. Experimental evaluations on a diverse set of real-world APIs demonstrate that CLGBT significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in terms of code coverage, fault detection, and vulnerability discovery. Notably, CLGBT identified 35 previously unknown vulnerabilities in popular open-source APIs. Our results underscore the importance of incorporating code coverage analysis into blackbox fuzzing, paving the way for more effective and efficient API security testing.

title: Semantics-Recovering Decompilation through Neural Machine Translation
text: Decompilation transforms low-level program languages (PL) (e.g., binary code) into high-level PLs (e.g., C/C++). It has been widely used when analysts perform security analysis on software (systems) whose source code is unavailable, such as vulnerability search and malware analysis. However, current decompilation tools usually need lots of experts' efforts, even for years, to generate the rules for decompilation, which also requires long-term maintenance as the syntax of high-level PL or low-level PL changes. Also, an ideal decompiler should concisely generate high-level PL with similar functionality to the source low-level PL and semantic information (e.g., meaningful variable names), just like human-written code. Unfortunately, existing manually-defined rule-based decompilation techniques only functionally restore the low-level PL to a similar high-level PL and are still powerless to recover semantic information. In this paper, we propose a novel neural decompilation approach to translate low-level PL into accurate and user-friendly high-level PL, effectively improving its readability and understandability. Furthermore, we implement the proposed approaches called SEAM. Evaluations on four real-world applications show that SEAM has an average accuracy of 94.41%, which is much better than prior neural machine translation (NMT) models. Finally, we evaluate the effectiveness of semantic information recovery through a questionnaire survey, and the average accuracy is 92.64%, which is comparable or superior to the state-of-the-art compilers.

title: Semantics-Recovering Decompilation through Neural Machine Translation
text: The decompilation process involves translating low-level program languages, such as binary code, into high-level languages like C/C++. This technique is crucial for security analysis of software systems with unavailable source code, including vulnerability detection and malware analysis. However, existing decompilation tools rely heavily on manual effort, requiring years of expert input to develop and maintain decompilation rules, which are sensitive to changes in high-level and low-level language syntax. Ideal decompilation should not only preserve the original functionality but also recover semantic information, such as meaningful variable names, to produce high-level code akin to human-written code. Current rule-based decompilation techniques fall short, merely restoring functional equivalence without recovering semantic information. This paper proposes a novel neural decompilation approach, implemented in the SEAM system, which translates low-level languages into accurate and readable high-level languages. Our evaluation on four real-world applications demonstrates an average accuracy of 94.41%, outperforming prior neural machine translation models. Furthermore, a questionnaire survey assessing the recovery of semantic information yields an average accuracy of 92.64%, comparable to or surpassing state-of-the-art compilers.

title: State Selection Algorithms and Their Impact on The Performance of Stateful Network Protocol Fuzzing
text: The statefulness property of network protocol implementations poses a unique challenge for testing and verification techniques, including Fuzzing. Stateful fuzzers tackle this challenge by leveraging state models to partition the state space and assist the test generation process. Since not all states are equally important and fuzzing campaigns have time limits, fuzzers need effective state selection algorithms to prioritize progressive states over others. Several state selection algorithms have been proposed but they were implemented and evaluated separately on different platforms, making it hard to achieve conclusive findings. In this work, we evaluate an extensive set of state selection algorithms on the same fuzzing platform that is AFLNet, a state-of-the-art fuzzer for network servers. The algorithm set includes existing ones supported by AFLNet and our novel and principled algorithm called AFLNetLegion. The experimental results on the ProFuzzBench benchmark show that (i) the existing state selection algorithms of AFLNet achieve very similar code coverage, (ii) AFLNetLegion clearly outperforms these algorithms in selected case studies, but (iii) the overall improvement appears insignificant. These are unexpected yet interesting findings. We identify problems and share insights that could open opportunities for future research on this topic.

title: State Selection Algorithms and Their Impact on The Performance of Stateful Network Protocol Fuzzing
text: The statefulness of network protocol implementations presents a significant hurdle for testing and verification methodologies, including fuzzing. To overcome this challenge, stateful fuzzers employ state models to partition the state space and inform the test generation process. Given the time constraints of fuzzing campaigns and the varying importance of states, the development of effective state selection algorithms is crucial for prioritizing progressive states. Despite the proposal of several state selection algorithms, their implementation and evaluation on disparate platforms have hindered the attainment of conclusive results. This study provides a comprehensive evaluation of a range of state selection algorithms, including novel and principled approaches, on the AFLNet platform, a state-of-the-art fuzzer for network servers. Experimental results on the ProFuzzBench benchmark reveal that existing AFLNet algorithms achieve comparable code coverage, while our AFLNetLegion algorithm demonstrates superior performance in select case studies, albeit with limited overall improvement. These findings, though unexpected, offer valuable insights and identify areas for future research.

title: Scene-Adaptive Attention Network for Crowd Counting
text: In recent years, significant progress has been made on the research of crowd counting. However, as the challenging scale variations and complex scenes existed in crowds, neither traditional convolution networks nor recent Transformer architectures with fixed-size attention could handle the task well. To address this problem, this paper proposes a scene-adaptive attention network, termed SAANet. First of all, we design a deformable attention in-built Transformer backbone, which learns adaptive feature representations with deformable sampling locations and dynamic attention weights. Then we propose the multi-level feature fusion and count-attentive feature enhancement modules further, to strengthen feature representation under the global image context. The learned representations could attend to the foreground and are adaptive to different scales of crowds. We conduct extensive experiments on four challenging crowd counting benchmarks, demonstrating that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance. Especially, our method currently ranks No.1 on the public leaderboard of the NWPU-Crowd benchmark. We hope our method could be a strong baseline to support future research in crowd counting. The source code will be released to the community.

title: Scene-Adaptive Attention Network for Crowd Counting
text: Crowd counting remains a formidable challenge in computer vision, despite significant advances in recent years. The inherent scale variations and complex scenes in crowds have proven difficult to tackle using traditional convolutional networks and fixed-size attention-based Transformer architectures. To overcome these limitations, we introduce SAANet, a scene-adaptive attention network that leverages deformable attention and dynamic feature representations. Our approach incorporates a deformable attention mechanism within a Transformer backbone, enabling adaptive feature learning with sampling locations and attention weights that adjust to the scene context. Furthermore, we propose multi-level feature fusion and count-attentive feature enhancement modules to strengthen feature representation under global image context. Experimental results on four challenging benchmarks demonstrate the efficacy of SAANet, achieving state-of-the-art performance and currently ranking first on the NWPU-Crowd benchmark leaderboard. We plan to release the source code, providing a strong baseline for future research in crowd counting.

title: Transfer learning of phase transitions in percolation and directed percolation
text: The latest advances of statistical physics have shown remarkable performance of machine learning in identifying phase transitions. In this paper, we apply domain adversarial neural network (DANN) based on transfer learning to studying non-equilibrium and equilibrium phase transition models, which are percolation model and directed percolation (DP) model, respectively. With the DANN, only a small fraction of input configurations (2d images) needs to be labeled, which is automatically chosen, in order to capture the critical point. To learn the DP model, the method is refined by an iterative procedure in determining the critical point, which is a prerequisite for the data collapse in calculating the critical exponent $ν_{\perp}$. We then apply the DANN to a two-dimensional site percolation with configurations filtered to include only the largest cluster which may contain the information related to the order parameter. The DANN learning of both models yields reliable results which are comparable to the ones from Monte Carlo simulations. Our study also shows that the DANN can achieve quite high accuracy at much lower cost, compared to the supervised learning.

title: Transfer learning of phase transitions in percolation and directed percolation
text: Percolation and directed percolation are fundamental models in statistical physics, exhibiting rich phase transition behavior that has far-reaching implications for network science and critical phenomena. Despite their importance, the computational complexity of simulating these systems hinders large-scale analysis and limits our understanding of their behavior. Recent advances in deep learning have demonstrated the potential for neural networks to approximate complex physical systems, but it remains unclear whether these models can capture the intricate phase transitions of percolation and directed percolation. We investigate the transfer learning of phase transitions in these systems, leveraging large-scale simulations to train convolutional neural networks on percolation and directed percolation configurations.
