Our results show that these networks can accurately predict the phase transition point and critical exponents, achieving state-of-the-art performance on benchmark systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate transferability of the learned representations across different lattice sizes, boundary conditions, and even to related models, such as the Ising model. Our findings open up new avenues for the application of deep learning to the study of critical phenomena, enabling rapid and accurate analysis of complex systems.

title: Inferring perceptual decision making parameters from behavior in production and reproduction tasks
text: Bayesian models of behavior have provided computational level explanations in a range of psychophysical tasks. One fundamental experimental paradigm is the production or reproduction task, in which subjects are instructed to generate an action that either reproduces a previously sensed stimulus magnitude or achieves a target response. This type of task therefore distinguishes itself from other psychophysical tasks in that the responses are on a continuum and effort plays an important role with increasing response magnitude. Based on Bayesian decision theory we present an inference method to recover perceptual uncertainty, response variability, and the cost function underlying human responses. Crucially, the cost function is parameterized such that effort is explicitly included. We present a hybrid inference method employing MCMC sampling utilizing appropriate proposal distributions and an inner loop utilizing amortized inference with a neural network that approximates the mode of the optimal response distribution. We show how this model can be utilized to avoid unidentifiability of experimental designs and that parameters can be recovered through validation on synthetic and application to experimental data. Our approach will enable behavioral scientists to perform Bayesian inference of decision making parameters in production and reproduction tasks.

title: Inferring perceptual decision making parameters from behavior in production and reproduction tasks
text: The development of Bayesian models has facilitated the provision of computational level explanations for a diverse range of psychophysical tasks. Among these, the production or reproduction task stands out due to its distinctive characteristics, wherein subjects are required to generate an action that either reproduces a previously sensed stimulus magnitude or achieves a target response. This paradigm is uniquely defined by its continuous response range and the critical role of effort in modulating response magnitude. By leveraging Bayesian decision theory, we introduce an inference methodology capable of recovering perceptual uncertainty, response variability, and the underlying cost function governing human responses, with effort explicitly parameterized within the cost function. Our hybrid inference approach combines Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling with amortized inference, employing a neural network to approximate the mode of the optimal response distribution. We demonstrate the utility of this model in avoiding experimental design unidentifiability and validate its parameter recovery through synthetic and experimental data. This framework enables behavioral scientists to perform Bayesian inference of decision-making parameters in production and reproduction tasks, thereby advancing our understanding of human behavior.

title: Transfer learning for cancer diagnosis in histopathological images
text: Transfer learning allows us to exploit knowledge gained from one task to assist in solving another but relevant task. In modern computer vision research, the question is which architecture performs better for a given dataset. In this paper, we compare the performance of 14 pre-trained ImageNet models on the histopathologic cancer detection dataset, where each model has been configured as a naive model, feature extractor model, or fine-tuned model. Densenet161 has been shown to have high precision whilst Resnet101 has a high recall. A high precision model is suitable to be used when follow-up examination cost is high, whilst low precision but a high recall/sensitivity model can be used when the cost of follow-up examination is low. Results also show that transfer learning helps to converge a model faster.

title: Transfer learning for cancer diagnosis in histopathological images
text: Cancer diagnosis from histopathological images relies heavily on the availability of large, well-annotated datasets, which are often scarce and expensive to obtain. Transfer learning has shown promise in alleviating this issue by leveraging pre-trained models and fine-tuning them on smaller target datasets. In this context, we investigate the efficacy of transfer learning for cancer diagnosis in histopathological images. We employ a range of pre-trained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and fine-tune them on a dataset of 1,500 images from the Cancer Genome Atlas. Our results demonstrate that transfer learning achieves state-of-the-art performance, with an average accuracy of 93.2% and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.97, outperforming traditional machine learning approaches by a significant margin. We also show that the choice of pre-trained model has a significant impact on performance, with models pre-trained on larger datasets yielding better results.

title: Scalable Deep Graph Clustering with Random-walk based Self-supervised Learning
text: Web-based interactions can be frequently represented by an attributed graph, and node clustering in such graphs has received much attention lately. Multiple efforts have successfully applied Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN), though with some limits on accuracy as GCNs have been shown to suffer from over-smoothing issues. Though other methods (particularly those based on Laplacian Smoothing) have reported better accuracy, a fundamental limitation of all the work is a lack of scalability. This paper addresses this open problem by relating the Laplacian smoothing to the Generalized PageRank and applying a random-walk based algorithm as a scalable graph filter. This forms the basis for our scalable deep clustering algorithm, RwSL, where through a self-supervised mini-batch training mechanism, we simultaneously optimize a deep neural network for sample-cluster assignment distribution and an autoencoder for a clustering-oriented embedding. Using 6 real-world datasets and 6 clustering metrics, we show that RwSL achieved improved results over several recent baselines. Most notably, we show that RwSL, unlike all other deep clustering frameworks, can continue to scale beyond graphs with more than one million nodes, i.e., handle web-scale. We also demonstrate how RwSL could perform node clustering on a graph with 1.8 billion edges using only a single GPU.

title: Scalable Deep Graph Clustering with Random-walk based Self-supervised Learning
text: The representation of web-based interactions as attributed graphs has sparked significant interest in node clustering, with Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) being a prominent approach. However, GCNs are plagued by over-smoothing issues, limiting their accuracy. Alternative methods, such as those based on Laplacian Smoothing, have reported improved accuracy but are hindered by scalability limitations. This paper bridges this gap by establishing a connection between Laplacian smoothing and Generalized PageRank, enabling the development of a scalable graph filter based on random walks. Our proposed algorithm, RwSL, leverages this filter to facilitate deep clustering through a self-supervised mini-batch training mechanism, jointly optimizing a deep neural network for sample-cluster assignment distribution and an autoencoder for clustering-oriented embedding. Empirical evaluation on six real-world datasets and six clustering metrics demonstrates the superiority of RwSL over recent baselines. Notably, RwSL exhibits scalability beyond graphs with over one million nodes, making it the first deep clustering framework capable of handling web-scale data. We further demonstrate RwSL's ability to perform node clustering on a massive graph with 1.8 billion edges using a single GPU.

title: Machine Learning Trivializing Maps: A First Step Towards Understanding How Flow-Based Samplers Scale Up
text: A trivializing map is a field transformation whose Jacobian determinant exactly cancels the interaction terms in the action, providing a representation of the theory in terms of a deterministic transformation of a distribution from which sampling is trivial. Recently, a proof-of-principle study by Albergo, Kanwar and Shanahan [arXiv:1904.12072] demonstrated that approximations of trivializing maps can be `machine-learned' by a class of invertible, differentiable neural models called \textit{normalizing flows}. By ensuring that the Jacobian determinant can be computed efficiently, asymptotically exact sampling from the theory of interest can be performed by drawing samples from a simple distribution and passing them through the network. From a theoretical perspective, this approach has the potential to become more efficient than traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling techniques, where autocorrelations severely diminish the sampling efficiency as one approaches the continuum limit. A major caveat is that it is not yet understood how the size of models and the cost of training them is expected to scale. As a first step, we have conducted an exploratory scaling study using two-dimensional $φ^4$ with up to $20^2$ lattice sites. Although the scope of our study is limited to a particular model architecture and training algorithm, initial results paint an interesting picture in which training costs grow very quickly indeed. We describe a candidate explanation for the poor scaling, and outline our intentions to clarify the situation in future work.

title: Machine Learning Trivializing Maps: A First Step Towards Understanding How Flow-Based Samplers Scale Up
text: Theoretical guarantees of MCMC algorithms often rely on the notion of conductance, which measures the mixing rate of a Markov chain. However, in practice, flow-based samplers have been observed to scale up remarkably well to high-dimensional problems, even when the conductance is poor. This discrepancy between theory and practice motivates our investigation into the role of trivializing maps in machine learning, which we hypothesize can help explain the scalability of flow-based methods. We introduce the concept of machine learning trivializing maps (MLTMs), which are learned transformations that simplify the geometry of the target distribution, making it more amenable to sampling. Our approach leverages a novel neural network architecture, designed to minimize the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the pushforward of the target distribution and a tractable reference distribution. We provide a theoretical analysis of MLTMs, establishing their connection to the conductance of the underlying Markov chain. Empirically, we evaluate the performance of MLTMs on a range of benchmark distributions, demonstrating significant improvements in sampling efficiency and quality compared to state-of-the-art methods. Notably, we observe that MLTMs can effectively trivialize complex distributions, rendering them accessible to simple sampling algorithms. Our results provide a first step towards understanding the scalability of flow-based samplers and have implications for the design of more efficient and robust sampling algorithms in high-dimensional spaces.

title: Machine learning based disease diagnosis: A comprehensive review
text: Globally, there is a substantial unmet need to diagnose various diseases effectively. The complexity of the different disease mechanisms and underlying symptoms of the patient population presents massive challenges to developing the early diagnosis tool and effective treatment. Machine Learning (ML), an area of Artificial Intelligence (AI), enables researchers, physicians, and patients to solve some of these issues. Based on relevant research, this review explains how Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) are being used to help in the early identification of numerous diseases. To begin, a bibliometric study of the publication is given using data from the Scopus and Web of Science (WOS) databases. The bibliometric study of 1216 publications was undertaken to determine the most prolific authors, nations, organizations, and most cited articles. The review then summarizes the most recent trends and approaches in Machine Learning-based Disease Diagnosis (MLBDD), considering the following factors: algorithm, disease types, data type, application, and evaluation metrics. Finally, the paper highlights key results and provides insight into future trends and opportunities in the MLBDD area.

title: Machine learning based disease diagnosis: A comprehensive review
text: The timely and accurate diagnosis of diseases remains a significant global health challenge, hindered by the intricate complexity of disease mechanisms and heterogeneous patient populations. Artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), offers a promising solution to address this unmet need. This review synthesizes the current state of ML-based disease diagnosis (MLBDD), leveraging a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of 1216 publications from Scopus and Web of Science databases. The analysis identifies prolific authors, nations, organizations, and highly cited articles, providing valuable insights into the field's evolution. We then distill recent trends and approaches in MLBDD, categorizing them by algorithm, disease type, data type, application, and evaluation metrics. Our review culminates in highlighting key findings and outlining future directions and opportunities in MLBDD, underscoring its potential to transform disease diagnosis and treatment.

title: on the effectiveness of generative adversarial network on anomaly detection
text: Identifying anomalies refers to detecting samples that do not resemble the training data distribution. Many generative models have been used to find anomalies, and among them, generative adversarial network (GAN)-based approaches are currently very popular. GANs mainly rely on the rich contextual information of these models to identify the actual training distribution. Following this analogy, we suggested a new unsupervised model based on GANs --a combination of an autoencoder and a GAN. Further, a new scoring function was introduced to target anomalies where a linear combination of the internal representation of the discriminator and the generator's visual representation, plus the encoded representation of the autoencoder, come together to define the proposed anomaly score. The model was further evaluated on benchmark datasets such as SVHN, CIFAR10, and MNIST, as well as a public medical dataset of leukemia images. In all the experiments, our model outperformed its existing counterparts while slightly improving the inference time.

title: on the effectiveness of generative adversarial network on anomaly detection
text: Anomaly identification involves distinguishing samples that deviate from the underlying distribution of the training data. Among various generative models employed for this task, generative adversarial network (GAN)-based approaches have garnered significant attention. By leveraging the rich contextual information inherent in these models, GANs effectively capture the actual training distribution. Building upon this concept, we propose a novel unsupervised model that integrates an autoencoder with a GAN. A new scoring function is introduced, which combines the internal representation of the discriminator, the generator's visual representation, and the encoded representation of the autoencoder to produce a comprehensive anomaly score. Empirical evaluations on benchmark datasets, including SVHN, CIFAR10, MNIST, and a public medical dataset of leukemia images, demonstrate the superiority of our model over existing counterparts, accompanied by a slight reduction in inference time.

title: OWLOOP: A Modular API to Describe OWL Axioms in OOP Objects Hierarchies
text: OWLOOP is an Application Programming Interface (API) for using the Ontology Web Language (OWL) by the means of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP). It is common to design software architectures using the OOP paradigm for increasing their modularity. If the components of an architecture also exploit OWL ontologies for knowledge representation and reasoning, they would require to be interfaced with OWL axioms. Since OWL does not adhere to the OOP paradigm, such an interface often leads to boilerplate code affecting modularity, and OWLOOP is designed to address this issue as well as the associated computational aspects. We present an extension of the OWL-API to provide a general-purpose interface between OWL axioms subject to reasoning and modular OOP objects hierarchies.

title: OWLOOP: A Modular API to Describe OWL Axioms in OOP Objects Hierarchies
text: The Web Ontology Language (OWL) is a cornerstone of the Semantic Web, enabling machines to interpret and reason about domain-specific knowledge. However, the complexity of OWL axioms hinders their adoption in software applications, particularly when integrating with object-oriented programming (OOP) principles. To bridge this gap, we introduce OWLOOP, a modular API that represents OWL axioms as OOP objects hierarchies. OWLOOP leverages a novel, graph-based approach to decompose axioms into modular, reusable components, facilitating their integration into software systems. Our evaluation on a suite of ontologies demonstrates OWLOOP's ability to reduce axiom representation complexity by up to 75% and improve reasoning performance by up to 30%. These findings have significant implications for the development of scalable, ontology-driven software applications.

title: Training and Generating Neural Networks in Compressed Weight Space
text: The inputs and/or outputs of some neural nets are weight matrices of other neural nets. Indirect encodings or end-to-end compression of weight matrices could help to scale such approaches. Our goal is to open a discussion on this topic, starting with recurrent neural networks for character-level language modelling whose weight matrices are encoded by the discrete cosine transform. Our fast weight version thereof uses a recurrent neural network to parameterise the compressed weights. We present experimental results on the enwik8 dataset.

title: Training and Generating Neural Networks in Compressed Weight Space
text: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for character-level language modeling can be scaled by leveraging indirect encodings or end-to-end compression of their weight matrices. We explore this concept using the discrete cosine transform to encode weight matrices of RNNs. Furthermore, we introduce a fast weight variant that employs an RNN to parameterize compressed weights, demonstrating its effectiveness through experimental results on the enwik8 dataset.

title: Improving Baselines in the Wild
text: We share our experience with the recently released WILDS benchmark, a collection of ten datasets dedicated to developing models and training strategies which are robust to domain shifts. Several experiments yield a couple of critical observations which we believe are of general interest for any future work on WILDS. Our study focuses on two datasets: iWildCam and FMoW. We show that (1) Conducting separate cross-validation for each evaluation metric is crucial for both datasets, (2) A weak correlation between validation and test performance might make model development difficult for iWildCam, (3) Minor changes in the training of hyper-parameters improve the baseline by a relatively large margin (mainly on FMoW), (4) There is a strong correlation between certain domains and certain target labels (mainly on iWildCam). To the best of our knowledge, no prior work on these datasets has reported these observations despite their obvious importance. Our code is public.

title: Improving Baselines in the Wild
text: This study presents key insights gleaned from experiments on the WILDS benchmark, a suite of ten datasets designed to develop robust models and training strategies against domain shifts. Focusing on the iWildCam and FMoW datasets, our investigation reveals several critical findings with broad implications for future WILDS research. Notably, we demonstrate the importance of separate cross-validation for each evaluation metric in both datasets. Furthermore, our results show that the correlation between validation and test performance can be weak, particularly in iWildCam, which may complicate model development. We also find that minor adjustments to hyper-parameter tuning can yield significant improvements to the baseline, primarily in FMoW. Additionally, our analysis uncovers a strong correlation between specific domains and target labels, mainly in iWildCam. These observations, to our knowledge, have not been previously reported, despite their significance. The code underlying this study is publicly available.

title: An Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Model based on Dual-module Adversarial Training
text: In this paper, we propose a dual-module network architecture that employs a domain discriminative feature module to encourage the domain invariant feature module to learn more domain invariant features. The proposed architecture can be applied to any model that utilizes domain invariant features for unsupervised domain adaptation to improve its ability to extract domain invariant features. We conduct experiments with the Domain-Adversarial Training of Neural Networks (DANN) model as a representative algorithm. In the training process, we supply the same input to the two modules and then extract their feature distribution and prediction results respectively. We propose a discrepancy loss to find the discrepancy of the prediction results and the feature distribution between the two modules. Through the adversarial training by maximizing the loss of their feature distribution and minimizing the discrepancy of their prediction results, the two modules are encouraged to learn more domain discriminative and domain invariant features respectively. Extensive comparative evaluations are conducted and the proposed approach outperforms the state-of-the-art in most unsupervised domain adaptation tasks.

title: An Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Model based on Dual-module Adversarial Training
text: We present a novel dual-module network architecture designed to enhance domain invariance in unsupervised domain adaptation. By incorporating a domain discriminative feature module, our approach encourages the domain invariant feature module to learn more robust and domain-agnostic representations. The proposed architecture is model-agnostic, applicable to any framework that relies on domain invariant features for unsupervised domain adaptation. Using the Domain-Adversarial Training of Neural Networks (DANN) model as a representative algorithm, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through extensive experiments. Specifically, we supply identical inputs to both modules and analyze their feature distributions and prediction results. A discrepancy loss is introduced to quantify the differences between the two modules' outputs, promoting adversarial training that maximizes feature distribution discrepancy and minimizes prediction result discrepancy. This strategy enables the modules to learn domain discriminative and domain invariant features, respectively. Our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in most unsupervised domain adaptation tasks.

title: SOK: On the Analysis of Web Browser Security
text: Web browsers are integral parts of everyone's daily life. They are commonly used for security-critical and privacy sensitive tasks, like banking transactions and checking medical records. Unfortunately, modern web browsers are too complex to be bug free (e.g., 25 million lines of code in Chrome), and their role as an interface to the cyberspace makes them an attractive target for attacks. Accordingly, web browsers naturally become an arena for demonstrating advanced exploitation techniques by attackers and state-of-the-art defenses by browser vendors. Web browsers, arguably, are the most exciting place to learn the latest security issues and techniques, but remain as a black art to most security researchers because of their fast-changing characteristics and complex code bases. To bridge this gap, this paper attempts to systematize the security landscape of modern web browsers by studying the popular classes of security bugs, their exploitation techniques, and deployed defenses. More specifically, we first introduce a unified architecture that faithfully represents the security design of four major web browsers. Second, we share insights from a 10-year longitudinal study on browser bugs. Third, we present a timeline and context of mitigation schemes and their effectiveness. Fourth, we share our lessons from a full-chain exploit used in 2020 Pwn2Own competition. and the implication of bug bounty programs to web browser security. We believe that the key takeaways from this systematization can shed light on how to advance the status quo of modern web browsers, and, importantly, how to create secure yet complex software in the future.

title: SOK: On the Analysis of Web Browser Security
text: The pervasive adoption of web browsers as a primary interface to the internet has made them an attractive target for malicious actors. Despite significant investments in browser security, the landscape of web browser vulnerabilities remains poorly understood. This knowledge gap hinders the development of effective countermeasures, perpetuating a cat-and-mouse game between browser vendors and attackers. This paper presents a systematic and comprehensive analysis of web browser security, focusing on the Chrome, Firefox, and Edge browsers. We employ a mixed-methods approach, combining static and dynamic analysis of browser binaries, as well as a large-scale study of publicly disclosed vulnerabilities. Our methodology involves decompiling and analyzing browser binaries to identify security-critical components, followed by a thorough examination of vulnerability reports and patches. Our findings indicate that browser security is largely dictated by the complexity of their architecture, with a disproportionate number of vulnerabilities stemming from the rendering engine and JavaScript interpreter. We identify a significant lack of diversity in browser security mechanisms, with all three browsers relying heavily on similar sandboxing and memory protection techniques. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the vulnerability disclosure process is often slow and ineffective, with a median patch time of 120 days. We also discover a concerning trend of vendors prioritizing features over security, as evidenced by the frequent introduction of new functionality despite lingering security issues. Our study provides a nuanced understanding of the web browser security landscape, highlighting the need for more effective vulnerability disclosure mechanisms, increased diversity in security mechanisms, and a shift in priorities towards security-centric design. Our findings have important implications for browser vendors, policymakers, and security practitioners, informing the development of more secure and resilient web browsers.

title: PCACE: A Statistical Approach to Ranking Neurons for CNN Interpretability
text: In this paper we introduce a new problem within the growing literature of interpretability for convolution neural networks (CNNs). While previous work has focused on the question of how to visually interpret CNNs, we ask what it is that we care to interpret, that is, which layers and neurons are worth our attention? Due to the vast size of modern deep learning network architectures, automated, quantitative methods are needed to rank the relative importance of neurons so as to provide an answer to this question. We present a new statistical method for ranking the hidden neurons in any convolutional layer of a network. We define importance as the maximal correlation between the activation maps and the class score. We provide different ways in which this method can be used for visualization purposes with MNIST and ImageNet, and show a real-world application of our method to air pollution prediction with street-level images.

title: PCACE: A Statistical Approach to Ranking Neurons for CNN Interpretability
text: The quest for interpretability in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has primarily centered on visualizing their internal workings. However, a crucial, yet understudied, aspect of this problem is identifying which layers and neurons warrant attention. The sheer scale of modern deep learning architectures necessitates automated, quantitative methods for ranking neuronal importance. This paper proposes a novel statistical approach for ranking hidden neurons within any convolutional layer. We operationalize importance as the maximum correlation between activation maps and class scores. The proposed method is demonstrated through various visualization strategies using MNIST and ImageNet datasets, and its practical applicability is showcased in a real-world scenario involving air pollution prediction from street-level images. Our approach offers a principled means of discerning informative neurons, thereby facilitating more effective network interpretation and optimization.

title: Fast Learning of MNL Model from General Partial Rankings with Application to Network Formation Modeling
text: Multinomial Logit (MNL) is one of the most popular discrete choice models and has been widely used to model ranking data. However, there is a long-standing technical challenge of learning MNL from many real-world ranking data: exact calculation of the MNL likelihood of \emph{partial rankings} is generally intractable. In this work, we develop a scalable method for approximating the MNL likelihood of general partial rankings in polynomial time complexity. We also extend the proposed method to learn mixture of MNL. We demonstrate that the proposed methods are particularly helpful for applications to choice-based network formation modeling, where the formation of new edges in a network is viewed as individuals making choices of their friends over a candidate set. The problem of learning mixture of MNL models from partial rankings naturally arises in such applications. And the proposed methods can be used to learn MNL models from network data without the strong assumption that temporal orders of all the edge formation are available. We conduct experiments on both synthetic and real-world network data to demonstrate that the proposed methods achieve more accurate parameter estimation and better fitness of data compared to conventional methods.

title: Fast Learning of MNL Model from General Partial Rankings with Application to Network Formation Modeling
text: The Multinomial Logit (MNL) model is a ubiquitous discrete choice model employed to analyze ranking data, yet exact likelihood computation for partial rankings poses a perennial technical hurdle. This limitation is particularly problematic in real-world applications, where partial rankings are common. We present a scalable method for approximating the MNL likelihood of general partial rankings in polynomial time complexity, thereby circumventing this computational bottleneck. Furthermore, we extend our approach to accommodate mixtures of MNL models. The proposed methods are particularly well-suited for choice-based network formation modeling, where edge formation is viewed as individuals making choices from a candidate set. In such contexts, learning mixtures of MNL models from partial rankings is a natural problem. By relaxing the assumption of complete temporal information on edge formation, our approach enables MNL model estimation from network data. Experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world network data demonstrate that our methods achieve superior parameter estimation and better data fit compared to conventional approaches.

title: How Infinitely Wide Neural Networks Can Benefit from Multi-task Learning -- an Exact Macroscopic Characterization
text: In practice, multi-task learning (through learning features shared among tasks) is an essential property of deep neural networks (NNs). While infinite-width limits of NNs can provide good intuition for their generalization behavior, the well-known infinite-width limits of NNs in the literature (e.g., neural tangent kernels) assume specific settings in which wide ReLU-NNs behave like shallow Gaussian Processes with a fixed kernel. Consequently, in such settings, these NNs lose their ability to benefit from multi-task learning in the infinite-width limit. In contrast, we prove that optimizing wide ReLU neural networks with at least one hidden layer using L2-regularization on the parameters promotes multi-task learning due to representation-learning - also in the limiting regime where the network width tends to infinity. We present an exact quantitative characterization of this infinite width limit in an appropriate function space that neatly describes multi-task learning.

title: How Infinitely Wide Neural Networks Can Benefit from Multi-task Learning -- an Exact Macroscopic Characterization
text: Theoretical guarantees for infinitely wide neural networks have recently been established, but their practical applications remain largely unexplored. We bridge this gap by investigating the benefits of multi-task learning in this regime. By leveraging the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) framework, we derive an exact macroscopic characterization of the interaction between tasks, capturing how the kernel matrices evolve during training. Our analysis reveals that, in the infinite-width limit, the tasks' covariance matrices converge to a fixed point, which we explicitly compute. This enables us to identify optimal task combinations that maximize the benefits of multi-task learning. Empirically, we validate our theoretical findings on various datasets, demonstrating significant performance improvements over single-task baselines. Our results provide a foundational understanding of the interplay between infinitely wide neural networks and multi-task learning, opening up new avenues for their practical application in real-world scenarios.

title: Importance of Empirical Sample Complexity Analysis for Offline Reinforcement Learning
text: We hypothesize that empirically studying the sample complexity of offline reinforcement learning (RL) is crucial for the practical applications of RL in the real world. Several recent works have demonstrated the ability to learn policies directly from offline data. In this work, we ask the question of the dependency on the number of samples for learning from offline data. Our objective is to emphasize that studying sample complexity for offline RL is important, and is an indicator of the usefulness of existing offline algorithms. We propose an evaluation approach for sample complexity analysis of offline RL.

title: Importance of Empirical Sample Complexity Analysis for Offline Reinforcement Learning
text: The practical viability of offline reinforcement learning (RL) hinges on understanding the sample complexity of learning from static datasets. Recent advances have shown that policies can be successfully learned directly from offline data, but the fundamental question of how the learning process depends on the dataset size remains unexplored. This study highlights the critical importance of investigating sample complexity in offline RL, as it serves as a key indicator of the efficacy of existing algorithms. We introduce a novel evaluation framework for rigorously analyzing the sample complexity of offline RL methods.

title: Single-Shot Pruning for Offline Reinforcement Learning
text: Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a powerful framework for solving complex real-world problems. Large neural networks employed in the framework are traditionally associated with better generalization capabilities, but their increased size entails the drawbacks of extensive training duration, substantial hardware resources, and longer inference times. One way to tackle this problem is to prune neural networks leaving only the necessary parameters. State-of-the-art concurrent pruning techniques for imposing sparsity perform demonstrably well in applications where data distributions are fixed. However, they have not yet been substantially explored in the context of RL. We close the gap between RL and single-shot pruning techniques and present a general pruning approach to the Offline RL. We leverage a fixed dataset to prune neural networks before the start of RL training. We then run experiments varying the network sparsity level and evaluating the validity of pruning at initialization techniques in continuous control tasks. Our results show that with 95% of the network weights pruned, Offline-RL algorithms can still retain performance in the majority of our experiments. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work utilizing pruning in RL retained performance at such high levels of sparsity. Moreover, pruning at initialization techniques can be easily integrated into any existing Offline-RL algorithms without changing the learning objective.

title: Single-Shot Pruning for Offline Reinforcement Learning
text: The efficacy of Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) in solving complex real-world problems is well established, but its reliance on large neural networks poses significant challenges. While these networks often exhibit better generalization capabilities, their size incurs substantial computational costs, including prolonged training durations, increased hardware requirements, and longer inference times. To mitigate these drawbacks, neural network pruning has emerged as a promising approach, wherein only essential parameters are retained. Although concurrent pruning techniques have demonstrated impressive results in applications with fixed data distributions, their application in RL remains largely unexplored. This paper bridges this gap by introducing a general pruning approach for Offline RL, leveraging a fixed dataset to prune neural networks prior to RL training. Through experiments varying network sparsity levels, we validate the effectiveness of pruning at initialization techniques in continuous control tasks, achieving remarkable performance retention with up to 95% network weight pruning. Notably, our approach can be seamlessly integrated into existing Offline-RL algorithms without modifying the learning objective, offering a significant advancement in the field.

title: 3-D Material Style Transfer for Reconstructing Unknown Appearance in Complex Natural Materials
text: We propose a 3-D material style transfer framework for reconstructing invisible (or faded) appearance properties in complex natural materials. Our algorithm addresses the technical challenge of transferring appearance properties from one object to another of the same material when both objects have intricate, noncorresponding color patterns. Eggshells, exoskeletons, and minerals, for example, have patterns composed of highly randomized layers of organic and inorganic compounds. These materials pose a challenge as the distribution of compounds that determine surface color changes from object to object and within local pattern regions. Our solution adapts appearance observations from a material property distribution in an exemplar to the material property distribution of a target object to reconstruct its unknown appearance. We use measured reflectance in 3-D bispectral textures to record changing material property distributions. Our novel implementation of spherical harmonics uses principles from chemistry and biology to learn relationships between color (hue and saturation) and material composition and concentration in an exemplar. The encoded relationships are transformed to the property distribution of a target for color recovery and material assignment. Quantitative and qualitative evaluation methods show that we replicate color patterns more accurately than methods that only rely on shape correspondences and coarse-level perceptual differences. We demonstrate applications of our work for reconstructing color in extinct fossils, restoring faded artifacts and generating synthetic textures.

title: 3-D Material Style Transfer for Reconstructing Unknown Appearance in Complex Natural Materials
text: Reconstructing the appearance properties of complex natural materials with intricate, non-corresponding color patterns is a challenging task, particularly when dealing with objects that exhibit highly randomized distributions of organic and inorganic compounds. Examples of such materials include eggshells, exoskeletons, and minerals, where the surface color is determined by the varying distribution of compounds across objects and within local pattern regions. To address this challenge, we introduce a 3-D material style transfer framework that adapts appearance observations from a material property distribution in an exemplar to the material property distribution of a target object, enabling the reconstruction of its unknown appearance. By leveraging measured reflectance in 3-D bispectral textures, our approach encodes relationships between color (hue and saturation) and material composition and concentration in the exemplar using principles from chemistry and biology. These relationships are then transformed to the property distribution of the target object, facilitating color recovery and material assignment. Our method outperforms existing approaches that rely solely on shape correspondences and coarse-level perceptual differences, as demonstrated through quantitative and qualitative evaluations. The proposed framework has promising applications in reconstructing color in extinct fossils, restoring faded artifacts, and generating synthetic textures.

title: A Neural Network Solves, Explains, and Generates University Math Problems by Program Synthesis and Few-Shot Learning at Human Level
text: We demonstrate that a neural network pre-trained on text and fine-tuned on code solves mathematics course problems, explains solutions, and generates new questions at a human level. We automatically synthesize programs using few-shot learning and OpenAI's Codex transformer and execute them to solve course problems at 81% automatic accuracy. We curate a new dataset of questions from MIT's largest mathematics courses (Single Variable and Multivariable Calculus, Differential Equations, Introduction to Probability and Statistics, Linear Algebra, and Mathematics for Computer Science) and Columbia University's Computational Linear Algebra. We solve questions from a MATH dataset (on Prealgebra, Algebra, Counting and Probability, Intermediate Algebra, Number Theory, and Precalculus), the latest benchmark of advanced mathematics problems designed to assess mathematical reasoning. We randomly sample questions and generate solutions with multiple modalities, including numbers, equations, and plots. The latest GPT-3 language model pre-trained on text automatically solves only 18.8% of these university questions using zero-shot learning and 30.8% using few-shot learning and the most recent chain of thought prompting. In contrast, program synthesis with few-shot learning using Codex fine-tuned on code generates programs that automatically solve 81% of these questions. Our approach improves the previous state-of-the-art automatic solution accuracy on the benchmark topics from 8.8% to 81.1%. We perform a survey to evaluate the quality and difficulty of generated questions. This work is the first to automatically solve university-level mathematics course questions at a human level and the first work to explain and generate university-level mathematics course questions at scale, a milestone for higher education.

title: A Neural Network Solves, Explains, and Generates University Math Problems by Program Synthesis and Few-Shot Learning at Human Level
text: Mathematics education is essential for various STEM fields, yet it often poses significant challenges for students, instructors, and educational resources. Automated systems that can generate, solve, and explain mathematical problems at a human level have the potential to revolutionize mathematics education. Recent advances in program synthesis and few-shot learning have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in generating code for specific tasks. However, these techniques have not been explored for solving and explaining university-level math problems. We present a neural network architecture that tackles this challenge by leveraging program synthesis and few-shot learning. Our model is trained on a dataset of university math problems and their solutions, and it can generate new problems, solve given problems, and provide step-by-step explanations for the solutions. Our approach combines a neural program synthesizer with a few-shot learning mechanism, enabling the model to learn from a small set of examples and generalize to unseen problems. Experiments on a diverse set of university math topics, including calculus, linear algebra, and differential equations, demonstrate that our model achieves human-level performance in solving and generating math problems. Moreover, our model's explanations are coherent and accurate, as evaluated by mathematics instructors. We also show that our model can generalize to new topics and problem types with minimal additional training data. Our work has significant implications for mathematics education, as it can facilitate personalized learning, reduce instructors' workload, and provide real-time feedback to students.

title: Triangular Flows for Generative Modeling: Statistical Consistency, Smoothness Classes, and Fast Rates
text: Triangular flows, also known as Knöthe-Rosenblatt measure couplings, comprise an important building block of normalizing flow models for generative modeling and density estimation, including popular autoregressive flow models such as real-valued non-volume preserving transformation models (Real NVP). We present statistical guarantees and sample complexity bounds for triangular flow statistical models. In particular, we establish the statistical consistency and the finite sample convergence rates of the Kullback-Leibler estimator of the Knöthe-Rosenblatt measure coupling using tools from empirical process theory. Our results highlight the anisotropic geometry of function classes at play in triangular flows, shed light on optimal coordinate ordering, and lead to statistical guarantees for Jacobian flows. We conduct numerical experiments on synthetic data to illustrate the practical implications of our theoretical findings.

title: Triangular Flows for Generative Modeling: Statistical Consistency, Smoothness Classes, and Fast Rates
text: The Knöthe-Rosenblatt measure coupling, also referred to as triangular flows, constitutes a fundamental component of normalizing flow models in generative modeling and density estimation, with prominent applications in autoregressive flow models such as Real NVP. This paper derives statistical guarantees and sample complexity bounds for triangular flow statistical models, thereby establishing the consistency and finite sample convergence rates of the Kullback-Leibler estimator for the Knöthe-Rosenblatt measure coupling. Leveraging empirical process theory, our analysis reveals the anisotropic geometric structure underlying function classes in triangular flows, provides insight into optimal coordinate ordering, and yields statistical guarantees for Jacobian flows. The practical implications of our theoretical findings are demonstrated through numerical experiments on synthetic data.

title: A Literature Review on Length of Stay Prediction for Stroke Patients using Machine Learning and Statistical Approaches
text: Hospital length of stay (LOS) is one of the most essential healthcare metrics that reflects the hospital quality of service and helps improve hospital scheduling and management. LOS prediction helps in cost management because patients who remain in hospitals usually do so in hospital units where resources are severely limited. In this study, we reviewed papers on LOS prediction using machine learning and statistical approaches. Our literature review considers research studies that focus on LOS prediction for stroke patients. Some of the surveyed studies revealed that authors reached contradicting conclusions. For example, the age of the patient was considered an important predictor of LOS for stroke patients in some studies, while other studies concluded that age was not a significant factor. Therefore, additional research is required in this domain to further understand the predictors of LOS for stroke patients.

title: A Literature Review on Length of Stay Prediction for Stroke Patients using Machine Learning and Statistical Approaches
text: Stroke is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with prolonged hospital stays contributing significantly to healthcare costs. Accurate prediction of length of stay (LOS) for stroke patients is crucial for optimizing resource allocation and improving patient outcomes. This literature review synthesizes existing research on machine learning and statistical approaches for LOS prediction in stroke patients, encompassing 35 studies published between 2010 and 2022. We systematically examined the methodologies, datasets, and performance metrics employed, as well as the predictive capabilities of different models. Our analysis reveals that machine learning algorithms, particularly random forests and neural networks, outperform statistical models in LOS prediction, with mean absolute errors ranging from 2.1 to 4.5 days. However, significant heterogeneity exists across studies, highlighting the need for standardized datasets and evaluation protocols. This review provides a comprehensive framework for future research, emphasizing the importance of multimodal data integration and external validation.

title: Leveraging Queue Length and Attention Mechanisms for Enhanced Traffic Signal Control Optimization
text: Reinforcement learning (RL) techniques for traffic signal control (TSC) have gained increasing popularity in recent years. However, most existing RL-based TSC methods tend to focus primarily on the RL model structure while neglecting the significance of proper traffic state representation. Furthermore, some RL-based methods heavily rely on expert-designed traffic signal phase competition. In this paper, we present a novel approach to TSC that utilizes queue length as an efficient state representation. We propose two new methods: (1) Max Queue-Length (M-QL), an optimization-based traditional method designed based on the property of queue length; and (2) AttentionLight, an RL model that employs the self-attention mechanism to capture the signal phase correlation without requiring human knowledge of phase relationships. Comprehensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach: (1) the M-QL method outperforms the latest RL-based methods; (2) AttentionLight achieves a new state-of-the-art performance; and (3) our results highlight the significance of proper state representation, which is as crucial as neural network design in TSC methods. Our findings have important implications for advancing the development of more effective and efficient TSC methods. Our code is released on Github ( com/LiangZhang1996/AttentionLight).

title: Leveraging Queue Length and Attention Mechanisms for Enhanced Traffic Signal Control Optimization
text: The burgeoning interest in reinforcement learning (RL) for traffic signal control (TSC) has led to a plethora of methods that primarily focus on optimizing the RL model architecture, often at the expense of adequate traffic state representation. The reliance on expert-designed traffic signal phase competition is another pervasive limitation of existing RL-based TSC approaches. This paper addresses these shortcomings by introducing a novel TSC framework that leverages queue length as a concise and effective state representation. We propose two complementary methods: Max Queue-Length (M-QL), a traditional optimization-based approach that exploits the inherent properties of queue length, and AttentionLight, an RL model that incorporates self-attention mechanisms to capture signal phase correlations without relying on human expertise. Our comprehensive evaluation on multiple real-world datasets reveals the superiority of our approach, with M-QL outperforming state-of-the-art RL-based methods and AttentionLight achieving unprecedented performance. Notably, our results underscore the critical importance of proper state representation in TSC, on par with neural network design. These findings have significant implications for the development of more efficient and effective TSC strategies.

title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
text: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
text: The knowledge distillation paradigm has been extended to leverage multiple teacher models, enabling the student model to benefit from diverse knowledge sources. However, existing approaches often combine teacher predictions through averaging or label-free strategies, which can be detrimental when low-quality teacher predictions are present. We propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), a novel framework that adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability weights to each teacher prediction based on their proximity to the ground-truth labels. By incorporating intermediate layers, CA-MKD stabilizes the knowledge transfer process, leading to improved student performance. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate the consistent superiority of CA-MKD over state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures, emphasizing its effectiveness in harnessing diverse knowledge sources.

title: A Lightweight and Accurate Spatial-Temporal Transformer for Traffic Forecasting
text: We study the forecasting problem for traffic with dynamic, possibly periodical, and joint spatial-temporal dependency between regions. Given the aggregated inflow and outflow traffic of regions in a city from time slots 0 to t-1, we predict the traffic at time t at any region. Prior arts in the area often consider the spatial and temporal dependencies in a decoupled manner or are rather computationally intensive in training with a large number of hyper-parameters to tune. We propose ST-TIS, a novel, lightweight, and accurate Spatial-Temporal Transformer with information fusion and region sampling for traffic forecasting. ST-TIS extends the canonical Transformer with information fusion and region sampling. The information fusion module captures the complex spatial-temporal dependency between regions. The region sampling module is to improve the efficiency and prediction accuracy, cutting the computation complexity for dependency learning from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n\sqrt{n})$, where n is the number of regions. With far fewer parameters than state-of-the-art models, the offline training of our model is significantly faster in terms of tuning and computation (with a reduction of up to $90\%$ on training time and network parameters). Notwithstanding such training efficiency, extensive experiments show that ST-TIS is substantially more accurate in online prediction than state-of-the-art approaches (with an average improvement of up to $9.5\%$ on RMSE, and $12.4\%$ on MAPE).

title: A Lightweight and Accurate Spatial-Temporal Transformer for Traffic Forecasting
text: This research addresses the challenging problem of forecasting traffic patterns in urban regions, where complex, dynamic, and potentially periodic dependencies exist between spatially and temporally correlated regions. Our goal is to predict traffic volumes at time t in any region, given aggregated inflow and outflow data from time slots 0 to t-1. Existing approaches often overlook the intricate interplay between spatial and temporal dependencies or require computationally intensive training with numerous hyper-parameters. We introduce ST-TIS, a novel, efficient, and accurate Spatial-Temporal Transformer architecture that integrates information fusion and region sampling for traffic forecasting. By extending the canonical Transformer, our model captures complex spatial-temporal dependencies through information fusion and improves efficiency and prediction accuracy via region sampling, reducing computational complexity from O(n^2) to O(n√n) for dependency learning. With significantly fewer parameters than state-of-the-art models, our offline training is substantially faster, with up to 90% reductions in training time and network parameters. Despite this training efficiency, extensive experiments demonstrate that ST-TIS achieves substantial online prediction accuracy improvements, with average reductions of up to 9.5% in RMSE and 12.4% in MAPE compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

title: Improving Deep Neural Network Classification Confidence using Heatmap-based eXplainable AI
text: This paper quantifies the quality of heatmap-based eXplainable AI (XAI) methods w.r.t image classification problem. Here, a heatmap is considered desirable if it improves the probability of predicting the correct classes. Different XAI heatmap-based methods are empirically shown to improve classification confidence to different extents depending on the datasets, e.g. Saliency works best on ImageNet and Deconvolution on Chest X-Ray Pneumonia dataset. The novelty includes a new gap distribution that shows a stark difference between correct and wrong predictions. Finally, the generative augmentative explanation is introduced, a method to generate heatmaps capable of improving predictive confidence to a high level.

title: Improving Deep Neural Network Classification Confidence using Heatmap-based eXplainable AI
text: We investigate the efficacy of heatmap-based eXplainable AI (XAI) methods in the context of image classification, where a desirable heatmap is defined as one that enhances the probability of correct class prediction. An empirical analysis of various XAI heatmap-based methods reveals that their impact on classification confidence varies across datasets, with Saliency exhibiting superior performance on ImageNet and Deconvolution on the Chest X-Ray Pneumonia dataset. We also introduce a novel gap distribution, which highlights a pronounced distinction between correct and incorrect predictions. Furthermore, we propose generative augmentative explanation, a method capable of generating heatmaps that significantly boost predictive confidence.

title: An Efficient Federated Distillation Learning System for Multi-task Time Series Classification
text: This paper proposes an efficient federated distillation learning system (EFDLS) for multi-task time series classification (TSC). EFDLS consists of a central server and multiple mobile users, where different users may run different TSC tasks. EFDLS has two novel components, namely a feature-based student-teacher (FBST) framework and a distance-based weights matching (DBWM) scheme. Within each user, the FBST framework transfers knowledge from its teacher's hidden layers to its student's hidden layers via knowledge distillation, with the teacher and student having identical network structure. For each connected user, its student model's hidden layers' weights are uploaded to the EFDLS server periodically. The DBWM scheme is deployed on the server, with the least square distance used to measure the similarity between the weights of two given models. This scheme finds a partner for each connected user such that the user's and its partner's weights are the closest among all the weights uploaded. The server exchanges and sends back the user's and its partner's weights to these two users which then load the received weights to their teachers' hidden layers. Experimental results show that the proposed EFDLS achieves excellent performance on a set of selected UCR2018 datasets regarding top-1 accuracy.

title: An Efficient Federated Distillation Learning System for Multi-task Time Series Classification
text: Multi-task time series classification has gained significant attention in recent years, particularly in applications such as IoT, finance, and healthcare, where data is often decentralized and heterogeneous. However, traditional centralized machine learning approaches are limited by data privacy, communication overhead, and scalability issues. To address these challenges, we propose an efficient federated distillation learning system for multi-task time series classification. Our system leverages a novel hierarchical distillation strategy, where a global model is trained using a federation of local models, each responsible for a specific task. We employ a task-aware attention mechanism to adaptively weigh the importance of each task and a knowledge distillation loss function to transfer knowledge from the global model to local models. Experimental results on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our system achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing federated learning and centralized approaches by up to 15% in terms of accuracy and 30% in terms of communication efficiency. Furthermore, our system exhibits robustness to non-IID data distributions and heterogeneous client resources, making it a promising solution for real-world multi-task time series classification applications.

title: MORAL: Aligning AI with Human Norms through Multi-Objective Reinforced Active Learning
text: Inferring reward functions from demonstrations and pairwise preferences are auspicious approaches for aligning Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents with human intentions. However, state-of-the art methods typically focus on learning a single reward model, thus rendering it difficult to trade off different reward functions from multiple experts. We propose Multi-Objective Reinforced Active Learning (MORAL), a novel method for combining diverse demonstrations of social norms into a Pareto-optimal policy. Through maintaining a distribution over scalarization weights, our approach is able to interactively tune a deep RL agent towards a variety of preferences, while eliminating the need for computing multiple policies. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of MORAL in two scenarios, which model a delivery and an emergency task that require an agent to act in the presence of normative conflicts. Overall, we consider our research a step towards multi-objective RL with learned rewards, bridging the gap between current reward learning and machine ethics literature.

title: MORAL: Aligning AI with Human Norms through Multi-Objective Reinforced Active Learning
text: The inference of reward functions from demonstrations and pairwise preferences has emerged as a promising approach for aligning Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents with human values. Nevertheless, existing methods tend to focus on learning a single reward model, thereby limiting their ability to balance competing objectives from multiple experts. To address this limitation, we introduce Multi-Objective Reinforced Active Learning (MORAL), a novel framework that integrates diverse demonstrations of social norms into a Pareto-optimal policy. By maintaining a distribution over scalarization weights, MORAL enables interactive tuning of a deep RL agent towards a range of preferences, eliminating the need to compute multiple policies. We evaluate MORAL in two scenarios, modeling delivery and emergency tasks that involve normative conflicts, and demonstrate its effectiveness. Our research contributes to the development of multi-objective RL with learned rewards, bridging the gap between reward learning and machine ethics.

title: Exploiting Bi-directional Global Transition Patterns and Personal Preferences for Missing POI Category Identification
text: Recent years have witnessed the increasing popularity of Location-based Social Network (LBSN) services, which provides unparalleled opportunities to build personalized Point-of-Interest (POI) recommender systems. Existing POI recommendation and location prediction tasks utilize past information for future recommendation or prediction from a single direction perspective, while the missing POI category identification task needs to utilize the check-in information both before and after the missing category. Therefore, a long-standing challenge is how to effectively identify the missing POI categories at any time in the real-world check-in data of mobile users. To this end, in this paper, we propose a novel neural network approach to identify the missing POI categories by integrating both bi-directional global non-personal transition patterns and personal preferences of users. Specifically, we delicately design an attention matching cell to model how well the check-in category information matches their non-personal transition patterns and personal preferences. Finally, we evaluate our model on two real-world datasets, which clearly validate its effectiveness compared with the state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, our model can be naturally extended to address next POI category recommendation and prediction tasks with competitive performance.

title: Exploiting Bi-directional Global Transition Patterns and Personal Preferences for Missing POI Category Identification
text: The proliferation of Location-based Social Network (LBSN) services has created opportunities for developing personalized Point-of-Interest (POI) recommender systems. However, existing approaches to POI recommendation and location prediction rely on past information to inform future suggestions or predictions from a single directional perspective. In contrast, identifying missing POI categories requires leveraging check-in information from both preceding and subsequent periods. This poses a significant challenge in real-world mobile user check-in data. To address this, we present a novel neural network approach that integrates bi-directional global non-personal transition patterns and personal user preferences to identify missing POI categories. Our design incorporates an attention matching cell to capture the alignment between check-in category information, non-personal transition patterns, and personal preferences. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our model compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Additionally, our approach can be seamlessly extended to tackle next POI category recommendation and prediction tasks with competitive performance.

title: TransLog: A Unified Transformer-based Framework for Log Anomaly Detection
text: Log anomaly detection is a key component in the field of artificial intelligence for IT operations (AIOps). Considering log data of variant domains, retraining the whole network for unknown domains is inefficient in real industrial scenarios especially for low-resource domains. However, previous deep models merely focused on extracting the semantics of log sequence in the same domain, leading to poor generalization on multi-domain logs. Therefore, we propose a unified Transformer-based framework for log anomaly detection (\ourmethod{}), which is comprised of the pretraining and adapter-based tuning stage. Our model is first pretrained on the source domain to obtain shared semantic knowledge of log data. Then, we transfer the pretrained model to the target domain via the adapter-based tuning. The proposed method is evaluated on three public datasets including one source domain and two target domains. The experimental results demonstrate that our simple yet efficient approach, with fewer trainable parameters and lower training costs in the target domain, achieves state-of-the-art performance on three benchmarks.

title: TransLog: A Unified Transformer-based Framework for Log Anomaly Detection
text: The detection of log anomalies is a crucial component in AIOps, yet prevailing deep models fall short in generalizing across multiple domains due to their focus on extracting semantics within a single domain. This limitation is particularly pronounced in industrial settings where retraining entire networks for unknown domains is impractical, especially for resource-constrained domains. To address this challenge, we introduce a unified Transformer-based framework, \ourmethod{}, which comprises pretraining and adapter-based tuning stages. By pretraining on a source domain, our model acquires shared semantic knowledge of log data, which is subsequently fine-tuned for target domains via adapter-based tuning. Evaluations on three public datasets, encompassing one source and two target domains, demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance with reduced trainable parameters and lower training costs in target domains.

title: Privacy-Protecting COVID-19 Exposure Notification Based on Cluster Events
text: We provide a rough sketch of a simple system design for exposure notification of COVID-19 infections based on copresence at cluster events -- locations and times where a threshold number of tested-positive (TP) individuals were present. Unlike other designs, such as DP3T or the Apple-Google exposure-notification system, this design does not track or notify based on detecting direct proximity to TP individuals. The design makes use of existing or in-development tests for COVID-19 that are relatively cheap and return results in less than an hour, and that have high specificity but may have lower sensitivity. It also uses readily available location tracking for mobile phones and similar devices. It reports events at which TP individuals were present but does not link events with individuals or with other events in an individual's history. Participating individuals are notified of detected cluster events. They can then compare these locally to their own location history. Detected cluster events can be publicized through public channels. Thus, individuals not participating in the reporting system can still be notified of exposure. A proper security analysis is beyond the scope of this design sketch. We do, however, discuss resistance to various adversaries and attacks on privacy as well as false-reporting attacks.

title: Privacy-Protecting COVID-19 Exposure Notification Based on Cluster Events
text: This paper outlines a novel system design for COVID-19 exposure notification, leveraging copresence at cluster events where a threshold number of tested-positive individuals were present. Diverging from existing approaches, such as DP3T and the Apple-Google exposure-notification system, our design eschews direct proximity tracking and notification. Instead, it utilizes rapid, cost-effective COVID-19 tests with high specificity, albeit potentially lower sensitivity, in conjunction with ubiquitous location tracking capabilities on mobile devices. The system reports cluster events where tested-positive individuals were present, without linking these events to specific individuals or their historical movements. Participating users receive notifications of detected cluster events, which they can then cross-reference with their personal location history. Moreover, publicizing detected cluster events through public channels enables non-participating individuals to also receive exposure notifications. While a comprehensive security analysis is beyond the scope of this design sketch, we discuss the system's resilience against various adversaries, privacy attacks, and false-reporting threats.

title: Stochastic convex optimization for provably efficient apprenticeship learning
text: We consider large-scale Markov decision processes (MDPs) with an unknown cost function and employ stochastic convex optimization tools to address the problem of imitation learning, which consists of learning a policy from a finite set of expert demonstrations. We adopt the apprenticeship learning formalism, which carries the assumption that the true cost function can be represented as a linear combination of some known features. Existing inverse reinforcement learning algorithms come with strong theoretical guarantees, but are computationally expensive because they use reinforcement learning or planning algorithms as a subroutine. On the other hand, state-of-the-art policy gradient based algorithms (like IM-REINFORCE, IM-TRPO, and GAIL), achieve significant empirical success in challenging benchmark tasks, but are not well understood in terms of theory. With an emphasis on non-asymptotic guarantees of performance, we propose a method that directly learns a policy from expert demonstrations, bypassing the intermediate step of learning the cost function, by formulating the problem as a single convex optimization problem over occupancy measures. We develop a computationally efficient algorithm and derive high confidence regret bounds on the quality of the extracted policy, utilizing results from stochastic convex optimization and recent works in approximate linear programming for solving forward MDPs.

title: Stochastic convex optimization for provably efficient apprenticeship learning
text: Apprenticeship learning, a paradigm for learning from expert demonstrations, has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its potential to solve complex decision-making problems in various domains. However, the lack of efficient and provably effective algorithms hinders its widespread adoption. In this context, we explore the use of stochastic convex optimization for apprenticeship learning, leveraging the power of convex analysis to provide robustness guarantees. We propose a novel algorithm, Stochastic Apprenticeship Learning (SAL), which combines the benefits of stochastic optimization with convex relaxation to efficiently learn a near-optimal policy. Our approach is based on a novel convex relaxation of the apprenticeship learning problem, which enables us to derive a stochastic optimization algorithm with provable convergence guarantees. We establish a convergence rate of O(1/√T) for SAL, significantly improving upon existing methods. Empirical evaluations on a range of benchmark problems demonstrate the efficacy of SAL, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of both convergence rate and final performance. Our results provide a significant step forward in developing efficient and provably effective algorithms for apprenticeship learning, with potential applications in robotics, healthcare, and finance.

title: Avoiding Catastrophe: Active Dendrites Enable Multi-Task Learning in Dynamic Environments
text: A key challenge for AI is to build embodied systems that operate in dynamically changing environments. Such systems must adapt to changing task contexts and learn continuously. Although standard deep learning systems achieve state of the art results on static benchmarks, they often struggle in dynamic scenarios. In these settings, error signals from multiple contexts can interfere with one another, ultimately leading to a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting. In this article we investigate biologically inspired architectures as solutions to these problems. Specifically, we show that the biophysical properties of dendrites and local inhibitory systems enable networks to dynamically restrict and route information in a context-specific manner. Our key contributions are as follows. First, we propose a novel artificial neural network architecture that incorporates active dendrites and sparse representations into the standard deep learning framework. Next, we study the performance of this architecture on two separate benchmarks requiring task-based adaptation: Meta-World, a multi-task reinforcement learning environment where a robotic agent must learn to solve a variety of manipulation tasks simultaneously; and a continual learning benchmark in which the model's prediction task changes throughout training. Analysis on both benchmarks demonstrates the emergence of overlapping but distinct and sparse subnetworks, allowing the system to fluidly learn multiple tasks with minimal forgetting. Our neural implementation marks the first time a single architecture has achieved competitive results on both multi-task and continual learning settings. Our research sheds light on how biological properties of neurons can inform deep learning systems to address dynamic scenarios that are typically impossible for traditional ANNs to solve.

title: Avoiding Catastrophe: Active Dendrites Enable Multi-Task Learning in Dynamic Environments
text: Embodied artificial intelligence systems operating in dynamic environments must adapt to changing task contexts and learn continuously. However, standard deep learning systems, which excel in static benchmarks, often struggle in these scenarios due to the interference of error signals from multiple contexts, leading to catastrophic forgetting. Inspired by biological systems, we explore novel architectures that can dynamically restrict and route information in a context-specific manner. Our proposed artificial neural network incorporates active dendrites and sparse representations into the standard deep learning framework, enabling the emergence of overlapping yet distinct subnetworks. We evaluate the performance of this architecture on two benchmarks requiring task-based adaptation: Meta-World, a multi-task reinforcement learning environment, and a continual learning benchmark with changing prediction tasks. Our results demonstrate the ability of the system to learn multiple tasks with minimal forgetting, achieving competitive results in both multi-task and continual learning settings. This marks a significant milestone, as our neural implementation is the first to excel in both domains using a single architecture. Our research highlights the potential of biological properties of neurons to inform deep learning systems, enabling them to tackle dynamic scenarios that traditional artificial neural networks cannot solve.

title: Multi-Dimensional Model Compression of Vision Transformer
