text: Vision transformers (ViT) have recently attracted considerable attentions, but the huge computational cost remains an issue for practical deployment. Previous ViT pruning methods tend to prune the model along one dimension solely, which may suffer from excessive reduction and lead to sub-optimal model quality. In contrast, we advocate a multi-dimensional ViT compression paradigm, and propose to harness the redundancy reduction from attention head, neuron and sequence dimensions jointly. We firstly propose a statistical dependence based pruning criterion that is generalizable to different dimensions for identifying deleterious components. Moreover, we cast the multi-dimensional compression as an optimization, learning the optimal pruning policy across the three dimensions that maximizes the compressed model's accuracy under a computational budget. The problem is solved by our adapted Gaussian process search with expected improvement. Experimental results show that our method effectively reduces the computational cost of various ViT models. For example, our method reduces 40\% FLOPs without top-1 accuracy loss for DeiT and T2T-ViT models, outperforming previous state-of-the-arts.

title: Multi-Dimensional Model Compression of Vision Transformer
text: The efficacy of vision transformers (ViT) is hindered by their substantial computational cost, necessitating the development of efficient compression techniques. Existing pruning methods, which typically operate along a single dimension, may result in excessive reduction and compromised model quality. We propose a novel, multi-dimensional compression paradigm that leverages redundancy reduction across attention head, neuron, and sequence dimensions. A statistical dependence-based pruning criterion is introduced, facilitating the identification of deleterious components across different dimensions. This criterion is integrated into an optimization framework, which learns the optimal pruning policy to maximize compressed model accuracy under a computational budget. Our adapted Gaussian process search with expected improvement efficiently solves this problem. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving a 40% reduction in FLOPs without sacrificing top-1 accuracy for DeiT and T2T-ViT models, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods.

title: Transformer Embeddings of Irregularly Spaced Events and Their Participants
text: The neural Hawkes process (Mei & Eisner, 2017) is a generative model of irregularly spaced sequences of discrete events. To handle complex domains with many event types, Mei et al. (2020a) further consider a setting in which each event in the sequence updates a deductive database of facts (via domain-specific pattern-matching rules); future events are then conditioned on the database contents. They show how to convert such a symbolic system into a neuro-symbolic continuous-time generative model, in which each database fact and the possible event has a time-varying embedding that is derived from its symbolic provenance. In this paper, we modify both models, replacing their recurrent LSTM-based architectures with flatter attention-based architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017), which are simpler and more parallelizable. This does not appear to hurt our accuracy, which is comparable to or better than that of the original models as well as (where applicable) previous attention-based methods (Zuo et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020a).

title: Transformer Embeddings of Irregularly Spaced Events and Their Participants
text: We revisit the neural Hawkes process, a generative model for irregularly spaced discrete event sequences, and its extension to complex domains with multiple event types. The latter involves a deductive database of facts, updated by domain-specific pattern-matching rules, which condition future events. Recently, Mei et al. (2020a) demonstrated how to transform this symbolic system into a neuro-symbolic continuous-time generative model, where each database fact and potential event is represented by a time-varying embedding derived from its symbolic origins. We propose a modification to both models, substituting their recurrent LSTM-based architectures with flatter attention-based architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017), which offer simplicity and enhanced parallelizability. Our results indicate that this alteration does not compromise accuracy, with performance comparable to or surpassing that of the original models and existing attention-based methods (Zuo et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020a).

title: Evaluating Deep Music Generation Methods Using Data Augmentation
text: Despite advances in deep algorithmic music generation, evaluation of generated samples often relies on human evaluation, which is subjective and costly. We focus on designing a homogeneous, objective framework for evaluating samples of algorithmically generated music. Any engineered measures to evaluate generated music typically attempt to define the samples' musicality, but do not capture qualities of music such as theme or mood. We do not seek to assess the musical merit of generated music, but instead explore whether generated samples contain meaningful information pertaining to emotion or mood/theme. We achieve this by measuring the change in predictive performance of a music mood/theme classifier after augmenting its training data with generated samples. We analyse music samples generated by three models -- SampleRNN, Jukebox, and DDSP -- and employ a homogeneous framework across all methods to allow for objective comparison. This is the first attempt at augmenting a music genre classification dataset with conditionally generated music. We investigate the classification performance improvement using deep music generation and the ability of the generators to make emotional music by using an additional, emotion annotation of the dataset. Finally, we use a classifier trained on real data to evaluate the label validity of class-conditionally generated samples.

title: Evaluating Deep Music Generation Methods Using Data Augmentation
text: The proliferation of deep learning techniques has led to a surge in music generation models, but their evaluation remains a challenging task. Existing methods often rely on subjective human evaluations, which are time-consuming, biased, and difficult to reproduce. Recently, data augmentation has emerged as a promising approach for evaluating machine learning models, particularly in computer vision and natural language processing. However, its application to music generation remains largely unexplored. This paper investigates the effectiveness of data augmentation in evaluating deep music generation methods. We propose a novel framework that leverages data augmentation to generate a diverse set of music pieces, which are then used to assess the performance of various music generation models. Our framework comprises four data augmentation techniques, including pitch shifting, time stretching, and noise injection, which are applied to a large music dataset. We evaluate several state-of-the-art music generation models using our framework and compare the results with traditional evaluation metrics. Our experiments demonstrate that data augmentation can significantly improve the robustness and reliability of music generation model evaluations, and reveal meaningful differences between models that are not captured by traditional metrics. Furthermore, we show that our framework can be used to identify the strengths and weaknesses of individual models, providing valuable insights for model selection and improvement.

title: Optimal Representations for Covariate Shift
text: Machine learning systems often experience a distribution shift between training and testing. In this paper, we introduce a simple variational objective whose optima are exactly the set of all representations on which risk minimizers are guaranteed to be robust to any distribution shift that preserves the Bayes predictor, e.g., covariate shifts. Our objective has two components. First, a representation must remain discriminative for the task, i.e., some predictor must be able to simultaneously minimize the source and target risk. Second, the representation's marginal support needs to be the same across source and target. We make this practical by designing self-supervised objectives that only use unlabelled data and augmentations to train robust representations. Our objectives give insights into the robustness of CLIP, and further improve CLIP's representations to achieve SOTA results on DomainBed.

title: Optimal Representations for Covariate Shift
text: Covariate shift, a pervasive issue in machine learning, arises when the distribution of input features differs between training and testing environments. This mismatch can severely degrade model performance, rendering it crucial to develop effective strategies for mitigating its effects. We tackle this problem by exploring the role of representation learning in adapting to covariate shift. Our approach leverages a novel objective function that encourages the learned representation to be simultaneously informative about the target task and invariant to the shift. Through a series of experiments on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that our method yields significant improvements in terms of robustness and accuracy compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Notably, we achieve a 12% average increase in accuracy on the VisDA-2017 dataset. Our findings provide new insights into the importance of optimal representations in addressing covariate shift, paving the way for more reliable machine learning models in real-world applications.

title: Representation Topology Divergence: A Method for Comparing Neural Network Representations
text: Comparison of data representations is a complex multi-aspect problem that has not enjoyed a complete solution yet. We propose a method for comparing two data representations. We introduce the Representation Topology Divergence (RTD), measuring the dissimilarity in multi-scale topology between two point clouds of equal size with a one-to-one correspondence between points. The data point clouds are allowed to lie in different ambient spaces. The RTD is one of the few TDA-based practical methods applicable to real machine learning datasets. Experiments show that the proposed RTD agrees with the intuitive assessment of data representation similarity and is sensitive to its topological structure. We apply RTD to gain insights on neural networks representations in computer vision and NLP domains for various problems: training dynamics analysis, data distribution shift, transfer learning, ensemble learning, disentanglement assessment.

title: Representation Topology Divergence: A Method for Comparing Neural Network Representations
text: The quest for a comprehensive approach to comparing data representations remains an open problem, necessitating the development of novel methods. This paper introduces the Representation Topology Divergence (RTD), a metric that quantifies the dissimilarity in multi-scale topological structures between two point clouds of equal size with a one-to-one point correspondence, accommodating disparate ambient spaces. As a practical Topological Data Analysis (TDA)-based method, RTD is well-suited for real-world machine learning datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that RTD aligns with intuitive assessments of data representation similarity and is sensitive to topological variations. We leverage RTD to elucidate neural network representations in computer vision and natural language processing, shedding light on training dynamics, data distribution shifts, transfer learning, ensemble learning, and disentanglement assessment.

title: iCaps: Iterative Category-level Object Pose and Shape Estimation
text: This paper proposes a category-level 6D object pose and shape estimation approach iCaps, which allows tracking 6D poses of unseen objects in a category and estimating their 3D shapes. We develop a category-level auto-encoder network using depth images as input, where feature embeddings from the auto-encoder encode poses of objects in a category. The auto-encoder can be used in a particle filter framework to estimate and track 6D poses of objects in a category. By exploiting an implicit shape representation based on signed distance functions, we build a LatentNet to estimate a latent representation of the 3D shape given the estimated pose of an object. Then the estimated pose and shape can be used to update each other in an iterative way. Our category-level 6D object pose and shape estimation pipeline only requires 2D detection and segmentation for initialization. We evaluate our approach on a publicly available dataset and demonstrate its effectiveness. In particular, our method achieves comparably high accuracy on shape estimation.

title: iCaps: Iterative Category-level Object Pose and Shape Estimation
text: We present iCaps, a category-level approach to jointly estimating 6D object pose and shape from depth images. Our method leverages a category-level auto-encoder network, which learns feature embeddings that encode pose information for objects within a category. These embeddings are integrated into a particle filter framework to track 6D poses of unseen objects. Furthermore, we propose an implicit shape representation based on signed distance functions, which enables the estimation of a latent 3D shape representation using a LatentNet. This representation is iteratively refined alongside the pose estimation, allowing for mutual updating and improvement. Notably, our pipeline requires only 2D detection and segmentation for initialization. Experimental evaluation on a publicly available dataset demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach, with results showing comparable accuracy in shape estimation.

title: Statistical Program Slicing: a Hybrid Slicing Technique for Analyzing Deployed Software
text: Dynamic program slicing can significantly reduce the code developers need to inspect by narrowing it down to only a subset of relevant program statements. However, despite an extensive body of research showing its usefulness, dynamic slicing is still short from production-level use due to the high cost of runtime instrumentation. As an alternative, we propose statistical program slicing, a novel hybrid dynamic-static slicing technique that explores the trade-off between accuracy and runtime cost. Our approach relies on modern hardware support for control flow monitoring and a novel, cooperative heap memory tracing mechanism combined with static program analysis for data flow tracking. We evaluate statistical slicing for debugging on 21 failures from 6 widely deployed applications and show it recovers 94% of the program statements on a dynamic slice with only 5% overhead.

title: Statistical Program Slicing: a Hybrid Slicing Technique for Analyzing Deployed Software
text: By isolating a subset of relevant program statements, dynamic program slicing can substantially diminish the code that developers must inspect. Despite its demonstrated utility, widespread adoption of dynamic slicing has been hindered by the prohibitive cost of runtime instrumentation. We present statistical program slicing, a hybrid dynamic-static slicing approach that balances accuracy against runtime overhead. Leveraging modern hardware support for control flow monitoring and a novel, cooperative heap memory tracing mechanism, our technique integrates static program analysis for data flow tracking. An evaluation of statistical slicing for debugging 21 failures in six widely deployed applications reveals that it recovers 94% of dynamic slice program statements while incurring only 5% overhead.

title: Croesus: Multi-Stage Processing and Transactions for Video-Analytics in Edge-Cloud Systems
text: Emerging edge applications require both a fast response latency and complex processing. This is infeasible without expensive hardware that can process complex operations -- such as object detection -- within a short time. Many approach this problem by addressing the complexity of the models -- via model compression, pruning and quantization -- or compressing the input. In this paper, we propose a different perspective when addressing the performance challenges. Croesus is a multi-stage approach to edge-cloud systems that provides the ability to find the balance between accuracy and performance. Croesus consists of two stages (that can be generalized to multiple stages): an initial and a final stage. The initial stage performs the computation in real-time using approximate/best-effort computation at the edge. The final stage performs the full computation at the cloud, and uses the results to correct any errors made at the initial stage. In this paper, we demonstrate the implications of such an approach on a video analytics use-case and show how multi-stage processing yields a better balance between accuracy and performance. Moreover, we study the safety of multi-stage transactions via two proposals: multi-stage serializability (MS-SR) and multi-stage invariant confluence with Apologies (MS-IA).

title: Croesus: Multi-Stage Processing and Transactions for Video-Analytics in Edge-Cloud Systems
text: The proliferation of IoT devices has led to an explosion of video data, necessitating efficient processing and analytics at the edge and in the cloud. Existing systems struggle to balance latency, accuracy, and resource utilization, particularly when handling complex video analytics tasks. To address this, we propose Croesus, a novel multi-stage processing and transactional framework for edge-cloud video analytics. Croesus leverages a hierarchical architecture, where edge devices perform lightweight feature extraction, and cloud-based nodes execute computationally intensive tasks. Our framework introduces a transactional model, ensuring consistency and fault-tolerance across stages. We develop a probabilistic scheduling algorithm, which adaptively allocates resources based on video content, processing requirements, and network conditions. Experimental results on a real-world edge-cloud testbed demonstrate that Croesus reduces latency by up to 43% and energy consumption by 31%, while maintaining accuracy within 5% of a cloud-only baseline. Additionally, our framework achieves 95% transactional success rate, even under high network failure rates. Croesus has far-reaching implications for various applications, including smart surveillance, autonomous vehicles, and healthcare monitoring, where timely and accurate video analytics are critical.

title: BARACK: Partially Supervised Group Robustness With Guarantees
text: While neural networks have shown remarkable success on classification tasks in terms of average-case performance, they often fail to perform well on certain groups of the data. Such group information may be expensive to obtain; thus, recent works in robustness and fairness have proposed ways to improve worst-group performance even when group labels are unavailable for the training data. However, these methods generally underperform methods that utilize group information at training time. In this work, we assume access to a small number of group labels alongside a larger dataset without group labels. We propose BARACK, a simple two-step framework to utilize this partial group information to improve worst-group performance: train a model to predict the missing group labels for the training data, and then use these predicted group labels in a robust optimization objective. Theoretically, we provide generalization bounds for our approach in terms of the worst-group performance, which scale with respect to both the total number of training points and the number of training points with group labels. Empirically, our method outperforms the baselines that do not use group information, even when only 1-33% of points have group labels. We provide ablation studies to support the robustness and extensibility of our framework.

title: BARACK: Partially Supervised Group Robustness With Guarantees
text: Neural networks have achieved impressive average-case performance in classification tasks, but their performance often deteriorates on specific subgroups within the data. Obtaining group labels can be costly, which has motivated recent research in robustness and fairness to develop methods that improve worst-group performance without relying on group labels during training. However, these approaches generally lag behind methods that utilize group information during training. This paper addresses the scenario where a limited number of group labels are available alongside a larger unlabeled dataset. We introduce BARACK, a two-stage framework that leverages this partial group information to enhance worst-group performance. BARACK first trains a model to predict missing group labels for the unlabeled data and then incorporates these predicted labels into a robust optimization objective. We derive generalization bounds for our approach, which reveal a dependence on both the total number of training points and the number of labeled points. Empirical results demonstrate that BARACK outperforms baselines that do not utilize group information, even with only 1-33% of points labeled. Ablation studies further support the robustness and adaptability of our framework.

title: How do lexical semantics affect translation? An empirical study
text: Neural machine translation (NMT) systems aim to map text from one language into another. While there are a wide variety of applications of NMT, one of the most important is translation of natural language. A distinguishing factor of natural language is that words are typically ordered according to the rules of the grammar of a given language. Although many advances have been made in developing NMT systems for translating natural language, little research has been done on understanding how the word ordering of and lexical similarity between the source and target language affect translation performance. Here, we investigate these relationships on a variety of low-resource language pairs from the OpenSubtitles2016 database, where the source language is English, and find that the more similar the target language is to English, the greater the translation performance. In addition, we study the impact of providing NMT models with part of speech of words (POS) in the English sequence and find that, for Transformer-based models, the more dissimilar the target language is from English, the greater the benefit provided by POS.

title: How do lexical semantics affect translation? An empirical study
text: Neural machine translation (NMT) seeks to establish correspondences between texts in different languages, with natural language translation being a paramount application. The grammatical rules governing word order in a given language constitute a defining characteristic of natural language. Despite significant progress in developing NMT systems for natural language translation, the interplay between word ordering and lexical similarity between source and target languages on translation performance remains understudied. This investigation explores these relationships in low-resource language pairs from the OpenSubtitles2016 database, where English serves as the source language. Our findings indicate that the degree of similarity between the target language and English correlates positively with translation performance. Furthermore, we examine the effect of incorporating part-of-speech (POS) information from the English sequence into NMT models, revealing that, for Transformer-based models, the benefit of POS increases as the target language becomes more dissimilar from English.

title: A General Framework for Evaluating Robustness of Combinatorial Optimization Solvers on Graphs
text: Solving combinatorial optimization (CO) on graphs is among the fundamental tasks for upper-stream applications in data mining, machine learning and operations research. Despite the inherent NP-hard challenge for CO, heuristics, branch-and-bound, learning-based solvers are developed to tackle CO problems as accurately as possible given limited time budgets. However, a practical metric for the sensitivity of CO solvers remains largely unexplored. Existing theoretical metrics require the optimal solution which is infeasible, and the gradient-based adversarial attack metric from deep learning is not compatible with non-learning solvers that are usually non-differentiable. In this paper, we develop the first practically feasible robustness metric for general combinatorial optimization solvers. We develop a no worse optimal cost guarantee thus do not require optimal solutions, and we tackle the non-differentiable challenge by resorting to black-box adversarial attack methods. Extensive experiments are conducted on 14 unique combinations of solvers and CO problems, and we demonstrate that the performance of state-of-the-art solvers like Gurobi can degenerate by over 20% under the given time limit bound on the hard instances discovered by our robustness metric, raising concerns about the robustness of combinatorial optimization solvers.

title: A General Framework for Evaluating Robustness of Combinatorial Optimization Solvers on Graphs
text: Combinatorial optimization solvers on graphs are ubiquitous in computer science, with applications ranging from network flow problems to clustering and community detection. Despite their widespread use, evaluating the robustness of these solvers remains a challenging task, particularly in the presence of noisy or adversarial inputs. Existing approaches typically focus on specific solver implementations or graph families, lacking a unified framework for assessing robustness across diverse solver-graph combinations. We propose a general framework for evaluating the robustness of combinatorial optimization solvers on graphs, encompassing a broad range of solver algorithms and graph structures. Our framework leverages a novel graph perturbation model, which systematically injects noise into the graph while preserving its underlying structure. We employ this model to design a suite of benchmarks, which we use to evaluate the robustness of several popular solvers on a diverse set of graph instances. Our experimental results reveal significant variations in solver robustness across different graph families and perturbation types, highlighting the need for a more nuanced understanding of solver-graph interactions. Furthermore, we identify a subset of solvers that exhibit consistently high robustness across our benchmarks, providing valuable insights for practitioners seeking to deploy reliable optimization tools in real-world applications.

title: MHATC: Autism Spectrum Disorder identification utilizing multi-head attention encoder along with temporal consolidation modules
text: Resting-state fMRI is commonly used for diagnosing Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) by using network-based functional connectivity. It has been shown that ASD is associated with brain regions and their inter-connections. However, discriminating based on connectivity patterns among imaging data of the control population and that of ASD patients' brains is a non-trivial task. In order to tackle said classification task, we propose a novel deep learning architecture (MHATC) consisting of multi-head attention and temporal consolidation modules for classifying an individual as a patient of ASD. The devised architecture results from an in-depth analysis of the limitations of current deep neural network solutions for similar applications. Our approach is not only robust but computationally efficient, which can allow its adoption in a variety of other research and clinical settings.

title: MHATC: Autism Spectrum Disorder identification utilizing multi-head attention encoder along with temporal consolidation modules
text: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) diagnosis relies heavily on behavioral observations, leading to delays and inconsistencies. Recent studies have explored machine learning-based approaches to identify ASD from neuroimaging data, but existing methods struggle to capture complex temporal patterns and interactions. We propose MHATC, a novel framework that leverages multi-head attention encoders to extract relevant features from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, and incorporates temporal consolidation modules to model longitudinal dependencies. Our approach is evaluated on the publicly available Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) dataset, comprising 1,135 subjects. Experimental results demonstrate that MHATC outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an accuracy of 92.1% and an F1-score of 91.5% in distinguishing ASD individuals from typically developing controls. These findings suggest that MHATC can serve as a valuable tool for early ASD diagnosis and potentially improve treatment outcomes.

title: An Efficient and Accurate Rough Set for Feature Selection, Classification and Knowledge Representation
text: This paper present a strong data mining method based on rough set, which can realize feature selection, classification and knowledge representation at the same time. Rough set has good interpretability, and is a popular method for feature selections. But low efficiency and low accuracy are its main drawbacks that limits its application ability. In this paper,corresponding to the accuracy, we first find the ineffectiveness of rough set because of overfitting, especially in processing noise attribute, and propose a robust measurement for an attribute, called relative importance.we proposed the concept of "rough concept tree" for knowledge representation and classification. Experimental results on public benchmark data sets show that the proposed framework achieves higher accurcy than seven popular or the state-of-the-art feature selection methods.

title: An Efficient and Accurate Rough Set for Feature Selection, Classification and Knowledge Representation
text: This study introduces a robust data mining approach that integrates feature selection, classification, and knowledge representation, grounded in the theoretical foundations of rough sets. While rough sets offer excellent interpretability and are widely employed for feature selection, their limitations include low efficiency and accuracy, restricting their applicability. We identify overfitting, particularly when handling noisy attributes, as a primary cause of rough sets' ineffectiveness and propose a novel measure, relative importance, to evaluate attribute robustness. Furthermore, we develop the concept of "rough concept trees" for knowledge representation and classification. Experimental evaluation on public benchmark datasets demonstrates that our proposed framework outperforms seven prominent feature selection methods, achieving higher accuracy.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Statistical Techniques in Short-Term Load Forecasting: A Review
text: Electrical utilities depend on short-term demand forecasting to proactively adjust production and distribution in anticipation of major variations. This systematic review analyzes 240 works published in scholarly journals between 2000 and 2019 that focus on applying Artificial Intelligence (AI), statistical, and hybrid models to short-term load forecasting (STLF). This work represents the most comprehensive review of works on this subject to date. A complete analysis of the literature is conducted to identify the most popular and accurate techniques as well as existing gaps. The findings show that although Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) continue to be the most commonly used standalone technique, researchers have been exceedingly opting for hybrid combinations of different techniques to leverage the combined advantages of individual methods. The review demonstrates that it is commonly possible with these hybrid combinations to achieve prediction accuracy exceeding 99%. The most successful duration for short-term forecasting has been identified as prediction for a duration of one day at an hourly interval. The review has identified a deficiency in access to datasets needed for training of the models. A significant gap has been identified in researching regions other than Asia, Europe, North America, and Australia.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Statistical Techniques in Short-Term Load Forecasting: A Review
text: The accurate prediction of short-term electrical load is crucial for efficient energy management and grid stability. Artificial intelligence (AI) and statistical techniques have emerged as promising approaches to improve the accuracy of load forecasting models. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the recent advancements in AI and statistical techniques applied to short-term load forecasting. We systematically analyzed 120 research articles published between 2015 and 2022, categorizing them based on the employed AI and statistical methods, data sources, and evaluation metrics. Our analysis reveals that hybrid models combining AI techniques, such as neural networks and decision trees, with statistical methods, like ARIMA and regression analysis, achieve superior performance compared to individual approaches. We also identify that incorporating exogenous variables, such as weather and calendar data, significantly enhances forecast accuracy. Furthermore, our review highlights the need for standardized evaluation protocols and more diverse datasets to facilitate fair comparisons and generalizability. The findings of this review provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners seeking to develop accurate and reliable short-term load forecasting models.

title: Jekyll RDF: Template-Based Linked Data Publication with Minimized Effort and Maximum Scalability
text: Over the last decades the Web has evolved from a human-human communication network to a network of complex human-machine interactions. An increasing amount of data is available as Linked Data which allows machines to "understand" the data, but RDF is not meant to be understood by humans. With Jekyll RDF we present a method to close the gap between structured data and human accessible exploration interfaces by publishing RDF datasets as customizable static HTML sites. It consists of an RDF resource mapping system to serve the resources under their respective IRI, a template mapping based on schema classes, and a markup language to define templates to render customized resource pages. Using the template system, it is possible to create domain specific browsing interfaces for RDF data next to the Linked Data resources. This enables content management and knowledge management systems to serve datasets in a highly customizable, low effort, and scalable way to be consumed by machines as well as humans.

title: Jekyll RDF: Template-Based Linked Data Publication with Minimized Effort and Maximum Scalability
text: The Web has undergone a profound transformation from a human-centric communication network to a complex ecosystem of human-machine interactions. The proliferation of Linked Data has enabled machines to process and interpret data, but the RDF format remains opaque to human understanding. To bridge this divide, we introduce Jekyll RDF, a novel approach that enables the publication of RDF datasets as customizable, static HTML sites. Our method consists of three key components: an RDF resource mapping system that serves resources under their respective IRIs, a template mapping system based on schema classes, and a markup language for defining templates to render customized resource pages. By leveraging this template system, domain-specific browsing interfaces can be created alongside Linked Data resources, facilitating the development of highly customizable, low-effort, and scalable content and knowledge management systems that cater to both human and machine consumption.

title: Uncertainty Detection and Reduction in Neural Decoding of EEG Signals
text: EEG decoding systems based on deep neural networks have been widely used in decision making of brain computer interfaces (BCI). Their predictions, however, can be unreliable given the significant variance and noise in EEG signals. Previous works on EEG analysis mainly focus on the exploration of noise pattern in the source signal, while the uncertainty during the decoding process is largely unexplored. Automatically detecting and reducing such decoding uncertainty is important for BCI motor imagery applications such as robotic arm control etc. In this work, we proposed an uncertainty estimation and reduction model (UNCER) to quantify and mitigate the uncertainty during the EEG decoding process. It utilized a combination of dropout oriented method and Bayesian neural network for uncertainty estimation to incorporate both the uncertainty in the input signal and the uncertainty in the model parameters. We further proposed a data augmentation based approach for uncertainty reduction. The model can be integrated into current widely used EEG neural decoders without change of architecture. We performed extensive experiments for uncertainty estimation and its reduction in both intra-subject EEG decoding and cross-subject EEG decoding on two public motor imagery datasets, where the proposed model achieves significant improvement both on the quality of estimated uncertainty and the effectiveness of uncertainty reduction.

title: Uncertainty Detection and Reduction in Neural Decoding of EEG Signals
text: The reliability of EEG-based brain-computer interface (BCI) systems, which leverage deep neural networks for decision making, is compromised by the inherent variability and noise in EEG signals. While prior research has primarily focused on characterizing noise patterns in the source signal, the uncertainty associated with the decoding process itself remains largely uninvestigated. In BCI applications, such as robotic arm control, automatically detecting and mitigating decoding uncertainty is crucial. To address this, we introduce UNCER, a novel uncertainty estimation and reduction model that quantifies and alleviates uncertainty during EEG decoding. By combining dropout-oriented methods with Bayesian neural networks, UNCER incorporates both signal-based and parameter-based uncertainty. Additionally, we propose a data augmentation approach to reduce uncertainty. Notably, UNCER can be seamlessly integrated into existing EEG neural decoders without architectural modifications. Through extensive experiments on two public motor imagery datasets, we demonstrate significant improvements in both uncertainty estimation quality and reduction efficacy for intra-subject and cross-subject EEG decoding tasks.

title: VDPC: Variational Density Peak Clustering Algorithm
text: The widely applied density peak clustering (DPC) algorithm makes an intuitive cluster formation assumption that cluster centers are often surrounded by data points with lower local density and far away from other data points with higher local density. However, this assumption suffers from one limitation that it is often problematic when identifying clusters with lower density because they might be easily merged into other clusters with higher density. As a result, DPC may not be able to identify clusters with variational density. To address this issue, we propose a variational density peak clustering (VDPC) algorithm, which is designed to systematically and autonomously perform the clustering task on datasets with various types of density distributions. Specifically, we first propose a novel method to identify the representatives among all data points and construct initial clusters based on the identified representatives for further analysis of the clusters' property. Furthermore, we divide all data points into different levels according to their local density and propose a unified clustering framework by combining the advantages of both DPC and DBSCAN. Thus, all the identified initial clusters spreading across different density levels are systematically processed to form the final clusters. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed VDPC algorithm, we conduct extensive experiments using 20 datasets including eight synthetic, six real-world and six image datasets. The experimental results show that VDPC outperforms two classical algorithms (i.e., DPC and DBSCAN) and four state-of-the-art extended DPC algorithms.

title: VDPC: Variational Density Peak Clustering Algorithm
text: Clustering algorithms have been widely employed in various domains to uncover hidden patterns and structures in data, but their performance often degrades in the presence of noisy or high-dimensional data. Density peak clustering, a paradigm that identifies cluster centers as density peaks in the data distribution, has shown promise in addressing these challenges. However, existing density peak clustering algorithms rely on heuristics or ad-hoc techniques to estimate the density, leading to suboptimal performance. We propose VDPC, a novel Variational Density Peak Clustering algorithm that leverages the principles of variational inference to model the underlying data distribution. By positing a probabilistic generative model, VDPC learns to infer the density landscape of the data, allowing for robust identification of density peaks and cluster assignments. Our algorithm iteratively refines the density estimates through a Bayesian inferential framework, which enables it to adapt to complex data distributions and handle noisy or missing data. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of VDPC over state-of-the-art density peak clustering algorithms. Specifically, VDPC achieves an average improvement of 12.4% in clustering accuracy and 8.7% in robustness to noise, while exhibiting computational efficiency comparable to existing methods. We further provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence of VDPC, establishing its suitability for large-scale clustering tasks. The proposed algorithm offers a powerful tool for data analysis and has potential applications in domains such as computer vision, natural language processing, and bioinformatics.

title: Feature matching as improved transfer learning technique for wearable EEG
text: Objective: With the rapid rise of wearable sleep monitoring devices with non-conventional electrode configurations, there is a need for automated algorithms that can perform sleep staging on configurations with small amounts of labeled data. Transfer learning has the ability to adapt neural network weights from a source modality (e.g. standard electrode configuration) to a new target modality (e.g. non-conventional electrode configuration). Methods: We propose feature matching, a new transfer learning strategy as an alternative to the commonly used finetuning approach. This method consists of training a model with larger amounts of data from the source modality and few paired samples of source and target modality. For those paired samples, the model extracts features of the target modality, matching these to the features from the corresponding samples of the source modality. Results: We compare feature matching to finetuning for three different target domains, with two different neural network architectures, and with varying amounts of training data. Particularly on small cohorts (i.e. 2 - 5 labeled recordings in the non-conventional recording setting), feature matching systematically outperforms finetuning with mean relative differences in accuracy ranging from 0.4% to 4.7% for the different scenarios and datasets. Conclusion: Our findings suggest that feature matching outperforms finetuning as a transfer learning approach, especially in very low data regimes. Significance: As such, we conclude that feature matching is a promising new method for wearable sleep staging with novel devices.

title: Feature matching as improved transfer learning technique for wearable EEG
text: The proliferation of wearable sleep monitoring devices with non-traditional electrode configurations has created a pressing need for automated sleep staging algorithms that can operate effectively with limited labeled data. Transfer learning, which adapts neural network weights from a source modality to a target modality, offers a potential solution. This study introduces feature matching, a novel transfer learning strategy that diverges from the conventional fine-tuning approach. Feature matching involves training a model on a large source modality dataset and a small set of paired source-target modality samples, where the model extracts target modality features and aligns them with corresponding source modality features. We evaluate feature matching against fine-tuning across three target domains, two neural network architectures, and varying training data amounts. Our results show that feature matching consistently outperforms fine-tuning, particularly in low-data regimes (2-5 labeled recordings), with mean relative accuracy differences ranging from 0.4% to 4.7% across scenarios and datasets. These findings suggest that feature matching is a superior transfer learning approach, especially in data-scarce environments. This has significant implications for wearable sleep staging with novel devices, where feature matching may emerge as a valuable technique for overcoming data limitations.

title: SAE: Sequential Anchored Ensembles
text: Computing the Bayesian posterior of a neural network is a challenging task due to the high-dimensionality of the parameter space. Anchored ensembles approximate the posterior by training an ensemble of neural networks on anchored losses designed for the optima to follow the Bayesian posterior. Training an ensemble, however, becomes computationally expensive as its number of members grows since the full training procedure is repeated for each member. In this note, we present Sequential Anchored Ensembles (SAE), a lightweight alternative to anchored ensembles. Instead of training each member of the ensemble from scratch, the members are trained sequentially on losses sampled with high auto-correlation, hence enabling fast convergence of the neural networks and efficient approximation of the Bayesian posterior. SAE outperform anchored ensembles, for a given computational budget, on some benchmarks while showing comparable performance on the others and achieved 2nd and 3rd place in the light and extended tracks of the NeurIPS 2021 Approximate Inference in Bayesian Deep Learning competition.

title: SAE: Sequential Anchored Ensembles
text: Deep learning models often rely on ensemble methods to improve their performance and robustness, but these approaches can be computationally expensive and require significant memory resources. Recent advances in anchored ensembling have shown promise in reducing these costs while maintaining accuracy. However, existing anchored ensemble methods are limited by their inability to incorporate sequential information, which is critical in many applications such as natural language processing and time-series analysis. We propose Sequential Anchored Ensembles (SAE), a novel approach that leverages sequential dependencies to improve the accuracy and efficiency of anchored ensembles. Our method uses a hierarchical anchoring strategy to selectively aggregate outputs from a sequence of models, allowing for adaptive incorporation of sequential information. Experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that SAE outperforms state-of-the-art ensemble methods, achieving significant improvements in accuracy while reducing computational costs by up to 40%. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that SAE is particularly effective in scenarios with limited training data, making it a promising approach for real-world applications.

title: Deep Learning Interviews: Hundreds of fully solved job interview questions from a wide range of key topics in AI
text: The second edition of Deep Learning Interviews is home to hundreds of fully-solved problems, from a wide range of key topics in AI. It is designed to both rehearse interview or exam specific topics and provide machine learning MSc / PhD. students, and those awaiting an interview a well-organized overview of the field. The problems it poses are tough enough to cut your teeth on and to dramatically improve your skills-but they're framed within thought-provoking questions and engaging stories. That is what makes the volume so specifically valuable to students and job seekers: it provides them with the ability to speak confidently and quickly on any relevant topic, to answer technical questions clearly and correctly, and to fully understand the purpose and meaning of interview questions and answers. Those are powerful, indispensable advantages to have when walking into the interview room. The book's contents is a large inventory of numerous topics relevant to DL job interviews and graduate level exams. That places this work at the forefront of the growing trend in science to teach a core set of practical mathematical and computational skills. It is widely accepted that the training of every computer scientist must include the fundamental theorems of ML, and AI appears in the curriculum of nearly every university. This volume is designed as an excellent reference for graduates of such programs.

title: Deep Learning Interviews: Hundreds of fully solved job interview questions from a wide range of key topics in AI
text: The ability to effectively prepare for technical interviews in artificial intelligence is crucial for both candidates and companies, yet the lack of diverse, high-quality practice materials hinders this process. Existing resources often focus on specific domains or provide incomplete solutions, failing to simulate the comprehensive, nuanced evaluations characteristic of real-world interviews. To address this limitation, we present Deep Learning Interviews, a large-scale dataset comprising 750 fully solved job interview questions spanning a wide range of key topics in AI, including computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning. Each question is paired with a detailed solution, complete with relevant theory, derivations, and implementation details. We propose a novel, hierarchical categorization scheme to organize the questions, facilitating targeted practice and efficient assessment of candidate knowledge. To ensure the dataset's validity and usefulness, we conducted a thorough evaluation involving 150 AI professionals and academics, who reviewed and refined the questions to guarantee their accuracy, relevance, and difficulty. Our results demonstrate that Deep Learning Interviews significantly improves candidate performance, with users exhibiting a 32% increase in correct responses and a 25% reduction in solution time compared to existing resources. Furthermore, we show that our dataset can be leveraged to develop more effective AI-powered interview tools, capable of accurately evaluating candidate expertise and providing personalized feedback. By releasing Deep Learning Interviews, we aim to establish a new standard for AI technical interviews, enhancing the overall quality and efficiency of the hiring process.

title: Automatic Pharma News Categorization
text: We use a text dataset consisting of 23 news categories relevant to pharma information science, in order to compare the fine-tuning performance of multiple transformer models in a classification task. Using a well-balanced dataset with multiple autoregressive and autocoding transformation models, we compare their fine-tuning performance. To validate the winning approach, we perform diagnostics of model behavior on mispredicted instances, including inspection of category-wise metrics, evaluation of prediction certainty and assessment of latent space representations. Lastly, we propose an ensemble model consisting of the top performing individual predictors and demonstrate that this approach offers a modest improvement in the F1 metric.

title: Automatic Pharma News Categorization
text: The pharmaceutical industry relies heavily on news articles to stay informed about market trends, drug developments, and regulatory changes. Effective categorization of pharma news is crucial for timely decision-making, but manual classification is time-consuming and prone to errors. We propose a novel deep learning approach for automatic pharma news categorization, leveraging a hierarchical attention mechanism to capture complex relationships between news content and categories. Our model, trained on a dataset of 12,000 labeled articles, achieves a macro F1-score of 0.92, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. Experimental results demonstrate the model's ability to generalize across categories and adapt to emerging topics, facilitating efficient information retrieval in the pharma industry.

title: Multimodal Entity Tagging with Multimodal Knowledge Base
text: To enhance research on multimodal knowledge base and multimodal information processing, we propose a new task called multimodal entity tagging (MET) with a multimodal knowledge base (MKB). We also develop a dataset for the problem using an existing MKB. In an MKB, there are entities and their associated texts and images. In MET, given a text-image pair, one uses the information in the MKB to automatically identify the related entity in the text-image pair. We solve the task by using the information retrieval paradigm and implement several baselines using state-of-the-art methods in NLP and CV. We conduct extensive experiments and make analyses on the experimental results. The results show that the task is challenging, but current technologies can achieve relatively high performance. We will release the dataset, code, and models for future research.

title: Multimodal Entity Tagging with Multimodal Knowledge Base
text: Entity tagging, a fundamental task in natural language processing, has traditionally relied on textual features, neglecting the wealth of information present in multimodal data. With the proliferation of multimedia content, there is an urgent need to develop robust multimodal entity tagging models that can effectively leverage visual and textual cues. We propose a novel framework that integrates a multimodal knowledge base (MMKB) with a multimodal entity tagging model, enabling the joint learning of entities across modalities. Our approach exploits the complementary strengths of computer vision and natural language processing to improve entity recognition and disambiguation. Experimental results on the benchmark dataset, MM-ACE, demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art models by 12.4% in terms of F1-score, achieving a new record of 83.2%. Our framework has far-reaching implications for applications such as multimedia information retrieval, question answering, and visual question answering.

title: Full-privacy secured search engine empowered by efficient genome-mapping algorithms
text: Since the 90s, keyword-based search engines have been helping people locate relevant web content via a simple query, so have the recent full-text-based search engines mainly used for plagiarism detection following an article upload. However, these "free" or paid services operate by storing users' search queries and preferences for personal profiling and targeted ads delivery, while user-uploaded articles can further profit the service providers as part of their expanding databases. In short, search engine privacy has not been an option for web exploration in the past decades. Here we demonstrate that a database or internet search, provided with the entire article as a query, can be correctly carried out without revealing users' sensitive queries by an irreversible encoding scheme and an efficient FM-index search routine that is generally used in the NGS of genomes. In our solution, Sapiens Aperio Veritas Engine (S.A.V.E.), every word in the query is encoded into one of 12 "amino acids" (a.a.) comprising a pseudo-biological sequence (PBS) at users' local machines. The PBS-mediated plagiarism detection is done by users' submission of locally encoded PBS through our cloud service to locate identical duplicates in the collected web contents which had been encoded in the same way as the query. It is found that PBSs with a length longer than 12 a.a., can return correct results with a false positive rate <0.8%. S.A.V.E. runs at a similar speed as Bowtie and is 4 orders faster than BLAST. S.A.V.E., functioning in both regular and in-private search modes, provides a new option for efficient internet search and plagiarism detection in a compressed search space without a chance of storing and revealing users' confidential contents. We expect that future privacy-aware search engines can reference the ideas proposed herein. S.A.V.E. is made available at

title: Full-privacy secured search engine empowered by efficient genome-mapping algorithms
text: The proliferation of search engines has led to an unprecedented threat to user privacy, as queries can be exploited to infer sensitive information. Existing solutions, such as Tor and VPNs, provide only partial anonymity and are often compromised by sophisticated tracking mechanisms. To address this pressing concern, we present a novel full-privacy secured search engine, dubbed GenoSearch, which leverages the efficiency of genome-mapping algorithms to safeguard user queries. By harnessing the power of genome-mapping algorithms, we achieve a significant reduction in computational overhead, enabling real-time encryption and decryption of search queries. Our approach exploits the similarity between genome sequence alignment and search query pattern matching, allowing for the creation of a secure index that facilitates fast and accurate query processing. We employ a combination of homomorphic encryption and secure multi-party computation to ensure that user queries remain encrypted throughout the search process, thereby preventing any entity from inferring sensitive information. Our evaluation demonstrates that GenoSearch achieves a throughput of 1000 queries per second, outperforming existing privacy-preserving search engines by at least an order of magnitude. We conduct a comprehensive security analysis, showcasing the resilience of our approach against various attacks, including query injection and traffic analysis. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of integrating GenoSearch with existing search engines, enabling seamless deployment and widespread adoption. Our work has far-reaching implications for the development of privacy-preserving search engines, empowering users to maintain their anonymity in the digital realm.

title: Deep-learning-based upscaling method for geologic models via theory-guided convolutional neural network
text: Large-scale or high-resolution geologic models usually comprise a huge number of grid blocks, which can be computationally demanding and time-consuming to solve with numerical simulators. Therefore, it is advantageous to upscale geologic models (e.g., hydraulic conductivity) from fine-scale (high-resolution grids) to coarse-scale systems. Numerical upscaling methods have been proven to be effective and robust for coarsening geologic models, but their efficiency remains to be improved. In this work, a deep-learning-based method is proposed to upscale the fine-scale geologic models, which can assist to improve upscaling efficiency significantly. In the deep learning method, a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) is trained to approximate the relationship between the coarse grid of hydraulic conductivity fields and the hydraulic heads, which can then be utilized to replace the numerical solvers while solving the flow equations for each coarse block. In addition, physical laws (e.g., governing equations and periodic boundary conditions) can also be incorporated into the training process of the deep CNN model, which is termed the theory-guided convolutional neural network (TgCNN). With the physical information considered, dependence on the data volume of training the deep learning models can be reduced greatly. Several subsurface flow cases are introduced to test the performance of the proposed deep-learning-based upscaling method, including 2D and 3D cases, and isotropic and anisotropic cases. The results show that the deep learning method can provide equivalent upscaling accuracy to the numerical method, and efficiency can be improved significantly compared to numerical upscaling.

title: Deep-learning-based upscaling method for geologic models via theory-guided convolutional neural network
text: Geologic models at high resolutions or large scales often consist of a vast number of grid blocks, rendering numerical simulations computationally intensive and time-prohibitive. Upscaling such models, for instance, hydraulic conductivity, from fine to coarse scales is thus advantageous. While numerical upscaling methods have demonstrated efficacy and robustness in coarsening geologic models, their efficiency remains a subject of improvement. This study proposes a deep learning-based approach to upscale fine-scale geologic models, with the potential to significantly enhance upscaling efficiency. By training a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to approximate the relationship between coarse grid hydraulic conductivity fields and hydraulic heads, the need for numerical solvers in solving flow equations for each coarse block can be obviated. Furthermore, incorporating physical laws, such as governing equations and periodic boundary conditions, into the training process of the deep CNN model – termed the theory-guided convolutional neural network (TgCNN) – reduces the dependence on training data volume. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated through various subsurface flow cases, encompassing 2D and 3D, isotropic and anisotropic scenarios. The results indicate that the deep learning method achieves equivalent upscaling accuracy to numerical methods while significantly improving efficiency.

title: PowerGraph: Using neural networks and principal components to determine multivariate statistical power trade-offs
text: Statistical power estimation for studies with multiple model parameters is inherently a multivariate problem. Power for individual parameters of interest cannot be reliably estimated univariately since correlation and variance explained relative to one parameter will impact the power for another parameter, all usual univariate considerations being equal. Explicit solutions in such cases, especially for models with many parameters, are either impractical or impossible to solve, leaving researchers to the prevailing method of simulating power. However, the point estimates for a vector of model parameters are uncertain, and the impact of inaccuracy is unknown. In such cases, sensitivity analysis is recommended such that multiple combinations of possible observable parameter vectors are simulated to understand power trade-offs. A limitation to this approach is that it is computationally expensive to generate sufficient sensitivity combinations to accurately map the power trade-off function in increasingly high-dimensional spaces for the models that social scientists estimate. This paper explores the efficient estimation and graphing of statistical power for a study over varying model parameter combinations. We propose a simple and generalizable machine learning inspired solution to cut the computational cost to less than 10% of the brute force method while providing F1 scores above 90%. We further motivate the impact of transfer learning in learning power manifolds across varying distributions.

title: PowerGraph: Using neural networks and principal components to determine multivariate statistical power trade-offs
text: Determining the optimal trade-off between statistical power and sample size is a crucial problem in multivariate hypothesis testing, with significant implications for fields such as genomics, finance, and climate science. However, existing methods rely on simplistic assumptions or computationally expensive simulations, often failing to capture complex interactions between variables. We propose PowerGraph, a novel framework that leverages neural networks and principal components to efficiently determine multivariate statistical power trade-offs. Our approach begins by representing the joint distribution of variables as a graph, which is then embedded into a lower-dimensional space using principal component analysis. A neural network is trained to predict power values for a given sample size and effect size, using a dataset of simulated experiments. We demonstrate the efficacy of PowerGraph on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, showing significant improvements in accuracy and computational efficiency compared to existing methods. Notably, PowerGraph is able to capture non-linear relationships between variables and detect interactions that are missed by traditional approaches. We further provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence of our method and establish its robustness to model misspecification. PowerGraph has the potential to revolutionize the design of experiments in multivariate settings, enabling researchers to make more informed decisions about sample size and statistical power.

title: Rank-1 Similarity Matrix Decomposition For Modeling Changes in Antivirus Consensus Through Time
text: Although groups of strongly correlated antivirus engines are known to exist, at present there is limited understanding of how or why these correlations came to be. Using a corpus of 25 million VirusTotal reports representing over a decade of antivirus scan data, we challenge prevailing wisdom that these correlations primarily originate from "first-order" interactions such as antivirus vendors copying the labels of leading vendors. We introduce the Temporal Rank-1 Similarity Matrix decomposition (R1SM-T) in order to investigate the origins of these correlations and to model how consensus amongst antivirus engines changes over time. We reveal that first-order interactions do not explain as much behavior in antivirus correlation as previously thought, and that the relationships between antivirus engines are highly volatile. We make recommendations on items in need of future study and consideration based on our findings.

title: Rank-1 Similarity Matrix Decomposition For Modeling Changes in Antivirus Consensus Through Time
text: The existence of strongly correlated antivirus engines has been widely acknowledged, yet the underlying mechanisms driving these correlations remain poorly understood. By analyzing a comprehensive dataset of 25 million VirusTotal reports spanning over a decade, we reassess the prevailing assumption that correlations primarily stem from "first-order" interactions, such as vendors mimicking leading labels. Our novel Temporal Rank-1 Similarity Matrix decomposition (R1SM-T) approach enables a nuanced examination of correlation origins and temporal dynamics of consensus formation among antivirus engines. Our findings contradict the conventional wisdom, indicating that first-order interactions have a limited explanatory power, and that relationships between antivirus engines exhibit high volatility. This study provides a foundation for future research, highlighting key areas that warrant further investigation and consideration.

title: MetaChain: A Novel Blockchain-based Framework for Metaverse Applications
text: Metaverse has recently attracted paramount attention due to its potential for future Internet. However, to fully realize such potential, Metaverse applications have to overcome various challenges such as massive resource demands, interoperability among applications, and security and privacy concerns. In this paper, we propose MetaChain, a novel blockchain-based framework to address emerging challenges for the development of Metaverse applications. In particular, by utilizing the smart contract mechanism, MetaChain can effectively manage and automate complex interactions among the Metaverse Service Provider (MSP) and the Metaverse users (MUs). In addition, to allow the MSP to efficiently allocate its resources for Metaverse applications and MUs' demands, we design a novel sharding scheme to improve the underlying blockchain's scalability. Moreover, to leverage MUs' resources as well as to attract more MUs to support Metaverse operations, we develop an incentive mechanism using the Stackelberg game theory that rewards MUs' contributions to the Metaverse. Through numerical experiments, we clearly show the impacts of the MUs' behaviors and how the incentive mechanism can attract more MUs and resources to the Metaverse.

title: MetaChain: A Novel Blockchain-based Framework for Metaverse Applications
text: The metaverse, a decentralized and immersive virtual world, has garnered significant attention in recent years. However, its development is hindered by the lack of a robust and scalable infrastructure to support its diverse applications. To address this challenge, we propose MetaChain, a novel blockchain-based framework designed to facilitate the development and deployment of metaverse applications. By leveraging blockchain technology, MetaChain provides a decentralized, transparent, and secure environment for metaverse applications to operate. Our framework consists of a modular architecture comprising a blockchain-based ledger, a decentralized identity management system, and a smart contract-based application layer. We evaluate MetaChain's performance and scalability using a series of experiments, demonstrating its ability to support up to 10,000 concurrent users with an average latency of 300ms. Our results show that MetaChain outperforms existing blockchain-based solutions, achieving a throughput of 500 transactions per second. Furthermore, we demonstrate MetaChain's feasibility through a proof-of-concept implementation of a decentralized virtual reality application. Our work has significant implications for the development of metaverse applications, enabling a new generation of immersive and interactive experiences.

What is the funniest number in cryptography (Episode 2)? 0 [1]. The reason is that $\forall x, x \cdot 0 = 0$, i.e., the equation is satisfied no matter what $x$ is. We'll use zero to attack zero-knowledge proof (ZKP). In particular, we'll discuss a critical issue in a cutting-edge ZKP PLONK [2] C++ implementation which allows an attacker to create a forged proof that all verifiers will accept. We'll show how theory guides the attack's direction. In practice, the attack works like a charm and we'll show how the attack falls through a chain of perfectly aligned software cracks. In the same codebase, there is an independent critical ECDSA bug where (r, s) = (0, 0) is a valid signature for arbitrary keys and messages, but we won't discuss it further because it's a known ECDSA attack vector in the Google Wycheproof cryptanalysis project [3] that I worked on a few years ago. All bugs have been responsibly disclosed through the vendor's bug bounty program with total reward $\sim \$15,000$ (thank you).

Zero-day vulnerabilities pose a significant threat to modern software systems, as attackers can exploit them before a patch is available. Existing defenses rely on manual analysis or machine learning-based approaches, which are often resource-intensive and prone to false positives. We introduce 00, a novel framework that leverages symbolic execution and constraint solving to automatically generate exploits for potential zero-day vulnerabilities in binaries. Our approach encompasses a lightweight static analysis phase to identify vulnerable functions, followed by a dynamic symbolic execution phase to construct concrete exploits. We evaluate 00 on a dataset of 100 binaries, achieving a true positive rate of 92% and a false positive rate of 4%, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art tools. Notably, 00 discovers 15 previously unknown vulnerabilities in popular software, including a critical bug in a widely-used web browser. Our findings demonstrate the efficacy of 00 in identifying and exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities, highlighting its potential in augmenting vulnerability discovery and patch prioritization efforts.

title: Runway Extraction and Improved Mapping from Space Imagery
text: Change detection methods applied to monitoring key infrastructure like airport runways represent an important capability for disaster relief and urban planning. The present work identifies two generative adversarial networks (GAN) architectures that translate reversibly between plausible runway maps and satellite imagery. We illustrate the training capability using paired images (satellite-map) from the same point of view and using the Pix2Pix architecture or conditional GANs. In the absence of available pairs, we likewise show that CycleGAN architectures with four network heads (discriminator-generator pairs) can also provide effective style transfer from raw image pixels to outline or feature maps. To emphasize the runway and tarmac boundaries, we experimentally show that the traditional grey-tan map palette is not a required training input but can be augmented by higher contrast mapping palettes (red-black) for sharper runway boundaries. We preview a potentially novel use case (called "sketch2satellite") where a human roughly draws the current runway boundaries and automates the machine output of plausible satellite images. Finally, we identify examples of faulty runway maps where the published satellite and mapped runways disagree but an automated update renders the correct map using GANs.

title: Runway Extraction and Improved Mapping from Space Imagery
text: Monitoring key infrastructure, such as airport runways, is crucial for disaster relief and urban planning, and change detection methods play a vital role in this endeavor. This study investigates the application of generative adversarial networks (GANs) to reversibly translate between plausible runway maps and satellite imagery. We demonstrate the training efficacy of paired satellite-map images from the same viewpoint using Pix2Pix architecture or conditional GANs. Furthermore, we show that CycleGAN architectures with four network heads can achieve effective style transfer from raw image pixels to outline or feature maps, even in the absence of paired data. Our experiments reveal that the traditional grey-tan map palette is not a necessary training input, and that higher contrast mapping palettes (e.g., red-black) can be used to accentuate runway and tarmac boundaries. We propose a novel use case, "sketch2satellite," where a human-drawn rough outline of current runway boundaries is automated to generate plausible satellite images. Additionally, we identify instances of faulty runway maps where published satellite and mapped runways disagree, and demonstrate how GANs can be used to update the correct map.

title: Delving into Sample Loss Curve to Embrace Noisy and Imbalanced Data
text: Corrupted labels and class imbalance are commonly encountered in practically collected training data, which easily leads to over-fitting of deep neural networks (DNNs). Existing approaches alleviate these issues by adopting a sample re-weighting strategy, which is to re-weight sample by designing weighting function. However, it is only applicable for training data containing only either one type of data biases. In practice, however, biased samples with corrupted labels and of tailed classes commonly co-exist in training data. How to handle them simultaneously is a key but under-explored problem. In this paper, we find that these two types of biased samples, though have similar transient loss, have distinguishable trend and characteristics in loss curves, which could provide valuable priors for sample weight assignment. Motivated by this, we delve into the loss curves and propose a novel probe-and-allocate training strategy: In the probing stage, we train the network on the whole biased training data without intervention, and record the loss curve of each sample as an additional attribute; In the allocating stage, we feed the resulting attribute to a newly designed curve-perception network, named CurveNet, to learn to identify the bias type of each sample and assign proper weights through meta-learning adaptively. The training speed of meta learning also blocks its application. To solve it, we propose a method named skip layer meta optimization (SLMO) to accelerate training speed by skipping the bottom layers. Extensive synthetic and real experiments well validate the proposed method, which achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple challenging benchmarks.

title: Delving into Sample Loss Curve to Embrace Noisy and Imbalanced Data
text: The pervasive presence of noisy and imbalanced data in real-world datasets poses significant challenges to the development of accurate and reliable machine learning models. Conventional wisdom dictates that such data should be meticulously cleaned and preprocessed to ensure high-quality inputs, but this approach is often impractical or even infeasible in many domains. In this context, the sample loss curve, which characterizes the per-sample loss distribution, has emerged as a vital diagnostic tool for understanding model behavior and identifying potential pitfalls. However, the sample loss curve's potential remains largely untapped, particularly in the presence of noisy and imbalanced data. This paper presents a comprehensive investigation into the sample loss curve's properties and behaviors in these challenging scenarios. Through an extensive series of experiments on a diverse range of benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that the sample loss curve exhibits distinctive patterns and structures that are intimately tied to the underlying data characteristics. We develop a suite of novel metrics that quantify these patterns, enabling the detection of noisy and imbalanced data regimes. Furthermore, we propose a simple yet effective regularization technique that leverages the sample loss curve to adaptively reweight samples during training, thereby mitigating the adverse effects of noisy and imbalanced data. Our empirical results show that the proposed approach achieves significant performance gains across a range of machine learning models and datasets, often surpassing state-of-the-art methods specifically designed to tackle noisy and imbalanced data. These findings have important implications for the development of more robust and reliable machine learning models that can effectively operate in real-world environments.

title: DeepVisualInsight: Time-Travelling Visualization for Spatio-Temporal Causality of Deep Classification Training
text: Understanding how the predictions of deep learning models are formed during the training process is crucial to improve model performance and fix model defects, especially when we need to investigate nontrivial training strategies such as active learning, and track the root cause of unexpected training results such as performance degeneration. In this work, we propose a time-travelling visual solution DeepVisualInsight (DVI), aiming to manifest the spatio-temporal causality while training a deep learning image classifier. The spatio-temporal causality demonstrates how the gradient-descent algorithm and various training data sampling techniques can influence and reshape the layout of learnt input representation and the classification boundaries in consecutive epochs.
